Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Khuddakanikāye

The Khuddaka Nikāya

Mahāniddesa-aṭṭhakathā

The Great Exposition Commentary

Ganthārambhakathā

Introduction to the Text

Avijjālaṅgiṃ [V 0.0001][P 1.0001][M 0.0001] ghātento, nandirāgañca mūlato;

Bhāventaṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ, phusi yo amataṃ padaṃ.

Destroying the bolt of ignorance, and uprooting delight and lust from the root, he who cultivated the Noble Eightfold Path touched the deathless state.

Pāpuṇitvā jino bodhiṃ, migadāyaṃ vigāhiya;

Dhammacakkaṃ pavattetvā, theraṃ koṇḍaññamādito.

Having attained enlightenment, the Victor, entering the Deer Park, set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma, beginning with the Elder Koṇḍañña.

Aṭṭhārasannaṃ koṭīnaṃ, bodhesi tāpaso tahiṃ;

Vandehaṃ sirasā tañca, sabbasattānamuttamaṃ.

There, the ascetic awakened eighteen crores of beings; I bow my head to him, the supreme one of all beings.

Tathā [V 0.0002] dhammuttamañceva, saṅghañcāpi anuttaraṃ;

Saṃkhittena hi yo vuttaṃ, dhammacakkaṃ vibhāgaso.

And likewise to the supreme Dhamma, and also to the unsurpassed Sangha. For the Wheel of Dhamma, which was spoken concisely, was expounded in detail.

Sāriputto mahāpañño, satthukappo jinatrajo;

Dhammacakkaṃ vibhājetvā, mahāniddesamabravi;

Pāṭho visiṭṭho niddeso, taṃnāmavisesito ca.

The greatly wise Sāriputta, equal to the Teacher, the Buddha's descendant, having analyzed the Wheel of Dhamma, spoke the Great Exposition. The text is excellent, an exposition, and also specifically designated by that name.

Taṃ sāriputtaṃ jinarājaputtaṃ, theraṃ thirānekaguṇādhivāsaṃ;

Paññāpabhāvuggatacārukittiṃ, sunīcavuttiñca atho namitvā.

Having paid homage to Sāriputta, the son of the King of Conquerors, the elder, the abode of numerous steadfast virtues, whose fair fame has risen through the power of wisdom, and who is of truly humble conduct.

Khamādayādiyuttena[M 0.0002], yuttamuttādivādinā;

Bahussutena therena, devena abhiyācito.

Requested by the learned elder Deva, endowed with patience, compassion, and other virtues, a speaker on what is proper, on liberation, and on other such topics,

Mahāvihāravāsīnaṃ[P 1.0002], sajjhāyamhi patiṭṭhito;

Gahetabbaṃ gahetvāna, porāṇesu vinicchayaṃ.

Established in the recitation of the residents of the Mahāvihāra, having taken up what should be taken from the judgments of the ancients,

Avokkamento samayaṃ sakañca, anāmasanto samayaṃ parañca;

Pubbopadesaṭṭhakathānayañca, yathānurūpaṃ upasaṃharanto.

Not distorting my own doctrine, nor misrepresenting the doctrine of others, and applying the method of the earlier commentaries appropriately,

Ñāṇappabhedāvahanassa tassa, yogīhi nekehi nisevitassa;

Atthaṃ apubbaṃ anuvaṇṇayanto, suttañca yuttiñca anukkamento.

Explaining the unique meaning of that [Mahāniddesa], which brings forth distinctions of knowledge and is frequented by many yogis, while following the Suttas and reasoning,

Ārabhissaṃ samāsena, mahāniddesavaṇṇanaṃ;

Saddhammabahumānena, nāttukkaṃsanakamyatā.

I will begin a brief explanation of the Great Exposition, out of great respect for the Good Dhamma, not from a desire for self-exaltation.

Vakkhāmahaṃ aṭṭhakathaṃ janassa, hitāya saddhammaciraṭṭhitatthaṃ;

Sakkacca saddhammapajotikaṃ taṃ, suṇātha dhāretha ca sādhu santoti.

I shall explain the commentary for the benefit of the people and for the long duration of the true Dhamma. O good people, listen attentively to that illuminator of the true Dhamma and retain it well.

Tattha “pāṭho visiṭṭho niddeso, taṃnāmavisesito cā”ti vuttattā duvidho pāṭho – byañjanapāṭho, atthapāṭho ca. Tesu byañjanapāṭho akkharapadabyañjanaākāraniruttiniddesavasena [V 0.0003] chabbidho. Atthapāṭho saṅkāsanapakāsanavivaraṇavibhajanauttānīkaraṇapaññattivasena chabbidho. Tattha tīsu dvāresu parisuddhapayogabhāvena visuddhakaruṇānaṃ cittena pavattitadesanā vācāhi akathitattā adesitattā akkharamiti saññitā, taṃ pārāyanikabrāhmaṇānaṃ manasā pucchitapañhānaṃ vasena bhagavatā ratanaghare nisīditvā sammasitapaṭṭhānamahāpakaraṇavasena ca akkharaṃ nāmāti gahetabbaṃ.

Here, because it is said 'the text is excellent, an exposition, and also specifically designated by that name,' the text is twofold: the verbal text and the meaning text. Among these, the verbal text is sixfold by way of letter, word, expression, mode, derivation, and exposition. The meaning text is sixfold by way of concise explanation, elucidation, elaboration, analysis, making clear, and designation. Here, the discourse, issued from a mind of purified compassion and perfectly expressed at the three doors, was not spoken, not taught, not uttered by words, hence it is designated 'letter' (akkhara). And that term should also be understood in relation to the questions asked mentally by the Pārāyana Brahmins, and to the Blessed One's contemplation, seated in the Jewel House, of the great Paṭṭhāna treatise.

Atha [M 0.0003] vā aparipuṇṇaṃ padaṃ akkharamiti gahetabbaṃ “saṭṭhivassasahassānī”ti [P 1.0003] evamādīsu (pe. va. 802; jā. 1.4.54; netti. 120) viya. Ettha hi sakāra nakāra sokārādīni akkharamiti, ekakkharaṃ vā padaṃ akkharamiti eke. “Yāyaṃ taṇhā ponobhavikā”ti evamādīsu (mahāva. 14; vibha. 203; ma. ni. 3.374; paṭi. ma. 2.30) vibhatyantaṃ atthajotakaṃ akkharapiṇḍaṃ padaṃ. “Nāmañca rūpañcā”ti evamādīsu (dha. sa. dukamātikā 109; su. ni. 878; mahāni. 107; cūḷani. ajitamāṇavapucchāniddeso 6; netti. 45) bahuakkharehi yuttaṃ padaṃ nāma. Saṃkhittena vuttaṃ padaṃ vibhāveti. Padena abhihitaṃ byañjayati byattaṃ pākaṭaṃ karotīti byañjanaṃ, vākyameva. “Cattāro iddhipādā”ti saṅkhepena kathitamatthaṃ. “Katame cattāro? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu chandasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti. Vīriyacittavīmaṃsasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāvetī”tiādīsu (vibha. 431; saṃ. ni. 5.813; dī. ni. 3.306; a. ni. 4.276) pākaṭakaraṇabhāvena byañjanaṃ nāma. Byañjanavibhāgapakāso ākāro. “Tattha katamo chando? Yo chando chandikatā kattukamyatā”ti evamādīsu (vibha. 433) kathitabyañjanaṃ anekavidhena vibhāgakaraṇaṃ ākāro nāma. Ākārābhihitassa nibbacanaṃ nirutti. “Phasso, vedanā”ti evamādīsu (dha. sa. 1) ākārena kathitaṃ “phusatīti phasso. Vediyatīti vedanā”ti nīharitvā vacanaṃ nirutti nāma. Nibbacanavitthāro nissesato desoti niddeso, vediyatīti vedanāti nibbacanaladdhapadaṃ “sukhā dukkhā adukkhamasukhā, sukhayatīti sukhā, dukkhayatīti dukkhā, neva dukkhayati na sukhayatīti adukkhamasukhā”ti atthavitthāro niravasesena kathitattā niddeso nāma.

Alternatively, an incomplete word should be understood as a letter (akkhara), as in examples like 'sixty thousand years'. Here, such as ‘sa’, ‘na’, ‘so’, are considered letters; or, some say, even a single-letter word is a letter. In phrases like 'that craving which leads to renewed existence', a word (pada) is a cluster of letters with an inflectional ending that illuminates the meaning. In expressions like 'name and form', a word is that which is constituted by multiple letters. A word elaborates what is stated concisely. Byañjana (expression) makes clear what is conveyed by a word, rendering it intelligible—it is essentially a sentence. 'The four bases of spiritual power'—this is the meaning stated concisely. When expanded, as in: 'What are the four? Here, monks, a monk develops the basis of spiritual power endowed with zeal, concentration, and volitional formations. He develops the basis of spiritual power endowed with energy, mind, and investigation...'—this is called byañjana because it makes the meaning clear. The ākāra (mode) is the way of dividing the expression. For instance, in the passage: 'Here, what is zeal? That which is zeal, zealfulness, the desire to act...'—the detailed classification of the expression is called the ākāra. The nirutti (derivation) is the etymological explanation of what is indicated by the mode. For example, in phrases like 'contact, feeling', the derivation is extracted by stating: ''Contact' because it touches, 'feeling' because it feels'—this is called nirutti. The niddesa (exposition) is the thorough explanation of the derivation without omission. For instance, having derived the word 'feeling' as 'that which feels', the full meaning is elaborated: 'pleasant, painful, neither-painful-nor-pleasant; 'pleasant' because it causes pleasure, 'painful' because it causes pain, 'neither-painful-nor-pleasant' because it causes neither pain nor pleasure.' Since this meaning is explained exhaustively, it is called a niddesa.

Evaṃ [P 1.0004] chabbidhāni byañjanapadāni jānitvā ca chasu atthapadesu saṅkhepato kāsanā dīpanā saṅkāsanā, “maññamāno kho, bhikkhu, bandho mārassa amaññamāno mutto pāpimato”ti evamādīsu saṅkhepena atthadīpanā saṅkāsanā nāma. Eso pana thero “buddhena bhagavatā [V 0.0004] evaṃ saṅkhepaṃ katvā vuttamatthaṃ ‘aññātaṃ bhagavā, aññātaṃ sugatā’”ti kathetuṃ samattho paṭivijjhi.

Thus, having known the six kinds of verbal expressions, among the six meaning-categories, the concise clarification and illumination is saṅkāsanā. In examples like ‘Bhikkhu, one who conceives is bound by Māra; one who does not conceive is freed from the Evil One,’ the concise illumination of meaning is called saṅkāsanā. Furthermore, that elder attained penetration so that he was capable of declaring the meaning spoken concisely by the Blessed One, saying, ‘It is understood, O Blessed One; it is understood, O Sugata!’

Upari [M 0.0004] vattabbamatthaṃ ādito kāsanā dīpanā pakāsanā, “sabbaṃ, bhikkhave, āditta”nti evamādīsu (mahāva. 54; saṃ. ni. 4.28) pacchā kathitabbamatthaṃ paṭhamavacanena dīpanā pakāsanā nāma. Evaṃ paṭhamaṃ dīpitaṃ atthaṃ puna pākaṭaṃ katvā dīpanena “kiñca, bhikkhave, sabbaṃ ādittaṃ? Cakkhuṃ, bhikkhave, ādittaṃ, rūpā ādittā”ti evamādīsu (mahāva. 54; saṃ. ni. 4.28) kathitesu “tikkhindriyo saṅkhepena vuttaṃ paṭivijjhatī”ti kathitattā dve atthapadāni tikkhindriyassa upakāravasena vuttāni.

The clarification and illumination from the beginning of a meaning to be expounded later is pakāsanā. This is exemplified by statements such as, 'Monks, all is burning,' where the meaning to be expounded later is illuminated by the initial statement. Thus, after first illuminating the meaning and then making it manifest again through elucidation, in statements such as, 'And what, monks, is all burning? The eye, monks, is burning; forms are burning,' etc., because it is stated that 'one with keen faculties penetrates what was stated concisely,' two meaning-terms are expressed as a help to one with keen faculties.

Saṃkhittassa vitthārābhidhānaṃ sakiṃ vuttassa ca punapi abhidhānaṃ vivaraṇaṃ, “kusalā dhammā”ti (dha. sa. 1) saṅkhepena nikkhittassa. “Katame dhammā kusalā? Yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hotī”ti (dha. sa. 1) niddesavasena vitthāraṇaṃ vitthāravasena puna kathanaṃ vivaraṇaṃ nāma.

The elaboration of a concise statement and the restatement of what was said once is called vivaraṇa (explanation). For instance, of the phrase 'wholesome states' concisely presented, the elaboration—that is, the restating in detail, carried out by way of exposition—such as: 'Which states are wholesome? At the time when a wholesome mind pertaining to the sense sphere has arisen,' is called vivaraṇa.

Taṃ vibhāgakaraṇaṃ vibhajanaṃ, “yasmiṃ samaye”ti (dha. sa. 1) vivarite kusale dhamme “tasmiṃ samaye phasso hoti, vedanā hotī”ti (dha. sa. 1) vibhāgakaraṇaṃ vibhajanaṃ nāma. Vivarassa vitthārābhidhānena vibhattassa ca upamābhidhānena [P 1.0005] paṭipādanaṃ uttānīkaraṇaṃ, vivaraṇena vivaritatthassa “katamo tasmiṃ samaye phasso hoti? Yo tasmiṃ samaye phasso phusanā samphusanā”ti (dha. sa. 2) ativivaritvā kathanañca vibhajanena vibhattassa “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, gāvī niccammā, evameva khvāhaṃ, bhikkhave, phassāhāro daṭṭhabboti vadāmī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.63) evamādiupamākathanañca uttānīkaraṇaṃ nāma. Dhammaṃ suṇantānaṃ dhammadesanena cittassa anekavidhena somanassauppādanañca atikhiṇabuddhīnaṃ anekavidhena ñāṇassa tikhiṇabhāvakaraṇañca paññatti nāma, tesaṃ suṇantānaṃ taṃcittatosanena taṃcittanisāmanena ca paññāyatīti paññatti. Tattha bhagavā akkharehi saṅkāsayati, padehi pakāsayati, byañjanehi vivarati, ākārehi vibhajati, niruttīhi uttānīkaroti, niddesehi paññāpayatīti. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Buddhā bhagavanto ekacce veneyye ekasmiṃ desane akkharehi atthasaṅkāsanaṃ karonti…pe… niddesehi atthapaññāpanaṃ karontīti ayamettha adhippāyo.

That which is a distinguishing, a dividing, is called analysis or classification. For example, when the wholesome states are explained with 'at which time' (Dhs. 1), and it is said 'at that time there is contact, there is feeling' (Dhs. 1), this is called analysis or classification. The presentation by way of detailed explanation of what has been opened up, and by way of simile for what has been distinguished, is called making plain. By extensively explaining what has been opened up—such as, 'What is the contact at that time? The contact at that time is touching, a touching, a thorough touching' (Dhs. 2)—and by illustrating with similes what has been distinguished by analysis—such as, 'Just as, monks, a cow without skin, so too, monks, I say that contact should be seen as food' (SN 2.63)—such illustrations are called making plain. Designation is the arousal of various kinds of joy in the minds of those listening to the Dhamma through the teaching of the Dhamma, and the sharpening of the knowledge of those with very keen intellects in various ways. It is called designation because for those listening, it is understood or known through the satisfaction and inclination of their minds. Therein, the Blessed One makes clear with syllables, reveals with words, explains with phrases, classifies with modes, makes plain with expressions, and designates with indications. What is meant? The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in teaching certain individuals to be trained, make the meaning clear with syllables… make the meaning known with indications—this is the intention here.

Atha [V 0.0005] vā akkharehi saṅkāsayitvā padehi pakāsayati, byañjanehi vivaritvā ākārehi vibhajati, niruttīhi uttānīkatvā niddesehi paññāpayati[M 0.0005]. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Evarūpena dhammadesanena ekaccesu ṭhānesu ekaccānaṃ veneyyānaṃ vinayatīti.

Or, having made clear with syllables, he reveals with words; having explained with phrases, he classifies by modes; having made plain with expressions, he designates with indications. What is meant? By such a teaching of the Dhamma, in certain instances, he trains certain individuals to be trained.

Atha vā akkharehi ugghāṭayitvā padehi pakāsento vinayati ugghaṭitaññuṃ, byañjanehi vivaritvā ākārehi vibhajanto vinayati vipañcitaññuṃ, niruttīhi uttānīkatvā niddesehi paññāpento vinayati neyyaṃ. Iti veneyyavasenapi yojetabbameva.

Or, by unfolding with syllables and revealing with words, he trains the one who understands quickly. By explaining with phrases and classifying by modes, he trains the one who understands through elaboration. By making plain with expressions and designating with indications, he trains the one who is to be led. Thus, it should be applied according to the disposition of the one to be led.

Atthato panettha katamo byañjanapāṭho, katamo atthapāṭhoti? Buddhānaṃ bhagavantānaṃ dhammaṃ desentānaṃ yo atthāvagamako saviññattikasaddo, so byañjanapāṭho[P 1.0006]. Yo tena abhisametabbo lakkhaṇarasādisahito dhammo, so atthapāṭhoti veditabbo. Punapi sandhāyabhāsito byañjanabhāsito sāvasesapāṭho anavasesapāṭho nīto neyyoti chabbidho pāṭho. Tattha anekatthavattā sandhāyabhāsito “mātaraṃ pitaraṃ hantvā, rājāno dve ca khattiye”ti evamādi (dha. pa. 294). Ekatthavattā byañjanabhāsito ‘manopubbaṅgamā dhammā”ti evamādi (dha. pa. 1.2; netti. 89, 92; peṭako. 14). Sāvaseso “sabbaṃ, bhikkhave, āditta”nti evamādi (mahāva. 54; saṃ. ni. 4.28). Viparīto anavaseso “sabbe dhammā sabbākārena buddhassa bhagavato ñāṇamukhe āpāthaṃ āgacchantī”ti evamādi (mahāni. 156; cūḷani. mogharājamāṇavapucchāniddeso 85; paṭi. ma. 3.5). Yathā vacanaṃ, tathā avagantabbo nīto “aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattā”ti evamādi. Yuttiyā anussaritabbo neyyo “ekapuggalo bhikkhave”ti evamādi (a. ni. 1.170).

Regarding meaning, what is the recitation of expressions, and what is the recitation of meaning? When the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, teach the Dhamma, the sound that conveys meaning along with expression is the recitation of expressions. The Dhamma that is to be understood through it, endowed with characteristics, function, and so on, is to be known as the recitation of meaning. Furthermore, the recitation is sixfold: spoken with an implied meaning, spoken literally, with remainder, without remainder, direct, and requiring inference. Among these, what is spoken with an implied meaning has multiple meanings, such as: 'Having slain mother and father, and two warrior kings' (Dhammapada 294). What is spoken literally has a single meaning, such as: 'Mind precedes all phenomena' (Dhammapada 1.2; Netti 89, 92; Peṭakopadesa 14). The one with remainder is like: 'Monks, all is burning' (Mahāvagga 54; Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.28). The opposite is the one without remainder, such as: 'All phenomena in every way come within the range of the Buddha’s knowledge' (Mahāniddesa 156; Cūḷaniddesa, Mogharājamāṇavapucchāniddesa 85; Paṭisambhidāmagga 3.5). What is to be understood just as it is spoken is the direct, such as: 'Impermanent, suffering, not-self.' What is to be inferred through reasoning is that requiring inference, such as: 'Monks, there is one person...' (Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.170).

Attho pana anekappakāro pāṭhattho sabhāvattho ñāyattho pāṭhānurūpo napāṭhānurūpo sāvasesattho niravasesattho nītattho neyyattho iccādi. Tattha yo appassatthassa ñāpanatthamuccāriyate, so pāṭhattho “sātthaṃ sabyañjana”ntiādīsu (pārā. 1; dī. ni. 1.190) viya. Rūpārūpadhammānaṃ lakkhaṇarasādisabhāvattho “sammādiṭṭhiṃ bhāvetī”tiādīsu (vibha. 485; saṃ. ni. 5.3) viya. Yo ñāyamāno hitāya saṃvattati, so ñātuṃ arahatīti ñāyattho – “atthavādī dhammavādī”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.9, 194; 3.238; ma. ni. 1.411) viya. Yathāpāṭhaṃ bhāsito pāṭhānurūpo “cakkhu[M 0.0006], bhikkhave, purāṇakamma”nti (saṃ. ni. 4.146) bhagavatā vuttaṃ. Tasmā cakkhumapi kammanti. Byañjanacchāyāya atthaṃ paṭibāhayamānena vutto attho napāṭhānurūpo, so pāṭhato ananuññāto akatapaṭikkhepo [V 0.0006] viyutto. So [P 1.0007] ca saṅgahetabbampi asaṅgahetvā, parivajjetabbampi vā kiñci aparivajjetvā parisesaṃ katvā vutto sāvasesattho “cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ (saṃ. ni. 4.60; mahāni. 107). Sabbe tasanti daṇḍassa, sabbe bhāyanti maccuno”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 129) viya. Viparīto niravasesattho “sandhāvitaṃ saṃsaritaṃ mamañceva tumhākañca (dī. ni. 2.155; mahāva. 287; netti. 114). Tatra, bhikkhave, ko mantā ko saddhātā…pe… aññatra diṭṭhapadehī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 7.66) viya. Saddavaseneva veditabbo nītattho “rūpā saddā rasā gandhā, phoṭṭhabbā ca manoramā”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.151, 165; mahāva. 33) viya. Sammutivasena veditabbo neyyattho “cattārome, bhikkhave, valāhakūpamā puggalā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.101-102) viya. Evamidha pāṭhañca atthañca vivaritvā ṭhito asaṃhīro bhavati paravādīhi dīgharattaṃ titthavāsena.

The meaning, however, is of various kinds: the literal meaning, the essential meaning, the beneficial meaning, the meaning conforming to the text, the meaning not conforming to the text, the meaning with remainder, the meaning without remainder, the explicit meaning, the implied meaning, and so on. Among these, what is expressed for the purpose of conveying the meaning of the text is the literal meaning, as in 'with meaning and phrasing' (Pārā. 1; Dī. Ni. 1.190) and the like. The inherent nature of material and immaterial phenomena, characterized by their marks, function, and so on, is the essential meaning, as in 'one develops right view' (Vibha. 485; Saṃ. Ni. 5.3) and the like. What, when understood, leads to benefit is the beneficial meaning—worthy of being known—as in 'one who speaks of meaning, one who speaks the Dhamma' (Dī. Ni. 1.9, 194; 3.238; Ma. Ni. 1.411) and the like. Spoken in accordance with the text is the meaning conforming to the text, as when the Blessed One said, 'Monks, the eye is old kamma' (Saṃ. Ni. 4.146). Therefore, even the eye is kamma. The meaning not conforming to the text is one spoken by one who obstructs the meaning through the semblance of phrasing; it is unauthorized by the text, not rejected, and disconnected. It is also the meaning with remainder when, without including what should be included or avoiding what should be avoided, a remainder is stated, as in 'dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises' (Saṃ. Ni. 4.60; Mahāni. 107) and 'All tremble at the rod, all fear death' (Dha. Pa. 129) and the like. The opposite is the meaning without remainder, as in 'Wandering and transmigrating, both mine and yours' (Dī. Ni. 2.155; Mahāva. 287; Netti. 114) and 'Here, monks, who is the thinker, who is the believer… except by way of what is seen?' (A. Ni. 7.66) and the like. The explicit meaning is to be understood merely by the words themselves, as in 'Forms, sounds, tastes, smells, and delightful touches' (Saṃ. Ni. 1.151, 165; Mahāva. 33) and the like. The implied meaning is to be understood by convention, as in 'Monks, these four persons are like clouds' (A. Ni. 4.101-102) and the like. Thus, having explained here both the text and the meaning, one stands unassailable by opponents, by long-term adherence to the teaching.

Iti asaṃhīrabhāvena yāva āgamādhigamasampadaṃ, tāva vattuṃ sakkoti. Saṅkhepavitthāranayena hetudāharaṇādīhi avabodhayituṃ samattho. Evaṃvidho attānañca parañca sodhetuṃ samatthabhāvena dussīlyadiṭṭhimalavirahitattā suci. Dussīlo hi attānaṃ upahanati, tena nādeyyavāco ca bhavati sabyohāramāno idha niccāturo vejjova. Duddiṭṭhi paraṃ upahanati, nāvassayo ca bhavati vāḷagahākulo iva kamalasaṇḍo. Ubhayavipanno pana sabbathāpi anupāsanīyo bhavati gūthagatamiva chavālātaṃ gūthagato viya ca kaṇhasappo. Ubhayasampanno pana sabbathāpi upāsanīyo sevitabbo ca viññūhi, nirupaddavo iva ratanākaro, evaṃ bhūto evaṃ amaccharo [P 1.0008] ahīnācariyamuṭṭhi. Suttasuttānulomaācariyavādaattanomatisaṅkhātānañca catunnaṃ apariccāgī, tesaṃ vasena byākhyāto.

Thus, by being unassailable, one is able to speak until the attainment of scriptural knowledge and accomplishment. He is capable of explaining concisely and in detail, with reasons and examples. Being thus capable of purifying both himself and others, he is pure—free from the defilements of misconduct and wrong view. For an immoral person harms himself, and thus his words are not to be accepted; and in his dealings here, he is like a physician who is always sick. One with wrong views harms others and is not a refuge, like a lotus pond crowded with fierce snakes. But one flawed in both ways is entirely unfit for association, like a burning brand fallen into dung or a black snake in dung. One accomplished in both, however, is entirely worthy of association and should be followed by the wise—like a jewel mine free from danger. Being such, he is without stinginess, not possessing the closed fist of a teacher. He does not abandon the four—namely, the suttas, what accords with the suttas, the tradition of the teachers, and his own considered judgment—and he expounds by way of these.

“Ekaṃsavacanaṃ ekaṃ, vibhajjavacanaṃ padaṃ;

Tatiyaṃ paṭipuccheyya, catutthaṃ pana ṭhāpaye”ti.

“One is a categorical statement, another is a statement requiring analysis; the third should be questioned in return, and the fourth should be set aside.”

Etesaṃ [M 0.0007] vā apariccāgī. Tato eva sotūnaṃ hite niyuttattā nesaṃ avabodhanaṃ pati akilāsu bhavatīti. Āha cettha –

Or, he does not abandon these. Therefore, because he is devoted to the welfare of the listeners, he is tireless in regard to their understanding. Here it is said:

“Pāṭhatthavidasaṃhīro, vattā suci amaccharo;

Catunnaṃ apariccāgī, desakassa hitānvito”ti.

“A knower of the text and meaning, unassailable, a speaker pure and unselfish; not abandoning the four, devoted to the welfare of others.”

Ettha [V 0.0007] desakassāti desako assa, bhaveyyāti attho. Hitānvitoti hite anugato hitacitto. So eso sucittā piyo, catunnaṃ apariccāgittā garu, asaṃhīrattā bhāvanīyo, desakattā vattā, hitānvitattā vacanakkhamo, pāṭhatthavidattā gambhīrakathaṃ kattā, amaccharattā na cāṭṭhāne niyojako iti –

Here, 'desakassa' means 'desako assa,' that is, 'he should be' is the meaning. 'Hitānvito' means 'one who follows what is beneficial, of beneficial mind.' Such a one, being of pure intention, is dear. Because of not abandoning the four, he is venerable. Because of not being timid, he is worthy of cultivation. Being a teacher, he is a speaker. Being endowed with what is beneficial, he is patient in speech. Knowing the text and its meaning, he is a speaker of profound discourse. Not being miserly, he does not assign tasks inappropriately.

“Piyo garu bhāvanīyo, vattā ca vacanakkhamo;

Gambhīrañca kathaṃ kattā, no cāṭṭhāne niyojako”ti. (a. ni. 7.37; netti. 113);

“Dear, venerable, worthy of cultivation, a speaker and patient in speech; a speaker of profound discourse, and one who does not assign tasks inappropriately.”

“Abhihito desako so, tāva dāni abhidhīyate”.

The speaker has been described; now the listener is described.

Tattha dhammagaruttā kathaṃ na paribhavati, ācariyagaruttā kathikaṃ na paribhavati, saddhāpaññādiguṇapaṭimaṇḍitattā attānaṃ na paribhavati, asaṭhāmāyāvittā amatābhimukhattā ca avikkhittacitto bhavati, sumedhattā yoniso manasi karotīti. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Herein, due to reverence for the Dhamma, one does not disparage the discourse; due to reverence for the teacher, one does not disparage the speaker; due to being adorned with qualities such as faith and wisdom, one does not disparage oneself; and due to being without deceit or trickery and facing towards the Deathless, one's mind becomes undistracted; due to great wisdom, one attends wisely. For this has been said:

“Pañcahi, bhikkhave, dhammehi samannāgato suṇanto saddhammaṃ bhabbo niyāmaṃ okkamituṃ kusalesu dhammesu sammattaṃ. Katamehi pañcahi? Na kathaṃ paribhoti, na kathikaṃ paribhoti, na attānaṃ paribhoti, avikkhittacitto [P 1.0009] dhammaṃ suṇāti ekaggacitto, yoniso manasi karotī”ti (a. ni. 5.151).

“Monks, endowed with five qualities, a listener of the true Dhamma is capable of entering the definite course in wholesome qualities, the right way. What five? He does not disparage the discourse, he does not disparage the speaker, he does not disparage himself, he listens to the Dhamma with an undistracted and concentrated mind, and he attends to it wisely.”

Taṃlakkhaṇappattattā bhāvanaṃ bhajatīti. Āha cettha –

Due to having attained those characteristics, one engages in cultivation. And here it is said:

“Dhammācariyagaru saddhāpaññādiguṇamaṇḍito;

Asaṭhāmāyāvikassa, sumedho amatābhimukho”. –

“Reverent towards the Dhamma and the teacher, adorned with qualities such as faith and wisdom; without deceit or trickery, wise, facing towards the Deathless.”

Iti vattā ca sotā ca.

Thus the speaker and the listener.

Evaṃ [M 0.0008] vuttappakāraṃ byañjanañca atthañca dassetvā idāni yo atiaggaṃ katvā kathitattā mahāsamuddamahāpathavī viya mahā ca so niddeso cāti mahāniddeso, taṃ mahāniddesaṃ vaṇṇayissāmi.

Having thus explained the expression and the meaning, I shall now comment on the Mahāniddesa, which is so called because it is a 'Great Exposition,' having been spoken with utmost excellence and being vast like the great ocean and the great earth.

Tadetaṃ [V 0.0008] mahāniddesaṃ atthasampannaṃ byañjanasampannaṃ gambhīraṃ gambhīratthaṃ lokuttarappakāsakaṃ suññatappaṭisaṃyuttaṃ paṭipattimaggaphalavisesasādhanaṃ paṭipattipaṭipakkhapaṭisedhanaṃ yogāvacarānaṃ ñāṇavararatanākarabhūtaṃ dhammakathikānaṃ dhammakathāvilāsavisesahetubhūtaṃ saṃsārabhīrukānaṃ dukkhanissaraṇatadupāyadassanena assāsajananatthaṃ tappaṭipakkhanāsanatthañca gambhīratthānañca anekesaṃ suttantapadānaṃ atthavivaraṇena sujanahadayaparitosajananatthaṃ, tathāgatena arahatā sammāsambuddhena sabbattha appaṭihatasabbaññutaññāṇamahādīpobhāsena sakalajanavitthatamahākaruṇāsinehena veneyyajanahadayagatakilesandhakāravidhamanatthaṃ samujjalitassa saddhammamahāpadīpassa tadadhippāyavikāsanasinehaparisekena pañcavassasahassamaticirasamujjalanamicchatā lokānukampakena satthukappena dhammarājassa dhammasenāpatinā āyasmatā sāriputtattherena bhāsitaṃ sutvā āyasmā ānando paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikāle yathāsutameva saṅgahaṃ āropesi.

This great exposition—rich in meaning and expression, profound and of deep meaning, revealing the supramundane, connected with emptiness, accomplishing the distinction of the path and fruit of practice, counteracting the hindrances to practice, a treasure mine of noble knowledge for meditators, a special cause for the delight of Dhamma preachers in their Dhamma talks, intended to give solace to those afraid of saṃsāra by showing the escape from suffering and its means, to dispel their opposing states, and to gladden the hearts of the good by explaining the profound meanings of many sutta passages—was spoken by the venerable elder Sāriputta, the general of the King of Dhamma, who is like the Teacher and compassionate towards the world. He spoke it with the wish that the great lamp of the true Dhamma—lit by the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, with the great light of his unobstructed omniscient knowledge and the affection of his great compassion for all beings, in order to dispel the darkness of defilements in the hearts of those to be trained—should blaze for a very long time, even beyond five thousand years, by being sprinkled with the oil of affection for unfolding its meaning. Having heard it, the venerable Ānanda, during the First Great Council, compiled it exactly as he had heard it.

So panesa vinayapiṭakaṃ suttantapiṭakaṃ abhidhammapiṭakanti [P 1.0010] tīsu piṭakesu suttantapiṭakapariyāpanno, dīghanikāyo majjhimanikāyo saṃyuttanikāyo aṅguttaranikāyo khuddakanikāyoti pañcasu mahānikāyesu khuddakamahānikāyapariyāpanno, suttaṃ geyyaṃ veyyākaraṇaṃ gāthā udānaṃ itivuttakaṃ jātakaṃ abbhutadhammaṃ vedallanti navasu satthusāsanaṅgesu yathāsambhavaṃ gāthaṅgaveyyākaraṇaṅgadvayasaṅgahito.

This, however, is included in the Suttanta Piṭaka, one of the three Piṭakas: the Vinaya Piṭaka, Suttanta Piṭaka, and Abhidhamma Piṭaka. Among the five great Nikāyas, namely, the Dīgha Nikāya, Majjhima Nikāya, Saṃyutta Nikāya, Aṅguttara Nikāya, and Khuddaka Nikāya, it is included in the Khuddaka Nikāya. Among the nine limbs of the Teacher’s Dispensation, namely, Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla, it is included, as appropriate, in the two limbs of Gāthā and Veyyākaraṇa.

“Dvāsīti buddhato gaṇhiṃ, dvesahassāni bhikkhuto;

Caturāsīti sahassāni, ye me dhammā pavattino”ti. (theragā. 1027) –

“Eighty-two thousand I received from the Buddha, two thousand from the monks; eighty-four thousand are the teachings that are current for me.”

Dhammabhaṇḍāgārikattherena pañcasu ṭhānesu etadaggaṃ āropitena paṭiññātānaṃ caturāsītiyā dhammakkhandhasahassānaṃ bhikkhuto gahitesu dvīsu dhammakkhandhasahassesu anekasatadhammakkhandhasaṅgahito. Tassa dve vaggā aṭṭhakavaggo pārāyanavaggo khaggavisāṇasuttañca, ekekasmiṃ vagge soḷasa soḷasa katvā khaggavisāṇasuttañcāti tettiṃsa suttāni kāmasuttādikhaggavisāṇasuttapariyosānāni[M 0.0009]. Evaṃ anekadhā vavatthāpitassa imassa mahāniddesassa anupubbapadatthavaṇṇanaṃ karissāmi. Ayañhi mahāniddeso pāṭhato atthato ca uddisantena niddisantena ca sakkaccaṃ uddisitabbo niddisitabbo ca, uggaṇhantenāpi sakkaccaṃ uggaṇhitabbo dhāretabbo ca. Taṃ kissa hetu? Gambhīrattā imassa mahāniddesassa lokahitāya loke ciraṭṭhitatthanti.

It is comprised of many hundreds of Dhamma aggregates from the two thousand Dhamma aggregates received from the monks, out of the eighty-four thousand Dhamma aggregates mastered by the Elder, the Treasurer of the Dhamma, who was declared foremost in five respects. It has two sections—the Aṭṭhakavagga and the Pārāyanavagga—and the Khaggavisāṇa Sutta. With sixteen suttas in each section, and including the Khaggavisāṇa Sutta, there are thirty-three suttas in total, from the Kāma Sutta to the Khaggavisāṇa Sutta. Having thus classified this Mahāniddesa in various ways, I will now provide a sequential explanation of the meaning of its words. For this Mahāniddesa must be carefully pointed out and explained by one who teaches it, both in terms of text and meaning, and it must also be diligently learned and retained by one who learns it. Why is this? Because of the profundity of this Mahāniddesa, for the welfare of the world and for its long-lasting benefit.

1. Aṭṭhakavaggo

1. The Chapter of Eights

1. Kāmasuttaniddesavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Exposition of the Kāma Sutta

Tattha [V 0.0009][P 1.0011] kāmasuttaṃ ādi. Tasmimpi “kāmaṃ kāmayamānassā”ti gāthā ādi. Sā uddesaniddesapaṭiniddesavasena tidhā ṭhitā. “Kāmaṃ kāmayamānassā”ti evamādi uddeso. “Kāmāti uddānato dve kāmā – vatthukāmā ca kilesakāmā cā”ti niddeso. “Katame vatthukāmā? Manāpikā rūpā”ti evamādi paṭiniddeso.

Herein, the Kāma Sutta is first. Within it, the verse beginning “kāmaṃ kāmayamānassa” is first. It stands threefold in terms of statement, explanation, and detailed exposition. “Kāmaṃ kāmayamānassa” and so forth is the statement. “Sensual pleasures—in summary, there are two kinds of sensual pleasures: sensual pleasures as objects and sensual pleasures as defilements” is the explanation. “What are sensual pleasures as objects? Pleasing forms,” and so forth, is the detailed exposition.

1. Tattha kāmanti manāpiyarūpāditebhūmakadhammasaṅkhātaṃ vatthukāmaṃ. Kāmayamānassāti icchamānassa. Tassa cetaṃ samijjhatīti tassa kāmayamānassa sattassa taṃ kāmasaṅkhātaṃ vatthu samijjhati ce, sace so taṃ labhatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Addhā pītimano hotīti ekaṃsaṃ tuṭṭhacitto hoti. Laddhāti labhitvā. Maccoti satto. Yadicchatīti yaṃ icchati. Idaṃ pana saṅkhepato padatthasambandhamattameva, vitthāro pana upari pāḷiyaṃ āgatanayeneva veditabbo. Yathā ca imasmiṃ, evaṃ ito paraṃ sabbesupīti.

1. Herein, 'kāma' refers to sensual pleasure as an object, designated as pleasing forms and other things pertaining to the three planes of existence. 'Kāmayamānassa' means 'of one who desires.' 'If this succeeds for him' means that if the object of desire succeeds for the being who desires it, that is, if he obtains it. 'Surely, he becomes joyful' means his mind becomes decidedly delighted. 'Laddhā' means 'having obtained.' 'Macco' means 'a mortal,' a being. 'Yadicchati' means 'whatever he desires.' This, in brief, is merely the connection of the word-meanings; the detailed explanation should be understood according to the method given above in the Pāli text. And as in this case, so too in all that follows.

Kāmāti uddisitabbapadaṃ. Uddānatoti niddisitabbapadaṃ. Uddānatoti vaggavasena “macchuddānaṃ kineyyā”ti ādīsu viya. Atha vā uparūpari dānato uddānaṃ, uddhaṃ uddhaṃ sodhanato byavadānaṭṭhena vodānaṃ viya. Vitthārakaraṇabhāvena vā. Kāmā iti pāṭhasesaṃ katvā vattabbaṃ. Dveti gaṇanaparicchedo[M 0.0010], na ekaṃ, na tayo. Vatthukāmā cāti manāpiyarūpādivatthukāmā ca. Upatāpanaṭṭhena vibādhanaṭṭhena ca kilesakāmā ca. Tesu vatthukāmo pariññeyyo, kilesakāmo [V 0.0010] pahātabbo. Tattha vatthukāmo [P 1.0012] kilesakāmena patthayitabboti kāmīyatīti kāmo. Kilesakāmo vatthukāmānaṃ paccāsīsanassa kāraṇabhāvena kāmīyate anenāti kāmo. Tattha rūpādikkhandhe saṅgahito vatthukāmo, saṅkhārakkhandhe saṅgahito kilesakāmo. Chahi viññāṇehi vijānitabbo vatthukāmo, manoviññāṇena jānitabbo kilesakāmo. Kilesānaṃ patiṭṭhaṭṭhena kāraṇaṭṭhena ārammaṇaṭṭhena ca vatthukāmo.

'Kāma' is a term to be stated. 'Uddāna' is a term to be explained. 'Uddāna' signifies enumeration, as in sections with phrases like 'macchuddānaṃ kineyyā' and so on. Alternatively, 'uddāna' means a summing up, just as 'vodāna' means purification in the sense of cleansing again and again. Or it may mean elaboration. The word 'Kāmā' is to be stated, taking it as the remainder of the text. 'Dve' indicates a numerical distinction—not one, not three. 'Vatthukāmā' refers to desirable objects such as pleasing forms, and 'kilesakāmā' refers to defilements in the sense of torment and affliction. Of these, object-desire is to be fully understood, and defilement-desire is to be abandoned. Here, object-desire is called 'kāma' because it is desired by defilement-desire. Defilement-desire is called 'kāma' because it is the cause of craving for object-desires. In this context, object-desire is included in the aggregates of form, etc., while defilement-desire is included in the aggregate of mental formations. Object-desire is to be known by the six types of consciousness, while defilement-desire is to be known by mental consciousness. Object-desire serves as the basis, cause, and object for defilements.

“Nete kāmā yāni citrāni loke, saṅkapparāgo purisassa kāmo;

Tiṭṭhanti citrāni tatheva loke, athettha dhīrā vinayanti chanda”nti. (a. ni. 6.63);

'The varied things in the world are not sensual pleasures; a person's lustful intention is sensual pleasure. The varied things remain just as they are in the world, while the wise subdue their desire for them.' (AN 6.63)

Nandamāṇavaka- (dha. pa. aṭṭha. 1.68 uppalavaṇṇattherīvatthu) soreyyaseṭṭhiputtādīnaṃ (dha. pa. 43) vatthūni cettha nidassanaṃ. Kilesakāmo tāpanaṭṭhena bādhanaṭṭhena ca sayaṃ kāmetīti kāmo. Vuttampi cetaṃ “ratto kho, brāhmaṇa, rāgena abhibhūto pariyādinnacitto attabyābādhāyapi ceteti, parabyābādhāyapi ceteti, ubhayabyābādhāyapi cetetī”ti ca “ratto kho, brāhmaṇa, pāṇampi hanati, adinnampi ādiyati, paradārampi gacchati, musāpi bhaṇatī”ti (a. ni. 3.54) ca evamādi nidassanaṃ.

The stories of the young man Nanda (DhpA. 1.68, Uppalavaṇṇattherīvatthu), the treasurer's son Soreyya (Dhp. 43), and others are examples here. Defilement-desire is called 'kāma' because it itself desires, in the sense of burning and oppressing. And this has been said: 'Lustful, brahmin, overcome by lust, with mind obsessed, one intends one’s own affliction, the affliction of others, and the affliction of both.' And: 'Lustful, brahmin, one kills living beings, takes what is not given, goes to another's wife, and speaks falsely.' (AN 3.54) Such are the examples.

Tameva paṭiniddesavasena vitthāretvā vattukāmo – “katame vatthukāmā”tiādimāha. Tattha katameti kathetukamyatāpucchā. Pañcavidhā hi pucchā, tāsaṃ vibhāgo upari pāḷiyaṃyeva āvi bhavissati. Tāsu ayaṃ kathetukamyatāpucchā. Tattha manāpikāti manaṃ appāyanti vaddhentīti manāpā, manāpā eva manāpikā. Rūpāti kammacittautuāhārasamuṭṭhānavasena catusamuṭṭhānikā rūpārammaṇā. Rūpayantīti rūpā, vaṇṇavikāraṃ āpajjamānā hadayaṅgatabhāvaṃ pakāsentīti attho.

Wishing to speak on this very point, expanding on it by way of detailed exposition, he says, beginning with: 'What are the objects of desire?' Here, 'what' is a question expressing the wish to speak. For there are five kinds of questions, and their classification will become clear later in the Pāli text itself. Among them, this is a question expressing the wish to speak. Here, 'manāpikā' means pleasing; because they satisfy and increase the mind, they are 'manāpā', and 'manāpā' are indeed 'manāpikā.' 'Rūpā' refers to form-objects of fourfold origin, arising from kamma, mind, temperature, and nutriment. They are called 'rūpā' because they manifest form, meaning they undergo changes of appearance and reveal their state of being captivating to the heart.

Tattha [M 0.0011] kenaṭṭhena rūpanti? Ruppanaṭṭhena. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

In what sense is it 'rūpa'? In the sense of being afflicted. For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Kiñca, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ vadetha? Ruppatīti kho, bhikkhave, tasmā ‘rūpa’nti vuccati. Kena ruppati? Sītenapi ruppati, uṇhenapi ruppati, jighacchāyapi [P 1.0013] ruppati, pipāsāyapi ruppati, ḍaṃsamakasavātātapasarīsapasamphassenapi ruppati. Ruppatīti kho, bhikkhave, tasmā ‘rūpa’nti vuccatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.79).

'And what, bhikkhus, do you call form? It is afflicted, bhikkhus, therefore it is called form. By what is it afflicted? It is afflicted by cold, by heat, by hunger, by thirst; it is afflicted by contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things. It is afflicted, bhikkhus, therefore it is called form.' (SN 22.79)

Tattha [V 0.0011] ruppatīti kuppati ghaṭṭīyati pīḷīyati, bhijjatīti attho. Sītena tāva ruppanaṃ lokantarikaniraye pākaṭaṃ. Mahiṃsakaraṭṭhādīsupi himapātasītalesu padesesu etaṃ pākaṭameva. Tattha hi sattā sītena bhinnachinnasarīrā jīvitakkhayampi pāpuṇanti.

There, 'ruppati' means it is agitated, struck, oppressed, and broken. First, affliction by cold is evident in the Lokantarika hell. It is also evident in regions like the Mahiṃsaka country and other places cold with snowfall. For there, beings with bodies broken and torn by the cold even meet with the destruction of life.

Uṇhena ruppanaṃ avīcimahāniraye pākaṭaṃ. Tattha hi tattāya lohapathaviyā nipajjāpetvā pañcavidhabandhanādikaraṇakāle sattā mahādukkhaṃ anubhavanti.

Affliction by heat is evident in the Avīci great hell. There, having been made to lie on the hot iron ground, beings experience great suffering at the time of the fivefold binding and other such acts.

Jighacchāya ruppanaṃ pettivisaye ceva dubbhikkhakāle ca pākaṭaṃ. Pettivisayasmiñhi sattā dve tīṇi buddhantarāni kiñcideva āmisaṃ hatthena gahetvā mukhe pakkhipantā nāma na honti, antoudaraṃ ādittasusirarukkho viya hoti. Dubbhikkhe kañjikamattampi alabhitvā maraṇasattānaṃ pamāṇaṃ natthi.

Affliction by hunger is evident in the realm of ghosts and during times of famine. In the realm of ghosts, for two or three Buddha-intervals, beings are not able to take any kind of food with their hands and put it in their mouths; their insides are like a burning hollow tree. During a famine, there is no counting the beings who die without obtaining even a measure of gruel.

Pipāsāya ruppanaṃ kālakañjikādīsu pākaṭaṃ. Tattha hi sattā dve tīṇi buddhantarāni hadayatemanamattaṃ vā jivhātemanamattaṃ vā udakabindumpi laddhuṃ na sakkonti. “Pānīyaṃ pivissāmā”ti nadiṃ gatānaṃ jalaṃ vālukātalaṃ sampajjati. Mahāsamuddaṃ pakkhantānampi samuddo piṭṭhipāsāṇoyeva hoti. Te sussantā balavadukkhapīḷitā viravanti. Ḍaṃsādīhi ruppanaṃ ḍaṃsamakkhikādibahulesu padesesu pākaṭaṃ. Taṃ pana – “katamaṃ taṃ rūpaṃ sanidassanaṃ? Sappaṭigha”nti ādinā nayena abhidhamme (dha. sa. 656, 658) vitthāritameva.

Affliction by thirst is evident among the Kālakañjika petas and others. There, for two or three Buddha-intervals, beings are unable to get even a drop of water sufficient to moisten the heart or to moisten the tongue. For those who go to a river thinking, 'We will drink water,' the water turns into a bed of sand. Even for those who enter the great ocean, the ocean becomes just a slab of rock. Parched and afflicted by intense suffering, they cry out. Affliction by gadflies and the like is evident in places teeming with gadflies, flies, and so on. This, however, is explained in detail in the Abhidhamma by the method beginning: 'What is that form which is visible and resistant?' and so on (Dhs. §656, §658).

Sappantīti saddā, udāharīyantīti attho. Utucittavasena dvisamuṭṭhānikā saddā. Gandhayantīti gandhā, attano vatthūni sūcayantīti attho. Rasanti te sattāti rasā, assādentīti attho. Phusīyantīti phoṭṭhabbā[M 0.0012]. Ete gandhādayo catusamuṭṭhānikāva[P 1.0014]. Tesaṃ vibhāgo abhidhamme (dha. sa. 622-624) vitthāritoyeva.

Sounds are called 'saddā' because they travel (`sappanti`); the meaning is that they are uttered. Sounds arise from two sources: temperature and mind. Scents are called 'gandhā' because they give off a scent (`gandhayanti`); the meaning is that they indicate their own bases. Flavors are called 'rasā' because beings relish (`rasanti`) them; the meaning is that they are savored. Tangibles (`phoṭṭhabbā`) are so called because they are touched (`phusīyanti`). These—scents and the rest—arise from four sources. Their classification is explained in detail in the Abhidhamma (Dhs. §622-624).

Tamevatthaṃ vitthāravasena dassento “attharaṇā pāvuraṇā”tiādimāha. Tattha attharitvā nipajjiyantīti attharaṇā. Sarīraṃ veṭhetvā pārupīyantīti pāvuraṇā. Antojātādayo cattāro dāsī ca dāso ca dāsidāsā. Khettaṃ nāma yasmiṃ pubbaṇṇaṃ ruhati. Vatthu nāma yasmiṃ aparaṇṇaṃ ruhati. Yattha vā ubhayampi ruhati, taṃ khettaṃ. Tadatthāya katabhūmibhāgo vatthu. Khettavatthusīsena cettha vāpītaḷākādīnipi saṅgahitāni. Hiraññanti kahāpaṇo. Suvaṇṇanti jātarūpaṃ. Tesaṃ gahaṇena lohamāsako jatumāsako dārumāsakoti sabbepi saṅgahaṃ gacchanti. Gāmanigamarājadhāniyoti [V 0.0012] ekakuṭikādi gāmo. Āpaṇayutto nigamo. Ekassa rañño āṇāpavattiṭṭhānaṃ rājadhānī. Raṭṭhanti janapadekadesaṃ. Janapadoti kāsikosalādijanapado. Kosoti catubbidho koso – hatthī asso ratho patti. Koṭṭhāgāranti tividhaṃ koṭṭhāgāraṃ – dhanakoṭṭhāgāraṃ dhaññakoṭṭhāgāraṃ vatthakoṭṭhāgāraṃ. Yaṃ kiñcīti anavasesapariyādānavacanaṃ. Rajanīyanti rañjetuṃ yuttaṭṭhena.

To show this same meaning in detail, he says, beginning with 'coverings and cloaks.' Here, 'coverings' (`attharaṇā`) are so called because, having been spread out, they are lain upon. 'Cloaks' (`pāvuraṇā`) are so called because, having wrapped the body, they are worn. Female and male slaves (`dāsidāsā`): the four kinds, beginning with those born in the household. A 'field' (`khetta`) is that in which early grain grows. A 'site' (`vatthu`) is that in which later grain grows. Or, where both grow is a 'field'; a plot of land prepared for that purpose is a 'site'. Under the heading of 'fields and sites,' reservoirs, ponds, and so on are also included. 'Hirañña' is a kahāpaṇa. 'Suvaṇṇa' is gold. By mentioning these, all coins—such as metal coins, lac coins, and wooden coins—are included. Village, town, and royal capital: a village is a single hut and so on. A town is endowed with shops. A royal capital is the place where the command of a single king prevails. 'Raṭṭha' is a part of a country. 'Janapada' is a country such as Kāsi or Kosala. The army (`koso`) is of four kinds: elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry. The storehouse (`koṭṭhāgāra`) is of three kinds: a treasury for wealth, a granary for grain, and a storehouse for cloth. 'Whatever' is a term indicating complete inclusion. 'Rajanīya' means in the sense of being fit to arouse passion.

Ito paraṃ tikavasena dassetuṃ atītattikaajjhattattikahīnattikaokāsattikasaṃyogattikakāmāvacarattikavasena chattike āha. Tattha atītattike tāva attano sabhāvaṃ uppādādikkhaṇaṃ vā patvā atikkantāti atītā. Tadubhayampi na āgatāti anāgatā. Taṃ taṃ kāraṇaṃ paṭicca uppannāti paccuppannā. Idaṃ bhavena paricchannaṃ. Paṭisandhito hi paṭṭhāya atītabhavesu nibbattā anantarabhave vā nibbattā hontu kappakoṭisatasahassamatthake vā, sabbe atītāyeva nāma. Cutito paṭṭhāya anāgatabhavesu nibbattanakā kāmā anantarabhave vā nibbattantu kappakoṭisatasahassamatthake vā, sabbe [P 1.0015] anāgatāyeva nāma. Cutipaṭisandhiantare pavattā kāmā paccuppannā nāma.

To further explain this by way of triplets, he states six triplets: the past triplet, the internal triplet, the inferior triplet, the spatial triplet, the associative triplet, and the sense-sphere triplet. Here, in the past triplet, first, having reached their own nature or the moment of arising and so forth, they have passed—thus, they are past. Both of those have not yet arrived—thus, they are future. Having arisen dependent on this or that cause—thus, they are present. This is delimited by existence. For, starting from rebirth-linking, those that have arisen in past existences, whether they arose in the immediately following existence or at the end of a hundred thousand crores of aeons, are all simply called past. Starting from death, those sensual pleasures destined to arise in future existences, whether they arise in the immediately following existence or at the end of a hundred thousand crores of aeons, are all simply called future. Those sensual pleasures occurring between rebirth-linking and death are called present.

Ajjhattattike “evaṃ pavattamānā mayaṃ attāti gahaṇaṃ gamissāmā”ti iminā viya adhippāyena attānaṃ adhikāraṃ katvā pavattā attano santāne [M 0.0013] pavattā pāṭipuggalikā kāmā ajjhattā kāmā nāma. Tato bahibhūtā pana indriyabaddhā vā anindriyabaddhā vā bahiddhā nāma. Tatiyapadaṃ tadubhayavasena vuttaṃ.

In the internal triplet, with the intention, as it were, 'As this continues, we will grasp at a self,' making the self the authority, the individual sensual pleasures occurring in one's own continuum are called internal sensual pleasures. But those external to that, whether bound by the sense faculties or not bound by the sense faculties, are called external. The third term is stated with reference to both.

Hīnattike hīnāti lāmakā. Majjhimāti hīnapaṇītānaṃ majjhe bhavāti majjhimā. Avasesā uttamaṭṭhena paṇītā. Api ca upādāyupādāya hīnamajjhimapaṇītatā veditabbā. Nerayikānañhi kāmā koṭippattā hīnā nāma. Te upādāya tiracchānesu nāgasupaṇṇānaṃ kāmā paṇītā nāma. Sesatiracchānagatānaṃ kāmā majjhimā nāma. Tesampi kāmā hīnā. Te upādāya mahesakkhapetānaṃ kāmā paṇītā nāma. Avasesānaṃ kāmā majjhimā nāma. Tesampi hīnā. Te upādāya jānapadānaṃ kāmā paṇītā nāma. Paccantavāsīnaṃ kāmā majjhimā nāma. Tesampi hīnā. Te upādāya gāmabhojakānaṃ kāmā paṇītā nāma. Tesaṃ paricārikānaṃ kāmā majjhimā nāma. Tesampi hīnā. Te upādāya janapadasāmikānaṃ kāmā paṇītā nāma. Tesaṃ paricārikānaṃ kāmā majjhimā nāma. Tesampi hīnā. Te upādāya padesarājūnaṃ kāmā paṇītā nāma. Tesaṃ amaccānaṃ kāmā majjhimā nāma. Tesampi hīnā. Te upādāya cakkavattirañño [V 0.0013] kāmā paṇītā nāma. Tassa amaccānaṃ kāmā majjhimā nāma. Tassapi hīnā. Te upādāya bhummadevānaṃ kāmā paṇītā nāma. Tesaṃ paricārikānaṃ devānaṃ kāmā majjhimā nāma. Tesampi hīnā. Te upādāya cātumahārājikānaṃ devānaṃ kāmā paṇītātiādinā nayena yāva akaniṭṭhadevānaṃ kāmā matthakappattā paṇītā nāma. Evaṃ upādāyupādāya hīnamajjhimapaṇītatā veditabbā.

In the inferior triplet, the inferior are the base. The middling are those that exist between the inferior and the refined. The rest are the refined in the sense of being excellent. Moreover, the inferior, middling, and refined should be understood relatively, depending on what is taken as a basis. For instance, the sensual pleasures of hell-beings, though extreme, are called inferior. Taking those as a basis, the sensual pleasures of animals like nāgas and garuḍas are called refined. The sensual pleasures of other animals are called middling. But even those sensual pleasures are inferior. Taking those as a basis, the sensual pleasures of powerful pretas are called refined. The sensual pleasures of the remaining pretas are called middling. But even those are inferior. Taking those as a basis, the sensual pleasures of people in the countryside are called refined. The sensual pleasures of those living on the borders are called middling. But even those are inferior. Taking those as a basis, the sensual pleasures of village headmen are called refined. The sensual pleasures of their attendants are called middling. But even those are inferior. Taking those as a basis, the sensual pleasures of district lords are called refined. The sensual pleasures of their attendants are called middling. But even those are inferior. Taking those as a basis, the sensual pleasures of local rulers are called refined. The sensual pleasures of their ministers are called middling. But even those are inferior. Taking those as a basis, the sensual pleasures of a wheel-turning king are called refined. The sensual pleasures of his ministers are called middling. But even his are inferior. Taking those as a basis, the sensual pleasures of earth-bound devas are called refined. The sensual pleasures of the devas who are their attendants are called middling. But even those are inferior. Taking those as a basis, the sensual pleasures of the devas of the Four Great Kings are called refined, and so on, up to the sensual pleasures of the Akaniṭṭha devas, which, having reached the ultimate peak, are called refined. Thus, the inferior, middling, and refined should be understood relatively, depending on what is taken as a basis.

Okāsattike āpāyikā kāmāti avaḍḍhisaṅkhātesu apagataayesu [P 1.0016] catūsu apāyesu nibbattakāmā āpāyikā. Manussesu nibbattakāmā mānusikā. Devesu nibbattakāmā dibbā.

In the spatial triplet, the sensual pleasures that arise in the four woeful states—known as 'non-growth' (avaḍḍhi) and 'loss of gain' (apagata-āya)—are called 'āpāyikā'. The sensual pleasures that arise among humans are called 'mānusikā'. The sensual pleasures that arise among the devas are called 'dibbā'.

Saṃyogattike paccupaṭṭhitānaṃ kāmānaṃ paribhuñjanato ṭhapetvā nerayike sesaapāyasattānaṃ manussānaṃ cātumahārājike deve upādāya yāva tusitakāyikānañca devānaṃ kāmā paccupaṭṭhitā kāmā nāma. Pakatipaṭiyattārammaṇato atirekena ramitukāmatākāle yathārucitaṃ ārammaṇaṃ nimminitvā nimminitvā ramantīti nimmānaratīnaṃ devānaṃ kāmā nimmitā kāmā nāma. Attano ajjhāsayaṃ ñatvā parehi nimmite ārammaṇe [M 0.0014] sevantīti paranimmitavasavattīnaṃ kāmā paranimmitā kāmā nāma. Pariggahitāti “mayhaṃ eta”nti gahitā kāmā. Apariggahitāti tathā apariggahitā uttarakurukānaṃ kāmā. Mamāyitāti taṇhāvasena “mama eta”nti gahitā. Amamāyitāti vuttapaṭipakkhā.

In the associative triplet, the sensual pleasures of beings in woeful states (excluding hell-beings), of humans, and of devas from the Cātumahārājika realm up to the Tusita realm, are called 'present sensual pleasures' (paccupaṭṭhitā kāmā). When they desire to delight beyond their naturally prepared objects, creating objects as they wish and repeatedly delighting in them, the sensual pleasures of the Nimmānaratī devas (devas who delight in creation) are called 'created sensual pleasures' (nimmitā kāmā). Knowing their own disposition, they enjoy objects created by others; thus, the sensual pleasures of the Paranimmitavasavattī devas (devas who wield power over others' creations) are called 'sensual pleasures created by others' (paranimmitā kāmā). 'Possessed' (pariggahitā) sensual pleasures are those grasped with the thought, "This is mine." 'Unpossessed' (apariggahitā) sensual pleasures are those not grasped in that way, such as the sensual pleasures of the Uttarakuru beings. 'Claimed' (mamāyitā) sensual pleasures are those seized through craving with the thought, "This is mine." 'Unclaimed' (amamāyitā) sensual pleasures are the opposite of what has been described.

Sabbepi kāmāvacarā dhammāti “heṭṭhato avīcinirayaṃ pariyantaṃ karitvā”tiādinā (dha. sa. 1287) nayena vuttesu kāmāvacaradhammesu pariyāpannā. Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho – uddānato dve kāmā, vatthukāmo ca kilesakāmo cāti. Tattha kilesakāmo atthato chandarāgo. Vatthukāmo tebhūmakaṃ vaṭṭaṃ. Kilesakāmo cettha kāmetīti kāmo. Itaro kāmīyatīti. Yasmiṃ pana padese duvidhopeso kāmo pavattivasena avacarati, so catunnaṃ apāyānaṃ manussānaṃ channañca devalokānaṃ vasena ekādasavidho padeso kāmo ettha avacaratīti kāmāvacaro. Tattha pariyāpannadhamme sandhāya “sabbepi kāmāvacarā dhammā”ti vuttaṃ. Attano sabhāvaṃ dhārentīti dhammā. Rūpāvacarā dhammāti “heṭṭhato brahmalokaṃ pariyantaṃ karitvā uparito akaniṭṭhe deve antokaritvā”tiādinā (dha. sa. 1289) nayena vuttānaṃ rūpāvacaradhammānaṃ vasena sabbepi dhammā rūpāvacarā. Arūpāvacarā dhammāti “heṭṭhato ākāsānañcāyatanupage deve pariyantaṃ karitvā uparito nevasaññānāsaññāyatanupage deve antokaritvā”tiādinā (dha. sa. 1291) nayena vuttā sabbepi arūpāvacarā dhammā[P 1.0017]. Tattha rūpe avacarantīti rūpāvacarā. Arūpe [V 0.0014] avacarantīti arūpāvacarā. Taṇhāvatthukāti patiṭṭhaṭṭhena kāraṇaṭṭhena ca taṇhāya vatthubhūtā. Taṇhārammaṇāti taṇhāpavattivasena taṇhāya ārammaṇabhūtā. Kāmanīyaṭṭhenāti paccāsīsitabbaṭṭhena. Rajanīyaṭṭhenāti rañjetuṃ yuttaṭṭhena. Madanīyaṭṭhenāti kulamadādimadaṃ uppādanīyaṭṭhena.

All phenomena pertaining to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacarā dhammā) are included in the sense-sphere phenomena, as stated by the method beginning with "having made the Avīci hell the lower limit" (Dhs. §1287). Herein, this is the meaning of the statement: in brief, there are two kinds of kāma: vatthukāma (sensual objects) and kilesakāma (sensual defilement). Herein, kilesakāma is, in essence, chandarāga (lustful desire). Vatthukāma is the threefold round of existence. In this context, kilesakāma is called kāma because it desires (kāmeti). The other is called kāma because it is desired (kāmīyati). The region where these two kinds of kāma operate by way of occurrence is the elevenfold region comprising the four states of deprivation, the human realm, and the six heavenly realms. This region is called kāmāvacara (sense-sphere) because kāma operates therein. With reference to the phenomena included therein, it is said, "All phenomena pertaining to the sense-sphere." They are called dhammā (phenomena) because they maintain their own nature (attano sabhāvaṃ dhārenti). The phenomena pertaining to the form-sphere (rūpāvacarā dhammā) are all phenomena included in the form-sphere phenomena, as stated by the method beginning with "having made the Brahmā world the lower limit and the Akaniṭṭha gods the upper limit" (Dhs. §1289). The phenomena pertaining to the formless-sphere (arūpāvacarā dhammā) are all phenomena included in the formless-sphere phenomena, as stated by the method beginning with "having made the gods of the base of infinite space the lower limit and the gods of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception the upper limit" (Dhs. §1291). Herein, those that operate in form (rūpe avacaranti) are called rūpāvacara (pertaining to the form-sphere). Those that operate in the formless (arūpe avacaranti) are called arūpāvacara (pertaining to the formless-sphere). 'Taṇhāvatthukā' (rooted in craving) means they are the foundation (patiṭṭhaṭṭhena) and cause (kāraṇaṭṭhena) of craving. 'Taṇhārammaṇā' (objects of craving) means they are the objects of craving by way of craving's occurrence (taṇhāpavattivasena). 'Kāmanīyaṭṭhena' (desirable in nature) means they are of a nature to be longed for (paccāsīsitabbaṭṭhena). 'Rajanīyaṭṭhena' (enticing in nature) means they are fit to delight (rañjetuṃ yuttaṭṭhena). 'Madanīyaṭṭhena' (intoxicating in nature) means they are of a nature to produce intoxication, such as clan pride and the like (kulamadādimadaṃ uppādanīyaṭṭhena).

Tattha “katame vatthukāmā? Manāpikā rūpā”tiādiṃ katvā “yaṃ kiñci rajanīyaṃ vatthū”ti pariyosānaṃ saviññāṇakaaviññāṇakavasena vuttaṃ. Avasesaṃ ekacatukkādikachattikanti veditabbaṃ.

Herein, the passage beginning with, "What are sensual objects? Appealing forms," and ending with, "whatever is an enticing object," has been stated in terms of both the animate and the inanimate. The remainder should be understood as the single item, the quadruples, and so on, up to the six triplets.

Evaṃ vatthukāmaṃ dassetvā kilesakāmaṃ dassetuṃ “katame kilesakāmā”tiādimāha. Tattha chandoti dubbalarāgo. Rāgoti tato balavataro[M 0.0015]. Upari tayopi rāgā imehi balavatarā. Kāmesūti pañcasu kāmaguṇesu. Kāmacchandoti kāmasaṅkhāto chando, na kattukamyatāchando, na dhammacchando. Kāmanavasena rajjanavasena ca kāmoyeva rāgo kāmarāgo. Kāmanavasena nandanavasena ca kāmoyeva nandī kāmanandī. Evaṃ sabbattha kāmatthaṃ viditvā taṇhāyanaṭṭhena kāmataṇhā. Sinehanaṭṭhena kāmasneho. Pariḍayhanaṭṭhena kāmapariḷāho. Mucchanaṭṭhena kāmamucchā. Gilitvā pariniṭṭhāpanaṭṭhena kāmajjhosānaṃ. Vaṭṭasmiṃ oghehi osīdāpetīti kāmogho. Vaṭṭasmiṃ yojetīti kāmayogo. Daḷhavasena taṇhādiṭṭhiggahaṇaṃ upādānaṃ. Cittaṃ nīvarati pariyonandhatīti nīvaraṇaṃ.

Having thus shown sensual objects (vatthukāma), to show sensual defilements (kilesakāma), it is said, “What are sensual defilements (kilesakāmā)?” Herein, desire (chanda) means weak lust (dubbalarāgo). Lust (rāga) is stronger than that. Moreover, the three types of lust mentioned above are even stronger than these. “In sensual pleasures” (kāmesu) refers to the five strands of sensual pleasure (pañcasu kāmaguṇesu). Sensual desire (kāmacchando) is the desire that is designated as sensual pleasure (kāma), not the desire to act (kattukamyatāchando), nor the desire for the Dhamma (dhammacchando). Through the aspect of desiring (kāmanavasena) and the aspect of attachment (rajjanavasena), sensual pleasure itself is sensual lust (kāmarāgo). Through the aspect of desiring (kāmanavasena) and the aspect of delighting (nandanavasena), delight itself is sensual delight (kāmanandī). Thus, understanding the meaning of “sensual” (kāma) in all these instances: sensual craving (kāmataṇhā) is craving in the sense of thirsting (taṇhāyanaṭṭhena). Sensual affection (kāmasneho) is affection in the sense of attachment (sinehanaṭṭhena). Sensual torment (kāmapariḷāho) is torment in the sense of burning (pariḍayhanaṭṭhena). Sensual infatuation (kāmamucchā) is infatuation in the sense of delusion (mucchanaṭṭhena). Sensual absorption (kāmajjhosānaṃ) is absorption in the sense of swallowing and consuming (gilitvā pariniṭṭhāpanaṭṭhena). It causes one to sink by means of the floods in the round of existence (vaṭṭasmiṃ oghehi osīdāpeti), hence it is the flood of sensuality (kāmogho). It yokes one to the round of existence (vaṭṭasmiṃ yojetīti), hence it is the yoke of sensuality (kāmayogo). Firm grasping by way of craving and views is clinging (upādāna). It obstructs (nīvarati) and envelops (pariyonandhati) the mind, hence it is a hindrance (nīvaraṇa).

Addasanti addakkhiṃ. Kāmāti ālapanaṃ. Teti tava. Mūlanti patiṭṭhaṃ. Saṅkappāti parikappena. Na taṃ saṅkappayissāmīti taṃ parikappanaṃ na karissāmi. Na hohisīti na bhavissasi.

Addasanti (they see) means addakkhiṃ (I saw). Kāmā (O sensual pleasure!) is a vocative. Te (your) means tava (of you). Mūlaṃ (the root) means patiṭṭhaṃ (the foundation). Saṅkappā ti (from intention) means parikappena (by conceptualization). Na taṃ saṅkappayissāmi (I will not form an intention of you) means taṃ parikappanaṃ na karissāmi (I will not make that conceptualization). Na hohisi (you will not be) means na bhavissasi (you will not come to be).

Icchamānassāti paccāsīsantassa. Sādiyamānassāti assādiyamānassa. Patthayamānassāti patthanaṃ uppādentassa. Pihayamānassāti pāpuṇituṃ icchaṃ uppādentassa. Abhijappamānassāti taṇhāvasena tittiṃ uppādentassa. Atha [P 1.0018] vā abhivadantassa.

Icchamānassa (of one desiring) means of one expecting (paccāsīsantassa). Sādiyamānassa (of one enjoying) means of one savoring (assādiyamānassa). Patthayamānassa (of one longing) means of one generating a longing (patthanaṃ uppādentassa). Pihayamānassa (of one yearning) means of one generating the desire to attain (pāpuṇituṃ icchaṃ uppādentassa). Abhijappamānassa (of one craving) means of one generating satisfaction through craving (taṇhāvasena tittiṃ uppādentassa). Alternatively, it means of one speaking out (abhivadantassa).

Khattiyassa vātiādi catujjātivasena vuttaṃ. Gahaṭṭhassa vā pabbajitassa vāti liṅgavasena vuttaṃ. Devassa vā manussassa vāti upapattivasena vuttaṃ. Ijjhatīti nipphajjati. Samijjhatīti sammā nipphajjati. Ijjhati visesarūpapaṭilābhavasena. Labhati dassanīyarūpapaṭilābhavasena. Paṭilabhati [V 0.0015] pasādanīyarūpapaṭilābhavasena. Adhigacchati saṇṭhānarūpapaṭilābhavasena. Vindati chavippasādarūpapaṭilābhavasena. Atha vā puññamahattena ijjhati. Jātimahattena labhati. Issariyamahattena paṭilabhati. Sukhamahattena adhigacchati. Sampattimahattena vindatīti.

“Whether of a warrior” (khattiyassa vā), and so on, is stated in terms of the four castes (catujjātivasena). “Whether a householder or a renunciate” (gahaṭṭhassa vā pabbajitassa vā) is stated in terms of status (liṅgavasena). “Whether a deva or a human” (devassa vā manussassa vā) is stated in terms of rebirth (upapattivasena). Ijjhati (succeeds) means it is accomplished (nipphajjati). Samijjhati (thoroughly succeeds) means it is fully accomplished (sammā nipphajjati). One succeeds (ijjhati) by way of gaining a distinctive form (visesarūpapaṭilābhavasena). One obtains (labhati) by way of gaining an attractive form (dassanīyarūpapaṭilābhavasena). One acquires (paṭilabhati) by way of gaining an inspiring form (pasādanīyarūpapaṭilābhavasena). One attains (adhigacchati) by way of gaining a well-proportioned form (saṇṭhānarūpapaṭilābhavasena). One finds (vindati) by way of gaining a radiant complexion (chavippasādapaṭilābhavasena). Alternatively, one succeeds (ijjhati) due to the greatness of merit (puññamahattena). One obtains (labhati) due to the greatness of birth (jātimahattena). One acquires (paṭilabhati) due to the greatness of power (issariyamahattena). One attains (adhigacchati) due to the greatness of happiness (sukhamahattena). One finds (vindati) due to the greatness of accomplishment (sampattimahattena).

Ekaṃsavacananti ekakoṭṭhāsavacanaṃ. “Ekaṃsaṃ cīvaraṃ katvā (pārā. 349, 367), ekaṃsabyākaraṇīyo pañho”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 3.312; a. ni. 4.42) viya anekaṃsagahaṇapaṭikkhepo. Nissaṃsayavacananti saṃsayavirahitavacanaṃ, sandehapaṭikkhepavacananti attho. Nikkaṅkhāvacananti “kathamidaṃ kathamida”nti kaṅkhāpaṭikkhepavacanaṃ. Advejjhavacananti dvidhābhāvaṃ [M 0.0016] dvejjhaṃ, taṃabhāvena advejjhavacanaṃ. Dvidhābhāvavirahitaṃ “advejjhavacanā buddhā”tiādīsu viya vimatipaṭikkhepo. Adveḷhakavacananti dvihadayābhāvena adveḷhakaṃ. “Itihāsa, itihāsā”ti dveḷhakapaṭikkhepavacanaṃ. Niyogavacananti ekasmiṃ atthe dve na yujjantīti niyogavacanaṃ dvidhāpathapaṭikkhepo. Aññattha pana “niyogā anāgatārammaṇā natthī”ti āgataṃ. Apaṇṇakavacananti palāsarahitaṃ sāravacanaṃ aviraddhakāraṇaṃ “apaṇṇakaṃ ṭhānameke”tiādīsu (jā. 1.1.1) viya, apaṇṇakamaṇi viya sappatiṭṭhavacanaṃ. Avatthāpanavacanametanti etaṃ vacanaṃ otaritvā patiṭṭhitaṃ santiṭṭhāpanaṃ ṭhapanaṃ.

Ekaṃsavacanaṃ (a definitive statement) means a statement of one part (ekakoṭṭhāsavacanaṃ). As in “having arranged the robe over one shoulder” (ekaṃsaṃ cīvaraṃ katvā; Pārā. 349, 367) and “a question to be answered definitively” (ekaṃsabyākaraṇīyo pañho; Dī. Ni. 3.312; A. Ni. 4.42), it is a rejection of grasping multiple sides (anekaṃsagahaṇapaṭikkhepo). Nissaṃsayavacanaṃ (a statement free from doubt) means a statement devoid of uncertainty (saṃsayavirahitavacanaṃ); the meaning is a statement that rejects indecision (sandehapaṭikkhepavacanaṃ). Nikkaṅkhāvacanaṃ (a statement without perplexity) means a statement that rejects perplexity (kaṅkhāpaṭikkhepavacanaṃ) about “how is this? how is that?” Advejjhavacanaṃ (a statement without ambiguity) means dvejjhaṃ (ambiguity) is a twofold state (dvidhābhāvaṃ); thus, advejjhavacanaṃ is a statement without that state. Being free from a twofold state (dvidhābhāvavirahitaṃ), as in “the Buddhas speak without ambiguity” (advejjhavacanā buddhā), it is a rejection of uncertainty (vimatipaṭikkhepo). Adveḷhakavacanaṃ (a statement without duplicity) means adveḷhakaṃ (without duplicity) by reason of not having a divided heart (dvihadayābhāvena). It is a statement rejecting duplicity (dveḷhakapaṭikkhepavacanaṃ) such as “so they say, so they say” (itihāsa, itihāsā). Niyogavacanaṃ (a binding statement) means that two interpretations do not fit one meaning (ekasmiṃ atthe dve na yujjanti); it is a statement that rejects a dual path (dvidhāpathapaṭikkhepo). Elsewhere, however, it is stated, “There are no binding statements (niyogā) that have future objects” (anāgatārammaṇā natthī). Apaṇṇakavacanaṃ (an infallible statement) means a statement free from superficiality (palāsarahitaṃ), a statement of essence (sāravacanaṃ), a cause without contradiction (aviraddhakāraṇaṃ), as in “some hold an infallible position” (apaṇṇakaṃ ṭhānameke; Jā. 1.1.1), like an infallible gem (apaṇṇakamaṇi viya), a well-established statement (sappatiṭṭhavacanaṃ). Avatthāpanavacanametaṃ (this is a statement of establishment) means this statement, having been set down (otaritvā), is firmly established (patiṭṭhitaṃ), a settling (santiṭṭhāpanaṃ), an establishment (ṭhapanaṃ).

Yāni [P 1.0019] imasmiṃ mahāniddese vibhattiṃ āropitāni padāni, tāni vibhattiṃ gacchantāni tīhi kāraṇehi vibhattiṃ gacchanti, nānā hontāni catūhi kāraṇehi nānā bhavanti. Aparadīpanā panettha dve ṭhānāni gacchanti. Kathaṃ? Tāni hi byañjanavasena upasaggavasena atthavasena vāti imehi tīhi kāraṇehi vibhattiṃ gacchanti. Tattha “kodho kujjhanā kujjhitattaṃ, doso dussanā dussitatta”nti (dha. sa. 1066) evaṃ byañjanavasena vibhattigamanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tattha hi ekova kodho byañjanavasena evaṃ vibhattiṃ labhati. “Ijjhati samijjhati labhati paṭilabhati gacchati adhigacchatī”ti evaṃ pana upasaggavasena vibhattigamanaṃ veditabbaṃ. “Paṇḍiccaṃ kosallaṃ nepuññaṃ vebhabyā cintā upaparikkhā”ti (dha. sa. 16) evaṃ atthavasena vibhattigamanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

The terms that are subjected to analysis (vibhattiṃ āropitāni padāni) in this Great Exposition (mahāniddese) undergo analysis (vibhattiṃ gacchanti) for three reasons, and in becoming distinct (nānā hontāni), they become distinct (nānā bhavanti) for four reasons. Furthermore, in this context, the further clarification (aparadīpanā) proceeds in two ways. How? These terms undergo analysis through these three means: by literal expression (byañjanavasena), by prefix (upasaggavasena), or by meaning (atthavasena). Herein, the process of analysis by literal expression (byañjanavasena vibhattigamanaṃ) should be understood through such examples as: “Anger (kodho) is being angry (kujjhanā), the state of being angry (kujjhitattaṃ); hatred (doso) is being hostile (dussanā), the state of being hostile (dussitattaṃ)” (Dhs. §1066). For here, the single concept of anger (ekova kodho) obtains such analysis (vibhattiṃ labhati) by way of literal expression. Moreover, the process of analysis by prefix (upasaggavasena vibhattigamanaṃ) should be understood through such examples as: “Ijjhati (succeeds), samijjhati (thoroughly succeeds), labhati (obtains), paṭilabhati (acquires), gacchati (goes), adhigacchati (attains).” And the process of analysis by meaning (atthavasena vibhattigamanaṃ) should be understood through such examples as: “Wisdom (paṇḍiccaṃ), skill (kosallaṃ), cleverness (nepuññaṃ), expertise (vebhabyā), thought (cintā), investigation (upanisā)” (Dhs. §16).

Tesu pītipadaniddese tāva imā tisso vibhattiyo labbhanti. Pīti pāmojjanti hi byañjanavasena vibhattigamanaṃ hoti. Āmodanā pamodanā pahāsoti upasaggavasena. Vitti tuṭṭhi odagyaṃ attamanatāti atthavasena. Iminā nayena sabbapadaniddesesu vibhattigamanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Among these, in the exposition of the term ‘joy’ (pītipadaniddese), these three types of analysis (vibhattiyo) are found. ‘Joy’ (pīti) and ‘gladness’ (pāmojja) exemplify the process of analysis by way of literal expression (byañjanavasena). ‘Delight’ (āmodanā), ‘rejoicing’ (pamodanā), and ‘mirth’ (pahāso) exemplify analysis by way of prefix (upasaggavasena). ‘Satisfaction’ (vitti), ‘contentment’ (tuṭṭhi), ‘elation’ (odagyaṃ), and ‘merriment’ (attamanatā) exemplify analysis by way of meaning (atthavasena). In this manner, the process of analysis should be understood in the expositions of all terms.

Nānā [V 0.0016] hontānipi nāmanānattena lakkhaṇanānattena kiccanānattena paṭikkhepanānattenāti imehi catūhi kāraṇehi nānā honti. Tattha “katamo tasmiṃ samaye byāpādo hoti? Yo tasmiṃ samaye doso dussanā”ti ettha byāpādoti vā dosoti vā dvepi ete kodho eva, nāmena pana nānattaṃ gatāti evaṃ nāmanānattena nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Things that become distinct do so for these four reasons: diversity in name (nāmanānatta), diversity in characteristic (lakkhaṇanānatta), diversity in function (kiccanānatta), and diversity in negation (paṭikkhepanānatta). Herein, regarding the passage: “What at that time is ill will (byāpādo)? Whatever at that time is hatred (doso), being hostile (dussanā)…” In this case, both ‘ill will’ and ‘hatred’ are simply anger (kodho), but they have become distinct by name. Thus, diversity should be understood in terms of diversity in name.

Rāsaṭṭhena [M 0.0017] ca pañcapi khandhā ekova khandho hoti. Ettha pana rūpaṃ ruppanalakkhaṇaṃ, vedanā vedayitalakkhaṇā, saññā sañjānanalakkhaṇā, cetanā cetayitalakkhaṇā, viññāṇaṃ vijānanalakkhaṇanti iminā lakkhaṇanānattena pañcakkhandhā honti. Evaṃ lakkhaṇanānattena nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ.

In the sense of a mass (rāsaṭṭhena), the five aggregates are just one aggregate. Here, however, form has the characteristic of being afflicted (ruppanalakkhaṇaṃ), feeling has the characteristic of feeling (vedayitalakkhaṇā), perception has the characteristic of perceiving (sañjānanalakkhaṇā), formations have the characteristic of forming (saṅkhāralakkhaṇā), and consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing (vijānanalakkhaṇaṃ). By this diversity in characteristic, there come to be five aggregates. In this way, diversity should be understood by diversity in characteristic.

“Cattāro sammappadhānā – idha bhikkhu anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppādāya…pe… cittaṃ paggaṇhāti [P 1.0020] padahatī”ti (vibha. 390; dī. ni. 2.402) ekameva vīriyaṃ kiccanānattena catūsu ṭhānesu āgataṃ. Evaṃ kiccanānattena nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ.

“The four right strivings—here, a monk… for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states… exerts and strives with his mind (cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati)” (Vibh. 390; Dī. Ni. 2.402). Here, one and the same energy (vīriyaṃ) is presented in four instances due to diversity in function. Thus, diversity should be understood in terms of diversity in function.

“Cattāro asaddhammā kodhagarutā, na saddhammagarutā, makkhagarutā, na saddhammagarutā, lābhagarutā, na saddhammagarutā, sakkāragarutā, na saddhammagarutā”ti evamādīsu (a. ni. 4.44) pana paṭikkhepanānattena nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ.

In passages such as, “The four qualities contrary to the true Dhamma are: esteeming anger (kodhagarutā), not esteeming the true Dhamma (na saddhammagarutā); esteeming contempt (makkhagarutā), not esteeming the true Dhamma; esteeming gain (lābhagarutā), not esteeming the true Dhamma; esteeming honor (sakkāragarutā), not esteeming the true Dhamma” (A. Ni. 4.44), diversity should be understood by way of diversity in negation.

Imāni pana cattāri nānattāni na pītiyāyeva labbhanti, sabbesupi yathālābhavasena labbhanti. Pītiyā hi pītīti nāmaṃ, cittassa cittanti nāmaṃ. Pīti ca pharaṇalakkhaṇā, vedanā vedayitalakkhaṇā, saññā sañjānanalakkhaṇā, cetanā cetayitalakkhaṇā, viññāṇaṃ vijānanalakkhaṇaṃ.

These four kinds of diversity, however, are not found only in the case of joy (pīti), but are found in all cases according to their respective applicability. For joy, the name is “joy”; for consciousness, the name is “consciousness.” Joy has the characteristic of suffusing (pharaṇalakkhaṇā); feeling has the characteristic of feeling (vedayitalakkhaṇā); perception has the characteristic of perceiving (sañjānanalakkhaṇā); formations have the characteristic of forming (saṅkhāralakkhaṇā); and consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing (vijānanalakkhaṇaṃ).

Tathā pīti pharaṇakiccā, vedanā anubhavanakiccā, saññā sañjānanakiccā, cetanā cetayitakiccā, viññāṇaṃ vijānanakiccanti evaṃ kiccanānattena nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ. Paṭikkhepanānattaṃ pītipade natthi.

Similarly, joy has the function of pervading, feeling has the function of experiencing, perception has the function of perceiving, volition has the function of intending, and consciousness has the function of cognizing. Thus, diversity should be understood by way of diversity in function. There is no diversity by way of negation in the case of the term 'pīti'.

Alobhādiniddese pana “alobho alubbhanā alubbhitatta”ntiādinā (dha. sa. 35) nayena [V 0.0017] labbhatīti evaṃ paṭikkhepanānattena nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ sabbapadaniddesesu labbhamānavasena catubbidhampi nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ.

In the four verses beginning with 'Sensual pleasures are your first army,' the meaning is this: Because from the very beginning, defilements of sensual desire delude beings who are householders in regard to sensual objects. For those who, having overcome these, have adopted the homeless life, dissatisfaction arises while dwelling in remote lodgings or in regard to certain higher wholesome states. And this has been said: 'Friend, for one who has gone forth, delight is difficult to find' (Saṃ. Ni. 4.331). Then, because their livelihood is dependent on others, hunger and thirst afflict them. For those afflicted by these, the craving for seeking wears out their mind. Then, for those with a weary mind, sloth and torpor descend. Then, for those not attaining distinction while dwelling in forest and woodland lodgings that are difficult to endure, fear associated with dread is born. For those who are suspicious and apprehensive, dwelling for a long time without savoring the taste of seclusion, doubt about the practice arises: 'Could this not be the path?' For those dwelling having dispelled that, through a slight attainment of distinction, conceit, contempt, and obstinacy are born. For those dwelling having dispelled these too, based on a higher attainment of distinction, gain, honor, and praise arise. Infatuated with gain and so on, displaying counterfeits of the Dhamma, they attain wrong renown, and established therein, they exalt themselves on account of birth and so on, and disparage others. Therefore, the state of sensual pleasures and so on as the first army and so on should be understood.

Aparadīpanā pana padatthuti vā hoti daḷhīkammaṃ vāti evaṃ dve ṭhānāni gacchati. Yaṭṭhikoṭiyā uppīḷentena viya hi sakimeva “pītī”ti vutte etaṃ padaṃ phullitamaṇḍitavibhūsitaṃ nāma na hoti, punappunaṃ byañjanavasena upasaggavasena atthavasena “pīti pāmojjaṃ āmodanā pamodanā hāso pahāso vittī”ti (dha. sa. 9) vutte phullitamaṇḍitavibhūsitaṃ nāma hoti. Yathā hi daharakumāraṃ nahāpetvā manoramaṃ vatthaṃ paridahāpetvā pupphāni piḷandhāpetvā akkhīni añjetvā athassa nalāṭe ekameva [M 0.0018] manosilābinduṃ kareyya, na tassa ettāvatā cittatilako nāma hoti, nānāvaṇṇehi pana parivāretvā bindūsu katesu cittatilako nāma hoti. Evaṃ sampadamidaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ayaṃ padatthuti nāma.

Furthermore, 'further explanation' comprises two aspects: either 'praise of the word' or 'strengthening.' For just as when pressing with the tip of a stick, if one says 'pīti' only once, this word is not said to be fully blossomed, adorned, and embellished. But when it is repeatedly stated by way of phrasing, prefixes, and meaning—'joy, delight, gladness, rejoicing, laughter, great laughter, satisfaction' (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 9)—then it is said to be fully blossomed, adorned, and embellished. For example, if one bathes a young boy, dresses him in pleasing clothes, adorns him with flowers, applies collyrium to his eyes, and then places just a single drop of red pigment on his forehead, this alone is not called a decorative mark. But when dots of various colors are arranged around it, then it is called a decorative mark. This is how this matter should be understood. This is called 'praise of the word.'

Byañjanavasena [P 1.0021] pana upasaggavasena atthavasena ca punappunaṃ bhaṇanameva daḷhīkammaṃ nāma. Yathā hi “āvuso”ti vā “bhante”ti vā “yakkho”ti vā “sappo”ti vā vutte daḷhīkammaṃ nāma na hoti, “āvuso āvuso, bhante bhante, yakkho yakkho, sappo sappo”ti vutte pana daḷhīkammaṃ nāma hoti, evameva sakiṃdeva yaṭṭhikoṭiyā uppīḷentena viya “pītī”ti vuttamatte daḷhīkammaṃ nāma na hoti, punappunaṃ byañjanavasena upasaggavasena atthavasena “pīti pāmojjaṃ āmodanā pamodanā hāso pahāso vittī”ti vutteyeva daḷhīkammaṃ nāma hotīti evaṃ aparadīpanā dve ṭhānāni gacchati. Etissāpi vasena labbhamānakapadaniddesesu sabbattha attho veditabbo.

However, repeated speaking by way of phrasing, prefixes, and meaning is indeed called strengthening. For just as when 'friend' or 'venerable sir' or 'yakkha' or 'snake' is said once, it is not called strengthening, but when 'friend, friend,' 'venerable sir, venerable sir,' 'yakkha, yakkha,' 'snake, snake' is said, then it is called strengthening. Similarly, just as when pressing once with the tip of a stick, merely saying 'pīti' is not called strengthening; only when 'joy, delight, gladness, rejoicing, laughter, great laughter, satisfaction' is repeatedly stated by way of phrasing, prefixes, and meaning is it called strengthening.
