Thus, 'further explanation' comprises two aspects. By means of this too, the meaning should be understood everywhere in the explanations of the terms as they are found.

Tattha pīnayatīti pīti. Sā sampiyāyanalakkhaṇā, kāyacittapīṇanarasā pharaṇarasā vā, odagyapaccupaṭṭhānā. Yā pañcakāmaguṇapaṭisaññuttāti yā rūpādipañcakāmakoṭṭhāsapaṭisaṃyuttā pīti, sā pīnayatīti pīti, idaṃ sabhāvapadaṃ. Pamuditassa bhāvo pāmojjaṃ. Āmodanākāro āmodanā. Pamodanākāro pamodanā. Yathā vā bhesajjānaṃ vā telānaṃ vā uṇhodakasītodakānaṃ vā ekato karaṇaṃ “modanā”ti vuccati, evamayampi pītidhammānaṃ ekato karaṇena modanā. Upasaggavasena pana maṇḍetvā “āmodanā pamodanā”ti vuttā.

Herein, that which gladdens is joy (pīti). It has the characteristic of endearment, its function is to gladden the body and mind or to suffuse, and its manifestation is elation. That joy which is connected with the five strands of sensual pleasure—that is, the joy associated with the fivefold range of sensual objects such as forms—is called joy (pīti) because it gladdens; this is a term for its inherent nature. The state of one who is delighted is 'pāmojja'. The mode of rejoicing is 'āmodanā'. The mode of great delight is 'pamodanā'. Or, just as the mixing of medicines, oils, hot water, or cold water is called 'modanā' (mixing), so too this is 'modanā' through the combination of joyful states. However, being embellished by way of prefixes, they are called 'āmodanā' and 'pamodanā'.

Hāsetīti hāso. Pahāsetīti pahāso, haṭṭhapahaṭṭhākārānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Vittīti vittaṃ, dhanassetaṃ [V 0.0018] nāmaṃ. Ayaṃ pana somanassapaccayattā vittisarikkhatāya vitti. Yathā hi dhanino dhanaṃ paṭicca somanassaṃ uppajjati, evaṃ pītimatopi pītiṃ paṭicca somanassaṃ uppajjati. Tasmā “vittī”ti vuttā. Tuṭṭhīti sabhāvasaṇṭhitāya pītiyā etaṃ nāmaṃ. Pītimā pana puggalo kāyacittānaṃ uggatattā abbhuggatattā “udaggo”ti vuccati, udaggassa bhāvo odagyaṃ.

That which causes laughter is 'hāso' (laughter). That which causes great laughter is 'pahāso' (great laughter); this is a designation for the states of being joyful and greatly joyful. 'Vitti' is from 'vitta' (wealth); this is a name for riches. This, however, is called 'vitti' because it is a condition for gladness and because of its similarity to wealth. For just as gladness arises for a wealthy person on account of their wealth, so too does gladness arise for one possessing joy on account of their joy. Therefore, it is called 'vitti.' 'Tuṭṭhi' (contentment) is a name for joy that is established in its own nature. A person filled with joy, due to the uplifting and exalting of body and mind, is called 'udagga' (uplifted). The state of being uplifted is 'odagya' (elation).

Attano manatā attamanatā. Anabhiraddhassa hi mano dukkhapadaṭṭhānattā na attano mano nāma hoti, abhiraddhassa sukhapadaṭṭhānattā attano [M 0.0019] mano nāma hoti, iti attano manatā [P 1.0022] attamanatā, sakamanatā, sakamanassa bhāvoti attho. Sā pana yasmā na aññassa kassaci attano manatā, cittasseva panesā bhāvo cetasiko dhammo, tasmā “attamanatā cittassā”ti vuttā.

'Attamanatā' is 'attano manatā' (one's own state of mind). For one who is displeased, the mind, being a basis for suffering, is not called 'one's own mind'; but for one who is pleased, the mind, being a basis for happiness, is called 'one's own mind.' Thus, 'attamanatā' means 'attano manatā,' 'sakamanatā' (having one's own mind); the meaning is the state of having one's own mind. And since this 'attamanatā' does not belong to anyone else, but is a state of the mind itself, a mental factor, it is therefore said, 'attamanatā is of the mind.'

Cittavicittatāya cittaṃ. Ārammaṇaṃ minamānaṃ jānātīti mano. Mānasanti mano eva, “antalikkhacaro pāso, yvāyaṃ carati mānaso”ti (mahāva. 33; saṃ. ni. 1.151) hi ettha pana sampayuttakadhammo “mānaso”ti vutto.

The mind is 'citta' because of its variegated (vicitta) nature. It is 'mano' because it measures (mināti) or knows the object. 'Mānasa' is indeed 'mano,' for it is said: 'The snare that moves in the sky, this which moves as the mind (mānaso)' (SN 4.15). Here, in that verse, the associated states are called 'mānasa.'

“Kathañhi bhagavā tuyhaṃ, sāvako sāsane rato;

Appattamānaso sekkho, kālaṃkayirā jane sutā”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.159) –

'How, Blessed One, could a disciple of yours, delighting in the teaching, a trainee who has not attained his goal, pass away? O Jina, hear us!' (SN 4.23).

Ettha arahattaṃ “mānasa”nti vuttaṃ. Idha pana mano eva mānasaṃ, byañjanavasena hetaṃ padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ.

Here [in that verse], Arahantship is called 'mānasa.' But here [in this context], 'mānasa' is simply 'mano'; the word is extended by way of its phrasing.

Hadayanti cittaṃ. “Cittaṃ vā te khipissāmi, hadayaṃ vā te phālessāmī”ti (su. ni. āḷavakasuttaṃ; saṃ. ni. 1.237; 246) ettha uro “hadaya”nti vuttaṃ. “Hadayā hadayaṃ maññe aññāya tacchatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.63) ettha cittaṃ. “Vakkaṃ hadaya”nti (khu. pā. 3.dvatiṃsākāro; dī. ni. 2.377; ma. ni. 1.110) ettha hadayavatthu. Idha pana cittameva abbhantaraṭṭhena “hadaya”nti vuttaṃ. Tameva parisuddhaṭṭhena paṇḍaraṃ, bhavaṅgaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Yathāha – “pabhassaramidaṃ, bhikkhave, cittaṃ, tañca kho āgantukehi upakkilesehi upakkiliṭṭha”nti (a. ni. 1.49). Tato nikkhantattā pana akusalampi [V 0.0019] gaṅgāya nikkhantā nadī gaṅgā viya godhāvarito nikkhantā godhāvarī viya ca “paṇḍara”ntveva vuttaṃ.

The heart (hadaya) is the mind (citta). In the phrase, “I will either agitate your mind or shatter your heart” (SN 10.1), the chest is referred to as “heart.” In, “From heart to heart, I think, knowing, he pierces” (MN 43), the mind is meant. In, “The kidney, the heart” (Khp 3), the heart-base is referred to. But here, the mind itself is called “heart” in the sense of being internal. That very mind, in the sense of being pure, is called “white” (paṇḍara), referring to the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). As it is said: “This mind, monks, is luminous, but it is defiled by adventitious defilements” (AN 1.49). Because it emerges from that, even the unwholesome is called “white,” just as a river emerging from the Ganges is still called the Ganges, and a river emerging from the Godhāvarī is still called the Godhāvarī.

Mano manāyatananti idha pana manoggahaṇaṃ manasseva āyatanabhāvadīpanatthaṃ. Tenetaṃ dīpeti “nayidaṃ devāyatanaṃ viya manassa āyatanattā manāyatanaṃ, atha kho mano eva āyatanaṃ manāyatana”nti. Tattha [P 1.0023] nivāsaṭṭhānaṭṭhena ākaraṭṭhena samosaraṇaṭṭhānaṭṭhena sañjātidesaṭṭhena kāraṇaṭṭhena ca āyatanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tathā hi loke “issarāyatanaṃ, vāsudevāyatana”ntiādīsu nivāsaṭṭhānaṃ “āyatana”nti vuccati. “Suvaṇṇāyatanaṃ, rajatāyatana”ntiādīsu ākaro. Sāsane pana “manorame āyatane, sevanti naṃ vibhaṅgamā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 5.38) samosaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ. “Dakkhiṇāpatho [M 0.0020] gunnaṃ āyatana”ntiādīsu sañjātideso. “Tatra tatreva sakkhibhabbataṃ pāpuṇāti sati satiāyatane”tiādīsu (a. ni. 3.102; 5.23; ma. ni. 3.158) kāraṇaṃ. Idha pana sañjātidesaṭṭhena samosaraṇaṭhānaṭṭhena kāraṇaṭṭhenāti tidhāpi vaṭṭati.

Regarding ‘mind-base’ (manāyatana): here, the inclusion of ‘mind’ (mano) is for the purpose of indicating the mind’s own nature as a base (āyatana). Thus, this clarifies: “This is not a mind-base in the way a temple is a base for a god (devāyatana), but rather, the mind itself is the base; therefore, it is the mind-base.” Herein, ‘base’ should be understood in the sense of a place of dwelling, a source, a meeting place, a place of origin, and a cause. For in the world, in expressions like “the abode of the lord,” “the abode of Vāsudeva,” etc., a place of dwelling is called a “base.” In phrases like “a gold mine,” “a silver mine,” etc., it means a source. In the Dispensation, in expressions such as “they frequent the delightful base, the analysis,” etc. (AN 5.38), it refers to a meeting place. In phrases like “the southern region is the place of origin of cattle,” etc., it means a place of origin. And in statements like “there, right there, he is capable of being a witness, when mindfulness is present as the base,” etc. (AN 3.102), it signifies a cause. Here, however, it applies in three ways: as a place of origin, as a meeting place, and as a cause.

Phassādayo hi dhammā ettha sañjāyantīti sañjātidesaṭṭhenapi etaṃ āyatanaṃ. Bahiddhā rūpasaddagandharasaphoṭṭhabbā ārammaṇabhāvenettha osarantīti samosaraṇaṭhānaṭṭhenapi āyatanaṃ. Phassādīnaṃ pana sahajātādipaccayaṭṭhena kāraṇattā kāraṇaṭṭhenapi āyatananti veditabbaṃ. Tadeva mananalakkhaṇe indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti indriyaṃ, mano eva indriyaṃ manindriyaṃ.

Contact and other phenomena arise here; hence, this is an āyatana also in the sense of a place of arising. External forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tactile objects enter here as objects; hence, it is an āyatana also in the sense of a place of confluence. Moreover, since it is a cause for contact and other phenomena in the sense of being a co-nascent condition, etc., it should be understood as an āyatana also in the sense of a cause. That very thing, having the characteristic of thinking, exercises supremacy; therefore, it is an indriya. The mind itself is the indriya, thus the mind-faculty (manindriya).

Vijānātīti viññāṇaṃ. Viññāṇameva khandho viññāṇakkhandho. Tassa rāsiādivasena attho veditabbo. “Mahāudakakkhandhotveva saṅkhaṃ gacchatī”ti (a. ni. 4.51) ettha hi rāsaṭṭhena khandho vutto. “Sīlakkhandho samādhikkhandho”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 3.555) guṇaṭṭhena. “Addasā kho bhagavā mahantaṃ dārukkhandha”nti (saṃ. ni. 4.241-242) ettha paṇṇattimattaṭṭhena. Idha pana ruḷhito khandho vutto. Rāsaṭṭhena hi viññāṇakkhandhassa ekadeso ekaṃ viññāṇaṃ. Tasmā yathā rukkhassa ekadesaṃ chindanto “rukkhaṃ chindatī”ti vuccati, evameva viññāṇakkhandhassa ekadesabhūtaṃ ekampi viññāṇaṃ rūḷhito “viññāṇakkhandho”ti vuttaṃ.

It cognizes, thus it is consciousness (viññāṇa). Consciousness itself is the aggregate, the aggregate of consciousness. Its meaning should be understood in terms of a heap (rāsi), etc. For in the phrase “it is reckoned as a great mass of water,” the term ‘aggregate’ (khandha) is used in the sense of a heap. In phrases like “the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration,” it is used in the sense of a quality. In the phrase “the Blessed One saw a great log,” it is used in the sense of a mere designation. Here, however, the term ‘aggregate’ is used in its conventional sense. For, in the sense of a heap, a single instance of consciousness is a part of the aggregate of consciousness. Therefore, just as one who cuts a part of a tree is said to “cut the tree,” so too, even a single instance of consciousness, being a part of the aggregate of consciousness, is conventionally called the “aggregate of consciousness.”

Tajjā manoviññāṇadhātūti tesaṃ phassādīnaṃ dhammānaṃ anucchavikā [P 1.0024] manoviññāṇadhātu. Imasmiñhi pade ekameva cittaṃ minanaṭṭhena mano, vijānanaṭṭhena viññāṇaṃ, sabhāvaṭṭhena nissattaṭṭhena [V 0.0020] vā dhātūti tīhi nāmehi vuttaṃ. Sahagatoti avijahito. Sahajātoti saddhiṃ niggato. Saṃsaṭṭhoti saṃsaggo hutvā ṭhito. Sampayuttoti samaṃ pakārehi yutto. Katamehi pakārehīti? Ekuppādādīhi. Natthi keci dhammā kehici dhammehi sampayuttāti? Āmantā. Iti hi imassa pañhassa paṭikkhepe “nanu atthi keci dhammā kehici dhammehi sahagatā sahajātā saṃsaṭṭhā ekuppādā ekanirodhā ekavatthukā ekārammaṇā”ti (kathā. 473) evaṃ ekuppādatādīnaṃ vasena sampayogattho vutto. Iti imehi ekuppādatādīhi [M 0.0021] samaṃ pakārehi yutto sampayutto. Ekuppādoti ekato uppanno, na vināti attho. Ekanirodhoti ekato nirodho. Ekavatthukoti hadayavatthuvasena ekavatthuko. Ekārammaṇoti rūpādivasena ekārammaṇo.

The corresponding mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu) is the mind-consciousness element that is suitable for those phenomena of contact, etc. In this phrase, a single consciousness is referred to by three names: as ‘mind’ (mano) in the sense of measuring, as ‘consciousness’ (viññāṇa) in the sense of cognizing, and as ‘element’ (dhātu) in the sense of intrinsic nature or non-substantiality. ‘Associated’ (sahagata) means not abandoned. ‘Co-arisen’ (sahajāta) means having arisen together. ‘Intermingled’ (saṃsaṭṭha) means existing in a state of connection. ‘Conjoined’ (sampayutta) means united in the same modes. By what modes? By arising together, etc. 'Are there no phenomena conjoined with any other phenomena?' 'Yes.' Thus, in rejecting this question, it is said: “Surely there are some phenomena that are associated, co-arisen, intermingled, arising together, ceasing together, having the same basis, and having the same object.” (Kathāvatthu 473) In this way, the meaning of conjunction is stated in terms of such modes as arising together. Thus, being united in the same modes—such as arising together—is called ‘conjoined.’ ‘Arising together’ (ekuppāda) means arising at the same time, not separately. ‘Ceasing together’ (ekanirodha) means cessation at the same time. ‘Having the same basis’ (ekavatthuka) means having the heart-basis as the same basis. ‘Having the same object’ (ekārammaṇa) means having the same object, such as form, etc.

Ettha sahagatasaddo tabbhāve, vokiṇṇe, ārammaṇe, nissaye, saṃsaṭṭheti pañcasu atthesu dissati jinavacane. “Yāyaṃ taṇhā ponobhavikā nandirāgasahagatā”ti (mahāva. 14; vibha. 203; ma. ni. 3.374; saṃ. ni. 5.1081; paṭi. ma. 2.30) ettha tabbhāve veditabbo, nandirāgabhūtāti attho. “Yā, bhikkhave, vīmaṃsā kosajjasahagatā kosajjasampayuttā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.832) ettha vokiṇṇe, antarantarā uppajjamānena kosajjena vokiṇṇāti ayamettha attho. “Lābhī hoti rūpasahagatānaṃ vā samāpattīnaṃ arūpasahagatānaṃ vā samāpattīna”nti (pu. pa. 3-6) ettha ārammaṇe, rūpārammaṇānaṃ arūpārammaṇānanti attho. “Aṭṭhikasaññāsahagataṃ satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāvetī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.238) ettha nissaye, aṭṭhikasaññaṃ nissāya aṭṭhikasaññaṃ bhāvetvā paṭiladdhanti attho. “Idaṃ sukhaṃ imāya pītiyā sahagataṃ hoti sahajātaṃ sampayutta”nti (vibha. 578) ettha saṃsaṭṭhe, saṃmissanti attho. Imasmimpi ṭhāne saṃsaṭṭhe āgato.

Here, the term 'sahagata' is found in five meanings in the words of the Jina: in the sense of being of that nature, of being mingled, of being an object, of being a basis, and of being intermingled. In 'This craving, which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust' (Mahāvagga 14; Vibhaṅga 203; Majjhima Nikāya 3.374; Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.1081; Paṭisambhidāmagga 2.30), it should be understood in the sense of being of that nature, meaning it is of the nature of delight and lust. In 'Bhikkhus, that investigation which is accompanied by sloth, connected with sloth' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.832), it is in the sense of being mingled; the meaning here is 'mingled with sloth arising intermittently.' In 'He gains meditative attainments associated with form or meditative attainments associated with the formless' (Puggalapaññatti 3-6), it is in the sense of being an object, meaning having form as object or the formless as object. In 'He develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor accompanied by the perception of bones' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.238), it is in the sense of being a basis, meaning attained by relying on and developing the perception of bones. In 'This happiness is accompanied by this joy, co-arisen, conjoined' (Vibhaṅga 578), it is in the sense of being intermingled, meaning mixed. In this present context as well, it has come in the sense of being intermingled.

Sahajātasaddo [P 1.0025] “sahajātaṃ purejātaṃ pacchājāta”nti (paṭṭha. 1.1.435) ettha viya sahajāte. Saṃsaṭṭhasaddo “gihīhi saṃsaṭṭho”ti ca, “evaṃ saṃsaṭṭho, bhante”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.3) cāti evamādīsu saṃsagge. “Kise thūle vivajjetvā saṃsaṭṭhā yojitā hayā”ti (jā. 2.22.70) ettha sadise.

The term ‘sahajāta’ (co-arisen) is used in the sense of ‘co-arisen’ as in the phrase “co-arisen, pre-arisen, post-arisen” (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.435). The term ‘saṃsaṭṭha’ (intermingled) is used in contexts like “associated with householders” and “thus associated, venerable sir” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.3), indicating association. In the phrase “avoiding the lean and the stout, the well-matched horses are yoked” (Jātaka 2.22.70), it denotes similarity.

“Pucimandaparivāro, ambo te dadhivāhana;

Mūlaṃ mūlena saṃsaṭṭhaṃ, sākhā sākhā nisevare”ti. (jā. 1.2.72) –

“The Pucimanda grove is your retinue, O mango tree, Dadhivāhana; root with root is intermingled, branch entwines with branch.” (Jātaka 1.2.72)

Ettha upacite. “Cittasaṃsaṭṭhā dhammā”ti (dha. sa. dukamātikā 59) ettha cittasampayuttadhamme[V 0.0021]. Idha pana yo phalappadāne aviyogadhammo vinibbhogaṃ akatvā ekuppādādidhammo hutvā “sampayutto”ti vuccati. Taṃvisayo. Atha vā “sahagato”ti vatvā pacchato pacchato āgatasuttena viya so na hotīti dassetuṃ [M 0.0022] “sahajāto”ti vuttaṃ. Ekato uppannarūpārūpaṃ viya sopi na hotīti dassetuṃ “saṃsaṭṭho”ti vuttaṃ.

Here, it is used in the sense of 'accumulated.' In 'phenomena associated with consciousness' (Dhammasaṅgaṇī, Duka Mātikā 59), it refers to phenomena conjoined with consciousness. In this context, however, that which is a state inseparable in the giving of results, not having been divided, and having become a state characterized by single arising, etc., is called 'conjoined' (sampayutta). That is its domain. Alternatively, having stated ‘sahagata’ (accompanied), to show that it is not something that follows behind, ‘sahajāta’ (co-arisen) is stated. To show that it is also not like form and non-form arising together, ‘saṃsaṭṭha’ (intermingled) is stated.

Khīrodakaṃ viya ca sopi na hotīti dassetuṃ “sampayutto”ti vuttaṃ. Vinibbhogaṃ kātuṃ asakkuṇeyyaṭṭhena hi sahuppannā dhammā sampayuttāpi atthi khīratelaṃ viya. Tathā vippayuttāpi khīrato apanītaṃ navanītaṃ viya. Evaṃ lakkhaṇasampayutto ekuppādādilakkhaṇoyeva hotīti dassetuṃ “ekuppādo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ettha ekuppādasahajātānaṃ kiṃ nānattaṃ? Uppāde antaravirahito ekuppādo. Khīrakālamuttassāpi dadhino mathane mathane pākaṭaṃ navanītaṃ viya purebhattapacchābhattavasena ekadivasameva jāto viya so na hotīti dassetuṃ ekakkhaṇe nibbattoti sahajāto. Ekavatthukoti patiṭṭhaṭṭhena ekaparicchedena ekavatthuko, dvinnaṃ [P 1.0026] bhikkhūnaṃ ekavatthukatā viya ṭhānantaravirahito. Ekārammaṇoti aniyatekārammaṇo na cakkhuviññāṇaṃ viyāti evameke vaṇṇayanti.

And to show that it is not like milk and water, the term 'conjoined' (sampayutta) is stated. For, in the sense of being impossible to separate, among co-arisen phenomena there are those that are conjoined, like milk and oil, and likewise those that are dissociated, like butter removed from milk. To show that what is conjoined with such characteristics has precisely the characteristics of single arising, etc., the terms 'single arising' and so on are stated. Here, what is the difference between single arising and co-arising? 'Single arising' means arising without an interval. To show that it is not like butter that becomes evident only from the constant churning of curd after the time for milk has passed, as if born on a single day in terms of 'before the meal' and 'after the meal,' it is said to be 'born in a single moment'—thus, 'co-arisen' (sahajāta). 'Having a single basis' (ekavatthuka) means having a single basis by way of a single delimitation as a foundation, like two bhikkhus having a single residence, without an intervening space. 'Having a single object' (ekārammaṇa) means not having an indeterminate object, unlike eye-consciousness. Thus some explain.

Maccoti mūlapadaṃ. Rūpādīsu satto laggo laggitoti satto. Vuttañhetaṃ “satto sattoti, bhante, vuccati, kittāvatā nu kho, bhante, ‘satto’ti vuccatīti? Rūpe kho, rādha, yo chando yo rāgo yā nandī yā taṇhā, tatra satto tatra visatto, tasmā ‘satto’ti vuccatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.161; mahāni. 7). Sattayogena vā satto. Sugatiduggatiṃ naratīti naro. Manuno puttoti mānavo. Upakaraṇena sayaṃ posayatīti poso. Puṃ vuccati nirayo, taṃ galatīti puggalo. Jīvitindriyaṃ dhāretīti jīvo. Cutito jātiṃ gacchatīti jāgu. Jiyatīti jantu. Indriyena gacchatīti indagu. Atha vā indabhūtena kammunā gacchatīti indagu. “Hindagū”tipi pāḷi. Hindanti maraṇaṃ, taṃ gacchatīti hindagu. Manuto jātoti manujo. Yaṃ sādiyatīti yaṃ rūpādiṃ assādiyati. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Ito paraṃ vuttamatthaṃ nigamento tenāha bhagavā –

'Maccu' (death) is the root word. A 'satta' (being) is one who is attached, clinging to forms and so on. For it has been said: 'Venerable sir, it is said, "a being, a being." In what way, venerable sir, is one called "a being"?' 'Rādha, whatever desire, passion, delight, or craving there is for form—there a being is attached, there it is clinging. Therefore, one is called "a being."' Or, 'satta' is so called because of the connection with attachment. One is called 'naro' because one goes to good and bad destinations. 'Māṇava' is a child of Manu. 'Poso' is one who sustains oneself by means of requisites. The hell realm is called 'puṃ,' and one who falls into it is called a 'puggala' (individual). 'Jīvo' is one who bears the life faculty. 'Jāgu' is one who goes from death to birth. 'Jantu' is one who is consumed by old age and death. 'Indagu' is one who goes by means of the faculties. Or, 'indagu' is one who goes by means of action, which is like a lord. The text also reads 'hindagū.' 'Hinda' means death, and one who goes to it is called 'hindagu.' 'Manujo' is one born from Manu. 'Yaṃ' is that which one savors, such as form. The rest is as previously explained. Beyond this, the Blessed One, summarizing the stated meaning, said—

“Kāmaṃ kāmayamānassa…pe… laddhā macco yadicchatī”ti;

'For one desiring sensual pleasures... a mortal obtains what he wishes.'

Ito paraṃ ettakampi avatvā visesamattameva vakkhāma.

Henceforth, without saying even this much, we will explain only the special points.

2. Tassa [V 0.0022][M 0.0023] ce kāmayānassāti tassa puggalassa kāme icchamānassa, kāmena vā yāyamānassa. Chandajātassāti jātataṇhassa. Jantunoti sattassa. Te kāmā parihāyantīti te kāmā parihāyanti ce. Sallaviddhova ruppatīti atha so ayomayādinā sallena viddho viya pīḷīyati. Ito paraṃ vuttaṃ vajjetvā avuttesu yaṃ yaṃ anuttānaṃ, taṃ tadeva kathayissāmi.

2. 'Tassa ce kāmayānassa' means for that individual desiring sensual pleasures, or striving for them through sensual pleasure. 'Chandajātassa' means for one in whom craving has arisen. 'Jantuno' means of a being. 'Te kāmā parihāyanti' means if those sensual pleasures decline. 'Sallaviddhova ruppati' means then he is afflicted like one pierced by a dart of iron or the like. Beyond this, setting aside what has been said, I will explain whatever is not clear among the unsaid points.

Cakkhupīṇanaṃ ārammaṇaṃ pāpuṇanavasena yāyati gacchati[P 1.0027]. Dassanīyavasena piyattaṃ ārammaṇavasena appāpetīti niyyati. Savanīyaṃ hutvā kaṇṇasotapīṇanaṃ ārammaṇavasena parikaḍḍhatīti vuyhati. Saritabbaṃ hutvā cittapīṇanaṃ ārammaṇavasena gahetvā upasaṃharīyatīti saṃharīyati. Yathāti opammatthe nipāto. Hatthinā yāyati gacchatīti hatthiyānena vā, vāiti vikappatthe. Assena yāyati gacchatīti assayānena vā. Goyuttaṃ vayhādiyānaṃ goyānaṃ, tena goyānena. Ajayānādīsupi eseva nayo. Iṭṭhavasena jāto sañjāto.

It goes, reaching the object that delights the eye. It is led in that it makes something dear by way of being visible, by way of the object, without having attained it. Having become audible, it is drawn by way of the object that delights the ear-channel. Having become memorable, it is gathered, taking hold of the object that delights the mind, and is brought near. 'Yathā' is a particle in the sense of comparison. 'Goes by elephant' means traveling by elephant vehicle; 'vā' is in the sense of an alternative. 'Goes by horse' means traveling by horse vehicle. An ox-yoke vehicle is an ox vehicle; thus, by ox vehicle. The same applies to goat vehicles and others. 'Sañjāta' means arisen by means of what is desired.

Ārammaṇapiyattavasena nibbatto abhinibbatto. Ārammaṇamanāpabhāvena pātubhūto. Atha vā kāmarāgavasena jāto sañjāto. Kāmanandivasena nibbatto abhinibbatto. Kāmataṇhāvasena kāmasinehavasena kāmacchandavasena kāmapariḷāhavasena ca pātubhūtoti veditabbo.

'Abhinibbatto' means produced due to the object's agreeableness. 'Pātubhūto' means manifested due to the object's pleasing nature. Or, 'sañjāta' means arisen due to sensual lust. 'Abhinibbatto' means produced due to delight in sensual pleasure. It should be understood as manifested due to sensual craving, sensual affection, sensual desire, and sensual burning.

Te vā kāmā parihāyantīti te vatthukāmādayo parihāyanti vigacchanti. So vā kāmehi parihāyatīti eso khattiyādipuggalo vatthukāmādikāmehi parihāyati vigacchati “pubbeva maccaṃ vijahanti bhogā, macco dhane pubbataraṃ jahātī”ti (jā. 1.5.2) evamādīsu viya. Kathanti kena pakārena. Tiṭṭhantassevāti dharantasseva. Te bhogeti te vatthukāmādayo bhoge. Rājāno vāti pathabyādirājāno. Harantīti gahetvā gacchanti, apaharanti vā. Corā vāti sandhicchedādikā. Aggi vāti dāvaggiādi. Dahatīti jhāpeti bhasmaṃ karoti. Udakaṃ vāti oghādiudakaṃ[P 1.0028]. Vahatīti gahetvā mahāsamuddaṃ pāpeti. Appiyā vāti akantā amanāpā. Dāyādā harantīti dāyajjavirahitā assāmikā haranti. Nihitaṃ [M 0.0024] vāti nidhānaṃ katvā ṭhapitaṃ. Nādhigacchatīti na vindati na paṭilabhati, na passatīti attho. Duppayuttāti visamapayogena yojitā kasivāṇijjādikammantā. Bhijjantīti bhedaṃ pāpuṇanti, na pavattantīti attho. “Bhañjanti rathaṃ ayānakā”tiādīsu (jā. 2.21.296) sambhavo veditabbo.

'Te vā kāmā parihāyanti' means those objects of sensual desire and the like fade away and disappear. Or, 'so vā kāmehi parihāyati' means that individual, whether a noble or other person, fades away and is separated from objects of sensual desire and the like, as in sayings such as: 'Even before death, wealth abandons a mortal, but a mortal abandons wealth even earlier.' 'Kathaṃ' means in what manner. 'Tiṭṭhantasseva' means while they endure. 'Te bhoge' means those objects of sensual desire and the like, which are riches. 'Rājāno' means kings, such as rulers of the land. 'Haranti' means they seize and carry them off, or they steal them. 'Corā' means thieves, such as burglars. 'Aggi' means fire, such as a forest fire. 'Dahati' means it burns, reduces to ashes. 'Udakaṃ' means water, such as a flood. 'Vahati' means it carries away, sweeping them to the great ocean. 'Appiyā' means those who are disliked or unwelcome. 'Dāyādā haranti' means heirs without rightful claim seize them. 'Nihitaṃ' means what was hidden away as a treasure. 'Nādhigacchati' means one does not find it, does not regain it, does not see it—this is the meaning. 'Duppayuttā' means mismanaged, such as farming or trade, which are improperly conducted. 'Bhijjanti' means they break down, they do not prosper—this is the meaning. As in the phrase, 'They break the chariot that does not move,' the sense should be understood accordingly.

Kule vā kulaṅgāro uppajjatīti khattiyādikule kulajhāpako kule antimapuriso nibbattati[V 0.0023]. “Kulaṅkaro”tipi pāḷi. Yo te bhoge vikiratīti yo eso kule pacchimako te hiraññādike bhoge khepeti. Vidhamatīti viyogaṃ karoti, dūre khipati. Viddhaṃsetīti nāseti adassanaṃ gameti. Atha vā itthidhutto hutvā vikirati. Surādhutto hutvā vidhamati. Akkhadhutto hutvā viddhaṃseti. Vikirati vā uppannaṃ āyaṃ ajānanena. Vidhamati vissajjanamukhaṃ ajānanena. Viddhaṃseti ṭhapitaṭṭhāne ārakkhaṃ asaṃvidhānenāti evamādinā yojetabbaṃ.

Or, 'kule vā kulaṅgāro uppajjati' means a family-destroyer, the last person in the family, is born in a noble or other family. 'Kulaṅkaro' is also a reading. 'Yo te bhoge vikirati' means this last person in the family wastes those riches like gold and the like. 'Vidhamati' means he separates them, throws them far away. 'Viddhaṃseti' means he annihilates them, makes them disappear. Or else, being a womanizer, he squanders; being a drunkard, he scatters; being a gambler, he destroys. Or, he squanders through ignorance of income; he scatters through ignorance of the means of expenditure; he destroys through a lack of planning to protect what has been stored. This should be understood in this way.

Aniccatāyeva aṭṭhamīti vināsabhāvo eva aṭṭhamo. Hāyantīti adassanaṃ yanti. Parihāyantīti na puna paññāyanti. Paridhaṃsentīti ṭhānato apagacchanti. Paripatantīti paggharanti. Antaradhāyantīti antaradhānaṃ adassanaṃ gacchanti. Vippalujjantīti cuṇṇavicuṇṇā hutvā apagacchanti.

'Aniccatā' (impermanence) itself is the eighth—meaning the nature of destruction is the eighth. 'Hāyanti' means they go to non-appearance. 'Parihāyanti' means they no longer appear. 'Paridhaṃsenti' means they depart from their place. 'Paripatanti' means they fall away, they drip away. 'Antaradhāyanti' means they go to disappearance, to non-appearance. 'Vippalujjanti' means having become powder and dust, they depart.

Tiṭṭhanteva [P 1.0029] te bhogeti tesaṃ dhanānaṃ ṭhitakāle “tiṭṭhante nibbute cāpī”ti evamādīsu (vi. va. 806) viya. Soti so bhogasāmiko puggalo. Cavati devalokato. Marati manussalokato. Vippalujjati nāgasupaṇṇādilokato. Atha vā hāyati dhaññakoṭṭhāgāravasena. Parihāyati dhanakoṭṭhāgāravasena. Paridhaṃsati balibaddahatthiassādivasena. Paripatati dāsidāsavasena. Antaradhāyati dārābharaṇavasena. Nassati udakādivasenāti eke vaṇṇayanti.

'Tiṭṭhanteva te bhoge' means while those riches are stable, as in phrases such as, 'They remain, and even when extinguished.' 'So' refers to that individual who owns the wealth. He passes away from the deva-world. He dies from the human world. He is utterly destroyed from the worlds of nāgas, supaṇṇas, and so on. Or alternatively, he declines with respect to granaries and storehouses; he dwindles with respect to treasuries; he is ruined with respect to oxen, elephants, horses, and so on; he is lost with respect to male and female servants; he vanishes with respect to wives and ornaments; he is ruined with respect to water and so on—thus some explain.

Ayomayenāti kāḷalohādinibbattena. Sallenāti kaṇḍena. Aṭṭhimayenāti manussaṭṭhiṃ ṭhapetvā avasesena. Dantamayenāti hatthidantādinā. Visāṇamayenāti govisāṇādinā. Kaṭṭhamayenāti veḷukaṭṭhādinā. Viddhoti vuttappakārasallānaṃ aññataraññatarena pahaṭo. Ruppatīti vikirati, vikāraṃ āpajjati. Kuppatīti calati, kopaṃ uppādeti. Ghaṭṭīyatīti [M 0.0025] ghaṭṭito hoti. Pīḷīyatīti pīḷito hoti, laddhappahāro kuppati. “Tatiyadivase salākaṃ pavesetvā dhovanakāle ghaṭṭīyati. Khārappadāne pīḷīyati. Pahāradhovane vā ruppati. Tasmiṃ dukkhuppādane kuppati. Salākapavesane pīḷīyati. Khārappadāne ghaṭṭīyatī”ti evameke vaṇṇayanti.

'Made of iron' means produced from black iron and the like. 'With a dart' means with an arrow. 'Made of bone' means made with the remainder after excluding human bones. 'Made of ivory' means from elephant tusks and the like. 'Made of horn' means from cow horns and the like. 'Made of wood' means from bamboo and the like. 'Pierced' means struck by one or another of the aforementioned darts. 'Is tormented' means is scattered, undergoes change. 'Is agitated' means moves, gives rise to anger. 'Is struck' means is rubbed. 'Is oppressed' means is oppressed; having received a blow, it is agitated. 'On the third day, when inserting the probe, it is rubbed during washing. When applying the caustic, it is oppressed. Or when washing the wound, it is tormented. When pain arises in it, it is agitated. When inserting the probe, it is oppressed. When applying the caustic, it is rubbed,' as some explain.

Byādhitoti laddhappahāro hutvā pīḷito. Domanassitoti domanassappatto. Vipariṇāmaññathābhāvāti pakatibhāvaṃ jahitvā aññathābhāvaṃ upanītena, antososādi soko ca vācāvippalāpo paridevo ca kāyapīḷanādi dukkhañca cittapīḷanādi domanassañca bhuso āyāso upāyāso ca. Ete vuttappakārā sokādayo uppajjanti samudācāraṃ gacchanti.

"Afflicted" means, having been struck, one is oppressed. "Distressed" means one has attained sadness. "Because of transformation and otherness of state" means that by being brought to another state after having abandoned its natural state, there arise sorrow such as inner sorrow, lamentation which is confused speech, pain such as bodily affliction, distress such as mental affliction, and great trouble and despair. These aforementioned sorrows and so forth arise and come into manifestation.

3. Tatiyagāthāyaṃ [V 0.0024] saṅkhepattho – yo pana ime kāme tattha chandarāgavikkhambhanena vā samucchedena vā attano pādena sappassa siraṃ viya parivajjeti, so bhikkhu sabbalokaṃ vipphāretvā [P 1.0030] ṭhitattā loke visattikāsaṅkhātaṃ taṇhaṃ sato hutvā samativattatīti.

3. The condensed meaning of the third verse: But whoever avoids these sensual pleasures through the suppression or eradication of desire and lust for them, as one avoids a snake's head with one's foot, that monk, because he abides having pervaded the entire world, mindfully overcomes craving, which is known as attachment in the world.

Yoti vibhajitabbaṃ padaṃ. Yo yādisotiādīni tassa vibhajanapadāni. Ettha ca yasmā yoti atthapadaṃ. tañca aniyamena puggalaṃ dīpeti. Tasmā tassa atthaṃ dassento aniyamena puggaladīpakaṃ yo-saddameva āha. Tasmā ettha evamattho veditabbo – yoti yo kocīti. Yasmā yo yo koci nāma, so avassaṃ yathāliṅgayathāyuttayathāvihitayathāppakārayaṃṭhānapattayaṃdhammasamannāgatavasena ekenākārena paññāyati, tasmā taṃ tattha ñāpetuṃ taṃ bhedaṃ pakāsento “yādiso”tiādimāha. Tattha yādisoti liṅgavasena yādiso vā tādiso vā hotu, dīgho vā rasso vā kāḷo vā odāto vā maṅguracchavi vā kiso vā thūlo vāti attho.

The word 'yo' is to be analyzed. The words for its analysis are 'yādiso' and so on. Here, since 'yo' is a word with meaning, and it indicates a person indefinitely, therefore, to show its meaning, the author states the word 'yo' itself, which indefinitely indicates a person. Hence, the meaning here should be understood thus: 'yo' means 'whoever.' Because whoever someone may be, that one is invariably known in one way according to characteristics, suitability, arrangement, manner, state attained, or qualities possessed. Therefore, to make that known in this context, revealing that distinction, the author states 'yādiso' and so on. Here, 'yādiso' means, in terms of characteristics, whether one is of this sort or that sort, tall or short, dark or fair, golden-skinned, thin, or fat—this is the meaning.

Yathāyuttoti yogavasena yena vā tena vā yutto hotu, navakammayutto vā uddesayutto vā vāsadhurayutto vāti attho. Yathāvihitoti yathāṭhapito navakammādhiṭṭhāyikādivasena. Yathāpakāroti yathāpakārena patiṭṭhito padīpanāyakādivasena. Yaṃṭhānappattoti [M 0.0026] yaṃ ṭhānantaraṃ patto senāpatiseṭṭhiṭṭhānādivasena. Yaṃdhammasamannāgatoti yena dhammena upāgato dhutaṅgādivasena.

"As is fit" means, by way of application, let him be engaged in this or that, whether engaged in new construction work, recitation, or the responsibility of residence—this is the meaning. "As arranged" means as appointed, such as being a supervisor of new construction and so on. "According to manner" means established in a certain manner, such as being a lamp-leader and so on. "Whatever position attained" means whatever rank he has attained, such as the position of a general or a wealthy merchant. "Whatever quality endowed with" means whatever quality he possesses, such as the ascetic practices.

Vikkhambhanato vāti upacārappanāsamādhīti kilesānaṃ dūrīkaraṇato vā ghaṭappahārena sevālānaṃ viya. Samucchedato vāti puna appavattiṃ katvā accantato maggena kilesānaṃ ucchinnamūlato pahānavasena samucchedato vā. Aṭṭhikaṅkalūpamā kāmātiādīni ekādasa padāni vipassanāvasena vuttāni.

"Or by suppression" means by making the defilements distant through access and absorption concentration, just as duckweed is scattered by the strike of a pot. "Or by eradication" means by abandoning the defilements, having made them not occur again, their roots having been completely cut off by the path; this is eradication. The eleven terms, beginning with "sensual pleasures are like a skeleton," are spoken by way of insight.

Buddhānussatiṃ bhāventopītiādīni cha padāni maraṇassatiṃ bhāventopi, upasamānussatiṃ bhāventopīti [P 1.0031] imāni ca upacārajjhānavasena vuttāni. Ānāpānassatiṃ bhāventopi, kāyagatāsatiṃ bhāventopi, paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ bhāventopītiādīni nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpattiṃ bhāventopīti pariyosānāni appanājjhānavasena vuttāni. Tattha aṭṭhikaṅkalūpamā kāmāti sunikkantaṃ nikkantaṃ nimmaṃsaṃ lohitamakkhitaṃ aṭṭhikaṅkalaṃ upamā etesaṃ kāmānanti aṭṭhikaṅkalūpamā kāmā. Appassādaṭṭhenāti “appaṃ parittaṃ sukhassādaṃ ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo”ti dassanaṭṭhena. Passantoti “yāvadeva pana so kukkuro kilamathassa vighātassa bhāgī assā”ti ñāṇacakkhunā passanto. Parivajjetīti dūraṅgameti. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

The six terms beginning with 'even while developing mindfulness of the Buddha,' and also 'even while developing mindfulness of death,' and 'even while developing mindfulness of peace'—these are spoken by way of access jhāna. 'Even while developing mindfulness of breathing,' 'even while developing mindfulness of the body,' 'even while developing the first jhāna,' and so on, ending with 'even while developing the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception'—these are spoken by way of absorption jhāna. Therein, "sensual pleasures are like a skeleton" means: a skeleton that is well-scraped, scraped clean, fleshless, and smeared with blood is the simile for these sensual pleasures. "In the sense of little satisfaction" means in the sense of seeing that "the enjoyment is small and limited, while the danger herein is greater." "Seeing" means seeing with the eye of wisdom that "that dog would only become a partaker of weariness and vexation." "Avoids" means keeps at a distance. For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Seyyathāpi[V 0.0025], gahapati, kukkuro jighacchādubbalyapareto goghātakasūnaṃ paccupaṭṭhito assa, tamenaṃ dakkho goghātako vā goghātakantevāsī vā aṭṭhikaṅkalaṃ sunikkantaṃ nikkantaṃ nimmaṃsaṃ lohitamakkhitaṃ upasumbheyya. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, gahapati, api nu kho so kukkuro amhaṃ aṭṭhikaṅkalaṃ sunikkantaṃ nikkantaṃ nimmaṃsaṃ lohitamakkhitaṃ palehanto jighacchādubbalyaṃ paṭivineyyā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Taṃ kissa hetu”? “Aduñhi, bhante, aṭṭhikaṅkalaṃ sunikkantaṃ nikkantaṃ nimmaṃsaṃ lohitamakkhitaṃ, yāvadeva pana so kukkuro kilamathassa vighātassa bhāgī assā”ti. “Evameva kho, gahapati, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati ‘aṭṭhikaṅkalūpamā kāmā vuttā bhagavatā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo’ti. Evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya disvā yāyaṃ upekkhā nānattā nānattasitā[M 0.0027], taṃ abhinivajjetvā yāyaṃ upekkhā ekattā ekattasitā, yattha sabbaso lokāmisupādānā aparisesā nirujjhanti, tamevūpekkhaṃ bhāvetī”ti (ma. ni. 2.42).

"Suppose, householder, a dog, overcome by hunger and weakness, were to attend upon a butcher’s stall. A skilled butcher or his apprentice might toss it a skeleton, well-scraped, scraped clean, fleshless, and smeared with blood. What do you think, householder? By licking that skeleton, well-scraped, scraped clean, fleshless, and smeared with blood, would that dog appease its hunger and weakness?" "No, venerable sir." "For what reason?" "Because, venerable sir, that skeleton is well-scraped, scraped clean, fleshless, and smeared with blood; the dog would only become a partaker of weariness and vexation." "So too, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus: 'The Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like a skeleton, of much suffering, of much despair, and that the danger in them is greater.' Having seen this as it actually is with right wisdom, he, avoiding that equanimity which is of diversity and is based on diversity, develops that very equanimity which is of unity and is based on unity, wherein all clinging to worldly bait ceases without remainder."

Gijjhādīhi sādhāraṇā maṃsapesi upamā etesanti maṃsapesūpamā. Bahūnaṃ sādhāraṇaṭṭhena bahusādhāraṇā. Ādittaṃ tiṇukkaṃ upamā etesanti tiṇukkūpamā. Anudahanaṭṭhenāti hatthādijhāpanaṭṭhena. Sādhikaporisappamāṇā [P 1.0032] vītaccikānaṃ vītadhūmānaṃ aṅgārānaṃ pūrā aṅgārakāsu upamā etesanti aṅgārakāsūpamā. Mahāpariḷāhaṭṭhenāti mahantaparitāpanaṭṭhena. Ārāmarāmaṇeyyādikaṃ supinaṃ upamā etesanti supinakūpamā. Ittarapaccupaṭṭhānaṭṭhenāti appatvā, na upagantvā tiṭṭhanaṭṭhena. Yācitena laddhaṃ yānādibhaṇḍaṃ upamā etesanti yācitakūpamā. Tāvakālikaṭṭhenāti anibandhanaṭṭhena. Sampannaphalarukkho upamā etesanti rukkhaphalūpamā. Sambhañjanaparibhañjanaṭṭhenāti sākhābhañjanaṭṭhena ceva samantato bhañjitvā rukkhapātanaṭṭhena ca. Asi ca sūnā ca upamā etesanti asisūnūpamā. Adhikuṭṭanaṭṭhenāti chindanaṭṭhena. Sattisūlaṃ upamā etesanti sattisūlūpamā. Vinivijjhanaṭṭhenāti nipatetvā gamanaṭṭhena. Bhayajananaṭṭhena sappasiraṃ upamā etesanti sappasirūpamā. Sappaṭibhayaṭṭhenāti saha abhimukhe bhayaṭṭhena. Dukkhajananaṃ aggikkhandhaṃ upamā etesanti aggikkhandhūpamā. Mahābhitāpanaṭṭhenāti mahantaabhitāpakāyapīḷāuppādanaṭṭhenāti kāmaṃ parivajjetīti. Vuttañhetaṃ –

A lump of flesh common to vultures and others is the simile, hence "simile of a lump of flesh." Because it is common to many, it is widely shared. A blazing grass torch is the simile, hence "simile of a grass torch"; this is because of its burning nature, that is, the burning of hands and so on. A pit of embers more than a man's height, full of embers free from flame and smoke, is the simile, hence "simile of a pit of embers"; this is because of its great scorching nature, that is, its great tormenting nature. A dream of a delightful park and so on is the simile, hence "simile of a dream"; this is because of its fleeting appearance, that is, because it stands without being attained or approached. Goods such as a vehicle obtained by borrowing are the simile, hence "simile of borrowed goods"; this is because of their temporary nature, that is, because they are not a permanent possession. A tree laden with fruit is the simile, hence "simile of a tree with fruit"; this is because of the breaking of its branches and its being felled by being broken all around. A sword and a butcher's block are the simile, hence "simile of a sword and butcher's block"; this is because of their chopping nature, that is, their cutting nature. A spear and a stake are the simile, hence "simile of a spear and stake"; this is because of their piercing-through nature, that is, their nature of felling and passing through. A snake's head is the simile, hence "simile of a snake's head"; this is because it is fear-producing. "Because it is terrifying" means because of the fear in confronting it. A mass of fire that produces suffering is the simile, hence "simile of a mass of fire"; this is because of its greatly tormenting nature, that is, because it produces great and intense bodily affliction. Thus one avoids sensual pleasure. And this was said:

“Seyyathāpi, gahapati, gijjho vā kaṅko vā kulalo vā maṃsapesiṃ ādāya uḍḍīyeyya, tamenaṃ gijjhāpi kaṅkāpi kulalāpi anupatitvā anupatitvā vitaccheyyuṃ vissajjeyyuṃ. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, gahapati, sace so gijjho vā kaṅko vā kulalo vā taṃ maṃsapesiṃ na khippameva paṭinissajjeyya, so tatonidānaṃ maraṇaṃ vā nigaccheyya[V 0.0026], maraṇamattaṃ vā dukkha”nti “evaṃ, bhante”. “Evameva kho, gahapati, ariyasāvako [P 1.0033] iti paṭisañcikkhati ‘maṃsapesūpamā kāmā vuttā bhagavatā…pe… tamevūpekkhaṃ bhāveti. Seyyathāpi, gahapati, puriso ādittaṃ tiṇukkaṃ ādāya paṭivātaṃ gaccheyya. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, gahapati, sace [M 0.0028] so puriso taṃ ādittaṃ tiṇukkaṃ na khippameva paṭinissajjeyya, tassa sā ādittā tiṇukkā hatthaṃ vā daheyya, bāhuṃ vā daheyya, aññataraṃ vā aññataraṃ vā aṅgapaccaṅgaṃ daheyya, so tatonidānaṃ maraṇaṃ vā nigaccheyya, maraṇamattaṃ vā dukkha”nti? “Evaṃ, bhante”. “Evameva kho, gahapati, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati ‘tiṇukkūpamā kāmā vuttā bhagavatā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā…pe… tamevūpekkhaṃ bhāveti. Seyyathāpi, gahapati, aṅgārakāsu sādhikaporisā pūrā aṅgārānaṃ vītaccikānaṃ vītadhūmānaṃ. Atha puriso āgaccheyya jīvitukāmo amaritukāmo sukhakāmo dukkhappaṭikkūlo, tamenaṃ dve balavanto purisā nānābāhāsu gahetvā aṅgārakāsuṃ upakaḍḍheyyuṃ. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi gahapati, api nu so puriso iti citi ceva kāyaṃ sannāmeyyā”ti? “Evaṃ, bhante”. “Taṃ kissahetu”? “Viditañhi, bhante, tassa purisassa ‘imañca ahaṃ aṅgārakāsuṃ papatissāmi, tatonidānaṃ maraṇaṃ vā nigacchissāmi maraṇamattaṃ vā dukkha’”nti. “Evameva kho gahapati ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati ‘aṅgārakāsūpamā kāmā vuttā bhagavatā…pe… tamevūpekkhaṃ bhāveti. Seyyathāpi, gahapati, puriso supinakaṃ passeyya ārāmarāmaṇeyyakaṃ vanarāmaṇeyyakaṃ bhūmirāmaṇeyyakaṃ pokkharaṇirāmaṇeyyakaṃ, so paṭibuddho na kiñci paṭipasseyya. Evameva kho, gahapati, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati ‘supinakūpamā kāmā vuttā bhagavatā…pe… tamevūpekkhaṃ bhāveti. Seyyathāpi, gahapati, puriso yācitakaṃ bhogaṃ yācitvā yānaṃ vā poriseyyaṃ pavaramaṇikuṇḍalaṃ. So tehi yācitakehi bhogehi purakkhato [P 1.0034] parivuto antarāpaṇaṃ paṭipajjeyya. Tamenaṃ jano disvā evaṃ vadeyya ‘bhogī vata bho puriso, evaṃ kira bho bhogino bhogāni bhuñjantī’ti. Tamenaṃ sāmikā yattha yattheva tāni passeyyuṃ, tattha tattheva tāni hareyyuṃ. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, gahapati, alaṃ nu kho tassa purisassa aññathattāyā”ti? “Evaṃ, bhante”. “Taṃ kissahetu”? “Sāmino hi, bhante, tāni harantī”ti. “Evameva kho, gahapati, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati ‘yācitakūpamā [M 0.0029] kāmā vuttā bhagavatā…pe… tamevūpekkhaṃ bhāveti. Seyyathāpi, gahapati, gāmassa vā nigamassa vā avidūre tibbo vanasaṇḍo, tatrassa rukkho sampannaphalo ca upapannaphalo ca. Na cassu kānici phalāni bhūmiyaṃ patitāni. Atha puriso [V 0.0027] āgaccheyya phalatthiko phalagavesī phalapariyesanaṃ caramāno. So taṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ ajjhogāhetvā taṃ rukkhaṃ passeyya sampannaphalañca upapannaphalañca. Tassa evamassa ‘ayaṃ kho rukkho sampannaphalo ca upapannaphalo ca, natthi ca kānici phalāni bhūmiyaṃ patitāni, jānāmi kho panāhaṃ rukkhaṃ āropituṃ. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ imaṃ rukkhaṃ ārohitvā yāvadatthañca khādeyyaṃ, ucchaṅgañca pūreyya’nti? So taṃ rukkhaṃ ārohitvā yāvadatthañca khādeyya, ucchaṅgañca pūreyya. Atha dutiyo puriso āgaccheyya phalatthiko phalagavesī phalapariyesanaṃ caramāno tiṇhaṃ kuṭhāriṃ ādāya. So taṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ ajjhogāhetvā taṃ rukkhaṃ passeyya sampannaphalañca upapannaphalañca. Tassa evamassa ‘ayaṃ kho rukkho sampannaphalo ca upapannaphalo ca, natthi ca kānici phalāni bhūmiyaṃ patitāni, na kho panāhaṃ jānāmi rukkhaṃ ārohituṃ. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ imaṃ rukkhaṃ mūlato chetvā yāvadatthañca khādeyyaṃ, ucchaṅgañca pūreyya’nti. So taṃ rukkhaṃ mūlatova chindeyya. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi[P 1.0035], gahapati, amuko so puriso paṭhamaṃ rukkhaṃ ārūḷho, sace so na khippameva oroheyya, tassa so rukkho papatanto hatthaṃ vā bhañjeyya pādaṃ vā bhañjeyya aññataraṃ vā aññataraṃ vā aṅgapaccaṅgaṃ bhañjeyya, so tatonidānaṃ maraṇaṃ vā nigaccheyya, maraṇamattaṃ vā dukkha”nti? “Evaṃ, bhante”. “Evameva kho, gahapati, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati ‘rukkhaphalūpamā kāmā vuttā bhagavatā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo’ti. Evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya disvā yāyaṃ upekkhā nānattā nānattasitā, taṃ abhinivajjetvā yāyaṃ upekkhā ekattā ekattasitā. Yattha sabbaso lokāmisūpādānā aparisesā nirujjhanti. Tamevūpekkhaṃ bhāvetī”ti (ma. ni. 2.43-48).

“Just as, householder, a vulture, a heron, or a hawk, having seized a piece of meat, would fly away, and other vultures, herons, or hawks would pursue it again and again, tearing and rending it. What do you think, householder? If that vulture, heron, or hawk does not quickly let go of that piece of meat, would it not thereby meet with death or suffering that is like death itself?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “In the same way, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘The Blessed One has compared sensual pleasures to a piece of meat…’ He cultivates that equanimity. “Just as, householder, a man would take a blazing grass torch and walk against the wind. What do you think, householder? If that man does not quickly let go of that blazing grass torch, would that blazing grass torch not burn his hand or arm or some other limb, and thereby he would meet with death or suffering that is like death itself?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “In the same way, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘The Blessed One has compared sensual pleasures to a blazing grass torch, of much suffering, much tribulation…’ He cultivates that equanimity. “Just as, householder, there were a pit of glowing coals, deeper than a man’s height, full of coals that were flame-free and smokeless. Then a man would come along, desiring to live, not wishing to die, desiring happiness and averse to pain. Two strong men would seize him by both arms and drag him towards that pit of coals. What do you think, householder, would that man not writhe and twist his body?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Why is that?” “Because, venerable sir, that man knows: ‘If I fall into this pit of coals, I will thereby meet death or suffering that is like death itself.’” “In the same way, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘The Blessed One has compared sensual pleasures to a pit of coals…’ He cultivates that equanimity. “Just as, householder, a man might see in a dream delightful parks, delightful forests, delightful grounds, delightful ponds. But upon waking, he would see nothing of them. In the same way, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘The Blessed One has compared sensual pleasures to a dream…’ He cultivates that equanimity. “Just as, householder, a man might borrow goods—a carriage or a palanquin, and excellent jeweled earrings. And, attended and surrounded by those borrowed goods, he would go to the marketplace. People, seeing him, would say: ‘This man is wealthy! For this is how the wealthy enjoy their wealth.’ But wherever the owners saw those goods, they would take them back. What do you think, householder, is there not cause for that man’s distress?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Why is that?” “Because, venerable sir, the owners are taking them back.” “In the same way, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘The Blessed One has compared sensual pleasures to borrowed goods…’ He cultivates that equanimity. “Just as, householder, not far from a village or town, there was a dense forest grove where a tree stood laden with abundant fruit, fully endowed with fruit. None of its fruit had fallen to the ground. Then a man would come along, seeking fruit, searching for fruit, wandering in search of fruit. Entering that grove, he would see that tree laden with abundant fruit and think: ‘This tree is laden with abundant fruit, fully endowed with fruit, but none of its fruit has fallen to the ground. I know how to climb a tree. Why don’t I climb this tree, eat as much as I want, and fill my lap?’ So he would climb the tree, eat as much as he wanted, and fill his lap. Then a second man would come along, seeking fruit, searching for fruit, carrying a sharp axe. Entering that grove, he would see that tree laden with abundant fruit and think: ‘This tree is laden with abundant fruit, fully endowed with fruit, but none of its fruit has fallen to the ground. I do not know how to climb a tree. Why don’t I chop this tree down at the root, eat as much as I want, and fill my lap?’ So he would chop the tree down at the root. What do you think, householder? If that first man who had climbed the tree does not come down quickly, would the falling tree not break his hand or foot or some other limb, and thereby he would meet with death or suffering that is like death itself?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “In the same way, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘The Blessed One has compared sensual pleasures to the fruits of a tree, of much suffering, much tribulation; the danger in them is greater.’ Seeing this as it truly is with right wisdom, rejecting the equanimity that is diverse and based on diversity, he cultivates the equanimity that is unified and based on unity, where all clinging to worldly acquisitions ceases without remainder. He cultivates that equanimity.”

Evaṃ [M 0.0030] aṭṭhikaṅkalādikaaggikkhandhūpamapariyosānato vipassanaṃ dassetvā idāni upacārasamādhiṃ dassento “buddhānussatiṃ bhāvento”tiādimāha.

Having thus shown insight meditation culminating in the simile of the mass of fire beginning with the skeleton, now, to explain access concentration, he said what begins with “developing recollection of the Buddha.”

Tattha punappunaṃ uppajjanato sati eva anussati. Pavattitabbaṭṭhānamhiyeva ca pavattattā saddhāpabbajitassa kulaputtassa anurūpā satītipi anussati. Buddhaṃ ārabbha uppannā anussati buddhānussati. Arahatādibuddhaguṇārammaṇāya satiyā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ, taṃ buddhānussatiṃ. Bhāventoti vaḍḍhento byūhento. Dhammaṃ ārabbha uppannā anussati dhammānussati, svākkhātatādidhammaguṇārammaṇāya satiyā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Saṅghaṃ ārabbha uppannā anussati saṅghānussati, suppaṭipannatādisaṅghaguṇārammaṇāya satiyā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sīlaṃ ārabbha uppannā anussati [V 0.0028] sīlānussati, attano akhaṇḍatādisīlaguṇārammaṇāya satiyā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Cāgaṃ ārabbha uppannā anussati cāgānussati, attano muttacāgatādicāgaguṇārammaṇāya satiyā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Devatā ārabbha uppannā anussati devatānussati, devatā sakkhiṭṭhāne [P 1.0036] ṭhapetvā attano saddhādiguṇārammaṇāya satiyā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Ānāpāne ārabbha uppannā sati ānāpānassati, ānāpānanimittārammaṇāya satiyā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Maraṇaṃ ārabbha uppannā sati maraṇassati, ekabhavapariyāpannajīvitindriyupacchedasaṅkhātamaraṇārammaṇāya satiyā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

Herein, because it arises repeatedly, mindfulness is recollection (anussati). And since it occurs precisely where it should for a faithful monastic, it is appropriate mindfulness, and thus also recollection. Recollection arising in connection with the Buddha is recollection of the Buddha. This is a designation for mindfulness that has the qualities of the Buddha—such as being an arahant—as its object; that is, recollection of the Buddha. “Developing” means increasing and expanding it. Recollection arising in connection with the Dhamma is recollection of the Dhamma; this is a designation for mindfulness that has the qualities of the Dhamma—such as being well-proclaimed—as its object. Recollection arising in connection with the Saṅgha is recollection of the Saṅgha; this is a designation for mindfulness that has the qualities of the Saṅgha—such as practicing rightly—as its object. Recollection arising in connection with virtue is recollection of virtue; this is a designation for mindfulness that has the qualities of one’s own unbroken virtue as its object. Recollection arising in connection with generosity is recollection of generosity; this is a designation for mindfulness that has the qualities of one’s own open-handed generosity as its object. Recollection arising in connection with deities is recollection of deities; this is a designation for mindfulness that has one’s own qualities, such as faith, as its object, taking deities as witnesses. Mindfulness arising in connection with the breath is mindfulness of breathing; this is a designation for mindfulness that has the sign of the breath as its object. Mindfulness arising in connection with death is mindfulness of death; this is a designation for mindfulness that has death—defined as the cessation of the life faculty comprised within a single existence—as its object.

Kucchitānaṃ kesādīnaṃ paṭikkūlānaṃ āyattā ākarattā kāyoti saṅkhaṃ gate sarīre gatā pavattā sati kāyagatāsati, tādisaṃ vā kāyaṃ gatā sati “kāyagatasatī”ti vattabbe rassaṃ akatvā “kāyagatāsatī”ti vuttaṃ. Kesādikesu kāyakoṭṭhāsesu paṭikkūlanimittārammaṇāya satiyā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Upasamaṃ ārabbha uppannā anussati. Upasamānussati, sabbadukkhūpasamārammaṇāya satiyā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

Mindfulness that has gone to and proceeds in the body—which is designated as 'body' because it is dependent on and a source of repulsive things such as hair and so forth—is called 'mindfulness of the body' (kāyagatāsati). Or, though it should be called 'kāyagatasati' (mindfulness gone to the body), it is said 'kāyagatāsati' without shortening the vowel. This is a designation for mindfulness whose object is the repulsive sign of bodily parts such as hair and so forth. Recollection arisen with reference to peace is 'recollection of peace' (upasamānussati); this is a designation for mindfulness whose object is the pacification of all suffering.

Vitakkavicārapītisukhacittekaggatāsampayuttaṃ paṭhamajjhānaṃ bhāvento. Pītisukhacittekaggatāsampayuttaṃ dutiyajjhānaṃ bhāvento. Sukhacittekaggatāsampayuttaṃ tatiyajjhānaṃ bhāvento. Upekkhācittekaggatāsampayuttaṃ catutthajjhānaṃ bhāvento…pe… nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ bhāventopi kāme parivajjetīti.

One who develops the first jhāna, associated with directed thought, sustained thought, rapture, bliss, and unification of mind, avoids sensual pleasures. One who develops the second jhāna, associated with rapture, bliss, and unification of mind, avoids sensual pleasures. One who develops the third jhāna, associated with bliss and unification of mind, avoids sensual pleasures. One who develops the fourth jhāna, associated with equanimity and unification of mind, avoids sensual pleasures… and so too, one who develops the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception avoids sensual pleasures.

Vikkhambhanappahānaṃ [M 0.0031] dassetvā idāni samucchedena kāmānaṃ pahānaṃ dassetuṃ “sotāpattimaggaṃ bhāventopī”tiādimāha. Tattha maggasotassa āpajjanaṃ sotāpatti, sotāpattiyā maggo sotāpattimaggo. Apāyagamanīye kāmeti yehi apāyaṃ gacchanti, te apāyagamanīye kāme samucchedato sotāpattimaggaṃ bhāvento parivajjeti. Paṭisandhivasena sakiṃyeva imaṃ lokaṃ āgacchatīti sakadāgāmī, tassa maggo sakadāgāmimaggo. Taṃ maggaṃ bhāvento. Oḷāriketi pariḷāhappatte. Paṭisandhivaseneva kāmabhavaṃ nāgacchatīti anāgāmī, tassa maggo anāgāmimaggo. Taṃ maggaṃ bhāvento. Anusahagateti sukhumabhāvappatte. Kilesehi ārakattā, kilesārīnaṃ hatattā, saṃsāracakkassa arānaṃ hatattā, pāpakaraṇe rahābhāvā, paccayādīnaṃ arahattā [P 1.0037] ca arahaṃ, arahato bhāvo arahattaṃ. Kiṃ taṃ? Arahattaphalaṃ. Arahattassa maggo arahattamaggo. Taṃ arahattamaggaṃ bhāvento. Sabbena sabbanti sabbenākārena sabbaṃ. Sabbathā sabbanti sabbappakārena sabbaṃ. Asesaṃ nissesanti niravasesaṃ gandhamattampi aṭṭhapetvā. Atha vā sabbena [V 0.0029] sabbaṃ mūlavasena. Sabbathā sabbaṃ ākāranippadesavasena. Asesaṃ nissesaṃ bhāvanānippadesavasena. Tathā purimena duccaritābhāvena. Dutiyena pariyuṭṭhānābhāvena. Tatiyena anusayābhāvena evameke vaṇṇayanti.

Having shown abandoning by suppression, now, to show the abandoning of sensual pleasures by eradication, he said: 'Even when developing the path of stream-entry,' and so on. Here, the attaining of the stream is stream-entry; the path to stream-entry is the path of stream-entry. Regarding 'sensual desires that lead to the lower realms'—those by which one goes to the lower realms—one developing the path of stream-entry abandons them by eradication. One who comes to this world only once by way of rebirth-linking is a 'once-returner' (sakadāgāmī); his path is the path of the once-returner. Developing that path. 'Gross' (oḷārika) means those that have reached the state of being inflamed. One who does not come back to sensual existence by way of rebirth-linking is a 'non-returner' (anāgāmī); his path is the path of the non-returner. Developing that path. Regarding 'accompanied' (anusahagata), this means those that have reached a subtle state. Because of being far from defilements, because of having slain the foes of defilements, because of having destroyed the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra, because of an absence of secrecy in doing evil, and because of being worthy of offerings—thus, one is an Arahant. The state of an Arahant is Arahantship. What is that? The fruit of Arahantship. The path to Arahantship is the path of Arahantship. Developing that path to Arahantship. 'Completely in every way' (sabbena sabbaṃ) means all in every manner. 'Totally in every way' (sabbathā sabbaṃ) means all in every mode. 'Without remainder, without exception' (asesaṃ nissesanti) means leaving not even a trace. Alternatively, 'completely all' refers to the root. 'Totally all' refers to the way of expression. 'Without remainder, without exception' refers to the way of development. Similarly, some explain: first, by the absence of misconduct; second, by the absence of obsession; third, by the absence of latent tendencies.

Sappo vuccati ahīti yo koci saranto gacchati. Kenaṭṭhenāti kena atthena. Saṃsappanto gacchatīti yasmā sammā saṃsaranto gacchatīti sappo. Bhujantoti vaṅkavaṅko hutvā. Pannasiroti nipannasīso hutvā. Sirena supatīti sīsaṃ bhogantare katvā supanabhāvena sirasā supatīti sarīsapo. Bile sayatīti bilāsayo. “Bilasayo”tipi pāḷi, taṃ sundaraṃ. Guhāyaṃ setīti guhāsayo. Dāṭhā tassa āvudhoti tassa sappassa duve dāṭhā paharaṇasatthasaṅkhāto āvudho. Visaṃ tassa ghoranti tassa sappassa byāpakasaṅkhātaṃ visaṃ dāruṇaṃ kakkhaḷaṃ. Jivhā tassa duvidhāti tassa sappassa dvedhā jivhā. Dvīhi jivhāhi rasaṃ sāyatīti duvidhāhi jivhāhi rasaṃ jānāti assādaṃ vindati sādiyatīti. Jīvituṃ kāmayatīti jīvitukāmo. Amarituṃ kāmayatīti amaritukāmo. Sukhaṃ kāmayatīti sukhakāmo. Dukkhappaṭikkūloti dukkhaṃ [M 0.0032] anicchamāno. Pādenāti attano pādena. Sappasiranti sappassa sīsaṃ. Vajjeyyāti dūrato vajjeyya. Vivajjeyyāti tassa pamāṇena. Parivajjeyyāti samantato. Abhinivajjeyyāti catutthappamāṇena. Atha vā purimena sīsato. Dutiyatatiyena dvīhi passehi. Catutthena pacchato. “Kāme pana appattassa pariyesanamūladukkhavatthubhāvena vajjeyya. Pattassa ārakkhamūladukkhavatthubhāvena [P 1.0038] vivajjeyya. Aññāṇapariḷāhadukkhavatthubhāvena parivajjeyya. Vināsamukhe piyavippayogadukkhavatthubhāvena abhinivajjeyyā”ti evameke vaṇṇayanti.

A serpent is called 'ahi,' meaning any creature that moves by creeping. By what meaning? Because it moves by creeping, it is called a 'serpent' (sappa). 'Crookedly' (bhujanto) means having become very crooked. 'With head down' (pannasiro) means having its head lowered. 'It sleeps with its head' (sirena supatīti) means placing its head within its coils, thus it is called a 'reptile' (sarīsapa). 'It dwells in holes' (bile sayatīti) means 'bilāsayo.' The Pāli also has 'bilasayo,' which is beautiful. 'It lies in caves' (guhāyaṃ setīti) means 'guhāsayo.' 'Its fangs are its weapons' (dāṭhā tassa āvudho) means the two fangs of that serpent are reckoned as its striking weapons. 'Its venom is deadly' (visaṃ tassa ghoraṃ) means the venom of that serpent, which is reckoned as destructive, is fierce and harsh. 'Its tongue is forked' (jivhā tassa duvidhā) means that serpent has a double tongue. 'With its two tongues, it tastes flavors' (dvīhi jivhāhi rasaṃ sāyati) means it discerns, enjoys, and relishes tastes with its forked tongues. 'It desires to live' (jīvituṃ kāmayati) means 'life-seeking' (jīvitukāmo). 'It desires not to die' (amarituṃ kāmayati) means 'death-averse' (amaritukāmo). 'It desires happiness' (sukhaṃ kāmayati) means 'pleasure-seeking' (sukhakāmo). 'It recoils from suffering' (dukkhappaṭikkūlo) means not wanting suffering. 'With one's own foot' (pādena) means with one's own foot. 'The serpent’s head' (sappasiraṃ) means the head of the serpent. 'One should avoid' (vajjeyya) means one should avoid from afar. 'One should completely avoid' (vivajjeyya) means by that measure. 'One should steer clear' (parivajjeyya) means all around. 'One should utterly avoid' (abhinivajjeyya) means by the fourth measure. Alternatively, the first is from the head. The second and third are from the two sides. The fourth is from behind. Some explain it thus: 'One should avoid sensual pleasures because of the suffering rooted in seeking unattained pleasures. One should completely avoid them because of the suffering rooted in guarding attained pleasures. One should steer clear of them because of the suffering rooted in the torment of ignorance. One should utterly avoid them because of the suffering rooted in separation from loved ones at the brink of destruction.'

Rañjanavasena rāgo. Balavarañjanaṭṭhena sārāgo. Visaye sattānaṃ anu anu nayanato anunayo. Anurujjhatīti anurodho, kāmetīti attho. Yattha katthaci bhave sattā etāya nandantīti nandī, sayaṃ vā nandatīti nandī. Nandī ca sā rañjanaṭṭhena rāgo cāti nandirāgo. Tattha ekasmiṃ ārammaṇe sakiṃ uppannā taṇhā nandī, punappunaṃ uppajjamānā nandirāgoti vuccati. Cittassa sārāgoti yo heṭṭhā “balavarañjanaṭṭhena sārāgo”ti vutto, so na sattassa, cittasseva sārāgoti attho.

Lust (rāga) is so called by way of coloring. Intense lust (sārāga) is by way of strong coloring. Affection (anunaya) is by way of leading beings repeatedly towards objects. Because it conforms, it is conformity (anurodha); the meaning is to desire. Wherever in any existence beings delight in this, that is delight (nandī); or it delights of itself—that is delight. That delight, and lust by way of coloring, is 'delight-lust' (nandirāga). Therein, craving that arises once in a single object is called delight; when it arises repeatedly, it is called delight-lust. The intense lust of the mind (cittassa sārāga) means that which was stated above as 'intense lust by way of strong coloring'—it is not of the being, but only of the mind—this is the meaning.

Icchanti etāya ārammaṇānīti icchā. Bahalakilesabhāvena mucchanti etāya pāṇinoti mucchā. Gilitvā pariniṭṭhapetvā gahaṇavasena ajjhosānaṃ. Iminā sattā gijjhanti gedhaṃ āpajjantīti gedho. Bahalaṭṭhena vā gedho. “Gedhaṃ vā pana pavanasaṇḍa”nti hi bahalaṭṭheneva vuttaṃ[V 0.0030]. Anantarapadaṃ upasaggavasena vaḍḍhitaṃ, sabbatobhāgena vā gedhoti paligedho. Sajjanti etenāti saṅgo. Lagganaṭṭhena vā saṅgo. Osīdanaṭṭhena paṅko. Ākaḍḍhanavasena ejā. “Ejā imaṃ purisaṃ parikaḍḍhati tassa tasseva bhavassa abhinibbattiyā”ti hi vuttaṃ. Vañcanaṭṭhena māyā. Vaṭṭasmiṃ sattānaṃ jananaṭṭhena janikā. “Taṇhā janeti purisaṃ, cittamassa vidhāvatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.55) hi vuttaṃ. Vaṭṭasmiṃ satte dukkhena saṃyojayamānā janetīti sañjananī. Ghaṭanaṭṭhena sibbinī. Ayañhi vaṭṭasmiṃ satte cutipaṭisandhivasena sibbati ghaṭeti tunnakāro viya pilotikāya pilotikaṃ, tasmā “ghaṭanaṭṭhena sibbinī”ti vuttā. Anekappakāraṃ [P 1.0039] visayajālaṃ taṇhāvipphanditanivesasaṅkhātaṃ vā jālamassā atthīti jālinī.

They desire objects through it; hence, it is desire (icchā). Through it, beings are deeply infatuated due to the abundance of defilements; hence, it is infatuation (mucchā). Absorption (ajjhosāna) is grasping by way of swallowing and consuming. Through this, beings become greedy and fall into avarice; hence, it is avarice (gedha). Or, it is avarice in the sense of abundance. For it is said, 'Avarice or a dense thicket,' which is stated in the sense of abundance. The subsequent term is augmented by a prefix, or it is avarice in every respect; thus, it is all-encompassing avarice (paligedho). They are attached by it; hence, it is attachment (saṅgo). Or, it is attachment in the sense of clinging. In the sense of sinking, it is mud (paṅko). In the sense of dragging, it is agitation (ejā). For it is said, 'Agitation drags this person toward the arising of this or that very existence.' In the sense of deceiving, it is illusion (māyā). In the sense of generating beings in the round of existence, it is the generator (janikā). For it is said, 'Craving generates a person; his mind runs about' (SN 1.55). It generates by joining beings with suffering in the round of existence; hence, it is the procreator (sañjananī). In the sense of stitching, it is the seamstress (sibbinī). For in the round of existence, it stitches beings together through death and rebirth, just as a tailor stitches one piece of cloth to another; therefore, it is said to be 'the seamstress in the sense of stitching.' It has a net of various kinds of sense objects, or it has what is reckoned as the net of craving's throbbing and settling; hence, it is the ensnarer (jālinī).

Ākaḍḍhanaṭṭhena [M 0.0033] sīghasotā saritā viyāti saritā. Allaṭṭhena vā saritā. Vuttañhetaṃ “saritāni sinehitāni ca somanassāni bhavanti jantuno”ti (dha. pa. 341). Allāni ceva siniddhāni cāti ayañhettha attho. Anayabyasanāpādanaṭṭhena kummānubandhasuttakaṃ viyāti suttaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ “suttanti kho, bhikkhave, nandirāgassetaṃ adhivacana”nti (saṃ. ni. 2.159). Rūpādīsu vitthataṭṭhena visatā. Tassa tassa paṭilābhatthāya satte āyūhāpetīti āyūhinī. Ukkaṇṭhituṃ apadānato sahāyaṭṭhena dutiyā. Ayañhi sattānaṃ vaṭṭasmiṃ ukkaṇṭhituṃ na deti, gatagataṭṭhāne piyasahāyo viya abhiramāpeti. Teneva vuttaṃ –

In the sense of dragging, it is a river (saritā), like a swift-flowing river. Or, it is a river in the sense of being moist. For it is said: 'For a being, there are streams and affectionate pleasures' (Dhp 341). Here, the meaning is both moist and affectionate. In the sense of causing misfortune and disaster, it is a thread (sutta), like the thread that snares a tortoise. For it is said: 'Bhikkhus, “thread” is a designation for delight and lust' (SN 22.121). In the sense of being spread out among forms and so on, it is the pervasive (visatā). Because it makes beings strive for the acquisition of this or that, it is the instigator (āyūhinī). In the sense of being a companion by not allowing weariness, it is the second (dutiyā). For it does not allow beings to become weary of the round of existence, but makes them delight in every place they go, like a dear companion. Therefore it is said:

“Taṇhādutiyo puriso, dīghamaddhānasaṃsaraṃ;

Itthabhāvaññathābhāvaṃ, saṃsāraṃ nātivattatī”ti. (itivu. 15; a. ni. 4.9; mahāni. 191; cūḷani. pāyāyanānugītigāthāniddesa 107);

A person with craving as his companion wanders for a long time; passing from this state to another, he does not transcend saṃsāra (Iti 15).

Paṇidhānakavasena paṇidhi. Bhavanettīti bhavarajju. Etāya hi sattā rajjuyā gīvāyaṃ baddhā goṇā viya icchiticchitaṭṭhānaṃ niyyanti. Taṃ taṃ ārammaṇaṃ vanati bhajati allīyatīti vanaṃ, vanati yācatīti vā vanaṃ. Vanathoti byañjanena padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ. Anatthadukkhānaṃ vā samuṭṭhāpanaṭṭhena gahanaṭṭhena ca vanaṃ viyāti vanaṃ. Balavataṇhāyetaṃ nāmaṃ. Gahanataraṭṭhena pana tato balavatarā vanatho nāma. Tena vuttaṃ –

In the sense of aspiration, it is aspiration (paṇidhi). The guide to existence (bhavanetti) is the rope of becoming. For by this rope, beings are led to whatever place they desire, like oxen bound by a rope at the neck. It is a jungle (vana) because it desires, resorts to, and clings to this or that object; or it is a jungle because it asks (vanati). The term 'vanatho' is augmented by a consonant. Or, like a jungle, it is a jungle (vana) in the sense of being a source of harm and suffering, and in the sense of being dense. This is a name for strong craving. But 'thicket' (vanatho) is a name for a craving that is even stronger than that, in the sense of being denser. Therefore, it is said:

“Vanaṃ chindatha mā rukkhaṃ, vanato jāyate bhayaṃ;

Chetvā vanañca vanathañca, nibbanā hotha bhikkhavo”ti. (dha. pa. 283);

Cut down the jungle, not the tree; from the jungle, fear is born. Having cut down the jungle and the thicket, be without jungle, O bhikkhus (Dhp 283).

Santhavanavasena [V 0.0031][P 1.0040] santhavo, saṃsaggoti attho. So duvidho – taṇhāsanthavo mittasanthavo ca. Tesu idha taṇhāsanthavo adhippeto. Sinehavasena sneho. Ālayakaraṇavasena kampamānā apekkhatīti apekkhā. Vuttampi cetaṃ “imāni te deva caturāsīti nagarasahassāni kusāvatīrājadhānippamukhāni, ettha deva chandaṃ janehi jīvite apekkhaṃ karohī”ti (dī. ni. 2.266). Ālayaṃ karohīti ayañhettha attho. Pāṭiyekke pāṭiyekke ārammaṇe bandhatīti paṭibandhu, ñātakaṭṭhena vā pāṭiyekko bandhūtipi paṭibandhu. Niccasannissitaṭṭhenapi sattānaṃ taṇhāsamo bandhu nāma natthi. Ārammaṇānaṃ [M 0.0034] asanato āsā. Ajjhottharaṇato ceva tittiṃ anugantvāva paribhuñjanato cāti attho. Āsīsanavasena āsīsanā. Āsīsitassa bhāvo āsīsitattaṃ.

In the sense of intimacy, it is intimacy (santhavo); the meaning is association. This is twofold: intimacy based on craving and intimacy based on friendship. Of these, intimacy based on craving is intended here. In the sense of affection, it is affection (sneho). In the sense of making an attachment, it is expectation (apekkhā), as in 'looking on while trembling.' And this is said: 'Your Majesty, these are your eighty-four thousand cities, with the royal capital Kusāvatī at their head. Here, Your Majesty, generate desire, make an expectation for life' (DN 17). Here, the meaning is 'make an attachment.' It is a bond (paṭibandhu) because it binds to each individual object; or, in the sense of a relative, an individual kinsman is also a bond (paṭibandhu). Indeed, for beings, there is no bond equal to craving in terms of constant dependence. Hope (āsā) is from the consuming of objects. The meaning is that it is from overwhelming and from consuming by pursuing satisfaction. In the sense of wishing, it is wishing (āsīsanā). The state of having wished is wished-for-ness (āsīsitattaṃ).

Idāni tassā pavattiṭṭhānaṃ dassetuṃ “rūpāsā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha āsīsanavasena āsāti āsāya atthaṃ gahetvā rūpe āsā rūpāsā. Evaṃ navapi padāni veditabbāni. Ettha ca purimāni pañca pañcakāmaguṇavasena vuttāni, parikkhāralobhavasena chaṭṭhaṃ. Taṃ visesato pabbajitānaṃ, tato parāni tīṇi atittiyavatthuvasena gahaṭṭhānaṃ. Na hi tesaṃ dhanaputtajīvitehi aññaṃ piyataraṃ atthi. “Idaṃ mayhaṃ, idaṃ mayha”nti vā “asukena me idaṃ dinnaṃ, idaṃ dinna”nti vā evaṃ satte jappāpetīti jappā. Parato dve padāni upasaggena vaḍḍhitāni, tato paraṃ aññenākārena vibhajituṃ āraddhattā puna “jappā”ti vuttaṃ. Jappanākāro jappanā. Jappitassa bhāvo jappitattaṃ. Punappunaṃ visaye lumpati ākaḍḍhatīti lolupo, lolupassa bhāvo loluppaṃ. Loluppanākāro loluppāyanā. Loluppasamaṅgino bhāvo loluppāyitattaṃ.

Now, to show its sphere of operation, 'hope for forms' and so on are stated. Therein, taking the meaning of 'āsā' in the sense of wishing, hope for forms is 'rūpāsā.' In this way, all nine terms should be understood. Here, the first five are stated in relation to the five strands of sensual pleasure, and the sixth in relation to greed for requisites, which applies especially to the ordained. The subsequent three pertain to householders, in relation to things of which they are insatiable. For them, there is nothing dearer than wealth, children, and life. It makes beings mutter, 'This is mine, this is mine,' or 'This was given to me by so-and-so'; hence, it is muttering (jappā). The two subsequent terms are augmented with prefixes. Then, because the analysis begins in another way, 'jappā' is stated again. The manner of muttering is 'jappanā.' The state of having muttered is 'jappitattaṃ.' One who repeatedly seizes or drags at sense objects is a greedy person (lolupo); the state of being greedy is greed (loluppaṃ). The manner of being greedy is greediness (loluppāyanā). The state of one endowed with greed is 'loluppāyitattaṃ.'

Pucchañjikatāti [P 1.0041] yāya taṇhāya lābhaṭṭhānesu pucchaṃ cālayamānā sunakhā viya kampamānā vicaranti, taṃ tassā kampanataṇhāya nāmaṃ. Sādhu manāpamanāpe visaye kāmetīti sādhukāmo, tassa bhāvo sādhukamyatā. Mātāmātucchātiādike ayuttaṭṭhāne rāgoti adhammarāgo. Yuttaṭṭhānepi balavā hutvā uppanno lobho visamalobho. “Rāgo visama”ntiādivacanato (vibha. 924) vā yuttaṭṭhāne vā ayuttaṭṭhāne vā uppanno chandarāgo adhammaṭṭhena adhammarāgo. Visamaṭṭhena visamalobhoti veditabbo. Ārammaṇānaṃ nikāmanavasena nikanti. Nikāmanākāro nikāmanā. Patthayanavasena patthanā. Pihāyanavasena pihanā. Suṭṭhu patthanā sampatthanā. Pañcasu kāmaguṇesu taṇhā kāmataṇhā. Rūpārūpabhavesu taṇhā bhavataṇhā. Ucchedasaṅkhāte vibhave taṇhā vibhavataṇhā. Suddhe rūpabhavasmiṃyeva taṇhā rūpataṇhā. Arūpabhave taṇhā arūpataṇhā. Ucchedadiṭṭhisahagato [V 0.0032] rāgo, nirodhe taṇhā nirodhataṇhā. Rūpe taṇhā rūpataṇhā. Sadde taṇhā saddataṇhā. Gandhataṇhādīsupi eseva nayo. Oghādayo vuttatthāva.

Tail-wagging (pucchañjikatā) is that craving by which beings wander about trembling, like a dog wagging its tail in places of gain; this is a name for that trembling craving. One who desires what is agreeable and disagreeable in the sense sphere is a 'fine-desirer' (sādhukāmo); the state of this is 'fine-desiring' (sādhukamyatā). Lust in an improper sphere, such as towards one's mother or maternal aunt, is unrighteous lust (adhammarāgo). Greed that has arisen strongly even in a proper sphere is improper greed (visamalobho). Or, from statements such as 'Lust is improper' (Vibh 924), desire-lust that arises in either a proper or an improper sphere is unrighteous lust in the sense of being unrighteous; it should be understood as improper greed in the sense of being improper. In the sense of liking objects, it is liking (nikanti). The manner of liking is 'nikāmanā.' In the sense of aspiring, it is aspiration (patthanā). In the sense of yearning, it is yearning (pihanā). Intense aspiration is 'sampatthanā.' Craving for the five strands of sensual pleasure is sensual craving (kāmataṇhā). Craving for form and formless becoming is craving for becoming (bhavataṇhā). Craving for non-becoming, reckoned as annihilation, is craving for non-becoming (vibhavataṇhā). Craving in the pure form-becoming alone is form-craving (rūpataṇhā). Craving in the formless becoming is formless-craving (arūpataṇhā). Lust accompanied by the annihilation view; craving for cessation is cessation-craving (nirodhataṇhā). Craving for form is form-craving (rūpataṇhā). Craving for sound is sound-craving (saddataṇhā). The same method applies to craving for smells and so on. The floods and so forth have the meaning already stated.

Kusaladhamme [M 0.0035] āvaratīti āvaraṇaṃ. Chādanavasena chadanaṃ. Satte vaṭṭasmiṃ bandhatīti bandhanaṃ. Cittaṃ upahantvā kilissati saṃkiliṭṭhaṃ karotīti upakkileso. Thāmagataṭṭhena anu anu setīti anusayo. Uppajjamānaṃ cittaṃ pariyuṭṭhātīti pariyuṭṭhānaṃ, uppajjituṃ apadānena kusalavāraṃ gaṇhātīti attho. “Corā magge pariyuṭṭhiṃsu, dhuttā magge pariyuṭṭhiṃsū”tiādīsu (cūḷava. 430) hi maggaṃ gaṇhiṃsūti attho. Evamidhāpi gahaṇaṭṭhena pariyuṭṭhānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Paliveṭhanaṭṭhena [P 1.0042] latā viyāti latā. “Latā uppajja tiṭṭhatī”ti (dha. pa. 340) āgataṭṭhānepi ayaṃ taṇhā latāti vuttā. Vividhāni vatthūni icchatīti vevicchaṃ. Vaṭṭadukkhassa mūlanti dukkhamūlaṃ. Tasseva dukkhassa nidānanti dukkhanidānaṃ. Taṃ dukkhaṃ ito pabhavatīti dukkhappabhavo. Bandhanaṭṭhena pāso viyāti pāso, mārassa pāso mārapāso. Duruggilanaṭṭhena baḷisaṃ viyāti baḷisaṃ, mārassa baḷisaṃ mārabaḷisaṃ. Taṇhābhibhūtā mārassa visayaṃ nātikkamanti, tesaṃ upari māro vasaṃ vattetīti iminā pariyāyena mārassa visayoti māravisayo. Sandanaṭṭhena taṇhāva nadī taṇhānadī. Ajjhottharaṇaṭṭhena taṇhāva jālaṃ taṇhājālaṃ. Yathā sunakhā gaddūlabaddhā yadicchakaṃ niyyanti, evaṃ taṇhābaddhā sattāti daḷhabandhanaṭṭhena gaddūlaṃ viyāti gaddūlaṃ, taṇhāva gaddūlaṃ taṇhāgaddūlaṃ. Duppūraṇaṭṭhena taṇhāva samuddo taṇhāsamuddo. Abhijjhāyanaṭṭhena abhijjhā. Lubbhanti etena, sayaṃ vā lubbhati, lubbhanamattameva vā tanti lobho. Sampayuttakānaṃ akusalānaṃ patiṭṭhaṭṭhena mūlaṃ.

It obstructs wholesome qualities, thus it is an obstruction (āvaraṇa). By way of covering, it is a cover (chadana). It binds beings in the cycle of rebirth, thus it is a bond (bandhana). It afflicts the mind and makes it defiled, thus it is a defilement (upakkileso). Due to its tenacious nature, it lies latent again and again, thus it is a latent tendency (anusayo). It arises and besieges the mind, thus it is a besieging (pariyuṭṭhāna); the meaning is that by preventing wholesome states from arising, it seizes their turn. As in the phrase, 'Thieves besieged the road, scoundrels besieged the road,' the meaning is that they took hold of the road. Similarly here, besieging should be understood in the sense of seizing. By the nature of entwining, it is like a creeper (latā). As stated in the phrase, 'A creeper arises and persists,' this craving is called a creeper. It desires various objects, thus it is varied craving (vevicchaṃ). It is the root of the suffering of the cycle, thus it is the root of suffering (dukkhamūla). It is the source of that suffering, thus it is the origin of suffering (dukkhanidāna). That suffering arises from this, thus it is the arising of suffering (dukkhappabhavo). By the nature of binding, it is like a snare (pāso)—the snare of Māra, thus it is Māra’s snare. By the nature of being hard to swallow, it is like a fishhook (baḷisaṃ)—the fishhook of Māra, thus it is Māra’s fishhook. Overcome by craving, beings do not escape Māra’s domain; Māra exercises power over them, and in this sense, it is Māra’s domain (māravisayo).
