By the nature of flowing, craving itself is a river—the river of craving (taṇhānadī). By the nature of covering over, craving itself is a net—the net of craving (taṇhājālaṃ). Just as dogs bound by a leash are led wherever one wishes, so too are beings bound by craving—thus, by the nature of a strong bond, it is like a leash (gaddūlaṃ); craving itself is the leash—the leash of craving (taṇhāgaddūlaṃ). By the nature of being hard to fill, craving itself is an ocean—the ocean of craving (taṇhāsamuddo). By the nature of desiring intensely, it is covetousness (abhijjhā). Through it, they are greedy, or it itself is greedy, or it is merely greed itself—thus it is greed (lobho). It is the root in the sense of being the foundation for associated unwholesome states.

Visattikātīti visattikā iti. Kenaṭṭhenāti kena sabhāvena. Visatāti vitthaṭā rūpādīsu. Visālāti vipulā. Visaṭāti tebhūmakabyāpakavasena visaṭā. Purimavacanameva takārassa ṭakāraṃ katvā byañjanavibhāgaṃ katvā vuttaṃ. Visakkatīti parisappati sahati vā. Ratto hi rāgavatthunā pādena tāḷiyamānopi sahati. Osakkanaṃ vipphandanaṃ vā “visakkana”ntipi vadanti. “Kusalākusalānaṃ patī”ti keci vaṇṇayanti. Visaṃharatīti tathā tathā kāmesu ānisaṃsaṃ passantī vividhehi ākārehi nekkhammābhimukhappavattito cittaṃ [P 1.0043] saṃharati saṅkhipati, visaṃ vā dukkhaṃ, taṃ harati, vahatīti attho. Visaṃvādikāti aniccādiṃ niccādito gaṇhantī visaṃvādikā hoti. Dukkhanibbattakassa kammassa hetubhāvato visamūlā[M 0.0036], visaṃ vā dukkhadukkhādibhūtā vedanā mūlaṃ etissāti visamūlā. Dukkhasamudayattā visaṃ phalaṃ etissāti [V 0.0033] visaphalā. Yāya taṇhāya rūpādikassa dukkhasseva paribhogo hoti, na amatassāti sā “visaparibhogā”ti vuttā. Sabbattha niruttivasena padasiddhi veditabbā.

It is called 'visattikā' because it clings. In what sense? By what nature? 'Visatā' means spread out among forms and so on. 'Visālā' means vast. 'Visaṭā' means spread out, pervading the three realms. The previous statement is made by changing the letter 'ta' to 'ṭa' and distinguishing the consonants. 'Visakkatī' means it crawls or endures. For even when a lustful person is struck with the foot by an object of lust, he endures it. Some also say 'visakkana' means retreating or struggling. Some describe it as 'the master of wholesome and unwholesome states.' 'Visaṃharatī' means that, seeing benefits in sensual pleasures, it withdraws or contracts the mind in various ways from proceeding towards renunciation; or it carries poison (visa), that is, suffering, meaning it bears it. 'Visaṃvādikā' is so called because, by grasping the impermanent as permanent and so on, it is deceptive. It is 'visamūlā' because it is the cause of kamma that produces suffering, or because poison (visa)—that is, feeling which is the suffering of suffering—is its root. Because it is the origin of suffering, its fruit is poison (visa), thus it is 'visaphalā'. The craving by which one enjoys only the suffering related to form and so on, and not the deathless, is called 'visaparibhogā' (enjoying poison). The formation of these words should be understood everywhere by way of etymology.

Tassā visayaṃ dassetukāmo “visālā vā pana sā taṇhā rūpe”tiādimāha. Tattha visālā vā panāti mahantī eva taṇhāyanaṭṭhena taṇhā, rūpādayo pañca pañcakāmaguṇikarāgavasena vuttā. Kule gaṇetiādīni ekādasa padāni loluppādavasena vuttāni. Kāmadhātuttiko kammavaṭṭavasena vibhatto, kāmabhavattiko vipākavaṭṭavasena vibhatto, saññābhavattiko saññāvasena vibhatto, ekavokārabhavattiko khandhavasena vibhatto. Atītattiko kālavasena, diṭṭhacatukko ārammaṇavasena, apāyattiko okāsavasena, khandhattiko nissattanijjīvavasena vibhattoti ñātabbaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepena atthadīpanā vibhāvanā ca –

Wishing to show its range, he said, 'Furthermore, that craving is vast in regard to forms,' and so on. Here, 'visālā vā pana' means that craving is indeed great; it is craving in the sense of craving. The five—form and so on—are mentioned in terms of passion for the five strands of sensual pleasure. The eleven terms beginning with 'kule gaṇe' are explained in terms of greed. It should be known that the triad pertaining to the sense-sphere is analyzed in terms of the round of kamma; the triad pertaining to sense-sphere existence is analyzed in terms of the round of result; the triad pertaining to existence with perception is analyzed in terms of perception; the triad pertaining to single-constituent existence is analyzed in terms of aggregates; the triad pertaining to the past is analyzed in terms of time; the tetrad pertaining to the seen is analyzed in terms of objects; the triad pertaining to the woeful states is analyzed in terms of location; and the triad pertaining to the aggregates is analyzed in terms of being without a being and without life. Herein, this is the brief elucidation of meaning and explanation:

“Tattha katamā kāmadhātu? Heṭṭhato avīcinirayaṃ pariyantaṃ karitvā uparito paranimmitavasavattideve antokaritvā yaṃ etasmiṃ antare etthāvacarā ettha pariyāpannā khandhadhātuāyatanā rūpaṃ vedanā saññā saṅkhārā viññāṇaṃ, ayaṃ vuccati kāmadhātu” (dha. sa. 1287).

Here, what is the sense-sphere realm? Below, having the Avīci hell as its boundary, and above, including the Paranimmitavasavatti deities—whatever aggregates, elements, and sense-bases are within this range, belonging to this realm, included herein—namely, form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness—this is called the sense-sphere realm (Dhs. 1287).

“Tattha katamā rūpadhātu? Heṭṭhato brahmalokaṃ pariyantaṃ karitvā uparito akaniṭṭhe deve antokaritvā yaṃ etasmiṃ antare [P 1.0044] etthāvacarā ettha pariyāpannā samāpannassa vā upapannassa vā diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārissa vā cittacetasikā dhammā, ayaṃ vuccati rūpadhātu” (dha. sa. 1289).

Here, what is the form realm? Below, having the Brahma world as its boundary, and above, including the Akaniṭṭha gods—whatever consciousness and mental factors are within this range, belonging to this realm, included herein, of one who has attained jhāna, or one who has been reborn there, or one who dwells happily in this very life—this is called the form realm (Dhs. 1289).

“Tattha katamā arūpadhātu? Heṭṭhato ākāsānañcāyatanupage deve pariyantaṃ karitvā uparito nevasaññānāsaññāyatanupage deve antokaritvā yaṃ etasmiṃ antare etthāvacarā ettha pariyāpannā samāpannassa vā upapannassa vā diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārissa vā cittacetasikā dhammā, ayaṃ vuccati arūpadhātū”ti (dha. sa. 1291). Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “kāmadhātūti kāmabhavo, pañcakkhandhā labbhanti. Rūpadhātūti rūpabhavo, pañcakkhandhā labbhanti. Arūpadhātūti arūpabhavo, cattāro khandhā labbhantī”ti vuttaṃ.

Here, what is the formless realm? Below, having the gods based in the sphere of infinite space as its boundary, and above, including the gods based in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—whatever consciousness and mental factors are within this range, belonging to this realm, included herein, of one who has attained jhāna, or one who has been reborn there, or one who dwells happily in this very life—this is called the formless realm (Dhs. 1291). In the commentary, however, it is stated: 'The sense-sphere realm is sense-sphere existence, where the five aggregates are obtained. The form realm is form existence, where the five aggregates are obtained. The formless realm is formless existence, where the four aggregates are obtained.'

Atha [M 0.0037] vā kāmarāgasaṅkhātena kāmena yuttā dhātu kāmadhātu, kāmasaṅkhātā vā dhātu kāmadhātu. Kāmaṃ pahāya rūpena yuttā dhātu rūpadhātu, rūpasaṅkhātā vā dhātu rūpadhātu. Kāmañca rūpañca [V 0.0034] pahāya arūpena yuttā dhātu arūpadhātu, arūpasaṅkhātā vā dhātu arūpadhātu. Tā eva dhātuyo puna bhavapariyāyena vuttā. Bhavantīti hi bhavāti vuccanti. Saññāya yutto bhavo, saññāvataṃ vā bhavo, saññā vā ettha bhave atthīti saññābhavo. So kāmabhavo ca asaññābhavamutto rūpabhavo ca nevasaññānāsaññābhavamutto arūpabhavo ca hoti.

Alternatively, the realm connected with desire, defined as sensual desire, is the sense-sphere realm; or the realm defined as desire is the sense-sphere realm. The realm connected with form, having abandoned desire, is the form realm; or the realm defined as form is the form realm. The realm connected with the formless, having abandoned desire and form, is the formless realm; or the realm defined as formless is the formless realm. These same realms are also described in terms of becoming. For what comes to be is called becoming. Becoming connected with perception, or the becoming of those with perception, or where perception exists in becoming—this is becoming with perception. That is, it is sense-sphere becoming, and form becoming (which is) free from non-percipient becoming, and formless becoming (which is) free from neither-perception-nor-non-perception becoming.

Na saññābhavo asaññābhavo, so rūpabhavekadeso. Oḷārikattābhāvato nevasaññā, sukhumattena sabbhāvato nāsaññāti nevasaññānāsaññā, tāya yutto bhavo nevasaññānāsaññābhavo. Atha vā oḷārikāya saññāya abhāvā sukhumāya ca bhāvā nevasaññānāsaññā asmiṃ bhaveti nevasaññānāsaññābhavo, so arūpabhavekadeso. Ekena rūpakkhandhena vokiṇṇo bhavo, eko vā vokāro, assa bhavassāti ekavokārabhavo, so asaññābhavova. Catūhi arūpakkhandhehi [P 1.0045] vokiṇṇo bhavo, cattāro vā vokārā assa bhavassāti catuvokārabhavo, so arūpabhavo eva. Pañcahi khandhehi vokiṇṇo bhavo, pañca vā vokārā assa bhavassāti pañcavokārabhavo, so kāmabhavo ca rūpabhavekadeso ca hoti. Atītattiko heṭṭhā vuttanayova. Diṭṭhanti catusamuṭṭhānikaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ. Sutanti dvisamuṭṭhānikaṃ saddārammaṇaṃ. Mutanti phusitvā gahetabbāni catusamuṭṭhānikāni gandharasaphoṭṭhabbārammaṇāni. Viññātabbaṃ nāma manasā jānitabbaṃ dhammārammaṇaṃ. Tesu diṭṭhasutamutaviññātabbesu dhammesu. Visaṭā vitthatāti mahantā patthaṭā.

Perception-becoming is not non-percipient becoming; the latter is a part of form becoming. Because of the absence of grossness, it is 'not perception'; because of the subtlety of its existence, it is 'not non-perception'—thus, it is 'neither-perception-nor-non-perception'. The becoming associated with that is the becoming of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Alternatively, because of the absence of gross perception and the presence of subtle perception, it is 'neither-perception-nor-non-perception'; the becoming in which this exists is the becoming of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, which is a part of formless becoming. A becoming intermingled with one aggregate of form, or a becoming having one constituent, is called the one-constituent becoming; this is indeed the non-percipient becoming. A becoming intermingled with the four formless aggregates, or a becoming having four constituents, is called the four-constituent becoming; this is indeed the formless becoming. A becoming intermingled with the five aggregates, or a becoming having five constituents, is called the five-constituent becoming; this is the sense-sphere becoming and a part of form becoming. The triad pertaining to the past is just as stated previously. 'Seen' refers to a form-object arising from four causes. 'Heard' refers to a sound-object arising from two causes. 'Sensed' refers to the objects of smell, taste, and touch, which arise from four causes and are to be grasped through contact. 'Cognized' refers to a mind-object to be cognized by the mind. Among these phenomena—the seen, heard, sensed, and cognized—'visaṭā' and 'vitthatā' mean great and widespread.

Apāyaloketi vaḍḍhisaṅkhātassa ayassa abhāvena apāyo, tasmiṃ apāyaloke. Khandhaloketi rāsaṭṭhena rūpādayo pañcakkhandhā eva loko. Dhātuloketi suññataṭṭhena cakkhudhātuādayo aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo eva loko. Āyatanaloketi āyatanādīhi kāraṇehi dvādasāyatanāni eva loko. Sabbepi lujjanapalujjanaṭṭhena loko, vuttappakāre loke visaṭā vitthaṭāti visattikā. Satoti saratīti sato, puggalena sati vuttā.

The world of misery is called 'apāya' because it is devoid of 'āya' (gain), which is known as 'vaḍḍhi' (growth); in that world of misery. The world of aggregates refers to the five aggregates—form and so on—as the world, in the sense of being a heap. The world of elements refers to the eighteen elements—beginning with the eye element—as the world, in the sense of being void. The world of sense bases refers to the twelve sense bases as the world, for reasons such as being sources. All these are called the world because of their nature of crumbling and dissolving. In the world described in this way, attachment (`visattikā`) is that which is spread out (`visaṭā`) and extensive (`vitthaṭā`). 'Mindful' (`sato`) is so called because one remembers (`sarati`). Mindfulness is spoken of with reference to a person.

Tattha [M 0.0038] saraṇalakkhaṇā sati. Saranti tāya, sayaṃ vā sarati, saraṇamattameva vā esāti sati. Sā panesā apilāpanalakkhaṇā, asammosanarasā, ārakkhapaccupaṭṭhānā, visayābhimukhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā vā, thirasaññāpadaṭṭhānā, kāyādisatipaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānā vā. Ārammaṇe daḷhapatiṭṭhitattā pana esikā viya, cakkhudvārādīnaṃ rakkhaṇato dovāriko viya ca daṭṭhabbā.

Herein, mindfulness has the characteristic of recollection. By it, one recollects, or it recollects by itself, or it is simply recollection—this is mindfulness. Moreover, it has the characteristic of non-superficiality, the function of non-confusion, and its manifestation is as protection, or as confronting the object. Its proximate cause is firm perception, or its proximate cause is the foundations of mindfulness concerning the body and so on. Because it stands firmly on its object, it should be seen as like a pillar. And because it guards the doors of the eye and other senses, it should be seen as like a gatekeeper.

Tassā pavattiṭṭhānaṃ dassento “kāye kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ bhāvento sato”tiādinā nayena [V 0.0035] catubbidhaṃ satipaṭṭhānamāha. Tattha kāyeti rūpakāye. Rūpakāyo hi idha aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ kesādīnañca dhammānaṃ samūhaṭṭhena hatthikāyarathakāyādayo viya “kāyo”ti adhippeto. Yathā ca samūhaṭṭhena, evaṃ kucchitānaṃ āyaṭṭhena. Kucchitānañhi paramajegucchānaṃ [P 1.0046] so āyotipi kāyo. Āyoti uppattideso. Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho – āyanti tatoti āyo. Ke āyantīti? Kucchitā kesādayo. Iti kucchitānaṃ kesādīnaṃ āyoti kāyo.

To explain its basis of occurrence, he speaks of the fourfold establishment of mindfulness by the method beginning, 'developing the establishment of mindfulness in the contemplation of the body in the body, being mindful.' Herein, 'in the body' refers to the material body. For here, the material body is intended by the term 'body' in the sense of a collection of limbs and parts, such as hair and so on, just like an elephant's body, a chariot's body, and so on. And just as it is in the sense of a collection, so too is it in the sense of being a source of repulsive things. For it is a source (`āya`) of utterly disgusting things, thus it is a 'body' (`kāya`). 'Āya' means the place of origin. Herein, this is the word's meaning: they come (`āyanti`) to it, thus it is a source (`āyo`). What comes to it? Repulsive things like hair and so on. Thus, because it is a source (`āya`) of repulsive things (`kucchita`) like hair and so on, it is a 'body' (`kāya`).

Kāyānupassanāti kāyassa anupassanā, kāyaṃ vā anupassanā, “kāye”ti ca vatvāpi puna “kāyānupassanā”ti dutiyaṃ kāyaggahaṇaṃ asammissato vavatthānaghanavinibbhogādidassanatthaṃ katanti veditabbaṃ.

"Contemplation of the body" means contemplation of the body, or contemplating the body. It should be understood that even after saying "in the body," the second mention of "body" in "contemplation of the body" is made for the purpose of showing its unmixed delimitation, the breaking down of compactness, and so on.

Tena na kāye vedanānupassanā cittadhammānupassanā vā, atha kho kāyānupassanāyevāti kāyasaṅkhāte vatthusmiṃ kāyānupassanākārasseva dassanena asammissato vavatthānaṃ dassitaṃ hoti, tathā na kāye aṅgapaccaṅgavinimuttaekadhammānupassanā, nāpi kesalomādivinimuttaitthipurisānupassanā. Yopi cettha kesalomādiko bhūtupādāyasamūhasaṅkhāto kāyo, tatthāpi na bhūtupādāyavinimuttaekadhammānupassanā, atha kho rathasambhārānupassakassa viya aṅgapaccaṅgasamūhānupassanā, nagarāvayavānupassakassa viya kesalomādisamūhānupassanā, kadalikkhandhapattavaṭṭivinibhujanakassa viya rittamuṭṭhiviniveṭhakassa viya ca bhūtupādāyasamūhānupassanāyevāti samūhavaseneva kāyasaṅkhātassa vatthuno nānappakārato dassentena ghanavinibbhogo dassito hoti. Na hettha yathāvuttasamūhavinimutto kāyo vā itthī vā puriso [M 0.0039] vā añño vā koci dhammo dissati, yathāvuttadhammasamūhamatteyeva pana tathā tathā sattā micchābhinivesaṃ karonti. Tenāhu porāṇā –

By this it is shown that in the body one does not contemplate feeling, mind, or mental phenomena, but rather only the body. Thus, the unmixed delimitation is shown by seeing only the aspect of body-contemplation in the object defined as the body. Likewise, it is not the contemplation of a single phenomenon in the body detached from limbs and parts, nor the contemplation of a woman or man detached from hair, body hair, and so on. Even in this body, which is designated as a collection of primary elements and derived matter, it is not the contemplation of a single phenomenon detached from the primary elements and derived matter. Rather, it is the contemplation of the collection of limbs and parts, like one who observes the components of a chariot; it is the contemplation of the collection of hair, body hair, and so on, like one who observes the parts of a city; and it is the contemplation of the collection of primary elements and derived matter, like one who peels a banana trunk or unwraps an empty fist. Thus, by showing the object designated as the body in various ways as a collection, the breaking down of compactness is demonstrated. Here, no body, woman, man, or any other phenomenon is seen detached from the aforementioned collections. Yet, beings wrongly fixate in various ways on these mere collections of phenomena. Therefore, the ancients have said:

“Yaṃ passati na taṃ diṭṭhaṃ, yaṃ diṭṭhaṃ taṃ na passati;

Apassaṃ bajjhate mūḷho, bajjhamāno na muccatī”ti. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.373; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.106);

"What one sees is not the truly seen; what is truly seen, one does not see. Not seeing, the fool is bound; being bound, one is not freed." (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 2.373; Ma. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.106)

Ghanavinibbhogādidassanatthanti vuttaṃ. Ādisaddena cettha ayampi attho veditabbo. Ayañhi etasmiṃ kāye kāyānupassanāyeva[P 1.0047], na aññadhammānupassanā. Yathā anudakabhūtāyapi marīciyā udakānupassanā hoti, na evaṃ aniccadukkhānattāsubhabhūteyeva imasmiṃ kāye niccasukhattasubhabhāvānupassanā[V 0.0036], atha kho kāyānupassanā aniccadukkhānattāsubhākārasamūhānupassanāyevāti vuttaṃ hoti.

It was said, "for the purpose of showing... the breaking down of compactness, and so on." By the term "and so on," this meaning should also be understood: In this body, there is only contemplation of the body, not contemplation of other phenomena. Just as in a mirage, which is not water, there is contemplation of water, it is not the case that in this body, which is impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure, one contemplates permanence, pleasure, self, or beauty. Rather, it is said that the contemplation of the body is the contemplation of a collection of aspects: impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity.

Atha vā yvāyaṃ mahāsatipaṭṭhāne “idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu araññagato vā…pe… so satova assasatī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 2.374; ma. ni. 1.107) nayena assāsapassāsādicuṇṇikajātaaṭṭhikapariyosāno kāyo vutto, yo ca paṭisambhidāyaṃ satipaṭṭhānakathāyaṃ “idhekacco pathavīkāyaṃ aniccato anupassati. Āpokāyaṃ. Tejokāyaṃ. Vāyokāyaṃ. Kesakāyaṃ. Lomakāyaṃ. Chavikāyaṃ. Cammakāyaṃ. Maṃsakāyaṃ. Ruhirakāyaṃ. Nhārukāyaṃ. Aṭṭhikāyaṃ. Aṭṭhimiñjakāya”nti kāyo vutto, tassa sabbassa imasmiṃyeva kāye anupassanato kāye kāyānupassanāti evampi attho daṭṭhabbo.

Alternatively, there is the body described in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta by the method beginning, 'Here, O bhikkhus, a bhikkhu gone to the forest... he breathes in mindful,' and so on, ending with the bones reduced to powder. And there is the body described in the Paṭisambhidāmagga, in the discourse on the foundations of mindfulness: 'Here, a certain person contemplates the body of earth as impermanent, the body of water, the body of fire, the body of air, the body of head hairs, the body of body hairs, the body of outer skin, the body of inner skin, the body of flesh, the body of blood, the body of sinews, the body of bones, the body of bone marrow.' Because all of that is contemplated within this very body, this too is the meaning of 'contemplation of the body in the body' that should be understood.

Atha vā kāye “aha”nti vā “mama”nti vā evaṃ gahetabbassa yassa kassaci anupassanato tassa tasseva pana kesalomādikassa nānādhammasamūhassa anupassanato kāye kesādisamūhasaṅkhātakāyānupassanāti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Api ca “imasmiṃ kāye aniccato anupassati, no niccato”tiādinā (paṭi. ma. 3.35) anukkamena paṭisambhidāyaṃ āgatanayassa sabbasseva aniccalakkhaṇādino ākārasamūhasaṅkhātassa kāyassa anupassanatopi kāye kāyānupassanāti evampi attho daṭṭhabbo. Ayaṃ pana catusatipaṭṭhānasādhāraṇo attho.

Alternatively, since in the body nothing is contemplated that could be grasped as 'I' or 'mine', but rather the contemplation is of that very collection of various phenomena such as hair and so on, therefore the meaning should be understood as 'in the body, the contemplation of the body' which is designated as the collection of hair, etc. Moreover, according to the method given in the Paṭisambhidāmagga, beginning, 'In this body, one contemplates impermanence, not permanence,' the contemplation of the body as a collection of characteristics such as impermanence should also be understood as 'contemplation of the body in the body'. This, however, is a meaning common to the four foundations of mindfulness.

Satipaṭṭhānanti [M 0.0040] tayo satipaṭṭhānā satigocaropi, tidhā paṭipannesu sāvakesu satthuno paṭighānunayavītivattatāpi, satipi. “Catunnaṃ, bhikkhave, satipaṭṭhānānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca desissāmi, taṃ suṇātha sādhukaṃ manasi karotha…pe… ko ca, bhikkhave, kāyassa samudayo? Āhārasamudayā kāyasamudayo”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 5.408) hi satigocaro “satipaṭṭhāna”nti vuccati[P 1.0048]. Tathā “kāyo upaṭṭhānaṃ, no sati, sati upaṭṭhānañceva sati cā”tiādīsupi (paṭi. ma. 3.35). Tassattho – patiṭṭhāti asminti paṭṭhānaṃ. Kā patiṭṭhāti? Sati. Satiyā paṭṭhānaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ, padhānaṭṭhānanti vā paṭṭhānaṃ, satiyā paṭṭhānaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ, hatthiṭṭhānaassaṭṭhānādīni viya.

The term 'satipaṭṭhāna' has three meanings: the domain of mindfulness, the Teacher's transcendence of aversion and attraction towards disciples practicing in three ways, and mindfulness itself. In passages such as, "Monks, I will teach you the arising and passing away of the four foundations of mindfulness. Listen carefully and pay close attention... What, monks, is the arising of the body? With the arising of food, there is the arising of the body" (SN 5.408), the domain of mindfulness is called 'the foundation of mindfulness.' Similarly, in passages such as, "The body is the establishment, not mindfulness; mindfulness is both the establishment and mindfulness itself" (Paṭi Ma 3.35). Its meaning is this: that in which something is established (patiṭṭhāti asmin'ti) is an establishment (paṭṭhāna). What is established? Mindfulness. The establishment of mindfulness is the foundation of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). Alternatively, 'establishment' (paṭṭhāna) means a principal place; the principal place of mindfulness is the foundation of mindfulness, just like an elephant's stand, a horse's stand, and so on.

“Tayo satipaṭṭhānā yadariyo sevati, yadariyo sevamāno satthā gaṇamanusāsitumarahatī”ti (ma. ni. 3.304, 311) ettha tidhā paṭipannesu sāvakesu satthuno paṭighānunayavītivattatā “satipaṭṭhāna”nti vuttā. Tassattho – paṭṭhapetabbato paṭṭhānaṃ, pavattayitabbatoti [V 0.0037] attho. Kena paṭṭhapetabboti? Satiyā, satiyā paṭṭhānaṃ satipaṭṭhānanti. “Cattāro satipaṭṭhānā bhāvitā bahulīkatā satta bojjhaṅge paripūrentī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.147) pana satiyeva “satipaṭṭhāna”nti vuccati. Tassattho – patiṭṭhātīti paṭṭhānaṃ, upaṭṭhāti okkantitvā pakkhanditvā pavattatīti attho. Satiyeva paṭṭhānanti satipaṭṭhānaṃ. Atha vā saraṇaṭṭhena sati, upaṭṭhānaṭṭhena paṭṭhānaṃ. Iti sati ca sā paṭṭhānañcātipi satipaṭṭhānaṃ. Idamidha adhippetaṃ. Taṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ. Bhāventoti vaḍḍhento. Ettha ca yaṃ tidhā paṭipannesu sāvakesu satthuno paṭighānunayavītivattatā “satipaṭṭhāna”nti vuttaṃ, taṃ iminā suttena gahetabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

"There are three foundations of mindfulness that a noble one cultivates, cultivating which the Teacher is worthy to instruct the assembly." Here, in relation to disciples practicing in three ways, the Teacher’s transcendence of aversion and attraction is called 'satipaṭṭhāna.' Its meaning is: because it is to be established (paṭṭhapetabbato), it is an establishment (paṭṭhāna); that is, it is to be set in motion. By what is it to be established? By mindfulness. The establishment by mindfulness is satipaṭṭhāna. In passages such as, "When the four foundations of mindfulness are developed and cultivated, they fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment," mindfulness itself is called 'satipaṭṭhāna.' Its meaning is: it is established (patiṭṭhāti), hence it is an establishment (paṭṭhāna); that is, it becomes present, and having entered and penetrated, it proceeds. Mindfulness itself is the establishment, hence satipaṭṭhāna. Alternatively, 'sati' is in the sense of recollection, and 'paṭṭhāna' is in the sense of presence. Thus, it is mindfulness and it is an establishment, hence 'satipaṭṭhāna.' This is what is intended here. That is 'satipaṭṭhāna.' 'Bhāvento' means developing or increasing. Here, what was said regarding the Teacher's transcendence of aversion and attachment in relation to disciples practicing in three ways as 'satipaṭṭhāna' should be understood through this discourse. For this was spoken by the Blessed One—

“Tayo satipaṭṭhānā yadariyo sevati, yadariyo sevamāno satthā gaṇamanusāsitumarahatī”ti (ma. ni. 3.304, 311) iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ. Idha, bhikkhave, satthā sāvakānaṃ dhammaṃ deseti anukampako hitesī anukampaṃ upādāya “idaṃ vo hitāya idaṃ vo sukhāyā”ti. Tassa sāvakā [M 0.0041] na sussūsanti, na sotaṃ odahanti, na aññā cittaṃ upaṭṭhapenti, vokkamma ca satthu sāsanā vattanti. Tatra, bhikkhave, tathāgato na ceva anattamano hoti, na ca anattamanataṃ paṭisaṃvedeti[P 1.0049], anavassuto ca viharati sato sampajāno. Idaṃ, bhikkhave, paṭhamaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ. Yadariyo…pe… marahati.

"There are three foundations of mindfulness that a noble one cultivates, cultivating which the Teacher is worthy to instruct the assembly—this has been said. With reference to what was this said? Here, monks, the Teacher teaches the Dhamma to the disciples, compassionate and seeking their welfare, out of compassion: 'This is for your welfare, this is for your happiness.' But his disciples do not listen, do not lend an ear, do not apply their minds to understanding, and they turn away from the Teacher's instruction. In this case, monks, the Tathāgata is neither displeased nor does he experience displeasure; he dwells untainted, mindful and fully aware. This, monks, is the first foundation of mindfulness that a noble one cultivates... is worthy to instruct.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, satthā…pe… idaṃ vo sukhāyāti. Tassa ekacce sāvakā na sussūsanti…pe… vattanti. Ekacce sāvakā sussūsanti…pe… na ca vokkamma satthu sāsanā vattanti. Tatra, bhikkhave, tathāgato na ceva anattamano hoti, na ca anattamanataṃ paṭisaṃvedeti, na ca attamano hoti, na ca attamanataṃ paṭisaṃvedeti. Anattamanatā ca attamanatā ca tadubhayaṃ abhinivajjetvā upekkhako viharati sato sampajāno. Idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, dutiyaṃ…pe….

"Furthermore, monks, the Teacher... 'This is for your welfare, this is for your happiness.' Some of his disciples do not listen... and they turn away from the Teacher's instruction. Some disciples listen... and do not turn away from the Teacher's instruction. In this case, monks, the Tathāgata is neither displeased nor does he experience displeasure; he is neither pleased nor does he experience pleasure. Having avoided both displeasure and pleasure, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and fully aware. This, monks, is called the second...

“Puna caparaṃ…pe… idaṃ vo sukhāyāti. Tassa sāvakā sussūsanti…pe… vattanti. Tatra, bhikkhave, tathāgato attamano ceva hoti, attamanatañca paṭisaṃvedeti, anavassuto ca viharati sato sampajāno. Idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, tatiya”nti (dī. ni. 3.311).

"Furthermore... 'This is for your welfare, this is for your happiness.' His disciples listen... and do not turn away from the Teacher's instruction. In this case, monks, the Tathāgata is both pleased and experiences pleasure, yet he dwells untainted, mindful and fully aware. This, monks, is called the third."

Evaṃ paṭighānunayehi anavassutatā niccaṃ upaṭṭhitasatitāya tadubhayaṃ vītivattatā “satipaṭṭhāna”nti [V 0.0038] vuttā. Buddhānameva kira niccaṃ upaṭṭhitasatitā hoti, na paccekabuddhādīnanti.

Thus, the untaintedness by aversion and attachment, and the transcendence of both through constantly present mindfulness, are called 'satipaṭṭhāna.' It is said that only Buddhas have constantly present mindfulness, not Paccekabuddhas and others.

Vedanāsu vedanānupassanātiādīsu vedanādīnaṃ puna vacane payojanaṃ kāyānupassanāyaṃ vuttanayeneva yathāyogaṃ yojetvā veditabbaṃ. Ayampi sādhāraṇattho. Sukhādīsu anekappabhedāsu vedanāsu visuṃ visuṃ aniccādito ekekavedanānupassanā. Sarāgādike soḷasappabhede citte visuṃ visuṃ aniccādito ekekacittānupassanā. Kāyavedanācittāni ṭhapetvā sesatebhūmakadhammesu visuṃ visuṃ aniccādito ekekadhammānupassanā satipaṭṭhānasuttante vuttanayena nīvaraṇādidhammānupassanāti. Ettha ca kāyeti ekavacanaṃ, sarīrassa ekattā[M 0.0042]. Citteti ekavacanaṃ, cittassa sabhāvabhedābhāvato jātiggahaṇena katanti veditabbaṃ. Yathā [P 1.0050] ca vedanādayo anupassitabbā, tathānupassanto vedanāsu vedanānupassanā, citte cittānupassanā, dhammesu dhammānupassanāti veditabbā. Kathaṃ vedanā anupassitabbā? Sukhā tāva vedanā dukkhato, dukkhā vedanā sallato, adukkhamasukhā aniccato anupassitabbā. Yathāha –

In phrases such as 'contemplation of feelings in feelings,' the purpose of repeating 'feelings' and so on should be understood by applying it appropriately, in the manner explained for the contemplation of the body. This is also a general meaning. Among the various kinds of feelings, such as pleasant, etc., the contemplation of each individual feeling as impermanent, etc., is the contemplation of feelings. In the sixteenfold classification of the mind, such as with lust, etc., the contemplation of each individual mind as impermanent, etc., is the contemplation of the mind. Apart from body, feelings, and mind, the contemplation of each individual phenomenon among the remaining phenomena of the three planes as impermanent, etc., is the contemplation of phenomena, as taught in the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta, such as the contemplation of the hindrances, etc. Here, 'body' is in the singular because the physical frame is a single entity. 'Mind' is in the singular because, there being no difference in its intrinsic nature, it is taken as a class. And just as feelings, etc., are to be contemplated, so it should be understood that one who contemplates them thus performs the 'contemplation of feelings in feelings,' the 'contemplation of mind in mind,' and the 'contemplation of phenomena in phenomena.' How are feelings to be contemplated? Pleasant feeling should be contemplated as suffering, painful feeling as a dart, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling as impermanent. As it is said—

“Yo sukhaṃ dukkhato adda, dukkhamaddakkhi sallato;

Adukkhamasukhaṃ santaṃ, addakkhi naṃ aniccato;

Sa ve sammaddaso bhikkhu, parijānāti vedanā”ti. (saṃ. ni. 4.253);

"He who saw pleasure as suffering, And saw suffering as a dart, Who saw the peaceful, neither-painful-nor-pleasant, As impermanent— That monk indeed sees rightly, And fully understands feelings."

Sabbā eva cetā dukkhatopi anupassitabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ “yaṃ kiñci vedayitaṃ, taṃ dukkhasminti vadāmī”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.259). Sukhadukkhatopi ca anupassitabbā. Yathāha “sukhā vedanā ṭhitisukhā, vipariṇāmadukkhā. Dukkhā vedanā ṭhitidukkhā, vipariṇāmasukhā. Adukkhamasukhā vedanā ñāṇasukhā, aññāṇadukkhā”ti (ma. ni. 1.465). Api ca aniccādisattavipassanāvasenāpi anupassitabbā. Cittadhammesupi cittaṃ tāva ārammaṇādhipatisahajātabhūmikammavipākakiriyādinānattabhedānaṃ aniccādisattānupassanānaṃ sarāgādisoḷasabhedānañca vasena anupassitabbaṃ. Dhammā salakkhaṇasāmaññalakkhaṇānaṃ suññatadhammassa aniccādisattānupassanānaṃ santāsantādīnañca vasena anupassitabbā.

All these feelings must also be contemplated as suffering. For it is said: "Whatever is felt, that I declare to be included in suffering" (SN 4.259). They must also be contemplated from the perspective of pleasure and suffering. As it is said: "Pleasant feeling is pleasant in its persistence, painful in its change. Painful feeling is painful in its persistence, pleasant in its change. Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is pleasant with knowledge, painful without knowledge" (MN 1.465). Moreover, they must be contemplated by way of the seven kinds of insight-contemplation beginning with impermanence. Regarding mind and phenomena: mind should be contemplated by way of the diverse distinctions of object, dominance, co-nascence, ground, kamma, result, functional consciousness, etc., by way of the seven contemplations beginning with impermanence, and by way of the sixteen aspects beginning with 'with lust.' Phenomena should be contemplated by way of their individual and general characteristics, the phenomenon of emptiness, the seven contemplations beginning with impermanence, and by way of presence, absence, and so on.

Ime cattāro satipaṭṭhānā pubbabhāge nānācittesu labbhanti. Aññeneva hi cittena kāyaṃ pariggaṇhāti, aññena vedanaṃ, aññena cittaṃ, aññena dhamme pariggaṇhāti, lokuttaramaggakkhaṇe [V 0.0039] pana ekacitteyeva labbhantīti. Ādito hi kāyaṃ pariggaṇhitvā āgatassa vipassanāsampayuttā sati kāyānupassanā nāma, tāya satiyā samannāgato puggalo kāyānupassī nāma. Vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā ariyamaggaṃ pattassa [P 1.0051] maggakkhaṇe maggasampayuttā sati kāyānupassanā nāma, tāya satiyā samannāgato puggalo kāyānupassī nāma.

These four foundations of mindfulness are obtained in the preliminary stage with differing minds. For with one mind one comprehends the body, with another feeling, with another the mind, and with yet another phenomena. However, at the moment of the supramundane path, they are obtained in a single mind. Initially, for one who has comprehended the body and thereby arrived at insight, mindfulness associated with insight is called contemplation of the body. A person endowed with that mindfulness is called one who contemplates the body. Having exerted insight and attained the noble path, at the moment of the path, mindfulness associated with the path is called contemplation of the body. A person endowed with that mindfulness is called one who contemplates the body.

Vedanaṃ pariggaṇhitvā cittaṃ pariggaṇhitvā dhamme pariggaṇhitvā āgatassa vipassanāsampayuttā sati dhammānupassanā nāma, tāya satiyā samannāgato puggalo dhammānupassī nāma. Vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā ariyamaggaṃ pattassa [M 0.0043] maggakkhaṇe maggasampayuttā sati dhammānupassanā nāma, tāya satiyā samannāgato puggalo dhammānupassī nāma, evaṃ tāva desanā puggale tiṭṭhati, kāye pana “subha”nti vipallāsappahānā kāyapariggāhikā sati maggena samijjhatīti kāyānupassanā nāma. Vedanāya “sukha”nti vipallāsappahānā vedanāpariggāhikā sati maggena samijjhatīti vedanānupassanā nāma. Citte “nicca”nti vipallāsappahānā cittapariggāhikā sati maggena samijjhatīti cittānupassanā nāma. Dhammesu “attā”ti vipallāsappahānā dhammapariggāhikā sati maggena samijjhatīti dhammānupassanā nāma. Iti ekāva maggasampayuttā sati catukiccasādhakaṭṭhena cattāri nāmāni labhati. Tena vuttaṃ “lokuttaramaggakkhaṇe pana ekacitteyeva labbhantī”ti.

For one who has arrived after comprehending feeling, comprehending mind, and comprehending phenomena, the mindfulness conjoined with insight is called contemplation of phenomena. A person endowed with that mindfulness is called one who contemplates phenomena. Having exerted insight and attained the noble path, at the moment of the path, the mindfulness conjoined with the path is called contemplation of phenomena. A person endowed with that mindfulness is called one who contemplates phenomena. Thus far, the teaching stands with regard to the person. As for the body, the mindfulness that comprehends the body, which is accomplished through the path by abandoning the perversion of perceiving it as 'beautiful,' is called contemplation of the body. As for feeling, the mindfulness that comprehends feeling, which is accomplished through the path by abandoning the perversion of perceiving it as 'pleasant,' is called contemplation of feeling. As for the mind, the mindfulness that comprehends the mind, which is accomplished through the path by abandoning the perversion of perceiving it as 'permanent,' is called contemplation of the mind. As for phenomena, the mindfulness that comprehends phenomena, which is accomplished through the path by abandoning the perversion of perceiving them as 'self,' is called contemplation of phenomena. Thus, the single mindfulness conjoined with the path, by virtue of accomplishing four tasks, obtains four names. Therefore it is said: 'However, at the moment of the supramundane path, they are obtained in a single mind.'

Puna upakāravasena ca aparihīnavasena ca guṇavasena ca apare tayo catukkā vuttā. Tattha asatiparivajjanāyāti na sati asati, sati ettha natthīti vā asati, muṭṭhassatiyā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Parivajjanāyāti samantato vajjanena. Bhattanikkhittakākasadise hi muṭṭhasatipuggale parivajjanena upaṭṭhitasatipuggalasevanena ṭhānanisajjādīsu satisamuṭṭhāpanatthaṃ ninnapoṇapabbhāracittatāya ca sati uppajjati. Satikaraṇīyānaṃ dhammānanti satiyā kātabbānaṃ dhammānaṃ. Katattāti katabhāvena. Catunnaṃ maggānaṃ katattā, bhāvitattāti attho. Satiparibandhānaṃ dhammānaṃ hatattāti kāmacchandādīnaṃ nāsitabhāvena. Satinimittānaṃ dhammānaṃ asammuṭṭhattāti satiyā kāraṇānaṃ kāyādiārammaṇānaṃ anaṭṭhabhāvena.

Again, three other tetrads are stated based on the aspect of assistance, the aspect of non-decline, and the aspect of qualities. Herein, 'by avoiding non-mindfulness' means that mindfulness is not non-mindfulness, or 'there is no mindfulness here' is non-mindfulness; this is a designation for lapsed mindfulness. 'By avoiding' means by completely avoiding. For mindfulness arises by avoiding a person with lapsed mindfulness, who is like a crow that has dropped its food; by associating with a person of established mindfulness; and, for the purpose of arousing mindfulness in postures such as standing and sitting, through the mind being inclined, sloping, and precipitous. 'Of things to be done by mindfulness' means of the things to be done by means of mindfulness. 'By having been done' means by the state of having been done, that is, by having developed the four paths. 'By the destruction of things that obstruct mindfulness' means by the destroyed state of things such as sensual desire. 'By non-confusion regarding the objects of mindfulness' means by the non-perished state of the objects such as the body, which are the causes of mindfulness.

Satiyā [P 1.0052] samannāgatattāti satiyā sammā āgatattā aparihīnattā ca. Vasitattāti vasibhāvappattena. Pāguññatāyāti paguṇabhāvena. Apaccorohaṇatāyāti anivattanabhāvena apaccosakkanabhāvena.

'Endowed with mindfulness' means being properly endowed with mindfulness, and not having declined. 'Mastery' means having attained a state of mastery. 'Through proficiency' means through a state of being well-practiced. 'Non-recoiling' means a state of not turning back, a state of not retreating.

Sattattāti [V 0.0040] sabhāvena vijjamānattā. Santattāti nibbutasabhāvattā. Samitattāti kilesānaṃ vūpasamitabhāvattā. Santadhammasamannāgatattāti sappurisadhammehi aparihīnattā. Buddhānussatiādayo heṭṭhā vuttanayā eva. Saraṇakavasena sati, idaṃ satiyā sabhāvapadaṃ. Punappunaṃ saraṇato anussaraṇavasena [M 0.0044] anussati. Abhimukhaṃ gantvā viya saraṇato paṭisaraṇavasena paṭissati. Upasaggavasena vā vaḍḍhitamattameva. Saraṇākāro saraṇatā. Yasmā pana saraṇatāti tiṇṇaṃ saraṇānampi nāmaṃ, tasmā taṃ paṭisedhetuṃ puna satiggahaṇaṃ kataṃ. Satisaṅkhātā saraṇatāti ayañhettha attho. Sutapariyattassa dhāraṇabhāvato dhāraṇatā. Anupavisanasaṅkhātena ogāhanaṭṭhena apilāpanabhāvo apilāpanatā. Yathā hi udake lābukaṭāhādīni palavanti, na anupavisanti, na tathā ārammaṇe sati. Ārammaṇañhi esā anupavisati, tasmā “apilāpanatā”ti vuttā. Cirakatacirabhāsitānaṃ na sammussanabhāvato asammussanatā. Upaṭṭhānalakkhaṇe jotanalakkhaṇe ca indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti indriyaṃ, satisaṅkhātaṃ indriyaṃ satindriyaṃ. Pamāde na kampatīti satibalaṃ. Yāthāvasati niyyānasati kusalasatīti sammāsati. Bujjhanakassa aṅgoti bojjhaṅgo, pasaṭṭho sundaro vā bojjhaṅgo sambojjhaṅgo, satiyeva sambojjhaṅgo satisambojjhaṅgo.

‘Being truly existent’ means existing by its own nature. ‘Being peaceful’ means having a nature that is extinguished. ‘Being calmed’ means the state of having pacified the defilements. ‘Being endowed with peaceful qualities’ means not having declined from the qualities of a good person. The recollections of the Buddha and so forth are in the manner explained below. Mindfulness (sati) is in the sense of remembering (saraṇa); this is the intrinsic term for mindfulness. Recollection (anussati) is in the sense of repeated remembering, from remembering again and again. Reflection (paṭissati) is in the sense of re-remembering, from remembering as if having gone towards the object; or, it is merely an intensification by way of the prefix. The mode of remembering is the state of recollection (saraṇatā). Since ‘state of recollection’ is also a name for the three refuges, the term ‘mindfulness’ (sati) is taken up again to preclude that. The meaning here is: the state of recollection designated as mindfulness. Retention (dhāraṇatā) is from the state of retaining what has been learned from scripture. Non-floating (apilāpanatā) is the state of not floating, in the sense of plunging in, which is described as entering into. For just as gourds and bowls float on water and do not sink in, mindfulness is not like that in regard to its object. For it enters into the object; therefore it is called ‘non-floating.’ Non-forgetfulness (asammussanatā) is the state of not forgetting things done and said long ago. A faculty (indriya) is so-called because it exercises sovereignty in the characteristic of presence and in the characteristic of illumination; the faculty designated as mindfulness is the faculty of mindfulness. The power of mindfulness (satibala) is so-called because it does not waver in the face of heedlessness. Right mindfulness (sammāsati) is mindfulness as it is, mindfulness that leads out, and wholesome mindfulness. An awakening factor (bojjhaṅga) is a factor of one who awakens. A supreme awakening factor (sambojjhaṅga) is an excellent or beautiful awakening factor. Mindfulness itself is a supreme awakening factor: the mindfulness-awakening-factor.

Ekāyanamaggoti ekamaggo, ayaṃ maggo na dvedhāpathabhūtoti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Atha vā ekena ayitabboti ekāyano. Ekenāti gaṇasaṅgaṇikaṃ pahāya vūpakaṭṭhena pavivittacittena. Ayitabbo paṭipajjitabbo, ayanti vā etenāti ayano, saṃsārato nibbānaṃ gacchatīti attho[P 1.0053]. Ekassa ayano ekāyano. Ekassāti seṭṭhassa. Sabbasattānaṃ seṭṭhova bhagavā, tasmā “bhagavato”ti vuttaṃ hoti. Kiñcāpi hi tena aññepi ayanti, evaṃ santepi bhagavatova so ayano tena uppāditattā. Yathāha “so hi brāhmaṇa bhagavā anuppannassa maggassa uppādetā”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 1.215; paṭi. ma. 3.5; ma. ni. 3.79). Ayatīti vā ayano, gacchati pavattatīti attho. Ekasmiṃ ayano ekāyano. Imasmiṃyeva dhammavinaye pavattati, na aññatthāti vuttaṃ hoti. Yathāha “imasmiṃ kho, subhadda, dhammavinaye ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo upalabbhatī”ti (dī. ni. 2.214). Desanābhedoyeva heso, atthato pana ekova. Api ca ekaṃ ayatīti ekāyano. Pubbabhāge nānāmukhabhāvanānayena pavattopi aparabhāge ekaṃ nibbānameva gacchatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Yathāha brahmā sahampati –

'The single path' (ekāyanamaggo) means a single path; this path is not of the nature of a divided road, thus the meaning should be understood. Alternatively, it is called 'ekāyana' because it is to be traversed by one. 'By one' means abandoning groups and gatherings, with a secluded and detached mind. 'To be traversed' means to be practiced; or 'ayana' means 'going,' thus it signifies going from saṃsāra to Nibbāna. 'Ekāyana' is the path of the one. 'Of the one' means of the best. The Blessed One is indeed the best among all beings, therefore it is said 'of the Blessed One.' Even though others may also travel it, even so, it is the Blessed One's path because it was originated by him. As it is said: 'For, brahmin, the Blessed One is the originator of the path that had not arisen before,' etc. (saṃ. ni. 1.215; paṭi. ma. 3.5; ma. ni. 3.79). Or, 'ayana' means 'going,' signifying that it proceeds or operates. 'Ekāyana' means operating in one thing—it operates only in this Dhamma-Vinaya, not elsewhere. As it is said: 'In this Dhamma-Vinaya, Subhadda, the noble eightfold path is found' (dī. ni. 2.214). Though the teachings may vary, in meaning, it is one. Moreover, 'ekāyana' means going to one thing. Though in the early stages it may proceed through various approaches of development, in the final stage, it leads solely to Nibbāna. As Brahmā Sahampati said:

“Ekāyanaṃ [V 0.0041][M 0.0045] jātikhayantadassī, maggaṃ pajānāti hitānukampī;

Etena maggena tariṃsu pubbe, tarissanti ye ca taranti ogha”nti. (saṃ. ni. 5.384, 409);

Seeing the end of birth, compassionate for the welfare of others, He knows the single path. By this path they crossed over before, and will cross, and are crossing the flood.

Maggoti kenaṭṭhena maggo? Nibbānaṃ gamanaṭṭhena, nibbānatthikehi magganīyaṭṭhena ca. Upetoti āsannaṃ gato. Samupetoti tato āsannataraṃ gato. Ubhayenapi satiyā aparihīnoti attho. Upagatoti upagantvā ṭhito. Samupagatoti sampayutto hutvā ṭhito. “Upāgato samupāgato”tipi pāḷi. Ubhayenāpi satisamīpaṃ āgatoti attho. Upapannoti aviyogāpanno. Samupapannoti paripuṇṇo. Samannāgatoti avikalo vijjamāno. “Upeto samupetoti dvīhi padehi pavattaṃ kathitaṃ. Upagato samupagatoti dvīhi padehi paṭivedho. Upapanno samupapanno samannāgatoti tīhi padehi paṭilābho kathito”ti evameke vaṇṇayanti.

'Path' (maggo)—in what sense is it a path? In the sense of going to Nibbāna, and in the sense of being sought by those seeking Nibbāna. 'Upeta' means 'approached.' 'Samupeta' means 'having approached even closer.' By both, the meaning is 'not having declined in mindfulness.' 'Upagata' means 'having approached and stood.' 'Samupagata' means 'having stood, fully conjoined.' The Pāli text also reads 'upāgato samupāgato.' By both, the meaning is 'having come near to mindfulness.' 'Upapanna' means 'having attained without separation.' 'Samupapanna' means 'fully complete.' 'Samannāgata' means 'undiminished, existing.' 'Upeta samupeta' is spoken of with two terms as engagement. 'Upagata samupagata' is penetration, spoken of with two terms. 'Upapanna samupapanna samannāgata' is acquisition, spoken of with three terms'—thus some explain.

Loke vā sā visattikāti yā esā anekappakārena vuttā visattikā, sā khandhaloke eva, na aññatra khandhehi pavattatīti [P 1.0054] attho. Loke vā taṃ visattikanti khandhaloke eva pavattaṃ etaṃ visattikasaṅkhātaṃ taṇhaṃ. Tarati kāme parivajjento. Uttarati kilese pajahanto. Patarati tesaṃ patiṭṭhāhetuṃ chindanto. Samatikkamati saṃsāraṃ atikkamanto. Vītivattati paṭisandhiabhabbuppattikaṃ karonto. Atha vā tarati uttarati kāyānupassanena. Patarati vedanānupassanena. Samatikkamati cittānupassanena. Atha vā tarati sīlena. Uttarati samādhinā. Patarati vipassanāya. Samatikkamati maggena. Vītivattati phalenāti evamādinā yojetabbaṃ.

Or, in the world, that craving—this craving, described in various ways—exists only in the world of aggregates, not apart from the aggregates. This is the meaning. Or, in the world, that craving—this craving, designated as attachment, operates solely within the world of aggregates. He crosses over desires by avoiding them. He rises above defilements by abandoning them. He overcomes by cutting off their causes of establishment. He transcends by going beyond the cycle of existence. He goes beyond by making rebirth impossible. Alternatively, he crosses over and rises above through contemplation of the body. He overcomes through contemplation of feelings. He transcends through contemplation of the mind. Alternatively, he crosses over through virtue. He rises above through concentration. He overcomes through insight. He transcends through the path. He goes beyond through the fruit. Thus, it should be interpreted in this way.

4. Catutthagāthāya ayaṃ saṅkhepattho – yo ekaṃ sālikhettādikhettaṃ vā gharavatthādivatthuṃ vā kahāpaṇasaṅkhātaṃ hiraññaṃ vā goassādibhedaṃ gavāssaṃ vā antojātādidāse vā bhatakādikammakare vā itthisaññitā thiyo vā ñātibandhavādibandhū vā aññe vā manāpiyarūpādike puthukāme [M 0.0046] anugijjhatīti. Sālikkhettanti yattha sāliyo viruhanti. Vīhikkhettādīsupi eseva nayo. Vīhīti avasesavīhayo. Modayatīti muggo. Gharavatthunti gharapatiṭṭhāpanatthaṃ katākatabhūmibhāgo. Koṭṭhakavatthādīsupi eseva nayo. Koṭṭhakoti dvārakoṭṭhādi. Pureti gharassa purato. Pacchāti gharassa pacchato. Ettha ārāmenti cittaṃ tosentīti ārāmo, pupphenapi phalenapi chāyāyapi dakenapi ramantīti attho.

4. The summary of the fourth verse is as follows: One who is intensely attached to a certain rice field or similar field, or a house site or similar property, or gold in the form of kahāpaṇas, or cattle such as oxen and horses, or slaves born within the household or hired laborers, or women, or relatives such as kin and kinsmen, or any other various desirable sensual pleasures such as pleasant forms. 'Rice field' means where rice plants grow. The same principle applies to other fields such as paddy fields, etc. 'Vīhi' means other kinds of paddy. 'Modayati' means mung bean. 'House site' means a portion of land prepared for establishing a house. The same principle applies to other sites such as storehouses, etc. 'Koṭṭhaka' means a gatehouse, etc. 'Front' means in front of the house. 'Rear' means behind the house. Here, 'ārāma' (garden) is so called because it delights or pleases the mind; it is a place where one enjoys flowers, fruits, shade, or water—that is the meaning.

Pasukādayoti [V 0.0042] eḷakādayo. Antojātakoti antogharadāsiyā kucchimhi jāto. Dhanakkītakoti dhanena kīṇitvā parivattetvā gahito. Sāmaṃ vāti sayaṃ vā. Dāsabyanti dāsassa bhāvo dāsabyaṃ, taṃ dāsabyaṃ. Upetīti upagacchati. Akāmako vāti attano aruciyā vā karamarānīto.

'Pasukādayo' (animals, etc.) means goats, etc. 'Antojāto' means born in the womb of a female house slave. 'Dhanakkīto' means bought with money, acquired by exchange. 'Sāmaṃ vā' means by oneself or personally. 'Dāsabyaṃ' means the state of being a slave, that is, slavery. 'Upeti' means approaches. 'Akāmako vā' means unwillingly or brought against one's own will.

Te [P 1.0055] cattāro punapi dassetuṃ “āmāya dāsāpi bhavanti heke”ti āha. Āmāya dāsāti antojātadāsā. “Yattha dāso āmajāto ṭhito thullāni gacchatī”ti etthāpi eteva vuttā. Dhanena kītāti dhanadāsā. Sāmañca eketi sayaṃ dāsā. Bhayāpaṇunnāti akāmadāsā. Bhayena paṇunnā khipitā.

To further explain these four, he said, "Some become slaves even by birth." 'Slaves by birth' means slaves born in the household. 'Where a slave born in the household stands and commits serious offenses'—here too, the same are meant. 'Bought with wealth' means slaves bought with money. 'And one who submits himself' means a self-enslaved person. 'Driven by fear' means unwilling slaves. They are driven, impelled by fear.

Bhatakāti bhatiyā jīvanakā. Kasikammādikammaṃ karontīti kammakarā. Upajīvinoti sammantanādinā upagantvā nissayaṃ katvā jīvantīti upajīvino.

'Bhatakā' (servants) are those who live on wages. Those who do work like farming are called 'kammakarā' (laborers). 'Upajīvino' (dependents) are those who live relying on another after approaching them for support, such as through agreement.

Itthīti thiyati etissaṃ gabbhoti itthī. Pariggahoti sahāyī sassāmikā. Mātāpitibandhavāpi ñātibandhu. Sagotto gottabandhu. Ekācariyakule vā ekajātimantaṃ vā uggahitamanto mantabandhu. Dhanusippādisaddhiṃ uggahitako sippabandhu. “Mittabandhavātipi bandhū”ti katthaci potthake pāṭho dissati.

'Itthī' (woman) is so called because the womb (gabbha) rests in her. 'Pariggaha' means a companion; a wife belonging to a husband. Relatives such as mother and father are 'ñātibandhu' (kin-kinsmen). Those of the same clan are 'gottabandhu' (clan-kinsmen). Those who have learned mantras together in the same teacher's lineage or are of the same birth are 'mantabandhu' (mantra-kinsmen). Those who have acquired skills like archery together are 'sippabandhu' (skill-kinsmen). In some books, the reading 'mittabandhavātipi bandhū' (friends and kinsmen are also kinsmen) is also found.

Gijjhatīti kilesakāmena pattheti. Anugijjhatīti anu anu gijjhati punappunaṃ pattheti. Paligijjhatīti samantato pattheti. Palibajjhatīti visesena pattheti. “Oḷārikattena nimittaggāhavasena gijjhati, anugijjhati, anubyañjanaggāhavasena paligijjhati, palibajjhatī”ti evameke vaṇṇayanti.

'Gijjhati' means to crave with the desire that is a defilement. 'Anugijjhati' means to crave again and again, repeatedly. 'Paligijjhati' means to crave from all sides. 'Palibajjhati' means to crave especially. Some describe it thus: 'By grasping the sign due to its grossness, one craves (gijjhati) and repeatedly craves (anugijjhati); by grasping the minor details, one craves from all sides (paligijjhati) and especially craves (palibajjhati).'

5. Pañcamagāthāyaṃ [M 0.0047] ayaṃ saṅkhepattho – taṃ puggalaṃ abalakhyā kilesā balīyanti sahanti maddanti. Saddhābalādivirahena vā abalaṃ taṃ puggalaṃ abalā kilesā balīyanti, abalattā balīyantīti attho. Atha vā taṃ kāmagiddhaṃ kāmarattaṃ [P 1.0056] kāmapariyesantañca sīhādayo ca pākaṭaparissayā, kāyaduccaritādayo ca apākaṭaparissayā maddanti. Tato apākaṭaparissayehi abhibhūtaṃ taṃ puggalaṃ jātiādidukkhaṃ bhinnaṃ nāvaṃ udakaṃ viya anveti.

5. The summary meaning of the fifth verse is this: That person, being weak, is overpowered, crushed, and oppressed by the strong defilements. Or, because that person lacks the strength of faith and so on, the weak defilements become strong; being weak, they grow strong—this is the meaning. Alternatively, that person, greedy for sensual pleasures, infatuated with sensual pleasures, and seeking sensual pleasures, is crushed by evident dangers like lions and so on, and by hidden dangers like bodily misconduct and so on. Then, overwhelmed by hidden dangers, that person is followed by the suffering of birth and so on, just as water follows a broken boat.

Abalāti natthi etesaṃ balanti abalā, balavirahitā. Dubbalāti mandapayogābalena kattabbakiccavirahitā[V 0.0043]. Appabalāti appaṃ parittaṃ etesaṃ balanti appabalā, yujjhituṃ asamatthā. Appathāmakāti appo paritto thāmo etesaṃ vāyāmo ussāhoti appathāmakā. Hīnā nihīnā payogahīnena. Omakā thāmahīnena. Lāmakā paccayahīnena. Chatukkā ajjhāsayahīnena. Parittā pattihīnena. Sahantīti maddanti ghaṭṭanaṃ uppādenti. Parisahantīti sabbato maddanti. Abhibhavanti aparāparaṃ uppattivasena. Ajjhottharanti punappunaṃ uppattivasena. Pariyādiyanti sussosetvā ṭhānena. Maddanti kusaluppattinivāraṇena.

'Abalā' (powerless) means those without strength; they are devoid of power. 'Dubbalā' (weak) means those lacking the ability to perform duties because of weak effort. 'Appabalā' (of little strength) means those with little strength; they are incapable of fighting. 'Appathāmakā' (of little energy) means those with little energy, exertion, or enthusiasm. 'Hīnā' (inferior) means base or lacking in effort. 'Omakā' (lowly) means lacking in strength. 'Lāmakā' (wretched) means lacking in requisites. 'Chatukkā' (worthless) means lacking in resolve. 'Parittā' (meagre) means lacking in accomplishment. 'Sahanti' means they crush and generate friction. 'Parisahanti' means they crush from all sides. 'Abhibhavanti' means they overpower through successive arising. 'Ajjhottharanti' means they overwhelm through repeated arising. 'Pariyādiyanti' means they take complete possession, causing one to be dried up. 'Maddanti' means they crush by preventing the arising of wholesome states.

Saddhābalanti saddahanti etāya, sayaṃ vā saddahati, saddahanamattameva vā esāti saddhā. Sā saddahanalakkhaṇā, okappanalakkhaṇā vā, sampasādanarasā udakappasādakamaṇi viya. Pakkhandanarasā vā oghuttaraṇo viya. Akālusiyapaccupaṭṭhānā, adhimuttipaccupaṭṭhānā vā. Saddheyyavatthupadaṭṭhānā, sotāpattiyaṅgapadaṭṭhānā vā. Sā hatthavittabījāni viya daṭṭhabbā. Asaddhiye na kampatīti saddhābalaṃ. Vīriyabalanti vīrassa bhāvo vīriyaṃ, vīrānaṃ vā kammaṃ vīriyaṃ, vidhinā vā nayena upāyena īrayitabbaṃ pavattayitabbanti vīriyaṃ. Taṃ panetaṃ upatthambhanalakkhaṇañca paggahaṇalakkhaṇañca vīriyaṃ, sahajātānaṃ upatthambhanarasaṃ, asaṃsīdanabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, “saṃviggo yoniso padahatī”ti vacanato (a. ni. 4.113) saṃvegapadaṭṭhānaṃ, vīriyārambhavatthupadaṭṭhānaṃ vā. Sammā āraddhaṃ sabbasampattīnaṃ mūlanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kosajje na kampatīti vīriyabalaṃ. Satiyā [P 1.0057] lakkhaṇādīni vuttāneva.

The power of faith: Faith (saddhā) is that by which one believes, or one believes by oneself, or it is merely belief. It has the characteristic of believing, or the characteristic of confidence. Its function is clarifying, like a water-purifying gem. Or its function is leaping forward, like one crossing a flood. It manifests as purity or as resolution. Its proximate cause is a trustworthy object or the factors of stream-entry. It should be seen as being like hands, wealth, and seeds. It does not waver in faithlessness—this is the power of faith. The power of energy: Energy (vīriya) is the state of the energetic, or the action of the energetic, or that which should be aroused and maintained by method, rule, or means. This energy has the characteristic of supporting and the characteristic of exertion. Its function is to support associated states. It manifests as non-collapse. Its proximate cause is a sense of urgency, according to the saying, 'Being stirred up, he strives wisely' (AN 4.113), or its proximate cause is the basis for initiating energy. It should be seen that, being rightly initiated, it is the root of all accomplishments. It does not waver in laziness—this is the power of energy. The characteristics of mindfulness and so on have already been stated.

Muṭṭhassacce [M 0.0048] na kampatīti satibalaṃ. Sahajātāni sammā ādhīyati ṭhapetīti samādhi. So pāmokkhalakkhaṇo avikkhepalakkhaṇo vā, sahajātānaṃ dhammānaṃ ārammaṇe sampiṇḍanaraso nhāniyacuṇṇānaṃ udakaṃ viya, upasamapaccupaṭṭhāno, ñāṇapaccupaṭṭhāno vā. “Samāhito yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti passatī”ti hi vuttaṃ. Visesato sukhapadaṭṭhāno nivāte padīpaccīnaṃ ṭhiti viya cetaso ṭhitīti daṭṭhabbo. Uddhacce na kampatīti samādhibalaṃ. Pajānātīti paññā. Kiṃ pajānāti? “Idaṃ dukkha”ntiādinā (mahāva. 15) nayena ariyasaccāni. Sā yathāsabhāvapaṭivedhalakkhaṇā, akkhalitapaṭivedhalakkhaṇā vā kusalissāsakhittausupaṭivedho viya, visayobhāsanarasā padīpo viya, asammohapaccupaṭṭhānā araññagatasudesako viya. Avijjāya na kampatīti paññābalaṃ. Hiribalaṃ ottappabalanti ahirike na kampatīti hiribalaṃ. Anottappe na kampatīti ottappabalaṃ. Ayaṃ ubhayavasena atthavaṇṇanā hoti. Kāyaduccaritādīhi hirīyatīti hirī, lajjāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tehi eva ottappatīti ottappaṃ, pāpato ubbegassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

Not wavering in forgetfulness is the power of mindfulness. Concentration is that which rightly places and establishes co-arisen states. It has the characteristic of being pre-eminent, or the characteristic of non-distraction. Its function is to unify co-arisen states on an object, like water binding bath powder. Its manifestation is tranquility, or knowledge. For it is said, 'One who is concentrated understands and sees things as they truly are.' Specifically, it should be seen as the stability of the mind, having happiness as its proximate cause, like the steadiness of a lamp's flame in a windless place. Not wavering in restlessness is the power of concentration. 'One understands'—this is wisdom. What does one understand? The noble truths, according to the method beginning with 'This is suffering.' Wisdom has the characteristic of penetrating things according to their intrinsic nature, or the characteristic of unerring penetration, like the penetration of an arrow shot by a skilled archer. Its function is to illuminate its object, like a lamp. Its manifestation is non-confusion, like a good guide in a forest. Not wavering in ignorance is the power of wisdom. The power of moral shame and the power of moral dread are as follows: not wavering in shamelessness is the power of moral shame; not wavering in lack of moral dread is the power of moral dread. This is the explanation of the meaning concerning both. One is ashamed of bodily misconduct and so on—this is moral shame (hiri); this is a synonym for shame (lajjā). One is fearful of those same things—this is moral dread (ottappa); this is a synonym for dread of evil.

Tesaṃ [V 0.0044] nānākaraṇadīpanatthaṃ – “samuṭṭhānaṃ adhipati, lajjādilakkhaṇena cā”ti imaṃ mātikaṃ ṭhapetvā ayaṃ vitthārakathā vuttā – ajjhattasamuṭṭhānā hirī nāma, bahiddhāsamuṭṭhānaṃ ottappaṃ nāma. Attādhipati hirī nāma, lokādhipati ottappaṃ nāma. Lajjāsabhāvasaṇṭhitā hirī nāma, bhayasabhāvasaṇṭhitaṃ ottappaṃ nāma. Sappatissavalakkhaṇā hirī nāma, vajjabhīrukabhayadassāvilakkhaṇaṃ ottappaṃ nāma.

To explain their differences, this detailed exposition is given, having set forth the outline: 'By origin, by dominance, and by the characteristic of shame, etc.' Moral shame is of internal origin; moral dread is of external origin. Moral shame has oneself as its ruler; moral dread has the world as its ruler. Moral shame is established in the nature of shame; moral dread is established in the nature of fear. Moral shame has the characteristic of reverence; moral dread has the characteristic of seeing danger and fear in faults.

Tattha ajjhattasamuṭṭhānaṃ hiriṃ catūhi kāraṇehi samuṭṭhāpeti – jātiṃ paccavekkhitvā, vayaṃ paccavekkhitvā, sūrabhāvaṃ paccavekkhitvā, bāhusaccaṃ paccavekkhitvā. Kathaṃ? “Pāpakaraṇaṃ nāmetaṃ na jātisampannānaṃ kammaṃ, hīnajaccānaṃ kevaṭṭādīnaṃ idaṃ kammaṃ, mādisassa jātisampannassa [P 1.0058] idaṃ kammaṃ kātuṃ na yutta”nti evaṃ tāva jātiṃ paccavekkhitvā pāṇātipātādipāpaṃ akaronto hiriṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Tathā “pāpakaraṇaṃ nāmetaṃ daharehi kattabbaṃ kammaṃ, mādisassa vaye ṭhitassa idaṃ kammaṃ kātuṃ na yutta”nti evaṃ vayaṃ paccavekkhitvā pāṇātipātādipāpaṃ akaronto hiriṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Tathā “pāpakammaṃ nāmetaṃ dubbalajātikānaṃ kammaṃ, mādisassa sūrabhāvasampannassa [M 0.0049] idaṃ kammaṃ kātuṃ na yutta”nti evaṃ sūrabhāvaṃ paccavekkhitvā pāṇātipātādipāpaṃ akaronto hiriṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Tathā “pāpakammaṃ nāmetaṃ andhabālānaṃ kammaṃ, na paṇḍitānaṃ. Mādisassa paṇḍitassa bahussutassa idaṃ kammaṃ kātuṃ na yutta”nti evaṃ bāhusaccaṃ paccavekkhitvā pāṇātipātādipāpaṃ akaronto hiriṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Evaṃ ajjhattasamuṭṭhānaṃ hiriṃ catūhi kāraṇehi samuṭṭhāpeti. Samuṭṭhāpetvā ca pana attano citte hiriṃ pavesetvā pāpakammaṃ na karoti. Evaṃ ajjhattasamuṭṭhānā hirī nāma hoti. Kathaṃ bahiddhāsamuṭṭhānaṃ ottappaṃ nāma? “Sace tvaṃ pāpakammaṃ karissasi, catūsu parisāsu garahappatto bhavissasi –

Herein, one gives rise to internally-arisen moral shame for four reasons: by reflecting on birth, by reflecting on age, by reflecting on heroism, and by reflecting on great learning. How? 'This evil action is not a deed for the well-born; this is a deed for those of low birth, like fishermen. For someone like me, who is well-born, it is not fitting to do such a deed.' Thus, by reflecting on birth and refraining from evil actions like killing living beings, one gives rise to moral shame. Similarly, 'This evil action is a deed to be done by the young; for someone like me, established in age, it is not fitting to do such a deed.' Thus, by reflecting on age and refraining from evil actions like killing living beings, one gives rise to moral shame. Likewise, 'This evil action is a deed for the weak; for someone like me, endowed with heroism, it is not fitting to do such a deed.' Thus, by reflecting on heroism and refraining from evil actions like killing living beings, one gives rise to moral shame. Similarly, 'This evil action is a deed for the blind and foolish, not for the wise. For someone like me, who is wise and of great learning, it is not fitting to do such a deed.' Thus, by reflecting on great learning and refraining from evil actions like killing living beings, one gives rise to moral shame. In this way, one gives rise to internally-arisen moral shame for these four reasons. And having caused it to arise, and having made moral shame enter one's own mind, one does not do evil actions. This is called internally-arisen moral shame. How is there externally-arisen moral dread? 'If you commit an evil deed, you will incur blame in the four assemblies—

“Garahissanti taṃ viññū, asuciṃ nāgariko yathā;

Vajjito sīlavantehi, kathaṃ bhikkhu karissasī”ti. (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1 kāmāvacarakusala dhammuddesakathā) –

'The wise will blame you, as a townsman would something impure; avoided by the virtuous, what will you do, O monk?'

Evaṃ paccavekkhanto hi bahiddhāsamuṭṭhitena ottappena pāpakammaṃ na karoti, evaṃ bahiddhāsamuṭṭhānaṃ ottappaṃ nāma hoti.

Thus, by reflecting in this way, one does not commit an evil deed due to externally arisen moral dread; in this way, it comes to be called externally arisen moral dread.

Kathaṃ attādhipati hirī nāma? Idhekacco kulaputto attānaṃ adhipatiṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā “mādisassa [V 0.0045] saddhāpabbajitassa bahussutassa dhutaṅgadharassa na yuttaṃ pāpakammaṃ [P 1.0059] kātu”nti pāpaṃ na karoti. Evaṃ attādhipati hirī nāma hoti. Tenāha bhagavā “so attānaṃyeva adhipatiṃ karitvā akusalaṃ pajahati, kusalaṃ bhāveti, sāvajjaṃ pajahati, anavajjaṃ bhāveti, suddhaṃ attānaṃ pariharatī”ti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1 kāmāvacarakusala dhammuddesakathā; a. ni. 3.40).

How is moral shame said to have oneself as ruler? Here, a certain clansman, making himself the ruler and chief, thinks, 'It is not fitting for one like me—who has gone forth in faith, is of great learning, and an observer of the ascetic practices—to do an evil deed,' and thus he does not do evil. In this way, moral shame is said to have oneself as ruler. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Having made oneself the ruler, one abandons the unwholesome, cultivates the wholesome, abandons the blameworthy, cultivates the blameless, and maintains oneself in purity.'

Kathaṃ lokādhipati ottappaṃ nāma? Idhekacco kulaputto lokaṃ adhipatiṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā pāpakammaṃ na karoti. Yathāha –

How is moral dread said to have the world as its ruler? Here, a certain clansman makes the world his ruler and chief, and so does not do an evil deed. As it is said:

“Mahā kho panāyaṃ lokasannivāso, mahantasmiṃ kho pana lokasannivāse santi samaṇabrāhmaṇā iddhimanto dibbacakkhukā paracittaviduno, te dūratopi passanti, āsannāpi na dissanti, cetasāpi cittaṃ jānanti. Tepi maṃ evaṃ jāneyyuṃ ‘passatha bho imaṃ kulaputtaṃ saddhāya agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito samāno vokiṇṇo viharati pāpakehi akusalehi dhammehī’ti. Devatāpi kho santi iddhimantiniyo dibbacakkhukā paracittaviduniyo, tā dūratopi passanti, āsannāpi [M 0.0050] na dissanti, cetasāpi cittaṃ jānanti. Tāpi maṃ evaṃ jāneyyuṃ ‘passatha bho imaṃ kulaputtaṃ saddhāya agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito samāno vokiṇṇo viharati pāpakehi akusalehi dhammehī’ti. So iti paṭisañcikkhati ‘āraddhaṃ kho pana me vīriyaṃ bhavissati asallīnaṃ, upaṭṭhitā sati asammuṭṭhā, passaddho kāyo asāraddho, samāhitaṃ cittaṃ ekagga’nti. So lokaṃyeva adhipatiṃ karitvā akusalaṃ pajahati, kusalaṃ bhāveti, sāvajjaṃ pajahati, anavajjaṃ bhāveti, suddhaṃ attānaṃ pariharatī”ti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1 kāmāvacarakusala dhammuddesakathā; a. ni. 3.40).

'Indeed, this world assembly is vast. In such a vast world assembly, there are ascetics and brahmins endowed with psychic power, the divine eye, and knowledge of the minds of others. They see from afar, and though near, are not seen; they know mind with mind. They might know me thus: ‘See, sirs, this clansman, who went forth out of faith from the household life into homelessness, yet lives entangled in evil, unwholesome states.’ There are also deities endowed with psychic power, the divine eye, and knowledge of the minds of others. They see from afar, and though near, are not seen; they know mind with mind. They too might know me thus: ‘See, sirs, this clansman, who went forth out of faith from the household life into homelessness, yet lives entangled in evil, unwholesome states.’ He reflects thus: ‘My energy will be aroused and unflagging, my mindfulness established and unconfused, my body tranquil and unperturbed, my mind concentrated and one-pointed.’ Making the world his ruler, he abandons the unwholesome, cultivates the wholesome, abandons the blameworthy, cultivates the blameless, and maintains himself in purity.'

Evaṃ lokādhipati ottappaṃ nāma hoti. “Lajjāsabhāvasaṇṭhitā hirī, bhayasabhāvasaṇṭhitaṃ ottappa”nti ettha pana lajjāti lajjanākāro, tena sabhāvena saṇṭhitā hirī. Bhayanti apāyabhayaṃ, tena sabhāvena saṇṭhitaṃ ottappaṃ. Tadubhayampi pāpaparivajjane pākaṭaṃ hoti. Ekacco hi yathā nāma eko kulaputto uccārapassāvādīni karonto lajjitabbayuttakaṃ ekaṃ disvā lajjanākārappatto bhaveyya hīḷito, evameva ajjhattaṃ lajjīdhammaṃ okkamitvā pāpakammaṃ na karoti. Ekacco apāyabhayabhīto hutvā pāpakammaṃ na karoti.

Thus, moral dread is said to have the world as its ruler. Now, as for the statement, 'Moral shame is established in the nature of shame, moral dread is established in the nature of fear,' herein, 'shame' refers to the state of being ashamed; thus, moral shame is established by that nature. 'Fear' means fear of the lower realms; thus, moral dread is established by that nature. Both become evident in the avoidance of evil. For instance, just as a certain clansman, while defecating and urinating, might see someone before whom it is proper to be ashamed and become filled with the state of shame, feeling humiliated—in the same way, one who has internally undertaken the quality of shame does not commit evil deeds. Similarly, another, being terrified by the fear of the lower realms, does not commit evil deeds.

Tatridaṃ [V 0.0046] opammaṃ – yathā hi dvīsu ayoguḷesu eko sītalo bhaveyya gūthamakkhito, eko uṇho āditto. Tattha paṇḍito sītalaṃ gūthamakkhitattā jigucchanto na gaṇhāti, itaraṃ ḍāhabhayena. Tattha sītalassa [P 1.0060] gūthamakkhanajigucchāya agaṇhanaṃ viya ajjhattaṃ lajjīdhammaṃ okkamitvā pāpassa akaraṇaṃ, uṇhassa ḍāhabhayena agaṇhanaṃ viya apāyabhayena pāpassa akaraṇaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Here is a simile: Just as, of two iron balls, one might be cold and smeared with excrement, and the other hot and ablaze. There, a wise person, disgusted by the cold one smeared with excrement, would not pick it up, nor the other for fear of being burned. There, not picking up the cold one due to disgust for the excrement smeared on it is to be understood as like not doing evil, having internally taken up the quality of moral shame; not picking up the hot one for fear of being burned is to be understood as like not doing evil out of fear of the lower realms.

“Sappatissavalakkhaṇā hirī, vajjabhīrukabhayadassāvilakkhaṇaṃ ottappa”nti idampi dvayaṃ pāpaparivajjane eva pākaṭaṃ hoti. Ekacco hi jātimahattapaccavekkhaṇā satthumahattapaccavekkhaṇā dāyajjamahattapaccavekkhaṇā sabrahmacārimahattapaccavekkhaṇāti catūhi kāraṇehi sappatissavalakkhaṇaṃ hiriṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā pāpaṃ na karoti. Ekacco attānuvādabhayaṃ parānuvādabhayaṃ daṇḍabhayaṃ duggatibhayanti catūhākārehi vajjabhīrukabhāvadassāvilakkhaṇaṃ ottappaṃ [M 0.0051] samuṭṭhāpetvā pāpaṃ na karoti. Tattha jātimahattapaccavekkhaṇādīni ceva attānuvādabhayādīni ca vitthāretvā kathetabbāni. Evaṃ vuttaṃ sattavidhaṃ balaṃ yassa puggalassa natthi, te kilesā taṃ puggalaṃ sahanti…pe… pariyādiyanti maddantīti.

“Moral shame (hirī) has the characteristic of reverence, while moral dread (ottappa) has the characteristic of fearing wrongdoing and seeing danger in faults.” This pair, too, becomes manifest precisely in the avoidance of evil. For some, reflecting on the greatness of their birth, the greatness of the Teacher, the greatness of the heritage, and the greatness of their fellow practitioners—by these four reasons—having aroused moral shame characterized by reverence, they do not commit evil. Others, fearing self-reproach, fearing others’ reproach, fearing punishment, and fearing a bad rebirth—by these four aspects—having aroused moral dread characterized by the fear of wrongdoing and the perception of danger in faults, they do not commit evil. Here, the reflections on the greatness of birth and so forth, as well as the fears of self-reproach and so forth, should be expounded in detail. Thus, when a person lacks the sevenfold strength that has been stated, those defilements overwhelm that person… they overcome and crush them.

Dve parissayāti pākaṭāpākaṭavasena dve eva upaddavā, na ekaṃ, na tīṇi. Te vibhāgato dassetuṃ “katame pākaṭaparissayā”tiādimāha. Tattha kokāti kekā. Ayameva vā pāṭho. Corāti coriyakammehi yuttā. Māṇavāti sāhasikakammehi yuttā. Katakammāti sandhicchedādikatacorikakammā. Akatakammāti taṃ kammaṃ kātuṃ nikkhantā. Ettha assūti bhaveyyunti attho. Cakkhurogoti cakkhusmiṃ uppannarogo, rujatīti rogo. Cakkhurogotiādayo vatthuvasena veditabbā. Nibbattitapasādānañhi rogo nāma natthi. Kaṇṇarogoti bahikaṇṇarogo. Mukharogoti mukhe uppannarogo. Dantarogoti dantasūlaṃ. Kāsoti khayarogo. Sāsoti svāso uggārarogo. Pināsoti bahināsikāya rogo. Ḍāhoti abbhantare uppajjanako uṇho. Mucchāti [P 1.0061] sativissajjanakā. Pakkhandikāti lohitapakkhandikā atisāro. Sūlāti āmasūlā kucchivāto. Visūcikāti mahanto virecanako. Kilāsoti sabalo. Sosoti sukkhanako sosabyādhi. Apamāroti amanussaggāho veriyakkhābādho. Daddūti daddupīḷakā. Kaṇḍūti khuddakapīḷakā. Kacchūti mahākacchu. Rakhasāti nakhehi vilikhitaṭṭhāne rogo. “Nakhasā”tipi pāḷi. Vitacchikāti hatthatalapādatalesu hīraṃ hīraṃ katvā phālento uppajjanakarogo. Lohitapittanti soṇitapittaṃ, rattapittanti [V 0.0047] vuttaṃ hoti. Madhumehoti sarīrabbhantare ukkaṭṭharogo. Vuttañhetaṃ “api ca madhumeho ābādho ukkaṭṭho”ti (pāci. 15).

There are two kinds of dangers (parissaya)—manifest and unmanifest—thus, there are only two afflictions, not one, not three. To show them by way of division, he said, “What are the manifest dangers?” and so forth. Here, “kokā” means “kekā.” Or this is the reading. Thieves (corā) are those engaged in acts of theft. Ruffians (māṇavā) are those engaged in violent acts. Those who have committed crimes (katakammā) are those who have committed acts of theft such as housebreaking. Those who have not committed crimes (akatakammā) are those who have set out to commit such crimes. Here, “assūti” means “bhaveyyunti,” that is, “they may be.” Eye disease (cakkhurogo) is a disease arisen in the eye; “rogo” means “it pains.” Eye disease and so forth should be understood in terms of their respective bases. For there is no disease, as it were, for the sense-faculties that have arisen. Ear disease (kaṇṇarogo) is a disease of the outer ear. Mouth disease (mukharogo) is a disease arisen in the mouth. Tooth disease (dantarogo) is toothache. Cough (kāso) is consumption. Asthma (sāso) is labored breathing, a respiratory disease. Catarrh (pināso) is a disease of the outer nose. Burning (ḍāho) is internal heat that arises. Fainting (mucchā) is loss of consciousness. Dysentery (pakkhandikā) is bloody dysentery, diarrhea. Colic (sūlā) is indigestion-colic, abdominal wind. Cholera (visūcikā) is severe purging. Leprosy (kilāso) is a skin disease with spots. Wasting (soso) is a drying wasting disease. Epilepsy (apamāro) is possession by non-humans, an affliction by yakkhas. Ringworm (daddū) is a ringworm eruption. Itch (kaṇḍū) is small eruptions. Scabies (kacchū) is severe itching. Scratches (rakhasā) is a disease in places scratched by nails. “Nakhasā” is also a reading. Fissures (vitacchikā) is a disease that arises causing the palms of the hands and soles of the feet to crack and split. Blood-bile (lohitapitta) is blood-bile; it is also called “red-bile.” Diabetes (madhumeho) is a severe internal disease. For it has been said: “Moreover, diabetes is a severe affliction” (Pāc. 15).

Aṃsāti arisarogo. Pīḷakāti lohitapīḷakā. Bhagaṃ dālayatīti bhagandalā, vaccamaggaṃ phāletīti attho. Pittasamuṭṭhānāti pittena samuṭṭhānaṃ uppatti etesanti pittasamuṭṭhānā. Te kira dvattiṃsa honti. Semhasamuṭṭhānādīsupi eseva nayo. Sannipātikāti vātapittasemhānaṃ sannipātena [M 0.0052] ekībhāvena uppannā. Ābādhaṭṭhena ābādhā. Utupariṇāmajāti utupariṇāmena. Accuṇhāti sītena uppajjanakarogā. Visamaparihārajāti atiṭṭhānanisajjādinā visamaparihārena jātā. Opakkamikāti vadhabandhanādinā upakkamena jātā. Kammavipākajāti balavakammavipākasambhūtā. Sītaṃ uṇhaṃ…pe… samphassoti ime pākaṭā eva. Iti vāti evaṃ vā. Ime vuccantīti nigamento āha.

Hemorrhoids (aṃsā) is a disease of hemorrhoids. Boils (pīḷakā) are blood boils. Fistula (bhagandalā) means “it splits the anus,” meaning “it splits the anal passage.” Diseases arisen from bile (pittasamuṭṭhānā) are those whose origin or arising is by bile. There are said to be thirty-two of these. The same method applies to those arisen from phlegm and so forth. Diseases of combined origin (sannipātikā) are those arisen from the combination, the coming together, of wind, bile, and phlegm. They are afflictions (ābādhā) in the sense of being afflictions. Diseases born of seasonal change (utupariṇāmajā) are those arisen by seasonal change. Diseases caused by excessive heat (accuṇhā) are diseases arising from cold. Diseases born of improper conduct (visamaparihārajā) are those arisen from improper conduct such as improper standing and sitting. Diseases caused by external assault (opakkamikā) are those arisen from assault such as killing and binding. Diseases born of kamma-result (kammavipākajā) are those arisen from the result of strong kamma. Cold, heat… contact—these are manifest. Or thus, or in this way. Thus, he concluded, “These are called…”

Katame paṭicchannaparissayāti apākaṭā acchāditaupaddavā [P 1.0062] katameti pucchati. Tattha kāyaduccaritanti pāṇātipātaadinnādānamicchācāracetanā veditabbā. Vacīduccaritanti musāvādapisuṇavācāpharusavācāsamphappalāpacetanā veditabbā. Manoduccaritanti abhijjhābyāpādamicchādiṭṭhiyo veditabbā. Kāye pavattaṃ, kāyato vā pavattaṃ, duṭṭhu caritaṃ, kilesapūtikattā vā duṭṭhu caritanti kāyaduccaritaṃ. Vacīmanoduccaritesupi eseva nayo.

“What are the concealed dangers?” It asks, “What are the unmanifest, covered-up afflictions?” Here, bodily misconduct (kāyaduccarita) should be understood as the intention of destroying life, taking what is not given, and sexual misconduct. Verbal misconduct (vacīduccarita) should be understood as the intention of false speech, malicious speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter. Mental misconduct (manoduccarita) should be understood as covetousness, ill will, and wrong view. Bodily misconduct is that which occurs by way of the body, or proceeds from the body, or is ill-conduct, or is ill-conduct because of being putrid with defilements. The same method applies to verbal and mental misconduct.

Kāmīyantīti kāmā, pañca kāmaguṇā. Kāmesu chando kāmacchando. Kāmayatīti vā kāmo, kāmo eva chando, kāmacchando na kattukamyatāchando, na dhammacchando vā. Kāmataṇhāva evaṃnāmikā. Kusaladhamme nīvaratīti nīvaraṇaṃ, kāmacchando eva nīvaraṇaṃ kāmacchandanīvaraṇaṃ. Evaṃ sesesupi.
