Byāpajjati tena cittaṃ pūtibhāvaṃ upagacchati, byāpādayati vā vinayācārarūpasampattihitasukhādīnīti vā byāpādo. Thinanatā thinaṃ. Middhanatā middhaṃ, anussāhasaṃhananatā asattivighātatā cāti attho. Thinañca middhañca thinamiddhaṃ. Tattha thinaṃ anussāhanalakkhaṇaṃ, vīriyavinodanarasaṃ, saṃsīdanapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Middhaṃ akammaññatālakkhaṇaṃ, onahanarasaṃ, līnabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, pacalāyikāniddāpaccupaṭṭhānaṃ vā. Ubhayampi aratitandīvijambhitādīsu ayonisomanasikārapadaṭṭhānanti.

They are called “sensual pleasures” (kāmā) because they are desired; these are the five strands of sensual pleasure. Desire for sensual pleasures is sensual desire (kāmacchando). Or, it is `kāma` because it desires; `kāma` itself is desire. Sensual desire is not the desire to act, nor the desire for the Dhamma. Sensual craving (kāmataṇhā) is named thus. It obstructs wholesome qualities, thus it is a hindrance (nīvaraṇa); sensual desire itself is the hindrance, the hindrance of sensual desire. The same applies to the rest. By it the mind becomes corrupted, it goes to a state of putrefaction, or it destroys the attainment of discipline, good behavior, beauty, welfare, and happiness—thus it is ill will (byāpādo). Sluggishness (thina) is the state of being sluggish. Drowsiness (middha) is the state of being drowsy; the meaning is lack of initiative, lack of application, and obstruction of energy. Sluggishness and drowsiness together are sluggishness-and-drowsiness (thīnamiddha). Here, sluggishness has the characteristic of lack of initiative, the function of hindering energy, and manifests as sinking. Drowsiness has the characteristic of unworkability, the function of enveloping, and manifests as lethargy, or as nodding and sleep. Both have unwise attention to discontent, laziness, yawning, and so forth, as their proximate cause.

Uddhatassa bhāvo uddhaccaṃ. Taṃ avūpasamalakkhaṇaṃ vātābhighātacalajalaṃ viya, anavaṭṭhānarasaṃ vātābhighātacaladhajapaṭākaṃ viya, bhantattapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ pāsāṇābhighātasamuddhatabhasmaṃ viya[V 0.0048], cetaso avūpasamo ayonisomanasikārapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Cittavikkhepoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kucchitaṃ kataṃ kukataṃ, tassa [M 0.0053] bhāvo kukkuccaṃ. Taṃ pacchānutāpalakkhaṇaṃ, katākatānusocanarasaṃ, vippaṭisārapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, katākatapadaṭṭhānaṃ dāsabyaṃ viya daṭṭhabbaṃ[P 1.0063]. Uddhaccañca kukkuccañca uddhaccakukkuccaṃ. Vigatā cikicchāti vicikicchā, sabhāvaṃ vā vicinanto etāya kicchati kilamatīti vicikicchā, sā saṃsayalakkhaṇā, saṃsappanarasā, anicchayapaccupaṭṭhānā, anekaṃsaggāhapaccupaṭṭhānā vā, ayonisomanasikārapadaṭṭhānā. Paṭipattiantarāyakarāti daṭṭhabbā.

The state of being agitated is restlessness (uddhacca). It has the characteristic of non-subsiding, like water agitated by wind; its function is instability, like a flag flapping in the wind; its manifestation is bewilderment, like ashes scattered by striking a stone. It is the non-subsiding of the mind, and its proximate cause is unwise attention. It should be seen as mental distraction. What is badly done is “ill-done” (kukata); the state of that is remorse (kukkucca). It has the characteristic of subsequent regret; its function is regretting what was done and not done; its manifestation is repentance; its proximate cause is what was done and not done. It should be seen as like slavery. Restlessness and remorse together constitute restlessness-and-remorse (uddhaccakukkucca). The absence of remedy is doubt (vicikicchā). Or, one who investigates nature with it struggles and toils—thus it is called doubt. It has the characteristic of uncertainty; its function is to waver; its manifestation is indecision, or grasping at multiple alternatives; its proximate cause is unwise attention. It should be seen as obstructing the practice.

Rajjanalakkhaṇo rāgo. Dussanalakkhaṇo doso. Muyhanalakkhaṇo moho. Kujjhanalakkhaṇo kodho, caṇḍikkalakkhaṇo vā, āghātakaraṇaraso, dūsanapaccupaṭṭhāno. Upanandhanalakkhaṇo upanāho, veraappaṭinissajjanaraso, kodhānubandhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno. Vuttañcetaṃ “pubbakālaṃ kodho, aparakālaṃ upanāho”tiādi (vibha. 891).

Lust (rāgo) has the characteristic of staining. Hatred (doso) has the characteristic of corrupting. Delusion (moho) has the characteristic of bewilderment. Anger (kodho) has the characteristic of being enraged, or the characteristic of fierceness; its function is producing resentment; its manifestation is defilement. Hostility (upanāho) has the characteristic of binding; its function is not relinquishing enmity; its manifestation is the state of adherence to anger. And it has been said: “Anger is of an earlier time, hostility is of a later time,” and so forth (Vibh. 891).

Paraguṇamakkhanalakkhaṇo makkho. Tesaṃ vināsanaraso, tadacchādanapaccupaṭṭhāno. Yugaggāhalakkhaṇo paḷāso, paraguṇehi attano guṇānaṃ samīkaraṇaraso, paresaṃ guṇappamāṇena upaṭṭhānapaccupaṭṭhāno.

Denigration (makkho) has the characteristic of disparaging others' virtues; its function is to destroy them; its manifestation is to conceal them. Competitiveness (paḷāso) has the characteristic of grasping for preeminence; its function is to equate one's own virtues with those of others; its manifestation is to present oneself by the measure of others' virtues.

Parasampattikhīyanalakkhaṇā issā, tassa akkhamanalakkhaṇā vā, tattha anabhiratirasā, tato vimukhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā. Attano sampattinigūhanalakkhaṇaṃ macchariyaṃ, attano sampattiyā parehi sādhāraṇabhāvaṃ akkhamanarasaṃ, saṅkocanapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ.

Jealousy (issā) has the characteristic of resenting others' success, or the characteristic of being unable to bear it; its function is dissatisfaction in that regard; its manifestation is the state of turning away from it. Stinginess (macchariyaṃ) has the characteristic of concealing one's own success; its function is being unable to bear sharing one's success with others; its manifestation is contraction.

Katapāpapaṭicchādanalakkhaṇā māyā, tassa nigūhanarasā, tadāvaraṇapaccupaṭṭhānā. Attano avijjamānaguṇappakāsanalakkhaṇaṃ sāṭheyyaṃ, tesaṃ samudāharaṇarasaṃ, sarīrākārehipi tesaṃ vibhūtakaraṇapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ.

Deceit (māyā) has the characteristic of concealing evil deeds that have been done; its function is to hide them; its manifestation is to cover them up. Fraud (sāṭheyyaṃ) has the characteristic of proclaiming non-existent qualities in oneself; its function is to declare them; its manifestation is to make them apparent even through bodily gestures.

Cittassa uddhumātabhāvalakkhaṇo thambho, appatissavavuttiraso, amaddavapaccupaṭṭhāno. Karaṇuttariyalakkhaṇo sārambho, vipaccanīkatāraso, agāravapaccupaṭṭhāno.

Obstinacy (thambho) has the characteristic of mental rigidity; its function is conduct of non-compliance; its manifestation is inflexibility. Domineering (sārambho) has the characteristic of striving to outdo; its function is opposition; its manifestation is irreverence.

Uṇṇatilakkhaṇo māno, ahaṃkāraraso, uddhumātabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno. Abbhuṇṇatilakkhaṇo atimāno, ativiya ahaṃkāraraso, accuddhumātabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno.

Conceit (māno) has the characteristic of self-elevation; its function is self-importance; its manifestation is a state of being puffed-up. Excessive conceit (atimāno) has the characteristic of extreme self-elevation; its function is exceedingly intense self-importance; its manifestation is an excessively puffed-up state.

Mattabhāvalakkhaṇo [V 0.0049][M 0.0054] mado, madaggahaṇaraso, ummādapaccupaṭṭhāno[P 1.0064]. Pañcasu kāmaguṇesu cittassa vossaggalakkhaṇo pamādo, vossaggānuppadanaraso, sativippavāsapaccupaṭṭhānoti evaṃ imesaṃ dhammānaṃ lakkhaṇādīni veditabbāni. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana “tattha katamo kodho”tiādinā vibhaṅge (vibha. 891) vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

Intoxication (mado) has the characteristic of the state of being intoxicated; its function is grasping at intoxication; its manifestation is derangement. Heedlessness (pamādo) has the characteristic of the mind's abandonment to the five strands of sensual pleasure; its function is to persist in that abandonment; its manifestation is the absence of mindfulness. Thus, the characteristics and so forth of these states should be understood. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation, however, should be understood in the manner stated in the Vibhaṅga, beginning with “Herein, what is anger?” (Vibh. 891).

Visesato cettha āmisagiddho attanā alabhanto aññassa lābhino kujjhati, tassa sakiṃ uppanno kodho kodhoyeva. Taduttari upanāho. So evaṃ kuddho upanayhanto ca santepi aññassa lābhino guṇaṃ makkheti “ahampi tādiso”ti ca yugaggāhaṃ gaṇhāti. Ayamassa makkho ca palāso ca, so evaṃ makkhī palāsī tassa lābhasakkārādīsu “kiṃ imassa iminā”ti issati padussati, ayamassa issā. Sace panassa kāci sampatti hoti, tassā tena sādhāraṇabhāvaṃ na sahati, idamassa maccheraṃ. Lābhahetu kho pana attano santepi dose paṭicchādeti, ayamassa māyā. Asantepi guṇe pakāseti, idamassa sāṭheyyaṃ. So evaṃ paṭipanno sace pana yathādhippāyaṃ lābhaṃ labhati, tena thaddho hoti amuducitto “na idaṃ evaṃ kātabba”nti ovadituṃ asakkuṇeyyo, ayamassa thambho. Sace pana naṃ koci kiñci vadati “na idaṃ evaṃ kātabba”nti, tena sāraddhacitto hoti, bhākuṭikamukho “ko me tva”nti pasayhabhāṇī, ayamassa sārambho. Tato thambhena “ahameva seyyo”ti attānaṃ maññanto mānī hoti. Sārambhena “ke ime”ti pare atimaññanto atimānī, ayamassa māno ca atimāno ca. So tehi mānātimānehi jātimadādianekarūpaṃ madaṃ janeti, matto samāno kāmaguṇādibhedesu vatthūsu pamajjati, ayamassa mado ca pamādo cāti veditabbaṃ.

Here, specifically, one who is greedy for material gains and, not obtaining them for oneself, becomes angry at another who does obtain them—that anger, once arisen, is simply anger. Beyond that, it is hostility. Being thus angry and hostile, he even disparages the virtues of another who gains, and saying, 'I too am such a one,' he engages in stubborn competition. This is his denigration and competitiveness. Being so denigrating and competitive, he becomes jealous and hostile regarding the gains and honors of the other, thinking, 'Why should this be for him?' This is his jealousy. If, however, some success comes to him, he cannot bear to share it—this is his stinginess. Moreover, for the sake of gain, he conceals his own faults even when they exist—this is his deceit. He also boasts of non-existent virtues—this is his fraud. Behaving thus, if he obtains the gains he desires, he becomes stubborn and unyielding, unable to be advised, 'This should not be done thus'—this is his obstinacy. If someone says something to him, such as, 'This should not be done this way,' he becomes vehement, scowling and speaking forcibly, 'Who are you to me?'—this is his domineering. Then, due to obstinacy, thinking, 'I alone am better,' he becomes conceited. Due to domineering, thinking, 'Who are these people?,' he becomes excessively conceited, looking down on others—this is his conceit and excessive conceit. Through this conceit and excessive conceit, he generates various kinds of intoxication, such as intoxication with birth. Being intoxicated, he becomes heedless regarding things such as the strands of sensual pleasure—this is his intoxication and heedlessness. It should be understood thus.

Sabbe kilesāti sabbepi akusalā dhammā. Upatāpanaṭṭhena vibādhanaṭṭhena ca kilesā. Kilesapūtikattā duccaritā. Kilesadarathakaraṇaṭṭhena darathā. Antoḍāhādikaraṇaṭṭhena [P 1.0065] pariḷāhā. Sadā tāpanaṭṭhena santāpā. Akosallasambhūtaṭṭhena abhisaṅkharaṇaṭṭhena ca sabbe akusalābhisaṅkhārā.

‘All defilements’ means all unwholesome states. They are ‘defilements’ (kilesā) in the sense that they torment and oppress. They are ‘evil conduct’ (duccaritā) because they are putrid with defilements. They are ‘distresses’ (darathā) in the sense that they cause distress through defilement. They are ‘burnings’ (pariḷāhā) in the sense that they cause inner burning and the like. They are ‘anguishes’ (santāpā) in the sense that they constantly torment. They are all ‘unwholesome formations’ (akusalābhisaṅkhārā) in the sense that they are born from unskillfulness and in the sense that they are formative.

Kenaṭṭhenāti [M 0.0055] kena atthena. Abhibhavanāditividhaṃ atthaṃ dassetuṃ “parisahantīti parissayā”tiādimāha. Parisahantīti dukkhaṃ uppādenti abhibhavanti. Parihānāya saṃvattantīti kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pariccajanāya saṃvattanti. Tatrāsayāti tasmiṃ sarīre akusalā dhammā āsayanti nivasanti uppajjantīti attho. Te parissayāti kāyaduccaritādayo upaddavā. Kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ antarāyāyāti upari vattabbānaṃ sammāpaṭipadādito kosallasambhūtānaṃ dhammānaṃ antaradhānāya adassanatthāya saṃvattanti. Sammāpaṭipadāyāti sundarāya pasaṭṭhāya vā paṭipadāya, na [V 0.0050] micchāpaṭipadāya. Anulomapaṭipadāyāti aviruddhapaṭipadāya, na paṭilomapaṭipadāya. Apaccanīkapaṭipadāyāti na paccanīkapaṭipadāya, apaccatthikapaṭipadāya. Anvatthapaṭipadāyāti atthaanugatāya paṭipadāya, uparūpari vaḍḍhitāya paṭipadāya. Yathā attho, tathā paṭipajjitabbāya paṭipadāyāti vuttaṃ hoti. “Attatthapaṭipadāyā”tipi pāḷi, taṃ na sundaraṃ. Dhammānudhammapaṭipadāyāti dhammo nāma navalokuttaradhammo. Anudhammo nāma vipassanādi. Tassa dhammassa anurūpā dhammapaṭipadā dhammānudhammapaṭipadā, tassā dhammānudhammapaṭipadāya.

‘By what meaning?’ means by what import. To show the threefold meaning of overcoming and so on, it is said: 'Because they overcome, they are dangers.' 'They overcome' means they produce suffering and overpower. 'They lead to decline' means they lead to abandoning wholesome qualities. 'Therein they dwell' means unwholesome states abide, reside, and arise in that body—this is the meaning. 'These dangers' refers to bodily misconduct and other afflictions. 'For the obstruction of wholesome qualities' means they lead to the disappearance and non-seeing of skillful qualities born of proper practice and so on, which are to be spoken of later. 'Proper practice' means beautiful or excellent practice, not wrong practice. 'Harmonious practice' means non-conflicting practice, not contrary practice. 'Non-opposing practice' means not an opposing practice, a practice without hostility. 'Practice in accordance with the goal' means practice that follows the meaning, practice that grows progressively. It is said to be the practice that should be followed just as the meaning requires. There is also the reading 'practice for one's own benefit,' but this is not elegant. 'Practice in accordance with the Dhamma and its concomitants': 'Dhamma' refers to the nine supramundane states. 'Concomitant Dhamma' refers to insight and so on. The practice of Dhamma that is in conformity with that Dhamma is the 'practice in accordance with the Dhamma and its concomitants'; the text refers to this very practice.

Sīlesu paripūrikāritāyāti pātimokkhasīlesu pāripūriṃ katvā ṭhitatāya. Indriyesu guttadvāratāyāti “cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.213; a. ni. 3.16; ma. ni. 2.24; cūḷani. mettagūmāṇavapucchāniddesa 18) nayena vuttesu manacchaṭṭhesu indriyesu sugopitadvārabhāvassa. Bhojane mattaññutāyāti paṭiggahaṇādīsu pamāṇayuttatāya. Alaṃsāṭakādiṃ muñcitvā mitabhojanatāya.

‘By fulfilling the precepts’ means by being established in the complete fulfillment of the Pātimokkha precepts. ‘Guarding the sense doors’ means the state of having well-guarded doors in the six sense faculties, including the mind, as spoken of in the manner of “having seen a form with the eye,” and so on (Dī. Ni. 1.213; A. Ni. 3.16; Ma. Ni. 2.24; Cūḷani. Mettagūmāṇavapucchāniddesa 18). ‘Moderation in eating’ means having an appropriate measure in receiving alms-food and so on, and eating moderately, having renounced fine garments and the like.

Jāgariyānuyogassāti “divasaṃ caṅkamena nisajjāya āvaraṇīyehi dhammehī”ti (a. ni. 3.16; ma. ni. 2.24) evamādinā nayena pañca jāgaraṇadhamme anuyogassa. Satisampajaññassāti [P 1.0066] sabbakammaṭṭhānabhāvanānuyuttānaṃ sabbayogīnaṃ sabbadā upakārakassa satisampajaññassa.

‘Of the practice of wakefulness’ means of devotion to the five wakeful states, in the manner of “during the day, by walking and sitting, he purifies his mind from obstructive states,” and so on (A. Ni. 3.16; Ma. Ni. 2.24). ‘Of mindfulness and clear comprehension’ means of the mindfulness and clear comprehension that is always helpful to all yogis devoted to the cultivation of all meditation subjects.

Satipaṭṭhānānanti ārammaṇesu okkantitvā pakkanditvā upaṭṭhānato paṭṭhānaṃ, satiyeva paṭṭhānaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ. Kāyavedanācittadhammesu panassā asubhadukkhāniccānattākāragahaṇavasena [M 0.0056] subhasukhaniccattasaññāpahānakiccasādhanavasena ca pavattito catudhā pabhedo hoti, tesaṃ catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ.

Of the foundations of mindfulness: establishment (paṭṭhāna) is from attending (upaṭṭhāna), having entered and plunged into the objects. Mindfulness itself is the establishment; hence, 'satipaṭṭhāna.' Moreover, its fourfold division occurs in relation to body, feelings, mind, and phenomena, by way of grasping the characteristics of unattractiveness, suffering, impermanence, and non-self, and by way of accomplishing the task of abandoning the perceptions of attractiveness, pleasure, permanence, and self. Of these four foundations of mindfulness.

Catunnaṃ sammappadhānānanti padahanti etenāti padhānaṃ, sobhanaṃ padhānaṃ sammappadhānaṃ, sammā vā padahanti etenāti sammappadhānaṃ, sobhanaṃ vā taṃ kilesavirūpattavirahato, padhānañca hitasukhanipphādakaṭṭhena seṭṭhabhāvāvahanato, padhānabhāvakaraṇato cāti sammappadhānaṃ, vīriyassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Uppannuppannānaṃ anuppannuppannānañca catunnaṃ akusalakusalānaṃ pahānānuppattiuppādaṭṭhitikiccasādhanavasena pavattito panassa catudhā pabhedo hoti, tesaṃ catunnaṃ sammappadhānānaṃ.

Of the four right strivings: 'Padhāna' is that by which one strives. Excellent striving is right striving. Or, it is right striving because one strives rightly by means of it. It is excellent because it is free from the distortion of defilements; and it is pre-eminent striving because it produces benefit and happiness, brings about the highest state, and constitutes the very act of striving. This is a designation for energy. Moreover, its fourfold division arises from accomplishing the tasks of abandoning arisen unwholesome states, preventing the arising of unarisen unwholesome states, generating unarisen wholesome states, and maintaining wholesome states that have arisen. Of these four right strivings.

Catunnaṃ iddhipādānanti ettha chandavīriyacittavīmaṃsāsu ekeko ijjhatīti iddhi, samijjhati [V 0.0051] nipphajjatīti attho. Ijjhanti vā etāya sattā iddhā vuddhā ukkaṃsagatā hontīti iddhi. Paṭhamena atthena iddhiyeva pādoti iddhipādo, iddhikoṭṭhāsoti attho. Dutiyena atthena iddhiyā pādoti iddhipādo, pādoti patiṭṭhā adhigamupāyoti attho. Tena hi yasmā uparūparivisesasaṅkhātaṃ iddhiṃ pajjanti pāpuṇanti, tasmā pādoti vuccati. Tesaṃ catunnaṃ iddhipādānaṃ.

Of the four bases of spiritual power: Here, in regard to desire, energy, mind, and investigation, each one succeeds (ijjhati), thus it is called 'iddhi' (success, spiritual power); the meaning is that it accomplishes and is fulfilled. Or, by this, beings succeed, become powerful, developed, and exalted, thus it is called 'iddhi'. In the first sense, 'iddhi' itself is the base (pāda), thus 'iddhipāda'; the meaning is a constituent of spiritual power. In the second sense, it is the base of 'iddhi', thus 'iddhipāda'; 'pāda' means foundation, the means of attainment. Therefore, because they proceed to and attain the 'iddhi' characterized by ever higher distinctions, it is called a 'base'. Of these four bases of spiritual power.

Sattannaṃ bojjhaṅgānanti bodhiyā, bodhissa vā aṅgāti bojjhaṅgā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti, yā esā dhammasāmaggī yāya lokuttaramaggakkhaṇe uppajjamānāya līnuddhaccapatiṭṭhānāyūhanakāmasukhattakilamathānuyogaucchedasassatābhinivesādīnaṃ anekesaṃ upaddavānaṃ paṭipakkhabhūtāya satidhammavicayavīriyapītipassaddhisamādhiupekkhāsaṅkhātāya dhammasāmaggiyā ariyasāvako bujjhatīti katvā “bodhī”ti [P 1.0067] vuccati, bujjhatīti kilesasantānaniddāya uṭṭhahati, cattāri vā ariyasaccāni paṭivijjhati, nibbānameva vā sacchikaroti, tassā dhammasāmaggisaṅkhātāya bodhiyā aṅgātipi bojjhaṅgā jhānaṅgamaggaṅgādīni viya. Yo panesa yathāvuttappakārāya etāya dhammasāmaggiyā bujjhatīti katvā ariyasāvako “bodhī”ti vuccati, tassa bodhissa aṅgātipi bojjhaṅgā senaṅgarathaṅgādayo viya. Tenāhu [M 0.0057] aṭṭhakathācariyā “bujjhanakassa puggalassa aṅgāti bojjhaṅgā”ti. Tesaṃ sattannaṃ bojjhaṅgānaṃ.

Of the seven factors of enlightenment: They are 'bojjhaṅgā' because they are the limbs (aṅga) of enlightenment (bodhi) or of one who awakens (bodhi). This is said: That harmony of dhammas—namely, mindfulness, investigation of dhammas, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity—is called 'bodhi' (enlightenment) because by it, when it arises at the moment of the supramundane path, the noble disciple awakens. This harmony is the opposite of many afflictions, such as sloth and agitation, unestablished striving, indulgence in sensual pleasures and self-mortification, and adherence to annihilationism and eternalism. To 'awaken' means to rise from the slumber of the continuum of defilements, or to penetrate the four noble truths, or to realize Nibbāna itself. The limbs of that 'bodhi', which is the harmony of dhammas, are also 'bojjhaṅgā', like the factors of jhāna or the factors of the path. Furthermore, because the noble disciple who awakens by means of this harmony of dhammas as described is called 'bodhi' (one who awakens), the limbs of that awakened one are also 'bojjhaṅgā', like the limbs of an army or a chariot. Therefore, the commentary teachers said, 'The limbs of the person who awakens are the factors of enlightenment.' Of these seven factors of enlightenment.

Ariyassa aṭṭhaṅgikassa maggassāti ariyoti taṃtaṃmaggavajjhakilesehi ārakattā ariyabhāvakarattā ariyaphalapaṭilābhakarattā ca ariyo. Aṭṭhaṅgāni assāti aṭṭhaṅgiko. Svāyaṃ caturaṅgikā viya senā, pañcaṅgikaṃ viya ca tūriyaṃ aṅgamattameva hoti, aṅgavinimutto natthi. Nibbānaṃ maggati, kilese vā mārento gacchatīti maggo, tassa ariyassa aṭṭhaṅgikassa maggassa bhāvanānuyogassa. Imesaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānanti vuttappakārānaṃ lokiyalokuttarakusaladhammānaṃ. Antarāyāyāti lokuttarakusaladhammānaṃ antarāyāya antaradhānāya lokiyakusaladhammānaṃ pariccāgāya.

Of the noble eightfold path: It is 'ariya' (noble) because it is far from the defilements to be abandoned by each respective path, because it produces the state of nobility, and because it brings about the attainment of noble fruits. It is 'aṭṭhaṅgika' (eightfold) because it has eight components. Just as an army has four divisions or a musical ensemble has five parts, this is merely a collection of components; there is nothing apart from these components. It is the 'magga' (path) because it seeks Nibbāna, or because it goes along destroying defilements. Of the cultivation and application of this noble eightfold path. 'Of these wholesome states' refers to the mundane and supramundane wholesome phenomena described. 'For an obstacle' means for the obstruction and disappearance of supramundane wholesome states, and for the abandonment of mundane wholesome states.

Tesu lokuttarakusaladhammānaṃ uppajjituṃ appadānaṭṭhena parissayā nāma. Te hi uppajjitvā nirujjhamānā upaddavaṃ nāvahanti. Tattheteti tasmiṃ attabhāve ete. Pāpakāti lāmakā. Attabhāvasannissayāti attabhāvaṃ upanissāya ārammaṇaṃ katvā uppajjantīti attabhāvasannissayā. Daketi udake.

Among these, they are called 'parissayā' (dangers) in the sense of not allowing supramundane wholesome states to arise. For those states, having arisen and ceasing, do not bring affliction. 'Tatthete' (therein, these) means 'in that individual existence, these'. 'Pāpakā' (evil) means base. 'Attabhāvasannissayā' (dependent on individual existence) means they arise depending on individual existence, having made it an object. 'Dake' means in water.

Vuttaṃ [V 0.0052] hetanti kathitañhi etaṃ. Sāntevāsikoti antevāsikasaṅkhātena kilesena saha vasatīti sāntevāsiko. Sācariyakoti samudācaraṇasaṅkhātena kilesena saha vasatīti sācariyako.

'This has been said': for this has been spoken. 'Sāntevāsiko' (one with a pupil) means one who dwells with the defilement designated as a 'pupil'. 'Sācariyako' (one with a teacher) means one who dwells with the defilement designated as 'conduct'.

Cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvāti cakkhuviññāṇena rūpaṃ passitvā. Upari sotena saddaṃ sutvātiādīsupi eseva nayo. Uppajjantīti samudācaranti. Sarasaṅkappāti nānārammaṇe saṃsaraṇavasena uppannā parikappā. Saṃyojaniyāti ārammaṇabhāvaṃ [P 1.0068] upagantvā saṃyojanasambandhanena saṃyojanānaṃ hitā. Tyassāti te pāpakā assa puggalassa. Anto vasantīti abbhantare citte nivasanti. Anvāsavantīti kilesasantānaṃ anugantvā bhusaṃ savanti anubandhanti. Te nanti taṃ puggalaṃ ete akusalā dhammā. Samudācarantīti sammā ācaranti pavattantīti attho.

'Having seen a form with the eye': that is, having seen a form with eye-consciousness. The same principle applies to the subsequent phrases: 'having heard a sound with the ear,' and so on. 'They arise': that is, they occur. 'Sarasaṅkappā' (wandering thoughts): means conceptions that have arisen by way of wandering among various objects. 'Saṃyojaniyā' (conducive to fetters): means, having become objects, they are beneficial to the fetters through connection with the fetters. 'Tyassa' (for him): 'te' means those evil states, 'assa' means for that person. 'Dwelling within': that is, they dwell internally in the mind. 'Flowing along': that is, following the continuum of defilements, they flow strongly and pursue. 'Te naṃ' (they... him): 'te' refers to these unwholesome states, 'naṃ' to that person. 'They occur': the meaning is they proceed fully, they are set in motion.

Kilissanaṭṭhena malā. Sattuatthena amittā. Veriatthena sapattā. Hananaṭṭhena vadhakā. Paccāmittaṭṭhena paccatthikā. Atha vā malā sūriyassopakkilesavalāhakā viya. Amittā sūriyassa dhūmaṃ viya. Sapattā [M 0.0058] sūriyassa himaṃ viya. Vadhakā sūriyassa rajaṃ viya. Paccatthikā sūriyassa rāhu viya. “Malā suvaṇṇassa malaṃ viya cittappabhānāsakā. Amittā kāḷalohamalaṃ viya citte siniddhabhāvanāsakā, sapattā yuganaddhaṃ yujjhantā sapattā viya citte patiṭṭhitadhammadhaṃsakā. Vadhakā manussaghātakā viya dhammaghātakā. Paccatthikā raññā upagatassa vināso viya mokkhamaggassa paṭisedhakā”ti evameke vaṇṇayanti.

They are 'stains' in the sense of defiling. They are 'foes' in the sense of being hostile. They are 'adversaries' in the sense of being rivals. They are 'murderers' in the sense of killing. They are 'enemies' in the sense of being opponents. Or alternatively: stains are like the sun's defiling clouds. Foes are like smoke to the sun. Adversaries are like frost to the sun. Murderers are like dust to the sun. Enemies are like Rāhu to the sun. Some explain it thus: 'Stains destroy the radiance of the mind like tarnish on gold. Foes destroy the mind's smooth quality like rust on black iron. Adversaries destroy the established Dhamma in the mind like rivals fighting yoked together. Murderers are destroyers of the Dhamma like killers of humans. Enemies are obstructors of the path to liberation, like the ruin of one who is confronted by a hostile king.'

Anatthajananoti na atthaṃ anatthaṃ, taṃ anatthaṃ uppādetīti anatthajanano. Ko so? Lobho. Cittappakopanoti cittassa pakopano calano, kusalaṃ nivāretvā cittaṃ rundhatīti attho. Bhayamantarato jātanti abbhantare attano citteyeva jātaṃ, anatthajananādibhayahetu. Taṃ jano nāvabujjhatīti taṃ bhayaṃ bālamahājano avagantvā otaritvā na jānāti. Atthanti luddho puggalo lokiyalokuttaraatthaṃ na jānāti. Dhammanti tassa hetuṃ. Andhatamanti bahalandhakāraṃ. Yanti yasmā, yaṃ naraṃ vā. Sahateti abhibhavati.

'Anatthajanano' (generator of harm): 'anattha' is what is not beneficial; it generates that harm, thus it is a 'generator of harm'. What is that? Greed. 'Cittappakopano' (agitator of the mind): it is the agitation and stirring of the mind; the meaning is that it prevents the wholesome and obstructs the mind. 'Bhayamantarato jātaṃ' (fear born from within): born internally in one's own mind, a cause of fear such as the generation of harm. 'Taṃ jano nāvabujjhati' (that, a person does not understand): the foolish masses do not know that fear, not having understood or penetrated it. 'Atthaṃ' (the benefit): a greedy person does not know worldly and supramundane benefit. 'Dhammaṃ' (the Dhamma): its cause. 'Andhatamaṃ' (deepest darkness): dense darkness. 'Yaṃ' (which/whom): means 'because', or 'which person'. 'Sahate' (overwhelms): means it overpowers.

Ajjhattanti sakasantāne. Uppajjamānā uppajjantīti pubbantato uddhaṃ uppajjamānā ahitāya uppajjanti dukkhāya[P 1.0069]. Tadubhayena aphāsuvihārāya. Ahitāyāti cetasikadukkhatthāya. Dukkhāyāti kāyikadukkhatthāya. Aphāsuvihārāyāti tadubhayena na sukhavihāratthāya. Atha vā “uppajjamānā uppajjantīti bhavaṅgacalanato paṭṭhāya yāva voṭṭhabbanā, tāva [V 0.0053] uppajjamānā nāma. Voṭṭhabbanaṃ pana patvā anivattanabhāvena uppajjanti nāmā”ti evameke vaṇṇayanti.

'Ajjhattaṃ' (internally) means within one's own continuity. 'Uppajjamānā uppajjanti' (arising, they arise) means that, arising from the beginning onward, they arise for harm and for suffering. By both, for an uncomfortable dwelling. 'Ahitāya' (for harm) means for mental suffering. 'Dukkhāya' (for suffering) means for physical suffering. 'Aphāsuvihārāya' (for an uncomfortable dwelling) means, by means of both, for not dwelling in comfort. Alternatively, some explain it thus: 'uppajjamānā' (arising) refers to the process from the disturbance of the life-continuum up to the stage of determining. Having reached determining, however, they are called 'uppajjanti' (they arise) because of their non-returning nature.

Tacasāraṃva samphalanti attano phalena nāsitaṃ tacasārasaṅkhātaṃ veḷu viya. Aratīti kusalesu dhammesu ukkaṇṭhitatā. Ratīti pañcakāmaguṇe abhirati. Lomahaṃsoti kaṇṭakasadiso hutvā uddhaggalomo. Itonidānāti ayaṃ attabhāvo nidānaṃ paccayo etesanti itonidānā. Itojāti ito attabhāvato jātā. Ito samuṭṭhāya manovitakkāti yathā dīghasuttakena pāde baddhaṃ kākaṃ kumārakā tassa suttassa pariyantaṃ aṅguliṃ veṭhetvā ossajjanti, so dūraṃ [M 0.0059] gantvāpi puna tesaṃ pādamūleyeva patati, evameva ito attabhāvato samuṭṭhāya pāpavitakkā cittaṃ ossajjanti.

'They bear fruit like the tacasāra' means like the tacasāra bamboo, which is destroyed by its own fruit. Discontent (arati) is dissatisfaction with wholesome qualities. Contentment (rati) is delight in the five strands of sensual pleasure. 'Horripilation' (lomahaṃso) means the hair of the body standing on end like thorns. 'Originating from this' (itonidānā) means this very existence is the source, the condition for them. 'Born from this' (itojāti) means born from this existence. 'Arising from this, mental thoughts' (ito samuṭṭhāya manovitakkā) means this: just as boys tie a crow’s foot with a long string, wrap the end of the string around their finger, and release the crow, and though it flies far, it falls back at their feet—so too, evil thoughts, arising from this very existence, release the mind.

“Sāntevāsiko”tiādikaṃ paṭhamasuttaṃ kilesena sahavāsaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. “Tayome, bhikkhave, antarāmalā”tiādikaṃ dutiyaṃ kusaladhammamalīnakaraṇavasena atthānatthassa ajānanavasena ca. “Tayo kho, mahārāja, purisassa dhammā ajjhattaṃ uppajjamānā”tiādikaṃ tatiyaṃ attano nissayaghātanavasena. “Rāgo ca doso ca itonidānā”tiādikaṃ catutthaṃ kilesānaṃ patiṭṭhādassanavasena vuttanti ñātabbaṃ.

The first discourse, beginning with 'a fellow resident' (sāntevāsiko), is said with reference to living together with defilements. The second, beginning with 'monks, these three are inner stains' (tayome, bhikkhave, antarāmalā), is said by way of defiling wholesome qualities and by way of not knowing what is beneficial and not beneficial. The third, beginning with 'great king, these three things arise internally in a person' (tayo kho, mahārāja, purisassa dhammā ajjhattaṃ uppajjamānā), is said by way of destroying one’s own support. The fourth, beginning with 'lust and hatred originate from this' (rāgo ca doso ca itonidānā), should be understood as being said by way of showing the foundation of defilements.

Tato tato parissayatoti tamhā tamhā upaddavā. Taṃ puggalanti vuttappakārakilesasamaṅgīpuggalaṃ. Dukkhaṃ anvetīti dukkhaṃ anu eti mātu pacchato khīrapivako viya. Anugacchatīti samīpaṃ gacchati coraghātako viya vajjhappattassa[P 1.0070]. Anvāyikaṃ hotīti sampattaṃ hoti dhammaganthikāya paricchedo viya. Jātidukkhanti jātisaddassa tāva aneke atthā paveditā. Yathā –

'From this and that peril' (tato tato parissayato) means from this and that misfortune. 'That person' (taṃ puggalaṃ) means an individual endowed with the kind of defilements described. 'Suffering follows' (dukkhaṃ anveti) means suffering comes after, like a milk-drinking calf after its mother. 'It pursues' (anugacchati) means it draws near, like an executioner to one sentenced to punishment. 'It is attendant' (anvāyikaṃ hoti) means it arrives, like the conclusion of a legal text. 'The suffering of birth' (jātidukkhaṃ): for the word 'birth' (jāti), many meanings have been declared. For example:

Bhavo kulaṃ nikāyo ca, sīlaṃ paññatti lakkhaṇaṃ;

Pasūti sandhi cevāti, jātiatthā paveditā.

Existence, family, sect, and virtue, designation, characteristic; parturition, and also linking—these are declared as the meanings of 'birth'.

Tathā hissa “ekampi jātiṃ dvepi jātiyo”tiādīsu (pārā. 12; dī. ni. 1.31; ma. ni. 2.257) bhavo attho. “Akkhitto anupakkuṭṭho jātivādenā”ti (dī. ni. 1.303) ettha kulaṃ. “Atthi, visākhe, nigaṇṭhā nāma samaṇajātī”ti (a. ni. 3.71) ettha nikāyo. “Yatohaṃ, bhagini, ariyāya jātiyā jāto nābhijānāmī”ti [V 0.0054] (ma. ni. 2.351) ettha ariyasīlaṃ. “Tiriyā nāma tiṇajāti nābhiyā uggantvā nabhaṃ āhacca ṭhitā ahosī”ti (a. ni. 5.196) ettha paññatti. “Jāti dvīhi khandhehi saṅgahitā”ti (dhātu. 71) ettha saṅkhatalakkhaṇaṃ. “Sampatijāto, ānanda, bodhisatto”ti (dī. ni. 2.31; ma. ni. 3.207) ettha pasūti. “Bhavapaccayā jātī”ti (mahāva. 1; udā. 1; ma. ni. 1.403; saṃ. ni. 2.53; vibha. 225; kathā. 450) ca, “jātipi dukkhā”ti (mahāva. 14; vibha. 190; dī. ni. 2.387; ma. ni. 2.373; saṃ. ni. 5.1081; paṭi. ma. 2.30) ca ettha pariyāyato paṭisandhikkhaṇo, nippariyāyato pana tattha tattha nibbattamānānaṃ sattānaṃ ye ye khandhā pātubhavanti, tesaṃ tesaṃ paṭhamapātubhāvo jāti nāma.

For instance, in passages such as 'one birth, two births' (Pārā. 12; Dī. Ni. 1.31; Ma. Ni. 2.257), the meaning is existence. In 'unreviled, unrebuked by talk of birth' (Dī. Ni. 1.303), it means lineage. In 'There are, Visākha, ascetics of the Nigaṇṭha kind' (A. Ni. 3.71), it means sect. In 'Sister, since I was born with the noble birth, I do not recall...' (Ma. Ni. 2.351), it means noble virtue. In 'A kind of grass called Tiriyā, having sprouted from the navel, stood reaching the sky' (A. Ni. 5.196), it means designation. In 'Birth is included in two aggregates' (Dhātu. 71), it means the characteristic of the conditioned. In 'Just born, Ānanda, was the Bodhisatta' (Dī. Ni. 2.31; Ma. Ni. 3.207), it means parturition. And in 'With becoming as condition, birth' (Mahāva. 1; etc.) and 'birth is suffering' (Mahāva. 14; etc.), it means, conventionally, the moment of rebirth-linking; but ultimately, the first appearance of whichever aggregates manifest for beings reborn here or there—this is what is called birth.

Kasmā [M 0.0060] panesā jāti dukkhāti ce? Anekesaṃ dukkhānaṃ vatthubhāvato. Anekāni hi dukkhāni. Seyyathidaṃ – dukkhadukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadukkhaṃ saṅkhāradukkhaṃ paṭicchannadukkhaṃ appaṭicchannadukkhaṃ pariyāyadukkhaṃ nippariyāyadukkhanti.

And why is this birth suffering? Because it is the basis for many sufferings. For there are many kinds of suffering, namely: suffering as suffering, the suffering of change, the suffering of formations, concealed suffering, unconcealed suffering, indirect suffering, and direct suffering.

Tattha kāyikacetasikā dukkhavedanā sabhāvato ca nāmato ca dukkhattā “dukkhadukkha”nti vuccati.

Therein, bodily and mental painful feeling is called 'suffering as suffering' because it is suffering both in its intrinsic nature and in name.

Sukhavedanā vipariṇāmena dukkhuppattihetuto vipariṇāmadukkhaṃ. Upekkhāvedanā ceva avasesā ca tebhūmakā saṅkhārā udayabbayapīḷitattā saṅkhāradukkhaṃ.

Pleasant feeling is the suffering of change because, through its transformation, it is a cause for the arising of suffering. Neutral feeling and the remaining conditioned phenomena of the three planes are the suffering of formations because they are oppressed by arising and passing away.

Kaṇṇasūladantasūlarāgajapariḷāhadosamohajapariḷāhādi [P 1.0071] kāyikacetasiko ābādho pucchitvā jānitabbato upakkamassa ca apākaṭabhāvato paṭicchannadukkhaṃ. Apākaṭadukkhantipi vuccati.

Bodily and mental affliction—such as earaches, toothaches, the burning distress born of lust, hatred, and delusion, and so on—is called concealed suffering because it must be learned of by asking, and because its onset is not manifest. It is also called unmanifest suffering.

Dvattiṃsakammakāraṇādisamuṭṭhāno ābādho apucchitvāva jānitabbato upakkamassa ca pākaṭabhāvato appaṭicchannadukkhaṃ. Pākaṭadukkhantipi vuccati.

Affliction arising from the thirty-two kinds of torture and so on is called unconcealed suffering because it can be known without asking, and because its onset is manifest. It is also called manifest suffering.

Ṭhapetvā dukkhadukkhaṃ sesaṃ dukkhasaccavibhaṅge āgataṃ jātiādi sabbampi tassa tassa dukkhassa vatthubhāvato pariyāyadukkhaṃ. Dukkhadukkhaṃ pana nippariyāyadukkhanti vuccati.

Excluding suffering as suffering, all the rest that is mentioned in the Analysis of the Truth of Suffering—such as birth and so on—is called indirect suffering, because it is the basis for each respective suffering. Suffering as suffering, however, is called direct suffering.

Tatrāyaṃ [V 0.0055] jāti yaṃ taṃ bālapaṇḍitasuttādīsu (ma. ni. 3.246 ādayo) bhagavatāpi upamāvasena pakāsitaṃ āpāyikaṃ dukkhaṃ, yañca sugatiyampi manussaloke gabbhokkantimūlakādibhedaṃ dukkhaṃ uppajjati, tassa vatthubhāvato dukkhā.

In this context, this birth is suffering because it is the basis for that suffering of the plane of misery—which the Blessed One has also explained by way of similes in discourses such as the Bālapaṇḍita Sutta (MN 3.246, etc.)—and for the suffering that arises even in a happy destiny, in the human world, which is differentiated as being rooted in descent into the womb and so on.

Tatridaṃ gabbhokkantimūlakādibhedaṃ dukkhaṃ – ayañhi satto mātukucchimhi nibbattamāno na uppalapadumapuṇḍarikādīsu nibbattati, atha kho heṭṭhā āmāsayassa upari pakkāsayassa udarapaṭalapiṭṭhikaṇṭakānaṃ vemajjhe paramasambādhe tibbandhakāre nānākuṇapagandhaparibhāvite asuciparamaduggandhapavanavicarite adhimattajegucche kucchippadese pūtimacchapūtikummāsacandanikādīsu kimi viya nibbattati. So tattha nibbatto dasa māse mātukucchisambhavena usmanā puṭapākaṃ viya paccamāno piṭṭhapiṇḍi viya sediyamāno samiñjanapasāraṇādivirahito [M 0.0061] adhimattaṃ dukkhaṃ paccanubhotīti, idaṃ tāva gabbhokkantimūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ.

Herein, the suffering differentiated as being rooted in descent into the womb is as follows: This being, being reborn in its mother’s womb, is not reborn among blue, red, or white lotuses. Rather, it is reborn in an extremely confined, pitch-dark space between the stomach below and the intestines above, amidst the abdominal lining and the spine; a place pervaded by the stench of various corpses, where an impure and extremely foul-smelling wind circulates, an utterly loathsome region of the belly, like a worm in rotting fish, spoiled gruel, or a cesspool. Having been reborn there, for ten months it is cooked by the heat of the womb as if in a sealed vessel, steamed like a lump of dough, and, deprived of bending and stretching, it experiences extreme suffering. This, in the first place, is the suffering rooted in descent into the womb.

Yaṃ pana so mātu sahasā upakkhalanagamananisīdanavuṭṭhānaparivattanādīsu surādhuttahatthagato eḷako viya ahituṇḍikahatthagato sappapotako viya ca ākaḍḍhanaparikaḍḍhanaodhunanaddhunanādinā upakkamena adhimattaṃ dukkhaṃ anubhavati, yañca mātu sītudakapānakāle sītanarakupapanno viya uṇhayāgubhattādiajjhoharaṇakāle aṅgāravuṭṭhisamparikiṇṇo viya loṇambilādiajjhoharaṇakāle khārāpaṭicchakādikammakāraṇapatto viya tibbaṃ dukkhaṃ anubhoti, idaṃ gabbhapariharaṇamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ.

Furthermore, when the mother suddenly stumbles, walks, sits, stands, or turns, the being suffers intensely, like a lamb seized by a drunkard’s hand or a young snake caught by a snake charmer, being dragged, pulled, shaken, and pressed down. And when the mother drinks cold water, he feels as if plunged into a freezing hell; when she consumes hot gruel and rice, it is like being showered with burning coals; when she eats salty or sour food, it is like being subjected to the torment of caustic liquids. This is the suffering rooted in being carried in the womb.

Yaṃ [P 1.0072] panassa mūḷhagabbhāya mātuyā mittāmaccasuhajjādīhipi adassanārahe dukkhuppattiṭṭhāne chedanaphālanādīhi dukkhaṃ uppajjati, idaṃ gabbhavipattimūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ.

Moreover, when the mother with an obstructed pregnancy undergoes cutting, splitting, or other painful procedures in places unfit to be seen even by friends, companions, and relatives, suffering arises for the being; this is suffering rooted in the misfortune of the fetus.

Yaṃ vijāyamānāya mātuyā kammajehi vātehi parivattetvā narakapapātaṃ viya atibhayānakaṃ yonimaggaṃ paṭipātiyamānassa paramasambādhena ca yonimukhena tāḷacchiggaḷena viya mahānāgassa nikaḍḍhiyamānassa narakasattassa viya ca saṅghātapabbatehi vicuṇṇiyamānassa dukkhaṃ uppajjati, idaṃ vijāyanamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ.

When the mother is giving birth, the being is turned by karma-born winds and forced through the extremely terrifying birth canal, like falling into a hellish abyss. It is as if a great elephant were being dragged through a keyhole, or a hell-being crushed between the clashing mountains—such suffering arises. This is the suffering rooted in the process of birth.

Yaṃ pana jātassa taruṇavaṇasadisasukhumālasarīrassa hatthaggahaṇanhāpanadhovanacoḷaparimajjanādikāle sūcimukhakhuradhārāhi vijjhanaphālanasadisaṃ dukkhaṃ uppajjati, idaṃ mātukucchito bahinikkhamanamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ.

And when, for the newborn whose body is as delicate as a fresh wound, suffering arises at the time of being handled, bathed, washed, and wiped with a cloth, a suffering like being pierced and slashed by needle points and razor edges, this is suffering rooted in emerging from the mother’s womb.

Yaṃ [V 0.0056] pana tato paraṃ pavattiyaṃ attanāva attānaṃ vadhentassa acelakavatādivasena ātāpanaparitāpanānuyogamanuyuttassa kodhavasena abhuñjantassa ubbandhantassa ca dukkhaṃ hoti, idaṃ attūpakkamamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ.

And whatever suffering arises thereafter in the course of life for one who afflicts himself—such as by engaging in the practice of naked asceticism, self-mortification, and extreme austerities, or by refusing to eat out of anger, or by hanging himself—this is suffering rooted in self-inflicted action.

Yaṃ pana parato vadhabandhanādīni anubhavantassa dukkhaṃ uppajjati, idaṃ parūpakkamamūlakaṃ dukkhanti.

And whatever suffering arises in one experiencing from others killing, imprisonment, and the like, this is suffering rooted in actions inflicted by others.

Iti imassa sabbassāpi dukkhassa ayaṃ jāti vatthumeva hoti, idaṃ jātidukkhaṃ anveti.

Thus, birth is the very basis for all this suffering. This is the suffering of birth.

Jarādukkhanti [M 0.0062] duvidhā jarā – saṅkhatalakkhaṇañca khaṇḍiccādisammato santatiyaṃ ekabhavapariyāpanno khandhapurāṇabhāvo ca, sā idha adhippetā. Sā panesā dukkhā saṅkhāradukkhabhāvato ceva dukkhavatthuto ca. Yaṃ hidaṃ aṅgapaccaṅgasithilabhāvato indriyavikāravirūpatā yobbanavināsabalūpaghātasatimativippavāsaparaparibhavādianekapaccayaṃ kāyikacetasikaṃ dukkhamuppajjati, jarā tassa vatthu. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

The suffering of aging: Aging is of two kinds: the characteristic of the conditioned, and the aging of the aggregates within the continuity of a single existence, which is understood as having broken teeth and so forth. Here, the latter is intended. This aging is suffering both because it is conditioned suffering and because it is a basis for suffering. For when, due to the loosening of limbs, the impairment of faculties, disfigurement, the loss of youth, the decline of strength, the loss of memory and intelligence, contempt from others, and other such factors, bodily and mental suffering arises, aging is its basis. Therefore, it is said:

“Aṅgānaṃ [P 1.0073] sithilabhāvā, indriyānaṃ vikārato;

Yobbanassa vināsena, balassa upaghātato.

“From the loosening of limbs, from the impairment of faculties; from the destruction of youth, from the decline of strength.

“Vippavāsā satādīnaṃ, puttadārehi attano;

Appasādanīyato ceva, bhiyyo bālattapattiyā.

“From the loss of memory and other faculties, from separation from one's own children and spouse; from being unpleasing, and from the increasing attainment of childishness.

“Pappoti dukkhaṃ yaṃ macco, kāyikaṃ mānasaṃ tathā;

Sabbametaṃ jarāhetu, yasmā tasmā jarā dukhā”ti. (vibha. aṭṭha. 192; visuddhi. 2.542);

“Whatever suffering, physical as well as mental, a mortal obtains, all of this is caused by aging. Therefore, aging is suffering.”

Idaṃ jarādukkhaṃ anvetīti sambandho. Byādhīti vividhaṃ dukkhaṃ ādahati vidahatīti byādhi. Byādhayati tāpayati kampayatīti vā byādhi.

This pertains to the suffering of aging; such is the connection. Illness: It is called ‘byādhi’ because it brings and inflicts various kinds of suffering. Or, it is called ‘byādhi’ because it afflicts, torments, and causes trembling.

Maraṇadukkhanti etthāpi duvidhaṃ maraṇaṃ saṅkhatalakkhaṇañca, yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “jarāmaraṇaṃ dvīhi [V 0.0057] khandhehi saṅgahita”nti (dhātu. 71). Ekabhavapariyāpannajīvitindriyapabandhavicchedo ca, yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “niccaṃ maraṇato bhaya”nti (su. ni. 581; jā. 1.11.88). Taṃ idha adhippetaṃ. Jātipaccayā maraṇaṃ upakkamamaraṇaṃ sarasamaraṇaṃ āyukkhayamaraṇaṃ puññakkhayamaraṇantipi tasseva nāmaṃ. Puna khaṇikamaraṇaṃ sammutimaraṇaṃ samucchedamaraṇanti ayampi bhedo veditabbo. Pavatte rūpārūpadhammānaṃ bhedo khaṇikamaraṇaṃ nāma. Tisso mato phusso matoti idaṃ paramatthato sattassa abhāvā, sassaṃ mataṃ, rukkho matoti idampi jīvitindriyassa abhāvā sammutimaraṇaṃ nāma. Khīṇāsavassa appaṭisandhikā kālakiriyā samucchedamaraṇaṃ nāma. Bāhirasammutimaraṇaṃ ṭhapetvā itaraṃ sammutimaraṇañca idha yathāvuttappabandhavicchedanabhāvena saṅgahitaṃ, dukkhassa pana vatthubhāvato dukkhaṃ. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

The suffering of death: Here too, death is of two kinds: the characteristic of the conditioned, which is referred to in the statement, ‘Aging and death are included in two aggregates’; and the severing of the continuity of the life faculty pertaining to a single existence, which is referred to in the statement, ‘There is constant fear of death.’ The latter is what is intended here. Death conditioned by birth is also called death due to external action, untimely death, death by exhaustion of lifespan, and death by exhaustion of merit. Furthermore, this classification should be understood: momentary death, conventional death, and death as final cutting off. The dissolution of material and immaterial phenomena in the course of existence is called momentary death. The statement ‘Tissa is dead, Phussa is dead’—since in an ultimate sense there is no being—and the statement ‘the crop is dead, the tree is dead’—since there is no life faculty—are called conventional death. The passing away of one whose taints are destroyed, which is without relinking, is called death as final cutting off. Setting aside external conventional death, the other conventional death is included here as the severing of the aforementioned continuity, and it is suffering because it is a basis for suffering. Therefore, it is said:

“Pāpassa [M 0.0063] pāpakammādi-nimittamanupassato;

Bhaddassāpasahantassa, viyogaṃ piyavatthukaṃ;

Mīyamānassa yaṃ dukkhaṃ, mānasaṃ avisesato.

“For the evil person who perceives the sign of evil kamma and so forth, and for the virtuous person who cannot endure separation from beloved things—whatever mental suffering arises without exception for one who is dying,

“Sabbesañcāpi [P 1.0074] yaṃ sandhi-bandhanacchedanādikaṃ;

Vitujjamānamammānaṃ, hoti dukkhaṃ sarīrajaṃ.

“And for all beings, whatever bodily suffering arises from the breaking of joints and ligaments, and from the piercing of vital spots.

“Asayhamappatikāraṃ, dukkhassetassidaṃ yato;

Maraṇaṃ vatthu tenetaṃ, dukkhamicceva bhāsita”nti. (vibha. aṭṭha. 193; visuddhi. 2.543);

“Since death is the basis of this unbearable and irremediable suffering, therefore it is spoken of as suffering.”

Sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsadukkhanti ettha sokādīsu soko nāma ñātibyasanādīhi phuṭṭhassa antonijjhānalakkhaṇo cittasantāpo. Dukkho panassa dukkhadukkhattā ceva dukkhassa ca vatthubhāvato. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

The suffering of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair: Here, among sorrow and the rest, sorrow is the mental anguish characterized by inner burning in one afflicted by the loss of relatives and so forth. It is suffering both because it is suffering in itself and because it is a basis for suffering. Therefore, it is said:

“Sattānaṃ hadayaṃ soko, sallaṃ viya vitujjati;

Aggitattova nārāco, bhusañca ḍahate puna.

“Sorrow pierces the hearts of beings like a dart; like a fire-heated arrow, it burns fiercely again and again.

“Samāvahati [V 0.0058] ca byādhi-jarāmaraṇabhedanaṃ;

Dukkhampi vividhaṃ yasmā, tasmā dukkhoti vuccatī”ti. (vibha. aṭṭha. 194; visuddhi. 2.544);

“And since it brings about destruction through disease, aging, and death, and also various kinds of suffering, therefore it is called suffering.”

Paridevo nāma ñātibyasanādīhi phuṭṭhassa vacīpalāpo. Dukkho panassa saṃsāradukkhabhāvato dukkhavatthuto ca. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

Lamentation is the verbal wailing of one afflicted by the loss of relatives and so forth. It is suffering both because it is conditioned suffering and because it is a basis for suffering. Therefore, it is said:

“Yaṃ sokasallavihato paridevamāno, kaṇṭhoṭṭhatālutalasosajamappasayhaṃ;

Bhiyyodhimattamadhigacchatiyeva dukkhaṃ, dukkhoti tena bhagavā paridevamāhā”ti. (vibha. aṭṭha. 195; visuddhi. 2.545);

“When one, struck by the dart of sorrow, laments, one experiences unbearable and greatly intensified suffering born of the drying of the throat, lips, palate, and tongue; therefore, the Blessed One declared lamentation to be suffering.”

Dukkhaṃ nāma kāyapīḷanalakkhaṇaṃ kāyikaṃ dukkhaṃ. Dukkhaṃ panassa dukkhadukkhattā ceva mānasadukkhāvahanato ca. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

Pain is physical suffering characterized by the affliction of the body. It is suffering both because it is suffering in itself and because it brings about mental suffering. Therefore, it is said:

“Pīḷeti kāyikamidaṃ, dukkhaṃ dukkhañca mānasaṃ bhiyyo;

Janayati yasmā tasmā, dukkhanti visesato vutta”nti. (vibha. aṭṭha. 196-197; visuddhi. 2.546);

“Since this physical suffering afflicts, and further generates mental suffering, therefore it is specifically called ‘suffering.’”

Domanassaṃ [P 1.0075][M 0.0064] nāma cittapīḷanalakkhaṇaṃ mānasaṃ dukkhaṃ. Dukkhaṃ panassa dukkhadukkhattā ceva kāyikadukkhāvahanato ca. Cetodukkhasamappitā hi kese pakiriya kandanti, urāni patipisenti, āvaṭṭanti, vivaṭṭanti, chinnapapātaṃ papatanti, satthaṃ āharanti, visaṃ khādanti, rajjuyā ubbandhanti, aggiṃ pavisanti, nānappakāraṃ dukkhaṃ anubhavanti. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

Grief is mental suffering characterized by the affliction of the mind. It is suffering both because it is suffering in itself and because it brings about bodily suffering. For those afflicted by mental suffering tear their hair, beat their breasts, writhe about, collapse, throw themselves down cliffs, take up weapons, consume poison, hang themselves with ropes, enter fire, and experience various kinds of suffering. Hence it is said:

“Pīḷeti yato cittaṃ, kāyassa ca pīḷanaṃ samāvahati;

Dukkhanti domanassampi, domanassaṃ tato ahū”ti. (vibha. aṭṭha. 196-197; visuddhi. 2.547);

“Since it afflicts the mind and brings affliction to the body, grief is also suffering; therefore, it is grief.”

Upāyāso nāma ñātibyasanādīhi phuṭṭhassa adhimattacetodukkhappabhāvito dosoyeva. Saṅkhārakkhandhapariyāpanno eko dhammoti eke. Dukkho panassa saṅkhāradukkhabhāvato cittaṃ paridahanato kāyassa vihananato ca. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

Despair is aversion arising from intense mental suffering in one afflicted by the loss of relatives and so forth. Some consider it a single phenomenon included in the aggregate of formations. It is suffering because of its nature as conditioned suffering, because it burns the mind, and because it torments the body. Hence it is said:

“Cittassa [V 0.0059] ca paridahanā, kāyassa vihananato ca adhimattaṃ;

Yaṃ dukkhamupāyāso, janeti dukkho tato vutto”ti. (vibha. aṭṭha. 198; visuddhi. 2.548);

“Because of the intense burning of the mind and tormenting of the body, the suffering that despair generates is therefore called suffering.”

Ettha ca mandagginā antobhājane pāko viya soko, tikkhagginā paccamānassa bhājanato bahi nikkhamanaṃ viya paridevo, bahi nikkhantāvasesassa nikkhamitumpi appahontassa antobhājaneyeva yāva parikkhayā pāko viya upāyāso daṭṭhabbo.

Here, sorrow is to be seen as like something cooking inside a pot over a slow fire; lamentation is like its boiling over the pot from a fierce fire; and despair is to be seen as like the remainder left inside, unable even to boil over, cooking until it is utterly destroyed.

Nerayikaṃ dukkhanti niraye pañcavidhabandhanādikaṃ dukkhaṃ anveti, taṃ devadūtasuttena dīpetabbaṃ. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

The suffering of hell-beings: This refers to the fivefold bondage and other suffering in hell, which should be illustrated by the Devadūta Sutta. Hence it is said:

“Jāyetha no ce narakesu satto, tatthaggidāhādikamappasayhaṃ;

Labhetha dukkhaṃ nu kuhiṃ patiṭṭhaṃ, iccāha dukkhāti munīdha jāti”nti. (vibha. aṭṭha. 191; visuddhi. 2.541);

“If a being were not born in hell, where could the unbearable suffering there, such as burning by fire, find a basis? Thus the Sage here declared birth to be suffering.”

Tiracchānayonikaṃ [P 1.0076] dukkhanti tiracchānesu kasāpatodatāḷanavijjhanādikaṃ anekavidhaṃ dukkhaṃ anveti, taṃ bālapaṇḍitasuttato gahetabbaṃ. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

The suffering of the animal realm: This refers to the various kinds of suffering that follow animals, such as whipping, goading, beating, and stabbing. This should be understood from the Bālapaṇḍita Sutta. Therefore, it is said:

“Dukkhaṃ [M 0.0065] tiracchesu kasāpatodadaṇḍābhighātādibhavaṃ anekaṃ;

Yaṃ taṃ kathaṃ tattha bhaveyya jātiṃ, vinā tahiṃ jāti tatopi dukkhā”ti. (vibha. aṭṭha. 191; visuddhi. 2.541);

“Manifold is the suffering in the animal realm, arising from whips, goads, beatings with sticks, and the like. How could that suffering exist there without birth? Therefore, birth in that realm is also suffering.”

Pettivisayikaṃ dukkhanti petesu pana khuppipāsa vātātapādinibbattaṃ dukkhañca lokantare tibbandhakāre asayhasītādidukkhañca anveti. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

Suffering pertaining to the realm of ghosts: this is the suffering that accompanies ghosts, arising from hunger, thirst, wind, heat, and so on, as well as the suffering in the world-interstice, in thick darkness, such as from unbearable cold. Therefore it is said:

“Petesu dukkhaṃ pana khuppipāsāvātātapādippabhavaṃ vicittaṃ;

Yasmā ajātassa na tattha atthi, tasmāpi dukkhaṃ muni jātimāha.

“For ghosts, suffering is varied, arising from hunger, thirst, wind, heat, and the like. Since it does not exist there for one who is unborn, therefore the Sage also declares birth to be suffering.”

“Tibbandhakāre [V 0.0060] ca asayhasīte, lokantare yaṃ asuresu dukkhaṃ;

Na taṃ bhave tattha na cassa jāti, yato ayaṃ jāti tatopi dukkhā”ti. (vibha. aṭṭha. 191; visuddhi. 2.541);

“And the suffering of the asuras in the world-interstice, in thick darkness and unbearable cold—that would not exist if one were not born there. For this reason, this birth is also suffering.”

Mānusikaṃ dukkhanti manussesu vadhabandhanādikaṃ dukkhaṃ. Gabbhokkantimūlakaṃ dukkhanti “ayañhi satto mātukucchimhi nibbattamāno na uppalapadumapuṇḍarikādīsu nibbattatī”tiādinā nayena yaṃ jātidukkhaṃ vuttaṃ, idaṃ tāva gabbhokkantimūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ anveti. Gabbhe ṭhitimūlakaṃ dukkhanti yaṃ pana “so mātu sahasā upakkhalanagamananisīdanā”tiādinā nayena yaṃ tibbaṃ dukkhaṃ vuttaṃ, idaṃ gabbhe ṭhitimūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ anveti. Gabbhā vuṭṭhānamūlakaṃ dukkhanti “yaṃ panassa mūḷhagabbhāya mātuyā mittāmaccasuhajjādīhipi adassanārahe dukkhuppattiṭṭhāne”tiādinā nayena yaṃ dukkhaṃ vuttaṃ, idaṃ [P 1.0077] mātukucchito bahi nikkhantamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ anveti. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

Human suffering refers to the suffering experienced by humans, such as execution, imprisonment, and so on. The suffering rooted in conception refers to the suffering of birth described in this way: “This being, being born in the mother’s womb, does not arise in a blue lotus, a red lotus, a white lotus, or other such flowers.” This suffering rooted in conception accompanies one. The suffering rooted in remaining in the womb refers to the intense suffering described in this way: “The mother’s sudden stumbling, walking, or sitting,” and so on. This suffering rooted in remaining in the womb accompanies one. The suffering rooted in emerging from the womb refers to the suffering described in this way: “When his mother, suffering from a difficult birth, is in a state unfit to be seen even by friends, ministers, or companions, in the place of the origin of suffering.” This suffering rooted in emerging from the mother’s womb accompanies one. Therefore, it is said:

“Yañcāpi gūthanarake viya mātugabbhe,

Satto vasaṃ ciramato bahi nikkhamanañca;

Pappoti dukkhamatighoramidampi natthi,

Jātiṃ vinā itipi jāti ayañhi dukkhā.

“A being dwells long in the mother’s womb as if in a hell of excrement; and emerging from there, attains extremely dreadful suffering. This too would not exist without birth; thus, this birth is indeed suffering.”

“Kiṃ [M 0.0066] bhāsitena bahunā nanu yaṃ kuhiñci,

Atthīdha kiñcirapi dukkhamidaṃ kadāci;

Nevatthi jātivirahe yadato mahesi,

Dukkhāti sabbapaṭhamaṃ imamāha jāti”nti. (vibha. aṭṭha. 191; visuddhi. 2.541);

“Why speak at length? Is it not so that whatever little suffering exists anywhere here, at any time—it does not exist in the absence of birth? Therefore, the Great Sage declared this birth to be suffering first of all.”

Jātassūpanibandhakaṃ dukkhanti jātassa upanibandhanaṃ nhānalepanakhādanapivanādijagganadukkhaṃ anveti. Jātassa parādheyyakaṃ dukkhanti parassa aññassa āyattaṃ issariyadukkhaṃ anveti. “Sabbaṃ paravasaṃ dukkha”nti hi vuttaṃ. Attūpakkamaṃ dukkhanti yaṃ attanāva attānaṃ vadhentassa acelakavatādivasena ātāpanaparitāpanānuyogamanuyuttassa kodhavasena abhuñjantassa ubbandhantassa ca dukkhaṃ hoti, idaṃ attūpakkamaṃ dukkhaṃ anveti. Parūpakkamaṃ dukkhanti yaṃ parato vadhabandhanādīni anubhavantassa uppajjati, idaṃ parūpakkamaṃ dukkhaṃ anveti. Dukkhadukkhanti [V 0.0061] kāyikacetasikā dukkhā vedanā sabhāvato ca nāmato ca dukkhattā dukkhadukkhaṃ, idaṃ dukkhadukkhaṃ anveti. Saṅkhāradukkhanti upekkhāvedanā ceva avasesā ca tebhūmakasaṅkhārā udayabbayapīḷitattā saṅkhāradukkhaṃ, idaṃ saṅkhāradukkhaṃ anveti. Vipariṇāmadukkhanti sukhavedanā vipariṇāmadukkhassa hetuto vipariṇāmadukkhaṃ, idaṃ vipariṇāmadukkhaṃ anveti.

The suffering bound up with one who is born means the suffering of tending to the body, such as bathing, anointing, eating, and drinking, accompanies the one who is born. The suffering of dependence on others for one who is born means the suffering of being subject to another’s authority, dependent on another, accompanies them. For it is said, “All that is dependent on others is suffering.” The suffering of self-inflicted harm means the suffering that arises when one harms oneself—through practices like naked asceticism, engaging in self-mortification and extreme austerities—or when one, due to anger, abstains from food, or hangs oneself. This suffering of self-inflicted harm accompanies one. The suffering of harm inflicted by others means the suffering that arises when one experiences execution, imprisonment, and the like from others. This suffering of harm inflicted by others accompanies one. The suffering of pain means bodily and mental painful feelings, which are suffering both in essence and in name. This suffering of pain accompanies one. The suffering of formations means equanimous feeling and all other formations of the three realms, which are oppressed by arising and passing away. This suffering of formations accompanies one. The suffering of change means pleasant feeling, which, being the cause of the suffering of change, is the suffering of change. This suffering of change accompanies one.

Mātumaraṇanti [P 1.0078] mātuyā maraṇaṃ. Pitumaraṇanti pituno maraṇaṃ. Bhātumaraṇanti jeṭṭhakaniṭṭhabhātūnaṃ maraṇaṃ. Bhaginimaraṇanti jeṭṭhakaniṭṭhabhaginīnaṃ maraṇaṃ. Puttamaraṇanti puttānaṃ maraṇaṃ. Dhītumaraṇanti dhītūnaṃ maraṇaṃ. Ñātibyasanaṃ dukkhanti ñātīnaṃ byasanaṃ, corarogabhayādīhi ñātikkhayo, ñātivināsoti attho. Tena ñātibyasanena phuṭṭhassa ajjhotthaṭassa abhibhūtassa uppannaṃ dukkhaṃ ñātibyasanaṃ dukkhaṃ, taṃ ñātibyasanaṃ dukkhaṃ anveti. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Ayaṃ pana viseso – bhogānaṃ byasanaṃ bhogabyasanaṃ, rājacorādivasena bhogakkhayo, bhogavināsoti attho. Vuttanayena taṃ bhogabyasanaṃ dukkhaṃ anveti. Rogabyasananti rogo eva byasanaṃ rogabyasanaṃ. Rogo hi ārogyaṃ byasati vināsetīti byasanaṃ, vuttanayena taṃ rogabyasanaṃ dukkhaṃ anveti. Sīlabyasanaṃ dukkhanti sīlassa byasanaṃ sīlabyasanaṃ, dussīlyassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Vuttanayena [M 0.0067] taṃ sīlabyasanaṃ dukkhaṃ anveti. Sammādiṭṭhiṃ vināsayamānā uppannā diṭṭhiyeva byasanaṃ diṭṭhibyasanaṃ, vuttanayena taṃ diṭṭhibyasanaṃ dukkhaṃ anveti. Ettha ca purimāni dve anipphannāni, pacchimāni tīṇi nipphannāni tilakkhaṇāhatāni. Purimāni ca tīṇi neva kusalāni nākusalāni. Sīladiṭṭhibyasanadvayaṃ akusalaṃ.

“The death of a mother” means the death of a mother. “The death of a father” means the death of a father. “The death of brothers” means the death of elder and younger brothers. “The death of sisters” means the death of elder and younger sisters. “The death of sons” means the death of sons. “The death of daughters” means the death of daughters. “The suffering of the ruin of relatives” means the ruin of relatives, that is, the destruction of relatives due to thieves, diseases, fears, and so on; the loss or destruction of relatives. The suffering that arises in one who is afflicted, overwhelmed, and overcome by such ruin of relatives is the suffering of the ruin of relatives. That suffering of the ruin of relatives accompanies one. The same method applies to the rest. Here, however, is the distinction: “the ruin of wealth” is the ruin of wealth, meaning the destruction of wealth due to kings, thieves, and so on; the loss or destruction of wealth. In the manner stated, that suffering of the ruin of wealth accompanies one. “The ruin of health” means illness itself is a misfortune, the ruin of health. For illness destroys health, hence it is called a misfortune. In the manner stated, that suffering of the ruin of health accompanies one. “The suffering of the ruin of virtue” means the ruin of virtue; this is a name for immorality. In the manner stated, that suffering of the ruin of virtue accompanies one. “The suffering of the ruin of view” is a misfortune of view; it is a view that arises while destroying right view. In the manner stated, that suffering of the ruin of view accompanies one. Here, the first two are unconditioned, while the latter three are conditioned and struck by the three characteristics. And the first three are neither wholesome nor unwholesome. The two, the ruin of virtue and the ruin of view, are unwholesome.

Yathāti opamme. Bhinnaṃ nāvanti sithilabandhanaṃ nāvaṃ, jajjarībhūtaṃ vā padarugghāṭimaṃ vā. Dakamesinti udakadāyiṃ udakappavesaniṃ. Tato tato udakaṃ anvetīti tato tato bhinnaṭṭhānato udakaṃ pavisati. Puratopīti nāvāya purimabhāgatopi. Pacchatopīti tassā pacchimabhāgatopi. Heṭṭhatopīti adhobhāgatopi. Passatopīti ubhayapassatopi. Yaṃ antarantarā na vuttaṃ, taṃ pāṭhānusārena veditabbaṃ.

The word ‘yathā’ (as) is used in the sense of a simile. ‘A broken boat’ means a boat with loose fastenings, or one that is worn out, or one with planks split apart. ‘Letting in water’ means yielding water, admitting water. ‘From here and there water enters’ means water enters from here and there, from the broken places. ‘From the front’ means from the front part of the boat. ‘From the back’ means from its rear part. ‘From below’ means from its lower part. ‘From the sides’ means from both sides. Whatever is not mentioned in between should be understood according to the text.

Tasmā [P 1.0079] kāyagatāsatiādibhāvanāya jantu, sadā sato hutvā vikkhambhanasamucchedavasena rūpādīsu vatthukāmesu sabbappakārampi kilesakāmaṃ parivajjento kāmāni parivajjeyya. Evaṃ te kāme pahāya tappahānakaramaggeneva catubbidhampi oghaṃ tareyya tarituṃ sakkuṇeyya. Tato yathā puriso garukaṃ nāvaṃ udakaṃ siñcitvā lahukāya nāvāya appakasireneva pāragū bhaveyya pāraṃ [V 0.0062] gaccheyya, evamevaṃ attabhāvanāvaṃ kilesūdakagarukaṃ siñcitvā lahukena attabhāvena pāragū bhaveyya. Sabbadhammapāraṃ nibbānaṃ gato bhaveyya, arahattappattiyā gaccheyya anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbānenāti arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi.

Therefore, by cultivating mindfulness directed to the body and other such meditations, a person, being always mindful, should abandon sensual pleasures by avoiding every kind of defilement-desire for sense-objects such as forms, etc., by way of suppression and eradication. Thus, having abandoned those sensual pleasures, one should cross, or be able to cross, the fourfold flood by the very path that leads to their abandonment. Then, just as a person, having bailed out the water from a heavy boat, would reach the far shore with little difficulty in a light boat, so too, having bailed out the water of defilements that makes the boat of one’s existence heavy, one would reach the far shore with a lightened existence. One would have gone to Nibbāna, the far shore of all phenomena; one would reach it by the attainment of Arahantship, by final Nibbāna in the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining. Thus he concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship.

Tasmāti yasmā jātiādikaṃ dukkhaṃ etaṃ puggalaṃ anveti, tasmā. Taṃkāraṇā taṃhetūtiādīsupi eseva nayo. Yasmā vuttappakāradukkhaṃ etaṃ anveti, taṃhetu. Yasmā anveti tappaccayā, yasmā anveti taṃnidānanti evaṃ padayojanā kātabbā. Hetūtiādīni kāraṇavevacanāni. Kāraṇañhi tena tassa phalaṃ hinoti pavattatīti hetu. Taṃ taṃ paṭicca phalaṃ eti pavattatīti paccayo. “Handa naṃ gaṇhathā”ti dassentaṃ viya attano phalaṃ nidetīti nidānaṃ.

‘Tasmā’ (therefore) means: because suffering such as birth accompanies this person, therefore. The same method applies to ‘taṃkāraṇā’ (for that reason), ‘taṃhetu’ (due to that cause), and so on. Because suffering of the stated kind accompanies this, that is the cause. Because it accompanies, that is the condition; because it accompanies, that is the source—thus the connection of the words should be made. ‘Hetu’ (cause) and so on are synonyms for ‘kāraṇa’ (reason). For a cause (`hetu`) is so called because through it its result is impelled and proceeds. A condition (`paccaya`) is so called because depending on that, the result comes to be and proceeds. A source (`nidāna`) is so called because it points out its own result, as if showing, “Here, take it.”

“Taṃkāraṇāti akāraṇanikkāraṇapaṭisedho. Taṃhetūti ahetumahābhūtahetupaṭisedho. Tappaccayāti appaccayena saddhiṃ asādhāraṇapaccayapaṭisedho[M 0.0068]. Taṃnidānāti anidānena saha āgamādhigamanidānapaṭisedho”ti evameke vaṇṇayanti. Etaṃ ādīnavaṃ sampassamānoti etaṃ vuttappakāraṃ upaddavaṃ vipassanāñāṇena sammā passamāno dakkhamāno.

‘Taṃkāraṇā’ means a refutation of groundlessness and causelessness. ‘Taṃhetu’ means a refutation of no-cause and of the great elements as cause. ‘Tappaccayā’ means a refutation of no-condition along with uncommon conditions. ‘Taṃnidānā’ means a refutation of no-origin along with origins based on scripture and personal attainment—thus some explain. ‘Seeing this danger’ means rightly seeing and perceiving with insight-knowledge this misfortune of the kind stated.

Sadāti mūlapadaṃ. Puna sadāti atthapadaṃ. Sadāti sabbadivase. Sabbadāti sabbasmiṃ kāle. Sabbakālanti pubbaṇhādisabbakālaṃ. Niccakālanti divase divase. Dhuvakālanti abbocchinnakālaṃ. Satatanti nirantaraṃ. Samitanti ekībhūtaṃ. Abbokiṇṇanti aññena asammissaṃ. Poṅkhānupoṅkhanti paṭipāṭiyā ghaṭitaṃ “poṅkhānupoṅkhaṃ avirādhitaṃ [P 1.0080] upaṭṭhātī”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 5.1115) viya. Udakūmikajātanti nibbattaudakaūmitaraṅgaṃ viya. Avīcīti aviraḷaṃ. Santatīti anupacchinnaṃ. Sahitanti ghaṭitaṃ ekībhūtaṃ vā “sahitaṃ me, asahitaṃ te”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.202) viya. Phassitanti phusitaṃ “nivāte phusitaggale”tiādīsu viya. Purebhattaṃ pacchābhattanti dve padāni divākālavibhāgavasena. Purimaṃ yāmaṃ majjhimaṃ yāmaṃ pacchimaṃ yāmanti tīṇi rattivibhāgavasena. Kāḷe juṇheti aḍḍhamāsavasena. Vasse…pe… gimheti tīṇi utuvasena. Purime vayokhandhe…pe… pacchime vayokhandheti tīṇi vayovibhāgavasena vuttānīti ñātabbaṃ.

‘Sadā’ is the root word. Again, ‘sadā’ is the word conveying the meaning. ‘Sadā’ means on every day. ‘Sabbadā’ means at all times. ‘Sabbakālaṃ’ means all periods of time, from morning onwards. ‘Niccakālaṃ’ means day after day. ‘Dhuvakālaṃ’ means an uninterrupted time. ‘Satataṃ’ means continuously. ‘Samitaṃ’ means unified. ‘Abbokiṇṇaṃ’ means unmixed with anything else. ‘Poṅkhānupoṅkhaṃ’ means connected in sequence, as in ‘it occurs in succession, uninterruptedly’ and so on. ‘Udakūmikajātaṃ’ means like the arising of waves in water. ‘Avīci’ means without gaps. ‘Santati’ means unbroken. ‘Sahitaṃ’ means connected or unified, as in ‘mine is coherent, yours is not’ and so on. ‘Phassitaṃ’ means touched, as in ‘in a windless place with the bolt fastened’ and so on. ‘Purebhattaṃ’ (before the meal) and ‘pacchābhattaṃ’ (after the meal) are two terms dividing the daytime. ‘Purimaṃ yāmaṃ’ (the first watch), ‘majjhimaṃ yāmaṃ’ (the middle watch), and ‘pacchimaṃ yāmaṃ’ (the last watch) are three divisions of the night. ‘Kāḷe’ (in the dark fortnight) and ‘juṇhe’ (in the bright fortnight) are according to the half-month. ‘Vasse’ (in the rainy season)... ‘gimhe’ (in the hot season) are three divisions according to the seasons. ‘Purime vayokhandhe’ (in the first stage of life)... ‘pacchime vayokhandhe’ (in the last stage of life) are three divisions according to the stages of life—this should be understood.

Satoti catūhi kāraṇehi sato. “Kāye kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ bhāvento sato”tiādīni “evaṃ samucchedato kāme parivajjeyyā”ti pariyosānāni vuttatthāneva. Api [V 0.0063] ca sattattā satoti tīsu vatthūsu sattabhāvena vā tayo kilese paṭikkamāpetuṃ sattibhāvena vā satattā sato. Santattāti kilesopakkilese palāpetvā ṭhānena ca ārammaṇena ca pamocetvā santattā sato. Samitattāti iṭṭhaphaladāyakapuññena ca aniṭṭhaphaladāyakapāpena ca samitattā sato. Santadhammasamannāgatoti sappurisadhamme bhajanato buddhādiariyapuggale sevanato santadhammasamannāgatattā sato.

‘Sato’ means mindful for four reasons. The passages beginning with ‘developing the foundation of mindfulness, the contemplation of the body in the body, one is mindful’ and concluding with ‘thus by eradication one should avoid sensual pleasures’ are to be understood as stated. Furthermore, one is mindful (`sato`) because of being attached (`sattattā`) to the three objects, or because of having the power (`sattibhāvena`) to make the three defilements retreat. One is mindful (`sato`) because of being tranquil (`santattā`), having driven away defilements and corruptions and being released from their location and object. One is mindful (`sato`) because of being pacified (`samitattā`) with regard to both merit that gives agreeable fruits and evil that gives disagreeable fruits. One is mindful (`sato`) because of being endowed with the qualities of the peaceful (`santadhammasamannāgatattā`), by cultivating the qualities of good people and associating with noble individuals such as the Buddha.

Vatthukāme parijānitvāti ete vuttappakāre tebhūmake vatthukāme tīraṇapariññāya jānitvā. Pahāyāti kilesakāme pahānapariññāya [M 0.0069] pariccajitvā. Pajahitvāti chaḍḍetvā. Kiṃ kacavaraṃ viya piṭakenāti? Na hi, api ca kho taṃ vinodetvā taritvā vijjhitvā nīharitvā. Kiṃ balibaddamiva patodenāti[P 1.0081]? Na hi, atha kho taṃ byantiṃ karitvā vigatantaṃ karitvā. Yathāssa antopi nāvasissati, antamaso bhaṅgamattampi, tathā taṃ karitvā. Kathaṃ pana taṃ tathā katanti? Anabhāvaṃ gahetvā anu abhāvaṃ gametvā. Samucchedappahānena yathā samucchinnā hoti, tathā karitvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Esa nayo kāmacchandanīvaraṇādīsu.

‘Having fully understood sense-objects’ means having known these sense-objects of the three realms, of the kind stated, by the full understanding of discernment. ‘Having abandoned’ means having relinquished the defilements of sensual desire by the full understanding of abandonment. ‘Having given up’ means having cast away. How? Like refuse with a basket? No, but rather by dispelling, crossing over, piercing through, and extracting them. How? Like an ox with a goad? No, but rather by making them cease, making them come to an end. So that not even a trace remains within, not even the slightest fragment, thus one does it. How then is it done thus? By taking it as non-existent, by leading it to non-existence. It is said that it is done by abandonment through eradication, so that it is utterly cut off. This is the method regarding the hindrance of sensual desire and so forth.

Kāmoghantiādīsu pañcakāmaguṇikarāgo avasīdanaṭṭhena “kāmogho”ti vuccati. Bhavoghoti rūpārūpabhavesu chandarāgo jhānanikanti ca. Diṭṭhoghoti sassatadiṭṭhādisahagatā bhave patthanāyeva, diṭṭhogho bhavoghe eva samodhānaṃ gacchati. Avijjogho catūsu saccesu aññāṇaṃ. Tattha kāmaguṇe assādato manasi karoto anuppanno ca kāmogho uppajjati, uppanno ca kāmogho saṃvaḍḍhati. Mahaggatadhamme assādato manasi karoto anuppanno ca bhavogho uppajjati, uppanno ca saṃvaḍḍhati. Tebhūmakadhammesu catuvipallāsapadaṭṭhānabhāvena anuppanno ca avijjogho uppajjati, uppanno ca saṃvaḍḍhatīti veditabbo. Vuttanayapaccanīkato sukkapakkho vitthāretabbo.

Among the floods, ‘kāmogha’ (flood of sensual pleasures) is said to be the lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure in the sense of sinking. ‘Bhavogha’ (flood of existence) is the lust for form and formless existences, as well as delight in meditative absorption. ‘Diṭṭhogha’ (flood of views) is the longing for existence associated with eternalist views and the like; the flood of views merges with the flood of existence. ‘Avijjogha’ (flood of ignorance) is the lack of knowledge regarding the four truths. Herein, for one who attends to the gratification of sensual pleasures, the unarisen flood of sensual pleasures arises, and the arisen flood of sensual pleasures grows. For one who attends to the gratification of exalted states, the unarisen flood of existence arises, and the arisen flood grows. Regarding the phenomena of the three realms, because they are the basis for the four perversions, it should be understood that the unarisen flood of ignorance arises, and the arisen flood grows. The bright side should be elaborated in opposition to the stated method.

Appaṇihitavimokkhaṃ paṭipanno kāmoghaṃ, animittavimokkhaṃ paṭipanno bhavoghaṃ, suññatavimokkhaṃ paṭipanno avijjoghañca tareyya. Paṭhamamaggavasena tareyya, dutiyamaggavasena uttareyya, tatiyamaggavasena patareyya, catutthamaggavasena samatikkameyya, phalavasena vītivatteyyāti. Atha vā “kāmoghavasena tareyya, bhavoghavasena uttareyya, diṭṭhoghavasena patareyya, avijjoghavasena samatikkameyya, sabboghavasena vītivatteyyā”ti evameke vaṇṇayanti.

One who has entered upon the desireless liberation would cross the flood of sensual pleasures; one who has entered upon the signless liberation would cross the flood of existence; and one who has entered upon the emptiness liberation would cross the flood of ignorance. By means of the first path, one would cross over; by means of the second path, one would rise above; by means of the third path, one would cross completely; by means of the fourth path, one would completely transcend; and by means of the fruit, one would go beyond. Alternatively, some explain it thus: ‘One would cross over the flood of sensual pleasures, rise above the flood of existence, cross completely the flood of views, completely transcend the flood of ignorance, and go beyond all floods.’

Garukanti na sallahukaṃ. Bhārikanti bhārabhaṇḍaṃ ettha ṭhapayantīti bhārikaṃ. Udakaṃ sitvāti [V 0.0064] udakaṃ [P 1.0082] siñcitvā. Osiñcitvāti atirekaṃ siñcitvā. Chaḍḍetvāti pātetvā. Lahukāyāti sallahukāya. Khippanti sīghaṃ. Lahunti taṃkhaṇaṃ. Appakasirenevāti nidukkheneva. Pāraṃ vuccati amataṃ nibbānanti sakkāyaorato pārabhūtaṃ pāraṃ. Taṇhāvānato nikkhantaṃ nibbānaṃ [M 0.0070] kathīyati. Yosoti yo eso. Sabbasaṅkhārasamathotiādi sabbaṃ nibbānameva. Yasmā hi taṃ āgamma sabbasaṅkhāravipphanditāni samanti vūpasamanti, tasmā “sabbasaṅkhārasamatho”ti vuccati. Yasmā cetaṃ āgamma sabbe upadhayo paṭinissaṭṭhā honti, sabbā taṇhā khīyanti, sabbe kilesarajjā virajjanti, sabbaṃ dukkhaṃ nirujjhati, tasmā “sabbūpadhipaṭinissaggo, taṇhakkhayo, virāgo, nirodho”ti vuccati. Yā panesā taṇhā bhavena bhavaṃ, phalena vā saddhiṃ kammaṃ vinati saṃsibbatīti katvā vānanti vuccati, tato nikkhantaṃ vānatoti nibbānaṃ. Pāraṃ gaccheyya nimittavasena ekato vuṭṭhānagotrabhuñāṇena nibbānapāraṃ pāpuṇeyya. Adhigaccheyya nimittapavattehi ubhatovuṭṭhānamaggañāṇena nibbānapāraṃ visesena pāpuṇeyya. Phuseyya nibbānārammaṇaphalacittavasena nibbānapāraṃ phuseyya. Sacchikareyya guṇavasena phusitvā paccavekkhaṇañāṇena nibbānapāraṃ paccakkhaṃ kareyya. Atha vā “paṭhamamaggena pāraṃ gaccheyya, dutiyena adhigaccheyya, tatiyena phuseyya, catutthena sacchi kareyyā”ti evameke vaṇṇayanti. Yopi pāraṃ gantukāmoti yo koci vipassanāñāṇe ṭhito puggalo nibbānapāraṃ gantukāmo, sopi avassaṃ tattha gamissatīti pāragū. Vuttañhetaṃ – “otiṇṇomhi jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehī”tiādi[P 1.0083]. Pubbabhāge ajjhāsayavasena vipassanāyogena ca, sopi pāragū nāma. Yopi pāraṃ gacchatīti yopi maggasamaṅgī nibbānapāraṃ gacchati, sopi pāragū nāma. Yopi pāraṃ gatoti yopi maggena kiccaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā phale ṭhito nibbānapāraṅgato, sopi pāragū nāma.

"Heavy" means not light. "Bhārika" means that which has a heavy burden placed upon it; therefore, it is called "bhārika." "Udakaṃ sitvā" means having sprinkled water. "Osiñcitvā" means having sprinkled excessively. "Chaḍḍetvā" means having thrown down. "Lahukāya" means very light. "Khippaṃ" means swiftly. "Lahuṃ" means instantly. "Appakasireneva" means without difficulty. The far shore is called the deathless Nibbāna—the far shore that has gone beyond the realm of the aggregates. Nibbāna is said to be the escape from the entanglement of craving. "Yoso" means "that which." "The calming of all formations," and so forth—all this is Nibbāna itself. For by relying on it, all the agitations of formations subside and cease; therefore, it is called "the calming of all formations." And because by relying on it, all attachments are relinquished, all cravings are exhausted, all defilements become dispassionate, and all suffering ceases; therefore, it is called "the relinquishment of all attachments, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation." Moreover, this craving, by means of existence, weaves existence, or, together with its result, binds kamma—thus it is called "vāna" (weaving/binding). That which has emerged from this "vāna" is Nibbāna.
