One may reach the far shore by means of the sign; through the knowledge of emergence (from the sign) and the gotrabhu-knowledge, one may attain the far shore of Nibbāna. One may realize it by means of the progression of the sign; through the knowledge of the path emerging on both sides, one may specially attain the far shore of Nibbāna. One may touch it by means of the fruition consciousness with Nibbāna as its object, thereby touching the far shore of Nibbāna. One may directly know it by means of its qualities, having touched it with reviewing knowledge, and make the far shore of Nibbāna evident. Alternatively, some explain it thus: "By the first path, one reaches the far shore; by the second, one realizes it; by the third, one touches it; by the fourth, one directly knows it." Whoever desires to go to the far shore—any person established in insight knowledge, wishing to go to the far shore of Nibbāna—they too will surely go there; thus, they are called "one who has gone beyond." For it is said: "I am immersed in birth, aging, death, sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs," and so forth. In the preliminary stage, by inclination and through the application of insight, they too are called "one who has gone beyond." Whoever is going to the far shore—whoever, endowed with the path, is going to the far shore of Nibbāna—they too are called "one who has gone beyond." Whoever has gone to the far shore—whoever, having completed the task by the path, stands in the fruition and has gone to the far shore of Nibbāna—they too are called "one who has gone beyond."

Taṃ jinavacanena dassetuṃ “vuttampi hetaṃ bhagavatā – tiṇṇo pāraṅgato thale tiṭṭhati brāhmaṇo”tiādimāha. Abhiññāpāragūti adhigatena ñāṇena ñātapariññāya nibbānapāraṃ gantukāmo gacchati, gatoti pāragū. Pariññāpāragūti sabbadhammānaṃ tīraṇapariññāya samatikkamitvā vuttanayena pāragū. Pahānapāragūti samudayapakkhikānaṃ kilesānaṃ pahānapariññāya samatikkamitvā vuttanayena pāragū. Yo hi sabbadhammaṃ parijānāti, so tīhi pariññāhi parijānāti ñātapariññāya tīraṇapariññāya pahānapariññāyāti. Tattha katamā ñātapariññā? Sabbadhammaṃ jānāti “ime ajjhattikā, ime bāhirā, idamassa lakkhaṇaṃ, imāni rasapaccupaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānānī”ti, ayaṃ [M 0.0071] ñātapariññā. Katamā tīraṇapariññā? Evaṃ ñātaṃ katvā labbhamānavasena sabbadhammaṃ tīreti “aniccato dukkhato rogato”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 3.122), ayaṃ [V 0.0065] tīraṇapariññā. Katamā pahānapariññā? Evaṃ tīrayitvā aggamaggena dhammesu chandarāgaṃ pajahati, ayaṃ pahānapariññāti. Imā pariññāyo sandhāya “so abhiññāpāragū pariññāpāragū pahānapāragū”ti āha.

To explain this through the words of the Victor, it is said: "Indeed, this was spoken by the Blessed One—'The brahmin has crossed over, gone beyond, and stands on firm ground.'" "Abhiññāpāragū" (one who has gone beyond by higher knowledge) means: one desiring to reach the far shore of Nibbāna by the knowledge that has been attained, through full understanding as knowing, goes and has gone; thus, he is one who has gone beyond. "Pariññāpāragū" (one who has gone beyond by full understanding) means: having transcended all phenomena by full understanding as thorough investigation, by the method described, he is one who has gone beyond. "Pahānapāragū" (one who has gone beyond by abandonment) means: having transcended the defilements associated with the side of arising by full understanding as abandonment, by the method described, he is one who has gone beyond. For whoever fully understands all phenomena does so through three kinds of full understanding: full understanding as knowing, full understanding as thorough investigation, and full understanding as abandonment. Herein, what is full understanding as knowing? One knows all phenomena thus: "These are internal, these are external, this is their characteristic, these are their function, manifestation, and proximate cause"—this is full understanding as knowing. What is full understanding as thorough investigation? Having known them thus, one thoroughly investigates all phenomena as they are found, [reflecting,] "as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease," and so on—this is full understanding as thorough investigation. What is full understanding as abandonment? Having thoroughly investigated thus, one abandons desire and lust for phenomena through the supreme path—this is full understanding as abandonment. With reference to these full understandings, it is said: "He is one who has gone beyond by higher knowledge, one who has gone beyond by full understanding, and one who has gone beyond by abandonment."

Bhāvanāpāragūti bhāvanāya koṭiṃ patvā maggavasena nibbānapāraṃ gato. Sacchikiriyāpāragūti phalanibbānavasena sacchi kiriyāphalanibbānapāraṃ gato. Samāpattipāragūti aṭṭhannaṃ samāpattīnaṃ pāraṃ patto. Sabbadhammānanti pañcakkhandhādisabbadhammānaṃ. Sabbadukkhānanti jātidukkhādisabbadukkhānaṃ. Sabbakilesānanti kāyaduccaritādisabbakilesānaṃ. Ariyamaggānanti sotāpattimaggādicatunnaṃ ariyamaggānaṃ[P 1.0084]. Nirodhassāti nibbānassa. Sabbasamāpattīnanti sabbāsampi aṭṭhannaṃ rūpārūpasamāpattīnaṃ. Soti so ariyo. Vasippattoti vasībhāvappatto. Atha vā kantabhāvaṃ issariyabhāvaṃ nipphannabhāvaṃ patto. Pāramippattoti pāramīti avasānaṃ niṭṭhānaṃ, uttamabhāvaṃ vā taṃ patto. Kattha pattoti āha “ariyasmiṃ sīlasmi”ntiādi. Tattha ariyasmiṃ sīlasminti niddose sīlasmiṃ. Ariyasmiṃ samādhisminti niddose samādhismiṃ. Ariyāya paññāyāti niddosāya paññāya. Ariyāya vimuttiyāti niddosāya phalavimuttiyā. Purimena vācākammantājīvā gahitā, dutiyena vāyāmasatisamādhayo gahitā, tatiyena vitakkasammādiṭṭhiyo gahitā, catutthena taṃsampayuttā sesadhammā gahitāti veditabbā.

"Bhāvanāpāragū" (one who has gone beyond by development) means having reached the culmination of development and attained the far shore of Nibbāna by way of the path. "Sacchikiriyāpāragū" (one who has gone beyond by direct realization) means having attained the far shore of Nibbāna, which is the fruit of direct realization, by way of the fruition Nibbāna. "Samāpattipāragū" (one who has gone beyond by attainments) means having reached the culmination of the eight attainments. "Of all phenomena" refers to all phenomena such as the five aggregates. "Of all sufferings" refers to all sufferings such as the suffering of birth. "Of all defilements" refers to all defilements such as bodily misconduct. "Of the noble paths" refers to the four noble paths, beginning with the path of stream-entry. "Of cessation" means of Nibbāna. "Of all attainments" means of all eight attainments, both form and formless. "He" refers to that noble one. "Vasippatto" (attained mastery) means having attained the state of mastery. Alternatively, it means having attained a state of desirability, sovereignty, or accomplishment. "Pāramippatto" (reached perfection) means having reached the culmination, the completion, or the highest state. "Where has he attained?" It is said: "In noble virtue," and so on. There, "in noble virtue" means in faultless virtue. "In noble concentration" means in faultless concentration. "In noble wisdom" means in faultless wisdom. "In noble liberation" means in faultless liberation through the fruit. By the first, right speech, right action, and right livelihood are understood; by the second, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration are understood; by the third, right thought and right view are understood; and by the fourth, the remaining qualities associated with them are understood. This should be known.

Antagatoti maggena saṅkhāralokantaṃ gato. Antappattoti tameva lokantaṃ phalena patto. Koṭigatoti maggena saṅkhārakoṭiṃ gato. Koṭippattoti tameva koṭiṃ phalena patto. Pariyantagatoti maggena khandhāyatanādilokapariyantaṃ paricchedaṃ parivaṭumaṃ katvā gato. Pariyantappattoti tameva lokaṃ phalena pariyantaṃ katvā patto. Vosānagatoti maggena avasānaṃ gato. Vosānappattoti phalena avasānaṃ patto. Tāṇagatoti maggena tāyanaṃ gato. Tāṇappattoti phalena tāyanaṃ patto. Leṇagatoti maggena nilīyanaṃ gato. Leṇappattoti taṃ phalena nilīyanaṃ patto. Saraṇagatoti maggena patiṭṭhaṃ gato. Saraṇappattoti phalena saraṇaṃ patto[M 0.0072]. Abhayagatoti maggena nibbhayaṃ gato. Abhayappattoti phalena nibbhayaṃ nibbānaṃ patto. Accutagatoti cutivirahitaṃ nibbānaṃ maggena gato. Accutappattoti taṃ phalena patto. Amatagatoti maraṇarahitaṃ nibbānaṃ maggena gato. Amatappattoti taṃ phalena patto. Nibbānagatoti taṇhāvānato nikkhantaṃ nibbānaṃ maggena gato. Nibbānappattoti tameva phalena patto. So [P 1.0085] vuṭṭhavāsoti so arahā dasasu ariyavāsesu vasi parivasi vuṭṭho vuṭṭhāti ca vuṭṭhavāso. Ciṇṇacaraṇoti sīlena saha aṭṭhasu samāpattīsu ciṇṇavasīti ciṇṇacaraṇo. Gataddhoti saṃsāraddhānaṃ [V 0.0066] atikkanto. Gatadisoti supinantenapi agatapubbaṃ nibbānadisaṃ gato. Gatakoṭikoti anupādisesanibbānakoṭiṃ gato hutvā ṭhito. Pālitabrahmacariyoti rakkhitabrahmacariyo. Uttamadiṭṭhippattoti uttamaṃ sammādiṭṭhiṃ patto. Paṭividdhākuppoti akuppaṃ acalanaṃ arahattaphalaṃ paṭivijjhitvā ṭhito. Sacchikatanirodhoti nirodhaṃ nibbānaṃ sacchikatvā ṭhito.

He has gone to the end: he has gone to the end of the world of conditioned phenomena by the path. He has attained the end: he has reached that very end of the world by the fruit. He has gone to the culmination: he has gone to the culmination of conditioned phenomena by the path. He has attained the culmination: he has reached that very culmination by the fruit. He has gone to the limit: he has gone by the path, having made the limit of the world—the aggregates, sense bases, and so forth—a boundary and enclosure. He has attained the limit: he has reached that very world, having made it a limit, by the fruit. He has gone to the conclusion: he has gone to the conclusion by the path. He has attained the conclusion: he has reached the conclusion by the fruit. He has gone to protection: he has gone to protection by the path. He has attained protection: he has reached protection by the fruit. He has gone to shelter: he has gone to a shelter by the path. He has attained shelter: he has reached that shelter by the fruit. He has gone to refuge: he has gone to a support by the path. He has attained refuge: he has reached refuge by the fruit. He has gone to safety: he has gone to fearlessness by the path. He has attained safety: he has reached the fearless Nibbāna by the fruit. He has gone to the immutable: he has gone to Nibbāna, free from passing away, by the path. He has attained the immutable: he has reached that by the fruit. He has gone to the deathless: he has gone to Nibbāna, free from death, by the path. He has attained the deathless: he has reached that by the fruit. He has gone to Nibbāna: he has gone to Nibbāna, which has emerged from the thicket of craving, by the path. He has attained Nibbāna: he has reached that very Nibbāna by the fruit. He is one who has completed dwelling: that Arahant has dwelt, lived completely, and emerged in the ten noble abodes; thus he is one who has completed dwelling. He is one of developed conduct: he has practiced mastery in the eight attainments along with virtue; thus he is one of developed conduct. He has traversed the path: he has gone beyond the journey of saṃsāra. He has gone to the direction: he has gone to the direction of Nibbāna, which was never reached before, not even in a dream. He is one who has reached the culmination: he stands having gone to the culmination of Nibbāna without residue. He is one who has protected the holy life: he is one who has protected the holy life. He has attained the highest view: he has attained the supreme right view. He has penetrated the unshakeable: he stands having penetrated the unshakeable, immovable fruit of arahantship. He has realized cessation: he stands having realized cessation, Nibbāna.

Dukkhaṃ tassa pariññātanti tividhaṃ dukkhaṃ tena samatikkamitvā paricchinnaṃ. Abhiññeyyanti sabhāvalakkhaṇāvabodhavasena sobhanena ākārena jānitabbaṃ. Abhiññātanti adhikena ñāṇena ñātaṃ. Pariññeyyanti sāmaññalakkhaṇāvabodhavasena kiccasamāpannavasena ca byāpitvā parijānitabbaṃ. Pariññātanti samantato ñātaṃ. Bhāvetabbanti vaḍḍhetabbaṃ. Sacchikātabbanti paccakkhaṃ kātabbaṃ. Duvidhā hi sacchikiriyā paṭilābhasacchikiriyā ārammaṇasacchikiriyā cāti.

Suffering has been fully understood by him: the threefold suffering has been overcome and fully comprehended by him. It is to be directly known: it should be known in an excellent way by way of understanding its intrinsic characteristics. It has been directly known: it has been known by higher knowledge. It is to be fully understood: it should be thoroughly understood by way of comprehending its general characteristics and by way of fulfilling its function. It has been fully understood: it has been known in all respects. It is to be developed: it is to be cultivated. It is to be realized: it is to be made manifest. For realization is twofold: realization by attainment and realization by object.

Ukkhittapalighoti ettha palighoti vaṭṭamūlikā avijjā. Ayañhi dukkhipanaṭṭhena “paligho”ti vuccati. Tenesa tassā ukkhittattā “ukkhittapaligho”ti vutto. Saṃkiṇṇaparikhoti parikhā vuccati punabbhavadāyako bhavesu jāyanavasena ceva saṃsaraṇavasena ca “jātisaṃsāro”ti laddhanāmānaṃ punabbhavakkhandhānaṃ paccayo kammābhisaṅkhāro. So hi punappunaṃ uppattikaraṇavasena parikkhipitvā ṭhitattā “parikhā”ti vuccati. Tenesa tassā saṃkiṇṇattā vikiṇṇattā “saṃkiṇṇaparikho”ti vutto. Abbūḷhesikoti esikāti vaṭṭamūlikā taṇhā. Ayañhi gambhīrānugataṭṭhena “esikā”ti vuccati. Tenesa tassā abbūḷhattā luñcitvā chaḍḍitattā “abbūḷhesiko”ti [M 0.0073] vuccati. Niraggaḷoti aggaḷaṃ vuccanti orambhāgajanakāni kāmabhave uppattipaccayāni orambhāgiyāni. Etāni hi mahākavāṭaṃ viya nagaradvāraṃ cittaṃ pidahitvā ṭhitattā “aggaḷa”nti vuccanti[P 1.0086]. Tenesa tesaṃ niraggaḷattā bhinnattā “niraggaḷo”ti vutto. Ariyoti nikkileso parisuddho. Pannaddhajoti pātitamānaddhajo. Pannabhāroti khandhabhārakilesabhāraabhisaṅkhārabhārapañcakāmaguṇabhārā pannā oropitā assāti pannabhāro. Api ca idha mānabhārasseva oropitattā “pannabhāro”ti adhippeto. Visaṃyuttoti catūhi yogehi sabbakilesehi ca visaṃyutto. Idha pana mānayogeneva visaṃyuttattā “visaṃyutto”ti adhippeto.

One whose bolt is removed: here, the bolt is ignorance, which is the root of the cycle of existence. Indeed, because it causes suffering, it is called a 'bolt.' Since this has been removed by him, he is called 'one whose bolt is removed.' One whose moat is scattered: the moat is said to be the kamma formations, the condition for the aggregates of future existence, which give future existence and have gained the name 'the cycle of birth and rebirth' by way of arising in existences and by way of wandering on. Indeed, because it stands encircling by way of repeatedly causing arising, it is called a 'moat.' Since this has been scattered and dispersed by him, he is called 'one whose moat is scattered.' One whose pillar is uprooted: the pillar is craving, the root of the cycle of existence. Indeed, because it has penetrated deeply, it is called a 'pillar.' Since this has been uprooted and cast away by him, he is called 'one whose pillar is uprooted.' Without a bar: the bar is said to be the lower fetters, which generate the lower part of existence and are conditions for arising in the sensual realm. Indeed, because they stand shutting the mind like a great gate-leaf at a city entrance, they are called a 'bar.' Since these have been broken by him, he is called 'one without a bar.' Noble: undefiled, purified. One whose banner is laid down: one whose banner of conceit is laid down. One whose burden is laid down: he is one whose burdens—the burden of the aggregates, the burden of defilements, the burden of volitional formations, and the burden of the five strands of sensual pleasure—have been laid down and put down. Here, however, it is specifically intended to mean the laying down of the burden of conceit, hence 'one whose burden is laid down.' Disjoined: he is disjoined from the four yokes and all defilements. Here, however, it is specifically intended to mean being disjoined from the yoke of conceit, hence 'disjoined'.

Ettāvatā therena maggena kilese khepetvā nirodhasayanavaragatassa khīṇāsavassa nibbānārammaṇaṃ [V 0.0067] phalasamāpattiṃ appetvā viharaṇakālo dassito. Yathā hi dve nagarāni ekaṃ coranagaraṃ, ekaṃ khemanagaraṃ. Atha ekassa mahāyodhassa evaṃ icchā uppajjeyya “yāvimaṃ coranagaraṃ tiṭṭhati, tāva khemanagaraṃ bhayato na muccati. Coranagaraṃ anagaraṃ karissāmī”ti sannāhaṃ katvā khaggaṃ gahetvā coranagaraṃ upasaṅkamitvā nagaradvāre ussāpite esikatthambhe khaggena chinditvā saddhiṃ dvārabāhāhi kavāṭaṃ bhinditvā palighaṃ ukkhipitvā pākāraṃ bhindanto parikhaṃ saṃkiritvā nagarasobhanatthāya ussāpite dhaje pātetvā nagaraṃ agginā jhāpetvā khemanagaraṃ pavisitvā uparipāsādamāruyha ñātigaṇaparivuto surasabhojanaṃ bhuñjeyya. Evaṃ coranagaraṃ viya sakkāyo, khemanagaraṃ viya nibbānaṃ, mahāyodho viya yogāvacaro. Tassevaṃ hoti “yāva sakkāyavaṭṭaṃ vaṭṭati, tāva dvattiṃsakammakāraṇehi aṭṭhanavutirogehi pañcavīsatimahabbhayehi ca parimuccanaṃ natthī”ti. So mahāyodho viya sannāhaṃ sīlasannāhaṃ katvā paññātiṇhakhaggaṃ gahetvā khaggena esikatthambhe viya arahattamaggena taṇhesikaṃ chinditvā, so yodho sadvārabāhakaṃ nagarakavāṭaṃ viya pañcorambhāgiyasaṃyojanaggaḷaṃ ugghoṭetvā, so yodho palighaṃ viya avijjāpalighaṃ ukkhipitvā, so yodho pākāraṃ bhindanto parikhaṃ [P 1.0087] viya kammābhisaṅkhārapākāraṃ bhindanto jātisaṃsāraparikhaṃ saṃkiritvā, so yodho nagarasobhanatthāya ussāpite dhaje viya mānaddhaje [M 0.0074] pātetvā sakkāyanagaraṃ jhāpetvā, so yodho khemanagaraṃ pavisitvā uparipāsāde surasabhojanaṃ bhuñjanto viya nibbānanagaraṃ pavisitvā amatanirodhārammaṇaṃ phalasamāpattisukhaṃ anubhavamāno kālaṃ vītināmeti. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā (a. ni. 5.71) –

By this much, the time of dwelling has been shown for the elder—one whose influxes are destroyed, who has gone to the supreme couch of cessation—who, having destroyed the defilements by the path, dwells having entered the fruition attainment with Nibbāna as its object. Just as there might be two cities—one a city of thieves, the other a city of safety. Then a great warrior might think: 'As long as this city of thieves stands, the city of safety is not free from danger. I will make this city of thieves no city!' Having donned his armor and taken up his sword, he would approach the city of thieves, cut down the pillar erected at the city gate with his sword, smash the gate-leaf together with its doorposts, lift the bolt, and, while breaking down the wall, scatter the moat, fell the banners raised for the city’s adornment, burn the city with fire, enter the city of safety, and, ascending to the upper palace surrounded by his kinsmen, enjoy delicious food. In the same way, the city of thieves is like the existing body, the city of safety is like Nibbāna, and the great warrior is like the practitioner. He thinks: 'As long as the cycle of the existing body revolves, there is no liberation from the thirty-two kinds of torture, the ninety-eight diseases, and the twenty-five great perils.' Like the great warrior, having donned the armor of virtue and taken up the sharp sword of wisdom, and like the warrior cutting the pillar with his sword, he cuts down the pillar of craving with the path to arahantship. Like the warrior smashing the city gate-leaf with its doorposts, he breaks open the bar of the five lower fetters. Like the warrior lifting the bolt, he removes the bolt of ignorance. Like the warrior breaking down the wall and scattering the moat, he breaks down the wall of kamma formations and scatters the moat of the cycle of birth and rebirth. Like the warrior felling the banners raised for the city’s adornment, he fells the banner of conceit. Having burned the city of the existing body, like the warrior entering the city of safety and enjoying delicious food in the upper palace, he enters the city of Nibbāna and spends his time experiencing the bliss of fruition attainment with the deathless cessation as its object. For this was said by the Blessed One (AN 5.71):

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu ukkhittapaligho hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno avijjā pahīnā hoti ucchinnamūlā tālāvatthukatā anabhāvaṃkatā āyatiṃ anuppādadhammā. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu ukkhittapaligho hoti.

And how, monks, is a monk one whose bolt is removed? Here, monks, a monk has abandoned ignorance, its root cut off, made like a palm stump, brought to non-existence, no longer subject to future arising. Thus, monks, a monk is one whose bolt is removed.

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu saṃkiṇṇaparikho hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno ponobhaviko jātisaṃsāro pahīno hoti…pe… evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu saṃkiṇṇaparikho hoti.

And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one whose moat is filled up? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has abandoned the cycle of rebirth leading to renewed existence... Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one whose moat is filled up.

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu abbūḷhesiko hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno taṇhā pahīnā hoti…pe… evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu abbūḷhesiko hoti.

And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one whose bar has been removed? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has abandoned craving... Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one whose bar has been removed.

“Kathañca[V 0.0068], bhikkhave, bhikkhu niraggaḷo hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno pañcorambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni pahīnāni honti…pe… evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu niraggaḷo hoti.

And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu unbolted? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has abandoned the five lower fetters... Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is unbolted.

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu ariyo pannaddhajo pannabhāro visaṃyutto hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno asmimāno pahīno hoti ucchinnamūlo tālāvatthukato anabhāvaṃkato āyatiṃ anuppādadhammo. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu ariyo pannaddhajo pannabhāro visaṃyutto hoti (a. ni. 5.71).

And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu noble, with banner lowered, burden laid down, unfettered? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has abandoned the conceit ‘I am,’ its root destroyed, made like a palm-tree stump, obliterated, subject to no further arising in the future. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is noble, with banner lowered, burden laid down, unfettered.

“Evaṃ vimuttacittaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhuṃ saindā devā sabrahmakā sapajāpatikā anvesaṃ nādhigacchanti ‘idaṃnissitaṃ tathāgatassa viññāṇa’”nti (ma. ni. 1.246).

Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu’s mind is thus liberated, the gods with Indra, with Brahmā, and with Prajāpati, though searching, do not find that the consciousness of the Tathāgata is supported by this.

Pañcaṅgavippahīnoti kāmacchandādipañcaṅgāni vividhehi upāyehi pajahitvā ṭhito. Vuttañhetaṃ –

‘Having abandoned the five factors’ means one who stands firm after abandoning the five factors, such as sensual desire, by various means. For this was said:

“Kathañcāvuso[M 0.0075], bhikkhu pañcaṅgavippahīno hoti? Idhāvuso, bhikkhuno kāmacchando pahīno hoti, byāpādo pahīno hoti, thinamiddhaṃ pahīnaṃ hoti, uddhaccakukkuccaṃ pahīnaṃ hoti, vicikicchā pahīnā [P 1.0088] hoti. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu pañcaṅgavippahīno hotī”ti (dī. ni. 3.348, 360).

And how, friend, is a bhikkhu one who has abandoned the five hindrances? Here, friend, a bhikkhu has abandoned sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt. Thus, friend, a bhikkhu is one who has abandoned the five hindrances.

Chaḷaṅgasamannāgatoti channaṃ aṅgānaṃ pūretvā chasu dvāresu rūpādiārammaṇe paṭighānunayaṃ vajjetvā upekkhāvasena sato sampajāno hutvā viharaṇavasena chaḷaṅgāni pūretvā paripuṇṇaṃ katvā ṭhitattā “chaḷaṅgasamannāgato”ti vutto. Vuttañhetaṃ –

‘Endowed with six factors’ means having fulfilled the six factors by avoiding repulsion and attraction toward visual forms and other objects at the six sense doors, dwelling with equanimity, mindful, and fully aware. Thus, being established in having completely fulfilled the six factors, he is called ‘endowed with six factors.’ For this was said:

“Kathañcāvuso, bhikkhu chaḷaṅgasamannāgato hoti? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā neva sumano hoti na dummano, upekkhako viharati sato sampajāno. Sotena saddaṃ sutvā…pe… ghānena gandhaṃ ghāyitvā, jivhāya rasaṃ sāyitvā, kāyena phoṭṭhabbaṃ phusitvā, manasā dhammaṃ viññāya neva sumano hoti na dummano, upekkhako viharati sato sampajāno. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu chaḷaṅgasamannāgato hotī”ti (dī. ni. 3.348, 360).

And how, friend, is a bhikkhu endowed with six factors? Here, friend, a bhikkhu, having seen a form with the eye, is neither pleased nor displeased, but dwells equanimous, mindful, and fully aware. Having heard a sound with the ear... having smelled an odor with the nose... having tasted a flavor with the tongue... having touched a tangible with the body... having cognized a mental object with the mind, he is neither pleased nor displeased, but dwells equanimous, mindful, and fully aware. Thus, friend, a bhikkhu is endowed with six factors.

Ekārakkhoti [V 0.0069] satiārakkhena eko uttamo ārakkho assāti ekārakkho. Vuttañhetaṃ –

‘One with a single guard’ means that having mindfulness as protection, one is possessed of a single, supreme protection; hence, ‘one with a single guard.’ As it is said:

“Kathañcāvuso, bhikkhu ekārakkho hoti? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu satārakkhena cetasā samannāgato viharati. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu ekārakkho hotī”ti (dī. ni. 3.348, 360).

And how, friend, is a bhikkhu one with a single guard? Here, friend, a bhikkhu dwells possessing a mind guarded by mindfulness. Thus, friend, a bhikkhu is one with a single guard.

Caturāpassenoti paññāya paṭisevanaparivajjanavinodanapajahanānaṃ vasena catunnaṃ apassayānaṃ ito cito ca aparivattamānānaṃ vasena caturāpasseno, tesaṃ pāpuṇitvā ṭhito. Vuttañhetaṃ –

‘One with four supports’ means one who has four supports, in that, by means of wisdom, he uses, avoids, dispels, and abandons; and in that the four supports are not turned away from here or there. Having attained them, he stands firm. As it is said:

“Kathañcāvuso, bhikkhu caturāpasseno hoti? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu saṅkhāyekaṃ paṭisevati, saṅkhāyekaṃ parivajjeti. Saṅkhāyekaṃ [M 0.0076] vinodeti, saṅkhāyekaṃ pajahatī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 3.348, 360) nayena vitthāretabbaṃ.

‘And how, friend, is a bhikkhu one who has four supports? Here, friend, a bhikkhu makes use of one thing after reflection, avoids one thing after reflection, gets rid of one thing after reflection, and gives up one thing after reflection.’ This should be elaborated in detail according to the method given in the Dīgha Nikāya (3.348, 360).

Paṇunnapaccekasaccoti “idameva dassanaṃ saccaṃ, idameva sacca”nti evaṃ pāṭiekkaṃ gahitattā paccekasaṅkhātāni diṭṭhisaccāni paṇunnāni nihaṭāni pahīnāni assāti paṇunnapaccekasacco.

‘One who has dispelled individual truths’ means one for whom those truths which are views, reckoned as individual because they are grasped individually with the thought, ‘This view alone is true, this alone is true,’ are dispelled, removed, and abandoned; therefore he is one who has dispelled individual truths.

Samavayasaṭṭhesanoti ettha avayāti anūnā. Saṭṭhāti vissaṭṭhā. Sammā avayā saṭṭhā esanā assāti samavayasaṭṭhesano. Sammā vissaṭṭhasabbaesanoti attho. Kevalīti [P 1.0089] paripuṇṇo. Vusitavāti vusitabrahmacariyo, garusaṃvāse ariyamaggepi dasasu ariyavāsesupi vusitavanto. Uttamapurisoti khīṇakilesattā visesapuriso ājaññapuriso. Paramapurisoti uttamapuriso, paramaṃ vā paṭilābhaṃ pattattā uttamaṃ pattabbaṃ arahattapaṭilābhaṃ patto anuttarapuññakkhettabhūto uttamapuriso, tenevatthena paramapuriso. Anuttaraṃ samāpattiṃ samāpajjituṃ amataṃ paṭilābhaṃ pattattā paramapattippatto. Atha vā “gharāvāse ādīnavaṃ sañjānitvā sāsanapavisanavasena uttamapuriso. Attabhāve ādīnavaṃ sañjānitvā vipassanāpavisanavasena paramapuriso. Kilese ādīnavaṃ sañjānitvā ariyabhūmantaraṃ paviṭṭho paramapattippattoti evameke vaṇṇayanti.

Here, ‘avayā’ means not incomplete. ‘Saṭṭhā’ means released. ‘Samavayasaṭṭhesano’ means one whose seeking is rightly not incomplete and released. The meaning is one whose every seeking is rightly released. ‘Kevalī’ means complete. ‘Vusitavā’ means one who has lived the holy life, having dwelt with a teacher, in the noble path, and in the ten noble dwellings. ‘Uttamapuriso’ means an excellent person, a distinguished person, a thoroughbred, due to the destruction of defilements. ‘Paramapuriso’ means the supreme person; or, because he has attained the supreme gain—having attained the supreme goal, the attainment of arahantship—he is an excellent person who has become an unsurpassed field of merit; for that reason he is the supreme person. Because he has attained the deathless gain in order to enter the unsurpassed attainment, he is one who has reached the supreme attainment. Alternatively, some explain it thus: ‘Having recognized the dangers in household life, one enters the dispensation and is therefore an excellent person. Having recognized the dangers in individual existence, one enters insight and is therefore a supreme person. Having recognized the dangers in defilements, one enters the noble sphere and has therefore attained the supreme achievement’—thus some explain.

Nevācinatīti [V 0.0070] kusalākusalānaṃ pahīnattā tesaṃ vipākaṃ na vaḍḍheti. Nāpacinatīti phale ṭhitattā na viddhaṃseti. Apacinitvā ṭhitoti paṭippassaddhipahāne ṭhitattā kilese viddhaṃsetvā ṭhito. Ito paraṃ tīhipi padehi maggaphalavaseneva yojetabbaṃ. Neva pajahatīti pahātabbābhāvena kilese na pajahati. Na upādiyatīti taṇhāmānadiṭṭhīhi gahetabbābhāvato tehi na gaṇhāti. Pajahitvā ṭhitoti cajitvā ṭhito. Neva saṃsibbatīti taṇhāvasena neva saṃsibbati. Na ussinetīti mānavasena na ukkaṃsati. Visinitvā ṭhitoti taṇhāsaṃsīvanaṃ akatvā ṭhitoti evameke vaṇṇayanti. Neva vidhūpetīti kilesaggiṃ na nibbāpeti. Na sandhūpetīti kilesaggiṃ na jālāpeti. Vidhūpetvā ṭhitoti taṃ nibbāpetvā ṭhito.

‘He does not accumulate’ means he does not increase the results of what is wholesome and unwholesome because of their abandonment. ‘He does not diminish’ means he does not destroy because he remains stable in the fruit. ‘Having eliminated and remaining’ means he remains after destroying the defilements by standing in relinquishment and calming. From here onward, these three phrases should be connected by way of the path and fruit. ‘He does not abandon’ means he does not abandon the defilements because there is nothing to be abandoned. ‘He does not grasp’ means he does not grasp because there is nothing to be grasped by craving, conceit, or views. ‘Having abandoned and remaining’ means he remains having relinquished. ‘He does not sew’ means he does not sew with craving. ‘He does not exalt’ means he does not elevate himself with conceit. ‘Having disentangled and remaining’ means he remains without creating the sewing of craving—so some explain. ‘He does not extinguish’ means he does not extinguish the fire of defilements. ‘He does not kindle’ means he does not ignite the fire of defilements. ‘Having extinguished and remaining’ means he remains having extinguished it.

Asekkhena [P 1.0090][M 0.0077] sīlakkhandhenāti sikkhitabbābhāvena asekkhena vācākammantājīvasīlakkhandhena sīlarāsinā samannāgatattā ṭhito, aparihīnabhāvena ṭhito. Samādhikkhandhenāti vāyāmasatīhi sampayuttena samādhinā. Vimuttikkhandhenāti phalavimuttisampayuttakkhandhena. Vimuttiñāṇadassanakkhandhenāti paccavekkhaṇañāṇena. Saccaṃ sampaṭipādiyitvāti catuariyasaccaṃ sabhāvavasena sakasantāne sampādiyitvā paṭivijjhitvā ṭhito. Ejaṃ samatikkamitvāti kampanataṇhaṃ atikkamitvā. Kilesagginti rāgādikilesaggiṃ. Pariyādiyitvāti khepetvā nibbāpetvā. Aparigamanatāyāti saṃsāre agamanabhāvena punāgamanābhāvenāti attho. Kaṭaṃ samādāyāti jayaggāhaṃ gahetvā. Muttipaṭisevanatāyāti sabbakilesehi muccitvā rūpādiārammaṇasevanavasena. Atha vā sabbakilesehi muttaphalasamāpattisevanavasena. Mettāya pārisuddhiyāti upakkilesamuttāya parisuddhabhāve ṭhitāya mettāya ṭhito. Karuṇādīsupi eseva nayo.

‘By the aggregate of virtue of the non-learner’ means that because there is nothing further to be trained, or because he is endowed with the aggregate of virtue of the non-learner—a mass of virtue consisting of right speech, right action, and right livelihood—he stands firm, not having declined. ‘By the aggregate of concentration’ means with concentration associated with effort and mindfulness. ‘By the aggregate of liberation’ means with the aggregate associated with the liberation of fruition. ‘By the aggregate of knowledge and vision of liberation’ means with the knowledge of reviewing. ‘Having fully realized the truth’ means having realized and penetrated the four noble truths in their true nature within his own continuity, he stands firm. ‘Having overcome this agitation’ means having transcended the agitation of craving. ‘The fire of defilements’ means the fire of defilements such as lust. ‘Having completely consumed’ means having exhausted and extinguished. ‘By not returning’ means by the state of not going again in the cycle of existence, meaning there is no coming back. ‘Taking up victory’ means having seized the victory. ‘By the enjoyment of liberation’ means being freed from all defilements and enjoying objects such as forms; or alternatively, by the enjoyment of the attainment of fruition, being freed from all defilements. ‘By the purity of loving-kindness’ means standing firm in loving-kindness, which is free from impurities and established in purity. The same method applies to compassion and the others.

Accantapārisuddhiyāti atikkantaparisuddhabhāvena parisuddhiyā antaṃ pāpuṇitvā ṭhito. Atammayatāyāti taṇhādiṭṭhimānā “tammayā”ti vuccanti. Tesaṃ abhāvo atammayatā, tāya taṇhādiṭṭhimānavirahitatāya ṭhito. Vuttañhetaṃ –

‘By utmost purity’ means having reached the limit of purity through a state of surpassing purity, he stands firm. ‘By non-identification’: craving, views, and conceit are called ‘identifications.’ Their absence is non-identification; by that, he stands firm, free from craving, views, and conceit. For this has been said:

“So tādiso lokavidū sumedho, sabbesu dhammesu atammayo munī”ti (a. ni. 3.40). Etthāpi taṇhāmānadiṭṭhivirahitoti attho. Vimuttattāti sabbakilesehi muttabhāvena. Santussitattāti yathālābhayathābalayathāsāruppasantosavasena santuṭṭhabhāvena ṭhito.

‘He is such, a knower of the world, of good wisdom, a sage not identifying with any phenomena.’ Here too, the meaning is being free from craving, conceit, and views. ‘By being liberated’: by the state of being freed from all defilements. ‘By being content’: he stands firm in a state of contentment, by way of contentment with whatever is obtained, according to one's strength, and with what is suitable.

Khandhapariyanteti [P 1.0091] ekacatupañcakkhandhānaṃ tīhi pariññaggīhi jhāpetvā ante avasāne ṭhito[V 0.0071], natthi etassa antoti vā pariyantaṃ, tasmiṃ pariyante. Dhātupariyantādīsupi eseva nayo. Ayaṃ pana viseso – dhātupariyanteti aṭṭhārasannaṃ dhātūnaṃ pariyante. Āyatanapariyanteti dvādasannaṃ āyatanānaṃ. Gatipariyanteti nirayādipañcannaṃ gatīnaṃ. Upapattipariyanteti sugatiduggatīsu nibbattiyā. Paṭisandhipariyanteti kāmarūpārūpabhavesu paṭisandhiyā[M 0.0078]. Bhavapariyanteti ekavokāracatupañcasaññāasaññānevasaññānāsaññākāmarūpaarūpabhavānaṃ. Saṃsārapariyanteti khandhadhātuāyatanānaṃ abbocchinnapavattiyā. Vaṭṭapariyanteti kammavipākakilesavaṭṭānaṃ pariyante. Antime bhaveti avasāne upapattibhave. Antime samussaye ṭhitoti avasāne samussaye sarīre ṭhito. Antimadehadharoti antimaṃ avasānadehaṃ sarīraṃ dhāretīti antimadehadharo. Arahāti ārakattā arīnaṃ, arānañca hatattā, paccayādīnaṃ arahattā, pāpakaraṇe rahābhāvā arahā.

‘With the aggregates as his limit’: he stands at the end, at the final point, having burned up the one, four, or five aggregates with the three fires of full understanding; or, there is no end or limit for him, at that limit. The same method applies to ‘with the elements as his limit’ and so forth. However, this is the distinction: ‘with the elements as his limit’ means at the limit of the eighteen elements. ‘With the sense bases as his limit’ means at the limit of the twelve sense bases. ‘With destinations as his limit’ means at the limit of the five destinations beginning with hell. ‘With rebirth as his limit’ means at the limit of rebirth in good or bad destinations. ‘With re-linking as his limit’ means at the limit of re-linking in the sensual, form, and formless existences. ‘With existence as his limit’ means at the limit of the existences of one-constituent, four-constituent, five-constituent, percipient, non-percipient, neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient, sensual, form, and formless. ‘With the cycle of existence as his limit’ means at the limit of the uninterrupted process of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases. ‘With the round as his limit’ means at the limit of the rounds of kamma, result, and defilements. ‘In his last existence’ means in the final existence of rebirth. ‘Standing in his last body’ means standing in the final collection, the body, at the end. ‘Bearing his last body’ means he bears the final, ultimate body; thus he is one who bears his last body. ‘Arahant’: because of being far from the defilements, because of having destroyed the spokes of the wheel of existence, because of being worthy of requisites, and because of the absence of secrecy in evil-doing, he is an Arahant.

Tassāyaṃ pacchimakoti tassa khīṇāsavassa ayaṃ samussayo attabhāvo avasāno. Carimoti appo mando carimo ālopo, carimaṃ kabaḷaṃ viya. Puna paṭisandhiyā natthibhāvaṃ sandhāya “jātimaraṇasaṃsāro, natthi tassa punabbhavo”ti āha. Jananaṃ jāti, maranti tenāti maraṇaṃ, khandhādīnaṃ abbocchinnā saṃsārapavatti ca tassa khīṇāsavassa puna natthīti vuttaṃ gāthaṃ nigamento āha tenāha bhagavā –

‘This is his last’: for that one whose taints are destroyed, this collection, this individuality, is the end. ‘Final’: like a small, slight, final morsel, like the last mouthful of food. Referring to the non-existence of further re-linking, it is said: ‘The cycle of birth and death; there is no more renewed existence for him.’ Being born is birth; death is that by which one dies; and the uninterrupted process of the aggregates and so forth, the cycle of existence—for that one whose taints are destroyed, this is no more. Concluding the verse that was spoken, he said—therefore the Blessed One said:

“Tasmā jantu…pe… nāvaṃ sitvāva pāragū”ti.

‘Therefore, a being…pe… having bailed out the boat, has gone to the far shore.’

Imasmiṃ sutte yaṃ antarantarā na vuttaṃ, taṃ pāṭhānusārena gahetabbaṃ.

In this discourse, whatever has been omitted in between should be understood according to the text.

Saddhammappajjotikāya mahāniddesaṭṭhakathāya

In the Saddhammappajjotikā, the commentary on the Mahāniddesa.

Kāmasuttaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Kāmasutta Niddesa is completed.

2. Guhaṭṭhakasuttaniddesavaṇṇanā

2. The Explanation of the Guhaṭṭhaka Sutta Niddesa

7. Dutiye [V 0.0072][P 1.0092] – sattoti laggo. Guhāyanti kāye. Kāyo hi rāgādīnaṃ vāḷānaṃ vasanokāsato “guhā”ti vuccati. Bahunābhichannoti bahunā rāgādikilesajātena abhicchanno. Etena ajjhattabandhanaṃ vuttaṃ. Tiṭṭhanti rāgādivasena tiṭṭhanto. Mohanasmiṃ pagāḷhoti mohanaṃ vuccati kāmaguṇo. Ettha hi devamanussā muyhanti tesu ajjhogāḷhā hutvā; etena bāhirabandhanaṃ vuttaṃ. Dūre vivekā hi tathāvidho soti so tathārūpo naro tividhāpi kāyavivekādivivekā dūre[M 0.0079], anāsanne. Kiṃkāraṇā? Kāmā hi loke na hi suppahāyāti yasmā loke kāmā suppahāyā na honti, tasmāti vuttaṃ hoti.

7. In the second verse: ‘Attached’ means clinging. ‘In the cave’ means in the body. The body is indeed called a ‘cave’ because it serves as a dwelling place for the beasts of lust and so on. ‘Covered by much’ means covered by the numerous kinds of defilements born of lust and so on. By this, internal bondage is stated. ‘Standing’ means standing by way of lust and so on. ‘Plunged into delusion’: sensual pleasure is called delusion. For in this, gods and humans are bewildered, having plunged into them; by this, external bondage is stated. ‘Such a one is far from seclusion’: such a person is far from, not near to, the threefold seclusion—seclusion of body and so on. For what reason? ‘Because sensual pleasures in the world are not easily abandoned’ means that because sensual pleasures in the world are not easy to abandon, it is thus stated.

Sattoti hi kho vuttanti “satto, naro, mānavo”ti evamādinā nayena kathitoyeva. Guhā tāva vattabbāti guhā tāva kathetabbā. Kāyoti vātiādīsu ayaṃ tāva padayojanā – kāyo iti vā guhā iti vā…pe… kumbho iti vāti. Tattha kāyoti “kucchitānaṃ āyoti kāyo”tiādinā heṭṭhā satipaṭṭhānakathāyaṃ vuttoyeva. Rāgādivāḷānaṃ vasanokāsaṭṭhena guhā, “paṭicchādanaṭṭhenā”tipi eke. “Dūraṅgamaṃ ekacaraṃ, asarīraṃ guhāsaya”ntiādīsu (dha. pa. 37) viya. Rāgādīhi jhāpanaṭṭhena deho “te hitvā mānusaṃ deha”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.332 thokaṃ visadisaṃ) viya. Pamattakaraṇaṭṭhena sandeho “bhijjati pūtisandeho, maraṇantañhi jīvita”ntiādīsu (dha. pa. 148) viya. Saṃsāre [P 1.0093] sañcaraṇaṭṭhena nāvā “siñca bhikkhu imaṃ nāvaṃ, sittā te lahumessatī”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 369) viya. Iriyāpathassa atthibhāvaṭṭhena ratho “ratho sīlaparikkhāro, jhānakkho cakkavīriyo”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 5.4) viya. Accuggataṭṭhena dhajo “dhajo rathassa paññāṇa”ntiādīsu (jā. 2.22.1841) viya.

The word ‘satto’ has indeed been explained by the method beginning with ‘a being,’ ‘a person,’ ‘a human,’ and so forth. ‘The cave should now be spoken of’ means the cave should now be discussed. Regarding ‘body’ and so on, this is the application of the terms: ‘body’ or ‘cave’… or ‘pot.’ Therein, ‘body’ has been explained below in the discussion on the foundations of mindfulness by the method beginning with ‘the body is a collection of disgusting things.’ It is a ‘cave’ in the sense of being a dwelling place for the beasts of lust and so on; some also say in the sense of concealing. As in such verses as: ‘Far-going, solitary, bodiless, dwelling in a cave’ (Dhammapada 37). It is a ‘body’ (deho) in the sense of being burned by lust and so on, as in: ‘Having abandoned the human body’ (Dīgha Nikāya 2.332, slightly different). It is a ‘heap’ (sandeho) in the sense of causing heedlessness, as in: ‘This putrid heap breaks apart, for death is indeed the end of life’ (Dhammapada 148). It is a ‘boat’ (nāvā) in the sense of traversing the cycle of existence, as in: ‘O monk, empty this boat; emptied, it will go swiftly’ (Dhammapada 369). It is a ‘chariot’ (ratho) in the sense of possessing the postures, as in: ‘The chariot is equipped with virtue, meditation its axle, energy its wheels’ (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.4). It is a ‘banner’ (dhajo) in the sense of being lofty, as in: ‘Wisdom is the banner of the chariot’ (Jātaka 2.22.1841).

Kimikulānaṃ āvāsabhāvena vammiko “vammikoti kho, bhikkhu, imassetaṃ cātumahābhūtikassa [V 0.0073] kāyassa adhivacana”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.251) viya. Yatheva hi bāhirako vammiko, vamati vantako vantussayo vantasinehasambaddhoti catūhi kāraṇehi “vammiko”ti vuccati. So hi ahinakulaundūragharagoḷikādayo nānappakāre pāṇake vamatīti vammiko. Upacikāhi vantakoti vammiko. Upacikāhi vamitvā mukhatuṇḍakehi ukkhittapaṃsucuṇṇena kaṭippamāṇenapi porisappamāṇenapi ussitoti vammiko. Upacikāhi vantakheḷasinehena ābaddhatāya sattasattāhaṃ deve vassantepi na vippakirīyati, nidāghepi tato paṃsumuṭṭhiṃ gahetvā [M 0.0080] tasmiṃ muṭṭhinā pīḷiyamāne sineho nikkhamati, evaṃ vantasinehena sambaddhoti vammiko. Evamayaṃ kāyopi “akkhimhā aggigūthako”tiādinā nayena nānappakāraṃ asucikalimalaṃ vamatīti vammiko. Buddhapaccekabuddhakhīṇāsavā imasmiṃ attabhāve nikantipariyādānena attabhāvaṃ chaḍḍetvā gatāti ariyehi vantakotipi vammiko. Yehi cāyaṃ tīhi aṭṭhisatehi ussito nahārusambaddho maṃsāvalepano allacammapariyonaddho chavirañjito satte vañceti, taṃ sabbaṃ ariyehi vantamevāti vantussayotipi vammiko. “Taṇhā janeti purisaṃ, cittamassa vidhāvatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.55-57) evaṃ taṇhāya janitattā ariyehi vanteneva taṇhāsinehena sambaddho ayanti vantasinehena sambaddhotipi vammiko. Yathā ca vammikassa anto nānappakārā pāṇakā tattheva jāyanti, uccārapassāvaṃ [P 1.0094] karonti, gilānā sayanti, matā nipatanti. Iti so tesaṃ sūtigharaṃ vaccakuṭi gilānasālā susānañca hoti. Evaṃ khattiyamahāsālādīnampi kāyo “ayaṃ gopitarakkhito maṇḍitapasādito mahānubhāvānaṃ kāyo”ti acintetvā chavinissitā pāṇā cammanissitā pāṇā maṃsanissitā pāṇā nahārunissitā pāṇā aṭṭhinissitā pāṇā aṭṭhimiñjanissitā pāṇāti evaṃ kulagaṇanāya asītimattāni kimikulasahassāni antokāyasmiṃyeva jāyanti, uccārapassāvaṃ karonti, gelaññena āturitāni sayanti, matāmatā nipatanti. Iti ayampi tesaṃ pāṇānaṃ sūtigharaṃ vaccakuṭi gilānasālā susānañca hotīti “vammiko”ti saṅkhaṃ gato.

The body is called an 'anthill' (vammiko) in the sense of being a dwelling place for families of worms, as in, 'Monk, “anthill” is a designation for this body composed of the four great elements' (MN 1.251), and so on. For just as an external anthill is called an 'anthill' for four reasons—because it ejects, because it is ejected, because it is a heap of ejected matter, and because it is bound by ejected moisture. It is called an anthill because it ejects various creatures like snakes, mongooses, rats, house lizards, and so on. It is called an anthill because it is ejected by termites. It is called an anthill because termites, after ejecting, pile up dust with their mandibles, raised to the height of the waist or even a person. It is called an anthill because it is bound by the ejected saliva-moisture, such that it does not scatter even when it rains for seven weeks, and even in the hot season, if one takes a handful of its dust and squeezes it, moisture comes out; thus, it is bound by ejected moisture. In the same way, this body is called an anthill because it ejects various kinds of impure filth, in the manner of 'eye-dirt from the eye,' and so on. Furthermore, since Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Arahants have departed, having abandoned this individual existence by the exhaustion of attachment, it is 'ejected by the noble ones.' And because this body—raised up with three hundred bones, bound by tendons, plastered with flesh, overlaid with moist skin, and painted with a complexion—deceives beings, all that is ejected by the noble ones; thus it is a 'heap of ejected matter.' Moreover, because it is said, 'Craving generates a person, his mind runs about' (SN 1.55-57), this body, being generated by craving, is bound by the moisture of craving, which is itself ejected by the noble ones; thus it is also 'bound by ejected moisture.' And just as inside an anthill various creatures are born, excrete, lie sick, and fall down dead—making it a birthing chamber, a latrine, a sickroom, and a cemetery for them—so too, in the body of even a great Khattiya noble, without considering, 'This is the body of one of great power, guarded, protected, adorned, and beautified,' creatures that depend on the skin, creatures that depend on the dermis, creatures that depend on the flesh, creatures that depend on the tendons, creatures that depend on the bones, and creatures that depend on the bone marrow—thus, by count of families, some eighty thousand families of worms are born right inside the body. They excrete, lie there afflicted with illness, and fall down dead. Thus, this body too is for those creatures a birthing chamber, a latrine, a sickroom, and a cemetery. For this reason, it has come to be designated an 'anthill'.

Manāpāmanāpapatanaṭṭhena nagaraṃ “sakkāyanagara”ntiādīsu viya. Rogādīnaṃ nīḷabhāvena kulāvakabhāvena nīḷaṃ “roganīḷaṃ pabhaṅgura”ntiādīsu (dha. pa. 148) viya. Paṭisandhiyā nivāsagehaṭṭhena kuṭi “pañcadvārāyaṃ kuṭikāyaṃ pasakkiyā”tiādīsu (theragā. 125) viya. Pūtibhāvena gaṇḍo “rogoti bhikkhave, gaṇḍoti bhikkhave, salloti bhikkhave, kāyassetaṃ adhivacana”ntiādīsu (a. ni. 9.15) viya. Bhijjanaṭṭhena kumbho “kumbhūpamaṃ kāyamimaṃ viditvā”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 40) viya. Kāyassetaṃ adhivacananti etaṃ vuttappakāraṃ catumahābhūtamayassa kucchitadhammānaṃ āyassa adhivacanaṃ, kathananti attho. Guhāyanti sarīrasmiṃ[V 0.0074][M 0.0081]. Sattoti allīno. Visattoti vaṇṇarāgādivasena vividho allīno. Saṇṭhānarāgavasena āsatto. Tattheva [P 1.0095] “subhaṃ sukha”nti gahaṇavasena laggo. Attaggahaṇavasena laggito. Palibuddhoti phassarāgavasena amuñcitvā ṭhito. Bhittikhileti bhittiyaṃ ākoṭitakhāṇuke. Nāgadanteti tatheva hatthidantasadise vaṅkadaṇḍake. Sattanti bhittikhile laggaṃ. Visattanti nāgadante laggaṃ. Āsattanti cīvaravaṃse laggaṃ. Lagganti cīvararajjuyā laggaṃ. Laggitanti pīṭhapāde laggaṃ. Palibuddhanti mañcapāde lagganti evamādinā nayena yojetabbaṃ.

The body is called a 'city' (nagara) in the sense of being a place where pleasant and unpleasant things fall, as in 'the city of one's own body' (sakkāyanagara), and so on. The body is called a 'nest' (nīḷa) because it is a nest, a bird's nest, for illnesses and so on, as in 'a nest of illness, fragile' (Dhp 148). The body is called a 'hut' (kuṭi) in the sense of being a dwelling place for rebirth-linking, as in 'in this hut with five doors' (Thag 125). Due to its putrid nature, it is called a 'boil' (gaṇḍa), as in '“Illness,” monks; “boil,” monks; “dart,” monks—this is a designation for this body' (AN 9.15), and so on. Due to its breakable nature, it is called a 'pot' (kumbha), as in 'knowing this body to be like a pot' (Dhp 40). 'This is a designation for the body' means this is a designation, a term, for this body which is composed of the four great elements and is a source of contemptible things. 'In the cave' means in the body. 'Satta' means adhering. 'Visatta' means diversely adhering due to lust for beauty and so on. 'Āsatta' means attached through lust for shape. 'Lagga' means stuck, through grasping it as 'beautiful' and 'pleasant.' 'Laggita' means made to stick, through grasping at a self. 'Palibuddha' means obstructed, standing unreleased due to lust for contact. 'Bhittikhila' means a peg hammered into a wall. 'Nāgadanta' means similarly, a curved peg like an elephant's tusk. 'Satta' means clinging to a wall peg. 'Visatta' means clinging to an elephant-tusk peg. 'Āsatta' means clinging to a robe-pole. 'Lagga' means clinging to a robe-rope. 'Laggita' means clinging to a chair leg. 'Palibuddha' means clinging to a bed leg—in this way it should be connected.

Lagganādhivacananti visesena allīyanakathanaṃ. Channoti vuttappakārehi kilesehi chādito. Punappunaṃ uppattivasena uparūpari channoti ucchanno. Āvutoti āvarito. Nivutoti vārito. Ophutoti avattharitvā chādito. Pihitoti bhājanena ukkhalimukhaṃ viya paliguṇṭhito. Paṭicchannoti āvaṭo. Paṭikujjitoti adhomukhaṃ ṭhapito. Tattha tiṇapaṇṇādīhi chāditaṃ viya channo. Ucchanno nadiṃ āvaraṇasetu viya. Āvuto janasañcaraṇamaggāvaraṇaṃ viya.

'Lagganādhivacana' means a specific explanation of adhering. 'Channo' means covered by the defilements of the types mentioned. 'Ucchanno' means covered repeatedly, over and over, due to arising again and again. 'Āvuto' means obstructed. 'Nivuto' means warded off. 'Ophuto' means covered by overspreading. 'Pihito' means wrapped, like the mouth of a cooking pot covered by a lid. 'Paṭicchanno' means covered. 'Paṭikujjito' means placed face down. There, 'channo' is like something covered by grass and leaves. 'Ucchanno' is like a dam obstructing a river. 'Āvuto' is like an obstruction blocking a public path.

Vinibaddho mānavasenāti nānāvidhena mānātimānavasena nānāvidhe ārammaṇe baddho hutvā tiṭṭhati. Parāmaṭṭho diṭṭhivasenāti dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhīnaṃ vasena parāmaṭṭho āmasitvā gahito. Vikkhepagato uddhaccavasenāti ārammaṇe asantiṭṭhanavasena cittavikkhepaṃ patto upagato. Aniṭṭhaṅgato vicikicchāvasenāti ratanattayādīsu kaṅkhāsaṅkhātāya vicikicchāya vasena sanniṭṭhānaṃ appatto. Thāmagato anusayavasenāti dunnīharaṇaappahīnānusayavasena thirabhāvaṃ patto upagato hutvā tiṭṭhati.

'Vinibaddho mānavasena' (bound by conceit) means standing bound to various objects by various kinds of conceit and excessive conceit. 'Parāmaṭṭho diṭṭhivasena' (grasped by views) means grasped and seized by way of the sixty-two views. 'Vikkhepagato uddhaccavasena' (distracted by restlessness) means having attained and arrived at distraction of mind due to inability to remain steady on an object. 'Aniṭṭhaṅgato vicikicchāvasena' (unsettled by doubt) means not having attained certainty due to doubt, which is hesitation concerning the Triple Gem and other matters. 'Thāmagato anusayavasena' (firmly rooted by latent tendencies) means having attained and arrived at a state of firmness due to latent tendencies that are difficult to remove and have not been abandoned, and thus standing.

Rūpūpayanti taṇhādiṭṭhūpayavasena rūpaṃ upagantvā ārammaṇaṃ katvā. Viññāṇaṃ tiṭṭhamānaṃ tiṭṭhatīti tasmiṃ ārammaṇe rūpārammaṇaṃ viññāṇaṃ tiṭṭhantaṃ tiṭṭhati. Rūpārammaṇaṃ [P 1.0096] rūpapatiṭṭhanti rūpameva ārammaṇaṃ ālambitvā rūpameva patiṭṭhaṃ katvā. Nandūpasecananti sappītikataṇhodakena āsittaṃ viññāṇaṃ. Vuddhinti vuddhibhāvaṃ. Virūḷhinti javanavasena uparito virūḷhibhāvaṃ. Vepullanti tadārammaṇavasena vepullaṃ.

Rūpūpayanti: by way of craving and views approaching form, having approached form and made it their object. Viññāṇaṃ tiṭṭhamānaṃ tiṭṭhatīti: consciousness stands established on that object, that is, consciousness stands established with form as its object. Rūpārammaṇaṃ rūpapatiṭṭhanti: having form as its object, established in form, by taking form as its object and making form its foundation. Nandūpasecananti: consciousness sprinkled with the water of craving accompanied by joy. Vuddhi: a state of growth. Virūḷhi: a state of flourishing upwards by way of impulsion. Vepulla: abundance by way of that object.

Atthi [M 0.0082] rāgotiādīni lobhasseva nāmāni. So hi rañjanavasena rāgo, nandanavasena nandī, taṇhāyanavasena taṇhāti vuccati. Patiṭṭhitaṃ tattha viññāṇaṃ virūḷhanti kammaṃ javāpetvā paṭisandhiākaḍḍhanasamatthatāya patiṭṭhitañceva virūḷhañca. Yatthāti tebhūmakavaṭṭe bhummaṃ. Sabbattha vā purimapade etaṃ bhummaṃ. Atthi tattha saṅkhārānaṃ vuddhīti idaṃ imasmiṃ vipākavaṭṭe ṭhitassa āyatiṃ [V 0.0075] vaṭṭahetuke saṅkhāre sandhāya vuttaṃ. Yattha atthi āyatiṃ punabbhavābhinibbattīti yasmiṃ ṭhāne āyatiṃ punabbhavābhinibbatti atthi. Tattha purimasuttaṃ rūpādiārammaṇalagganavasena vuttaṃ, dutiyasuttaṃ tadevārammaṇaṃ abhinandanavasena vuttaṃ, tatiyaṃ viññāṇapatiṭṭhānavasena vuttaṃ, catutthaṃ catubbidhaāhāravasena, kusalākusalaviññāṇapatiṭṭhānavasena vuttanti ñātabbaṃ.

Atthi rāgotiādīni: these and other terms like 'lust' are names for greed. Indeed, it is called lust due to its nature of coloring, delight due to its nature of enjoying, and craving due to its nature of thirsting. Patiṭṭhitaṃ tattha viññāṇaṃ virūḷhanti: consciousness established there grows, meaning it is both established and grown by having propelled kamma and being capable of attracting rebirth-linking. Yattha: this is the locative case, referring to the round of the three planes. Or, in all cases, this locative case refers to the preceding term. Atthi tattha saṅkhārānaṃ vuddhī: this is said with reference to the formations that are causes for the round in the future, for one abiding in this round of results. Yattha atthi āyatiṃ punabbhavābhinibbattīti: in that place where future rebirth arises. It should be understood that the first discourse is spoken with reference to clinging to forms and other objects; the second discourse, with reference to delighting in that same object; the third, with reference to the establishment of consciousness; and the fourth, with reference to the four kinds of nutriment and the establishment of wholesome and unwholesome consciousness.

Yebhuyyenāti pāyena. Muyhantīti mohaṃ āpajjanti. Sammuyhantīti visesena muyhanti. Sampamuyhantīti sabbākārena muyhanti. Atha vā rūpārammaṇaṃ paṭicca muyhanti, saddārammaṇaṃ paṭicca sammuyhanti, mutārammaṇaṃ paṭicca sampamuyhanti. Avijjāya andhīkatāti aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu aññāṇāya avijjāya andhīkatā. “Gatā”ti vā pāṭho, andhabhāvaṃ upagatāti attho. Pagāḷhoti paviṭṭho. Ogāḷhoti heṭṭhābhāgaṃ paviṭṭho. Ajjhogāḷhoti adhiogāhitvā avattharitvā visesena paviṭṭho nimuggoti adhomukhaṃ hutvā paviṭṭho. Atha vā dassanasaṃsaggena [P 1.0097] ogāḷho. Savanasaṃsaggena ajjhogāḷho. Vacanasaṃsaggena nimuggo. Sappurisasaṃsaggavirahito vā ogāḷho. Saddhammasevanavirahito vā ajjhogāḷho. Dhammānudhammapaṭipattivirahito vā nimuggo.

Yebhuyyena: generally. Muyhanti: they fall into delusion. Sammuyhanti: they are especially deluded. Sampamuyhanti: they are deluded in every way. Alternatively, they are deluded on account of a form as object, especially deluded on account of a sound as object, and completely deluded on account of what is sensed by the nose, tongue, and body as object. Avijjāya andhīkatā: blinded by ignorance, by unknowing in eight instances. 'Gatā' is also a reading, meaning they have gone to a state of blindness. Pagāḷha: entered. Ogāḷha: entered the lower part. Ajjhogāḷha: having deeply penetrated, having pervaded, especially entered. Nimugga: having entered face-down. Alternatively, 'ogāḷha' is through contact with sight; 'ajjhogāḷha' is through contact with hearing; 'nimugga' is through contact with speech. Or, one is 'ogāḷha' by being devoid of association with good people; 'ajjhogāḷha' by being devoid of association with the true Dhamma; and 'nimugga' by being devoid of the practice in accordance with the Dhamma.

Vivekāti vivitti, viviccanaṃ vā viveko. Tayoti gaṇanaparicchedo. Kāyavivekoti kāyena vivitti, vinā apasakkanaṃ. Cittavivekādīsupi eseva nayo. Idha bhikkhūti imasmiṃ sāsane. Saṃsāre bhayaṃ ikkhanato bhikkhu. Vivittanti suññaṃ, appasaddaṃ appanigghosanti attho. Etadeva hi sandhāya vibhaṅge “vivittanti santike cepi senāsanaṃ hoti, tañca anākiṇṇaṃ gahaṭṭhehi pabbajitehi, tena taṃ vivitta”nti (vibha. 526) vuttaṃ. Seti ceva āsati ca etthāti senāsanaṃ, mañcapīṭhādīnametamadhivacanaṃ. Tenāha –

Viveka: seclusion or separation. Tayo: an enumeration. Kāyaviveka: seclusion by body, that is, withdrawal. The same principle applies to cittaviveka and others. Idha bhikkhu: in this Dispensation. A bhikkhu is one who sees danger in saṃsāra. Vivitta: empty, quiet, and free from noise—this is the meaning. With this in mind, it is said in the Vibhaṅga: 'Even if a dwelling is nearby, if it is not crowded with householders or renunciants, then it is secluded' (Vibhaṅga 526). Senāsana: a place where one both lies down and sits; this is a term for beds, chairs, and the like. Hence it is said—

“Senāsananti [M 0.0083] mañcopi senāsanaṃ, pīṭhampi… bhisipi… bibbohanampi… vihāropi… aḍḍhayogopi… pāsādopi… aṭṭopi… māḷopi… leṇampi… guhāpi… rukkhamūlampi… veḷugumbopi… yattha vā pana bhikkhū paṭikkamanti, sabbametaṃ senāsana”nti (vibha. 527).

"A dwelling place includes a couch, a chair, a cushion, a bolster, a monastery, a gabled building, a palace, a flat-roofed dwelling, a storied building, a rock shelter, a cave, the foot of a tree, a bamboo grove—or wherever monks retire, all that is a dwelling place" (Vibhaṅga 527).

Api ca vihāro aḍḍhayogo pāsādo hammiyaṃ guhāti idaṃ vihārasenāsanaṃ nāma. Mañco pīṭhaṃ bhisi bibbohananti idaṃ mañcapīṭhasenāsanaṃ nāma. Cimilikā cammakhaṇḍo tiṇasanthāro paṇṇasanthāroti idaṃ santhatasenāsanaṃ nāma. Yattha vā pana bhikkhū paṭikkamanti, idaṃ okāsasenāsanaṃ [V 0.0076] nāmāti evaṃ catubbidhaṃ senāsanaṃ hoti. Taṃ sabbampi senāsanaggahaṇena gahitameva.

Furthermore, a monastery, a gabled building, a palace, a mansion, a cave—this is called a monastery-dwelling. A couch, a seat, a mattress, a pillow—this is called a couch-and-seat dwelling. A screen, a piece of hide, a grass mat, a leaf mat—this is called a mat-dwelling. Or wherever monks retire, this is called an open-space dwelling. Thus there are four kinds of dwellings. All of these are included in the term 'dwelling'.

Idha panassa sakuṇasadisassa cātuddisassa bhikkhuno anucchavikasenāsanaṃ dassento “araññaṃ rukkhamūla”ntiādimāha. Tattha araññanti “nikkhamitvā bahi indakhīlā sabbametaṃ arañña”nti (vibha. 529) idaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ vasena āgataṃ. “Āraññakaṃ nāma senāsanaṃ pañcadhanusatikaṃ pacchima”nti (pārā. 654) idaṃ [P 1.0098] pana imassa bhikkhuno anurūpaṃ. Tassa lakkhaṇaṃ visuddhimagge dhutaṅganiddese (visuddhi. 1.31) vuttaṃ. Rukkhamūlanti yaṃkiñci santacchāyaṃ vivittaṃ rukkhamūlaṃ. Pabbatanti selaṃ. Tattha hi udakasoṇḍīsu udakakiccaṃ katvā sītāya rukkhacchāyāya nisinnassa nānādisāsu khāyamānāsu sītena vātena bījiyamānassa cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti. Kandaranti kaṃ vuccati udakaṃ, tena dāritaṃ, udakena bhinnaṃ pabbatapadesaṃ. Yaṃ “nadītumba”ntipi “nadīkuñja”ntipi vadanti. Tattha hi rajatapaṭṭasadisā vālukā hoti, matthake maṇivitānaṃ viya vanagahanaṃ, maṇikhandhasadisaṃ udakaṃ sandati. Evarūpaṃ kandaraṃ oruyha pānīyaṃ pivitvā gattāni sītāni katvā vālukaṃ ussāpetvā paṃsukūlacīvaraṃ paññapetvā nisinnassa samaṇadhammaṃ karoto cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti. Giriguhanti dvinnaṃ pabbatānaṃ antaraṃ, ekasmiṃyeva vā umaṅgasadisaṃ mahāvivaraṃ. Susānalakkhaṇaṃ visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.34) vuttaṃ.

Here, for a monk who is like a bird, free in all directions, a suitable dwelling is described, beginning with 'the wilderness, the foot of a tree.' In this context, arañña, 'the wilderness,' is defined as: 'having gone beyond the city boundary post, all that lies outside is wilderness' (Vibhaṅga 529). This is stated with reference to nuns. 'A wilderness dwelling is a lodging at a minimum distance of five hundred bow-lengths' (Pārājika 654); this, however, is appropriate for this monk. Its characteristics are explained in the Visuddhimagga, in the section on the ascetic practices (Visuddhimagga 1.31). Rukkhamūla: any quiet, shaded foot of a tree. Pabbata: a mountain. There, after performing water-related duties at the water channels, sitting in the cool shade of a tree while various directions are visible, fanned by the cool breeze, the mind becomes unified. Kandara: a ravine, so called because 'kaṃ' means water, and it is split by it—a mountain area broken by water. It is also referred to as a 'river-basin' or a 'river-grove.' There, the sand is like silver plates, the dense forest canopy above is like a jeweled canopy, and the flowing water resembles a mass of jewels. Descending into such a ravine, drinking water, cooling the limbs, piling up sand, spreading out the rag-robe, and sitting while practicing the ascetic’s duties, the mind becomes unified. Giriguha: the space between two mountains, or in a single mountain a large opening resembling a tunnel. The characteristics of a charnel ground are explained in the Visuddhimagga (Visuddhimagga 1.34).

Vanapatthanti gāmantaṃ atikkamitvā manussānaṃ anupacāraṭṭhānaṃ yattha na kasanti na vapanti. Tenevāha “vanapatthanti dūrānametaṃ senāsanānaṃ adhivacana”ntiādi (vibha. 531). Abbhokāsanti acchannaṃ. Ākaṅkhamāno panettha cīvarakuṭiṃ [M 0.0084] katvā vasati. Palālapuñjanti palālarāsiṃ. Mahāpalālapuñjato hi palālaṃ nikkaḍḍhitvā pabbhāraleṇasadise ālaye karonti, gacchagumbādīnampi upari palālaṃ pakkhipitvā heṭṭhā nisinnā samaṇadhammaṃ karonti. Sabbametaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “kāyena vivitto viharatī”tiādi. Eko caṅkamaṃ adhiṭṭhāti pavattayatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Iriyatīti iriyāpathaṃ vattayati. Vattatīti iriyāpathavuttiṃ uppādeti. Pāletīti iriyāpathaṃ rakkhati. Yapetīti yapayati. Yāpetīti yāpayati.

Vanapattha: a place beyond the village boundaries, a place not frequented by people, where they do not plow or sow. Hence it is said, 'Vanapattha is a term for remote dwellings,' and so on (Vibhaṅga 531). Abbhokāsa: an uncovered space. One who wishes may build a robe-hut there and dwell. Palālapuñja: a pile of straw. For they pull out straw from a large heap of straw and make dwellings resembling rock overhangs, or they place straw over the tops of bushes, shrubs and the like, then sit beneath and practice the ascetic life. All this is said with reference to the statement, 'He dwells secluded in body,' and so on. Eko caṅkamaṃ adhiṭṭhāti: one undertakes walking meditation. This means one sets it in motion. Iriyati: one maintains a posture. Vattati: one generates the conduct of a posture. Pāleti: one guards the posture. Yapeti: one maintains oneself. Yāpeti: one keeps oneself going.

Paṭhamaṃ [P 1.0099] jhānaṃ samāpannassāti kusalajjhānasamaṅgissa. Nīvaraṇehi cittaṃ vivittanti upacārena nīvaraṇehi vivittampi samānaṃ antoappanāyaṃ suṭṭhu vivittaṃ nāma hotīti dassetuṃ “paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa nīvaraṇehi cittaṃ vivittaṃ hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Eseva nayo vitakkavicārapītisukhadukkhehi [V 0.0077] dutiyatatiyacatutthajjhānāni samāpannānanti. Rūpasaññāyāti kusalavipākakiriyavasena pañcadasannaṃ rūpāvacarajjhānānaṃ saññāya. Paṭighasaññāyāti cakkhurūpādisaṅghaṭṭanena uppannāya kusalākusalavipākavasena dvipañcaviññāṇasaṅkhātāya paṭighasaññāya ca. Nānattasaññāyāti nānārammaṇe pavattāya catucattālīsakāmāvacarasaññāya ca cittaṃ vivittaṃ hoti suññaṃ hoti.

One who has attained the first jhāna: for one endowed with a wholesome jhāna. 'The mind is secluded from the hindrances': although it is secluded from the hindrances by way of access concentration, it is called truly secluded within absorption. To show this, it is said: 'For one who has attained the first jhāna, the mind is secluded from the hindrances.' The same principle applies to those who have attained the second, third, and fourth jhānas, from applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, happiness, and suffering. 'From perceptions of form': from the perception of the fifteen form-sphere jhānas, whether wholesome, resultant, or functional. 'From perceptions of resistance': and from the perception of resistance that arises through the contact of the eye with forms, etc., which is designated as the two sets of five consciousnesses, whether wholesome, unwholesome, or resultant. 'From perceptions of diversity': and from the forty-four sense-sphere perceptions that occur with diverse objects, the mind is secluded; it is empty.

Ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samāpannassāti ettha nāssa antoti anantaṃ, ākāsaṃ anantaṃ ākāsānantaṃ, ākāsānantameva ākāsānañcaṃ, taṃ ākāsānañcaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena āyatanamassa sasampayuttadhammassa jhānassa devānaṃ devāyatanamivāti ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ, kasiṇugghāṭimākāsārammaṇajhānassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Taṃ ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samāpannassa kusalakiriyajhānaṃ samāpannassa. Rūpasaññāyāti saññāsīsena rūpāvacarajjhānato ceva tadārammaṇato ca. Rūpāvacarajjhānampi hi “rūpa”nti vuccati “rūpī rūpāni passatī”tiādīsu (paṭi. ma. 1.209), tassa ārammaṇampi “bahiddhā rūpāni passati suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇānī”tiādīsupi (paṭi. ma. 1.209). Tasmā idha rūpe saññā rūpasaññāti evaṃ saññāsīsena rūpāvacarajjhānassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Rūpe saññā assāti rūpasaññaṃ, rūpamassa nāmanti vuttaṃ hoti. Evaṃ pathavīkasiṇādibhedassa tadārammaṇassa [M 0.0085] cetaṃ adhivacananti veditabbaṃ. Etāya kusalavipākakiriyāvasena pañcadasavidhāya [P 1.0100] jhānasaṅkhātāya rūpasaññāya. Etāya ca pathavīkasiṇādivasena aṭṭhavidhāya ārammaṇasaṅkhātāya rūpasaññāya.

One who has attained the base of infinite space: here, 'no end' means infinite; space is infinite, thus 'infinite space.' Infinite space itself is the 'base of infinite space.' That is called the base because it serves as a foundation for this jhāna and its associated states, just as a divine abode is for the gods. This is a designation for the jhāna whose object is space revealed by the removal of the kasiṇa. One who has attained this base of infinite space: one who has attained this wholesome or functional jhāna. 'From perception of form': this refers, in terms of perception, to both the form-sphere jhānas and their objects. For even the form-sphere jhāna is called 'form,' as in passages like 'one with form sees forms' (Paṭis I 209), and its object also, as in 'one sees external forms, beautiful and ugly' (Paṭis I 209). Therefore, here 'perception of form' means perception related to form, and this is a designation for the form-sphere jhāna in terms of perception. 'One has perception of form' means that form is its name. Thus, it should be understood that this is a designation for its object, such as the earth-kasiṇa and others. [The mind is secluded] from this perception of form, which is of fifteen kinds classified as jhānas—wholesome, resultant, or functional; and from this perception of form, which is of eight kinds classified by objects, such as the earth-kasiṇa.

Paṭighasaññāyāti cakkhādīnaṃ vatthūnaṃ rūpādīnaṃ ārammaṇānañca paṭighātena samuppannā saññā paṭighasaññā, rūpasaññādīnaṃ etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Yathāha – “tattha katamā paṭighasaññā? Rūpasaññā saddasaññā gandhasaññā rasasaññā phoṭṭhabbasaññā, imā vuccanti paṭighasaññāyo”ti (vibha. 603). Tā kusalavipākā pañca akusalavipākā pañcāti etāya paṭighasaññāya.

From perception of resistance: Perception that arises through the impact between the bases, such as the eye, and their objects, such as forms, is perception of resistance. This is a designation for perceptions of form, and so on. As it is said: 'Therein, what is perception of resistance? Perception of form, perception of sound, perception of smell, perception of taste, perception of the tangible—these are called perceptions of resistance' (Vibh 603). [The mind is secluded] from this perception of resistance, of which there are five that are wholesome-resultant and five that are unwholesome-resultant.

Nānattasaññāyāti nānatte gocare pavattāya saññāya, nānattāya vā saññāya. Yathāha – “tattha katamā nānattasaññā? Asamāpannassa manodhātusamaṅgissa vā manoviññāṇadhātusamaṅgissa vā saññā sañjānanā sañjānitattaṃ, imā vuccanti nānattasaññāyo”ti (vibha. 604) evaṃ vibhaṅge vibhajitvā vuttā. Tā idha adhippetā. Asamāpannassa manodhātumanoviññāṇadhātusaṅgahitā saññā rūpasaddādibhede nānatte nānāsabhāve gocare pavattanti. Yasmā cesā aṭṭha kāmāvacarakusalasaññā, dvādasa akusalasaññā, ekādasa kāmāvacarakusalavipākasaññā, dve akusalavipākasaññā[V 0.0078], ekādasa kāmāvacarakiriyasaññāti evaṃ catucattālīsampi saññā nānattā nānāsabhāvā aññamaññaṃ asadisā, tasmā “nānattasaññā”ti vuttā, tāya nānattasaññāya.

From perception of diversity: from perception occurring in a diverse domain, or from perception that is itself diverse. As it is said: 'Therein, what is perception of diversity? For one who has not attained absorption, who is endowed with the mind-element or endowed with the mind-consciousness-element, the perception, the act of perceiving, the state of having perceived—these are called perceptions of diversity' (Vibh 604). Thus it is stated, having been analyzed in the Vibhaṅga. These are what is intended here. The perception included in the mind-element and mind-consciousness-element of one who has not attained absorption occurs in a diverse domain, in the various distinct natures such as forms, sounds, and so on. Because these forty-four perceptions—eight wholesome sense-sphere perceptions, twelve unwholesome perceptions, eleven wholesome-resultant sense-sphere perceptions, two unwholesome-resultant perceptions, and eleven functional sense-sphere perceptions—are diverse, of various natures, and dissimilar to one another, they are called 'perception of diversity.' [The mind is secluded] from that perception of diversity.

Cittaṃ vivittaṃ hotīti ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samāpannassa rūpasaññāpaṭighasaññānānattasaññāsaṅkhātāhi saññāhi jhānacittaṃ vivittaṃ hoti vinā hoti apasakkanaṃ hoti. Viññāṇañcāyatananti etadeva viññāṇaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena āyatanamassāti viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ, ākāse pavattaviññāṇārammaṇassa jhānassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Taṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa vuttappakārāya ākāsānañcāyatanasaññāya cittaṃ vivittaṃ hoti.

The mind is secluded: for one who has attained the base of infinite space, the jhāna-mind is secluded, devoid, and withdrawn from the perceptions designated as perception of form, perception of resistance, and perception of diversity. The base of infinite consciousness: that very consciousness is a base for it in the sense of being a foundation, thus it is the 'base of infinite consciousness.' This is a designation for the jhāna that has as its object the consciousness that occurred in relation to infinite space. For one who has attained that jhāna, the mind is secluded from the aforesaid perception of the base of infinite space.

Ākiñcaññāyatananti [P 1.0101] ettha pana nāssa kiñcananti akiñcanaṃ, antamaso bhaṅgamattampi assa avasiṭṭhaṃ natthīti vuttaṃ hoti. Akiñcanassa bhāvo ākiñcaññaṃ, ākāsānañcāyatanaviññāṇāpagamassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Taṃ ākiñcaññaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena āyatanamassāti ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ, ākāse [M 0.0086] pavattitaviññāṇāpagamārammaṇajhānassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Taṃ ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samāpannassa tāya viññāṇañcāyatanasaññāya cittaṃ vivittaṃ.

The base of nothingness: Here, 'there is nothing of it' means 'nothing' (akiñcanaṃ); it is said that not even a mere fragment remains. The state of 'nothing' is 'nothingness' (ākiñcaññaṃ); this is a designation for the absence of the consciousness of the base of infinite space. That nothingness is a base (āyatana) for it in the sense of being a foundation, thus it is the 'base of nothingness' (ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ). This is a designation for the jhāna whose object is the absence of the consciousness that had occurred in relation to space. For one who has attained that base of nothingness, the mind is secluded from that perception of the base of infinite consciousness.

Nevasaññānāsaññāyatananti ettha pana yāya saññāya bhāvato taṃ “nevasaññānāsaññāyatana”nti vuccati, yathāpaṭipannassa sā saññā hoti, taṃ tāva dassetuṃ vibhaṅge (vibha. 620) “nevasaññīnāsaññī”ti uddharitvā taññeva “ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ santato manasi karoti, saṅkhārāvasesasamāpattiṃ bhāveti, tena vuccati nevasaññīnāsaññī”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha santato manasi karotīti “santovatāyaṃ samāpatti, yatra hi nāma natthibhāvampi ārammaṇaṃ karitvā vasatī”ti evaṃ santārammaṇatāya naṃ “santā”ti manasi karoti. Taṃ nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ appetvā nisinnassa tāya ākiñcaññāyatanasaññāya jhānacittaṃ suññaṃ hoti.

The base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception: Here, it is called 'the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception' on account of the state of that perception. To show that this perception exists for one who has practiced accordingly, having cited 'neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient' in the Vibhaṅga (Vibh 620), it is then said: 'He attends to the base of nothingness as peaceful, he develops the attainment with residual formations; for that reason he is called 'neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient.'' Therein, 'attends to it as peaceful' means he attends to it as 'peaceful' on account of its peaceful object, thinking: 'Peaceful indeed is this attainment, wherein one abides having made even a state of non-existence its object.' For one who is sitting having attained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the jhāna-mind is empty of that perception of the base of nothingness.

Sotāpannassāti sotāpattiphalaṃ pattassa. Sakkāyadiṭṭhiyāti vīsativatthukāya sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā. Vicikicchāyāti aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu kaṅkhāya. Sīlabbataparāmāsāti “sīlena suddhi, vatena suddhī”ti parāmasitvā uppajjanakadiṭṭhi. Diṭṭhānusayāti appahīnaṭṭhena santāne anusayakā diṭṭhānusayā. Tathā vicikicchānusayā. Tadekaṭṭhehi cāti tehi sakkāyadiṭṭhiādīhi ekato [V 0.0079] ṭhitehi ca. Upatāpenti vibādhenti cāti kilesā, tehi sakkāyadiṭṭhiyādikilesehi cittaṃ vivittaṃ suññaṃ hoti. Ettha “tadekaṭṭha”nti duvidhaṃ ekaṭṭhaṃ pahānekaṭṭhaṃ sahajekaṭṭhañca. Apāyagamanīyā hi kilesā yāva sotāpattimaggena na pahīyanti, tāva diṭṭhivicikicchāhi saha ekasmiṃ puggale ṭhitāti pahānekaṭṭhā. Dasasu hi kilesesu idha diṭṭhivicikicchā [P 1.0102] eva āgatā. Anusayesu diṭṭhānusayavicikicchānusayā āgatā. Sesā pana apāyagamanīyo lobho doso moho māno thinaṃ uddhaccaṃ ahirikaṃ anottappanti aṭṭha kilesā diṭṭhivicikicchāhi saha pahānekaṭṭhā hutvā dvīhi anusayehi saddhiṃ sotāpattimaggena pahīyanti. Rāgadosamohapamukhesu vā diyaḍḍhesu kilesasahassesu sotāpattimaggena diṭṭhiyā pahīyamānāya diṭṭhiyā saha vicikicchā pahīnā, diṭṭhānusayavicikicchānusayehi saha apāyagamanīyā sabbakilesā pahānekaṭṭhavasena pahīyanti. Sahajekaṭṭhā [M 0.0087] pana diṭṭhiyā saha vicikicchāya ca saha ekekasmiṃ citte ṭhitā avasesakilesā.

“Of a stream-enterer” means one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry. “Identity-view” refers to the twenty-factored identity-view. “Doubt” means uncertainty regarding eight matters. “Clinging to rites and rituals” is the wrong view that arises from clinging to the belief, “Purity comes through virtue and vows.” “The underlying tendency to views” refers to the unabandoned underlying tendency to views that lies dormant in the mental continuum. Similarly, the “underlying tendency to doubt.” “And by those that are one with them” means with those—identity-view and the others—standing together. “They afflict and oppress” refers to the defilements; by these defilements such as identity-view, the mind becomes secluded and empty. Here, “one with them” is twofold: one in abandonment and one in co-arising. For defilements leading to the lower realms, as long as they are not abandoned by the path of stream-entry, they remain together with wrong view and doubt in a single individual—thus, they are “one in abandonment.” Among the ten defilements, here only wrong view and doubt are mentioned. Among the underlying tendencies, the underlying tendencies to views and doubt are mentioned. The remaining defilements leading to the lower realms—greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and recklessness, eight in total—being one in abandonment with wrong view and doubt, are abandoned by the path of stream-entry along with the two underlying tendencies. Or, among the one and a half thousand defilements headed by greed, hatred, and delusion, when wrong view is abandoned by the path of stream-entry, doubt is abandoned together with it. Along with the underlying tendencies to views and doubt, all defilements leading to the lower realms are abandoned by way of being one in abandonment. “One in co-arising,” however, refers to the remaining defilements that are present together with wrong view and doubt in each single moment of consciousness.

Sotāpattimaggena hi cattāri diṭṭhisahagatāni vicikicchāsahagatañcāti pañca cittāni pahīyanti. Tattha dvīsu diṭṭhisampayuttaasaṅkhārikacittesu pahīyamānesu tehi sahajāto lobho moho uddhaccaṃ ahirikaṃ anottappanti ime kilesā sahajekaṭṭhavasena pahīyanti, dvīsu diṭṭhisampayuttasasaṅkhārikacittesu pahīyamānesu tehi sahajāto lobho moho thinaṃ uddhaccaṃ ahirikaṃ anottappanti ime kilesā sahajekaṭṭhavasena pahīyanti, vicikicchāsahagatacitte pahīyamāne tena sahajāto moho uddhaccaṃ ahirikaṃ anottappanti ime kilesā sahajekaṭṭhavasena pahīyanti. Tehi duvidhekaṭṭhehi kilesehi cittaṃ vivittaṃ hotīti maggacittaṃ viviccati, phalacittaṃ vivittaṃ viyuttaṃ apasakkitaṃ suññaṃ hotīti attho.

Indeed, by the path of stream-entry, five types of consciousness are abandoned: four associated with wrong view and one associated with doubt. Among these, when the two types of unprompted consciousness associated with wrong view are abandoned, the defilements that arise together with them—greed, delusion, restlessness, shamelessness, and recklessness—are abandoned by way of being one in co-arising. When the two types of prompted consciousness associated with wrong view are abandoned, the defilements that arise together with them—greed, delusion, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and recklessness—are abandoned by way of being one in co-arising. When the type of consciousness associated with doubt is abandoned, the defilements that arise together with it—delusion, restlessness, shamelessness, and recklessness—are abandoned by way of being one in co-arising. By these defilements that are one in two ways, the mind becomes secluded; this means that the path-consciousness becomes secluded, and the fruition-consciousness becomes secluded, detached, withdrawn, and empty.

Sakadāgāmissa oḷārikā kāmarāgasaññojanāti oḷārikabhūtā kāyadvāre vītikkamassa paccayabhāvena thūlabhūtā methunarāgasaṅkhātā saññojanā. So hi kāmabhave saññojetīti “saññojana”nti vuccati. Paṭighasaññojanāti byāpādasaññojanā. So hi ārammaṇe paṭihaññatīti “paṭigha”nti vuccati. Te eva thāmagataṭṭhena santāne anusentīti anusayā. Aṇusahagatāti sukhumabhūtā kāmarāgasaññojanā paṭighasaññojanā aṇusahagatā kāmarāgānusayā paṭighānusayāti appahīnaṭṭhena santāne anusayanavasena sukhumabhūtā kāmarāgapaṭighānusayā.
