Tadekaṭṭhehi cāti vuttatthehi duvidhekaṭṭhehi kilesehi cittaṃ vivittaṃ suññaṃ hoti.

For the once-returner, “the gross fetter of sensual desire” refers to the fetter known as sexual desire, which is gross because it is a condition for transgression through the body door. It fetters one to the realm of sensual pleasure, hence it is called a “fetter.” “The fetter of ill will” refers to the fetter of aversion. It strikes against its object, hence it is called “ill will.” These same, being firmly established, lie dormant in the mental continuum as underlying tendencies. “Accompanied by the subtle” refers to the subtle fetters of sensual desire and ill will. It also refers to the underlying tendencies of sensual desire and ill will, which are subtle because they are unabandoned and lie dormant in the mental continuum. “And by those that are one with them” means that by the defilements that are one in the two ways previously explained, the mind becomes secluded and empty.

Arahatoti [P 1.0103] kilesārīnaṃ hatattā “arahā”ti laddhanāmassa. Rūparāgāti rūpabhave chandarāgā[V 0.0080]. Arūparāgāti arūpabhave chandarāgā. Mānāti arahattamaggavajjhā mānā eva. Tathā uddhaccaavijjāmānānusayādayo arahattamaggavajjhā. Etesu uṇṇatilakkhaṇo māno. Avūpasamalakkhaṇaṃ uddhaccaṃ. Andhabhāvalakkhaṇā avijjā. Rūparāgaarūparāgavasena pavattā bhavarāgānusayā. Tadekaṭṭhehi cāti tehi ekato ṭhitehi [M 0.0088] ca kilesehi. Bahiddhā ca sabbanimittehīti ajjhattacittasantāne akusalakkhandhe upādāya “bahiddhā”ti saṅkhaṃ gatehi ajjhattaṃ muñcitvā bahiddhā pavattehi sabbasaṅkhāranimittehi maggacittaṃ viviccati vinā hoti apasakkati, phalacittaṃ vivittaṃ viyuttaṃ apasakkitaṃ hoti.

“Of an Arahant” means of one who has gained the name “Arahant” because of having destroyed the enemies, the defilements. “Craving for form” is desire and lust for existence in the form realm. “Craving for the formless” is desire and lust for existence in the formless realm. “Conceit” refers to the conceit that is to be abandoned by the path of Arahantship. Similarly, restlessness, ignorance, the underlying tendency of conceit, and so on, are to be abandoned by the path of Arahantship. Among these, conceit has the characteristic of haughtiness; restlessness has the characteristic of non-tranquility; ignorance has the characteristic of blindness. The underlying tendency of craving for existence operates by way of craving for form and craving for the formless. “And by those that are one with them” means by those defilements that stand together with them. “And from all external signs” means: with reference to the unwholesome aggregates in the internal mental continuum, which are designated as ‘external’; from all conditioned signs that, having abandoned the internal, occur externally. From these defilements and signs, the path-consciousness becomes secluded, free, and withdrawn; the fruition-consciousness becomes secluded, detached, and withdrawn.

Tattha kilesapaṭipāṭiyā maggapaṭipāṭiyā cāti dvidhā anusayānaṃ abhāvo veditabbo. Kilesapaṭipāṭiyā hi kāmarāgānusayapaṭighānusayānaṃ tatiyamaggena abhāvo hoti, mānānusayassa catutthamaggena, diṭṭhānusayavicikicchānusayānaṃ paṭhamamaggena, bhavarāgānusayāvijjānusayānaṃ catutthamaggeneva. Maggapaṭipāṭiyā pana paṭhamamaggena diṭṭhānusayavicikicchānusayānaṃ abhāvo hoti, dutiyamaggena kāmarāgānusayapaṭighānusayānaṃ tanubhāvo, tatiyamaggena sabbaso abhāvo, catutthamaggena mānānusayabhavarāgānusayāvijjānusayānaṃ abhāvo hoti. Cittavivekoti mahaggatalokuttaracittānaṃ kilesehi suññabhāvo, tucchabhāvoti attho.

Herein, the absence of underlying tendencies should be understood in two ways: according to the sequence of defilements and according to the sequence of paths. According to the sequence of defilements, the absence of the underlying tendencies of sensual desire and aversion occurs through the third path; the absence of the underlying tendency of conceit, through the fourth path; the absence of the underlying tendencies of wrong view and doubt, through the first path; and the absence of the underlying tendencies of craving for existence and ignorance, through the fourth path alone. According to the sequence of paths, however, the absence of the underlying tendencies of wrong view and doubt occurs through the first path; the weakening of the underlying tendencies of sensual desire and aversion, through the second path; their complete absence, through the third path; and the absence of the underlying tendencies of conceit, craving for existence, and ignorance, through the fourth path. “Seclusion of mind” means the state of sublime and supramundane consciousness being empty of defilements; its meaning is voidness.

Upadhivivekoti kilesakkhandhaabhisaṅkhārasaṅkhātānaṃ upadhīnaṃ suññabhāvo. Upadhiṃ tāva dassetuṃ “upadhi vuccanti kilesā cā”tiādimāha. Rāgādayo yassa uppajjanti, taṃ upatāpenti vibādhentīti kilesā ca. Upādānagocarā rūpādayo pañcakkhandhā ca. Upādānasambhūtā puññāpuññaāneñjābhisaṅkhārā ca. Amatanti natthi etassa maraṇasaṅkhātaṃ matanti amataṃ, kilesavisapaṭipakkhattā agadantipi amataṃ. Saṃsārayonigatiupapattiviññāṇaṭṭhitisattāvāsesu saṃsibbati vinatīti taṇhā “vāna”nti vuccati, taṃ tattha natthīti nibbānaṃ. Vivekaṭṭhakāyānanti [P 1.0104] gaṇasaṅgaṇikāya apagatasarīrānaṃ. Nekkhammābhiratānanti nekkhamme kāmādito nikkhante paṭhamajjhānādike abhiratānaṃ tanninnānaṃ. Paramavodānappattānanti uttamaparisuddhabhāvaphalaṃ pāpuṇitvā ṭhitānaṃ. “Upakkilesābhāvena parisuddhacittānaṃ, kilesehi muttabhāvena paramavodānappattānaṃ. Vikkhambhanappahānena parisuddhacittānaṃ, samucchedappahānena paramavodānappattāna”nti evameke vaṇṇayanti. Nirūpadhīnanti vigatūpadhīnaṃ. Visaṅkhāragatānanti saṅkhārārammaṇaṃ cajitvā vigatasaṅkhāraṃ nibbānaṃ ārammaṇavasena upagatānaṃ. Visaṅkhāragataṃ cittanti etthapi hi nibbānameva “visaṅkhāra”nti vuttaṃ.

“Seclusion from the substrates” is the emptiness of the substrates, which are known as defilements, aggregates, and volitional formations. First, to show what the substrates are, it is said: “The substrates are called defilements,” and so on. Defilements are lust and so on, which, when they arise for someone, torment and afflict them. The five aggregates—form and so on—which are the sphere of clinging, are also substrates. The meritorious, demeritorious, and imperturbable volitional formations born of clinging are also substrates. “The deathless” (amata) means that for which there is no so-called death (mata); because it is the antidote (agada) to the poison of defilements, it is also called the deathless. Craving is called “weaving” (vāna) because it sews (saṃsibbati) and weaves (vināti) one through the cycles of rebirth, destinations, states of existence, stations of consciousness, and abodes of beings; Nibbāna is where that weaving is not. “Of those whose being is secluded” means of those whose bodies have departed from crowds and company. “Of those who delight in renunciation” means of those who are inclined towards and delight in renunciation, that is, the first jhāna and so on, which is an escape from sensual pleasures. “Of those who have attained supreme purification” means of those who have reached and abide in the fruit which is the state of utmost purity. Some explain it thus: “Their minds are purified through the absence of imperfections; they have attained supreme purification through freedom from defilements. Their minds are purified through abandonment by suppression; they have attained supreme purification through abandonment by eradication.” “Of those without substrates” means of those whose substrates are gone. “Of those who have gone to the unconditioned” means of those who, having relinquished formations as their object, have approached Nibbāna, which is free from formations, by way of it being their object. Regarding “the mind that has gone to the unconditioned,” here too Nibbāna itself is called “the unconditioned” (visaṅkhāra).

Vidūreti [V 0.0081][M 0.0089] vividhe dūre. Suvidūreti suṭṭhu vidūre. Na santiketi na samīpe. Na sāmantāti na ekapasse. Anāsanneti anaccantasamīpe. Vivekaṭṭheti atidūre, vigateti attho. Tādisoti taṃsadiso. Tassaṇṭhitoti tena ākārena ṭhito. Tappakāroti tena pakārena ṭhito. Tappaṭibhāgoti taṃkoṭṭhāsiko. Atha vā “attabhāvaguhāya laggabhāvena tādiso. Kilesehi channabhāvena tassaṇṭhito. Mohanasmiṃ pagāḷhabhāvena tappakāro. Tīhi vivekehi dūrabhāvena tappaṭibhāgoti evameke vaṇṇayanti.

Vidūre means far away in various ways. Suvidūre means very far away. Na santike means not close by. Na sāmanta means not on one side. Anāsanne means not extremely close. Vivekaṭṭhe means very far away; the meaning is 'gone away.' Tādiso means similar to that. Tassaṇṭhito means established in that manner. Tappakāro means of that kind. Tappaṭibhāgo means belonging to that portion. Alternatively, some explain it thus: 'Tādiso means similar, due to being attached to the cave of selfhood. Tassaṇṭhito means established in that, due to being concealed by defilements. Tappakāro means of that kind, due to being deeply immersed in delusion. Tappaṭibhāgo means belonging to that portion, due to being far from the three kinds of seclusion.'

Duppahāyāti sukhena pahātabbā na honti. Duccajjāti sukhena jahituṃ na sakkā. Duppariccajjāti sabbākārena jahituṃ na sakkā. Dunnimmadayāti nimmadaṃ amadaṃ kātuṃ na sakkā. Dubbiniveṭhayāti viniveṭhanaṃ mocanaṃ kātuṃ na sakkā. Duttarāti uttaritvā atikkantuṃ na sakkā. Duppatarāti visesetvā tarituṃ na sakkā. Dussamatikkamāti dukkhena atikkamitabbā. Dubbinivattāti nivattetuṃ dukkhā. Atha [P 1.0105] vā “pakativasena duppariccajjā. Goṇapatāsaṃ viya dunnimmadayā. Nāgapāsaṃ viya dubbiniveṭhayā. Gimhasamaye marukantāraṃ viya duttarā duppatarā. Byagghapariggahitā aṭavī viya dussamatikkamā. Samuddavīci viya dubbinivattāti evameke vaṇṇayanti.

Duppahāya means they are not easily abandoned. Duccajja means they cannot be easily given up. Duppariccajja means they cannot be abandoned in every way. Dunnimmadaya means they cannot be made free from intoxication. Dubbiniveṭhaya means they cannot be disentangled or freed. Duttara means they cannot be crossed over or surpassed. Duppatara means they cannot be especially traversed. Dussamatikkama means they are difficult to overcome. Dubbinivatta means they are difficult to turn away from. Alternatively, some describe it thus: 'Duppariccajja, due to their inherent nature. Dunnimmadaya, like a bull's tether. Dubbiniveṭhaya, like a serpent's noose. Duttara and Duppatara, like a desert in the hot season. Dussamatikkama, like a forest seized by a tiger. Dubbinivatta, like ocean waves.'

8. Evaṃ paṭhamagāthāya “dūre vivekā hi tathāvidho”ti sādhetvā puna tathāvidhānaṃ sattānaṃ dhammataṃ āvi karonto “icchānidānā”tiādigāthamāha. Tattha icchānidānāti taṇhāhetukā. Bhavasātabaddhāti sukhavedanādimhi bhavasātena baddhā. Te duppamuñcāti te bhavasātavatthubhūtā dhammā. Te vā tattha baddhā icchānidānā sattā duppamocayā. Na hi aññamokkhāti aññe ca mocetuṃ na sakkonti. Kāraṇavacanaṃ vā etaṃ. Te sattā duppamuñcā. Kasmā? Yasmā aññena mocetabbā na honti. Yadi sattā muñceyyuṃ, sakena thāmena muñceyyunti ayamassa attho. Pacchā pure vāpi apekkhamānāti anāgate atīte vā kāme apekkhamānā. Ime va kāme purime va jappanti ime vā paccuppanne kāme purime vā duvidhepi atītānāgate balavataṇhāya patthayamānā. Imesañca dvinnaṃ padānaṃ “te duppamuñcā na hi aññamokkhā”ti [M 0.0090] imināva saha sambandho veditabbo. Itarathā apekkhamānā jappaṃ kiṃ karonti, kiṃ vā katāti na paññāyeyyuṃ.

8. Having thus established in the first verse that 'far away is seclusion for one of such a kind,' he then reveals the nature of beings of such a kind by saying the verse beginning with 'rooted in desire,' and so on. Herein, 'rooted in desire' (icchānidānā) means caused by craving. 'Bound by existence's delight' (bhavasātabaddhā) means bound by the delight of existence in pleasant feelings and the like. 'They are hard to release' (te duppamuñcā) refers to those things that serve as the basis for the delight of existence. Or, it refers to those beings, rooted in desire and bound therein, who are hard to liberate. 'For they are not freed by another' (na hi aññamokkhā) means they cannot be freed by another. Or this is a statement of reason: 'Those beings are hard to release.' Why? Because they are not to be freed by another. If beings were to be freed, they would be freed by their own strength—this is the meaning. 'Expecting things in the future or the past' (pacchā pure vāpi apekkhamānā) means looking to future or past sensual pleasures. 'They yearn for these sensual pleasures or the former ones' (ime va kāme purime va jappanti) means, with strong craving, they long for these present sensual pleasures or for the former two kinds, past and future. The connection of these two phrases should be understood together with this very phrase: 'they are hard to release, for they are not freed by another.' Otherwise, it would not be clear what those who are expectant do by yearning, or what they have done.

Bhavasātabaddhāti bhave sātaṃ bhavasātaṃ, tena bhavasātena sukhassādena baddhā hutvā ṭhitā. Taṃ bhājetvā dassetuṃ “ekaṃ bhavasātaṃ – sukhā vedanā”tiādimāha. Yobbanabhāvo yobbaññaṃ. Arogabhāvo [V 0.0082] ārogyaṃ. Jīvitindriyassa pavattabhāvo jīvitaṃ. Lābhoti [P 1.0106] catunnaṃ paccayānaṃ lābho. Yasoti parivāro. Pasaṃsāti kitti. Sukhanti kāyikacetasikaṃ sukhaṃ. Manāpikā rūpāti manavaḍḍhanakā rūpā. Sesesupi eseva nayo.

'Bound to delight in existence' (bhavasātabaddhā) means delight in existence (bhavasāta) is delight in being; by that delight in existence, by the taste of pleasure, they are bound and remain. To explain this by analyzing it, it is said: 'One delight in existence—pleasant feeling,' and so on. Youthfulness (yobbañña) is the state of being young. Health (ārogya) is the state of being free from disease. Life (jīvita) is the functioning of the life faculty. Gain (lābha) is the acquisition of the four requisites. Fame (yasa) is one's retinue. Praise (pasaṃsā) is renown. Happiness (sukha) is bodily and mental pleasure. Pleasing forms (manāpikā rūpā) are forms that enhance the mind. The same method applies to the rest.

Cakkhusampadāti cakkhussa sampadā. “Mayhaṃ cakkhu sampannaṃ maṇivimāne ugghāṭitasīhapañjaraṃ viya khāyatī”ti uppannaṃ sukhassādaṃ sandhāya “cakkhusampadā”ti vuttaṃ. Sotasampadādīsupi eseva nayo. Sukhāya vedanāya sātabaddhā…pe… vibaddhāti vividhākārena baddhā. Ābaddhāti visesena ādito baddhā. Laggāti ārammaṇena saddhiṃ appitā. Laggitāti nāgadante phāṇitavārako viya laggitā. Yamettha ca avuttaṃ, taṃ satto visattotiādimhi vuttanayena gahetabbaṃ.

'Excellence of the eye' (cakkhusampadā) is the excellence of the eye. Referring to the taste of pleasure that has arisen, as in 'My eye is excellent, it appears like a jeweled palace with its lion-window opened,' it is called 'excellence of the eye' (cakkhusampadā). The same method applies to excellence of the ear and so on. 'Bound to the delight of pleasant feeling' (sukhāya vedanāya sātabaddhā)... and so on... 'diversely bound' (vibaddhā) means bound in diverse ways. 'Strongly bound' (ābaddhā) means specially bound from the beginning. 'Adhering' (laggā) means fixed upon the object. 'Clinging' (laggitā) means clinging like a lump of molasses to an elephant’s tusk. And whatever is not stated here should be understood in the way explained in 'a being is attached, thoroughly attached' (satto visatto), and so on.

Na hi aññamokkhāti na parehi mokkhā. Te vā bhavasātavatthū duppamuñcāti bhave sukhassādavatthubhūtā dhammā te muñcituṃ dukkhā. Sattā vā etto dummocayāti sattā eva vā etasmā bhavasātavatthuto mocetuṃ dukkhā.

'For they are not freed by another' (na hi aññamokkhā) means they are not freed by others. Alternatively, 'those things that are the basis for delight in existence are hard to release' (te vā bhavasātavatthū duppamuñcā) means those phenomena that are the basis for the taste of pleasure in existence are difficult to relinquish. Or, 'beings are hard to liberate from this' (sattā vā etto dummocayā) means that beings are difficult to liberate from this basis for delight in existence.

Duruddharāti uddharituṃ dukkhā. Dussamuddharāti samantato chinnataṭe narakāvāṭe patito viya uddhaṃ katvā uddharituṃ dukkhā. Dubbuṭṭhāpayāti uṭṭhāpetuṃ dukkhā. Dussamuṭṭhāpayāti sukhumaattabhāvaṃ pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhāpanaṃ viya ussāpetuṃ ativiya dukkhā.

'Hard to pull out' (duruddharā) means difficult to extract. 'Hard to completely pull out' (dussamuddharā) means, like one fallen into a hell-pit with its banks cut off all around, it is difficult to lift them up and pull them out. 'Hard to raise up' (dubbuṭṭhāpayā) means difficult to make them stand up. 'Hard to fully raise up' (dussamuṭṭhāpayā) means it is extremely difficult to raise them up, like establishing a subtle individuality on the earth.

Te attanā palipapalipannāti gambhīrakaddame yāva sīsato nimuggā na sakkonti. Paraṃ palipapalipannaṃ uddharitunti aparaṃ tatheva nimuggaṃ hatthe vā sīse vā gahetvā uddharitvā thale patiṭṭhāpetuṃ na sakkonti. So vata cundāti soti vattabbākārapuggalaniddeso. Tassa “yo”ti imaṃ uddesavacanaṃ āharitvā yo attanā palipapalipanno, so vata[M 0.0091], cunda, paraṃ palipapalipannaṃ uddharissatīti. Evaṃ sesapadesu sambandho veditabbo. Palipapalipannoti gambhīrakaddame nimuggo vuccati. Yathā, cunda, koci puriso yāva [P 1.0107] sīsato gambhīrakaddame nimuggo, parampi tatheva nimuggaṃ hatthe vā sīse vā gahetvā uddharissatīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Na hi taṃ kāraṇamatthi, yena so taṃ uddharitvā thale patiṭṭhāpeyyāti. Adanto avinīto aparinibbutoti ettha pana anibbisevanatāya adanto. Asikkhitavinayatāya avinīto. Anibbutakilesatāya aparinibbutoti veditabbo. So tādiso paraṃ damessati nibbisevanaṃ karissati, vinessati tisso sikkhā sikkhāpessati. Parinibbāpessati tassa kilese nibbāpessati.

Regarding 'One who is himself mired in the mire': they are sunk in deep mud up to their heads and are unable to pull out another who is mired in the mire, that is, they are unable to grasp another who is similarly sunk by the hand or head, pull them out, and set them on dry ground. Regarding 'That one, indeed, Cunda': this is the designation of a person of a certain type. Bringing in the relative pronoun 'who,' the sentence is constructed thus: 'That one, Cunda, who is himself mired in the mire, will pull out another mired in the mire'—this is impossible. The connection in the remaining phrases should be understood in the same way. 'Mired in the mire' refers to one submerged in deep mud. Just as, Cunda, if some man were submerged in deep mud up to his head, that he could pull out another similarly submerged by grasping his hand or head—this is impossible. Indeed, there is no reason by which he could pull him out and set him on dry ground. Regarding 'untamed, untrained, unextinguished': here, 'untamed' should be understood as due to not having practiced restraint; 'untrained' as due to not having been trained in the discipline; 'unextinguished' as due to not having extinguished the defilements. That such a one would tame another, bring them to restraint; would train another, make them train in the three trainings; would bring another to final extinguishment, would extinguish their defilements—this is impossible.

Natthañño [V 0.0083] kocīti añño koci puggalo mocetuṃ samattho natthi. Sakena thāmenāti attano ñāṇathāmena. Balenāti ñāṇabalena. Vīriyenāti ñāṇasampayuttacetasikavīriyena. Purisaparakkamenāti paraṃ paraṃ ṭhānaṃ akkamanena mahantavīriyena.

'There is no other' means there is no other person capable of liberating. 'By one's own strength' means by the strength of one's own wisdom. 'By power' means by the power of wisdom. 'By energy' means by the mental energy associated with wisdom. 'By manly effort' means by great energy in advancing to higher and higher states.

Nāhaṃ sahissāmīti ahaṃ na sahissāmi na sakkomi, na vāyamissāmīti vuttaṃ hoti. Pamocanāyāti pamocetuṃ. Kathaṃkathinti sakaṅkhaṃ. Dhotakāti ālapanaṃ. Taresīti tareyyāsi.

'I will not endure' means 'I do not endure, I am not able, I will not strive,' is what is said. 'For release' means 'to release.' 'With doubt' means 'with uncertainty.' 'Dhotaka' is a form of address. 'You would cross over' means 'you could cross over.'

“Attanā hi kataṃ pāpaṃ, attanā saṃkilissati;

Attanā akataṃ pāpaṃ, attanāva visujjhati;

Suddhī asuddhi paccattaṃ, nāñño aññaṃ visodhaye”ti. (dha. pa. 165; kathā. 743) –

By oneself, indeed, is evil done; by oneself is one defiled. By oneself is evil not done; by oneself is one purified. Purity and impurity are individual matters; no one can purify another.

Etthāyamattho – yena attanā akusalaṃ kammaṃ kataṃ hoti, so catūsu apāyesu dukkhaṃ anubhavanto attanāva saṃkilissati. Yena pana attanā akataṃ pāpaṃ, so sugatiñceva agatiñca gacchanto attanāva visujjhati. Kusalakammasaṅkhātā suddhi akusalakammasaṅkhātā ca asuddhi paccattaṃ kārakasattānaṃ attaniyeva vipaccati. Añño puggalo aññaṃ puggalaṃ na visodhaye neva visodheti, na kilesetīti vuttaṃ hoti.

Herein, this is the meaning: one by whom an unwholesome deed has been done is defiled by oneself while experiencing suffering in the four woeful states. But one by whom evil has not been done is purified by oneself while going to a happy destination and not a woeful one. Purity, reckoned as wholesome kamma, and impurity, reckoned as unwholesome kamma, ripens individually within the very self of the beings who are the doers. Another person does not purify another person, nor does one defile another; thus it is said.

Tiṭṭhateva nibbānanti amatamahānibbānaṃ tiṭṭhatiyeva. Nibbānagāmimaggoti pubbabhāgavipassanāto paṭṭhāya ariyamaggo. Tiṭṭhāmahaṃ samādapetāti ahaṃ gaṇhāpetā patiṭṭhāpetā tiṭṭhāmi. Evaṃ [P 1.0108] ovadiyamānā evaṃ anusāsiyamānāti [M 0.0092] mayā evaṃ ovadiyamānā evaṃ anusāsiyamānā. Ettha uppanne vatthusmiṃ vadanto ovadati nāma, anuppanne vatthusmiṃ anusāsanto “ayasopi te bhavissatī”tiādivasena anāgataṃ dassento anusāsati nāma. Sammukhā vadantopi ovadati nāma, parammukhā dūtasāsanaṃ vā pesento anusāsati nāma. Sakiṃ vadantopi ovadati nāma, punappunaṃ vadanto anusāsati nāma. Ovadanto eva vā anusāsati nāma. Appekacceti api ekacce, eketi attho. Accantaniṭṭhaṃ nibbānaṃ ārādhentīti khayavayasaṅkhātaṃ antaṃ atītanti accantaṃ, accantañca taṃ sabbasaṅkhārānaṃ appavattiṭṭhānattā niṭṭhañcāti accantaniṭṭhaṃ, ekantaniṭṭhaṃ, satataniṭṭhanti attho. Taṃ accantanibbānaṃ ārādhenti sampādenti. Nārādhentīti na sampādenti, na paṭilabhantīti attho. Ettha kyāhanti etesu kiṃ ahaṃ, kiṃ karomīti attho. Maggakkhāyīti paṭipadāmaggakkhāyī[V 0.0084]. Ācikkhati katheti. Attanā paṭipajjamānā muñceyyunti paṭipajjantā mayaṃ muñceyyuṃ.

'Nibbāna exists' means the deathless, great Nibbāna indeed exists. 'The path leading to Nibbāna' means the noble path beginning from the preliminary stage of insight. 'I stand, causing to undertake' means 'I stand, causing to take up, causing to establish.' 'Being thus advised, thus instructed' means being advised and instructed by me in this way. Here, speaking about a matter that has arisen is called advising, while instructing about a matter that has not arisen by showing the future, such as 'this too will be yours,' is called instructing. Speaking face-to-face is called advising, while sending a message or instruction from afar is called instructing. Speaking once is called advising, while speaking repeatedly is called instructing. Or, advising is itself instructing. 'Some' means 'also some,' the meaning is 'some.' 'They accomplish the ultimate Nibbāna' means: 'ultimate' (accanta) because it has gone beyond the end reckoned as decay and passing away; and it is 'final' (niṭṭha) because it is the state of the non-occurrence of all formations, hence 'absolutely final,' 'unconditionally final,' 'perpetually final'—this is the meaning. They accomplish that ultimate Nibbāna, they achieve it. 'They do not accomplish it' means 'they do not achieve it, they do not attain it'—this is the meaning. Here, 'what am I to do?' means 'among these, what am I, what can I do?'—this is the meaning. 'The proclaimer of the path' means 'the proclaimer of the path of practice.' He declares, he speaks. 'Practicing by themselves, they would be freed' means 'practicing, we would be freed.'

Atītaṃ upādāyāti atītaṃ paṭicca. Kathaṃ pure apekkhaṃ karotīti kena pakārena ikkhaṃ olokanaṃ karoti. Evaṃrūpo ahosinti dīgharassaaṇukathūlādivasena evaṃjātiko evarūpo abhaviṃ. Tattha nandiṃ samannānetīti tasmiṃ rūpārammaṇe taṇhaṃ sammā ānayati upaneti. Vedanādīsupi eseva nayo.

'Based on the past' means depending on the past. 'How does he look back?' means 'in what manner does he look or observe?' 'I was of such a form' means 'I was of such a kind, such as long, short, subtle, or coarse; I was of such a form.' There, 'he brings delight' means he rightly brings and applies craving to that form-object. The same principle applies to feelings and so on.

“Iti me cakkhū”tiādayo vatthuārammaṇavasena taṇhuppattiṃ dassento āha. Iti rūpātīti evaṃ rūpā iti. Tattha chandarāgapaṭibaddhanti tesu cakkhurūpesu dubbalasaṅkhāto chando ca balavasaṅkhāto rāgo ca, tena chandarāgena paṭibaddhaṃ allīnaṃ. Viññāṇanti javanacittaṃ. Chandarāgapaṭibaddhattā viññāṇassāti tassa javanaviññāṇassa chandarāgena baddhabhāvā. Tadabhinandatīti taṃ ārammaṇaṃ taṇhāvasena abhinandati.

'Thus, 'this is my eye',' etc., he says, showing the arising of craving in dependence on the base and the object. 'Thus, forms' means 'thus are forms.' There, 'bound by desire and lust' means in those eyes and forms, desire (chanda) reckoned as a weaker state and lust (rāga) reckoned as a stronger state; by that desire and lust it is bound, clinging. 'Consciousness' means the impulsion-consciousness. 'Because consciousness is bound by desire and lust' means because that impulsion-consciousness is in a state of being bound by desire and lust. 'He delights in that' means he delights in that object through craving.

Yānissa [P 1.0109] tānīti yāni assa tāni. Pubbeti atīte. Saddhinti ekato. Hasitalapitakīḷitānīti dantavidaṃsādihasitāni ca, vacībhedaṃ katvā lapitāni ca, kāyakhiḍḍādikīḷitāni ca. Tadassādetīti taṃ assādayati assādaṃ vindati sādiyati. Taṃ nikāmetīti taṃ nikāmayati paccāsīsati. Vittiṃ āpajjatīti tuṭṭhiṃ pāpuṇāti.

'Yānissa tānīti' means 'those which are his.' 'Pubbeti' means 'formerly, in the past.' 'Saddhinti' means 'together.' 'Hasitalapitakīḷitānīti' refers to laughter, such as showing the teeth; talk, such as various kinds of speech; and play, such as bodily sport. 'Tadassādetīti' means 'he savors that, finds gratification in it, relishes it.' 'Taṃ nikāmetīti' means 'he desires that, longs for it.' 'Vittiṃ āpajjatīti' means 'he attains joy.'

Siyanti [M 0.0093] bhaveyyaṃ. Appaṭiladdhassa paṭilābhāyāti appattassa pāpuṇanatthāya. Cittaṃ paṇidahatīti cittaṃ ṭhapeti. Cetaso paṇidhānapaccayāti cittassa ṭhapanakāraṇā.

'Siyanti' means 'may I be.' 'Appaṭiladdhassa paṭilābhāyāti' means 'for the sake of attaining what has not been attained.' 'Cittaṃ paṇidahatīti' means 'he directs his mind.' 'Cetaso paṇidhānapaccayāti' means 'due to the cause of the mind's direction.'

Sīlena vāti pañcasīlādisīlena vā. Vatena vāti dhutaṅgasamādānena vā. Tapena vāti vīriyasamādānena vā. Brahmacariyena vāti methunaviratiyā vā. Devo vāti mahānubhāvo devarājā vā. Devaññataro vāti tesaṃ aññataro vā.

'Sīlena vā' means 'or by virtue, such as the five precepts and so on.' 'Vatena vā' means 'or by undertaking an observance, such as the ascetic practices.' 'Tapena vā' means 'or by undertaking energy.' 'Brahmacariyena vā' means 'or by abstinence from sexual intercourse.' 'Devo vā' means 'or a deva of great power, or a king of devas.' 'Devaññataro vā' means 'or a certain one among them.'

Jappantāti guṇavasena kathentā. Pajappantāti pakārena kathentā. Abhijappantāti visesena kathentā, upasaggavasena vā vaḍḍhitaṃ.

'Jappantāti' means 'speaking by way of virtues.' 'Pajappantāti' means 'speaking in various ways.' 'Abhijappantāti' means 'speaking in a special way,' or it is augmented by way of a prefix.

9. Evaṃ paṭhamagāthāya “dūre vivekā hi tathāvidho”ti sādhetvā dutiyagāthāya ca tathāvidhānaṃ [V 0.0085] dhammataṃ āvi katvā idāni tesaṃ pāpakaraṇaṃ āvi karonto “kāmesu giddhā”ti gāthamāha.

9. Thus, having established in the first verse that 'such a one is indeed far from seclusion,' and having revealed the nature of such ones in the second verse, now, revealing their evil-doing, he speaks the verse beginning with 'kāmesu giddhā.'

Tassattho – te sattā kāmesu paribhogataṇhāya giddhā, pariyesanādimanuyuttattā pasutā, sammohamāpannattā pamūḷhā, avagamanatāya macchariyatāya buddhādīnaṃ vacanaṃ anādiyatāya ca avadāniyā, kāyavisamādimhi visame niviṭṭhā, antakāle maraṇadukkhūpanītā, “kiṃsu bhavissāma ito cutāse”ti paridevayantīti.

The meaning is this: Those beings are greedy for sensual pleasures due to craving for enjoyment, intent on pursuit and so on, and deluded by confusion; they are impure on account of their lack of understanding, stinginess, and disregard for the words of the Buddha and others; they are entrenched in what is crooked, such as bodily misconduct, and are overtaken by the suffering of death at the end of their time, lamenting, 'What will become of us after passing from here?'

Giddhāti kāmarāgena giddhā. Gadhitāti saṅkapparāgena paccāsīsamānā hutvā gadhitā. Mucchitāti kāmataṇhāya mucchāparetā. Ajjhosannāti kāmanandiyā adhiosannā ajjhotthaṭā. Laggāti kāmasinehena allīnā. Laggitāti kāmapariḷāhena ekībhūtā. Palibuddhāti kāmasaññāya āvaṭṭitā. Atha vā “diṭṭhidassane giddhā. Abhiṇhadassane gadhitā. Saṃsaggakiriyasmiṃ [P 1.0110] mucchitā. Vissāsakiriyasmiṃ ajjhosannā. Sinehavaḷañjasmiṃ laggā. Dvayaṃdvayasamāpattimhi laggitā. Aparāparaṃ amuñcamānā hutvā palibuddhā”ti evameke vaṇṇayanti.

"Giddhā" means "greedy with sensual lust." "Gadhitā" means "greedy, being expectant and longing with conceptual desire." "Mucchitā" means "infatuated, overcome by sensual craving." "Ajjhosannā" means "overwhelmed and steeped in sensual delight." "Laggā" means "clinging with sensual affection." "Laggitā" means "become one with the fever of sensual desire." "Palibuddhā" means "ensnared by perceptions of sensual pleasure." Alternatively, some explain it thus: "greedy in seeing views; longing in frequent seeing; infatuated in the act of association; overwhelmed in the act of intimacy; clinging in the use of affection; attached in the act of sexual union; and ensnared by not letting go again and again."

Esantīti paccāsīsanti. Gavesantīti maggayanti. Pariyesantīti sabbākārena icchanti patthenti. Atha vā diṭṭhārammaṇe subhāsubhaṃ atthi, natthīti esanti. Subhāsubhārammaṇe paccakkhaṃ katvā vaḷañjanatthāya piyaṃ karontā gavesanti[M 0.0094]. Cittavasena esanti. Payogavasena gavesanti. Karaṇavasena pariyesanti. Te duvidhe kāme paṭicca otaritvā carantīti taccaritā. Te ca kāme bahulaṃ yebhuyyena vaḍḍhenti pavattayantīti tabbahulā. Te ca kāme garuṃ katvā rahantīti taggarukā. Tesu kāmesu ninnā namitā hutvā vasantīti tanninnā. Tesu kāmesu sanninnā hutvā vasantīti tappoṇā. Tesu kāmesu avalambitā hutvā tesuyeva namitā vasantīti tappabbhārā. Tesu kāmesu avattharitvā mucchāparetappasaṅgā hutvā vadantīti tadadhimuttā. Te ca kāme adhipatiṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā vasantīti tadadhipateyyā. Atha vā “ārammaṇassa iṭṭhabhāvena taccaritā. Ārammaṇassa kantabhāvena tabbahulā. Ārammaṇassa manāpabhāvena taggarukā. Ārammaṇassa piyabhāvena tanninnā. Ārammaṇassa kāmupasaṃhitabhāvena tappoṇā. Ārammaṇassa rajanīyabhāvena tappabbhārā. Ārammaṇassa mucchanīyabhāvena tadadhimuttā. Ārammaṇassa bandhanīyabhāvena tadadhipateyyā”ti evameke vaṇṇayanti.

They seek, meaning they anticipate. They search, meaning they investigate. They seek out, meaning they desire and long for in every way. Or alternatively, regarding a visible object, they seek, thinking, 'There is the beautiful and the ugly,' or 'There is not.' They search by directly experiencing objects of beauty or ugliness, seeking to indulge in them, making them dear. They seek by way of the mind. They search by way of effort. They seek out by way of action. Having descended upon and conducting themselves in relation to these two kinds of sensual pleasures, they are 'those who conduct themselves accordingly.' They frequently and for the most part cultivate and promote these sensual pleasures—thus they are 'those who abound in them.' They dwell holding these sensual pleasures as important—thus they are 'those who hold them in esteem.' They dwell inclined and bent toward these sensual pleasures—thus they are 'those who are inclined to them.' They dwell deeply immersed in these sensual pleasures—thus they are 'those who are immersed in them.' They dwell clinging to these sensual pleasures, bent upon them—thus they are 'those who are prone to them.' They dwell overwhelmed, infatuated, and attached to these sensual pleasures—thus they are 'those who are resolved on them.' They dwell making these sensual pleasures their chief and foremost—thus they are 'those who are under their dominion.' Alternatively, some explain thus: 'Because the object is pleasing, they conduct themselves accordingly. Because the object is delightful, they abound in them. Because the object is agreeable, they hold them in esteem. Because the object is dear, they are inclined to them. Because the object is connected with sensual desire, they are immersed in them. Because the object is enticing, they are prone to them. Because the object is infatuating, they are resolved on them. Because the object is binding, they are under its dominion.'

Rūpe [V 0.0086] pariyesantītiādīsu pariyesantīti aladdhassa lābhāya esanavasena. Paṭilabhantīti hatthagatavasena. Paribhuñjantīti vaḷañjanavasena vuttanti ñātabbaṃ. Kalahaṃ vivādaṃ karotīti kalahakārako. Tasmiṃ niyuttoti kalahapasuto. Kammakārakādīsupi eseva nayo. Gocare carantoti vesiyādigocare, satipaṭṭhānādigocare vā [P 1.0111] caramāno. Tesu niyutto gocarapasuto. Ārammaṇūpanijjhānavasena jhānaṃ assa atthīti jhāyī. Tasmiṃ niyutto jhānapasuto.

In the phrases 'they seek out forms,' etc., 'they seek out' is meant by way of searching for the acquisition of what has not yet been obtained. 'They obtain' is meant by way of taking into possession. 'They enjoy' is meant by way of using—this should be understood. One who engages in quarrels and disputes is a quarrel-maker. One engaged in that is 'devoted to quarreling.' The same principle applies to 'they are workers,' etc. 'They wander in the pasture' means moving about in the pasture of prostitutes and so on, or in the pasture of the foundations of mindfulness and so on. One engaged in these is 'devoted to the pasture.' One who has absorption by way of contemplating an object is a meditator. One engaged in that is 'devoted to meditation.'

Avagacchantīti apāyaṃ gacchanti. Maccharinoti sakasampattiṃ niguhantā. Vacananti kathanaṃ. Byapathanti vākyapathaṃ. Desananti vissajjanaovādaṃ. Anusiṭṭhinti anusāsaniṃ. Nādiyantīti na gaṇhanti na garuṃ karonti. “Na paṭissantī”ti vā pāṭho, soyeva attho. Vatthuto macchariyadassanatthaṃ “pañca macchariyāni āvāsamacchariya”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha āvāse macchariyaṃ āvāsamacchariyaṃ. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo.

"They go to ruin" means they go to the lower realms. "Stingy" means those who conceal their own possessions. "Speech" means speaking. "Conversation" means the path of speech. "Instruction" means giving advice and exhortation. "Anusiṭṭhi" means instruction. "They do not heed" means they do not accept or respect. Alternatively, the reading is "they do not receive"—the meaning is the same. To show the basis for stinginess, it is said, "There are five kinds of stinginess, beginning with stinginess regarding dwellings." Herein, stinginess regarding dwellings is called "dwelling-stinginess." The same principle applies to the remaining instances.

Āvāso [M 0.0095] nāma sakalārāmopi pariveṇampi ekovarakopi rattiṭṭhānādīnipi. Tesu vasantā sukhaṃ vasanti, paccaye labhanti. Eko bhikkhu vattasampannasseva pesalassa bhikkhuno tattha āgamanaṃ na icchati, āgatopi “khippaṃ gacchatū”ti cintesi, idaṃ āvāsamacchariyaṃ nāma. Bhaṇḍanakārakādīnaṃ pana tattha vāsaṃ anicchato āvāsamacchariyaṃ nāma na hoti.

A dwelling means the entire monastery, a monastic residence, a single room, or places for overnight stays, and so on. Those who dwell there live comfortably and obtain requisites. If a monk does not wish for another virtuous and well-behaved monk to come there, or if upon his arrival thinks, 'Let him leave quickly,' this is called stinginess regarding dwellings. However, if one does not wish for quarrelsome individuals and so on to stay there, it is not called stinginess regarding dwellings.

Kulanti upaṭṭhākakulampi ñātikulampi. Tattha aññassa upasaṅkamanaṃ anicchato kulamacchariyaṃ hoti. Pāpapuggalassa pana upasaṅkamanaṃ anicchatopi macchariyaṃ nāma na hoti. So hi tesaṃ pasādabhedāya paṭipajjati. Pasādaṃ rakkhituṃ samatthasseva pana bhikkhuno tattha upasaṅkamanaṃ anicchato macchariyaṃ nāma hoti.

A family means either a supporting family or a family of relatives. In that regard, for one who does not wish another to approach them, it is called stinginess regarding families. But if one does not wish a wicked person to approach, it is not called stinginess. For such a person acts to destroy their faith. However, for a monk who is himself capable of protecting their faith, if he does not wish another to approach them, it is called stinginess.

Lābhoti catupaccayalābhova. Taṃ aññasmiṃ sīlavanteyeva labhante “mā labhatū”ti cintentassa lābhamacchariyaṃ hoti. Yo pana saddhādeyyaṃ vinipāteti, aparibhogadupparibhogādivasena vināseti, pūtibhāvaṃ gacchantampi aññassa na deti, taṃ disvā “sace imaṃ esa na labheyya, añño sīlavā labheyya, paribhogaṃ gaccheyyā”ti cintentassa macchariyaṃ nāma natthi.

'Gain' refers to the gain of the four requisites. When another virtuous one is obtaining it, for one who thinks, 'May he not receive it,' this is called stinginess regarding gains. But if someone squanders offerings given in faith, destroys them through non-use, misuse, and so on, or does not give them to another even as they are going to waste, and upon seeing this one thinks, 'If this person did not receive this, another virtuous one might receive it and it would be put to use,' this is not called stinginess.

Vaṇṇo [P 1.0112] nāma sarīravaṇṇopi guṇavaṇṇopi. Tattha sarīravaṇṇe maccharī “paro pāsādiko rūpavā”ti [V 0.0087] vutte taṃ na kathetukāmo hoti. Guṇavaṇṇamaccharī parassa sīlena dhutaṅgena paṭipadāya ācārena vaṇṇaṃ na kathetukāmo hoti.

'Vaṇṇa' means both physical appearance and good qualities. A person stingy about physical appearance, when another is said to be 'pleasing and handsome,' does not wish to speak of it. One stingy about good qualities does not wish to speak of another's virtue, ascetic practices, practice, or conduct.

Dhammoti pariyattidhammo ca paṭivedhadhammo ca. Tattha ariyasāvakā paṭivedhadhammaṃ na maccharāyanti, attanā paṭividdhadhamme sadevakassa lokassa paṭivedhaṃ icchanti. Taṃ pana paṭivedhaṃ “pare jānantū”ti icchanti, tantidhammeyeva pana dhammamacchariyaṃ nāma hoti. Tena samannāgato puggalo yaṃ guḷhaṃ ganthaṃ vā kathāmaggaṃ vā jānāti, taṃ aññe na jānāpetukāmo hoti. Yo pana puggalaṃ upaparikkhitvā dhammānuggahena dhammaṃ vā upaparikkhitvā puggalānuggahena na deti, ayaṃ dhammamaccharī nāma na hoti. Tattha ekacco puggalo lolo hoti, kālena samaṇo hoti[M 0.0096], kālena brāhmaṇo, kālena nigaṇṭho. Yo hi bhikkhu “ayaṃ puggalo paveṇiāgataṃ tantiṃ saṇhaṃ sukhumaṃ dhammantaraṃ bhinditvā āluḷessatī”ti na deti, ayaṃ puggalaṃ upaparikkhitvā dhammānuggahena na deti nāma. Yo pana “ayaṃ dhammo saṇho sukhumo, sacāyaṃ puggalo gaṇhissati, aññaṃ byākaritvā attānaṃ āvi katvā nassissatī”ti na deti, ayaṃ dhammaṃ upaparikkhitvā puggalānuggahena na deti nāma. Yo pana “sacāyaṃ imaṃ dhammaṃ gaṇhissati, amhākaṃ samayaṃ bhindituṃ samattho bhavissatī”ti na deti, ayaṃ dhammamaccharī nāma hoti.

'The Dhamma' is twofold: the Dhamma of learning and the Dhamma of realization. Herein, noble disciples are not stingy with the Dhamma of realization; having realized the Dhamma themselves, they wish for the realization of the Dhamma by the world with its gods. They wish, 'Let others know it too.' But it is precisely regarding the Dhamma of learning that what is called 'stinginess with the Dhamma' occurs. A person possessed of this does not wish to make known to others what he knows—be it a hidden text or a path of discussion. However, one who, after examining a person, does not give the Dhamma out of consideration for the Dhamma, or who, after examining the Dhamma, does not give it out of consideration for the person—this is not called stinginess with the Dhamma. Herein, a certain person is fickle—sometimes an ascetic, sometimes a brahmin, sometimes a naked ascetic. If a monk does not give the Dhamma, thinking, 'This person will break and confuse this subtle and delicate point of the traditional doctrine,' this is called not giving out of consideration for the Dhamma after examining the person. If one does not give, thinking, 'This Dhamma is subtle and delicate; if this person grasps it, he will misinterpret it, reveal himself, and come to ruin,' this is called not giving out of consideration for the person after examining the Dhamma. But if one does not give, thinking, 'If this person grasps this Dhamma, he will become capable of breaking our doctrine,' this is what is called stinginess with the Dhamma.

Imesu pañcasu macchariyesu āvāsamacchariyena tāva yakkho vā peto vā hutvā tasseva āvāsassa saṅkāraṃ sīsena ukkhipitvā vicarati. Kulamacchariyena tasmiṃ kule aññesaṃ dānamānanādīni karonte disvā “bhinnaṃ vatidaṃ kulaṃ mamā”ti cintayato lohitampi mukhato uggacchati, kucchivirecanampi hoti, antānipi khaṇḍākhaṇḍāni hutvā nikkhamanti. Lābhamacchariyena saṅghassa vā gaṇassa vā santake lābhe maccharāyitvā puggalikaparibhogaṃ viya paribhuñjitvā yakkho vā peto vā mahāajagaro vā hutvā nibbattati. Sarīravaṇṇaguṇavaṇṇamaccharena [P 1.0113] pana pariyattidhammamacchariyena ca attanova vaṇṇaṃ vaṇṇeti, paresaṃ vaṇṇe “kiṃ vaṇṇo eso”ti taṃ taṃ dosaṃ vadanto pariyattidhammañca kassaci kiñci adento dubbaṇṇo ceva eḷamūgo ca hoti.

Among these five kinds of stinginess, first, through stinginess with dwellings, one becomes a yakkha or a peta and wanders about carrying the filth of that very dwelling on one's head. Through stinginess with families, when seeing others giving gifts, honor, and the like to that family, one thinks, 'Alas, this family of mine is ruined!' Blood then gushes from one's mouth, one suffers from diarrhea, and one's intestines come out in pieces. Through stinginess with gains, if one is stingy with gains belonging to the Sangha or a group and uses them for personal enjoyment, one is reborn as a yakkha, a peta, or a great serpent. As for stinginess regarding physical appearance and good qualities, and stinginess with the Dhamma of learning, one praises only one's own appearance and qualities. Regarding the qualities of others, one says, 'What quality is that?' and speaks of various faults. And by not giving any of the Dhamma of learning to anyone, one becomes ugly and mute.

Api ca āvāsamacchariyena lohagehe paccati, kulamacchariyena appalābho hoti, lābhamacchariyena gūthaniraye nibbattati, vaṇṇamacchariyena bhave bhave nibbattassa vaṇṇo nāma na hoti, dhammamacchariyena kukkuḷaniraye nibbattatīti.

Moreover, due to stinginess with dwellings, one is tormented in a copper house; due to stinginess with families, one has little gain; due to stinginess with gains, one is reborn in a dung hell; due to stinginess regarding beauty, one who is reborn in existence after existence has no beauty; and due to stinginess with the Dhamma, one is reborn in the ember hell.

Maccharāyanavasena [V 0.0088] macchariyaṃ. Maccharāyanākāro maccharāyanā. Maccharena ayitassa maccherasamaṅgino bhāvo maccharāyitattaṃ. “Mayhameva hontu, mā aññassā”ti sabbāpi attano sampattiyo byāpetuṃ na icchatīti viviccho, vivicchassa bhāvo vevicchaṃ, mudumacchariyassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Kadariyo vuccati anādaro, tassa bhāvo kadariyaṃ, thaddhamacchariyassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Tena hi samannāgato puggalo parampi paresaṃ dadamānaṃ nivāreti. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Miserliness is so called because of the act of being miserly. The mode of being miserly is maccharāyanā. The state of one affected by miserliness, of one endowed with miserliness, is maccharāyitatta. The unwillingness to let any of one’s possessions extend to others—"Let these things be mine alone, not another's"—is called viviccha; the state of one possessing that is veviccha, which is a name for mild miserliness. Kadariya is said to be one who is disrespectful; the state of that person is kadariya, which is a name for hardened miserliness. A person endowed with that even prevents another from giving to others. And this was said:

“Kadariyo [M 0.0097] pāpasaṅkappo, micchādiṭṭhianādaro;

Dadamānaṃ nivāreti, yācamānāna bhojana”nti. (saṃ. ni. 1.132);

"The miser, of evil intention, holding wrong views and being disrespectful, prevents one who is giving and obstructs the food for those who are begging." (Saṃ. Ni. 1.132)

Yācake disvā kaṭukabhāvena cittaṃ añcati saṅkocetīti kaṭukañcuko, tassa bhāvo kaṭukañcukatā. Aparo nayo – kaṭukañcukatā vuccati kaṭacchuggāho. Samatittikapuṇṇāya hi ukkhaliyā bhattaṃ gaṇhanto sabbatobhāgena saṅkuṭitena aggakaṭacchunā gaṇhāti pūretvā gahetuṃ na sakkoti, evaṃ maccharipuggalassa cittaṃ saṅkucati, tasmiṃ saṅkucite kāyopi tatheva saṅkucati paṭikuṭati paṭinivaṭṭati na sampasārīyatīti maccheraṃ “kaṭukañcukatā”ti vuttaṃ.

Seeing a beggar, the mind bends and contracts with harshness; thus, one is called kaṭukañcuka. Its nature is kaṭukañcukatā. Another explanation: kaṭukañcukatā is called taking with a ladle (kaṭacchuggāha). Just as one taking rice from a pot filled to the brim takes it with the tip of a ladle that is constricted on all sides and cannot take a full amount, so too the mind of a miser shrinks. When the mind shrinks, the body also contracts in that way, curls up, recoils, and does not expand—thus, miserliness is called kaṭukañcukatā.

Aggahitattaṃ cittassāti paresaṃ upakārakaraṇe dānādinā ākārena yathā na sampasārīyati, evaṃ āvaritvā gahitabhāvo cittassa. Yasmā pana maccharipuggalo attano santakaṃ paresaṃ [P 1.0114] adātukāmo hoti, parasantakaṃ gaṇhitukāmo. Tasmā “idaṃ acchariyaṃ mayhameva hotu, mā aññassā”ti pavattivasenassa attasampattinigūhanalakkhaṇatā parasampattiggahaṇalakkhaṇatā ca veditabbā.

The mind's state of being ungrasped means that the mind does not expand towards helping others through generosity and so on, but is a state of being held back by obstruction. Because a miserly person is unwilling to give their own possessions to others and desires to take others' possessions, it should be understood that its characteristic is concealing one's own possessions and seizing others' possessions, with the thought prevailing, "Let this wonder be mine alone, not another's."

Khandhamacchariyampi macchariyanti attano pañcakkhandhasaṅkhātaṃ upapattibhavaṃ aññehi asādhāraṇaṃ “acchariyaṃ mayhameva hotu, mā aññassā”ti pavattaṃ macchariyaṃ khandhamacchariyaṃ nāma. Dhātuāyatanamacchariyesupi eseva nayo. Gāhoti gāhanicchayavasena gahaṇaṃ. Avadaññutāyāti sabbaññubuddhānampi kathitaṃ ajānanabhāvena. Yācakānaṃ adadamāno hi tehi kathitaṃ na jānāti nāma. Janā pamattāti sativippavāsā janā. Vacananti saṅkhepavacanaṃ. Byappathanti vitthāravacanaṃ. Desananti upamaṃ dassetvā atthasandassanavacanaṃ. Anusiṭṭhinti punappunaṃ saṃlakkhāpanavacanaṃ. Atha vā dassetvā kathanaṃ vacanaṃ nāma. Gaṇhāpetvā kathanaṃ byappathaṃ nāma. Tosetvā kathanaṃ desanaṃ nāma. Padassetvā kathanaṃ anusiṭṭhi nāma. Atha vā paritāpadukkhaṃ nāsetvā kathanaṃ vacanaṃ nāma. Pariḷāhadukkhaṃ nāsetvā kathanaṃ byappathaṃ nāma. Apāyadukkhaṃ nāsetvā kathanaṃ desanaṃ nāma. Bhavadukkhaṃ nāsetvā [V 0.0089] kathanaṃ anusiṭṭhi nāma. Atha vā dukkhasaccapariññāpaṭivedhayuttaṃ vacanaṃ. Samudayasaccapahānapaṭivedhayuttaṃ byappathaṃ. Nirodhasaccasacchikiriyapaṭivedhayuttaṃ desanaṃ. Maggasaccabhāvanāpaṭivedhayuttaṃ anusiṭṭhīti evamādinā nayena eke vaṇṇayanti.

Stinginess regarding the aggregates is also stinginess—the stinginess that arises with the thought, "Let this wonder, my own existence in rebirth which is reckoned as the five aggregates and is not shared with others, be exclusive to me, not another’s." The same principle applies to stinginess regarding the elements and sense bases. "Grasping" (gāha) means grasping by way of the desire to grasp. "Unresponsiveness" (avadaññutā) means the state of not knowing what has been spoken even by the Omniscient Buddhas—for one who does not give to beggars indeed does not know what has been spoken by them. "People are heedless" means people are devoid of mindfulness. "Speech" refers to concise speech. "Elaboration" refers to detailed speech. "Explanation" refers to speech that illustrates meaning by presenting a simile. "Admonition" refers to speech that repeatedly clarifies. Alternatively, speaking after showing is called "speech." Speaking after making one grasp is called "elaboration." Speaking after pleasing is called "explanation." Speaking after pointing out the way is called "admonition." Or, speaking that destroys the suffering of minor torment is called "speech." Speaking that destroys the suffering of burning torment is called "elaboration." Speaking that destroys the suffering of the lower realms is called "explanation." Speaking that destroys the suffering of existence is called "admonition." Alternatively, some explain it thus: Speech is connected with the penetration of fully understanding the truth of suffering. Elaboration is connected with the penetration of abandoning the truth of the origin. Explanation is connected with the penetration of realizing the truth of cessation. Admonition is connected with the penetration of developing the truth of the path—and so on.

Na [M 0.0098] sussusantīti na suṇanti. Na sotaṃ odahantīti savanatthaṃ kaṇṇasotaṃ na ṭhapenti. Na aññā cittaṃ upaṭṭhapentīti jānanatthaṃ cittaṃ na patiṭṭhapenti. Anassavāti ovādaṃ asuṇamānā. Avacanakarāti suṇamānāpi vacanaṃ na karontīti avacanakarā. Paṭilomavuttinoti paṭāṇī hutvā pavattanakā[P 1.0115]. Aññeneva mukhaṃ karontīti karontāpi mukhaṃ na dentīti attho.

They do not wish to hear—they do not hear. They do not incline the ear—they do not set the ear’s channel for hearing. They do not establish the mind for understanding—they do not fix the mind for knowing. They are unreceptive—not listening to advice. They do not act on what is said—even when they hear, they do not act on what is said. They act contrary—they are ones who behave in opposition. They turn their faces away—meaning that even when doing something, they do not give face.

Visameti kāyasucaritādisammatassa samassa paṭipakkhattā visamaṃ, tasmiṃ visame. Niviṭṭhāti paviṭṭhā dunnīharā. Kāyakammeti kāyato pavatte, kāyena vā pavatte kāyakamme. Vacīkammādīsupi eseva nayo.

In 'uneven' (visame): it is uneven because it is the opposite of the even, which is approved as good bodily conduct and so on; in that unevenness. "Established" (niviṭṭhā) means entered, difficult to remove. "Bodily action" (kāyakamma) means originating from the body, or performed by the body; the same principle applies to actions of speech, etc.

Tattha kāyakammavacīkammamanokammāni duccaritavasena vibhattāni, pāṇātipātādayo dasaakusalakammapathavasena vibhattāti ñātabbaṃ. Ayaṃ tāvettha sādhāraṇapadavaṇṇanā, asādhāraṇesu pana pāṇassa atipāto pāṇātipāto, pāṇavadho pāṇaghātoti vuttaṃ hoti. Pāṇoti cettha vohārato satto, paramatthato jīvitindriyaṃ. Tasmiṃ pana pāṇe pāṇasaññino jīvitindriyupacchedakaupakkamasamuṭṭhāpitā kāyavacīdvārānaṃ aññataradvārapavattā vadhakacetanā pāṇātipāto. So guṇavirahitesu tiracchānagatādīsu pāṇesu khuddake pāṇe appasāvajjo, mahāsarīre mahāsāvajjo. Kasmā? Payogamahantatāya, payogasamattepi vatthumahantatāya. Guṇavantesu manussādīsu appaguṇe pāṇe appasāvajjo, mahāguṇe mahāsāvajjo. Sarīraguṇānaṃ pana samabhāve sati kilesānaṃ upakkamānañca mudutāya appasāvajjo, tibbatāya mahāsāvajjoti veditabbo.

Herein, bodily action, verbal action, and mental action are distinguished by way of misconduct; and it should be understood that the ten unwholesome courses of action, beginning with the destruction of life, are distinguished as such. This, first, is a general exposition of the term. But regarding the specifics, the destruction of life (pāṇātipāta) means the killing of a being, the slaying of life. Herein, 'life' (pāṇa) means a being in conventional terms, but in the ultimate sense it is the life faculty. But in regard to that life, when one perceives a being as a living being, the volition to kill, which arises from an effort initiated to sever the life faculty and occurs through either the body or speech door, is the destruction of life. That is of slight blame in the case of beings devoid of qualities, such as animals, and in the case of small creatures; it is of great blame in the case of large-bodied beings. Why? Because of the magnitude of the effort; and even when the effort is equal, because of the greatness of the object. In beings endowed with virtues, such as humans, it is of slight blame in the case of a being of little virtue, but of great blame in the case of a being of great virtue. But when physical and virtuous qualities are equal, it should be understood that it is of slight blame if the defilements and effort are mild, but of great blame if they are intense.

Tassa pañca sambhārā honti – pāṇo pāṇasaññitā vadhakacittaṃ upakkamo tena maraṇanti. Chappayogā – sāhatthiko āṇattiko nissaggiyo thāvaro vijjāmayo iddhimayoti. Imasmiṃ panatthe vitthāriyamāne atipapañco hoti, tasmā naṃ na vitthārayissāma. Aññañca evarūpaṃ[V 0.0090], atthikehi pana samantapāsādikaṃ vinayaṭṭhakathaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.172) oloketvā gahetabbaṃ.

There are five constituents of it: a living being, the perception of a living being, the thought to kill, the effort, and death resulting from that. There are six modes of application: by one's own hand, by command, by means of a missile, by means of a trap, by means of sorcery, or by psychic power. However, elaborating on this matter would lead to excessive proliferation, therefore we shall not elaborate on it. Other similar cases should be understood by those who are interested by referring to the Vinaya commentary, the Samantapāsādikā (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.172).

Adinnassa [M 0.0099] ādānaṃ adinnādānaṃ, parassa haraṇaṃ theyyaṃ corikāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha adinnanti parapariggahitaṃ, yattha paro yathākāmakāritaṃ āpajjanto adaṇḍāraho anupavajjo ca hoti, tasmiṃ pana parapariggahite parapariggahitasaññino tadādāyakaupakkamasamuṭṭhāpikā theyyacetanā [P 1.0116] adinnādānaṃ. Taṃ hīne parasantake vatthusmiṃ appasāvajjaṃ, paṇīte mahāsāvajjaṃ. Kasmā? Vatthupaṇītatāya, vatthusamatte sati guṇādhikānaṃ santake vatthusmiṃ mahāsāvajjaṃ. Taṃ taṃ guṇādhikaṃ upādāya tato tato hīnaguṇassa santake vatthusmiṃ appasāvajjaṃ.

Taking what is not given is adinnādāna; it is said to be the taking of another's property, stealing, or theft. Herein, 'what is not given' (adinna) means what is possessed by another, in regard to which the other is not liable to punishment or blame when acting as they wish. In that which is possessed by another, the volition to steal, which is initiated by the effort of taking it, when one perceives it as possessed by another, constitutes taking what is not given. This is of slight blame when the object is an inferior possession of another, and of great blame when it is a superior one. Why? Because of the excellence of the object. When the objects are of equal value, it is of great blame if taken from the possession of one of superior qualities. Depending on those superior qualities, it is of slight blame if taken from the possession of one of correspondingly inferior qualities.

Tassa pañca sambhārā honti – parapariggahitaṃ parapariggahitasaññitā theyyacittaṃ upakkamo tena haraṇanti. Chappayogā sāhatthikādayova. Te ca kho yathānurūpaṃ theyyāvahāro pasayhāvahāro paṭicchannāvahāro parikappāvahāro kusāvahāroti imesaṃ pañcannaṃ avahārānaṃ vasena pavattanti. Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthāro pana samantapāsādikāyaṃ vutto.

It has five constituents: what is possessed by another, the perception of it as possessed by another, the volition to steal, the effort, and the taking away by that means. The six modes of application are the same as those beginning with direct action. These acts occur in accordance with five modes of taking: stealthy taking, forcible taking, concealed taking, scheming taking, and deceptive taking. This is the summary here. The detailed explanation, however, is stated in the Samantapāsādikā.

Kāmesumicchācāroti ettha pana kāmesūti methunasamācāresu. Micchācāroti ekantanindito lāmakācāro. Lakkhaṇato pana asaddhammasevanādhippāyena kāyadvārappavattā agamanīyaṭṭhānavītikkamacetanā kāmesumicchācāro.

As for sexual misconduct, here 'in sensual pleasures' refers to sexual intercourse. 'Misconduct' means an utterly blameworthy, base act. By way of characteristic, however, sexual misconduct is the volition to transgress regarding an improper place, a volition that occurs through the body-door with the intention of engaging in unrighteous practice.

Tattha agamanīyaṭṭhānaṃ nāma purisānaṃ tāva māturakkhitā piturakkhitā mātāpiturakkhitā bhāturakkhitā bhaginirakkhitā ñātirakkhitā gottarakkhitā dhammarakkhitā sārakkhā saparidaṇḍāti māturakkhitādayo dasa, dhanakkītā chandavāsinī bhogavāsinī paṭavāsinī odapattakinī obhatacumbaṭakā dāsī ca bhariyā kammakārī ca bhariyā dhajāhaṭā muhuttikāti etā dhanakkītādayo dasāti vīsati itthiyo. Itthīsu pana dvīnnaṃ sārakkhasaparidaṇḍānaṃ dasannañca dhanakkītādīnanti dvādasannaṃ itthīnaṃ aññe purisā, idaṃ agamanīyaṭṭhānaṃ nāma.

Here, an 'improper place' for men refers to twenty types of women. First, these ten: one protected by a mother, one protected by a father, one protected by both parents, one protected by a brother, one protected by a sister, one protected by relatives, one protected by lineage, one protected by the Dhamma, one with a guardian, and one under penalty. And also these ten: one bought with wealth, one cohabiting by consent, one cohabiting for maintenance, one cohabiting for clothing, one married by the water ceremony, one who has had her head-pad removed, a slave who is also a wife, a worker who is also a wife, a war captive, and a temporary wife. For women, however—namely for the two types, 'one with a guardian' and 'one under penalty,' and for the ten types beginning with 'one bought with wealth'—for these twelve women, other men are what is called an 'improper place'.

So panesa micchācāro sīlādiguṇarahite agamanīyaṭṭhāne appasāvajjo, sīlādiguṇasampanne mahāsāvajjo. Tassa cattāro sambhārā [M 0.0100] – agamanīyavatthu tasmiṃ sevanacittaṃ sevanapayogo maggena maggapaṭipattiadhivāsananti. Eko payogo sāhatthiko eva.

This misconduct is of slight offense when directed toward an improper person devoid of virtues such as morality, but of grave offense when toward one endowed with such virtues. Its four constituents are: an improper object, the volition to engage with it, the effort to engage, and the consent to the union of the sexual organs.

Musāti [V 0.0091] visaṃvādanapurekkhārassa atthabhañjanako vacīpayogo kāyapayogo vā. Visaṃvādanādhippāyena panassa paravisaṃvādakakāyavacīpayogasamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā musāvādo. Aparo nayo – musāti abhūtaṃ atacchaṃ vatthu. Vādoti [P 1.0117] tassa bhūtato tacchato viññāpanaṃ. Lakkhaṇato pana atathaṃ vatthuṃ tathato paraṃ viññāpetukāmassa tathāviññattisamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā musāvādo. So yamatthaṃ bhañjati, tassa appatāya appasāvajjo, mahantatāya mahāsāvajjo. Api ca gahaṭṭhānaṃ attano santakaṃ adātukāmatāya “natthī”tiādinayappavatto appasāvajjo, sakkhinā hutvā atthabhañjanatthaṃ vutto mahāsāvajjo. Pabbajitānaṃ appakampi telaṃ vā sappiṃ vā labhitvā hasādhippāyena “ajja gāme telaṃ nadī maññe sandatī”ti pūraṇakathānayena pavatto appasāvajjo, adiṭṭhaṃyeva pana diṭṭhantiādinā nayena vadantānaṃ mahāsāvajjo.

Lying is the use of speech or bodily action, preceded by the intention to deceive, which destroys another's welfare. The volition that gives rise to bodily or verbal action with the intention to deceive others is false speech. Another way of putting it: 'lying' is an unreal, untrue thing. 'Speech' is the communication of that as real and true. By way of characteristic, false speech is the volition, in one who wishes to make another perceive an untrue thing as true, that gives rise to such a communication. According to the welfare it destroys, it is of slight offense when the welfare is minor, and of grave offense when it is major. Moreover, for householders, saying 'I don't have it,' and so forth, out of unwillingness to give away what is their own, is of slight offense; but if one, acting as a witness, speaks to destroy another’s welfare, it is of grave offense. For monastics, having obtained even a small amount of oil or ghee, and then joking, 'Today, I think a river of oil flows in the village,' proceeding by way of exaggeration, is of slight offense; however, saying that they have seen what was not seen, and so forth, is of grave offense.

Tassa cattāro sambhārā honti – atathaṃ vatthu visaṃvādanacittaṃ tajjo vāyāmo parassa tadatthavijānananti. Eko payogo sāhatthikova. So ca kāyena vā kāyapaṭibaddhena vā vācāya vā paravisaṃvādakakiriyākaraṇe daṭṭhabbo. Tāya ce kiriyāya paro tamatthaṃ jānāti, ayaṃ kiriyasamuṭṭhāpikā cetanākkhaṇeyeva musāvādakammunā bajjhati.

It has four constituents: an untrue matter, a deceptive volition, the corresponding effort, and the other person's understanding of that matter. The single mode of application is by oneself alone. This should be understood as the act of deceiving another by body, by something connected with the body, or by speech. If by that action the other person understands the matter, then at the very moment of the volition that gives rise to the action, one is bound by the kamma of false speech.

Pisuṇavācātiādīsu yāya vācāya yassa taṃ vācaṃ bhāsati, tassa hadaye attano piyabhāvaṃ parassa ca suññabhāvaṃ karoti, sā pisuṇavācā. Yāya pana attānampi parampi pharusaṃ karoti, yā vācā sayampi pharusā neva kaṇṇasukhā na hadayaṅgamā, ayaṃ pharusavācā. Yena samphaṃ palapati niratthakaṃ, so samphappalāpo. Tesaṃ mūlabhūtāpi cetanā pisuṇavācādināmameva labhati, sā eva idha adhippetāti.

Among malicious speech and so forth, malicious speech is the speech by which one who speaks creates affection for themselves in the heart of the listener, while causing estrangement from the other person. Harsh speech, on the other hand, is speech that is rough, hurting both oneself and others; speech that is itself rough, neither pleasing to the ear nor endearing to the heart. Idle chatter is that by which one speaks frivolous and meaningless things. The underlying volition for these also obtains the name of malicious speech and so forth; that volition itself is what is intended here.

Tattha saṃkiliṭṭhacittassa paresaṃ vā bhedāya attano piyakamyatāya vā kāyavacīpayogasamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā pisuṇavācā. Sā yassa bhedaṃ karoti[M 0.0101], tassa appaguṇāya appasāvajjā, mahāguṇatāya mahāsāvajjā.

Therein, for one with a defiled mind, the volition that gives rise to bodily and verbal action for the purpose of dividing others or from the desire to be liked is malicious speech. It is of slight offense when it causes division in one of little virtue, and of grave offense when in one of great virtue.

Tassā cattāro sambhārā honti – bhinditabbo paro “iti ime nānā bhavissanti vinā bhavissantī”ti bhedapurekkhāratā vā, “iti ahaṃ piyo bhavissāmi vissāsiko”ti viyakamyatā vā, tajjo vāyāmo, tassa tadatthavijānananti.

It has four requisites: another person to be divided; the intention, being either the aim to cause division, thinking, 'Thus they will be separate, they will be apart,' or the desire to be liked, thinking, 'Thus I will be liked and trusted'; the corresponding effort; and the listener's understanding of that meaning.

Parassa mammacchedakakāyavacīpayogasamuṭṭhāpikā ekantapharusacetanā [P 1.0118] pharusavācā. Mammacchedakopi [V 0.0092] payogo cittasaṇhatāya pharusavācā na hoti. Mātāpitaro hi kadāci puttake evampi vadanti “corā vo khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ karontū”ti, uppalapattampi ca nesaṃ upari patantaṃ na icchanti. Ācariyupajjhāyā ca kadāci nissitake evaṃ vadanti “kiṃ ime ahirikā anottappino caranti, niddhamatha ne”ti. Atha ca nesaṃ āgamādhigamasampattiṃ icchanti. Yathā ca cittasaṇhatāya pharusavācā na hoti, evaṃ vacanasaṇhatāya apharusavācāpi na hoti. Na hi mārāpetukāmassa “imaṃ sukhaṃ sayāpethā”ti vacanaṃ apharusavācā hoti, cittapharusatāya panesā pharusavācāva, sā yaṃ sandhāya pavattitā. Tassa appaguṇatāya appasāvajjā, mahāguṇatāya mahāsāvajjā. Tassā tayo sambhārā – akkositabbo paro kupitacittaṃ akkosananti.

The utterly harsh volition, arising from bodily and verbal action, that pierces the vitals of another is harsh speech. Even a piercing act, if done with a gentle mind, is not harsh speech. For sometimes parents say to their children, 'May thieves cut you into pieces!'—yet they do not even wish a lotus petal to fall upon them. Similarly, teachers and preceptors sometimes say to their dependents, 'Why do these shameless ones, without moral dread, behave so? Drive them away!'—yet they still desire their acquisition and attainment of the Dhamma. Just as speech is not harsh when the mind is gentle, so too speech is not unharsh merely because the words are gentle. For someone who wishes to have another killed, saying, 'Let this one sleep peacefully,' is not unharsh speech—it is harsh speech due to the harshness of the mind, since it is directed toward that person. It is of slight offense when directed at one of little virtue, and of grave offense when at one of great virtue. It has three requisites: another person to be reviled, an angry mind, and the act of reviling.

Anatthaviññāpikā kāyavacīpayogasamuṭṭhāpikā akusalacetanā samphappalāpo. So āsevanamandatāya appasāvajjo, āsevanamahantatāya mahāsāvajjo. Tassa dve sambhārā honti – bhāratayuddhasītāharaṇādiniratthakakathāpurekkhāratā tathārūpīkathākathanañcāti.

The unwholesome volition, arising from bodily and verbal action, that communicates what is unbeneficial, is frivolous talk. It is of slight offense due to weakness in its practice, and of grave offense due to strength in its practice. It has two requisites: the prioritizing of meaningless talk, such as talk about the Mahābhārata war or the abduction of Sītā; and the engaging in such talk.

Abhijjhāyatīti abhijjhā, parabhaṇḍābhimukhī hutvā tanninnatāya pavattatīti attho. Sā “aho vata idaṃ mamāssā”ti evaṃ parabhaṇḍābhijjhāyanalakkhaṇā. Adinnādānaṃ viya appasāvajjā mahāsāvajjā ca. Tassā dve sambhārā honti – parabhaṇḍaṃ attano pariṇāmanañcāti. Parabhaṇḍavatthuke hi lobhe uppannepi na tāva kammapathabhedo hoti, yāva “aho vatidaṃ mamāssā”ti attano na pariṇāmeti.

It covets, thus it is covetousness; this means that it proceeds with an inclination towards another's goods, having turned towards them. It is characterized by longing for another's possessions with the thought, 'Oh, if only this were mine!' Like taking what is not given, it can be of little blame or of great blame. It has two requisites: another's goods, and appropriating them to oneself. For even when greed arises in relation to another's belongings, there is no breach of the path of action until one appropriates them to oneself with the thought, 'Oh, if only this were mine!'.

Hitasukhaṃ [M 0.0102] byāpādayatīti byāpādo, so paravināsāya manopadosalakkhaṇo. Pharusavācā viya appasāvajjo mahāsāvajjo ca. Tassa dve sambhārā honti – parasatto ca tassa ca vināsacintāti. Parasattavatthuke hi kodhe uppannepi na tāva kammapathabhedo [P 1.0119] hoti, yāva “aho vatāyaṃ ucchijjeyya vinasseyyā”ti tassa vināsaṃ na cintesi.

It harms welfare and happiness, thus it is ill will; it is characterized by corruption of mind aimed at another's destruction. Like harsh speech, it can be of little blame or of great blame. It has two requisites: another being, and the thought of that one's destruction. For even when anger arises in relation to another being, the breach of the path of action does not occur until one thinks, 'Oh, may this one be utterly destroyed, may this one perish!' and contemplates their ruin.

Yathābhuccagahaṇābhāvena micchā passatīti micchādiṭṭhi. Sā “natthi dinna”ntiādinā nayena viparītadassanalakkhaṇā. Samphappalāpo viya appasāvajjā mahāsāvajjā ca.

It sees wrongly due to the absence of grasping things as they truly are, thus it is wrong view. It is characterized by distorted seeing, in the manner of 'there is nothing given,' and so on. Like frivolous talk, it is of little blame and of great blame.

Saññī, asaññī, nevasaññīnāsaññī bhavissāmāti rūpādivasena kaṅkhanti. Bhavissāma nu kho mayantiādinā attānaṃ kaṅkhanti. Tattha bhavissāma nu kho. Na nu kho bhavissāmāti tassa [V 0.0093] sassatākārañca ucchedākārañca nissāya anāgate attānaṃ vijjamānatañca avijjamānatañca kaṅkhanti. Kiṃ nu kho bhavissāmāti jātiliṅgupapattiyo nissāya “khattiyā nu kho bhavissāma, brāhmaṇavessasuddagahaṭṭhapabbajitadevamanussānaṃ aññatarā”ti kaṅkhanti. Kathaṃ nu kho bhavissāmāti saṇṭhānākāraṃ nissāya “dīghā nu kho bhavissāma, rassaodātakaṇhapamāṇikaappamāṇikādīnaṃ aññatarā”ti kaṅkhanti. Keci pana “issaranimmānādīni nissāya ‘kena nu kho kāraṇena bhavissāmā’ti hetuto kaṅkhantī”ti vadanti. Kiṃ hutvā kiṃ bhavissāma nu kho mayanti jātiādīni nissāya “khattiyā hutvā nu kho brāhmaṇā bhavissāma…pe… devā hutvā manussā”ti attano paramparaṃ kaṅkhanti. Sabbattheva pana addhānanti kālādhivacanametaṃ.

They doubt, based on form and so forth, 'Will we be percipient, non-percipient, or neither percipient nor non-percipient?' They doubt about the self, saying, 'Will we exist or not?' Herein, relying on the notions of eternalism and annihilationism, they doubt about the existence or non-existence of the self in the future, saying, 'Will we exist? Will we not exist?' Relying on birth, gender, and rebirth, they doubt, 'What will we be? Will we be khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, suddas, householders, renunciants, devas, or humans?' Relying on shape and appearance, they doubt, 'How will we be? Will we be tall, short, fair, dark, of limited size, or unlimited, and so on?' Some, however, say: 'Relying on creation by a supreme being and so forth, they doubt about the cause: "By what cause will we come to be?"' Relying on birth and so forth, they doubt about their own succession of states, saying, 'Having been what, what will we become? Having been khattiyas, will we become brahmins?... Having been devas, will we become humans?' In all cases, 'addhāna' is a term referring to time.

10. Yasmā etadeva tasmā hi sikkhetha…pe… āhu dhīrāti. Tattha sikkhethāti tisso sikkhā āvajjeyya. Idhevāti imasmiṃyeva sāsane. Tattha sikkhitabbāti sikkhā. Tissoti gaṇanaparicchedo. Adhisīlasikkhāti adhikaṃ uttamaṃ sīlanti adhisīlaṃ, adhisīlañca taṃ sikkhitabbaṭṭhena sikkhā cāti adhisīlasikkhā. Esa nayo adhicittaadhipaññāsikkhāsu.

10. Since this is so, therefore, one should train... so the wise declare. Herein, 'one should train' means one should apply oneself to the three trainings. 'Here' means in this very dispensation. Herein, that which should be trained is training. 'Three' denotes a numerical distinction. Higher virtue training: virtue that is superior and excellent is higher virtue; and since it is higher virtue and that which should be trained, it is higher virtue training. The same principle applies to higher mind training and higher wisdom training.

Katamaṃ panettha sīlaṃ, katamaṃ adhisīlaṃ, katamaṃ cittaṃ, katamaṃ adhicittaṃ, katamā paññā, katamā adhipaññāti? Vuccate – pañcaṅgadasaṅgasīlaṃ tāva sīlameva[M 0.0103]. Tañhi buddhe uppannepi anuppannepi loke pavattati[P 1.0120]. Uppanne buddhe tasmiṃ sīle buddhāpi sāvakāpi mahājanaṃ samādapenti, anuppanne buddhe paccekabuddhā ca kammavādino ca dhammikā samaṇabrāhmaṇā ca cakkavattī ca mahārājāno mahābodhisattā ca samādapenti, sāmampi paṇḍitā samaṇabrāhmaṇā samādiyanti. Te taṃ kusalaṃ dhammaṃ paripūretvā devesu ca manussesu ca sampattiṃ anubhonti.

What then is virtue, what is higher virtue, what is mind, what is higher mind, what is wisdom, what is higher wisdom? It is said: The five-factored and ten-factored virtue is simply virtue. For it exists in the world whether a Buddha has arisen or not. When a Buddha has arisen, both the Buddha and his disciples encourage the multitude in this virtue. When no Buddha has arisen, paccekabuddhas, those who affirm kamma, righteous ascetics and brahmins, wheel-turning monarchs, great kings, and great bodhisattas encourage it. Wise ascetics and brahmins also undertake it themselves. Having fulfilled that wholesome quality, they experience prosperity among devas and humans.

Pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlaṃ pana “adhisīla”nti vuccati. Tañhi sūriyo viya pajjotānaṃ sineru viya pabbatānaṃ sabbalokiyasīlānaṃ adhikañceva uttamañca, buddhuppādeyeva ca pavattati, na vinā buddhuppādā. Na hi taṃ paññattiṃ uddharitvā añño satto ṭhapetuṃ sakkoti. Buddhāyeva pana sabbaso kāyavacīdvāraajjhācārasotaṃ chinditvā tassa tassa vītikkamassa anucchavikaṃ taṃ sīlasaṃvaraṃ paññapenti. Pātimokkhasaṃvaratopi ca maggaphalasampayuttameva sīlaṃ adhisīlaṃ.

The virtue of Pātimokkha restraint, however, is called 'higher virtue.' For just as the sun is superior to lights and Mount Sineru is superior to mountains, so too is this superior and supreme among all worldly virtues. Moreover, it arises only with the appearance of a Buddha; it does not arise without the appearance of a Buddha. Indeed, no other being can establish that rule after having drawn it up. Only the Buddhas, having completely severed the stream of transgressions through the doors of body and speech, prescribe that virtue-restraint appropriate for each transgression. And even beyond the restraint of the Pātimokkha, the virtue associated with the path and fruition is itself 'higher virtue.'

Kāmāvacarāni [V 0.0094] pana aṭṭha kusalacittāni lokiyaaṭṭhasamāpatticittāni ca ekajjhaṃ katvā cittamevāti veditabbāni. Buddhuppādānuppāde cassa pavatti, samādapanaṃ samādānañca sīle vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

The eight wholesome consciousnesses of the sense sphere and the consciousnesses of the eight worldly meditative attainments should be understood collectively as simply mind. Its occurrence, whether a Buddha has arisen or not, and its instigation and undertaking, should be understood in the same way as explained regarding virtue.

Vipassanāpādakaṃ aṭṭhasamāpatticittaṃ pana “adhicitta”nti vuccati. Tañhi adhisīlaṃ viya sīlānaṃ, sabbalokiyacittānaṃ adhikañceva uttamañca, buddhuppādeyeva ca hoti, na vinā buddhuppādā. Tatopi ca maggaphalacittameva adhicittaṃ.

The consciousness of the eight attainments that serves as the basis for insight is called 'the higher mind.' For just as higher virtue is superior among virtues, so too is this superior and supreme among all mundane consciousnesses, and it exists only with the arising of a Buddha, not without the arising of a Buddha. And beyond that, the path and fruition consciousness is itself the higher mind.

“Atthi dinnaṃ atthi yiṭṭha”ntiādinayappavattaṃ (ma. ni. 2.94) pana kammassakatāñāṇaṃ paññā. Sā hi buddhe uppannepi anuppannepi loke pavattati. Uppanne buddhe tassā paññāya buddhāpi sāvakāpi mahājanaṃ samādapenti, anuppanne buddhe paccekabuddhā ca kammavādino ca dhammikā samaṇabrāhmaṇā ca cakkavattī ca mahārājāno mahābodhisattā ca samādapenti, sāmampi paṇḍitā sattā samādiyanti. Tathā hi aṅkuro dasavassasahassāni mahādānaṃ adāsi. Velāmo vessantaro aññe ca bahū paṇḍitamanussā mahādānāni adaṃsu. Te taṃ kusalaṃ dhammaṃ paripūretvā devesu ca manussesu ca sampattiṃ anubhaviṃsu.

The knowledge of kamma as one's own, expressed in phrases like 'there is giving, there is sacrifice,' is wisdom. For this wisdom exists in the world whether a Buddha has arisen or not. When a Buddha has arisen, both the Buddha and his disciples encourage the multitude in this wisdom. When no Buddha has arisen, Paccekabuddhas, advocates of kamma, righteous ascetics and brahmins, wheel-turning monarchs, great kings, and great bodhisattas encourage it, and wise beings undertake it themselves. Thus, for example, Aṅkura gave great gifts for ten thousand years. Velāma, Vessantara, and many other wise humans also gave great gifts. Having fully perfected that wholesome quality, they experienced prosperity among gods and humans.

Tilakkhaṇākāraparicchedakaṃ [M 0.0104] pana [P 1.0121] vipassanāñāṇaṃ “adhipaññā”ti vuccati. Sā hi adhisīlaadhicittāni viya sīlacittānaṃ, sabbalokiyapaññānaṃ adhikā ceva uttamā ca, na ca vinā buddhuppādā loke pavattati. Tatopi ca maggaphalapaññāva adhipaññā.

The insight knowledge that discerns the three characteristics, however, is called 'higher wisdom.' For just as higher virtue and higher mind are superior to virtue and consciousness, so too is this higher wisdom superior and supreme to all worldly wisdom, and it does not occur in the world without the arising of a Buddha. Moreover, the wisdom of the path and fruition itself is higher wisdom.

Idāni ekekaṃ dassento “katamā adhisīlasikkhā – idha bhikkhu sīlavā hoti, pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto viharatī”tiādimāha. Idhāti vacanaṃ pubbabhāgakaraṇīyasampadāya sampannassa sabbapakārasīlaparipūrakassa puggalassa sannissayabhūtasāsanaparidīpanaṃ, aññasāsanassa ca tathābhāvapaṭisedhanaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ – “idheva, bhikkhave, samaṇo…pe… suññā parappavādā samaṇebhi aññehī”ti (ma. ni. 1.139-140). Bhikkhūti tassa sīlassa paripūrakassa puggalassa paridīpanaṃ. Pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutoti idamassa pātimokkhasaṃvare patiṭṭhitabhāvaparidīpanaṃ. Viharatīti idamassa tadanurūpavihārasamaṅgībhāvaparidīpanaṃ. Ācāragocarasampannoti idamassa pātimokkhasaṃvarassa upakārakadhammaparidīpanaṃ. Aṇumattesu vajjesu bhayadassāvīti idamassa pātimokkhato acavanadhammatāparidīpanaṃ. Samādāyāti idamassa sikkhāpadānaṃ [V 0.0095] anavasesato ādānaparidīpanaṃ. Sikkhatīti idamassa sikkhāya samaṅgībhāvaparidīpanaṃ. Sikkhāpadesūti idamassa sikkhitabbadhammaparidīpanaṃ.

Now, explaining each one, he says: “What is the higher training in virtue? Here, a monk is virtuous, restrained with the restraint of the Pātimokkha…” and so on. The word 'here' illuminates the teaching as the foundation for a person who has fulfilled the preparatory duties and perfected virtue in every way, while also refuting that other teachings are the same. For it is said: “Here alone, monks, is the ascetic… empty are the doctrines of other ascetics.” 'Monk' illuminates the person who has perfected that virtue. 'Restrained with the restraint of the Pātimokkha' illuminates his firm establishment in the restraint of the Pātimokkha. 'He dwells' illuminates his possession of a lifestyle in accordance with that. 'Endowed with good conduct and resort' illuminates the qualities that assist the restraint of the Pātimokkha. 'Seeing danger in the slightest faults' illuminates his nature of not deviating from the Pātimokkha. 'Having undertaken' illuminates his complete acceptance of the precepts. 'He trains' illuminates his possession of training. 'In the training rules' illuminates the qualities to be trained in.

Tattha bhikkhūti saṃsāre bhayaṃ ikkhatīti bhikkhu. Sīlamassa atthīti sīlavāti ettha sīlanti sīlanaṭṭhena sīlaṃ. Kimidaṃ sīlanaṃ nāma? Samādhānaṃ vā, kāyakammādīnaṃ susīlyavasena avippakiṇṇatāti attho. Upadhāraṇaṃ vā, kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ patiṭṭhāvasena ādhārabhāvoti attho. Etadeva hi ettha atthadvayaṃ saddalakkhaṇavidū anujānanti. Aññe pana “adhisevanaṭṭhena ācāraṭṭhena [P 1.0122] sīlanaṭṭhena siraṭṭhena sītalaṭṭhena sivaṭṭhena sīla”nti vaṇṇayanti.

Here, a monk is one who sees fear in the cycle of existence. He is virtuous, possessing virtue—here, virtue means virtue in the sense of ordering. What is this ordering? It is either the composing, or the non-scattering, of bodily actions and so forth by way of good conduct.
