Or it is the state of being a foundation, serving as a support for wholesome qualities, the meaning being the state of a basis. Indeed, the wise in language acknowledge these two meanings here. Others, however, describe virtue as 'virtue in the sense of adhesion, in the sense of conduct, in the sense of ordering, in the sense of eminence, in the sense of coolness, in the sense of safety.'

Sīlanaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ tassa, bhinnassāpi anekadhā;

Sanidassanattaṃ rūpassa, yathā bhinnassanekadhā.

Its characteristic is ordering, even when it is diverse in many ways; just as visibility is for form, even when it is diverse in many ways.

Yathā hi nīlapītādibhedenanekadhā bhinnassāpi rūpāyatanassa sanidassanattaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ nīlādibhedena bhinnassāpi sanidassanabhāvānatikkamanato. Tathā sīlassa cetanādibhedena anekadhā bhinnassāpi yadetaṃ [M 0.0105] kāyakammādīnaṃ samādhānavasena, kusalānañca dhammānaṃ patiṭṭhāvasena vuttaṃ sīlanaṃ, tadeva lakkhaṇaṃ cetanādibhedena bhinnassāpi samādhānapatiṭṭhābhāvānatikkamanato. Evaṃ lakkhaṇassa panassa –

For just as the form-base, though divided in many ways by distinctions such as blue and yellow, has visibility as its characteristic because it does not transcend the state of being visible even though divided by distinctions of blue and so on, so too virtue, though divided in many ways by distinctions such as volition, has as its characteristic that very ordering which is spoken of in terms of the composing of bodily actions and so forth, and in terms of being a foundation for wholesome qualities, because it does not transcend the state of composing and being a foundation even though divided by distinctions of volition and so on. Thus, regarding its characteristic—

Dussīlyaviddhaṃsanatā, anavajjaguṇo tathā;

Kiccasampattiatthena, raso nāma pavuccati.

The destruction of immorality, and likewise its faultless quality, is called its function in the sense of the accomplishment of its task.

Tasmā idaṃ sīlaṃ nāma kiccaṭṭhena rasena dussīlyaviddhaṃsanarasaṃ, sampattiatthena rasena anavajjarasanti veditabbaṃ.

Therefore, this virtue should be understood as having the function of destroying immorality, in the sense of its task; and as having the function of being blameless, in the sense of its accomplishment.

Soceyyapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, tayidaṃ tassa viññubhi;

Ottappañca hirī ceva, padaṭṭhānanti vaṇṇitaṃ.

Its manifestation is purity, this is declared by the wise; and fear of wrongdoing and shame are described as its proximate cause.

Tañhidaṃ sīlaṃ “kāyasoceyyaṃ vacīsoceyyaṃ manosoceyya”nti evaṃ vuttasoceyyapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, soceyyabhāvena paccupaṭṭhāti gahaṇabhāvaṃ gacchati. Hirottappañca pana tassa viññūhi padaṭṭhānanti vaṇṇitaṃ, āsannakāraṇanti attho. Hirottappe hi sati sīlaṃ uppajjati [V 0.0096] ceva tiṭṭhati ca, asati neva uppajjati ceva na tiṭṭhati cāti evaṃvidhena sīlena sīlavā hoti. Etaṃ sīlaṃ nāma pāṇātipātādīhi vā viramantassa, vattapaṭipattiṃ vā pūrentassa cetanādayo [P 1.0123] dhammā veditabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ paṭisambhidāyaṃ “kiṃ sīlanti? Cetanā sīlaṃ, cetasikaṃ sīlaṃ, saṃvaro sīlaṃ, avītikkamo sīla”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.39).

This virtue has as its manifestation the purity spoken of as 'purity of body, purity of speech, purity of mind'; it manifests as a state of purity and becomes graspable. Furthermore, shame and fear of wrongdoing are described by the wise as its proximate cause, meaning its immediate cause. For when shame and fear of wrongdoing exist, virtue arises and endures; when they do not exist, it neither arises nor endures. Thus, one is virtuous through such virtue. This virtue, in the case of one who abstains from killing living beings, etc., or who fulfills the prescribed duties, should be understood as the mental factors beginning with volition. For it was said in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: "What is virtue? Volition is virtue, mental factors are virtue, restraint is virtue, non-transgression is virtue."

Tattha cetanā sīlaṃ nāma pāṇātipātādīhi vā viramantassa vattapaṭipattiṃ vā pūrentassa cetanā. Cetasikaṃ sīlaṃ nāma pāṇātipātādīhi viramantassa virati. Api ca cetanā sīlaṃ nāma pāṇātipātādīni pajahantassa sattakammapathacetanā. Cetasikaṃ sīlaṃ nāma “abhijjhaṃ pahāya vigatābhijjhena cetasā viharatī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.217) nayena saṃyuttamahāvagge vuttā anabhijjhābyāpādasammādiṭṭhidhammā. Saṃvaro sīlanti ettha pañcavidhena saṃvaro veditabbo – pātimokkhasaṃvaro satisaṃvaro ñāṇasaṃvaro khantisaṃvaro vīriyasaṃvaro. Tassa nānākaraṇaṃ upari āvi bhavissati. Avītikkamo sīlanti samādinnasīlassa kāyikavācasiko avītikkamo. Ettha ca saṃvarasīlaṃ, avītikkamasīlanti idameva nippariyāyato [M 0.0106] sīlaṃ. Cetanāsīlaṃ, cetasikaṃ sīlanti pariyāyato sīlanti veditabbaṃ.

Therein, volition as virtue is the volition of one who abstains from killing living beings and so forth, or who fulfills a course of conduct. Virtue as a mental factor is the abstinence of one who abstains from killing living beings and so forth. Moreover, volition as virtue is the volition of the seven wholesome courses of action of one who abandons killing living beings and so forth. Virtue as a mental factor comprises the qualities of non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view, as stated in the Mahāvagga of the Saṃyutta Nikāya in the manner beginning with 'abandoning covetousness, one dwells with a mind free from covetousness...' Restraint as virtue—here, restraint is to be understood as fivefold: restraint by the Pātimokkha, restraint by mindfulness, restraint by knowledge, restraint by patience, and restraint by energy. Its various distinctions will become clear later. Non-transgression as virtue is the bodily and verbal non-transgression of one who has undertaken virtue. Herein, restraint as virtue and non-transgression as virtue are indeed virtue in the direct sense. Volition as virtue and virtue as a mental factor are to be understood as virtue in a figurative sense.

Pātimokkhanti sikkhāpadasīlaṃ. Tañhi yo naṃ pāti rakkhati, taṃ mokkheti moceti āpāyikādīhi dukkhehi, tasmā “pātimokkha”nti vuttaṃ. Pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutoti pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlena samannāgato. Ācāragocarasampannoti ācārena ceva gocarena ca sampanno. Aṇumattesūti appamattakesu. Vajjesūti akusaladhammesu. Bhayadassāvīti bhayadassī. Samādāyāti sammā ādiyitvā. Sikkhati sikkhāpadesūti taṃ taṃ sikkhāpadaṃ samādiyitvā sikkhati. Api ca samādāya sikkhati sikkhāpadesūti yaṃkiñci sikkhāpadesu sikkhākoṭṭhāsesu sikkhitabbaṃ kāyikaṃ vā cetasikaṃ vā, taṃ sabbaṃ samādāya sikkhati.

The Pātimokkha is the virtue of the training rules. For whoever protects (pāti) it, that releases (mokkheti) and frees them from the sufferings of the lower realms and so on; therefore, it is called "Pātimokkha." 'Restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha' means endowed with the virtue of Pātimokkha restraint. 'Accomplished in conduct and resort' means accomplished in both conduct and resort. 'In the slightest' means in insignificant matters. 'In faults' means in unwholesome qualities. 'Seeing danger' means one who sees danger. 'Undertaking' means properly undertaking. 'Trains in the training rules' means undertaking each training rule and training in it. Moreover, 'undertakes and trains in the training rules' means whatever is to be trained—whether bodily or mental—in the training rules or training sections, one undertakes and trains in all of it.

Khuddako sīlakkhandhoti saṅghādisesādisāvaseso sīlakkhandho. Mahantoti pārājikādiniravaseso. Yasmā pana pātimokkhasīlena bhikkhu sāsane patiṭṭhāti nāma[P 1.0124], tasmā taṃ “patiṭṭhā”ti vuttaṃ. Patiṭṭhahati vā ettha bhikkhu, kusalā dhammā eva vā ettha patiṭṭhahantīti patiṭṭhā. Ayamattho “sīle patiṭṭhāya naro sapañño”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.23, 192) ca, “patiṭṭhānalakkhaṇaṃ, mahārāja, sīlaṃ sabbesaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammāna”nti (mi. pa. 2.1.9) ca[V 0.0097], “sīle patiṭṭhito kho, mahārāja…pe… sabbe kusalā dhammā na parihāyantī”ti (mi. pa. 2.1.9) ca ādisuttavasena veditabbo.

The minor section of virtue (sīlakkhandha) is the section of virtue that leaves a remainder, such as the Saṅghādisesa rules. The major section is that which is without remainder, such as the Pārājika rules. Since it is by means of the Pātimokkha virtue that a bhikkhu is said to be established in the Dispensation, it is therefore called 'establishment' (patiṭṭhā). Either a bhikkhu becomes established therein, or wholesome states become established therein; thus it is 'establishment'. This meaning should be understood by way of such discourses as: 'A wise person established in virtue' (SN 1.23, 192); 'Virtue, O great king, has establishment as its characteristic for all wholesome states' (Miln 2.1.9); and 'Established in virtue, O great king... all wholesome states do not decline' (Miln 2.1.9).

Tadetaṃ pubbuppattiatthena ādi. Vuttampi cetaṃ “tasmātiha tvaṃ uttiya ādimeva visodhehi kusalesu dhammesu. Ko cādi kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ, sīlañca suvisuddhaṃ diṭṭhi ca ujukā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.382). Yathā hi nagaravaḍḍhakī nagaraṃ māpetukāmo paṭhamaṃ nagaraṭṭhānaṃ sodheti, tato aparabhāge vīthicatukkasiṅghāṭakādiparicchedena vibhajitvāva nagaraṃ māpeti. Evameva yogāvacaro ādito sīlaṃ visodheti, tato aparabhāge samādhivipassanāmaggaphalanibbānāni sacchikaroti. Yathā vā pana rajako paṭhamaṃ tīhi khārehi vatthaṃ dhovitvā parisuddhe vatthe yadicchakaṃ raṅgajātaṃ upaneti, yathā vā pana cheko cittakāro rūpaṃ likhitukāmo āditova bhittiparikammaṃ karoti, tato aparabhāge rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Evameva yogāvacaro [M 0.0107] āditova sīlaṃ visodhetvā aparabhāge samathavipassanādayo dhamme sacchikaroti. Tasmā sīlaṃ “ādī”ti vuttaṃ.

This is called 'beginning' (ādi) in the sense of its prior arising. And it has been said: 'Therefore, Uttiya, purify the very beginning in wholesome states. And what is the beginning of wholesome states? Perfectly purified virtue and upright view' (SN 5.382). Just as a city builder, wishing to construct a city, first clears the city site, and then afterwards, having divided it by means of streets, squares, crossroads, and so forth, constructs the city; even so, the yogin first purifies virtue, and then afterwards realizes concentration, insight, the paths, their fruits, and Nibbāna. Or just as a dyer first washes a cloth with three kinds of lye and then applies any desired dye to the purified cloth; or just as a skilled painter, wishing to paint a figure, first prepares the wall and then afterwards creates the figure; even so, the yogin, having first purified virtue, afterwards realizes the states of serenity, insight, and so forth. Therefore, virtue is called the 'beginning'.

Tadetaṃ caraṇasarikkhatāya caraṇaṃ. Caraṇāti hi pādā vuccanti. Yathā hi chinnacaraṇassa purisassa disaṃ gamanābhisaṅkhāro na jāyati, paripuṇṇapādasseva jāyati, evameva yassa sīlaṃ bhinnaṃ hoti khaṇḍaṃ aparipuṇṇaṃ, tassa nibbānagamanāya ñāṇagamanaṃ na sampajjati. Yassa pana taṃ abhinnaṃ hoti akhaṇḍaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ, tassa nibbānagamanāya ñāṇagamanaṃ sampajjati. Tasmā sīlaṃ “caraṇa”nti vuttaṃ.

This is called 'conduct' (caraṇa) because of its resemblance to feet (caraṇa). For 'caraṇa' means feet. Just as for a person whose feet are cut off, the volitional formation for going in a direction does not arise, but it arises only for one with complete feet; even so, for one whose virtue is broken, flawed, and incomplete, the movement of knowledge for going to Nibbāna does not succeed. But for one whose virtue is unbroken, unflawed, and complete, the movement of knowledge for going to Nibbāna succeeds. Therefore, virtue is called 'conduct'.

Tadetaṃ saṃyamanavasena saṃyamo. Saṃvaraṇavasena saṃvaroti ubhayenāpi sīlasaṃyamo ceva sīlasaṃvaro ca kathito. Vacanattho panettha saṃyameti vītikkamavipphandanaṃ[P 1.0125], puggalaṃ vā saṃyameti vītikkamavasena tassa vipphandituṃ na detīti saṃyamo. Vītikkamassa pavesanadvāraṃ saṃvarati pidahatīti saṃvaro.

This is called 'restraint' (saṃyama) in the sense of restraining. It is 'guarding' (saṃvara) in the sense of covering. Thus, both virtue as restraint and virtue as guarding are explained. The meaning of the word here is: 'restraint' (saṃyamo) restrains the agitation of transgression, or it restrains a person, not allowing them to become agitated by way of transgression. 'Guarding' (saṃvaro) covers, or closes, the door of entry for transgression.

Mokkhanti uttamaṃ mukhabhūtaṃ vā. Yathā hi sattānaṃ catubbidho āhāro mukhena pavisitvā aṅgamaṅgāni pharati, evaṃ yoginopi catubhūmakakusalaṃ sīlamukhena pavisitvā atthasiddhiṃ sampādeti. Tena “mokkha”nti. Pamukhe sādhūti pāmokkhaṃ, pubbaṅgamaṃ seṭṭhaṃ padhānanti attho. Kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ samāpattiyāti catubhūmakakusalānaṃ paṭilābhatthāya pāmokkhaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ seṭṭhaṃ padhānanti veditabbaṃ.

It is called 'mokkha' (foremost), or that which is the highest, or that which is like a mouth. For just as the four kinds of nutriment for beings enter through the mouth and pervade the limbs, so too for a yogī, the wholesome states of the four planes, entering through the mouth of virtue, bring about the accomplishment of the goal. Hence it is called 'mokkha'. 'Pāmokkha' means 'excellent in the forefront'; the meaning is 'leading,' 'supreme,' 'principal.' It should be understood that it is foremost, leading, supreme, and principal for the sake of attaining wholesome states, that is, for the acquisition of the wholesome states of the four planes.

Vivicceva [V 0.0098] kāmehīti kāmehi vivicca vinā hutvā apakkamitvā. Yo panāyamettha evakāro, so niyamatthoti veditabbo. Yasmā ca niyamattho, tasmā tasmiṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharaṇasamaye avijjamānānampi kāmānaṃ tassa paṭhamajjhānassa paṭipakkhabhāvaṃ kāmapariccāgeneva cassa adhigamaṃ dīpeti. Kathaṃ? “Vivicceva kāmehī”ti evañhi niyame kariyamāne idaṃ paññāyati, nūnimassa jhānassa kāmā paṭipakkhabhūtā, yesu sati idaṃ na pavattati andhakāre sati padīpobhāso viya, tesaṃ pariccāgeneva cassa adhigamo hoti orimatīrapariccāgena pārimatīrasseva. Tasmā niyamaṃ karotīti.

'Secluded from sensual pleasures' (vivicceva kāmehi) means being separated from sensual pleasures, being without them, or having withdrawn from them. The particle 'eva' here should be understood as having the meaning of restriction (niyamattha). And because it has the meaning of restriction, it indicates that even when sensual pleasures are absent at the time of attaining and abiding in the first jhāna, they are still opponents of that first jhāna, and that its attainment is achieved only by abandoning sensual pleasures. How so? For when such a restriction as 'secluded from sensual pleasures' is made, this becomes clear: that sensual pleasures are indeed opponents of this jhāna, such that when they are present, this jhāna does not arise, just as the light of a lamp does not appear when there is darkness; and its attainment is achieved only by abandoning them, just as the far shore is reached only by abandoning the near shore. Therefore, it makes a restriction.

Tattha [M 0.0108] siyā “kasmā panesa pubbapadeyeva vutto na uttarapade, kiṃ akusalehi dhammehi aviviccāpi jhānaṃ upasampajja vihareyyā”ti? Na kho panetaṃ evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Taṃnissaraṇato hi pubbapade eva esa vutto. Kāmadhātusamatikkamanato hi kāmarāgapaṭipakkhato ca idaṃ jhānaṃ kāmānameva nissaraṇaṃ. Yathāha – “kāmānametaṃ nissaraṇaṃ yadidaṃ nekkhamma”nti (itivu. 72). Uttarapadepi pana yathā [P 1.0126] “idheva, bhikkhave, samaṇo, idha dutiyo samaṇo”ti (ma. ni. 1.139) ettha evakāro ānetvā vuccati, evaṃ vattabbo. Na hi sakkā ito aññehipi nīvaraṇasaṅkhātehi akusalehi dhammehi avivicca jhānaṃ upasampajja viharituṃ. Tasmā vivicceva kāmehi vivicceva akusalehi dhammehīti evaṃ padadvayepi esa daṭṭhabbo. Padadvayepi ca kiñcāpi viviccāti iminā sādhāraṇavacanena tadaṅgavivekādayo kāyavivekādayo ca sabbepi vivekā saṅgahaṃ gacchanti, tathāpi pubbabhāge kāyavivekacittavivekavikkhambhanavivekā daṭṭhabbā. Lokuttaramaggakkhaṇe kāyavivekacittavivekasamucchedavivekanissaraṇavivekā.

Here, one might ask: 'Why is this stated only in the earlier phrase and not in the later phrase? Could one attain and abide in jhāna even without being secluded from unwholesome states?' But this should not be seen in such a way. For it is stated in the earlier phrase precisely because it is the escape from them. For this jhāna is indeed the escape from sensual pleasures, by transcending the sensual realm and by being the antidote to sensual lust. As it is said: 'This is the escape from sensual pleasures, namely, renunciation' (Itiv. 72). In the later phrase, however, just as the particle 'eva' is brought in and used in 'Here, bhikkhus, is the ascetic; here is the second ascetic' (MN 1.139), so too it should be supplied. For it is impossible to attain and abide in jhāna without being secluded from other unwholesome states, namely, the hindrances. Therefore, it should be understood that it applies to both phrases: 'secluded from sensual pleasures' and 'secluded from unwholesome states'. And although in both phrases, by this general expression 'secluded' (vivicca), all kinds of seclusion are included, such as seclusion by substitution of opposites (tadaṅgaviveka) and bodily seclusion (kāyaviveka), etc., nevertheless, in the preliminary stage, bodily seclusion, mental seclusion, and seclusion by suppression should be understood. At the moment of the supramundane path, bodily seclusion, mental seclusion, seclusion by eradication, and seclusion by escape are to be understood.

Kāmehīti iminā pana padena ye ca idha “katame vatthukāmā manāpikā rūpā”tiādinā nayena vatthukāmā vuttā, ye ca idheva vibhaṅge “chando kāmo rāgo kāmo chandarāgo kāmo saṅkappo kāmo rāgo kāmo saṅkapparāgo kāmo”ti evaṃ kilesakāmā vuttā, te sabbepi saṅgahitā icceva daṭṭhabbā. Evañhi sati vivicceva kāmehīti vatthukāmehipi viviccevāti attho yujjati. Tena kāyaviveko vutto hoti.

By this phrase 'from sensual pleasures' (kāmehi), it should be understood that all are included: both the sensual pleasures as objects mentioned here by way of 'What are the sensual pleasures as objects? Pleasing forms, etc.' and the sensual pleasures as defilements stated in the Vibhaṅga as 'Desire is sensual pleasure, lust is sensual pleasure, desire-lust is sensual pleasure, intention is sensual pleasure, lust is sensual pleasure, intention-lust is sensual pleasure'. When this is the case, the meaning 'secluded from sensual pleasures' applies, that is, secluded even from sensual pleasures as objects. Thereby, bodily seclusion is spoken of.

Vivicca akusalehi dhammehīti kilesakāmehi sabbākusalehi vā viviccāti attho yujjati. Tena cittaviveko vutto hoti. Purimena cettha vatthukāmehi vivekavacanato eva kāmasukhapariccāgo, dutiyena kilesakāmehi vivekavacanato nekkhammasukhapariggaho vibhāvito hoti[V 0.0099]. Evaṃ vatthukāmakilesakāmavivekavacanatoyeva ca etesaṃ paṭhamena saṃkilesavatthuppahānaṃ, dutiyena saṃkilesappahānaṃ. Paṭhamena lolabhāvassa hetupariccāgo, dutiyena bālabhāvassa. Paṭhamena ca payogasuddhi, dutiyena āsayaposanaṃ vibhāvitaṃ hotīti ñātabbaṃ[M 0.0109]. Esa tāva nayo “kāmehī”ti ettha vuttakāmesu vatthukāmapakkhe[P 1.0127].

'Secluded from unwholesome states' (vivicca akusalehi dhammehi) means seclusion from sensual pleasures as defilements or from all unwholesome states; this meaning fits. Thereby, mental seclusion is spoken of. And here, by the statement of seclusion from sensual pleasures as objects in the first instance, the abandonment of sensual pleasure is made clear; and by the statement of seclusion from sensual pleasures as defilements in the second instance, the acceptance of the bliss of renunciation is made clear. Thus, by the very statements of seclusion from sensual pleasures as objects and sensual pleasures as defilements, the first refers to the abandoning of the basis for defilement, and the second to the abandoning of defilement itself. By the first, the cause of greed is relinquished; by the second, foolishness. And by the first, purity of effort is made clear; by the second, the nurturing of one's disposition. This should be understood. This, then, is the method regarding the sensual pleasures as objects among the sensual pleasures mentioned in 'from sensual pleasures'.

Kilesakāmapakkhe pana chandoti ca rāgoti ca evamādīhi anekabhedo kāmacchandova “kāmo”ti adhippeto. So ca akusalapariyāpannopi samāno “tattha katamo kāmacchando, kāmo”tiādinā nayena vibhaṅge jhānapaṭipakkhato visuṃ vutto. Kilesakāmattā vā purimapade vutto, akusalapariyāpannattā dutiyapade. Anekabhedato cassa kāmatoti avatvā kāmehīti vuttaṃ. Aññesampi ca dhammānaṃ akusalabhāve vijjamāne “tattha katame akusalā dhammā, kāmacchando”tiādinā nayena vibhaṅge (vibha. 564) uparijhānaṅgānaṃ paccanīkapaṭipakkhabhāvadassanato nīvaraṇāneva vuttāni. Nīvaraṇāni hi jhānaṅgapaccanīkāni tesaṃ jhānaṅgāneva paṭipakkhāni, viddhaṃsakāni vighātakānīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tathā hi “samādhi kāmacchandassa paṭipakkho, pīti byāpādassa, vitakko thinamiddhassa, sukhaṃ uddhaccakukkuccassa, vicāro vicikicchāyā”ti peṭake vuttaṃ.

In the case of sensual pleasures as defilements, however, 'kāma' is intended to mean sensual desire (kāmacchanda), which is of many kinds, such as desire (chanda) and lust (rāga). Although it is included among the unwholesome, in the Vibhaṅga it is mentioned separately, as in 'Herein, what is sensual desire, sensual pleasure?' and so forth, because it is an opponent of jhāna. It is mentioned in the first phrase because it is a sensual pleasure as defilement, and in the second phrase because it is included among the unwholesome. And because it is of many kinds, it is said 'from sensual pleasures' (kāmehi) instead of 'from sensual pleasure' (kāmato). Even though other states are also unwholesome, in the Vibhaṅga (Vibh. 564) only the hindrances are mentioned, as in 'Herein, what are the unwholesome states? Sensual desire...' and so forth, because they show the state of being the direct opponents of the jhāna factors. For the hindrances are indeed opponents of the jhāna factors, and the jhāna factors are their opponents, their destroyers and obstructors. Thus, in the Peṭaka, it is stated: 'Concentration is the opponent of sensual desire, joy of ill will, applied thought of sloth and torpor, happiness of restlessness and remorse, and sustained thought of doubt.'

Evamettha vivicceva kāmehīti iminā kāmacchandassa vikkhambhanaviveko vutto hoti, vivicca akusalehi dhammehīti iminā pañcannampi nīvaraṇānaṃ. Aggahitaggahaṇena pana paṭhamena kāmacchandassa, dutiyena sesanīvaraṇānaṃ. Tathā paṭhamena tīsu akusalamūlesu pañcakāmaguṇabhedavisayassa lobhassa, dutiyena āghātavatthubhedādivisayānaṃ dosamohānaṃ. Oghādīsu vā dhammesu paṭhamena kāmoghakāmayogakāmāsavakāmupādānaabhijjhākāyaganthakāmarāgasaṃyojanānaṃ, dutiyena avasesaoghayogāsavaupādānaganthasaṃyojanānaṃ. Paṭhamena ca taṇhāya taṃsampayuttakānañca, dutiyena avijjāya taṃsampayuttakānañca. Api ca paṭhamena lobhasampayuttaaṭṭhacittuppādānaṃ, dutiyena sesānaṃ catunnaṃ akusalacittuppādānaṃ vikkhambhanaviveko vutto hotīti veditabbo.

Herein, by 'secluded from sensual pleasures' (vivicceva kāmehi) is meant the seclusion by suppression of sensual desire, and by 'secluded from unwholesome states' (vivicca akusalehi dhammehi) is meant the seclusion from all five hindrances. By way of including what was not included, the first phrase refers to sensual desire, and the second to the remaining hindrances. Similarly, by the first phrase is meant greed, which has as its object the five strands of sensual pleasure among the three unwholesome roots; by the second, hatred and delusion, which have as their object grounds for resentment and so forth. Or, among the states such as floods, by the first phrase are meant the flood of sensuality, the yoke of sensuality, the taint of sensuality, the clinging to sensuality, the bodily tie of covetousness, and the fetter of sensual lust; by the second, the remaining floods, yokes, taints, clingings, ties, and fetters. And by the first phrase are meant craving and its associated states, and by the second, ignorance and its associated states. Moreover, by the first phrase is meant the seclusion by suppression of the eight types of consciousness associated with greed, and by the second, the seclusion by suppression of the remaining four types of unwholesome consciousness. This should be understood.

Ettāvatā ca paṭhamassa jhānassa pahānaṅgaṃ dassetvā idāni sampayogaṅgaṃ dassetuṃ “savitakkaṃ savicāra”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ārammaṇe [M 0.0110] cittassa abhiniropanalakkhaṇo vitakko, ārammaṇānumajjanalakkhaṇo vicāro. Santepi ca nesaṃ katthaci aviyoge oḷārikaṭṭhena pubbaṅgamaṭṭhena [P 1.0128] ca ghaṇḍābhighāto viya cetaso paṭhamābhinipāto vitakko, sukhumaṭṭhena [V 0.0100] anumajjanasabhāvena ca ghaṇḍānuravo viya anupabandho vicāro. Vipphāravā cettha vitakko paṭhamuppattikāle paripphandanabhūto cittassa, ākāse uppatitukāmassa pakkhino pakkhavikkhepo viya, padumābhimukhapāto viya ca gandhānubandhacetaso bhamarassa. Santavutti vicāro nātiparipphandanabhāvo cittassa, ākāse uppatitassa pakkhino pakkhappasāraṇaṃ viya, paribbhamanaṃ viya ca padumābhimukhapatitassa bhamarassa padumassa uparibhāge.

Having thus shown the factors of abandonment of the first jhāna, now, in order to show its associated factors, it is said: 'with applied thought, with sustained thought' and so forth. Herein, applied thought has the characteristic of directing the mind onto the object, and sustained thought has the characteristic of repeatedly engaging the mind with the object. Even when they are not separate in some cases, applied thought, being coarse and leading, is like the initial striking of a bell, the mind's first impact on the object; sustained thought, being subtle and having the nature of repeatedly engaging, is like the subsequent reverberation of a bell, a continuous engagement. Here, applied thought is expansive, causing the mind to flutter at the moment of its first arising, like the flapping of a bird's wings when it desires to take flight into the sky, or like the descent of a bee, its mind following the scent, towards a lotus. Sustained thought is tranquil in its activity, not causing excessive fluttering in the mind, like the spreading of a bird's wings once it has taken flight in the sky, or like the hovering of a bee on the surface of the lotus after descending towards it.

Dukanipātaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “ākāse gacchato mahāsakuṇassa ubhohi pakkhehi vātaṃ gahetvā pakkhe sannisīdāpetvā gamanaṃ viya ārammaṇe cetaso abhiniropanabhāvena pavatto vitakko, vātaggahaṇatthaṃ pakkhe phandāpayamānassa gamanaṃ viya anumajjanabhāvena pavatto vicāro”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ anuppabandhena pavattiyaṃ yujjati. So pana nesaṃ viseso paṭhamadutiyajjhānesu pākaṭo hoti. Api ca malaggahitaṃ kaṃsabhājanaṃ ekena hatthena daḷhaṃ gahetvā itarena hatthena cuṇṇatelavālaṇḍupakena parimajjantassa daḷhaggahaṇahattho viya vitakko. Parimajjanahattho viya vicāro. Tathā kumbhakārassa daṇḍappahārena cakkaṃ bhamayitvā bhājanaṃ karontassa uppīḷanahattho viya vitakko. Ito cito ca sañcaraṇahattho viya vicāro. Tathā maṇḍalaṃ karontassa majjhe sannirumbhitvā ṭhitakaṇṭako viya abhiniropano vitakko. Bahi paribbhamanakaṇṭako viya anumajjamāno vicāro. Iti iminā ca vitakkena iminā ca vicārena saha vattati rukkho viya pupphena ca phalena cāti idaṃ jhānaṃ “savitakkaṃ savicāra”nti vuccati.

In the commentary on the Dukanipāta, however, it is said: 'Applied thought (vitakka) proceeds by way of directing the mind onto the object, like a great bird flying in the sky, which, having caught the wind with both wings, proceeds with its wings stilled; sustained thought (vicāra) proceeds by way of repeatedly engaging, like the bird flapping its wings in order to catch the wind.' This is fitting for its continuous occurrence. Their distinction, however, becomes clear in the first and second jhānas. Moreover, just as when one rubs a tarnished bronze vessel with a cloth containing powder and oil, firmly grasping it with one hand, the hand that firmly grasps is like applied thought, and the hand that rubs is like sustained thought. Similarly, when a potter spins the wheel with a stick and makes a vessel, the hand that presses down is like applied thought, and the hand that moves here and there is like sustained thought. Likewise, when drawing a circle, the thorn fixed in the center is like applied thought, which directs, and the thorn moving around the outside is like sustained thought, which repeatedly engages. Thus, because this jhāna abides together with this applied thought and this sustained thought, like a tree with its flowers and fruits, it is called 'with applied thought, with sustained thought' (savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ).

Vivekajanti ettha vivitti viveko, nīvaraṇavigamoti attho. Vivittoti vā viveko, nīvaraṇavivitto jhānasampayuttadhammarāsīti attho. Tasmā vivekā, tasmiṃ vā viveke jātanti vivekajaṃ. Pītisukhanti ettha piṇayatīti pīti, sā sampiyāyanalakkhaṇā. Sā [P 1.0129] panesā khuddikāpīti[M 0.0111], khaṇikāpīti, okkantikāpīti, ubbegāpīti, pharaṇāpītīti pañcavidhā hoti.

Herein, regarding 'born of seclusion' (vivekajaṃ): seclusion (viveka) is withdrawal (vivitti), meaning the removal of the hindrances. Or, seclusion (viveka) means secluded (vivitta), meaning the aggregate of states associated with jhāna, which is separated from the hindrances. Therefore, 'born of seclusion' means born from that seclusion or born in that seclusion. Regarding 'joy and happiness' (pītisukhaṃ): here, joy (pīti) is so called because it gladdens (piṇayati); its characteristic is delight. And this joy is fivefold: minor joy, momentary joy, showering joy, uplifting joy, and pervading joy.

Tattha khuddikāpīti sarīre lomahaṃsamattameva kātuṃ sakkoti. Khaṇikāpīti khaṇe khaṇe vijjuppādasadisā hoti. Okkantikāpīti samuddatīraṃ vīci viya, kāyaṃ okkamitvā okkamitvā bhijjati. Ubbegāpīti balavatī hoti, kāyaṃ uddhaggaṃ katvā ākāse laṅghāpanappamāṇapattā.

Among these, minor joy (khuddikāpīti) is only able to cause the hairs on the body to stand on end. Momentary joy (khaṇikāpīti) is like a flash of lightning, occurring from moment to moment. Showering joy (okkantikāpīti) is like a wave on the seashore; it breaks upon the body again and again. Uplifting joy (ubbegāpīti) is powerful, reaching the point of making the body leap into the air after lifting it up.

Pharaṇāpīti [V 0.0101] atibalavatī hoti. Tāya hi uppannāya sakalasarīraṃ dhamitvā pūritavatthi viya mahatā udakoghena pakkhandapabbatakucchi viya ca anuparipphuṭaṃ hoti. Sā panesā pañcavidhā pīti gabbhaṃ gaṇhantī paripākaṃ gacchantī duvidhaṃ passaddhiṃ paripūreti kāyapassaddhiñca cittapassaddhiñca, passaddhi gabbhaṃ gaṇhantī paripākaṃ gacchantī duvidhampi sukhaṃ paripūreti kāyikaṃ cetasikañca, sukhaṃ gabbhaṃ gaṇhantaṃ paripākaṃ gacchantaṃ tividhaṃ samādhiṃ paripūreti khaṇikasamādhiṃ upacārasamādhiṃ appanāsamādhiñcāti. Tāsu yā appanāsamādhissa mūlaṃ hutvā vaḍḍhamānā samādhisampayogaṅgatā pharaṇāpīti, ayaṃ imasmiṃ atthe adhippetā pītīti.

Pervading joy (pharaṇāpīti) is extremely powerful. For when it has arisen, the entire body is completely pervaded, like an inflated bladder, or like a mountain cavern flooded by a great torrent of water. And this fivefold joy, when it takes hold and matures, fulfills two kinds of tranquility: bodily tranquility and mental tranquility. Tranquility, when it takes hold and matures, fulfills two kinds of happiness: bodily and mental. Happiness, when it takes hold and matures, fulfills three kinds of concentration: momentary concentration, access concentration, and absorption concentration. Among these, it is pervading joy—which, having become the root of absorption concentration, grows and becomes a factor associated with concentration—that is intended as 'joy' in this context.

Itaraṃ pana sukhayatīti sukhaṃ, yassa uppajjati, taṃ sukhitaṃ karotīti attho. Sukhanaṃ vā sukhaṃ, suṭṭhu vā khādati khaṇati ca kāyacittābādhanti sukhaṃ, somanassavedanāyetaṃ nāmaṃ. Taṃ sātalakkhaṇaṃ. Santepi ca nesaṃ katthaci avippayoge iṭṭhārammaṇapaṭilābhatuṭṭhi pīti, paṭiladdharasānubhavanaṃ sukhaṃ. Yattha pīti, tattha sukhaṃ, yattha sukhaṃ, tattha na niyamato pīti. Saṅkhārakkhandhasaṅgahitā pīti, vedanākkhandhasaṅgahitaṃ sukhaṃ. Kantārakhinnassa vanantodakadassanasavanesu viya pīti, vanacchāyappavesanaudakaparibhogesu viya sukhaṃ. Tasmiṃ tasmiṃ samaye pākaṭabhāvato cetaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Iti ayañca pīti idañca sukhaṃ assa jhānassa, asmiṃ vā jhāne [P 1.0130] atthīti idaṃ jhānaṃ “pītisukha”nti vuccati.

As for the other, it is called happiness (sukha) because it makes one happy (sukhayati); the meaning is that it makes happy the one in whom it arises. Or, the state of being happy (sukhanaṃ) is happiness. Or, it is happiness because it thoroughly consumes (khādati) and digs up (khaṇati) bodily and mental afflictions; this is a name for pleasant mental feeling (somanassavedanā). Its characteristic is agreeableness. Even when they are not separate in some cases, joy (pīti) is the delight in acquiring a desirable object; happiness (sukha) is the experiencing of the taste of what has been acquired. Where there is joy, there is happiness; but where there is happiness, there is not necessarily joy. Joy is included in the aggregate of formations, while happiness is included in the aggregate of feeling. Joy is like the sight and sound of water in a forest to one exhausted in a wilderness; happiness is like entering the forest shade and partaking of the water. And it should be understood that this is stated based on what is manifest at each particular time. Thus, because this joy and this happiness belong to this jhāna, or exist in this jhāna, this jhāna is called 'with joy and happiness'.

Atha vā pīti ca sukhañca pītisukhaṃ dhammavinayādayo viya. Vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ assa jhānassa, asmiṃ vā jhāne atthīti evampi vivekajaṃpītisukhaṃ. Yatheva hi jhānaṃ, evaṃ pītisukhampettha vivekajameva hoti, tañcassa atthi, tasmā [M 0.0112] alopasamāsaṃ katvā ekapadeneva “vivekajaṃpītisukha”ntipi vattuṃ yujjati.

Alternatively, 'joy and happiness' (pītisukhaṃ) is a compound like 'Dhamma and Vinaya' (dhammavinaya), and so on. The joy and happiness born of seclusion belongs to this jhāna, or exists in this jhāna; in this way too, it is 'joy-and-happiness born of seclusion'. For just as the jhāna, so too the joy and happiness here is born of seclusion, and this belongs to it. Therefore, by forming a compound without elision of the case ending, it is also appropriate to say 'joy-and-happiness-born-of-seclusion' (vivekajaṃpītisukhaṃ) as a single term.

Paṭhamanti gaṇanānupubbatā paṭhamaṃ, idaṃ paṭhamaṃ uppannantipi paṭhamaṃ. Jhānanti duvidhaṃ jhānaṃ ārammaṇūpanijjhānaṃ lakkhaṇūpanijjhānañcāti. Tattha aṭṭha samāpattiyo pathavīkasiṇādiārammaṇaṃ upanijjhāyantīti ārammaṇūpanijjhānanti saṅkhyaṃ gatā. Vipassanāmaggaphalāni pana lakkhaṇūpanijjhānaṃ nāma. Tattha vipassanā aniccādilakkhaṇassa upanijjhānato lakkhaṇūpanijjhānaṃ. Vipassanāya katakiccassa maggena ijjhanato maggo lakkhaṇūpanijjhānaṃ, phalaṃ pana nirodhasaccaṃ tathalakkhaṇaṃ upanijjhāyatīti lakkhaṇūpanijjhānaṃ. Tesu idha pubbabhāge ārammaṇūpanijjhānaṃ, lokuttaramaggakkhaṇe lakkhaṇūpanijjhānaṃ adhippetaṃ. Tasmā ārammaṇūpanijjhānato ca lakkhaṇūpanijjhānato ca paccanīkajhāpanato ca jhānanti veditabbaṃ.

'First' (paṭhamaṃ) means first in numerical sequence; it also means that which has arisen first. 'Jhāna' is twofold: absorption by intently contemplating an object (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna) and absorption by intently contemplating characteristics (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna). Therein, the eight attainments are designated as 'absorption by intently contemplating an object' because they intently contemplate objects such as the earth kasiṇa. But insight, path, and fruition are called 'absorption by intently contemplating characteristics'. Therein, insight is 'absorption by intently contemplating characteristics' because of its intent contemplation of characteristics such as impermanence. The path is 'absorption by intently contemplating characteristics' because the task done by insight is accomplished by the path. Fruition is 'absorption by intently contemplating characteristics' because it intently contemplates the truth of cessation, which has that characteristic. Of these, 'absorption by intently contemplating an object' is intended here in the preliminary part, and 'absorption by intently contemplating characteristics' is intended at the moment of the supramundane path. Therefore, it should be understood as 'jhāna' because of intently contemplating an object, intently contemplating characteristics, and burning away opposing states.

Upasampajjāti [V 0.0102] upagantvā, pāpuṇitvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Upasampādayitvā vā, nipphādetvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Viharatīti tadanurūpena iriyāpathavihārena iriyati, vuttappakārajhānasamaṅgī hutvā attabhāvassa iriyanaṃ vuttiṃ abhinipphādeti.

'Having entered upon' (upasampajja) means having approached, having attained. Or, it means having brought about, having produced. 'Dwells' (viharati) means one comports oneself with a mode of conduct in accordance with it; that is, being endowed with the aforementioned jhāna, one brings about the continuation of one's personal existence.

Taṃ panetaṃ paṭhamajjhānaṃ pañcaṅgavippahīnaṃ pañcaṅgasamannāgataṃ tividhakalyāṇaṃ, dasalakkhaṇasampannaṃ. Tattha kāmacchando byāpādo thinamiddhaṃ uddhaccakukkuccaṃ vicikicchāti imesaṃ pañcannaṃ nīvaraṇānaṃ pahānavasena pañcaṅgavippahīnatā veditabbā. Na hi etesu appahīnesu jhānaṃ uppajjati. Tenassetāni pahānaṅgānīti vuccanti. Kiñcāpi hi jhānakkhaṇe aññepi akusalā dhammā pahīyanti, tathāpi etāneva visesena jhānantarāyakarāni. Kāmacchandena hi nānāvisayappalobhitaṃ cittaṃ na ekattārammaṇe [P 1.0131] samādhiyati, kāmacchandābhibhūtaṃ vā, taṃ na kāmadhātuppahānāya paṭipadaṃ paṭipajjati. Byāpādena vā ārammaṇe paṭihaññamānaṃ na nirantaraṃ pavattati. Thinamiddhābhibhūtaṃ akammaññaṃ hoti. Uddhaccakukkuccaparetaṃ avūpasantameva hutvā paribbhamati. Vicikicchāya upahataṃ jhānādhigamasādhikaṃ paṭipadaṃ nārohati. Iti visesena jhānantarāyakarattā etāneva pahānaṅgānīti vuttāni.

But this first jhāna is free from five factors, endowed with five factors, threefold excellent, and complete with ten characteristics. Herein, its being free from five factors should be understood as the abandonment of these five hindrances: sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt. For unless these are abandoned, jhāna does not arise. Therefore, these are called its factors of abandonment. Although other unwholesome states are also abandoned at the moment of jhāna, these five are specifically obstructive to jhāna. For a mind allured by sensual desire, enticed by various objects, does not become concentrated on a single object; or overcome by sensual desire, it does not enter upon the path leading to the abandonment of the sensual realm. Or when hindered by ill will toward the object, it does not continue uninterrupted. Overcome by sloth and torpor, it becomes unworkable. Afflicted by restlessness and remorse, it remains unquiet and wanders about. Afflicted by doubt, it does not undertake the practice that accomplishes the attainment of jhāna. Thus, because they are specifically obstructive to jhāna, these alone are called the factors of abandonment.

Yasmā pana vitakko ārammaṇe cittaṃ abhiniropeti, vicāro anupabandhati, tehi avikkhepāya sampāditapayogassa cetaso payogasampattisambhavā [M 0.0113] pīti pīṇanaṃ sukhañca upabrūhanaṃ karoti. Athassa sesasampayuttadhammā etehi abhiniropanānubandhanapīṇanupabrūhanehi anuggahitā ekaggatā ekattārammaṇe samaṃ sammā ca ādhiyati. Tasmā vitakko vicāro pīti sukhaṃ cittekaggatāti imesaṃ pañcannaṃ uppattivasena pañcaṅgasamannāgatatā veditabbā. Uppannesu hi etesu pañcasu jhānaṃ uppannaṃ nāma hoti. Tenassa etāni pañcaṅgasamannāgatānīti vuccanti. Tasmā na etehi samannāgataṃ aññadeva jhānaṃ nāma atthīti gahetabbaṃ. Yathā pana aṅgamattavaseneva caturaṅginī senā, pañcaṅgikaṃ tūriyaṃ, aṭṭhaṅgiko ca maggoti vuccati, evamidampi aṅgamattavaseneva pañcaṅgikanti vā pañcaṅgasamannāgatanti vā vuccatīti veditabbaṃ.

Since initial application directs the mind onto the object and sustained application keeps it engaged, joy gladdens and happiness invigorates; this is possible due to the successful endeavor of a mind that has accomplished its application for non-distraction by means of these two. Then, its remaining associated states and its one-pointedness, supported by this directing, engaging, gladdening, and invigorating, are placed evenly and rightly upon a single object. Therefore, its being endowed with five factors should be understood as the arising of these five: initial application, sustained application, joy, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind. For when these five arise, the jhāna is said to have arisen. Hence, these are called its 'endowed with five factors'. Therefore, it should not be understood that there is another jhāna apart from these, which is called jhāna. Just as an army is called 'four-limbed' (caturaṅginī senā), a musical instrument 'five-factored' (pañcaṅgikaṃ tūriyaṃ), and the path 'eight-factored' (aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo) merely by virtue of their factors, so too this jhāna is called 'five-factored' or 'endowed with five factors' merely by virtue of its factors.

Etāni ca pañcaṅgāni kiñcāpi upacārakkhaṇepi atthi, atha kho upacāre pakaticittato balavatarāni. Idha pana upacāratopi balavatarāni rūpāvacaralakkhaṇappattāni nipphannāni. Ettha hi vitakko suvisadena ākārena ārammaṇe cittaṃ abhiniropayamāno uppajjati. Vicāro ativiya ārammaṇaṃ anumajjamāno. Pītisukhaṃ sabbāvantampi kāyaṃ pharamānaṃ[V 0.0103]. Tenevāha – “nāssa kiñci sabbāvato kāyassa vivekajena pītisukhena apphuṭaṃ hotī”ti (dī. ni. 1.226). Cittekaggatāpi heṭṭhimamhi samuggapaṭale [P 1.0132] uparimaṃ samuggapaṭalaṃ viya ārammaṇesu phusitā hutvā uppajjati, ayametesaṃ itarehi viseso. Tattha cittekaggatā kiñcāpi “savitakkaṃ savicāra”nti imasmiṃ pāṭhe na niddiṭṭhā, tathāpi vibhaṅge (vibha. 565) “jhānanti vitakko vicāro pīti sukhaṃ cittekaggatā”ti evaṃ vuttattā aṅgameva. Yena hi adhippāyena bhagavatā uddeso kato, soyeva tena vibhaṅge pakāsitoti.

Even though these five factors are present in the access moment, in access concentration they are stronger than in the ordinary state of mind. Here, however, they are even stronger than in access concentration, having attained the characteristic of the form-sphere and being fully developed. For here, initial application arises directing the mind toward the object in a very clear manner. Sustained application intensely examines the object. Joy-and-happiness pervades the entire body. Therefore, it is said: 'There is no part of his entire body that is not suffused with the joy-and-happiness born of seclusion.' One-pointedness of mind also arises having made contact with the objects like the upper lid of a box pressing upon the lower lid. This is their distinction from the others. Here, although one-pointedness of mind is not explicitly mentioned in the passage 'with initial application and sustained application,' nevertheless, in the Vibhaṅga (Vibh. 565), it is stated: 'Jhāna consists of initial application, sustained application, joy, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind.' Thus, it is indeed a factor. For the intention with which the Blessed One made the summary, that very intention is what is explained in the Vibhaṅga.

Tividhakalyāṇaṃ

Threefold Excellence

Tividhakalyāṇaṃ dasalakkhaṇasampannanti ettha pana ādimajjhapariyosānavasenatividhakalyāṇatā. Tesaṃyeva ca ādimajjhapariyosānānaṃ lakkhaṇavasena dasalakkhaṇasampannatā veditabbā. Tatrāyaṃ pāḷi –

The threefold excellence, endowed with the ten characteristics—here, the threefold excellence is in terms of its beginning, middle, and end. And the possession of the ten characteristics should be understood in terms of the characteristics of those very beginning, middle, and end. The text here is:

“Paṭhamassa jhānassa paṭipadāvisuddhi ādi, upekkhānubrūhanā majjhe, sampahaṃsanā pariyosānaṃ, paṭhamassa jhānassa paṭipadāvisuddhi ādi. Ādissa kati lakkhaṇāni? Ādissa tīṇi lakkhaṇāni – yo [M 0.0114] tassa paripantho, tato cittaṃ visujjhati, visuddhattā cittaṃ majjhimaṃ samathanimittaṃ paṭipajjati, paṭipannattā tattha cittaṃ pakkhandati. Yañca paripanthato cittaṃ visujjhati, yañca visuddhattā cittaṃ majjhimaṃ samathanimittaṃ paṭipajjati, yañca paṭipannattā tattha cittaṃ pakkhandati. Paṭhamassa jhānassa paṭipadāvisuddhi ādi, ādissa imāni tīṇi lakkhaṇāni. Tena vuccati – ‘paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ ādikalyāṇañceva hoti tilakkhaṇasampannañcā’ti.

“The purification of the path of the first jhāna is its beginning, the development of equanimity its middle, and thorough satisfaction its end. The purification of the path of the first jhāna is its beginning. How many characteristics does the beginning have? The beginning has three characteristics: the mind is purified from its obstacle; because it is purified, the mind enters upon the middle sign of serenity; and because it has entered, the mind inclines towards it. That the mind is purified from the obstacle, that because it is purified the mind enters upon the middle sign of serenity, and that because it has entered the mind inclines towards it—these are the three characteristics of the beginning. Therefore it is said: ‘The first jhāna is beautiful in the beginning and endowed with three characteristics.’

“Paṭhamassa jhānassa upekkhānubrūhanā majjhe. Majjhassa kati lakkhaṇāni? Majjhassa tīṇi lakkhaṇāni – visuddhaṃ cittaṃ ajjhupekkhati, samathapaṭipannaṃ ajjhupekkhati, ekattupaṭṭhānaṃ ajjhupekkhati. Yañca visuddhaṃ cittaṃ ajjhupekkhati, yañca samathapaṭipannaṃ ajjhupekkhati, yañca ekattupaṭṭhānaṃ ajjhupekkhati. Paṭhamassa jhānassa upekkhānubrūhanā majjhe, majjhassa imāni tīṇi lakkhaṇāni. Tena vuccati – ‘paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ majjhekalyāṇañceva hoti tilakkhaṇasampannañcā’ti.

“The development of equanimity is the middle of the first jhāna. How many characteristics does the middle have? The middle has three characteristics: it looks upon the purified mind with equanimity; it looks upon that which has entered upon serenity with equanimity; and it looks upon the establishment of oneness with equanimity. That it looks upon the purified mind with equanimity, that it looks upon that which has entered upon serenity with equanimity, and that it looks upon the establishment of oneness with equanimity—these are the three characteristics of the middle. Therefore it is said: ‘The first jhāna is beautiful in the middle and endowed with three characteristics.’

“Paṭhamassa jhānassa sampahaṃsanā pariyosānaṃ. Pariyosānassa kati lakkhaṇāni? Pariyosānassa [V 0.0104] cattāri lakkhaṇāni – tattha [P 1.0133] jātānaṃ dhammānaṃ anativattanaṭṭhena sampahaṃsanā, indriyānaṃ ekarāsaṭṭhena sampahaṃsanā, tadupagavīriyavāhanaṭṭhena sampahaṃsanā, āsevanaṭṭhena sampahaṃsanā. Paṭhamassa jhānassa sampahaṃsanā pariyosānaṃ, pariyosānassa imāni cattāri lakkhaṇāni. Tena vuccati ‘paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ pariyosānakalyāṇañceva hoti catulakkhaṇasampannañcā’”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.158).

“Thorough satisfaction is the end of the first jhāna. How many characteristics does the end have? The end has four characteristics: thorough satisfaction by way of not overstepping the phenomena that have arisen there, thorough satisfaction by way of the unification of the faculties, thorough satisfaction by way of the driving force of the energy that supports it, and thorough satisfaction by way of cultivation. Thorough satisfaction is the end of the first jhāna, and the end has these four characteristics. Therefore it is said: ‘The first jhāna is beautiful in its end and endowed with four characteristics.’

“Tatra paṭipadāvisuddhi nāma sasambhāriko upacāro. Upekkhānubrūhanā nāma appanā. Sampahaṃsanā nāma paccavekkhaṇā”ti evameke vaṇṇayanti. Yasmā pana “ekattagataṃ cittaṃ paṭipadāvisuddhipakkhandañceva hoti upekkhānubrūhitañca ñāṇena ca sampahaṃsita”nti pāḷiyaṃ vuttaṃ, tasmā antoappanāyameva āgamanavasena paṭipadāvisuddhi, tatramajjhattupekkhāya kiccavasena upekkhānubrūhanā, dhammānaṃ anativattanādibhāvasādhanena pariyodāpakassa ñāṇassa kiccanipphattivasena sampahaṃsanā ca veditabbā.

“Here, ‘purification of the path’ means access concentration with its requisites. ‘Development of equanimity’ means absorption. ‘Thorough satisfaction’ means reviewing.” Thus some explain. However, since it is said in the Pāli, “The mind that has attained unification both plunges into the purification of the path, is developed by equanimity, and is thoroughly gladdened by knowledge,” therefore, purification of the path should be understood as the arrival within absorption itself; development of equanimity as the function of neutrality towards that; and thorough satisfaction as the accomplishment of the function of the purifying knowledge, which establishes the state of non-transgression of phenomena, and so on.

Kathaṃ[M 0.0115]? Yasmiñhi vāre appanā uppajjati, tasmiṃ yo nīvaraṇasaṅkhāto kilesagaṇo tassa jhānassa paripantho, tato cittaṃ visujjhati. Visuddhattā āvaraṇavirahitaṃ hutvā majjhimaṃ samathanimittaṃ paṭipajjati. Majjhimasamathanimittaṃ nāma samappavatto appanāsamādhiyeva. Tadanantaraṃ pana purimacittaṃ ekasantatipariṇāmanayena tathattaṃ upagacchamānaṃ majjhimaṃ samathanimittaṃ paṭipajjati nāma, evaṃ paṭipannattā tathattupagamanena tattha pakkhandati nāma. Evaṃ tāva purimacitte vijjamānākāranipphādikā paṭhamassa jhānassa uppādakkhaṇeyeva āgamanavasena paṭipadāvisuddhi veditabbā.

How? For at the time when absorption arises, the mind is purified from that group of defilements called the hindrances, which is an obstacle to that jhāna. Because it is purified, having become free from obstructions, it enters upon the middle sign of serenity. The middle sign of serenity is simply the absorption concentration that has just arisen. Immediately afterward, the previous mind, by way of the transformation of a single continuum, approaches that state and is said to enter upon the middle sign of serenity. Having entered upon it in this way, it is said to plunge into that state by the attainment of suchness. Thus, the purification of the path should be understood as the production of the qualities present in the previous mind, by way of its arrival at the very moment of the arising of the first jhāna.

Evaṃ visuddhassa pana tassa puna visodhetabbābhāvato visodhane byāpāraṃ akaronto visuddhaṃ cittaṃ ajjhupekkhati nāma. Samathabhāvūpagamanena samathapaṭipannassa puna samādhāne byāpāraṃ akaronto samathapaṭipannaṃ ajjhupekkhati nāma. Samathapaṭipannabhāvato eva cassa kilesasaṃsaggaṃ pahāya ekattena upaṭṭhitassa puna ekattupaṭṭhāne [P 1.0134] byāpāraṃ akaronto ekattupaṭṭhānaṃ ajjhupekkhati nāma. Evaṃ tatramajjhattupekkhāya kiccavasena upekkhānubrūhanā veditabbā.

Since the mind is thus purified, there being no further need to purify it, not engaging in the activity of purifying, one is said to equanimously regard the purified mind. When that which has entered upon serenity attains the state of serenity, there being no further need to engage in establishing concentration, not engaging in the activity of establishing concentration, one is said to equanimously regard that which has entered upon serenity. Because of having entered upon serenity, having abandoned contact with defilements, and being established in oneness, there being no further need to engage in establishing oneness, not engaging in the activity of establishing oneness, one is said to equanimously regard the establishment in oneness. Thus, the strengthening of equanimity should be understood by way of the function of that specific equanimity.

Ye panete evaṃ upekkhānubrūhite tattha jātā samādhipaññāsaṅkhātā yuganaddhadhammā aññamaññaṃ anativattamānā hutvā pavattā, yāni ca saddhādīni indriyāni nānākilesehi vimuttattā vimuttirasena ekarasāni hutvā pavattāni, yañcesa tadupagaṃ tesaṃ anativattanaekarasabhāvānaṃ [V 0.0105] anucchavikaṃ vīriyaṃ vāhayati, yā cassa tasmiṃ khaṇe pavattā āsevanā, sabbepi te ākārā yasmā ñāṇena saṃkilesavodānesu taṃ taṃ ādīnavañca ānisaṃsañca disvā tathā tathā sampahaṃsitattā visodhitattā pariyodāpitattā nipphannāva, tasmā “dhammānaṃ anativattanādibhāvasādhanena pariyodāpakassa ñāṇassa kiccanipphattivasena sampahaṃsanā veditabbā”ti vuttaṃ.

And those yoked-together states of concentration and wisdom that have arisen there, thus strengthened by equanimity, proceed without surpassing each other; and those faculties of faith and so forth, having become free from various defilements, proceed with a single taste of liberation; and whatever effort is appropriate to that state, maintaining their nature of not surpassing each other and their single taste, is carried on; and whatever cultivation occurs at that moment—all these aspects, since they are thoroughly gladdened, purified, and cleansed by knowledge seeing the respective dangers and benefits in both defilement and purification in that way—are thus accomplished. Therefore it is said: “Gladdening should be understood as the accomplishment of the function of knowledge that purifies by means of establishing the state of non-transgression of phenomena, etc.”

Vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamāti vitakkassa ca vicārassa cāti imesaṃ dvinnaṃ vūpasamā samatikkamā, dutiyajjhānakkhaṇe apātubhāvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha kiñcāpi dutiyajjhāne sabbepi paṭhamajjhānadhammā na santi, aññeyeva hi paṭhamajjhāne phassādayo, aññe idha. Oḷārikassa pana oḷārikassa aṅgassa samatikkamā paṭhamajjhānato paresaṃ dutiyajjhānādīnaṃ adhigamo hotīti dassanatthaṃ “vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā”ti [M 0.0116] evaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Ajjhattanti idha niyakajjhattaṃ adhippetaṃ, vibhaṅge pana “ajjhattaṃ paccatta”nti (vibha. 573) ettakameva vuttaṃ. Yasmā niyakajjhattaṃ adhippetaṃ, tasmā attani jātaṃ, attano santāne nibbattanti ayamettha attho.

“With the calming of initial and sustained thought” means the calming and overcoming of these two—initial thought and sustained thought—that is, their non-manifestation at the moment of the second jhāna. Here, although all the factors of the first jhāna are not present in the second jhāna—for the contacts and other factors in the first jhāna are different from those here—it should be understood that it is said, “with the calming of initial and sustained thought,” in order to show that the attainment of the second jhāna and beyond occurs by overcoming the grosser factors of the first jhāna. “Internally” here refers to one’s own internal state. In the Vibhaṅga, however, it is simply stated as “internal, personal.” Since it refers to one’s own internal state, the meaning here is that it arises within oneself, originates in one’s own continuum.

Sampasādananti sampasādanaṃ vuccati saddhā. Sampasādanayogato jhānampi sampasādanaṃ, nīlavaṇṇayogato nīlavatthaṃ viya. Yasmā vā taṃ jhānaṃ sampasādanasamannāgatattā vitakkavicārakkhobhavūpasamanena ca ceto sampasādayati, tasmāpi “sampasādana”nti [P 1.0135] vuttaṃ. Imasmiñca atthavikappe sampasādanaṃ cetasoti evaṃ padasambandho veditabbo. Purimasmiṃ pana atthavikappe cetasoti etaṃ ekodibhāvena saddhiṃ yojetabbaṃ.

Confidence is called ‘sampasādana,’ that is, faith. Due to its association with confidence, jhāna is also called ‘sampasādana,’ just as a cloth is called ‘blue’ due to its association with the color blue. Or because that jhāna, being endowed with confidence and calming the disturbance caused by initial and sustained thought, pacifies the mind, it is therefore called ‘sampasādana.’ In this alternative meaning, the connection of the words should be understood thus: 'sampasādanaṃ cetaso' (confidence of the mind). In the previous alternative meaning, however, ‘of the mind’ should be connected with ‘one-pointedness.’

Tatrāyaṃ atthayojanā – eko udetīti ekodi, vitakkavicārehi anajjhārūḷhattā aggo seṭṭho hutvā udetīti attho. Seṭṭhopi hi loke ekoti vuccati. Vitakkavicāravirahito vā eko asahāyo hutvātipi vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Atha vā sampayuttadhamme udāyatīti udi, uṭṭhāpetīti attho. Seṭṭhaṭṭhena eko ca so udi cāti ekodi, samādhissetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Iti imaṃ ekodiṃ bhāveti vaḍḍhetīti idaṃ dutiyajjhānaṃ ekodibhāvaṃ. So panāyaṃ ekodi yasmā cetaso, na sattassa, na jīvassa. Tasmā etaṃ “cetaso ekodibhāva”nti vuttaṃ.

Here is the explanation of the meaning: ‘One arises’ (eko udeti) means ‘ekodi,’ because it arises as supreme and excellent by not being overcome by initial and sustained thought. For in the world, even the supreme is called ‘one.’ Alternatively, it can be said that it is ‘one’ because it is devoid of initial and sustained thought, or because it is without a companion. Or else, ‘udi’ means it causes associated states to arise—that is, it uplifts them. ‘Ekodi’ means it is both ‘one’ in the sense of being supreme and ‘udi’ (uplifting). This is a designation for concentration. Thus, one develops and cultivates this ‘ekodi’—this is the second jhāna, the state of one-pointedness. However, this ‘ekodi’ pertains to the mind, not to a being or a life-principle. Therefore, it is called ‘the one-pointedness of mind.’

Nanu cāyaṃ saddhā paṭhamajjhānepi atthi, ayañca ekodināmako samādhi, atha kasmā idameva [V 0.0106] “sampasādanaṃ cetaso ekodibhāva”nti vuttanti? Vuccate – aduñhi paṭhamajjhānaṃ vitakkavicārakkhobhena vīcitaraṅgasamākulamiva jalaṃ na suppasannaṃ hoti, tasmā satiyāpi saddhāya sampasādananti na vuttaṃ. Na suppasannattāyeva cettha samādhipi na suṭṭhu pākaṭo, tasmā ekodibhāvantipi na vuttaṃ. Imasmiṃ pana jhāne vitakkavicārapalibodhābhāvena laddhokāsā balavatī saddhā, balavasaddhāsahāyapaṭilābheneva ca samādhipi pākaṭo. Tasmā idameva evaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

But is not this faith also present in the first jhāna, and this concentration one-pointed? So why is it said of just this, “confidence and one-pointedness of mind”? It is said—because the first jhāna, disturbed by the agitation of initial and sustained thought, is like water roiled by waves, not very clear. Therefore, even though faith is present, it is not called “confidence.” Due to its lack of clarity, the concentration here is not very apparent, so it is not called “one-pointedness.” In this jhāna, however, because there is no encumbrance of initial and sustained thought, faith, having gained an opportunity, is strong. And because concentration has gained the support of strong faith, it becomes apparent. Therefore, it should be understood that only this is described in this way.

Avitakkaṃ avicāranti bhāvanāya pahīnattā etasmiṃ, etassa vā vitakko natthīti avitakkaṃ. Imināva nayena avicāraṃ. Etthāha “nanu ca ‘vitakkavicārānaṃ [M 0.0117] vūpasamā’ti imināpi ayamattho siddho. Atha kasmā puna vuttaṃ ‘avitakkaṃ avicāra’”nti? Vuccate – evametaṃ, siddhovāyamattho. Na panetaṃ tadatthadīpakaṃ, nanu avocumha “oḷārikassa pana oḷārikassa aṅgassa samatikkamā paṭhamajjhānato paresaṃ dutiyajjhānādīnaṃ samadhigamo hotīti dassanatthaṃ ‘vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā’ti evaṃ vutta”nti.

“Without initial thought, without sustained thought”—because, through development, they have been abandoned in this state, or because initial thought is absent for it, it is called “without initial thought.” In the same way, it is “without sustained thought.” Here it may be asked: “But is not this meaning already established by ‘with the calming of initial and sustained thought’? So why is ‘without initial thought, without sustained thought’ further stated?” It is said: yes, this meaning is established. However, this is not a mere elucidation of that meaning. Did we not say: “To show that the attainment of the second jhāna and so on beyond the first jhāna occurs by overcoming the grosser and grosser factors, it is stated thus: ‘with the calming of initial and sustained thought’?”

Api [P 1.0136] ca vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā idaṃ sampasādanaṃ, na kilesakālussiyassa. Vitakkavicārānañca vūpasamā ekodibhāvaṃ, na upacārajjhānamiva nīvaraṇappahānā, na paṭhamajjhānamiva ca aṅgapātubhāvāti evaṃ sampasādanaekodibhāvānaṃ hetuparidīpakamidaṃ vacanaṃ. Tathā vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā idaṃ avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ, na tatiyacatutthajjhānāni viya cakkhuviññāṇādīni viya ca abhāvāti, evaṃ avitakkaavicārabhāvassa hetuparidīpakañca, na vitakkavicārābhāvamattaparidīpakaṃ. Vitakkavicārābhāvamattaparidīpakameva pana “avitakkaṃ avicāra”nti idaṃ vacanaṃ. Tasmā purimaṃ vatvāpi puna vattabbamevāti.

Moreover, this confidence is from the calming of initial and sustained thought, not from the calming of the turbidity of defilements. And this unification is from the calming of initial and sustained thought—not, as in access concentration, from the abandoning of the hindrances, nor, as in the first jhāna, from the manifestation of the factors. Thus, this statement clarifies the cause of the confidence and unification. Similarly, this state of being without initial and sustained thought is from the calming of initial and sustained thought, not from their mere absence as in the third and fourth jhānas or in eye-consciousness and so on. Thus, this statement clarifies the cause of the state of being without initial and sustained thought, not merely the fact of their absence. The statement 'without initial thought, without sustained thought,' however, merely clarifies the fact of the absence of initial and sustained thought. Therefore, even though the former was stated, this must be stated again.

Samādhijanti paṭhamajjhānasamādhito sampayuttasamādhito vā jātanti attho. Tattha kiñcāpi paṭhamampi sampayuttasamādhito jātaṃ, atha kho ayameva samādhi “samādhī”ti vattabbataṃ arahati, vitakkavicārakkhobhavirahena ativiya acalattā suppasannattā ca. Tasmā imassa vaṇṇabhaṇanatthaṃ idameva “samādhija”nti vuttaṃ. Pītisukhanti idaṃ vuttanayameva.

“Born of concentration” means born from the concentration of the first jhāna, or from associated concentration. Although the first jhāna is also born from associated concentration, only this concentration deserves to be called “concentration,” being exceedingly unshaken and very serene, free from the agitation of applied and sustained thought. Therefore, for the purpose of extolling it, only this is said to be “born of concentration.” “Rapture and happiness” are to be understood in the manner already stated.

Dutiyanti gaṇanānupubbatā dutiyaṃ. Idaṃ dutiyaṃ uppannantipi dutiyaṃ.

“Second” means second in numerical order. It is also second in that it is the second to have arisen.

Pītiyā ca virāgāti virāgo nāma vuttappakārāya pītiyā jigucchanaṃ vā samatikkamo vā[V 0.0107]. Ubhinnaṃ pana antarā ca-saddo sampiṇḍanattho, so vūpasamaṃ vā sampiṇḍeti vitakkavicāravūpasamaṃ vā. Tattha yadā vūpasamameva sampiṇḍeti, tadā pītiyā virāgā ca, kiñca bhiyyo vūpasamā cāti evaṃ yojanā veditabbā. Imissā ca yojanāya virāgo jigucchanattho hoti, tasmā pītiyā jigucchanā ca samatikkamā cāti ayamattho daṭṭhabbo. Yadā pana vitakkavicāravūpasamaṃ sampiṇḍeti, tadā pītiyā ca virāgā, kiñca bhiyyo vitakkavicārānañca vūpasamāti evaṃ yojanā veditabbā. Imissā [M 0.0118] ca yojanāya virāgo samatikkamanattho hoti, tasmā pītiyā ca samatikkamā vitakkavicārānañca vūpasamāti ayamattho daṭṭhabbo.

“And from dispassion for rapture” means that dispassion is either disgust with or transcendence of rapture of the kind described. The word “ca” (and) has a collective sense; it connects either with “cessation” or with “the cessation of applied and sustained thought.” Therein, when it connects with “cessation,” the construction should be understood as: “and from dispassion for rapture, and furthermore, from cessation.” In this construction, “dispassion” has the sense of disgust; therefore, the meaning should be seen as: “from disgust with rapture and from transcendence.” But when it connects with “the cessation of applied and sustained thought,” the construction should be understood as: “and from dispassion for rapture, and furthermore, from the cessation of applied and sustained thought.” In this construction, “dispassion” has the sense of transcendence; therefore, the meaning should be seen as: “and from the transcendence of rapture and from the cessation of applied and sustained thought.”

Kāmañcete vitakkavicārā dutiyajjhāneyeva [P 1.0137] vūpasantā, imassa pana jhānassa maggaparidīpanatthaṃ vaṇṇabhaṇanatthañcetaṃ vuttaṃ. “Vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā”ti hi vutte idaṃ paññāyati “nūna vitakkavicāravūpasamo maggo imassa jhānassā”ti. Yathā ca tatiye ariyamagge appahīnānampi sakkāyadiṭṭhādīnaṃ “pañcannaṃ orambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ pahānā”ti (ma. ni. 2.132-133) evaṃ pahānaṃ vuccamānaṃ vaṇṇabhaṇanaṃ hoti, tadadhigamāya ussukkānaṃ ussāhajanakaṃ, evameva idha avūpasantānampi vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamo vuccamāno vaṇṇabhaṇanaṃ hoti, tenāyamattho vutto “pītiyā ca samatikkamā vitakkavicārānañca vūpasamā”ti.

Although applied and sustained thought have already ceased in the second jhāna itself, this is stated here to clarify the path to this jhāna and for the sake of praise. For when “from the cessation of applied and sustained thought” is said, it is understood: “Surely the cessation of applied and sustained thought is the path to this jhāna.” And just as, in connection with the third noble path, the abandoning of the five lower fetters is mentioned (cf. MN 2.132–133)—which serves as a praise and generates enthusiasm in those striving for its attainment, even though some of those fetters have already been abandoned—so too here, the cessation of applied and sustained thought, which are already stilled, is mentioned for the sake of praise. Therefore, this meaning is stated as: “from the transcendence of rapture and from the cessation of applied and sustained thought.”

Upekkhako ca viharatīti ettha upapattito ikkhatīti upekkhā, samaṃ passati, apakkhapatitā hutvā passatīti attho. Tāya visadāya vipulāya thāmagatāya samannāgatattā tatiyajjhānasamaṅgī “upekkhako”ti vuccati.

“And he dwells equanimous”: Here, upekkhā (equanimity) means he sees impartially, he sees equally, meaning he sees without siding with any party. Because one who is endowed with the third jhāna is furnished with that clear, abundant, and firmly established equanimity, he is called “equanimous.”

Upekkhā pana dasavidhā hoti – chaḷaṅgupekkhā brahmavihārupekkhā bojjhaṅgupekkhā vīriyupekkhā saṅkhārupekkhā vedanupekkhā vipassanupekkhā tatramajjhattupekkhā jhānupekkhā pārisuddhupekkhāti.

Now, equanimity is of ten kinds: six-factored equanimity, equanimity of the divine abidings, equanimity as an enlightenment factor, equanimity of effort, equanimity towards formations, equanimity of feeling, equanimity of insight, equanimity as specific neutrality, equanimity of jhāna, and equanimity of purity.

Tattha yā “idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā neva sumano hoti na dummano, upekkhako ca viharati sato sampajāno”ti (ma. ni. 6.1) evamāgatā khīṇāsavassa chasu dvāresu iṭṭhāniṭṭhachaḷārammaṇāpāthe parisuddhapakatibhāvāvijahanākārabhūtā upekkhā, ayaṃ chaḷaṅgupekkhā nāma.

Herein, the equanimity described as: “Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having seen a form with the eye, is neither gladdened nor saddened, but dwells equanimous, mindful, and fully aware” (MN 6.1)—which, for one whose taints are destroyed, is characterized by not abandoning its pure natural state in the presence of agreeable and disagreeable objects at the six sense doors—this is called six-factored equanimity.

Yā [V 0.0108] pana “upekkhāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharatī”ti (dī. ni. 1.556; ma. ni. 1.77) evamāgatā sattesu majjhattākārabhūtā upekkhā, ayaṃ brahmavihārupekkhā nāma.

The equanimity described as: “With a mind accompanied by equanimity, one dwells pervading one direction” (DN 1.556; MN 1.77), which is characterized by a neutral attitude toward beings—this is called equanimity as a divine abiding.

Yā [M 0.0119] pana “upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekanissita”nti (ma. ni. 2.247) evamāgatā sahajātānaṃ dhammānaṃ majjhattākārabhūtā upekkhā, ayaṃ bojjhaṅgupekkhā nāma.

The equanimity described as: “One develops the equanimity enlightenment factor, dependent on seclusion” (MN 2.247), which is characterized by a neutral attitude toward co-arisen states—this is called the equanimity enlightenment factor.

Yā pana “kālena kālaṃ upekkhānimittaṃ manasi karotī”ti (a. ni. 3.103) evamāgatā [P 1.0138] anaccāraddhanātisithilavīriyasaṅkhātā upekkhā, ayaṃ vīriyupekkhā nāma.

The equanimity described as: “From time to time, one attends to the sign of equanimity” (AN 3.103), and which is known as effort that is neither over-strenuous nor too relaxed—this is called equanimity of effort.

Yā pana “kati saṅkhārupekkhā samathavasena uppajjanti, kati saṅkhārupekkhā vipassanāvasena uppajjanti? Aṭṭha saṅkhārupekkhā samathavasena uppajjanti, dasa saṅkhārupekkhā vipassanāvasena uppajjantī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.57) evamāgatā nīvaraṇādipaṭisaṅkhāsantiṭṭhanāgahaṇe majjhattabhūtā upekkhā, ayaṃ saṅkhārupekkhā nāma.

The equanimity that comes in the passage: “How many kinds of equanimity towards formations arise by way of serenity? How many kinds of equanimity towards formations arise by way of insight? Eight kinds of equanimity towards formations arise by way of serenity; ten kinds of equanimity towards formations arise by way of insight” (Paṭis I 57)—and which is neutral in apprehending the settling down of the hindrances and so on by way of reflection—this is called equanimity towards formations.

Yā pana “yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti upekkhāsahagata”nti (dha. sa. 150) evamāgatā adukkhamasukhasaṅkhātā upekkhā, ayaṃ vedanupekkhā nāma.

The equanimity described as: “At the time when a wholesome consciousness pertaining to the sense-sphere arises accompanied by equanimity” (Dhs §150), which is known as neither-painful-nor-pleasant—this is called equanimity of feeling.

Yā pana “yadatthi yaṃ bhūtaṃ, taṃ pajahati, upekkhaṃ paṭilabhatī”ti (ma. ni. 3.71-72; a. ni. 7.55) evamāgatā vicinane majjhattabhūtā upekkhā, ayaṃ vipassanupekkhā nāma.

The equanimity described thus: “One abandons what exists, what has come to be, and attains equanimity” (MN 3.71–72; AN 7.55), which is neutral in investigation—this is called equanimity of insight.

Yā pana chandādīsu yevāpanakesu āgatā sahajātānaṃ samavāhitabhūtā upekkhā, ayaṃ tatramajjhattupekkhā nāma.

The equanimity that occurs among incidental factors such as desire, and which consists in balancing the co-arisen states—this is called equanimity as specific neutrality.

Yā pana “upekkhako ca viharatī”ti evamāgatā aggasukhepi tasmiṃ apakkhapātajananī upekkhā, ayaṃ jhānupekkhā nāma.

The equanimity described as: “And one dwells equanimous,” which, even in that supreme happiness, generates no partiality—this is called equanimity of jhāna.

Yā pana “upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ catutthaṃ jhāna”nti (dha. sa. 165; dī. ni. 1.232) evamāgatā [V 0.0109] sabbapaccanīkaparisuddhā paccanīkavūpasamanepi abyāpārabhūtā upekkhā, ayaṃ pārisuddhupekkhā nāma.

The equanimity that comes as: “the fourth jhāna, which is the purity of mindfulness through equanimity” (Dhs §165; DN 1.232), which is purified of all opposing states and is non-active even in the calming of opposing states—this is called equanimity of purity.

Tattha chaḷaṅgupekkhā ca brahmavihārupekkhā ca bojjhaṅgupekkhā ca tatramajjhattupekkhā ca jhānupekkhā ca pārisuddhupekkhā ca atthato ekā, tatramajjhattupekkhāva hoti. Tena tena avatthābhedena panassā ayaṃ bhedo[M 0.0120]. Ekassāpi sato sattassa kumārayuvatherasenāpatirājādivasena bhedo viya, tasmā tāsu yattha chaḷaṅgupekkhā, na tattha bojjhaṅgupekkhādayo. Yattha vā pana bojjhaṅgupekkhā, na tattha chaḷaṅgupekkhādayo hontīti veditabbā.

Herein, six-factored equanimity, equanimity of the divine abidings, equanimity as an enlightenment factor, equanimity as specific neutrality, equanimity of jhāna, and equanimity of purity are one in meaning—they are simply equanimity as specific neutrality. However, this distinction among them is due to different circumstances. It is like the distinctions for a single being, who may be a child, a youth, an elder, a general, or a king. Therefore, among these, where there is six-factored equanimity, there is not equanimity as an enlightenment factor and so on. And where there is equanimity as an enlightenment factor, there is not six-factored equanimity and so on; so it should be understood.

Yathā cetāsaṃ atthato ekībhāvo, evaṃ saṅkhārupekkhāvipassanupekkhānampi. Paññā eva hi esā, kiccavasena dvidhā bhinnā, yathā hi purisassa sāyaṃ gehaṃ paviṭṭhaṃ sappaṃ ajapadadaṇḍaṃ [P 1.0139] gahetvā pariyesamānassa taṃ thusakoṭṭhake nipannaṃ disvā “sappo nu kho no”ti avalokentassa sovatthikattayaṃ disvā nibbematikassa “sappo na sappo”ti vicinane majjhattatā uppajjati, evameva yā āraddhavipassakassa vipassanāñāṇena lakkhaṇattaye diṭṭhe saṅkhārānaṃ aniccabhāvādivicinane majjhattatā uppajjati, ayaṃ vipassanupekkhā. Yathā pana tassa purisassa ajapadadaṇḍakena gāḷhaṃ sappaṃ gahetvā “kintāhaṃ imaṃ sappaṃ aviheṭhento attānañca iminā aḍaṃsāpento muñceyya”nti muñcanākārameva pariyesato gahaṇe majjhattatā hoti, evameva yā lakkhaṇattayassa diṭṭhattā āditte viya tayo bhave passato saṅkhāraggahaṇe majjhattatā, ayaṃ saṅkhārupekkhā. Iti vipassanupekkhāya siddhāya saṅkhārupekkhāpi siddhāva hoti. Iminā panesā vicinanaggahaṇesu majjhattatāsaṅkhātena kiccena dvidhā bhinnāti. Vīriyupekkhā pana vedanupekkhā ca aññamaññañca avasesāhi ca atthato bhinnāyevāti. Āha cettha –

Just as these are one in meaning, so too are equanimity towards formations and equanimity of insight. For this is just wisdom, divided in two by way of function. For example, when a man enters his house in the evening and, taking a goat's-foot staff, searches for a snake, and upon seeing it lying in a heap of chaff, he looks at it wondering, 'Is this a snake or not?'—upon seeing the three markings on its hood and becoming free from doubt, equanimity arises in the investigation 'Is it a snake or not a snake?'. In the same way, for a meditator who has undertaken insight, when the three characteristics are seen with insight knowledge, equanimity arises in the investigation of the impermanent nature, etc., of formations—this is equanimity of insight. And just as that man, having firmly grasped the snake with the goat's-foot staff, thinks, 'How can I release this snake without harming it and without being bitten by it myself?'—equanimity arises in the act of grasping while he is seeking a way to release it. Similarly, for one who sees the three kinds of existence as if ablaze because the three characteristics have been seen, equanimity arises in the grasping of formations—this is equanimity towards formations. Thus, when equanimity of insight is accomplished, equanimity towards formations is also accomplished. By this function, characterized as equanimity in investigating and in grasping, it is divided in two. But equanimity of energy and equanimity of feeling are different in meaning from each other and from the rest. And it is said here:

“Majjhattabrahmabojjhaṅgachaḷaṅgajhānasuddhiyo;

Vipassanā ca saṅkhāravedanāvīriyaṃ iti.

“Specific neutrality, the divine abiding, the enlightenment factor, the six-factored, of jhāna, and of purity; and insight, formations, feeling, and energy.”

“Vitthārato dasopekkhā-chamajjhattādito tato;

Duve paññā tato dvīhi, catassova bhavantimā”ti.

“In detail, the kinds of equanimity are ten. The six beginning with specific neutrality form one group; two are wisdom; then with the other two, these become four.”

Iti imāsu upekkhāsu jhānupekkhā idha adhippetā. Sā majjhattalakkhaṇā, anābhogarasā[V 0.0110], abyāpārapaccupaṭṭhānā, pītivirāgapadaṭṭhānāti. Etthāha – “nanu cāyaṃ atthato tatramajjhattupekkhāva hoti, sā ca paṭhamadutiyajjhānesupi atthi. Tasmā tatrāpi ‘upekkhako ca viharatī’ti evamayaṃ vattabbā siyā, sā kasmā na vuttā”ti? Aparibyattakiccato. Aparibyattañhi [M 0.0121] tassā tattha kiccaṃ, vitakkādīhi abhibhūtattā. Idha panāyaṃ vitakkavicārapītīhi anabhibhūtattā ukkhittasirā viya hutvā paribyattakiccā jātā, tasmā vuttāti.

Among these kinds of equanimity, it is equanimity of jhāna that is intended here. It has the characteristic of neutrality, the function of non-inclination, the manifestation of impartiality, and the fading away of joy as its proximate cause. Here it is asked: “But is this not, in meaning, just specific neutrality? And that exists also in the first and second jhānas. Therefore, it should be said there too, ‘and he dwells equanimous.’ Why is this not said?” Because its function is not manifest. For there its function is not manifest since it is overwhelmed by applied thought, etc. But here, since it is not overwhelmed by applied thought, sustained thought, and joy, its function becomes manifest, like one who has lifted his head. Therefore it is stated.

Sato [P 1.0140] ca sampajānoti ettha saratīti sato. Sampajānātīti sampajāno. Iti puggalena sati ca sampajaññañca vuttaṃ. Tattha saraṇalakkhaṇā sati, asammussanarasā ārakkhapaccupaṭṭhānā. Asammohalakkhaṇaṃ sampajaññaṃ, tīraṇarasaṃ, pavicayapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ.

And mindful and clearly comprehending: here, 'mindful' means one who remembers. 'Clearly comprehending' means one who comprehends clearly. Thus mindfulness and clear comprehension are stated in terms of the person. Therein, mindfulness has the characteristic of remembering, the function of not forgetting, and manifestation as guarding. Clear comprehension has the characteristic of non-delusion, the function of investigating, and manifestation as scrutiny.

Tattha kiñcāpi idaṃ satisampajaññaṃ purimajjhānesupi atthi, muṭṭhassatissa hi asampajānassa upacāramattampi na sampajjati, pageva appanā. Oḷārikattā pana tesaṃ jhānānaṃ bhūmiyaṃ viya purisassa cittassa gati sukhā hoti, abyattaṃ tattha satisampajaññakiccaṃ. Oḷārikaṅgappahānena pana sukhumattā imassa jhānassa purisassa khuradhārāyaṃ viya satisampajaññakiccapariggahitā eva cittassa gati icchitabbāti idheva vuttaṃ. Kiñca bhiyyo – yathā dhenupago vaccho dhenuto apanīto arakkhiyamāno punadeva dhenuṃ upagacchati, evamidaṃ tatiyajjhānasukhaṃ pītito apanītampi satisampajaññārakkhena arakkhiyamānaṃ punadeva pītiṃ upagaccheyya, pītisampayuttameva siyā, sukhe vāpi sattā sārajjanti. Idañca atimadhurasukhaṃ, tato paraṃ sukhābhāvā. Satisampajaññānubhāvena panettha sukhe asārajjanā hoti, no aññathāti imampi atthavisesaṃ dassetuṃ idamidheva vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

Although this mindfulness and clear comprehension exist also in the preceding jhānas—for one with lapsed mindfulness and no clear comprehension, not even access concentration is accomplished, still less absorption—yet because of the coarseness of those jhānas, the mind's progress is easy, like a person on level ground, and the function of mindfulness and clear comprehension is not manifest there. But since the coarse factors have been abandoned, this jhāna is subtle; thus the mind's progress must be guided by the function of mindfulness and clear comprehension, like a person on a razor's edge. That is why this is stated only here. Furthermore, just as a suckling calf that has been taken from the cow, if unguarded, goes back to the cow again, so this happiness of the third jhāna, though removed from joy, if it is not protected by mindfulness and clear comprehension, might go back to joy again and become associated with joy; or beings might become attached to the happiness. And this happiness is exceedingly sweet, since there is no happiness beyond it. It is by the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension that there is no attachment to happiness here, not otherwise. To show this special meaning, this was stated only here, so it should be understood.

Idāni sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedetīti ettha kiñcāpi tatiyajjhānasamaṅgino sukhapaṭisaṃvedanābhogo natthi, evaṃ santepi yasmā tassa nāmakāyena sampayuttaṃ sukhaṃ. Yaṃ vā taṃ nāmakāyasampayuttaṃ sukhaṃ, taṃsamuṭṭhānenassa yasmā atipaṇītena rūpena rūpakāyo phuṭo, yassa phuṭattā jhānā vuṭṭhitopi sukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedeyya, tasmā etamatthaṃ dassento “sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedetī”ti āha.

Now, as to 'and he feels pleasure with the body': here, although one endowed with the third jhāna has no deliberate experience of feeling pleasure, still there is pleasure associated with his mental body. Or, because his physical body is pervaded by a very refined form originated by that pleasure associated with the mental body, and because of this pervasion, even after emerging from the jhāna he would feel pleasure. Therefore, to show this meaning, it was said: 'and he feels pleasure with the body.'
