Idāni yaṃ taṃ ariyā ācikkhanti upekkhako satimā sukhavihārīti ettha yaṃjhānahetu yaṃjhānakāraṇā [V 0.0111] taṃ tatiyajjhānasamaṅgīpuggalaṃ buddhādayo ariyā ācikkhanti desenti paññapenti [P 1.0141] paṭṭhapenti vivaranti vibhajanti uttānīkaronti pakāsenti, pasaṃsantīti adhippāyo. Kinti? Upekkhako [M 0.0122] satimā sukhavihārīti. Taṃ tatiyajjhānaṃ upasampajja viharatīti evamettha yojanā veditabbā.

Now, as to 'that of which the noble ones declare, “He is equanimous, mindful, a happy dweller”': here, on account of that jhāna, for the reason of that jhāna, the noble ones—the Buddhas and others—describe, teach, make known, establish, open up, analyze, make plain, and show—that is, they praise—the person endowed with the third jhāna. As what? As 'equanimous, mindful, a happy dweller.' The connection of the words here should be understood thus: 'He enters and dwells in that third jhāna.'

Kasmā pana taṃ te evaṃ pasaṃsantīti? Pasaṃsārahato. Ayañhi yasmā atimadhurasukhe sukhapāramippattepi tatiyajjhāne upekkhako, na tattha sukhābhisaṅgena ākaḍḍhīyati. Yathā ca pīti na uppajjati, evaṃ upaṭṭhitasatitāya satimā. Yasmā ca ariyakantaṃ ariyajanasevitameva ca asaṃkiliṭṭhaṃ sukhaṃ nāmakāyena paṭisaṃvedeti, tasmā pasaṃsāraho. Iti pasaṃsārahato naṃ ariyā te evaṃ pasaṃsāhetubhūte guṇe pakāsento “upekkhako satimā sukhavihārī”ti evaṃ pasaṃsantīti veditabbaṃ. Tatiyanti gaṇanānupubbatā tatiyaṃ, idaṃ tatiyaṃ uppannantipi tatiyaṃ.

And why do they praise him thus? Because he is worthy of praise. For he is equanimous in the third jhāna even when it has reached the peak of pleasure, an exceedingly sweet pleasure, and he is not drawn away by attachment to that pleasure. And he is mindful with well-established mindfulness so that joy does not arise. And because he feels with the mental body a pleasure that is dear to the noble ones, frequented by noble persons, and undefiled, he is worthy of praise. Thus, because he is worthy of praise, it should be understood that the noble ones praise him by proclaiming the qualities that are the reason for praise, saying: 'equanimous, mindful, a happy dweller.' 'Third' means third in numerical order; and it is the third to have arisen, thus it is third.

Sukhassa ca pahānā dukkhassa ca pahānāti kāyikasukhassa ca kāyikadukkhassa ca pahānā. Pubbevāti tañca kho pubbeva, na catutthajjhānakkhaṇe. Somanassadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamāti cetasikasukhassa ca cetasikadukkhassa cāti imesampi dvinnaṃ pubbeva atthaṅgamā, pahānā icceva vuttaṃ hoti.

“With the abandoning of pleasure and pain” means with the abandoning of bodily pleasure and bodily pain. “Previously” means that this occurred before, not at the moment of the fourth jhāna. “With the disappearance of joy and grief” means with the disappearance of mental pleasure and mental pain. The disappearance of these two also occurred previously, and “disappearance” is stated here with the same meaning as “abandoning.”

Kadā pana nesaṃ pahānaṃ hoti? Catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ upacārakkhaṇe. Somanassañhi catutthajjhānassa upacārakkhaṇeyeva pahīyati, dukkhadomanassasukhāni paṭhamadutiyatatiyajjhānānaṃ upacārakkhaṇesu. Evametesaṃ pahānakkamena avuttānaṃ, indriyavibhaṅge pana indriyānaṃ uddesakkameneva idhāpi vuttānaṃ sukhadukkhasomanassadomanassānaṃ pahānaṃ veditabbaṃ.

But when does their abandoning occur? At the access moments of the four jhānas. For joy is abandoned at the very access moment of the fourth jhāna, while pain, grief, and pleasure are abandoned at the access moments of the first, second, and third jhānas respectively. Thus, though they are not stated here in the order of their abandoning, the abandoning of pleasure, pain, joy, and grief, which are stated here, should be understood to be in the same order as the exposition of the faculties in the Analysis of the Faculties.

Yadi panetāni tassa tassa jhānassa upacārakkhaṇeyeva pahīyanti, atha kasmā “kattha cuppannaṃ dukkhindriyaṃ aparisesaṃ nirujjhati? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi…pe… paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati, ettha cuppannaṃ dukkhindriyaṃ aparisesaṃ nirujjhati. Kattha cuppannaṃ domanassindriyaṃ… sukhindriyaṃ… somanassindriyaṃ aparisesaṃ [P 1.0142] nirujjhati? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu, sukhassa ca pahānā…pe… catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ettha cuppannaṃ somanassindriyaṃ aparisesaṃ nirujjhatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.510) evaṃ [V 0.0112] jhānesveva nirodho vuttoti. Atisayanirodhattā. Atisayanirodho hi nesaṃ paṭhamajjhānādīsu, na nirodhoyeva. Nirodhoyeva pana upacārakkhaṇe nātisayanirodho.

But if these are abandoned at the very access moment of each respective jhāna, then why is it said: “Where, bhikkhus, does the arisen faculty of pain cease without remainder? Here, a bhikkhu, secluded from sensual pleasures … enters and dwells in the first jhāna. It is here that the arisen faculty of pain ceases without remainder. … Where does the arisen faculty of joy cease without remainder? Here, a bhikkhu, with the abandoning of pleasure … enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna. It is here that the arisen faculty of joy ceases without remainder” (SN 48:40)? It is because of the superior cessation. For in the first jhāna and so on their cessation is a superior cessation, not mere cessation. But at the access moment there is only cessation, not a superior cessation.

Tathā [M 0.0123] hi nānāvajjane paṭhamajjhānūpacāre niruddhassāpi dukkhindriyassa ḍaṃsamakasādisamphassena vā visamāsanupatāpena vā siyā uppatti, na tveva antoappanāyaṃ. Upacāre vā niruddhampetaṃ na suṭṭhu niruddhaṃ hoti, paṭipakkhena avihatattā. Antoappanāyaṃ pana pītipharaṇena sabbo kāyo sukhokkanto hoti, sukhokkantakāyassa ca suṭṭhu niruddhaṃ hoti dukkhindriyaṃ, paṭipakkhena vihatattā. Nānāvajjaneyeva ca dutiyajjhānūpacāre pahīnassāpi domanassindriyassa yasmā etaṃ vitakkavicārapaccayepi kāyakilamathe cittupaghāte ca sati uppajjati, vitakkavicārābhāve neva uppajjati. Yattha pana uppajjati, tattha vitakkavicārabhāve. Appahīnāyeva ca dutiyajjhānūpacāre vitakkavicārāti tatthassa siyā uppatti, na tveva dutiyajjhāne, pahīnappaccayattā. Tathā tatiyajjhānūpacāre pahīnassāpi sukhindriyassa pītisamuṭṭhānapaṇītarūpaphuṭakāyassa siyā uppatti, na tveva tatiyajjhāne. Tatiyajjhāne hi sukhassa paccayabhūtā pīti sabbaso niruddhāti. Tathā catutthajjhānūpacāre pahīnassāpi somanassindriyassa āsannattā, appanāpattāya upekkhāya abhāvena sammā anatikkantattā ca siyā uppatti, na tveva catutthajjhāne. Tasmā eva ca “etthuppannaṃ dukkhindriyaṃ aparisesaṃ nirujjhatī”ti tattha tattha aparisesaggahaṇaṃ katanti.

For in access concentration for the first jhāna, even though the faculty of pain has been suppressed, it might arise from contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like, or from the affliction of an unsuitable posture, but not within absorption itself. Or, being suppressed in access concentration, it is not well suppressed, because it has not been overcome by its opposing factor. Within absorption, however, the whole body is pervaded with pleasure by the suffusion of rapture, and for one whose body is pervaded with pleasure, the faculty of pain is well suppressed, having been overcome by its opposing factor. And in access concentration for the second jhāna, even though the faculty of displeasure has been abandoned, it arises when there is bodily fatigue and mental affliction, which are also conditioned by applied and sustained thought, but it does not arise in the absence of applied and sustained thought. Where it does arise, it is in the presence of applied and sustained thought. And since applied and sustained thought are not yet abandoned in access concentration for the second jhāna, it might arise there, but not in the second jhāna itself, as its conditions have been abandoned. Similarly, in access concentration for the third jhāna, even though the faculty of pleasure has been abandoned, it might arise for one whose body is pervaded by the subtle matter born of rapture, but not in the third jhāna itself. For in the third jhāna, rapture, the condition for pleasure, has ceased completely. Similarly, in access concentration for the fourth jhāna, even though the faculty of joy has been abandoned, it might arise due to its nearness and because it has not been rightly transcended, owing to the absence of the equanimity that has attained absorption, but not in the fourth jhāna itself. That is why the phrase “the arisen faculty of pain ceases without remainder” has been included in each case.

Etthāha – “athevaṃ tassa tassa jhānassupacāre pahīnāpi etā vedanā idha kasmā samāhaṭā”ti? Sukhaggahaṇatthaṃ. Yā hi ayaṃ adukkhamasukhanti ettha adukkhamasukhā vedanā vuttā, sā sukhumā dubbiññeyyā, na sakkā sukhena gahetuṃ, tasmā [P 1.0143] yathā nāma duṭṭhassa yathā vā tathā vā upasaṅkamitvā gahetuṃ asakkuṇeyyassa goṇassa sukhagahaṇatthaṃ gopo ekasmiṃ vaje sabbā gāvo samāharati, athekekaṃ nīharanto paṭipāṭiyā āgataṃ “ayaṃ so gaṇhatha na”nti tampi gāhāpeti, evameva bhagavā sukhaggahaṇatthaṃ sabbā etā samāharīti. Evañhi samāhaṭā etā dassetvā “yaṃ neva sukhaṃ, na dukkhaṃ, na somanassaṃ, na domanassaṃ, ayaṃ adukkhamasukhā vedanā”ti sakkā hoti esā gāhayituṃ.

Here it is said: “But if these feelings are abandoned even in the access concentration for each jhāna, why are they collected together here?” For the sake of easy grasping. For this feeling called neither-painful-nor-pleasant is subtle and difficult to discern; it cannot be easily grasped. It is as though a cowherd, unable to catch a fierce bull by approaching it this way or that, gathers all the cattle into one pen for the sake of catching it easily; then, as he lets them out one by one, when the bull comes in its turn, he has it caught, saying, ‘This is it, catch it!’ So too, the Blessed One collected all these feelings together for the sake of easy grasping. For when they have been collected together and shown in this way, it is possible to make this feeling understood: ‘That which is neither pleasure nor pain, neither joy nor displeasure—this is the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.’”

Api ca adukkhamasukhāya cetovimuttiyā paccayadassanatthañcāpi etā vuttāti veditabbā. Dukkhappahānādayo hi tassā paccayā. Yathāha – “cattāro [M 0.0124] kho, āvuso, paccayā adukkhamasukhāya cetovimuttiyā samāpattiyā. Idhāvuso, bhikkhu sukhassa ca pahānā [V 0.0113] …pe… catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ime kho, āvuso, cattāro paccayā adukkhamasukhāya cetovimuttiyā samāpattiyā”ti (ma. ni. 1.458). Yathā vā aññattha pahīnāpi sakkāyadiṭṭhiādayo tatiyamaggassa vaṇṇabhaṇanatthaṃ “tattha pahīnā”ti vuttā, evaṃ vaṇṇabhaṇanatthampetassa jhānassetā idha vuttātipi veditabbā. Paccayaghātena vā ettha rāgadosānaṃ atidūrabhāvaṃ dassetumpetā vuttāti veditabbā. Etāsu hi sukhaṃ somanassassa paccayo, somanassaṃ rāgassa, dukkhaṃ domanassassa, domanassaṃ dosassa. Sukhādighātena ca te sappaccayā rāgadosā hatāti atidūre hontīti.

Furthermore, it should be understood that these are stated also to show the conditions for the neither-painful-nor-pleasant liberation of mind. For the abandonment of pain and so on are its conditions. As it is said: ‘Friend, there are four conditions for the attainment of the neither-painful-nor-pleasant liberation of mind. Here, friend, a bhikkhu, with the abandoning of pleasure… enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna. These, friend, are the four conditions for the attainment of the neither-painful-nor-pleasant liberation of mind’ (MN 44). Or, just as elsewhere identity view and so on, though already abandoned, are mentioned as ‘abandoned there’ for the sake of extolling the third path, so too it should be understood that these feelings are mentioned here for the sake of extolling this jhāna. Or again, it should be understood that they are mentioned to show the extreme remoteness from lust and hatred through the destruction of their conditions. For among these, pleasure is a condition for joy, and joy for lust; pain is a condition for displeasure, and displeasure for hatred. And with the destruction of pleasure and so on, lust and hatred together with their conditions are destroyed, and thus they become extremely remote.

Adukkhamasukhanti dukkhābhāvena adukkhaṃ, sukhābhāvena asukhaṃ. Etenettha sukhadukkhapaṭipakkhabhūtaṃ tatiyavedanaṃ dīpeti, na dukkhasukhābhāvamattaṃ. Tatiyavedanā nāma adukkhamasukhā, upekkhātipi vuccati. Sā iṭṭhāniṭṭhaviparītānubhavanalakkhaṇā, majjhattarasā, avibhūtapaccupaṭṭhānā, sukhanirodhapadaṭṭhānāti veditabbā.

Neither-painful-nor-pleasant: it is not-painful (adukkhaṃ) because of the absence of pain (dukkha), and not-pleasant (asukhaṃ) because of the absence of pleasure (sukha). By this is indicated the third kind of feeling, which is the opposite of pleasure and pain, not the mere absence of pleasure and pain. This third kind of feeling is called neither-painful-nor-pleasant; it is also called equanimity (upekkhā). It should be understood as having the characteristic of experiencing an object that is neither desirable nor undesirable, the function of neutrality, the manifestation of being unapparent, and the proximate cause of the cessation of pleasure.

Upekkhāsatipārisuddhinti upekkhāya janitasatipārisuddhiṃ. Imasmiñhi jhāne suparisuddhā sati, yā ca tassā satiyā [P 1.0144] pārisuddhi, sā upekkhāya katā, na aññena. Tasmā etaṃ “upekkhāsatipārisuddhi”nti vuccati. Yāya ca upekkhāya ettha sati pārisuddhi hoti, sā atthato tatramajjhattatāti veditabbā. Na kevalañcettha tāya satiyeva parisuddhā, api ca kho sabbepi sampayuttadhammā, satisīsena pana desanā vuttā.

Purity of mindfulness due to equanimity: this means the purity of mindfulness generated by equanimity. For in this jhāna mindfulness is very pure, and the purity of that mindfulness is produced by equanimity, not by anything else. Therefore it is called ‘purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.’ The equanimity by which mindfulness becomes pure here should be understood as being in reality specific neutrality (tatramajjhattatā). And not only mindfulness is purified by it here, but all associated states as well; however, the teaching is given with mindfulness as the heading.

Tattha kiñcāpi ayaṃ upekkhā heṭṭhāpi tīsu jhānesu vijjati, yathā pana divā sūriyappabhābhibhavā sommabhāvena ca attano upakārakattena vā sabhāgāya rattiyā alābhā divā vijjamānāpi candalekhā aparisuddhā hoti apariyodātā, evamayampi tatramajjhattupekkhācandalekhā vitakkādipaccanīkadhammatejābhibhavā sabhāgāya ca upekkhāvedanārattiyā apaṭilābhā vijjamānāpi paṭhamajjhānādibhedesu aparisuddhā hoti. Tassā ca aparisuddhāya divā aparisuddhacandalekhāya pabhā viya sahajātāpi satiādayo [M 0.0125] aparisuddhāva honti. Tasmā tesu ekampi “upekkhāsatipārisuddhi”nti na vuttaṃ. Idha pana vitakkādipaccanīkadhammatejābhibhavābhāvā sabhāgāya ca upekkhāvedanārattiyā paṭilābhā ayaṃ tatramajjhattupekkhācandalekhā ativiya parisuddhā, tassā parisuddhattā parisuddhacandalekhāya pabhā viya sahajātāpi satiādayo parisuddhā honti pariyodātā. Tasmā idameva “upekkhāsatipārisuddhi”nti [V 0.0114] vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Catutthanti gaṇanānupubbatā catutthaṃ. Idaṃ catutthaṃ uppannantipi catutthaṃ.

Here, although this equanimity exists in the three lower jhānas, it is not pure. Just as the crescent moon, though present during the day, is not pure and bright because it is overpowered by the sun’s radiance and because it does not obtain the kindred night that would assist it, so the crescent moon of specific neutrality, though present in the first jhāna and the others, is not pure because it is overpowered by the radiance of the opposing states beginning with applied thought, and because it does not obtain the kindred night of equanimous feeling. And as the light of the impure crescent moon by day is impure, so the co-nascent states of mindfulness and so on are also impure. Therefore none of those jhānas is called ‘purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.’ But here, since it is not overpowered by the radiance of the opposing states beginning with applied thought, and since it obtains the kindred night of equanimous feeling, this crescent moon of specific neutrality is exceedingly pure. Because it is pure, the co-nascent states of mindfulness and so on are also pure and bright, like the light of a pure crescent moon. Therefore it should be understood that this jhāna alone is called ‘purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.’ Fourth: it is the fourth in numerical sequence. It is also the fourth because it is the fourth to have arisen.

Paññavā hotīti paññā assa atthīti paññavā. Udayatthagāminiyāti udayagāminiyā ceva atthagāminiyā ca. Samannāgatoti paripuṇṇo. Ariyāyāti niddosāya. Nibbedhikāyāti nibbedhapakkhikāya. Dukkhakkhayagāminiyāti nibbānagāminiyā. So idaṃ dukkhanti evamādīsu “ettakaṃ dukkhaṃ na ito bhiyyo”ti sabbampi dukkhasaccaṃ sarasalakkhaṇapaṭivedhena yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti paṭivijjhati. Tassa ca dukkhassa nibbattikaṃ taṇhaṃ “ayaṃ dukkhasamudayo”ti. Tadubhayampi yaṃ ṭhānaṃ patvā nirujjhati, taṃ tesaṃ appavattiṃ [P 1.0145] nibbānaṃ “ayaṃ dukkhanirodho”ti. Tassa ca sampāpakaṃ ariyamaggaṃ “ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā”ti sarasalakkhaṇapaṭivedhena yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti paṭivijjhatīti evamattho veditabbo.

‘He is wise’: he has wisdom (paññā), thus he is wise (paññavā). ‘Leading to arising and passing away’: leading to arising and leading to passing away. ‘Endowed with’: complete. ‘Noble’: faultless. ‘Penetrative’: siding with penetration. ‘Leading to the destruction of suffering’: leading to Nibbāna. He understands and penetrates as it really is the entire truth of suffering, by penetrating its individual essence and characteristic, in such ways as: ‘This is suffering,’ and ‘So much is suffering, no more than this.’ He understands and penetrates as it really is, ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ namely, the craving that generates that suffering. He understands and penetrates as it really is, ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ namely, Nibbāna, the state reached where both of these cease, their non-occurrence. He understands and penetrates as it really is, ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering,’ namely, the Noble Path that brings one to its attainment. This is how the meaning should be understood.

Evaṃ sarūpato saccāni dassetvā idāni kilesavasena pariyāyato dassento “ime āsavā”tiādimāha. Te vuttanayeneva veditabbā. Evaṃ tisso sikkhāyo dassetvā idāni tāsaṃ pāripūrikkamaṃ dassetuṃ “imā tisso sikkhāyo āvajjanto sikkheyyā”tiādimāha. Tassattho – paccekaṃ paripūretuṃ āvajjantopi sikkheyya, āvajjitvāpi “ayaṃ nāma sikkhā”ti jānantopi sikkheyya, jānitvā punappunaṃ passantopi sikkheyya, passitvā yathādiṭṭhaṃ paccavekkhantopi sikkheyya, paccavekkhitvā tattheva cittaṃ acalaṃ katvā patiṭṭhapentopi sikkheyya, taṃtaṃsikkhāsampayuttasaddhāvīriyasatisamādhipaññāhi sakasakakiccaṃ karontopi sikkheyya, abhiññeyyābhijānanakālepi taṃ taṃ kiccaṃ karontopi tisso sikkhāyo sikkheyya, adhisīlaṃ ācareyya, adhicittaṃ sammā careyya, adhipaññaṃ samādāya vatteyya.

Having thus shown the truths in their own nature, now, showing them discursively by way of the defilements, he says, ‘These are the cankers,’ and so on. These should be understood in the way already stated. Having thus shown the three trainings, now, to show the course for their fulfillment, he says, ‘Adverting to these three trainings, one should train,’ and so on. The meaning is this: One should train by adverting in order to fulfill each training individually; having adverted, by knowing, ‘This is such a training’; having known, by seeing it again and again; having seen, by reviewing it as seen; having reviewed, by making the mind unshaken and establishing it right there; one should train by carrying out the respective tasks with the faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom associated with each particular training; even at the time of directly knowing what is to be directly known, one should train in the three trainings by carrying out the respective tasks. One should practice the higher virtue, conduct oneself rightly in the higher mind, and undertake and practice the higher wisdom.

Idhāti [M 0.0126] mūlapadaṃ. Imissā diṭṭhiyātiādīhi dasahi padehi sikkhattayasaṅkhātaṃ sabbaññubuddhasāsanameva kathitaṃ. Tañhi buddhena bhagavatā diṭṭhattā diṭṭhīti vuccati. Tasseva khamanavasena khanti, ruccanavasena ruci, gahaṇavasena ādāyo, sabhāvaṭṭhena dhammo, sikkhitabbaṭṭhena vinayo, tadubhayenapi dhammavinayo, pavuttavasena pāvacanaṃ, seṭṭhacariyaṭṭhena brahmacariyaṃ, anusiṭṭhidānavasena satthusāsananti vuccati. Tasmā “imissā diṭṭhiyā”tiādīsu imissā buddhadiṭṭhiyā imissā buddhakhantiyā imissā buddharuciyā imasmiṃ buddhaādāye imasmiṃ buddhadhamme imasmiṃ buddhavinaye.

‘Here’ is the root term. By ‘of this view,’ and so forth—with these ten terms—the entire dispensation of the Omniscient Buddha, comprised of the threefold training, is spoken of. For since it was seen by the Blessed One, the Buddha, it is called a view. Due to its being approved of, it is called patience; due to its being pleasing, it is called delight; due to its being taken up, it is called acceptance; in the sense of its own nature, it is called the Dhamma; in the sense of what should be trained in, it is called the Discipline; by both of these, it is called the Dhamma and Discipline; in the sense of its being proclaimed, it is called the Teaching; in the sense of supreme conduct, it is called the holy life; and in the sense of giving instruction, it is called the Teacher’s Dispensation. Therefore, in such phrases as ‘of this view,’ it means: of this Buddha-view, of this Buddha-patience, of this Buddha-delight, in this Buddha-acceptance, in this Buddha-Dhamma, in this Buddha-Discipline.

“Ye [V 0.0115] kho tvaṃ, gotami, dhamme jāneyyāsi ‘ime dhammā sarāgāya saṃvattanti, no virāgāya, saññogāya saṃvattanti, no visaññogāya, ācayāya saṃvattanti, no apacayāya, mahicchatāya saṃvattanti, no appicchatāya, asantuṭṭhiyā saṃvattanti, no santuṭṭhiyā, saṅgaṇikāya saṃvattanti[P 1.0146], no pavivekāya, kosajjāya saṃvattanti, no vīriyārambhāya, dubbharatāya saṃvattanti, no subharatāyā’ti. Ekaṃsena, gotami, dhāreyyāsi ‘neso dhammo, neso vinayo, netaṃ satthusāsana’nti.

Gotami, as to those teachings that you might know thus: ‘These teachings lead to passion, not to dispassion; to fettering, not to unfettering; to accumulation, not to diminution; to great desire, not to fewness of wishes; to discontent, not to contentment; to sociability, not to seclusion; to laziness, not to arousal of energy; to being difficult to support, not to being easy to support’—you may definitely hold, Gotami: ‘This is not the Dhamma, this is not the Discipline, this is not the Teacher’s Dispensation’.

“Ye ca kho tvaṃ, gotami, dhamme jāneyyāsi ‘ime dhammā virāgāya saṃvattanti, no sarāgāya…pe… subharatāya saṃvattanti, no dubbharatāyā’ti. Ekaṃsena, gotami, dhāreyyāsi ‘eso dhammo, eso vinayo, etaṃ satthusāsana’”nti (a. ni. 8.53; cūḷava. 406) –

But, Gotami, as to those teachings that you might know thus: ‘These teachings lead to dispassion, not to passion … to being easy to support, not to being difficult to support’—you may definitely hold, Gotami: ‘This is the Dhamma, this is the Discipline, this is the Teacher’s Dispensation’.

Evaṃ vutte imasmiṃ buddhadhammavinaye imasmiṃ buddhapāvacane imasmiṃ buddhabrahmacariye imasmiṃ buddhasāsaneti evamattho veditabbo.

When this is said, the meaning should be understood thus: in this Buddha-Dhamma-and-Discipline, in this Buddha’s Teaching, in this Buddha’s holy life, in this Buddha’s Dispensation.

Api cetaṃ sikkhattayasaṅkhātaṃ sakalaṃ sāsanaṃ bhagavatā diṭṭhattā sammādiṭṭhipaccayattā sammādiṭṭhipubbaṅgamattā ca diṭṭhi. Bhagavato khamanavasena khanti. Ruccanavasena ruci. Gahaṇavasena ādāyo. Attano kārakaṃ apāyesu apatamānaṃ katvā dhāretīti dhammo. Sova saṃkilesapakkhaṃ vinetīti vinayo. Dhammo ca so vinayo cāti dhammavinayo. Kusaladhammehi vā akusaladhammānaṃ esa vinayoti dhammavinayo. Teneva vuttaṃ –

Moreover, this entire dispensation, designated as the threefold training, is a ‘view’ because it was seen by the Blessed One, because it has right view as its condition, and because it has right view as its forerunner. By way of the Blessed One’s approval, it is ‘patience.’ By way of its being pleasing, it is ‘delight.’ By way of its being taken up, it is ‘acceptance.’ Because it holds its practitioner, preventing them from falling into the planes of misery, it is ‘Dhamma.’ And it removes the side of defilement, thus it is ‘Discipline.’ It is both Dhamma and Discipline, thus ‘Dhamma-and-Discipline.’ Or, it is the removal of unwholesome states by means of wholesome states, thus ‘Dhamma-and-Discipline.’ Thus it is said:

“Ye [M 0.0127] ca kho tvaṃ, gotami, dhamme jāneyyāsi ‘ime dhammā virāgāya saṃvattanti, no sarāgāya…pe… ekaṃsena gotami dhāreyyāsi ‘eso dhammo, eso vinayo, etaṃ satthusāsana’”nti (a. ni. 8.53; cūḷava. 406).

But, Gotami, as to those teachings that you might know thus: ‘These teachings lead to dispassion, not to passion … to being easy to support, not to being difficult to support’—you may definitely hold, Gotami: ‘This is the Dhamma, this is the Discipline, this is the Teacher’s Dispensation’.

Dhammena vā vinayo, na daṇḍādīhīti dhammavinayo. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Or, the discipline is by means of the Dhamma, not by the rod and so on; thus it is ‘Dhamma-and-Discipline.’ And this too has been said:

“Daṇḍeneke damayanti, aṅkusehi kasāhi ca;

Adaṇḍena asatthena, nāgo danto mahesinā”ti. (cūḷava. 342; ma. ni. 2.352);

Some tame with the rod, with goads, and with whips; but the great being was tamed by the Great Seer without a rod, without a weapon.

Tathā [V 0.0116] –

Likewise:

“Dhammena nīyamānānaṃ, kā usūyā vijānata”nti. (mahāva. 63);

For those who are guided by the Dhamma, what envy can there be for one who understands?

Dhammāya vā vinayo dhammavinayo. Anavajjadhammatthañhesa vinayo, na bhavabhogāmisatthaṃ. Tenāha bhagavā “nayidaṃ, bhikkhave, brahmacariyaṃ vussati janakuhanattha”nti [P 1.0147] (a. ni. 4.25) vitthāro. Puṇṇattheropi āha “anupādāparinibbānatthaṃ kho, āvuso, bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.259). Visiṭṭhaṃ vā nayatīti vinayo. Dhammato vinayo dhammavinayo. Saṃsāradhammato hi sokādidhammato vā esa visiṭṭhaṃ nibbānaṃ nayati. Dhammassa vā vinayo, na titthakarānanti dhammavinayo. Dhammabhūto hi bhagavā, tasseva vinayo.

Or, the Discipline is for the sake of the Dhamma; hence, Dhamma-and-Discipline. This Discipline is for the sake of the blameless goal, not for the sake of existence, enjoyment, and material gain. Therefore, the Blessed One said in detail: 'Monks, this holy life is not lived for the sake of deceiving people…' (AN 4.25). The Elder Puṇṇa also said: 'Friend, the holy life is lived under the Blessed One for the sake of final Nibbāna without clinging' (MN 24). Or, because it leads in a special way, it is the Discipline. The Discipline that comes from the Dhamma is the Dhamma-and-Discipline. For it leads in a special way from the state of saṃsāra, or from the state of sorrow and the like, to Nibbāna. Or it is the Discipline belonging to the Dhamma, not to the sectarians, that is the Dhamma-and-Discipline. For the Blessed One has become Dhamma, and this is his Discipline.

Yasmā vā dhammā eva abhiññeyyā pariññeyyā pahātabbā bhāvetabbā sacchikātabbā ca, tasmā esa dhammesu vinayo, na sattesu na jīvesu cāti dhammavinayo. Sātthasabyañjanatādīhi aññesaṃ vacanato padhānaṃ vacananti pavacanaṃ, pavacanameva pāvacanaṃ. Sabbacariyāhi visiṭṭhacariyabhāvena brahmacariyaṃ. Devamanussānaṃ satthubhūtassa bhagavato sāsananti satthusāsanaṃ. Satthubhūtaṃ vā sāsanantipi satthusāsanaṃ. “So vo mamaccayena satthāti (dī. ni. 2.216) hi dhammavinayova satthā”ti vuttoti evametesaṃ padānaṃ attho veditabbo.

Or, since it is precisely states that are to be directly known, fully understood, abandoned, developed, and realized, this is a discipline in regard to states, not in regard to beings or souls; hence, 'Dhamma-and-Discipline.' Because it is the principal speech that leads others by being complete in meaning and phrasing, it is 'the Teaching' (pavacanaṃ); the word pavacanaṃ is also written pāvacanaṃ. Because it is the superior conduct among all kinds of conduct, it is 'the holy life.' It is the dispensation of the Blessed One, who has become the teacher of gods and humans, thus 'the Teacher’s Dispensation.' Or, it is the dispensation that has become the teacher, thus also 'the Teacher’s Dispensation.' For it is said: 'That will be your teacher after my passing,' and here the Dhamma-and-Discipline itself is said to be the teacher. Thus the meaning of these terms should be understood.

Yasmā pana imasmiṃyeva sāsane sabbappakārajjhānanibbattako bhikkhu dissati, na aññatra, tasmā tattha tattha “imissā”ti ca “imasmi”nti ca ayaṃ niyamo katoti veditabbo.

But since in this very dispensation a bhikkhu who brings forth all kinds of jhānas is seen, and not elsewhere, therefore it should be understood that this specific determination 'of this' and 'in this' is made in various places.

Jīvanti [M 0.0128] tena taṃsampayuttakā dhammāti jīvitaṃ. Anupālanalakkhaṇe indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti indriyaṃ. Jīvitameva indriyaṃ jīvitindriyaṃ. Taṃ pavattasantatādhipateyyaṃ hoti. Lakkhaṇādīhi pana attanā avinibhuttānaṃ dhammānaṃ anupālanalakkhaṇaṃ jīvitindriyaṃ, tesaṃ pavattanarasaṃ, tesaṃyeva ṭhapanapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, yāpayitabbadhammapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Santepi ca anupālanalakkhaṇādimhi vidhāne atthikkhaṇeyeva taṃ te dhamme anupāleti, udakaṃ viya uppalādīni. Yathāsakaṃ paccayehi uppannepi ca dhamme pāleti, dhāti viya kumāraṃ, sayaṃpavattitadhammasambandheneva [P 1.0148] ca pavattati, niyāmako viya nāvaṃ. Na bhaṅgato uddhaṃ pavattayati, attano ca pavattayitabbānañca abhāvā. Na bhaṅgakkhaṇe ṭhapeti, sayaṃ bhijjamānattā, khīyamāno viya vaṭṭisineho padīpasikhaṃ, na ca anupālanapavattanaṭṭhapanānubhāvavirahitaṃ[V 0.0117], yathāvuttakkhaṇe tassa tassa sādhanatoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ṭhitiparittatāya vāti ṭhitikkhaṇassa mandatāya thokatāya. Appakanti mandaṃ lāmakaṃ. Sarasaparittatāya vāti attano paccayabhūtānaṃ kiccānaṃ sampattīnaṃ vā appatāya dubbalatāya.

Associated states live by means of it; therefore, it is 'life.' It exercises sovereignty in the sense of maintaining, hence it is a 'faculty.' Life itself is a faculty; it is the life faculty. It has sovereignty over the continuity of occurrence. However, with respect to its characteristics, etc., the life faculty has the characteristic of maintaining those states that are inseparable from it; its function is to make them occur; its manifestation is the establishing of those very states; and its proximate cause is the states that are to be sustained. And although it has the characteristic of maintaining, etc., it maintains those states only at the moment of their presence, like water maintains lotuses and the like. And it protects the states that have arisen by their respective conditions, like a nurse protects a child; and it proceeds only in connection with the states that have arisen by themselves, like a helmsman steers a boat. It does not proceed beyond dissolution, due to the absence of itself and of those that are to be made to proceed. It does not establish at the moment of dissolution, because it itself is breaking up, like the oil in the wick being consumed does not establish the lamp’s flame. And it should be seen that it is not devoid of the power to maintain, make proceed, and establish, since it accomplishes each of these at its respective moment as stated. Or, due to the briefness of its duration—that is, due to the weakness or briefness of the moment of presence—it is slight, feeble, and inferior. Or, due to the paucity of its own essence—that is, due to the deficiency and weakness in the accomplishment of the functions of its own conditions—it is weak and inadequate.

Tesaṃ dvinnaṃ kāraṇaṃ vibhāgato dassetuṃ “kathaṃ ṭhitiparittatāyā”tiādimāha. Tattha “atīte cittakkhaṇe jīvitthāti evamādi pañcavokārabhave pavattiyaṃ cittassa nirujjhanakāle sabbasmiṃ rūpārūpadhamme anirujjhantepi rūpato arūpassa paṭṭhānabhāvena arūpajīvitaṃ sandhāya, cuticittena vā saddhiṃ sabbesaṃ rūpārūpānaṃ nirujjhanabhāvena pañcavokārabhave cuticittaṃ sandhāya, catuvokārabhave rūpassa abhāvena catuvokārabhavaṃ sandhāya kathita”nti veditabbaṃ. Atīte cittakkhaṇeti atītacittassa bhaṅgakkhaṇasamaṅgīkāle taṃsamaṅgīpuggalo “jīvittha” iti vattuṃ labbhati. Na jīvatīti “jīvatī”tipi vattuṃ na labbhati. Na jīvissatīti “jīvissatī”tipi vattuṃ na labbhati. Anāgate cittakkhaṇe jīvissatīti anāgatacittassa anuppajjanakkhaṇasamaṅgīkāle “jīvissatī”ti vattuṃ labbhati. Na jīvatīti “jīvatī”ti vattuṃ na labbhati. Na jīvitthāti “jīvittha”itipi vattuṃ na labbhati. Paccuppanne cittakkhaṇeti paccuppannacittakkhaṇasamaṅgīkāle. Jīvatīti “idāni jīvatī”ti vattuṃ labbhati. Na jīvitthāti “jīvittha”iti vattuṃ na labbhati. Na jīvissatīti “jīvissatī”tipi vattuṃ na labbhati.

To show the distinction between these two reasons, the text begins, 'How is it brief in duration?' Herein, it should be understood that the passage beginning 'in a past mind-moment, one lived' is spoken with reference to several cases: with reference to the five-constituent existence during the course of becoming, where, at the time of a mind-moment's cessation, even though not all material and immaterial states cease, the statement is made with reference to the immaterial life faculty due to its being a condition in relation to the material; or with reference to the death-consciousness in the five-constituent existence, because all material and immaterial states cease along with it; or with reference to the four-constituent existence, due to the absence of materiality there. 'In a past mind-moment' means: at the time one is endowed with the dissolution-moment of a past consciousness, it is possible to say of the person endowed with that moment, 'he lived.' It is not possible to say 'he lives,' nor is it possible to say 'he will live.' 'In a future mind-moment, he will live' means: at the time one is endowed with the moment of non-arising of a future consciousness, it is possible to say 'he will live.' It is not possible to say 'he lives,' nor is it possible to say 'he lived.' 'In the present mind-moment' means: at the time one is endowed with the present mind-moment. It is possible to say 'now he lives.' It is not possible to say 'he lived,' nor is it possible to say 'he will live.'

Jīvitaṃ [M 0.0129] attabhāvo ca sukhadukkhā cāti ayaṃ gāthā pañcavokārabhavaṃ amuñcitvā labbhamānāya dukkhāya vedanāya gahitattā [P 1.0149] pañcavokārabhavameva sandhāya vuttāti veditabbā. Kathaṃ? Jīvitanti jīvitasīsena saṅkhārakkhandho. Attabhāvoti rūpakkhandho. “Upekkhā pana santattā, sukhamicceva bhāsitā”ti (vibha. aṭṭha. 232) vuttattā upekkhāvedanā antokaritvā sukhadukkhā cāti vedanākkhandho, cittaṃ iti viññāṇakkhandho vutto. Imesaṃ catunnaṃ khandhānaṃ kathitattāyeva khandhalakkhaṇena ekalakkhaṇabhāvena lakkhaṇākāravasena saññākkhandhopi kathitoti veditabbo. Evaṃ vuttesu pañcasu khandhesu arūpadhammaṃ muñcitvā kammasamuṭṭhānādirūpassa appavattanabhāvena ekacittasamāyuttāti arūpapadhānabhāvo kathito hoti. Kathaṃ? Asaññasatte rūpampi idhupacitakammabalaṃ amuñcitvāva pavattati, nirodhasamāpannānaṃ rūpampi paṭhamasamāpannasamāpattibalaṃ amuñcitvāva pavattati. Evaṃ attano appavattiṭṭhānepi rūpapavattiṃ attano santakameva katvā pavattanasabhāvassa arūpadhammassa attano pavattiṭṭhāne rūpapavattiyā padhānakāraṇabhāvena ekacittasamāyuttāti cittapadhānabhāvo kathitoti veditabbo.

This verse—'Life and individual existence, and pleasure and pain'—should be understood as spoken in reference to the five-constituent existence, because it is taken in terms of the painful feeling that is obtained without abandoning the five-constituent existence. How so? 'Life' is the aggregate of formations, with life as its head. 'Individual existence' is the aggregate of form. Since it is said, 'Equanimity, being tranquil, is spoken of as pleasure,' by including equanimous feeling, 'pleasure and pain' is the aggregate of feeling; 'mind' is said to be the aggregate of consciousness. Because these four aggregates have been stated, it should be understood that the aggregate of perception is also stated by way of its characteristic mode, as having a single characteristic in common with them. Thus, when these five aggregates are spoken of, because form originating from kamma and so on does not occur apart from formless phenomena, the state of being 'conjoined with a single mind' is said to have formless phenomena as primary. How so? For non-percipient beings, form occurs only by not abandoning the power of kamma accumulated here. For those who have attained cessation, form also occurs only by not abandoning the power of the attainment of the first jhāna. Thus, it should be understood that the primacy of mind is stated by the phrase 'conjoined with a single mind,' because the formless phenomenon—which has the nature of causing occurrence—makes the occurrence of form its own even in a state of its own non-occurrence, and is the primary cause for the occurrence of form in its own sphere of occurrence.

Evaṃ [V 0.0118] pañcavokārabhave pavattiyaṃ rūpapavattiyā padhānabhūtacittanirodhena rūpe dharamāneyeva pavattānaṃ nirodho nāma hotīti arūpadhammavasena eva “lahuso vattate khaṇo”ti vuttaṃ. Atha vā pañcavokārabhave cuticittaṃ sandhāya kathitāti veditabbā. Evaṃ kathiyamāne sukhadukkhā cāti kāyikacetasikasukhavedanā ca kāyikacetasikadukkhavedanā ca cuticittakkhaṇe ahontīpi ekasantativasena cuticittena saddhiṃ nirujjhatīti kathitā. Catuvokārabhavaṃ vā sandhāya kathitātipi veditabbā. Kathaṃ[P 1.0150]? Aññasmiṃ ṭhāne attabhāvoti saññākkhandhassa vuttabhāvena attabhāvoti saññākkhandhova gahito. Brahmaloke kāyikasukhadukkhadomanassaṃ ahontampi sukhadukkhā cāti vedanāsāmaññato labbhamāno vedanākkhandho gahitoti veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ vuttasadisameva. Imesu ca tīsu vikappesu kevalāti dhuvasukhasubhaattā natthi, kevalaṃ tehi avomissā. Lahuso vattati khaṇoti vuttanayena ekacittakkhaṇikatāya lahuko atiparitto jīvitādīnaṃ khaṇo vattati.

Thus, in the five-constituent existence, since the cessation of what is occurring takes place while form is still present through the cessation of the mind that is primary for the occurrence of form, it is said, 'The moment passes quickly,' by way of the formless phenomena. Alternatively, it should be understood as spoken in reference to the death-consciousness in the five-constituent existence. When explained thus, 'pleasure and pain'—that is, bodily and mental pleasant feeling and bodily and mental painful feeling—are said to cease along with the death-consciousness by way of a single continuum, even though they are not present at the moment of the death-consciousness. Or it should be understood as spoken in reference to the four-constituent existence. How? Since in another place 'individual existence' is said to be the aggregate of perception, 'individual existence' is taken as just the aggregate of perception. It should be understood that in the Brahma-world, although bodily pleasure, pain, and displeasure are not present, 'pleasure and pain' is taken as the aggregate of feeling, which is obtained from the generality of feeling. The rest is just as has been said. And in these three alternatives, 'only' means there is no permanent pleasure, beauty, or self; they are merely unmixed with those. By the method stated as 'The moment passes quickly,' the moment of life and so on is fleeting, extremely brief, because of being momentary for a single mind-moment.

Ekato [M 0.0130] dvinnaṃ cittānaṃ appavattiṃ dassento “cullāsītisahassānī”ti gāthamāha. Cullāsītisahassāni, kappā tiṭṭhanti ye marūti ye devagaṇā caturāsīti kappasahassāni āyuṃ gahetvā nevasaññānāsaññāyatane tiṭṭhanti. “Ye narā”tipi pāḷi. Na tveva tepi jīvanti, dvīhi cittasamohitāti tepi devā dvīhi cittehi samohitā ekato hutvā yuganaddhena cittena na tu eva jīvanti, ekenekena cittena jīvantīti attho.

To show the non-occurrence of two minds at once, he states the verse beginning, 'Eighty-four thousand.' 'Eighty-four thousand aeons they remain, those Maruts': this means those hosts of devas who, having taken a lifespan of eighty-four thousand aeons, abide in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. 'Those men' is also a textual reading. 'Yet even they do not live, conjoined with two minds': those devas, being conjoined with two minds, do not live with a mind yoked together as one. The meaning is: they live with one mind at a time.

Idāni maraṇakālaṃ dassento “ye niruddhā”ti gāthamāha. Tattha ye niruddhāti ye khandhā niruddhā atthaṅgatā. Marantassāti matassa. Tiṭṭhamānassa vāti dharamānassa vā. Sabbepi sadisā khandhāti cutito uddhaṃ niruddhakkhandhā vā pavatte niruddhakkhandhā vā puna ghaṭetuṃ asakkuṇeyyaṭṭhena sabbepi khandhā sadisā. Gatā appaṭisandhikāti niruddhakkhandhānaṃ puna āgantvā paṭisandhānābhāvena gatā appaṭisandhikāti vuccanti.

Now, showing the time of death, he states the verse beginning, 'Those that have ceased.' Herein, 'those that have ceased' means those aggregates that have ceased, passed away. 'Of the dying' means of the dead. 'Or of one standing' means of one who is still living. 'All aggregates are alike': all aggregates are alike in the sense that they cannot be put together again, whether they are the aggregates that have ceased after death or the aggregates that have ceased during the continuity of life. 'Gone without relinking': because the ceased aggregates do not come back again for relinking, they are called 'gone without relinking.'

Idāni tīsu kālesu niruddhakkhandhānaṃ nānattaṃ natthīti dassetuṃ “anantarā”ti gāthamāha. Tattha anantarā ca ye bhaggā, ye ca bhaggā anāgatāti ye khandhā anantarātītā hutvā [P 1.0151] bhinnā niruddhā, ye ca anāgatā khandhā bhijjissanti. Tadantareti tesaṃ antare niruddhānaṃ paccuppannakhandhānaṃ. Vesamaṃ natthi lakkhaṇeti visamassa bhāvo vesamaṃ, taṃ vesamaṃ natthi, tehi nānattaṃ natthīti attho. Lakkhīyatīti lakkhaṇaṃ, tasmiṃ lakkhaṇe.

Now, to show that there is no difference among the ceased aggregates in the three times, he states the verse beginning, 'Immediately.' Herein, 'those that have broken immediately, and those that will break in the future' means those aggregates that, having just passed, are broken and ceased, and those future aggregates that will break. 'In between them' refers to the present aggregates that have ceased in the interval between them. 'There is no unevenness in characteristic': 'unevenness' (vesamaṃ) is the state of being uneven (visamassa bhāvo); that unevenness is absent. The meaning is: there is no difference among them. 'Characteristic' (lakkhaṇa) is that which is characterized (lakkhīyati); in that characteristic.

Idāni [V 0.0119] anāgatakkhandhānaṃ vattamānakkhandhehi asammissabhāvaṃ kathento “anibbattena na jāto”ti gāthamāha. Anibbattena na jātoti ajātena apātubhūtena anāgatakkhandhena na jāto na nibbatto. Etena anāgatakkhandhassa vattamānakkhandhena asammissabhāvaṃ kathesi. Paccuppannena jīvatīti khaṇapaccuppannena vattamānakkhandhena jīvati. Etena ekakkhaṇe dvīhi cittehi na jīvatīti kathitaṃ. Cittabhaggā matoti dvīhi cittehi ekakkhaṇe ajīvanabhāvena cittabhaṅgena mato. “Uparito cittabhaṅgā”tipi pāḷi, taṃ ujukameva. Paññatti paramatthiyāti “rūpaṃ jīrati maccānaṃ, nāmagottaṃ na jīratī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.76) vacanakkamena paṇṇattimattaṃ na jīraṇasabhāvena paramā ṭhiti etissāti paramatthiyā, sabhāvaṭṭhitikāti attho. “Datto [M 0.0131] mato, mitto mato”ti paṇṇattimattameva hi tiṭṭhati. Atha vā paramatthiyāti paramatthikā. Paramo attho etissāti paramatthikā. Ajaṭākāsoti paññattiyā natthidhammaṃ paṭicca kathanaṃ viya matoti paññatti natthidhammaṃ paṭicca na kathiyati, jīvitindriyabhaṅgasaṅkhātaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca kathiyati.

Now, explaining the unmixed nature of future aggregates with present aggregates, he states the verse beginning, 'Not born of the unproduced.' 'Not born of the unproduced' means not born, not produced by the future aggregate, which is unborn and unmanifest. By this he has explained the unmixed nature of the future aggregate with the present aggregate. 'He lives by the present' means he lives by the present aggregate in the present moment. By this it is said that one does not live by two minds in a single moment. 'Dead by the breaking of mind' means one is dead by the breaking of the mind because of not living with two minds in a single moment. 'From the breaking of mind onwards' is also a textual reading; that is straightforward. 'Concept is ultimate': in accordance with the statement, 'The form of mortals decays, but their name and clan does not decay,' a mere concept has ultimate stability because it does not have a nature of decaying; this is the meaning of 'ultimate' (paramatthiyā), having stability in its own nature. For 'Datta is dead, Mitta is dead' is a mere concept that remains. Alternatively, 'ultimate' (paramatthiyā) means 'of ultimate meaning' (paramatthikā), because it has the highest meaning. Unlike a concept such as 'unentangled space,' which is spoken of in dependence on a non-existent thing, the concept 'dead' is not spoken of in dependence on a non-existent thing, but in dependence on the phenomenon called the breaking of the life faculty.

Anidhānagatā [P 1.0152] bhaggāti ye khandhā bhinnā, te nidhānaṃ nihitaṃ nicayaṃ na gacchantīti anidhānagatā. Puñjo natthi anāgateti anāgatepi nesaṃ puñjabhāvo rāsibhāvo natthi. Nibbattāyeva tiṭṭhantīti paccuppannavasena uppannā ṭhitikkhaṇe vayadhammāva hutvā tiṭṭhanti. Kimiva? Āragge sāsapūpamāti sūcimukhe sāsapo viya.

'Broken, they do not go to a store': those aggregates that are broken do not go to a store, a deposit, an accumulation; thus they are 'those that do not go to a store.' 'There is no heap in the future': even in the future, there is no state of being a heap or a mass for them. 'They exist only as produced': having arisen in the present, they exist at the moment of duration only as being of a nature to vanish. Like what? 'Like a mustard seed on an awl-point': that is, like a mustard seed on the point of a needle.

Idāni khandhānaṃ dassanabhāvaṃ dassento “nibbattāna”nti gāthamāha. Tattha nibbattānaṃ dhammānanti paccuppannānaṃ khandhānaṃ. Bhaṅgo nesaṃ purakkhatoti etesaṃ bhedo purato katvā ṭhapito. Palokadhammāti nassanasabhāvā. Purāṇehi adhissitāti pure uppannehi khandhehi na missitā na saṃsaggā.

Now, showing the visible nature of the aggregates, he states the verse beginning, 'Of the produced.' Herein, 'of produced phenomena' means of the present aggregates. 'Their breaking is set before them': their dissolution is placed before them. 'Of a nature to crumble': of a nature to perish. 'Not dependent on the old': not mixed, not associated with previously arisen aggregates.

Idāni khandhānaṃ adassanabhāvaṃ dassento “adassanato āyantī”ti gāthamāha. Tattha adassanato āyantīti adissamānāyeva āgacchanti uppajjanti. Bhaṅgā gacchantidassananti bhedā bhaṅgato uddhaṃ adassanabhāvaṃ gacchanti. Vijjuppādova ākāseti vivaṭākāse vijjulatāniccharaṇaṃ viya. Uppajjanti vayanti cāti pubbantato uddhaṃ uppajjanti ca bhijjanti ca, nassantīti attho. “Udeti āpūrati veti cando”ti (jā. 1.5.3) evamādīsu viya.

Now, showing the invisible nature of the aggregates, he states the verse beginning, 'They come from the unseen.' Herein, 'they come from the unseen' means they come, they arise, while being unseen. 'Having broken, they go to the unseen': after dissolution, they go to a state of being unseen. 'Like the arising of lightning in the sky': like the flashing of a streak of lightning in the open sky. 'They arise and pass away': from the prior end onwards, they arise and break up; they perish, this is the meaning. As in such phrases as 'The moon rises, waxes full, and wanes.'

Evaṃ [V 0.0120] ṭhitiparittataṃ dassetvā idāni sarasaparittataṃ dassento “kathaṃ sarasaparittatāyā”tiādimāha. Tattha assāsūpanibandhaṃ jīvitanti abbhantarapavisananāsikavātapaṭibaddhaṃ jīvitindriyaṃ. Passāsoti bahinikkhamananāsikavāto. Assāsapassāsoti tadubhayaṃ. Mahābhūtūpanibandhanti catusamuṭṭhānikānaṃ pathavīāpatejavāyānaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ paṭibaddhaṃ jīvitaṃ. Kabaḷīkārāhārūpanibandhanti asitapītādikabaḷīkāraāhārena upanibandhaṃ. Usmūpanibandhanti [P 1.0153] kammajatejodhātūpanibandhaṃ. Viññāṇūpanibandhanti bhavaṅgaviññāṇūpanibandhaṃ. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “āyu usmā ca viññāṇaṃ, yadā kāyaṃ jahantima”nti (saṃ. ni. 3.95).

Having thus shown the brevity of their duration, now showing the brevity of their substance, he says, 'How by the brevity of substance?' and so on. Herein, 'life bound to the in-breaths' means the life faculty connected to the wind of the nostrils that enters within. 'Out-breath' is the wind of the nostrils that goes out. 'In-breath and out-breath' is both of them. 'Bound to the great elements' is life bound to the great elements of earth, water, fire, and air, which arise from four causes. 'Bound to physical nutriment' is that which is bound up with physical nutriment such as what is eaten and drunk. 'Bound to heat' is that which is bound up with the heat element born of kamma. 'Bound to consciousness' is that which is bound up with the life-continuum consciousness. In reference to this it is said: 'When life, heat, and consciousness abandon this body.'

Idāni [M 0.0132] nesaṃ dubbalakāraṇaṃ dassento “mūlampi imesaṃ dubbala”ntiādimāha. Tattha mūlampīti patiṭṭhaṭṭhena mūlabhūtampi. Assāsapassāsānañhi karajakāyo mūlaṃ. Mahābhūtādīnaṃ avijjākammataṇhāhārā. Imesanti vuttappakārānaṃ assāsādīnaṃ jīvitindriyapavattikāraṇavasena vuttānaṃ. Etesu hi ekekasmiṃ asati jīvitindriyaṃ na tiṭṭhati. Dubbalanti appathāmaṃ. Pubbahetūpīti atītajātiyaṃ imassa vipākavaṭṭassa hetubhūtā kāraṇasaṅkhātā avijjāsaṅkhārataṇhupādānabhavāpi. Imesaṃ dubbalā ye paccayā tepi dubbalāti ye ārammaṇādisādhāraṇapaccayā. Pabhāvikāti padhānaṃ hutvā uppādikā bhavataṇhā. Sahabhūmīti sahabhavikāpi rūpārūpadhammā. Sampayogāpīti ekato yuttāpi arūpadhammā. Sahajāpīti saddhiṃ ekacitte uppannāpi. Yāpi payojikāti cutipaṭisandhivasena yojetuṃ niyuttāti payojikā, vaṭṭamūlakā taṇhā. Vuttañhetaṃ “taṇhādutiyo puriso”ti (itivu. 15, 105). Niccadubbalāti nirantarena dubbalā. Anavaṭṭhitāti na avaṭṭhitā, otaritvā na ṭhitā. Paripātayanti imeti ime aññamaññaṃ pātayanti khepayanti. Aññamaññassāti añño aññassa, eko ekassāti attho. Hi-iti kāraṇatthe nipāto. Natthi tāyitāti tāyano rakkhako natthi. Na cāpi ṭhapenti aññamaññanti aññe aññaṃ ṭhapetuṃ na sakkonti. Yopi [P 1.0154] nibbattako so na vijjatīti yopi imesaṃ uppādako dhammo, so idāni natthi.

Now, to show their weak cause, he says, “even their root is weak,” etc. Herein, “even their root” means that which is the root in the sense of a foundation. For the in-and-out breaths, the body produced by kamma is the root. For the great elements and so on, the roots are ignorance, kamma, craving, and nutriment. “These”—referring to the aforementioned in-and-out breaths, etc.—are said to be the causes for the functioning of the life faculty. For if even one of these is absent, the life faculty does not persist. “Weak” means lacking strength. “Past causes too”—the ignorance, formations, craving, clinging, and becoming that were causes in a past life for this resultant round, are also weak. “Their conditions are weak too”—the common conditions such as objects, etc. “The generative force”—the craving for existence, which arises as the predominant producer. “Coexistent”—the material and immaterial phenomena that arise together. “Associated too”—the immaterial phenomena connected together. “Co-nascent too”—those that arise simultaneously in the same mind. “And what is the yoker”—that which is appointed to connect through death and rebirth, the craving that is the root of the round. For it is said: “A person with craving as a second” (Iti 1.15). “Always weak”—continuously weak. “Unstable”—not steady, not remaining after descending. “They destroy each other”—they cause each other to fall, to perish. “Each other”—one destroys another, meaning one destroys the other. “For”—this is a particle indicating reason. “There is no protector”—no protector or defender. “Nor can they sustain each other”—they cannot uphold one another. “And their producer does not exist”—that is, the phenomenon that produces them does not exist now.

Na ca kenaci koci hāyatīti koci ekopi kassaci vasena na parihāyati. Gandhabbā ca ime hi sabbasoti sabbe hi ime khandhā sabbākārena bhaṅgaṃ pāpuṇituṃ yuttā. Purimehi pabhāvitā imeti pubbahetupaccayehi ime vattamānakā uppādikā. Yepi pabhāvikāti yepi ime vattamānakā uppādakā pubbahetupaccayā. Te pure matāti te vuttappakārapaccayā vattamānaṃ apāpuṇitvā paṭhamameva maraṇaṃ pattā. Purimāpi ca pacchimāpi cāti purimā pubbahetupaccayāpi [V 0.0121] ca pacchimā vattamāne paccayasamuppannā ca. Aññamaññaṃ na kadāci maddasaṃsūti aññamaññaṃ kismiñci kāle na diṭṭhapubbā. Ma-kāro padasandhivasena vutto.

“No one is diminished by anyone else,” meaning not a single one declines on account of anyone else. “And these aggregates”—indeed, all of them—are fit to completely disintegrate in every way. “These are produced by previous causes,” meaning these present phenomena are producers due to past causes and conditions. “And those that are generative,” meaning these present producers are also due to prior causes and conditions. “They died before,” meaning those aforesaid conditions, not reaching the present, met their death first. “Both the former and the latter,” meaning the former, past causes and conditions, and the latter, phenomena dependently arisen in the present. “They never saw each other,” meaning they had never seen each other at any time. The syllable “ma” is used for the sake of euphonic combination.

Cātumahārājikānaṃ devānanti dhataraṭṭhavirūḷhakavirūpakkhakuverasaṅkhātā catumahārājā issarā etesanti cātumahārājikā. Rūpādīhi dibbanti kīḷantīti [M 0.0133] devā. Te sinerupabbatassa vemajjhe honti. Tesu atthi pabbataṭṭhakāpi, atthi ākāsaṭṭhakāpi. Tesaṃ paramparā cakkavāḷapabbataṃ pattā. Khiḍḍāpadosikā manopadosikā sītavalāhakā uṇhavalāhakā candimā devaputto sūriyo devaputtoti ete sabbepi cātumahārājikadevalokaṭṭhā eva tesaṃ cātumahārājikānaṃ jīvitaṃ. Upādāyāti paṭicca. Parittakanti vuddhipaṭisedho. Thokanti mandakālaṃ, dīghadivasapaṭisedho. Khaṇikanti mandakālaṃ, kālantarapaṭisedho. Lahukanti sallahukaṃ, alasapaṭisedho. Itaranti sīghabalavapaṭisedho[P 1.0155]. Anaddhanīyanti kālavasena na addhānakkhamaṃ. Naciraṭṭhitikanti divasena ciraṃ na tiṭṭhatīti naciraṭṭhitikaṃ, divasapaṭisedho.

“The devas of the Four Great Kings”: these are the four great kings known as Dhataraṭṭha, Virūḷhaka, Virūpakkha, and Kuvera, who are lords over them; hence, they are called the devas of the Four Great Kings. They are called devas because they play (`dibbanti`) and enjoy divine things such as forms. They dwell in the middle of Mount Sineru. Among them, some dwell on mountain surfaces, while others dwell in the sky. Their successive ranks extend to the Cakkavāḷa mountain. The Khiḍḍāpadosikā, Manopadosikā, Sītavalāhakā, Uṇhavalāhakā, the moon-deva Candimā, and the sun-deva Sūriya—all these abide in the world of the Four Great Kings. “Dependent on” (`upādāya`) means on account of (`paṭicca`). “Trifling” (`parittaka`) is a negation of increase. “Short” (`thoka`) means a short time, a negation of a long day. “Momentary” (`khaṇika`) means a short time, a negation of a long duration. “Quick” (`lahuka`) means light, a negation of laziness. “Insignificant” (`itara`) is a negation of swift and strong. “Not long-lasting” (`anaddhanīya`) means not capable of lasting for a long time. “Not of long duration” (`naciraṭṭhitika`) means not lasting long for a day, a negation of a day.

Tāvatiṃsānanti tettiṃsajanā tattha upapannāti tāvatiṃsā. Api ca tāvatiṃsāti tesaṃ devānaṃ nāmamevātipi vuttaṃ. Tepi atthi pabbataṭṭhakā, atthi ākāsaṭṭhakā, tesaṃ paramparā cakkavāḷapabbataṃ pattā. Tathā yāmādīnaṃ. Ekadevalokepi hi devānaṃ paramparā cakkavāḷapabbataṃ appattā nāma natthi. Dibbasukhaṃ yātā payātā sampattāti yāmā. Tuṭṭhā pahaṭṭhāti tusitā. Pakatipaṭiyattārammaṇato atirekena nimmitukāmakāle yathārucite bhoge nimminitvā ramantīti nimmānaratī. Cittācāraṃ ñatvā parehi nimmitesu bhogesu vasaṃ vattentīti paranimmitavasavattī. Brahmakāye brahmaghaṭāya niyuttāti brahmakāyikā. Sabbepi pañcavokārabrahmāno gahitā.

“The Tāvatiṃsa devas”: they are called Tāvatiṃsa because thirty-three (`tettiṃsa`) beings were reborn there. Moreover, it is said that “Tāvatiṃsa” is simply the name of those devas. Some of them dwell on mountains, some in the sky, and their successive ranks extend up to the Cakkavāḷa mountain. The same applies to the Yāma devas and the others. Indeed, in any one deva-world there are no devas whose successive ranks do not reach the Cakkavāḷa mountain. “Yāmā” means those who have gone (`yātā`), fared to (`payātā`), and attained (`sampattā`) divine bliss. “Tusitā” means those who are pleased (`tuṭṭhā`) and delighted (`pahaṭṭhā`). “Nimmānaratī” refers to those who, when desiring to create pleasures exceeding those naturally provided, create enjoyments according to their liking and delight in them. “Paranimmitavasavattī” means those who, knowing the minds of others, wield power over the enjoyments created by those others. “Brahmakāyikā” are those belonging to the Brahmā group, assigned to the Brahmā-assembly. All Brahmās of the five-constituent existence are included.

Gamaniyoti gandhabbo. Samparāyoti paraloko. Yo bhikkhave ciraṃ jīvati, so vassasatanti yo ciraṃ tiṭṭhamāno, so vassasatamattaṃ tiṭṭhati. Appaṃ vā bhiyyoti vassasatato upari tiṭṭhamāno dve vassasatāni tiṭṭhamāno nāma natthi. Hīḷeyya nanti naṃ jīvitaṃ avaññātaṃ kareyya, lāmakato cinteyya. “Hīḷeyyāna”nti ca paṭhanti. Accayantīti atikkamanti. Ahorattāti rattindivaparicchedā. Uparujjhatīti jīvitindriyaṃ nirujjhati, abhāvaṃ upagacchati. Āyu khiyyati maccānanti sattānaṃ āyusaṅkhāro khayaṃ yāti. Kunnadīnaṃva odakanti yathā udakacchinnāya kunnadiyā udakaṃ, evaṃ maccānaṃ āyu khiyyati. Paramatthato hi atiparitto sattānaṃ jīvitakkhaṇo ekacittakkhaṇikamattoyeva. Yathā nāma rathacakkaṃ pavattamānampi [V 0.0122][M 0.0134] ekeneva nemipadesena pavattati, tiṭṭhamānampi ekeneva tiṭṭhati, evameva ekacittakkhaṇikaṃ sattānaṃ jīvitaṃ [P 1.0156] tasmiṃ citte niruddhamatte satto niruddhoti vuccati.

“Leader” (`gamaniya`) means a celestial musician (`gandhabba`). “The next life” (`samparāya`) means the other world (`paraloko`). “Whoever, bhikkhus, lives long, lives for a hundred years”: one who remains long, remains for about a hundred years. “Or a little more”: there is no one who remains beyond a hundred years who remains for two hundred years. “One should not despise it”: one should not treat that life with contempt, one should not think of it as inferior. Some read “Hīḷeyyāna.” “They pass by”: they pass away. “Days and nights”: the divisions of day and night. “Is interrupted”: the life faculty ceases, it comes to non-existence. “The lifespan of mortals is depleted”: the life-formation of beings goes to destruction. “Like the water of small rivers”: just as the water of a small river with its supply cut off, so the lifespan of mortals is depleted. For in the ultimate sense, the life-moment of beings is extremely short, lasting for just a single moment of consciousness. Just as a rolling chariot wheel rolls on only one point of its rim, and when it is standing still it also stands on only one point, so the life of beings lasts for a single moment of consciousness. When that consciousness has ceased, a being is said to have ceased.

Dhīrāti dhīrā iti. Puna dhīrāti paṇḍitā. Dhitimāti dhiti assa atthīti dhitimā. Dhitisampannāti paṇḍiccena samannāgatā. Dhīkatapāpāti garahitapāpā. Taṃyeva pariyāyaṃ dassetuṃ “dhī vuccati paññā”tiādimāha. Tattha pajānātīti paññā. Kiṃ pajānāti? “Idaṃ dukkha”ntiādinā nayena ariyasaccāni. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “paññāpanavasena paññā”ti vuttā. Kinti paññāpeti? “Aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattā”ti paññāpeti. Sāva avijjāya abhibhavanato adhipatiyaṭṭhena indriyaṃ, dassanalakkhaṇe vā indaṭṭhaṃ kāretītipi indriyaṃ, paññāva indriyaṃ paññindriyaṃ. Sā panesā obhāsanalakkhaṇā, pajānanalakkhaṇā ca; yathā hi catubhittike gehe rattibhāge dīpe jalite andhakāraṃ nirujjhati, āloko pātubhavati, evameva obhāsanalakkhaṇā paññā. Paññobhāsasamo obhāso nāma natthi. Paññavato hi ekapallaṅkena nisinnassa dasasahassilokadhātu ekālokā hoti. Tenāha thero –

“The wise” (`dhīrā`): the wise indeed. Again, “the wise” means the discerning (`paṇḍitā`). “Resolute” (`dhitimā`): one who has resolution (`dhiti`). “Endowed with fortitude” (`dhitisampannā`): possessed of discernment (`paṇḍiccena`). “Those who have censured evil” (`dhīkatapāpā`): those who have censured evil (`garahitapāpā`). To explain this very synonym, he says, “`dhī` is called wisdom (`paññā`),” and so on. Herein, “one understands” (`pajānāti`), therefore it is wisdom (`paññā`). What does one understand? The noble truths in the way beginning with “This is suffering.” But in the commentary, it is said: “Wisdom (`paññā`) is so called because it makes known (`paññāpanavasena`).” How does it make known? It makes known thus: “Impermanent, suffering, non-self.” This wisdom is a faculty (`indriya`) because it overcomes ignorance by exercising sovereignty, or it is a faculty because it exercises lordship in its characteristic of seeing; thus wisdom is a faculty, the faculty of wisdom. Moreover, this has the characteristic of illumination and the characteristic of understanding. Just as in a house with four walls, when a lamp is lit at night, darkness ceases and light appears, so too wisdom has the characteristic of illumination. There is no light equal to the light of wisdom. For one endowed with wisdom, seated in a single cross-legged posture, the ten-thousandfold world system becomes a single radiance. Therefore, the elder said:

“Yathā, mahārāja, puriso andhakāre gehe telappadīpaṃ paveseyya, paviṭṭho padīpo andhakāraṃ viddhaṃseti, obhāsaṃ janeti, ālokaṃ vidaṃseti, pākaṭāni ca rūpāni karoti; evameva kho, mahārāja, paññā uppajjamānā avijjandhakāraṃ viddhaṃseti, vijjobhāsaṃ janeti, ñāṇālokaṃ vidaṃseti, pākaṭāni ariyasaccāni karoti. Evaṃ kho, mahārāja, obhāsanalakkhaṇā paññā”ti (mi. pa. 2.1.15).

“Just as, great king, if a person were to bring an oil lamp into a dark house, the lamp upon entering would dispel the darkness, produce light, spread radiance, and make forms visible; just so, great king, when wisdom arises, it dispels the darkness of ignorance, produces the light of knowledge, spreads the radiance of knowledge, and makes the Noble Truths apparent. Thus, great king, wisdom has the characteristic of illumination.”

Yathā pana cheko bhisakko āturānaṃ sappāyāsappāyāni bhojanādīni jānāti, evaṃ paññā uppajjamānā kusalākusale sevitabbāsevitabbe hīnappaṇītakaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāgaappaṭibhāge dhamme pajānāti. Vuttampi cetaṃ dhammasenāpatinā “pajānāti pajānātīti kho, āvuso, tasmā paññavāti vuccati. Kiñca pajānāti? Idaṃ dukkhanti pajānātī”ti (ma. ni. 1.449) vitthāretabbaṃ. Evamassā pajānanalakkhaṇatā veditabbā.

Just as a skilled physician knows what is suitable and unsuitable in food and so forth for the sick, so too, when wisdom arises, it understands wholesome and unwholesome states, states that should be cultivated and should not be cultivated, inferior and superior states, and dark and bright states with their counterparts. And this was said by the General of the Dhamma: ‘One understands, one understands—thus, friend, one is called a person of wisdom. And what does one understand? One understands: “This is suffering.”’ This should be elaborated. Thus, its characteristic of understanding should be known.

Aparo [P 1.0157][M 0.0135] nayo – yathāsabhāvapaṭivedhalakkhaṇā paññā, akkhalitapaṭivedhalakkhaṇā vā, kusalissāsakhittausupaṭivedho viya. Visayobhāsarasā, padīpo viya. Asammohapaccupaṭṭhānā, araññagatasudesako viya.

Another method: wisdom has the characteristic of penetrating things according to their intrinsic nature, or the characteristic of unerring penetration, like the penetration of an arrow shot by a skilled archer. Its function is to illuminate the object, like a lamp. Its manifestation is non-delusion, like a guide in the wilderness.

Khandhadhīrāti [V 0.0123] pañcasu khandhesuñāṇaṃ pavattentīti khandhadhīrā. Aṭṭhārasasu dhātūsu ñāṇaṃ pavattentīti dhātudhīrā. Sesesupi iminā nayena attho netabbo. Te dhīrā evamāhaṃsūti ete paṇḍitā evaṃ kathayiṃsu. Kathentīti “appakaṃ parittaka”nti kathayanti. Bhaṇantīti “thokaṃ khaṇika”nti bhāsanti. Dīpayantīti “lahukaṃ ittara”nti patiṭṭhapenti. Voharantīti “anaddhanikaṃ naciraṭṭhitika”nti nānāvidhena byavaharanti.

Those wise in the aggregates: they exercise knowledge in regard to the five aggregates; thus they are wise in the aggregates. Those wise in the elements: they exercise knowledge in regard to the eighteen elements; thus they are wise in the elements. The meaning in the remaining cases should be understood in the same way. Those wise ones spoke thus: these learned ones spoke in this way. They speak: they say, ‘It is little, trifling.’ They declare: they state, ‘It is a trifle, momentary.’ They illuminate: they establish, ‘It is insignificant, transient.’ They express: they use various expressions such as, ‘It is not long-lasting, not of long duration.’

11. Idāni ye tathā na karonti, tesaṃ byasanuppattiṃ dassento “passāmī”ti gāthamāha. Tattha passāmīti maṃsacakkhuādīhi pekkhāmi. Loketi apāyādimhi. Pariphandamānanti ito cito ca phandamānaṃ. Pajaṃ imanti imaṃ sattakāyaṃ. Taṇhāgatanti taṇhāya gataṃ abhibhūtaṃ nipātitanti adhippāyo. Bhavesūti kāmabhavādīsu. Hīnā narāti hīnakammantā narā. Maccumukhe lapantīti antakāle sampatte maraṇamukhe paridevanti. Avītataṇhāseti avigatataṇhā. Bhavāti kāmabhavādikā. Bhavesūti kāmabhavādikesu. Atha vā bhavābhavesūti bhavabhavesu, punappunabhavesūti vuttaṃ hoti.

11. Now, to show the arising of misfortune for those who do not act thus, he spoke the verse beginning ‘I see.’ Herein, ‘I see’ means I behold with the fleshly eye and so on. ‘In the world’ means in the plane of misery and so on. ‘Struggling’ means quivering this way and that. ‘This generation’ means this host of beings. ‘Gone to craving’ means gone to craving, overcome and felled by it; this is the intention. ‘In states of existence’ means in the states of sensual existence and so on. ‘Inferior people’ means people of inferior deeds. ‘They wail in the mouth of death’ means they lament in the mouth of death when their time has come. ‘For whom craving has not passed’ means for whom craving has not departed. ‘Existence’ refers to sensual existence and the like. ‘In states of existence’ refers to the states of sensual existence and the like. Or alternatively, ‘in this or that state of existence’ means in repeated existences; so it is said.

Passāmīti maṃsacakkhunāpi passāmīti duvidhaṃ maṃsacakkhu – sasambhāracakkhu pasādacakkhūti. Tattha yoyaṃ akkhikūpake patiṭṭhito heṭṭhā akkhikūpakaṭṭhikena upari bhamukaṭṭhikena ubhato akkhikūṭehi bahiddhā akkhilomehi paricchinno akkhikūpakamajjhā nikkhantena nhārusuttakena matthaluṅge ābaddho setakaṇhamaṇḍalavicitto maṃsapiṇḍo, idaṃ sasambhāracakkhu nāma. Yo pana [P 1.0158] ettha sito ettha paṭibaddho catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ upādāya pasādo, idaṃ pasādacakkhu nāma. Idamadhippetaṃ. Tadetaṃ tassa sasambhāracakkhuno setamaṇḍalaparikkhittassa kaṇhamaṇḍalassa majjhe abhimukhe ṭhitānaṃ sarīrasaṇṭhānuppattipadese diṭṭhamaṇḍale sattasu [M 0.0136] picupaṭalesu āsittatelaṃ picupaṭalāni viya sattakkhipaṭalāni byāpetvā pamāṇato ūkāsiramattaṃ cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ yathārahaṃ vatthudvārabhāvaṃ sādhayamānaṃ tiṭṭhati.

‘I see’ means I see with the fleshly eye: there are two kinds of fleshly eye: the composite eye and the sensitive eye. Herein, that lump of flesh established in the eye socket—bounded below by the bone of the eye socket, above by the bone of the eyebrow, on both sides by the corners of the eye, and externally by the eyelashes, connected to the brain by a sinew-thread that comes out from the middle of the eye socket, variegated with white and black circles—this is called the composite eye. But the sensitivity situated and bound there, which is derived from the four great elements—this is called the sensitive eye. This is what is intended here. This sensitive eye stands in the middle of the black circle, which is surrounded by the white circle of that composite eye, in the pupil, the place where the images of bodily forms appear when they are in front of it. It pervades the seven layers of the eye, like oil that has been sprinkled on seven cotton wicks, and is about the size of a louse’s head. It serves appropriately as the physical basis and door for eye-consciousness and so on.

Taṃ cakkhatīti cakkhu, tena maṃsacakkhunā passāmi. Dibbacakkhunāti “addasaṃ kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, dibbena cakkhunā visuddhenā”ti (ma. ni. 1.284) evaṃvidhena dibbacakkhunā. Paññācakkhunāti “virajaṃ vītamalaṃ dhammacakkhuṃ udapādī”ti (ma. ni. 2.395; mahāva. 16) evaṃ āgatena paññācakkhunā. Buddhacakkhunāti “addasaṃ kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ volokento”ti (ma. ni. 1.283) evamāgatena buddhacakkhunā. Samantacakkhunāti “samantacakkhu vuccati sabbaññutaññāṇa”nti (cūḷani. dhotakamāṇavapucchāiddesa 32; mogharājamāṇavapucchāniddesa 85) evamāgatena [V 0.0124] samantacakkhunā. Passāmīti maṃsacakkhunā hatthatale ṭhapitāmalakaṃ viya rūpagataṃ maṃsacakkhunā. Dakkhāmīti sañjānāmi dibbena cakkhunā cutūpapātaṃ. Olokemīti avalokemi paññācakkhunā catusaccaṃ. Nijjhāyāmīti cintemi buddhacakkhunā saddhāpañcamakāni indriyāni. Upaparikkhāmīti samantato ikkhāmi pariyesāmi samantacakkhunā pañca neyyapathe.

It sees (cakkhati), thus it is the eye (cakkhu); with this fleshly eye, I see. With the divine eye: as in the passage, ‘Bhikkhus, with the divine eye, which is purified… I saw,’ with such a divine eye. With the eye of wisdom: as in the passage, ‘The dust-free, stainless eye of the Dhamma arose,’ with such an eye of wisdom. With the Buddha-eye: as in the passage, ‘Bhikkhus, surveying the world with the Buddha-eye… I saw,’ with such a Buddha-eye. With the all-around eye: as in the passage, ‘The all-around eye is a term for the knowledge of omniscience,’ with such an all-around eye. I see: with the fleshly eye I see a form that has come into range as clearly as an āmalaka fruit placed on the palm of the hand. I behold: with the divine eye I discern the passing away and reappearance of beings. I look upon: with the eye of wisdom I survey the Four Noble Truths. I contemplate: with the Buddha-eye I reflect upon the five faculties headed by faith. I examine: with the all-around eye I investigate all around and search for the five dispositions of those to be guided.

Taṇhāphandanāya phandamānanti taṇhācalanāya calamānaṃ. Ito paraṃ diṭṭhiphandanādidiṭṭhibyasanena dukkhena phandamānapariyosānaṃ vuttanayattā uttānameva. Samphandamānanti punappunaṃ phandamānaṃ. Vipphandamānanti nānāvidhena calamānaṃ. Vedhamānanti kampamānaṃ. Pavedhamānanti padhānena kampamānaṃ. Sampavedhamānanti [P 1.0159] punappunaṃ kampamānaṃ. Upasaggena vā padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ.

‘Struggling with the agitation of craving’ means trembling with the movement of craving. Further, the passage beginning with ‘the struggling of views’ and ending with ‘struggling with the suffering that is the calamity of views’ is clear because of the method already stated. ‘Struggling completely’ means struggling again and again. ‘Struggling in various ways’ means trembling in diverse ways. ‘Quaking’ means trembling. ‘Quaking violently’ means trembling intensely. ‘Quaking repeatedly’ means trembling again and again. Or the word is augmented by a prefix.

Taṇhānugatanti taṇhāya anupaviṭṭhaṃ. Taṇhāyānusaṭanti taṇhāya anupatthaṭaṃ. Taṇhāyāsannanti taṇhāya nimuggaṃ. Taṇhāya pātitanti taṇhāya khittaṃ. “Paripātita”nti vā pāṭho. Abhibhūtanti taṇhāya madditaṃ ajjhotthaṭaṃ. Pariyādinnacittanti khepetvā gahitacittaṃ. Atha vā oghena gataṃ viya taṇhāgataṃ. Upādiṇṇakarūpapaccayehi patitvā gataṃ viya taṇhānugataṃ. Udakapiṭṭhiṃ chādetvā patthaṭanīlikā udakapiṭṭhi viya taṇhānusaṭaṃ. Vaccakūpe nimuggaṃ viya taṇhāyāsannaṃ. Rukkhaggato patitvā narake patitaṃ viya taṇhāpātitaṃ. Upādiṇṇakarūpaṃ saṃyogaṃ viya taṇhāya abhibhūtaṃ. Upādiṇṇakarūpapariggāhakassa uppannavipassanaṃ viya taṇhāya pariyādinnacittaṃ. Atha vā kāmacchandena taṇhāgataṃ. Kāmapipāsāya taṇhānugataṃ. Kāmāsavena [M 0.0137] taṇhānusaṭaṃ. Kāmapariḷāhena taṇhāyāsannaṃ. Kāmajjhosānena taṇhāya pātitaṃ. Kāmoghena taṇhāya abhibhūtaṃ. Kāmupādānena taṇhāya pariyādinnacittanti evameke vaṇṇayanti. Kāmabhaveti kāmāvacare. Rūpabhaveti rūpāvacare. Arūpabhaveti arūpāvacare. Tesaṃ nānattaṃ heṭṭhā pakāsitaṃyeva.

‘Followed by craving’ means entered into by craving. ‘Pervaded by craving’ means spread over by craving. ‘Sunken in craving’ means immersed in craving. ‘Felled by craving’ means cast down by craving. Or the reading is ‘completely felled.’ ‘Overcome’ means crushed and overwhelmed by craving. ‘With mind mastered’ means with the mind seized and exhausted. Or alternatively: ‘gone to craving’ is like being carried away by a flood. ‘Followed by craving’ is like having fallen and gone on account of conditioned things born of clinging. ‘Pervaded by craving’ is like the surface of water covered and spread over with duckweed. ‘Sunken in craving’ is like being immersed in a cesspit. ‘Felled by craving’ is like having fallen from a treetop into hell. ‘Overcome by craving’ is like the fetter of form born of clinging. ‘With mind mastered by craving’ is like the arising of insight for one who is comprehending form born of clinging. Or some explain it thus: one is gone to craving through sensual desire; followed by craving through thirst for sensual pleasures; pervaded by craving through the taint of sensuality; sunken in craving through the fever of sensuality; felled by craving through addiction to sensuality; overcome by craving through the flood of sensuality; with mind mastered by craving through clinging to sensuality. ‘In sensual existence’ means in the sense-sphere realm. ‘In form existence’ means in the form realm. ‘In formless existence’ means in the formless realm. Their diversity has already been explained below.

Bhavābhavesūti bhavābhaveti bhavoti kāmadhātu. Abhavoti rūpārūpadhātu. Atha vā bhavoti kāmadhātu rūpadhātu. Abhavoti arūpadhātu. Tesu bhavābhavesu. Kammabhaveti kammavaṭṭe. Punabbhaveti ponobhavike vipākavaṭṭe. Kāmabhaveti kāmadhātuyā. Kammabhaveti kammavaṭṭe. Tattha kammabhavo bhāvayatīti bhavo. Kāmabhave punabbhaveti kāmadhātuyā upapattibhave vipākavaṭṭe. Vipākabhavo bhavatīti bhavo. Rūpabhavādīsupi eseva nayo. Ettha ca “kāmabhave rūpabhave arūpabhave”ti [V 0.0125] okāsabhavaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tīsupi “kammabhave”ti kammabhavaṃ[P 1.0160], tathā “punabbhave”ti upapattibhavaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Punappunabbhaveti aparāparaṃ uppattiyaṃ. Gatiyāti pañcagatiyā aññatarāya. Attabhāvābhinibbattiyāti attabhāvānaṃ abhinibbattiyā. Avītataṇhāti mūlapadaṃ. Avigatataṇhāti khaṇikasamādhi viya khaṇikappahānābhāvena na vigatā taṇhā etesanti avigatataṇhā. Acattataṇhāti tadaṅgappahānābhāvena apariccattataṇhā. Avantataṇhāti vikkhambhanappahānābhāvena na vantataṇhāti avantataṇhā. Amuttataṇhāti accantasamucchedappahānābhāvena na muttataṇhā. Appahīnataṇhāti paṭippassaddhippahānābhāvena na pahīnataṇhā. Appaṭinissaṭṭhataṇhāti nissaraṇappahānābhāvena bhave patiṭṭhitaṃ anusayakilesaṃ appaṭinissajjitvā ṭhitattā appaṭinissaṭṭhataṇhā.

In this or that state of existence: 'existence' is the sense-sphere realm; 'non-existence' is the form and formless realms. Or, 'existence' is the sense-sphere and form realms; 'non-existence' is the formless realm. In these states of existence. 'In kamma-existence' means in the round of kamma. 'In renewed existence' means in the round of result that generates a new existence. 'In sensual existence' means in the sense-sphere realm. 'In kamma-existence' means in the round of kamma. Therein, kamma-existence makes exist (bhāvayati), thus it is 'existence' (bhavo). 'In renewed existence in sensual existence' means in the rebirth-existence that is the round of result in the sense-sphere realm. Resultant existence comes to be (bhavati), thus it is 'existence' (bhavo). This same method applies to form existence and so on. Here, 'in sensual existence, in form existence, in formless existence' is said with reference to existence as a location (okāsa-bhava). In all three, 'in kamma-existence' is said with reference to kamma-existence, and similarly 'in renewed existence' is said with reference to rebirth-existence. 'In repeated existence' means in one birth after another. 'In a destination' means in any of the five destinations. 'In the generation of an individual existence' means in the generation of individual existences. 'For whom craving has not passed' is the base term. 'With craving not departed': they are those for whom craving has not departed, due to the absence of momentary abandonment. 'With craving not given up': they are those with craving not given up, due to the absence of abandonment by substitution of opposites. 'With craving not vomited': they are those with craving not vomited, due to the absence of abandonment by suppression. 'With craving not released': they are those with craving not released, due to the absence of abandonment by eradication. 'With craving not abandoned': they are those with craving not abandoned, due to the absence of abandonment by tranquillization. 'With craving not relinquished': they are those with craving not relinquished because, due to the absence of abandonment by escape, they stand without having relinquished the underlying defilement established in existence.

12. Idāni yasmā avigatataṇhā evaṃ phandanti ca lapanti ca, tasmā taṇhāvinaye samādapento “mamāyite”ti gāthamāha. Tattha mamāyiteti taṇhādiṭṭhimamattehi “mama”nti pariggahite vatthusmiṃ. Passathāti sotāre ālapanto āha. Etampīti etampi ādīnavaṃ. Sesaṃ pākaṭameva.

12. Now, since those for whom craving has not departed struggle and lament in this way, therefore, in order to get them to undertake the removal of craving, he spoke the verse beginning 'In what is held as mine.' Herein, 'in what is held as mine' means in an object grasped as 'mine' through the 'my-making' of craving and views. 'See': he speaks this addressing the listeners. 'This too' means this danger too. The rest is evident.

Dve mamattāti dve ālayā. Yāvatāti paricchedaniyamatthe nipāto. Taṇhāsaṅkhātenāti taṇhākoṭṭhāsena, saṅkhā saṅkhātanti atthato [M 0.0138] ekaṃ “saññānidānā hi papañcasaṅkhā”tiādīsu (su. ni. 880) viya. Sīmakatanti aparicchedadosavirahitaṃ mariyādakataṃ “tiyojanaparamaṃ sīmaṃ sammannitu”nti ādīsu (mahāva. 140) viya. Odhikatanti vacanaparicchedadosavirahitaṃ paricchedakataṃ [P 1.0161] sīmantarikarukkho viya. Pariyantakatanti paricchedakataṃ. Sīmantarikarukkho pana dvinnaṃ sādhāraṇaṃ, ayaṃ pana ekābaddhatālapanti viya katanti pariyantakataṃ. Pariggahitanti kālantarepi parāyattaṃ muñcitvā sabbākārena gahitaṃ. Mamāyitanti ālayakataṃ vassūpagataṃ senāsanaṃ viya. Idaṃ mamanti samīpe ṭhitaṃ. Etaṃ mamanti dūre ṭhitaṃ. Ettakanti parikkhāraniyamanaṃ “ettakampi nappaṭibhāseyyā”ti viya. Ettāvatāti paricchedatthepi nipātaniyamanaṃ “ettāvatā kho mahānāmā”ti viya. Kevalampi mahāpathavinti sakalampi mahāpathaviṃ.

There are two kinds of possessiveness, meaning two kinds of clinging. "Yāvatā" is a particle indicating limitation of extent. "Taṇhāsaṅkhātena" means by the designation of craving; "saṅkhā" and "saṅkhāta" are one in essence, as in passages like "for conceptual proliferation is rooted in perception" (Snp. 880). "Sīmakatanti" means free from the fault of being unbounded, demarcated, as in "let the boundary be fixed at three leagues" (Mhv. 140). "Odhikatanti" means free from the fault of verbal limitation, defined, like a boundary-marking tree. "Pariyantakatanti" means bounded. A boundary-marking tree, however, is common to both sides, whereas this is made like a single connected row of palmyra trees—thus, it is bounded. "Pariggahita" means grasped in every way, having freed it from being under another's control even at a later time. "Mamāyita" means clung to, like a dwelling used during the rains. "Idaṃ mama" refers to what is near. "Etaṃ mama" refers to what is far. "Ettaka" indicates a limitation of requisites, as in "one should not speak even this much."
