"Ettāvatā" is a particle indicating limitation of extent, as in "thus far, Mahānāma." "Kevalampi mahāpathaviṃ" means the entire great earth.

Aṭṭhasataṃ taṇhāvicaritanti aṭṭhuttarasataṃ taṇhāgamanavitthāraṃ. Aṭṭhuttarasataṃ kathaṃ hotīti ce? Rūpataṇhā…pe… dhammataṇhāti evaṃ cakkhudvārādīsu javanavīthiyā pavattā taṇhā “seṭṭhiputto, brāhmaṇaputto”ti evamādīsu pitito laddhanāmā viya pitusadisārammaṇe bhūtā. Ettha [V 0.0126] ca rūpārammaṇā rūpe taṇhāti rūpataṇhā. Sā kāmarāgabhāvena rūpaṃ assādentī pavattamānā kāmataṇhā. Sassatadiṭṭhisahagatarāgabhāvena “rūpaṃ niccaṃ dhuvaṃ sassata”nti evaṃ assādentī pavattamānā bhavataṇhā. Ucchedadiṭṭhisahagatarāgabhāvena “rūpaṃ ucchijjati vinassati pacchedaṃ bhavissatī”ti evaṃ assādentī pavattamānā vibhavataṇhāti evaṃ tividhā hoti. Yathā ca rūpataṇhā, tathā saddataṇhādayopīti etāni aṭṭhārasa taṇhāvicaritāni honti. Tāni ajjhattarūpādīsu aṭṭhārasa, bahiddhārūpādīsu aṭṭhārasāti chattiṃsa, iti atītāni chattiṃsa, anāgatāni chattiṃsa, paccuppannāni chattiṃsāti aṭṭhasataṃ. Ajjhattikassa upādāya “asmī”ti hoti, “itthasmī”ti hotīti vā evamādīni ajjhattikarūpādinissitāni aṭṭhārasa, bāhirassupādāya iminā “asmī”ti hoti, iminā “itthasmī”ti hotīti bāhirarūpādinissitāni aṭṭhārasāti chattiṃsa. Iti atītāni chattiṃsa, anāgatāni chattiṃsa, paccuppannāni chattiṃsāti evampi aṭṭhasatataṇhāvicaritāni honti.

The craving that wanders in one hundred and eight ways means the detailed course of craving in one hundred and eight. How does it become one hundred and eight? Craving for forms... craving for mental phenomena—thus, the craving that arises in the cognitive process through the eye-door and other doors is like one who has received a name from his father, such as 'the merchant's son' or 'the brahmin's son,' having arisen with an object that is like its progenitor. Here, craving that takes a form as its object is called craving for forms. When it arises savoring forms as sensual lust, it is sensual craving. When it arises savoring forms with the lust accompanied by eternalist views, thinking 'forms are permanent, stable, eternal,' it is craving for existence. When it arises savoring forms with the lust accompanied by annihilationist views, thinking 'forms are annihilated, destroyed, will be cut off,' it is craving for non-existence. Thus, it is threefold. Just as craving for forms, so too craving for sounds and the rest: these make eighteen modes of craving. These eighteen apply to internal forms and so on, and another eighteen to external forms and so on, making thirty-six. Thus, past ones are thirty-six, future ones are thirty-six, and present ones are thirty-six—totaling one hundred and eight. For the internal, clinging gives rise to 'I am,' or 'I am thus'—these are the eighteen dependent on internal forms and so on. For the external, clinging gives rise to 'by this, I am,' or 'by this, I am thus'—these are the eighteen dependent on external forms and so on, making thirty-six. Thus, past ones are thirty-six, future ones are thirty-six, and present ones are thirty-six—in this way too, craving wanders in one hundred and eight ways.

Vīsativatthukā [P 1.0162][M 0.0139] sakkāyadiṭṭhīti rūpādīnaṃ pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ ekekampi “rūpaṃ attato samanupassatī”tiādinā (paṭi. ma. 1.130-131) nayena catudhā gāhavasena pavattāni vatthūni katvā uppannā vijjamānaṭṭhena sati khandhapañcakasaṅkhāte kāye diṭṭhīti sakkāyadiṭṭhi. Dasavatthukā micchādiṭṭhīti “natthi dinnaṃ, natthi yiṭṭha”ntiādinayappavattā micchādiṭṭhi, ayāthāvadiṭṭhi virajjhitvā gahaṇato vā vitathā diṭṭhi micchādiṭṭhi, anatthāvahattā paṇḍitehi kucchitā diṭṭhītipi micchādiṭṭhi. Sā ayoniso abhinivesalakkhaṇā, parāmāsarasā, micchābhinivesapaccupaṭṭhānā, ariyānamadassanakāmatādipadaṭṭhānā, paramavajjāti daṭṭhabbā. Dasavatthukā antaggāhikā diṭṭhīti sassato loko, asassato loko, antavā loko”ti ādinayappavattā ekekaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ patiṭṭhaṃ katvā gahaṇavasena evaṃ pavattā diṭṭhi dasavatthukā antaggāhikā diṭṭhi. Yā evarūpā diṭṭhīti yā evaṃjātikā diṭṭhi. Diṭṭhigatanti diṭṭhīsu gataṃ. Idaṃ dassanaṃ dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhiantogadhattāti diṭṭhigataṃ, diṭṭhiyeva duratikkamanaṭṭhena gahanaṃ diṭṭhigahanaṃ tiṇagahanavanagahanapabbatagahanāni viya. Sāsaṅkasappaṭibhayaṭṭhena diṭṭhikantāraṃ corakantāravāḷakantāranirudakakantāradubbhikkhakantārā viya. Sammādiṭṭhiyā vinivijjhanaṭṭhena vilomanaṭṭhena ca diṭṭhivisūkāyikaṃ. Micchādassanañhi uppajjamānaṃ sammādassanaṃ vinivijjhati ceva vilometi ca. Kadāci sassatassa, kadāci ucchedassa gahaṇato diṭṭhiyā virūpaṃ phanditanti diṭṭhivipphanditaṃ. Diṭṭhigatiko hi ekasmiṃ patiṭṭhātuṃ na sakkoti. Kadāci sassataṃ anussarati, kadāci ucchedaṃ. Diṭṭhiyeva bandhanaṭṭhena saṃyojananti diṭṭhisaṃyojanaṃ. Susumārādayo [P 1.0163] viya purisaṃ ārammaṇaṃ daḷhaṃ gaṇhātīti gāho. Patiṭṭhahanato patiṭṭhāho. Ayañhi [V 0.0127] balavapavattibhāvena patiṭṭhahitvā gaṇhāti. Niccādivasena abhinivisatīti abhiniveso. Dhammasabhāvaṃ atikkamitvā niccādivasena parato āmasatīti parāmāso. Anatthāvahattā kucchito maggo, kucchitānaṃ vā apāyānaṃ maggoti kummaggo. Ayāthāvapathato micchāpatho. Yathā hi disāmūḷhena “ayaṃ asukagāmassa nāma patho”ti gahitopi taṃ gāmaṃ na sampāpeti, evaṃ diṭṭhigatikena “sugatipatho”ti gahitāpi diṭṭhi sugatiṃ na pāpetīti ayāthāvapathato micchāpatho. Micchāsabhāvato micchattaṃ. Tattheva paribbhamanato [M 0.0140] taranti ettha bālāti titthaṃ, titthañca taṃ anatthānañca āyatananti titthāyatanaṃ, titthiyānaṃ vā sañjātidesaṭṭhena nivāsaṭṭhānaṭṭhena ca āyatanantipi titthāyatanaṃ. Vipariyesabhūto gāho, vipariyesato vā gāhoti vipariyesaggāho. Asabhāvagāhoti viparītaggāho. “Anicce nicca”nti ādinayappavattavasena parivattetvā gāho vipallāsaggāho. Anupāyagāho micchāgāho. Ayāthāvakasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ na sabhāvasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ tathaṃ yāthāvakaṃ sabhāvanti gāho “ayāthāvakasmiṃ yāthāvaka”nti gāho. Yāvatāti yattakā. Dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhigatānīti brahmajāle (dī. ni. 1.29 ādayo) āgatāni dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhigatāni.

The twentyfold basis of personality view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) is the view that arises by taking each of the five aggregates—form, etc.—as its basis, considering each of them in four ways according to the method beginning with ‘He regards form as self,’ etc. (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.130-131). It is called personality view because it is a view that arises concerning the body, which is designated as the five aggregates, existing as a real entity. The tenfold wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) is the view that arises according to the method beginning with ‘There is no giving, no sacrifice,’ etc. It is called wrong view because it grasps what is contrary to reality, or because it is a false view, or because it is despised by the wise as unbeneficial. It has the characteristic of unwise adherence, the function of obstinate clinging, the manifestation of wrong conviction, and the proximate cause of not wanting to see the noble ones. It should be regarded as the supreme fault. The tenfold extreme view (antaggāhikā diṭṭhi) is the view that arises by grasping one-sided positions such as ‘The world is eternal,’ ‘The world is not eternal,’ ‘The world is finite,’ etc., establishing each portion as a support. It is called extreme view because it thus holds to one extreme. ‘Such a view’ means a view of such a kind. ‘Gone to views’ (diṭṭhigata) means gone into views; this view is called ‘gone to views’ because it is included among the sixty-two views. The thicket of views (diṭṭhigahanaṃ) is so called because view itself is a thicket, being hard to overcome, like thickets of grass, jungle thickets, or mountain thickets. The wilderness of views (diṭṭhikantāraṃ) is so called because it is fraught with danger and fear, like wildernesses infested with thieves, wild beasts, waterless wildernesses, or famine-stricken wildernesses. The writhing of views (diṭṭhivisūkāyikaṃ) is so called because it pierces and goes against right view. For when wrong view arises, it both pierces and goes against right view. The vacillation of views (diṭṭhivipphanditaṃ) is so called because of the view's unsteady flickering, sometimes grasping eternalism, sometimes annihilationism. One who has gone to views cannot stand firm in one position; sometimes he inclines to eternalism, sometimes to annihilationism. The fetter of views (diṭṭhisaṃyojanaṃ) is so called because view itself acts as a fetter. Like a crocodile, etc., it firmly seizes a person as its object—that is grasping (gāho). Adherence (patiṭṭhāho) is so called because it establishes itself (patiṭṭhahanato); for it grasps by establishing itself with powerful momentum. Dogmatic clinging (abhiniveso) is so called because one adheres in terms of permanence, etc. Misapprehension (parāmāso) is so called because, transgressing the nature of things, one ‘touches upon’ (āmasati) something else in terms of permanence, etc. The wrong path (kummaggo) is so called because it is a despised path, being unbeneficial, or the path to the despised states of misery. The wrong way (micchāpatho) is so called because it is a path deviating from reality. Just as a person confused about directions, even though he has grasped what he thinks is the path to a certain village, does not reach that village, so too one gone to views, even though he has grasped a view he thinks is the path to a good destination, does not reach a good destination; thus it is called the wrong way. Wrongness (micchattaṃ) is so called because of its nature of being wrong. A ford (tittha) is so called because fools wander about and cross over right there. A sectarian ground (titthāyatanaṃ) is so called because it is both a ford and a basis of harm; or a sectarian ground is so called because it is the dwelling place of sectarians in the sense of being a place of assembly or a place of dwelling. Misconception (vipariyesaggāho) is so called because it is a grasp that is a perversion, or a grasp because of perversion. Wrong grasp (viparītaggāho) is so called because it is a grasp that is not in accordance with reality. Perversion (vipallāsaggāho) is so called because it grasps by inverting according to the method beginning with ‘The impermanent as permanent,’ etc. Wrong grasp (micchāgāha) is so called because it is a grasp of an inappropriate means. ‘Grasping what is not real as real’ is so called because it is a grasp in an unreal thing—that is, a thing that is not its own nature—taking it as its own nature, as real. ‘All’ means as many as there are. ‘The sixty-two views’ refers to the sixty-two views mentioned in the Brahmajāla Sutta (Dīgha Nikāya 1.29, etc.).

Acchedasaṃkinopi phandantīti acchinditvā pasayha balakkārena gaṇhissantīti uppannasaṃkinopi calanti. Acchindantepīti vuttanayena acchijjantepi. Acchinnepīti vuttanayena acchinditvā gahitepi. Vipariṇāmasaṃkinopīti parivattetvā aññathābhāvena āsaṃkinopi[P 1.0164]. Vipariṇāmantepīti viparivattanakālepi. Vipariṇatepīti viparivattitepi. Phandantīti calanti. Samphandantīti sabbākārena calanti. Vipphandantīti vividhākārena phandanti. Vedhantīti bhayaṃ disvā kampanti. Pavedhantīti chambhitattā bhayena visesena kampanti. Sampavedhantīti lomahaṃsanabhayena sabbākārena kampanti. Phandamāneti upayogabahuvacanaṃ. Appodaketi mandodake. Parittodaketi luḷitodake. Udakapariyādāneti khīṇodake. Balākāhi vāti vuttāvasesāhi pakkhijātīhi. Paripātiyamānāti vihiṃsiyamānā ghaṭṭiyamānā. Ukkhipiyamānāti kaddamantarato nīhariyamānā giliyamānā vā. Khajjamānāti khādiyamānā. Phandanti kākehi. Samphandanti kulalehi. Vipphandanti balākāhi. Vedhanti tuṇḍena gahitakāle maraṇavasena. Pavedhanti vijjhanakāle. Sampavedhanti maraṇasamīpe.

Even those apprehensive of being seized tremble: this means that even those who are apprehensive, thinking, 'They will seize us by force, violently,' they tremble. Even while being seized: this means while being seized in the way stated. Even when seized: this means after being seized and taken in the way stated. Even those apprehensive of change: this means apprehensive of being transformed into another state. Even while changing: this means during the time of transformation. Even when changed: this means after being transformed. They tremble means they shake. They convulse means they shake in every way. They thrash means they tremble in various ways. They shudder means they tremble upon seeing danger. They quake means they tremble especially out of fear because of being startled. They tremble violently means they shake all over with hair-raising terror. 'Trembling': this is a plural of usage. 'In little water' means in meager water. 'In scanty water' means in roiled water. 'When the water is exhausted' means when the water is depleted. 'Or by herons' means by the remaining species of birds mentioned. 'Being harassed' means being harmed, buffeted. 'Being lifted up' means being dragged out from the mud or being swallowed. 'Being devoured' means being eaten. Crows make them tremble. Hawks make them convulse. Herons make them thrash. They shudder when seized by the beak, on account of death. They quake when being pierced. They tremble violently when near death.

Passitvāti aguṇaṃ passitvā. Tulayitvāti guṇāguṇaṃ tulayitvā. Tīrayitvāti guṇāguṇaṃ vitthāretvā. Vibhāvayitvāti vatthuhānabhāgiṃ muñcitvā vajjetvā. Vibhūtaṃ katvāti nipphattiṃ pāpetvā āveṇikaṃ katvā. Atha vā saṃkiṇṇadosaṃ mocetvā vatthuvibhāgakaraṇena passitvā. Aparicchedadosaṃ [V 0.0128] mocetvā pamāṇakaraṇavasena tulayitvā. Vatthudosaṃ mocetvā vibhāgakaraṇavasena tīrayitvā. Sammohadosaṃ mocayitvā [M 0.0141] aggavibhāgakaraṇavasena vibhāvayitvā. Ghanadosaṃ mocetvā pakativibhāgakaraṇena vibhūtaṃ katvā. Pahāyāti pajahitvā. Paṭinissajjitvāti nissajjitvā. Amamāyantoti taṇhādiṭṭhīhi ālayaṃ akaronto. Agaṇhantoti diṭṭhiyā pubbabhāge paññāya taṃ na gaṇhanto. Aparāmasantoti vitakkena ūhanaṃ akaronto. Anabhinivesantoti niyāmokkantidiṭṭhivasena nappavisanto.

Having seen means having seen the defect. Having weighed means having weighed the good and bad qualities. Having judged means having elaborated on the good and bad qualities. Having discerned means having released and avoided the portion that belongs to decline. Having made it manifest means having brought it to completion and made it distinct. Alternatively, having freed it from the defect of confusion by seeing through the division of the subject matter; having freed it from the defect of non-delimitation by weighing by way of measuring; having freed it from the defect of the subject matter by judging by way of division; having freed it from the defect of delusion by discerning by way of the supreme division; having freed it from the defect of compactness by making it manifest by way of natural division. Having abandoned means having given it up. Having relinquished means having let it go. Not regarding as 'mine' means not making an attachment through craving and views. Not grasping means not grasping it with the wisdom that is the preliminary part of a view. Not misapprehending means not making a consideration with thought. Not adhering means not entering by way of a view that has entered a fixed course.

Akubbamānoti pariggāhataṇhāvasena akaronto. Ajanayamānoti ponobhavikataṇhāvasena ajanayamāno. Asañjanayamānoti [P 1.0165] visesena asañjanayamāno. Anibbattayamānoti patthanātaṇhāvasena na nibbattayamāno. Anabhinibbattayamānoti sabbākārena na abhinibbattayamāno. Upasaggavasena vā etāni padāni vaḍḍhitāni. Evamettha paṭhamagāthāya assādaṃ.

Not making means not making by way of craving for grasping. Not generating means not generating by way of craving for renewed existence. Not co-generating means not generating in a special way. Not bringing into existence means not bringing into existence by way of craving for aspiration. Not bringing into full existence means not bringing into existence in any way. Or, these terms are augmented by way of prefixes. Thus, in the first verse, the gratification is shown.

13. Tato parāhi catūhi gāthāhi ādīnavañca dassetvā idāni saupāyaṃ nissaraṇaṃ nissaraṇānisaṃsañca dassetuṃ, sabbāhi vā etāhi kāmānaṃ ādīnavaṃ okāraṃ saṃkilesañca dassetvā idāni nekkhamme ānisaṃsaṃ dassetuṃ “ubhosu antesū”ti gāthādvayamāha. Tattha ubhosu antesūti phassaphassasamudayādīsu dvīsu, dvīsu paricchedesu. Vineyya chandanti chandarāgaṃ vinetvā. Phassaṃ pariññāyāti cakkhusamphassādiphassaṃ, phassānusārena vā taṃsampayutte sabbepi arūpadhamme, tesaṃ vatthudvārārammaṇavasena rūpadhamme cāti sakalampi nāmarūpaṃ tīhi pariññāhi parijānitvā. Anānugiddhoti rūpādīsu sabbadhammesu agiddho. Yadattagarahī tadakubbamānoti yaṃ attanā garahati, taṃ akurumāno. Na limpatī diṭṭhasutesu dhīroti so evarūpo dhitisampanno dhīro diṭṭhesu ca sutesu ca dhammesu dvinnaṃ lepānaṃ ekenāpi lepena na limpati, ākāsamiva nirupalitto accantavodānappatto hoti.

13. Then, with the subsequent four verses having shown the danger, now in order to show the escape with its means and the benefit of escape—or, with all these verses having shown the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, now in order to show the benefit in renunciation—he spoke the pair of verses beginning 'At both ends.' Herein, 'at both ends' means at the two ends, the two divisions, namely, contact and the origin of contact. 'Having subdued desire' means having subdued sensual desire. 'Having fully understood contact' means having fully understood with the three kinds of full understanding all of name-and-form: that is, eye-contact and other kinds of contact, or, in accordance with contact, all immaterial phenomena associated with it, and the material phenomena by way of their base, door, and object. 'Not greedy' means not being greedy for any phenomena, such as form and so on. 'What he himself censures, that he does not do' means not doing what one censures in oneself. 'The wise one is not smeared by what is seen and heard' means: such a wise one, endowed with fortitude, is not smeared by what is seen and heard with either of the two kinds of smearing, not even with a single smearing; like space, he is unblemished, having reached ultimate purity.

Phasso eko antoti phasso ekaparicchedo. Phusatīti phasso. Svāyaṃ phusanalakkhaṇo, saṅghaṭṭanaraso, sannipātapaccupaṭṭhāno, āpāthagatavisayapadaṭṭhāno. Ayañhi arūpadhammopi samāno ārammaṇe [M 0.0142] phusanākāreneva pavattatīti phusanalakkhaṇo. Ekadeseneva anallīyamānopi rūpaṃ viya cakkhuṃ, saddo viya ca sotaṃ cittaṃ ārammaṇañca saṅghaṭṭetīti saṅghaṭṭanaraso, vatthārammaṇasaṅghaṭṭanato vā uppannattā sampattiatthenapi rasena “saṅghaṭṭanaraso”ti veditabbo. Vuttañhetaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ –

'Contact is one end' means contact is one division. It touches, thus it is 'contact.' It has the characteristic of touching, the function of impacting, the manifestation of conjunction, and an object that has come into range as its proximate cause. For this, though an immaterial phenomenon, occurs in the manner of touching an object; thus its characteristic is touching. It impacts the mind and the object just as form impacts the eye and sound the ear; thus its function is impacting. Or, because it arises from the impact of the base and the object, it should be understood to have the function of impacting also in the sense of accomplishment. This is stated in the commentary:

“Catubhūmakaphasso [V 0.0129] no phusanalakkhaṇo nāma natthi, saṅghaṭṭanaraso pana pañcadvārikova hoti. Pañcadvārikassa hi phusanalakkhaṇotipi saṅghaṭṭanarasotipi nāmaṃ. Manodvārikassa phusanalakkhaṇotveva nāmaṃ, na saṅghaṭṭanaraso”ti [P 1.0166] (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1, kāmāvacarakusala, dhammuddesakathā).

For contact belonging to the four planes, it is not that there is no such thing as a 'characteristic of touching'; the function of impacting, however, belongs only to the five-door process. For the five-door process, there is both the name 'characteristic of touching' and 'function of impacting.' For the mind-door process, there is only the name 'characteristic of touching,' not 'function of impacting.'

Idañca vatvā idaṃ suttaṃ (mi. pa. 2.3.8) ābhataṃ –

And having said this, this passage is cited:

“Yathā, mahārāja, dve meṇḍā yujjheyyuṃ, yathā eko meṇḍo, evaṃ cakkhu daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yathā dutiyo meṇḍo, evaṃ rūpaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yathā tesaṃ sannipāto, evaṃ phasso daṭṭhabbo. Evaṃ phusanalakkhaṇo ca phasso saṅghaṭṭanaraso ca. Yathā, mahārāja, dve sammā vajjeyyuṃ, dve pāṇī vajjeyyuṃ. Yathā eko pāṇi, evaṃ cakkhu daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yathā dutiyo pāṇi, evaṃ rūpaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yathā tesaṃ sannipāto, evaṃ phasso daṭṭhabbo. Evaṃ phusanalakkhaṇo ca phasso saṅghaṭṭanaraso cā”ti vitthāro.

'Just as, great king, two rams might fight: the eye should be seen as the one ram, form should be seen as the second ram, and contact should be seen as their collision. Thus contact has the characteristic of touching and the function of impacting. Just as, great king, two cymbals might be struck, or two hands might be clapped: the eye should be seen as the one hand, form should be seen as the second hand, and contact should be seen as their collision. Thus contact has the characteristic of touching and the function of impacting.' This is the detailed account.

Yathā vā “cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 1352, 1354) cakkhuviññāṇādīni cakkhuādināmena vuttāni, evamidhāpi tāni cakkhuādināmeneva vuttānīti veditabbāni. Tasmā “evaṃ cakkhu daṭṭhabba”ntiādīsu evaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ daṭṭhabbanti iminā nayena attho veditabbo. Evaṃ sante cittārammaṇasaṅghaṭṭanato imasmimpi sutte kiccaṭṭheneva rasena “saṅghaṭṭanaraso”ti siddho hoti. Tiṇṇaṃ sannipātasaṅkhātassa pana attano kāraṇassa vasena paveditattā sannipātapaccupaṭṭhāno. Ayañhi tattha tattha “tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso”ti evaṃ kāraṇasseva vasena paveditoti. Imassa ca suttapadassa tiṇṇaṃ saṅgatiyā phassoti ayamattho, na saṅgatimattameva phasso.

Or, just as in such passages as 'having seen a form with the eye,' eye-consciousness and so on are spoken of by the name 'eye' and so on, so too here they should be understood as being spoken of by the name 'eye' and so on. Therefore, in such passages as 'thus the eye should be seen,' the meaning should be understood in this way: 'thus eye-consciousness should be seen.' This being so, because of the impact of mind and object, in this passage too 'function of impacting' is established as the function in the sense of its role. But because it is made known by way of its own cause, designated as the conjunction of the three, its manifestation is conjunction. For here and there it is made known in terms of its cause thus: 'Contact is the meeting of the three.' The meaning of this sutta passage is that contact arises from the meeting of the three, not that the mere meeting is contact.

Evaṃ [M 0.0143] paveditattā pana tenevākārena paccupaṭṭhātīti “sannipātapaccupaṭṭhāno”ti vutto. Phalaṭṭhena pana paccupaṭṭhānenesa vedanāpaccupaṭṭhāno nāma hoti. Vedanaṃ hesa paccupaṭṭhāpeti, uppādetīti attho. Uppādayamāno ca yathā bahiddhā uṇhapaccayāpi samānā lākhāsaṅkhātadhātunissitā usmā attano nissaye mudubhāvakārī hoti, na attano paccayabhūtepi bahiddhā vītaccitaṅgārasaṅkhāte uṇhabhāve. Evaṃ vatthārammaṇasaṅkhātaaññapaccayopi samāno cittanissitattā attano nissayabhūte citte eva esa vedanuppādako hoti, na attano paccayabhūtepi vatthumhi ārammaṇevāti [V 0.0130] veditabbo. Tajjena [P 1.0167] samannāhārena pana indriyena ca parikkhate visaye anantarāyena uppajjanato esa “āpāthagatavisayapadaṭṭhāno”ti vuccati.

But because it is made known in this way, it manifests in that same manner, thus it is said to have 'conjunction as manifestation.' In terms of its manifestation as a result, however, it has feeling as its manifestation. For it causes feeling to manifest, that is, it produces it. When it produces it, it is like this: just as heat, which is dependent on the element called lac, though it has external heat as its condition, produces softness in its own support, but not in the external heat, the glowing embers, which is its own condition. So too, though having other conditions, namely the base and the object, since it is dependent on the mind, it produces feeling only in its own support, the mind, not in its own conditions, the base and the object—this is how it should be understood. And because it arises without obstruction in a field defined by the sense faculty and the appropriate attention born of that, it is said to have 'an object that has come into range as its proximate cause.'

Phasso yato samudeti uppajjati, so “phassasamudayo”ti vuccati. Vuttañhetaṃ – “saḷāyatanapaccayā phasso”ti (mahāva. 1; vibha. 225). Atītaduko kālavasena vutto. Vedanāduko “upekkhā pana santattā, sukhamicceva bhāsitā”ti (vibha. aṭṭha. 232) vuttattā upekkhāvedanaṃ sukhameva katvā sukhadukkhavasena, nāmarūpaduko rūpārūpavasena, āyatanaduko saṃsārapavattivasena, sakkāyaduko pañcakkhandhavasena vuttoti veditabbo. Tattha sukhayatīti sukhā. Vedayatīti vedanā. Dukkhayatīti dukkhā. Namanalakkhaṇaṃ nāmaṃ. Ruppanalakkhaṇaṃ rūpaṃ. Cakkhāyatanādīni cha ajjhattikāni. Rūpāyatanādīni cha bāhirāni. Rūpakkhandhādayo pañcakkhandhā vijjamānaṭṭhena sakkāyo. Avijjākammataṇhāāhāraphassanāmarūpā sakkāyasamudayo.

That from which contact originates, arises, is called the 'origin of contact.' This is stated: 'Conditioned by the sixfold sense base, contact comes to be.' The pair concerning the past is stated in terms of time. The pair concerning feeling is stated in terms of pleasure and pain, by treating equanimous feeling as pleasure since it is said: 'Equanimity, being peaceful, is spoken of as pleasure itself.' The pair concerning name-and-form is stated in terms of the material and immaterial. The pair concerning the sense bases is stated in terms of the continuation of saṃsāra. The pair concerning identity should be understood as stated in terms of the five aggregates. Herein: it makes pleasant, thus it is pleasure. It is felt, thus it is feeling. It makes painful, thus it is pain. Name has the characteristic of bending. Form has the characteristic of being afflicted. The six internal sense bases are the eye base and so on. The six external sense bases are the form base and so on. The five aggregates, beginning with the form aggregate, are identity in the sense of their existing. Ignorance, kamma, craving, nutriment, contact, and name-and-form are the origin of identity.

Cakkhusamphassoti cakkhatīti cakkhu, rūpaṃ assādeti vibhāveti cāti attho. Cakkhuto pavatto samphasso cakkhusamphasso. So pana attanā sampayuttāya vedanāya sahajātaaññamaññanissayavipākaāhārasampayuttaatthiavigatavasena aṭṭhadhā paccayo hoti. Suṇātīti sotaṃ. Taṃ sasambhārasotabilassa anto tanutambalomācite aṅguliveṭhakasaṇṭhāne padese sotaviññāṇādīnaṃ yathārahaṃ vatthudvārabhāvaṃ sādhayamānaṃ tiṭṭhati. Sotato pavatto samphasso sotasamphasso. Ghānasamphassādīsupi eseva nayo. Ghāyatīti ghānaṃ[M 0.0144]. Taṃ sasambhārabilassa anto ajapadasaṇṭhāne padese ghānaviññāṇādīnaṃ yathārahaṃ vatthudvārabhāvaṃ sādhayamānaṃ tiṭṭhati. Jīvitamavhāyatīti jivhā, sāyanaṭṭhena vā jivhā. Sā sasambhārajivhāya atiaggamūlapassāni vajjetvā uparimatalamajjhe bhinnauppaladalaggasaṇṭhāne padese jivhāviññāṇādīnaṃ [P 1.0168] yathārahaṃ vatthudvārabhāvaṃ sādhayamānā tiṭṭhati. Kucchitānaṃ sāsavadhammānaṃ āyoti kāyo. Āyoti uppattideso. Yāvatā imasmiṃ kāye upādiṇṇapavatti nāma atthi, tattha yebhuyyena kāyappasādo kāyaviññāṇādīnaṃ yathārahaṃ vatthudvārabhāvaṃ sādhayamāno tiṭṭhati. Munātīti mano, vijānātīti attho. Manoti sahāvajjanabhavaṅgaṃ; manato pavatto samphasso manosamphasso.

Eye-contact: 'Cakkhu' means 'that which sees' (cakkhati); it also means 'that which savors and distinguishes forms' (rūpaṃ assādeti vibhāveti). Contact that has arisen from the eye is eye-contact. It is a condition in eight ways for the feeling associated with it: by way of co-nascence, mutuality, support, result, nutriment, association, presence, and non-disappearance. Ear: 'Sota' means 'that which hears' (suṇāti). It is situated within the cavity of the ear with its apparatus, in a place lined with fine copper-colored hairs and shaped like a finger-ring, where it serves to establish the appropriate base and door for ear-consciousness and so on. Contact that has arisen from the ear is ear-contact. The same method applies to nose-contact and so on. Nose: 'Ghāna' means 'that which smells' (ghāyati). It is situated inside the cavity of the nose with its apparatus, in a place shaped like a goat's footprint, where it serves to establish the appropriate base and door for nose-consciousness and so on. Tongue: 'Jivhā' means 'that which calls for life' (jīvitamavhāyati), or it is 'jivhā' in the sense of tasting (sāyana). It is situated in the middle of the upper surface of the tongue—avoiding the very tip, root, and sides—in a place shaped like the tip of a torn lotus petal, where it serves to establish the appropriate base and door for tongue-consciousness and so on. Body: 'Kāya' means 'the source (āyo) of contemptible, tainted phenomena' (kucchitānaṃ sāsavadhammānaṃ). 'Āyo' means the place of origin. Insofar as there is clung-to occurrence in this body, the body-sensitivity for the most part is situated there, where it serves to establish the appropriate base and door for body-consciousness and so on. Mind: 'Mano' means 'that which knows' (munāti), that is, 'that which cognizes' (vijānāti). By 'mind' is meant the bhavaṅga together with adverting. Contact that has arisen from the mind is mind-contact.

Chabbidhampi phassaṃ duvidhameva hotīti dassetuṃ “adhivacanasamphasso paṭighasamphasso”ti āha[V 0.0131]. Manodvāriko adhivacanasamphasso. Pañcadvāriko vatthārammaṇādipaṭighena uppajjanato paṭighasamphasso.

To show that contact, though sixfold, is just twofold, he said: 'designation-contact and resistance-contact.' Contact at the mind door is designation-contact. Contact at the five doors is resistance-contact because it arises from the impact of the physical base, object, and so on.

Sukhavedanāya ārammaṇe sukhavedanīyo. Dukkhavedanāya ārammaṇe dukkhavedanīyo. Adukkhamasukhavedanāya ārammaṇe adukkhamasukhavedanīyo. Tattha sukhayatīti sukhaṃ, yassuppajjati, taṃ sukhitaṃ karotīti attho. Suṭṭhu vā khanati, khādati ca kāyacittābādhanti sukhaṃ. Dukkhayatīti dukkhaṃ, yassuppajjati, taṃ dukkhitaṃ karotīti attho. Na dukkhaṃ na sukhanti adukkhamasukhaṃ, ma-kāro padasandhivasena vutto.

In the case of a pleasant feeling, the object is to be felt as pleasant. In the case of a painful feeling, the object is to be felt as painful. In the case of a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, the object is to be felt as neither-painful-nor-pleasant. Herein, 'pleasant' (sukhaṃ) is that which makes one happy (sukhayati); the meaning is that it makes happy the one in whom it arises. Or, 'pleasant' (sukhaṃ) is so called because it thoroughly (suṭṭhu) digs up (khanati) and consumes physical and mental afflictions. 'Painful' (dukkhaṃ) is that which causes pain (dukkhayati); the meaning is that it makes pained the one in whom it arises. 'Neither-painful-nor-pleasant' (adukkhamasukhaṃ) is that which is not painful and not pleasant; the 'ma' is stated for the sake of euphonic conjunction.

Kusalotiādayo jātivasena vuttā. Tattha kusaloti ekavīsatikusalacittasampayutto. Akusaloti dvādasākusalacittasampayutto. Abyākatoti avasesavipākakiriyābyākatacittasampayutto.

'Wholesome,' and so on, are stated by way of class. Herein, 'wholesome' is that which is associated with the twenty-one wholesome consciousnesses. 'Unwholesome' is that which is associated with the twelve unwholesome consciousnesses. 'Indeterminate' is that which is associated with the remaining resultant and functional indeterminate consciousnesses.

Puna bhavappabhedavasena niddisanto “kāmāvacaro”tiādimāha. Catupaññāsakāmāvacaracittasampayutto kāmāvacaro. Kāmaṃ pahāya rūpe avacaratīti rūpāvacaro, kusalābyākatavasena pañcadasarūpāvacaracittasampayutto. Kāmañca rūpañca pahāya arūpe avacaratīti arūpāvacaro, kusalābyākatavasena dvādasārūpāvacaracittasampayutto.

Again, indicating by way of the divisions of existence, he says, 'of the sense sphere,' and so on. 'Of the sense sphere' is that which is associated with the fifty-four sense-sphere consciousnesses. 'Of the form sphere' (rūpāvacaro) is so called because one resorts to the form sphere (rūpe avacarati) after having abandoned the sense sphere (kāmaṃ); it is that which is associated with the fifteen form-sphere consciousnesses by way of wholesome and indeterminate. 'Of the formless sphere' (arūpāvacaro) is so called because one resorts to the formless sphere (arūpe avacarati) after having abandoned the sense sphere and the form sphere; it is that which is associated with the twelve formless-sphere consciousnesses by way of wholesome and indeterminate.

Idāni [M 0.0145] abhinivesavasena dassento “suññato”tiādimāha. Tattha suññatoti rāgadosamohehi suññattā suññato. Rāgadosamohanimittehi animittattā animitto. Rāgadosamohapaṇidhīnaṃ abhāvato appaṇihitoti vuccati.

Now, showing it by way of adherence, he says, 'void,' and so on. Here, it is called 'void' because it is void of lust, hatred, and delusion. It is called 'signless' because it is devoid of the signs of lust, hatred, and delusion. It is called 'desireless' because of the absence of aspirations for lust, hatred, and delusion.

Idāni vaṭṭapariyāpannaapariyāpannavasena dassento “lokiyo”tiādimāha. Loko vuccati lujjanapalujjanaṭṭhena vaṭṭaṃ[P 1.0169], tasmiṃ pariyāpannabhāvena loke niyuttoti lokiyo. Uttiṇṇoti uttaro, loke apariyāpannabhāvena lokato uttaroti lokuttaro. Phusanāti phusanākāro. Samphusanā samphusitattanti upasaggena padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ.

Now, showing by way of inclusion and non-inclusion in the round, he says, 'mundane,' and so on. The round is called 'the world' (loko) in the sense of crumbling and disintegrating (lujjana-palujjana); because it is included in that, it is engaged in the world, hence 'mundane' (lokiyo). 'Transcended' (uttiṇṇo) means 'higher' (uttaro); because it is not included in the world, it is 'higher than the world' (lokato uttaro), hence 'supramundane' (lokuttaro). 'Touching' (phusanā) is the mode of touching. 'Contact' (samphusanā) means the state of having been contacted (samphusitattaṃ); the word is augmented with a prefix.

Evaṃ ñātaṃ katvāti evaṃ pākaṭaṃ katvā jānanto tīreti tīrayati, upari vattabbākārena cinteti. Aniccantikatāya ādiantavantatāya ca aniccato tīreti. Uppādavayapaṭipīḷanatāya dukkhavatthutāya ca dukkhato. Paccayayāpanīyatāya rogamūlatāya ca rogato. Dukkhatāsūlayogitāya [V 0.0132] kilesāsucipaggharatāya uppādajarābhaṅgehi uddhumātaparipakkapabhinnatāya ca gaṇḍato. Pīḷājanakatāya antotudanatāya dunnīharaṇīyatāya ca sallato. Vigarahaṇīyatāya avaḍḍhiāvahanatāya aghavatthutāya ca aghato. Aseribhāvajanakatāya ābādhapadaṭṭhānatāya ca ābādhato. Avasatāya avidheyyatāya ca parato. Byādhijarāmaraṇehi lujjanapalujjanatāya palokato. Anekabyasanāvahanatāya ītito. Aviditānaṃyeva vipulānaṃ anatthānaṃ āvahanato sabbūpaddavavatthutāya ca upaddavato. Sabbabhayānaṃ ākaratāya ca dukkhavūpasamasaṅkhātassa paramassāsassa paṭipakkhabhūtatāya ca bhayato. Anekehi anatthehi anubaddhatāya dosūpasaṭṭhatāya, upasaggo viya anadhivāsanārahatāya ca upasaggato. Byādhijarāmaraṇehi ceva lābhādīhi ca lokadhammehi pacalitatāya calato. Upakkamena ceva sarasena ca pabhaṅgupagamanasīlatāya pabhaṅguto. Sabbāvatthāvinipātitāya, thirabhāvassa ca abhāvatāya adhuvato. Atāyanatāya ceva alabbhaneyyakhematāya ca [M 0.0146] atāṇato. Allīyituṃ anarahatāya, allīnānampi ca leṇakiccākāritāya aleṇato. Nissitānaṃ bhayasārakattābhāvena asaraṇato. Yathāparikappitehi dhuvasubhasukhattabhāvehi [P 1.0170] rittatāya rittato. Rittatāyeva tucchato, appakattā vā. Appakampi hi loke “tuccha”nti vuccati. Sāminivāsivedaka kārakādhiṭṭhāyakavirahitatāya suññato.

Having thus made it known, having made it evident, knowing, he judges, he decides; he contemplates in the manner to be described. He judges it as impermanent because of its impermanent nature and because it has a beginning and an end. He judges it as suffering because it is oppressed by arising and passing away and because it is a basis for suffering. He judges it as a disease because it must be sustained by conditions and is the root of illness. He judges it as a tumor because it is connected to the stake of suffering, because of the oozing of the impurity of defilements, and because it is swollen, ripened, and burst by arising, aging, and breaking up. He judges it as a dart because it produces affliction, pricks within, and is hard to extract. He judges it as a calamity because it is reprehensible, brings decline, and is a basis for misery. He judges it as an affliction because it produces a state of dependence and is a basis for ailments. He judges it as alien because it is uncontrollable and not submissive. He judges it as disintegrating because it crumbles and breaks up through sickness, aging, and death. He judges it as a plague because it brings many misfortunes. He judges it as a disaster because it brings vast and unknown harms and is a basis for all calamities. He judges it as fearful because it is a mine of all fears and is the opponent of the supreme solace designated as the calming of suffering. He judges it as a menace because it is followed by many harms, is afflicted by faults, and is unfit to be endured, like a disease. He judges it as unstable because it is shaken by sickness, aging, and death, and by the worldly conditions such as gain. He judges it as perishable because it is disposed to break up both by external attack and by its own nature. He judges it as unlasting because it falls away in all states and because of the absence of a stable nature. He judges it as no protection because it is no safeguard and because security is unobtainable from it. He judges it as no shelter because it is unfit to be clung to and because even those who cling to it are made to perform the function of a shelter. He judges it as no refuge because it has no core of safety for those who rely on it. He judges it as empty because it is devoid of the states of permanence, beauty, and happiness as imagined. He judges it as vain because it is empty, or because it is insignificant; for even what is small is called 'vain' in the world. He judges it as void because it is devoid of an owner, a dweller, an experiencer, a doer, or a controller.

Sayañca asāmikabhāvāditāya anattato. Pavattidukkhatāya, dukkhassa ca ādīnavatāya ādīnavato. Atha vā ādīnaṃ vāti gacchati pavattatīti ādīnavo, kapaṇamanussassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Khandhāpi ca kapaṇāyevāti ādīnavasadisatāya ādīnavato. Jarāya ceva maraṇena cāti dvedhā pariṇāmapakatitāya vipariṇāmadhammato. Dubbalatāya, pheggu viya sukhabhañjanīyatāya ca asārakato. Aghahetutāya aghamūlato. Mittamukhasapatto viya vissāsaghātitāya vadhakato. Vigatabhavatāya vibhavasambhūtatāya ca vibhavato. Āsavapadaṭṭhānatāya sāsavato. Hetupaccayehi abhisaṅkhatatāya saṅkhatato. Maccumārakilesamārānaṃ āmisabhūtatāya mārāmisato. Jātijarābyādhimaraṇapakatitāya jātijarābyādhimaraṇadhammato. Sokaparidevaupāyāsahetutāya sokaparidevaupāyāsadhammato. Taṇhādiṭṭhiduccaritasaṃkilesānaṃ visayadhammatāya saṃkilesadhammato. Avijjākammataṇhāsaḷāyatanavasena uppattito samudayato. Tesaṃ abhāvena atthaṅgamato. Phasse chandarāgavasena madhurassādena assādato. Phassassa vipariṇāmena ādīnavato. Ubhinnaṃ nissaraṇena nissaraṇato tīretīti sabbesu ca imesu “tīretī”ti pāṭhaseso daṭṭhabbo.

And he judges it as not-self because it is without ownership, and so on. He judges it as a danger because of the suffering of the process of existence and because of the danger of suffering. Or, 'danger' (ādīnavo) is so called because it goes towards and proceeds to misery (ādīnaṃ); this is a term for a wretched person. And since the aggregates are indeed wretched, he judges them as a danger because they are like a danger. He judges it as subject to change because its nature is to be transformed in two ways, namely, by aging and death. He judges it as coreless because of its weakness and because it is as easily broken as pith. He judges it as the root of misery because it is a cause of misery. He judges it as a murderer because it destroys trust, like an enemy with the face of a friend. He judges it as annihilation because its being has passed away and because it is a product of annihilation. He judges it as subject to taints because it is a basis for the taints. He judges it as conditioned because it is formed by causes and conditions. He judges it as Māra's bait because it is the bait for the Māra of death and the Māra of defilements. He judges it as subject to birth, aging, sickness, and death because its nature is birth, aging, sickness, and death. He judges it as subject to sorrow, lamentation, and despair because it is a cause of sorrow, lamentation, and despair. He judges it as subject to defilement because it is an object for the defilements of craving, views, and misconduct. He judges it as origination because it arises by way of ignorance, kamma, craving, and the six sense bases. He judges it as cessation because of the absence of these. He judges it as gratification because of the sweet taste of contact by way of desire and lust. He judges it as danger because of the change of contact. He judges it as escape because of the escape from both. And in all these cases, the remainder of the text, 'he judges,' should be understood.

Pajahatīti sakasantānato nīharati. Vinodetīti tudati. Byantiṃ karotīti vigatantaṃ [V 0.0133] karoti. Anabhāvaṃ gametīti anu anu abhāvaṃ gameti. Ariyamaggasatthena ucchinnaṃ taṇhāavijjāmayaṃ mūlametesanti ucchinnamūlā. Tālavatthu viya nesaṃ vatthu katanti tālāvatthukatā. Yathā hi tālarukkhaṃ samūlaṃ uddharitvā tassa vatthumatte tasmiṃ padese kate na puna tassa tālassa uppatti paññāyati, evaṃ ariyamaggasatthena samūle rūpādirase uddharitvā tesaṃ pubbe uppannapubbabhāvena vatthumatte cittasantāne kate sabbepi te “tālāvatthukatā”ti vuccanti. Yassesoti [P 1.0171] yassa [M 0.0147] puggalassa eso gedho. Samucchinnoti ucchinno. Vūpasantoti phalena vūpasanto. Paṭipassaddhoti paṭipassaddhippahānena paṭipassambhito. Upasaggena vā padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ. Abhabbuppattikoti puna uppajjituṃ abhabbo. Ñāṇagginā daḍḍhoti maggañāṇagginā jhāpito. Atha vā visanikkhittaṃ bhājanena saha chaḍḍitaṃ viya vatthunā saha pahīno. Mūlacchinnavisavalli viya samūlacchinnoti samucchinno. Uddhane udakaṃ siñcitvā nibbāpitaaṅgāraṃ viya vūpasanto. Nibbāpitaaṅgāre patitaudakaphusitaṃ viya paṭipassaddho. Aṅkuruppattiyā hetucchinnabījaṃ viya abhabbuppattiko. Asanipātavisarukkho viya ñāṇagginā daḍḍhoti evameke vaṇṇayanti.

'To abandon' means to remove from one’s own continuity. 'To dispel' means to pierce. 'To make an end' means to make it past its end. 'To bring to non-existence' means to lead it again and again to non-existence. Their root consisting of craving and ignorance has been cut off by the sword of the noble path: thus they are with root cut off. Their base has been made like the stump of a palm tree: thus they are made like a palm-tree stump. For just as when a palm tree has been uprooted, and its base has been made a mere site in that place, the arising of that palm tree is no longer discerned, so too, when the taste for forms, etc., has been uprooted by the sword of the noble path, and their mental continuum, in which they formerly arose, has been made a mere site, they are all said to be ‘made like a palm-tree stump.’ 'For whom' means for whichever person this greed is. 'Utterly cut off' means cut off. 'Pacified' means pacified by the fruit. 'Calmed' means stilled by the abandoning that is calming. Or the word is augmented by a prefix. 'Incapable of arising' means unable to arise again. 'Burnt by the fire of knowledge' means consumed by the fire of path-knowledge. Alternatively, some explain it thus: it is abandoned along with its base, like a vessel containing poison that is discarded along with it. It is utterly cut off, like a poison creeper cut off at the root. It is pacified, like an ember extinguished by sprinkling water on a brazier. It is calmed, like a drop of water that has fallen on an extinguished ember. It is incapable of arising, like a seed whose cause of sprouting has been cut off. It is burnt by the fire of knowledge, like a poison tree struck by lightning.

Vītagedhoti idaṃ sakabhāvapariccajanavasena vuttaṃ. Vigatagedhoti idaṃ ārammaṇe sālayabhāvapariccajanavasena. Cattagedhoti idaṃ puna anādiyanabhāvadassanavasena. Muttagedhoti idaṃ santatito vinimocanavasena. Pahīnagedhoti idaṃ muttassāpi kvaci anavaṭṭhānadassanavasena. Paṭinissaṭṭhagedhoti idaṃ ādinnapubbassa nissaggadassanavasena vuttaṃ. Vītarāgo vigatarāgo cattarāgoti vuttanayena yojetabbaṃ. Tattha gijjhanavasena gedho. Rañjanavasena rāgo. Nicchātoti nittaṇho. “Nicchado”tipi pāṭho, taṇhāchadanavirahitoti attho. Nibbutoti nibbutasabhāvo. Sītibhūtoti sītasabhāvo. Sukhapaṭisaṃvedīti kāyikacetasikasukhaṃ anubhavanasabhāvo. Brahmabhūtenāti uttamasabhāvena. Attanāti cittena.

'Without greed': this is said in the sense of abandoning its own nature. 'With greed departed': this is said in the sense of abandoning the state of attachment to an object. 'With greed relinquished': this is said in the sense of showing the state of not taking up again. 'With greed released': this is said in the sense of liberation from the continuity. 'With greed abandoned': this is said in the sense of showing the non-establishment anywhere even of what is released. 'With greed cast off': this is said in the sense of showing the relinquishment of what was previously taken up. 'Without lust, with lust departed, with lust relinquished' should be connected in the way stated. Here, greed is in the sense of avarice. Lust is in the sense of attachment. 'Without desire' means without craving. There is also the reading ‘nicchado,’ meaning devoid of the covering of craving. 'Extinguished' means of an extinguished nature. 'Become cool' means of a cool nature. 'Experiencing bliss' means of a nature to experience bodily and mental happiness. 'Become supreme' means of the highest nature. 'By oneself' means by the mind.

Katattā cāti pāpakammānaṃ katabhāvena ca. Akatattā cāti kusalānaṃ akatabhāvena ca. Kataṃ me kāyaduccaritaṃ, akataṃ me kāyasucaritantiādayo dvāravasena avirativirativasena kammapathavasena ca vuttā. Sīlesumhi na paripūrakārītiādayo catupārisuddhisīlavasena. Jāgariyamananuyuttoti pañcajāgaraṇavasena. Satisampajaññenāti sātthakādisampajaññavasena[P 1.0172]. Cattāro satipaṭṭhānātiādayo bodhipakkhiyadhammā lokiyalokuttaravasena. Dukkhaṃ me apariññātantiādayo cattāro ariyasaccavasena vuttāti veditabbaṃ. Te atthato tattha tattha vuttanayattā pākaṭāyeva.

'And because of having done': because of the fact that evil kamma has been done. 'And because of not having done': because of the fact that wholesome kamma has not been done. ‘Bodily misconduct has been done by me, bodily good conduct has not been done by me,’ and so on, are stated in terms of the doors, in terms of non-restraint and restraint, and in terms of the courses of kamma. ‘I am not a fulfiller in regard to the virtues,’ and so on, are stated in terms of the fourfold purity of virtue. 'Devoted to wakefulness' is stated in terms of the five kinds of wakefulness. 'With mindfulness and clear comprehension' is stated in terms of clear comprehension of purpose, etc. ‘The four establishments of mindfulness,’ and so on, are the aids to enlightenment, stated in terms of the mundane and the supramundane. ‘Suffering has not been fully understood by me,’ and so on, should be understood as stated in terms of the four noble truths. Their meaning is evident because of the method stated in the respective passages.

Dhīro [V 0.0134][M 0.0148] paṇḍitoti satta padā vuttatthāyeva. Api ca dukkhe akampiyaṭṭhena dhīro. Sukhe anuppilavaṭṭhena paṇḍito. Diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikatthe kataparicayaṭṭhena paññavā. Attatthaparatthe niccalaṭṭhena buddhimā. Gambhīrauttānatthe apaccosakkanaṭṭhena ñāṇī. Guḷhapaṭicchannatthe obhāsanaṭṭhena vibhāvī. Nikkilesabyavadānaṭṭhena tulāsadisoti medhāvī. Na limpatīti sajātiyā na limpati ākāse lekhā viya. Na palimpatīti visesena na limpati. Na upalimpatīti saññogo hutvāpi na limpati hatthatale lekhā viya. Alittoti saññogo hutvāpi na kilissati kāsikavatthe ṭhapitamaṇiratanaṃ viya. Apalittoti visesena na kilissati maṇiratane paliveṭhitakāsikavatthaṃ viya. Anupalittoti upagantvāpi na allīyati pokkharapatte udakabindu viya. Nikkhantoti bahi nikkhanto bandhanāgārato palāto viya. Nissaṭoti pāpapahīno amittassa paṭicchāpitakiliṭṭhavatthu viya. Vippamuttoti suṭṭhu mutto gayhūpage vatthumhi ratiṃ nāsetvā puna nāgamanaṃ viya. Visaññuttoti kilesehi ekato na yutto byādhinā muttagilāno viya. Vimariyādikatena cetasāti vigatamariyādakatena cittena, sabbabhavena sabbārammaṇena sabbakilesehi muttacittenāti attho.

'The wise, the sage': the meaning of these seven terms is as stated. Furthermore, one is wise (dhīro) in the sense of being unshaken by suffering. One is a sage (paṇḍito) in the sense of not being carried away by happiness. One is endowed with wisdom (paññavā) in the sense of having gained familiarity with matters of this life and the future life. One is intelligent (buddhimā) in the sense of being steadfast in what concerns oneself and others. One is possessed of knowledge (ñāṇī) in the sense of not shrinking back from matters profound and plain. One is discerning (vibhāvī) in the sense of illuminating what is hidden and concealed. One is sagacious (medhāvī) in the sense of being like a balance in being without defilement and being pure. 'He is not smeared': he is not smeared by his own kind, like a line in the sky. 'He is not besmeared': he is not smeared in a special way. 'He is not defiled': even having come into contact, he is not smeared, like a line on the palm of the hand. 'Unsmeared': even having come into contact, he is not soiled, like a jewel placed on a Kāsī cloth. 'Unbesmeared': he is not soiled in a special way, like a Kāsī cloth wrapped around a jewel. 'Undefiled': even having approached, he does not adhere, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf. 'Gone forth': he has gone out, like one who has fled from a prison. 'Escaped': he has abandoned evil, like a soiled cloth entrusted to an enemy. 'Fully released': well released, like one who, having destroyed delight in a graspable object, does not return again. 'Disjoined': not yoked together with the defilements, like a sick person released from a disease. 'With a mind that has transcended limits': with a mind whose limits are gone, that is, with a mind released from all states of being, all objects, and all defilements—this is the meaning.

14. Saññaṃ pariññāti gāthāya pana ayaṃ saṅkhepattho – na kevalañca phassameva, api ca kho pana kāmasaññādibhedaṃ saññaṃ, saññānusārena vā pubbe vuttanayeneva nāmarūpaṃ tīhi pariññāhi parijānitvā imāya paṭipadāya catubbidhampi [P 1.0173] vitareyya oghaṃ, tato so tiṇṇogho taṇhādiṭṭhipariggahesu taṇhādiṭṭhikilesappahānena anupalitto khīṇāsavamuni rāgādisallānaṃ abbūḷhattā abbūḷhasallo, sativepullappattiyā appamatto caraṃ, pubbabhāge vā appamatto caranto tena appamādacārena abbūḷhasallo hutvā sakaparattabhāvādibhedaṃ nāsīsati lokamimaṃ parañca, aññadatthu carimacittanirodhā nirupādānova jātavedo parinibbātīti arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi, dhammanettiṭhapanameva karonto; na tu imāya desanāya maggaṃ vā phalaṃ vā uppādesi, khīṇāsavassa desitattāti.

14. But of the verse ‘Having fully understood perception,’ this is the concise meaning: not only contact, but also perception of various kinds such as perception of sensual pleasure, or, in accordance with perception, having fully understood name-and-form by the three kinds of full understanding in the way stated before, by this practice one might cross over the fourfold flood. Then, having crossed the flood, unsmeared by the appropriations of craving and views through the abandoning of the defilements of craving and views, the sage whose taints are destroyed, having drawn out the darts of lust, etc., is one with dart drawn out. Dwelling heedfully through the attainment of abundant mindfulness, or, dwelling heedfully in the preliminary stage, by that heedful conduct he becomes one with dart drawn out. He does not long for this world or the next, which are distinguished as one’s own being, another’s being, and so on. Indeed, with the cessation of the final consciousness, he attains final Nibbāna without fuel, like a fire. Thus he concluded the discourse with the pinnacle of arahantship, merely establishing the guideline of the Dhamma; but by this discourse he did not produce the path or the fruit, because it was taught to one whose taints are destroyed.

Nīlādibhedaṃ [M 0.0149] ārammaṇaṃ sañjānātīti saññā. Sā sañjānanalakkhaṇā paccābhiññāṇarasā. Catubhūmikasaññā hi nosañjānanalakkhaṇā nāma natthi, sabbā sañjānanalakkhaṇāva. Yā panettha abhiññāṇena sañjānāti, sā paccābhiññāṇarasā nāma hoti. Tassā vaḍḍhakissa dārumhi abhiññāṇaṃ katvā puna tena abhiññāṇena taṃ paccābhijānanakāle, purisassa kāḷatilakādiabhiññāṇaṃ sallakkhetvā puna tena abhiññāṇena “asuko nāma eso”ti tassa paccābhijānanakāle, rañño piḷandhanagopakabhaṇḍāgārikassa [V 0.0135] tasmiṃ tasmiṃ piḷandhane nāmapaṇṇakaṃ bandhitvā “asukaṃ piḷandhanaṃ nāma āharā”ti vutte dīpaṃ jāletvā sāragabbhaṃ pavisitvā paṇṇaṃ vācetvā tassa tasseva piḷandhanassa āharaṇakāle ca pavatti veditabbā.

It perceives an object distinguished as blue, etc.: thus it is perception. It has the characteristic of perceiving, and the function of recognizing. For there is no perception in the four planes that does not have the characteristic of perceiving; all have the characteristic of perceiving. The one among them that perceives by means of a sign has the function of recognizing. Its occurrence should be understood from the time when a carpenter, having made a sign on a piece of wood, recognizes it again by that sign; from the time when a person, having noted a sign such as a black mole on another, recognizes him again by that sign, thinking, ‘This is so-and-so’; and from the time when a king’s keeper of the regalia, having tied a name-tag to each ornament, when told, ‘Bring such-and-such an ornament,’ lights a lamp, enters the strong room, reads the tag, and brings that very ornament.

Aparo nayo – sabbasaṅgāhikavasena hi sañjānanalakkhaṇā saññā, punasañjānanapaccayanimittakaraṇarasā dāruādīsu tacchakādayo viya, yathāgahitanimittavasena abhinivesakaraṇapaccupaṭṭhānā hatthidassakaandho viya, ārammaṇe anogāḷhavuttitāya aciraṭṭhānapaccupaṭṭhānā vā vijju viya, yathāupaṭṭhitavisayapadaṭṭhānā tiṇapurisakesu migapotakānaṃ purisāti uppannasaññā viya. Yā panettha ñāṇasampayuttā hoti, sā ñāṇameva anuvattati, sasambhārapathavīādīsu sesadhammā pathavīādīni viyāti veditabbā.

Another method: In an all-inclusive sense, perception has the characteristic of perceiving. Its function is to make a sign as a condition for perceiving again, like carpenters with wood, etc. It is manifested as the act of adhering to the sign as it was grasped, like a blind man who has seen an elephant. Or it is manifested as being of short duration because of its not plunging into the object, like lightning. Its proximate cause is the object as it has appeared, like the perception ‘a man’ that arises in young deer with respect to a scarecrow. That perception which is associated with knowledge follows knowledge, just as the other phenomena follow the earth element, etc., in the case of the earth element with its components. This should be understood.

Kāmapaṭisaññuttā saññā kāmasaññā. Byāpādapaṭisaññuttā saññā byāpādasaññā. Vihiṃsāpaṭisaññuttā saññā vihiṃsāsaññā[P 1.0174]. Tesu dve sattesupi saṅkhāresupi uppajjanti. Kāmasaññā hi piye manāpe satte vā saṅkhāre vā vitakkentassa uppajjati. Byāpādasaññā appiye amanāpe satte vā saṅkhāre vā kujjhitvā olokanakālato paṭṭhāya yāva vināsanā uppajjati. Vihiṃsāsaññā saṅkhāresu na uppajjati. Saṅkhāro hi dukkhāpetabbo nāma natthi. “Ime sattā haññantu vā, ucchijjantu vā, vinassantu vā, mā vā ahesu”nti cintanakāle pana sattesu uppajjati. Nekkhammapaṭisaññuttā saññā nekkhammasaññā, sā asubhapubbabhāge kāmāvacarā hoti, asubhajhāne rūpāvacarā, taṃ jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā uppannamaggaphalakāle lokuttarā. Abyāpādapaṭisaññuttā saññā abyāpādasaññā, sā mettāpubbabhāge kāmāvacarā hoti, mettājhāne rūpāvacarā, taṃ jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā uppannamaggaphalakāle [M 0.0150] lokuttarā. Avihiṃsāpaṭisaññuttā saññā avihiṃsāsaññā, sā karuṇāpubbabhāge kāmāvacarā, karuṇājhāne rūpāvacarā, taṃ jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā uppannamaggaphalakāle lokuttarā. Yadā alobho sīsaṃ hoti, tadā itare dve tadanvāyikā bhavanti. Yadā mettā sīsaṃ hoti, tadā itare dve tadanvāyikā bhavanti. Yadā karuṇā sīsaṃ hoti, tadā itare dve tadanvāyikā bhavanti. Rūpārammaṇaṃ ārabbha uppannā saññā rūpasaññā. Saddasaññādīsupi eseva nayo. Idaṃ tassāyeva ārammaṇato nāmaṃ. Ārammaṇānaṃ vuttattā cakkhusamphassajādivatthūnipi vuttāneva honti.

Perception connected with sensual desire is sensual perception. Perception connected with ill will is perception of ill will. Perception connected with harmfulness is perception of harmfulness. Of these, the first two arise in regard to both beings and formations. For sensual perception arises when one thinks about beings or formations that are dear and pleasing. Perception of ill will arises from the moment of looking with anger at beings or formations that are not dear or pleasing, up until their destruction. Perception of harmfulness does not arise in regard to formations, for there is no such thing as a formation that can be made to suffer. However, it arises toward beings when one thinks: “May these beings be struck down, may they be annihilated, may they be destroyed, may they not exist!” Perception connected with renunciation is perception of renunciation; in its preliminary stage of contemplating unattractiveness it is of the sense sphere; in the jhāna on unattractiveness it is of the form sphere; and when it arises at the time of path and fruition based on that jhāna, it is supramundane. Perception connected with non-ill will is perception of non-ill will; in its preliminary stage of loving-kindness it is of the sense sphere; in the jhāna on loving-kindness it is of the form sphere; and when it arises at the time of path and fruition based on that jhāna, it is supramundane. Perception connected with non-harming is perception of non-harming; in its preliminary stage of compassion it is of the sense sphere; in the jhāna on compassion it is of the form sphere; and when it arises at the time of path and fruition based on that jhāna, it is supramundane. When non-greed is primary, the other two follow it. When loving-kindness is primary, the other two follow it. When compassion is primary, the other two follow it. Perception that arises in dependence on a form-object is perception of form. The same method applies to perception of sound and so on. This is its name based on its object. Since the objects have been stated, the bases, such as things born of eye-contact, are also thereby stated.

Yā evarūpā saññāti aññāpi “paṭighasamphassajā saññā adhivacanasamphassajā saññā”ti evamādikā veditabbā. Tattha adhivacanasamphassajā saññātipi pariyāyena chadvārikāyeva[V 0.0136]. Tayo hi arūpino khandhā sayaṃ piṭṭhivaṭṭakā hutvā attanā sahajātasaññāya “adhivacanasamphassajā saññā”ti nāmaṃ karonti, nippariyāyena pana paṭighasamphassajā saññā nāma pañcadvārikā saññā, adhivacanasamphassajā saññā nāma manodvārikā saññā. Etā atirekasaññā pariggahitāti veditabbā.

Such a kind of perception should also be understood as “perception born of resistance-contact” and “perception born of designation-contact,” and so on. Herein, perception born of designation-contact is, by way of figurative speech, six-doored. For the three formless aggregates, having become a support, themselves provide the name “perception born of designation-contact” for the co-arisen perception. But in a literal sense, perception born of resistance-contact is five-doored perception, while perception born of designation-contact is mind-door perception. It should be understood that these are additional perceptions that are included here.

Saññāti [P 1.0175] sabhāvanāmaṃ. Sañjānanāti sañjānanākāro. Sañjānitattanti sañjānitabhāvo.

‘Perception’ is its name from its intrinsic nature. ‘Perceiving’ is its mode of functioning. ‘The state of having perceived’ is its state of being.

Avijjoghanti pūretuṃ ayuttaṭṭhena kāyaduccaritādi avindiyaṃ nāma, aladdhabbanti attho. Taṃ avindiyaṃ vindatīti avijjā. Tabbiparītato kāyasucaritādi vindiyaṃ nāma, taṃ vindiyaṃ na vindatīti avijjā. Khandhānaṃ rāsaṭṭhaṃ, āyatanānaṃ āyatanaṭṭhaṃ, dhātūnaṃ suññaṭṭhaṃ, indriyānaṃ adhipatiyaṭṭhaṃ, saccānaṃ tathaṭṭhaṃ aviditaṃ karotītipi avijjā. Dukkhādīnaṃ pīḷanādivasena vuttaṃ catubbidhaṃ atthaṃ aviditaṃ karotītipi avijjā. Antavirahite saṃsāre yonigatibhavaviññāṇaṭṭhitisattāvāsesu satte javāpetīti avijjā. Paramatthato avijjamānesu itthipurisādīsu javati, vijjamānesu khandhādīsu na javatīti avijjā. Api ca cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ vatthārammaṇānaṃ paṭiccasamuppādapaṭiccasamuppannānañca dhammānaṃ chādanatopi avijjā, taṃ avijjoghaṃ. Kāmoghavasena uttareyya. Bhavoghavasena patareyya. Diṭṭhoghavasena samatikkameyya. Avijjoghavasena vītivatteyya. Atha vā sotāpattimaggena [M 0.0151] pahānavasena uttareyya. Sakadāgāmimaggena pahānavasena patareyya. Anāgāmimaggena pahānavasena samatikkameyya. Arahattamaggena pahānavasena vītivatteyya. Atha vā “tareyyādipañcapadaṃ tadaṅgādipañcapahānena yojetabba”nti keci vadanti.

Regarding the flood of ignorance: Bodily misconduct and so on are called ‘not to be found’ (avindiyaṃ) in the sense that they are improper; the meaning is ‘not to be obtained.’ Ignorance (avijjā) is that which finds what is not to be found. Conversely, wholesome bodily conduct and the like are called ‘to be found’ (vindiyaṃ); ignorance is not finding what is to be found. Ignorance is also that which fails to understand: the characteristic of the aggregates as a mass, the characteristic of the sense bases as their own nature, the characteristic of the elements as void, the characteristic of the faculties as governing, and the characteristic of the truths as suchness. It is also ignorance that fails to understand the fourfold meaning of the truths—oppression, etc.—spoken of in relation to suffering and so on. Ignorance drives beings through the endless cycle of existence—through rebirths, destinies, states of becoming, stations of consciousness, and abodes of beings. In ultimate reality, it rushes toward what does not exist, such as a woman or a man, but does not rush toward what does exist, such as the aggregates. Moreover, ignorance is so called because it conceals the bases and objects of eye-consciousness and the like, and it conceals dependently originated and dependently arisen phenomena. That is the flood of ignorance. One should cross over the flood of sensuality, traverse the flood of existence, surmount the flood of views, and pass beyond the flood of ignorance. Alternatively, one should cross over by abandoning through the path of stream-entry, traverse by abandoning through the path of a once-returner, surmount by abandoning through the path of a non-returner, and pass beyond by abandoning through the path of arahantship. Or again, some say that the five terms beginning with ‘cross over’ should be connected with the five kinds of abandoning, beginning with that by substitution of opposites.

“Monaṃ vuccati ñāṇa”nti vatvā taṃ pabhedato dassetuṃ “yā paññā pajānanā”tiādimāha. Taṃ vuttanayameva ṭhapetvā “amoho dhammavicayo”ti padaṃ. Amoho kusalesu dhammesu abhāvanāya paṭipakkho bhāvanāhetu. Amohena aviparītaṃ gaṇhāti mūḷhassa viparītaggahaṇato. Amohena yāthāvaṃ yāthāvato dhārento yathāsabhāve pavattati. Mūḷho hi “tacchaṃ atacchaṃ, atacchañca taccha”nti gaṇhāti; tathā icchitālābhadukkhaṃ na hoti. Amūḷhassa “taṃ kutettha labbhā”ti evamādipaccavekkhaṇasambhavato maraṇadukkhaṃ na hoti. Sammohamaraṇañhi dukkhaṃ, na ca taṃ amūḷhassa hoti. Pabbajitānaṃ sukhasaṃvāso hoti, tiracchānayoniyaṃ nibbatti na hoti. Mohena hi niccasammūḷhā tiracchānayoniṃ upapajjanti[V 0.0137][P 1.0176]. Mohapaṭipakkho ca amoho mohavasena amajjhattabhāvassa abhāvakaro. Amohena avihiṃsāsaññā dhātusaññā majjhimāya paṭipattiyā paṭipajjanaṃ, pacchimaganthadvayassa pabhedanañca hoti. Pacchimāni dve satipaṭṭhānāni tasseva ānubhāvena ijjhanti. Amoho dīghāyukatāya paccayo hoti. Amūḷho hi hitāhitaṃ ñatvā ahitaṃ parivajjento hitañca paṭisevamāno dīghāyuko hoti, attasampattiyā aparihīno hoti. Amūḷho hi attano hitameva karonto attānaṃ sampādeti. Ariyavihārassa paccayo hoti, udāsinapakkhesu nibbuto hoti amūḷhassa sabbābhisaṅgatāya abhāvato. Amohena anattadassanaṃ hoti. Asammūḷho hi yāthāvagahaṇakusalo apariṇāyakaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ apariṇāyakato bujjhati. Yathā ca etena anattadassanaṃ, evaṃ attadassanaṃ mohena. Ko hi nāma attasuññataṃ bujjhitvā puna sammohaṃ āpajjeyyāti.

Having said, ‘Sagehood is called knowledge,’ to show its analysis he said, ‘That which is wisdom, understanding…,’ and so on. The method of explanation is the same as that already given, except for the terms ‘non-delusion’ and ‘investigation of phenomena.’ Non-delusion is the opposite of the non-cultivation of wholesome states and is the cause for their cultivation. Through non-delusion one grasps things without distortion, for a deluded person grasps things with distortion. By upholding things as they really are through non-delusion, one proceeds in accordance with their intrinsic nature. A deluded person takes the true as false and the false as true. Thus, for an undeluded person, there is no suffering from not obtaining what is desired, because it is possible for them to reflect, ‘How could that be obtained here?’ Nor is there the suffering of death, for death with delusion is suffering, and that does not happen to one who is undeluded. For the renunciants, there is pleasant living, and there is no rebirth in the animal realm; for those constantly deluded by delusion are reborn in the animal realm. Non-delusion, the opposite of delusion, brings about the absence of a non-neutral state caused by delusion. Through non-delusion there arise the perception of non-harming, the perception of the elements, the practice of the middle path, and the breaking of the last two ties. The last two foundations of mindfulness are accomplished through its power. Non-delusion is a condition for long life. For one who is undeluded, knowing what is beneficial and what is harmful, avoids the harmful and pursues the beneficial, and thus becomes long-lived and does not fall away from personal attainment. For the undeluded person, by doing only what is for their own welfare, accomplishes their own good. It is a condition for the noble abiding. One is at peace regarding indifferent things, since for the undeluded there is no attachment at all. Through non-delusion there is the vision of not-self. For one who is not confused, being skilled in grasping things as they are, understands the five aggregates to be without a guide, from their being unguided. And just as through this there is the vision of not-self, so through delusion there is the vision of self. For who, having understood the emptiness of self, would again fall into delusion?

Tena ñāṇena samannāgatoti etena vuttappakārena ñāṇena samaṅgībhūto sekkhādayo muni. Monappattoti paṭiladdhañāṇo munibhāvaṃ [M 0.0152] patto. Tīṇīti gaṇanaparicchedo. Moneyyānīti munibhāvakarā moneyyakarā paṭipadā dhammā. Kāyamoneyyantiādīsu viññattikāyarūpakāyavasena paññāpetabbaṃ kāyamoneyyaṃ. Viññattivācāsaddavācāvasena paññāpetabbaṃ vacīmoneyyaṃ. Manodvārikacittādivasena paññāpetabbaṃ manomoneyyaṃ. Tividhakāyaduccaritānaṃ pahānanti pāṇātipātādividhānaṃ kāyato pavattānaṃ duṭṭhu caritānaṃ pajahanaṃ. Kāyasucaritanti kāyato pavattaṃ suṭṭhu caritaṃ. Kāyārammaṇe ñāṇanti kāyaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā aniccādivasena pavattaṃ kāyārammaṇe ñāṇaṃ. Kāyapariññāti kāyaṃ ñātatīraṇappahānapariññāhi jānanavasena pavattaṃ ñāṇaṃ. Pariññāsahagato maggoti ajjhattikaṃ kāyaṃ sammasitvā uppāditamaggo pariññāsahagato. Kāye chandarāgassa pahānanti kāye taṇhāchandarāgassa pajahanaṃ. Kāyasaṅkhāranirodhoti [P 1.0177] assāsapassāsānaṃ nirodho āvaraṇo, catutthajjhānasamāpattisamāpajjanaṃ. Vacīsaṅkhāranirodhoti vitakkavicārānaṃ nirodho āvaraṇo, dutiyajjhānasamāpattisamāpajjanaṃ. Cittasaṅkhāranirodhoti saññāvedanānaṃ nirodho āvaraṇo, saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpattisamāpajjanaṃ.

Endowed with that knowledge: a trainee and others endowed with knowledge of the kind described are a sage. Having attained sagehood: one who has obtained knowledge and has attained the state of a sage. Three: this is a numerical determination. Qualities of a sage: practices and principles that produce the state of a sage, that make one a sage. Bodily sagehood, etc.: Bodily sagehood should be designated in terms of bodily intimation and the physical body. Verbal sagehood should be designated in terms of verbal intimation and speech as sound. Mental sagehood should be designated in terms of mind-door consciousness, etc. The abandoning of the threefold bodily misconduct: the abandonment of evil conduct performed with the body, of the kind beginning with the destruction of life. Good bodily conduct: good conduct performed with the body. Knowledge regarding the body: knowledge that proceeds by way of impermanence, etc., taking the body as its object. Full understanding of the body: knowledge that proceeds by way of knowing the body through the full understanding of it as to be known, as to be investigated, and as to be abandoned. The path accompanied by full understanding: the path produced by contemplating the internal body is accompanied by full understanding. The abandoning of desire and lust for the body: the abandonment of sensual desire and lust for the body. Cessation of the bodily formation: the cessation and obstruction of in-breaths and out-breaths, which is the attainment of the fourth jhāna. Cessation of the verbal formation: the cessation and obstruction of thought and examination, which is the attainment of the second jhāna. Cessation of the mental formation: the cessation and obstruction of perception and feeling, which is the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.

Paṭhamagāthāya kāyamunintiādīsu kāyaduccaritappahānavasena kāyamuni. Vacīduccaritappahānavasena vācāmuni. Manoduccaritappahānavasena manomuni. Sabbākusalappahānavasena anāsavamuni. Moneyyasampannanti jānitabbaṃ jānitvā phale ṭhitattā moneyyasampannaṃ. Āhu sabbappahāyinanti sabbakilese pajahitvā ṭhitattā sabbappahāyinaṃ kathayanti.

In the first verse, in such phrases as ‘a sage in body,’ a sage in body is one by means of abandoning bodily misconduct. A sage in speech is one by means of abandoning verbal misconduct. A sage in mind is one by means of abandoning mental misconduct. A taintless sage is one by means of abandoning all unwholesome states. Accomplished in sagehood: one is accomplished in sagehood because, having known what is to be known, one is established in the fruit. They call him one who has abandoned all: because he stands having abandoned all the defilements, they call him one who has abandoned all.

Dutiyagāthāya [V 0.0138] ninhātapāpakanti yo ajjhattabahiddhasaṅkhāte sabbasmimpi āyatane ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇavasena uppattirahāni sabbapāpakāni maggañāṇena ninhāya dhovitvā ṭhitattā ninhātapāpakaṃ āhūti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Agāramajjhe vasantā agāramunino. Pabbajjupagatā anagāramunino. Tattha sekkhā sekkhamunino. Arahanto asekkhamunino. Paccekabuddhā paccekamunino. Sammāsambuddhā munimunino.

By the second verse, 'one who has washed away evil': this is the meaning to be understood. It refers to one who, in every sense sphere classified as internal and external, has washed away all evils with the knowledge of the path, making them devoid of arising in relation to internal and external objects, and thus stands purified. Those dwelling in a house are householder-sages. Those who have gone forth into homelessness are homeless-sages. Among them, trainees are trainee-sages. Arahants are non-trainee-sages. Paccekabuddhas are solitary-sages. Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddhas are the sage of sages.

Puna kathetukamyatāpucchāvasena “katame agāramunino”ti āha. Agārikāti kasigorakkhādiagārikakamme niyuttā. Diṭṭhapadāti diṭṭhanibbānā[M 0.0153]. Viññātasāsanāti viññātaṃ sikkhattayasāsanaṃ etesanti viññātasāsanā. Anagārāti kasigorakkhādiagāriyakammaṃ etesaṃ natthīti pabbajitā “anagārā”ti vuccanti. Satta sekkhāti sotāpannādayo satta. Tīsu sikkhāsu sikkhantīti sekkhā. Arahanto na sikkhantīti asekkhā. Taṃ taṃ kāraṇaṃ paṭicca ekakāva anācariyakāva catusaccaṃ bujjhitavantoti paccekabuddhā paccekamunino.

Again, out of a desire to speak further, he asks by way of a question: 'Who are the householder-sages?' 'Householders' are those engaged in household work such as agriculture and cattle-herding. 'They have seen the state' means they have seen Nibbāna. 'They have understood the teaching' means the teaching of the threefold training has been understood by them. 'Homeless ones': because they have no household work such as agriculture and cattle-herding, those who have gone forth are called 'homeless ones.' The 'seven trainees' are the stream-enterer and the other six. Because they train in the three trainings, they are 'trainees.' Arahants do not train, thus they are 'non-trainees.' Because, depending on this or that condition, they have awakened to the Four Noble Truths by themselves and without a teacher, paccekabuddhas are solitary sages.

Munimunino vuccanti tathāgatāti ettha aṭṭhahi kāraṇehi bhagavā tathāgato – tathā āgatoti tathāgato, tathā gatoti tathāgato, tathalakkhaṇaṃ āgatoti tathāgato, tathadhamme yāthāvato [P 1.0178] abhisambuddhoti tathāgato, tathadassitāya tathāgato, tathavāditāya tathāgato, tathākāritāya tathāgato, abhibhavanaṭṭhena tathāgatoti.

The Tathāgatas are called 'the sage of sages.' Herein, the Blessed One is the Tathāgata for eight reasons: because he has 'come thus'; because he has 'gone thus'; because he has arrived at the 'characteristic of suchness'; because he has 'perfectly awakened to the true Dhamma as it really is'; because he 'sees what is true'; because he 'speaks what is true'; because he 'acts in truth'; and in the sense of 'overcoming'.

Kathaṃ bhagavā tathā āgatoti tathāgato? Yathā sabbalokahitāya ussukkamāpannā purimakā sammāsambuddhā āgatā. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yenābhinīhārena purimakā bhagavanto āgatā, teneva amhākampi bhagavā āgato. Atha vā yathā purimakā bhagavanto dānasīlanekkhammapaññāvīriyakhantisaccādhiṭṭhānamettupekkhāsaṅkhātā dasa pāramiyo dasa upapāramiyo dasa paramatthapāramiyoti samatiṃsapāramiyo pūretvā aṅgapariccāgaṃ nayanadhanarajjaputtadārapariccāganti ime pañca mahāpariccāge pariccajitvā pubbayogapubbacariyadhammakkhānañātatthacariyādayo pūretvā buddhicariyāya koṭiṃ patvā āgatā, tathā amhākampi bhagavā āgato. Yathā ca purimakā bhagavanto cattāro satipaṭṭhāne, cattāro sammappadhāne, cattāro iddhipāde, pañcindriyāni, pañca balāni, satta bojjhaṅge, ariyaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ bhāvetvā pūretvā āgatā, tathā amhākampi bhagavā āgato. Evaṃ tathā āgatoti tathāgato.

How is the Blessed One the Tathāgata, one who has 'come thus'? Just as the previous Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddhas came, striving for the welfare of the whole world. What is meant? Our Blessed One has come with the very same aspiration with which the previous Blessed Ones came. Or, just as the previous Blessed Ones came—having fulfilled the thirty perfections (the ten perfections, the ten higher perfections, and the ten ultimate perfections); having made the five great sacrifices (the sacrifice of limbs, eyes, wealth, kingdom, and sons and wife); and having fulfilled former practices, former conduct, the declaration of the Dhamma, conduct for the benefit of relatives, and so on, thereby reaching the peak of the conduct of wisdom—so too has our Blessed One come. And just as the previous Blessed Ones came, having developed and fulfilled the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right strivings, the four bases of spiritual power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven enlightenment factors, and the Noble Eightfold Path, so too has our Blessed One come. In this way he is the Tathāgata, one who has 'come thus.'

“Yathā [V 0.0139] ca dīpaṅkarabuddhaādayo, sabbaññubhāvaṃ munayo idhāgatā;

Tathā ayaṃ sakyamunīpi āgato, tathāgato vuccati tena cakkhumā”ti.

Just as the Buddhas Dīpaṅkara and others, sages who came here having attained omniscience, so too has this Sakyan sage come; therefore the One with Vision is called the Tathāgata.

Kathaṃ [M 0.0154] tathā gatoti tathāgato? Yathā sampatijātā purimakā bhagavanto gatā. Kathañca te gatā? Te hi sampatijātā samehi pādehi pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhāya uttarābhimukhā sattapadavītihārena gatā. Yathāha –

How is he the Tathāgata, one who has 'gone thus'? Just as the previous Blessed Ones went immediately upon being born. And how did they go? Immediately upon being born, they stood firmly on the earth with even feet and went seven strides facing north. As it is said:

“Sampatijāto, ānanda, bodhisatto samehi pādehi pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhahitvā uttarābhimukho sattapadavītihārena gacchati, setamhi chatte anudhāriyamāne sabbā ca disā anuviloketi, āsabhiñca vācaṃ bhāsati – ‘aggohamasmi lokassa, jeṭṭhohamasmi lokassa, seṭṭhohamasmi lokassa, ayamantimā jāti, natthi dāni punabbhavo’”ti (dī. ni. 2.31; ma. ni. 3.207).

As soon as he is born, Ānanda, the Bodhisatta stands firmly with even feet on the earth and, facing north, takes seven strides. While a white parasol is held over him, he surveys all the quarters and utters a bull-like utterance: ‘I am the foremost in the world, I am the eldest in the world, I am the best in the world. This is my last birth; now there is no more renewed existence.’

Tañcassa gamanaṃ tathaṃ ahosi avitathaṃ anekesaṃ visesādhigamānaṃ [P 1.0179] pubbanimittabhāvena. Yañhi so sampatijāto samehi pādehi patiṭṭhāti, idamassa caturiddhipādapaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ. Uttaramukhabhāvo panassa sabbalokuttarabhāvassa pubbanimittaṃ. Sattapadavītihāro sattabojjhaṅgaratanapaṭilābhassa. “Suvaṇṇadaṇḍā vītipatanti cāmarā”ti (su. ni. 693) ettha vuttacāmarukkhepo pana sabbatitthiyanimmadanassa. Setacchattadhāraṇaṃ arahattavimuttivaravimalasetacchattapaṭilābhassa. Sabbadisānuvilokanaṃ sabbaññutānāvaraṇañāṇapaṭilābhassa. Āsabhivācābhāsanaṃ pana appaṭivattiyavaradhammacakkapavattanassa pubbanimittaṃ. Tathā ayaṃ bhagavāpi gato. Tañcassa gamanaṃ tathaṃ ahosi avitathaṃ tesaṃyeva visesādhigamānaṃ pubbanimittabhāvena. Tenāhu porāṇā –

And his going was true, not false, being a forerunner for the attainment of many special qualities. For his standing firmly with even feet just after birth was a forerunner for his attainment of the four bases for spiritual power. His facing north was a forerunner for his state of being supreme in all the world. The seven-step stride was a forerunner for his attainment of the seven jewel-like enlightenment factors. The tossing of the whisks, mentioned in the verse 'And whisks with golden handles wave,' was a forerunner for his crushing of all sectarians. The holding of the white parasol was a forerunner for his attainment of the excellent, immaculate white parasol of the liberation of arahantship. His surveying of all directions was a forerunner for his attainment of the unobstructed knowledge of omniscience. His uttering of the bull-like utterance was a forerunner for his setting in motion the excellent, irreversible Wheel of Dhamma. In this way this Blessed One also went. And his going was true, not false, being a forerunner for the attainment of those very same special qualities. Therefore the ancients have said:

“Muhuttajātova gavampatī yathā, samehi pādehi phusī vasundharaṃ;

So vikkamī satta padāni gotamo, setañca chattaṃ anudhārayuṃ marū.

Just as a lord of bulls, just born, touches the earth with even feet, so Gotama strode seven steps, while the Maruts held a white parasol aloft.

“Gantvāna so satta padāni gotamo, disā vilokesi samā samantato;

Aṭṭhaṅgupetaṃ giramabbhudīrayi, sīho yathā pabbatamuddhaniṭṭhito”ti. (paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 1.1.37; itivu. aṭṭha. 38);

Having gone seven steps, Gotama surveyed the directions all around. He uttered speech endowed with eight factors, like a lion standing on a mountain peak.

Evaṃ [V 0.0140][M 0.0155] tathā gatoti tathāgato.
