Thus, in the sense that he has 'gone thus,' he is the Tathāgata.

Atha vā yathā purimakā bhagavanto, ayampi bhagavā tatheva nekkhammena kāmacchandaṃ…pe… paṭhamajjhānena nīvaraṇe…pe… aniccānupassanāya niccasaññaṃ…pe… arahattamaggena sabbakilese pahāya gato, evampi tathā gatoti tathāgato.

Or else, just as the previous Blessed Ones went, so this Blessed One too has gone in the very same way: having abandoned sensual desire by means of renunciation... having abandoned the hindrances by means of the first jhāna... having abandoned the perception of permanence by means of the contemplation of impermanence... having abandoned all defilements by means of the path of arahantship. In this way too, in the sense that he has 'gone thus,' he is the Tathāgata.

Kathaṃ tathalakkhaṇaṃ āgatoti tathāgato? Pathavīdhātuyā kakkhaḷattalakkhaṇaṃ tathaṃ avitathaṃ, āpodhātuyā paggharaṇalakkhaṇaṃ, tejodhātuyā uṇhattalakkhaṇaṃ, vāyodhātuyā vitthambhanalakkhaṇaṃ, ākāsadhātuyā asamphuṭṭhalakkhaṇaṃ, viññāṇadhātuyā vijānanalakkhaṇaṃ.

How is he the Tathāgata as one who has arrived at the characteristic of suchness? The characteristic of hardness of the earth element is true, not otherwise; the characteristic of cohesion of the water element; the characteristic of heat of the fire element; the characteristic of distension of the wind element; the characteristic of being untouched of the space element; the characteristic of cognizing of the consciousness element.

Rūpassa [P 1.0180] ruppanalakkhaṇaṃ, vedanāya vedayitalakkhaṇaṃ, saññāya sañjānanalakkhaṇaṃ, saṅkhārānaṃ abhisaṅkharaṇalakkhaṇaṃ, viññāṇassa vijānanalakkhaṇaṃ.

The characteristic of material form is being afflicted; of feeling, being felt; of perception, perceiving; of formations, forming; of consciousness, cognizing.

Vitakkassa abhiniropanalakkhaṇaṃ, vicārassa anumajjanalakkhaṇaṃ, pītiyā pharaṇalakkhaṇaṃ, sukhassa sātalakkhaṇaṃ, cittekaggatāya avikkhepalakkhaṇaṃ, phassassa phusanalakkhaṇaṃ.

The characteristic of initial application is directing onto; of sustained application, continued examination; of rapture, pervading; of pleasure, gratification; of one-pointedness of mind, non-distraction; of contact, touching.

Saddhindriyassa adhimokkhalakkhaṇaṃ, vīriyindriyassa paggahalakkhaṇaṃ, satindriyassa upaṭṭhānalakkhaṇaṃ, samādhindriyassa avikkhepalakkhaṇaṃ, paññindriyassa pajānanalakkhaṇaṃ.

The characteristic of the faith faculty is resolving; of the energy faculty, exerting; of the mindfulness faculty, establishing; of the concentration faculty, non-distraction; of the wisdom faculty, understanding.

Saddhābalassa assaddhiye akampiyalakkhaṇaṃ, vīriyabalassa kosajje, satibalassa muṭṭhassacce, samādhibalassa uddhacce, paññābalassa avijjāya akampiyalakkhaṇaṃ.

The characteristic of the power of faith is being unshakable by faithlessness; of the power of energy, by laziness; of the power of mindfulness, by forgetfulness; of the power of concentration, by restlessness; of the power of wisdom, by ignorance.

Satisambojjhaṅgassa upaṭṭhānalakkhaṇaṃ, dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa pavicayalakkhaṇaṃ, vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa paggahalakkhaṇaṃ, pītisambojjhaṅgassa pharaṇalakkhaṇaṃ, passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa upasamalakkhaṇaṃ, samādhisambojjhaṅgassa avikkhepalakkhaṇaṃ, upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa paṭisaṅkhānalakkhaṇaṃ.

The characteristic of the mindfulness enlightenment factor is establishing; of the investigation-of-dhammas enlightenment factor, discerning; of the energy enlightenment factor, exertion; of the rapture enlightenment factor, pervading; of the tranquility enlightenment factor, pacification; of the concentration enlightenment factor, non-distraction; of the equanimity enlightenment factor, reflecting.

Sammādiṭṭhiyā dassanalakkhaṇaṃ, sammāsaṅkappassa abhiniropanalakkhaṇaṃ, sammāvācāya pariggahalakkhaṇaṃ, sammākammantassa samuṭṭhānalakkhaṇaṃ, sammāājīvassa vodānalakkhaṇaṃ, sammāvāyāmassa [V 0.0141] paggahalakkhaṇaṃ, sammāsatiyā upaṭṭhānalakkhaṇaṃ, sammāsamādhissa avikkhepalakkhaṇaṃ.

The characteristic of right view is seeing; of right intention, directing onto; of right speech, embracing; of right action, originating; of right livelihood, cleansing; of right effort, exerting; of right mindfulness, establishing; of right concentration, non-distraction.

Avijjāya [M 0.0156] aññāṇalakkhaṇaṃ, saṅkhārānaṃ cetanālakkhaṇaṃ, viññāṇassa vijānanalakkhaṇaṃ, nāmassa namanalakkhaṇaṃ, rūpassa ruppanalakkhaṇaṃ, saḷāyatanassa āyatanalakkhaṇaṃ, phassassa phusanalakkhaṇaṃ, vedanāya vedayitalakkhaṇaṃ, taṇhāya hetulakkhaṇaṃ, upādānassa gahaṇalakkhaṇaṃ, bhavassa āyūhanalakkhaṇaṃ, jātiyā nibbattilakkhaṇaṃ, jarāya jīraṇalakkhaṇaṃ, maraṇassa cutilakkhaṇaṃ.

The characteristic of ignorance is unknowing; of formations, volition; of consciousness, cognizing; of name, inclining; of form, being afflicted; of the sixfold sense base, being a sphere; of contact, touching; of feeling, being felt; of craving, being a cause; of clinging, grasping; of becoming, accumulating; of birth, generation; of aging, decaying; of death, passing away.

Dhātūnaṃ suññatalakkhaṇaṃ, āyatanānaṃ āyatanalakkhaṇaṃ, satipaṭṭhānānaṃ upaṭṭhānalakkhaṇaṃ, sammappadhānānaṃ padahanalakkhaṇaṃ, iddhipādānaṃ ijjhanalakkhaṇaṃ, indriyānaṃ adhipatilakkhaṇaṃ, balānaṃ akampiyalakkhaṇaṃ, bojjhaṅgānaṃ niyyānalakkhaṇaṃ, maggassa hetulakkhaṇaṃ.

The characteristic of the elements is emptiness. The characteristic of the bases is that of a base. The characteristic of the foundations of mindfulness is establishing. The characteristic of the right strivings is exertion. The characteristic of the bases for spiritual power is accomplishment. The characteristic of the faculties is sovereignty. The characteristic of the powers is unshakability. The characteristic of the factors of enlightenment is deliverance. The characteristic of the path is being a cause.

Saccānaṃ tathalakkhaṇaṃ, samathassa avikkhepalakkhaṇaṃ, vipassanāya anupassanālakkhaṇaṃ, samathavipassanānaṃ ekarasalakkhaṇaṃ, yuganaddhānaṃ anativattanalakkhaṇaṃ.

The characteristic of the truths is suchness. The characteristic of serenity is non-distraction. The characteristic of insight is contemplation. The characteristic of serenity and insight is a single function. The characteristic of their coupling is non-transgression.

Sīlavisuddhiyā saṃvaraṇalakkhaṇaṃ, cittavisuddhiyā avikkhepalakkhaṇaṃ, diṭṭhivisuddhiyā dassanalakkhaṇaṃ, khaye ñāṇassa samucchedalakkhaṇaṃ, anuppāde ñāṇassa passaddhilakkhaṇaṃ, chandassa mūlalakkhaṇaṃ.

The characteristic of the purification of virtue is restraint. The characteristic of the purification of mind is non-distraction. The characteristic of the purification of view is seeing. The characteristic of the knowledge of destruction is extirpation. The characteristic of the knowledge of non-arising is tranquility. The characteristic of zeal is being a root.

Manasikārassa samuṭṭhānalakkhaṇaṃ, phassassa [P 1.0181] samodhānalakkhaṇaṃ, vedanāya samosaraṇalakkhaṇaṃ, samādhissa pamukhalakkhaṇaṃ, satiyā ādhipateyyalakkhaṇaṃ, paññāya tatuttariyalakkhaṇaṃ, vimuttiyā sāralakkhaṇaṃ, amatogadhassa nibbānassa pariyosānalakkhaṇaṃ tathaṃ avitathaṃ, etaṃ tathalakkhaṇaṃ ñāṇagatiyā āgato avirajjhitvā patto anuppattoti tathāgato. Evaṃ tathalakkhaṇaṃ āgatoti tathāgato.

The characteristic of attention is originating. The characteristic of contact is confluence. The characteristic of feeling is convergence. The characteristic of concentration is being foremost. The characteristic of mindfulness is sovereignty. The characteristic of wisdom is its superiority. The characteristic of liberation is the essence. The characteristic of Nibbāna, the immersion in the Deathless, is consummation. This is so, not otherwise; this is the characteristic of suchness. Because he has come by way of knowledge and, without deviating, has attained what was to be attained, he is a Tathāgata. Thus, because he has come to the characteristic of suchness, he is a Tathāgata.

Kathaṃ tathadhamme yāthāvato abhisambuddhoti tathāgato? Tathadhammā nāma cattāri ariyasaccāni. Yathāha –

How is he a Tathāgata in the sense that he has perfectly awakened to the true Dhamma as it really is? The true Dhamma is the Four Noble Truths. As it is said:

“Cattārimāni, bhikkhave, tathāni avitathāni anaññathāni. Katamāni cattāri? ‘Idaṃ [V 0.0142] dukkha’nti, bhikkhave, tathametaṃ avitathametaṃ anaññathameta”nti vitthāro (saṃ. ni. 5.1090).

“Bhikkhus, these four things are actual, not unactual, not otherwise. What four? ‘This is suffering,’ bhikkhus, is actual, not unactual, not otherwise… (The full passage should be expanded here, as in SN 56.20).”

Tāni [M 0.0157] ca bhagavā abhisambuddhoti tathānaṃ abhisambuddhattā tathāgatoti vuccati. Abhisambuddhattho hi ettha gatasaddo.

And the Blessed One has perfectly awakened to these. Because he has perfectly awakened to these actualities, he is called a Tathāgata. For here the word gata has the meaning of ‘perfectly awakened.’

Api ca jarāmaraṇassa jātipaccayasambhūtasamudāgataṭṭho tatho avitatho anaññatho…pe… saṅkhārānaṃ avijjāpaccayasambhūtasamudāgataṭṭho tatho avitatho anaññatho. Tathā avijjāya saṅkhārānaṃ paccayaṭṭho…pe… jātiyā jarāmaraṇassa paccayaṭṭho tatho avitatho anaññatho. Taṃ sabbaṃ bhagavā abhisambuddho, tassāpi tathānaṃ abhisambuddhattā tathāgato. Evaṃ tathadhamme yāthāvato abhisambuddhoti tathāgato.

Furthermore, the fact that aging-and-death is produced and arisen from birth as its condition is actual, not unactual, not otherwise… and so on… the fact that volitional formations are produced and arisen from ignorance as their condition is actual, not unactual, not otherwise. Similarly, the fact that ignorance is a condition for volitional formations… and so on… the fact that birth is a condition for aging-and-death is actual, not unactual, not otherwise. The Blessed One has perfectly awakened to all this. Because he has perfectly awakened to these actualities, he is a Tathāgata. Thus he is a Tathāgata in the sense that he has perfectly awakened to the true Dhamma as it really is.

Kathaṃ tathadassitāya tathāgato? Bhagavā yaṃ sadevake loke…pe… sadevamanussāya pajāya aparimāṇāsu lokadhātūsu aparimāṇānaṃ sattānaṃ cakkhudvāre āpāthaṃ āgacchantaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ nāma atthi, taṃ sabbākārena jānāti passati. Evaṃ jānatā passatā ca tena taṃ iṭṭhāniṭṭhādivasena vā diṭṭhasutamutaviññātesu labbhamānakapadavasena vā “katamaṃ taṃ rūpaṃ rūpāyatanaṃ? Yaṃ rūpaṃ catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ upādāya vaṇṇanibhā sanidassanaṃ sappaṭighaṃ nīlaṃ pītaka”ntiādinā (dha. sa. 616) nayena anekehi nāmehi terasahi vārehi dvipaññāsāya nayehi vibhajjamānaṃ tathameva hoti, vitathaṃ natthi. Esa nayo sotadvārādīsupi āpāthamāgacchantesu [P 1.0182] saddādīsu. Vuttampi cetaṃ bhagavatā –

How is he a Tathāgata in the sense that he sees what is actual? Whatever form-object comes into the range of the eye-door of countless beings in countless world-systems—in this world with its gods… and so on… with its generation of gods and humans—the Blessed One knows and sees it in all its aspects. And as he thus knows and sees it, whether in terms of the desirable and undesirable, etc., or in terms of the items obtainable among things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized, it is just so; it is not unactual. It is analyzed by numerous terms, in thirteen sections, by fifty-two methods, as in the passage beginning: ‘What is that form, the form-base? That form which is derived from the four great elements, having color, visible and impinging, such as blue, yellow…’ (Dhs §616). This same method applies to sounds and other objects that come into the range of the ear-door and the other sense doors. And this was said by the Blessed One:

“Yaṃ, bhikkhave, sadevakassa lokassa…pe… sadevamanussāya pajāya diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ mutaṃ viññātaṃ pattaṃ pariyesitaṃ anuvicaritaṃ manasā, tamahaṃ jānāmi…pe… tamahaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ. Taṃ tathāgatassa viditaṃ, taṃ tathāgato na upaṭṭhāsī”ti (a. ni. 4.24).

“Bhikkhus, whatever in this world with its devas… and so on… with its generation of devas and humans, has been seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought, and mentally explored—that I know… that I have directly known. That is known to the Tathāgata, but the Tathāgata did not take a stand on it” (AN 4.24).

Evaṃ tathadassitāya tathāgato. Tattha tathadassīatthe tathāgatoti padasambhavo veditabbo.

Thus he is a Tathāgata in the sense that he sees what is actual. Here the formation of the word should be understood: Tathāgata in the sense of tathā-dassī, one who sees what is actual.

Kathaṃ tathavāditāya tathāgato? Yaṃ rattiṃ bhagavā bodhimaṇḍe aparājitapallaṅke nisinno catunnaṃ mārānaṃ matthakaṃ madditvā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddho, yañca rattiṃ yamakasālānamantare [V 0.0143] anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyi, etthantare pañcacattālīsavassaparimāṇe kāle [M 0.0158] paṭhamabodhiyampi majjhimabodhiyampi pacchimabodhiyampi yaṃ bhagavatā bhāsitaṃ suttaṃ geyyaṃ…pe… vedallaṃ. Sabbaṃ taṃ atthato byañjanato ca anupavajjaṃ anūnamanadhikaṃ sabbākāraparipuṇṇaṃ rāgamadanimmadanaṃ dosamohamadanimmadanaṃ, natthi tattha vālaggamattampi pakkhalitaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ ekamuddikāya lañchitaṃ viya, ekanāḷiyā mitaṃ viya, ekatulāya tulitaṃ viya ca tathameva hoti avitathaṃ anaññathaṃ. Yathāha –

How is he a Tathāgata in the sense that he speaks what is actual? During the interval of forty-five years—from the night when the Blessed One, sitting on the unconquerable seat at the site of awakening, crushed the heads of the four Māras and perfectly awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, to the night when he passed into the Nibbāna-element with no residue remaining between the twin sāl trees—whatever was spoken by the Blessed One in the first, middle, and last periods of his enlightenment, that is, suttas, mixed prose and verse… and so on… vedallas, all of it is faultless in meaning and phrasing, neither deficient nor excessive, complete in all respects, crushing the vanity of lust, hatred, and delusion. There is not even a hair’s tip of error in it. All of it is just so, not unactual, not otherwise, as if stamped with a single seal, measured with a single measure, or weighed with a single balance. As it is said:

“Yañca, cunda, rattiṃ tathāgato anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambujjhati, yañca rattiṃ anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyati, yaṃ etasmiṃ antare bhāsati lapati niddisati, sabbaṃ taṃ tatheva hoti no aññathā, tasmā ‘tathāgato’ti vuccatī”ti (dī. ni. 3.188).

“Cunda, in the interval between the night when the Tathāgata perfectly awakens to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment and the night when he passes away into the Nibbāna-element with no residue remaining, whatever he speaks, utters, and explains, all that is just so and not otherwise. Therefore he is called the ‘Tathāgata’” (DN 29).

Gadaattho hi ettha gatasaddo. Evaṃ tathavāditāya tathāgato.

For here the word gata has the meaning of ‘spoken.’ Thus he is a Tathāgata in the sense that he speaks what is actual.

Api ca āgadanaṃ āgado, vacananti attho. Tatho aviparīto āgado assāti dakārassa takāraṃ katvā tathāgatoti evametasmiṃ atthe padasiddhi veditabbā.

Furthermore, āgada means speaking; the meaning is ‘speech.’ The formation of the word Tathāgata in this sense should be understood thus: his speech (āgado) is actual (tatho) and not distorted, and the ‘d’ is changed to a ‘t’.

Kathaṃ tathākāritāya tathāgato? Bhagavato hi vācāya kāyo anulometi, kāyassāpi vācā. Tasmā yathāvādī tathākārī, yathākārī tathāvādī ca hoti. Evaṃbhūtassa cassa yathā vācā[P 1.0183], kāyopi tathā gato pavattoti attho. Yathā ca kāyo, vācāpi tathā gatā pavattāti tathāgato. Tenevāha – “yathāvādī, bhikkhave, tathāgato tathākārī, yathākārī tathāvādī. Iti yathāvādī tathākārī, yathākārī tathāvādī. ‘Tasmā tathāgato’ti vuccatī”ti (a. ni. 4.23). Evaṃ tathākāritāya tathāgato.

How is he a Tathāgata in the sense that he acts in accordance with his speech? The Blessed One’s body conforms to his speech, and his speech to his body. Therefore he is one who does as he says and says as he does. Being such, the meaning is that as his speech is, so (tathā) his body has gone (gato), that is, it proceeds. And as his body is, so (tathā) his speech has gone (gatā), that is, it proceeds; hence he is a Tathāgata. For this reason it is said: “Bhikkhus, as the Tathāgata says, so he does; as he does, so he says. Since he does as he says and says as he does, therefore he is called the ‘Tathāgata’” (AN 4.23). Thus he is a Tathāgata in the sense that he acts in accordance with his speech.

Kathaṃ abhibhavanaṭṭhena tathāgato? Upari bhavaggaṃ heṭṭhā avīciṃ pariyantaṃ katvā tiriyaṃ aparimāṇāsu lokadhātūsu sabbasatte abhibhavati sīlena samādhinā paññāya vimuttiyā vimuttiñāṇadassanena, na tassa tulā vā pamāṇaṃ vā atthi, atha kho atulo appameyyo anuttaro rājātirājā devānaṃ atidevo sakkānaṃ atisakko brahmānaṃ atibrahmā. Tenāha –

How is he a Tathāgata in the sense of overcoming? He overcomes all beings—up to the peak of existence above and down to the Avīci hell below, and across in the immeasurable world-systems—by his virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and knowledge and vision of liberation. There is no one who can equal or measure him. On the contrary, he is the incomparable, the immeasurable, the unsurpassed, the king of kings, the deva of devas, the Sakka of Sakkas, the Brahmā of Brahmās. For this reason it is said:

“Sadevake[M 0.0159], bhikkhave, loke…pe… sadevamanussāya pajāya tathāgato abhibhū anabhibhūto [V 0.0144] aññadatthudaso vasavattī, tasmā ‘tathāgato’ti vuccatī”ti (a. ni. 4.23).

“Bhikkhus, in this world with its devas… and so on… with its generation of devas and humans, the Tathāgata is the overcomer, the unovercome, the all-seeing, the wielder of power. Therefore he is called the ‘Tathāgata’” (AN 4.23).

Tatthevaṃ padasiddhi veditabbā – agado viya agado. Ko panesa? Desanāvilāso ceva puññussayo ca. Tena hesa mahānubhāvo bhisakko dibbāgadena sappe viya sabbaparappavādino sadevakañca lokaṃ abhibhavati. Iti sabbalokābhibhavane tatho aviparīto desanāvilāsamayo ceva puññamayo ca agado assāti dakārassa takāraṃ katvā tathāgatoti veditabbo. Evaṃ abhibhavanaṭṭhena tathāgato.

Here the formation of the word should be understood thus: he is an antidote (agado), like a medicine. What is this antidote? It is the grace of his teaching and his store of merit. For this great physician of great power, with his divine antidote, overcomes all the tenets of others and the world with its devas, just as a snake-charmer overcomes snakes. Thus, because in overcoming the whole world his antidote—which consists of the grace of his teaching and his merit—is actual (tatho) and not distorted, the word Tathāgata is to be understood by changing the ‘d’ to a ‘t’. Thus he is a Tathāgata in the sense of overcoming.

Api ca tathāya gatotipi tathāgato, tathaṃ gatotipi tathāgato. Gatoti avagato, atīto patto paṭipannoti attho. Tattha sakalaṃ lokaṃ tīraṇapariññāya tathāya gato avagatoti tathāgato, lokasamudayaṃ pahānapariññāya tathāya gato atītoti tathāgato, lokanirodhaṃ sacchikiriyāya tathāya gato pattoti tathāgato, lokanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ tathaṃ gato paṭipannoti tathāgato. Tena yaṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatā –

Furthermore, he is a Tathāgata because he has gone to the truth (tathāya gato), and because he has gone thus (tathaṃ gato). Here, ‘gone’ (gato) means understood, passed beyond, attained, and entered upon. In this regard: (1) he is a Tathāgata because, by the full understanding of scrutinizing, he has gone to the truth, that is, he has understood the entire world; (2) he is a Tathāgata because, by the full understanding of abandoning, he has gone to the truth, that is, he has passed beyond the origin of the world; (3) he is a Tathāgata because, by the full understanding of realization, he has gone to the truth, that is, he has attained the cessation of the world; (4) he is a Tathāgata because he has gone thus, that is, he has entered upon the path leading to the cessation of the world. Therefore, what was said by the Blessed One—

“Loko, bhikkhave, tathāgatena abhisambuddho, lokasmā tathāgato visaṃyutto. Lokasamudayo, bhikkhave, tathāgatena abhisambuddho, lokasamudayo tathāgatassa pahīno. Lokanirodho, bhikkhave, tathāgatena abhisambuddho, lokanirodho tathāgatassa sacchikato. Lokanirodhagāminī [P 1.0184] paṭipadā, bhikkhave, tathāgatena abhisambuddhā, lokanirodhagāminī paṭipadā tathāgatassa bhāvitā. Yaṃ, bhikkhave, sadevakassa lokassa…pe… anuvicaritaṃ manasā, sabbaṃ taṃ tathāgatena abhisambuddhaṃ. Tasmā ‘tathāgato’ti vuccatī”ti (a. ni. 4.23).

“Bhikkhus, the world has been fully understood by the Tathāgata; from the world the Tathāgata is disengaged. Bhikkhus, the origin of the world has been fully understood by the Tathāgata; the origin of the world has been abandoned by the Tathāgata. Bhikkhus, the cessation of the world has been fully understood by the Tathāgata; the cessation of the world has been realized by the Tathāgata. Bhikkhus, the path leading to the cessation of the world has been fully understood by the Tathāgata; the path leading to the cessation of the world has been developed by the Tathāgata. Whatever, bhikkhus, in this world with its devas… pondered over by the mind, all that has been fully understood by the Tathāgata. That is why he is called the ‘Tathāgata.’” (AN 4.23)

Tassa [M 0.0160] evampi attho veditabbo. Idampi ca tathāgatassa tathāgatabhāvadīpena mukhamattameva. Sabbākārena pana tathāgatova tathāgatassa tathāgatabhāvaṃ vaṇṇeyya. Yasmā pana sabbabuddhā tathāgataguṇenāpi samasamā, tasmā sabbesaṃ vasena “tathāgatā”ti āha.

This meaning should also be understood in this way. And this is just a mere glimpse of the Tathāgata’s state as a Tathāgata, shown by the light of that state. Only a Tathāgata could describe in all its aspects the Tathāgata’s state as a Tathāgata. But since all Buddhas are perfectly equal in the qualities of a Tathāgata, he therefore spoke of “Tathāgatas” with reference to them all.

Arahantoti kilesehi ārakattā, arīnaṃ arānañca hatattā, paccayādīnaṃ arahattā, pāpakaraṇe rahābhāvā tathāgato arahaṃ. Ārakā hi so sabbakilesehi suvidūravidūre ṭhito maggena savāsanānaṃ kilesānaṃ viddhaṃsitattāti ārakattā arahaṃ.

The Tathāgata is an Arahant because he is far (ārakattā) from the defilements, because he has destroyed (hatattā) the enemies (ari) and the spokes (ara), because he is worthy (arahattā) of requisites and so on, and because of the absence of secret (raha) evil-doing. For he stands far, very far from all defilements, having destroyed by the path the defilements along with their latent dispositions; thus he is an Arahant because he is far (ārakattā).

“So [V 0.0145] tato ārakā nāma, yassa yenāsamaṅgitā;

Asamaṅgī ca dosehi, nātho tenārahaṃ mato”.

“He is called ‘far’ from that with which he is unassociated; and since he is unassociated with faults, the Protector is for that reason deemed an Arahant.”

Te cānena kilesārayo maggena hatāti arīnaṃ hatattāpi arahaṃ.

And since he has destroyed by the path those enemies, the defilements, he is also an Arahant because the enemies have been destroyed.

“Yasmā rāgādisaṅkhātā, sabbepi arayo hatā;

Paññāsatthena nāthena, tasmāpi arahaṃ mato”.

“Because all enemies, designated as lust and so on, have been slain by the Protector with the sword of wisdom, for that reason too he is deemed an ‘Arahant.’”

Yañcetaṃ avijjābhavataṇhāmayanābhiṃ puññādiabhisaṅkhārānaṃ jarāmaraṇanemiṃ āsavasamudayamayena akkhena vijjhitvā tibhavarathe samāyojitaṃ anādikālappavattaṃ saṃsāracakkaṃ, tassānena bodhimaṇḍe vīriyapādehi sīlapathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhāya saddhāhatthena kammakkhayakaraṃ ñāṇapharasuṃ gahetvā sabbe arā hatāti arahaṃ.

There is the wheel of saṃsāra, which has been turning since beginningless time. It is yoked to the chariot of the three kinds of existence, fitted with an axle made of the origin of the taints, with a nave of ignorance and craving for existence, and a rim of aging and death. At the site of enlightenment, standing on the ground of virtue with the feet of energy, he took up with the hand of faith the axe of knowledge that brings about the destruction of kamma and with it destroyed all the spokes of that wheel—the meritorious and other formations. Because he has destroyed the spokes (arā), he is an Arahant.

“Arā saṃsāracakkassa, hatā ñāṇāsinā yato;

Lokanāthena tenesa, ‘araha’nti pavuccati”.

“Since the spokes of saṃsāra’s wheel have been destroyed by the Protector of the World with the sword of knowledge, for that reason he is called an ‘Arahant.’”

Aggadakkhiṇeyyattā [P 1.0185] ca cīvarādipaccaye arahati pūjāvisesañca, teneva ca uppanne tathāgate ye keci mahesakkhā devamanussā, na te aññattha pūjaṃ karonti. Tathā hi brahmā sahampati sinerumattena ratanadāmena tathāgataṃ pūjesi, yathābalañca aññe devā ca manussā ca bimbisārakosalarājādayo. Parinibbutampi ca bhagavantaṃ uddissa channavutikoṭidhanaṃ vissajjetvā asokamahārājā sakalajambudīpe caturāsītivihārasahassāni patiṭṭhāpesi. Ko pana vādo aññesaṃ pūjāvisesānanti paccayādīnaṃ arahattāpi arahaṃ.

Because he is the foremost recipient of offerings, he is worthy of requisites such as robes, and of special veneration. For that very reason, when a Tathāgata has arisen, whatever devas and humans of great power there are, they do not make offerings elsewhere. Indeed, Brahmā Sahampati worshipped the Tathāgata with a jeweled garland the size of Mount Sineru, and other devas and humans, such as King Bimbisāra and the king of Kosala, did so according to their ability. And even after the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna, having spent ninety-six crores of wealth in his honor, the great King Asoka established eighty-four thousand monasteries throughout all of Jambudīpa. What need be said of other special acts of veneration? Thus, because he is worthy of requisites and so on, he is an Arahant.

“Pūjāvisesaṃ [M 0.0161] saha paccayehi, yasmā ayaṃ arahati lokanātho;

Atthānurūpaṃ arahanti loke, tasmā jino arahati nāmametaṃ”.

“Because the Protector of the World is worthy of special veneration along with requisites, and is worthy in the world in a way that befits his attainment, therefore the Conqueror is worthy of this name.”

Yathā ca loke ye keci paṇḍitamānino bālā asilokabhayena raho pāpaṃ karonti, evamesa na kadāci pāpaṃ karotīti pāpakaraṇe rahābhāvatopi arahaṃ.

Just as in the world some fools who fancy themselves wise commit evil in secret out of fear of a bad reputation, this one never commits evil. Thus, because of the absence of any secret evil-doing, he is also an Arahant.

“Yasmā natthi raho nāma, pāpakammesu tādino;

Rahābhāvena tenesa, arahaṃ iti vissuto”.

“Because for the Such-like One in evil deeds there is no such thing as secrecy; for that absence of secrecy he is renowned as an ‘Arahant.’”

Evaṃ [V 0.0146] sabbathāpi –

Thus, in all ways:

“Ārakattā hatattā ca, kilesārīna so muni;

Hatasaṃsāracakkāro, paccayādīna cāraho;

Na raho karoti pāpāni, arahaṃ tena vuccatī”ti.

“Because he is far, and has destroyed the enemies that are the defilements, that sage; has destroyed the spokes of saṃsāra’s wheel, and is worthy of requisites and so on; he does no evil deeds in secret: for these reasons he is called an ‘Arahant.’”

Yasmā pana sabbe buddhā arahattaguṇenāpi samasamā, tasmā sabbesampi vasena “arahanto”ti āha. Sammāsambuddhāti sammā sāmañca sabbadhammānaṃ buddhattā sammāsambuddho. Tathā hesa sabbadhamme sammāsambuddho, abhiññeyye dhamme abhiññeyyato, pariññeyye dhamme pariññeyyato, pahātabbe dhamme pahātabbato, sacchikātabbe dhamme sacchikātabbato, bhāvetabbe dhamme bhāvetabbato. Tenevāha –

Moreover, since all Buddhas are perfectly equal in the quality of Arahantship, he therefore spoke of “Arahants” with reference to them all. A Perfectly Self-Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) is one who is perfectly self-enlightened because he has understood all things rightly and by himself. Indeed, he has perfectly understood all things: he has directly known those things that are to be directly known; he has fully understood those things that are to be fully understood; he has abandoned those things that are to be abandoned; he has realized those things that are to be realized; and he has developed those things that are to be developed. Therefore it was said:

“Abhiññeyyaṃ [P 1.0186] abhiññātaṃ, bhāvetabbañca bhāvitaṃ;

Pahātabbaṃ pahīnaṃ me, tasmā buddhosmi brāhmaṇā”ti. (su. ni. 563; ma. ni. 2.399);

“What was to be directly known, I have directly known; what was to be developed, I have developed; what was to be abandoned, I have abandoned; therefore, brahmin, I am a Buddha.” (Snp 563; MN 92)

Atha vā cakkhu dukkhasaccaṃ, tassa mūlakāraṇabhāvena samuṭṭhāpikā purimataṇhā samudayasaccaṃ, ubhinnaṃ appavatti nirodhasaccaṃ, nirodhapajānanā paṭipadā maggasaccanti evaṃ ekekapaduddhārenāpi sabbadhamme sammā sāmañca buddho. Esa nayo sotaghānajivhākāyamanesu. Eteneva ca nayena rūpādīni cha āyatanāni, cakkhuviññāṇādayo cha viññāṇakāyā, cakkhusamphassādayo cha phassā, cakkhusamphassajā vedanādayo cha vedanā, rūpasaññādayo [M 0.0162] cha saññā, rūpasañcetanādayo cha cetanā, rūpataṇhādayo cha taṇhākāyā, rūpavitakkādayo cha vitakkā, rūpavicārādayo cha vicārā, rūpakkhandhādayo pañcakkhandhā, dasa kasiṇāni, dasa anussatiyo, uddhumātakasaññādivasena dasa saññā, kesādayo dvattiṃsākārā, dvādasāyatanāni, aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo, kāmabhavādayo nava bhavā, paṭhamādīni cattāri jhānāni, mettābhāvanādayo catasso appamaññāyo, catasso arūpasamāpattiyo, paṭilomato jarāmaraṇādīni, anulomato avijjādīni paṭiccasamuppādaṅgāni ca yojetabbāni.

Alternatively, the eye is the truth of suffering; the preceding craving that is its root cause is the truth of origin; the non-occurrence of both is the truth of cessation; and the path that is the understanding of cessation is the truth of the path. Thus, by analyzing each term, he understood all phenomena rightly and by himself. This same method applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. In the same way, the following should be connected accordingly: the six sense bases such as form; the six classes of consciousness such as eye-consciousness; the six contacts such as eye-contact; the six kinds of feeling such as feeling born of eye-contact; the six kinds of perception such as perception of form; the six kinds of volition such as volition regarding form; the six bodies of craving such as craving for forms; the six kinds of thought such as thought about forms; the six kinds of examination such as examination of forms; the five aggregates such as the form aggregate; the ten kasiṇas; the ten recollections; the ten perceptions such as the perception of a bloated corpse; the thirty-two parts of the body; the twelve sense bases; the eighteen elements; the nine kinds of existence such as existence in the sensual realm; the four jhānas beginning with the first; the four immeasurables such as the development of loving-kindness; the four formless attainments; and the links of dependent origination in reverse order beginning with aging-and-death, and in forward order beginning with ignorance.

Tatrāyaṃ ekapadayojanā – jarāmaraṇaṃ dukkhasaccaṃ, jāti samudayasaccaṃ, ubhinnaṃ nissaraṇaṃ nirodhasaccaṃ, nirodhapajānanā paṭipadā maggasaccanti evaṃ ekekapaduddhārena sabbadhamme sammā sāmañca [V 0.0147] buddho anubuddho paṭividdho. Yaṃ vā pana kiñci atthi neyyaṃ nāma, sabbassa sammā sambuddhattā vimokkhantikañāṇavasena sammāsambuddho. Tesaṃ pana vibhāgo upari āvi bhavissati. Yasmā pana sabbabuddhā sammāsambuddhaguṇenāpi samasamā, tasmā sabbesampi vasena “sammāsambuddhā”ti āha.

Herein, this is the application of single terms: aging-and-death is the truth of suffering, birth is the truth of origin, the escape from both is the truth of cessation, and the path that is the understanding of cessation is the truth of the path. Thus, by analyzing each term, he understood, sequentially understood, and penetrated all phenomena rightly and by himself. Or, whatever is knowable, because he has perfectly understood it all by means of the knowledge that culminates in deliverance, he is a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. The analysis of these will become clear below. And since all Buddhas are perfectly equal in the quality of being a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, he therefore spoke of “Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones” with reference to them all.

Monenāti kāmañhi moneyyapaṭipadāsaṅkhātena maggañāṇamonena muni nāma hoti, idha pana tuṇhībhāvaṃ sandhāya “na monenā”ti vuttaṃ. Mūḷharūpoti tuccharūpo. Aviddasūti [P 1.0187] aviññū. Evarūpo hi tuṇhībhūtopi muni nāma na hoti. Atha vā moneyyamuni nāma na hoti, tucchabhāvo ca pana aññāṇī ca hotīti attho. Yo ca tulaṃva paggayhāti yathā hi tulaṃ gahetvā ṭhito atirekaṃ ce hoti, harati, ūnaṃ ce hoti, pakkhipati; evameva so atirekaṃ haranto viya pāpaṃ harati parivajjeti, ūnake pakkhipanto viya kusalaṃ paripūreti. Evañca pana karonto sīlasamādhipaññāvimuttivimuttiñāṇadassanasaṅkhātaṃ varaṃ uttamameva ādāya pāpāni akusalakammāni parivajjeti sa muni nāmāti attho. Tena so munīti kasmā pana so munīti ce? Yaṃ heṭṭhā vuttakāraṇaṃ, tena so munīti attho. Yo munāti ubho loketi yo puggalo imasmiṃ khandhādiloke tulaṃ āropetvā minanto viya “ime ajjhattikā khandhā, ime bāhirā”tiādinā nayena ime [M 0.0163] ubho atthe munāti. Muni tena pavuccatīti tena pana kāraṇena “munī”ti vuccatiyevāti attho.

Regarding 'by sagacity': it is true that one becomes a sage (muni) by the sagacity of the knowledge of the path, designated as the practice of sagacity. Here, however, 'not by sagacity' is said with reference to mere silence. 'Of deluded form' means of base form. 'Unlearned' means unwise. For such a one, even if silent, is not called a sage. Or else, he is not called a sage through sagacity, but is of base nature and ignorant—this is the meaning. As for 'he who, having taken up the scale': just as one standing holding a scale removes any excess and adds to any deficiency, so too he removes and avoids evil as if taking away an excess, and fulfills the wholesome as if adding to a deficiency. And in so doing, having taken up what is excellent and supreme—namely, virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—he avoids evil, unwholesome deeds. He is a sage—this is the meaning. As for 'by that he is a sage': if it is asked, 'Why then is he a sage?' It is because of the reason stated below—this is the meaning. As for 'He who knows both worlds': this means a person who knows both these aspects in this world of aggregates, etc., as if weighing them on a scale, in the way beginning: 'These are the internal aggregates, these are the external.' As for 'by that he is called a sage': the meaning is that for that very reason he is indeed called a 'sage.'

Asatañcāti gāthāya ayaṃ saṅkhepattho – yvāyaṃ akusalakusalappabhedo, asatañca satañca dhammo, taṃ “ajjhattaṃ bahiddhā”ti imasmiṃ sabbaloke pavicayañāṇena asatañca satañca ñatvā dhammaṃ. Tassa ñātattā eva, rāgādibhedato sattavidhaṃ saṅgaṃ taṇhādiṭṭhibhedato duvidhaṃ jālañca aticca atikkamitvā ṭhito, so tena monasaṅkhātena pavicayañāṇena samannāgatattā muni. Devamanussehi pūjitoti idaṃ panassa thutivacanaṃ. So hi khīṇāsavamunittā devamanussānaṃ pūjāraho hoti, tasmā evaṃ vuttoti.

This is the summary meaning of the verse beginning 'And the bad…': Having known that dhamma—the bad and the good, the distinction between the unwholesome and the wholesome—internally and externally in this whole world with the knowledge of investigation. Just because of having known that, having gone beyond and overcome the sevenfold attachment distinguished as lust, etc., and the twofold net distinguished as craving and views, he stands transcendent. He is a sage because he is endowed with that knowledge of investigation called sagacity. As for 'honored by devas and humans,' this is a statement in praise of him. For, being a sage whose taints are destroyed, he is worthy of honor by devas and humans; therefore it is said thus.

Sallanti mūlapadaṃ. Satta sallānīti gaṇanaparicchedo. Rāgasallanti rañjanaṭṭhena rāgo ca pīḷājanakatāya antotudanatāya dunnīharaṇatāya sallañcāti rāgasallaṃ. Dosasallādīsupi eseva nayo. Abbūḷhasalloti mūlapadaṃ. Abbahitasalloti nīhaṭasallo. Uddhatasalloti uddhaṃ haṭasallo uddharitasallo. Samuddhatasalloti upasaggavasena vutto. Uppāṭitasalloti luñcitasallo. Samuppāṭitasalloti upasaggavaseneva.

'Dart' is the root term. 'Seven darts': this is an enumeration. 'The dart of lust': it is lust in the sense of attachment, and a dart in the sense of causing affliction, of piercing within, and of being difficult to extract; thus it is the dart of lust. The same method applies to 'the dart of hatred' and so on. 'With dart unextracted' is the root term. 'With dart pulled out' means one whose dart has been removed. 'With dart extracted' means one whose dart has been drawn out, whose dart has been extracted. 'With dart thoroughly extracted' is stated with a prefix. 'With dart uprooted' means one whose dart has been torn out. 'With dart thoroughly uprooted' is likewise stated with a prefix.

Sakkaccakārīti [V 0.0148][P 1.0188] dānādīnaṃ kusaladhammānaṃ bhāvanāya puggalassa vā deyyadhammassa vā sakkaccakaraṇavasena sakkaccakārī. Satatabhāvakaraṇena sātaccakārī. Aṭṭhitakaraṇena aṭṭhitakārī. Yathā nāma kakaṇṭako thokaṃ gantvā thokaṃ tiṭṭhati, na nirantaraṃ gacchati; evameva yo puggalo ekadivasaṃ dānaṃ datvā pūjaṃ vā katvā dhammaṃ vā sutvā samaṇadhammaṃ vā katvā puna cirassaṃ karoti, taṃ na nirantaraṃ pavatteti. So “asātaccakārī, anaṭṭhitakārī”ti vuccati. Ayaṃ evaṃ na karotīti aṭṭhitakārī. Anolīnavuttikoti nirantarakaraṇasaṅkhātassa vipphārassa bhāvena na līnavuttikoti anolīnavuttiko. Anikkhittacchandoti kusalakaraṇe vīriyacchandassa anikkhittabhāvena anikkhittacchando. Anikkhittadhuroti vīriyadhurassa anoropanena anikkhittadhuro, anosakkitamānasoti attho. Yo tattha chando ca vāyāmo cāti yo tesu kusaladhammesu kattukamyatādhammacchando ca payattasaṅkhāto vāyāmo ca. Ussahanavasena [M 0.0164] ussāho ca. Adhimattussahanavasena ussoḷhī ca. Vāyāmo ceso pāraṃ gamanaṭṭhena. Ussāho ceso pubbaṅgamanaṭṭhena. Ussoḷhī ceso adhimattaṭṭhena. Appaṭivāni cāti anivattanā ca. Sati ca sampajaññanti saratīti sati. Sampajānātīti sampajaññaṃ, samantato pakārehi jānātīti attho. Sātthakasampajaññaṃ sappāyasampajaññaṃ gocarasampajaññaṃ asammohasampajaññanti imassa sampajānassa vasena bhedo veditabbo. Ātappanti kilesatāpanavīriyaṃ. Padhānanti uttamavīriyaṃ. Adhiṭṭhānanti kusalakaraṇe patiṭṭhābhāvo. Anuyogoti anuyuñjanaṃ. Appamādoti nappamajjanaṃ, satiyā avippavāso.

One who acts carefully: One is 'one who acts carefully' on account of acting carefully in the development of wholesome states such as giving, with respect to either the person or the gift. On account of acting with constancy, one is 'one who acts constantly.' On account of acting persistently, one is 'one who acts persistently.' Just as a chameleon walks a little and stops a little, not proceeding continuously, so too, a person who gives a gift, or makes an offering, or listens to the Dhamma, or undertakes the ascetic's duties for one day and then does so again only after a long time, does not maintain it continuously. He is called 'one who does not act constantly, one who does not act persistently.' This one does not act in such a way; thus he is 'one who acts persistently.' 'Of resolute conduct': one is 'of resolute conduct' because one's conduct is not sluggish, owing to the expansion of continuous practice. 'Not having thrown off the desire': one is 'one not having thrown off the desire' because one has not thrown off the desire for exertion in doing what is wholesome. 'Not having laid down the yoke': one is 'one not having laid down the yoke' because one has not set down the yoke of energy; the meaning is that one's mind has not shrunk back. 'The desire and effort therein': this is the desire for the state of wanting to do those wholesome states, and the effort defined as exertion. And 'endeavor' on account of striving. And 'exertion' on account of intense striving. This 'effort' is in the sense of going to the far shore. This 'endeavor' is in the sense of going foremost. This 'exertion' is in the sense of what is intense. And 'unrelenting' is non-turning back. And 'mindfulness and clear comprehension': 'one remembers,' thus 'mindfulness'; 'one clearly comprehends,' thus 'clear comprehension,' the meaning is that one knows in all ways, from every side. The distinction of this clear comprehension should be understood by way of clear comprehension of purpose, clear comprehension of suitability, clear comprehension of the resort, and clear comprehension of non-delusion. 'Ardor' is the energy that scorches the defilements. 'Striving' is supreme energy. 'Determination' is the state of being established in doing what is wholesome. 'Application' is devotion. 'Heedfulness' is non-negligence, the non-absence of mindfulness.

Imaṃ lokaṃ nāsīsatīti mūlapadaṃ. Sakattabhāvanti attano attabhāvaṃ. Parattabhāvanti paraloke attabhāvaṃ. Sakarūpavedanādayo attano pañcakkhandhe, pararūpavedanādayo ca paraloke pañcakkhandhe. Kāmadhātunti kāmabhavaṃ. Rūpadhātunti rūpabhavaṃ. Arūpadhātunti arūpabhavaṃ. Puna rūpārūpavasena dukaṃ [P 1.0189] dassetuṃ kāmadhātuṃ rūpadhātuṃ ekaṃ katvā, arūpadhātuṃ ekaṃ katvā vuttaṃ. Gatiṃ vāti patiṭṭhānavasena pañcagati vuttā. Upapattiṃ vāti nibbattivasena catuyoni vuttā. Paṭisandhiṃ vāti tiṇṇaṃ bhavānaṃ ghaṭanavasena paṭisandhi vuttā. Bhavaṃ vāti kammabhavavasena. Saṃsāraṃ vāti khandhādīnaṃ abbocchinnavasena. Vaṭṭaṃ vāti tebhūmakavaṭṭaṃ nāsīsatīti.

'He does not hope for this world' is the root phrase. 'One's own existence' means one's own individual existence. 'Another's existence' means individual existence in another world. One's own form, feeling, etc., are one's own five aggregates; another's form, feeling, etc., are the five aggregates in another world. 'The sense-sphere realm' means the sense-sphere existence. 'The form realm' means the form existence. 'The formless realm' means the formless existence. Again, to show the pair by way of form and formless, it is stated after making the sense-sphere realm and the form realm one, and the formless realm one. Or 'destination': the five destinations are stated on account of being a footing. Or 'rebirth': the four modes of generation are stated on account of arising. Or 're-linking consciousness': re-linking consciousness is stated on account of connecting the three kinds of existence. Or 'existence': on account of kamma-existence. Or 'saṃsāra': on account of the uninterruptedness of the aggregates, etc. Or 'the round': he does not hope for the round of the three planes.

Saddhammappajjotikāya mahāniddesaṭṭhakathāya

In the Saddhammappajjotikā, the Commentary on the Mahāniddesa.

Guhaṭṭhakasuttaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Niddesa on the Guhaṭṭhaka Sutta is concluded.

3. Duṭṭhaṭṭhakasuttaniddesavaṇṇanā

3. The Explanation of the Niddesa on the Duṭṭhaṭṭhaka Sutta

15. Duṭṭhaṭṭhake [V 0.0149][P 1.0190] paṭhamagāthāyaṃ tāva tattha vadantīti bhagavantaṃ bhikkhusaṅghañca upavadanti. Duṭṭhamanāpi eke, athopi ve saccamanāti ekacce duṭṭhacittā, ekacce tathasaññinopi hutvā titthiyā tuṭṭhacittā, ye tesaṃ sutvā saddahiṃsu, te saccamanāti adhippāyo. Vādañca jātanti etaṃ akkosavādaṃ uppannaṃ. Muni no upetīti akārakatāya ca akuppanatāya ca buddhamuni na upeti. Tasmā munī natthi khilo kuhiñcīti tena kāraṇena ayaṃ muni, rāgādikhilehi natthi khilo kuhiñcīti veditabbo.

15. In the first verse of the Duṭṭhaṭṭhaka: 'They speak there': they disparage the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. 'Some with corrupt minds, and others truly with truthful minds': some have corrupt minds; others, though perceiving it as so, are sectarians with pleased minds; the intention is that those who heard them and gained faith are 'with truthful minds.' 'And a dispute has arisen': this abusive dispute has arisen. 'The sage does not get involved': the sage, the Buddha, does not get involved because he is not the agent and is imperturbable. 'Therefore for the sage there is no barrenness anywhere': for that reason, it should be understood that this sage has no barrenness anywhere on account of the barrenness of lust, etc.

Duṭṭhamanāti [M 0.0165] uppannehi dosehi dūsitacittā. Viruddhamanāti tehi kilesehi kusalassa dvāraṃ adatvā āvaritacittā. Paṭiviruddhamanāti upasaggavasena padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ. Āhatamanāti paṭighena āhataṃ cittaṃ etesanti āhatamanā. Paccāhatamanāti upasaggavaseneva. Āghātitamanāti vihiṃsāvasena āghātitaṃ manaṃ etesanti āghātitamanā. Paccāghātitamanāti upasaggavaseneva. Atha vā “kodhavasena duṭṭhamanā, upanāhavasena paduṭṭhamanā, makkhavasena viruddhamanā, paḷāsavasena paṭiviruddhamanā, dosavasena āhatapaccāhatamanā, byāpādavasena āghātitapaccāghātitamanā. Paccayānaṃ alābhena duṭṭhamanā paduṭṭhamanā, ayasena viruddhamanā paṭiviruddhamanā, garahena āhatapaccāhatamanā, dukkhavedanāsamaṅgībhāvena āghātitapaccāghātitamanā”ti evamādinā nayena eke vaṇṇayanti. Upavadantīti garahaṃ uppādenti. Abhūtenāti asaṃvijjamānena.

'With corrupt minds' means with minds corrupted by arisen hatred. 'With opposed minds' means with minds obstructed, not having given an opening to the wholesome because of those defilements. 'With thoroughly opposed minds': the word is augmented by a prefix. 'With afflicted minds': they are 'with afflicted minds' because their minds are afflicted by aversion. 'With thoroughly afflicted minds': likewise by way of a prefix. 'With hateful minds': they are 'with hateful minds' because their minds are filled with hate on account of cruelty. 'With thoroughly hateful minds': likewise by way of a prefix. Alternatively, some explain thus: 'with corrupt minds' on account of anger, 'with depraved minds' on account of malice, 'with opposed minds' on account of contempt, 'with thoroughly opposed minds' on account of spite, 'with afflicted and thoroughly afflicted minds' on account of hatred, 'with hateful and thoroughly hateful minds' on account of ill will. Or: 'with corrupt and depraved minds' from not obtaining requisites; 'with opposed and thoroughly opposed minds' from disrepute; 'with afflicted and thoroughly afflicted minds' from censure; 'with hateful and thoroughly hateful minds' from being endowed with painful feeling. 'They disparage' means they generate censure. 'With what is not factual' means with what is non-existent.

Saddahantāti pasādavasena saddhaṃ uppādentā. Okappentāti [P 1.0191] guṇavasena otaritvā avakappayantā. Adhimuccantāti sampasādanavasena sanniṭṭhānaṃ katvā tesaṃ kathaṃ adhivāsentā. Saccamanāti tacchamanā. Saccasaññinoti tacchasaññino. Tathamanāti aviparītamanā. Bhūtamanāti bhūtatthamanā. Yāthāvamanāti niccalamanā. Aviparītamanāti nicchayamanā. Tattha “saccamanā [V 0.0150] saccasaññino”ti saccavādiguṇaṃ, “tathamanā tathasaññino”ti saccasaddhāguṇaṃ, “bhūtamanā bhūtasaññino”ti ṭhitaguṇaṃ, “yāthāvamanā yāthāvasaññino”ti paccayikaguṇaṃ, “aviparītamanā aviparītasaññino”ti avisaṃvādaguṇaṃ kathitanti ñātabbaṃ.

'They have faith' means generating faith on account of confidence. 'They place trust' means having entered into it by way of virtue, they form a conviction. 'They are resolved' means having made a firm decision on account of serene confidence, they assent to their talk. 'With truthful minds' means with genuine minds. 'Perceiving truth' means perceiving what is genuine. 'With minds on what is so' means with non-perverted minds. 'With minds on what is factual' means with minds on the factual meaning. 'With minds on what is as it is' means with unwavering minds. 'With non-perverted minds' means with minds of certainty. Herein, it should be known that by 'with truthful minds, perceiving truth,' the quality of speaking truth is stated; by 'with minds on what is so, perceiving what is so,' the quality of true faith is stated; by 'with minds on what is factual, perceiving what is factual,' the quality of steadfastness is stated; by 'with minds on what is as it is, perceiving what is as it is,' the quality of being trustworthy is stated; by 'with non-perverted minds, perceiving without perversion,' the quality of being non-deceptive is stated.

Paratoghosoti aññesaṃ santikā uppannasaddo. Akkosoti jātiādīsu dasasu akkosesu aññataro. Yo vādaṃ upetīti yo puggalo upavādaṃ upagacchati. Kārako vāti katadoso vā. Kārakatāyāti dosassa katabhāvena vuccamānoti kathiyamāno. Upavadiyamānoti dosaṃ upavajjamāno. Kuppatīti kopaṃ karoti.

'A sound from another' means a sound that has arisen from others. 'Abuse' means one of the ten grounds for abuse, such as birth, etc. 'One who gets involved in a dispute' means a person who takes up a disparaging statement. Or 'as the agent' means or as one who has committed a fault. 'Because of being the agent' means being spoken of, being described, on account of being the one who has done the fault. 'Being disparaged' means being reproached with a fault. 'He becomes perturbed' means he gets angry.

Khīlajātatāpi [M 0.0166] natthīti cittabandhabhāvacittakacavarabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ paṭighakhilaṃ jātaṃ assāti khilajāto, tassa bhāvo khilajātatā, tāpi natthi na santi. Pañcapi cetokhilāti kāme avītarāgo, kāye avītarāgo, rūpe avītarāgo, yāvadatthaṃ udarāvadehakaṃ bhuñjitvā seyyasukhaṃ passasukhaṃ middhasukhaṃ anuyutto viharati, aññataraṃ devanikāyaṃ paṇidhāya brahmacariyaṃ carati “imināhaṃ sīlena vā vatena vā tapena vā brahmacariyena vā devo vā bhavissāmi, devaññataro vā”ti (ma. ni. 1.186) evarūpā pañcapi cittassa bandhabhāvakacavarabhāvasaṅkhātā cetokhilā natthi.

'The state of being barren also does not exist': one for whom the mental barrenness of aversion—defined as a state of mental bondage and mental refuse—has arisen is 'one who has become barren'; the state of that is 'the state of being barren.' That too does not exist, is not found. The five mental barrennesses are also not found: (i) one is not without lust for sensual pleasures; (ii) one is not without lust for the body; (iii) one is not without lust for form; (iv) having eaten as much as his belly can hold, he dwells committed to the pleasure of lying down, the pleasure of reclining, and the pleasure of torpor; (v) he lives the spiritual life aspiring to some order of deities, thinking: 'By this virtue or observance or austerity or spiritual life, I will become a deva or one among the devas' (cf. MN 16, i 101). These five mental barrennesses, defined as states of mental bondage and mental refuse, are not found.

16. Imañca gāthaṃ vatvā bhagavā ānandattheraṃ pucchi – “evaṃ khuṃsetvā vambhetvā vuccamānā bhikkhū, ānanda, kiṃ [P 1.0192] vadantī”ti, “na kiñci bhagavā”ti. “Na, ānanda, ‘ahaṃ sīlavā’ti sabbattha tuṇhī bhavitabbaṃ. Loke hi nābhāsamānaṃ jānanti, missaṃ bālehi paṇḍita”nti (saṃ. ni. 2.241) vatvā “bhikkhū, ānanda, te manusse evaṃ paṭicodentū”ti dhammadesanatthāya “abhūtavādī nirayaṃ upetī”ti (dha. pa. 306; udā. 38; itivu. 48; su. ni. 666) imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi. Thero taṃ uggahetvā bhikkhū āha – “manussā tumhehi imāya gāthāya paṭicodetabbā”ti. Bhikkhū tathā akaṃsu. Paṇḍitamanussā tuṇhī ahesuṃ. Rājāpi rājapurise sabbattha pesetvā yesaṃ dhuttānaṃ lañjaṃ datvā titthiyā taṃ mārāpesuṃ, te gahetvā niggayha taṃ pavattiṃ ñatvā titthiye paribhāsi. Manussāpi titthiye disvā leḍḍunā hananti, paṃsunā okiranti “bhagavato ayasaṃ uppādesu”nti. Ānandatthero taṃ disvā bhagavato ārocesi, bhagavā therassa imaṃ gāthamabhāsi “sakañhi diṭṭhiṃ…pe… vadeyyā”ti.

16. Having spoken this verse, the Blessed One asked the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, when the bhikkhus are reviled and scorned in this way, what do they say?” “Nothing, Blessed One.” “Ānanda, one should not remain silent everywhere, thinking, ‘I am virtuous.’ For in the world, one who does not speak is not recognized, the wise person among fools” (cf. SN 7.2). Then, for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma, he recited this verse: “One who speaks what is not true goes to hell” (Dhp 306; Ud 4.8; Iti 48; Sn 3.11). The elder, having learned this, told the bhikkhus: “You should reproach those people with this verse.” The bhikkhus did so. The wise people remained silent. The king, having sent his men everywhere, seized and subdued the scoundrels to whom the sectarians had given a bribe to have her killed. Having learned of the affair, he reviled the sectarians. People, too, upon seeing the sectarians, would strike them with clods of earth and cover them with dust, saying, “They have brought disgrace upon the Blessed One.” The Venerable Ānanda, seeing this, reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then spoke this verse to the elder: “For one’s own view … he would speak.”

Tassa [V 0.0151] attho – yāyaṃ diṭṭhi titthiyajanassa “sundariṃ māretvā samaṇānaṃ sakyaputtiyānaṃ avaṇṇaṃ pakāsetvā etenupāyena laddhaṃ sakkāraṃ sādiyissāmā”ti so taṃ diṭṭhiṃ kathaṃ atikkameyya? Atha kho so ayaso tameva titthiyajanaṃ paccāgato taṃ diṭṭhiṃ accetuṃ asakkontaṃ. Yo vā sassatādivādī, sopi sakaṃ diṭṭhiṃ kathamaccayeyya, tena diṭṭhichandena anunīto tāya ca diṭṭhiruciyā niviṭṭho, api ca kho pana sayaṃ samattāni pakubbamāno attanāva paripuṇṇāni tāni diṭṭhigatāni karonto yathā jāneyya, tatheva vadeyyāti.

Its meaning is this: How could that sectarian person overcome this view of his: ‘Having had Sundarī killed and having proclaimed the disrepute of the Sakyan ascetics, by this means we will enjoy the honor we have gained’? But that disgrace returned to that very sectarian person, who was unable to overcome that view. Or how could one who holds a view of eternalism and so on overcome his own view, being led on by desire for that view and entrenched in his preference for that view? And making those views complete and perfect himself, he would speak just as he knows.

Avaṇṇaṃ [M 0.0167] pakāsayitvāti aguṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ katvā. Sakkāranti catunnaṃ paccayānaṃ sakkaccakaraṇaṃ. Sammānanti cittena bahumānanaṃ. Paccāharissāmāti etaṃ lābhādiṃ nibbattessāma. Evaṃdiṭṭhikāti evaṃladdhikā. Yathā taṃ “lābhādiṃ nibbattessāmā”ti evaṃ ayaṃ laddhi tesaṃ atthi, tathā “atthi me vuttappakāro dhammo”ti etesaṃ khamati ceva ruccati ca, evaṃsabhāvameva vā tesaṃ cittaṃ “atthi me citta”nti. Tadā tesaṃ diṭṭhi vā, diṭṭhiyā [P 1.0193] saha khanti vā, diṭṭhikhantīhi saddhiṃ ruci vā, diṭṭhikhantirucīhi saddhiṃ laddhi vā, diṭṭhikhantiruciladdhīhi saddhiṃ ajjhāsayo vā, diṭṭhikhantiruciladdhiajjhāsayehi saddhiṃ adhippāyo vā hotīti dassento “evaṃdiṭṭhikā…pe… evaṃadhippāyā”ti āha. Sakaṃ diṭṭhinti attano dassanaṃ. Sakaṃ khantinti attano sahanaṃ. Sakaṃ rucinti attano ruciṃ. Sakaṃ laddhinti attano laddhiṃ. Sakaṃ ajjhāsayanti attano ajjhāsayaṃ. Sakaṃ adhippāyanti attano bhāvaṃ. Atikkamitunti samatikkamituṃ. Atha kho sveva ayasoti so eva ayaso ekaṃsena. Te paccāgatoti tesaṃ patiāgato. Teti sāmiatthe upayogavacanaṃ.

'Having proclaimed disrepute' means having made a lack of virtue evident. 'Honor' means the respectful providing of the four requisites. 'Respect' means high regard in the mind. 'We will bring back' means we will produce this gain, etc. 'One with such a view' means one with such a doctrine. Just as they have the doctrine, ‘We will produce gain, etc.,’ so too they approve and prefer this, thinking, ‘There is for me a Dhamma of the kind described,’ or their mind is of such a nature, thinking, ‘This is my mind.’ To show that at that time they have either a view, or forbearance along with the view, or preference along with forbearance and the view, or a doctrine along with preference and forbearance, or a disposition along with a doctrine, preference, and forbearance, or an intention along with a disposition, doctrine, preference, and forbearance, he said: ‘one with such a view … one with such an intention.’ 'One’s own view' means one’s own seeing. 'One’s own forbearance' means one’s own endurance. 'One’s own preference' means one’s own liking. 'One’s own doctrine' means one’s own tenet. 'One’s own disposition' means one’s own inclination. 'One’s own intention' means one’s own state of being. 'To overcome' means to transcend completely. 'But that very disgrace' means that very disgrace, certainly. 'Returned to them' means returned to them. 'Them' is a dative of reference in the sense of possession.

Atha vāti atthantaradassanaṃ. Sassatoti nicco dhuvo. Lokoti attabhāvo. Idameva saccaṃ, moghamaññanti idaṃ eva tacchaṃ tathaṃ, aññaṃ tucchaṃ. Samattāti sampuṇṇā. Samādinnāti sammā ādinnā. Gahitāti upagantvā gahitā.

'Or' means showing another meaning. 'Eternal' means permanent, stable. 'The world' means personal existence. 'This alone is true, the other is futile' means this is genuine, real; the other is empty. 'Complete' means perfected. 'Undertaken' means rightly taken up. 'Grasped' means having approached and grasped.

Parāmaṭṭhāti sabbākārena parāmasitvā gahitā. Abhiniviṭṭhāti visesena laddhappatiṭṭhā. Asassatoti vuttavipariyāyena veditabbo.

Misapprehended means grasped after considering it in every way. Adhered to means having gained a special footing. Non-eternal should be understood in the opposite way to what has been stated.

Antavāti saanto. Anantavāti vuddhianantavā. Taṃ jīvanti so jīvo, liṅgavipallāso kato. Jīvoti ca attāyeva. Tathāgatoti satto, “araha”nti eke. Paraṃ maraṇāti maraṇato uddhaṃ, paraloketi attho. Na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇāti maraṇato uddhaṃ na [V 0.0152] hoti. Hoti ca na ca hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇāti maraṇato uddhaṃ hoti ca na hoti ca. Neva hoti na na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇāti ucchedavasena neva hoti, takkikavasena na na hoti.

Finite means with an end. Infinite means infinite in extent. ‘That is the life principle’ means ‘that is the soul’; a change of gender has been made. And ‘life principle’ is just the self. ‘Tathāgata’ means a being; some say, ‘an arahant.’ ‘After death’ means beyond death; the meaning is ‘in the world beyond.’ ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death’ means he does not exist beyond death. ‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death’ means he both exists and does not exist beyond death. ‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’ means: in the sense of annihilationism, he does not exist; in the sense of the sophists, he does not not-exist.

Sakāya [M 0.0168] diṭṭhiyātiādayo karaṇavacanaṃ. Allīnoti ekībhūto.

‘By his own view,’ etc., is the instrumental case. Clinging means having become one with.

Sayaṃ samattaṃ karotīti attanā ūnabhāvaṃ mocetvā sammā attaṃ samattaṃ karoti. Paripuṇṇanti atirekadosaṃ mocetvā sampuṇṇaṃ. Anomanti hīnadosaṃ mocetvā alāmakaṃ. Agganti ādiṃ. Seṭṭhanti padhānaṃ niddosaṃ. Visesanti jeṭṭhakaṃ[P 1.0194]. Pāmokkhanti adhikaṃ. Uttamanti visesaṃ na heṭṭhimaṃ. Pavaraṃ karotīti atirekena uttamaṃ karoti. Atha vā “āsayadosamocanena aggaṃ, saṃkilesadosamocanena seṭṭhaṃ, upakkilesadosamocanena visesaṃ, pamattadosamocanena pāmokkhaṃ, majjhimadosamocanena uttamaṃ, uttamamajjhimadosamocanena pavaraṃ karotī”ti evameke vaṇṇayanti. Ayaṃ satthā sabbaññūti ayaṃ amhākaṃ satthā sabbajānanavasena sabbaññū. Ayaṃ dhammo svākkhātoti ayaṃ amhākaṃ dhammo suṭṭhu akkhāto. Ayaṃ gaṇo suppaṭipannoti ayaṃ amhākaṃ gaṇo suṭṭhu paṭipanno. Ayaṃ diṭṭhi bhaddikāti ayaṃ amhākaṃ laddhi sundarā. Ayaṃ paṭipadā supaññattāti ayaṃ amhākaṃ pubbabhāgā attanta pādipaṭipadā suṭṭhu paññattā. Ayaṃ maggo niyyānikoti ayaṃ amhākaṃ niyyāmokkantiko maggo niyyānikoti sayaṃ samattaṃ karoti.

‘He makes it complete himself’ means that, having freed it from deficiency himself, he makes it properly complete. ‘Perfect’ means, having freed it from the fault of excess, it is complete. ‘Not inferior’ means, having freed it from the fault of inferiority, it is not base. ‘Highest’ means first. ‘Best’ means principal, faultless. ‘Excellent’ means chief. ‘Principal’ means superior. ‘Supreme’ means special, not low. ‘He makes it excellent’ means he makes it surpassingly supreme. Alternatively, some explain it thus: ‘By freeing it from the fault of disposition, he makes it highest; by freeing it from the fault of defilement, he makes it best; by freeing it from the fault of subsidiary defilement, he makes it excellent; by freeing it from the fault of negligence, he makes it principal; by freeing it from the fault of mediocrity, he makes it supreme; by freeing it from the fault of supreme mediocrity, he makes it most excellent.’ ‘This Teacher is all-knowing’ means this Teacher of ours is all-knowing in the sense of knowing all. ‘This Dhamma is well-expounded’ means this Dhamma of ours is well-expounded. ‘This Sangha is practicing the good way’ means this Sangha of ours is practicing the good way. ‘This view is good’ means this doctrine of ours is beautiful. ‘This practice is well-declared’ means this preliminary practice of ours, which is the basis for the goal, is well-declared. ‘This path is emancipating’ means this path of ours that leads out is emancipating; thus he makes it complete himself.

Katheyya “sassato loko”ti. Bhaṇeyya “idameva saccaṃ moghamañña”nti. Dīpeyya “antavā loko”ti. Vohareyya nānāvidhena gaṇhāpeyya “hoti ca na ca hotī”ti.

He would speak, ‘The world is eternal.’ He would say, ‘This alone is true; the other is futile.’ He would explain, ‘The world is finite.’ He would use language and in various ways get others to accept, ‘He both exists and does not exist.’

17. Atha rājā sattāhaccayena taṃ kuṇapaṃ chaḍḍāpetvā sāyanhasamayaṃ vihāraṃ gantvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā āha – “nanu, bhante, īdise ayase uppanne mayhampi ārocetabbaṃ siyā”ti? Evaṃ vutte bhagavā “na, mahārāja, ‘ahaṃ sīlavā guṇasampanno’ti paresaṃ ārocetuṃ ariyānaṃ paṭirūpa”nti vatvā tassā aṭṭhuppattiyā “yo attano sīlavatānīti avasesagāthāyo abhāsi.

17. Then, after seven days had passed, the king had the corpse discarded and, in the evening, went to the monastery. Having paid homage to the Blessed One, he said: “Venerable sir, when such a disgrace arose, should I not have been informed?” When this was said, the Blessed One replied: “No, great king, it is not proper for noble ones to announce to others, ‘I am virtuous, endowed with good qualities.’” Having said this, in connection with that occasion, he recited the remaining verses, beginning: “One who by his own virtues and observances….”

Tattha sīlavatānīti pātimokkhādīni sīlāni, āraññikādīni dhutaṅgavatāni ca. Anānupuṭṭhoti apucchito. Pāvāti vadati. Anariyadhammaṃ kusalā tamāhu, yo ātumānaṃ sayameva pāvāti [V 0.0153] yo evaṃ attānaṃ [M 0.0169] sayameva vadati, tassa taṃ vādaṃ “anariyadhammo eso”ti kusalā evaṃ kathenti.

Therein, ‘by virtues and observances’ refers to the kinds of virtue such as the Pātimokkha, and the ascetic practices such as the forest-dweller’s observance. ‘Unasked’ means not having been questioned. ‘Proclaims’ means speaks. ‘The skilled call it an ignoble quality, one who proclaims himself’ means: as to one who thus speaks proclaiming himself, the skilled describe that speech of his thus: ‘This is an ignoble quality.’”

Atthi sīlañceva vatañcāti sīlanaṭṭhena sīlañceva atthi, samādānaṭṭhena vatañca atthi, vataṃ na sīlanti vuttatthena vataṃ atthi, taṃ na sīlaṃ. Katamanti [P 1.0195] kathetukamyatāpucchā. Idha bhikkhu sīlavātiādayo vuttanayā eva. Saṃvaraṭṭhenāti saṃvaraṇaṭṭhena, vītikkamadvāraṃ pidahanaṭṭhena. Samādānaṭṭhenāti taṃ taṃ sikkhāpadaṃ sammā ādānaṭṭhena. Āraññikaṅganti araññe nivāso sīlaṃ assāti āraññiko, tassa aṅgaṃ āraññikaṅgaṃ. Piṇḍapātikaṅganti bhikkhāsaṅkhātānaṃ paraāmisapiṇḍānaṃ pāto piṇḍapāto, parehi dinnānaṃ piṇḍānaṃ patte nipatananti vuttaṃ hoti. Taṃ piṇḍapātaṃ uñchati taṃ taṃ kulaṃ upasaṅkamanto gavesatīti piṇḍapātiko, piṇḍāya vā patituṃ vatametassāti piṇḍapātī. Patitunti carituṃ. Piṇḍapātī eva piṇḍapātiko, tassa aṅgaṃ piṇḍapātikaṅgaṃ. Aṅganti kāraṇaṃ vuccati. Tasmā yena samādānena so piṇḍapātiko hoti, tassetaṃ adhivacananti veditabbaṃ. Eteneva nayena rathikāsusānasaṅkārakūṭādīnaṃ yattha katthaci paṃsūnaṃ upari ṭhitattā abbhuggataṭṭhena tesu paṃsukūlamivāti paṃsukūlaṃ. Atha vā paṃsu viya kucchitabhāvaṃ ulatīti paṃsukūlaṃ, kucchitabhāvaṃ gacchatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Evaṃ laddhanibbacanassa paṃsukūlassa dhāraṇaṃ paṃsukūlaṃ, paṃsukūlaṃ sīlamassāti paṃsukūliko, paṃsukūlikassa aṅgaṃ paṃsukūlikaṅgaṃ. Saṅghāṭiuttarāsaṅgaantaravāsakasaṅkhātaṃ ticīvaraṃ sīlamassāti tecīvariko, tecīvarikassa aṅgaṃ tecīvarikaṅgaṃ. Sapadānacārikaṅganti dānaṃ vuccati avakhaṇḍanaṃ, apetaṃ dānato apadānaṃ, anavakhaṇḍananti attho. Saha apadānena sapadānaṃ, avakhaṇḍanavirahitaṃ, anugharanti vuttaṃ hoti. Sapadānaṃ carituṃ idamassa sīlanti sapadānacārī, sapadānacārīyeva sapadānacāriko, tassa aṅgaṃ sapadānacārikaṅgaṃ. Khalupacchābhattikaṅganti khalūti paṭisedhanatthe nipāto. Pavāritena satā pacchā laddhaṃ bhattaṃ pacchābhattaṃ nāma, tassa pacchābhattassa bhojanaṃ pacchābhattabhojanaṃ, tasmiṃ pacchābhattabhojane pacchābhattasaññaṃ katvā pacchābhattaṃ sīlamassāti pacchābhattiko, na pacchābhattiko [P 1.0196] khalupacchābhattiko, samādānavasena paṭikkhittātirittabhojanassetaṃ nāmaṃ, tassa aṅgaṃ khalupacchābhattikaṅgaṃ[M 0.0170]. Nesajjikaṅganti sayanaṃ paṭikkhipitvā nisajjāya viharituṃ sīlamassāti nesajjiko, tassa aṅgaṃ nesajjikaṅgaṃ. Yathāsanthatikaṅganti yadeva santhataṃ yathāsanthataṃ, “idaṃ tuyhaṃ pāpuṇātī”ti evaṃ paṭhamaṃ uddiṭṭhasenāsanassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tasmiṃ yathāsanthate viharituṃ sīlamassāti yathāsanthatiko, tassa aṅgaṃ yathāsanthatikaṅgaṃ. Sabbāneva panetāni tena tena samādānena dhutakilesattā dhutassa bhikkhuno aṅgāni, kilesadhunanato vā dhutanti laddhavohāraṃ ñāṇaṃ aṅgaṃ etesanti dhutaṅgāni. Atha [V 0.0154] vā dhutāni ca tāni paṭipakkhānaṃ dhunanato aṅgāni ca paṭipattiyātipi dhutaṅgāni. Evaṃ tāvettha atthato viññātabbo vinicchayo. Sabbāneva cetāni samādānacetanālakkhaṇāni. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

There is both virtue and observance: in the sense of virtue, there is virtue; and in the sense of undertaking, there is observance. According to the saying, 'observance is not virtue,' there is observance, but it is not virtue. 'Which?' is a question asked out of a desire to explain. Here, 'a bhikkhu is virtuous,' and so forth, are to be understood in the way already stated. 'In the sense of restraint' means in the sense of guarding, in the sense of closing the door to transgression. 'In the sense of undertaking' means in the sense of properly taking up each training rule. The forest-dweller's practice: dwelling in the forest is his virtue, thus he is a forest-dweller; his factor is the forest-dweller's practice. The alms-food-eater's practice: the falling of lumps of food from others, known as alms, is alms-food; it is said to be the falling into the bowl of lumps of food given by others. He who gleans that alms-food, approaching and seeking it from various households, is an alms-food-eater; or, he whose observance it is to go for alms is an alms-goer. 'To go' means to walk. An alms-goer is an alms-food-eater; his factor is the alms-food-eater's practice. 'Factor' is said to mean cause. Therefore, it should be understood that this is the designation for that undertaking by which he becomes an alms-food-eater. By this same method, regarding the rag-robe-wearer's practice: because it is found on top of dust anywhere in places like streets, cemeteries, and rubbish heaps, and is prominent because it lies upon them, it is like a dust-heap, hence 'paṃsukūla.' Alternatively, because it goes to a despised state like dust, it is 'paṃsukūla'; it is said that it goes to a despised state. The wearing of a 'paṃsukūla,' which has this etymology, is the 'paṃsukūla' practice. The rag-robe is his virtue, thus he is a rag-robe-wearer; his factor is the rag-robe-wearer's practice. The three-robe-wearer's practice: the three robes—namely the outer robe, the upper robe, and the inner robe—are his virtue, thus he is a three-robe-wearer; his factor is the three-robe-wearer's practice. The house-to-house-goer's practice: 'dāna' is said to mean breaking; 'apadāna' is without breaking, meaning 'uninterrupted.' 'Sapadāna' is with non-breaking, free from interruption; it is said to be going from house to house in order. To walk without interruption is his virtue, thus he is a house-to-house-goer; a house-to-house-goer is indeed a `sapadānacāriko`; his factor is the house-to-house-goer's practice. The refuser-of-later-food's practice: 'khalu' is a particle in the sense of prohibition. Food received after one has indicated one is satisfied is called 'later food.' Eating that later food is 'eating later food.' Regarding that eating of later food, having the perception of it as later food, later food is his virtue, thus he is a 'later-food-eater.' Not a 'later-food-eater' is a 'refuser-of-later-food.' This is the name for one who has rejected extra food by way of undertaking; his factor is the refuser-of-later-food's practice. The sitter's practice: his virtue is to dwell by sitting, having rejected lying down, thus he is a sitter; his factor is the sitter's practice. The any-lodging-user's practice: whatever is spread out is 'as spread.' 'This falls to your lot'—this is the designation for the lodging first assigned. To dwell in that 'as spread' lodging is his virtue, thus he is an any-lodging-user; his factor is the any-lodging-user's practice. All these, through their respective undertakings, are factors of a monk who has shaken off defilements, because they themselves have shaken off defilements. Or, they are 'ascetic factors' because knowledge, which has received the designation 'shaken off' from shaking off defilements, is their factor. Alternatively, they are also 'ascetic factors' because they are 'shaken off' by shaking off their opposites, and they are 'factors' of the practice. Thus, the analysis here is to be understood in terms of its meaning. All these have the characteristic of the volition of undertaking. And it is said:

“Yo samādiyati, so puggalo. Yena samādiyati, cittacetasikā ete dhammā. Yā samādānacetanā, taṃ dhutaṅgaṃ. Yaṃ paṭikkhipati, taṃ vatthu”nti (visuddhi. 1.23).

He who undertakes is the person. That by which he undertakes—these are mind and mental factors. The volition of undertaking is the ascetic factor. That which he rejects is the object.

Sabbāneva ca loluppaviddhaṃsanarasāni, nilloluppabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānāni, appicchatādiariyadhammapadaṭṭhānāni. Evamettha lakkhaṇādīhi vinicchayo veditabbo.

All these have the function of destroying greed, the manifestation of being without greed, and the proximate cause of noble qualities such as having few wants. Thus, the analysis should be understood here by their characteristics and so on.

Vīriyasamādānampīti vīriyaggahaṇampi. Kāmanti ekaṃsatthe nipāto. Taco ca nhāru cāti chavi ca nhāruvalliyo ca. Aṭṭhi cāti sabbā aṭṭhiyo ca. Avasissatūti tiṭṭhatu. Upasussatu maṃsalohitanti sabbaṃ maṃsañca lohitañca sukkhatu. “Taco”ti ekaṃ aṅgaṃ, “nhārū”ti ekaṃ, “aṭṭhī”ti ekaṃ, “upasussatu maṃsalohita”nti ekaṃ aṅgaṃ. Yaṃ tanti upari vattabbapadena sambandho. Purisathāmenāti purisassa kāyikena balena, balenāti ñāṇabalena. Vīriyenāti cetasikañāṇavīriyatejena. Parakkamenāti paraṃ paraṃ ṭhānaṃ akkamanena ussāhappattavīriyena. Pattabbanti [P 1.0197] yaṃ taṃ pāpuṇitabbaṃ. Na taṃ apāpuṇitvāti taṃ pattabbaṃ appatvā. Vīriyassa saṇṭhānaṃ bhavissatīti vuttappakārassa vīriyassa sithilattaṃ osīdanaṃ na bhavissati. “Paṭṭhāna”ntipi pāṭho, ayamevattho. Cittaṃ paggaṇhātīti cittaṃ ussāhaṃ gaṇhāpeti. Padahatīti patiṭṭhāpeti.

'Even the undertaking of energy' means the grasping of energy. 'Kāmaṃ' is a particle in the sense of certainty. 'Skin and sinews' means the skin and the sinew-creepers. 'And bones' means all the bones. 'Let it remain' means let it stay. 'Let flesh and blood dry up' means let all the flesh and blood dry up. 'Skin' is one part, 'sinews' is one, 'bones' is one, and 'let flesh and blood dry up' is one part. The word 'that' (yaṃ) is connected with a word to be stated further on. 'With human strength' means with the bodily strength of a man; 'with strength' means with the strength of knowledge. 'With energy' means with the power of mental energy associated with knowledge. 'With striving' means with the energy of effort achieved by advancing to higher and higher states. 'What is to be attained' means that which is to be reached. 'Not without attaining it' means without having attained that which is to be attained. The phrase 'there will be no stopping of energy' means there will be no slackening or sinking down of the aforesaid kind of energy. 'Paṭṭhāna' (resolve) is also a reading; this is the same meaning. 'He uplifts the mind' means he makes the mind take up exertion. 'He strives' means he establishes it.

Nāsissanti [M 0.0171] na khādissāmi na bhuñjissāmi. Na pivissāmīti yāgupānādīni na pivissāmi. Vihārato na nikkhameti senāsanato bahi na nikkhameyyaṃ. Napi passaṃ nipātessanti passaṃ mañce vā pīṭhe vā bhūmiyaṃ vā kaṭasantharake vā pātanaṃ ṭhapanaṃ na karissāmi. Taṇhāsalle anūhateti taṇhāsaṅkhāte kaṇḍe anuddhaṭe, avigateti attho.

“I will not eat” means I will not chew, I will not consume. “I will not drink” means I will not drink gruel, beverages, and so on. “I will not leave the dwelling” means I will not go outside the lodging. “Nor will I lay down my side” means I will not make a placing, a setting down of my side on a bed, a chair, the ground, or a mat-spread. “The dart of craving not being removed” means the arrow known as craving not being pulled out; the meaning is 'not having departed'.

Imaṃ pallaṅkanti samantato ābhujitaṃ ūrubaddhāsanaṃ. Na bhindissāmīti na vijahissāmi. Yāva me na anupādāyāti catūhi upādānehi gahaṇaṃ aggahetvā. Āsavehīti kāmāsavādīhi catūhi āsavehi. Vimuccissatīti samucchedavimuttiyā na muccissati. Na tāvāhaṃ imamhā āsanā vuṭṭhahissāmīti ādiṃ katvā yāva rukkhamūlā nikkhamissāmīti okāsavasena [V 0.0155] vuttā. Imasmiññeva pubbaṇhasamayaṃ ariyadhammaṃ āharissāmīti ādiṃ katvā yāva gimheti kālavasena vuttā. Purime vayokhandhetiādayo vayavasena vuttā. Tattha āsanā na vuṭṭhahissāmīti nisinnāsanā na uṭṭhahissāmi. Aḍḍhayogāti nikuṇḍagehā. Pāsādāti dīghapāsādā. Hammiyāti muṇḍacchadanagehā. Guhāyāti paṃsuguhāya. Leṇāti mariyādachinnacchiddā pabbataleṇā. Kuṭiyāti ullittādikuṭiyā. Kūṭāgārāti kaṇṇikaṃ āropetvā katagehato. Aṭṭāti dvāraṭṭālakā. Māḷāti vaṭṭagehā. Uddaṇḍo nāma eko patissayaviseso. “Tichadanageho”tipi eke. Upaṭṭhānasālāti sannipātasālā bhojanasālā vā. Maṇḍapādayo pākaṭāyeva. Ariyadhammanti [P 1.0198] anavajjadhammaṃ, ariyānaṃ vā buddhapaccekabuddhabuddhasāvakānaṃ dhammaṃ. Āharissāmīti mama cittasamīpaṃ ānayissāmi sīlena. Samāharissāmīti visesena ānayissāmi samādhinā. Adhigacchissāmīti paṭilābhavasena gamissāmi tadaṅgena. Phassayissāmīti phusissāmi maggena. Sacchikarissāmīti paccakkhaṃ karissāmi phalena. Atha vā sotāpattimaggena āharissāmi. Sakadāgāmimaggena samāharissāmi, anāgāmimaggena adhigacchissāmi, arahattamaggena phassayissāmi, paccavekkhaṇena sacchikarissāmi. Dvīsupi nayesu phassayissāmīti nāmakāyena nibbānaṃ phusissāmīti attho.

“This seat” means the cross-legged posture, completely surrounding and bound by the thighs. “I will not break it” means I will not abandon it. “Until… without clinging” means without grasping by the four kinds of clinging. “From the taints” means from the four taints, starting with the taint of sensual desire. “Will be liberated” means will be liberated by the liberation of eradication. “I will not rise from this seat” and so forth, up to “I will leave the foot of the tree,” are stated in terms of place. “In this very morning, I will bring forth the noble Dhamma” and so forth, up to “in the hot season,” are stated in terms of time. “The former stages of life” and so forth are stated in terms of age. There, “I will not rise from the seat” means I will not rise from the seated posture. “Aḍḍhayoga” refers to a house with a niche. “Pāsāda” means a long palace. “Hammiya” refers to a flat-roofed house. “Guhā” means a cave of earth. “Leṇa” refers to mountain shelters with openings cut within defined limits. “Kuṭi” means a plastered hut, etc. “Kūṭāgāra” refers to a house built with a pinnacle erected. “Aṭṭa” means gate-towers. “Māḷa” refers to round houses. “Uddaṇḍa” is a specific type of dwelling. Some say, “a house with three roofs.” “Upaṭṭhānasālā” means an assembly hall or a dining hall. “Maṇḍapa” and so forth are obvious. “Noble Dhamma” means blameless Dhamma, or the Dhamma of the noble ones—Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, or disciples of the Buddha. “I will bring forth” means I will bring it near to my mind through virtue. “I will gather” means I will especially bring it near through concentration. “I will attain” means I will reach it through acquisition, by means of that factor. “I will touch” means I will touch it through the path. “I will realize” means I will directly experience it through the fruit. Alternatively, I will bring it forth through the path of stream-entry, gather it through the path of once-returning, attain it through the path of non-returning, touch it through the path of arahantship, and realize it through reviewing. In both methods, “I will touch” means I will touch Nibbāna with the mental body—that is the meaning.

Apuṭṭhoti mūlapadaṃ, tassa apucchitoti attho. Apucchitoti ajānāpito. Ayācitoti anāyācito. Anajjhesitoti anāṇāpito[M 0.0172], “na icchito”ti eke. Apasāditoti na pasādāpito. Pāvadatīti kathayati. Ahamasmīti ahaṃ asmi bhavāmi. Jātiyā vāti khattiyabrāhmaṇajātiyā vā. Gottena vāti gotamādigottena vā. Kolaputtiyena vāti kulaputtabhāvena vā. Vaṇṇapokkharatāya vāti sarīrasundaratāya vā. Dhanena vāti dhanasampattiyā vā. Ajjhenena vāti ajjhāyakaraṇena vā. Kammāyatanena vāti kammameva kammāyatanaṃ, tena kammāyatanena, kasigorakkhakammādinā vā. Sippāyatanena vāti dhanusippādinā vā. Vijjāṭṭhānena vāti aṭṭhārasavijjāṭṭhānena vā. Sutena vāti bahussutaguṇena vā. Paṭibhānena vāti kāraṇākāraṇapaṭibhānasaṅkhātañāṇena vā. Aññataraññatarena vā vatthunāti jātiādīnaṃ ekekena vatthunā vā.

“Unasked” is the root term, meaning “not questioned.” “Not questioned” means not informed. “Unsolicited” means not requested. “Uninvited” means not commanded; some say, “not wished for.” “Not rejected” means not caused to be pleased. “He proclaims” means he declares. “I am” means “I am, I exist.” “By birth” means by birth as a noble or a brahmin. “By clan” means by a clan such as the Gotama clan. “By being a son of a good family” means by the state of being a son of a good family. “By beauty” means by bodily beauty. “By wealth” means by possession of wealth. “By study” means by the practice of recitation. “By sphere of work” means work itself is the sphere of work; by this sphere of work, such as farming and cattle-herding. “By sphere of craft” means by a craft such as archery. “By a branch of knowledge” means by the eighteen branches of knowledge. “By learning” means by the quality of being very learned. “By intelligence” means by the knowledge reckoned as intelligence regarding cause and non-cause. “Or by some other ground” means by any single one of these grounds, such as birth.

Uccā kulāti khattiyabrāhmaṇakulā, etena jātigottamahattaṃ dīpeti. Mahābhogakulāti gahapatimahāsālakulā, etena aḍḍhamahattaṃ dīpeti. Uḷārabhogakulāti avasesavessādikulā, etena pahūtajātarūparajatādiṃ dīpeti. Caṇḍālāpi hi uḷārabhogā honti. Ñātoti pākaṭo. Yassassīti parivārasampanno. Suttantikoti [P 1.0199] suttante niyutto. Vinayadharoti vinayapiṭakadharo. Dhammakathikoti [V 0.0156] ābhidhammiko. Āraññikotiādayo dhutaṅgapubbaṅgamapaṭipattidassanatthaṃ vuttā. Paṭhamassa jhānassa lābhītiādayo rūpārūpaaṭṭhasamāpattiyo dassetvā paṭivedhadassanavasena vuttā. Pāvadatīti mūlapadaṃ. Kathetīti “piṭakācariyosmī”ti kathayati. Bhaṇatīti “dhutaṅgikomhī”ti pākaṭaṃ karoti. Dīpayatīti “rūpajjhānaṃ lābhīmhī”ti paridīpayati. Voharatīti “arūpajjhānaṃ lābhīmhī”ti vākyabhedaṃ karoti.

“High families” are noble and brahmin families; this indicates greatness of birth and clan. “Families of great wealth” are the families of householders and great magnates; this indicates greatness of affluence. “Families of vast wealth” are the remaining merchant families and the like; this indicates abundant gold, silver, and so on.
