For even caṇḍālas can have vast wealth. “Known” means famous. “Renowned” means endowed with a retinue. “One versed in the suttas” means one devoted to the Sutta Piṭaka. “A bearer of the Vinaya” means one who upholds the Vinaya Piṭaka. “A speaker on the Dhamma” means one versed in the Abhidhamma. “A forest-dweller” and so on are mentioned to show the practice that gives precedence to the ascetic practices. “One who has attained the first jhāna” and so on are stated to show penetration, having illustrated the eight form and formless attainments. “He proclaims” is the root term. “He declares”: he says, “I am a teacher of the Piṭakas.” “He states”: he makes it known, “I am an ascetic practitioner.” “He illuminates”: he makes manifest, “I have attained a form jhāna.” “He expresses”: he makes a distinction in speech, “I have attained a formless jhāna.”

Khandhakusalāti pañcasu khandhesu salakkhaṇasāmaññalakkhaṇesu chekā, ñātatīraṇapahānavasena kusalāti attho. Dhātuāyatanapaṭiccasamuppādādīsupi eseva nayo. Nibbānakusalāti nibbāne chekā. Anariyānanti na ariyānaṃ. Eso dhammoti eso sabhāvo. Bālānanti apaṇḍitānaṃ. Asappurisānanti na sobhanapurisānaṃ. Attāti attānaṃ.

“Skilled in the aggregates” means skilled in the five aggregates in regard to their individual and general characteristics; the meaning is skilled by way of full understanding, investigation, and abandoning. The same method applies to the elements, sense bases, dependent origination, and so on. “Skilled in Nibbāna” means skilled in Nibbāna. “Of the non-noble” means of those who are not noble ones. “This is the Dhamma” means this is the nature. “Of fools” means of the unwise. “Of untrue persons” means of those who are not good persons. “Self” means oneself.

18. Santoti rāgādikilesūpasamena santo. Tathā abhinibbutatto. Iti’hanti sīlesu akatthamānoti “ahamasmi sīlasampanno”tiādinā [M 0.0173] nayena iti sīlesu akatthamāno, sīlanimittaṃ attupanāyikaṃ vācaṃ abhāsamānoti vuttaṃ hoti. Tamariyadhammaṃ kusalā vadantīti tassa taṃ akatthanaṃ “ariyadhammo eso”ti buddhādayo khandhādikusalā vadanti. Yassussadā natthi kuhiñci loketi yassa khīṇāsavassa rāgādayo sattussadā kuhiñci loke natthi. Tassa taṃ akatthanaṃ “ariyadhammo eso”ti evaṃ kusalā vadantīti sambandho.

18. “Peaceful”: he is peaceful through the calming of the defilements such as lust. Similarly, “one whose self is extinguished.” “Thus not boasting about his virtues”: this means not boasting about his virtues in such ways as, “I am accomplished in virtue”; it is said to mean not uttering speech that takes virtue as a sign and is self-referential. “That noble Dhamma the skillful declare”: the Buddhas and others skilled in the aggregates and so on declare that non-boasting to be “a noble Dhamma.” “For whom there are no protuberances anywhere in the world”: for which arahant, whose taints are destroyed, the seven protuberances beginning with lust do not exist anywhere in the world. The connection is: the skillful declare that non-boasting of his to be “a noble Dhamma.”

Santoti mūlapadaṃ. Rāgassa samitattāti rañjanalakkhaṇassa rāgassa samitabhāvena. Dosādīsupi eseva nayo. Vijjhātattāti sabbapariḷāhānaṃ jhāpitattā. Nibbutattāti sabbasantāpānaṃ nibbāpitabhāvena. Vigatattāti sabbākusalābhisaṅkhārānaṃ vigatabhāvena dūrabhāvena. Paṭipassaddhattāti sabbākārena abhabbuppattikabhāvena. Sattannaṃ [P 1.0200] dhammānaṃ bhinnattā bhikkhūti upari vattabbānaṃ sattadhammānaṃ bhinditvā ṭhitabhāvena bhikkhu. Sakkāyadiṭṭhivicikicchāsīlabbataparāmāsoti ime tayo kilesā sotāpattimaggena bhinnā, rāgo dosoti ime dve kilesā oḷārikā sakadāgāmimaggena bhinnā, te eva aṇusahagatā anāgāmimaggena bhinnā, moho mānoti ime dve kilesā arahattamaggena bhinnā. Avasese kilese dassetuṃ “bhinnāssa honti pāpakā akusalā dhammā”ti āha. Saṃkilesikāti kilesapaccayā. Ponobhavikāti punabbhavadāyikā. Sadarāti kilesadarathā ettha santīti sadarā. “Saddarā”tipi pāṭho, sahadarathāti attho. Dukkhavipākāti phalakāle dukkhadāyikā. Āyatiṃ jātijarāmaraṇiyāti anāgate jātijarāmaraṇassa paccayā.

“Peaceful” is the root term. “Because lust is pacified”: because lust, which has the characteristic of staining, has been pacified. The same method applies to hatred and so on. “Because it is burnt out”: because all fevers have been burnt out. “Because it is extinguished”: because all torments have been extinguished. “Because it has departed”: because all unwholesome formations have departed and are far away. “Because it is tranquil”: because it has become incapable of arising in any way. “A bhikkhu is one who has broken seven things”: a bhikkhu is one who stands having broken the seven things to be mentioned below. The three defilements—identity view, doubt, and adherence to rules and observances—are broken by the path of stream-entry. The two gross defilements—lust and hatred—are broken by the path of the once-returner. These same two, together with their subtle forms, are broken by the path of the non-returner. The two defilements—delusion and conceit—are broken by the path of arahantship. To show the remaining defilements, he says: “His evil, unwholesome states are broken.” “Defiling”: because they are a condition for the defilements. “Leading to renewed existence”: because they produce a new existence. “Fraught with anguish”: because anguish from the defilements is present in them. There is also the reading “saddarā,” meaning accompanied by anguish. “Resulting in suffering”: because they yield suffering at the time of their fruit. “Pertaining to future birth, aging, and death”: because they are a condition for birth, aging, and death in the future.

Pajjena [V 0.0157] katena attanāti gāthāya ayaṃ piṇḍattho – yo attanā bhāvitena maggena parinibbānaṃ gato, kilesaparinibbānaṃ patto, parinibbānagatattā eva ca vitiṇṇakaṅkho, vipattisampattihānivuddhiucchedasassataapuññapuññappabhedaṃ bhavañca vibhavañca vippahāya maggavāsaṃ vusitavā khīṇapunabbhavoti etesaṃ thutivacanānaṃ araho so bhikkhūti.

Regarding 'by oneself the path is made,' this is the summary meaning of the verse: That bhikkhu who, by the path developed by himself, has gone to final Nibbāna, has attained the final Nibbāna of the defilements; and just because he has gone to final Nibbāna, he has crossed over doubt; having abandoned the distinctions of failure and success, decline and growth, annihilationism and eternalism, demerit and merit, and existence and non-existence, he has lived the life of the path and is one whose renewed existence is destroyed—such a bhikkhu is worthy of these words of praise.

Itihanti[M 0.0174], idahantīti duvidho pāṭho. Itīti padasandhiādayo sandhāya “idaha”nti pāṭhaṃ na rocenti. Tattha itīti yaṃ vuttaṃ. Padasandhīti padānaṃ sandhi padasandhi, padaghaṭananti attho. Padasaṃsaggoti padānaṃ ekībhāvo. Padapāripūrīti padānaṃ paripūraṇaṃ dvinnaṃ padānaṃ ekībhāvo. Akkharasamavāyoti ekībhūtopi aparipuṇṇopi hoti, ayaṃ na evaṃ. Akkharānaṃ samavāyo sannipāto hotīti dassanatthaṃ “akkharasamavāyo”ti āha. Byañjanasiliṭṭhatāti byañjanasamuccayo padamīti vuttānaṃ byañjanānaṃ atthabyañjanānaṃ atthabyattikāraṇānaṃ vā madhurabhāvattā pāṭhassa mudubhāvo. Padānupubbatā [P 1.0201] metanti padānaṃ anupubbabhāvo padānupubbatā, padapaṭipāṭibhāvoti attho. Metanti etaṃ. Katamanti ce? Itīti idaṃ. Metanti ettha ma-kāro padasandhivasena vutto. Katthī hotīti “ahamasmi sīlasampanno”ti attānaṃ ukkaṃsetvā kathanasīlo hoti. Katthatīti vuttanayena kathayati. Vikatthatīti vividhā kathayati. Katthanāti kathanā. Āratoti dūrato rato. Viratoti ṭhānasaṅkantivasena vigatabhāvena rato. Paṭiviratoti tato nivattitvā sabbākārena viyutto hutvā rato. Tattha pisācaṃ viya disvā palāto ārato. Hatthimhi maddante viya paridhāvitvā gato virato. Yodhasampahāraṃ viya pothetvā maddetvā gato paṭivirato.

'Iti'haṃ' and 'idahaṃ' are the two readings. Referring to the joining of words and so on with 'iti,' they do not approve of the reading 'idahaṃ.' Herein, 'iti' means what has been said. 'Joining of words' (padasandhi) means the conjunction of words; the meaning is the connection of words. 'Association of words' (padasaṃsaggo) is the unification of words. 'Completion of a phrase' (padapāripūrī) is the filling out of a phrase, the unification of two words. 'Combination of letters' (akkharasamavāyo): something can be unified yet still incomplete, but this is not so here. To show that there is a combination, an assembly of letters, it says 'combination of letters.' 'Smoothness of consonants' (byañjanasiliṭṭhatā): because of the sweetness of the consonants that are said to be the word—the consonants that convey the meaning or cause the meaning to be expressed—the recitation is smooth. 'The sequence of words is this' (padānupubbatā metanti): the sequential nature of the words is the sequence of words; the meaning is the orderly arrangement of words. 'Is this' (metanti) means this. If it is asked, 'What is this?' It is this 'iti.' Here, in 'metanti,' the letter 'm' is stated for the sake of word-joining. 'He is a boaster': he is disposed to boasting, exalting himself by saying, 'I am accomplished in virtue.' 'He boasts' (katthati): he speaks in the way stated. 'He boasts variously' (vikatthati): he speaks in various ways. 'Boasting' (katthanā) is the act of boasting. 'Remote' (ārato): delighting from afar. 'Abstaining' (virato): delighting in having departed by changing place. 'Fully abstaining' (paṭivirato): delighting in having turned back from that and become detached in every way. Herein, one who flees upon seeing a demon is 'remote.' One who runs away as if being crushed by an elephant is 'abstaining.' One who departs after striking and crushing as in a battle of warriors is 'fully abstaining.'

Khīṇāsavassāti khīṇakilesāsavassa. Kammussadoti puññābhisaṅkhāraapuññābhisaṅkhāraāneñjābhisaṅkhārasaṅkhātānaṃ kammānaṃ ussado ussannatā. Yassimeti yassa khīṇāsavassa ime ussadā.

'Of one whose taints are destroyed' means of one whose taints, which are defilements, are destroyed. 'Protuberance of kamma' means the protuberance, the abundance, of kammas reckoned as meritorious formations, demeritorious formations, and imperturbable formations. 'For whom these' means: for which one whose taints are destroyed these protuberances do not exist.

19. Evaṃ khīṇāsavapaṭipattiṃ dassetvā idāni diṭṭhigatikānaṃ titthiyānaṃ paṭipattiñca dassento āha “pakappitā saṅkhatā”ti. Tattha pakappitāti parikappitā. Saṅkhatāti paccayābhisaṅkhatā. Yassāti yassa kassaci diṭṭhigatikassa. Dhammāti diṭṭhiyo. Purakkhatāti purato katā. Santīti saṃvijjanti. Avīvadātāti avodātā. Yadattani passati ānisaṃsaṃ, taṃ nissito kuppapaṭiccasantinti yassete diṭṭhidhammā ‘purakkhatā avodātā santi, so evaṃvidho yasmā attani tassā diṭṭhiyā diṭṭhadhammikañca sakkārādiṃ, samparāyikañca gativisesādiṃ [V 0.0158] ānisaṃsaṃ sampassati, tasmā tañca ānisaṃsaṃ, tañca kuppatāya ca paṭiccasamuppannatāya ca sammutisantitāya ca kuppapaṭiccasantisaṅkhātaṃ [M 0.0175] diṭṭhiṃ nissito ca hoti. So taṃ nissitattā attānaṃ vā ukkaṃseyya, pare vā vambheyya abhūtehipi guṇadosehi.

19. Having thus shown the practice of one whose taints are destroyed, now, to show the practice of the sectarians who are given to views, he says, 'concocted and conditioned.' Herein, 'concocted' means devised. 'Conditioned' means conditioned by causes. 'Of whomever' means of any adherent of a view. 'States' means views. 'Held in front' means placed foremost. 'Are' means they exist. 'Not fully purified' means not cleansed. 'Whatever benefit he sees in himself, relying on that which is unstable and dependent': for whomever these views are 'held in front' and 'not fully purified,' such a person, because he sees for himself the benefit of that view in this very life, such as honor, and the future benefit, such as a special destination, therefore relies on that benefit and on that view, which is reckoned as 'unstable and dependent' because it is unstable, dependently arisen, and conventionally existing. Because he relies on that, he might exalt himself or disparage others with non-existent virtues and faults.

Saṅkhatāti mūlapadaṃ. Saṅkhatāti paccayehi samāgantvā katā. Upasaggavasena padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ. Abhisaṅkhatāti [P 1.0202] paccayehi abhikatā. Saṇṭhapitāti paccayavaseneva sammā ṭhapitā. Aniccāti hutvā abhāvena. Paṭiccasamuppannāti vatthārammaṇaṃ paṭicca uppannā. Khayadhammāti kamena khayasabhāvā. Vayadhammāti pavattivasena parihāyanasabhāvā. Virāgadhammāti anivattī hutvā vigacchanasabhāvā. Nirodhadhammāti nirujjhanasabhāvā, anuppattidhammā hutvā nirujjhanasabhāvāti attho. Diṭṭhigatikassāti dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhiyo gahetvā ṭhitapuggalassa.

“Conditioned” is the root term. “Conditioned” means made by the coming together of conditions. The word is expanded by way of a prefix. “Fabricated” means thoroughly made by conditions. “Established” means properly established by the force of conditions. “Impermanent” means having come into being and then ceasing to be. “Dependently arisen” means arisen dependent on a basis and object. “Subject to destruction” means having the nature of gradual destruction. “Subject to vanishing” means having the nature of deterioration through the process of becoming. “Subject to fading away” means having the nature of departing without returning. “Subject to cessation” means having the nature of ceasing, meaning having the nature of ceasing after having come into existence. “For one who holds to views” refers to a person established in holding the sixty-two views.

Purekkhārāti pure katā. Taṇhādhajoti ussāpitaṭṭhena taṇhādhajo, taṇhāpaṭākā assa atthīti taṇhādhajo. Purecārikaṭṭhena taṇhā eva ketu assāti taṇhāketu. Taṇhādhipateyyoti chandādhipativasena, taṇhā adhipatito āgatāti vā taṇhādhipateyyo, taṇhādhipati vā etassa atthīti taṇhādhipateyyo. Diṭṭhidhajādīsupi eseva nayo. Avodātāti aparisuddhā. Saṃkiliṭṭhāti sayaṃ kiliṭṭhā. Saṃkilesikāti tapanīyā.

“Purekkhārā” means placed in front. “Taṇhādhajo” means one whose banner is craving, because craving is raised high—thus, one with craving as a banner or flag. “Taṇhāketu” means one whose standard is craving, because craving goes before. “Taṇhādhipateyyo” means by way of the dominance of desire, or because it comes from craving as a dominant factor, or because one has craving as a dominant factor. The same principle applies to “diṭṭhidhaja” and others. “Avodātā” means impure. “Saṃkiliṭṭhā” means self-defiled. “Saṃkilesikā” means tormenting.

Dve ānisaṃse passatīti dve guṇe dakkhati. Diṭṭhadhammikañca ānisaṃsanti imasmiṃyeva attabhāve paccakkhadhammānisaṃsañca. Samparāyikanti paraloke pattabbaṃ ānisaṃsañca. Yaṃdiṭṭhiko satthā hotīti satthā yathāladdhiko bhavati. Taṃdiṭṭhikā sāvakā hontīti tassa vacanaṃ suṇantā sāvakāpi tathāladdhikā honti. Sakkarontīti sakkārappattaṃ karonti. Garuṃ karontīti garukārappattaṃ karonti. Mānentīti manasā piyāyanti. Pūjentīti catupaccayābhihārapūjāya pūjenti. Apacitiṃ karontīti apacitippattaṃ karonti. Tattha yassa cattāro paccaye sakkaritvā suabhisaṅkhate paṇīte katvā denti, so sakkato. Yasmiṃ garubhāvaṃ paṭṭhapetvā denti, so garukato. Yaṃ manasā piyāyanti, so mānito. Yassa sabbampetaṃ karonti, so pūjito. Yassa abhivādanapaccupaṭṭhānaañjalikammādivasena [P 1.0203] paramanipaccakāraṃ karonti, so apacito. Keci [M 0.0176] “sakkaronti kāyena, garuṃ karonti vācāya, mānenti cittena, pūjenti lābhenā”ti vaṇṇayanti. Alaṃ nāgattāya vāti nāgabhāvāya nāgarājabhāvāya vā alaṃ pariyattaṃ. Supaṇṇattāya vāti supaṇṇarājabhāvāya. Yakkhattāya vāti yakkhasenāpatibhāvāya. Asurattāya [V 0.0159] vāti asurabhāvāya. Gandhabbattāya vāti gandhabbadevaghaṭe nibbattabhāvāya. Mahārājattāya vāti catunnaṃ mahārājānaṃ aññatarabhāvāya. Indattāya vāti sakkabhāvāya. Brahmattāya vāti brahmakāyikādīnaṃ aññatarabhāvāya. Devattāya vāti sammutidevādīnaṃ aññatarabhāvāya. Suddhiyāti parisuddhabhāvāya alaṃ pariyattaṃ. Visuddhiyāti sabbamalarahitaaccantaparisuddhabhāvāya. Parisuddhiyāti sabbākārena parisuddhabhāvāya.

'He sees two benefits' means he will see two benefits. 'The visible benefit' refers to the direct advantage in this very life. 'The future benefit' refers to the advantage attainable in the next life. 'A teacher who has such a view' means a teacher who holds that view. 'Disciples who have such a view' means the disciples who listen to his words also hold that view. 'They honor' means they treat with respect. 'They revere' means they treat with reverence. 'They esteem' means they hold dear in their minds. 'They venerate' means they honor with offerings of the four requisites. 'They pay homage' means they show the utmost respect. Here, one to whom the four requisites are offered with care, prepared well and given refined, is honored. One in whom a sense of reverence is established and then given to, is revered. One who is held dear in the mind is esteemed. One to whom all these are done is venerated. One to whom the highest homage is paid through gestures like bowing, attending, and raising joined palms is paid homage. Some explain it thus: “They honor with the body, revere with speech, esteem with the mind, and venerate with material support.” 'Sufficient for attaining the state of a nāga' means sufficient for becoming a nāga or a nāga king. 'Sufficient for attaining the state of a supaṇṇa' means sufficient for becoming a supaṇṇa king. 'Sufficient for attaining the state of a yakkha' means sufficient for becoming a yakkha general. 'Sufficient for attaining the state of an asura' means sufficient for becoming an asura. 'Sufficient for attaining the state of a gandhabba' means sufficient for being reborn among the gandhabba devas. 'Sufficient for attaining the state of a great king' means sufficient for becoming one of the four great kings. 'Sufficient for attaining the state of Indra' means sufficient for becoming Sakka. 'Sufficient for attaining the state of Brahmā' means sufficient for becoming one of the Brahmā beings. 'Sufficient for attaining the state of a deva' means sufficient for becoming one of the devas by convention. 'Sufficient for purity' means sufficient for a state of purity. 'Sufficient for purification' means sufficient for an utterly pure state entirely free from stains. 'Sufficient for complete purity' means sufficient for a state of purity in every way.

Tattha tiracchānayoniyaṃ adhipaccattaṃ suddhiyā. Devaloke adhipaccattaṃ visuddhiyā. Brahmaloke adhipaccattaṃ parisuddhiyā. Caturāsītikappasahassāni atikkamitvā muccanatthaṃ muttiyā. Antarāyābhāvena muccanatthaṃ vimuttiyā. Sabbākārena muttiyā parimuttiyā. Sujjhantīti tasmiṃ samaye pabbajitabhāvena suddhiṃ pāpuṇanti. Visujjhantīti pabbajjaṃ gahetvā paṭipattiyā yuttabhāvena vividhena sujjhanti. Parisujjhantīti nipphattiṃ pāpetvā sabbākārena sujjhanti. Muccanti tesaṃ samayantaradhammena. Vimuccanti etassa satthuno ovādena. Parimuccanti etassa satthuno anusāsanena. Sujjhissāmītiādayo anāgatavasena vuttā. Āyatiṃ phalapāṭikaṅkhīti anāgate vipākaphalamākaṅkhamāno. Idaṃ diṭṭhigatikānaṃ icchāmattaṃ. Diṭṭhigatañhi ijjhamānaṃ nirayaṃ vā tiracchānayoniṃ vā nipphādeti.

Here, mastery in the animal realm is for purification. Mastery in the divine realm is for thorough purification. Mastery in the Brahma realm is for complete purification. Having passed through eighty-four thousand eons, they are freed for the sake of liberation. Through the absence of obstacles, they are freed for the sake of deliverance. In every way, by liberation for the sake of final liberation. ‘They become purified’—at that time, they attain purity through the state of having gone forth. ‘They become thoroughly purified’—having undertaken the going forth, they are purified in various ways through being devoted to the practice. ‘They become completely purified’—having attained fulfillment, they are purified in every way. ‘They are freed’—by the doctrine of another school. ‘They are liberated’—by the instruction of this Teacher. ‘They are fully liberated’—by the guidance of this Teacher. ‘I will be purified,’ and so on, are said with reference to the future. ‘Longing for the fruit in the future’—desiring the fruit of ripening in the future. This is merely the wish of those whose destination is determined by views. For a view, when it succeeds, produces either hell or the animal realm.

Accantasantīti atiantanissaraṇasanti. Tadaṅgasantīti paṭhamajjhānādiguṇaṅgena nīvaraṇādiaguṇaṅgaṃ sametīti jhānaṃ tadaṅgasanti. Sammutisantīti samāhāravasena diṭṭhisanti. Tā vibhāgato dassetuṃ “katamā accantasantī”tiādimāha. Amataṃ [P 1.0204] nibbānanti evamādayo heṭṭhā vuttatthāyeva. Paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa nīvaraṇā santā hontīti evamādayo anto appanāyaṃ atisayavasena vuttā. Api ca sammutisanti imasmiṃ atthe adhippetā, santīti itare dve santiyo paṭikkhipitvā sammutisantimeva dīpeti. Kuppasantinti vipākajanakavasena parivattanavasena calasantiṃ[M 0.0177]. Pakuppasantinti visesena calasantiṃ. Eritasantinti kampanasantiṃ. Sameritasantinti visesena kampitasantiṃ. Calitasantinti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Ghaṭṭitasantinti pīḷitasantiṃ. Santiṃ nissitoti diṭṭhisaṅkhātaṃ santiṃ nissito. Assitoti āsito visesena nissito. Allīnoti ekībhūto.

‘Accantasantī’ means the peace that is the ultimate escape, the uttermost release. ‘Tadaṅgasantī’ refers to the peace where the hindrances and other unwholesome factors are pacified by the qualities of the first jhāna and so forth; thus, jhāna is called a peace by substitution of factors. ‘Sammutisantī’ denotes the peace of a view by way of convention. To explain their distinctions, it is said: ‘What is the ultimate peace?’ and so on. ‘The deathless, Nibbāna,’ and similar terms have the meanings already explained above. For one who has attained the first jhāna, the hindrances are pacified—this and similar statements are made with emphasis within absorption. Moreover, in this context, ‘sammutisanti’ is what is intended; by saying ‘peace,’ it indicates only conventional peace, rejecting the other two types of peace. ‘Kuppasantī’ means a wavering peace, due to its nature of producing results and its liability to change. ‘Pakuppasantī’ means an especially wavering peace. ‘Eritasantī’ means a trembling peace. ‘Sameritasantī’ means an especially trembling peace. ‘Calitasantī’ is a synonym for the same. ‘Ghaṭṭitasantī’ means an oppressed peace. ‘Santiṃ nissito’ means relying on peace, which is reckoned as a view. ‘Assito’ means especially relying upon. ‘Allīno’ means having become one with it.

20. Evaṃ nissite tāva “diṭṭhīnivesā…pe… ādiyatī ca dhamma”nti tattha diṭṭhīnivesāti idaṃsaccābhinivesasaṅkhātāni diṭṭhinivesanāni. Na hi svātivattāti sukhena ativattitabbā na honti. Dhammesu niccheyya samuggahītanti dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhigatesu taṃ taṃ samuggahitaṃ [V 0.0160] abhiniviṭṭhadhammaṃ nicchinitvā pavattā diṭṭhinivesā na hi svātivattāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tasmā naro tesu nivesanesu, nirassatī ādiyatī ca dhammanti yasmā na hi svātivattā, tasmā naro tesuyeva diṭṭhinivesanesu ajasīlagosīlakukkurasīlapañcātapamaruppapātaukkuṭikappadhānakaṇṭakāpassayādibhedaṃ satthāraṃ dhammakkhānaṃ gaṇādibhedañca taṃ taṃ dhammaṃ nirassati ca ādiyati ca jahati ca gaṇhāti ca vanamakkaṭo viya taṃ taṃ sākhanti vuttaṃ hoti.

20. Thus, for one who relies on this, ‘adherence to views… and grasps a doctrine.’ Therein, ‘adherence to views’ means the adherences to views reckoned as the insistence that ‘this alone is true.’ ‘Not easily overcome’ means they are not to be easily surpassed. Regarding ‘having decided among doctrines what is firmly grasped,’ this means that the adherences to views, which proceed from having decided upon this or that firmly grasped and adhered-to doctrine among the sixty-two views, are said to be ‘not easily overcome.’ Therefore, regarding ‘a person in these adherences rejects and grasps doctrines,’ because they are not easily overcome, it is said that a person in these very adherences to views rejects and grasps, abandons and takes up, this or that doctrine—concerning the teacher, the exposition of the Dhamma, the group, and so on, with their various distinctions such as the goat-practice, the cow-practice, the dog-practice, the five-fire austerity, falling from a cliff, the squatting exertion, and lying on a bed of thorns—like a forest monkey grabbing and letting go of various branches.

Evaṃ nirassanto ca ādiyanto ca anavaṭṭhitacittattā asantehipi [P 1.0205] guṇadosehi attano vā parassa vā yasāyasaṃ uppādeyya. Durativattāti atikkamituṃ dukkhā. Duttarāti duuttarā. Duppatarā dussamatikkamā dubbinivattāti upasaggena vaḍḍhitā.

Thus, rejecting and grasping, due to an unsettled mind, one might generate fame or infamy for oneself or for others, even with regard to non-existent virtues or faults. ‘Hard to overcome’ means difficult to transcend. ‘Hard to cross’ means very hard to cross. ‘Hard to pass over,’ ‘hard to get beyond,’ and ‘hard to turn back from’ are terms intensified by prefixes.

Nicchinitvāti sassatavasena nicchayaṃ katvā. Vinicchinitvāti attavasena nānāvidhena vinicchayaṃ katvā. Vicinitvāti pariyesitvā. Pavicinitvāti attaniyavasena sabbākārena pariyesitvā. “Nicinitvā viccinitvā”tipi pāṭho. Odhiggāhoti avadhiyitvā gāho. Bilaggāhoti koṭṭhāsavasena gāho “bilaso vibhajitvā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.378; ma. ni. 1.111) viya. Varaggāhoti uttamagāho. Koṭṭhāsaggāhoti avayavavasena gāho. Uccayaggāhoti rāsivasena gāho. Samuccayaggāhoti koṭṭhāsavasena rāsivasena ca gāho. Idaṃ saccanti idameva sabhāvaṃ. Tacchanti tathabhāvaṃ aviparītasabhāvaṃ. Tathanti vipariṇāmarahitaṃ. Bhūtanti vijjamānaṃ. Yāthāvanti yathāsabhāvaṃ. Aviparītanti na viparītaṃ.

‘Nicchinitvā’ means having made a determination in terms of eternalism. ‘Vinicchinitvā’ means having made an investigation in various ways in terms of self. ‘Vicinitvā’ means having sought. ‘Pavicinitvā’ means having sought in every way in terms of what belongs to self. There is also the reading: ‘nicinitvā viccinitvā’ (having accumulated, having explored). ‘Odhiggāho’ means grasping by setting a limit. ‘Bilaggāho’ means grasping by portions, as in ‘having divided into portions’ (Dī. Ni. 2.378; Ma. Ni. 1.111). ‘Varaggāho’ means the supreme grasping. ‘Koṭṭhāsaggāho’ means grasping by parts. ‘Uccayaggāho’ means grasping by accumulation. ‘Samuccayaggāho’ means grasping by both portions and accumulation. ‘This is truth’ means this alone is the true nature. ‘Real’ means the state of being so, a nature that is not contrary. ‘So’ means devoid of change. ‘Actual’ means existing. ‘As it is’ means according to its own nature. ‘Not contrary’ means not inverted.

Nirassatīti [M 0.0178] niassati vikkhipati. Paravicchindanāya vāti parehi vissajjāpanena. Anabhisambhuṇanto vāti asampāpuṇanto vā asakkonto vā vissajjeti. Paro vicchindetīti añño viyogaṃ karoti. Natthetthāti natthi ettha. Sīlaṃ anabhisambhuṇantoti sīlaṃ asampādento. Sīlaṃ nirassatīti sīlaṃ vissajjeti. Ito paresupi eseva nayo.

‘Nirassati’ means casts away, discards. Or ‘for the cutting off by another’ means by causing it to be abandoned by others. Or ‘not accomplishing’ means, not attaining or not being able, one abandons. ‘Another cuts off’ means another causes a separation. ‘There is nothing here’ means there is nothing in this. ‘Not accomplishing virtue’ means not fulfilling virtue. ‘Rejects virtue’ means abandons virtue. The same method applies to the following cases.

21. Yo panāyaṃ sabbadiṭṭhigatādidosadhunanāya paññāya samannāgatattā dhono, tassa dhonassa hi…pe… anūpayo so. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Dhonadhammasamannāgamā dhonassa dhutasabbapāpassa arahato katthaci loke tesu tesu bhavesu [P 1.0206] saṃkappanā diṭṭhi natthi. So tassā diṭṭhiyā abhāvā, yāya ca attanā kataṃ pāpakammaṃ paṭicchādentā titthiyā māyāya vā mānena vā evaṃ agatiṃ gacchanti, tampi māyañca mānañca pahāya dhono rāgādīnaṃ dosānaṃ kena [V 0.0161] gaccheyya, diṭṭhadhamme samparāye vā nirayādīsu gativisesesu kena saṅkhaṃ gaccheyya, anūpayo so, so hi taṇhādiṭṭhiupayānaṃ dvinnaṃ abhāvena anūpayoti.

21. But this one, who is ‘cleansed’ (dhono) because he is endowed with the wisdom that shakes off all faults such as wrong views, for that cleansed one... he is without attachment. What is meant by this? Because he is endowed with the qualities of the cleansed, for the cleansed one, the Arahant who has shaken off all evil, there is no conception or view anywhere in the world regarding this or that state of existence. Due to the absence of that view—by which sectarians, concealing the evil deeds done by themselves, go to a wrong course through deceit or conceit—and having abandoned that deceit and conceit, by what means would the cleansed one go astray among the faults such as lust? In the present life or in the future, in particular destinations such as hell, by what means could he be reckoned? He is without attachment, for he is without attachment due to the absence of the two attachments: craving and views.

Kiṃ kāraṇāti kena kāraṇena. Dhonā vuccati paññāti dhonā iti kiṃkāraṇā paññā kathīyati. Tāya paññāya kāyaduccaritanti tāya vuttappakārāya paññāya kāyato pavattaṃ duṭṭhu kilesapūtikattā vā caritanti kāyaduccaritaṃ. Dhūtañca dhotañcāti kampitañca dhovitañca. Sandhotañcāti sammā dhovitañca. Niddhotañcāti visesena suṭṭhu niddhotañca. Rāgo dhuto cātiādayo catunnaṃ maggānaṃ vasena yojetabbā.

‘For what reason?’ means by what reason. ‘Wisdom is called cleansed’ means for what reason is wisdom said to be ‘cleansed’? By that wisdom, bodily misconduct—that is, conduct proceeding from the body that is corrupt, or so called because of the putrid nature of the defilements—is shaken and washed, that is, agitated and cleansed. ‘Thoroughly washed’ means properly washed. ‘Completely washed’ means especially well washed. ‘Lust is shaken off,’ and so on—these should be connected by way of the four paths.

Sammādiṭṭhiyā micchādiṭṭhi dhutā cāti maggasampayuttāya sammādiṭṭhiyā micchādiṭṭhi kampitā calitā dhovitā. Sammāsaṅkappādīsupi eseva nayo. Vuttañhetaṃ “sammādiṭṭhikassa, bhikkhave, micchādiṭṭhi nijjiṇṇā hotī”ti suttaṃ (a. ni. 10.106; dī. ni. 3.360) vitthāretabbaṃ. Sammāñāṇenāti maggasampayuttañāṇena, paccavekkhaṇañāṇena vā. Micchāñāṇanti viparītañāṇaṃ ayāthāvañāṇaṃ, pāpakiriyāsu upacintāvasena pāpaṃ katvā “sukataṃ mayā”ti paccavekkhaṇākārena ca [M 0.0179] uppanno moho. Sammāvimuttiyā micchāvimuttīti samucchedavimuttiyā viparītā ayāthāvavimuttiyeva cetovimuttisaññitā.

Through right view, wrong view is dispelled—that is, by right view associated with the path, wrong view is shaken, dislodged, and washed away. The same principle applies to right intention and the rest. As it is said: "For one with right view, wrong view is overcome"—this sutta (A. Ni. 10.106; Dī. Ni. 3.360) should be elaborated. By right knowledge is meant knowledge associated with the path, or knowledge of reviewing. Wrong knowledge is perverted knowledge, untrue knowledge, the delusion that arises from contemplating evil deeds, and from reviewing evil after having done it with the thought, "I have done well." Through right liberation, wrong liberation is dispelled; this wrong liberation is the opposite of liberation by cutting off, a false and untrue liberation designated as 'liberation of mind'.

Arahā imehi dhoneyyehi dhammehīti rāgādīhi kilesehi dūre ṭhito arahā imehi vuttappakārehi kilesadhovanehi dhammehi upeto hoti. Dhonoti dhono puggalo, teneva “so dhutarāgo”tiādayo āha.

The Arahant is endowed with these cleansing qualities; that is, the Arahant, standing far from defilements such as lust, is endowed with these qualities that cleanse defilements as described. 'Dhono' means a purified person; hence it is said, "he has shaken off lust," and so on.

Māyā vuccati vañcanikācariyāti vañcanakiriyaṃ vañcanakaraṇaṃ assā atthīti vañcanikācariyā. Tassa paṭicchādanahetūti [P 1.0207] tesaṃ duccaritānaṃ appakāsanakāraṇā. Pāpikaṃ icchaṃ paṇidahatīti lāmakaṃ patthanaṃ patiṭṭhāpeti. “Mā maṃ jaññā”ti icchatīti “mayhaṃ kataṃ pāpaṃ pare mā jāniṃsū”ti paccāsīsati. Saṅkappetīti vitakkaṃ uppādeti. Vācaṃ bhāsatīti jānaṃyeva paṇṇattiṃ vītikkamanto bhikkhu bhāriyaṃ karoti. “Amhākaṃ vītikkamaṭṭhānaṃ nāma natthī”ti upasanto viya bhāsati. Kāyena parakkamatīti “mayā kataṃ idaṃ pāpakammaṃ mā keci jāniṃsū”ti kāyena vattaṃ karoti. Vijjamānadosapaṭicchādanato cakkhumohanamāyā assāti māyāvī, māyāvino bhāvo māyāvitā. Katvā pāpaṃ puna paṭicchādanato aticca assarati etāya sattoti accasarā. Kāyavācākiriyāhi aññathā dassanato vañcetīti vañcanā[V 0.0162]. Etāya sattā nikarontīti nikati, micchā karontīti attho. “Nāhaṃ evaṃ karomī”ti pāpānaṃ vikkhipanato nikiraṇā. “Nāhaṃ evaṃ karomī”ti parivajjanato pariharaṇā. Kāyādīhi saṃharaṇato gūhanā. Samabhāgena gūhanā parigūhanā. Tiṇapaṇṇehi viya gūthaṃ kāyavacīkammehi pāpaṃ chādetīti chādanā. Sabbato bhāgena chādanā paricchādanā. Na uttāniṃ katvā dassetīti anuttānikammaṃ. Na pākaṭaṃ katvā dassetīti anāvikammaṃ. Suṭṭhu chādanā vocchādanā. Katapaṭicchādanavasena punapi pāpassa karaṇato pāpakiriyā. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ katapaṭicchādanalakkhaṇā māyā nāma vuccati, yāya samannāgato puggalo bhasmapaṭicchanno viya aṅgāro, udakapaṭicchanno viya khāṇu, pilotikapaliveṭhitaṃ viya ca satthaṃ hoti.

Deception is called 'deceitful practice' (vañcanikācariyā); that is, it has the act of deceiving and the means of deceiving, hence it is deceitful practice. It serves to conceal their misconduct—the reason for not exposing their misdeeds. They harbor wicked desires—they establish base aspirations. Wishing, "May they not know me," they hope, "May others not know the evil I have done." They plan—they generate thoughts. They speak words—knowing and violating the precepts, a bhikkhu commits a grave offense. They speak as if restrained, saying, "There is no place where we transgress." They strive with the body—acting with the thought, "May no one know the evil deed I have done." Because they conceal existing faults, they have deception (māyā) which blinds the eye, thus they are called deceitful (māyāvī)—the state of being deceitful is deceitfulness (māyāvitā). Having done evil, they further conceal it—thus they are called 'transgressors' (accasarā), for with this a being goes beyond. They deceive by showing something false through actions of body and speech—this is deception (vañcanā). By this, beings act fraudulently—this is trickery (nikati), meaning they act falsely. They scatter their evil, saying, "I do not do this"—this is scattering (nikiraṇā). They avoid, saying, "I do not do this"—this is avoidance (pariharaṇā). They conceal with body and so forth—this is hiding (gūhanā). They conceal completely—this is total concealment (parigūhanā). They cover evil with actions of body and speech, like hiding dung with grass and leaves—this is covering (chādanā). They conceal thoroughly—this is complete covering (paricchādanā). They do not reveal openly—this is non-disclosure (anuttānikammaṃ). They do not make it evident—this is non-exposure (anāvikammaṃ). They cover well—this is thorough covering (vocchādanā). Because by concealing what they have done, they commit evil again—this is evil action (pāpakiriyā). This is called—this characteristic of concealment is known as deceit (māyā). A person endowed with this is like an ember covered with ashes, a stump hidden by water, or a sword wrapped in rags.

Ekavidhena [M 0.0180] mānoti ekaparicchedena ekakoṭṭhāsena māno. Yā cittassa unnatīti yā cittassa abbhussāpanā, ayaṃ mānoti attho. Ettha puggalaṃ anāmasitvā nibbattitamānova vutto.

Pride is of one kind, meaning pride is a single determination or a single portion. The phrase "the exaltation of the mind" refers to the raising up of the mind—this is the meaning of pride. Here, it is stated as pride that arises without reference to a person.

Attukkaṃsanamānoti attānaṃ upari ṭhapanamāno. Paravambhanamānoti pare lāmakakaraṇamāno. Ime dve mānā yebhuyyena tathā pavattākāravasena vuttā.

Self-exaltation is the conceit of placing oneself above others. Disparaging others is the conceit of making others seem inferior. These two kinds of conceit are generally spoken of in terms of the way they manifest.

“Seyyohamasmī”ti mānoti jātiādīni nissāya “ahamasmi seyyo”ti [P 1.0208] uppanno māno. Sadisamānādīsupi eseva nayo. Evamimepi tayo mānā puggalavisesaṃ anissāya tathā pavattākāravasena vuttā. Tesu ekeko tiṇṇampi seyyasadisahīnānaṃ uppajjati. Tattha “seyyohamasmī”ti māno seyyasseva yāthāvamāno, sesānaṃ ayāthāvamāno. “Sadisohamasmī”ti māno sadisasseva yāthāvamāno, sesānaṃ ayāthāvamāno. “Hīnohamasmī”ti māno hīnasseva yāthāvamāno, sesānaṃ ayāthāvamāno.

The conceit "I am superior" is the conceit that arises based on things such as birth, with the thought, "I am superior." The same method applies to the conceits of equality and inferiority. Thus, these three conceits are spoken of according to how they occur, without depending on individual distinctions. Each one of them arises in relation to the superior, the equal, and the inferior. Of these, the conceit "I am superior" is a conceit according to reality only for one who is superior, but a conceit not according to reality for the others. The conceit "I am equal" is a conceit according to reality only for one who is equal, but a conceit not according to reality for the others. The conceit "I am inferior" is a conceit according to reality only for one who is inferior, but a conceit not according to reality for the others.

Catubbidhena māno lokadhammavasena vutto. Pañcavidhena māno pañcakāmaguṇavasena vutto. Chabbidhena māno cakkhādisampattivasena vutto. Tattha mānaṃ janetīti mānaṃ uppādeti.

Conceit is spoken of in four ways, in connection with worldly conditions. Conceit is spoken of in five ways, in connection with the five strands of sensual pleasure. Conceit is spoken of in six ways, in connection with the accomplishment of the eye and so forth. Here, 'it generates conceit' means 'it produces conceit'.

Sattavidhena mānaniddese mānoti unnamo. Atimānoti “jātiādīhi mayā sadiso natthī”ti atikkamitvā maññanavasena uppanno māno. Mānātimānoti “ayaṃ pubbe mayā sadiso, idāni ahaṃ seṭṭho, ayaṃ hīnataro”ti uppanno māno. Ayaṃ bhārātibhāro viya purimaṃ [V 0.0163] sadisamānaṃ upādāya mānātimāno nāmāti dassetuṃ “mānātimāno”ti āha. Omānoti hīnamāno. Yo “hīnohamasmī”ti māno nāma vutto, ayaṃ omāno nāma. Api cettha “tvaṃ jātimā, kākajāti viya te jāti. Tvaṃ gottavā, caṇḍālagottaṃ viya te gottaṃ. Tuyhaṃ saro atthi, kākasaro viya te saro”ti evaṃ attānaṃ heṭṭhā katvā pavattanavasena ayaṃ “omāno”ti veditabbo.

In the sevenfold classification of conceit, "conceit" is elevation. "Excessive conceit" is the conceit that arises from thinking surpassingly, "There is no one equal to me in birth and other qualities." "Conceit above conceit" is the conceit that arises thinking, "This person was once equal to me, but now I am superior, and this one is inferior." To show that this is called "conceit above conceit" by taking the previous conceit of equality as a basis, like an extra burden upon a burden, the term "mānātimāno" is used. "Inferiority conceit" is conceit of inferiority. The conceit that is expressed as, "I am inferior," is called "inferiority conceit." Furthermore, it should be understood as 'inferiority conceit' when it proceeds by way of debasing oneself, for example, by thinking, 'Though you are of high birth, your birth is like that of a crow. Though you have a lineage, your lineage is like that of an outcast. Though you have a voice, your voice is like that of a crow.'

Adhimānoti cattāri saccāni appatvā pattasaññissa, catūhi maggehi kattabbe kicce akateyeva katasaññissa, catusaccadhamme anadhigate adhigatasaññissa[M 0.0181], arahatte asacchikate sacchikatasaññissa uppanno adhigatamāno adhimāno nāma. Ayaṃ pana kassa uppajjati, kassa na uppajjatīti? Ariyasāvakassa tāva na uppajjati. So hi maggaphalanibbānapahīnakilesāvasiṭṭhakilesapaccavekkhaṇena sañjātasomanasso ariyaguṇapaṭivedhe nikkaṅkho, tasmā sotāpannādīnaṃ “ahaṃ sakadāgāmī”tiādivasena māno na uppajjati, dussīlassa ca na uppajjati. So hi ariyaguṇādhigame nirāsova. Sīlavatopi pariccattakammaṭṭhānassa niddārāmatādimanuyuttassa na uppajjati[P 1.0209], parisuddhasīlassa pana kammaṭṭhāne appamattassa nāmarūpaṃ vavatthapetvā paccayapariggahena vitiṇṇakaṅkhassa tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā saṅkhāre sammasantassa āraddhavipassakassa uppajjati, uppanne ca suddhasamathalābhī suddhavipassanālābhī vā antarā ṭhapeti. So hi dasapi vassāni vīsampi vassāni tiṃsampi vassāni asītipi vassāni kilesasamudācāraṃ apassanto “ahaṃ sotāpanno”ti vā “sakadāgāmī”ti vā “anāgāmī”ti vā maññati, samathavipassanālābhī pana arahatteyeva ṭhapeti. Tassa hi samādhibalena kilesā vikkhambhitā, vipassanābalena saṅkhārā supariggahitā, tasmā saṭṭhipi vassāni asītipi vassāni vassasatampi kilesā na samudācaranti, khīṇāsavasseva cittācāro hoti. So evaṃ dīgharattaṃ kilesasamudācāraṃ apassanto antarā aṭṭhatvāva “arahā aha”nti maññati.

Over-estimation (adhimāna) is the conceit that arises in one who, not having attained the four truths, has the perception of having attained them; who, not having done what should be done by the four paths, has the perception of having done it; who, not having realized the dhammas of the four truths, has the perception of having realized them; who, not having realized arahantship, has the perception of having realized it. Now, to whom does it arise, and to whom does it not arise? Firstly, it does not arise in a noble disciple. For such a one, being joyful from reviewing the defilements abandoned by the path, fruit, and Nibbāna, and the defilements that remain, is without doubt concerning the penetration of noble qualities. Therefore, in stream-enterers and others, conceit does not arise in the form of thinking, 'I am a once-returner,' and so forth. Nor does it arise in the immoral, for such a one is without hope of attaining noble qualities. It also does not arise in a virtuous person who has given up their meditation subject and is devoted to indolence and the like. But it does arise in one of purified virtue, diligent in their meditation subject, who, having defined name-and-form and overcome doubt by grasping conditions, contemplates formations by applying the three characteristics, and has thus undertaken insight meditation. And when it arises, one who has attained only pure serenity or only pure insight establishes it at an intermediate stage. For such a person, not seeing the defilements arise for ten, twenty, thirty, or even eighty years, thinks, 'I am a stream-enterer,' or 'a once-returner,' or 'a non-returner.' But one who has attained both serenity and insight establishes it only at arahantship. For them, defilements are suppressed by the power of concentration, and formations are well-grasped by the power of insight. Thus, even for sixty, eighty, or a hundred years, defilements do not arise, and their mental conduct is like that of one whose taints are destroyed. Not seeing the defilements arise for such a long time, having established it at an intermediate stage, they think, 'I am an arahant.'

Asmimānoti rūpe asmītiādinā nayena pañcasu khandhesu “ahaṃ rūpādayo”ti uppanno māno. Micchāmānoti pāpakehi kammāyatanasippāyatanavijjāṭṭhānasutapaṭibhānasīlabbatehi, pāpikāya ca diṭṭhiyā uppanno māno. Tattha pāpakaṃ kammāyatanaṃ nāma kevaṭṭamacchabandhanesādānaṃ kammaṃ. Pāpakaṃ sippāyatanaṃ nāma macchajālakhipakumīnakaraṇesu ceva pāsaoḍḍanasūlāropanādīsu ca chekatā. Pāpakaṃ vijjāṭṭhānaṃ nāma yā kāci parūpaghātavijjā. Pāpakaṃ sutaṃ nāma bhāratayuddhasītāharaṇādipaṭisaṃyuttaṃ. Pāpakaṃ paṭibhānaṃ nāma dubbhāsitayuttaṃ kappanāṭakavilappanādipaṭibhānaṃ[V 0.0164]. Pāpakaṃ sīlaṃ nāma ajasīlaṃ gosīlaṃ. Vatampi ajavatagovatameva. Pāpikā diṭṭhi pana dvāsaṭṭhiyā diṭṭhigatesu yākāci diṭṭhi. Aṭṭhavidhamāno uttānatthoyeva.

The conceit 'I am' (asmimāna) is the conceit that arises in the five aggregates—form and so on—with the notion 'I am form, etc.' Wrong conceit (micchāmāna) is the conceit that arises from unwholesome bases of action, unwholesome crafts, unwholesome branches of knowledge, unwholesome learning, unwholesome eloquence, unwholesome moral practices and vows, and from unwholesome views. Herein, an unwholesome base of action is action such as that of fishermen, fish-trappers, and hunters. An unwholesome craft is skill in making fishing nets and fish-traps, as well as expertise in setting snares and impaling. An unwholesome branch of knowledge refers to any knowledge used to harm others. Unwholesome learning includes material connected with the Bharata war, the abduction of Sītā, and similar stories. Unwholesome eloquence consists of ingenuity connected with improper speech, theatrical performances, and lamentations. Unwholesome moral practice is goat-like morality and cow-like morality. Vows, too, are merely goat-like vows and cow-like vows. An unwholesome view, however, is any of the sixty-two kinds of views. The eightfold conceit is clear in meaning.

Navavidhena [M 0.0182] mānaniddese seyyassa “seyyohamasmī”tiādayo nava mānā puggalaṃ nissāya vuttā. Ettha pana seyyassa “seyyohamasmī”ti māno rājānañceva pabbajitānañca uppajjati. Rājā hi “raṭṭhena vā dhanavāhanehi vā ko [P 1.0210] mayā sadiso atthī”ti etaṃ mānaṃ karoti. Pabbajitopi “sīladhutaṅgādīhi ko mayā sadiso atthī”ti etaṃ mānaṃ karoti.

In the exposition of the ninefold conceit, the nine conceits—such as 'I am superior' in one who is superior—are stated in reference to a person. Here, the conceit 'I am superior' in one who is superior arises in both kings and renunciants. A king thinks, 'Who is equal to me in kingdom, wealth, or vehicles?' and thus harbors this conceit. A renunciant also thinks, 'Who is equal to me in virtue, ascetic practices, and so on?' and thus harbors this conceit.

Seyyassa “sadisohamasmī”ti mānopi etesaṃyeva uppajjati. Rājā hi “raṭṭhena vā dhanavāhanehi vā aññarājūhi saddhiṃ mayhaṃ kiṃ nānākaraṇa”nti etaṃ mānaṃ karoti. Pabbajitopi “sīladhutaṅgādīhi aññena bhikkhunā mayhaṃ kiṃ nānākaraṇa”nti etaṃ mānaṃ karoti.

The conceit 'I am equal' in one who is superior also arises in these same individuals. A king thinks, 'What distinction is there between me and other kings in terms of kingdom, wealth, or vehicles?' and thus harbors this conceit. A renunciant also thinks, 'What distinction is there between me and another monk in terms of virtue, ascetic practices, and so on?' and thus harbors this conceit.

Seyyassa “hīnohamasmī”ti mānopi etesaṃyeva uppajjati. Yassa hi rañño raṭṭhaṃ vā dhanavāhanādīni vā nātisampannāni honti, so “mayhaṃ rājāti vohārasukhamattakameva, kiṃ rājā nāma aha”nti etaṃ mānaṃ karoti. Pabbajitopi appalābhasakkāro “ahaṃ dhammakathiko, bahussuto, mahātheroti kathāmattameva, kiṃ dhammakathiko nāmāhaṃ, kiṃ bahussuto nāmāhaṃ, kiṃ mahāthero nāmāhaṃ, yassa me lābhasakkāro natthī”ti etaṃ mānaṃ karoti.

The conceit 'I am inferior' in one who is superior also arises in these same individuals. A king whose kingdom, wealth, vehicles, and so on, are not very prosperous thinks, 'The title 'king' is merely a pleasant convention for me—what kind of king am I?' and thus harbors this conceit. A renunciant with little gain and honor thinks, 'The titles 'Dhamma speaker,' 'learned,' and 'great elder' are mere words—what kind of Dhamma speaker am I? What kind of learned one am I? What kind of great elder am I, since I receive no gain or honor?' and thus harbors this conceit.

Sadisassa “seyyohamasmī”ti mānādayo amaccādīnaṃ uppajjanti. Amacco vā hi raṭṭhiyo vā “bhogayānavāhanādīhi ko mayā sadiso añño rājapuriso atthī”ti vā, “mayhaṃ aññehi saddhiṃ kiṃ nānākaraṇa”nti vā, “amaccoti nāmameva mayhaṃ, ghāsacchādanamattampi me natthi, kiṃ amacco nāmāha”nti vā ete māne karoti.

For one who is equal, conceits such as 'I am superior' and so on arise in ministers and the like. For a minister or a provincial governor might think, 'Who else among the king's men is equal to me in terms of wealth, carriages, vehicles, and so on?' or, 'What distinction is there between me and others?' or, 'The name 'minister' is all I have, I do not even have enough for food and clothing; what kind of minister am I?'—thus they harbor these conceits.

Hīnassa “seyyohamasmī”ti mānādayo dāsādīnaṃ uppajjanti. Dāso hi “mātito vā pitito vā ko mayā sadiso añño dāso nāma atthi, aññe jīvituṃ asakkontā kucchihetu dāsā nāma jātā, ahaṃ pana paveṇīāgatattā seyyo”ti vā, “paveṇīāgatabhāvena ubhatosuddhikadāsattena asukadāsena nāma saddhiṃ ki mayhaṃ nānākaraṇa”nti vā, “kucchivasenāhaṃ dāsabyaṃ upagato, mātāpitukoṭiyā pana me dāsaṭṭhānaṃ natthi[V 0.0165], kiṃ dāso nāma aha”nti vā ete māne karoti. Yathā ca dāso, evaṃ pukkusacaṇḍālādayopi ete māne karontiyeva.

For one who is inferior, conceits such as 'I am superior' and so on arise in slaves and the like. A slave might think, 'Who else is equal to me as a slave, whether from the mother's side or the father's side? Others become slaves for the sake of their bellies, being unable to make a living, but I am superior because I come from a traditional lineage,' or, 'Coming from a traditional lineage and being a slave of pure birth on both sides, what distinction is there between me and such-and-such a slave?' or, 'I have entered into servitude on account of my belly, but on my mother's and father's side there is no slave status; what kind of slave am I?'—thus they harbor these conceits. Just as a slave does, so too do Pukkusas, Caṇḍālas, and the like harbor these conceits.

Ettha [M 0.0183] ca seyyassa “seyyohamasmī”ti uppannamānova yāthāvamāno, itare dve ayāthāvamānā. Tathā sadisassa “sadisohamasmī”ti, hīnassa “hīnohamasmī”ti uppannamānova yāthāvamāno, itare dve ayāthāvamānā. Tattha yāthāvamānā arahattamaggavajjhā, ayāthāvamānā sotāpattimaggavajjhā.

Here, the conceit 'I am superior' that arises in one who is superior is a conceit in accordance with reality, while the other two are not in accordance with reality. Similarly, the conceit 'I am equal' that arises in one who is equal, and the conceit 'I am inferior' that arises in one who is inferior, are conceits in accordance with reality, while the other two in each case are not in accordance with reality. Among these, conceits in accordance with reality are abandoned by the path of arahantship, while conceits not in accordance with reality are abandoned by the path of stream-entry.

Ettha [P 1.0211] ca seyyassa “seyyohamasmī”ti māno uttamassa uttamaṭṭhena “ahaṃ seyyo”ti evaṃ uppannamāno, seyyassa “sadisohamasmī”ti māno uttamassa samaṭṭhena “ahaṃ sadiso”ti evaṃ uppannamāno. Seyyassa “hīnohamasmī”ti māno uttamassa lāmakaṭṭhena “ahaṃ hīno”ti evaṃ uppannamāno. Evaṃ seyyamāno sadisamāno hīnamānoti ime tayo mānā seyyassa uppajjanti. Sadisassāpi ahaṃ seyyo, sadiso, hīnoti tayo mānā uppajjanti. Hīnassāpi ahaṃ hīno, sadiso, seyyoti tayo mānā uppajjanti.

Here, the conceit 'I am superior' in one who is superior arises as 'I am superior' in the sense of being superior. The conceit 'I am equal' in one who is superior arises as 'I am equal' in the sense of being equal. The conceit 'I am inferior' in one who is superior arises as 'I am inferior' in the sense of being inferior. Thus, these three conceits—the conceit of superiority, the conceit of equality, and the conceit of inferiority—arise in one who is superior. In one who is equal, too, the three conceits 'I am superior,' 'I am equal,' and 'I am inferior' arise. In one who is inferior, too, the three conceits 'I am inferior,' 'I am equal,' and 'I am superior' arise.

Dasavidhamānaniddese idhekacco mānaṃ janetīti ekacco puggalo mānaṃ janayati. Jātiyā vāti khattiyabhāvādijātisampattiyā vā. Gottena vāti gotamagottādinā ukkaṭṭhagottena vā. Kolaputtiyena vāti mahākulabhāvena vā. Vaṇṇapokkharatāya vāti vaṇṇasampannasarīratāya vā. Sarīrañhi “pokkhara”nti vuccati, tassa vaṇṇasampattiyā abhirūpabhāvenāti attho. Dhanena vāti dhanasampannabhāvena vā, mayhaṃ nidhānagatassa dhanassa pamāṇaṃ natthīti attho. Ajjhenena vāti ajjhāyanavasena vā. Kammāyatanena vāti “avasesā sattā chinnapakkhakākasadisā, ahaṃ pana mahiddhiko mahānubhāvo”ti vā, “ahaṃ yaṃ yaṃ kammaṃ karomi, taṃ taṃ samijjhatī”ti vā evamādinayappavattena kammāyatanena vā. Sippāyatanena vāti “avasesā sattā nisippā, ahaṃ sippavā”ti evamādinayappavattena sippāyatanena vā. Vijjāṭṭhānena vāti idaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayameva. Sutena vāti “avasesā sattā appassutā, ahaṃ pana bahussuto”ti evamādisutena vā. Paṭibhānena vāti “avasesā sattā appaṭibhānā, mayhaṃ pana paṭibhānappamāṇaṃ natthī”ti evamādipaṭibhānena vā. Aññataraññatarena vā vatthunāti avuttena aññena vatthunā vā. Yo evarūpo mānoti mānakaraṇavasena māno. Maññanā maññitattanti ākārabhāvaniddeso. Ussitaṭṭhena unnati. Yassuppajjati, taṃ [M 0.0184] puggalaṃ unnāmeti ukkhipitvā ṭhapetīti unnāmo. Samussitaṭṭhena dhajo. Ukkhipanaṭṭhena cittaṃ sampaggaṇhātīti sampaggāho. Ketu [V 0.0166] vuccati bahūsu dhajesu accuggatadhajo[P 1.0212]. Mānopi punappunaṃ uppajjamāno aparāpare upādāya accuggataṭṭhena ketu viyāti ketu, taṃ ketuṃ icchatīti ketukamyaṃ, tassa bhāvo ketukamyatā. Sā pana cittassa, na attano. Tena vuttaṃ “ketukamyatā cittassā”ti. Mānasampayuttañhi cittaṃ ketuṃ icchati, tassa bhāvo, ketusaṅkhāto mānoti. Dhono māyañca mānañca pahāya pajahitvā yo so dhono arahā heṭṭhā vuttanayena vinodanabyantikaraṇādivasena kilese pajahitvā ṭhito, so tena rāgādinā kilesena gaccheyya.

In the exposition of the tenfold conceit, 'here a certain person generates conceit' means a certain individual generates conceit. By birth: or by the attainment of good birth, such as being a khattiya. By clan: or by a distinguished clan such as the Gotama clan. By family lineage: or by belonging to a great family. By beauty of complexion: or by possessing a body endowed with beauty of complexion. For the body is called 'pokkhara,' and the meaning is the excellence of beauty, being handsome. By wealth: or by being wealthy, meaning 'there is no measure to the wealth stored up for me.' By learning: or by way of study. By means of work: or by thinking, 'Other beings are like crows with clipped wings, but I am of great power and might,' or 'Whatever work I do succeeds,' and so on, by such means of engaging in work. By means of craft: or by thinking, 'Other beings are unskilled, but I am skilled,' and so on, by such means of engaging in craft. By means of knowledge: this is by the same method as explained above. By learning (suta): or by thinking, 'Other beings are unlearned, but I am widely learned,' and so on, by such learning. By eloquence: or by thinking, 'Other beings lack eloquence, but there is no limit to my eloquence,' and so on, by such eloquence. By any other ground: or by some other unmentioned thing. Such is conceit: conceit in the sense of the act of making conceit. Conceiving, the state of being conceited: this is a description of the way of conceiving. By the characteristic of elevation, it is 'pride' (unnati). That which arises in a person elevates them, lifting them up and placing them high: thus, it is 'elevation' (unnāmo). By the characteristic of being raised high, it is a 'banner' (dhajo). By the act of lifting up, it seizes the mind: thus, it is 'grasping' (sampaggāho). A 'ketu' is called the highest banner among many banners. Conceit, arising repeatedly, being supported again and again, becomes like a banner due to its very elevated nature: thus, it is 'ketu.' Desiring such a banner is 'ketukamya,' and its state is 'ketukamyatā.' But this belongs to the mind, not to itself. Therefore, it is said, 'ketukamyatā is of the mind.' For the mind associated with conceit desires a banner; its state is conceit, designated as a banner. The purified one, having abandoned deceit and conceit—that purified one, the Arahant, stands, having abandoned defilements by the method described above, by way of dispelling, bringing to an end, and so on. He would not proceed by way of such defilements as lust.

Nerayikoti vāti niraye nibbattakasattoti vā. Tiracchānayonikādīsupi eseva nayo. So hetu natthīti yena janakahetunā gatiyādīsu nibbatteyya, so hetu natthi. Paccayoti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Kāraṇanti ṭhānaṃ. Kāraṇañhi tadāyattavuttitāya attano phalassa ṭhānanti vuccati. Tasmā yena hetunā yena paccayena gatiyādīsu nibbatteyya, taṃ kāraṇaṃ natthi.

'A hell-dweller' (nerayiko) means one who is born in hell. The same method applies to the animal realm and the like. 'There is no cause' means there is no generating cause by which one would be born in a destination or the like; that cause does not exist. 'Condition' (paccaya) is a synonym for that same thing. 'Reason' (kāraṇa) means basis. For a reason is called the basis of its effect because the effect's existence is dependent on it. Therefore, there is no cause, no condition by which one would be born in a destination or the like; that reason does not exist.

22. Yo pana nesaṃ dvinnaṃ upayānaṃ bhāvena upayo hoti, so upayo hi…pe… diṭṭhimidheva sabbanti. Tattha upayoti taṇhādiṭṭhinissito. Dhammesu upeti vādanti “ratto”ti vā “duṭṭho”ti vā evaṃ tesu tesu dhammesu upeti vādaṃ. Anūpayaṃ kena kathaṃ vadeyyāti taṇhādiṭṭhippahānena pana anūpayaṃ khīṇāsavaṃ kena rāgena vā dosena vā kathaṃ “ratto”ti vā “duṭṭho”ti vā vadeyya. Evaṃ anupavajjo ca so kiṃ titthiyā viya katapaṭicchādako bhavissatīti adhippāyo. Attā nirattā na hi tassa atthīti tassa hi attadiṭṭhi vā ucchedadiṭṭhi vā natthi, gahaṇamuñcanaṃ vāpi attanirattasaññitaṃ natthi. Kiṃ kāraṇā natthīti ce? Adhosi so diṭṭhimidheva sabbanti. Yasmā so idheva attabhāve ñāṇambunā sabbadiṭṭhigataṃ adhosi pajahi vinodesīti arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi. Taṃ sutvā rājā attamano bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā pakkāmīti.

22. Now, whatever serves as a means (upaya) for these two—craving and views—that means indeed... (the passage continues with) 'all is merely views right here.' Here, 'means' (upaya) refers to being rooted in craving and views. One engages with phenomena by saying, 'attached' or 'averse,' thus making a claim about these various phenomena. 'How could one who is without means speak in any way?' means: But through the abandonment of craving and views, how could one who is without means and whose defilements are destroyed—by what lust or hatred—say, 'attached' or 'averse'? Thus, being blameless, how could that person be like sectarians, who conceal their faults? This is the meaning. 'For him there is neither self nor not-self' means: for that person there is no view of self or annihilation, nor any grasping or releasing perceived as self or not-self. If one asks, 'What is the reason for this?' (the answer is) 'Because that person has eradicated all views right here.' Since that person has extinguished, abandoned, and dispelled all views in this very existence with the water of knowledge, the teaching is concluded with the pinnacle of arahantship. Hearing this, the king, delighted, paid homage to the Blessed One and departed.

Rattoti vāti rāgena rattoti vā. Duṭṭhoti vātiādīsupi eseva [P 1.0213] nayo. Te abhisaṅkhārā appahīnāti ye puññāpuññaāneñjābhisaṅkhārā, te [M 0.0185] appahīnā. Abhisaṅkhārānaṃ appahīnattāti tesaṃ vuttappakārānaṃ kammābhisaṅkhārānaṃ na pahīnabhāvena. Gatiyā vādaṃ upetīti pañcannaṃ gatīnaṃ aññatarāya kathanaṃ upagacchati. Tenevāha – “nerayikoti vā…pe… vādaṃ upeti upagacchatī”ti. Vadeyyāti katheyya. Gahitaṃ natthīti gahetabbaṃ natthi. Muñcitabbaṃ natthīti muñcitvā ṭhitattā mocetabbaṃ natthi.

'Attached' (ratto) means stained by lust. The same principle applies to 'corrupt' (duṭṭho) and so on. 'Those formations are unabandoned' means that the meritorious, demeritorious, and imperturbable formations are unabandoned. 'Because the formations are unabandoned' means because the karmic formations of the types mentioned have not been abandoned. 'Goes to assertion of a destination' means he undertakes speaking about one of the five destinations. Hence it is said: 'He goes to the assertion "a hell-being"... he engages in talk.' 'Would speak' (vadeyya) means he would speak. 'There is nothing grasped' (gahitaṃ natthi) means there is nothing to be grasped. 'There is nothing to release' (muñcitabbaṃ natthi) means because, having released, he stands, there is nothing to be freed.

Yassatthi [V 0.0167] gahitanti yassa puggalassa “ahaṃ mamā”ti gahitaṃ atthi. Tassatthi muñcitabbanti tassa puggalassa mocetabbaṃ atthi. Upari padāni parivattetvā yojetabbāni. Gahaṇaṃ muñcanā samatikkantoti gahaṇamocanā arahā atikkanto. Buddhiparihānivītivattoti vaḍḍhiñca parihāniñca atikkamitvā pavatto. So vuṭṭhavāsotiādiṃ katvā ñāṇagginā daḍḍhānīti pariyosānaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayameva. Adhosīti kantesi. Dhuni sandhuni niddhunīti upasaggena padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ.

'For whom there is grasping' means for that individual, there is grasping in the sense of 'I' and 'mine.' 'For them, there is release' means for that individual, there is something to be freed. The words above should be rearranged and connected accordingly. 'Grasping and releasing have been transcended' means the Arahant has gone beyond grasping and releasing. 'Having overcome the decline of wisdom' means having transcended both growth and decline, one proceeds. The conclusion, 'He who has emerged from dwelling,' etc., up to 'things burned by the fire of knowledge,' follows the method explained above. 'Adhosīti' means 'he cut off.' 'Dhuni, sandhuni, niddhuni'—the word is augmented by a prefix.

Saddhammappajjotikāya mahāniddesaṭṭhakathāya

In the Saddhammappajjotikā, the commentary on the Mahāniddesa.

Duṭṭhaṭṭhakasuttaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of the Duṭṭhaṭṭhaka Sutta is finished.

4. Suddhaṭṭhakasuttaniddesavaṇṇanā

4. Explanation of the Exposition of the Suddhaṭṭhaka Sutta

23. Catutthe [V 0.0168][P 1.0214] suddhaṭṭhake paṭhamagāthāya tāvattho – na, bhikkhave, evarūpena dassanena suddhi hoti, api ca kho kilesamalīnattā asuddhaṃ, kilesarogānaṃ adhigamā sarogameva candābhaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ, aññaṃ vā evarūpaṃ disvā diṭṭhigatiko bālo abhijānāti “passāmi suddhaṃ paramaṃ arogaṃ, tena ca diṭṭhisaṅkhātena dassanena saṃsuddhi narassa hotī”ti, so evaṃ abhijānanto taṃ dassanaṃ “parama”nti ñatvā tasmiṃ dassane suddhānupassī samāno taṃ dassanaṃ “maggañāṇa”nti pacceti. Taṃ pana maggañāṇaṃ na hoti.

23. In the fourth Suddhaṭṭhaka, the meaning of the first verse is this: ‘No, bhikkhus, purity does not come about by such a view. Rather, being stained by defilements, it is impure. Having acquired the diseases of defilements, the brahmin Candābha is indeed diseased, or seeing another such one, a fool clinging to views understands: “I perceive the pure, the supreme, the free from disease; and through this view, so-called sight, a person attains complete purity.”’ Thus, understanding this, knowing that view to be ‘supreme,’ and contemplating purity in that view, he accepts that view as ‘knowledge of the path.’ But that is not knowledge of the path.

Paramaṃ ārogyappattanti uttamaṃ nibyādhiṃ pāpuṇitvā ṭhitaṃ. Tāṇappattanti tathā pālanappattaṃ. Leṇappattanti nilīyanappattaṃ.Saraṇappattanti patiṭṭhāpattaṃ, dukkhanāsanaṃ vā pattaṃ. Abhayappattanti nibbhayabhāvappattaṃ. Accutappattanti niccalabhāvaṃ pattaṃ. Amatappattanti amataṃ mahānibbānaṃ pattaṃ. Nibbānappattanti vānavirahitaṃ pattaṃ.

‘Having attained supreme health’ means having reached the highest state free from disease and being established therein. ‘Having attained protection’ means having reached such protection. ‘Having attained shelter’ means having reached a place of concealment. ‘Having attained refuge’ means having reached a foundation, or having reached the destruction of suffering. ‘Having attained fearlessness’ means having reached a state free from fear. ‘Having attained the immutable’ means having reached a state of constancy. ‘Having attained the deathless’ means having reached the deathless, the great Nibbāna. ‘Having attained Nibbāna’ means having reached the state free from craving.

Abhijānantoti [M 0.0186] visesena jānanto. Ājānantoti ājānamāno. Vijānantoti anekavidhena jānamāno. Paṭivijānantoti taṃ taṃ paṭicca vijānamāno. Paṭivijjhantoti hadaye kurumāno.

‘Abhijānanto’ means knowing distinctly. ‘Ājānantoti’ means knowing fully. ‘Vijānanto’ means knowing in various ways. ‘Paṭivijānanto’ means knowing specifically in relation to each. ‘Paṭivijjhanto’ means penetrating.

Cakkhuviññāṇaṃ rūpadassanenāti cakkhuviññāṇena rūpadassanaṃ. Ñāṇanti paccetīti paññā iti saddahati. Maggoti paccetīti “upāyo”ti saddahati. Pathoti sañcāro. Nīyānanti gahetvā yātīti nīyānaṃ. “Niyyāna”nti vā pāṭho.

‘Eye-consciousness by seeing forms’ means the seeing of forms by eye-consciousness. ‘He accepts it as knowledge’ means he believes it is wisdom. ‘He accepts it as the path’ means he believes it is a means. ‘Path’ means the course. ‘Nīyāna’ means that by which one is led, hence ‘nīyāna’. Alternatively, the reading is ‘niyyāna’.

24. “Diṭṭhena [P 1.0215] ce suddhī”ti dutiyagāthā. Tassattho – tena rūpadassanasaṅkhātena diṭṭhena yadi kilesasuddhi narassa hoti, tena vā ñāṇena so yadi jātiādidukkhaṃ pajahāti, evaṃ sante [V 0.0169] ariyamaggato aññena asuddhimaggeneva so sujjhati, rāgādīhi upadhīhi saupadhiko eva samāno sujjhatīti vattabbataṃ āpanno hoti, na ca evaṃvidho sujjhati. Tasmā diṭṭhī hi naṃ pāva tathā vadānaṃ, sā naṃ diṭṭhiyeva “micchādiṭṭhiko aya”nti katheti, diṭṭhianurūpaṃ “sassato loko”tiādinā nayena tathā tathā vadatīti.

24. ‘If by sight there is purity’ is the second verse. Its meaning is: If a person attains purity from defilements through what is called ‘sight’—namely, the seeing of forms—or if through that knowledge he abandons the suffering of birth and so forth, then, if this were so, he would be purified by a path other than the Noble Path, an impure path. Being still bound by attachments such as greed, he would have to be said to attain purity—but such a one does not truly become pure. Therefore, the view itself indeed proclaims those who speak thus; that very view proclaims him as ‘one with wrong view’. In accordance with their view, they speak in various ways, such as ‘the world is eternal,’ and so on.

Rāgena saha vattatīti sarāgo, rāgavāti attho. Sadosotiādīsupi eseva nayo.

‘Sarāgo’ means ‘one who exists with greed’; the meaning is ‘greedy’. The same method applies to ‘sadoso’ (with hatred) and so on.

25. Na brāhmaṇoti tatiyagāthā. Tassattho – yo pana bāhitapāpattā brāhmaṇo hoti, so maggena adhigatāsavakkhayo khīṇāsavabrāhmaṇo ariyamaggañāṇato aññena abhimaṅgalasammatarūpasaṅkhāte diṭṭhe, tathāvidhasaddasaṅkhāte sute, avītikkamasaṅkhāte sīle, hatthivatādibhede vate, pathaviādibhede mute ca uppannena micchāñāṇena suddhiṃ na āhāti. Sesamassa brāhmaṇassa vaṇṇabhaṇanāya vuttaṃ. So hi tedhātukapuññe sabbasmiñca pāpe anūpalitto, kasmā? Tassa pahīnattā tassa attadiṭṭhiyā, yassa kassaci vā gahaṇassa pahīnattā attañjaho, puññābhisaṅkhārādīnaṃ akaraṇato “nayidha pakubbamāno”ti vuccati. Tasmā naṃ evaṃ pasaṃsanto āha. Sabbasseva cassa purimapādena sambandho veditabbo – puññe ca pāpe ca anūpalitto attañjaho [M 0.0187] nayidha pakubbamāno na brāhmaṇo aññato suddhimāhāti. Nāti paṭikkhepoti na iti paṭisedho.

25. ‘Not a brahmin’ is the third verse. Its meaning is: A brahmin is one who has abandoned evil. He, a brahmin whose taints are destroyed, having attained the destruction of taints through the Noble Path, does not claim purity through wrong knowledge arisen in regard to what is seen, such as forms considered auspicious; what is heard, such as certain sounds; virtue, such as unbroken precepts; vows, such as those of an elephant-keeper; or what is cognized, such as perceptions of earth and other elements. The rest is said in praise of such a brahmin. For he is unstained by all merit in the threefold world or any evil—why? Because he has abandoned self-view and all grasping, having relinquished the self. He does not engage in meritorious formations or the like, as it is said, ‘He does nothing here.’ Therefore, praising him thus, it is said: It should be understood that the entire preceding line relates to him – ‘He is unstained by merit or evil, having abandoned the self, doing nothing here—such a one does not claim purity from another.’ ‘Na’ (not) is a denial, a negation.

Bāhitvā sabbapāpakānīti gāthāyattho – yo catutthamaggena bāhitvā sabbapāpakāni ṭhitatto ṭhitoicceva vuttaṃ hoti. Bāhitapāpattā eva ca vimalo vimalabhāvaṃ brahmabhāvaṃ seṭṭhabhāvaṃ patto, paṭinissaṭṭhasamādhivikkhepakarakilesamalena [P 1.0216] aggamaggaphalasamādhinā sādhusamāhito, saṃsārahetusamatikkamena saṃsāramaticca pariniṭṭhitakiccatāya kevalīti ca, taṇhādiṭṭhīhi anissitattā anissitoti ca, lokadhammehi nibbikārattā tādīti ca pavuccati. Evaṃ thutiraho sa brahmā so brāhmaṇoti.

‘Having abandoned all evil’ is the meaning of the verse: One who, through the fourth path, has abandoned all evil, is said to be ‘steadfast,’ having attained steadfastness. Having abandoned evil, he is truly pure, having attained purity, the state of Brahma, the supreme state. With the defilements that disturb concentration expelled by the concentration of the highest path and fruition, he is well-composed, complete in his task through the transcendence of the causes of saṃsāra, therefore ‘a perfected one’. Unattached to craving and views, he is called ‘unattached’. Unaffected by worldly conditions, he is called ‘such a one’. Thus, he is praised: ‘He is Brahma, he is a brahmin’.

Aññatra satipaṭṭhānehīti cattāro satipaṭṭhāne muñcitvā. Sammappadhānādīsupi eseva nayo.

‘Except for the establishments of mindfulness’ means excluding the four establishments of mindfulness. The same method applies to the right exertions and so on.

Santeke samaṇabrāhmaṇāti ekacce lokasaṅketena “samaṇabrāhmaṇā”ti laddhavohārā saṃvijjanti. Diṭṭhasuddhikāti diṭṭhena suddhiṃ icchamānā. Te ekaccānaṃ rūpānaṃ dassananti ete diṭṭhasuddhikā [V 0.0170] etesaṃ rūpārammaṇānaṃ olokanaṃ. Maṅgalaṃ paccentīti iddhikāraṇaṃ buddhikāraṇaṃ sabbasampattikāraṇaṃ patiṭṭhāpenti. Amaṅgalaṃ paccentīti aniddhikāraṇaṃ na buddhikāraṇaṃ na sampattikāraṇaṃ patiṭṭhāpenti. Te kālato vuṭṭhahitvāti ete diṭṭhādimaṅgalikā puretarameva uṭṭhahitvā. Abhimaṅgalagatānīti visesena vuḍḍhikāraṇagatāni. Rūpāni passantīti nānāvidhāni rūpārammaṇāni dakkhanti. Cāṭakasakuṇanti evaṃnāmakaṃ. Phussaveḷuvalaṭṭhinti phussanakkhattena uppannaṃ taruṇabeḷuvalaṭṭhiṃ. Gabbhinitthinti sagabbhaṃ itthiṃ. Kumārakaṃ khandhe āropetvā gacchantanti taruṇadārakaṃ aṃse ussāpetvā gacchamānaṃ. Puṇṇaghaṭanti udakapuṇṇaghaṭaṃ. Rohitamacchanti rattarohitamacchaṃ. Ājaññarathanti sindhavayuttarathaṃ. Usabhanti maṅgalausabhaṃ. Gokapilanti kapilagāviṃ.

‘There are some ascetics and brahmins’ means some exist who are called ‘ascetics and brahmins’ by worldly convention. ‘Diṭṭhasuddhikā’ means those desiring purity through sight. ‘The seeing of certain forms’ means the looking at these visible objects by these ‘diṭṭhasuddhikā’. ‘They establish auspiciousness’ means they establish it as the cause of success, intelligence, and all attainments. ‘They establish inauspiciousness’ means they establish it as the cause of failure, lack of intelligence, and lack of attainments. ‘These rise from the time’ means these sight-and-so-forth-auspicious-practitioners rise early. ‘Deeply absorbed in auspicious signs’ means those that are particularly the cause of increase. ‘They see forms’ means they will see various visible objects. ‘The cāṭaka bird’ means a bird so named. ‘A bamboo shoot grown under the Phussa constellation’ means a young bamboo shoot born under the Phussa constellation. ‘A pregnant woman’ means a woman with child. ‘A child carried on the shoulder’ means a young boy being carried on the shoulder while walking. ‘A full pot’ means a pot filled with water. ‘A red rohita fish’ means a red rohita fish. ‘A noble chariot’ means a chariot yoked with Sindh horses. ‘A bull’ means an auspicious bull. ‘A tawny cow’ means a tawny cow.

Palālapuñjanti thusarāsiṃ. Takkaghaṭanti gotakkādipūritacāṭiṃ. Rittaghaṭanti [P 1.0217] tucchaghaṭaṃ. Naṭanti naṭakādiṃ. “Dhuttakiriya”nti eke. Naggasamaṇakanti niccoḷasamaṇaṃ[M 0.0188]. Kharanti gadrabhaṃ. Kharayānanti gadrabhayuttaṃ vayhādikaṃ. Ekayuttayānanti ekena vāhanena saṃyuttaṃ yānaṃ. Kāṇanti ekakkhiubhayakkhikāṇaṃ. Kuṇinti hatthakuṇiṃ. Khañjanti khañjapādaṃ tiriyagatapādaṃ. Pakkhahatanti pīṭhasappiṃ. Jiṇṇakanti jarājiṇṇaṃ. Byādhikanti byādhipīḷitaṃ. Matanti kālaṅkataṃ.

‘A heap of straw’ means a pile of chaff. ‘A pot of buttermilk’ means a jar filled with buttermilk and so on. ‘An empty pot’ means a hollow pot. ‘An actor’ means a dancer and so on. Some say ‘the work of a cheat’. ‘A naked ascetic’ means a permanently unclothed ascetic. ‘A donkey’ means a donkey. ‘A donkey-drawn cart’ means a vehicle and so on yoked to a donkey. ‘A single-yoked cart’ means a vehicle yoked to one animal. ‘A blind person’ means one with one eye or both eyes blind. ‘A cripple’ means one with a crooked hand. ‘A lame person’ means one with a lame foot, one with a sideways gait. ‘A paralytic’ means one who crawls on his buttocks. ‘An old person’ means one worn out by old age. ‘A sick person’ means one afflicted by disease. ‘A dead person’ means one who has died.

Sutasuddhikāti sotaviññāṇena sutena suddhiṃ icchamānā. Saddānaṃ savananti saddārammaṇānaṃ savanaṃ. Vaḍḍhāti vātiādayo loke pavattasaddamattāni gahetvā vuttā. Amaṅgalaṃ pana “kāṇo”tiādinā tena tena nāmena vuttasaddāyeva. “Chinda”nti vāti hatthapādādicchinnanti vā. “Bhinda”nti vāti sīsādibhinnanti vā. “Daḍḍha”nti vāti agginā jhāpitanti vā. “Naṭṭha”nti vāti corādīhi vināsitanti vā. “Natthī”ti vāti na vijjatīti vā.

‘Sutasuddhikā’ means those desiring purity through what is heard by ear-consciousness. ‘Hearing sounds’ means the hearing of sound-objects. ‘Grows’ and similar words are spoken by taking merely those conventional sounds that prevail in the world. But ‘inauspicious’ refers to sounds expressed by those various names, such as ‘blind,’ and so on. ‘Cut’ means ‘cut off’ (as in hands, feet, etc.). ‘Break’ means ‘broken’ (as in head, etc.). ‘Burned’ means ‘burned by fire’. ‘Lost’ means ‘destroyed by thieves and so on’. ‘Non-existent’ means ‘it does not exist’.

Sīlasuddhikāti sīlena visuddhiṃ icchanakā. Sīlamattenāti saṃvaraṇamattena. Saṃyamamattenāti uparamamattena. Saṃvaramattenāti dvārathakanamattena. Avītikkamamattenāti na atikkamitamattena. Samaṇo muṇḍikāputtoti mātito laddhanāmaṃ. Sampannakusalanti paripuṇṇakusalaṃ. Paramakusalanti uttamakusalaṃ. Uttamapattippattanti uttamaṃ arahattaṃ pāpuṇitabbataṃ patvā ṭhitaṃ. Ayojjanti parājetuṃ asakkuṇeyyaṃ samaṇaṃ.

‘Sīlasuddhikā’ means those desiring purity through virtue. ‘Merely by virtue’ means merely by restraint. ‘Merely by self-restraint’ means merely by abstaining. ‘Merely by restraint’ means merely by closing the doors. ‘Merely by non-transgression’ means merely by not transgressing. ‘The ascetic Muṇḍikāputta’ means he whose name was received from his mother. ‘Endowed with skill’ means fully skilled. ‘Supremely skilled’ means the highest skill. ‘Having attained the highest attainment’ means having reached and standing in the supreme state that is to be attained, arahantship. ‘Cannot be defeated’ means an ascetic who cannot be defeated.

Vatasuddhikāti samādānena vatena suddhiṃ icchanakā. Hatthivatikā vāti samādinnaṃ hatthivataṃ [V 0.0171] etesaṃ atthīti hatthivatikā, sabbahatthikiriyaṃ karontīti attho. Kathaṃ? “Ajja [P 1.0218] paṭṭhāya hatthīhi kātabbaṃ karissāmī”ti evaṃ uppannacittā hatthīnaṃ gamanākāraṃ tiṭṭhanākāraṃ nisīdanākāraṃ sayanākāraṃ uccārapassāvakaraṇākāraṃ, aññe hatthī disvā soṇḍaṃ ussāpetvā gamanākārañca sabbaṃ karontīti hatthivatikā. Assavatikādīsupi labbhamānavasena yathāyogaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Tesu avasāne disāvatikā vāti puratthimādidisānaṃ namassanavasena samādinnadisāvatikā, etesaṃ vuttappakārānaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ vatasamādānaṃ sampajjamānaṃ hatthiādīnaṃ sahabyataṃ upaneti. Sace kho panassa micchādiṭṭhi hoti “imināhaṃ sīlavatasamādānabrahmacariyena devo vā devaññataro vā homī”ti cintayantassa nirayatiracchānayonīnaṃ aññataro hotīti ñātabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā (ma. ni. 2.79) –

‘Purification by vows’ means those who desire purity through undertaking a vow. ‘Elephant-vowed’ means those who have undertaken the elephant vow; that is, they perform all the actions of an elephant. How? With the thought, ‘From today onwards, I will do what should be done by elephants,’ they imitate the way elephants walk, stand, sit, lie down, and excrete; seeing other elephants, they raise their trunks and do everything like them—therefore they are called elephant-vowed. The same should be applied appropriately to those vowed to horses and so on, as is applicable. At the end of these, ‘direction-vowed’ means those who have undertaken the direction vow of revering the eastern and other directions. The undertaking of vows by these ascetics and brahmins of the kinds mentioned, when successful, leads to companionship with elephants and so on. But if one has wrong view, thinking, ‘By this virtue, vow, and celibacy, I will become a god or some other divine being,’ it should be known that one will be reborn in hell or the animal realm. For this was said by the Blessed One (MN 2.79):

“Idha[M 0.0189], puṇṇa, ekacco kukkuravataṃ bhāveti paripuṇṇaṃ abbokiṇṇaṃ, kukkurasīlaṃ bhāveti paripuṇṇaṃ abbokiṇṇaṃ, kukkuracittaṃ bhāveti paripuṇṇaṃ abbokiṇṇaṃ, kukkurākappaṃ bhāveti paripuṇṇaṃ abbokiṇṇaṃ. So kukkuravataṃ bhāvetvā paripuṇṇaṃ abbokiṇṇaṃ, kukkurasīlaṃ bhāvetvā paripuṇṇaṃ abbokiṇṇaṃ, kukkuracittaṃ bhāvetvā paripuṇṇaṃ abbokiṇṇaṃ, kukkurākappaṃ bhāvetvā paripuṇṇaṃ abbokiṇṇaṃ kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā kukkurānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapajjati. Sace kho panassa evaṃdiṭṭhi hoti ‘imināhaṃ sīlena vā vatena vā tapena vā brahmacariyena vā devo vā bhavissāmi devaññataro vā’ti, sāssa hoti micchādiṭṭhi. Micchādiṭṭhissa kho ahaṃ, puṇṇa, dvinnaṃ gatīnaṃ aññataraṃ gatiṃ vadāmi nirayaṃ vā tiracchānayoniṃ vā. Iti kho, puṇṇa, sampajjamānaṃ kukkuravataṃ kukkurānaṃ sahabyataṃ upaneti, vipajjamānaṃ niraya”nti.

“Here, Puṇṇa, someone cultivates the dog-vow fully and uninterruptedly, cultivates the dog-like moral habit fully and uninterruptedly, cultivates the dog-like mind fully and uninterruptedly, cultivates the dog-like manner fully and uninterruptedly. Having cultivated the dog-vow fully and uninterruptedly, the dog-like moral habit fully and uninterruptedly, the dog-like mind fully and uninterruptedly, and the dog-like manner fully and uninterruptedly, on the dissolution of the body, after death, one is reborn in the company of dogs. But if one has such a view: ‘By this virtue or vow or austerity or spiritual life, I will become a god or some other divine being,’ that is one's wrong view. For one with wrong view, Puṇṇa, I declare one of two destinations: hell or the animal realm. Thus, Puṇṇa, when the dog-vow is successful, it leads to the company of dogs; when it fails, it leads to hell.”

Gandhabbavatikādayo gandhabbādīnaṃ sahabyataṃ upagacchantīti attho na gahetabbo, micchādiṭṭhiyā gahitattā nirayatiracchānayonimeva upagacchantīti gahetabbo.

The meaning that those who undertake the gandhabba-vow and the like attain the company of gandhabbas and the like should not be taken, because it is grasped by wrong view. Instead, it should be understood that they go only to hell or the animal realm.

Mutasuddhikāti [P 1.0219] phusitena suddhikā. Pathaviṃ āmasantīti sasambhārikaṃ mahāpathaviṃ kāyena phusanti. Haritanti allanīlasaddalaṃ. Gomayanti gavādigomayaṃ. Kacchapanti aṭṭhikacchapādianekavidhaṃ. Phālaṃ akkamantīti ayaphālaṃ maddanti. Tilavāhanti tilasakaṭaṃ tilarāsiṃ vā. Phussatilaṃ khādantīti maṅgalapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ tilaṃ khādanti. Phussatelaṃ makkhentīti tathārūpaṃ tilatelaṃ sarīrabbhañjanaṃ karonti. Dantakaṭṭhanti dantapoṇaṃ. Mattikāya nhāyantīti kuṅkuṭṭhādikāya [V 0.0172] saṇhamattikāya sarīraṃ ubbaṭṭetvā nhāyanti. Sāṭakaṃ nivāsentīti maṅgalapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ vatthaṃ paridahanti. Veṭhanaṃ veṭhentīti sīsaveṭhanaṃ pattuṇṇādipaṭaṃ sīse ṭhapenti paṭimuccanti.
