‘Purification by touch’ means purification by contact. ‘Touching the earth’ means they touch the great earth with their bodies, along with its constituent elements. ‘Green’ means fresh, blue-green grass. ‘Cow dung’ means the dung of cows and the like. ‘Tortoise’ means various kinds, such as bone-tortoise and the like. ‘Trampling the plowshare’ means they crush an iron plowshare. ‘Sesame-carrier’ means a sesame cart or a heap of sesame. ‘Eating auspicious sesame seeds’ means they eat sesame seeds associated with auspicious occasions. ‘Anointing with auspicious sesame oil’ means they apply such sesame oil to their bodies as an unguent. ‘Tooth-stick’ means a tooth cleaner. ‘Bathing with clay’ means they rub their bodies with fine clay like kuṅkuṭṭha and bathe. ‘Wearing a garment’ means they put on cloth associated with auspicious occasions. ‘Wrapping a turban’ means they place a head-wrap, a cloth of wool and the like, on their heads and fasten it.

Tedhātukaṃ kusalābhisaṅkhāranti kāmadhāturūpadhātuarūpadhātūsu paṭisandhidāyakaṃ kosallasambhūtaṃ paccayābhisaṅkhāraṃ. Sabbaṃ akusalanti dvādasavidhaṃ akosallasambhūtaṃ akusalaṃ. Yatoti yadā. Te dasavidho [M 0.0190] puññābhisaṅkhāro ca, dvādasavidho apuññābhisaṅkhāro ca, catubbidho āneñjābhisaṅkhāro ca yathānurūpaṃ samucchedappahānena pahīnā honti. Attadiṭṭhijahoti “eso me attā”ti gahitadiṭṭhiṃ jaho. Gāhaṃ jahoti “esohamasmī”ti mānasampayuttagahaṇaṃ jaho. Puna attañjahoti “etaṃ mamā”ti taṇhāgahaṇavasena ca diṭṭhigahaṇavasena ca parāmasitvā gahitaṃ, parato āmaṭṭhañca, tasmiṃ abhiniviṭṭhañca, balavataṇhāvasena gilitvā ajjhositañca, balavamucchitañca. Sabbaṃ taṃ cattaṃ hotītiādayo vuttanayāyeva.

‘Skillful volitional formations pertaining to the three realms’ means the conditioned volitional formations born of skillfulness that give rise to rebirth in the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm. ‘All unwholesome’ refers to all the twelve types of unwholesome states born of unskillfulness. ‘When’ means at the time when. Those, the ten kinds of meritorious volitional formations, the twelve kinds of demeritorious volitional formations, and the four kinds of imperturbable volitional formations, are abandoned by means of abandonment by eradication, as is appropriate. ‘One abandons the view of self’ means one abandons the view grasped as ‘This is my self.’ ‘One abandons grasping’ means one abandons the grasping connected with conceit, thinking ‘I am this.’ ‘Again, one abandons self’ means that which is grasped through craving and view as ‘This is mine,’ clung to, influenced by others, and firmly adhered to; swallowed and consumed through strong craving, and with which one is strongly infatuated. ‘All that is relinquished’: these and other explanations are as previously stated.

26. Evaṃ “na brāhmaṇo aññato suddhimāhā”ti vatvā idāni ye diṭṭhigatikā aññato suddhiṃ bruvanti, tesaṃ tassā diṭṭhiyā anibbāhakabhāvaṃ [P 1.0220] dassento “purimaṃ pahāyā”ti gāthamāha. Tassattho – tehi aññato suddhivādā samānāpi yassā diṭṭhiyā appahīnattā gahaṇamuñcanaṃ hoti, tāya purimaṃ satthārādiṃ pahāya aparaṃ nissitā, ejāsaṅkhātāya taṇhāya anugatā abhibhūtā rāgādibhedaṃ na taranti saṅgaṃ, tañca atarantā taṃ taṃ dhammaṃ uggaṇhanti ca nirassajanti ca makkaṭova sākhanti.

26. Having stated, ‘A brahmin does not claim purity from another,’ now, to show the ineffectiveness of the views of those who are adherents of views and claim purity from another, the verse ‘abandoning the former’ is spoken. Its meaning is: although they speak of purity from another, because they have not abandoned that view, grasping and releasing occur. Having abandoned the former—such as the Teacher—they rely on another. Followed and overcome by craving, which is known as agitation, they do not cross over the attachment which is divided into lust and other defilements. And not crossing it, they grasp and discard various teachings like a monkey on a branch.

Purimaṃ satthāraṃ pahāyāti purimagahitaṃ satthupaṭiññaṃ vajjetvā. Paraṃ satthāraṃ nissitāti aññaṃ satthupaṭiññaṃ nissitā allīnā. Purimaṃ dhammakkhānaṃ pahāyātiādīsupi eseva nayo.

‘Having abandoned the former teacher’ means having rejected the one formerly accepted who claims to be a teacher. ‘Relying on another teacher’ means relying on and being attached to another who claims to be a teacher. For ‘Having abandoned the former teaching’ and so on, the same principle applies.

Ejānugāti taṇhāya anugā. Ejānugatāti taṇhāya anugatā. Ejānusaṭāti taṇhāya anusaṭā pakkhandā vā. Ejāya pannā patitāti taṇhāya nimuggā ca nikkhipitā ca.

‘Following agitation’ means following craving. ‘Those who go along with agitation’ means those who follow craving. ‘Swept along by agitation’ means swept along by craving or plunging into it. ‘Fallen into agitation’ means sunk in and cast down by craving.

Makkaṭoti vānaro. Araññeti vipine. Pavaneti mahāvane. Caramānoti gacchamāno. Evamevāti opammasaṃsandanaṃ. Puthūti nānā. Puthudiṭṭhigatānīti nānāvidhāni diṭṭhigatāni. Gaṇhanti ca muñcanti cāti gahaṇavasena gaṇhanti ca cajanavasena muñcanti ca. Ādiyanti ca nirassajanti cāti palibodhaṃ karonti ca vissajjenti ca khipanti ca.

‘Monkey’ means a monkey. ‘In the wilderness’ means in the forest. ‘In the wood’ means in the great forest. ‘Wandering’ means going about. ‘Just so’—this is the connection of the simile. ‘Many’ means various. ‘Many views’ means diverse kinds of views. ‘They grasp and release’ means they grasp by way of taking and release by way of abandoning. ‘They take up and cast off’ means they create an entanglement and then release it, they discard it.

27. Pañcamagāthāya [V 0.0173] ca sambandho – yo ca so “diṭṭhī hi naṃ pāva tathā vadāna”nti vutto, so sayaṃ samādāyāti. Tattha sayanti sāmaṃ[M 0.0191]. Samādāyāti gahetvā. Vatānīti hatthivatādīni. Uccāvacanti aparāparaṃ, hīnapaṇītaṃ vā satthārato satthārādiṃ. Saññasattoti kāmasaññādīsu laggo. Vidvā ca vedehi samecca dhammanti paramatthavidvā ca arahā catūhi maggañāṇavedehi catusaccadhammaṃ abhisameccāti. Sesaṃ pākaṭameva.

27. The connection with the fifth verse is this: the one who is spoken of as ‘For views, indeed, lead one astray, thus they say,’ is one who ‘personally adopts’ them. Here, ‘personally’ means by oneself. ‘Adopts’ means taking hold. ‘Vows’ refers to elephant vows and the like. ‘High and low’ means one after another, or inferior and superior, from teacher to teacher and so on. ‘Perception-bound’ means attached to sensual perceptions and so on. ‘The wise one, having comprehended the Dhamma with knowledges’ refers to the arahant, the knower of the ultimate truth, who fully comprehends the Dhamma of the four truths with the four path-knowledges. The rest is clear enough.

Sāmaṃ samādāyāti sayameva gahetvā. Ādāyāti ādiyitvā gaṇhitvā. Samādāyāti sammā ādāya. Ādiyitvāti palibodhaṃ [P 1.0221] katvā. Samādiyitvāti sammā palibodhaṃ katvā. Gaṇhitvāti avissajjetvā. Parāmasitvāti dassitvā. Abhinivisitvāti patiṭṭhahitvā. Kāmasaññādayo vuttanayā eva.

‘Personally adopts’ means taking hold by oneself. ‘Takes up’ means seizing and grasping. ‘Adopts’ means properly taking hold. ‘Having taken up’ means making it an encumbrance. ‘Having firmly adopted’ means properly making it an encumbrance. ‘Having grasped’ means not relinquishing. ‘Misapprehended’ means having seen wrongly. ‘Adhered to’ means having established. Sensual perceptions and the like are as previously explained.

Vidvāti medhāvī. Vijjāgatoti vijānanabhāvaṃ gato. Ñāṇīti paññāsampanno. Vibhāvīti ñāṇena vīmaṃsako. Medhāvīti aniccādīhi tulitañāṇo. Paññātiādayo heṭṭhā vuttanayāyeva. Catusaccadhammaṃ vicinātīti dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgo. Bojjhaṅgattho heṭṭhā vuttova. Vīmaṃsāti catusaccadhammavicinanā paññāva. “Vīmaṃsā dhammacintanā”ti hi vuttā. Vipassanāti maggasampayuttā vividhākārena passanā paññāva. Sammādiṭṭhīti sobhanā pasaṭṭhā sundarā maggasampayuttā sammādiṭṭhi. Tehi vedehīti eteheva catūhi maggañāṇehi. Antagatoti jātijarāmaraṇassa pariyosānaṃ gato. Koṭigatotiādayo heṭṭhā vuttanayāva. Vedānaṃ vā antagatoti jānitabbānaṃ avasānappatto. Vedehi vā antagatoti catūhi maggañāṇavedehi vaṭṭadukkhassa pariyantabhāvena antasaṅkhātaṃ nibbānaṃ gato. Viditattāti viditabhāvena jānitabhāvena.

‘Wise’ means intelligent. ‘Possessed of knowledge’ means having attained the state of knowing. ‘Knowledgeable’ means endowed with wisdom. ‘Discerning’ means one who examines with wisdom. ‘Intelligent’ means one whose knowledge is weighed by impermanence and so on. The explanations of ‘wisdom’ and the rest are as previously stated. ‘Examines the truth of the four noble truths’ refers to the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor. The meaning of ‘enlightenment factors’ is as previously stated. ‘Examination’ means the wisdom that investigates the four noble truths. For it is said, ‘Examination is reflection on the Dhamma.’ ‘Insight’ means the wisdom associated with the path, seeing in various ways. ‘Right view’ means the beautiful, excellent, and lovely right view associated with the path. ‘With those knowledges’ means with those very fourfold path-knowledges. ‘Gone to the end’ means having reached the conclusion of birth, aging, and death. ‘Reached the culmination’ and the rest are as previously explained. ‘Gone to the end of what is to be known’ means having reached the limit of what should be known. ‘Gone to the end with knowledges’ means having reached Nibbāna, designated as the end due to being the limit of the suffering of the cycle, through the fourfold path-knowledges. ‘Because it is known’ means by the fact of being known, by the state of being known.

Vedāni viceyya kevalānīti gāthāya ayamattho – yo catūhi maggañāṇavedehi kilesakkhayaṃ karonto gato, so paramatthato vedagū nāma hoti. Sova sabbasamaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ satthasaññitāni vedāni tāyeva maggabhāvanāya kiccato aniccādivasena viceyya. Tattha chandarāgappahānena tameva sabbaṃ vedamaticca yāpi vedapaccayā, aññathā vā uppajjanti vedanā, tāsu sabbavedanāsu vītarāgo hoti. Tasmā tamatthaṃ dassento “kiṃ pattinamāhu vedagu”nti (su. ni. 533) puṭṭho “idaṃ pattina”nti avatvā [M 0.0192] “vedāni viceyya…pe… vedagū so”ti āha. Yasmā vā yo pavicayapaññāya vedāni viceyya, tattha chandarāgappahānena sabbaṃ vedamaticca vattati. So satthasaññitāni vedāni gato ñāto atikkantova hoti. Yo vedanāsu [V 0.0174] vītarāgo, sopi vedanāsaññitāni vedāni gato atikkanto[P 1.0222], ativedanaṃ gatotipi vedagū. Tasmā tampi atthaṃ dassento “idaṃ pattina”nti avatvā “vedāni viceyya…pe… vedagū so”ti āha.

This is the meaning of the verse, 'Having examined all the Vedas completely': One who has gone, making an end of the defilements by means of the four path-knowledges, is in the ultimate sense called a 'knower of the Vedas' (vedagū). That very one, by means of that same development of the path, having functionally examined the Vedas—esteemed as scripture by all ascetics and brahmins—by way of impermanence and so on, transcends that entire Veda by abandoning desire and lust for it. Whatever feelings arise, whether conditioned by the Vedas or otherwise, he is dispassionate towards all those feelings. Therefore, to show this meaning, when asked, 'What attainment do they call a knower of the Vedas?' (Sn. 533), instead of saying, 'This is the attainment,' he said, 'Having examined all the Vedas... he is a knower of the Vedas.' Alternatively, one who, having examined the Vedas with investigative wisdom, lives having transcended all the Vedas by abandoning desire and lust for them, has thereby gone beyond, known, and surpassed the Vedas esteemed as scripture. One who is dispassionate towards feelings has also gone beyond and surpassed the 'vedas' designated as feelings; having gone beyond feeling, he is a 'knower of the Vedas'. Therefore, to show that meaning as well, instead of saying, 'This is the attainment,' he said, 'Having examined all the Vedas... he is a knower of the Vedas.'

Sameccāti ñāṇena samāgantvā. Abhisameccāti ñāṇena paṭivijjhitvā. Dhammanti catusaccadhammaṃ. Sabbe saṅkhārāti sabbe sappaccayā dhammā. Te hi saṅkhatasaṅkhārā nāma. Paccayehi saṅgamma karīyantīti saṅkhārā, te evaṃ paccayehi saṅgamma katattā “saṅkhatā”ti visesetvā vuttā. “Kammanibbattā tebhūmakarūpārūpadhammā abhisaṅkhatasaṅkhārā”ti (visuddhi. 2.587) aṭṭhakathāsu vuttā. Tepi “aniccā vata saṅkhārā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.221, 272; saṃ. ni. 1.186) saṅkhatasaṅkhāresu saṅgahaṃ gacchanti. “Avijjāgatoyaṃ, bhikkhave, purisapuggalo puññañce saṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharotī”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 2.51) avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārāva āgatā. Tebhūmikakusalākusalacetanā abhisaṅkharaṇakasaṅkhārā nāma. “Yāvatikā abhisaṅkhārassa gati, tāvatikaṃ gantvā akkhāhataṃ maññe aṭṭhāsī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 3.15) āgataṃ kāyikacetasikavīriyaṃ payogābhisaṅkhāro nāma. “Saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samāpannassa kho, āvuso visākha, bhikkhuno paṭhamaṃ nirujjhati vacīsaṅkhāro, tato kāyasaṅkhāro, tato cittasaṅkhāro”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.464) āgatā vitakkavicārā vācaṃ saṅkharontīti vacīsaṅkhārā, assāsapassāsā kāyena saṅkharīyantīti kāyasaṅkhārā, saññā ca vedanā ca cittena saṅkharīyantīti cittasaṅkhārā. Idha pana saṅkhatasaṅkhārā adhippetā. Aniccā hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena. Dukkhā paṭipīḷanaṭṭhena. Sabbe dhammāti nibbānampi antokatvā vuttā. Anattā avasavattanaṭṭhena. Avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārāti ettha yaṃ paṭicca phalameti, so paccayo. Paṭiccāti na vinā, apaccakkhitvāti attho. Etīti uppajjati ceva pavattati cāti attho. Apica upakārakaṭṭho paccayaṭṭho. Avijjā ca sā paccayo cāti avijjāpaccayo, tasmā [M 0.0193] avijjāpaccayā. Saṅkhārā sambhavantīti nibbattanti, evaṃ sambhavantisaddassa sesapadehipi yojanā kātabbā.

Samecca means 'having come together with knowledge.' Abhisamecca means 'having penetrated with knowledge.' Dhamma means the Four Noble Truths. 'All formations' means all phenomena with conditions. For these are called conditioned formations. They are called formations because they are formed by conditions; and because they are thus made by coming together with conditions, they are specifically termed 'conditioned.' In the commentaries, it is said: 'The material and immaterial phenomena of the three realms, produced by kamma, are constructed formations (abhisaṅkhatasaṅkhārā)' (Vism. 2.587). These too are included among the conditioned formations in statements such as 'Indeed, all formations are impermanent' (DN 2.221, 272; SN 1.186). In passages such as 'Monks, this person, gone to ignorance, constructs even a meritorious formation' (SN 2.51), formations dependent on ignorance are meant. Wholesome and unwholesome volitions (cetanā) of the three realms are called constructing formations. In statements such as 'As far as the range of construction extends, having gone that far, it is as if struck down and comes to rest' (AN 3.15), the bodily and mental effort that arises is called the formation of exertion (payogābhisaṅkhāro). In passages such as 'Friend Visākha, for a bhikkhu who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, first the verbal formation ceases, then the bodily formation, and then the mental formation' (MN 1.464), thoughts and examination, which form speech, are called verbal formations; in-and-out breaths, which are formed by the body, are called bodily formations; and perception and feeling, which are formed by the mind, are called mental formations. Here, however, conditioned formations are intended. They are impermanent in the sense of having no lasting existence. Suffering in the sense of oppression. 'All phenomena' is stated including Nibbāna. Non-self in the sense of not being subject to control. Regarding 'Dependent on ignorance, formations arise': here, that which is relied upon to produce the result is the condition. 'Dependent' means 'not without'; the meaning is 'not having disregarded.' 'Arises' means both 'originates' and 'continues'—this is the meaning. Furthermore, the characteristic of a condition is to be helpful. Ignorance is the condition—thus, 'dependent on ignorance.' 'Formations come into being' means 'they are produced.' In this way, the term 'come into being' should be applied to the remaining phrases as well.

Tattha [P 1.0223] katamā avijjā? Dukkhe aññāṇaṃ, dukkhasamudaye aññāṇaṃ, dukkhanirodhe aññāṇaṃ, dukkhanirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāya aññāṇaṃ, pubbante aññāṇaṃ, aparante aññāṇaṃ, pubbantāparante aññāṇaṃ, idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppannesu dhammesu aññāṇaṃ. Katame saṅkhārā? Puññābhisaṅkhāro apuññābhisaṅkhāro āneñjābhisaṅkhāro, kāyasaṅkhāro vacīsaṅkhāro cittasaṅkhāro, aṭṭha kāmāvacarakusalacetanā, pañca rūpāvacarakusalacetanā puññābhisaṅkhāro, dvādasa akusalacetanā [V 0.0175] apuññābhisaṅkhāro, catasso arūpāvacarakusalacetanā āneñjābhisaṅkhāro, kāyasañcetanā kāyasaṅkhāro, vacīsañcetanā vacīsaṅkhāro, manosañcetanā cittasaṅkhāro.

Herein, what is ignorance? Not knowing suffering, not knowing the origin of suffering, not knowing the cessation of suffering, not knowing the path leading to the cessation of suffering, not knowing the past, not knowing the future, not knowing the past and the future, not knowing the dependently arisen phenomena. What are formations? Meritorious formation, demeritorious formation, imperturbable formation; bodily formation, verbal formation, mental formation. The eight wholesome volitions pertaining to the sense sphere and the five wholesome volitions pertaining to the form sphere are the meritorious formation. The twelve unwholesome volitions are the demeritorious formation. The four wholesome volitions pertaining to the formless sphere are the imperturbable formation. Bodily volition is the bodily formation, verbal volition is the verbal formation, mental volition is the mental formation.

Tattha siyā – kathaṃ panetaṃ jānitabbaṃ “ime saṅkhārā avijjāpaccayā hontī”ti? Avijjābhāve bhāvato. Yassa hi dukkhādīsu avijjāsaṅkhātaṃ aññāṇaṃ appahīnaṃ hoti, so dukkhe tāva pubbantādīsu ca aññāṇena saṃsāradukkhaṃ sukhasaññāya gahetvā tasseva hetubhūte tividhepi saṅkhāre ārabhati. Samudaye aññāṇena dukkhahetubhūtepi taṇhāparikkhāre saṅkhāre sukhahetuto maññamāno ārabhati. Nirodhe pana magge ca aññāṇena dukkhassa anirodhabhūtepi gativisese dukkhanirodhasaññī hutvā nirodhassa ca amaggabhūtesupi yaññāmaratapādīsu nirodhamaggasaññī hutvā dukkhanirodhaṃ patthayamāno yaññāmaratapādimukhena tividhepi saṅkhāre ārabhati.

Here it might be asked: How then is it to be known that 'these formations are conditioned by ignorance'? By their arising when ignorance is present. For one in whom non-knowledge, termed ignorance regarding suffering and so on, has not been abandoned, he, due to non-knowledge of suffering itself and of the past and so on, grasps the suffering of saṃsāra as pleasant, and thus engages in the threefold formations that are the cause of that suffering. Due to non-knowledge of the origin, though the formations that are the requisites of craving are causes of suffering, he perceives them as causes of happiness and thus engages in them. And due to non-knowledge of cessation and the path, though specific destinations are not the cessation of suffering, he perceives cessation in them; and though sacrifices, self-mortification, and the like are not the path to cessation, he perceives the path in them. Thus, desiring the cessation of suffering, he engages in the threefold formations through sacrifices, self-mortification, and so on.

Api ca so tāya catūsu saccesu appahīnāvijjatāya visesato jātijarārogamaraṇādianekādīnavavokiṇṇampi puññaphalasaṅkhātaṃ dukkhaṃ dukkhato ajānanto tassa adhigamāya kāyavacīcittasaṅkhārabhedaṃ puññābhisaṅkhāraṃ ārabhati devaccharakāmako viya maruppapātaṃ. Sukhasammatassāpi ca tassa puññaphalassa ante mahāpariḷāhajanikaṃ vipariṇāmadukkhataṃ appassādatañca apassantopi tappaccayaṃ vuttappakārameva puññābhisaṅkhāraṃ ārabhati salabho viya dīpasikhābhinipātaṃ, madhubindugiddho viya ca madhulittasatthadhārālehanaṃ.

Moreover, not having abandoned ignorance regarding the Four Noble Truths, he does not know as suffering the suffering designated as the fruit of merit, though it is especially beset with birth, aging, sickness, death, and countless other dangers. To attain it, he undertakes meritorious formations—the diversity of bodily, verbal, and mental formations—like one desiring a celestial nymph falling from a mountain precipice. And not seeing that the fruit of merit, though regarded as happiness, ultimately brings great torment due to change and offers little satisfaction, he still, conditioned by that, undertakes meritorious formations in the way previously described, just as a moth falls upon a flame, or like one greedy for a drop of honey licking a honey-smeared razor's edge.

Kāmupasevanādīsu [M 0.0194] ca savipākesu ādīnavaṃ apassanto sukhasaññāya ceva kilesābhibhūtatāya ca dvārattayappavattampi apuññābhisaṅkhāraṃ ārabhati bālo [P 1.0224] viya gūthakīḷanaṃ, maritukāmo viya ca visakhādanaṃ. Āruppavipākesu cāpi saṅkhāravipariṇāmadukkhataṃ anavabujjhamāno sassatādivipallāsena cittasaṅkhārabhūtaṃ āneñjābhisaṅkhāraṃ ārabhati disāmūḷho viya pisācanagarābhimukhamaggagamanaṃ. Evaṃ yasmā avijjābhāvatova saṅkhārabhāvo, na abhāvato. Tasmā jānitabbametaṃ “ime saṅkhārā avijjāpaccayā hontī”ti.

Not seeing the danger in indulging in sensual pleasures and other actions with their results, the fool, overwhelmed by the perception of pleasure and by defilements, engages in demeritorious formations through the three doors—like a child playing with filth or one wishing to die consuming poison. And not understanding the suffering in the change of formations, even in the results of the formless attainments, one engages in the imperturbable formation, which is a mental formation, due to the distortion of eternalism and so forth—like one confused in direction traveling towards a city of demons. Thus, because the existence of formations is only due to the existence of ignorance, not due to its absence, it should be understood: 'These formations are conditioned by ignorance.'

Etthāha – gaṇhāma tāva etaṃ “avijjā saṅkhārānaṃ paccayo”ti, kiṃ panāyamekāva avijjā saṅkhārānaṃ paccayo, udāhu aññepi paccayā santīti? Kiṃ panettha yadi tāva ekāva, ekakāraṇavādo āpajjati. Atha aññepi santi, “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”ti ekakāraṇaniddeso nupapajjatīti? Na nupapajjati. Kasmā? Yasmā –

Here it is said: 'Let us first accept this: "Ignorance is a condition for formations." But is ignorance alone a condition for formations, or are there other conditions as well?' What then? If it is alone, then the doctrine of a single cause is incurred. But if there are other conditions as well, how is the designation of a single cause, 'formations are conditioned by ignorance,' justified? It is justified. Why? Because—

“Ekaṃ [V 0.0176] na ekato idha, nānekamanekatopi no ekaṃ;

Phalamatthi atthi pana eka-hetuphaladīpane attho”. (vibha. aṭṭha. 226, saṅkhārapadaniddesa; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 1.1.105; visuddhi. 2.617);

'Here, one is not from one, nor are many from many, nor is one from many; a result exists, and there is meaning in explaining a single cause for a result.' (VibhA. 226, Saṅkhārapadaniddesa; PaṭisA. 1.1.105; Vism. 2.617)

Bhagavā hi katthaci padhānattā, katthaci pākaṭattā, katthaci asādhāraṇattā desanāvilāsassa ca veneyyānañca anurūpato ekameva hetuṃ vā phalaṃ vā dīpeti. Tasmā ayamidha avijjā vijjamānesupi aññesu vatthārammaṇasahajātadhammādīsu saṅkhārakāraṇesu “assādānupassino taṇhā pavaḍḍhatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.52) ca, “avijjāsamudayā āsavasamudayo”ti (ma. ni. 1.104) ca vacanato aññesampi taṇhādīnaṃ saṅkhārahetūnaṃ hetūti padhānattā, “avidvā, bhikkhave, avijjāgato puññābhisaṅkhārampi abhisaṅkharotī”ti pākaṭattā, asādhāraṇattā ca saṅkhārānaṃ hetubhāvena dīpitāti veditabbā. Eteneva ca ekekahetuphaladīpanaparihāravacanena sabbattha ekekahetuphaladīpane payojanaṃ veditabbanti.

For the Blessed One reveals only one cause or one result, sometimes because of its pre-eminence, sometimes because of its obviousness, sometimes because of its uniqueness, and in accordance with the elegance of the teaching and the suitability of the trainees. Therefore, here, ignorance is to be understood as having been revealed as the cause of formations due to its pre-eminence—because it is the cause of other causes of formations such as craving, as stated in 'for one who dwells contemplating enjoyment, craving increases' (SN 2.52) and 'with the arising of ignorance, the taints arise' (MN 1.104)—even though other causes of formations such as basis, object, and co-arisen phenomena exist; due to its obviousness, as stated in 'an ignorant person, monks, overcome by ignorance, fabricates even meritorious formations'; and due to its uniqueness as the cause of formations. And by this very statement that provides the explanation for revealing a single cause for a single result, the purpose in revealing a single cause for a single result in all instances should be understood.

Etthāha – evaṃ santepi ekantāniṭṭhaphalāya sāvajjāya avijjāya kathaṃ puññāneñjābhisaṅkhārapaccayattaṃ yujjati? Na hi nimbabījato ucchu uppajjatīti. Kathaṃ na yujjissati? Lokasmiñhi –

Here it is said: Even so, how can ignorance, which has an entirely undesirable result and is blameworthy, be a condition for meritorious and imperturbable formations? For a sugarcane does not arise from a neem seed. How should it not be justified? For in the world—

“Viruddho [M 0.0195] cā viruddho ca, sadisāsadiso tathā;

Dhammānaṃ paccayo siddho, vipākā eva te ca na”.

"Opposed and unopposed, and likewise similar and dissimilar; a condition for phenomena is established, and these are not results."

Iti [P 1.0225] ayaṃ avijjā vipākavasena ekantāniṭṭhaphalā, sabhāvavasena ca sāvajjāpi samānā sabbesampi etesaṃ puññābhisaṅkhārādīnaṃ yathānurūpaṃ ṭhānakiccasabhāvaviruddhāviruddhapaccayavasena, sadisāsadisapaccayavasena ca paccayo hotīti veditabbā. Api ca ayaṃ aññopi pariyāyo –

Thus, this ignorance, which by way of result has an entirely undesirable outcome, and which by nature is blameworthy, is to be understood as a condition for all these meritorious formations and the like, by way of conditions that are opposed or unopposed, and similar or dissimilar, in accordance with their respective position, function, and nature. Moreover, there is this other method:

“Cutūpapāte saṃsāre, saṅkhārānañca lakkhaṇe;

Yo paṭiccasamuppanna-dhammesu ca vimuyhati.

"One who is deluded concerning passing away and reappearance in saṃsāra, and concerning the characteristics of formations, and concerning dependently arisen phenomena;

“Abhisaṅkharoti so ete, saṅkhāre tividhe yato;

Avijjā paccayo tesaṃ, tividhānampayaṃ tato.

"Because he fabricates these threefold formations, therefore this ignorance is the condition for these threefold [formations]."

“Yathāpi [V 0.0177] nāma jaccandho, naro apariṇāyako;

Ekadā yāti maggena, ummaggenāpi ekadā.

"Just as a man born blind, without a guide, sometimes goes by the path and sometimes by a wrong path,

“Saṃsāre saṃsaraṃ bālo, tathā apariṇāyako;

Karoti ekadā puññaṃ, apuññamapi ekadā.

"So too the fool, wandering in saṃsāra without a guide, sometimes does merit, and sometimes demerit."

“Yadā ca ñatvā so dhammaṃ, saccāni abhisamessati;

Tadā avijjūpasamā, upasanto carissatī”ti.

"But when, having known the Dhamma, he fully understands the truths, then, with the calming of ignorance, he will fare calmed."

Saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇanti chaviññāṇakāyā cakkhuviññāṇaṃ sotaviññāṇaṃ ghānaviññāṇaṃ jivhāviññāṇaṃ kāyaviññāṇaṃ manoviññāṇaṃ. Tattha cakkhuviññāṇaṃ kusalavipākaṃ akusalavipākanti duvidhaṃ. Tathā sotaghānajivhākāyaviññāṇāni. Manoviññāṇaṃ pana dve vipākamanodhātuyo, tisso ahetukavipākamanoviññāṇadhātuyo, aṭṭha sahetukavipākacittāni, pañca rūpāvacaravipākacittāni, cattāri arūpāvacaravipākacittānīti bāvīsatividhaṃ. Iti sabbāni bāttiṃsalokiyavipākaviññāṇāni.

"Conditioned by formations, consciousness arises"—this refers to the six classes of consciousness: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness. Therein, eye-consciousness is twofold: wholesome-resultant and unwholesome-resultant. Likewise for ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness. Mind-consciousness, however, is of twenty-two kinds: two resultant mind-elements, three rootless resultant mind-consciousness-elements, eight resultant consciousnesses with roots, five fine-material-sphere resultant consciousnesses, and four immaterial-sphere resultant consciousnesses. Thus, there are in all thirty-two mundane resultant consciousnesses.

Tattha siyā – kathaṃ panetaṃ jānitabbaṃ “idaṃ vuttappakāraṃ viññāṇaṃ saṅkhārapaccayā hotī”ti? Upacitakammābhāve vipākābhāvato. Vipākañhetaṃ, vipākañca na upacitakammābhāve uppajjati, yadi uppajjeyya, sabbesaṃ [M 0.0196] sabbavipākāni uppajjeyyuṃ, na ca uppajjantīti jānitabbametaṃ “saṅkhārapaccayā idaṃ viññāṇaṃ hotī”ti. Sabbameva hi idaṃ pavattipaṭisandhivasena dvedhā pavattati[P 1.0226]. Tattha dve pañcaviññāṇāni, dve manodhātuyo, somanassasahagatā ahetukamanoviññāṇadhātūti imāni terasa pañcavokārabhave pavattiyaṃyeva pavattanti. Sesāni ekūnavīsati tīsu bhavesu yathānurūpaṃ pavattiyampi paṭisandhiyampi pavattanti.

Here, one might ask: "How, then, is it to be known that 'this consciousness, described in this way, is conditioned by formations'?" Because in the absence of accumulated kamma, there is no result. For this is a result, and a result does not arise in the absence of accumulated kamma. If it were to arise, all results would arise for everyone, but they do not. Therefore, it is to be known that "this consciousness is conditioned by formations." Indeed, all this consciousness occurs in two ways: in the course of life and at rebirth-linking. Among these, the two sets of five sense-consciousnesses, the two mind-elements, and the rootless mind-consciousness-element accompanied by joy—these thirteen occur only in the course of life in the five-aggregate existence. The remaining nineteen occur in the three kinds of existence, both in the course of life and at rebirth-linking, as appropriate.

“Laddhappaccayamiti dhamma-mattametaṃ bhavantaramupeti;

Nāssa tato saṅkanti, na tato hetuṃ vinā hoti”.

"Having obtained its conditions, this mere phenomenon proceeds to another existence; there is no transmigration for it from there, nor does it arise from there without a cause."

Iti hetaṃ laddhappaccayaṃ rūpārūpadhammamattaṃ uppajjamānaṃ “bhavantaramupetī”ti vuccati, na satto na jīvo. Tassa ca nāpi atītabhavato idha saṅkanti atthi, nāpi tato hetuṃ vinā idha [V 0.0178] pātubhāvo. Ettha ca purimaṃ cavanato cuti, pacchimaṃ bhavantarādipaṭisandhānato paṭisandhīti vuccati.

Thus, this conditioned phenomenon, consisting merely of material and immaterial states, arising, is said to "proceed to another existence"—not a being, not a soul. And for it, there is no transmigration from a past existence to here, nor is there a manifestation here from there without a cause. Here, the former, from its falling away, is called 'passing away' (cuti), and the latter, from its relinking to the beginning of another existence, is called 'rebirth-linking' (paṭisandhi).

Etthāha – nanu evaṃ asaṅkantipātubhāve sati ye imasmiṃ manussattabhāve khandhā, tesaṃ niruddhattā, phalapaccayassa ca kammassa tattha agamanato, aññassa aññato ca taṃ phalaṃ siyā, upabhuñjake ca asati kassa taṃ phalaṃ siyā, tasmā na sundaramidaṃ vidhānanti? Tatridaṃ vuccati –

Here it may be asked: "If there is manifestation without transmigration, then since the aggregates in this human existence have ceased, and since the kamma that is a condition for the result does not go there, that result would be for another and from another. And if there is no experiencer, for whom would that result be? Therefore, this arrangement is not sound." To this, the following is said:

“Santāne yaṃ phalaṃ etaṃ, nāññassa na ca aññato;

Bījānaṃ abhisaṅkhāro, etassatthassa sādhako.

"This result, which is in the continuum, is not for another nor from another; the conditioning of seeds is the proof of this meaning."

“Phalassuppattiyā eva, siddhā bhuñjakasammuti;

Phaluppādena rukkhassa, yathā phalati sammutī”ti.

“By the arising of the result itself, the designation ‘experiencer’ is established; just as by the production of fruit from a tree, the designation ‘fruitful’ is established.”

Yopi vadeyya “evaṃ santepi ete saṅkhārā vijjamānā vā phalassa paccayā siyuṃ, avijjamānā vā. Yadi ca vijjamānā, pavattikkhaṇeyeva nesaṃ vipākena bhavitabbaṃ. Atha avijjamānā, pavattito pubbe pacchā ca niccaṃ phalāvahā siyu”nti. So evaṃ vattabbo –

And if someone should say: “Even so, these formations, whether existing or non-existing, could be conditions for the fruit. If existing, their result should occur in the very moment of their occurrence. But if non-existing, they would constantly produce fruit before and after their occurrence.” To him, one should reply:

“Katattā paccayā ete, na ca niccaṃ phalāvahā;

Pāṭibhogādikaṃ tattha, veditabbaṃ nidassana”nti.

“These are conditions because they have been done, but they are not constantly fruit-bearing; there, an example like a surety should be understood.”

Viññāṇapaccayā [P 1.0227][M 0.0197] nāmarūpanti idha vedanāsaññāsaṅkhārakkhandhā nāmaṃ, cattāri mahābhūtāni catunnañca mahābhūtānaṃ upādāyarūpaṃ rūpaṃ. Abhāvakagabbhaseyyakānaṃ aṇḍajānañca paṭisandhikkhaṇe vatthudasakaṃ kāyadasakanti vīsati rūparūpāni, tayo ca arūpino khandhāti ete tevīsati dhammā “viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpa”nti veditabbā. Sabhāvakānaṃ bhāvadasakaṃ pakkhipitvā tettiṃsa, opapātikasattesu brahmakāyikādīnaṃ paṭisandhikkhaṇe cakkhusotavatthudasakāni jīvitindriyanavakañcāti ekūnacattālīsa rūparūpāni, tayo ca arūpino khandhāti ete bācattālīsa dhammā “viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpa”nti veditabbā. Kāmabhave pana sesaopapātikānaṃ, saṃsedajānaṃ vā sabhāvakaparipuṇṇāyatanānaṃ paṭisandhikkhaṇe cakkhusotaghānajivhākāyavatthubhāvadasakānīti sattati rūparūpāni, tayo ca arūpino khandhāti ete [V 0.0179] tesattati dhammā “viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpa”nti veditabbā. Esa ukkaṃso, avakaṃsena pana taṃtaṃdasakavikalānaṃ tassa tassa vasena hāpetvā hāpetvā paṭisandhiyaṃ viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpasaṅkhā veditabbā. Arūpīnaṃ pana tayova arūpino khandhā. Asaññīnaṃ rūpato jīvitindriyanavakamevāti. Esa tāva paṭisandhiyaṃ nayo.

“With consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises.” Here, the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations are ‘name,’ while the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements are ‘form.’ For sexless womb-born beings and for egg-born beings, at the moment of rebirth-linking, there are the base decad and the body decad, making twenty material phenomena, and the three immaterial aggregates—thus, these twenty-three phenomena should be understood as ‘name-and-form conditioned by consciousness.’ For those with sex, including the sex decad, it becomes thirty-three. For spontaneously born beings such as those in the Brahmā realms, at the moment of rebirth-linking, there are the eye, ear, and base decads, and the life-faculty nonad, making thirty-nine material phenomena, and the three immaterial aggregates—thus, these forty-two phenomena should be understood as ‘name-and-form conditioned by consciousness.’ In the desire realm, for the remaining spontaneously born beings and for moisture-born beings who possess sex and have complete sense bases, at the moment of rebirth-linking, the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, base, and sex decads make seventy material phenomena, along with the three immaterial aggregates—thus, these seventy-three phenomena should be understood as ‘name-and-form conditioned by consciousness.’ This is the maximum count. In the minimum count, for those deficient in this or that decad, by omitting them accordingly, the enumeration of name-and-form conditioned by consciousness at rebirth-linking should be understood. For the formless beings, there are only the three immaterial aggregates. For the non-percipient beings, as to form, there is only the life-faculty nonad. This, then, is the method regarding rebirth-linking.

Pavatte pana sabbattha rūpapavattidese paṭisandhicittassa ṭhitikkhaṇe paṭisandhicittena saha pavattaututo utusamuṭṭhānaṃ suddhaṭṭhakaṃ pātubhavati. Paṭhamabhavaṅgato pabhuti cittasamuṭṭhānaṃ suddhaṭṭhakaṃ, saddapātubhāvakāle ututo ceva cittato ca saddanavakaṃ, kabaḷīkārāhārūpajīvīnaṃ āhārasamuṭṭhānaṃ suddhaṭṭhakanti evaṃ āhārasamuṭṭhānassa, suddhaṭṭhakassa, utucittasamuṭṭhānānañca dvinnaṃ navakānaṃ vasena chabbīsatividhaṃ, ekekacitte tikkhattuṃ uppajjamānaṃ vuttakammasamuṭṭhānañca sattatividhanti channavutividhaṃ rūpaṃ, tayo ca arūpino khandhāti navanavutidhammā yathāsambhavaṃ “viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpa”nti veditabbā.

But in the course of existence, in all instances where material phenomena occur, at the static phase of the rebirth-linking consciousness, the temperature-originated pure octad appears from the temperature that arises together with the rebirth-linking consciousness. From the first life-continuum onward, the mind-originated pure octad arises. At the time sound appears, the sound nonad arises from both temperature and mind. For those who live on physical food, the food-originated pure octad arises. Thus, by way of the food-originated pure octad, the [kamma-originated] pure octad, and the two nonads originating from temperature and mind, there are twenty-six types of material phenomena. And with the seventy types of kamma-originated material phenomena which are said to arise three times in every single moment of consciousness, there are ninety-six types of material phenomena. These, together with the three immaterial aggregates, are ninety-nine phenomena that should be understood, according to their occurrence, as ‘name-and-form conditioned by consciousness.’

Tattha siyā – kathaṃ panetaṃ jānitabbaṃ “paṭisandhināmarūpaṃ viññāṇapaccayā hotī”ti? Suttato yuttito ca. Sutte [P 1.0228] hi “cittānuparivattino dhammā”tiādinā (dha. sa. dukamātikā 62) nayena bahudhā vedanādīnaṃ viññāṇapaccayatā siddhā. Yuttito pana –

Here, it may be asked: How then should it be known that “rebirth-linking name-and-form is conditioned by consciousness”? By the Suttas and by reasoning. For in the Suttas, by way of statements like “phenomena that revolve around consciousness” (Dhs. Dukamātikā 62), the fact that feeling and other states are conditioned by consciousness is established in many ways. And by reasoning—

“Cittajena [M 0.0198] hi rūpena, idha diṭṭhena sijjhati;

Adiṭṭhassāpi rūpassa, viññāṇaṃ paccayo itī”ti.

“For by mind-originated form seen here, it is established that consciousness is a condition for unseen form as well.”

Nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatananti nāmaṃ vuttameva. Idha pana rūpaṃ niyamato cattāri mahābhūtāni, cha vatthūni, jīvitindriyanti ekādasavidhaṃ. Saḷāyatanaṃ pana cakkhāyatanaṃ sotaghānajivhākāyamanāyatanaṃ.

“With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise.” Name is as stated before. Here, however, form is specifically of eleven kinds: the four great elements, the six bases, and the life faculty. The six sense bases are the eye base, ear base, nose base, tongue base, body base, and mind base.

Tattha siyā – kathaṃ panetaṃ jānitabbaṃ “nāmarūpaṃ saḷāyatanassa paccayo”ti? Nāmarūpabhāve bhāvato. Tassa tassa hi nāmassa rūpassa ca bhāve taṃ taṃ āyatanaṃ hoti, na aññathāti.

Here one might ask: But how is it to be known that “name-and-form is a condition for the six sense bases?” By the existence of name-and-form. For when that particular name and form are present, then that particular sense base exists, not otherwise.

Saḷāyatanapaccayā phassoti –

“With the six sense bases as condition, contact arises.”

“Chaḷeva [V 0.0180] phassā saṅkhepā, cakkhusamphassaādayo;

Viññāṇamiva bāttiṃsa, vitthārena bhavanti te”.

“In brief, there are just six contacts: eye-contact and so on; like consciousness, they become thirty-two when expanded in detail.”

Phassapaccayā vedanāti –

“With contact as condition, feeling arises.”

“Dvārato vedanā vuttā, cakkhusamphassajādikā;

Chaḷeva tā pabhedena, idha bāttiṃsa vedanā”.

“Feeling is spoken of in terms of the doors, such as that born of eye-contact; there are just six such kinds, but here, by way of division, they become thirty-two.”

Vedanāpaccayā taṇhāti –

“With feeling as condition, craving arises.”

“Rūpataṇhādibhedena, cha taṇhā idha dīpitā;

Ekekā tividhā tattha, pavattākārato matā.

“Here, craving is expounded as sixfold, beginning with craving for forms. Each of these is regarded as threefold in terms of its mode of occurrence.”

“Dukkhī sukhaṃ patthayati, sukhī bhiyyopi icchati;

Upekkhā pana santattā, sukhamicceva bhāsitā.

“One who is suffering longs for pleasure; one who is happy desires even more. But equanimity, being serene, is itself declared to be happiness.”

“Taṇhāya paccayā tasmā, honti tissopi vedanā;

Vedanāpaccayā taṇhā, iti vuttā mahesinā”ti.

“Therefore, the three feelings are conditions for craving. ‘With feeling as condition, craving arises’—so it was said by the Great Sage.”

Taṇhāpaccayā upādānanti cattāri upādānāni kāmupādānaṃ diṭṭhupādānaṃ sīlabbatupādānaṃ attavādupādānaṃ. Upādānapaccayā bhavoti idha kammabhavo adhippeto, upapattibhavo pana paduddhāravasena vutto. Bhavapaccayā jātīti kammabhavapaccayā jāti paṭisandhikhandhānaṃ pātubhavo.

“With craving as condition, clinging arises”: the four kinds of clinging are clinging to sensual pleasures, clinging to views, clinging to precepts and vows, and clinging to a doctrine of self. “With clinging as condition, becoming arises”: here, kamma-becoming is intended, while rebirth-becoming is mentioned by way of a supplementary statement. “With becoming as condition, birth arises”: birth conditioned by kamma-becoming is the manifestation of the aggregates at rebirth.

Tattha [P 1.0229] siyā – kathaṃ panetaṃ jānitabbaṃ “bhavo jātiyā paccayo”ti ce? Bāhirapaccayasamattepi hīnapaṇītatādivisesadassanato. Bāhirānañhi janakajananisukkasoṇitāhārādīnaṃ paccayānaṃ samattepi sattānaṃ yamakānampi [M 0.0199] sataṃ hīnapaṇītatādiviseso dissati. So ca na ahetuko sabbadā ca sabbesañca abhāvato, na kammabhavato aññahetuko tadabhinibbattakasattānaṃ ajjhattasantāne aññassa kāraṇassa abhāvatoti kammabhavahetukova. Kammañhi sattānaṃ hīnapaṇītatādivisesassa hetu. Tenāha bhagavā – “kammaṃ satte [V 0.0181] vibhajati yadidaṃ hīnapaṇītatāyā”ti (ma. ni. 3.289). Tasmā jānitabbametaṃ “bhavo jātiyā paccayo”ti.

Here one might ask: But how is it to be known that “becoming is a condition for birth”? Because distinctions such as inferiority and superiority are observed even when external conditions are the same. For even when external conditions such as the parents’ semen and blood, nourishment, etc., are the same, distinctions of inferiority and superiority are seen among beings, even in the case of twins. And this is not without a cause, for it is not always and for all the same; nor is there any other cause apart from kamma-becoming, since there is no other cause in the internal continuum of beings produced by it. Thus, it must be due to kamma-becoming alone. For kamma is the cause of distinctions such as inferiority and superiority among beings. Therefore, the Blessed One said: “Kamma divides beings, that is, into inferiority and superiority” (MN 135). Therefore, it is to be understood that “becoming is a condition for birth.”

Jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇantiādīsu yasmā asati jātiyā jarāmaraṇañceva sokādayo ca dhammā na honti, jātiyā pana sati jarāmaraṇañceva jarāmaraṇasaṅkhātadukkhadhammaphuṭṭhassa bālassa jarāmaraṇādisambandhā vā tena tena dukkhadhammena phuṭṭhassa anabhisambandhā vā sokādayo ca dhammā honti. Tasmā jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇanti. Samecca abhisamecca dhammanti ñāṇena samāgantvā catusaccadhammaṃ paṭivijjhitvā.

In “With birth as condition, aging and death arise,” and so forth: because when there is no birth, aging and death, as well as sorrow and other states, do not exist. But when there is birth, aging and death occur; and for the fool afflicted by the states of suffering known as aging and death—whether in connection with aging and death or when afflicted by various states of suffering without such connection—sorrow and other states arise. Therefore, “With birth as condition, aging and death arise.” “Having fully understood, thoroughly understood the Dhamma” means having approached with knowledge and penetrated the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths.

Evaṃ dvādasapadikaṃ paccayākārappavattiṃ dassetvā idāni vivaṭṭavasena avijjādīnaṃ nirodhadassanatthaṃ “avijjānirodhā saṅkhāranirodhoti samecca abhisamecca dhamma”ntiādimāha. Tattha avijjānirodhāti avijjāya anuppādanirodhā puna appavattinirodhena. Saṅkhāranirodhoti saṅkhārānaṃ anuppādanirodho hoti. Evaṃ sesapadesupi. Idaṃ dukkhantiādayo pubbe vuttanayā eva. Ime dhammā abhiññeyyāti ime tebhūmakā dhammā sabhāvalakkhaṇāvabodhavasena sobhanākārena, adhikena ñāṇena vā sabhāvato jānitabbā. Pariññeyyāti sāmaññalakkhaṇāvabodhavasena, kiccasamāpanavasena ca byāpitvā jānitabbā. Ime dhammā pahātabbāti ime samudayapakkhikā dhammā tena tena guṇaṅgena pahātabbā. Bhāvetabbāti [P 1.0230] vaḍḍhetabbā. Sacchikātabbāti paccakkhaṃ kātabbā. Duvidhā sacchikiriyā paṭilābhasacchikiriyā ca ārammaṇasacchikiriyā ca. Channaṃ phassāyatanānanti cakkhādīnaṃ channaṃ āyatanānaṃ. Samudayañca atthaṅgamañcāti uppādañca nirodhañca.

Having thus shown the twelve-factored cycle of dependent origination, now, to demonstrate the cessation of ignorance and so forth by way of reversal, it is said: “With the cessation of ignorance, formations cease,” and so on, “having fully understood, thoroughly understood the Dhamma.” Herein, “with the cessation of ignorance” means the cessation of ignorance by non-arising, and further, cessation by non-occurrence. “Formations cease” means the cessation of formations by non-arising. The same applies to the remaining terms. “This is suffering,” and so forth, are as previously explained. “These phenomena are to be fully known”: these phenomena pertaining to the three worlds are to be known in their intrinsic nature through clear comprehension of their specific characteristics, or known in their true nature with heightened wisdom. “They are to be thoroughly understood”: they are to be known by encompassing them through the comprehension of their general characteristics and the completion of their function. “These phenomena are to be abandoned”: these phenomena belonging to the side of origination are to be abandoned by their respective qualities. “They are to be developed”: they are to be increased. “They are to be realized”: they are to be directly experienced. There are two kinds of realization: realization by attainment and realization by object. “Of the six sense bases”: of the six bases beginning with the eye. “Arising and passing away”: both arising and cessation.

Bhūripaññoti bhūri viyāti bhūri, tāya bhūripaññāya samannāgato bhūripañño. Mahāpaññotiādīsu mahāpaññādīhi samannāgatoti attho.

Bhūripañño means possessing abundant wisdom, because bhūri means abundant; thus, one endowed with abundant wisdom is called bhūripañño. Regarding mahāpañño and similar terms, the meaning is: endowed with great wisdom and so forth.

Tatridaṃ [M 0.0200] mahāpaññādīnaṃ nānattaṃ – katamā mahāpaññā? Mahante atthe pariggaṇhātīti mahāpaññā. Mahante dhamme…pe… mahantā niruttiyo… mahantāni paṭibhānāni pariggaṇhātīti mahāpaññā. Mahante sīlakkhandhe pariggaṇhātīti mahāpaññā. Mahante samādhikkhandhe…pe… paññākkhandhe… vimuttikkhandhe… vimuttiñāṇadassanakkhandhe pariggaṇhātīti mahāpaññā. Mahantāni ṭhānāṭhānāni…pe… mahāvihārasamāpattiyo… mahantāni ariyasaccāni… mahante satipaṭṭhāne… sammappadhāne… iddhipāde… mahantāni indriyāni [V 0.0182]… balāni… bojjhaṅgāni… mahante ariyamagge… mahantāni sāmaññaphalāni… mahāabhiññāyo… mahantaṃ paramatthaṃ nibbānaṃ pariggaṇhātīti mahāpaññā.

Herein, this is the diversity of great wisdom and others: What is great wisdom? It is called great wisdom because it comprehends great meanings. It comprehends great qualities... great expressions... great inspirations—thus it is great wisdom. It comprehends the great aggregate of virtue—thus it is great wisdom. It comprehends the great aggregate of concentration... the aggregate of wisdom... the aggregate of liberation... the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation—thus it is great wisdom. It comprehends great possibilities and impossibilities... great meditative attainments... the great noble truths... the great foundations of mindfulness... the great right efforts... the great bases of power... the great faculties... the great powers... the great factors of enlightenment... the great noble path... the great fruits of recluseship... the great supernormal knowledges... the great ultimate meaning, Nibbāna—thus it is great wisdom.

Katamā puthupaññā? Puthunānākhandhesu ñāṇaṃ pavattatīti puthupaññā. Puthunānādhātūsu…pe… puthunānāāyatanesu… puthunānāpaṭiccasamuppādesu… puthunānāsuññatamanupalabbhesu… puthunānāatthesu… dhammesu… niruttīsu… paṭibhānesu… puthunānāsīlakkhandhesu… puthunānāsamādhipaññāvimuttivimuttiñāṇadassanakkhandhesu… puthunānāṭhānāṭhānesu… puthunānāvihārasamāpattīsu… puthunānāariyasaccesu… puthunānāsatipaṭṭhānesu… sammappadhānesu… iddhipādesu… indriyesu… balesu… bojjhaṅgesu… puthunānāariyamaggesu… sāmaññaphalesu… abhiññāsu… puthunānājanasādhāraṇe dhamme samatikkamma paramatthe nibbāne ñāṇaṃ pavattatīti puthupaññā.

What is extensive wisdom? Extensive wisdom is so called because knowledge functions in diverse aggregates. It functions in diverse elements... diverse bases... diverse dependent originations... diverse perceptions of emptiness... diverse meanings... diverse teachings... diverse expressions... diverse inspirations... diverse aggregates of virtue... diverse aggregates of concentration, wisdom, liberation, and knowledge and vision of liberation... diverse possibilities and impossibilities... diverse meditative attainments... diverse noble truths... diverse foundations of mindfulness... diverse right efforts... diverse bases of power... diverse faculties... diverse powers... diverse factors of enlightenment... diverse noble paths... diverse fruits of recluseship... diverse supernormal knowledges... knowledge functions by transcending diverse ordinary worldly phenomena and reaching the ultimate reality, Nibbāna—thus it is extensive wisdom.

Katamā [P 1.0231] hāsapaññā? Idhekacco hāsabahulo vedabahulo tuṭṭhibahulo pāmojjabahulo sīlaṃ paripūreti. Indriyasaṃvaraṃ paripūreti. Bhojane mattaññutaṃ…pe… jāgariyānuyogaṃ… sīlakkhandhaṃ… samādhikkhandhaṃ… paññākkhandhaṃ… vimuttikkhandhaṃ… vimuttiñāṇadassanakkhandhaṃ paripūretīti hāsapaññā. Hāsabahulo…pe… pāmojjabahulo ṭhānāṭhānaṃ paṭivijjhatīti hāsapaññā. Hāsabahulo vihārasamāpattiyo paripūretīti hāsapaññā. Hāsabahulo ariyasaccāni paṭivijjhatīti hāsapaññā. Satipaṭṭhāne bhāveti sammappadhāne… iddhipāde… indriyāni… balāni… bojjhaṅge… ariyamaggaṃ bhāvetīti hāsapaññā, hāsabahulo sāmaññaphalāni sacchikarotīti hāsapaññā, abhiññāyo paṭivijjhatīti hāsapaññā, hāsabahulo paramatthaṃ nibbānaṃ sacchikarotīti hāsapaññā.

What is wisdom accompanied by mirth? Here, someone who is frequently mirthful, frequently joyous, frequently content, and frequently delighted fulfills virtue. They fulfill sense restraint. They fulfill moderation in eating... devotion to wakefulness... the aggregate of virtue... the aggregate of concentration... the aggregate of wisdom... the aggregate of liberation... the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation—this is wisdom accompanied by mirth. Being frequently mirthful... they penetrate what is possible and what is impossible—this is wisdom accompanied by mirth. Being frequently mirthful, they fulfill the meditative attainments—this is wisdom accompanied by mirth. Being frequently mirthful, they penetrate the noble truths—this is wisdom accompanied by mirth. They develop the foundations of mindfulness... right efforts... bases of power... faculties... powers... enlightenment factors... the noble path—this is wisdom accompanied by mirth. Being frequently mirthful, they realize the fruits of recluseship—this is wisdom accompanied by mirth. They penetrate the supernormal knowledges—this is wisdom accompanied by mirth. Being frequently mirthful, they realize the ultimate goal, Nibbāna—this is wisdom accompanied by mirth.

Katamā [M 0.0201] javanapaññā? Yaṃ kiñci rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā oḷārikaṃ vā sukhumaṃ vā hīnaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā yaṃ dūre santike vā, sabbaṃ rūpaṃ aniccato khippaṃ javatīti javanapaññā. Dukkhato, anattato khippaṃ javatīti javanapaññā. Yā kāci vedanā…pe… yā kāci saññā… ye keci saṅkhārā… yaṃ kiñci viññāṇaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ…pe… yaṃ dūre santike vā, sabbaṃ viññāṇaṃ aniccato… dukkhato… anattato khippaṃ javatīti javanapaññā. Cakkhuṃ…pe… jarāmaraṇaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ aniccato… dukkhato… anattato khippaṃ javatīti javanapaññā.

What is swift wisdom? Whatever form—past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—it swiftly penetrates all form as impermanent: this is swift wisdom. It swiftly penetrates it as suffering, as non-self: this is swift wisdom. Whatever feeling… whatever perception… whatever formations… whatever consciousness—past, future, or present… far or near—it swiftly penetrates all consciousness as impermanent… as suffering… as non-self: this is swift wisdom. The eye… aging-and-death—past, future, or present—it swiftly penetrates as impermanent… as suffering… as non-self: this is swift wisdom.

Rūpaṃ [V 0.0183] atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ aniccaṃ khayaṭṭhena, dukkhaṃ bhayaṭṭhena, anattā asārakaṭṭhenāti tulayitvā tīrayitvā vibhāvayitvā vibhūtaṃ katvā rūpanirodhe nibbāne khippaṃ javatīti javanapaññā. Vedanā… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ… cakkhuṃ…pe… jarāmaraṇaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ aniccaṃ khayaṭṭhena, dukkhaṃ bhayaṭṭhena, anattā asārakaṭṭhenāti tulayitvā…pe… vibhūtaṃ katvā jarāmaraṇanirodhe nibbāne khippaṃ javatīti javanapaññā.

Form—past, future, or present—is impermanent in the sense of destruction, suffering in the sense of fear, non-self in the sense of insubstantiality. Having weighed, examined, and discerned it, having made it clear, one swiftly penetrates the cessation of form, Nibbāna: this is swift wisdom. Feeling… perception… formations… consciousness… the eye… aging-and-death—past, future, or present—is impermanent in the sense of destruction, suffering in the sense of fear, non-self in the sense of insubstantiality. Having weighed… and made it clear, one swiftly penetrates the cessation of aging-and-death, Nibbāna: this is swift wisdom.

Rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ aniccaṃ saṅkhataṃ paṭiccasamuppannaṃ khayadhammaṃ vayadhammaṃ virāgadhammaṃ nirodhadhammanti tulayitvā…pe… [P 1.0232] vibhūtaṃ katvā rūpanirodhe nibbāne khippaṃ javatīti javanapaññā. Vedanā…pe… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ… cakkhuṃ…pe… jarāmaraṇaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ aniccaṃ…pe… nirodhadhammanti tulayitvā…pe… vibhūtaṃ katvā jarāmaraṇanirodhe nibbāne khippaṃ javatīti javanapaññā.

Form—past, future, or present—is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to decay, vanishing, dispassion, and cessation. Having weighed… and made it clear, one swiftly penetrates the cessation of form, Nibbāna: this is swift wisdom. Feeling… perception… formations… consciousness… the eye… aging-and-death—past, future, or present—is impermanent… subject to cessation. Having weighed… and made it clear, one swiftly penetrates the cessation of aging-and-death, Nibbāna: this is swift wisdom.

Katamā tikkhapaññā? Khippaṃ kilese chindatīti tikkhapaññā. Uppannaṃ kāmavitakkaṃ nādhivāseti. Uppannaṃ byāpādavitakkaṃ… uppannaṃ vihiṃsāvitakkaṃ… uppannuppanne pāpake akusale dhamme… uppannaṃ rāgaṃ… uppannaṃ dosaṃ… mohaṃ… kodhaṃ… upanāhaṃ… makkhaṃ… paḷāsaṃ… issaṃ… macchariyaṃ… māyaṃ… sāṭheyyaṃ… thambhaṃ… sārambhaṃ… mānaṃ… atimānaṃ… madaṃ… pamādaṃ… sabbe kilese… sabbe duccarite… sabbe abhisaṅkhāre… sabbe bhavagāmikamme nādhivāseti pajahati vinodeti byantīkaroti anabhāvaṃ gametīti tikkhapaññā. Ekamhi āsane cattāro ariyamaggā, cattāri ca sāmaññaphalāni, catasso ca paṭisambhidāyo, cha abhiññāyo adhigatā honti sacchikatā phassitā paññāyāti tikkhapaññā.

What is keen wisdom? It quickly cuts off defilements; thus it is keen wisdom. It does not tolerate arisen sensual thoughts, arisen thoughts of ill-will, arisen thoughts of harm, arisen unwholesome states, arisen lust, arisen hatred, arisen delusion, arisen anger, arisen resentment, arisen hypocrisy, arisen spite, arisen envy, arisen stinginess, arisen deceit, arisen fraud, arisen obstinacy, arisen rivalry, arisen conceit, arisen arrogance, arisen intoxication, arisen heedlessness, all defilements, all misconduct, all formations, all actions leading to continued existence. It does not tolerate them, but abandons, dispels, eliminates, and brings them to an end; thus it is keen wisdom. Through wisdom, on a single seat, the four noble paths, the four fruits of recluseship, the four analytical knowledges, and the six higher knowledges are attained, realized, and experienced; thus it is keen wisdom.

Katamā [M 0.0202] nibbedhikapaññā? Idhekacco sabbasaṅkhāresu ubbegabahulo hoti uttāsabahulo ukkaṇṭhanabahulo aratibahulo anabhiratibahulo bahimukho na ramati sabbasaṅkhāresu, anibbiddhapubbaṃ apadālitapubbaṃ lobhakkhandhaṃ nibbijjhati padāletīti nibbedhikapaññā. Anibbiddhapubbaṃ apadālitapubbaṃ dosakkhandhaṃ…pe… mohakkhandhaṃ… kodhaṃ… upanāhaṃ…pe… sabbe bhavagāmikamme nibbijjhati padāletīti nibbedhikapaññā.

What is penetrative wisdom? Here, someone is abundant in dismay regarding all conditioned things, abundant in terror, abundant in weariness, abundant in displeasure, abundant in lack of delight; they are turned away and do not delight in any conditioned things. Having not previously been disgusted with, nor previously broken through the mass of greed, they become disgusted with and break through it—this is penetrative wisdom. Having not previously been disgusted with, nor previously broken through the mass of hatred… the mass of delusion… anger… resentment… all actions leading to continued existence—they become disgusted with and break through them—this is penetrative wisdom.

28. Sa sabbadhammesu visenibhūto, yaṃ kiñci diṭṭhaṃ va sutaṃ mutaṃ vāti so bhūripañño khīṇāsavo yaṃ kiñci diṭṭhaṃ vā sutaṃ vā mutaṃ vā tesu sabbadhammesu mārasenaṃ vināsetvā ṭhitabhāvena [V 0.0184] visenibhūto. Tameva dassinti taṃ eva visuddhadassiṃ. Vivaṭaṃ carantanti taṇhāchadanādivigamena vivaṭaṃ hutvā carantaṃ. Kenīdha lokasmi vikappayeyyāti [P 1.0233] kena idha loke taṇhākappena vā diṭṭhikappena vā koci vikappeyya, tesaṃ vā pahīnattā rāgādinā pubbe vuttenāti.

28. Regarding 'He is free from the army in all phenomena—whatever is seen, heard, or cognized': that one of vast wisdom, whose taints are destroyed, whatever is seen, heard, or cognized—in all these phenomena, having vanquished Māra’s army, he is established as one free from the army. Regarding 'He sees just that': it means that very one of purified vision. Regarding 'He moves uncovered': it means moving having become uncovered through the removal of the coverings of craving and so on. Regarding 'By what could one conceive of him here in the world?': by what conceiving of craving or conceiving of view could anyone conceive of him here in the world? For these—lust and so on—have been abandoned, as was previously stated.

Kāmā te paṭhamā senātiādīsu catūsu gāthāsu ayamattho – yasmā āditova agāriyabhūte satte vatthukāmesu kilesakāmā mohayanti, te abhibhuyya anagāriyabhāvaṃ upagatānaṃ pantesu vā senāsanesu, aññataraññataresu vā adhikusalesu dhammesu arati uppajjati. Vuttañcetaṃ – “pabbajitena kho, āvuso, abhirati dukkarā”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.331). Tato te parapaṭibaddhajīvikattā khuppipāsā bādheti, tāya bādhitānaṃ pariyesanataṇhā cittaṃ kilamayati, atha nesaṃ kilantacittānaṃ thinamiddhaṃ okkamati tato visesamanadhigacchantānaṃ durabhisambhavesu araññavanapatthesu senāsanesu viharataṃ utrāsasaññitā bhīru jāyati, tesaṃ ussaṅkitaparisaṅkitānaṃ dīgharattaṃ vivekarasamanassādayamānānaṃ viharataṃ “na siyā nu kho esa maggo”ti paṭipattiyaṃ vicikicchā uppajjati, taṃ vinodetvā viharataṃ appamattakena visesādhigamena mānamakkhathambhā jāyanti, tepi vinodetvā viharataṃ tato adhikataraṃ visesādhigamaṃ nissāya lābhasakkārasilokā uppajjanti, lābhādimucchitā dhammapaṭirūpakāni pakāsentā micchāyasaṃ adhigantvā tattha ṭhitā jātiādīhi attānaṃ ukkaṃsenti, paraṃ vambhenti. Tasmā kāmādīnaṃ paṭhamasenādibhāvo veditabbo.

In the four verses beginning with 'Kāmā te paṭhamā senā,' the meaning is this: From the very beginning, sensual objects and defilements of sensual desire delude beings who are still householders. Having overcome these and adopted the homeless life, dissatisfaction arises in them while dwelling in remote lodgings, or in regard to certain higher wholesome states. As it is said: 'Friend, it is difficult for one gone forth to find delight' (Saṃ. Ni. 4.331). Then, because their livelihood depends on others, hunger and thirst afflict them. Afflicted by these, the craving for seeking wears down their mind. When their mind is worn down, sloth and torpor overcome them. Not attaining distinction, while dwelling in hard-to-endure forest and woodland lodgings, fear accompanied by dread arises in them. Being suspicious and apprehensive, dwelling for a long time without savoring the taste of seclusion, doubt arises in them about the practice: 'Could this be the wrong path?' Having dispelled that and dwelling with a slight attainment of distinction, conceit, contempt, and obstinacy arise in them. Having dispelled these too and dwelling with a higher attainment of distinction, based on that, gain, honor, and praise arise. Infatuated with gain and such, they display semblances of the Dhamma, achieve wrong repute, and remaining there, they exalt themselves with birth and so on, while disparaging others. Therefore, it should be understood that sensual pleasures and the rest constitute the first army and so on.

Evametaṃ [M 0.0203] dasavidhaṃ senaṃ uddisitvā yasmā sā kaṇhadhammasamannāgatattā kaṇhassa namucino upakārāya saṃvattati, tasmā naṃ “tava senā”ti niddisanto āha – “esā namuci te senā, kaṇhassābhippahārinī”ti. Tattha abhippahārinīti samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ ghātinī nippothinī, antarāyakarīti attho. Na naṃ asūro jināti, jetvāva labhate sukhanti evaṃ tava senaṃ asūro kāye ca jīvite ca sāpekkho puriso na jināti, sūro pana jināti, jetvāva maggasukhaṃ phalasukhañca adhigacchati.

Having thus described this tenfold army, because it is associated with dark qualities and conduces to the benefit of the dark one, Namuci, therefore, pointing it out as 'your army,' he says: 'This, Namuci, is your army, the striking force of the dark one.' Here, 'striking force' means it is the slayer and destroyer of ascetics and brahmins, and creates obstacles. Regarding 'Not a non-hero conquers it, but having conquered it, one attains happiness': thus, a person who is a non-hero, attached to body and life, does not conquer your army; but the hero conquers it and, having conquered, attains the happiness of the path and the fruit.

Yato [P 1.0234] catūhi ariyamaggehīti yadā catūhi niddosanibbānamagganasaṅkhātehi maggehi. Mārasenāti mārassa senā vacanakarā kilesā. Paṭisenikarāti paṭipakkhakarā. Jitā cāti parājayamānā hanitā ca. Parājitā cāti niggahitā ca. Bhaggāti bhinnā. Vippaluggāti cuṇṇavicuṇṇā. Parammukhāti vimukhabhāvaṃ pāpitā. Visenibhūtoti nikkileso hutvā ṭhito.

Regarding 'When by the four noble paths': that is, when by the four paths reckoned as the faultless paths to Nibbāna. Regarding 'Māra's army': the defilements that are Māra's army, doing his bidding. Regarding 'Opponents': those who act as opponents. Regarding 'And conquered': defeated and slain. Regarding 'And routed': and destroyed. Regarding 'Broken': shattered. Regarding 'Scattered': reduced to powder. Regarding 'Turned their backs': brought to a state of having turned away. Regarding 'Become free from the army': having become without defilements, he stands.

Vodātadassinti [V 0.0185] byavadātadassiṃ. Tāni chadanānīti etāni taṇhādikilesachadanāni. Vivaṭānīti pākaṭīkatāni. Viddhaṃsitānīti ṭhitaṭṭhānato apahatāni. Ugghāṭitānīti uppāṭitāni. Samugghāṭitānīti visesena uppāṭitāni.

Regarding 'One who sees the pure': it means one who sees the purified. Regarding 'Those coverings': these are the coverings of craving and other defilements. Regarding 'Uncovered': made apparent. Regarding 'Destroyed': removed from their standing place. Regarding 'Uprooted': extracted. Regarding 'Thoroughly uprooted': specially extracted.

29. Na kappayantīti gāthāya sambandho attho ca – kiñca bhiyyo? Te hi tādisā santo dvinnaṃ kappānaṃ purekkhārānañca kenaci na kappayanti, na purekkharonti. Paramatthaṃ accantasuddhiṃ adhigatattā anaccantasuddhiṃyeva akiriyasassatadiṭṭhiṃ “accantasuddhī”ti na te vadanti. Ādānaganthaṃ gatitaṃ visajjāti catubbidhampi rūpādīnaṃ ādāyakattā ādānaganthaṃ attano cittasantāne gathitaṃ baddhaṃ ariyamaggasatthena vissajja chinditvā. Sesaṃ pākaṭameva.

29. Regarding 'They do not conceive': the connection and meaning of the verse is this. And what more? Such beings, being thus, do not conceive by means of any of the two kinds of conceiving, nor do they prioritize. Because they have attained the ultimate, absolute purity, they do not declare the non-absolute purity—namely, the views of inaction and eternalism—to be 'absolute purity.' Regarding 'Having released the fastened bond of grasping': having released and severed with the sword of the noble path the bond of grasping—so-called because it grasps the fourfold things such as form—which is fastened and bound in one's own mental continuum. The rest is evident.

Accantasuddhinti accantaṃ paramatthaṃ suddhiṃ. Saṃsārasuddhinti saṃsārato suddhiṃ. Akiriyadiṭṭhinti karoto na karīyati pāpanti akiriyadiṭṭhiṃ. Sassatavādanti “nicco dhuvo sassato”ti vacanaṃ. Na vadanti na kathenti.

Regarding 'Absolute purity': it means the absolute, ultimate purity. Regarding 'Purity from saṃsāra': it means purity from saṃsāra. Regarding 'The view of inaction': it means the view that 'for one who acts, no evil is done.' Regarding 'The doctrine of eternalism': it means the statement, 'permanent, stable, eternal.' Regarding 'They do not speak': they do not say.

Ganthāti [M 0.0204] nāmakāyaṃ ganthenti, cutipaṭisandhivasena vaṭṭasmiṃ ghaṭentīti ganthā. Abhijjhā ca sā nāmakāyaghaṭanavasena gantho cāti abhijjhākāyagantho. Hitasukhaṃ byāpādayatīti byāpādo. Byāpādo ca so vuttanayena gantho cāti byāpādo kāyagantho. Sīlabbataparāmāsoti “ito bahiddhā samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ sīlena suddhi vatena suddhī”ti (dha. sa. 1143, 1222) parato āmāso. Idaṃsaccābhinivesoti sabbaññubhāsitampi paṭikkhipitvā “sassato loko, idameva saccaṃ, moghamañña”nti [P 1.0235] (dha. sa. 1144) iminā ākārena abhiniveso idaṃsaccābhiniveso. Attano diṭṭhiyā rāgoti attanā abhinivisitvā gahitāya diṭṭhiyā chandarāgo. Paravādesu āghātoti parassa vacanesu kopo. Appaccayoti atuṭṭhākāro. Attano sīlaṃ vāti attanā samādinnaṃ gosīlādisīlaṃ vā. Attano diṭṭhīti attanā gahitā parāmaṭṭhā diṭṭhi. Tehi ganthehīti etehi vuttehi nāmakāyaghaṭanehi. Rūpaṃ ādiyantīti catusamuṭṭhānikaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ ādiyanti gaṇhanti. Upādiyantīti upagantvā gaṇhanti taṇhāgahaṇena. Parāmasanti diṭṭhigahaṇena. Abhinivisanti mānagahaṇena. Vaṭṭanti tebhūmakavaṭṭaṃ. Gantheti bandhane.

Regarding 'Bonds' (ganthā): they bind (ganthenti) the mental body; they fasten (ghaṭenti) it to the cycle by way of death and rebirth-linking—thus they are called bonds. Covetousness, and it is a bond by way of fastening the mental body—thus, the bodily bond of covetousness. Regarding 'Ill-will' (byāpādo): it harms (byāpādayati) welfare and happiness. And that ill-will is a bond in the way described—thus, the bodily bond of ill-will. Regarding 'Grasping at rules and observances': it is the grasping from elsewhere, with the thought, 'Outside of this teaching, purity for ascetics and brahmins comes through virtue, purity comes through rites' (Dhs. 1143, 1222). Regarding 'Insistence that this alone is true': it is the insistence of this kind—rejecting even what was spoken by the Omniscient One—'The world is eternal, this alone is true, the other is false' (Dhs. 1144). Regarding 'Lust for one's own view': it is desire and lust for a view that one has personally adhered to and grasped. Regarding 'Anger at others' doctrines': it is wrath at the words of another. Regarding 'Discontent': it is the state of dissatisfaction. Regarding 'One's own virtue': it is virtue such as the cow-practice undertaken by oneself. Regarding 'One's own view': it is a view personally grasped and held. Regarding 'By those bonds': by these aforementioned fasteners of the mental body. Regarding 'They grasp form': they take up and grasp form as an object, which arises from four causes. Regarding 'They cling': they approach and grasp with the grasp of craving. Regarding 'They grasp': with the grasp of views. Regarding 'They insist': with the grasp of conceit. Regarding 'They revolve': in the cycle of the three planes. Regarding 'Gantheti': it is in the sense of binding.

Vosajjitvā vāti sammā vissajjitvā vā. Gathiteti bandhane. Ganthiteti ganthanena ganthite. Vibandheti visesena bandhe. Ābandheti anekavidhena bandhe. Palibuddheti amuñcite. Bandhane poṭayitvāti taṇhāmānadiṭṭhibandhanāni pappoṭayitvā. Visajjāti cajitvā.

Regarding 'Or having released': it means or having rightly dismissed. Regarding 'Gathite': it is in the sense of binding. Regarding 'Ganthite': it means bound by a bond. Regarding 'Vibandhe': it is in the sense of a special bond. Regarding 'Ābandhe': it is in the sense of a manifold bond. Regarding 'Palibuddhe': it is in the sense of being unreleased. Regarding 'Having burst the bonds': it means having burst the bonds of craving, conceit, and views. Regarding 'Visajja': it means having abandoned.

Ime [V 0.0186] pana cattāro ganthe kilesapaṭipāṭiyāpi āharituṃ vaṭṭati, maggapaṭipāṭiyāpi – kilesapaṭipāṭiyā abhijjhākāyagantho arahattamaggena pahīyati, byāpādo kāyagantho anāgāmimaggena, sīlabbataparāmāso kāyagantho idaṃsaccābhiniveso kāyagantho sotāpattimaggena. Maggapaṭipāṭiyā sīlabbataparāmāso kāyagantho idaṃsaccābhiniveso kāyagantho sotāpattimaggena, byāpādo kāyagantho anāgāmimaggena, abhijjhākāyagantho arahattamaggenāti. Ete cattāro ganthā yassa saṃvijjanti, taṃ cutipaṭisandhivasena vaṭṭasmiṃ ganthenti ghaṭentīti ganthā. Te catuppabhedā abhijjhāyanti etāya, sayaṃ vā abhijjhāyati, abhijjhāyanamattameva vā esāti abhijjhā. Lobhoyeva [M 0.0205] nāmakāyaṃ gantheti cutipaṭisandhivasena vaṭṭasmiṃ ghaṭetīti kāyagantho. Byāpajjati tena cittaṃ pūtibhāvaṃ gacchati, byāpādayati [P 1.0236] vā vinayācārarūpasampattihitasukhādīnīti byāpādo. “Ito bahiddhā samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ sīlena suddhi vatena suddhī”ti parāmasanaṃ sīlabbataparāmāso, sabbaññubhāsitampi paṭikkhipitvā “sassato loko, idameva saccaṃ, moghamañña”ntiādinā ākārena abhinivisatīti idaṃsaccābhiniveso. Yathā vayhaṃ vātiādiṃ vayhādivisaṅkharaṇaṃ ganthānaṃ viyogakaraṇe upamaṃ dassento āha.

These four bonds can also be brought up according to the sequence of defilements and the sequence of the path. In the sequence of defilements, the bodily bond of covetousness is abandoned by the path of arahantship; the bodily bond of ill will by the path of non-returning; the bodily bond of clinging to rites and rituals and the bodily bond of dogmatic adherence to 'this is true' by the path of stream-entry. In the sequence of the path, the bodily bond of clinging to rites and rituals and the bodily bond of dogmatic adherence to 'this is true' are abandoned by the path of stream-entry; the bodily bond of ill will by the path of non-returning; the bodily bond of covetousness by the path of arahantship. These four bonds, for whom they exist, bind and fasten that one in the cycle of existence by way of death and rebirth—thus they are called bonds. They are of four kinds. Covetousness (abhijjhā): one covets by means of it, or one covets oneself, or it is merely coveting. Greed itself binds the mental group (nāmakāya) and fastens it in the cycle of existence by way of death and rebirth—thus it is a bodily bond (kāyagantho). Ill will (byāpāda): through it the mind becomes corrupt and goes to a state of putrefaction, or it destroys virtuous conduct, proper behavior, physical beauty, welfare, and happiness. Clinging to rites and rituals (sīlabbataparāmāso) is the grasping that 'Outside of this teaching, there is purity for ascetics and brahmins through virtue or through vows.' Dogmatic adherence to 'this is true' (idaṃsaccābhiniveso) is when, rejecting even what was spoken by the Omniscient One, one dogmatically adheres in the manner of 'The world is eternal,' 'This alone is true, all else is false,' and so on. He spoke, showing the verse beginning 'Just as a burden...' as an analogy for bringing about separation from the bonds, which is the dismantling of the burden and so on.

Na janentīti na uppādenti. Na sañjanentīti na nibbattenti. Nābhinibbattentīti upasaggavasena padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ. Na sañjanentīti uppādakkhaṇaṃ. Na nibbattenti nābhinibbattentīti pavattikkhaṇaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ.

'Na janenti' means they do not generate. 'Na sañjanenti' means they do not produce. 'Nābhinibbattenti' is a word expanded by means of a prefix. 'Na sañjanenti' refers to the moment of arising. 'Na nibbattenti nābhinibbattenti' is stated with reference to the moment of continuation.

30. Sīmātigoti gāthā ekapuggalādhiṭṭhānāya desanāya vuttā. Pubbasadiso eva panassā sambandho, so evaṃ atthavaṇṇanāya saddhiṃ veditabbo – kiñca bhiyyo? So īdiso bhūripañño catunnaṃ kilesasīmānaṃ atītattā sīmātigo, bāhitapāpattā ca brāhmaṇo, itthambhūtassa ca tassa natthi, paracittapubbenivāsañāṇehi ñatvā vā maṃsadibbacakkhūhi disvā vā kiñci samuggahītaṃ, abhiniviṭṭhanti vuttaṃ hoti. So ca kāmarāgābhāvato na rāgarāgī rūpārūparāgābhāvato na virāgaratto, yato evaṃvidhassa tassa “idaṃ parama”nti kiñci idha uggahītaṃ natthīti arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi.

30. The verse 'Sīmātigo' (One who has crossed the boundary) was spoken as a teaching based on a single individual. Its connection is indeed similar to the previous one, and it should be understood thus, along with the explanation of the meaning—what more? Such a one, being of vast wisdom, is called 'one who has crossed the boundary' because he has gone beyond the four boundaries of defilements, and a 'brahmin' because he has warded off evil. For such a one of this kind, there is nothing grasped or adhered to, whether known through the knowledge of others' minds and past lives, or seen with the physical eye or the divine eye. And being free from sensual lust, he is not lustful with lust; being free from lust for form and formlessness, he is not attached to dispassion. Since for such a one nothing here is grasped as 'this is supreme,' he concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of arahantship.

Catasso sīmāyoti cattāro paricchedā. Diṭṭhānusayoti diṭṭhi ca sā appahīnaṭṭhena anusayo cāti diṭṭhānusayo. Vicikicchānusayādīsupi eseva nayo. Kenaṭṭhena anusayā? Anusayanaṭṭhena. Ko esa anusayaṭṭho nāmāti? Appahīnaṭṭho. Ete hi appahīnaṭṭhena tassa tassa [V 0.0187] santāne anusenti nāma, tasmā “anusayā”ti vuccanti. Anusentīti anurūpaṃ kāraṇaṃ labhitvā uppajjantīti attho. Athāpi siyā – anusayaṭṭho nāma appahīnākāro, appahīnākāro ca “uppajjatī”ti vattuṃ na yujjati, tasmā na anusayā uppajjantīti. Tatridaṃ paṭivacanaṃ – appahīnākāro anusayo, anusayoti pana appahīnaṭṭhena thāmagatā kilesā vuccanti. So cittasampayutto sārammaṇo sappaccayaṭṭhena [M 0.0206] sahetuko ekantākusalo atītopi hoti anāgatopi paccuppannopi, tasmā “uppajjatī”ti vattuṃ yujjati.

'Four boundaries' means four limits. 'Latent tendency to wrong view' means that it is wrong view and also a latent tendency in the sense of being unabandoned—thus it is the latent tendency to wrong view. The same method applies to the latent tendency to doubt and so on. In what sense are they latent tendencies? In the sense of lying dormant. What is this sense of 'lying dormant'? It is the sense of being unabandoned. For these, in the sense of being unabandoned, indeed lie dormant in the continuity of each being—therefore they are called 'latent tendencies' (anusayā). 'They lie dormant' means they arise upon obtaining a suitable condition. Alternatively, it might be said: the sense of a latent tendency is an unabandoned mode, and an unabandoned mode cannot properly be said to 'arise,' therefore latent tendencies do not arise. To that, here is the reply: the unabandoned mode is the latent tendency, but 'latent tendency' refers to defilements that have become strong by way of being unabandoned. It is associated with consciousness, has an object, is conditioned and thus has a cause, is exclusively unwholesome, and can be past, future, or present. Therefore, it is correct to say that it 'arises.'

Tatridaṃ [P 1.0237] pamāṇaṃ – paṭisambhidāyaṃ tāva abhisamayakathāyaṃ (paṭi. ma. 3.21) “paccuppanne kilese pajahatī”ti pucchitvā anusayānaṃ paccuppannabhāvassa atthitāya “thāmagato anusayaṃ pajahatī”ti vuttaṃ. Dhammasaṅgaṇiyaṃ mohassa padabhājane (dha. sa. 390) “avijjānusayo avijjāpariyuṭṭhānaṃ, avijjālaṅgī moho akusalamūlaṃ, ayaṃ tasmiṃ samaye moho hotī”ti akusalacittena saddhiṃ avijjānusayassa uppannabhāvo vutto. Kathāvatthusmiṃ “anusayā abyākatā anusayā ahetukā anusayā cittavippayuttā”ti (kathā. 605) sabbe vādā paṭisedhitā. Anusayayamake sattannaṃ mahāvārānaṃ aññatarasmiṃ uppajjanavāre “yassa kāmarāgānusayo uppajjati tassa paṭighānusayo uppajjatī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tasmā “anusentīti anurūpaṃ kāraṇaṃ labhitvā uppajjantī”ti yaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ iminā tantippamāṇena suvuttanti veditabbaṃ. Yampi “cittasampayutto sārammaṇo”tiādi vuttaṃ, tampi suvuttameva. Anusayo hi nāmesa parinipphanno cittasampayutto akusaladhammoti niṭṭhamettha gantabbaṃ.

Here is the authority: In the Paṭisambhidāmagga, in the discourse on full understanding, after asking, 'Does one abandon defilements in the present?' it is stated, because of the existence of latent tendencies in the present, 'one abandons the latent tendency when it has become strong.' In the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, in the analysis of delusion, it is said: 'The latent tendency to ignorance is the obsession of ignorance; the bolt of ignorance, delusion, is an unwholesome root—this is delusion at that time.' Here, the arising of the latent tendency to ignorance along with an unwholesome consciousness is described. In the Kathāvatthu, all the assertions that 'latent tendencies are indeterminate, rootless, and dissociated from consciousness' are refuted. In the Anusaya Yamaka, in one of the seven great sections on arising, it is said: 'For whom the latent tendency to sensual lust arises, for him the latent tendency to aversion arises,' and so on. Therefore, what was stated, '“They lie dormant” means they arise when they obtain a suitable condition,' should be understood as well-expounded by this canonical authority. Likewise, what was stated, 'they are associated with consciousness and have an object,' is also well-expounded. For this latent tendency is indeed a fully developed unwholesome state associated with consciousness—this is the conclusion to be drawn here.

Tattha diṭṭhānusayo catūsu diṭṭhisampayuttesu, vicikicchānusayo vicikicchāsahagate, avijjānusayo dvādasasu akusalacittesu sahajātavasena ārammaṇavasena ca; tayopi avasesatebhūmakadhammesu ārammaṇavasena diṭṭhivicikicchāmohā. Kāmarāgānusayo cettha lobhasahagatacittesu sahajātavasena ārammaṇavasena ca, manāpesu avasesakāmāvacaradhammesu ārammaṇavasena uppajjamāno lobho. Paṭighānusayo domanassasahagatacittesu sahajātavasena ārammaṇavasena ca, amanāpesu avasesakāmāvacaradhammesu ārammaṇavaseneva uppajjamāno doso. Mānānusayo diṭṭhivippayuttalobhasahagatacittesu sahajātavasena ārammaṇavasena ca, dukkhavedanāvajjesu avasesakāmāvacaradhammesu rūpārūpāvacaradhammesu ca ārammaṇavaseneva uppajjamāno māno. Bhavarāgānusayo catūsu diṭṭhivippayuttesu uppajjamānopi [P 1.0238][M 0.0207] sahajātavasena vutto. Ārammaṇavaseneva pana rūpārūpāvacaradhammesu uppajjamāno lobho vutto.
