Here, the latent tendency to wrong view arises in the four types of consciousness associated with wrong view; the latent tendency to doubt in consciousness accompanied by doubt; and the latent tendency to ignorance in the twelve types of unwholesome consciousness both by way of co-nascence and by way of object. These three—wrong view, doubt, and delusion—also arise by way of object in the remaining states of the three planes. The latent tendency to sensual lust arises here in consciousness accompanied by greed both by way of co-nascence and by way of object, and it is the greed that arises by way of object in the remaining desirable sense-sphere states. The latent tendency to aversion arises in consciousness accompanied by displeasure both by way of co-nascence and by way of object, and it is the aversion that arises by way of object only in the remaining undesirable sense-sphere states. The latent tendency to conceit arises in consciousness accompanied by greed dissociated from wrong view both by way of co-nascence and by way of object, and it is the conceit that arises by way of object only in the remaining sense-sphere states excluding painful feeling, as well as in the form and formless sphere states. The latent tendency to craving for existence is described by way of co-nascence as that which arises in the four types of consciousness dissociated from wrong view; and it is described as the greed that arises by way of object only with regard to the form and formless sphere states.

Tattha [V 0.0188] diṭṭhānusayoti dvāsaṭṭhividhā diṭṭhi. Vicikicchānusayoti aṭṭhavatthukā vicikicchā. Tadekaṭṭhā ca kilesāti sahajekaṭṭhavasena diṭṭhiyā vicikicchāya, sahajekaṭṭhavasena ekato ṭhitā. Mānānusayoti navavidhamāno. Paramatthañāṇena vā ñatvāti paresaṃ cittācārajānanapaññāya jānitvā, cetopariyañāṇena jānitvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇena vāti atīte nivuṭṭhakkhandhānussaraṇañāṇena jānitvā. Maṃsacakkhunā vāti pakaticakkhunā. Dibbacakkhunā vāti dibbasadisena dibbavihārasannissitena vā dibbacakkhunā passitvā. Rāgarattāti rāgena rañjitā. Ye pañcasu kāmaguṇesūti ye pañcasu rūpādivatthukāmakoṭṭhāsesu. Virāgarattāti virāgasaṅkhātāsu rūpārūpasamāpattīsu atirattā allīnā. Yato kāmarāgo cāti yadā kāmabhave rāgo ca. Rūpārūparāgesupi eseva nayo.

Here, 'diṭṭhānusaya' (latent tendency to wrong view) refers to the sixty-two kinds of wrong views. 'Vicikicchānusaya' (latent tendency to doubt) refers to doubt based on eight grounds. And those defilements, being of one foundation with these, stand united with wrong view and doubt by way of having a co-nascent single foundation. 'Mānānusaya' (latent tendency to conceit) refers to the nine kinds of conceit. 'By knowing with the knowledge of another's mind' means knowing through the wisdom that discerns others' minds and conduct; that is, knowing through the knowledge of others' thoughts. 'Or by the knowledge of recollection of past lives' means knowing through the knowledge that recollects past aggregates. 'With the physical eye' means with the ordinary eye. 'With the divine eye' means seeing with the divine eye, which resembles the divine, or is based upon divine abidings. 'Rāgarattā' (attached to lust) means those stained by lust. 'Who indulge in the five strands of sensual pleasure' refers to those who indulge in the five portions of sensual pleasure which have forms and other objects as their basis. 'Virāgarattā' (attached to dispassion) means those excessively attached and clinging to the so-called dispassionate states of form and formless attainments. 'When lust for sensual pleasures arises' refers to when lust arises in the realm of sensual existence. The same method applies to lust for form and formless realms.

Saddhammappajjotikāya mahāniddesaṭṭhakathāya

The Saddhammappajjotikā, the Commentary on the Mahāniddesa.

Suddhaṭṭhakasuttaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the exposition on the Suddhaṭṭhaka Sutta is concluded.

5. Paramaṭṭhakasuttaniddesavaṇṇanā

5. Explanation of the Exposition on the Paramaṭṭhaka Sutta

31. Pañcame [V 0.0189][P 1.0239] paramaṭṭhakasutte paramanti diṭṭhīsu paribbasānoti idaṃ paramanti gahetvā sakāya sakāya diṭṭhiyā vasamāno. Yaduttariṃ kuruteti yaṃ attano satthārādiṃ seṭṭhaṃ karoti. Hīnāti aññe tato sabbamāhāti taṃ attano satthārādiṃ ṭhapetvā tato aññe sabbe “hīnā ime”ti āha. Tasmā vivādāni avītivattoti tena kāraṇena so diṭṭhikalahe avītivattova hoti.

31. In the fifth Paramaṭṭhaka Sutta, regarding 'dwelling in views, [holding something as] supreme': this means, taking 'this is supreme', one dwells dominated by one's own view. 'Yaduttariṃ kurute' means whatever one makes superior, such as one’s own teacher and so forth. 'Hīnāti aññe tato sabbamāhāti' means, setting aside one’s own teacher and so forth, one declares all others to be 'inferior'. 'Tasmā vivādāni avītivatto' means that for that reason one has not gone beyond disputes concerning views.

Vasantīti paṭhamuppannadiṭṭhivasena vasanti. Pavasantīti pavisitvā vasanti. Āvasantīti visesena vasanti. Parivasantīti sabbabhāgena vasanti. Taṃ upamāya sādhento “yathā āgārikā vā”tiādimāha. Āgārikā vāti gharasāmikā. Gharesu vasantīti attano gharesu āsaṅkavirahitā hutvā nivasanti. Sāpattikā vāti āpattibahulā. Sakilesā vāti [M 0.0208] rāgādikilesabahulā. Uttariṃ karotīti atirekaṃ karoti. Ayaṃ satthā sabbaññūti ‘ayaṃ amhākaṃ satthā sabbaṃ jānāti’.

‘Vasanti’ means they dwell by way of a view that has arisen first. ‘Pavasanti’ means they dwell having entered. ‘Āvasanti’ means they dwell especially. ‘Parivasanti’ means they dwell in every way. Illustrating this with an analogy, he says, ‘just as householders,’ and so forth. ‘Āgārikā vā’ means masters of the house. ‘Gharesu vasanti’ means they dwell in their own homes, being free from apprehension. ‘Sāpattikā vā’ means full of offenses. ‘Sakilesā vā’ means full of defilements such as lust and so forth. ‘Uttariṃ karoti’ means one makes something additional. ‘Ayaṃ satthā sabbaññū’ means ‘this teacher of ours knows everything’.

Sabbe parappavāde khipatīti sabbā paraladdhiyo chaḍḍeti. Ukkhipatīti nīharati. Parikkhipatīti parammukhe karoti. Diṭṭhimedhagānīti diṭṭhivihesakāni.

‘Sabbe parappavāde khipati’ means one rejects all doctrines of others. ‘Ukkhipati’ means one removes. ‘Parikkhipati’ means one makes them turn away. ‘Diṭṭhimedhagāni’ means things that cause strife regarding views.

32. Dutiyagāthāyattho – evaṃ avītivatto ca yaṃ diṭṭhe sute sīlavate muteti etesu catūsu vatthūsu uppannadiṭṭhisaṅkhāte attani pubbe vuttappakāraṃ ānisaṃsaṃ passati, tadeva so tattha sakāya diṭṭhiyā ānisaṃsaṃ “idaṃ seṭṭha”nti abhinivisitvā aññaṃ sabbaṃ parasatthārādikaṃ nihīnato passati.

32. The meaning of the second verse: Thus, not having gone beyond disputes, one perceives in oneself a benefit of the kind previously stated in what is seen, heard, in virtue and vows, or sensed—in these four bases, which are designated as an arisen view. Then, clinging to that very benefit therein in one’s own view, considering it ‘the best,’ one regards all else—such as others’ teachers and so forth—as inferior.

Dve ānisaṃse passatīti dve guṇe oloketi. Diṭṭhadhammikañcāti [P 1.0240] diṭṭhe paccakkhe attabhāve [V 0.0190] vipaccanakaraṇaṃ. Samparāyikañcāti paraloke paṭilabhitabbaguṇañca. Yaṃdiṭṭhiko satthāti yaṃladdhiko titthāyatanasāmiko. Alaṃ nāgattāya vāti nāgarājabhāvāya vā pariyattaṃ. Supaṇṇattādīsupi eseva nayo. Devattāya vāti sammutidevādibhāvāya. Āyatiṃ phalapāṭikaṅkhī hotīti anāgate vipākaphalaṃ patthayāno hoti. Diṭṭhasuddhiyāpi dve ānisaṃse passatīti cakkhuviññāṇena diṭṭharūpāyatanassa vasena suddhiyā hetuttāpi attano gahitagahaṇena dve guṇe oloketi. Sutasuddhiyādīsupi eseva nayo.

‘Dve ānisaṃse passati’ means one observes two qualities. ‘Diṭṭhadhammikañca’ means the ripening in the present, visible existence. ‘Samparāyikañca’ means also the quality to be obtained in the next world. ‘Yaṃdiṭṭhiko satthā’ means a master of a school who holds such a doctrine. ‘Alaṃ nāgattāya vā’ means sufficient for the state of a nāga-king. The same method applies to the state of a supaṇṇa and so forth. ‘Devattāya vā’ means for the state of a conventional deity and so forth. ‘Āyatiṃ phalapāṭikaṅkhī hoti’ means one hopes for the fruit of ripening in the future. ‘Diṭṭhasuddhiyāpi dve ānisaṃse passati’ means that also because of being a cause for purity by means of the visible object as apprehended by eye-consciousness, one observes two qualities by one’s own grasping. The same method applies to purity of hearing and so forth.

33. Tatiyagāthāyattho – evaṃ passato ca yaṃ attano satthārādiṃ nissito aññaṃ parasatthārādiṃ hīnaṃ passati, taṃ pana dassanaṃ ganthameva kusalā vadanti, bandhananti vuttaṃ hoti. Yasmā etadeva, tasmā hi diṭṭhaṃ va sutaṃ mutaṃ vā, sīlabbataṃ bhikkhu na nissayeyya, nābhiniveseyyāti vuttaṃ hoti.

33. The meaning of the third verse: Thus, for one who sees, that very seeing—where one relies on one’s own teacher and so forth and sees another’s teacher and so forth as inferior—the wise call that a fetter; it is said to be a bond. Because this is so, therefore, it is said that a bhikkhu should not rely on what is seen, heard, or sensed, or on virtue and vows, nor should he be attached to them.

Kusalāti khandhādijānane chekā. Khandhakusalāti rūpādīsu pañcasu khandhesu kusalā. Dhātuāyatanapaṭiccasamuppādasatipaṭṭhānasammappadhānaiddhipādaindriyabalabojjhaṅgamaggaphalanibbānesupi eseva nayo. Tattha maggakusalāti catūsu maggesu. Phalakusalāti catūsu phalesu. Nibbānakusalāti duvidhe nibbāne chekā. Te kusalāti te etesu vuttappakāresu [M 0.0209] chekā. Evaṃ vadantīti evaṃ kathenti. Gantho esoti passato ca attano satthārādinissitañca aññaṃ parasatthārādiṃ hīnato dassanañca gantho bandhano esoti vadanti. Lagganaṃ etanti etaṃ vuttappakāraṃ nāgadante laggitaṃ viya adholambanaṃ. Bandhanaṃ etanti nicchindituṃ dukkhaṭṭhena saṅkhalikādibandhanaṃ [P 1.0241] viya etaṃ bandhanaṃ. Palibodho esoti saṃsārato nikkhamituṃ appadānaṭṭhena eso palibodho.

‘Kusalā’ means those skilled in understanding aggregates and so forth. ‘Khandhakusalā’ means those skilled in the five aggregates such as form and so forth. The same method applies to elements, sense bases, dependent origination, foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of psychic power, faculties, powers, enlightenment factors, path, fruition, and Nibbāna. There, ‘maggakusalā’ means those skilled in the four paths. ‘Phalakusalā’ means those skilled in the four fruits. ‘Nibbānakusalā’ means those skilled in the twofold Nibbāna. ‘Te kusalā’ means they are skilled in these stated categories. ‘Evaṃ vadanti’ means thus they declare. ‘Gantho eso’ means they say that this seeing—where one relies on one’s own teacher and so forth and sees another’s teacher and so forth as inferior—is a fetter, a bond. ‘Lagganaṃ etaṃ’ means this is a hanging down, like something stuck on an elephant's tusk. ‘Bandhanaṃ etaṃ’ means this is a bond, like bondage with chains and so forth, in the sense of being difficult to cut through. ‘Palibodho eso’ means this is an obstacle, in the sense of not allowing one to get out of saṃsāra.

34. Catutthagāthāyattho – na kevalaṃ diṭṭhasutādīsu na nissayeyya, apica kho pana asañjātaṃ uparūpari diṭṭhimpi lokasmiṃ na kappayeyya, na janeyyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Kīdisaṃ? Ñāṇena vā sīlavatena vāpi, samāpattiñāṇādiñāṇena vā sīlavatena vā yā kappiyati, etaṃ diṭṭhiṃ na kappeyya. Na kevalañca diṭṭhiṃ na kappayeyya, apica kho pana mānenapi jātiādīhi vatthūhi samoti attānamanūpaneyya, hīno na maññetha visesi vāpīti.

34. The meaning of the fourth verse: It is said that one should not only not rely on what is seen, heard, and so forth, but also should not fabricate, or generate, any unarisen view in the world, one on top of another. What kind? One should not fabricate such a view that is fabricated through knowledge or through virtue and vows, or through knowledge such as that of meditative attainments, or through virtue and vows. And not only should one not fabricate a view, but also, through conceit, one should not compare oneself as equal to others based on birth and other grounds, nor should one think oneself inferior or superior.

Aṭṭhasamāpattiñāṇena vāti paṭhamajjhānādīnaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ samāpattīnaṃ sampayuttapaññāya vā. Pañcābhiññāñāṇena vāti lokiyānaṃ pañcannaṃ abhiññānaṃ sampayuttapaññāya vā. Micchāñāṇena vāti [V 0.0191] viparītasabhāvena pavattāya paññāya amutte muttaṃ passāti evaṃ uppannena micchāñāṇena vā.

‘Aṭṭhasamāpattiñāṇena vā’ means by the wisdom associated with the eight attainments, beginning with the first jhāna. ‘Pañcābhiññāñāṇena vā’ means by the wisdom associated with the five mundane supernormal knowledges. ‘Micchāñāṇena vā’ means by wrong knowledge that has arisen in such a way, by wisdom that functions with a perverted nature, such as seeing the unliberated as liberated.

35. Pañcamagāthāyattho – evañhi diṭṭhiṃ akappento amaññamāno ca attaṃ pahāya anupādiyāno yaṃ pubbe gahitaṃ, taṃ pahāya paraṃ aggaṇhanto tasmimpi vuttappakāre ñāṇe duvidhaṃ nissayaṃ no karoti, akaronto ca sa ve viyattesu nānādiṭṭhivasena bhinnesu sattesu na vaggasārī chandādivasena agacchanadhammo hutvā dvāsaṭṭhiyā diṭṭhīsu kiñci diṭṭhiṃ na pacceti, na paccāgacchatīti vuttaṃ hoti.

35. The meaning of the fifth verse: Thus, not fabricating a view and not conceiving, having abandoned self and not clinging, having abandoned what was previously grasped and not grasping anything further, one does not make a twofold reliance on that knowledge of the kind described. Not doing so, that person, being one whose nature is not to follow a faction due to desire and so forth, is not a partisan among beings who are distinct and divided by diverse views. It is said that one does not accept any of the sixty-two views, nor return to them.

Catūhi upādānehīti kāmupādānādīhi catūhi bhusaṃ gahaṇehi sa ve viyattesūti so puggalo nicchitesu. Bhinnesūti dvidhā bhinnesu.

‘Catūhi upādānehi’ means by the four kinds of strong grasping, beginning with sensual clinging. ‘Sa ve viyattesu’ means that person among those who are clearly decided. ‘Bhinnesu’ means among those split into two.

36. Idāni yo so imāya gāthāya vutto khīṇāsavo, tassa vaṇṇabhaṇanatthaṃ “yassūbhayante”tiādikā tisso gāthāyo āha. Tattha paṭhamagāthāya yassūbhayanteti pubbe vutte phassādibhede. Paṇidhīti [M 0.0210] taṇhā. Bhavābhavāyāti punappunabhavāya[P 1.0242]. Idha vā huraṃ vāti sakattabhāvādibhede idha vā parattabhāvādibhede parattha vā.

36. Now, in order to praise that one with destroyed taints who was described in this verse, he stated three verses beginning with ‘yassūbhayante’. Therein, in the first verse, ‘yassūbhayante’ refers to the previously mentioned distinctions of contact and so forth. ‘Paṇidhi’ is craving. ‘Bhavābhavāya’ is for repeated becoming. ‘Idha vā huraṃ vā’ refers to distinctions such as one’s own state of being here, or another’s state of being there.

Phasso eko antoti cakkhusamphassādiko eko koṭṭhāso. Phassasamudayoti vatthārammaṇo. Yato samudeti uppajjati, so samudayo. Dutiyo antoti dutiyo koṭṭhāso. Atītanti ati itaṃ atītaṃ, atikkantanti vuttaṃ hoti. Anāgatanti na āgataṃ, anuppannanti vuttaṃ hoti. Sukhā vedanādayo visabhāgavasena. Nāmarūpadukaṃ namanaruppanavasena. Ajjhattikādayo ajjhattabāhiravasena. Sakkāyādayo khandhapañcakānaṃ pavattisamudayavasena vuttāti veditabbā.

‘Phasso eko anto’ is one part, such as eye-contact and so forth. ‘Phassasamudayo’ is the base and object. That from which it arises, that is its origin. ‘Dutiyo anto’ is the second part. ‘Atītaṃ’ is ‘ati itaṃ’, meaning that which has passed. ‘Anāgataṃ’ is ‘na āgataṃ’, meaning that which has not yet arisen. Pleasant feelings and so forth are by way of being dissimilar. The pair of name-and-form is by way of bending and being afflicted. The internal and so forth are by way of internal and external. Self-identity and so forth are described in terms of the occurrence and origin of the five aggregates—this should be understood.

Sakattabhāvoti attano attabhāvo. Parattabhāvoti parassa attabhāvo.

‘Sakattabhāva’ is one’s own existence. ‘Parattabhāva’ is another’s existence.

37. Dutiyagāthāya diṭṭhe vāti diṭṭhasuddhiyā vā. Esa nayo sutādīsu. Saññāti saññāsamuṭṭhāpikā diṭṭhi.

37. In the second verse, ‘diṭṭhe vā’ means by purity of the seen. This same method applies to the heard and so forth. ‘Saññā’ is the view that originates from perception.

Aparāmasantanti [V 0.0192] taṇhāmānadiṭṭhīhi na parāmasantaṃ. Anabhinivesantanti teheva anabhinivisantaṃ.

‘Aparāmasantaṃ’ is not grasping by means of craving, conceit, and views. ‘Anabhinivesantaṃ’ is not adhering to them.

“Vinibaddho”ti vāti mānena vinibaddhoti vā. “Parāmaṭṭho”ti vāti parato niccasukhasubhādīhi parāmaṭṭhoti vā. Vikkhepagatoti uddhaccavasena. Aniṭṭhaṅgatoti vicikicchāvasena. Thāmagatoti anusayavasena. Gatiyāti gantabbavasena.

‘Vinibaddho’ is being bound by conceit. ‘Parāmaṭṭho’ is being grasped by another regarding permanence, pleasure, beauty, and so forth. ‘Vikkhepagato’ is having gone to distraction, by way of restlessness. ‘Aniṭṭhaṅgato’ is having gone to the undesirable, by way of doubt. ‘Thāmagato’ is having gone to firmness, by way of underlying tendencies. ‘Gatiyā’ is by way of what is to be gone to.

38. Tatiyagāthāya dhammāpi tesaṃ na paṭicchitāseti dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhigatadhammāpi tesaṃ “idameva saccaṃ, moghamañña”nti (udā. 54) evaṃ na paṭicchitā. Pāraṅgato na pacceti tādīti nibbānapāraṃ gato tena tena maggena pahīne kilese puna nāgacchati pañcahi ca ākārehi tādī hotīti. Sesaṃ pākaṭameva.

38. In the third verse, ‘dhammāpi tesaṃ na paṭicchitā’ means that even the doctrines associated with the sixty-two views are not accepted by them with the thought, ‘This alone is true, all else is false’ (Udāna 54). ‘Pāraṅgato na pacceti tādī’ means that one who has gone to the further shore of Nibbāna does not return to the defilements abandoned by that particular path, and in five ways is ‘such a one’. The rest is clear.

Vīsativatthukā sakkāyadiṭṭhīti “rūpaṃ attato samanupassatī”tiādinā (paṭi. ma. 1.132) nayena ekekasmiṃ khandhe catūhi catūhi ākārehi pañcakkhandhe patiṭṭhaṃ katvā pavattā vijjamāne kāye diṭṭhi. Dasavatthukā [P 1.0243] micchādiṭṭhīti “natthi [M 0.0211] dinna”ntiādinayappavattā (dha. sa. 1221) diṭṭhi. Antaggāhikādiṭṭhīti “sassato loko idameva saccaṃ, moghamañña”ntiādinayappavattā (ma. ni. 3.27) ekekaṃ antaṃ atthīti gahetvā pavattā diṭṭhi. Yā evarūpā diṭṭhīti idāni vuccamānānaṃ ekūnavīsapadānaṃ sādhāraṇaṃ mūlapadaṃ. Yā diṭṭhi, tadeva diṭṭhigataṃ; yā diṭṭhi, tadeva diṭṭhigahananti sabbesaṃ sambandho kātabbo. Yā ayāthāvadassanaṭṭhena diṭṭhi, tadeva diṭṭhīsu gataṃ dassanaṃ dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhiyā antogatattāti diṭṭhigataṃ. Heṭṭhāpissa attho vuttoyeva.

The identity view with twenty bases is the view that occurs with regard to the existing body, established in the five aggregates by taking each aggregate in four ways, in the manner beginning with 'one regards form as self' (Patisambhidamagga 1.132). The wrong view with ten bases is the view that occurs in the manner beginning with 'there is nothing given' (Dhammasangani 1221). The view that grasps at extremes is the view that occurs in the manner beginning with 'the world is eternal, this alone is true, all else is false' (Majjhima Nikaya 3.27), by grasping each extreme as existing. The phrase 'such a view' is the common root term for the nineteen terms now being mentioned. Whatever is a view, that itself is a viewpoint; whatever is a view, that itself is a thicket of views—this connection should be made for all. Whatever is a view in the sense of not seeing things as they are, that is a viewpoint because it is a seeing that has gone among views, being included within the sixty-two views. Its meaning has also been stated below.

Dvinnaṃ antānaṃ ekantagatattātipi diṭṭhigataṃ. Tattha sassatoti nicco. Lokoti attā. “Idha sarīraṃyeva nassati, attā pana idha parattha ca soyevā”ti maññanti. So hi sāmaññeva āloketīti katvā lokoti maññati. Asassatoti anicco. Attā sarīreneva saha nassatīti maññanti. Antavāti paritte kasiṇe jhānaṃ uppādetvā taṃ parittakasiṇārammaṇaṃ cetanaṃ “sapariyanto attā”ti maññanti. Ananta vāti na antavā appamāṇe kasiṇe jhānaṃ uppādetvā taṃ appamāṇakasiṇārammaṇaṃ cetanaṃ “apariyanto attā”ti maññanti. Taṃ jīvaṃ taṃ sarīranti jīvo ca sarīrañca taṃyeva. Jīvoti attā, liṅgavipallāsena napuṃsakavacanaṃ kataṃ. Sarīranti rāsaṭṭhena khandhapañcakaṃ. Aññaṃ jīvaṃ aññaṃ sarīranti añño jīvo aññaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ[V 0.0193]. Hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇāti khandhā idheva vinassanti, satto maraṇato paraṃ hoti vijjati na nassati, tathāgatoti cetaṃ sattādhivacananti. Keci pana “tathāgatoti arahā”ti vadanti. Ime na hotīti pakkhe dosaṃ disvā evaṃ gaṇhanti. Na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇāti khandhāpi idheva nassanti[P 1.0244], tathāgato ca maraṇato paraṃ na hoti ucchijjati. Ime hotīti pakkhe dosaṃ disvā evaṃ gaṇhanti. Hoti ca na ca hotīti ime ekekapakkhapariggahe dosaṃ disvā ubhayapakkhaṃ gaṇhanti. Neva hoti na na hotīti ime ubhayapakkhapariggahe ubhayadosāpattiṃ disvā “hoti ca na hotī”ti ca “neva hoti na na hotī”ti ca amarāvikkhepapakkhaṃ gaṇhanti.

It is also a viewpoint because it has gone to one of the two extremes. Therein, 'eternal' is permanent. 'World' is self. They think, 'Here, only the body perishes, but the self remains the very same here and hereafter.' For they consider it the 'world' because it illuminates by itself. 'Annihilationist' is impermanent. They think, 'The self perishes together with the body.' 'Finite' is when, having produced jhāna on a limited kasiṇa, they regard that consciousness with a limited kasiṇa as its object as 'the self is finite.' 'Infinite' is when, having produced jhāna on an unlimited kasiṇa, they regard that consciousness with an unlimited kasiṇa as its object as 'the self is infinite.' 'The life is the body' means the life and the body are the very same. 'Life' is the self; the neuter word is used due to a change of gender. 'Body' refers to the five aggregates in the sense of a mass. 'The life is one thing, the body another' means the life is one thing and the five aggregates another. 'The Tathāgata exists after death' means the aggregates perish right here, but the being exists after death; it exists, it is not annihilated—'Tathāgata' being a designation for a being. Some, however, say, 'The Tathāgata is an arahant.' These, seeing a fault in the position that 'he does not exist,' adopt this view. 'The Tathāgata does not exist after death' means the aggregates also perish right here, and the Tathāgata does not exist after death; he is annihilated. These, seeing a fault in the position that 'he exists,' adopt this view. 'Both exists and does not exist': these, seeing a fault in grasping each single position, adopt both positions. 'Neither exists nor does not exist': these, seeing the double fault in grasping both positions, adopt the position of evasive ambiguity, which is ‘both exists and does not exist’ and ‘neither exists nor does not exist’.

Ayaṃ panettha aṭṭhakathānayo (paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 2.1.113) – “sassato loko”ti vātiādīhi dasahākārehi diṭṭhipabhedova vutto. Tattha sassato lokoti [M 0.0212] ca khandhapañcakaṃ lokoti gahetvā “ayaṃ loko nicco dhuvo sabbakāliko”ti gaṇhantassa sassatanti gahaṇākārappavattā diṭṭhi. Asassatoti tameva lokaṃ “ucchijjati vinassatī”ti gaṇhantassa ucchedaggahaṇākārappavattā diṭṭhi. Antavāti parittakasiṇalābhino suppamatte vā sarāvamatte vā kasiṇe samāpannassa antosamāpattiyaṃ pavattitarūpārūpadhamme “loko”ti ca kasiṇaparicchedantena “antavā”ti ca gaṇhantassa “antavā loko”ti gahaṇākārappavattā diṭṭhi. Sā sassatadiṭṭhipi hoti ucchedadiṭṭhipi. Vipulakasiṇalābhino pana tasmiṃ kasiṇe samāpannassa antosamāpattiyaṃ pavattitarūpārūpadhamme “loko”ti ca kasiṇaparicchedantena ca “ananto”ti gaṇhantassa “anantavā loko”ti gahaṇākārappavattā diṭṭhi. Sā sassatadiṭṭhi hoti, ucchedadiṭṭhipi. Taṃ jīvaṃ taṃ sarīranti bhedanadhammassa sarīrasseva “jīva”nti gahitattā “sarīre ucchijjamāne jīvampi ucchijjatī”ti ucchedaggahaṇākārappavattā diṭṭhi. Dutiyapadena sarīrato aññassa jīvassa gahitattā “sarīre ca ucchijjamānepi jīvaṃ na ucchijjatī”ti sassatagahaṇākārappavattā diṭṭhi. Hoti tathāgatotiādīsu “satto tathāgato nāma, so paraṃ maraṇā hotī”ti gaṇhato paṭhamā sassatadiṭṭhi. “Na hotī”ti gaṇhato dutiyā ucchedadiṭṭhi. “Hoti ca na ca hotī”ti gaṇhato tatiyā ekaccasassatadiṭṭhi. “Neva hoti na na hotī”ti gaṇhato catutthā amarāvikkhepadiṭṭhīti vuttappakārā dasavidhā diṭṭhi. Yathāyogaṃ bhavadiṭṭhi ca vibhavadiṭṭhi cāti dvidhā hoti. Tāsu ekāpi tesaṃ khīṇāsavānaṃ na paṭicchitāti attho.

Herein, the method of the commentary (Patisambhidamagga Atthakatha 2.1.113) is as follows: the divisions of views are explained in ten ways, beginning with 'the world is eternal,' and so forth. In this context, the view that 'the world is eternal' arises from grasping the five aggregates as the world, thinking, 'This world is permanent, stable, and everlasting'; it is a view that proceeds from a mode of grasping that affirms eternalism. The view that 'the world is not eternal' arises from grasping that same world as 'cut off, annihilated'; it is a view that proceeds from a mode of grasping that affirms annihilation. The view that 'the world is finite' arises when one who has attained a limited kasiṇa, such as one the size of a platter or a bowl, perceives the material and immaterial phenomena occurring within that attainment as 'the world' and, due to the limitation of the kasiṇa, grasps it as 'finite'; it is a view that proceeds from a mode of grasping that 'the world is finite.' This can be either an eternalist view or an annihilationist view. For one who has attained an extensive kasiṇa, however, perceiving the material and immaterial phenomena within that attainment as 'the world' and, due to the boundlessness of the kasiṇa, grasping it as 'infinite,' it is a view that proceeds from a mode of grasping that 'the world is infinite.' This can be an eternalist view or an annihilationist view. The view that 'the soul is the same as the body' arises from having grasped the perishable body itself as the 'soul,' thus it is a view that proceeds from a mode of grasping annihilation, thinking 'when the body is cut off, the soul is also cut off.' By the second phrase, since a soul other than the body is grasped, it is a view that proceeds from a mode of grasping eternalism, thinking 'even when the body is cut off, the soul is not cut off.' In the statements 'the Tathāgata exists after death,' and so forth, for one who grasps that 'the being called the Tathāgata exists after death,' the first is an eternalist view. For one who grasps 'he does not exist,' the second is an annihilationist view. For one who grasps 'he both exists and does not exist,' the third is a partially eternalist view. For one who grasps 'he neither exists nor does not exist,' the fourth is the view of evasive equivocation. Thus, there are ten kinds of views of the type stated. As is appropriate, they are twofold: the view of existence and the view of annihilation. Not even one of these is accepted by those whose cankers are destroyed—this is the meaning.

Ye kilesāti ye kilesā sotāpattimaggena pahīnā, te kilese[P 1.0245]. Na punetīti na puna eti[V 0.0194]. Na paccetīti puna nibbattetvā na paṭieti, na paccāgacchatīti paccabhave nāgacchati. Pañcahākārehi tādīti pañcahi kāraṇehi koṭṭhāsehi vā sadiso. Iṭṭhāniṭṭhe tādīti iṭṭhārammaṇe ca aniṭṭhārammaṇe ca anunayapaṭighaṃ muñcitvā ṭhitattā dvīsu sadiso. Cattāvīti kilese cajitavā. Tiṇṇāvīti saṃsāraṃ atikkamitavā. Muttāvīti rāgādito muttavā. Taṃniddesā tādīti tena tena sīlasaddhādinā niddisitvā niddisitvā kathetabbato sadiso.

The phrase 'those defilements' (ye kilesā) refers to those defilements abandoned by the path of stream-entry. 'Does not return' (na puneti) means does not come again. 'Does not come back' (na pacceti) means one does not return to be reborn; one does not come back, that is, one does not come to a future existence. 'Like that in five ways' (pañcahākārehi tādī) means similar in five reasons or parts. 'Like that in the pleasant and unpleasant' (iṭṭhāniṭṭhe tādī) means being similar in two respects, in that one stands firm having abandoned attraction and repulsion toward pleasant and unpleasant objects. 'One who has abandoned' (cattāvī) means one who has abandoned defilements. 'One who has crossed over' (tiṇṇāvī) means one who has transcended saṃsāra. 'One who is freed' (muttāvī) means one who is freed from lust and so on. 'Like that by that designation' (taṃniddesā tādī) means similar on account of being spoken of by being repeatedly designated with virtues such as morality and faith.

Taṃ [M 0.0213] pañcavidhaṃ vitthāretvā kathetukāmo “kathaṃ arahā iṭṭhāniṭṭhe tādī”tiādimāha. Tattha lābhepīti catunnaṃ paccayānaṃ lābhepi. Alābhepīti tesaṃ alābhepi. Yasepīti parivārepi. Ayasepīti parivāravipattiyāpi. Pasaṃsāyapīti vaṇṇabhaṇanāyapi. Nindāyapīti garahāyapi. Sukhepīti kāyikasukhepi. Dukkhepīti kāyikadukkhepi. Ekañce bāhaṃ gandhena limpeyyunti sace ekaṃ bāhaṃ catujātiyagandhena lepaṃ uparūpari dadeyyuṃ. Vāsiyā taccheyyunti yadi ekaṃ bāhaṃ vaḍḍhakī vāsiyā tacchetvā tacchetvā tanuṃ kareyyuṃ. Amusmiṃ natthi rāgoti amusmiṃ gandhalepane sineho natthi na saṃvijjati. Amusmiṃ natthi paṭighanti amusmiṃ vāsiyā tacchane paṭihananasaṅkhātaṃ paṭighaṃ kopaṃ natthi na saṃvijjati. Anunayapaṭighavippahīnoti sinehañca kopañca pajahitvā ṭhito. Ugghātinighātivītivattoti anunayavasena anuggahañca paṭighavasena niggahañca atikkamitvā ṭhito. Anurodhavirodhasamatikkantoti anunayañca paṭighañca sammā atikkanto.

Wishing to elaborate and explain that fivefold way, he says, 'How is an arahant like that in the pleasant and unpleasant?' and so on. Herein, 'in gain' (lābhepi) means even in the gain of the four requisites. 'In loss' (alābhepi) means even in their loss. 'In fame' (yasepi) means even in having a retinue. 'In disrepute' (ayasepi) means even in the loss of a retinue. 'In praise' (pasaṃsāyapi) means even in being praised. 'In blame' (nindāyapi) means even in being censured. 'In pleasure' (sukhepi) means even in bodily pleasure. 'In pain' (dukkhepi) means even in bodily pain. 'If they were to anoint one arm with perfume' (ekaṃce bāhaṃ gandhena limpeyyuṃ) means if they were to repeatedly apply the four kinds of perfumes to one arm. 'Were to cut with an adze' (vāsiyā taccheyyuṃ) means if a carpenter were to repeatedly shave one arm with an adze, making it thin. 'There is no lust in that' (amusmiṃ natthi rāgo) means there is no affection, no attachment, in that anointing with perfume. 'There is no aversion in that' (amusmiṃ natthi paṭighaṃ) means there is no anger, no repulsion designated as striking back, in that shaving with an adze. 'Having abandoned attraction and repulsion' (anunayapaṭighavippahīno) means he stands having given up affection and anger. 'Having overcome favor and disfavor' (ugghātinighātivītivatto) means he stands having transcended both favor through attraction and disfavor through repulsion. 'Having gone beyond approval and disapproval' (anurodhavirodhasamatikkanto) means having rightly transcended both attraction and repulsion.

Sīle satīti sīle saṃvijjamāne. Sīlavāti sīlasampanno. Tena niddesaṃ kathanaṃ labhatīti tādī. Saddhāya sati saddhoti evamādīsupi eseva nayo.

'When there is virtue' (sīle sati) means when virtue is present. 'Virtuous' (sīlavā) means endowed with virtue. By that, he obtains a designation, a way of speaking; thus, 'like that' (tādī). 'When there is faith, faithful' (saddhāya sati saddho)—the same method applies in these and similar cases.

Saddhammappajjotikāya mahāniddesaṭṭhakathāya

From the Saddhammappajjotikā, the Commentary on the Mahāniddesa.

Paramaṭṭhakasuttaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Exposition of the Paramaṭṭhaka Sutta is concluded.

6. Jarāsuttaniddesavaṇṇanā

6. The Explanation of the Exposition of the Jarā Sutta

39. Chaṭṭhe [V 0.0195][P 2.0247] jarāsutte appaṃ vata jīvitaṃ idanti idaṃ vata manussānaṃ jīvitaṃ appakaṃ parittaṃ ṭhitiparittatāya sarasaparittatāyāti guhaṭṭhakasuttepi vuttanayametaṃ. Oraṃ vassasatāpi miyyatīti vassasatā oraṃ kalalādikālepi miyyati. Aticcāti vassasataṃ atikkamitvā. Jarasāpi miyyatīti jarāya miyyati. Ito paraṃ guhaṭṭhakasuttavaṇṇanāya vuttanayeneva gahetabbaṃ.

39. In the sixth Jarā Sutta, it is said: “Truly, this life is short!” This human life is indeed brief and limited, due to its limited duration and limited essence—this is the same method stated in the Guhaṭṭhaka Sutta. “One dies even before a hundred years”: one dies even before a hundred years, even in the kalala stage and so on. “Exceeding”: having passed a hundred years. “One dies of old age”: one dies due to old age. From here onwards, it should be understood in the same way as stated in the explanation of the Guhaṭṭhaka Sutta.

Appanti [M 0.0214] mandaṃ. Gamanīyo samparāyoti paraloko gantabbo. Kalalakālepīti ettha kalalakālaṃ nāma paṭisandhikkhaṇe tīhi jātiuṇṇaṃsūhi katasuttagge ṭhitatelabinduppamāṇaṃ acchaṃ vippasannakalalaṃ hoti. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ –

“Appaṃ” means slight. “The next life must be gone to” means the other world is to be gone to. “Even in the kalala stage”: here, the kalala stage is a clear, very pure kalala, the size of a drop of oil resting on the tip of a thread made from three strands of fine wool, at the moment of rebirth-linking. Concerning which it is said:

“Tilatelassa yathā bindu, sappimaṇḍo anāvilo;

Evaṃ vaṇṇappaṭibhāgaṃ, kalalaṃ sampavuccatī”ti. (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.235; vibha. aṭṭha. 26 pakiṇṇakakathā);

“As is a drop of sesame oil, or the clear surface of ghee, so, resembling it in appearance, is the kalala said to be.”

Tasmiṃ [V 0.0196] kalalakālepi. Cavatīti jīvitaṃ gaḷati. Maratīti jīvitaviyogaṃ āpajjati. Antaradhāyatīti adassanaṃ pāpuṇāti. Vippalujjatīti chijjati. “Aṇḍajayoniyā cavati. Jalābujayoniyā marati. Saṃsedajayoniyā antaradhāyati. Opapātikayoniyā vippalujjatī”ti evameke vaṇṇayanti. Abbudakālepīti abbudaṃ nāma kalalato sattāhaccayena maṃsadhovanaudakavaṇṇaṃ hoti, kalalanti nāmaṃ antaradhāyati. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Even in that kalala stage. “Passes away” (cavati) means life drips away. “Dies” (marati) means one undergoes separation from life. “Disappears” (antaradhāyati) means one reaches invisibility. “Is destroyed” (vippalujjati) means it is cut off. “In the case of egg-birth, one passes away. In the case of womb-birth, one dies. In the case of moisture-birth, one disappears. In the case of spontaneous birth, one is destroyed.” Thus some explain it. “Even in the abbuda stage”: the abbuda is what, after seven days from the kalala, becomes the color of meat-washing water, and the name ‘kalala’ disappears. And this has also been said:

“Sattāhaṃ [P 2.0248] kalalaṃ hoti, paripakkaṃ samūhataṃ;

Vivaṭṭamānaṃ tabbhāvaṃ, abbudaṃ nāma jāyatī”ti. (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.235);

“For seven days it is a kalala, fully ripened and collected; developing from that state, what is called an ‘abbuda’ arises.”

Tasmiṃ abbudakālepi. Pesikālepīti tasmāpi abbudā sattāhaccayena vilīnatipusadisā pesi nāma sañjāyati. Sā maricaphāṇitena dīpetabbā. Gāmadārikā hi supakkāni maricāni gahetvā sāṭakante bhaṇḍikaṃ katvā pīḷetvā maṇḍaṃ ādāya kapāle pakkhipitvā ātape ṭhapenti, taṃ sukkhamānaṃ sabbabhāgehi muccati. Evarūpā pesi hoti, abbudanti nāmaṃ antaradhāyati. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Even in that abbuda stage. “Even in the pesi stage”: from that abbuda, after seven days, what is called a pesi, resembling melted lead, arises. It should be illustrated with pepper molasses. For village girls, taking well-ripened peppers, making a bundle in the corner of their garment, squeezing them, taking the liquid, putting it in a potsherd, and placing it in the sun—as it dries, it detaches from all sides. Such a pesi comes into being, and the name ‘abbuda’ disappears. And this has also been said:

“Sattāhaṃ abbudaṃ hoti, paripakkaṃ samūhataṃ;

Vivaṭṭamānaṃ tabbhāvaṃ, pesi nāma pajāyatī”ti. (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.235);

“For seven days it is an abbuda, fully ripened and collected; developing from that state, what is called a ‘pesi’ is born.”

Tasmiṃ pesikālepi. Ghanakālepīti tatopi pesito sattāhaccayena kukkuṭaṇḍasaṇṭhāno ghano nāma maṃsapiṇḍo nibbattati, pesīti nāmaṃ antaradhāyati. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Even in that pesi stage. “Even in the ghana stage”: from that pesi, after seven days, a ghana, a lump of flesh the size of a hen’s egg, arises, and the name ‘pesi’ disappears. And this has also been said—

“Sattāhaṃ [M 0.0215] pesi bhavati, paripakkaṃ samūhataṃ;

Vivaṭṭamānaṃ tabbhāvaṃ, ghanoti nāma jāyati.

“For seven days it is a pesi, fully developed and collected; developing into that state, it is called a ghana.”

“Yathā kukkuṭiyā aṇḍaṃ, samantā parimaṇḍalaṃ;

Evaṃ ghanassa saṇṭhānaṃ, nibbattaṃ kammapaccayā”ti. (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.235);

“Just as a hen’s egg is perfectly round all around, so is the shape of the ghana, produced by the force of kamma.”

Tasmiṃ ghanakālepi. Pasākhakālepīti pañcame sattāhe dvinnaṃ dvinnaṃ hatthapādānaṃ sīsassa catthāya pañca pīḷakā jāyanti, yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “pañcame, bhikkhave, sattāhe pañca pīḷakā saṇṭhahanti kammato”ti. Tasmiṃ pasākhakālepi. Tato paraṃ chaṭṭhasattamādīni sattāhāni atikkamma desanaṃ saṅkhipitvā dvācattālīsasattāhe pariṇatakāle kesalomanakhādīnaṃ uppattikālañca. Tassa ca nābhito uṭṭhito nāḷo mātu udarapaṭalena ekābaddho hoti, so uppaladaṇḍako viya chiddo, tena āhāraraso saṃsaritvā āhārasamuṭṭhānarūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Evaṃ so dasamāse yāpeti, taṃ [P 2.0249] sabbaṃ avatvā “sūtighare”ti āha. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ –

Even in that ghana stage. “Even in the limb stage”: in the fifth week, five protuberances arise for the two hands, two feet, and the head, concerning which it is said: “Monks, in the fifth week, five protuberances become established due to kamma.” Even in that limb stage. After that, having passed the sixth, seventh, and subsequent weeks, summarizing the teaching, at the forty-second week, the time of maturation, and the time for the arising of hair, body hair, nails, and so forth. And a tube risen from his navel is bound together with the mother’s uterine lining; it is hollow like a lotus stalk, and through it, the nutrient essence flows, producing nutriment-originated matter. Thus he passes ten months. Without saying all that, it is said, “in the maternity room.” Concerning which it is said—

“Kesā [V 0.0197] lomā nakhāni ca”;

“Yañcassa bhuñjatī mātā, annaṃ pānañca bhojanaṃ;

Tena so tattha yāpeti, mātukucchigato naro”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.235; kathā. 692);

“Hairs of the head, body hairs, and nails”; “Whatever food and drink the mother consumes, he lives on that, a person gone into the mother’s womb.”

Tattha sūtighareti sūtikaghare, vijāyanaghareti attho. “Sūtikāghare”ti vā pāṭho, sūtikāyāti padacchedo. Addhamāsikopīti jātadivasato paṭṭhāya addhamāso etassa atthīti addhamāsiko. Dvemāsikādīsupi eseva nayo. Jātadivasato paṭṭhāya ekaṃ saṃvaccharaṃ etassa atthīti saṃvacchariko. Upari dvevassikādīsupi eseva nayo.

Here, “in the lying-in room” means in the delivery room, the place of birth. Alternatively, the reading may be “sūtikāghare,” with the word division as “sūtikāya” (of the woman in childbirth). “Half-a-month-old” means that from the day of birth, half a month has passed for him—thus, half-a-month-old. The same principle applies to “two-month-old” and so forth. From the day of birth, one full year has passed for him—thus, year-old. The same principle applies to “two-year-old” and so forth.

Yadā jiṇṇo hotīti yasmiṃ kāle jarājiṇṇo bhavati jajjarībhūto. Vuddhoti vayovuddho. Mahallakoti jātimahallako. Addhagatoti tayo addhe atikkanto. Vayoanuppattoti tatiyaṃ vayaṃ anuppatto. Khaṇḍadantoti antarantarā patitā dantā phālitā ca jarānubhāvena khaṇḍā dantā jātā assāti khaṇḍadanto. Palitakesoti paṇḍarakeso. Vilūnanti luñcitvā gahitakesā viya khallāṭasīso[M 0.0216]. Khalitasiroti mahākhallāṭasīso. Valinanti sañjātavali. Tilakāhatagattoti setatilakakāḷatilakehi vikiṇṇasarīro. Bhoggoti bhaggo, imināpissa vaṅkabhāvaṃ dīpeti. Daṇḍaparāyaṇoti daṇḍapaṭissaraṇo daṇḍadutiyo. So jarāyapīti so puggalo jarāyapi abhibhūto marati. Natthi maraṇamhā mokkhoti maraṇato muñcanupāyo natthi nupalabbhati.

“When he is aged” means at the time when he is worn out by old age, become decrepit. “Old” means advanced in age. “Elderly” means elderly by birth. “Past his prime” means having passed the three stages. “Having reached his last stage” means having arrived at the third age. “With broken teeth” means that due to the effect of aging, his teeth have fallen out here and there, and have become split and broken—thus, with broken teeth. “Gray-haired” means with white hair. “Bald” means with a bald head, like one whose hair has been plucked out. “With a bald head” means with a greatly bald head. “Wrinkled” means with wrinkles formed. “With a body marked with age-spots” means a body speckled with white and black age-spots. “Bent” means bent over, indicating his crooked posture. “Leaning on a staff” means relying on a staff, using the staff as a companion. “That person, too, is overcome by old age and dies.” “There is no escape from death” means no means of release from death is found.

Phalānamiva pakkānaṃ, pāto patanato bhayanti paripākagatānaṃ sithilavaṇṭānaṃ panasaphalādipakkānaṃ paccūsakāle avassaṃ patissantīti phalasāmikānaṃ bhāyamānānaṃ viya. Evaṃ jātāna maccānaṃ, niccaṃ maraṇato bhayanti evameva uppannānaṃ sattānaṃ maccusaṅkhātamaraṇato satataṃ kālaṃ bhayaṃ.

“Just as owners fear ripe fruits falling in the morning”: just as owners fear that ripe jackfruits and other ripe fruits, whose stalks have loosened, will surely fall at dawn. “So too, for mortals who are born, there is always fear of death”: just so, for beings who have arisen, there is always fear of death, which is called mortality.

Yathāpi [P 2.0250] kumbhakārassāti yathā nāma mattikābhājanaṃ karontassa. Kataṃ mattikabhājananti (su. ni. 582) tena niṭṭhāpitabhājanaṃ. Sabbaṃ bhedanapariyantanti pakkāpakkaṃ sabbaṃ bhedanaṃ bhijjapariyantaṃ avasānaṃ assāti bhedanapariyantaṃ. Evaṃ maccāna jīvitanti evameva sattānaṃ āyusaṅkhāraṃ.

“Of a potter”: that is, of one making earthenware vessels. “A finished earthen vessel” (Su. Ni. 582) means a vessel completed by him. “All ending in breakage” means all, whether baked or unbaked, have breakage as their end, as their conclusion. “So too is the life of mortals”—just so is the life-span of beings.

Daharā [V 0.0198] ca mahantā cāti taruṇā ca mahallakā ca. Ye bālā ye ca paṇḍitāti ye ca assāsapassāsāyattā jīvitā bālā ye ca paṇḍiccena samannāgatā buddhādayo. Sabbe maccuvasaṃ yantīti ete vuttappakārā daharādayo sabbe maccuno issariyaṃ upagacchanti.

“The young and the old”: both the youthful and the aged. “The foolish and the wise”: those foolish ones whose lives depend on in-and-out breathing, and those endowed with wisdom, like the Buddhas and others. “All come under the power of death”: all these aforementioned, the young and others, come under the authority of death.

Tesaṃ maccuparetānanti etesaṃ maccunā parivāritānaṃ. Gacchataṃ paralokatoti ito manussalokato paralokaṃ gacchantānaṃ. Na pitā tāyate puttanti pitā puttaṃ na rakkhati. Ñātī vā pana ñātaketi mātāpitipakkhikā ñātī vā teyeva ñātake rakkhituṃ na sakkonti.

“Of those afflicted by death”: of these who are surrounded by death. “Of those going to the other world”: of those going from this human world to the other world. “A father cannot protect his son” means a father does not protect his son. “Nor relatives their kin” means relatives, whether on the mother’s or father’s side, are not able to protect those relatives.

Pekkhataññeva ñātīnanti vuttavidhānaṃyeva ñātīnaṃ pekkhantānaṃyeva olokentānaṃyeva. Passa lālappataṃ puthūti passāti ālapanaṃ. Lālapantānaṃ vilapantānaṃ puthūnaṃ nānappakārānaṃ. Ekamekova maccānaṃ, govajjho viya niyyatīti sattānaṃ ekameko vadhāya niyyamānagoṇo viya maraṇāya niyyati pāpuṇīyati. Evamabbhāhato lokoti [M 0.0217] evameva sattaloko bhusaṃ āhato. Maccunā ca jarāya cāti maraṇena ca jarāya ca abhibhūto.

“Of the relatives merely looking on”: of the relatives, as stated, merely looking on, merely observing. “See the many lamenting”: “Passa” (see) is an address. Of the many lamenting, wailing, of various kinds. “Alone, indeed, does each of mortals go, like a cow led to slaughter”: each individual of beings goes to death, reaches it, like a cow being led to slaughter. “Thus stricken is the world”: just so the world of beings is greatly stricken. “By death and decay”: overcome by death and decay.

40. Mamāyiteti mamāyitavatthukāraṇā. Vinābhāvaṃ santamevidanti santaṃ vijjamānaṃ vinābhāvameva idaṃ, na sakkā avinābhāvena bhavitunti vuttaṃ hoti.

40. “Because of what is held as mine”: this is said because the objects held as mine are the cause. “This existing thing is only separation” means this existing thing is indeed separation; it is said that it is not possible for it to be without separation.

Socantīti cittena socanaṃ karonti. Kilamantīti kāyena kilamathaṃ pāpuṇanti. Paridevantīti nānāvidhaṃ vācāvilāpaṃ bhaṇanti. Urattāḷiṃ kandantīti uraṃ tāḷetvā tāḷetvā kandanti. Sammohaṃ āpajjantīti sammohabhāvaṃ pāpuṇanti.

“They grieve” means they grieve in their minds. “They become fatigued” means they undergo bodily fatigue. “They lament” means they utter various lamentations. “They beat their breasts and cry” means they cry, striking their chests repeatedly. “They fall into delusion” means they attain a state of delusion.

Aniccoti hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena. Saṅkhatoti paccayehi saṅgamma kato. Paṭiccasamuppannoti paccayasāmaggiṃ paṭicca na paccakkhāya saha sammā ca uppanno. Khayadhammoti [P 2.0251] khayaṃ gamanasabhāvo. Vayadhammoti vayaṃ gamanasabhāvo, bhaṅgavasena bhaṅgagamanasabhāvoti attho. Virāgadhammoti virajjanasabhāvo. Nirodhadhammoti nirujjhanasabhāvo. Yvāyaṃ pariggahoti yo ayaṃ pariggaho. “Yāya pariggaho”tipi pāṭho, ayameva padacchedo. Niccoti satatakāliko. Dhuvoti thiro. Sassatoti acavano. Avipariṇāmadhammoti pakatiajahanasabhāvo. Sassati samaṃ tatheva ṭhassatīti candasūriyasinerumahāsamuddapathavīpabbatādayo viya tiṭṭheyya.

Impermanent (anicca) in the sense of non-existence after having been. Conditioned (saṅkhata) in the sense of being made by the coming together of conditions. Dependently arisen (paṭiccasamuppanna) in the sense of having arisen rightly and together in dependence on an assemblage of conditions, not rejecting them. Subject to destruction (khayadhamma) in the sense of having the nature of going to destruction. Subject to vanishing (vayadhamma) in the sense of having the nature of going to vanishing; that is, having the nature of going to dissolution by way of breaking up. Subject to fading away (virāgadhamma) in the sense of having the nature of fading away. Subject to cessation (nirodhadhamma) in the sense of having the nature of ceasing. The phrase `yvāyaṃ pariggaho` means `yo ayaṃ pariggaho` (this grasping). There is also the reading `yāya pariggaho` (by which grasping); this (`yo ayaṃ`) is the correct word division. Permanent (nicca) in the sense of being continuous in time. Stable (dhuva) in the sense of being firm. Eternal (sassata) in the sense of being unchanging. Not subject to change (avipariṇāmadhamma) in the sense of having the nature of not abandoning its natural state. It would stand eternally, just the same, like the moon, sun, Mount Sineru, the great ocean, the earth, mountains, and so on.

Nānābhāvoti jātiyā nānābhāvo. Vinābhāvoti maraṇena viyogabhāvo. Aññathābhāvoti [V 0.0199] sabbhāvato aññathābhāvo. Purimānaṃ purimānaṃ khandhānanti anantare pure uppannānaṃ khandhānaṃ. Vipariṇāmaññathābhāvāti pakatibhāvaṃ jahitvā aññathābhāvena. Pacchimā pacchimā khandhādayo pavattanti uppajjantīti sambandho.

Diversity (nānābhāva) in the sense of diversity by birth. Separation (vinābhāva) in the sense of the state of separation by death. Otherness (aññathābhāva) in the sense of being otherwise than its own nature. 'Of the former aggregates' (purimānaṃ purimānaṃ khandhānaṃ) means of the aggregates that arose immediately before. Transformation and alteration (vipariṇāmaññathābhāva), meaning by abandoning their natural state and becoming otherwise. The subsequent aggregates and so forth continue and arise—this is the connection.

Sabbaṃ gharāvāsapalibodhanti sakalaṃ gihibhāvajaṭaṃ. Ñātimittāmaccapalibodhanti mātāpitupakkhikā ñātī, mittā sahāyā, amaccā bhaccā. Sannidhipalibodhanti nidhānajaṭaṃ chinditvā. Kesamassuṃ ohāretvāti kese ca massūni ca oropayitvā. Kāsāyāni vatthānīti kasāyarasapītāni vatthāni.

'All the household bonds' means the entire entanglement of household life. 'The bonds of relatives, friends, and attendants' means relatives on the side of mother and father, friends as companions, and attendants as servants. 'The bond of accumulation': having cut off the entanglement of stored wealth. 'Having shaved off hair and beard' means having removed hair and beard. 'The ochre robes' means cloths dyed with an astringent juice.

41. Māmakoti [M 0.0218] mama upāsako bhikkhu vāti saṅkhaṃ gato, buddhādīni vā vatthūni mamāyamāno.

41. 'Māmako' means one who is considered 'my lay follower' or 'my monk,' or one who appropriates things such as the Buddha and so forth.

Tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānanti anekesaṃ sattānaṃ sādhāraṇaniddeso. “Yaññadattassa maraṇaṃ, somadattassa maraṇa”nti evañhi divasampi kathiyamāne neva sattā pariyādānaṃ gacchanti, na sabbaṃ aparattadīpanaṃ sijjhati. Imehi pana dvīhi padehi na koci satto apariyādinno hoti, na kiñci aparattādīpanaṃ na sijjhati. Tamhā tamhāti ayaṃ gativasena anekesaṃ nikāyānaṃ sādhāraṇaniddeso. Sattanikāyāti sattānaṃ nikāyā, sattaghaṭā sattasamūhāti attho. Cutīti [P 2.0252] cavanavasena vuttaṃ. Ekacatupañcakkhandhāya cutiyā sāmaññavacanametaṃ. Cavanatāti bhāvavacanena lakkhaṇanidassanaṃ. Bhedoti cutikhandhānaṃ bhaṅguppattiparidīpanaṃ. Antaradhānanti ghaṭassa viya bhinnassa bhinnānaṃ khandhānaṃ yena kenaci pariyāyena ṭhānābhāvaparidīpanaṃ. Maccumaraṇanti maccusaṅkhātaṃ maraṇaṃ, na khaṇikamaraṇaṃ. Kālo nāma antako, tassa kiriyāti kālaṃkiriyā. Ettāvatā sammutimaraṇaṃ dīpitaṃ. Idāni paramatthena dīpetuṃ “khandhānaṃ bhedo”tiādimāha. Paramatthena hi khandhāyeva bhijjanti, na satto nāma koci marati. Khandhesu pana bhijjamānesu satto marati, bhinnesu “mato”ti vohāro hoti.

'Of those very beings' means a general designation for many beings. For even if one were to speak all day, saying, 'Yaññadatta's death, Somadatta's death,' beings would not be exhausted, nor would the entire matter be illuminated. But by these two terms, no being is left unincluded, and nothing regarding the full illumination is left unaccomplished. 'From that very place' means this is a general designation for many groups by way of their destination. 'Groups of beings' means collections of beings, crowds of beings, or masses of beings. 'Passing away' is said in the sense of ceasing. This is a general term for the passing away related to one, four, or five aggregates. 'The state of passing away' is a demonstration of the characteristic by way of an abstract term. 'Disintegration' is an illustration of the breaking up and arising of the aggregates that are passing away. 'Disappearance' is an illustration of the non-existence of a place for the broken aggregates, in any way whatsoever, like a shattered pot. 'Death' means the death reckoned as 'maccu,' not momentary death. Time is the end-maker; its action is 'kālaṃkiriyā.' Thus far, conventional death has been explained. Now, to explain it in the ultimate sense, it is said, 'the breaking up of the aggregates,' and so forth. For in the ultimate sense, only the aggregates break apart; no being whatsoever dies. Yet, when the aggregates are breaking apart, a being is said to die; when they are broken, the expression 'he has died' is used.

Ettha ca catuvokārapañcavokāravasena khandhānaṃ bhedo, ekavokāravasena kaḷevarassa nikkhepo. Catuvokāravasena vā khandhānaṃ bhedo, sesadvayavasena kaḷevarassa nikkhepo veditabbo. Kasmā? Kāmarūpabhavadvayepi rūpakāyasaṅkhātassa kaḷevarassa sabbhāvato. Yasmā vā cātumahārājikādīsu khandhā bhijjanteva, na kiñci nikkhipanti, tasmā tesaṃ vasena khandhānaṃ bhedo, manussādīsu kaḷevarassa [V 0.0200] nikkhepo. Ettha ca kaḷevarassa nikkhepakaraṇato maraṇaṃ “kaḷevarassa nikkhepo”ti vuttaṃ. Jīvitindriyassupacchedoti iminā indriyabaddhasseva maraṇaṃ nāma hoti, anindriyabaddhassa maraṇaṃ nāma natthīti dasseti. “Sassaṃ mataṃ, rukkho mato”ti idaṃ pana vohāramattameva. Atthato pana evarūpāni vacanāni sassādīnaṃ khayavayabhāvameva dīpenti. Rūpagatanti rūpameva rūpagataṃ. Vedanāgatantiādīsupi eseva nayo.

Here, the breaking up of the aggregates is in the case of the four-constituent and five-constituent existences, while the laying down of the body is in the case of the one-constituent existence. Alternatively, the breaking up of the aggregates is in the case of the four-constituent existence, and the laying down of the body should be understood as in the case of the remaining two. Why? Because in both the desire-sphere and form-sphere existences, the body, designated as the form-body, exists. Or, because in realms like that of the Four Great Kings and so forth, the aggregates only break apart and they do not lay down anything, therefore, in their case, there is the breaking up of the aggregates, while in the case of humans and others, there is the laying down of the body. And here, because it is the act of laying down the body, death is called 'the laying down of the body.' By 'the cutting off of the life faculty,' it is shown that death occurs only for that which is bound by faculties; for that which is not bound by faculties, there is no such thing as death. Phrases like 'the crop is dead, the tree is dead' are merely conventional expressions. In reality, however, such statements indicate only the state of decay and passing away of crops and the like. 'Gone to form' means it is form itself that is gone to form. The same principle applies to 'gone to feeling' and so on.

Tattha [M 0.0219] pubbeva maccanti maccaṃ vā bhogā pubbeva paṭhamataraññeva vijahanti. Macco vā te bhoge pubbataraṃ jahati. Kāmakāmīti corarājānaṃ ālapati. Ambho kāme kāmayamāna kāmakāmi bhogino nāma loke asassatā, bhogesu vā naṭṭhesu jīvamānā ca abhogino honti. Bhoge vā pahāya sayaṃ nassanti, tasmā ahaṃ mahājanassa sokakālepi na socāmīti attho.

Therein, 'beforehand from the mortal' means: either wealth abandons the mortal beforehand, that is, first of all; or the mortal abandons that wealth even earlier. 'Kāmakāmī' addresses the king of thieves, saying: 'O you who desire pleasures, Kāmakāmī, possessors of wealth in this world are impermanent. When their wealth is lost while they are still alive, they become without wealth. Or, having abandoned their wealth, they themselves perish. Therefore, even in a time of sorrow for the multitude, I do not grieve'—that is the meaning.

Viditā [P 2.0253] mayā sattuka lokadhammāti corarājānaṃ ālapanto āha. Ambho sattuka mayā lābho alābho yaso ayasotiādayo lokadhammā viditā. Yatheva hi cando udeti ca pūrati ca puna ca khīyati, yathā ca sūriyo andhakāraṃ vidhamento mahantaṃ lokappadesaṃ tapitvāna puna sāyaṃ atthaṃ paleti atthaṃ gacchati na dissati, evameva bhogā uppajjanti ca vinassanti ca, tattha kiṃ sokena, tasmā na socāmīti attho.

Addressing the king of thieves, he said: 'The worldly conditions are understood by me, O enemy.' 'O enemy, gain and loss, fame and disgrace, and other such worldly conditions have been understood by me. Just as the moon rises, waxes full, and then wanes, and just as the sun, dispelling the darkness and heating the vast region of the world, again in the evening sets, goes to rest, and is no longer seen, so too does wealth arise and perish. What is the use of sorrow in that? Therefore, I do not grieve'—that is the meaning.

Taṇhāmaññanāya maññatīti taṇhāya janitamānamaññanāya maññati. Mānaṃ karoti diṭṭhimaññanāyāti diṭṭhiṃ upanissayaṃ katvā uppannāya maññanāya. Mānamaññanāyāti sahajātamānamaññanāya. Kilesamaññanāyāti vuttappakārāya upatāpanaṭṭhena kilesamaññanāya maññati.

'He conceives through craving-conceiving' means he conceives through the conceit-conceiving born of craving. 'He creates conceit through view-conceiving' means through the conceiving that has arisen having made view its support. 'Through conceit-conceiving' means through the co-nascent conceit-conceiving. 'He conceives through defilement-conceiving' means he conceives through the defilement-conceiving of the type described, which has the characteristic of tormenting.

Kuhāti vimhāpakā. Thaddhāti khāṇu viya thaddhā. Lapāti paccayanimittena lapanakā.

'Kuhā' means one who bewilders. 'Thaddhā' means one who is obstinate like a tree stump. 'Lapā' means one who chatters, making hints for the sake of requisites.

42. Saṅgatanti samāgataṃ, diṭṭhaṃ phuṭṭhaṃ vā. Piyāyitanti piyakataṃ.

42. 'Saṅgata' means come together, seen, or touched. 'Piyāyita' means made dear.

Saṅgatanti sammukhībhūtaṃ. Samāgatanti samīpaṃ āgataṃ. Samāhitanti ekībhūtaṃ. Sannipatitanti piṇḍitaṃ. Supinagatoti supinaṃ paviṭṭho. Senābyūhaṃ passatīti senāsannivesaṃ dakkhati. Ārāmarāmaṇeyyakanti pupphārāmādīnaṃ ramaṇīyabhāvaṃ. Vanarāmaṇeyyakādīsupi eseva nayo. Petanti ito paralokaṃ gataṃ. Kālaṅkatanti mataṃ.

'Saṅgata' means having come face to face. 'Samāgata' means having come near. 'Samāhita' means having become unified. 'Sannipatita' means having gathered together. 'Supinagata' means having entered a dream. 'He sees the army array' means one sees the arrangement of the army. 'The delightfulness of a park' means the pleasing nature of flower gardens and so forth. The same principle applies to 'the delightfulness of a forest' and similar terms. 'Peta' means gone from this world to the next. 'Kālaṅkata' means dead.

43. Nāmaṃyevāvasissati[V 0.0201], akkheyyanti sabbaṃ rūpādidhammajātaṃ pahīyati, nāmamattameva tu avasissati “buddharakkhito dhammarakkhito”ti evaṃ akkhātuṃ kathetuṃ.

43. 'Only the name remains to be declared' means that the entire class of phenomena such as form is abandoned, and only the mere name remains to be declared and spoken, thus: 'Buddharakkhita,' 'Dhammarakkhita.'

Ye [M 0.0220] cakkhuviññāṇābhisambhūtāti ye sayaṃ cakkhuviññāṇena abhisambhūtā rāsikatā diṭṭhā catusamuṭṭhānikā rūpā. Sotaviññāṇābhisambhūtāti paratoghosena sotaviññāṇena rāsikatā sutā dvisamuṭṭhānikā saddā.

'Those arisen from eye-consciousness' means those forms with four origins, which are seen, accumulated, and arisen by one's own eye-consciousness. 'Those arisen from ear-consciousness' means those sounds with two origins, which are heard and accumulated by ear-consciousness through the voice of another.

44. Munayoti khīṇāsavamunayo. Khemadassinoti nibbānadassino.

44. 'Munis' means the sages whose taints are destroyed. 'Seers of security' means those who see Nibbāna.

Sokoti sokaniddese – byasatīti byasanaṃ, hitasukhaṃ khipati [P 2.0254] viddhaṃsetīti attho. Ñātīnaṃ byasanaṃ ñātibyasanaṃ, corarogabhayādīhi ñātikkhayo ñātivināsoti attho. Tena ñātibyasanena. Phuṭṭhassāti ajjhotthaṭassa, abhibhūtassa samannāgatassāti attho. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Ayaṃ pana viseso – bhogānaṃ byasanaṃ bhogabyasanaṃ, rājacorādivasena bhogakkhayo bhogavināsoti attho. Rogoyeva byasanaṃ rogabyasanaṃ. Rogo hi ārogyaṃ byasati vināsetīti byasanaṃ. Sīlassa byasanaṃ sīlabyasanaṃ, dussilyassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Sammādiṭṭhiṃ vināsayamānā uppannā diṭṭhiyeva byasanaṃ diṭṭhibyasanaṃ. Ettha ca purimāni dve anipphannāni, pacchimāni tīṇi nipphannāni tilakkhaṇabbhāhatāni. Purimāni ca tīṇi neva kusalāni nākusalāni, sīladiṭṭhibyasanadvayaṃ akusalaṃ.

'Sorrow': in the exposition of sorrow, 'byasana' (misfortune) is so called because it brings ruin ('byasati'); the meaning is that it casts away and destroys welfare and happiness. The misfortune of relatives is 'ñātibyasana'; the meaning is the loss and ruin of relatives due to thieves, disease, fear, and so forth. 'By that misfortune of relatives.' 'Phuṭṭhassa' means affected, overwhelmed, overcome, or possessed; that is the meaning. The same principle applies to the rest. This, however, is the distinction: the misfortune of wealth is 'bhogabyasana'; the meaning is the loss and ruin of wealth due to kings, thieves, and so forth. Disease itself is a misfortune, 'rogabyasana,' for disease ruins and destroys health; hence, it is a 'byasana.' The misfortune of virtue is 'sīlabyasana'; this is a name for immorality. A view that has arisen destroying right view is itself a misfortune, 'diṭṭhibyasana.' Here, the first two are not produced phenomena, while the latter three are produced phenomena, afflicted by the three characteristics. The first three are neither wholesome nor unwholesome, while the two misfortunes concerning virtue and view are unwholesome.

Aññataraññatarenāti gahitesu vā yena kenaci aggahitesu vā mittāmaccabyasanādīsu yena kenaci. Samannāgatassāti samanubandhassa aparimuccamānassa. Aññataraññatarena dukkhadhammenāti yena kenaci sokadukkhassa uppattihetunā. Sokoti socanakavasena soko. Idaṃ tehi kāraṇehi uppajjanakasokassa sabhāvapaccattaṃ. Socanāti socanākāro. Socitattanti socitabhāvo. Antosokoti abbhantarasoko. Dutiyapadaṃ upasaggena vaḍḍhitaṃ. So hi abbhantaraṃ sukkhāpento viya parisukkhāpento viya uppajjatīti “antosoko antoparisoko”ti vuccati. Antodāhoti abbhantaradāho. Dutiyapadaṃ upasaggena vaḍḍhitaṃ. Cetaso parijjhāyanāti cittassa jhānanākāro. Soko hi uppajjamāno aggi viya cittaṃ jhāpeti [M 0.0221] dahati, “cittaṃ me jhāmaṃ, na me kiñci paṭibhātī”ti vadāpeti. Dukkhito mano dummano, tassa bhāvo domanassaṃ. Anupaviṭṭhaṭṭhena sokova sallanti sokasallaṃ.

'By one or another' (aññataraññatarena) means by any whatsoever, whether concerning things held dear or not, or by any of the calamities concerning friends, relatives, and so on. 'Possessed of' (samannāgatassa) means being pursued by, not being released from. 'By one or another state of suffering' (aññataraññatarena dukkhadhammena) means by any cause for the arising of sorrow and suffering. 'Sorrow' (soka) means sorrow in the sense of lamenting. This is the inherent nature of sorrow arising from those causes. 'Lamenting' (socanā) means the act of lamenting. 'The state of having lamented' (socitatta) means the state of being one who has lamented. 'Inner sorrow' (antosoka) means internal sorrow. The second term is intensified by a prefix. For it arises as if drying up the interior, as if completely drying it up—thus it is called 'inner sorrow, inner desolation' (antosoka, antoparisoka). 'Inner burning' (antodāha) means internal burning. The second term is intensified by a prefix. 'The mind's anguish' (cetaso parijjhāyanā) means the mind's state of being scorched. For sorrow, when arising, scorches and burns the mind like fire, making one say, 'My mind is scorched, nothing occurs to me.' 'An afflicted mind is a sad mind' (dukkhito mano dummano); the state of that is dejection (domanassa). Because of its meaning of penetrating, sorrow itself is a dart—a sorrow-dart (sokasalla).

Paridevaniddese [V 0.0202] – “mayhaṃ dhītā, mayhaṃ putto”ti evaṃ ādissa ādissa devanti rodanti etenāti ādevo. Taṃ taṃ vaṇṇaṃ parikittetvā parikittetvā devanti etenāti paridevo. Tato parāni dve dve padāni purimadvayasseva ākārabhāvaniddesavasena vuttāni. Vācāti vacanaṃ. Palāpoti tucchaṃ niratthakavacanaṃ[P 2.0255]. Uppaḍḍhabhaṇitaaññabhaṇitādivasena virūpo palāpo vippalāpo. Lālappoti punappunaṃ lapanaṃ. Lālappanākāro lālappanā. Lālappitassa bhāvo lālappitattaṃ. Macchariyādīni vuttatthāneva.

In the exposition of lamentation: 'My daughter, my son,' thus repeatedly specifying, they lament and weep; hence it is called lamentation (ādeva). By repeatedly extolling this and that quality, they lament; hence it is called lamentation (parideva). Thereafter, the next two pairs of terms are stated in the same way as the previous pair, by way of indicating the mode and state. 'Speech' (vācā) means utterance. 'Chatter' (palāpa) means empty, meaningless speech. 'Distorted chatter' (vippalāpa) is distorted speech, such as half-spoken words or speaking of other things. 'Babbling' (lālappa) means repeated chatter. The manner of babbling is lālappanā. The state of one who has babbled is lālappitatta. Stinginess and the like are as explained in their respective places.

45. Sattamagāthā evaṃ maraṇabbhāhate loke anurūpapaṭipattidassanatthaṃ vuttā. Tattha patilīnacarassāti tato tato patilīnaṃ cittaṃ katvā carantassa. Bhikkhunoti kalyāṇaputhujjanassa vā sekkhassa vā. Sāmaggiyamāhu tassa taṃ, yo attānaṃ bhavane na dassayeti tassetaṃ patirūpamāhu, yo evaṃpaṭipanno nirayādibhede bhavane attānaṃ na dassaye. Evañhi so imamhā maraṇā mucceyyāti adhippāyo.

45. The seventh verse is spoken to show the appropriate practice in a world afflicted by death. Here, 'of one who lives withdrawn' (patilīnacarassa) means of one who moves having withdrawn the mind from this and that. 'Of a monk' (bhikkhuno) refers either to a virtuous ordinary person or to a trainee. 'They call that concord for him, who does not show himself in existence': they say this is fitting for him, who, practicing thus, does not show himself in the various realms of existence, such as hell. For thus he may be freed from this death—this is the intention.

Patilīnacarā vuccantīti tato tato līnacittācārā kathīyanti. Satta sekkhāti adhisīlādīsu tīsu sikkhāsu sikkhantīti sotāpattimaggaṭṭhaṃ ādiṃ katvā yāva arahattamaggaṭṭhā satta sekkhā. Arahāti phalaṭṭho. So niṭṭhitacittattā patilīno. Sekkhānaṃ patilīnacaraṇabhāve kāraṇaṃ dassento “kiṃ kāraṇā”tiādimāha. Te tato tatoti te satta sekkhā tehi tehi ārammaṇehi cittaṃ patilīnentāti attano cittaṃ nilīnentā. Patikuṭentāti saṅkocentā. Pativaṭṭentāti kaṭasārakaṃ viya ābhujentā. Sanniruddhantāti sannirujjhantā. Sannigaṇhantāti niggahaṃ kurumānā. Sannivārentāti vārayamānā. Rakkhantāti rakkhaṃ kurumānā. Gopentāti cittamañjūsāya gopayamānā.

'Those of withdrawn conduct' (patilīnacarā) are said—they are called those whose conduct is with a mind withdrawn from this and that. 'Seven trainees' (satta sekkhā) are those training in the three trainings of higher virtue, etc.; they are the seven trainees starting from the one on the path of stream-entry up to the one on the path of arahantship. 'An arahant' (arahā) is one at the fruition stage. He is withdrawn because his mind is perfected. Showing the reason for the withdrawn conduct of trainees, he says, 'What is the reason?' and so on. 'They from this and that' (te tato tato) means those seven trainees withdraw their minds from those various objects, thus concealing their own minds. 'They recoil' (patikuṭenti) means they contract. 'They turn away' (pativaṭṭenti) means they bend back like a mat. 'They restrain' (sanniruddhanti) means they are completely restrained. 'They control' (sannigaṇhanti) means they exercise control. 'They ward off' (sannivārenti) means they ward off. 'They protect' (rakkhanti) means they provide protection. 'They guard' (gopenti) means they guard it as in a casket of the mind.

Idāni [M 0.0222] dvāravasena dassento “cakkhudvāre”tiādimāha. Tattha cakkhudvāreti cakkhuviññāṇadvāre. Sotadvārādīsupi eseva nayo. Bhikkhunoti puthujjanakalyāṇakassa vā bhikkhuno, sekkhassa vā bhikkhunoti bhikkhusaddassa vacanatthaṃ avatvā idhādhippetabhikkhuyeva dassito. Tattha puthujjano ca so kilesānaṃ asamucchinnattā, kalyāṇo ca sīlādipaṭipattiyuttattāti [P 2.0256] puthujjanakalyāṇova puthujjanakalyāṇako, tassa puthujjanakalyāṇakassa. Adhisīlādīni sikkhatīti sekkho, tassa sekkhassa vā sotāpannassa vā sakadāgāmino vā anāgāmino vā.

Now, showing this by way of the doors, he says, 'at the eye-door,' and so on. Here, 'at the eye-door' (cakkhudvāre) means at the door of eye-consciousness. The same method applies to the ear-door and so on. As for 'of a bhikkhu' (bhikkhuno), without stating the etymological meaning of the word 'bhikkhu,' only the bhikkhu intended here is indicated: either a bhikkhu who is a virtuous ordinary person or one who is a trainee. Here, he is an ordinary person (puthujjano) because the defilements are not severed, and he is virtuous (kalyāṇo) because he is endowed with the practice of virtue, etc.; thus, a virtuous ordinary person (puthujjanakalyāṇako)—of that virtuous ordinary person. One who trains (sikkhati) in higher virtue, etc., is a trainee (sekkho)—of that trainee, whether a stream-enterer, a once-returner, or a non-returner.

Āsanti [V 0.0203] nisīdanti etthāti āsanaṃ. Yatthāti yesu mañcapīṭhādīsu. Mañcotiādīni āsanassa pabhedavacanāni. Mañcopi hi nisajjāyapi okāsattā idha āsanesu vutto, so pana masārakabundikābaddhakuḷīrapādakaāhaccapādakānaṃ aññataro. Pīṭhampi tesaṃ aññatarameva. Bhisīti uṇṇabhisi coḷabhisi vākabhisi tiṇabhisi paṇṇabhisīnaṃ aññatarā. Taṭṭikāti tālapaṇṇādīhi vinitvā katā. Cammakhaṇḍoti nisajjāraho yo koci cammakhaṇḍo. Tiṇasanthārādayo tiṇādīni gumbetvā katā. Asappāyarūpadassanenāti asappāyānaṃ iṭṭharūpānaṃ olokanena. Rittanti abbhantarato tucchaṃ. Vivittanti bahiddhāpavesanena suññaṃ. Pavivittanti koci gahaṭṭho tattha natthīti atirekena suññaṃ. Asappāyasaddassavanepi eseva nayo. Pañcahi kāmaguṇehīti itthirūpasaddagandharasaphoṭṭhabbehi pañcahi kāmakoṭṭhāsehi. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

'They sit, they sit down here' (āsanti, nisīdanti ettha)—thus, a seat (āsana). 'Where' (yattha) means on which, such as on beds and chairs. 'Bed' (mañca) and so on are terms for different types of seats. For even a bed is mentioned here among seats because it provides space for sitting; it is one of those with cord-woven legs, crab-like legs, or inserted legs. A chair (pīṭha) is likewise one of those. 'A cushion' (bhisī) refers to any one of these: a woolen cushion, a cotton cushion, a bark-fibre cushion, a grass cushion, or a leaf cushion. 'A mat' (taṭṭikā) is one made by weaving palm leaves or similar materials. 'A piece of leather' (cammakhaṇḍa) is any piece of leather suitable for sitting. 'A grass spread' (tiṇasanthāra) and the like are those made by bundling grass and other materials. 'By seeing unsuitable forms' (asappāyarūpadassanena) means by looking at unsuitable, desirable forms. 'Empty' (ritta) means empty inside. 'Secluded' (vivitta) means empty by preventing external entry. 'Very secluded' (pavivitta) means exceedingly empty, as no householder is present there. The same method applies to 'hearing unsuitable sounds' (asappāyasaddassavana). 'With the five strands of sensual pleasure' (pañcahi kāmaguṇehi) refers to the five portions of sensual pleasure: a woman's form, sound, smell, taste, and touch. And this has also been said:

“Rūpā saddā rasā gandhā, phoṭṭhabbā ca manoramā;

Pañca kāmaguṇā loke, itthirūpasmiṃ dissare”ti. (a. ni. 5.55);

“Forms, sounds, tastes, smells, and touches, which are delightful—

These five strands of sensual pleasure in the world

Are found in a woman’s form.”

Bhajatoti cittena sevanaṃ karontassa. Sambhajatoti sammā sevantassa. Sevatoti upasaṅkamantassa. Nisevatoti nissayaṃ katvā sevantassa. Saṃsevatoti suṭṭhu sevantassa. Paṭisevatoti punappunaṃ upasaṅkamantassa.

'Associates with' (bhajati) means of one who serves with the mind. 'Associates with properly' (sambhajati) means of one who serves properly. 'Serves' (sevāti) means of one who approaches. 'Serves devotedly' (nisevati) means of one who serves having taken it as a support. 'Serves well' (saṃsevāti) means of one who serves excellently. 'Indulges in' (paṭisevati) means of one who approaches again and again.

Gaṇasāmaggīti samaṇānaṃ ekībhāvo samaggabhāvo. Dhammasāmaggīti sattatiṃsabodhipakkhiyadhammānaṃ samūhabhāvo. Anabhinibbattisāmaggīti anibbattamānānaṃ [M 0.0223] anuppajjamānānaṃ anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbutānaṃ arahantānaṃ samūho. Samaggāti kāyena aviyogā. Sammodamānāti cittena suṭṭhu modamānā tussamānā. Avivadamānāti vācāya [P 2.0257] vivādaṃ akurumānā. Khīrodakībhūtāti khīrena saṃsaṭṭhaudakasadisā.

'Harmony of the group' (gaṇasāmaggī) means the unity and concord of ascetics. 'Harmony of the Dhamma' (dhammasāmaggī) means the collective nature of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. 'Harmony in non-rearising' (anabhinibbattisāmaggī) means the assembly of arahants who are not reborn, do not arise, and have attained final Nibbāna with the Nibbāna element without remainder. 'In harmony' (samaggā) means inseparable in body. 'Rejoicing together' (sammodamānā) means being well-pleased and delighted in mind. 'Not quarreling' (avivadamānā) means not engaging in disputes with speech. 'Having become like milk and water' (khīrodakībhūtā) means like water mixed with milk.

Te ekato pakkhandantīti te bodhipakkhiyadhammā ekaṃ ārammaṇaṃ pavisanti. Pasīdantīti tasmiṃyeva ārammaṇe pasādamāpajjanti. Anupādisesāyāti upādivirahitāya.

'They enter together' (te ekato pakkhandanti) means those factors of enlightenment enter a single object. 'They become serene' (pasīdanti) means they attain serenity in that very object. 'Without remainder' (anupādisesāya) means devoid of any basis for renewed existence.

Nibbānadhātuyāti amatamahānibbānadhātuyā. Ūnattaṃ vāti ettha unabhāvo ūnattaṃ, aparipuṇṇabhāvoti attho. Puṇṇattaṃ vāti paripuṇṇabhāvo puṇṇattaṃ, puṇṇabhāvo vā na paññāyati natthīti attho.

'Of the Nibbāna element' (nibbānadhātuyā) means of the deathless, great Nibbāna element. 'Or deficiency' (ūnattaṃ vā): here, deficiency is the state of being deficient, meaning the state of being incomplete. 'Or fullness' (puṇṇattaṃ vā): fullness is the state of being complete; or, the state of fullness is not discerned, meaning it does not exist.

Nerayikānanti [V 0.0204] niraye nibbattanakakammānaṃ atthibhāvena. Nirayaṃ arahantīti nerayikā, tesaṃ nerayikānaṃ. Nirayo bhavananti nirayo eva tesaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gharaṃ. Tiracchānayonikānantiādīsupi eseva nayo. Tassesā sāmaggīti tassa khīṇāsavassa esā nibbānasāmaggī. Etaṃ channanti etaṃ anucchavikaṃ. Patirūpanti sadisaṃ paṭibhāgaṃ, asadisaṃ appaṭibhāgaṃ na hoti. Anucchavikanti etaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ vā dhammānaṃ, maggaphalanibbānasāsanadhammānaṃ vā anucchavikaṃ. Tesaṃ chaviṃ chāyaṃ sundarabhāvaṃ anveti anugacchati, atha kho santikāva tehi dhammehi anucchavikattā eva ca anulomaṃ. Tesañca anulometi, atha kho na vilomaṃ na paccanīkabhāve ṭhitaṃ.

“Those destined for hell” (nerayikānaṃ) means due to the existence of actions that cause rebirth in hell. They deserve hell, therefore they are called “those destined for hell” (nerayikā). “Hell is their dwelling” means hell itself is their dwelling place, their home. The same method applies to “those destined for the animal realm” (tiracchānayonikānaṃ), and so on. “This is his harmony” (tassesā sāmaggī) refers to the Nibbāna-harmony of that one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava). “This is suitable” (etaṃ channaṃ) means this is appropriate. “Suitable” (patirūpaṃ) means similar, a counterpart; it is not dissimilar, not an opposite part. “Suitable” (anucchavikaṃ) means it is suitable for the qualities of ascetics and brahmins, or for the Dhammas of the path, fruition, Nibbāna, and the dispensation. It follows their complexion, shade, and beauty; furthermore, being near to those Dhammas and because of its suitability, it is indeed in conformity. And it conforms to them; indeed, it does not stand in opposition or antagonism.

46. Idāni “yo attānaṃ bhavane na dassaye”ti evaṃ khīṇāsavo vibhāvito, tassa vaṇṇabhaṇanatthaṃ ito parā tisso gāthāyo āha. Tattha paṭhamagāthāya sabbatthāti dvādasasu āyatanesu. Na piyaṃ kubbati nopi appiyanti niddese piyāti citte pītikarā. Te vibhāgato dassento “katame sattā piyā, idha yassa te hontī”ti āha. Tattha yassa teti ye assa te. Hontīti bhavanti. Atthakāmāti vaḍḍhikāmā. Hitakāmāti sukhakāmā. Phāsukāmāti sukhavihārakāmā. Yogakkhemakāmāti catūhi yogehi khemaṃ nibbhayaṃ kāmā. Mamāyatīti [P 2.0258] mātā. Piyāyatīti pitā. Bhajatīti bhātā. Bhaginīti [M 0.0224] etthāpi eseva nayo. Puṃ tāyati rakkhatīti putto. Kulavaṃsaṃ dhāretīti dhītā. Mittā sahāyā. Amaccā bhaccā. Ñātī pitupakkhikā. Sālohitā mātipakkhikā. Ime sattā piyāti ime sattā pītijanakā. Vuttavipariyāyena appiyā veditabbā.

46. Now, the one whose taints are destroyed has been thus explained with the phrase “one who would not display oneself in any abode”; to speak his praise, three verses are stated hereafter. Therein, in the first verse, “everywhere” refers to the twelve bases. In the explanation of “neither makes dear nor undear,” “dear” means pleasing to the mind. Showing this by way of analysis, it is said: “Which beings are dear? Here, those who are his.” Therein, “those who are his” means those who belong to him. “They are” means they exist. “Desiring their welfare” (atthakāmā) means desiring their growth. “Desiring their benefit” (hitakāmā) means desiring their happiness. “Desiring their comfort” (phāsukāmā) means desiring their pleasant living. “Desiring their security from bondage” (yogakkhemakāmā) means desiring security and fearlessness from the four bonds. A “mother” (mātā) is one who regards as “mine” (mamāyati). A “father” (pitā) is one who is dear (piyāyati). A “brother” (bhātā) is one who associates (bhajati). For “sister” (bhaginī), the same method applies here. A “son” (putto) is one who protects (tāyati) from the hell named Puṃ. A “daughter” (dhītā) is one who upholds (dhāreti) the family lineage. “Friends” (mittā) are companions. “Ministers” (amaccā) are servants. “Relatives” (ñātī) are those on the father’s side. “Kin” (sālohitā) are those on the mother’s side. “These beings are dear” means these beings generate joy. The undear should be understood as the opposite of what has been said.

47. Yadidaṃ diṭṭhasutamutesu vāti ettha pana yadidaṃ diṭṭhasutaṃ, ettha vā mutesu vā dhammesu; evaṃ muni na upalimpatīti evaṃ sambandho veditabbo.

47. Here, regarding “Whatever is seen, heard, or sensed,” the connection should be understood in this way: the sage is not stained by whatever is seen and heard, or by phenomena that are sensed.

Udakathevoti udakassa thevo. “Udakatthevako”tipi pāṭho. Padumapatteti paduminipatte.

“A drop of water” (udakathevo) means a drop of water (udakassa thevo). There is also the reading “udakatthevako.” “On a lotus leaf” (padumapatte) means on a lotus-plant’s leaf (paduminipatte).

48. Dhono na hi tena maññati, yadidaṃ diṭṭhasutamutesu vāti atrāpi yadidaṃ diṭṭhasutaṃ, tena vatthunā na maññati, mutesu vā dhammesu na maññatīti evameva sambandho veditabbo. Na hi so rajjati, no virajjatīti bālaputhujjano viya na rajjati, kalyāṇaputhujjanasekkhā viya na virajjati, rāgassa khīṇattā “viratto”tveva saṅkhaṃ gacchati. Sesaṃ pākaṭamevāti.

48. Regarding “The cleansed one does not conceive by that, whatever is seen, heard, or sensed”: here too, the connection should be understood in this way: he does not conceive by that object which is seen or heard, nor does he conceive in regard to sensed phenomena. Regarding “He is not attached, nor is he becoming dispassionate”: he is not attached like a foolish worldling; he is not becoming dispassionate like virtuous worldlings and trainees. Because lust is destroyed, he is accounted as simply “dispassionate” (viratto). The rest is evident.

Tāya [V 0.0205] paññāya kāyaduccaritanti sampayuttāya pubbabhāgāyeva vā paññāya pariggahetabbe pariggaṇhanto yogī tividhaṃ kāyaduccaritaṃ samucchedavasena dhunāti. Ayañca puggalo vipannadhammaṃ desanādhammesu dhunantesu taṃdhammasamaṅgīpuggalopi dhunāti nāma. Te ca dhamme paññāya attano pavattikkhaṇe dhunitumāraddho dhutāti vuccati, yathā bhuñjitumāraddho bhuttoti vuccati. Lakkhaṇaṃ panettha saddasatthato veditabbaṃ. Dhutanti kattusādhanaṃ. Dhutaṃ paṭhamamaggena. Dhotaṃ dutiyamaggena. Sandhotaṃ tatiyamaggena. Niddhotaṃ catutthamaggena.

Regarding “by that wisdom, bodily misconduct”: the yogi, grasping what is to be grasped with wisdom that is associated with it or even preliminary to it, shakes off the threefold bodily misconduct by way of eradication. And this person, in shaking off corrupt qualities according to the teachings, is also said to shake off the individual endowed with those qualities. And when he has begun to shake off those qualities with wisdom at the moment of their arising, he is called “shaken off” (dhuta), just as one who has begun to eat is called “having eaten” (bhutto).
