Here, the grammatical form should be understood from the science of words. “Shaken off” (dhuta) is an agentive derivation. Defilements are “shaken off” (dhutaṃ) by the first path, “washed” (dhotaṃ) by the second path, “thoroughly washed” (sandhotaṃ) by the third path, and “completely cleansed” (niddhotaṃ) by the fourth path.

Dhono diṭṭhaṃ na maññatīti arahā maṃsacakkhunā diṭṭhaṃ [P 2.0259] dibbacakkhunā diṭṭhaṃ rūpāyatanaṃ na maññati tīhi maññanāhi, kathaṃ? Rūpāyatanaṃ subhasaññāya sukhasaññāya ca passanto na tattha chandarāgaṃ janeti na taṃ assādeti nābhinandati, evaṃ diṭṭhaṃ taṇhāmaññanāya na maññati. “Iti me rūpaṃ siyā anāgatamaddhāna”nti vā panettha nandiṃ na samannāneti. Rūpasampadaṃ vā ākaṅkhamāno dānaṃ na deti, sīlaṃ na samādiyati, uposathakammaṃ na karoti. Evampi [M 0.0225] diṭṭhaṃ taṇhāmaññanāya na maññati, attano pana parassa ca rūpasampattivipattiṃ nissāya mānaṃ na janeti. “Imināhaṃ seyyosmīti vā, sadisosmīti vā, hīnosmīti vā”ti evaṃ diṭṭhaṃ mānamaññanāya na maññati. Rūpāyatanaṃ pana “niccaṃ dhuvaṃ sassata”nti na maññati. Attānaṃ “attaniya”nti na maññati. Maṅgalaṃ “amaṅgala”nti na maññati. Evaṃ diṭṭhaṃ diṭṭhimaññanāya na maññati. Diṭṭhasmiṃ na maññatīti rūpasmiṃ attānaṃ samanupassananayena amaññanto diṭṭhasmiṃ na maññati. Yathā vā thane thaññaṃ, evaṃ rūpasmiṃ rāgādayoti amaññantopi diṭṭhasmiṃ na maññati. Tasmiṃyeva panassa diṭṭhimaññanāya amaññite vatthusmiṃ sinehaṃ mānañca na uppādayato taṇhāmānamaññanāpi natthīti veditabbā. Evaṃ diṭṭhasmiṃ na maññati. Diṭṭhato na maññatīti ettha pana diṭṭhatoti nissakkavacanaṃ. Tasmā saupakāraṇassa attano vā parassa vā yathāvuttappabhedato diṭṭhato upapatti vā niggamanaṃ vā diṭṭhato vā añño attāti amaññamāno diṭṭhato na maññatīti veditabbo. Ayamassa na diṭṭhimaññanā. Tasmiṃyeva panassa diṭṭhimaññanāya amaññite vatthusmiṃ sinehaṃ mānañca na uppādayato na taṇhāmānamaññanāpi veditabbā.

“The cleansed one does not conceive the seen”: the Arahant does not conceive the form-base seen with the fleshly eye or seen with the divine eye by the three kinds of conceiving. How? Seeing the form-base with the perception of beauty and the perception of pleasure, he does not generate desire and lust for it, does not relish it, does not delight in it; thus, he does not conceive the seen by the conceiving of craving. He does not bring forth delight in it, thinking, “May such form be mine in the future.” Or, desiring the attainment of form, he does not give gifts, does not undertake the moral precepts, does not perform the Uposatha observance. In this way too, he does not conceive the seen by the conceiving of craving. Furthermore, based on the success or failure regarding form for himself or others, he does not generate conceit, thinking, “By this I am better,” or “I am equal,” or “I am inferior.” Thus, he does not conceive the seen by the conceiving of conceit. Furthermore, he does not conceive the form-base as “permanent, stable, eternal.” He does not conceive a self or “what belongs to self.” He does not conceive an auspicious sign as an inauspicious one. Thus, he does not conceive the seen by the conceiving of views. “He does not conceive in the seen” means that, by not regarding a self in form, he does not conceive in the seen. Or, just as there is no milk in a cow’s horn, so too, by not conceiving that lust and so on are in form, he does not conceive in the seen. Moreover, it should be understood that in that very object where, for him, the conceiving of views does not occur, since he does not produce affection and conceit, the conceiving of craving and the conceiving of conceit are also absent. Thus, he does not conceive in the seen. “He does not conceive from the seen”: here, “from the seen” is an ablative expression. Therefore, it should be understood that he does not conceive from the seen by not conceiving that for oneself or another, with its basis, according to the distinctions mentioned, there is an arising from the seen or a departure from the seen, or that self is other than the seen. This is his non-conceiving of views. Moreover, it should be understood that in that very object where, for him, the conceiving of views does not occur, since he does not produce affection and conceit, the conceiving of craving and the conceiving of conceit are also absent.

Diṭṭhā meti na maññatīti ettha pana “etaṃ mamā”ti taṇhāvasena amamāyamāno diṭṭhaṃ taṇhāmaññanāya na maññati. Sutanti [P 2.0260] maṃsasotenapi sutaṃ, dibbasotenapi sutaṃ, saddāyatanassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Mutanti mutvā munitvā ca gahitaṃ āhacca upagantvāti attho. Indriyānaṃ ārammaṇānañca aññamaññaṃ saṃkilese viññātanti vuttaṃ hoti. Gandharasaphoṭṭhabbāyatanānaṃ [V 0.0206] etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Viññātanti manasā viññātaṃ, sesānaṃ sattānaṃ āyatanānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ, dhammārammaṇassa vā, idha pana sakkāyapariyāpannameva labbhati. Vitthāro panettha diṭṭhavāre vuttanayena veditabbo.

Regarding “He does not conceive, ‘It is seen by me’”: here, by not making it “mine” through craving, he does not conceive of the seen by the conceiving of craving. “Heard” refers to what is heard by the fleshly ear as well as what is heard by the divine ear; this is a designation for the sound-base. “Sensed” means grasped by having sensed and known; the meaning is “having encountered and approached.” It is said to be what is cognized in the mutual conjunction of the sense faculties and their objects. This is a designation for the smell, taste, and touch bases. “Cognized” refers to what is cognized by the mind; this is a designation for the remaining sense bases of beings, or for the mental object. Here, however, only what is included in the personal identity is meant. The detailed explanation here should be understood in the same way as stated in the section on the seen.

Idāni bhagavatā vuttasuttavasena dassento “asmīti bhikkhave”tiādimāha. Tattha asmīti bhavāmi, niccassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Maññitametanti diṭṭhikappanaṃ etaṃ. Ayamahamasmīti ayaṃ ahaṃ asmi bhavāmi.

Now, showing this by way of a sutta spoken by the Blessed One, the commentator says, “‘Monks, “I am”’ and so on. Therein, ‘I am’ means I exist; this is a designation for permanence. ‘This is a conceiving’ means this is a fabrication of view. ‘This I am’ means this is ‘I am,’ I exist.

Aññatra satipaṭṭhānehīti ṭhapetvā catusatipaṭṭhāne.

“Apart from the foundations of mindfulness” means setting aside the four foundations of mindfulness.

Sabbe bālaputhujjanā rajjantīti sakalā andhabālā nānājanā lagganti. Satta sekkhā virajjantīti sotāpannādayo satta ariyajanā virāgaṃ āpajjanti[M 0.0226]. Arahā neva rajjati no virajjatīti kilesānaṃ parinibbāpitattā ubhayampi na karoti. Khayā rāgassātiādayo tividhāpi nibbānameva.

‘All foolish worldlings are attached’ means all blind, ignorant people cling to various things. ‘The seven trainees are dispassionate’ means the seven noble ones, beginning with stream-enterers, attain dispassion. ‘The Arahant neither clings nor is dispassionate’ means because the defilements have been completely extinguished, he does neither. ‘With the destruction of lust,’ and so on, all three are simply Nibbāna.

Saddhammappajjotikāya mahāniddesaṭṭhakathāya

The Saddhammappajjotikā, the Commentary on the Mahāniddesa.

Jarāsuttaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Jarāsutta Niddesa is concluded.

7. Tissametteyyasuttaniddesavaṇṇanā

7. The Explanation of the Tissametteyya Sutta Niddesa

49. Sattame [V 0.0207][P 2.0261] tissametteyyasutte methunamanuyuttassāti methunadhammaṃ samāyuttassa. Itīti evamāha. Āyasmāti piyavacanametaṃ. Tissoti nāmaṃ tassa therassa. Sopi hi tissoti nāmena. Metteyyoti gottaṃ, gottavaseneva esa pākaṭo ahosi. Tasmā aṭṭhuppattiyaṃ (su. ni. aṭṭha. 2.821) vuttaṃ – “tissametteyyā nāma dve sahāyā”ti. Vighātanti upaghātaṃ. Brūhīti ācikkha. Mārisāti piyavacanametaṃ, niddukkhāti vuttaṃ hoti. Sutvāna tava sāsananti tava vacanaṃ sutvā. Viveke sikkhissāmaseti sahāyaṃ ārabbha dhammadesanaṃ yācanto bhaṇati, so pana sikkhitasikkhoyeva.

49. In the seventh Tissametteyya Sutta, ‘one devoted to sexual intercourse’ (methunamanuyuttassa) means one associated with sexual activity (methunadhammaṃ samāyuttassa). ‘Iti’ (thus) means he said thus. ‘Āyasmā’ (Venerable) is a term of endearment. ‘Tissa’ is the name of that elder; for he too was known by the name Tissa. ‘Metteyya’ is the clan name; he became well-known by his clan name alone. Therefore, in the Aṭṭhuppatti (SnA 2.821), it is said: ‘Tissa and Metteyya were two friends.’ ‘Vighāta’ means ‘upaghāta’ (harm). ‘Brūhi’ (tell) means ‘ācikkha’ (relate). ‘Mārisa’ (dear sir) is a term of endearment; it means ‘niddukkha’ (free from suffering). ‘Having heard your teaching’ (sutvāna tava sāsanaṃ) means having heard your words (tava vacanaṃ sutvā). ‘We will train in seclusion’ (viveke sikkhissāmase) – he speaks thus, requesting a teaching of the Dhamma from his friend, though he himself was already well-trained.

Methunadhammo nāmāti idaṃ niddisitabbassa methunadhammassa upadesapadaṃ. Asaddhammoti asataṃ nīcajanānaṃ dhammo. Gāmadhammoti gāmavāsīnaṃ sevanadhammo. Vasaladhammoti vasalānaṃ dhammo, kilesavassanato vā sayameva vasalo dhammoti vasaladhammo. Duṭṭhulloti duṭṭho ca kilesehi duṭṭhattā, thūlo ca anipuṇabhāvatoti duṭṭhullo. Yasmā ca tassa dhammassa parivārabhūtaṃ dassanampi gahaṇampi āmasanampi phusanampi ghaṭṭanampi duṭṭhullaṃ, tasmāpi duṭṭhullo so methunadhammo. Odakantikoti udakaṃ assa ante suddhatthaṃ ādiyatīti udakanto, udakantoyeva odakantiko. Raho paṭicchanne okāse kattabbatāya rahasso. Vinaye pana “duṭṭhullaṃ odakantikaṃ rahassa”nti (pārā. 39) pāṭho. Tattha tīsu padesu yo soti padaṃ parivattetvā yaṃ tanti [P 2.0262] katvā yojetabbaṃ “yaṃ taṃ duṭṭhullaṃ, so methunadhammo, yaṃ taṃ odakantikaṃ so methunadhammo, yaṃ taṃ rahassaṃ[M 0.0227], so methunadhammo”ti. Idha pana “yo so asaddhammo, so methunadhammo…pe… yo so rahasso, so methunadhammo”ti evaṃ yojanā veditabbā. Dvayena dvayena samāpajjitabbato dvayaṃdvayasamāpatti. Tattha yojanā – yā sā dvayaṃdvayasamāpatti, so methunadhammo nāmāti. Kiṃkāraṇā vuccati methunadhammoti kena kāraṇena kena pariyāyena methunadhammoti kathīyati. Taṃ kāraṇaṃ dassento “ubhinnaṃ rattāna”ntiādimāha. Tattha ubhinnaṃ rattānanti [V 0.0208] dvinnaṃ itthipurisānaṃ rāgena rañjitānaṃ. Sārattānanti visesena suṭṭhu rañjitānaṃ. Avassutānanti kilesena tintānaṃ. Pariyuṭṭhitānanti kusalācāraṃ pariyādiyitvā madditvā ṭhitānaṃ “magge corā pariyuṭṭhitā”tiādīsu viya. Pariyādinnacittānanti kusalacittaṃ pariyādiyitvā khepetvā ṭhitacittānaṃ. Ubhinnaṃ sadisānanti dvinnaṃ kilesena sadisānaṃ. Dhammoti sabhāvo. Taṃ kāraṇāti tena kāraṇena. Taṃ upamāya sādhento “ubho kalahakārakā”tiādimāha. Tattha ubho kalahakārakāti pubbabhāge kalahakārakā dve. Methunakāti vuccantīti sadisāti vuccanti. Bhaṇḍanakārakāti tattha tattha gantvā bhaṇḍanaṃ karontā. Bhassakārakāti vācākalahaṃ karontā. Vivādakārakāti nānāvacanaṃ karontā. Adhikaraṇakārakāti vinicchayapāpuṇanavisesakāraṇaṃ karontā. Vādinoti vādapaṭivādino. Sallāpakāti vācaṃ kathentā evamevanti upamāsaṃsandanaṃ.

‘Methunadhamma’ (sexual intercourse) is the word indicating the sexual intercourse to be defined. ‘Asaddhamma’ (unwholesome conduct) means the conduct of ignoble, base people. ‘Gāmadhamma’ (village conduct) refers to conduct frequented by villagers. ‘Vasaladhamma’ (outcaste conduct) means the conduct of outcastes, or because it is defiled by defilements, the conduct itself is an outcaste, hence ‘vasaladhamma’. ‘Duṭṭhulla’ (obscene) means both corrupted—because it is corrupted by defilements—and coarse—due to its unrefined nature, hence ‘duṭṭhulla’. Moreover, because even the acts associated with that conduct—such as seeing, taking hold of, stroking, touching, or rubbing—are obscene, therefore, that sexual intercourse is also called ‘duṭṭhulla’ (obscene). ‘Odakantika’ (water’s edge) refers to one who takes water at the edge for purification, hence ‘udakanta’; ‘udakanta’ itself is ‘odakantika’. ‘Rahassa’ (secret) means it should be done in a concealed, private place. In the Vinaya, however, the reading is: ‘duṭṭhullaṃ odakantikaṃ rahassaṃ’ (Pārā. 39). There, in the three instances, the word ‘yo so’ should be transformed into ‘yaṃ taṃ,’ and it should be construed as: ‘Whatever is obscene, that is sexual intercourse; whatever is water’s edge, that is sexual intercourse; whatever is secret, that is sexual intercourse.’ Here, however, the construction should be understood as: ‘Whatever is unwholesome conduct, that is sexual intercourse… whatever is secret, that is sexual intercourse.’ ‘Dvayaṃdvayasamāpatti’ (two-by-two engagement) refers to the fact that it is engaged in two-by-two. There, the construction is: ‘Whatever is two-by-two engagement, that is called ‘methunadhamma’ (sexual intercourse).’ ‘For what reason is it called sexual intercourse?’ (kiṃkāraṇā vuccati methunadhammo) – by what reason or manner is it spoken of as ‘methunadhamma’? To explain that reason, he says: ‘When both are impassioned’ (ubhinnaṃ rattānaṃ), and so forth. There, ‘ubhinnaṃ rattānaṃ’ means when both the man and woman are colored by passion. ‘Sārattānaṃ’ (very impassioned) means they are especially and thoroughly colored. ‘Avassutānaṃ’ (drenched) means they are saturated by defilements. ‘Pariyuṭṭhitānaṃ’ (beset) means they are beset, having overcome and crushed wholesome conduct, as in phrases such as ‘thieves beset the road’. ‘Pariyādinnacittānaṃ’ (with minds encompassed) means their wholesome minds are encompassed, destroyed, and fixed. ‘Ubhinnaṃ sadisānaṃ’ (similar) means the two are similar in defilement. ‘Dhamma’ means inherent state. ‘Taṃ kāraṇa’ (for that reason) means because of that reason. Confirming this with a simile, he says: ‘Both are quarrel-makers’ (ubho kalahakārakā), and so forth. There, ‘ubho kalahakārakā’ means the two are quarrel-makers from the beginning. ‘Methunakā’ (those who engage in sexual intercourse) means they are said to be similar. ‘Bhaṇḍanakārakā’ (disputers) means they go about making disputes here and there. ‘Bhassakārakā’ (brawlers) means they make verbal disputes. ‘Vivādakārakā’ (contenders) means they make various statements. ‘Adhikaraṇakārakā’ (those who cause legal disputes) means they create a special cause for reaching a judgment. ‘Vādino’ (debaters) means those who debate and counter-debate. ‘Sallāpakā’ (conversers) means those who speak words; thus is the connection of the simile.

Yuttassāti saññuttassa. Payuttassāti ādarena yuttassa. Āyuttassāti visesena yuttassa. Samāyuttassāti ekato yuttassa. Taccaritassāti taṃcaritaṃ karontassa. Tabbahulassāti taṃbahulaṃ karontassa. Taggarukassāti taṃgaruṃ karontassa. Tanninnassāti tasmiṃ natacittassa. Tappoṇassāti tasmiṃ natakāyassa. Tappabbhārassāti [P 2.0263] tasmiṃ abhimukhakāyassa. Tadadhimuttassāti tasmiṃ adhiharitassa. Tadadhipateyyassāti taṃ adhipatiṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā pavattassa.

‘Yuttassa’ means ‘saññutta’ (connected). ‘Payuttassa’ means ‘ādarena yutta’ (diligently connected). ‘Āyuttassa’ means ‘visesena yutta’ (especially connected). ‘Samāyuttassa’ means ‘ekato yutta’ (connected together). ‘Taccaritassa’ means one who performs that action (‘taṃcaritaṃ karonta’). ‘Tabbahulassa’ means one who frequently does that (‘taṃbahulaṃ karonta’). ‘Taggarukassa’ means one who regards that as weighty (‘taṃgaruṃ karonta’). ‘Tanninnassa’ means one whose mind is inclined to that (‘tasmiṃ natacitta’). ‘Tappoṇassa’ means one whose body is inclined to that (‘tasmiṃ natakāya’). ‘Tappabbhārassa’ means one whose body is directed to that (‘tasmiṃ abhimukhakāya’). ‘Tadadhimuttassa’ means one who is resolved on that (‘tasmiṃ adhiharita’). ‘Tadadhipateyyassa’ means one who proceeds making that the dominant factor (‘taṃ adhipatiṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā pavatta’).

Vighātanti niddesassa uddesavacanaṃ. Vighātanti pīḷanaṃ. Upaghātanti samīpaṃ katvā pīḷanaṃ. Pīḷananti ghaṭṭanaṃ. Ghaṭṭananti pīḷanaṃ. Sabbaṃ aññamaññavevacanaṃ. Upaddavanti hiṃsanaṃ. Upasagganti tattha tattha upagantvā pīḷanākāraṃ. Brūhīti kathehi. Ācikkhāti [M 0.0228] vissajjehi. Desehīti dassehi. Paññapehīti ñāpehi. Paṭṭhapehīti ṭhapehi. Vivarāti pākaṭaṃ karohi. Vibhajāti bhājehi. Uttānīkarohīti tīraṃ pāpehi. Pakāsehīti pākaṭaṃ karohi.

‘Vighāta’ is the statement of the subject for the exposition. ‘Vighāta’ means ‘pīḷana’ (affliction). ‘Upaghāta’ means ‘samīpaṃ katvā pīḷana’ (afflicting by coming close). ‘Pīḷana’ means ‘ghaṭṭana’ (rubbing). ‘Ghaṭṭana’ means ‘pīḷana’ (affliction). All these are synonyms for each other. ‘Upaddava’ means ‘hiṃsana’ (injuring). ‘Upasagga’ means a mode of affliction by approaching here and there (‘tattha tattha upagantvā pīḷanākāraṃ’). ‘Brūhi’ means ‘kathehi’ (speak). ‘Ācikkha’ means ‘vissajjehi’ (declare). ‘Desehi’ means ‘dassehi’ (point out). ‘Paññapehi’ means ‘ñāpehi’ (make known). ‘Paṭṭhapehi’ means ‘ṭhapehi’ (establish). ‘Vivara’ means ‘pākaṭaṃ karohi’ (make open). ‘Vibhaja’ means ‘bhājehi’ (distinguish). ‘Uttānīkarohi’ means ‘tīraṃ pāpehi’ (bring to the shore). ‘Pakāsehi’ means ‘pākaṭaṃ karohi’ (make manifest).

Tuyhaṃ vacananti tava vācaṃ. Byappathanti vacanaṃ. Desananti ācikkhanaṃ. Anusāsananti ovādaṃ. Anusiṭṭhanti anusāsanaṃ. Sutvāti sotena sutvā. Suṇitvāti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Uggahetvāti sammā gahetvā. Upadhārayitvāti anāsetvā. Upalakkhayitvāti sallakkhetvā.

‘Tuyhaṃ vacanaṃ’ (your speech) means ‘tava vācaṃ’ (your words). ‘Byappatha’ means ‘vacana’ (speech). ‘Desana’ means ‘ācikkhana’ (teaching). ‘Anusāsana’ means ‘ovāda’ (advice). ‘Anusiṭṭhi’ means ‘anusāsana’ (instruction). ‘Sutvā’ means ‘sotena sutvā’ (having heard with the ear). ‘Suṇitvā’ is another word for the same. ‘Uggahetvā’ means ‘sammā gahetvā’ (having rightly grasped). ‘Upadhārayitvā’ means ‘anāsetvā’ (having retained). ‘Upalakkhayitvā’ means ‘sallakkhetvā’ (having noticed).

50. Mussate vāpi sāsananti pariyattipaṭipattito duvidhampi sāsanaṃ nassati. Vāpīti padapūraṇamattaṃ. Etaṃ tasmiṃ anariyanti tasmiṃ puggale etaṃ anariyaṃ, yadidaṃ micchāpaṭipadā. Gāravādhivacananti guṇavisiṭṭhasabbasattuttamagarugāravādhivacanaṃ. Tenāhu porāṇā –

50. ‘Mussate vāpi sāsanaṃ’ (the teaching is lost) means the twofold teaching—both textual learning (pariyatti) and practice (paṭipatti)—is lost. ‘Vāpi’ is merely a particle for filling out the verse. ‘Etaṃ tasmiṃ anariyaṃ’ (this is ignoble in him) means in that person, this is ignoble, that is, wrong practice (micchāpaṭipadā). ‘Gāravādhivacana’ means a term of reverence for the Teacher, who is supreme among all beings and endowed with excellent qualities. Therefore, the ancients said:

“Bhagavāti [V 0.0209] vacanaṃ seṭṭhaṃ, bhagavāti vacanamuttamaṃ;

Garu gāravayutto so, bhagavā tena vuccatī”ti. (visuddhi. 1.142);

‘The word “Blessed One” (Bhagavā) is the best, the word “Blessed One” is supreme; He is venerable and endowed with reverence, therefore he is called “Blessed One.”’ (Vism. 1.142)

Catubbidhaṃ vā nāmaṃ āvatthikaṃ, liṅgikaṃ, nemittikaṃ, adhiccasamuppannanti. Adhiccasamuppannaṃ nāma lokiyavohārena “yadicchaka”nti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha vaccho, dammo, balībaddhoti evamādi āvatthikaṃ, daṇḍī, chattī, sikhī, karīti evamādi liṅgikaṃ, tevijjo, chaḷabhiññoti evamādi nemittikaṃ, sirivaḍḍhako, dhanavaḍḍhakoti evamādi [P 2.0264] vacanatthaṃ anapekkhitvā pavattaṃ adhiccasamuppannaṃ. Idaṃ pana bhagavāti nāmaṃ nemittikaṃ, na mahāmāyāya, na suddhodanamahārājena, na asītiyā ñātisahassehi kataṃ, na sakkasantusitādīhi devatāvisesehi kataṃ. Vakkhati ca “bhagavāti netaṃ nāmaṃ mātarā kataṃ…pe… paṭilābhā sacchikā paññatti yadidaṃ bhagavā”ti (mahāni. 84).

Names are fourfold: ‘āvatthika’ (based on occasion), ‘liṅgika’ (based on characteristic), ‘nemittika’ (based on sign), and ‘adhiccasamuppanna’ (arbitrarily arisen). The arbitrarily arisen name is called ‘yadicchaka’ (according to wish) in worldly speech. Here, names like ‘vaccha’ (calf), ‘damma’ (untamed one), and ‘balībadda’ (ox) are ‘āvatthika’. Names like ‘daṇḍī’ (staff-bearer), ‘chattī’ (umbrella-bearer), ‘sikhī’ (crested one), and ‘karī’ (elephant) are ‘liṅgika’. Names like ‘tevijja’ (one with threefold knowledge) and ‘chaḷabhiñña’ (one with sixfold direct knowledges) are ‘nemittika’. Names like Sirivaḍḍhaka and Dhanavaḍḍhaka arise arbitrarily (‘adhiccasamuppanna’), without regard for the meaning of the word. But this name ‘Bhagavā’ (Blessed One) is ‘nemittika’ (based on sign); it was not given by Mahāmāyā, nor by King Suddhodana, nor by eighty thousand relatives, nor by distinguished deities like Sakka or Santusita. And it will be said, ‘The name “Bhagavā” was not given by his mother… It is an attainment, a realization, a designation—that is, “Bhagavā.”’ (MhN 84)

“Bhāgyavā bhaggavā yutto, bhagehi ca vibhattavā;

Bhattavā vantagamano, bhavesu bhagavā tato”ti. (visuddhi. 1.144);

He is fortunate (bhāgyavā), has broken (defilements) (bhaggavā), is endowed with fortunes (bhagehi yutto), and has analyzed (dhammas) (vibhattavā); he has frequented (noble states) (bhattavā), and has abandoned going in existences (vantagamano bhavesu); therefore, he is the Bhagavā.

Tattha –

Here—

“Vaṇṇāgamo vaṇṇavipariyāyo, dve cāpare vaṇṇavikāranāsā;

Dhātūnamatthātisayena yogo, taduccate pañcavidhaṃ nirutti”nti. –

‘The insertion of a letter (vaṇṇāgama), the transposition of a letter (vaṇṇavipariyāya), and two others—the alteration (vaṇṇavikāra) and elision (vaṇṇanāsa) of a letter; the connection of roots with intensified meaning (dhātūnamatthātisayena yogo)—this is called the fivefold etymology (pañcavidhaṃ nirutti).’

Evaṃ [M 0.0229] vuttaniruttilakkhaṇaṃ gahetvā padasiddhi veditabbā. Tattha “nakkhattarājāriva tārakāna”nti ettha rakārāgamo viya avijjamānassa akkharassa āgamo vaṇṇāgamo nāma. “Hiṃsanā, hiṃso”ti vattabbe “sīho”ti viya vijjamānakkharānaṃ heṭṭhupariyavasena parivattanaṃ vaṇṇavipariyāyo nāma. “Nave channake dānaṃ diyyatī”ti ettha akārassa ekārāpajjanatā viya aññakkharassa aññakkharāpajjanatā vaṇṇavikāro nāma. “Jīvanassa mūto jīvanamūto”ti vattabbe “jīmūto”ti vakāranakārānaṃ vināso viya vijjamānakkharavināso vaṇṇavināso nāma. “Pharusāhi vācāhi pakrubbamāno āsajja maṃ tvaṃ vadasi kumārā”ti ettha pakrubbamānoti padassa abhibhavamānoti atthapaṭipādanaṃ viya tattha tattha yathāyogaṃ visesatthayogo dhātūnaṃ atthātisayena yogo nāma.

Having grasped the characteristics of such stated etymology, the formation of words should be understood. Here, in the phrase ‘nakkhattarājāriva tārakānaṃ’ (like the king of stars among the stars), the insertion of the letter ‘ra’—like the insertion of a non-existent letter—is called ‘vaṇṇāgama’ (letter insertion). In the case where ‘hiṃsanā, hiṃso’ should be said, but ‘sīho’ (lion) is used instead—like the transformation of existing letters by their lower and upper forms—is called ‘vaṇṇavipariyāya’ (letter transposition). In the phrase ‘nave channake dānaṃ diyyatī’ (a gift is given to a new roof), the change of the letter ‘a’ to ‘e’—like the substitution of one letter for another—is called ‘vaṇṇavikāra’ (letter alteration). Where ‘jīvanassa mūto jīvanamūto’ (dead of life, dead from life) should be said, but ‘jīmūto’ (cloud) is used—like the omission of the letters ‘va’ and ‘na’—the loss of existing letters is called ‘vaṇṇavināsa’ (letter elision). In the phrase ‘pharusāhi vācāhi pakrubbamāno āsajja maṃ tvaṃ vadasi kumārā’ (you speak to me, young man, assailing me with harsh words, being angry), the interpretation of the word ‘pakrubbamāno’ as ‘abhibhavamāno’ (overpowering)—like the appropriate application of special meaning to roots here and there—is called ‘dhātūnaṃ atthātisayena yogo’ (the connection of roots with intensified meaning).

Evaṃ [V 0.0210] niruttilakkhaṇaṃ gahetvā saddanayena vā pisodarādinissito patiṭṭhānīti pisodarādipakkhepalakkhaṇaṃ gahetvā yasmā lokiyalokuttarasukhābhinibbattakaṃ [P 2.0265] dānasīlādipārappattaṃ bhāgyamassa atthi, tasmā “bhāgyavā”ti vattabbe “bhagavā”ti vuccatīti ñātabbaṃ.

Having grasped the characteristic of etymology in this way, or having grasped the characteristic of inclusion in the pisodarādi group of irregular formations, it should be understood that since he possesses the fortune that produces worldly and supramundane happiness, perfected through giving, virtue, and so forth, when he should be called 'bhāgyavā' (fortunate one), he is called 'Bhagavā'.

Yasmā pana lobhadosamohaviparītamanasikāraahirikānottappakodhūpanāhamakkhapaḷāsaissā- macchariyamāyāsāṭheyyathambhasārambhamānātimānamadapamādataṇhāavijjātividhākusalamūladuccarita- saṃkilesamalavisamasaññāvitakkapapañcacatubbidhavipariyesaāsavaganthaoghayogaagati- taṇhuppādupādānapañcacetokhīlavinibandhanīvaraṇābhinandanachavivādamūlataṇhākāyasattānusaya- aṭṭhamicchattanavataṇhāmūlakadasākusalakammapathadvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhigataaṭṭhasatataṇhāvicaritappabhesabbadaratha- pariḷāhakilesasatasahassāni, saṅkhepato vā pañca kilesakhandhaabhisaṅkhāradevaputtamaccumāre abhañji, tasmā bhaggattā etesaṃ parissayānaṃ “bhaggavā”ti vattabbe “bhagavā”ti vuccati. Āha cettha –

Since he has shattered greed, hatred, and delusion, distorted attention, lack of shame and fear of wrongdoing, anger, resentment, hypocrisy, envy, stinginess, deception, dishonesty, obstinacy, rivalry, arrogance, excessive pride, intoxication, negligence, craving, ignorance, the three unwholesome roots, misconduct, defilements, impurities, wrong perceptions, proliferating thoughts, the four inversions, the influxes, the bonds, the floods, the yokes, wrong paths, the arising of craving, clinging, the five mental barrennesses, the ties, the hindrances, delight in disputes, the body of craving, the seven latent tendencies, the eight wrongnesses, the nine cravings rooted in craving, the ten unwholesome courses of action, the sixty-two wrong views, the hundred and eight cravings, various kinds of torments, burnings, and defilements, even hundreds of thousands of them—or in brief, the five aggregates of defilement, and the Māras of formations, the divine son, and death—therefore, because he has shattered these dangers, when he should be called 'bhaggavā' (one who has shattered), he is called 'Bhagavā.' Here it is said:

“Bhaggarāgo bhaggadoso, bhaggamoho anāsavo;

Bhaggāssa pāpakā dhammā, bhagavā tena vuccatī”ti. (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.96; visuddhi. 1.144);

Lust shattered, hatred shattered, delusion shattered, without taints; His evil qualities are shattered, therefore he is called 'Bhagavā.'

Bhāgyavantatāya cassa satapuññajalakkhaṇavarassa rūpakāyasampatti dīpitā hoti. Bhaggadosatāya dhammakāyasampatti. Tathā lokiyasarikkhakānaṃ bahumatabhāvo[M 0.0230], gahaṭṭhapabbajitehi abhigamanīyatā, abhigatānañca nesaṃ kāyacittadukkhāpanayane paṭibalabhāvo, āmisadānadhammadānehi upakāritā, lokiyalokuttarasukhehi ca saññojanasamatthatā dīpitā hoti.

By his fortune, the perfection of his physical form adorned with the one hundred marks of merit is revealed. By the shattering of defilements, the perfection of his Dhamma-body is shown. Likewise, his high esteem among worldly people, his worthiness of being approached by both householders and renunciates, his ability to relieve the physical and mental suffering of those who approach him, his beneficence through material gifts and Dhamma gifts, and his capacity to connect people with both worldly and supramundane happiness are all revealed.

Yasmā ca loke issariyadhammayasasirikāmapayattesu chasu dhammesu bhagasaddo pavattati, paramañcassa sakacitte issariyaṃ, aṇimālaṅghimādikaṃ vā lokiyasammataṃ sabbākāraparipūraṃ atthi, tathā lokuttaro dhammo, lokattayabyāpako yathābhuccaguṇādhigato ativiya parisuddho yaso, rūpakāyadassanabyāvaṭajananayanappasādajananasamatthā sabbākāraparipūrā sabbaṅgapaccaṅgasirī, yaṃ yaṃ etena icchitaṃ patthitaṃ attahitaṃ parahitaṃ vā, tassa tassa tatheva abhinipphannattā [P 2.0266] icchiticchitatthanipphattisaññito kāmo, sabbalokagarubhāvappattihetubhūto sammāvāyāmasaṅkhāto payatto ca atthi, tasmā imehi bhagehi yuttattāpi bhagā assa santīti iminā atthena “bhagavā”ti vuccati.

Moreover, since the term 'bhaga' is used in the world concerning six things—sovereignty, Dhamma, fame, beauty, pleasure, and exertion—and because he possesses supreme sovereignty over his own mind, along with worldly accepted perfections such as the powers of minuteness, lightness, and so forth, and because he possesses the supramundane Dhamma, which pervades the three worlds, is attained through truly existing qualities, is exceedingly pure fame, and because his physical form, when seen, is capable of generating delight in the eyes of people, being perfect in every way with all limbs and features radiant beauty—whatever he wishes or aspires to, whether for his own welfare or that of others, comes to fruition exactly as intended—thus, he possesses pleasure that brings about the fruition of intended aims. Because he is the cause of attaining reverence from the entire world and is endowed with right effort, called 'payatta,' therefore, being endowed with these 'bhagas,' he is called 'Bhagavā' in this sense as well.

Yasmā [V 0.0211] pana kusalādīhi bhedehi sabbadhamme, khandhāyatanadhātusaccaindriyapaṭiccasamuppādādīhi vā kusalādidhamme, pīḷanasaṅkhatasantāpavipariṇāmaṭṭhena vā dukkhamariyasaccaṃ, āyūhananidānasaṃyogapalibodhaṭṭhena samudayaṃ, nissaraṇavivekāsaṅkhataamataṭṭhena nirodhaṃ, niyyānikahetudassanādhipateyyaṭṭhena maggaṃ vibhattavā, vibhajitvā vivaritvā desitavāti vuttaṃ hoti, tasmā “vibhattavā”ti vattabbe “bhagavā”ti vuccati.

Since he has analyzed, explained, and taught all phenomena—whether classified by divisions such as wholesome or otherwise, or by wholesome phenomena such as aggregates, sense bases, elements, truths, faculties, dependent origination, and so forth; or by defining the Noble Truth of Suffering as having the characteristic of oppression, conditioned distress, and change; the Truth of Origin as having the characteristic of accumulation, cause, connection, and encumbrance; the Truth of Cessation as having the characteristic of escape, detachment, the unconditioned, and the deathless; and the Path as having the characteristic of leading forth, cause, vision, and supremacy—therefore, when he should be called 'vibhattavā' (the Analyzer), he is called 'Bhagavā.'

Yasmā ca esa dibbabrahmaariyavihāre kāyacittaupadhiviveke suññatappaṇihitānimittavimokkhe aññe ca lokiyalokuttare uttarimanussadhamme bhaji sevi bahulamakāsi, tasmā “bhattavā”ti vattabbe “bhagavā”ti vuccati.

Moreover, because he cultivated, frequented, and practiced abundantly the divine, Brahma, and noble abodes, solitude of body, mind, and acquisitions, emptiness, the signless, the undirected liberation, and other mundane and supramundane qualities surpassing human states, therefore, when he should be called 'bhattavā' (one who has cultivated), he is called 'Bhagavā'.

Yasmā pana tīsu bhavesu taṇhāsaṅkhātaṃ gamanaṃ anena vantaṃ, tasmā “bhavesu vantagamano”ti vattabbe bhavasaddato bhakāraṃ gamanasaddato gakāraṃ vantasaddato vakārañca dīghaṃ katvā ādāya “bhagavā”ti vuccati, yathā loke “mehanassa khassa mālā”ti vattabbe “mekhalā”ti vuccati.

Furthermore, because by him the wandering, consisting of craving, in the three realms of existence is abandoned, therefore, when he should be called 'bhavesu vantagamano' (one whose going in existences is abandoned), taking the 'bha' from the word bhava (existence), the 'ga' from the word gamana (going), and the lengthened 'vā' from the word vanta (abandoned), he is called 'Bhagavā,' just as in the world, when it should be said 'the garland of the urine-drinker,' it is called 'mekhalā.'

Puna [M 0.0231] aparampi pariyāyaṃ niddisanto “api ca bhaggarāgoti bhagavā”tiādimāha. Tattha bhaggo rāgo assāti bhaggarāgo. Bhaggadosādīsupi eseva nayo. Kaṇḍakoti vinivijjhanaṭṭhena kilesā eva. Bhajīti uddesavasena vibhāgaṃ katvā bhājesi. Vibhajīti niddesavasena vividhā bhājesi. Pavibhajīti paṭiniddesavasena pakārena vibhaji. Ugghaṭitaññūnaṃ vasena bhaji. Vipañcitaññūnaṃ vasena vibhaji. Neyyānaṃ vasena pavibhaji.

Presenting yet another explanation, he said, beginning with: 'Furthermore, the Blessed One is one who has shattered lust.' Here, 'bhaggarāga' means one whose lust is shattered. The same method applies to one who has shattered hatred, and so forth. 'Thorns' (kaṇḍaka) are indeed the defilements in the sense of piercing. 'He apportioned' (bhaji) means he divided, having made a division by way of summary. 'He analyzed' (vibhajī) means he divided variously, by way of detailed exposition. 'He thoroughly analyzed' (pavibhajī) means he divided in a particular way, by way of re-exposition. He apportioned for those capable of understanding quickly, analyzed for those capable of understanding with elaboration, and thoroughly analyzed for those who require guidance.

Dhammaratananti –

The Jewel of the Dhamma, namely:

“Cittīkataṃ mahagghañca, atulaṃ dullabhadassanaṃ;

Anomasattaparibhogaṃ, ratanaṃ tena vuccatī”ti. (khu. pā. aṭṭha. 6.3; dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.33) –

"It is esteemed, of great value, incomparable, and rare to see. It is enjoyed by the noblest of beings; therefore it is called a jewel."

Evaṃ vaṇṇitaṃ dhammaratanaṃ tividhena bhājesi. Bhavānaṃ [P 2.0267] antakaroti kāmabhavādīnaṃ navannaṃ bhavānaṃ paricchedaṃ pariyantaṃ parivaṭumaṃ kārako. Bhāvitakāyoti vaḍḍhitakāyo. Tathā itaresupi. Bhajīti sevi. Araññavanapatthānīti gāmassa vā nagarassa vā indakhīlato bahi araññaṃ. Vanapatthāni manussūpacārātikkantāni [V 0.0212] vanasaṇḍāni. Pantānīti yattha manussā na kasanti na vapanti dūrāni senāsanāni. Keci pana “vanapattānīti yasmā yattha byagghādayo atthi, taṃ vanaṃ te pālayanti rakkhanti, tasmā tehi rakkhitattā vanapattānī”ti vadanti. Senāsanānīti seti ceva āsati ca etthāti senāsanāni. Appasaddānīti vacanasaddena appasaddāni. Appanigghosānīti gāmanagaranigghosasaddena appanigghosāni. Vijanavātānīti antosañcaraṇajanassa sarīravātena virahitāni. “Vijanavādānī”tipi pāṭho, “antojanavādena virahitānī”ti attho. “Vijanapātānī”tipi pāṭho, “janasañcāravirahitānī”ti attho. Manussarāhasseyyakānīti manussānaṃ rahassakaraṇaṭṭhānāni. Paṭisallānasāruppānīti vivekānurūpāni. Bhāgī vāti “bhāgo cīvarādikoṭṭhāso assa atthī”ti bhāgī. “Paṭilābhavasena attharasādibhāgo assa atthī”ti bhāgī. Attharasassāti hetuphalasampattisaṅkhātassa attharasassa. Dhammarasassāti hetusampattisaṅkhātassa dhammarasassa. Vuttañhetaṃ “hetuphale ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidā, hetumhi ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā”ti (vibha. 720). Vimuttirasassāti phalasampattisaṅkhātassa vimuttirasassa. Vuttampi cetaṃ “kiccasampattiatthena, raso nāma pavuccatī”ti (paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 1.1.2 mātikāvaṇṇanā; visuddhi. 1.8).

Thus, he divided the Dhamma-jewel, praised in this way, in three ways. He is the end-maker of existences, the one who makes an end, a boundary, a limit to the nine existences such as the realm of sensual desire. "Developed in body" means the body has grown. Similarly for the others. "Frequented" means he cultivates. "Remote forest and wilderness areas" refers to the wilderness outside the boundary-marker of a village or town. "Wilderness areas" are thick forests beyond human habitation. "Secluded" refers to dwellings far away where people do not plow or sow. Some say, "'Vanapattāni' (forest-protected) is so called because where there are tigers and so forth, they protect and guard that forest; thus, they are called vanapattāni because they are protected by them." "Dwellings" are places where one both lies down and sits. "Quiet" means with little sound of speech. "Tranquil" means with little noise from villages or towns. "Free from human disturbance" means devoid of the bodily wind of people moving about inside. Another reading is "free from human voices," meaning devoid of the sound of people inside. Another variant is "free from human contact," meaning devoid of human traffic. "Places of human secrecy" means places for humans to do secret things. "Fit for seclusion" means suitable for withdrawal. "Having a share" means "he has a share, a portion of robes and the like." Alternatively, it means "he has a share in the essence of meaning and so forth, by way of gain." "The essence of meaning" refers to the essence of meaning known as the attainment of cause and result. "The essence of the Dhamma" refers to the essence of the Dhamma known as the attainment of the cause. As it is said: "Knowledge of cause and result is the analysis of meaning; knowledge of the cause is the analysis of the Dhamma" (Vibhanga 720). "The essence of liberation" refers to the essence of liberation known as the attainment of the fruit. And it was said, "Because it accomplishes its purpose, it is called the essence" (Patisambhidamagga Atthakatha 1.1.2, Mātikāvaṇṇanā; Visuddhimagga 1.8).

Catunnaṃ [M 0.0232] jhānānanti paṭhamajjhānādīnaṃ catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ. Catunnaṃ appamaññānanti mettādīnaṃ pharaṇappamāṇavirahitānaṃ catunnaṃ brahmavihārānaṃ. Catunnaṃ arūpasamāpattīnanti ākāsānañcāyatanādīnaṃ catunnaṃ arūpajjhānānaṃ. Aṭṭhannaṃ vimokkhānanti “rūpī rūpāni passatī”tiādinā (dha. sa. 248) nayena vuttānaṃ ārammaṇavimuttānaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ vimokkhānaṃ. Abhibhāyatanānanti [P 2.0268] ettha abhibhūtāni āyatanāni etesaṃ jhānānanti abhibhāyatanāni, jhānāni. Āyatanānīti adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena āyatanasaṅkhātāni kasiṇārammaṇāni. Ñāṇuttariko hi puggalo visadañāṇoti kiṃ ettha ārammaṇe samāpajjitabbaṃ, na mayi cittekaggatākaraṇe bhāro atthīti tāni ārammaṇāni abhibhavitvā samāpajjati. Saha nimittuppādenevettha appanaṃ nibbattetīti attho. Evaṃ uppāditāni jhānāni abhibhāyatanānīti vuccanti, tesaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ abhibhāyatanānaṃ. Navannaṃ anupubbavihārasamāpattīnanti pubbaṃ pubbaṃ anu anupubbaṃ, anupubbaṃ viharitabbato samāpajjitabbato anupubbavihārasamāpatti, anupaṭipāṭiyā samāpajjitabbāti attho, tāsaṃ navannaṃ anupubbavihārasamāpattīnaṃ. Dasannaṃ saññābhāvanānanti girimānandasutte (a. ni. 10.60) āgatānaṃ aniccasaññādīnaṃ dasannaṃ saññābhāvanānaṃ. Dasannaṃ kasiṇasamāpattīnanti sakalaṭṭhena kasiṇasaṅkhātānaṃ pathavīkasiṇajjhānādīnaṃ dasannaṃ jhānānaṃ. Ānāpānassatisamādhissāti ānāpānassatisampayuttasamādhissa[V 0.0213]. Asubhasamāpattiyāti asubhajjhānasamāpattiyā. Dasannaṃ tathāgatabalānanti dasabalabalānaṃ dasannaṃ. Catunnaṃ vesārajjānanti visāradabhāvānaṃ catunnaṃ vesārajjānaṃ. Catunnaṃ paṭisambhidānanti paṭisambhidāñāṇānaṃ catunnaṃ. Channaṃ abhiññāṇānanti iddhividhādīnaṃ channaṃ abhiññāṇānaṃ. Channaṃ buddhadhammānanti “sabbaṃ kāyakammaṃ ñāṇānuparivattī”tiādinā (cūḷani. mogharājamāṇavapucchāniddesa 85; netti. 15) nayena upari āgatānaṃ channaṃ buddhadhammānaṃ.

Of the four jhānas: the four jhānas, beginning with the first jhāna. Of the four immeasurables: the four divine abodes—loving-kindness and so forth—devoid of measure through pervasion. Of the four formless attainments: the four formless jhānas, beginning with the base of infinite space. Of the eight liberations: the eight liberations, freed by their objects, as stated in the way beginning with, "One with form sees forms" (Dhs. 248). Of the masteries: here, the masteries are jhānas, because these jhānas master sense bases. The sense bases: the kasiṇa objects, designated as sense bases in the sense of being foundations. For a person superior in knowledge, whose knowledge is clear, what is there to be attained in this object? The burden does not lie in unifying the mind upon himself, but rather in mastering those objects and attaining absorption. Here, absorption arises simultaneously with the appearance of the sign—this is the meaning. Thus, the jhānas produced in this way are called masteries—there are eight such masteries. Of the nine successive abidings: because they are to be dwelt in successively, one after another, to be attained gradually, they are called successive abidings—they are to be attained in sequence. There are nine such successive abidings. Of the ten perceptions: the ten perceptions, such as the perception of impermanence, found in the Girimānanda Sutta (AN 10.60). Of the ten kasiṇa attainments: the ten jhānas, such as the earth-kasiṇa jhāna, designated as kasiṇas in their entirety. Of the concentration through mindfulness of breathing: the concentration associated with mindfulness of breathing. Of the foul attainment: the foul jhāna attainment. Of the ten powers of the Tathāgata: the ten powers, which are the strengths. Of the four confidences: the four kinds of confidence. Of the four analytical knowledges: the four analytical knowledges. Of the six direct knowledges: the six direct knowledges, such as psychic power. Of the six Buddha-qualities: the six Buddha-qualities, as stated above in the way beginning with, "All bodily actions are preceded by knowledge" (Cūḷaniddesa 85; Netti. 15).

Tattha cīvarādayo bhāgyasampattivasena vuttā. Attharasatiko [P 2.0269] paṭivedhavasena vutto. Adhisīlatiko paṭipattivasena. Jhānattiko rūpārūpajjhānavasena. Vimokkhattiko samāpattivasena. Saññācatukko upacārappanāvasena. Satipaṭṭhānādayo sattatiṃsabodhipakkhiyadhammavasena. Tathāgatabalānantiādayo āveṇikadhammavasena vuttāti veditabbā.

Here, robes and so forth are spoken of as possessions due to fortune. The three regarding meaning are spoken of in terms of penetration. The three regarding higher virtue are spoken of in terms of practice. The three regarding jhāna are spoken of in terms of form and formless jhānas. The three regarding liberation are spoken of in terms of attainment. The four perceptions are spoken of in terms of proximity and full absorption. The foundations of mindfulness and so forth are spoken of in terms of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. Likewise, the powers of the Tathāgata and so forth are spoken of in terms of the unique qualities—this should be understood.

Ito [M 0.0233] paraṃ bhagavāti netaṃ nāmantiādi “atthamanugatā ayaṃ paññattī”ti ñāpanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha samaṇā pabbajjupagatā. Brāhmaṇā bhovādino samitapāpabāhitapāpā vā. Devatā sakkādayo brahmāno ca. Vimokkhantikanti vimokkho arahattamaggo, vimokkhassa anto arahattaphalaṃ, tasmiṃ vimokkhante bhavaṃ vimokkhantikaṃ nāmaṃ. Sabbaññubhāvo hi arahattamaggena sijjhati, arahattaphalādhigamena siddho hoti. Tasmā sabbaññubhāvo vimokkhante bhavo hoti. Taṃ nemittikampi nāmaṃ vimokkhante bhavaṃ nāma hoti. Tena vuttaṃ – “vimokkhantikametaṃ buddhānaṃ bhagavantāna”nti. Bodhiyā mūle saha sabbaññutaññāṇassa paṭilābhāti mahābodhirukkhamūle yathāvuttakkhaṇe sabbaññutaññāṇassa paṭilābhena saha. Sacchikā paññattīti arahattaphalasacchikiriyāya sabbadhammasacchikiriyāya vā jātā paññatti. Yadidaṃ bhagavāti yā ayaṃ bhagavāti paññatti.

From here onward, the phrase "Bhagavā—this is not merely a name," etc., is spoken to indicate that "this designation is based on meaning." Herein, ascetics are those who have gone forth. Brahmins are those who use the term 'bho' or have eliminated evil. Devas are like Sakka and others, and Brahmās as well. "Culmination of liberation" means liberation is the path to arahantship, the end of liberation is the fruit of arahantship; existence in that culmination of liberation is called "culmination of liberation." For omniscience is achieved through the path to arahantship and is accomplished by the attainment of the fruit of arahantship. Therefore, omniscience is existence in the culmination of liberation. That is also a characteristic name, a name that exists at the culmination of liberation. Hence it is said: "This is the culmination of liberation for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones." "At the foot of the Bodhi tree, together with the attainment of omniscient knowledge" means at the foot of the great Bodhi tree, at the aforementioned moment, together with the attainment of omniscient knowledge. "The designation realized" means the designation arisen from the realization of the fruit of arahantship or the realization of all phenomena. "Namely, the Blessed One" means this designation "the Blessed One."

Dvīhi kāraṇehīti dvīhi koṭṭhāsehi. Pariyattisāsananti tepiṭakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ. Paṭipattīti paṭipajjati etāyāti paṭipatti. Yaṃ tassa pariyāpuṭanti tena puggalena yaṃ pariyāpuṭaṃ sajjhāyitaṃ karaṇatthe sāmivacanaṃ. “Pariyāpuṭṭa”ntipi pāṭho. Suttanti ubhatovibhaṅganiddesakhandhakaparivārā, suttanipāte maṅgalasutta- (khu. pā. 5.1 ādayo; su. ni. 261 ādayo) ratanasutta- (khu. pā. 6.1 ādayo) tuvaṭakasuttāni (su. ni. 921 ādayo), aññampi ca suttanāmakaṃ tathāgatavacanaṃ suttanti veditabbaṃ. Geyyanti sabbampi sagāthakaṃ suttaṃ geyyanti veditabbaṃ, visesena saṃyuttake sakalopi sagāthāvaggo. Veyyākaraṇanti [P 2.0270] sakalaṃ abhidhammapiṭakaṃ niggāthakaṃ suttaṃ, yañca aññampi aṭṭhahi aṅgehi asaṅgahitaṃ buddhavacanaṃ[V 0.0214], taṃ “veyyākaraṇa”nti veditabbaṃ. Gāthāti dhammapadaṃ, theragāthā, therīgāthā, suttanipāte nosuttanāmikā suddhikagāthā ca “gāthā”ti veditabbā. Udānanti somanassañāṇamayikagāthāpaṭisaṃyuttā dveasīti suttantā “udāna”nti veditabbaṃ. Itivuttakanti “vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā”tiādinayappavattā (itivu. 1 ādayo) dasuttarasatasuttantā “itivuttaka”nti veditabbaṃ. Jātakanti apaṇṇakajātakādīni (jā. 1.1.1) paṇṇāsādhikāni pañcajātakasatāni “jātaka”nti veditabbaṃ. Abbhutadhammanti “cattārome[M 0.0234], bhikkhave, acchariyā abbhutadhammā ānande”tiādinayappavattā (dī. ni. 2.209; a. ni. 4.129) sabbepi acchariyaabbhutadhammapaṭisaṃyuttā suttantā “abbhutadhamma”nti veditabbaṃ. Vedallanti cūḷavedalla- (ma. ni. 1.460 ādayo) mahāvedalla- (ma. ni. 1.449 ādayo) sammādiṭṭhi- (ma. ni. 1.89 ādayo) sakkapañha- (dī. ni. 2.344 ādayo) saṅkhārabhājaniyamahāpuṇṇamasuttādayo (ma. ni. 3.85 ādayo) sabbepi vedañca tuṭṭhiñca laddhā laddhā pucchitasuttantā “vedalla”nti veditabbaṃ. Idaṃ pariyattisāsananti idaṃ vuttappakāraṃ tepiṭakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ pariyāpuṇitabbaṭṭhena pariyatti, anusāsanaṭṭhena sāsananti katvā pariyattisāsanaṃ. Tampi mussatīti tampi pariyattisāsanaṃ nassati. Sammussatīti ādito nassati. Paribāhiro hotīti parammukho hoti.

For two reasons—that is, in two aspects. The teaching of scripture—this refers to the Tipiṭaka, the word of the Buddha. Practice—this means 'one proceeds by it,' hence it is called practice. What has been learned by him—this refers to what has been studied and recited by that person; the genitive is used in the sense of the agent. The reading 'pariyāpuṭṭa' is also found. Sutta—this includes the Ubhatovibhaṅga, Niddesa, Khandhaka, and Parivāra; in the Sutta Nipāta, the Maṅgala Sutta (Khuddakapāṭha 5.1, etc.; Sutta Nipāta 261, etc.), the Ratana Sutta (Khuddakapāṭha 6.1, etc.), and the Tuvaṭaka Sutta (Sutta Nipāta 921, etc.), and any other discourses named 'sutta' that are the word of the Tathāgata, should be understood as 'sutta.' Geyya—all discourses with verses should be understood as 'geyya,' especially the entire Sagāthāvagga in the Saṃyutta Nikāya. Veyyākaraṇa—this includes the entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka, discourses without verses, and any other word of the Buddha not included in the other eight divisions—these should be understood as 'veyyākaraṇa.' Gāthā—this includes the Dhammapada, Theragāthā, Therīgāthā, and the purely metrical verses in the Sutta Nipāta that are not named 'suttas'—these should be understood as 'gāthā.' Udāna—the eighty-two discourses connected with verses expressing joy and knowledge should be understood as 'udāna.' Itivuttaka—the one hundred and ten discourses beginning with 'Thus was said by the Blessed One' should be understood as 'itivuttaka.' Jātaka—the Apaṇṇaka Jātaka (Jātaka 1.1.1) and the five hundred and fifty Jātakas should be understood as 'jātaka.' Abbhutadhamma—all discourses connected with marvelous and wonderful phenomena, such as those beginning with 'Monks, these four astonishing and wonderful things are in Ānanda,' should be understood as 'abbhutadhamma.' Vedalla—the Cūḷavedalla (Majjhima Nikāya 1.460, etc.), Mahāvedalla (Majjhima Nikāya 1.449, etc.), Sammādiṭṭhi (Majjhima Nikāya 1.89, etc.), Sakkapañha (Dīgha Nikāya 2.344, etc.), Saṅkhārabhājaniya and Mahāpuṇṇama Suttas (Majjhima Nikāya 3.85, etc.), and all discourses where questions are asked after gaining knowledge and delight—these should be understood as 'vedalla.' This is the teaching of scripture—this refers to the Tipiṭaka, the Buddha’s word, called 'pariyatti' in the sense of being learned and 'sāsana' in the sense of instruction, hence 'pariyattisāsana.' Even that is forgotten—even that teaching of scripture is lost. Completely forgotten—lost from the very beginning. He becomes an outsider—he turns away.

Katamaṃ paṭipattisāsananti lokuttaradhammato pubbabhāgo tadatthaṃ paṭipajjīyatīti paṭipatti. Sāsīyanti ettha veneyyāti sāsanaṃ. Sammāpaṭipadātiādayo vuttanayā eva.

What is the teaching of practice? The preliminary part of the supramundane Dhamma is 'practice' because one practices for that purpose. It is 'teaching' (sāsana) because in it those who are to be trained are instructed (sāsīyanti). 'Right practice' and so forth are to be understood in the way already stated.

Pāṇampi hanatīti jīvitindriyampi ghāteti. Adinnampi ādiyatīti parapariggahitampi vatthuṃ gaṇhāti. Sandhimpi chindatīti gharasandhimpi chindati. Nillopampi haratīti gāme paharitvā mahāvilopampi karoti. Ekāgārikampi [P 2.0271] karotīti paṇṇāsamattehipi saṭṭhimattehipi parivāretvā jīvaggāhaṃ gahetvāpi dhanaṃ āharāpeti. Paripanthepi tiṭṭhatīti panthadūhanakammaṃ karoti. Paradārampi gacchatīti paradāresu cārittaṃ āpajjati. Musāpi bhaṇatīti atthabhañjanakaṃ musāpi vadati. Anariyadhammoti anariyasabhāvo.

He kills living beings—he destroys the life faculty. He takes what is not given—he takes objects possessed by others. He breaks into houses—he breaks through the walls of houses. He commits robbery—he plunders villages and commits great robbery. He attacks a single house—he surrounds it with about fifty or sixty men and, even taking the owner captive, makes him bring out his wealth. He waylays—he commits the act of making roads unsafe. He commits adultery—he engages in misconduct with others' wives. He speaks falsely—he speaks falsehood that destroys welfare. An ignoble quality—this is an ignoble nature.

51. Eko pubbe caritvānāti pabbajjāsaṅkhātena vā gaṇāvavassaggaṭṭhena vā pubbe loke viharitvā. Yānaṃ bhantaṃva taṃ loke, hīnamāhu puthujjananti taṃ vibbhantakaṃ puggalaṃ yathā hatthiyānādiyānaṃ adantaṃ visamampi ārohati, ārohanakampi bhañjati, papātepi papatati, evaṃ [V 0.0215] kāyaduccaritādivisamārohanena nirayādīsu, atthabhañjanena jātipapātādīsu papatanena ca yānaṃ bhantaṃva hīnaṃ puthujjanañca āhūti.

51. "Having once lived alone"—having previously lived in the world either through what is termed renunciation or in the sense of forsaking a group. "Like a runaway chariot in the world, they call him a lowly ordinary person"—just as an untamed vehicle, such as a chariot, climbs uneven terrain, breaks its rider, and falls into a chasm, so too does that confused person, by climbing the uneven terrain of bodily misconduct and the like, fall into hell and the like; and by destroying his welfare, he falls into the chasm of birth and so forth. Thus, like a runaway chariot, they call him lowly and an ordinary person.

Pabbajjāsaṅkhātena vāti pabbajjākoṭṭhāsena vā “pabbajito samaṇo”ti gaṇanāropanena vā. Gaṇāvavassaggaṭṭhena vāti gaṇasaṅgaṇikārāmataṃ vissajjetvā vassaggaṭṭhena vā.

By what is termed renunciation—that is, by the aspect of renunciation, or by being reckoned as 'a renunciant, an ascetic.' Or in the sense of abandoning a group—that is, by giving up the pleasure of association with a group.

Eko [M 0.0235] paṭikkamatīti ekakova gāmato nivattati. Yo nisevatīti niddesassa uddesapadaṃ. Aparena samayenāti aññasmiṃ kāle aparabhāge. Buddhanti sabbaññubuddhaṃ. Dhammanti svākkhātatādiguṇayuttaṃ dhammaṃ. Saṅghanti suppaṭipannatādiguṇayuttaṃ saṅghaṃ. Sikkhanti adhisīlādisikkhitabbaṃ sikkhaṃ. Paccakkhāyāti buddhādiṃ paṭikkhipitvā. Hīnāyāti hīnatthāya gihibhāvāya. Āvattitvāti nivattitvā. Sevati ekavāraṃ sevati. Nisevati anekavidhena sevati. Saṃsevati allīyitvā sevati. Paṭisevati punappunaṃ sevati.

"He returns alone" means he turns back from the village by himself. "Who associates" is the subject term for the exposition. "At a later time" means at another time, in a subsequent period. "The Buddha" means the Omniscient Buddha. "The Dhamma" means the Dhamma endowed with qualities such as being well-proclaimed. "The Saṅgha" means the Saṅgha endowed with qualities such as practicing rightly. "The training" means the training to be undertaken, such as higher virtue. "Having rejected" means having rejected the Buddha and so forth. "To a low state" means for a low purpose, for the household life. "Having turned back" means having reverted. "He associates" (sevati) means he associates once. "He associates closely" (nisevati) means he associates in many ways. "He consorts with" (saṃsevati) means he associates while clinging. "He resorts to" (paṭisevati) means he associates again and again.

Bhantanti vibbhantaṃ. Adantanti dantabhāvaṃ anupanītaṃ. Akāritanti susikkhitakiriyaṃ asikkhāpitaṃ. Avinītanti na vinītaṃ ācārasampattiyā asikkhitaṃ. Uppathaṃ gaṇhātīti vuttappakāraṃ yānaṃ adantātiyuttaṃ bhantaṃ visamamaggaṃ upeti. Visamaṃ khāṇumpi pāsāṇampi abhiruhatīti visamaṃ hutvā ṭhitaṃ kharakhāṇumpi tathā [P 2.0272] pabbatapāsāṇampi ārohati. Yānampi ārohanakampi bhañjatīti vayhādiyānaṃ ārohantassa pājentassa hatthapādādimpi bhindati. Papātepi papatatīti ekatocchinnapabbhārapapātepi pāteti. So vibbhantakoti so paṭikkantako. Bhantayānapaṭibhāgoti anavaṭṭhitayānasadiso. Uppathaṃ gaṇhātīti kusalakammapathato paṭikkamitvā apāyapathabhūtaṃ uppathaṃ micchāmaggaṃ upeti. Visamaṃ kāyakammaṃ abhiruhatīti samassa paṭipakkhaṃ kāyaduccaritasaṅkhātaṃ visamaṃ kāyakammaṃ ārohati. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Niraye attānaṃ bhañjatīti nirassādasaṅkhāte niraye attabhāvaṃ cuṇṇavicuṇṇaṃ karoti. Manussaloke attānaṃ bhañjatīti vividhakammakāraṇavasena bhañjati. Devaloke attānaṃ bhañjatīti piyavippayogādidukkhavasena. Jātipapātampi papatatīti jātipapātepi pāteti. Jarāpapātādīsupi eseva nayo. Manussaloketi idha adhippetalokameva dasseti.

"Bhanta" means deviated, gone astray. "Adanta" means untamed, not brought to a state of discipline. "Akārita" means untrained in well-practiced actions, uninstructed. "Avinīta" means undisciplined, not trained in proper conduct. "It takes the wrong path" means that such a vehicle, being untamed and so on, goes astray and takes a crooked path. "It climbs over an uneven stump and rock" means it ascends a harsh stump that is unevenly placed and likewise a mountain rock. "It breaks the vehicle and the rider" means it breaks the limbs, such as the hands and feet, of the one mounting and driving the vehicle. "It falls into a chasm" means it causes a fall into a precipice, a cliff sheer on one side. "That deviated one" means that one who has turned back. "Like a runaway chariot" means similar to an unstable vehicle. "He takes the wrong path" means, having turned back from the path of skillful action, he enters the wrong path, the false path that has become the way to the plane of misery. "He engages in uneven bodily action" means he undertakes uneven bodily action, known as bodily misconduct, which is the opposite of what is even. The same method applies to the rest. "He breaks himself in hell" means he smashes his personal existence to powder in the hell known as 'joyless.' "He breaks himself in the human world" means he is broken by way of various punishments. "He breaks himself in the world of gods" means by way of suffering from separation from loved ones and so on. "He falls into the chasm of birth" means he causes himself to fall into the chasm of birth. The same method applies to the chasms of aging and so on. "In the human world" here indicates only the world intended in this context.

Puthujjanāti niddesassa uddesapadaṃ. Tattha puthujjanāti –

"Puthujjana" is the subject term for the exposition. Therein, "puthujjana" means:

Puthūnaṃ [V 0.0216] jananādīhi, kāraṇehi puthujjano;

Puthujjanantogadhattā, puthuvāyaṃ jano iti.

He is an ordinary person (puthujjana) for reasons such as generating a multitude (puthū) of defilements; and because he is included among the mass of ordinary people, this person (jano) is thus 'separate' (puthu).

So [M 0.0236] hi puthūnaṃ nānappakārānaṃ kilesādīnaṃ jananādīhipi kāraṇehi puthujjano. Taṃ vibhāgato dassetuṃ “puthu kilese janentī”tiādimāha. Tattha bahūnaṃ nānappakārānaṃ sakkāyadiṭṭhīnaṃ avihatattā vā tā janenti, tāhi janitāti vā puthujjanā. Avihatamevatthaṃ janasaddo vadati. Puthu satthārānaṃ mukhullokikāti ettha puthū nānājanā satthupaṭiññā etesanti puthujjanāti vacanattho. Puthu sabbagatīhi avuṭṭhitāti ettha janetabbā janayanti etthāti janā, gatiyo. Puthū janā etesanti puthujjanā. Ito pare jāyanti etehīti janā, abhisaṅkhārādayo. Te etesaṃ vijjantīti puthujjanā. Abhisaṅkharaṇādiattho eva vā janasaddo daṭṭhabbo. Nānāsantāpehi santapantīti rāgaggiādayo santāpā. Te eva vā sabbepi vā kilesā pariḷāhā. Puthu [P 2.0273] pañcasu kāmaguṇesūti ettha jāyatīti jano, rāgo gedhoti evamādiko, puthu jano etesanti puthujjanā. Puthu jātā rattāti evaṃ rāgādiattho eva vā janasaddo daṭṭhabbo. Palibuddhāti sambaddhā. Āvutāti āvaritā. Nivutāti vāritā. Ovutāti uparito pihitā. Pihitāti heṭṭhābhāgena pihitā. Paṭicchannāti apākaṭā. Paṭikujjitāti adhomukhagatā.

Indeed, one is an ordinary person for reasons such as generating various kinds of defilements in abundance. To show this in detail, it is said, “they generate defilements widely,” and so forth. Here, they are called “ordinary people” either because they generate many different kinds of identity views that remain unremoved, or because they are generated by them. The word “jana” here conveys the meaning of what is unremoved. Regarding “those who look to the faces of various teachers”: here, the meaning of the word “puthujjanā” is that they have various (puthu) teachers (janā). Regarding “unrisen from all destinations”: here, “janā” refers to destinations, wherein beings are generated. They are called “ordinary people” because they have many such destinations. Furthermore, “janā” means that from which beings are born, namely formations and so forth. They are called “ordinary people” because these exist for them. Alternatively, the term “jana” should be understood as having the meaning of forming and so forth. Regarding “tormented by various torments”: here, the torments refer to the fires of lust and so forth, or all defilements are fevers. Regarding “widely in the five strands of sensual pleasure”: here, “jana” refers to that which is born, such as lust, greed, and so on; and they are called “ordinary people” because they have this in abundance. Alternatively, the term “jana” should be understood as having the meaning of lust and so forth, in the sense of being “widely born and impassioned.” “Palibuddhā” means connected. “Āvutā” means enveloped. “Nivutā” means obstructed. “Ovutā” means covered over from above. “Pihitā” means covered over from below. “Paṭicchannā” means concealed. “Paṭikujjitā” means turned face-down.

Atha vā puthūnaṃ vā gaṇanapathamatītānaṃ ariyadhammaparammukhānaṃ nīcadhammasamācārānaṃ janānaṃ antogadhattāpi puthujjanā. Puthu vā ayaṃ visuṃyeva saṅkhaṃ gato, visaṃsaṭṭho sīlasutādiguṇayuttehi ariyehi janotipi puthujjano.

Or alternatively, they are called ordinary people because they are included among the innumerable people who are averse to the noble Dhamma and whose conduct is base. Or alternatively, this person is called an ordinary person because he is counted separately, unassociated with the noble ones who are endowed with virtues such as morality and learning.

Evaṃ ye te –

Thus, those—

“Duve puthujjanā vuttā, buddhenādiccabandhunā;

Andho puthujjano eko, kalyāṇeko puthujjano”ti. –

“Two kinds of ordinary people are spoken of by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun: one is a blind ordinary person, the other is a virtuous ordinary person.”

Dveva puthujjanā vuttā, tesu andhaputhujjano vutto hotīti veditabbo.

Two kinds of ordinary people are spoken of; among them, the blind ordinary person should be understood as being spoken of.

52. Yaso kitti cāti lābhasakkāro pasaṃsā ca. Pubbeti pabbajitabhāve. Hāyate vāpi tassa sāti tassa vibbhantakassa sato so [M 0.0237] ca yaso sā ca kitti hāyati. Etampi disvāti [V 0.0217] etampi pubbe yasakittīnaṃ lābhaṃ pacchā ca hāniṃ disvā. Sikkhetha methunaṃ vippahātaveti tisso sikkhāyo sikkhetha. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Methunaṃ vippahātave, methunappahānatthāyāti vuttaṃ hoti.

52. “Fame and reputation” means gain, honor, and praise. “Formerly” means in the state of having gone forth. “It declines for him too” means that for one who has gone astray, his fame and reputation decline. “Having seen this too” means having seen this gain of fame and reputation formerly and their loss later. “Train to abandon sexual intercourse” means one should train in the three trainings. For what reason? To abandon sexual intercourse; it is said for the sake of abandoning sexual intercourse.

Kittivaṇṇagatoti bhagavā kittivaṇṇo, kittisaddañceva guṇañca ukkhipitvā vadanto hotīti attho. Cittaṃ nānānayena kathanaṃ assa atthīti cittakathī. Kalyāṇapaṭibhānoti sundarapañño.

“Kittivaṇṇagato” means the Blessed One is of renowned fame; the meaning is that he speaks while exalting both his renown and his virtues. “Cittakathī” means an eloquent speaker, one who possesses diverse ways of speaking. “Kalyāṇapaṭibhāno” means one of beautiful eloquence, one who possesses beautiful wisdom.

Hāyatīti niddesassa uddesapadaṃ. Parihāyatīti samantato hāyati. Paridhaṃsatīti adhopathaviṃ patati. Paripatatīti [P 2.0274] samantato apagacchati. Antaradhāyatīti adassanaṃ yāti. Vippalujjatīti ucchijjati.

“Hāyati” is the subject term for the exposition. “Parihāyati” means it declines on all sides. “Paridhaṃsati” means it falls to the ground. “Paripatati” means it departs on all sides. “Antaradhāyati” means it goes to invisibility. “Vippalujjati” means it is destroyed.

Khuddako sīlakkhandhoti thullaccayādi. Mahanto sīlakkhandhoti pārājikasaṃṅghādiseso.

“The minor section on virtue” refers to offenses such as the grave offense and so forth. “The major section on virtue” refers to the Pārājika and Saṅghādisesa offenses.

Methunadhammassa pahānāyāti tadaṅgādipahānena pajahanatthāya. Vūpasamāyāti malānaṃ vūpasamanatthāya. Paṭinissaggāyāti pakkhandanapariccāgapaṭinissaggatthāya. Paṭipassaddhiyāti paṭipassaddhisaṅkhātassa phalassa atthāya.

“For abandoning sexual intercourse” means for abandoning by way of temporary abandonment and so forth. “For calming” means for calming defilements. “For relinquishing” means for the purpose of abandoning, renouncing, and relinquishing. “For pacification” means for the sake of the fruit known as pacification.

53. Yo hi methunaṃ na vippajahati saṅkappehi…pe… tathāvidho. Tattha paretoti samannāgato. Paresaṃ nigghosanti upajjhāyādīnaṃ nindāvacanaṃ. Maṅku hotīti dummano hoti.

53. One who does not abandon sexual intercourse, even in thought… such a one. There, “pareto” means possessed. “Paresaṃ nigghosa” refers to the reproachful words of others, such as the preceptor. “Maṅku hoti” means he becomes downcast.

Kāmasaṅkappenāti kāmapaṭisaṃyuttena vitakkena. Upariṭṭhepi eseva nayo. Phuṭṭhoti vitakkehi phusito. Paretoti aparihīno. Samohitoti sammā ohito anto paviṭṭho. Kapaṇo viyāti duggatamanusso viya. Mando viyāti aññāṇī viya. Momūho viyāti sammohabhūto viya. Jhāyatīti cinteti. Pajjhāyatīti bhusaṃ cinteti. Nijjhāyatīti anekavidhena cinteti. Apajjhāyatīti tato apagantvā cinteti. Ulūkoti ulūkasakuṇo. Rukkhasākhāyanti rukkhe uṭṭhitasākhāya, viṭape vā. Mūsikaṃ magayamānoti mūsikaṃ gavesamāno, “maggayamāno”tipi paṭhanti. Kotthūti siṅgālo. Biḷāroti babbu. Sandhisamalasaṅkaṭireti [M 0.0238] dvinnaṃ gharānaṃ antare ca udakaniddhamanacikkhallakacavaranikkhipanaṭṭhāne ca thaṇḍile ca. Vahacchinnoti piṭṭhigīvamaṃsacchinno. Ito parā gāthā pākaṭasambandhā eva.

“Kāmasaṅkappena” means with thought connected to sensual pleasures. The same method applies to the terms above. “Phuṭṭho” means touched by thoughts. “Pareto” means not diminished. “Samohito” means well-placed, having entered within. “Kapaṇo viya” means like a miserable person. “Mando viya” means like an ignorant one. “Momūho viya” means like one overcome by delusion. “Jhāyati” means he contemplates. “Pajjhāyati” means he contemplates intensely. “Nijjhāyati” means he contemplates in various ways. “Apajjhāyati” means he contemplates after turning away from it. “Ulūko” means an owl. “Rukkhasākhāya” means on a branch of a tree, or in the foliage. “Mūsikaṃ magayamāno” means seeking a mouse; some also read it as “maggayamāno”. “Kotthū” means a jackal. “Biḷāro” means a cat. “Sandhisamalasaṅkaṭire” means in the space between two houses, and in a place where water drains away, a muddy spot, a place for throwing rubbish, and on bare ground. “Vahacchinno” means with the flesh of the back and neck cut off. The verses after this are clearly connected.

54. Tāsu [V 0.0218] satthānīti kāyaduccaritādīni. Tāni hi attano paresañca chedanaṭṭhena “satthānī”ti vuccanti. Tesu vāyaṃ visesena tāva ādito musāvacanasatthāneva karoti, “iminā kāraṇenāhaṃ vibbhanto”ti bhaṇanto. Tenevāha – “esa khvassa mahāgedho[P 2.0275], mosavajjaṃ pagāhatī”ti. Tattha esa khvassāti esa kho assa. Mahāgedhoti mahābandhanaṃ. Katamoti ce? Yadidaṃ mosavajjaṃ pagāhati, svāyaṃ musāvādajjhogāho “mahāgedho”ti veditabbo.

54. “Among those weapons” refers to bodily misconduct and so forth. Indeed, these are called “weapons” because they cut oneself and others. Among them, he especially first engages in the weapon of false speech, saying, “For this reason, I have gone astray.” Therefore, it is said: “Indeed, this is his great bond; he plunges into false speech.” There, “esa khvassa” means “this indeed is his”. “Mahāgedho” means a great bondage. What is it? It is this plunging into false speech. This immersion in false speech should be understood as a “great bond”.

Tīṇi satthānīti tayo chedakā. Kāyaduccaritaṃ kāyasatthaṃ. Vacīsatthādīsupi eseva nayo. Taṃ vibhāgato dassetuṃ “tividhaṃ kāyaduccaritaṃ kāyasattha”nti āha. Sampajānamusā bhāsatīti jānanto tucchaṃ vācaṃ bhāsati. Abhirato ahaṃ bhante ahosiṃ pabbajjāyāti sāsane pabbajjāya anabhirativirahito ahaṃ āsiṃ. Mātā me posetabbāti mātā mayā posetabbā. Tenamhi vibbhantoti bhaṇatīti tena kāraṇena paṭikkanto asmītipi katheti. Pitā me posetabbotiādīsupi eseva nayo.

“Three weapons” means three cutters. Bodily misconduct is a bodily weapon. The same method applies to verbal weapons and so forth. To show this in detail, it is said: “Threefold bodily misconduct is a bodily weapon.” “Knowingly speaks falsely” means that knowing, he speaks empty words. “Delighted, venerable sir, I was with the going forth” means: “I was without lack of delight in the going forth in the Dispensation.” “My mother should be supported” means: “My mother should be supported by me.” “Therefore I have gone astray,” he says—meaning, for that reason, he also says: “I have returned.” The same method applies to “My father should be supported” and so forth.

Eso tassa mahāgedhoti tassa puggalassa eso mahābandho. Mahāvananti mahantaṃ duṭṭhavanaṃ. Gahananti duratikkamaṃ. Kantāroti corakantārādisadiso. Visamoti kaṇṭakavisamo. Kuṭiloti vaṅkakaṭakasadiso. Paṅkoti pallalasadiso. Palipoti kaddamasadiso. Palibodhoti mahādukkho. Mahābandhananti mahantaṃ dumocayabandhanaṃ. Yadidaṃ sampajānamusāvādoti yo ayaṃ sampajānamusāvādo.

“That is his great bond” means that person’s great bondage. “The great forest” means a vast, wicked forest. “The thicket” means something hard to overcome. “The wilderness” means something like a robber-infested wilderness. “The uneven ground” means something rough with thorns. “The crooked path” means something like a bent bracelet. “The mire” means something like a puddle. “The mud” means something like mire. “The entanglement” means great suffering. “The great bondage” means a massive, hard-to-release bondage. “Namely, deliberate lying” means this deliberate lying.

Sabhaggato vāti sabhāyaṃ ṭhito vā. Parisaggato vāti gāmaparisāyaṃ ṭhito vā. Ñātimajjhagato vāti dāyādānaṃ majjhe ṭhito vā. Pūgamajjhagato vāti senīnaṃ majjhe ṭhito vā. Rājakulamajjhagato vāti rājakulassa majjhe mahāvinicchaye ṭhito vā. Abhinītoti pucchanatthāya nīto. Sakkhipuṭṭhoti sakkhiṃ katvā pucchito. Ehambho purisāti [M 0.0239] ālapanametaṃ. Attahetu vā parahetu vāti attano vā parassa vā hatthapādādihetu vā dhanahetu vā. Āmisakiñcikkhahetu vāti ettha āmisanti lābho adhippeto. Kiñcikkhanti yaṃ vā taṃ vā appamattakaṃ, antamaso tittiravaṭṭakasappipiṇḍanavanītapiṇḍādimattakassapi lābhassa hetūti [P 2.0276] attho. Sampajānamusā bhāsatīti jānantoyeva musāvādaṃ karoti.

“In an assembly” means standing in an assembly. “In a group” means standing in a village assembly. “Among relatives” means standing among one’s heirs. “In a company” means standing among a guild. “In the royal court” means standing in the midst of the royal family during a great trial. “Brought forward” means brought for questioning. “Questioned as a witness” means questioned after being made a witness. “Come here, good man”—this is an address. “For one’s own sake or another’s sake” means for the sake of oneself or for the sake of another, whether for reasons concerning hands, feet, and so forth, or for wealth. “For some trifling gain”—here, “gain” refers to profit. “Some trifle” means anything small, even as little as the gain from a partridge, a quail, a lump of ghee, a lump of fresh butter, or similar things. “Knowingly speaks falsely” means knowingly utters falsehood.

Puna aññaṃ pariyāyaṃ dassento “api ca tīhākārehi musāvādo hoti, pubbevassa hotī”tiādimāha. Tattha tīhākārehīti sampajānamusāvādassa aṅgabhūtehi tīhi kāraṇehi. Pubbevassa [V 0.0219] hotīti pubbabhāgeyeva assa puggalassa evaṃ hoti “musā bhaṇissa”nti. Bhaṇantassa hotīti bhaṇamānassa hoti. Bhaṇitassa hotīti bhaṇite assa hoti. Yaṃ vattabbaṃ tasmiṃ vutte hotīti attho. Atha vā bhaṇitassāti vuttavato niṭṭhitavacanassa hotīti. Yo evaṃ pubbabhāgepi jānāti, bhaṇantopi jānāti, pacchāpi jānāti “musā mayā bhaṇita”nti, so evaṃ vadanto musāvādakammunā bajjhatīti ayamettha attho dassito. Kiñcāpi dassito, atha kho ayamettha viseso – pucchā tāva hoti, “musā bhaṇissa”nti pubbabhāgo atthi, “musā mayā bhaṇita”nti pacchābhāgo natthi. Vuttamattameva hi koci pamussati kiṃ tassa musāvādo hoti, na hotīti? Sā evaṃ aṭṭhakathāsu vissajjitā – pubbabhāge “musā bhaṇissa”nti ca, bhaṇantassa “musā bhaṇāmī”ti ca jānato pacchābhāge “musā mayā bhaṇita”nti na sakkā na bhavituṃ, sacepi na hoti, musāvādoyeva. Purimameva hi aṅgadvayaṃ pamāṇaṃ. Yassāpi pubbabhāge “musā bhaṇissa”nti ābhogo natthi, bhaṇanto pana “musā bhaṇāmī”ti jānāti. Bhaṇitepi “musā mayā bhaṇita”nti jānāti. So musāvādena na kāretabbo. Pubbabhāgo hi pamāṇataro. Tasmiṃ asati davā bhaṇitaṃ vā, ravā bhaṇitaṃ vā hotīti.

Furthermore, to explain another method, it is said: “Indeed, false speech occurs in three ways: ‘before it is spoken,’ and so forth.” Herein, “in three ways” refers to the three factors that constitute intentional false speech. “Before it is spoken” means that even in the initial stage, the person has this thought: “I will speak falsely.” “While speaking” means that this occurs as one is speaking. “After it is spoken” means that it occurs once it has been spoken. The meaning is that it occurs when what should be said is said. Alternatively, “after it is spoken” means that it occurs for one who has finished speaking and whose speech is completed. Whoever knows thus in the initial stage, knows while speaking, and knows afterward, thinking, “I have spoken falsely”—such a person, speaking thus, is bound by the kamma of false speech. This is the meaning shown here. Although this is shown, there is a distinction here: first, there is the question: if the initial stage, “I will speak falsely,” exists, but the later stage, “I have spoken falsely,” does not exist because someone merely forgets what was just said, does false speech occur for them, or not? This is how it is resolved in the commentaries: if in the initial stage one thinks, “I will speak falsely,” and while speaking one knows, “I am speaking falsely,” then in the later stage, it is impossible for the thought “I have spoken falsely” not to occur; even if it does not occur, it is still false speech. For the first two factors alone are the measure. Even for one who has no intention in the initial stage, thinking, “I will speak falsely,” but while speaking knows, “I am speaking falsely,” and after speaking knows, “I have spoken falsely”—such a person should not be considered as engaging in the kamma of false speech. The initial stage is the more decisive measure. When that is absent, what is spoken is either uttered through carelessness or haste.

Ettha ca taṃñāṇatā ca ñāṇasamodhānañca pariccajitabbaṃ. Taṃñāṇatā pariccajitabbāti yena cittena “musā bhaṇissa”nti jānāti, teneva “musā bhaṇāmī”ti ca, “musā mayā bhaṇita”nti ca jānātīti evaṃ ekacitteneva tīsu khaṇesu jānātīti ayaṃ taṃñāṇatā pariccajitabbā. Na [M 0.0240] hi sakkā teneva cittena taṃ cittaṃ jānituṃ, yathā na sakkā teneva asinā so asi chinditunti. Purimaṃ purimaṃ pana cittaṃ pacchimassa pacchimassa cittassa tathā uppattiyā paccayo hutvā nirujjhati. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

Here, both “that-knowledge” and the “conjunction of knowledge” should be relinquished. “That-knowledge should be relinquished” means the idea that with the same mind one knows “I will speak falsely,” and with that same mind “I am speaking falsely,” and “I have spoken falsely.” Thus, that-knowledge, which is knowing in three moments with one mind, should be relinquished. For it is not possible with that very mind to know that very mind, just as it is not possible with that very sword to cut that very sword. However, each preceding mind, having served as a condition for the arising of each subsequent mind, ceases. Therefore, it is said:

“Pamāṇaṃ [P 2.0277] pubbabhāgova, tasmiṃ sati na hessati;

Sesadvayanti nattheta, miti vācā tivaṅgikā”ti. (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.200);

“The initial stage is the measure; when that is present, the remaining two will not be absent. Thus is the measure of speech with its three factors.”

Ñāṇasamodhānaṃ pariccajitabbanti etāni tīṇi cittāni ekakkhaṇe uppajjantīti na gahetabbāni. Idañhi cittaṃ nāma –

“The conjunction of knowledge should be relinquished” means that these three states of mind should not be taken as arising in a single moment. For this, namely mind:

“Aniruddhamhi paṭhame, na uppajjati pacchimaṃ;

Nirantaruppajjanato, ekaṃ viya pakāsatī”ti. (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.200);

“When the first has not ceased, the subsequent one does not arise; from continuous arising, it appears as one.”

Ito [V 0.0220] paraṃ pana yvāyaṃ ajānaṃyeva “jānāmī”tiādinā nayena sampajānamusā bhaṇati, yasmā so “idaṃ abhūta”nti evaṃdiṭṭhiko hoti, tassa hi attheva ayaṃ laddhi. Tathā “idaṃ abhūta”nti evamassa khamati ceva ruccati ca. Evamassa saññā, evaṃsabhāvameva cassa cittaṃ “idaṃ abhūta”nti. Yadā pana musā vattukāmo hoti, tadā taṃ diṭṭhiṃ vā diṭṭhiyā saha khantiṃ vā diṭṭhikhantīhi saddhiṃ ruciṃ vā diṭṭhikhantirucīhi saddhiṃ saññaṃ vā diṭṭhikhantirucisaññāhi saddhiṃ bhāvaṃ vā vinidhāya nikkhipitvā paṭicchādetvā abhūtaṃ katvā bhaṇati. Tasmā tesampivasena aṅgabhedaṃ dassetuṃ “api ca catūhākārehī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Beyond this, however, whoever, while not knowing, speaks a deliberate lie in the manner of “I know,” and so forth—since such a person holds the view that “this is untrue,” for them, this view is indeed established. Similarly, they accept and approve that “this is untrue.” Such is their perception, and the very nature of their mind is “this is untrue.” But when they wish to speak falsely, they set aside that view, or the acceptance along with the view, or the preference along with the view and acceptance, or the perception along with the view, acceptance, and preference, or the very nature itself—setting it aside, putting it down, concealing it, and, having made it untrue, they speak. Therefore, to show the distinction of the factors by way of these, it is said: “Moreover, in four ways…”

Ettha ca vinidhāya diṭṭhinti balavadhammavinidhānavasenetaṃ vuttaṃ. Vinidhāya khantintiādīni tato dubbaladubbalānaṃ vinidhānavasena. Vinidhāya saññanti idaṃ panettha sabbadubbaladhammavinidhānavasena. Saññāmattampi nāma avinidhāya sampajānamusā bhāsissatīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati.

Here, “setting aside the view” is said with reference to setting aside a strong quality. “Setting aside acceptance” and so forth are said by way of setting aside progressively weaker qualities. “Setting aside perception” here is said by way of setting aside the weakest quality of all. For it is impossible that one would speak a deliberate lie without setting aside even a mere perception; such a situation is not possible.

55. Mandova parikissatīti pāṇavadhādīni karonto tatonidānañca dukkhamanubhonto bhogapariyesanārakkhaṇāni ca karonto momūho viya parikilissati.

55. “Like a fool, he toils” means that by engaging in killing living beings and so forth, experiencing suffering as a result, and striving to acquire and protect wealth, he toils like one utterly deluded.

Tamenaṃ rājāno gahetvā vividhā kammakāraṇā kārentīti na rājāno karonti, rājādhīnapurisā nānāvidhāni kammakāraṇāni karonti. Kasāhipi [M 0.0241] tāḷentīti kasādaṇḍakehipi vitajjenti. Vettehīti vettalatāhi. Addhadaṇḍakehīti [P 2.0278] muggarehi, pahārasādhanatthaṃ vā catuhatthadaṇḍaṃ dvedhā chetvā gahitadaṇḍakehi. Bilaṅgathālikanti kañjiyaukkhalikakammakāraṇaṃ. Taṃ [V 0.0221] karontā sīsakapālaṃ uppāṭetvā tattaṃ ayoguḷaṃ saṇḍāsena gahetvā tattha pakkhipanti, tena matthaluṅgaṃ pakkuṭṭhitvā upari uttarati. Saṅkhamuṇḍikanti saṅkhamuṇḍakammakāraṇaṃ. Taṃ karontā uttaroṭṭhaubhatokaṇṇacūḷikagalavāṭakaparicchedena cammaṃ chinditvā sabbakese ekato gaṇṭhiṃ katvā daṇḍakena veṭhetvā uppāṭenti, saha kesehi cammaṃ uṭṭhahati. Tato sīsakaṭāhaṃ thūlasakkharāhi ghaṃsitvā dhovantā saṅkhavaṇṇaṃ karonti. Rāhumukhanti rāhumukhakammakāraṇaṃ. Taṃ karontā saṅkunā mukhaṃ vivaritvā antomukhe dīpaṃ jālenti, kaṇṇacūḷikāhi vā paṭṭhāya mukhaṃ nikhādanena khananti, lohitaṃ paggharitvā mukhaṃ pūreti.

“Then the kings, having seized him, inflict various tortures”—but it is not the kings who do this; it is the men under the king’s authority who inflict the various tortures. “They strike him with whips” means they torment him with whip-sticks. “With canes” means with rattan vines. “With clubs” means with mallets, or with a four-cubit staff split in two and used as a weapon. “The gruel pot” means the torture of the gruel pot. While doing this, they tear off his skull, take a red-hot iron ball with tongs, and drop it inside, causing his brains to boil over and spill out. “The conch-shell tonsure” means the torture of the conch-shell tonsure. While doing this, they cut the skin with an incision from the upper lip to both ear-tips and the nape of the neck, gather all his hair into a single knot, wrap it around a stick, and pull it up—the skin comes off with the hair. Then they scrape his skull with coarse gravel, wash it, and make it as white as a conch shell. “Rahu’s mouth” means the torture of Rahu’s mouth. While doing this, they pry open his mouth with a spike and light a lamp inside it, or, starting from the ear-tips, they dig at his mouth with stakes until blood gushes out and fills his mouth.

Jotimālikanti sakalasarīraṃ telapilotikāya veṭhetvā ālimpenti. Hatthapajjotikanti hatthe telapilotikāya veṭhetvā dīpaṃ viya pajjālenti. Erakavattikanti erakavattakammakāraṇaṃ. Taṃ karontā heṭṭhāgīvato paṭṭhāya cammavaṭṭe kantitvā gopphake pātenti. Atha naṃ yottehi bandhitvā kaḍḍhanti. So attano cammavaṭṭe akkamitvā akkamitvā patati. Cirakavāsikanti cirakavāsikakammakāraṇaṃ. Taṃ karontā tatheva cammavaṭṭe kantitvā kaṭiyaṃ ṭhapenti, kaṭito paṭṭhāya kantitvā gopphakesu ṭhapenti, uparimehi heṭṭhimasarīraṃ cirakanivāsananivatthaṃ viya hoti. Eṇeyyakanti eṇeyyakakammakāraṇaṃ. Taṃ karontā ubhosu kapparesu ca ubhosu jaṇṇukesu ca ayavalayāni datvā ayasūlāni koṭṭenti, so catūhi ayasūlehi bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhahati. Atha naṃ parivāretvā aggiṃ karonti. “Eṇeyyako jotipariggaho yathā”ti āgataṭṭhānepi idameva vuttaṃ. Taṃ sandhito sandhito sūlāni apanetvā catūhi aṭṭhikoṭīhiyeva ṭhapenti. Evarūpā kammakāraṇā nāma natthi.

Jotimālikanti: They wrap the entire body with oil-soaked cloths and set it alight. Hatthapajjotikanti: They wrap the hands with oil-soaked cloths and light them like lamps.
