Erakavattikanti: The Erakavattika punishment. In doing this, they cut a strip of skin from below the neck down to the ankles. Then, binding him with cords, they pull him. He falls, stepping again and again on his own strip of skin. Cirakavāsikanti: The Cirakavāsika punishment. In doing this, they similarly cut a strip of skin and place it at the waist; then, cutting from the waist down, they place it at the ankles. The lower body appears as if clothed in a bark-cloth garment. Eṇeyyakanti: The Eṇeyyaka punishment. In doing this, they fix iron rings on both elbows and both knees and hammer in iron stakes. He stands on the ground supported by the four iron stakes. Then, surrounding him, they light a fire. Where the phrase “like a deer surrounded by flames” occurs, this very thing is meant. They remove the stakes one by one from the joints and leave him supported only by the four bone-ends. Such forms of punishment do not exist.

Baḷisamaṃsikanti [P 2.0279] ubhatomukhehi baḷisehi paharitvā cammamaṃsanhārūni uppāṭenti. Kahāpaṇikanti sakalasarīraṃ tiṇhāhi vāsīhi koṭito paṭṭhāya kahāpaṇamattaṃ kahāpaṇamattaṃ pātentā koṭṭenti. Khārāpatacchikanti sarīraṃ [M 0.0242] tattha tattha āvudhehi paharitvā kocchehi khāraṃ ghaṃsenti, cammamaṃsanhārūni paggharitvā pasavanti, aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikāva tiṭṭhati. Palighaparivattikanti ekena passena nipajjāpetvā kaṇṇacchiddena ayasūlaṃ koṭṭetvā pathaviyā ekābaddhaṃ karonti. Atha naṃ pāde gahetvā āviñchanti. Palālapīṭhakanti chekā kāraṇikā chavicammaṃ acchinditvā nisadapotakāhi aṭṭhīni chinditvā kesesu gahetvā ukkhipanti, maṃsarāsiyeva hoti. Atha naṃ keseheva pariyonandhitvā gaṇhanti, palālapīṭhaṃ viya katvā paliveṭhenti. Sunakhehipīti katipayāni divasāni āhāraṃ adatvā chātasunakhehi khādāpenti. Te muhuttena aṭṭhisaṅkhalikameva karonti. Evampi kissatīti evampi vighātaṃ pāpuṇāti. Parikissatīti sabbabhāgena vighātaṃ pāpuṇāti. Parikilissatīti upatāpaṃ pāpuṇāti.

Baḷisamaṃsikanti: They strike with double-pointed hooks and tear off skin, flesh, and sinews. Kahāpaṇikanti: They cut the entire body with sharp adzes, starting from the crown of the head, and chop it piece by piece, each the size of a kahāpaṇa coin. Khārāpatacchikanti: They strike the body with weapons in various places, then rub it with caustic substances using brushes; the skin, flesh, and sinews ooze and flow away, leaving only a chain of bones. Palighaparivattikanti: They make the person lie on one side and drive an iron stake through the ear hole into the ground, fixing him to it. Then they grab his feet and whirl him around. Palālapīṭhakanti: Skillful executioners strip off the outer skin and hide, break the bones with grindstones, and lift the body by the hair, so that it becomes just a heap of flesh. Then, wrapping it up completely with his own hair, they seize it, making it like a straw mat, and roll it up. Sunakhehipi: They starve dogs for some days and then have them devour the person. In a moment, they reduce him to a mere skeleton. Evampi kissati means he is thus tormented. Parikissati means he is completely tormented. Parikilissati means he experiences affliction.

Puna aññaṃ kāraṇaṃ dassento “atha vā kāmataṇhāya abhibhūto”tiādimāha. Tattha kāmataṇhāyāti pañcakāmaguṇikalobhena. Abhibhūtoti tena maddito. Pariyādinnacittoti kusalācāraṃ khepetvā gahitacitto. Bhoge pariyesantoti dhanaṃ gavesamāno. Nāvāya mahāsamuddaṃ pakkhandatīti taraṇīsaṅkhātāya nāvāya mahantaṃ loṇasāgaraṃ pavisati. Sītassa purakkhatoti sītaṃ purato katvā. Uṇhassa purakkhatoti uṇhaṃ purato katvā. Ḍaṃsāti piṅgalamakkhikā. Makasāti makasā eva. Pīḷiyamānoti ḍaṃsādisamphassehi vihesiyamāno. Khuppipāsāya miyyamānoti khuddāpipāsāya maramāno. Tigumbaṃ gacchatītiādīni mūlapadaṃ gacchatītipariyosānāni catuvīsati padāni raṭṭhanāmena vuttāni. Marukantāraṃ [P 2.0280] gacchatīti vālukakantāraṃ tārakasaññāya gacchati[V 0.0222]. Jaṇṇupathanti jāṇūhi gantabbamaggaṃ. Ajapathanti ajehi gantabbamaggaṃ. Meṇḍapathepi eseva nayo.

Then, presenting another reason, he says, “Or else, overcome by craving for sensual pleasures,” and so on. Here, kāmataṇhāya means through greed for the five strands of sensual pleasure. Abhibhūto means crushed by it. Pariyādinnacitto means his mind is seized, having abandoned virtuous conduct. Bhoge pariyesanto means seeking wealth. Nāvāya mahāsamuddaṃ pakkhandati means he enters the great saltwater ocean by means of a ship, which is known as a taraṇī. Sītassa purakkhato means having put cold before him. Uṇhassa purakkhato means having put heat before him. Ḍaṃsā refers to gadflies, which are reddish-brown flies. Makasā means mosquitoes. Pīḷiyamāno means being harassed, vexed by the contact of gadflies and so on. Khuppipāsāya miyyamāno means dying from hunger and thirst. The twenty-four terms from “Tigumbaṃ gacchati” up to “mūlapadaṃ gacchati” are spoken as names of regions. Marukantāraṃ gacchati means he traverses a sandy wasteland, guided by the stars. Jaṇṇupatha means a path to be travelled on one's knees. Ajapatha means a path to be travelled by goats. The same principle applies to Meṇḍapatha.

Saṅkupathanti khāṇuke koṭṭetvā tehi uggamitabbaṃ khāṇumaggaṃ, taṃ gacchanto pabbatapāde ṭhatvā ayasiṅghāṭakaṃ yottena bandhitvā uddhaṃ khipitvā pabbate laggāpetvā yottenāruyha vajiraggena lohadaṇḍena pabbataṃ vijjhitvā khāṇukaṃ koṭṭetvā tattha ṭhatvā siṅghāṭakaṃ ākaḍḍhitvā puna upari laggāpetvā tattha ṭhito cammayottaṃ olambetvā taṃ ādāya otaritvā heṭṭhimakhāṇuke bandhitvā vāmahatthena yottaṃ gahetvā dakkhiṇahatthena muggaraṃ ādāya yottaṃ paharitvā khāṇukaṃ nīharitvā puna [M 0.0243] abhiruhati. Etenupāyena pabbatamatthakaṃ abhiruyha parato otaranto purimanayeneva paṭhamaṃ pabbatamatthake khāṇukaṃ koṭṭetvā cammapasibbake yottaṃ bandhitvā khāṇuke veṭhetvā sayaṃ antopasibbake nisīditvā makkaṭakānaṃ suttavissajjanākārena yottaṃ viniveṭhetvā otarati. Tena vuttaṃ – “khāṇuke koṭṭetvā tehi uggamitabbaṃ khāṇumagga”nti. Chattapathanti cammachattena vātaṃ gāhāpetvā sakuṇehi viya otaritabbaṃ maggaṃ. Vaṃsapathanti veṇugumbachedanasatthena chinditvā rukkhaṃ pharasunā koṭṭetvā maggaṃ karonto veḷuvane nisseṇiṃ katvā veḷugumbe āruyha veḷuṃ chinditvā aparassa veḷugumbassa upari pātetvā veḷugumbamatthakeneva gantabbaṃ maggaṃ sandhāya “vaṃsapathaṃ gacchatī”ti vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

Saṅkupathanti means a stake-path, which is a path to be ascended by means of hammered-in stakes. To traverse it, one stands at the foot of a mountain, fastens an iron grappling hook with a rope, throws it upwards to make it catch, and then climbs up by the rope. With a diamond-tipped iron rod, one pierces the mountain, hammers in a stake, and stands on it. One then pulls back the hook and makes it catch higher up. Standing there, one lowers a leather strap, takes it, descends, fastens it to the lower stake, holds the strap with the left hand, takes a mallet with the right hand, strikes the strap to dislodge the stake, removes it, and climbs up again. By this method, one reaches the mountain peak. When descending on the other side, following the same method, one first hammers a stake into the mountain peak, fastens a rope to a leather bag, wraps it around the stake, sits inside the bag, and then descends by unwinding the rope in the manner of a monkey releasing a thread. Hence it is said: “a stake-path to be ascended by means of hammered-in stakes.” Chattapathanti means an umbrella-path, a path to be descended like birds by catching the wind with a leather umbrella. Vaṃsapathanti: It should be understood that when it is said, “He goes by the bamboo-path,” this refers to a path that must be traversed right over the tops of bamboo clumps, which one makes by cutting a bamboo from a clump one has climbed—having made a ladder in the bamboo grove—and letting it fall onto another bamboo clump, thus making a path by cutting through bamboo thickets with a bamboo-splitting knife and chopping down trees with an axe.

Gavesanto na vindati, alābhamūlakampi dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedetīti avindanamūlakampi kāyikacetasikaṃ dukkhaṃ paṭilabhati.

Seeking but not finding, he experiences suffering and distress rooted in non-attainment; this means he obtains physical and mental suffering rooted in not finding.

Laddhāti labhitvā. Ārakkhamūlakanti rakkhaṇamūlakampi. Kinti me bhogeti kena upāyena mama bhoge. Neva rājāno hareyyuṃ…pe… na appiyā dāyādā hareyyunti. Gopayatoti mañjūsādīhi gopayantassa. Vippalujjantīti vinassanti.

Laddhāti means having obtained. Ārakkhamūlakaṃ means rooted in guarding. Kinti me bhoge means: “By what means might my wealth be such that neither kings would take it… nor would unloved heirs take it?” Gopayato refers to one who is guarding it with chests and so on. Vippalujjanti means they are destroyed.

56. Etamādīnavaṃ [P 2.0281] ñatvā, muni pubbāpare idhāti etaṃ “yaso kitti ca yā pubbe, hāyate vāpi tassa sā”ti ito pabhuti vutte pubbāpare idha imasmiṃ sāsane pubbato apare samaṇabhāvato vibbhantakabhāve ādīnavaṃ muni ñatvā.

56. “Knowing this danger, the sage, earlier and later, here” means: the sage, knowing the danger in the state of having strayed from the state of a recluse—which is later than the former state—within this Dispensation, as described from the passage, “Whatever fame and praise one had before, that too declines for him,” onwards.

Daḷhaṃ kareyyāti niddesapadassa uddesapadaṃ. Thiraṃ kareyyāti asithilaṃ kareyya. Daḷhaṃ samādāno assāti thirapaṭiñño bhaveyya. Avaṭṭhitasamādānoti sanniṭṭhānapaṭiñño.

“Make it firm” is the term being defined. “Make it steady” means to make it not slack. “One should undertake it firmly” means one should be of firm resolve. “Unwavering commitment” means resolute in decision.

57. Etaṃ [V 0.0223] ariyānamuttamanti yadidaṃ vivekacariyā, etaṃ buddhādīnaṃ ariyānaṃ uttamaṃ. Tasmā vivekaṃyeva sikkhethāti adhippāyo. Na tena seṭṭho maññethāti tena ca vivekena attānaṃ “seṭṭho aha”nti na maññeyya, tena mānathaddho na bhaveyyāti vuttaṃ hoti.

57. “This is the supreme for the noble ones” means this practice of seclusion is supreme for the noble ones, such as the Buddha and others. Therefore, the intention is that one should train only in seclusion. “One should not think oneself best on account of that” means that one should not think of oneself, “I am the best,” because of that seclusion. The meaning is that one should not become stiff with conceit on account of it.

Unnatinti [M 0.0244] ussāpanaṃ. Unnamanti uggantvā paṭṭhapanaṃ. Mānanti ahaṃkāraṃ. Thāmanti balakkāraṃ. Thambhanti thaddhakaraṇaṃ. Thaddhoti amaddavo. Patthaddhoti visesena amaddavo. Paggahitasiroti uṭṭhitasīso. Sāmantāti na ārakā. Āsanneti na dūre. Avidūreti samīpe. Upakaṭṭheti santike.

"Unnatinti" means raising up. "Unnamanti" means raising up and establishing. "Mānanti" means conceit. "Thāmanti" means force. "Thambhanti" means making rigid. "Thaddhoti" means inflexible. "Patthaddhoti" means especially inflexible. "Paggahitasiroti" means with head uplifted. "Sāmantāti" means not remote. "Āsanneti" means not far. "Avidūreti" means near. "Upakaṭṭheti" means very near.

58. Rittassāti vivittassa, kāyaduccaritādīhi virahitassa. Oghatiṇṇassa pihayanti, kāmesu gadhitā pajāti vatthukāmesu laggā sattā tassa caturoghatiṇṇassa pihayanti iṇāyikā viya āṇaṇyassāti arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi.

58. "Of the empty" means of the secluded, devoid of bodily misconduct and the like. People attached to sensual pleasures envy one who has crossed the flood; that is, beings attached to the objects of sensual pleasure envy that one who has crossed the four floods, just as debtors envy one who is free from debt. Thus, he concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship.

Rittassāti sabbakilesehi tucchassa. Vivittassāti suññassa. Pavivittassāti ekakassa. Idāni yehi ritto hoti, te dassento “kāyaduccaritena rittassā”tiādimāha. Tattha kilesapaṭipāṭiyā maggapaṭipāṭiyāti dvidhā rittatā veditabbā. Kilesapaṭipāṭiyā tāva rāgo moho thambho sārambho māno madoti, imehi chahi kilesehi arahattamaggena ritto hoti; doso kodho upanāho pamādoti, imehi catūhi kilesehi anāgāmimaggena [P 2.0282] ritto hoti; atimāno makkho paḷāso issā macchariyaṃ māyā sāṭheyyanti, imehi sattahi sotāpattimaggena ritto hoti.

"Of the empty" means of one devoid of all defilements. "Of the secluded" means of the empty. "Of the quite secluded" means of one who is alone. Now, to show what one is empty of, he said: "empty of bodily misconduct," and so on. Herein, emptiness should be understood in two ways: by the sequence of defilements and by the sequence of paths. First, by the sequence of defilements: one is empty of these six defilements—lust, delusion, rigidity, rivalry, conceit, and intoxication—by the path of Arahantship; one is empty of these four defilements—hatred, anger, resentment, and negligence—by the path of non-returning; one is empty of these seven—contempt, denigration, spite, envy, stinginess, deceit, and dishonesty—by the path of stream-entry.

Maggapaṭipāṭiyā pana sotāpattimaggena atimāno makkho paḷāso issā macchariyaṃ māyā sāṭheyyanti; imehi sattahi ritto hoti, anāgāmimaggena doso kodho upanāho pamādoti, imehi catūhi ritto hoti; arahattamaggena rāgo moho thambho sārambho māno madoti, imehi chahi ritto hoti. Tīṇi duccaritāni sabbakilesehītiādinā nayena avasesāpi yathāyogaṃ yojetabbā.

Furthermore, by the sequence of paths, one is empty of these seven by the path of stream-entry: contempt, denigration, spite, envy, stinginess, deceit, and dishonesty. One is empty of these four by the path of non-returning: hatred, anger, resentment, and negligence. One is empty of these six by the path of Arahantship: lust, delusion, rigidity, rivalry, conceit, and intoxication. The remaining defilements should also be connected as appropriate, according to the method beginning with 'the three kinds of misconduct, all defilements,' and so forth.

Vatthukāme [M 0.0245] parijānitvāti tebhūmake vatthukāme ñātatīraṇapariññāhi samāpanavasena jānitvā. Kilesakāme pahāyāti chandādayo kilesakāme pahānapariññāya jahitvā. Byantiṃ karitvāti vigatantaṃ vigatakoṭiṃ karitvā.

"Having fully understood the objects of sensual pleasure" means having known the objects of sensual pleasure belonging to the three planes by means of the full understanding of knowing and the full understanding of judging, by way of accomplishment. "Having abandoned the defilements of sensual pleasure" means having abandoned the defilements of sensual pleasure, such as desire, by means of the full understanding of abandoning. "Having made an end of them" means having made a gone-end, having made a gone-limit.

Kāmoghaṃ [V 0.0224] tiṇṇassāti anāgāmimaggena avasānasaṅkhātaṃ kāmoghaṃ taritvā ṭhitassa. Bhavoghanti arahattamaggena. Diṭṭhoghanti sotāpattimaggena. Avijjoghanti arahattamaggena. Sabbaṃ saṃsārapathanti sabbakhandhadhātuāyatanapaṭipāṭisaṅkhātaṃ pathaṃ arahattamaggeneva taritvā ṭhitassa. Sotāpattimaggena uttiṇṇassa. Sakadāgāmimaggena nittiṇṇassa. Anāgāmimaggena kāmadhātuṃ atikkantassa. Arahattamaggena sabbabhavaṃ samatikkantassa. Phalasamāpattivasena vītivattassa. Pāraṃgatassātiādīni nibbānavasena vuttāni. Yathā iṇāyikā āṇaṇyanti pavaḍḍhakaiṇaṃ ādāya vicarantā āṇaṇyaṃ. Patthentīti patthanaṃ uppādenti. Ābādhikā ārogyanti pittādirogāturo bhesajjakiriyāya taṃrogavūpasamanatthaṃ ārogyaṃ. Yathā bandhanabaddhāti nakkhattadivase bandhanāgāre baddhapurisā. Yathā dāsā bhujissanti yasmā bhujissā purisā yaṃ icchanti, taṃ karonti, na naṃ koci balakkārena tato nivatteti, tasmā dāsā bhujissabhāvaṃ patthenti. Yathā kantāraddhānapakkhandāti yasmā balavanto purisā hatthabhāraṃ gahetvā sajjāvudhā saparivārā [P 2.0283] kantāraṃ paṭipajjanti, te corā dūratova disvā palāyanti. Te sotthinā kantāraṃ nittharitvā khemantaṃ patvā haṭṭhatuṭṭhā honti. Tasmā kantārapakkhandā khemantabhūmiṃ patthenti. Desanāpariyosāne tisso sotāpattiphalaṃ patvā pacchā pabbajitvā arahattaṃ sacchākāsi.

"Of one who has crossed the flood of sensuality" means of one who, by the path of the non-returner, having crossed the flood of sensuality, which is designated as the end, stands firm. "The flood of existence" is by the Arahant path. "The flood of views" is by the stream-entry path. "The flood of ignorance" is by the Arahant path. "The entire path of saṃsāra" refers to the entire course designated as the sequence of all aggregates, elements, and sense bases, of one who has crossed it and stands firm by the Arahant path alone. Of one who has crossed over by the stream-entry path. Of one who has completely crossed over by the once-returner path. Of one who has gone beyond the realm of sensual desire by the non-returner path. Of one who has completely transcended all existence by the Arahant path. Of one who has passed beyond by way of the attainment of fruition. "Gone to the far shore" and similar terms are spoken with reference to Nibbāna. Just as debtors long for freedom from debt—those wandering having taken on increasing debt long for freedom from debt. "They long for" means they generate a longing. The sick long for health—one afflicted by illnesses of bile, etc., seeks health through the action of medicine for the purpose of pacifying that illness. Just as those bound in bonds—men bound in a prison on a festival day. Just as slaves long for freedom—since free men do whatever they wish, and no one forcibly turns them back from it, therefore slaves long for the state of being free. Just as those setting out on a wilderness path—since strong men, having taken up a load, armed and with a retinue, proceed into the wilderness, and thieves, seeing them from afar, flee. They, having safely crossed the wilderness and reached a place of safety, are delighted and happy. Thus, those setting out on a wilderness path long for a place of safety. At the end of the discourse, three women attained the fruit of stream-entry; later they went forth and realized Arahantship.

Saddhammapajjotikāya mahāniddesaṭṭhakathāya

In the Saddhammapajjotikā, the Commentary on the Mahāniddesa.

Tissametteyyasuttaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Niddesa on the Tissametteyya Sutta is concluded.

8. Pasūrasuttaniddesavaṇṇanā

8. The Explanation of the Niddesa on the Pasūra Sutta.

59. Aṭṭhame [V 0.0225][P 2.0284] pasūrasuttaniddese paṭhamagāthāya tāva saṅkhepo – ime diṭṭhigatikā attano diṭṭhiṃ sandhāya “idheva suddhī”ti vadanti. Aññesu pana dhammesu visuddhiṃ nāhu, evaṃ yaṃ attano satthārādiṃ nissitā, tattheva “esa vādo subho”ti evaṃ subhavādā hutvā puthū samaṇabrāhmaṇā “sassato loko”tiādīsu paccekasaccesu niviṭṭhā.

59. In the eighth, the Niddesa on the Pasūra Sutta, first the summary of the first verse is as follows: these adherents of views, with reference to their own view, declare, "Purity is here alone." But in other doctrines, they said there is no purity. Thus, relying on their own teachers and the like, right there they become proponents of an excellent doctrine, saying, "This doctrine is excellent." Various ascetics and brahmins are established in individual truths, such as "the world is eternal," and so on.

Sabbe [M 0.0246] paravāde khipantīti sabbā paraladdhiyo chaḍḍenti. Ukkhipantīti dūrato khipanti. Parikkhipantīti samantato khipanti. Subhavādāti niddesassa uddesapadaṃ. Sobhanavādāti “etaṃ sundara”nti kathentā. Paṇḍitavādāti “paṇḍitā maya”nti evaṃ kathentā. Thiravādāti “niddosavādaṃ vadāmā”ti kathentā. Ñāyavādāti “yuttavādaṃ vadāmā”ti kathentā. Hetuvādāti “kāraṇasahitaṃ vadāmā”ti kathentā. Lakkhaṇavādāti “sallakkhetabbaṃ vadāmā”ti vadantā. Kāraṇavādāti “udāharaṇayuttavādaṃ vadāmā”ti kathentā. Ṭhānavādāti “pakkamituṃ asakkuṇeyyavādaṃ vadāmā”ti vadantā.

"They reject all others' views" means they abandon all others' doctrines. "Ukkhipanti" means they cast away from afar. "Parikkhipanti" means they cast away from all sides. "Subhavādā" is the term to be explained of the Niddesa. "Sobhanavādā" means those who say, "This is beautiful." "Paṇḍitavādā" means those who say, "We are wise." "Thiravādā" means those who say, "We speak a faultless doctrine." "Ñāyavādā" means those who say, "We speak a fitting doctrine." "Hetuvādā" means those who say, "We speak with reason." "Lakkhaṇavādā" means those who say, "We speak what should be discerned." "Kāraṇavādā" means those who say, "We speak a doctrine accompanied by examples." "Ṭhānavādā" means those who say, "We speak a doctrine from which it is impossible to depart."

Niviṭṭhāti antopaviṭṭhā. Patiṭṭhitāti tattheva ṭhitā.

"Niviṭṭhā" means entered within. "Patiṭṭhitā" means standing right there.

60. Evaṃ niviṭṭhā ca “te vādakāmā”ti dutiyagāthā. Tattha bālaṃ dahantī mithu aññamaññanti “ayaṃ bālo, ayaṃ bālo”ti evaṃ dvepi janā aññamaññaṃ bālaṃ dahanti, bālato passanti. Vadanti te aññasitā kathojjanti te aññamaññasatthārādinissitā kalahaṃ vadanti. Pasaṃsakāmā kusalāvadānāti pasaṃsatthikā ubhopi “mayaṃ kusalāvadānā paṇḍitavādā”ti evaṃ saññino hutvā.

60. And thus established, the second verse is "they are desirous of debate." Therein, "fools they set down mutually, one another" means both people set down each other as a fool, seeing each other as a fool, thinking, "This one is a fool, this one is a fool." "They speak, relying on another, a quarrelsome speech" means, relying on each other's teachers and so forth, they speak a quarrel. "Desiring praise, skilled in speech" means both, being desirous of praise, become conscious thus: "we are skilled in speech, proponents of a wise doctrine."

Vādatthikāti vādena atthikā. Vādādhippāyāti vādajjhāsayā. Vādapurekkhārāti vādameva purato [V 0.0226] katvā caramānā[P 2.0285]. Vādapariyesanaṃ carantāti vādameva gavesanaṃ caramānā. Vigayhāti pavisitvā. Ogayhāti otaritvā. Ajjhogāhetvāti nimujjitvā. Pavisitvāti antokatvā.

"Vādatthikā" means they have a need for debate. "Vādādhippāyā" means their intention is debate. "Vādapurekkhārā" means they live having put debate first. "Vādapariyesanaṃ carantā" means they live searching for debate. "Vigayha" means having entered. "Ogayha" means having descended. "Ajjhogāhetvā" means having immersed. "Pavisitvā" means having entered within.

Anojavantīti nihīnaojavatī, tejavirahitāti attho. Sā kathāti esā vācā. Kathojjaṃ vadantīti nittejaṃ bhaṇanti. Evaṃ vadānesu ca tesu eko niyamato eva.

"Anojavantī" means having inferior power; devoid of vigor is the meaning. "Sā kathā" means this utterance. "Kathojjaṃ vadantī" means they speak without vigor. And among those speaking thus, one is invariably so.

61. Yutto kathāyanti gāthā. Tattha yutto kathāyanti vādakathāya ussukko. Pasaṃsamicchaṃ vinighāti hotīti attano pasaṃsaṃ icchanto “kathaṃ nu kho niggahessāmī”tiādinā nayena pubbeva vādā kathaṃkathī vinighātī hoti. Apāhatasminti pañhavīmaṃsakehi “atthāpagataṃ te bhaṇitaṃ, byañjanāpagataṃ te bhaṇita”ntiādinā nayena apaharite [M 0.0247] vāde. Nindāya so kuppatīti evaṃ apāhatasmiñca vāde uppannāya nindāya so kuppati. Randhamesīti yassa randhameva gavesanto.

61. "Yutto kathāya" is a verse. Here, "yutto kathāya" means zealous for debate. "Pasaṃsamicchaṃ vinighāti hoti" means one who, desiring praise, becomes doubtful and destructive of the debate beforehand, in the manner of "How indeed shall I refute them?" "Apāhatasmiṃ" means when the debate is refuted by those who examine questions, in the manner of "Your statement lacks meaning, your statement lacks clarity." "Nindāya so kuppati" means he becomes angry at the criticism that arises when the debate is thus refuted. "Randhamesī" means one who seeks only for flaws.

Thomananti vaṇṇabhaṇanaṃ. Kittinti pākaṭakaraṇaṃ. Vaṇṇahāriyanti guṇavaḍḍhanaṃ. Pubbeva sallāpāti sallāpato puretarameva. “Kathamidaṃ kathamida”nti kathaṃkathā assa atthīti kathaṃkathī. Jayo nu kho meti mama jayo. Kathaṃ niggahanti kena pakārena niggaṇhanaṃ. Paṭikammaṃ karissāmīti mama laddhiṃ parisuddhiṃ karissāmi. Visesanti atirekaṃ. Paṭivisesanti punappunaṃ visesaṃ. Āveṭhiyaṃ karissāmīti pariveṭhanaṃ karissāmi. Nibbeṭhiyanti mama nibbeṭhanaṃ mocanaṃ nikkhamanaṃ. Chedanti vādachindanaṃ. Maṇḍalanti vādasaṅghātaṃ. Pārisajjāti paricārikā. Pāsārikāti kāraṇitā. Apaharantīti paṭibāhanti.

"Thomanā" means praise. "Kitti" means making manifest. "Vaṇṇahāriyā" means increasing virtues. "Pubbeva sallāpa" means even before the conversation. "Kathaṃkathī" means he is doubtful, having doubts like "How is this? How is that?" "Jayo nu kho me" means "my victory." "Kathaṃ niggaha" means by what manner is the refutation. "Paṭikammaṃ karissāmi" means "I will purify my doctrine." "Visesa" means exceeding. "Paṭivisesa" means repeatedly exceeding. "Āveṭhiyaṃ karissāmi" means "I will envelop." "Nibbeṭhiyā" means my unwrapping, release, escape. "Cheda" means cutting off the argument. "Maṇḍala" means a clash of arguments. "Pārisajjā" means attendants. "Pāsārikā" means one who is an agent. "Apaharantī" means warding off.

Atthāpagatanti atthato apagataṃ[P 2.0286], attho natthīti. Atthato apaharantīti atthamhā paṭibāhanti. Attho te dunnitoti tava attho na sammā upanīto. Byañjanaṃ te duropitanti tava byañjanaṃ duppatiṭṭhāpitaṃ. Niggaho te akatoti tayā niggaho na kato. Paṭikammaṃ te dukkaṭanti tayā attano laddhipatiṭṭhāpanaṃ duṭṭhu kataṃ. Visamakathaṃ dukkathitanti na sammā kathitaṃ. Dubbhaṇitanti bhaṇantenapi duṭṭhu bhaṇitaṃ. Dullapitanti na sammā vissajjitaṃ. Duruttanti aññathā bhaṇitaṃ. Dubbhāsitanti virūpaṃ bhāsitaṃ.

"Atthāpagata" means gone from the meaning; it has no meaning. "Atthato apaharantī" means they ward off from the meaning. "Attho te dunnito" means your meaning is not well presented. "Byañjanaṃ te duropita" means your expression is poorly established. "Niggaho te akato" means a refutation was not made by you. "Paṭikammaṃ te dukkaṭa" means the establishment of your own doctrine is poorly done by you. "Visamakathaṃ dukkathita" means not properly spoken. "Dubbhaṇita" means poorly spoken even in the speaking. "Dullapita" means not properly answered. "Durutta" means spoken otherwise. "Dubbhāsita" means improperly spoken.

Nindāyāti garahaṇena. Garahāyāti dosakathanena. Akittiyāti aguṇakathanena. Avaṇṇahārikāyāti aguṇavaḍḍhanena.

"Nindāya" means by censure. "Garahāya" means by speaking of faults. "Akittiyā" means by speaking of non-virtues. "Avaṇṇahārikāya" means by increasing non-virtues.

Kuppatīti [V 0.0227] pakatibhāvaṃ jahetvā calati. Byāpajjatīti dosavasena pūtibhāvaṃ āpajjati. Patiṭṭhīyatīti kodhavasena gaṇabhāvaṃ gacchati. Kopañcāti kupitabhāvaṃ. Dosañcāti dūsanaṃ. Apaccayañcāti atuṭṭhākārañca. Pātukarotīti pākaṭaṃ karoti. Randhamesīti antaragavesī. Virandhamesīti chiddagavesī. Aparaddhamesīti guṇaṃ apanetvā dosameva gavesī. Khalitamesīti pakkhalanagavesī. Gaḷitamesīti patanagavesī. “Ghaṭṭitamesī”tipi pāṭho, tassa pīḷanagavesīti attho. Vivaramesīti dosagavesī.

"Kuppati" means abandoning the natural state and becoming agitated. "Byāpajjati" means reaching a state of corruption through hatred. "Patiṭṭhīyati" means reaching a hardened state through anger. "Kopa" means a state of anger. "Dosa" means corruption. "Apaccaya" means a state of displeasure. "Pātukaroti" means making manifest. "Randhamesī" means seeking an opening. "Virandhamesī" means seeking a fissure. "Aparaddhamesī" means seeking only faults after removing virtues. "Khalitamesī" means seeking a stumble. "Gaḷitamesī" means seeking a fall. "Ghaṭṭitamesī" is also a reading; its meaning is seeking oppression. "Vivaramesī" means seeking a defect.

62. Na [M 0.0248] kevalañca so kuppati, apica kho pana “yamassa vāda”nti gāthā. Tattha parihīnamāhu, apāhatanti atthabyañjanādito apāhataṃ parihīnaṃ vadanti. Paridevatīti tatonimittaṃ so “aññaṃ mayā āvajjita”ntiādīhi vippalapati. Socatīti “tassa jayo”tiādīni ārabbha socati. “Upaccagā ma”nti anutthunātīti “so maṃ vādena vādaṃ atikkanto”tiādinā nayena suṭṭhutaraṃ vippalapati.

62. Not only does he become angry, but also there is the verse, "Whatever his argument is." Therein, "diminished" they say; they call it rejected and diminished in terms of meaning, phrasing, and so on. "He laments" means that, for that reason, he babbles with phrases such as, "Something else was considered by me." "He grieves" means he grieves concerning such things as, "His is the victory." "'He has surpassed me,' he laments" means he babbles excessively in the manner of, "He has surpassed me in argument after argument."

Parihāpitanti na vaḍḍhitaṃ. Aññaṃ mayā āvajjitanti aññaṃ kāraṇaṃ mayā avanamitaṃ. Cintitanti vīmaṃsitaṃ. Mahāpakkhoti mahanto ñātipakkho etassāti mahāpakkho. Mahāparisoti mahāparicārikapariso. Mahāparivāroti mahādāsadāsiparivāro. Parisā cāyaṃ vaggāti ayañca parisā vaggā, na ekā. Puna bhañjissāmīti puna bhindissāmi.

"Parihāpita" means not increased. "Aññaṃ mayā āvajjita" means "I have inclined towards another reason." "Cintita" means investigated. "Mahāpakkha" means "he has a large group of relatives," hence "mahāpakkha." "Mahāparisa" means a large assembly of attendants. "Mahāparivāra" means a large entourage of male and female slaves. "Parisā cāyaṃ vaggā" means "this assembly is divided," that is, not unified. "Puna bhañjissāmi" means "I will break it again."

63. Ete [P 2.0287] vivādā samaṇesūti ettha pana samaṇā vuccanti bāhiraparibbājakā. Etesu ugghātinighāti hotīti etesu vādesu jayaparājayādivasena cittaugghātanighātaṃ vā pāpuṇanto ugghāti ca nighāti ca hoti. Virame kathojjanti pajaheyya kalahaṃ. Na haññadatthatthi pasaṃsalābhāti na hi ettha pasaṃsalābhato añño attho atthi. Uttāno vāti na gambhīroti attho “pañcime kāmaguṇā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 6.63) viya.

63. "Ete vivādā samaṇesu": Here, "samaṇā" refers to external wanderers. "Etesu ugghātinighāti hoti" means that in these disputes, by attaining an uplifting and a striking down of the mind due to victory, defeat, and so on, one becomes uplifted and struck down. "Virame kathojja" means one should abandon quarreling. "Na haññadatthatthi pasaṃsalābhā" means that here there is indeed no other purpose than the gain of praise. "Uttāno" means not profound, as in the passage beginning "these five strands of sensual pleasure" (AN 6.63).

Gambhīro vāti duppaveso appatiṭṭho paṭiccasamuppādo viya. Gūḷho vāti paṭicchanno hutvā ṭhito “abhirama nanda ahaṃ te pāṭibhogo”tiādīsu (udā. 22) viya. Paṭicchanno vāti apākaṭo “mātaraṃ pitaraṃ hantvā”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 294; netti. 113) viya. Neyyo vāti nīharitvā kathetabbo “asaddho akataññū cā”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 97) viya. Nīto vāti pāḷiyā ṭhitaniyāmena kathetabbo “cattārome, bhikkhave, ariyavaṃsā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.28) viya. Anavajjo vāti niddosattho “kusalā dhammā”tiādīsu [V 0.0228] (dha. sa. tikamātikā 1) viya. Nikkileso vāti kilesavirahito vipassanā viya. Vodāno vāti [M 0.0249] parisuddho lokuttaraṃ viya. Paramattho vāti uttamattho uttamatthabhūto attho khandhadhātuāyatananibbānāni viya.

"Profound" means difficult to penetrate and unestablished, like dependent origination. "Hidden" means concealed, as in "Rejoice, Nanda, I am your guarantor" (Ud 2.2). "Concealed" means unmanifest, as in "having killed mother and father" (Dhp 294). "Requiring interpretation" means to be spoken after drawing out the meaning, as in "the faithless and ungrateful" (Dhp 97). "Explicit" means to be spoken according to the established method in the Pāli text, as in "these four noble lineages, monks" (AN 4.28). "Blameless" means having a faultless meaning, as in "wholesome states" (Dhs Tikamātikā 1). "Undefiled" means devoid of defilements, like insight meditation. "Purified" means completely pure, like the supramundane. "Ultimate meaning" means the highest meaning, the meaning that is ultimate reality, such as the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and Nibbāna.

64. Chaṭṭhagāthāyattho – yasmā ca na haññadatthatthi pasaṃsalābhā, tasmā paramaṃ lābhaṃ labhantopi “sundaro aya”nti tattha diṭṭhiyā pasaṃsito vā pana hotīti taṃ vādaṃ parisāya majjhe dīpetvā tato so tena jayatthena tuṭṭhiṃ vā dantavidaṃsakaṃ vā āpajjanto hassati, mānena ca unnamati. Kiṃ kāraṇaṃ? Yasmā taṃ jayatthaṃ pappuyya yathāmano jāto.

64. The meaning of the sixth verse: Because there is no other purpose than the gain of praise, therefore, even when obtaining the highest gain, he is praised for that view with "This is beautiful." Having declared that statement in the midst of the assembly, then through that gain of victory, he laughs, experiencing either delight or a baring of the teeth, and is uplifted with pride. What is the reason? Because, having obtained that victory, he has become as he wished.

Thambhayitvāti pūretvā. Brūhayitvāti vaḍḍhetvā. Imissā gāthāya niddeso uttānattho.

"Thambhayitvā" means having filled. "Brūhayitvā" means having increased. The explanation of this verse is straightforward in meaning.

65. Evaṃ unnamato ca “yā unnatī”ti gāthā. Tattha mānātimānaṃ vadate panesoti eso pana taṃ unnatiṃ “vighātabhūmī”ti abujjhamāno mānañca atimānañca vadati. Evaṃ imissāpi gāthāya niddeso uttānattho.

65. Thus, concerning one who is uplifted, there is the verse, "Whatever uplifting." Here, "this one speaks of pride and excessive pride," not understanding that uplifting as "a ground for ruin." Thus, the explanation of this verse is also straightforward in meaning.

66. Evaṃ vāde dosaṃ dassetvā idāni tassa vādaṃ asampaṭicchanto [P 2.0288] “sūro”ti gāthamāha. Tattha rājakhādāyāti rājakhādanīyena, bhattavetanenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Abhigajjameti paṭisūramicchanti yathā so paṭisūraṃ icchanto abhigajjanto eti, evaṃ diṭṭhigatiko diṭṭhigatikanti dasseti. Yeneva so tena palehīti yena so tuyhaṃ paṭisūro, tena gaccha. Pubbeva natthi yadidaṃ yudhāyāti yaṃ pana kilesajātaṃ yuddhāya siyā, taṃ idha pubbeva natthi, bodhimūleyevassa pahīnanti dasseti.

66. Having thus shown the fault in debate, now, not accepting that debate, he speaks the verse beginning with "hero." Here, "rājakhādāya" means by royal sustenance, that is, by food and wages. "Abhigajjameti" means they desire a counter-hero; just as one, desiring a counter-hero, comes roaring, so too, he shows, one who adheres to a view is like another who adheres to a view. "Yeneva so tena palehi" means "Go with him, who is your counter-hero." "Pubbeva natthi yadidaṃ yudhāya" means that whatever group of defilements would be for battle, that does not exist here beforehand; it shows that it was abandoned for him at the very root of awakening.

Sūroti niddesassa uddesapadaṃ. Suṭṭhu uro sūro, vissaṭṭhauro ninnauroti attho. Vīroti parakkamavanto. Vikkantoti saṅgāmaṃ pavisanto. Abhīrūtiādayo vuttanayā eva. Puṭṭhoti niddesassa uddesapadaṃ. Positoti thūlakato. Āpāditoti upaḍḍhabalito paṭipādito. Vaḍḍhitoti tato tato bhāvito.

'Sūra' is the heading of the explanation. 'Sūra' (hero) means 'one with a good chest,' that is, one with a broad chest or a prominent chest. 'Vīra' (brave) means one who is energetic. 'Vikkanta' (valiant) means one who enters battle. 'Abhīru' (fearless) and the rest are as previously stated. 'Puṭṭha' (nourished) is the heading of the explanation. 'Posita' (nourished) means made stout. 'Āpādita' (brought up) means provided for from half-growth. 'Vaḍḍhita' (increased) means developed further from that point.

Gajjantoti [M 0.0250] abyattasarena gajjanto. Uggajjantoti ukkuṭṭhiṃ karonto. Abhigajjantoti sīhanādaṃ karonto. Etīti āgacchati. Upetīti tato samīpaṃ gacchati. Upagacchatīti tato samīpaṃ [V 0.0229] gantvā na nivattati. Paṭisūranti nibbhayaṃ. Paṭipurisanti sattupurisaṃ. Paṭisattunti sattu hutvā abhimukhe ṭhitaṃ. Paṭimallanti paṭisedhaṃ hutvā yujjhantaṃ. Icchantoti ākaṅkhamāno.

'Roaring' means roaring with an indistinct voice. 'Roaring loudly' means making a loud cry. 'Roaring greatly' means making a lion’s roar. 'Comes' means arrives. 'Approaches' means goes near to that. 'Goes up to' means having gone near to that, one does not turn back. 'Paṭisūra' means fearless. 'Paṭipurisa' means an enemy. 'Paṭisattu' means becoming a foe and standing face-to-face. 'Paṭimalla' means fighting as an opponent. 'Desiring' means longing.

Palehīti gaccha. Vajāti mā tiṭṭha. Gacchāti samīpaṃ upasaṅkama. Abhikkamāti parakkamaṃ karohi.

'Palehi' means go. 'Vaja' means do not stand. 'Gaccha' means approach. 'Abhikkama' means make an effort.

Bodhiyā mūleti mahābodhirukkhassa samīpe. Ye paṭisenikarā kilesāti ye kilesā paṭipakkhakarā. Paṭilomakarāti paṭāṇīkarā. Paṭikaṇṭakakarāti vinivijjhanakarā. Paṭipakkhakarāti sattukarā.

At the root of the Bodhi tree means near the great Bodhi tree. 'Those defilements that are hostile' means those defilements that act as opponents. 'Acting contrary' means acting to bring one down. 'Acting as a thorn' means acting to pierce through. 'Acting as an opponent' means acting as an enemy.

67. Ito paraṃ sesagāthā pākaṭasambandhā eva. Tattha vivādayantīti vivadanti. Paṭisenikattāti paṭilomakārakā. “Na tvaṃ imaṃ dhammavinayaṃ ājānāsī”tiādinā nayena viruddhavacanaṃ vivādo.

67. The remaining verses from here onwards are clearly connected. Therein, 'vivādayanti' means they dispute. 'Paṭisenikattā' means acting contrary. Dispute refers to contradictory speech, such as saying, 'You do not understand this Dhamma and Vinaya,' and so on.

Sahitaṃ meti mama vacanaṃ atthasaṃhitaṃ. Asahitaṃ teti tava vacanaṃ anatthasaṃhitaṃ. Adhiciṇṇaṃ te viparāvattanti [P 2.0289] yaṃ taṃ adhiciṇṇaṃ cirakālasevanavasena paguṇaṃ, taṃ mama vādaṃ āgamma nivattaṃ. Āropito te vādoti tuyhaṃ upari mayā doso āropito. Cara vādappamokkhāyāti bhattapuṭaṃ ādāya taṃ taṃ upasaṅkamitvā vādā pamokkhatthāya uttaraṃ pariyesamāno vicara. Nibbeṭhehi vāti atha vā mayā āropitadosato attānaṃ mocehi. Sace pahosīti sace sakkosi.

'Sahitaṃ me' means my words are connected with meaning. 'Asahitaṃ te' means your words are not connected with meaning. 'Adhiciṇṇaṃ te viparāvatta' means that which you have long practiced, that which is habitual through long association, has been overturned by encountering my doctrine. 'Āropito te vādo' means a fault has been imputed to you by me. 'Cara vādappamokkhāya' means taking your food parcel and approaching various people, wander seeking an answer for release from the debate. 'Nibbeṭhehi vā' means or else, free yourself from the fault imputed by me. 'Sace pahosi' means if you are able.

Āveṭhiyāya āveṭhiyanti āveṭhetvā nivattanena nivattanaṃ. Nibbeṭhiyāya nibbeṭhiyanti dosato mocanena mocanaṃ. Chedena chedanti evamādi heṭṭhā vuttanayattā yathāyogaṃ yojetabbaṃ.

'Āveṭhiyāya āveṭhiyanti' means a turning back by means of entwining and turning back. 'Nibbeṭhiyāya nibbeṭhiyanti' means a release by means of releasing from a fault. 'Chedena cheda' and so on should be applied appropriately, as the method has been stated below.

68. Visenikatvāti kilesasenaṃ vināsetvā. Kiṃ labhethāti paṭimallaṃ kiṃ labhissasi. Pasūrāti taṃ paribbājakaṃ ālapati. Yesīdha natthīti yesaṃ idha natthi. Imāyapi gāthāya niddeso uttānatthoyeva.

68. 'Visenikatvā' means having destroyed the army of defilements. 'Kiṃ labhetha' means 'what opponent will you gain?' 'Pasūra' means he addresses that wanderer. 'Yesīdha natthi' means 'for whom there is nothing here.' The explanation of this verse is also of straightforward meaning.

69. Pavitakkanti [M 0.0251] “jayo nu kho me bhavissatī”tiādīni vitakkento. Dhonena yugaṃ samāgamāti dhutakilesena buddhena saddhiṃ yugaggāhaṃ samāpanno. Na hi tvaṃ sakkhasi sampayātaveti [V 0.0230] kotthuādayo viya sīhādīhi dhonena saha yugaṃ gahetvā ekapadampi sampayātuṃ yugaggāhameva vā sampādetuṃ na sakkhissasīti.

69. 'Pavitakkanti' means thinking, 'Will there be victory for me?' and so on. 'Dhonena yugaṃ samāgamā' means having entered into a contest with the Buddha, who has shaken off defilements. 'Na hi tvaṃ sakkhasi sampayātaveti' means that, like jackals with lions, you will not be able to proceed even a single step having taken up a yoke with the purified one, nor will you be able to accomplish the yoking itself.

Manoti niddesassa uddesapadaṃ. Cittanti cittatāya cittaṃ. “Ārammaṇaṃ minamānaṃ jānātī”ti mano. Mānasanti mano eva. “Antalikkhacaro pāso, yvāyaṃ carati mānaso”ti (mahāva. 33; saṃ. ni. 1.151) hi ettha pana sampayuttakadhammo mānasoti vutto.

'Mano' is the heading of the explanation. 'Citta' is so called because it thinks. 'It knows, measuring the object'—thus, it is called 'mano' (mind). 'Mānasa' is simply the mind itself. In the verse, 'The snare that moves in the sky, that which moves as the mind,' however, the associated phenomena are called 'mānasa.'

“Kathañhi bhagavā tuyhaṃ, sāvako sāsane rato;

Appattamānaso sekkho, kālaṃkayirā janesutā”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.159) –

'How, indeed, Blessed One, could your disciple, devoted to the teaching, a learner who has not attained the goal, die among the people?'

Ettha [P 2.0290] arahattaṃ mānasanti vuttaṃ. Idha pana manova mānasaṃ, byañjanavasena hetaṃ padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ.

Here, arahantship is called 'mānasa.' But in this context, 'mano' itself is 'mānasa'; this term has been expanded by way of its letters.

Hadayanti cittaṃ. “Cittaṃ vā te khipissāmi, hadayaṃ vā te phālessāmī”ti (su. ni. āḷavakasutta; saṃ. ni. 1.237) ettha uro hadayanti vuttaṃ. “Hadayā hadayaṃ maññe aññāya tacchatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.63) ettha cittaṃ. “Vakkaṃ hadaya”nti (dī. ni. 2.377; ma. ni. 1.110; khu. pā. 3.dvattiṃsākāra) ettha hadayavatthu. Idha pana cittameva abbhantaraṭṭhena “hadaya”nti vuttaṃ. Tameva parisuddhaṭṭhena paṇḍaraṃ, bhavaṅgaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Yathāha “pabhassaramidaṃ, bhikkhave, cittaṃ, tañca kho āgantukehi upakkilesehi upakkiliṭṭha”nti (a. ni. 1.49). Tato nikkhantattā pana akusalampi gaṅgāya nikkhantā nadī gaṅgā viya godhāvarito nikkhantā godhāvari viya ca “paṇḍara”ntveva vuttaṃ.

'Hadaya' means the mind (citta). In the phrase, “I will either disturb your mind or split your heart,” ‘heart’ is said to mean the chest. In, “From heart to heart, I think, knowing, he carves it,” it means the mind. In, “The kidney, the heart,” it means the physical heart-base. But here, the mind itself is called ‘heart’ in the sense of being internal. That very mind, in the sense of being pure, is called ‘white’ (paṇḍara); this is said with reference to the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). As it is said: “This mind, monks, is luminous, but it is defiled by adventitious defilements.” Because even the unwholesome emerges from that, it is still called ‘white,’ just as a river emerging from the Ganges is called the Ganges, or one emerging from the Godhāvarī is called the Godhāvarī.

Mano manāyatananti idha pana manogahaṇaṃ manasseva āyatanabhāvadīpanatthaṃ. Tenetaṃ dīpeti “nayidaṃ devāyatanaṃ viya manassa āyatanattā manāyatanaṃ, atha kho mano eva āyatanaṃ manāyatana”nti. Tattha nivāsaṭṭhānaṭṭhena ākaraṭṭhena samosaraṇaṭṭhānaṭṭhena sañjātidesaṭṭhena kāraṇaṭṭhena ca āyatanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tathā hi loke “issarāyatanaṃ vāsudevāyatana”ntiādīsu nivāsaṭṭhānaṃ āyatananti vuccati[M 0.0252]. “Suvaṇṇāyatanaṃ rajatāyatana”ntiādīsu ākaro. Sāsane pana “manorame āyatane, sevanti naṃ vihaṅgamā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 5.38) samosaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ. “Dakkhiṇāpatho gunnaṃ āyatana”ntiādīsu sañjātideso. “Tatra tatreva sakkhibhabbataṃ [V 0.0231] pāpuṇāti sati satiāyatane”tiādīsu (a. ni. 3.102; ma. ni. 3.158) kāraṇaṃ. Idha pana sañjātidesaṭṭhena samosaraṇaṭṭhānaṭṭhena kāraṇaṭṭhenāti tidhāpi vaṭṭati.

Mind, the mind-base: Here, the taking up of ‘mind’ (mano) is for the purpose of showing that the mind itself has the nature of a base. Thus it is shown: “This is not a mind-base (manāyatana) in the sense of being a base for the mind, like a divine abode; rather, the mind itself is the base, hence ‘mind-base’.” Here, ‘base’ (āyatana) should be understood in the sense of a dwelling place, a source, a meeting place, a place of origin, and a cause. For example, in the world, in phrases such as “the abode of the Lord” or “the abode of Vāsudeva,” ‘āyatana’ means a dwelling place. In phrases such as “a source of gold” or “a source of silver,” it means a source. But in the Dispensation, in passages such as “in delightful resorts, birds dwell,” it refers to a meeting place. In phrases such as “the Southern Path is the place of origin for cattle,” it refers to a place of origin. In passages such as “he attains the ability to bear witness whenever there is a cause for mindfulness,” it refers to a cause. Here, however, it applies in three ways: as a place of origin, a meeting place, and a cause.

Phassādayo hi dhammā ettha sañjāyantīti sañjātidesaṭṭhenapi etaṃ āyatanaṃ. Bahiddhā rūpasaddagandharasaphoṭṭhabbā ārammaṇabhāvenettha osarantīti samosaraṇaṭṭhānaṭṭhenapi āyatanaṃ[P 2.0291]. Phassādīnaṃ pana sahajātādipaccayaṭṭhena kāraṇattā kāraṇaṭṭhenāpi āyatananti veditabbaṃ. Manindriyaṃ vuttatthameva.

For phenomena such as contact arise here—thus, it is a base in the sense of a place of origin. External forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tactile objects enter here as objects—thus, it is also a base in the sense of a meeting place. Moreover, because it is a cause for contact and other phenomena by way of conditions such as co-nascence, it should be understood as a base also in the sense of a cause. The mind faculty (manindriya) has the same meaning as explained.

Vijānātīti viññāṇaṃ. Viññāṇameva khandho viññāṇakkhandho. Tassa rāsiādivasena attho veditabbo. “Mahāudakakkhandhotveva saṅkhaṃ gacchatī”ti (a. ni. 4.51) ettha hi rāsaṭṭhena khandho vutto. “Sīlakkhandho samādhikkhandho”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 3.355) guṇaṭṭhena. “Addasa kho bhagavā mahantaṃ dārukkhandha”nti (saṃ. ni. 4.241) ettha paṇṇattimattaṭṭhena. Idha pana rūḷhito khandho vutto. Rāsaṭṭhena hi viññāṇakkhandhassa ekadeso ekaṃ viññāṇaṃ. Tasmā yathā rukkhassa ekadesaṃ chindanto rukkhaṃ chindatīti vuccati, evameva viññāṇakkhandhassa ekadesabhūtaṃ ekampi viññāṇaṃ rūḷhito viññāṇakkhandhoti vuttaṃ.

It cognizes, thus it is consciousness (viññāṇa). Consciousness itself is the aggregate (khandha), the consciousness aggregate (viññāṇakkhandha). Its meaning should be understood in terms of a heap, etc. For in the phrase “It comes to be reckoned as a great mass of water,” ‘aggregate’ (khandha) is used in the sense of a heap. In phrases such as “the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration,” it is used in the sense of a quality. In the phrase “The Blessed One saw a large log,” it is used in the sense of a mere designation. Here, however, ‘aggregate’ is used in the conventional sense. For in the sense of a heap, a single instance of consciousness is a part of the consciousness aggregate. Therefore, just as one who cuts a part of a tree is said to cut the tree, so too, a single instance of consciousness, being a part of the consciousness aggregate, is conventionally called the consciousness aggregate.

Tajjā manoviññāṇadhātūti tesaṃ phassādīnaṃ dhammānaṃ anucchavikā manoviññāṇadhātu. Imasmiñhi pade ekameva cittaṃ minanaṭṭhena mano, vijānanaṭṭhena viññāṇaṃ, sabhāvaṭṭhena nissattaṭṭhena vā dhātūti tīhi nāmehi vuttaṃ.

The mind-consciousness element associated with them (tajjā manoviññāṇadhātu) refers to the mind-consciousness element that is suitable to those phenomena such as contact. For in this passage, a single consciousness (citta) is referred to by three names: as ‘mind’ (mano) in the sense of measuring, as ‘consciousness’ (viññāṇa) in the sense of cognizing, and as ‘element’ (dhātu) in the sense of its intrinsic nature or being without a living entity.

Saddhiṃ yugaṃ samāgamanti ekappahārena saddhiṃ. Sammāgantvāti pāpuṇitvā. Yugaggāhaṃ gaṇhitvāti yugapaṭibhāgaṃ gahetvā. Sākacchetunti saddhiṃ kathetuṃ. Sallapitunti allāpasallāpaṃ kātuṃ. Sākacchaṃ samāpajjitunti saddhiṃ kathanaṃ paṭipajjituṃ. Na paṭibalabhāve kāraṇaṃ dassetuṃ “taṃ kissahetu, pasūro paribbājako hīno”tiādimāha. So hi bhagavā aggo [M 0.0253] cāti asadisadānaaggattā asamānapaññattā aggo ca. Seṭṭho cāti sabbaguṇehi appaṭisamaṭṭhena seṭṭho ca. Mokkho cāti savāsanehi kilesehi muttattā mokkho ca. Uttamo cāti attano uttaritaravirahitattā uttamo ca. Pavaro cāti sabbalokena abhipatthanīyattā pavaro ca. Mattena [P 2.0292] mātaṅgenāti pabhinnamadena hatthinā.

‘They meet together in pairs’ means together, at one stroke. ‘Having met’ means having arrived. ‘Having taken hold of the yoke’ means having taken hold of a share of the yoke. ‘To converse’ means to speak together. ‘To chat’ means to engage in friendly conversation. ‘To enter into conversation’ means to engage in speech together. To show the reason for his inability, it is said: “Why is that? Because Pasūra the wanderer is inferior,” and so on. For the Blessed One is the foremost (agga), being foremost due to his incomparable giving and unequalled wisdom. He is the best (seṭṭha), being best due to being unequalled in all virtues. He is liberated (mokkha), being liberated from defilements with their latent tendencies. He is the supreme (uttama), being supreme due to lacking anyone superior to himself. He is the most excellent (pavara), being most excellent due to being desired by the whole world. ‘By an elephant in rut’ means by an elephant with dripping ichor.

Kotthukoti [V 0.0232] jiraṇasiṅgālo. Sīhena migaraññā saddhinti kesarasīhena migarājena saha. Taruṇakoti chāpako. Dhenupakoti khīrapako. Usabhenāti maṅgalasammatena usabhena. Calakakunā saddhinti calamānakakunā saddhiṃ. Dhaṅkoti kāko. Garuḷena venateyyena saddhinti ettha garuḷenāti jātivasena nāmaṃ. Venateyyenāti gottavasena. Caṇḍāloti chavacaṇḍālo. Raññā cakkavattināti cātuddīpikacakkavattinā. Paṃsupisācakoti kacavarachaḍḍanaṭṭhāne nibbattako yakkho. Indena devaraññā saddhinti sakkena devarājena saha. So hi bhagavā mahāpaññotiādīni chappadāni heṭṭhā vitthāritāni. Tattha paññāpabhedakusaloti attano anantavikappe paññābhede cheko. Pabhinnañāṇoti anantappabhedapattañāṇo. Etena paññāpabhedakusalattepi sati tāsaṃ paññānaṃ anantabhedattaṃ dasseti. Adhigatapaṭisambhidoti paṭiladdhaaggacatupaṭisambhidañāṇo. Catuvesārajjappattoti cattāri visāradabhāvasaṅkhātāni ñāṇāni patto. Yathāha –

‘Kotthuka’ means an old jackal. ‘With the lion, king of beasts’ means with the mane-lion, king of beasts. ‘A young one’ means a cub. ‘Dhenupaka’ means a suckling calf. ‘With the bull’ means with the bull regarded as auspicious. ‘With the swift kakuṇa’ means with the swift-moving kakuṇa. ‘A crow’ means a crow. ‘With the Garuḷa, the Venateyya’—here, ‘Garuḷa’ is a name by birth, ‘Venateyya’ by clan. ‘An outcaste’ means a charnel-ground outcaste. ‘With the king, the wheel-turning monarch’ means with the universal monarch ruling the four continents. ‘A dust-demon’ means a yakkha born in a place where rubbish is thrown. ‘With Indra, the king of gods’ means with Sakka, the king of gods. For he, the Blessed One, is of great wisdom, etc.—these six terms are explained in detail below. There, ‘skilled in the distinctions of wisdom’ means expert in the infinite distinctions of his own wisdom. ‘Of distinguished knowledge’ means having attained knowledge of infinite distinctions. By this, even while being skilled in the distinctions of wisdom, he shows the infinite distinctions of those wisdoms. ‘Attained the paṭisambhidā’ means having obtained the supreme four knowledges of paṭisambhidā. ‘Achieved the four confidences’ means having attained the four knowledges known as states of confidence (visārada). As it is said:

“Sammāsambuddhassa te paṭijānato ‘ime dhammā anabhisambuddhā’ti, tatra vata maṃ samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā devo vā māro vā brahmā vā koci vā lokasmiṃ sahadhammena paṭicodessatīti nimittametaṃ, bhikkhave, na samanupassāmi, etamahaṃ, bhikkhave, nimittaṃ asamanupassanto khemappatto abhayappatto vesārajjappatto viharāmi.

“For me, who claims to be a Perfectly Enlightened One, I do not see any ground, bhikkhus, that any ascetic or brahmin, god or Māra or Brahmā, or anyone in the world, could rightfully rebuke me on the principle that ‘these phenomena have not been fully awakened to.’ Not seeing such a ground, bhikkhus, I dwell having attained safety, attained fearlessness, attained assurance.”

“Khīṇāsavassa te paṭijānato ‘ime āsavā aparikkhīṇā’ti…pe… ‘ye kho pana te antarāyikā dhammā vuttā, te paṭisevato nālaṃ antarāyāyā”ti…pe… yassa kho pana [M 0.0254] te atthāya dhammo desito, so na niyyāti takkarassa sammā dukkhakkhayāyāti, tatra vata maṃ samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā devo vā māro vā brahmā vā koci vā lokasmiṃ sahadhammena paṭicodessatīti nimittametaṃ, bhikkhave, na samanupassāmi, etamahaṃ, bhikkhave, nimittaṃ asamanupassanto khemappatto abhayappatto vesārajjappatto viharāmī”ti (a. ni. 4.8; ma. ni. 1.150).

“For me, who claims to be one whose taints are destroyed, I do not see any ground, bhikkhus, that any ascetic or brahmin, god or Māra or Brahmā, or anyone in the world, could rightfully rebuke me on the principle that ‘these taints are not fully extinguished’… or that ‘those things declared by you as obstructions are not able to cause an obstruction for one who partakes of them’… or that ‘the Dhamma taught by you for a certain purpose does not lead the one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering.’ Not seeing such a ground, bhikkhus, I dwell having attained safety, attained fearlessness, attained assurance.”

Dasabalabaladhārīti [P 2.0293] dasa balāni etesanti dasabalā, dasabalānaṃ balāni dasabalabalāni, tāni dasabalabalāni dhārayatīti dasabalabaladhārī, dasabalañāṇabaladhārīti attho. Etehi tīhi vacanehi anantappabhedānaṃ neyyānaṃ pabhedamukhamattaṃ dassitaṃ. Soyeva paññāpayogavasena abhimaṅgalasammataṭṭhena purisāsabho. Asantāsaṭṭhena purisasīho. Mahantaṭṭhena purisanāgo. Pajānanaṭṭhena purisājañño. Lokakiccadhuravahanaṭṭhena purisadhorayho.

‘The bearer of the strength of the ten powers’ (dasabalabaladhārī) means: those who have ten powers are ‘dasabalā’; the strengths of the ten powers are ‘dasabalabalāni’; and one who bears those strengths of the ten powers is ‘dasabalabaladhārī,’ meaning the bearer of the knowledge-strength of the ten powers. By these three expressions, only a mere indication of the endless varieties of those to be guided has been shown. He himself is the bull among men (purisāsabha) due to being esteemed as auspicious by virtue of the application of his wisdom. He is the lion among men (purisasīha) due to his fearlessness. He is the great being among men (purisanāga) due to his greatness. He is the thoroughbred among men (purisājañña) due to his faculty of knowing. He is the leader among men (purisadhorayha) due to bearing the burden of the world’s tasks.

Atha [V 0.0233] tejādikaṃ anantañāṇato laddhaṃ guṇavisesaṃ dassetukāmo tesaṃ tejādīnaṃ anantañāṇamūlabhāvaṃ dassento “anantañāṇo”ti vatvā “anantatejo”tiādimāha. Tattha anantañāṇoti gaṇanavasena ca pabhāvavasena ca antavirahitañāṇo. Anantatejoti veneyyasantāne mohatamavidhamanena anantañāṇatejo. Anantayasoti paññāguṇeheva lokattayavitthatānantakittighoso. Aḍḍhoti paññādhanasamiddhiyā samiddho. Mahaddhanoti paññādhanavaḍḍhattepi pabhāvamahattena mahantaṃ pavattapaññādhanamassāti mahaddhano. “Mahādhano”ti vā pāṭho. Dhanavāti pasaṃsitabbapaññādhanavattā niccayuttapaññādhanavattā atisayabhāvena paññādhanavattā dhanavā. Etesupi hi tīsu atthesu idaṃ vacanaṃ saddavidū icchanti.

Then, wishing to show the special qualities, such as radiance, gained from infinite knowledge, and showing that these, such as radiance, are rooted in infinite knowledge, he says "infinite knowledge," and then "infinite radiance," and so on. Here, "infinite knowledge" means knowledge without limit in terms of calculation and in terms of power. "Infinite radiance" is the radiance of infinite knowledge that dispels the darkness of delusion in the minds of those to be trained. "Infinite fame" signifies boundless renown spread throughout the three worlds through the qualities of wisdom. "Wealthy" means rich through the abundance of the wealth of wisdom. "Greatly wealthy" refers to one who possesses great, active wisdom due to the greatness of power, and whose wealth of wisdom is immense. Alternatively, the reading may be "mahādhano." "Possessor of wealth" means one endowed with praiseworthy wealth of wisdom, constantly applied wealth of wisdom, and surpassingly abundant wealth of wisdom. Indeed, experts in language consider that this term applies in these three senses.

Evaṃ paññāguṇena bhagavato attasampattisiddhiṃ dassetvā puna paññāguṇeneva lokahitasampattisiddhiṃ dassento “netā”tiādimāha. Tattha veneyye saṃsārasaṅkhātabhayaṭṭhānato nibbānasaṅkhātaṃ khemaṭṭhānaṃ netā[M 0.0255]. Tattha nayanakāle eva saṃvaravinayapahānavinayavasena veneyye vinetā. Dhammadesanākāle eva saṃsayacchedanena anunetā. Saṃsayaṃ chinditvā saññāpetabbaṃ atthaṃ paññāpetā. Tathā paññāpitānaṃ nicchayakaraṇena nijjhāpetā. Tathā nijjhāpitassa atthassa paṭipattipayojanavasena [P 2.0294] pekkhetā. Tathāpaṭipanne paṭipattibalena pasādetā. So hi bhagavāti ettha hi-kāro anantaraṃ vuttassa atthassa kāraṇopadese nipāto.

Having thus shown the Blessed One's accomplishment of his own welfare through the quality of wisdom, he further shows the accomplishment of the world's welfare through that same quality of wisdom, beginning with "the leader." Herein, he is the leader (netā) who leads those to be trained from the fearful place known as saṃsāra to the secure place known as Nibbāna. At the very time of leading, he is the trainer (vinetā) who trains those to be trained through the training of restraint and the training of abandoning. At the very time of teaching the Dhamma, he is the persuader (anunetā) who guides them by cutting off doubt. Having cut off doubt, he is the illuminator (paññāpetā) who makes known the meaning to be understood. Likewise, having made it known, he is the one who causes contemplation (nijjhāpetā) by settling their understanding. Likewise, having caused them to contemplate the meaning, he is the overseer (pekkhetā) who watches over them in terms of the benefit of practice. Likewise, for those who have so practiced, he is the one who gladdens (pasādetā) them through the power of practice. In 'So hi bhagavā,' the particle 'hi' is a particle indicating the reason in the explanation of the meaning that was stated immediately before.

Anuppannassa maggassa uppādetāti sakasantāne nauppannapubbassa chaasādhāraṇañāṇahetubhūtassa ariyamaggassa bodhimūle lokahitatthaṃ sakasantāne uppādetā. Asañjātassa maggassa sañjanetāti veneyyasantāne asañjātapubbassa sāvakapāramīñāṇahetubhūtassa ariyamaggassa dhammacakkappavattanato pabhuti yāvajjakālā veneyyasantāne sañjanetā. Sāvakaveneyyānampi hi santāne bhagavatā vuttavacaneneva ariyamaggassa sañjananato bhagavā sañjanetā nāma hoti. Anakkhātassa maggassa akkhātāti aṭṭhadhammasamannāgatānaṃ buddhabhāvāya kathābhinīhārānaṃ bodhisattānaṃ buddhabhāvāya byākaraṇaṃ datvā anakkhātapubbassa pāramitāmaggassa “buddho bhavissatī”ti byākaraṇamatteneva bodhimūle uppajjitabbassa ariyamaggassa akkhātā. Ayaṃ nayo paccekabodhisattabyākaraṇepi labbhatiyeva. Maggaññūti paccavekkhaṇāvasena attano uppāditassa ariyamaggassa ñātā. Maggavidūti veneyyasantāne janetabbassa ariyamaggassa kusalo. Maggakovidoti bodhisattānaṃ akkhātabbamagge vicakkhaṇo. Atha vā abhisambodhipaṭipatti maggaññū, paccekabodhipaṭipatti maggavidū, sāvakabodhipaṭipatti maggakovido. Atha vā –

The arouser of the unarisen path—he arouses in his own continuum the noble path, which has never before arisen in his own continuum, is the cause of the sixfold knowledge not shared by others, and is for the welfare of the world at the root of enlightenment. The producer of the unproduced path—from the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma up to the present time, he produces in the continuum of those to be trained the noble path, which has never before been produced in their continuum and is the cause of the knowledge of a disciple's perfection. For the Blessed One is called the producer because he produces the noble path in the continuum of disciples to be trained by means of the word spoken by the Blessed One. The expounder of the unexpounded path—having given a prediction of Buddhahood to bodhisattas endowed with eight qualities who have made the verbal aspiration for Buddhahood, he expounds the path of perfections, which was never expounded before, and the noble path that is to arise at the root of enlightenment merely by the declaration, 'He will become a Buddha.' This method is also found in the prediction of Paccekabodhisattas. Knower of the path—he is a knower of the noble path he has aroused, by way of reviewing it. Skilled in the path—he is skilled in the noble path to be produced in the continuum of those to be trained. Expert in the path—he is discerning in the path to be expounded to bodhisattas. Alternatively, the knower of the path pertains to the practice for full enlightenment; the skilled in the path, to the practice for Paccekabodhi; the expert in the path, to the practice for the enlightenment of a disciple. Or alternatively—

“Etena [V 0.0234] maggena tariṃsu pubbe,

Tarissanti ye ca taranti ogha”nti. (saṃ. ni. 5.409) –

"By this path the ancients crossed over, and those who will cross and those who are now crossing the flood."

Vacanato yathāyogaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannabuddhapaccekabuddhasāvakānaṃ maggavasena ca suññatānimittaappaṇihitamaggavasena [P 2.0295] ca ugghaṭitaññūvipañcitaññūneyyapuggalānaṃ maggavasena ca yathākkamenettha yojanaṃ karonti[M 0.0256]. Maggānugā ca panassāti bhagavato gatamaggānugāmino hutvā. Ettha ca-saddo hetuatthe nipāto, etena ca bhagavatā magguppādanādiguṇādhigamāya hetu vutto hoti. Pana-saddo katatthe nipāto, tena bhagavatā katamaggakaraṇaṃ vuttaṃ hoti. Pacchā samannāgatāti paṭhamaṃ gatassa bhagavato pacchā sīlādiguṇena samannāgatā. Iti thero “anuppannassa maggassa uppādetā”tiādīhi yasmā sabbepi bhagavato sīlādayo guṇā arahattamaggameva nissāya āgatā, tasmā arahattamaggameva nissāya guṇaṃ kathesi.

According to the wording, they apply the interpretation here in due order: by way of the path of past, future, and present Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples; by way of the path of emptiness, the signless, and the desireless; and by way of the path for individuals of quick understanding, of expanded understanding, and the trainable. The phrase 'And his followers of the path' means: having become followers of the path trodden by the Blessed One. Here, the particle 'ca' is a particle in the sense of cause; by this, the cause for the Blessed One's acquisition of qualities such as the arising of the path is stated. The particle 'pana' is a particle in the sense of what has been done; by this, the making of the path done by the Blessed One is stated. 'Endowed afterward' means endowed afterward with virtues such as morality, following the Blessed One who went first. Thus the Elder, with phrases like 'the arouser of the unarisen path,' etc., expounded the quality dependent on the path to arahantship, because all the qualities of the Blessed One, such as morality, have come about dependent on the path to arahantship alone.

Jānaṃ jānātīti jānitabbaṃ jānāti, sabbaññutāya yaṃkiñci paññāya jānitabbaṃ nāma atthi, taṃ sabbaṃ pañcaneyyapathabhūtaṃ paññāya jānātīti attho. Passaṃ passatīti passitabbaṃ passati, sabbadassāvitāya taṃyeva neyyapathaṃ cakkhunā diṭṭhaṃ viya karonto paññācakkhunā passatīti attho. Yathā vā ekacco viparītaṃ gaṇhanto jānantopi na jānāti, passantopi na passati, na evaṃ bhagavā. Bhagavā pana yathāsabhāvaṃ gaṇhanto jānanto jānātiyeva, passanto passatiyeva. Svāyaṃ nayana pariṇāyakaṭṭhena cakkhubhūto. Viditatādiatthena ñāṇabhūto. Aviparītasabhāvaṭṭhena vā pariyattidhammapavattanato hadayena cintetvā vācāya nicchāritadhammamayoti vā dhammabhūto. Seṭṭhaṭṭhena brahmabhūto. Atha vā cakkhu viya bhūtoti cakkhubhūto. Ñāṇaṃ viya bhūtoti ñāṇabhūto. Aviparītadhammo viya bhūtoti dhammabhūto. Brahmā viya bhūtoti brahmabhūto. Yvāyaṃ dhammassa vacanato vattanato vā vattā. Nānappakārehi vacanato vattanato vā pavattā. Atthaṃ nīharitvā dassanato atthassa ninnetā. Amatādhigamāya paṭipattidesanato, amatappakāsanāya vā dhammadesanāya amatassa adhigamāpanato [P 2.0296] amatassa dātā. Lokuttarassa dhammassa uppāditattā veneyyānurūpena yathāsukhaṃ lokuttaradhammassa dānena ca dhammesu issaroti dhammassāmī. Tathāgatapadaṃ heṭṭhā vuttatthaṃ.

'Knowing, he knows' means he knows what is to be known. The meaning is: through omniscience, whatever there is to be known by wisdom, all of that, having come into the range of what is knowable, he knows by wisdom. 'Seeing, he sees' means he sees what is to be seen. The meaning is: through his all-seeing quality, making that very domain of the knowable as if seen with the physical eye, he sees with the eye of wisdom. For just as someone grasping things wrongly does not know even when knowing, and does not see even when seeing, it is not so for the Blessed One. The Blessed One, grasping things according to their true nature, when knowing, truly knows, and when seeing, truly sees. He, by his quality of leading and guiding, has become the Eye. By his quality of being known, etc., he has become Knowledge. By his quality of having an unperverted nature, or because he is made of the Dhamma declared by voice after reflecting in his heart due to the turning of the Dhamma of the scriptures, he has become Dhamma. By his quality of being the best, he has become Brahma. Or, having become like an eye, he is the Eye. Having become like knowledge, he is Knowledge. Having become like the unperverted Dhamma, he is Dhamma. Having become like Brahma, he is Brahma. He is the Speaker because he speaks or acts in accordance with the Dhamma. He is the Proclaimer because he speaks or acts in accordance with various methods. He is the Guide of the meaning because he extracts and reveals the meaning. He is the Giver of the Deathless because he teaches the practice for attaining the Deathless, or because he enables the attainment of the Deathless by teaching the Dhamma for its revelation. He is the Lord of the Dhamma because he has generated the supramundane Dhamma and because he gives the supramundane Dhamma as is suitable, according to the disposition of those to be trained. The term 'Tathāgata' has the meaning explained below.

Idāni “jānaṃ jānātī”tiādīhi vuttaguṇaṃ sabbaññutāya visesetvā dassetukāmo sabbaññutaṃ sādhento “natthī”tiādimāha. Evaṃbhūtassa hi [M 0.0257] tassa bhagavato pāramitāpuññaphalappabhāvanipphannena arahattamaggañāṇena sabbadhammesu savāsanassa sammohassa vihatattā asammohato [V 0.0235] sabbadhammānaṃ ñātattā aññātaṃ nāma natthi. Tatheva ca sabbadhammānaṃ cakkhunā viya ñāṇacakkhunā diṭṭhattā adiṭṭhaṃ nāma natthi. Ñāṇena pattattā aviditaṃ nāma natthi. Asammohasacchikiriyāya sacchikatattā asacchikataṃ nāma natthi. Asammohapaññāya phuṭṭhattā paññāya aphassitaṃ nāma natthi.

Now, wishing to show the quality mentioned in phrases like 'knowing, he knows' by specifying it as omniscience, and thus establishing that omniscience, he says, 'There is nothing...' For with such a Blessed One, because delusion with its latent tendencies regarding all phenomena has been destroyed by the knowledge of the path of arahantship—produced by the power of the fruit of the merit of the perfections—and because, due to this non-delusion, all phenomena are known, there is nothing that is unknown. And likewise, because all phenomena are seen with the eye of knowledge as if with the physical eye, there is nothing that is unseen. Because they are attained by knowledge, there is nothing that is uncomprehended. Because they are realized by the realization of non-delusion, there is nothing that is unrealized. Because they are touched by the wisdom of non-delusion, there is nothing untouched by wisdom.

Paccuppannanti paccuppannaṃ kālaṃ vā dhammaṃ vā. Upādāyāti ādāya, antokatvāti attho. Upādāyavacaneneva kālavinimuttaṃ nibbānampi gahitameva hoti. “Atītā”divacanāni ca “natthī”tiādivacaneneva ghaṭiyanti, “sabbe”tiādivacanena vā. Sabbe dhammāti sabbasaṅkhatāsaṅkhatadhammapariyādānaṃ. Sabbākārenāti sabbadhammesu ekekasseva dhammassa aniccākārādisabbākārapariyādānaṃ. Ñāṇamukheti ñāṇābhimukhe. Āpāthaṃ āgacchantīti osaraṇaṃ upenti. Jānitabbanti padaṃ neyyanti padassa atthavivaraṇatthaṃ vuttaṃ.

‘Present’ refers to the present time or a present phenomenon. ‘With reference to’ means taking up; the sense is ‘including.’ By this very expression ‘with reference to,’ even Nibbāna, which is timeless, is included. The words ‘past,’ and so on, are connected with the words ‘there is not,’ and so on, or with the word ‘all.’ ‘All phenomena’ means the complete inclusion of all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena. ‘In every way’ means the complete inclusion of all aspects—such as impermanence—of each and every phenomenon. ‘In the face of knowledge’ means directed towards knowledge. ‘They come into range’ means they enter the field. The term ‘to be known’ is stated to explain the meaning of the word ‘knowable’.

Attattho vātiādīsu vā-saddo samuccayattho. Attatthoti attano attho. Paratthoti paresaṃ tiṇṇaṃ lokānaṃ attho. Ubhayatthoti attano ca paresañcāti sakiṃyeva ubhinnaṃ attho. Diṭṭhadhammikoti diṭṭhadhamme niyutto, diṭṭhadhammappayojano vā attho. Samparāye niyutto, samparāyappayojano vā samparāyiko. Uttānotiādīsu vohāravasena vattabbo sukhapatiṭṭhattā uttāno[P 2.0297]. Vohāraṃ atikkamitvā vattabbo suññatāpaṭisaṃyutto dukkhapatiṭṭhattā gambhīro. Lokuttaro accantatirokkhattā gūḷho. Aniccatādiko ghanādīhi paṭicchannattā paṭicchanno. Apacuravohārena vattabbo yathārutaṃ aggahetvā adhippāyassa netabbato neyyo. Pacuravohārena vattabbo vacanamatteneva adhippāyassa nītattā nīto. Suparisuddhasīlasamādhivipassanattho tadaṅgavikkhambhanavasena vajjavirahitattā anavajjo. Kilesasamucchedanato ariyamaggattho nakkileso. Kilesapaṭippassaddhattā ariyaphalattho vodāno. Saṅkhatāsaṅkhatesu aggadhammattā nibbānaṃ paramattho. Parivattatīti buddhañāṇassa visayabhāvato abahibhūtattā antobuddhañāṇe byāpitvā vā samantā vā alaṅkaritvā vā visesena vā vattati.

In phrases such as 'attattho vā,' the word 'vā' has a conjunctive meaning. 'Attattho' means one's own benefit. 'Parattho' means the benefit of others, that is, of the three worlds. 'Ubhayattho' means the benefit of both oneself and others—thus, the benefit of both at once. 'Diṭṭhadhammiko' refers to what is connected with the present life, or has the present life as its purpose. 'Samparāyiko' refers to what is connected with the future life, or has the future life as its purpose. In phrases like 'uttāno,' it is said to be 'plain' in the conventional sense, because it is established in happiness. Transcending convention, it is said to be 'profound' because, being connected with emptiness, it is established in suffering. The supramundane is 'hidden' because it is completely concealed. The characteristic of impermanence and so on is 'concealed' because it is covered by compactness and so on. 'Neyyo' (requiring interpretation) is spoken of with infrequent usage, because the meaning must be inferred towards the intention, not grasped literally. 'Nīto' (explicit) is spoken of with frequent usage, because the intention is conveyed by the mere word. The meaning of perfectly pure virtue, concentration, and insight is 'faultless' (anavajjo) because it is free from fault by way of suppression by those respective factors. The meaning of the noble path is 'undefiled' (nakkileso) because of the eradication of defilements. The meaning of the noble fruit is 'purified' (vodāno) because of the stilling of defilements. Nibbāna is the ultimate meaning because it is the foremost phenomenon among conditioned and unconditioned things. 'It revolves' (parivattati) means it operates by pervading within the Buddha's knowledge, or all around it, or adorning it, or in a special way, because it is the domain of the Buddha's knowledge and is not external to it.

“Sabbaṃ [M 0.0258] kāyakamma”ntiādīhi bhagavato ñāṇavisayataṃ dasseti. Ñāṇānuparivattīti ñāṇaṃ anuparivatti, ñāṇavirahitaṃ na hotīti attho. Appaṭihatanti nirāvaraṇataṃ dasseti. Puna sabbaññutaṃ upamāya sādhetukāmo “yāvataka”ntiādimāha. Tattha jānitabbanti neyyaṃ. Neyyapariyanto neyyāvasānamassa atthīti neyyapariyantikaṃ. Asabbaññūnaṃ pana neyyāvasānameva natthi. Ñāṇapariyantikepi eseva nayo. Purimayamake vuttatthameva iminā yamakena visesetvā dasseti[V 0.0236], tatiyayamakena paṭisedhavasena niyametvā dasseti. Ettha ca neyyaṃ ñāṇassa pathattā neyyapatho. Aññamaññapariyantaṭṭhāyinoti neyyañca ñāṇañca khepetvā ṭhānato aññamaññassa pariyante ṭhānasīlā.

By phrases such as 'all bodily action,' the text shows that these are the domain of the Blessed One's knowledge. 'Revolving in accordance with knowledge' means it revolves along with knowledge; the meaning is, it is not devoid of knowledge. 'Unobstructed' shows its unhindered nature. Again, wishing to establish omniscience by means of a simile, he says, 'as far as,' and so on. Here, 'what is to be known' is the knowable. 'Limited by the knowable' means it has a limit of the knowable, it has an end to the knowable. For non-omniscient beings, however, there is no end to the knowable. The same method applies to 'limited by knowledge.' The meaning stated in the first pair is shown as distinguished by this pair, and by the third pair it is shown as defined by way of negation. Here, the knowable is the path for knowledge, hence 'the path of the knowable.' 'Standing at each other’s limits' means that the knowable and knowledge, having exhausted their respective domains, have the characteristic of standing at each other’s limits.

Āvajjanapaṭibaddhāti manodvārāvajjanāyattā, āvajjitānantarameva jānātīti attho. Ākaṅkhapaṭibaddhāti ruciāyattā[P 2.0298], āvajjanānantaraṃ javanañāṇena jānātīti attho. Itarāni dve padāni imesaṃ dvinnaṃ padānaṃ yathākkamena atthappakāsanatthaṃ vuttāni. Āsayaṃ jānātīti ettha āsayanti nissayanti etthāti āsayo, micchādiṭṭhiyā sammādiṭṭhiyā kāmādīhi nekkhammādīhi vā paribhāvitassa santānassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sattasantānaṃ anusenti anupavattentīti anusayā, thāmagatānaṃ kāmarāgādīnaṃva etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Anusayaṃ jānātīti anusayakathā heṭṭhā vuttāyeva.

“Dependent on attention” means dependent on mind-door attention; the meaning is that one knows immediately after attending. “Dependent on desire” means dependent on inclination; the meaning is that one knows through javana-cognition immediately after attention. The other two terms are stated in order to clarify the meaning of these two terms respectively. In “knows the disposition,” āsaya (disposition) is so called because one dwells (āsayanti) or relies (nissayanti) on it. This is a designation for the mental continuum of one pervaded by wrong view or right view, or by sensual desires and so on or renunciation and so on. Anusayā (latent tendencies) are so called because they lie latent in (anusenti) and persist in (anupavattenti) the mental continuum of beings; this is a designation for deeply rooted sensual lust and the like. The discussion on “knows the latent tendencies” has already been stated previously.

Caritanti pubbe katakusalākusalakammaṃ. Adhimuttinti sampati kusale akusale vā cittavosaggo. Apparajakkheti paññāmaye akkhimhi appaṃ rāgādirajo etesanti apparajakkhā. Appaṃ rāgādirajo etesanti vā apparajakkhā, te apparajakkhe. Mahārajakkheti ñāṇamaye akkhimhi mahantaṃ rāgādirajo etesanti mahārajakkhā. Mahantaṃ rāgādirajo etesanti vā mahārajakkhā, te mahārajakkhe. Tikkhindriye mudindriyeti tikkhāni saddhādīni indriyāni etesanti tikkhindriyā. Mudūni saddhādīni indriyāni etesanti mudindriyā. Svākāre dvākāreti sundarā saddhādayo ākārā koṭṭhāsā etesanti svākārā. Kucchitā garahitā asaddhādayo ākārā koṭṭhāsā etesanti dvākārā. Suviññāpaye duviññāpayeti ye kathitaṃ kāraṇaṃ sallakkhenti [M 0.0259] sukhena sakkā honti viññāpetuṃ, te suviññāpayā. Tabbiparītā duviññāpayā. Bhabbābhabbeti bhabbe ca abhabbe ca. Ariyāya jātiyā bhavanti jāyantīti bhabbā. Vattamānasamīpe vattamānavacanaṃ. Bhavissanti jāyissanti vāti bhabbā, bhājanabhūtāti attho. Ye ariyamaggapaṭivedhassa anucchavikā upanissayasampannā, te bhabbā. Vuttapaṭipakkhā abhabbā.

Carita (disposition) means past wholesome and unwholesome kamma. Adhimutti (inclination) means the mind's resolve towards wholesome or unwholesome things at present. Apparajakkha (those with little dust) means those in whose eye of wisdom there is little dust of passion and the like. Alternatively, it means those who have little dust of passion and the like; these are the apparajakkha. Mahārajakkha (those with much dust) means those in whose eye of knowledge there is much dust of passion and the like. Alternatively, it means those who have much dust of passion and the like; these are the mahārajakkha. Tikkhindriya (those with sharp faculties) means those whose faculties such as faith are sharp. Mudindriya (those with dull faculties) means those whose faculties such as faith are dull. Svākāra (of good disposition) means those whose aspects or divisions such as faith are beautiful. Dvākāra (of bad disposition) means those whose aspects or divisions such as faithlessness are ugly and blameworthy. Suviññāpaya (easily instructed) means those who, when a reason is explained, consider it and can easily be instructed. The opposite of these are duviññāpaya (difficult to instruct). Bhabbā (capable) and abhabbā (incapable) means the capable and the incapable. Bhabbā means those who are born or arise in the noble lineage. The present tense is used for what is close to the present. Bhabbā also means 'they will be born' or 'they will arise,' signifying they are fit vessels. Those who are suitable and endowed with supporting conditions for the penetration of the noble path are bhabbā. Those who are the opposite of what has been stated are abhabbā.

Satte pajānātīti rūpādike ārammaṇe lagge laggite satte pajānāti. Sadevako [P 2.0299] lokoti saha devehi sadevako. Saha mārena samārako. Saha brahmunā sabrahmako. Saha samaṇabrāhmaṇehi sassamaṇabrāhmaṇī. Pajātattā pajā. Saha devamanussehi sadevamanussā. “Pajā”ti sattalokassa pariyāyavacanametaṃ. Tattha sadevakavacanena pañcakāmāvacaradevaggahaṇaṃ, samārakavacanena [V 0.0237] chaṭṭhakāmāvacaradevaggahaṇaṃ. Sabrahmakavacanena brahmakāyikādibrahmaggahaṇaṃ. Sassamaṇabrāhmaṇīvacanena sāsanassa paccatthikapaccāmittasamaṇabrāhmaṇaggahaṇaṃ samitapāpabāhitapāpasamaṇabrāhmaṇaggahaṇañca. Pajāvacanena sattalokaggahaṇaṃ. Sadevamanussavacanena sammutidevaavasesamanussaggahaṇaṃ. Evamettha tīhi padehi okāsaloko. Dvīhi pajāvasena sattaloko gahitoti veditabbo.

'He understands beings' (satte pajānāti) means he understands beings who are attached and clinging to objects such as form. 'The world with its devas' (sadevako loko) means together with the devas. 'With Māra' (samārako) means together with Māra. 'With Brahmā' (sabrahmako) means together with Brahmā. 'With ascetics and brahmins' (sassamaṇabrāhmaṇī) means together with ascetics and brahmins. 'Beings' (pajā) are so called because they are born (pajātattā). 'With devas and humans' (sadevamanussā) means together with devas and humans. The term 'pajā' is a synonym for the world of beings. Here, by the term 'with its devas,' the devas of the five sense-sphere realms are included. By the term 'with Māra,' the devas of the sixth sense-sphere realm are included. By the term 'with Brahmā,' the Brahmās beginning with the Brahmākāyika devas are included. By the term 'with ascetics and brahmins,' the ascetics and brahmins who are opponents and adversaries of the Teaching are included, as well as the ascetics and brahmins who have calmed and eliminated evil. By the term 'beings,' the world of beings is included. By the term 'with devas and humans,' conventional devas and the remaining humans are included. Thus, in this context, the world as location is included by three terms, and the world of beings is to be understood as included by two terms.

Aparo nayo – sadevakaggahaṇena arūpāvacaraloko gahito, samārakaggahaṇena chakāmāvacaraloko, sabrahmakaggahaṇena rūpāvacarabrahmaloko, sassamaṇabrāhmaṇādiggahaṇena catuparisavasena sammutidevehi vā saha manussaloko, avasesasabbasattaloko vā. Api cettha sadevakavacanena ukkaṭṭhaparicchedato sabbassapi lokassa antobuddhañāṇe parivattanabhāvaṃ sādheti. Tato yesaṃ siyā “māro mahānubhāvo chakāmāvacarissaro vasavattī, kiṃ sopi antobuddhañāṇe parivattatī”ti. Tesaṃ vimatiṃ vidhamento “samārako”ti āha. Yesaṃ pana siyā “brahmā mahānubhāvo, ekaṅguliyā ekasmiṃ cakkavāḷasahasse ālokaṃ pharati. Dvīhi…pe… dasahi aṅgulīhi dasasu cakkavāḷasahassesu ālokaṃ pharati, anuttarañca jhānasamāpattisukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti, kiṃ sopi antobuddhañāṇe parivattatī”ti. Tesaṃ vimatiṃ vidhamento “sabrahmako”ti āha. Tato yesaṃ [M 0.0260] siyā “puthū samaṇabrāhmaṇā sāsanapaccatthikā, kiṃ tepi antobuddhañāṇe parivattantī”ti.
