Tesaṃ vimatiṃ vidhamento “sassamaṇabrāhmaṇī pajā”ti āha.

Another method: by the inclusion of 'with devas,' the formless realm is included; by the inclusion of 'with Māra,' the six sense-sphere realms are included; by the inclusion of 'with Brahmā,' the Brahmā world of the form realm is included; by the inclusion of 'with ascetics and brahmins,' the human world is included, either by way of the four assemblies or together with conventional devas, or all remaining worlds of beings. Moreover, here, by the term 'with devas,' it is established, from the highest perspective, that the entire world revolves within the Buddha's knowledge. Then, for those who might think, 'Māra is of great power, the lord of the six sense-sphere realms, the ruler Vasavattī—could even he revolve within the Buddha’s knowledge?'—to dispel their uncertainty, it is said, 'with Māra.' For those who might think, 'Brahmā is of great power; with one finger, he illuminates a thousand world-systems; with two… up to ten fingers, he illuminates ten thousand world-systems; and he experiences the unsurpassed bliss of meditative attainment—could even he revolve within the Buddha’s knowledge?'—to dispel their uncertainty, it is said, 'with Brahmā.' Then, for those who might think, 'There are many ascetics and brahmins who are adversaries of the teaching—could even they revolve within the Buddha’s knowledge?'—to dispel their uncertainty, it is said, 'the beings with ascetics and brahmins'.

Evaṃ ukkaṭṭhānaṃ antobuddhañāṇe parivattanabhāvaṃ pakāsetvā atha sammutideve avasesamanusse ca upādāya ukkaṭṭhaparicchedavasena sesasattalokassa antobuddhañāṇe [P 2.0300] parivattanabhāvaṃ pakāsento “sadevamanussā”ti āha. Ayamettha anusandhikkamo. Porāṇā panāhu “sadevakoti devatāhi saddhiṃ avasesaloko. Samārakoti mārena saddhiṃ avasesaloko. Sabrahmakoti brahmehi saddhiṃ avasesaloko. Evaṃ sabbepi tibhavūpage satte tīhākārehi tīsu padesu pakkhipitvā puna dvīhākārehi pariyādātuṃ ‘sassamaṇabrāhmaṇī pajā sadevamanussā’ti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ pañcahi padehi tena tena ākārena tedhātukameva pariyādinnaṃ hotī”ti.

Having thus shown the state of the highest beings revolving within the Buddha's knowledge, then, taking the conventional devas and the remaining humans, and explaining the state of the rest of the world of beings revolving within the Buddha's knowledge by way of the highest distinction, he says, 'with devas and humans.' This is the sequence of connection here. But the ancients say: 'Sadevako (with devas) means the rest of the world together with deities. Samārako (with Māra) means the rest of the world together with Māra. Sabrahmako (with Brahmā) means the rest of the world together with Brahmās. Thus, having included all beings subject to the three realms in three ways within three terms, then to encompass them in two ways, it is said: 'the beings with ascetics and brahmins, with devas and humans.' In this way, through five terms, the three realms themselves are encompassed in various ways.

Antamasoti uparimantena. Timitimiṅgalanti ettha timi nāma ekā macchajāti, timiṃ gilituṃ samatthā tato mahantasarīrā timiṅgalā nāma ekā macchajāti, timiṅgalampi gilituṃ samatthā pañcayojanasatikasarīrā timitimiṅgalā nāma ekā macchajāti. Idha jātiggahaṇena ekavacanaṃ [V 0.0238] katanti veditabbaṃ. Garuḷaṃ venateyyanti ettha garuḷoti jātivasena nāmaṃ. Venateyyoti gottavasena. Padeseti ekadese. Sāriputtasamāti sabbabuddhānaṃ dhammasenāpatitthere gahetvā vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Sesasāvakā hi paññāya dhammasenāpatittherena samā nāma natthi. Yathāha – “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ mahāpaññānaṃ yadidaṃ sāriputto”ti (a. ni. 1.188-189). Aṭṭhakathāyañca (visuddhi. 1.171; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 2.3.5) vuttaṃ –

Even to the highest limit. Timitimiṅgala: Here, 'timi' is the name of a certain kind of fish; 'timiṅgala' is the name of a certain kind of fish with a larger body, capable of swallowing a timi; and 'timitimiṅgala' is the name of a certain kind of fish with a body five hundred yojanas in size, capable of swallowing a timiṅgala. Here, it should be understood that the singular is used to denote the species. Garuḷa and Venateyya: Here, 'Garuḷa' is a name based on species, and 'Venateyya' is based on lineage. 'Padeseti' means 'in one part'. 'Equal to Sāriputta': It should be understood that this is said with reference to the Elder, the General of the Dhamma of all Buddhas. For among the remaining disciples, there is no one equal in wisdom to the Elder, the General of the Dhamma. As it is said: 'Monks, among my bhikkhu disciples who are great in wisdom, Sāriputta is the foremost' (A. Ni. 1.188–189). And in the commentary (Visuddhi. 1.171; Paṭi. Ma. Aṭṭha. 2.3.5), it is said:

“Lokanāthaṃ ṭhapetvāna, ye caññe santi pāṇino;

Paññāya sāriputtassa, kalaṃ nāgghanti soḷasi”nti.

“Excepting the Protector of the World, whatever other beings there are, they are not worth a sixteenth part of Sāriputta’s wisdom.”

Pharitvāti buddhañāṇaṃ sabbadevamanussānampi paññaṃ pāpuṇitvā ṭhānato tesaṃ paññaṃ pharitvā byāpitvā tiṭṭhati. Abhibhavitvāti sabbadevamanussānampi paññaṃ atikkamitvā, tesaṃ avisayabhūtampi sabbaṃ neyyaṃ abhibhavitvā tiṭṭhatīti attho.

'Having pervaded': The Buddha’s wisdom, having reached even the wisdom of all gods and humans, stands having pervaded and spread through their wisdom from its own standpoint. 'Having overcome': It stands having surpassed even the wisdom of all gods and humans, having overcome all that is knowable and beyond their scope—this is the meaning.

Paṭisambhidāyaṃ [M 0.0261] (paṭi. ma. 3.5) pana “atighaṃsitvā”ti pāṭho, ghaṃsitvā tuditvāti attho. Yepi tetiādīhi evaṃ pharitvā abhibhavitvā ṭhānassa paccakkhakāraṇaṃ dasseti. Tattha paṇḍitāti paṇḍiccena samannāgatā[P 2.0301]. Nipuṇāti saṇhasukhumabuddhino sukhume atthantare paṭivijjhanasamatthā. Kataparappavādāti viññātaparappavādā ceva parehi saddhiṃ katavādaparicayā ca. Vālavedhirūpāti vālavedhidhanuggahasadisā. Vo bhindantā maññe caranti paññāgatena diṭṭhigatānīti vālavedhī viya vālaṃ sukhumānipi paresaṃ diṭṭhigamanāni attano paññāgamanena bhindantā viya carantīti attho. Atha vā “gūthagataṃ muttagata”ntiādīsu (a. ni. 9.11) viya paññā eva paññāgataṃ. Diṭṭhiyo eva diṭṭhigatāni. Pañhe abhisaṅkharitvā abhisaṅkharitvāti dvipadampi tipadampi catupadampi pucchaṃ racayitvā tesaṃ pañhānaṃ atibahukattā sabbasaṅgahatthaṃ dvikkhattuṃ vuttaṃ. Gūḷhāni ca paṭicchannāni ca atthajātānīti pāṭhaseso. Tesaṃ tathā vinayaṃ disvā attanā abhisaṅkhataṃ pañhaṃ pucchantīti evaṃ bhagavatā adhippetattā pañhaṃ pucchanti. Aññesaṃ pana pucchāya okāsameva adatvā bhagavā upasaṅkamantānaṃ dhammaṃ deseti. Yathāha –

In the Paṭisambhidāmagga (Paṭi. Ma. 3.5), however, the reading is 'atighaṃsitvā,' meaning 'having rubbed' or 'having struck'. With the words beginning 'Ye pi te,' he shows the direct evidence for this state of having thus pervaded and overcome. Therein, 'paṇḍitā' means 'endowed with wisdom'. 'Nipuṇā' means 'those with subtle and refined intellect, capable of penetrating subtle meanings and distinctions'. 'Kataparappavādā' means 'those who understand others’ doctrines and have experience in conducting debates with others'. 'Vālavedhirūpā' means 'resembling an archer skilled in splitting a hair'. 'They seem to shatter as they move, using wisdom to penetrate views': This means that like a hair-splitter splitting a hair, they go about shattering even the most subtle views of others with the penetration of their own wisdom. Alternatively, just as in 'gūthagataṃ muttagataṃ' and so forth (A. Ni. 9.11), wisdom itself is 'paññāgataṃ,' and views themselves are 'diṭṭhigatāni'. ‘Having composed and composed questions’ means having formulated questions of two, three, or four parts; because these questions are very numerous, the word is repeated to encompass all of them. 'Gūḷhāni ca paṭicchannāni ca atthajātānīti' is the remaining text. Seeing their method thus, they ask questions formulated by themselves—this is what the Blessed One intended, hence they ask questions. But to others, without even giving an opening for questions, the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma to those who approach. As it is said:

“Te pañhaṃ abhisaṅkharonti ‘imaṃ mayaṃ pañhaṃ samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ upasaṅkamitvā pucchissāma, sace no samaṇo gotamo evaṃ puṭṭho evaṃ byākarissati, evamassa mayaṃ vādaṃ [V 0.0239] āropessāma, evaṃ cepi no puṭṭho evaṃ byākarissati, evampissa mayaṃ vādaṃ āropessāmā’ti. Te suṇanti ‘samaṇo khalu bho gotamo amukaṃ nāma gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā osaṭo’ti. Te yena samaṇo gotamo tenupasaṅkamanti. Te samaṇo gotamo dhammiyā kathāya sandasseti samādapeti samuttejeti sampahaṃseti. Te samaṇena gotamena dhammiyā kathāya sandassitā samādapitā samuttejitā sampahaṃsitā na ceva samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ pañhaṃ pucchanti, kutossa vādaṃ āropessanti, aññadatthu samaṇasseva gotamassa sāvakā sampajjantī”ti (ma. ni. 1.289).

“They prepare a question, thinking, ‘We will approach the ascetic Gotama and ask him this question. If the ascetic Gotama, when asked thus, answers us thus, we will confute him in this way. And even if, when asked thus, he answers us thus, we will still confute him in this way.’ They hear, ‘Indeed, the ascetic Gotama has arrived at such and such a village or town.’ They approach the ascetic Gotama. The ascetic Gotama instructs, urges, inspires, and gladdens them with a Dhamma talk. Having been instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened by the ascetic Gotama with a Dhamma talk, they do not even ask the ascetic Gotama a question—how then could they confute him? Instead, they become disciples of the ascetic Gotama.” (MN 1.289)

Kasmā pañhe na pucchantīti ce? Bhagavā kira parisamajjhe dhammaṃ desento parisāya ajjhāsayaṃ oloketi, tato passati “ime paṇḍitā gūḷhaṃ rahassaṃ pañhaṃ ovaṭṭikasāraṃ katvā āgatā”ti. So tehi apuṭṭhoyeva [M 0.0262] “pañhapucchāya ettakā dosā, vissajjane ettakā, atthe, pade, akkhare ettakāti; imaṃ pañhaṃ pucchanto evaṃ puccheyya, vissajjento [P 2.0302] evaṃ vissajjeyyā”ti; iti ovaṭṭikasāraṃ katvā ānīte pañhe dhammakathāya antare pakkhipitvā dasseti. Te paṇḍitā “seyyā vata no, ye mayaṃ ime pañhe na pucchimhā. Sacepi mayaṃ puccheyyāma, appatiṭṭhite no katvā samaṇo gotamo khipeyyā”ti attamanā bhavanti.

If you ask, 'Why do they not ask questions?' It is said that when the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma in the midst of an assembly, he surveys the inclinations of the assembly and then sees, 'These wise ones have come having prepared hidden, profound questions, making them like the pith of a quail egg.' Without being asked by them, he says: 'There are this many faults in asking a question, this many in answering, this many in meaning, word, and syllable. One who asks this question should ask thus, and one who answers should answer thus.' Thus, he reveals the questions they had brought, prepared like the pith of a quail egg, by inserting them into the Dhamma talk. Those wise ones think, 'Indeed, it is better for us that we did not ask these questions. Even if we had asked, the ascetic Gotama would have refuted us, leaving us without a footing.' They become pleased.

Api ca buddhā nāma dhammaṃ desentā parisaṃ mettāya pharanti. Mettāpharaṇena dasabalesu mahājanassa cittaṃ pasīdati. Buddhā nāma rūpaggappattā honti dassanasampannā madhurassarā mudujivhā suphusitadantāvaraṇā, amatena hadayaṃ siñcantā viya dhammaṃ kathenti. Tatra nesaṃ mettāpharaṇena pasannacittānaṃ evaṃ hoti – “evarūpaṃ advejjhakathaṃ amoghakathaṃ niyyānikakathaṃ kathentena bhagavatā saddhiṃ na sakkhissāma paccanīkaggāhaṃ gaṇhitu”nti attano pasannabhāveneva pañhe na pucchantīti.

Moreover, the Buddhas, when teaching the Dhamma, pervade the assembly with loving-kindness. Through the pervasion of loving-kindness, the minds of the great multitude become serene towards the Ten-Powered One. The Buddhas are those who have attained the height of beauty, are endowed with a pleasing appearance, have sweet voices, soft tongues, and well-formed lips; they teach the Dhamma as if sprinkling the heart with ambrosia. There, for those whose minds are serene through his pervasion of loving-kindness, it occurs to them thus: 'We will not be able to take a contrary position against the Blessed One, who teaches such unequivocal, unfailing, and liberating talk.' Thus, due to their own serene state, they do not ask questions.

Kathitā vissajjitā vāti “evaṃ tumhe pucchathā”ti apucchitapañhānaṃ uccāraṇena te pañhā bhagavatā kathitā eva honti. Yathā ca te vissajjetabbā, tathā vissajjitā eva honti. Niddiṭṭhakāraṇāti iminā kāraṇena iminā hetunā evaṃ hontīti evaṃ sahetukaṃ katvā vissajjanena bhagavatā niddiṭṭhakāraṇā eva honti te pañhā. Upakkhittakā ca te bhagavato sampajjantīti khattiyapaṇḍitādayo bhagavato pañhavissajjaneneva bhagavato samīpe khittakā pakkhittakā sampajjanti; sāvakā vā sampajjanti, upāsakā vāti attho; sāvakasampattiṃ vā [V 0.0240] pāpuṇanti, upāsakasampattiṃ vāti vuttaṃ hoti. Athāti anantaratthe, tesaṃ upakkhittakasampattisamanantaramevāti attho. Tatthāti tasmiṃ ṭhāne, tasmiṃ adhikāre vā. Atirocatīti ativiya jotati pakāsati. Yadidaṃ paññāyāti yāyaṃ bhagavato paññā, tāya paññāya bhagavāva atirocatīti attho. Iti-saddo kāraṇattho, iminā kāraṇenāti attho. Sesaṃ sabbattha pākaṭamevāti.

'Spoken and answered': Even without being asked, those questions are indeed spoken by the Blessed One by prompting them, saying, 'Ask thus.' And they are indeed answered just as they should be answered. 'Having stated the reason': By stating a reasoned answer, saying 'it is thus because of this reason, because of this cause,' the Blessed One has indeed stated the cause for those questions. 'And they are well-placed before the Blessed One': This means that the wise khattiyas and others, through the Blessed One's answering of questions, become placed and established in the presence of the Blessed One. Or they become disciples, or lay followers—this is the meaning. Or it is said that they attain the accomplishment of discipleship or the accomplishment of lay followers. 'Atha' (Then): In the sense of immediately after; meaning, immediately after their accomplishment of being well-placed. 'Tattha' (There): In that place, or in that context. 'Atirocati' (Shines exceedingly): It shines and radiates very brightly. 'Namely, with wisdom': This means that by that wisdom of the Blessed One, the Blessed One himself shines exceedingly. The word 'iti' denotes reason, meaning 'for this reason.' The rest is clear throughout.

Saddhammappajjotikāya mahāniddesaṭṭhakathāya

The Saddhammappajjotikā, a commentary on the Mahāniddesa.

Pasūrasuttaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Pasūrasutta-niddesa is concluded.

9. Māgaṇḍiyasuttaniddesavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Exposition of the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta

70. Navame [V 0.0241][P 2.0303][M 0.0263] māgaṇḍiyasuttaniddese paṭhamagāthāya tāva ajapālanigrodhamūle nānārūpāni nimminitvā abhikāmaṃ āgataṃ māradhītaraṃ disvāna taṇhaṃ aratiṃ ragañca chandamattampi methunasmiṃ nāhosi, kimevidaṃ imissā dārikāya muttakarīsapuṇṇaṃ rūpaṃ disvā bhavissati, sabbathā pādāpi naṃ samphusituṃ na icche, kutonena saṃvasitunti.

70. In the ninth, the exposition of the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta, regarding the first verse: At the foot of the Ajapāla banyan tree, when Māra’s daughter, having created various forms, arrived with desire, upon seeing her, there arose not even the slightest inclination for sexual intercourse—for craving, discontent, and passion. 'What could come of seeing this form of a girl filled with urine and excrement? In no way would I wish to touch her even with my foot, so how much less to cohabit with her!'

Muttapuṇṇanti āhārautuvasena vatthipuṭantaraṃ pūretvā ṭhitamuttena pūritaṃ. Karīsapuṇṇanti pakkāsayasaṅkhāte heṭṭhānābhipiṭṭhikaṇṭakamūlānaṃ antare ubbedhena aṭṭhaṅgulamatte antāvasāne ṭhitavaccena puṇṇaṃ. Semhapuṇṇanti udarapaṭale ṭhitaekapattappamāṇena semhena pūritaṃ. Ruhirapuṇṇanti yakanassa heṭṭhābhāgaṃ pūretvā hadayavakkapapphāsānaṃ upari thokaṃ thokaṃ paggharantena vakkahadayayakanapapphāse temayamānena ṭhitena ekapattassa pūraṇamattena sannicitalohitasaṅkhātena ca kesalomanakhadantānaṃ maṃsavinimuttaṭṭhānañceva thaddhasukkhacammañca ṭhapetvā dhamanījālānusārena sabbaṃ upādiṇṇakasarīraṃ pharitvā ṭhitasaṃsaraṇalohitasaṅkhātena ca duvidhena ruhirena puṇṇaṃ.

“Filled with urine” means filled with urine that has filled the inside of the bladder-pouch according to food and season. “Filled with excrement” means filled with feces, which is located in the large intestine, between the lower navel and the base of the spine, accumulated to a height of eight finger-widths at the end of the intestines. “Filled with phlegm” means filled with phlegm the measure of a single bowl, located in the abdominal membrane. “Filled with blood” means filled with two kinds of blood: first, the blood that, having filled the lower part of the liver, drips little by little onto the heart, kidneys, and lungs above, moistening the kidneys, heart, liver, and lungs, enough to fill a single bowl, and also what is called accumulated blood; second, the circulating blood that flows through the network of veins, permeating the entire appropriated body, except for the flesh-free areas of hair, body hair, nails, and teeth, and the tough, dry skin.

Aṭṭhisaṅghātanti sakalasarīre heṭṭhā aṭṭhīnaṃ upariṭṭhitāni sādhikāni tīṇi aṭṭhisatāni, tehi aṭṭhīhi ghaṭitaṃ. Nhārusambandhanti sakalasarīre aṭṭhīni ābandhitvā ṭhitāni nava nhārusatāni, tehi nhārūhi sambandhaṃ ābandhaṃ. Rudhiramaṃsāvalepananti saṃsaraṇalohitena ca sādhikāni tīṇi aṭṭhisatāni anulimpetvā ṭhitena navamaṃsapesisatena ca anulittaṃ sarīraṃ. Cammavinaddhanti sakalasarīraṃ pariyonandhitvā pākaṭakilomakassa upari chaviyā heṭṭhā [P 2.0304] ṭhitaṃ cammaṃ, tena cammena vinaddhaṃ pariyonaddhaṃ. “Cammāvanaddha”ntipi pāḷi. Chaviyā paṭicchannanti atisukhumachaviyā paṭicchannaṃ chādetvā ṭhitaṃ. Chiddāvachiddanti anekachiddaṃ. Uggharantanti akkhimukhādīhi uggharantaṃ. Paggharantanti adhobhāgena paggharantaṃ. Kimisaṅghanisevitanti sūcimukhādīhi [V 0.0242] nānāpāṇakulasamūhehi āsevitaṃ. Nānākalimalaparipūranti anekavidhehi asucikoṭṭhāsehi pūritaṃ.

“A mass of bones” means joined together by the more than three hundred bones that stand in the entire body. “Bound by sinews” refers to being bound by the nine hundred sinews that stand binding the bones in the entire body. “Plastered with flesh and blood” refers to the body being smeared with circulating blood and with the nine hundred lumps of flesh that plaster the bones. “Wrapped in skin” means the entire body is completely enveloped by the skin that is below the epidermis and above the manifest membranes, wrapped and enveloped by that skin. “Covered with hide” is also a reading. “Covered by epidermis” means covered and concealed by the very fine epidermis. “Full of holes” means having many holes. “Oozing” refers to oozing from the eyes, mouth, and so on. “Dripping” refers to dripping from the lower parts. “Frequented by swarms of worms” means inhabited by multitudes of different groups of creatures, such as needle-mouthed worms. “Filled with various impurities” means filled with various kinds of impure parts.

71. Tato [M 0.0264] māgaṇḍiyo “pabbajitā nāma mānusake kāme pahāya dibbakāmatthāya pabbajanti, ayañca dibbepi kāme na icchati, idampi itthiratanaṃ, kā nu assa diṭṭhī”ti pucchituṃ dutiyaṃ gāthamāha. Tattha etādisaṃ ce ratananti dibbitthiratanaṃ sandhāya bhaṇati. Nārinti attano dhītaraṃ sandhāya. Diṭṭhigataṃ sīlavataṃ nu jīvitanti diṭṭhiñca sīlañca vatañca jīvitañca. Bhavūpapattiñca vadesi kīdisanti attano bhavūpapattiṃ vā tuvaṃ kīdisaṃ vadesi.

71. Then Māgaṇḍiya thought, “Renunciates, having abandoned human pleasures, go forth for the sake of divine pleasures, but this one does not desire even divine pleasures. And this here is a jewel of a woman—what could his view be?” To ask this, he spoke the second verse. Therein, “such a jewel” refers to the divine jewel of a woman. “This woman” refers to his own daughter. “View, virtue, or life” means view, virtue, observance, and life. “And what kind of arising in existence do you declare?” means “what kind of arising in existence do you declare for yourself?”

72. Ito parā dve gāthā vissajjanapucchānayena pavattattā pākaṭasambandhāyeva. Tāsu paṭhamagāthāya saṅkhepattho – tassa mayhaṃ māgaṇḍiya dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhigatadhammesu nicchinitvā “idameva saccaṃ, moghamañña”nti (ma. ni. 3.27, 301) evaṃ idaṃ vadāmīti samuggahītaṃ na hoti natthi na vijjati, kiṃ kāraṇā? Ahañhi passanto diṭṭhīsu ādīnavaṃ kañci diṭṭhiṃ aggahetvā saccāni pavicinanto ajjhattaṃ rāgādīnaṃ santibhāvena ajjhattasantisaṅkhātaṃ nibbānameva addasanti.

72. The next two verses proceed by way of question and answer, so their connection is quite clear. Of these, the condensed meaning of the first verse is: “Māgaṇḍiya, for me, among the sixty-two tenets of views, there is nothing held after having decided, ‘This I declare,’ in the manner of ‘This alone is true, the other is futile.’ For what reason? Because I, seeing the danger in views, not grasping any view, and while investigating the truths, saw Nibbāna itself, known as internal peace, through the internal calming of lust and so forth.”

Ādīnavanti upaddavaṃ. Sadukkhanti kāyikadukkhena sadukkhaṃ. Savighātanti cetasikadukkhena sahitaṃ. Saupāyāsanti upāyāsasahitaṃ. Sapariḷāhanti sadarathaṃ. Na nibbidāyāti na vaṭṭe nibbindanatthāya. Na virāgāyāti na vaṭṭe virāgatthāya. Na nirodhāyāti na vaṭṭassa nirodhatthāya. Na upasamāyāti na vaṭṭassa upasamatthāya. Na abhiññāyāti na vaṭṭassa abhijānanatthāya. Na sambodhāyāti na kilesaniddāvigamena vaṭṭato sambujjhanatthāya[P 2.0305]. Na nibbānāyāti na amatanibbānatthāya. Ettha pana “nibbidāyā”ti vipassanā. “Virāgāyā”ti maggo. “Nirodhāya upasamāyā”ti nibbānaṃ. “Abhiññāya sambodhāyā”ti maggo. “Nibbānāyā”ti nibbānameva. Evaṃ ekasmiṃ ṭhāne vipassanā, tīsu maggo, tīsu nibbānaṃ vuttanti evaṃ vavatthānakathā veditabbā. Pariyāyena pana sabbānipetāni maggavevacanānipi nibbānavevacanānipi hontiyeva.

“Danger” means affliction. “With suffering” means accompanied by bodily suffering. “With distress” means associated with mental suffering. “With despair” means accompanied by despair. “With fever” means accompanied by burning. “Not for disenchantment” means not for the purpose of disenchantment with the round. “Not for dispassion” means not for the purpose of dispassion towards the round. “Not for cessation” means not for the purpose of the cessation of the round. “Not for peace” means not for the purpose of the pacification of the round. “Not for direct knowledge” means not for the purpose of directly knowing the round. “Not for awakening” means not for the purpose of awakening from the round through the dispelling of the sleep of defilements. “Not for Nibbāna” means not for the purpose of deathless Nibbāna. Here, “for disenchantment” refers to insight. “For dispassion” refers to the path. “For cessation and for peace” refer to Nibbāna. “For direct knowledge and for awakening” refer to the path. “For Nibbāna” refers to Nibbāna itself. Thus, this should be understood as an explanation of the distinctions: in one instance, insight is stated; in three, the path; and in three, Nibbāna. However, by way of alternative meaning, all these terms can also be synonyms for the path and for Nibbāna.

Ajjhattaṃ rāgassa santinti ajjhattarāgassa santabhāvena nibbutabhāvena ajjhattasantisaṅkhātaṃ nibbānaṃ olokesiṃ. Dosassa santintiādīsupi eseva nayo. Pacinanti niddesassa uddesapadaṃ. Vicinantoti saccāni vaḍḍhento vibhāvento. Pavicinantoti tāneva paccekaṃ vibhāvento[V 0.0243]. Keci [M 0.0265] “gavesanto”ti vaṇṇayanti. Adassanti olokesiṃ. Adakkhinti vinivijjhiṃ. Aphassinti paññāya phusiṃ. Paṭivijjhinti ñāṇena paccakkhaṃ akāsiṃ.

“The internal calming of lust” means: I saw Nibbāna, which is called internal peace, by means of the calmed and quenched state of internal lust. The same method applies to “the calming of hatred,” and so on. “Pacinanti” is the summary term of the exposition. “Vicinanto” means developing and analyzing the truths. “Pavicinanto” means analyzing them individually. Some explain it as “seeking.” “Adassaṃ” means I saw. “Adakkhiṃ” means I penetrated. “Aphassiṃ” means I touched with wisdom. “Paṭivijjhīṃ” means I realized it directly with knowledge.

73. Dutiyagāthāya saṅkhepattho – yānimāni diṭṭhigatāni tehi tehi sattehi vinicchinitvā gahitattā “vinicchayā”ti ca attano paccayehi abhisaṅkhatabhāvādinā nayena “pakappitānī”ti ca vuccanti, te ve munī diṭṭhigatadhamme aggahetvā ajjhattasantīti yametamatthaṃ brūsi, ācikkha me, kathaṃ nu dhīrehi paveditaṃ taṃ kathaṃ pakāsitaṃ dhīrehīti vadati.

73. The summary of the second verse is: These views, because they are determined and grasped by various beings, are called 'determinations' (vinicchayā); and because they are constructed by their own conditions and so on, they are also called 'constructions' (pakappitāni). You speak of this meaning, 'inner peace,' for the sage who does not grasp these phenomena that are views. Tell me, how is that declared by the wise? How is it made known by the wise? — thus he speaks.

Imissā gāthāya niddeso uttānattho ṭhapetvā paramatthapadaṃ. Tattha yaṃ paramatthanti yaṃ uttamaṃ nibbānaṃ.

The explanation of this verse is clear in meaning, except for the ultimate term. Here, 'the ultimate' refers to the supreme Nibbāna.

74. Athassa bhagavā yathā yena upāyena taṃ padaṃ dhīrehi pakāsitaṃ, taṃ upāyaṃ sapaṭipakkhaṃ dassento “na diṭṭhiyā”ti gāthamāha. Tattha na diṭṭhiyātiādīhi diṭṭhisutiaṭṭhasamāpattiñāṇabāhirasīlabbatāni paṭikkhipati. “Suddhimāhā”ti ettha vuttaṃ āha-saddaṃ sabbattha nakārena saddhiṃ yojetvā purimapadattayaṃ netvā “diṭṭhiyā suddhiṃ nāha [P 2.0306] na kathemī”ti evamattho veditabbo. Yathā cettha, evaṃ uttarapadesupi. Tattha ca adiṭṭhiyā nāhāti dasavatthukaṃ sammādiṭṭhiṃ vinā na kathemi. Tathā assutiyāti navaṅgaṃ savanaṃ vinā. Añāṇāti kammassakatasaccānulomikañāṇaṃ vinā. Asīlatāti pātimokkhasaṃvaraṃ vinā. Abbatāti dhutaṅgavataṃ vinā. Nopi tenāti tesu ekamekena diṭṭhiādimattenāpi na kathemīti evamattho veditabbo. Ete ca nissajja anuggahāyāti ete ca purimadiṭṭhiādibhede kaṇhapakkhike dhamme samugghātakaraṇena nissajja, pacchime adiṭṭhiādibhede sukkapakkhikepi atammayatāpajjanena anuggahāya. Santo anissāya bhavaṃ na jappeti imāya paṭipattiyā rāgādivūpasamena santo cakkhādīsu kañci dhammaṃ anissāya ekampi bhavaṃ na jappe, apihetuṃ apatthetuṃ samattho siyā, ayamassa ajjhattasantīti adhippāyo.

74. Then the Blessed One, showing the method with its counterpoint by which the wise have revealed that path, spoke the verse, “Not by view.” Herein, “not by view,” and so on, reject views, hearsay, attainments, knowledge, and external virtue and vows. In the phrase, “declares purity,” the word “declares” should be connected with the negative particle throughout, and the first three terms should be taken together to mean: “I do not declare purity by view.” The same applies to the following terms. Therein, “not without view” means I do not declare it without the tenfold right view. Similarly, “not without hearing” means without hearing the ninefold teaching. “Not without knowledge” means without the knowledge of the ownership of kamma and knowledge in conformity with the truths. “Not without virtue” means without the restraint of the monastic code. “Not without vows” means without the practice of ascetic observances. “Nor even by that” means I do not declare it even by any one of these—view and so on—alone. “Having abandoned these, not grasping” means having abandoned the former divisions of view and so on, which belong to the dark side, by utterly destroying them, and, on the bright side, not grasping the latter divisions of right view and so on, by not identifying with them. “Peaceful, not relying, he does not long for existence” — being peaceful through the calming of lust and so on by this practice, and not relying on any phenomenon regarding the eye and so on, he would not long for even a single existence, and would be capable of not desiring or seeking it. This is the meaning of his inner peace.

Savanampi icchitabbanti suttādivasena suṇanampi ākaṅkhitabbaṃ. Sambhārā ime dhammāti sammādiṭṭhiādikā ime dhammā upakāraṭṭhena sambhārā honti[M 0.0266]. Kaṇhapakkhikānanti akusalapakkhe bhavānaṃ. Samugghātato pahānaṃ icchitabbanti sammā hananato samucchedato pahānaṃ ākaṅkhitabbaṃ. Tedhātukesu kusalesu dhammesūti kāmarūpārūpasaṅkhātesu tebhūmakesu kosallasambhūtesu. Atammayatāti nittaṇhabhāvo.

“One should also desire to listen” means one should wish to hear through discourses and the like. “These states are requisites” means these states, right view and so forth, are requisites in the sense of being helpful. “Of those belonging to the dark side” means of those belonging to the unwholesome side. “One should desire abandonment by eradication” means one should wish for abandonment through proper destruction and complete cutting off. “In the wholesome states pertaining to the three realms” means in those states arisen from skillfulness in the three planes, designated as the realms of sensuality, form, and formlessness. “Non-identification” means the state of being free from craving.

75. Evaṃ [V 0.0244] vutte vacanatthaṃ asallakkhento māgaṇḍiyo “no ce kirā”ti gāthamāha. Tattha diṭṭhādīni vuttanayāneva. Kaṇhapakkhikāniyeva pana sandhāya ubhayatrāpi āha. Āha-saddaṃ pana “no ce”ti saddena yojetvā no ce kira āha no ce kira kathesīti evaṃ attho daṭṭhabbo. Momūhanti atimūḷhaṃ, mohanaṃ vā. Paccentīti jānanti. Imissāpi gāthāya niddeso uttāno.

75. When this was said, Māgaṇḍiya, not considering the meaning of the words, spoke the verse, “If indeed not…” Here, 'views, etc.' are to be understood in the manner already stated. However, he spoke in both instances with reference to the dark aspect. The word 'āha' (he declared), however, should be connected with the words 'no ce' (if not), and the meaning should be understood thus: 'if indeed he does not declare,' or 'if indeed he does not speak.' 'Momūha' means extremely deluded, or causing delusion. 'Paccenti' means they know. The explanation of this verse is also clear.

76. Athassa [P 2.0307] bhagavā taṃ diṭṭhiṃ nissāya pucchaṃ paṭikkhipanto “diṭṭhiñca nissāyā”ti gāthamāha. Tassattho – tvaṃ māgaṇḍiya diṭṭhiṃ nissāya punappunaṃ pucchamāno yāni te diṭṭhigatāni samuggahitāni, tesveva samuggahītesu pamohaṃ āgato tvaṃ ito ca mayā vuttaajjhattasantito paṭipattito dhammadesanato vā aṇumpi yuttasaññaṃ na passasi, tena kāraṇena tvaṃ imaṃ dhammaṃ momūhato passasīti.

76. Then, rejecting his question based on that view, the Blessed One spoke this verse: “Relying on views…” Its meaning is: “You, Māgaṇḍiya, relying on a view, repeatedly ask questions. Having fallen into delusion concerning those very views you have grasped, you do not see even a particle of what is fitting, whether from the inner peace spoken of by me, or from the practice, or from the teaching of the Dhamma. For that reason, you see this Dhamma as utterly deluded.”

Lagganaṃ nissāya laggananti diṭṭhilagganaṃ allīyitvā diṭṭhilagganaṃ. Bandhananti diṭṭhibandhanaṃ. Palibodhanti diṭṭhipalibodhaṃ.

“Relying on clinging, there is clinging” means: having adhered to the clinging of views, there is the clinging of views. “Bondage” means the bondage of views. “Obstruction” means the obstruction of views.

Andhakāraṃ pakkhandosīti bahalandhakāraṃ paviṭṭhosi. Yuttasaññanti samaṇadhamme yuttasaññaṃ. Pattasaññanti samaṇadhamme paṭiladdhasaññaṃ. Lagganasaññanti sañjānitasaññaṃ. Kāraṇasaññanti hetusaññaṃ. Ṭhānasaññanti kāraṇasaññaṃ. Na paṭilabhasīti na vindasi. Kuto ñāṇanti maggañāṇaṃ pana kena kāraṇena labhissasi. Aniccaṃ vāti hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena pañcakkhandhā aniccaṃ. Aniccasaññānulomaṃ vāti “pañcakkhandhā aniccā”ti uppannā saññā aniccasaññā, tāya saññāya anulomaṃ appaṭikkūlaṃ aniccasaññānulomaṃ. Kiṃ taṃ? Vipassanāñāṇaṃ. Dvinnaṃ vipassanāñāṇānaṃ dukkhānattasaññānulomānampi eseva nayo.

“You have plunged into darkness” means you have entered deep darkness. “Perception of what is fitting” means perception of what is fitting in the ascetic’s life. “Perception of what is attained” means perception of what has been gained in the ascetic’s life. “Perception of clinging” means perception that has been cognized. “Perception of a cause” means perception of a reason. “Perception of a basis” means perception of a cause. “You do not obtain” means you do not find. “From where will knowledge come?” means by what cause will you attain the knowledge of the path? “Impermanent” means the five aggregates are impermanent in the sense of becoming nonexistent after having come to be. “Or in conformity with the perception of impermanence” means the perception that arises as “the five aggregates are impermanent” is the perception of impermanence; conformity with that perception, not being opposed to it, is conformity with the perception of impermanence. What is that? It is the knowledge of insight. This same method applies also to the two conformities with the perceptions of suffering and non-self, which are insight knowledges.

77. Evaṃ samuggahitesu pamohena māgaṇḍiyassa vivādāpattiṃ dassetvā idāni tesu aññesu ca dhammesu vigatappamohassa attano nibbivādataṃ [M 0.0267] dassento “samo visesī”ti gāthamāha. Tassattho – yo evaṃ tidhā mānena vā diṭṭhiyā vā puggalena vā maññati, so tena mānena tāya vā diṭṭhiyā tena vā puggalena vivadeyya. Yo pana amhādiso imāsu tīsu vidhāsu avikampamāno, samo visesīti na tassa hoti, na ca hīnoti pāṭhaseso. Imissāpi gāthāya niddeso uttānova.

77. Having thus shown Māgaṇḍiya’s falling into contention due to delusion regarding what has been grasped, now, indicating his own freedom from contention towards those and other things, being without delusion, he speaks the verse, “Equal, superior…” Its meaning is: whoever thus conceives in three ways—by conceit, by view, or by a person—would contend by that conceit, by that view, or by that person. But for one like us, unwavering in these three ways, the thought 'I am equal' or 'I am superior' does not occur; “nor inferior” is the remainder of the text. The explanation of this verse is also clear.

78. Kiñca [V 0.0245] bhiyyo – “saccanti so”ti gāthā. Tassattho – so evarūpo pahīnamānadiṭṭhiko “mādiso ‘bāhitapāpattā’dinā nayena brāhmaṇo, idameva sacca”nti kiṃ vadeyya kiṃ vatthuṃ bhaṇeyya, kena [P 2.0308] vā kāraṇena bhaṇeyya, “mayhaṃ saccaṃ, tuyhaṃ musā”ti vā kena mānena diṭṭhiyā puggalena vā vivadeyya. Yasmiṃ mādise khīṇāsave “sadisohamasmī”ti pavattiyā samaṃ vā, itaradvayabhāvena pavattiyā visamaṃ vā maññitaṃ natthi, samānādīsu kena vādaṃ paṭisaṃyujeyya paṭipphareyyāti. Imissāpi gāthāya niddeso uttāno.

78. Furthermore, the verse is, “That truth…” Its meaning is: what could such a one, who has abandoned conceit and views, say? What could he speak of, or for what reason would he declare: “A brahmin like me (in the sense of ‘one who has barred evil,’ etc.) knows that this alone is true”? With what conceit, view, or person would he contend, saying, “My truth, yours is false”? In one like me, whose defilements are destroyed, there is no conceiving of equality, through the occurrence of “I am equal,” or of inequality, through the occurrence of the state of the other two. Among equals and the like, with whom would he engage in dispute or argue? The explanation of this verse is also clear.

79. Nanu ekaṃseneva evarūpo puggalo? “Okaṃ pahāyā”ti gāthā. Tattha okaṃ pahāyāti rūpadhātvādiviññāṇassokāsaṃ tatra chandarāgappahānena chaḍḍetvā. Aniketasārīti rūpanimittaniketādīni taṇhāvasena asaranto. Gāme akubbaṃ muni santhavānīti gāme gihisanthavāni akaronto. Kāmehi rittoti kāmesu chandarāgābhāvena sabbakāmehi puthubhūto. Apurakkharānoti āyatiṃ attabhāvaṃ anabhinibbattento. Kathaṃ na viggayha janena kayirāti janena saddhiṃ viggāhikakathaṃ na katheyya.

79. Is such a person not invariably so? The verse is, “Having abandoned a home…” Here, “having abandoned a home” means having discarded the abode for consciousness in the form realm, etc., by abandoning desire and lust for it. “Faring without a shelter” means not resorting to shelters like the sign of form, etc., through the power of craving. “The sage, not forming intimacies in the village” means not cultivating intimacies with householders in the village. “Devoid of sensual pleasures” means being separate from all sensual pleasures due to the absence of desire and lust for them. “Not putting anything forward” means not generating a future existence. “How could he contend with people?” means he would not engage in quarrelsome talk with people.

Hāliddakānīti evaṃnāmako gahapati. Yenāyasmā mahākaccāno tenupasaṅkamīti yenāti bhummatthe karaṇavacanaṃ. Tasmā yattha mahākaccāno, tattha upasaṅkamīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Yena vā kāraṇena mahākaccāno devamanussehi upasaṅkamitabbo, tena kāraṇena upasaṅkamīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Kena ca kāraṇena [M 0.0268] mahākaccāno upasaṅkamitabbo? Nānappakāraguṇavisesādhigamādhippāyena, sāduphalūpabhogādhippāyena dijagaṇehi niccaphalitamahārukkho viya. Upasaṅkamīti ca gatoti vuttaṃ hoti. Upasaṅkamitvāti upasaṅkamanapariyosānadīpanaṃ. Atha vā evaṃ gato tato āsannataraṃ ṭhānaṃ mahākaccānassa samīpasaṅkhātaṃ gantvātipi vuttaṃ hoti.

'Hāliddakāni' means a householder of that name. 'He approached the Venerable Mahākaccāna'—here, 'yena' is an instrumental case in the sense of location. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as: 'he approached where Mahākaccāna was.' Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood as: 'he approached for the reason that Mahākaccāna should be approached by gods and humans.' And for what reason should Mahākaccāna be approached? With the intention of attaining various excellent qualities, just as a great, ever-fruitful tree is approached by flocks of birds with the intention of enjoying its delicious fruit. 'Upasaṅkamī' (he approached) means it is said that he went. 'Upasaṅkamitvā' (having approached) indicates the conclusion of the act of approaching. Alternatively, it is also said to mean: having gone thus, he went to a place closer, which is designated as the vicinity of Mahākaccāna.

Abhivādetvāti pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā. Idāni yenatthena mahākaccānassa upaṭṭhānaṃ āgato, taṃ pucchitukāmo dasanakhasamodhānasamujjalaṃ añjaliṃ sirasi patiṭṭhāpetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantanti bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso [P 2.0309] “visamaṃ candimasūriyā parivattantī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.7) viya. Tasmā yathā nisinno ekamantaṃ nisinno hoti, evaṃ nisīdīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Bhummatthe vā etaṃ upayogavacanaṃ. Nisīdīti nisajjaṃ kappesi. Paṇḍitā hi devamanussā garuṭṭhāniyaṃ upasaṅkamitvā āsanakusalatāya ekamantaṃ nisīdanti. Ayañca gahapati tesaṃ aññataro, tasmā ekamantaṃ nisīdi.

'Having paid respects' means having bowed down with the five-point prostration. Now, wishing to ask about the purpose for which he had come to attend upon Mahākaccāna, he placed on his head the añjali gesture, resplendent with his ten fingernails brought together, and sat down to one side. 'Ekamantaṃ' (to one side) is an adverbial neuter designation, like in the phrase, 'The sun and moon revolve unevenly,' and so on (AN 4.7). Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as: he sat down in such a way as to be sitting to one side. Alternatively, this is a locative case indicating usage. 'Nisīdi' (he sat down) means he took a seat. For wise gods and humans, when approaching one worthy of respect, sit down to one side due to their skill in seating. And this householder was one of them; therefore, he sat down to one side.

Kathaṃ [V 0.0246] nisinno ca pana ekamantaṃ nisinno hotīti? Cha nisajjadose vajjetvā. Seyyathidaṃ? Atidūraṃ accāsannaṃ uparivātaṃ unnatappadesaṃ atisammukhaṃ atipacchāti. Atidūre nisinno hi sace kathetukāmo hoti, uccāsaddena kathetabbaṃ hoti. Accāsanne nisinno saṅghaṭṭanaṃ karoti. Uparivāte nisinno sarīragandhena bādhati. Unnatappadese nisinno agāravaṃ pakāseti. Atisammukhā nisinno sace daṭṭhukāmo hoti, cakkhunā cakkhuṃ āhacca daṭṭhabbaṃ hoti. Atipacchā nisinno sace daṭṭhukāmo hoti, gīvaṃ pasāretvā daṭṭhabbaṃ hoti. Tasmā ayampi ete cha nisajjadose vajjetvā nisīdi. Tena vuttaṃ – “ekamantaṃ nisīdī”ti.

And how does one who is seated sit to one side? By avoiding the six faults of sitting. What are these? Being too far, too close, upwind, on a higher seat, directly in front, or directly behind. For if one sits too far and wishes to speak, one must speak in a loud voice. If one sits too close, one causes physical contact. If one sits upwind, one offends with bodily odor. If one sits on a higher seat, one displays disrespect. If one sits directly in front and wishes to look, one must look by meeting eye to eye. If one sits directly behind and wishes to look, one must stretch one’s neck to see. Therefore, this person also avoided these six faults of sitting and sat down. Hence it is said: 'He sat down to one side.'

Etadavocāti etaṃ avoca. Vuttamidaṃ bhante kaccāna bhagavatā aṭṭhakavaggiye māgaṇḍiyapañheti aṭṭhakavaggiyamhi māgaṇḍiyapañho nāma atthi, tasmiṃ pañhe.

'He said this' means this he said. 'Venerable Kaccāna, this was said by the Blessed One in the Aṭṭhakavagga, in the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta' means: in the Aṭṭhakavagga there is a sutta named the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta; it was said in that sutta.

Rūpadhātūti rūpakkhandho adhippeto. Rūpadhāturāgavinibandhanti rūpadhātumhi rāgena vinibaddhaṃ. Viññāṇanti kammaviññāṇaṃ. Okasārīti gehasārī ālayasārī. Kasmā panettha “viññāṇadhātu kho gahapatī”ti na vuttanti? Sammohavighātatthaṃ. “Oko”ti hi atthato paccayo vuccati, purejātañca [M 0.0269] kammaviññāṇaṃ pacchājātassa kammaviññāṇassapi vipākaviññāṇassapi, vipākaviññāṇañca vipākaviññāṇassapi kammaviññāṇassapi paccayo hoti, tasmā “kataraṃ nu kho idha viññāṇa”nti sammoho bhaveyya. Tassa vighātatthaṃ taṃ aggahetvā asambhinnāva desanā katāti. Apica vipākaārammaṇavasena catasso abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇaṭṭhitiyoti vuttāti tā dassetumpi idha viññāṇaṃ na gahitaṃ.

'The element of form' is intended as the form aggregate. 'Bound by lust for the element of form' means bound by lust in the element of form. 'Consciousness' means kamma-consciousness. 'One who frequents a home' means one who frequents a house, one who partakes of attachment. Why, then, was it not said here, 'Householder, the element of consciousness'? To eliminate confusion. For 'home' (oka), in its meaning, is said to be a condition. And previously arisen kamma-consciousness is a condition for later arisen kamma-consciousness and for resultant consciousness; and resultant consciousness is a condition for resultant consciousness and for kamma-consciousness. Therefore, confusion might arise as to 'which consciousness is meant here?' To eliminate this, the teaching was given without including it, thus remaining unmixed. Furthermore, consciousness was not included here also in order to show the four stations of consciousness related to formations, which are spoken of in terms of a resultant object.

Upayupādānāti [P 2.0310] taṇhūpayadiṭṭhūpayavasena dve upayā, kāmupādānādīni cattāri upādānāni ca. Cetaso adhiṭṭhānābhinivesānusayāti akusalacittassa adhiṭṭhānabhūtā ceva abhinivesabhūtā ca anusayabhūtā ca. Tathāgatassāti sammāsambuddhassa. Sabbesampi hi khīṇāsavānaṃ ete pahīnāva, satthu pana khīṇāsavabhāvo loke atipākaṭoti uparimakoṭiyā evaṃ vuttaṃ. Viññāṇadhātuyāti idha viññāṇaṃ kasmā gahitaṃ? Kilesappahānadassanatthaṃ. Kilesā hi na kevalaṃ catūsuyeva khandhesu pahīnā pahīyanti, pañcasupi pahīyantiyevāti kilesappahānadassanatthaṃ gahitaṃ. Evaṃ kho gahapati anokasārī hotīti evaṃ kammaviññāṇena okaṃ asarantena anokasārī nāma hoti.

'Approaches and clinging' refers to the two approaches—the approach of craving and the approach of views—and the four kinds of clinging beginning with sensual clinging. 'The mind's resolves, adherences, and underlying tendencies' refers to that which is the basis for resolve, adherence, and underlying tendencies of an unwholesome mind. 'Of the Tathāgata' means of the Perfectly Enlightened One. For all whose taints are destroyed, these are indeed abandoned; but since the Teacher's state of having destroyed the taints is exceptionally manifest in the world, it is stated in this supreme manner. Why is the element of consciousness included here? To show the abandonment of the defilements. For the defilements are abandoned not only in the four aggregates, but they are abandoned in all five. Thus, it is included to show the abandonment of the defilements. 'Thus, householder, one is not a frequenter of a home' means that one is called 'not a frequenter of a home' by not frequenting a 'home' by means of kamma-consciousness.

Rūpanimittaniketavisāravinibandhāti rūpameva kilesānaṃ paccayaṭṭhena nimittaṃ, ārammaṇakiriyasaṅkhātena [V 0.0247] nivāsaṭṭhena niketanti rūpanimittaniketaṃ. Visāro ca vinibandho ca visāravinibandhā. Ubhayenapi hi kilesānaṃ patthaṭabhāvo ca vinibandhanabhāvo ca vutto, rūpanimittanikete visāravinibandhāti rūpanimittaniketavisāravinibandhā, tasmā rūpanimittaniketamhi uppannena kilesavisārena ceva kilesavinibandhanena cāti attho. Niketasārīti vuccatīti ārammaṇakaraṇavasena nivāsaṭṭhānaṭṭhena niketasārīti vuccati. Pahīnāti te rūpanimittanikete kilesavisāravinibandhā pahīnā.

'Diffusion and bondage regarding the sign and abode of form' means: form itself is a 'sign' (nimitta) in the sense of being a condition for the defilements, and it is an 'abode' (niketa) in the sense of being a dwelling place, which is designated by its function as an object; thus 'sign-and-abode of form' (rūpanimittaniketa). 'Diffusion' (visāra) and 'bondage' (vinibandha) are 'diffusion-and-bondage' (visāravinibandhā). By both of these are expressed the state of spreading and the state of being bound of the defilements. 'Diffusion and bondage regarding the sign and abode of form' are the diffusion and bondage in the sign-and-abode of form. Therefore, the meaning is: by the diffusion of defilements and the bondage of defilements that have arisen in the sign-and-abode of form. 'Is called one who frequents an abode' means one is called a 'frequenter of an abode' in the sense of it being a dwelling place by way of making it an object. 'Are abandoned' means that that diffusion and bondage of defilements in the sign-and-abode of form are abandoned.

Kasmā panettha pañcakkhandhā ca “okā”ti vuttā, cha ārammaṇāni “niketa”nti? Chandarāgassa balavadubbalatāya. Samānepi hi etesaṃ ālayaṭṭhena visayabhāve okoti nippariyāyena suddhaṃ gehameva vuccati, niketanti [M 0.0270] “ajja asukaṭṭhāne kīḷissāmā”ti katasaṅketānaṃ nivāsanaṭṭhānaṃ uyyānādi. Tattha yathā puttadāradhanadhaññapuṇṇagehe chandarāgo balavā hoti, evaṃ ajjhattikesu khandhesu. Yathā pana uyyānaṭṭhānādīsu tato dubbalataro hoti, evaṃ bāhiresu [P 2.0311] chasu ārammaṇesūti chandarāgassa balavadubbalatāya evaṃ desanā katāti veditabbā.

Why here are the five aggregates called a 'home' (oka) and the six sense objects an 'abode' (niketa)? Because of the strength and weakness of desire and lust. For although these are similar in being objects and a basis for attachment, 'home' (oka) is said to be simply a house in the unqualified sense, whereas 'abode' (niketa) is a dwelling place for those who have made an arrangement, such as a park, as in, 'Today we will amuse ourselves in such-and-such a place.' Just as desire and lust are strong in a house full of children, a wife, wealth, and grain, so too are they strong regarding the internal aggregates. And just as desire and lust are weaker in relation to places like parks, so too are they weaker regarding the six external sense objects. Thus, it should be understood that the teaching was given in this way because of the strength and weakness of desire and lust.

Sukhitesu sukhitoti upaṭṭhākesu dhanadhaññalābhādivasena sukhitesu “idānāhaṃ manāpaṃ cīvaraṃ manāpaṃ bhojanaṃ labhissāmī”ti gehassitasukhena sukhito hoti, tehi pattasampattiṃ attanā anubhavamāno viya carati. Dukkhitesu dukkhitoti tesaṃ kenacideva kāraṇena dukkhe uppanne sayaṃ dviguṇena dukkhena dukkhito hoti. Kiccakaraṇīyesūti kiccasaṅkhātesu karaṇīyesu. Voyogaṃ āpajjatīti upayogaṃ sayaṃ tesaṃ kiccānaṃ kattabbataṃ āpajjati.

'Happy among the happy': When his supporters are happy on account of gains of wealth, grain, and so on, he becomes happy with a household-based happiness, thinking, 'Now I will receive a pleasing robe and pleasing food.' He acts as if he himself were experiencing the success they have attained. 'Sorrowful among the sorrowful': When suffering arises for them for some reason, he himself becomes sorrowful with a twofold suffering. 'In duties to be performed': in tasks designated as duties. 'He applies himself': he personally undertakes the performance of their duties.

Kāmesūti vatthukāmesu. Evaṃ kho gahapati kāmehi aritto hotīti evaṃ kilesakāmehi aritto hoti.

'In sensual pleasures' means in objective sensual pleasures. 'Thus, householder, one is not devoid of sensual pleasures' means one is thus not devoid of the defilements of sensual pleasure.

Anto kāmānaṃ bhāvena atuccho. Sukkapakkho tesaṃ abhāvena ritto tucchoti veditabbo.

Because of the presence of sensual pleasures within, one is not void. The bright side, due to their absence, should be understood as empty and void.

Purakkharānoti vaṭṭaṃ purato kurumāno. Evaṃrūpo siyantiādīsu dīgharassakāḷodātādīsu rūpesu evaṃrūpo nāma bhaveyyanti pattheti. Sukhādīsu vedanāsu evaṃvedano nāma. Nīlasaññādīsu saññāsu evaṃsañño nāma. Puññābhisaṅkhārādīsu saṅkhāresu evaṃsaṅkhāro nāma. Cakkhuviññāṇādīsu viññāṇesu evaṃviññāṇo nāma bhaveyyanti pattheti.

'Purakkharānoti' means making the round of rebirths foremost. In the case of forms such as long, short, black, and white, one aspires: 'May I become of such a form.' In the case of feelings such as pleasure, one aspires: 'May I become of such a feeling.' In the case of perceptions such as the perception of blue, one aspires: 'May I become of such a perception.' In the case of formations such as meritorious volitional formations, one aspires: 'May I become of such a formation.' In the case of consciousnesses such as eye-consciousness, one aspires: 'May I become of such a consciousness.'

Apurakkharānoti [V 0.0248] vaṭṭaṃ purato akurumāno. Sahitaṃ me, asahitaṃ teti tuyhaṃ vacanaṃ asahitaṃ asiliṭṭhaṃ, mayhaṃ sahitaṃ siliṭṭhaṃ madhuraṃ madhurapānasadisaṃ. Adhiciṇṇaṃ te viparāvattanti yaṃ tuyhaṃ dīghena kālena paricitaṃ suppaguṇaṃ, taṃ mama vādaṃ āgamma sabbaṃ khaṇena viparāvattaṃ nivattaṃ. Āropito te vādoti tuyhaṃ doso mayā āropito. Cara vādappamokkhāyāti taṃ taṃ ācariyaṃ upasaṅkamitvā uttaraṃ pariyesanto imassa vādassa mokkhāya cara āhiṇḍa. Nibbeṭhehi vā sace pahosīti atha sayameva pahosi, idheva nibbeṭhehīti.

'Apurakkharānoti' means not putting the round of rebirths foremost. 'Sahitaṃ me, asahitaṃ te' means your words are incoherent and disjointed, while mine are coherent, connected, sweet, like a honeyed drink. 'Adhiciṇṇaṃ te viparāvattanti' means what you have long practiced and become well-acquainted with, all that, upon encountering my argument, has in an instant been overturned and reversed. 'Āropito te vādo' means your fault has been imputed by me. 'Cara vādappamokkhāya' means approaching various teachers, seeking a rebuttal, wander about for release from this argument. 'Nibbeṭhehi vā sace pahosi' means then, if you yourself are able, unravel it right here.

80. So [M 0.0271] evarūpo “yehi vivitto”ti gāthā. Tattha yehīti yehi diṭṭhigatādīhi. Vivitto vicareyyāti ritto careyya. Na tāni [P 2.0312] uggayha vadeyya nāgoti “āguṃ na karotī”tiādinā (cūḷani. bhadrāvudhamāṇavapucchāniddesa 70; pārāyanānugītiniddesa 102) nayena nāgo tāni diṭṭhigatāni uggahetvā na careyya. Elambujanti elasaññite ambumhi jātaṃ kaṇṭakanāḷaṃ vārijaṃ, padumanti vuttaṃ hoti. Yathā jalena paṅkena canūpalittanti taṃ padumaṃ yathā jalena ca paṅkena ca anupalittaṃ hoti. Evaṃ muni santivādo agiddhoti evaṃ ajjhattasantivādo muni gedhābhāvena agiddho. Kāme ca loke ca anūpalittoti duvidhepi kāme apāyādike ca loke dvīhi silesehi anupalitto hoti.

80. For one of such a nature, there is the verse beginning 'yehi vivitto'. Herein, 'yehi' refers to those wrong views and the like. 'Vivitto vicareyya' means one should wander free. 'Na tāni uggayha vadeyya nāgo' means, as explained in the Cūḷaniddesa (Bhadrāvudhamāṇavapucchāniddesa 70; Pārāyanānugītiniddesa 102) with the phrase 'āguṃ na karoti' and the like, the Nāga does not take up those wrong views and act upon them. 'Elambuja' refers to a water-born plant with a thorny stalk, born in water called 'ela'; it is said to be a lotus. 'Yathā jalena paṅkena canūpalittaṃ' means just as that lotus is unstained by water and mud. 'Evaṃ muni santivādo agiddho' means so too is the sage, an inwardly peaceful speaker, not greedy due to the absence of greed. 'Kāme ca loke ca anūpalitto' means he is unstained by both kinds of sensual pleasures and by the world, such as the woeful states, being unstained by the two adhesions.

Āguṃ na karotīti akusalādidosaṃ na karoti. Na gacchatīti agativasena na gacchati. Nāgacchatīti pahīnakilese na upeti. Pāpakāti lāmakā. Akusalāti akosallasambhūtā. Te kilese na punetīti ye kilesā pahīnā, te kilese puna na eti. Na paccetīti paṭi na upeti. Na paccāgacchatīti puna na nivattati.

'Āguṃ na karoti' means he does not commit faults such as unwholesome deeds. 'Na gacchati' means he does not go by way of wrong courses. 'Nāgacchati' means he does not approach the abandoned defilements. 'Pāpakā' means base. 'Akusalā' means born of unskillfulness. 'Te kilese na puneti' means he does not return to those defilements that have been abandoned. 'Na pacceti' means he does not go back. 'Na paccāgacchati' means he does not turn back again.

Kharadaṇḍoti kharapattadaṇḍo pharusadaṇḍo. Cattagedhoti vissaṭṭhagedho. Vantagedhoti vamitagedho. Muttagedhoti chinnabandhanagedho. Pahīnagedhoti pajahitagedho. Paṭinissaṭṭhagedhoti yathā na puna cittaṃ āruhati, evaṃ paṭivissajjitagedho. Upari vītarāgādīsupi eseva nayo. Sabbāneva tāni gahitaggahaṇassa vissaṭṭhabhāvavevacanāni.

'Kharadaṇḍo' means a rough-leaved stick, a coarse stick. 'Cattagedho' means one whose greed is relinquished. 'Vantagedho' means one who has vomited out greed. 'Muttagedho' means one whose greed, which is a bond, is severed. 'Pahīnagedho' means one who has abandoned greed. 'Paṭinissaṭṭhagedho' means one whose greed is cast aside such that it does not arise in the mind again; it is utterly relinquished. The same principle applies to being free from passion and the like. All these terms are synonyms signifying the relinquished state of grasping.

81. Kiñca bhiyyo – “na vedagū”ti gāthā. Tattha na vedagū diṭṭhiyāyakoti catumaggavedagū mādiso diṭṭhiyāyako na hoti, diṭṭhiyā gacchanto vā, taṃ sārato paccento vā na hoti. Tattha vacanattho – yāyatīti yāyako. Karaṇavacanena diṭṭhiyā yāyatīti diṭṭhiyāyako. Upayogatthe sāmivacanenapi diṭṭhiyā yātītipi diṭṭhiyāyako. Na mutiyā sa mānametīti [V 0.0249] mutarūpādibhedāya mutiyāpi so mānaṃ na eti. Na hi tammayo soti taṇhādiṭṭhivasena tammayo hoti tapparāyaṇo, ayaṃ pana na tādiso. Na kammunā nopi [P 2.0313] sutena neyyoti puññābhisaṅkhārādinā kammunā vā, sutasuddhiādinā sutena vā [M 0.0272] so netabbo na hoti. Anūpanīto sa nivesanesūti so dvinnampi upayānaṃ pahīnattā sabbesu taṇhādiṭṭhinivesanesu anupanīto.

81. What more? There is the verse beginning 'na vedagū'. Herein, 'na vedagū diṭṭhiyāyako' means one like me, who has attained knowledge through the four paths, is not a proponent of views, nor does he proceed by views or rely on them as an essence. The etymology is: 'yāyati' means he goes, thus 'yāyako', a goer. By the instrumental case, 'diṭṭhiyā yāyati' means one who goes by views, a 'diṭṭhiyāyako'. In the sense of connection, by the genitive case, 'diṭṭhiyā yāti' also means one who goes by views. 'Na mutiyā sa mānameti' means he does not come to conceit even through what is cognized, which is divided into odors, tastes, and so on. 'Na hi tammayo so' means he is not identified with that, by way of craving and views, nor is he devoted to that; this one is not like that. 'Na kammunā nopi sutena neyyo' means he is not to be led by action, such as meritorious formations, or by learning, such as purity through learning. 'Anūpanīto sa nivesanesūti' means, having abandoned both kinds of attachment, he is not led into any abodes of craving and views.

Mutarūpena vāti ettha mutarūpaṃ nāma gandharasaphoṭṭhabbāni. Mānaṃ netīti asmimānaṃ na eti. Na upetīti samīpaṃ na eti. Na upagacchatīti upagantvā na tiṭṭhati. Tammayoti tappakato.

'Mutarūpena vā'—here 'mutarūpa' refers to odors, tastes, and tangible objects. 'Mānaṃ neti' means he does not come to the conceit 'I am'. 'Na upeti' means he does not come near. 'Na upagacchati' means having approached, he does not stay. 'Tammayo' means made of that.

82. Tassa ca evaṃvidhassa “saññāvirattassā”ti gāthā. Tattha saññāvirattassāti nekkhammasaññāpubbaṅgamāya bhāvanāya pahīnakāmādisaññassa. Iminā padena ubhatobhāgavimutto samathayāniko adhippeto. Paññāvimuttassāti vipassanāpubbaṅgamāya bhāvanāya sabbakilesehi vimuttassa. Iminā sukkhavipassako adhippeto. Saññañca diṭṭhiñca ye aggahesuṃ, te ghaṭṭamānā vicaranti loketi ye pana kāmasaññādikaṃ saññaṃ aggahesuṃ, te visesato gahaṭṭhā kāmādhikaraṇaṃ, ye ca diṭṭhiṃ aggahesuṃ, te visesato pabbajitā dhammādhikaraṇaṃ aññamaññaṃ ghaṭṭentā vicarantīti.

82. For one of such a nature, there is the verse beginning 'saññāvirattassa'. Herein, 'saññāvirattassa' refers to one who has abandoned perceptions of sensuality and so on, through development preceded by the perception of renunciation. By this phrase, one liberated in both ways, who travels by serenity, is intended. 'Paññāvimuttassa' refers to one liberated from all defilements through development preceded by insight. By this, the dry-insight meditator is intended. 'Saññañca diṭṭhiñca ye aggahesuṃ, te ghaṭṭamānā vicaranti loke' means those who have grasped perception and views wander clashing in the world. Specifically, those who grasp perception, such as sensual perception—especially householders, in disputes about sensuality—and those who grasp views—especially renunciants, in disputes about doctrine—wander about clashing with one another.

Yo samathapubbaṅgamaṃ ariyamaggaṃ bhāvetīti yo puggalo samathapubbaṅgamaṃ purecārikaṃ katvā sahavipassanaṃ ariyamaggaṃ bhāveti, paṭhamaṃ samādhiṃ uppādetvā pacchā sahavipassanaṃ ariyamaggaṃ uppādetīti attho. Tassa āditoti tassa puggalassa paṭhamajjhānādito. Upādāyāti paṭicca āgamma. Ganthā vikkhambhītā hontīti ganthā dūrīkatā bhavanti. Arahatte patteti arahattaphalaṃ patte. Arahatoti arahattaphale ṭhitassa. Ganthā ca mohā cātiādayo sabbe kilesā pahīnā honti.

'One who develops the noble path preceded by serenity' means a person who develops the noble path together with insight, having made serenity the forerunner; the meaning is that, having first generated concentration, he then generates the noble path together with insight. 'Tassa ādito' means from the beginning for that person, from the first jhāna onwards. 'Upādāya' means depending on, relying on. 'Ganthā vikkhambhītā honti' means the ties are suppressed, that is, the ties are kept at a distance. 'Arahatte patte' means when he has attained the fruit of arahantship. 'Arahato' means for one established in the fruit of arahantship. 'Ganthā ca mohā ca', the ties and delusions, etc.—all defilements are abandoned.

Yo vipassanāpubbaṅgamaṃ ariyamaggaṃ bhāvetīti yo puggalo vipassanaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ purecārikaṃ katvā ariyamaggaṃ bhāveti, paṭhamaṃ vipassanaṃ uppādetvā pacchā ariyamaggasampayuttaṃ samādhiṃ bhāvetīti attho. Tassa ādito upādāyāti tassa puggalassa vipassanato paṭṭhāya vipassanaṃ [P 2.0314] paṭicca. Mohā vikkhambhitā hontīti ettha vikkhambhitāti dūraṃ pāpitā saññāvasena. Ghaṭṭentīti ye kāmasaññādiṃ gaṇhanti, te saññāvasena pīḷenti. Saṅghaṭṭentīti tato tato pīḷenti[V 0.0250]. Idāni ghaṭṭente dassetuṃ “rājānopi [M 0.0273] rājūhi vivadantī”tiādinā nayena vitthāro vutto. Aññamaññaṃ pāṇīhipi upakkamantīti ettha aññamaññaṃ hatthehi paharanti. Leḍḍūhīti kapālakhaṇḍehi. Daṇḍehīti aḍḍhadaṇḍakehi. Satthehīti ubhatodhārehi satthehi.

'One who develops the noble path preceded by insight' means a person who develops the noble path, having made insight the forerunner; the meaning is that, having first generated insight, he then cultivates concentration associated with the noble path. 'Tassa ādito upādāya' means for that person, starting from insight, relying on insight. 'Mohā vikkhambhitā honti'—here, 'vikkhambhitā' means pushed far away by means of perception. 'Ghaṭṭenti' means they strike; that is, those who grasp sensual perceptions, etc., torment by means of perception. 'Saṅghaṭṭenti' means they clash; that is, they torment from here and there. Now, to illustrate those who strike, the detailed explanation is given in the manner of 'kings quarrel with kings,' etc. 'Aññamaññaṃ pāṇīhipi upakkamanti' means they attack each other with hands, that is, they strike each other with their hands. 'Leḍḍūhi' means with clods, that is, with shards of pottery. 'Daṇḍehi' means with sticks, that is, with clubs. 'Satthehi' means with weapons, that is, with double-edged weapons.

Abhisaṅkhārānaṃ appahīnattāti puññādiabhisaṅkhārānaṃ appahīnabhāvena. Gatiyā ghaṭṭentīti gantabbāya patiṭṭhābhūtāya gatiyā pīḷenti ghaṭṭanaṃ āpajjanti. Nirayādīsupi eseva nayo. Sesamettha vuttanayattā uttānameva.

'Abhisaṅkhārānaṃ appahīnattā' means due to the non-abandonment of volitional formations such as the meritorious. 'Gatiyā ghaṭṭenti' means they are struck by their destiny; that is, they are oppressed and encounter affliction through the destiny that is their foundation and destination. The same principle applies to hell and other realms. The remainder here is self-explanatory, as the method has been stated.

Saddhammappajjotikāya mahāniddesaṭṭhakathāya

In the Saddhammappajjotikā, the Commentary on the Mahāniddesa.

Māgaṇḍiyasuttaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta Exposition is completed.

10. Purābhedasuttaniddesavaṇṇanā

10. The Explanation of the Purābheda Sutta Exposition

83. Dasame [V 0.0251][P 2.0315] purābhedasuttaniddese kathaṃdassīti imassa suttassa ito paresañca pañcannaṃ kalahavivādacūḷabyūhamahābyūhatuvaṭakaattadaṇḍasuttānaṃ sammāparibbājanīyasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ (su. ni. aṭṭha. 2.362 ādayo) vuttanayeneva sāmaññato uppatti veditabbā. Visesato pana yatheva tasmiṃ mahāsamaye rāgacaritadevatānaṃ sappāyavasena dhammaṃ desetuṃ nimmitabuddhena attānaṃ pucchāpetvā sammāparibbājanīyasuttanta- (su. ni. 361 ādayo) mabhāsi, evaṃ tasmiṃyeva mahāsamaye “kiṃ nu kho purā sarīrabhedā kattabba”nti uppannacittānaṃ devatānaṃ cittaṃ ñatvā tāsaṃ anuggahatthaṃ aḍḍhateḷasabhikkhusataparivāraṃ nimmitabuddhaṃ ākāsena ānetvā tena attānaṃ pucchāpetvā imaṃ suttamabhāsi.

83. In the explanation of the Purābheda Sutta, the tenth, concerning the phrase 'kathaṃdassī' in this sutta, and also concerning the origin of the following five suttas—Kalahavivāda, Cūḷabyūha, Mahābyūha, Tuvaṭaka, and Attadaṇḍa—the origin should be understood in a general way according to the method described in the commentary on the Sammāparibbājanīya Sutta (Sutta Nipāta Aṭṭhakathā 2.362, etc.). Specifically, just as in that great assembly, to teach the Dhamma in a way suitable to deities with a lustful disposition, the Blessed One, having had himself questioned by a created Buddha, expounded the Sammāparibbājanīya Sutta (Sutta Nipāta 361, etc.); so too in that very same great assembly, knowing the minds of deities in whom the thought had arisen, 'What should be done before the breaking up of the body?', for their benefit, he brought a created Buddha attended by twelve hundred and fifty monks through the sky, and having had himself questioned by that one, he expounded this sutta.

Kathaṃ? Buddhā nāma mahantā ete sattavisesā, yaṃ sadevakassa lokassa diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ mutaṃ viññātaṃ pattaṃ pariyesitaṃ anuvicaritaṃ manasā na kiñci katthaci nīlādivasena vibhattarūpārammaṇesu vibhattarūpārammaṇaṃ vā, bherisaddādivasena vibhattasaddārammaṇādīsu saddādiārammaṇaṃ vā atthi, yaṃ etesaṃ ñāṇamukhe āpāthaṃ nāgacchati. Yathāha – “yaṃ, bhikkhave, sadevakassa lokassa…pe… sadevamanussāya diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ mutaṃ viññātaṃ pattaṃ pariyesitaṃ anuvicaritaṃ [M 0.0274] manasā, tamahaṃ jānāmi tamahaṃ abbhaññāsi”nti (a. ni. 4.24). Evaṃ sabbattha appaṭihatañāṇo bhagavā sabbāpi tā devatā bhabbābhabbavasena dve koṭṭhāse akāsi. “Kammāvaraṇena vā samannāgatā”tiādinā (pu. pa. 12) hi nayena vuttā sattā abhabbā nāma. Te ekavihāre vasantepi buddhā na olokenti. Viparītā pana bhabbā nāma. Te dūre vasantepi gantvā saṅgaṇhanti. Tasmiṃ devatāsannipāte ye abhabbā, te [P 2.0316] pahāya bhabbe pariggahesi. Pariggahetvā “ettakā ettha rāgacaritā, ettakā dosādicaritā”ti cariyavasena cha koṭṭhāse akāsi. Atha nesaṃ sappāyadhammadesanaṃ upadhārento “rāgacaritānaṃ devānaṃ sammāparibbājanīyasuttaṃ (su. ni. 361 ādayo) kathessāmi, dosacaritānaṃ kalahavivādasuttaṃ [V 0.0252] (su. ni. 868 ādayo), mohacaritānaṃ mahābyūhasuttaṃ (su. ni. 901 ādayo), vitakkacaritānaṃ cūḷabyūhasuttaṃ (su. ni. 884 ādayo), saddhācaritānaṃ tuvaṭakasuttaṃ (su. ni. 921 ādayo), buddhicaritānaṃ purābhedasuttaṃ (su. ni. 854 ādayo) kathessāmī”ti desanaṃ vavatthāpetvā puna taṃ parisaṃ manasākāsi “attajjhāsayena nu kho jāneyya, parajjhāsayena, aṭṭhuppattikena, pucchāvasenā”ti. Tato “pucchāvasena jāneyyā”ti ñatvā “atthi nu kho koci devatānaṃ ajjhāsayaṃ gahetvā cariyavasena pañhaṃ pucchituṃ samattho”ti “tesu pañcasatesu bhikkhūsu ekopi na sakkotī”ti addasa. Tato asītimahāsāvake, dve aggasāvake ca samannāharitvā “tepi na sakkontī”ti disvā cintesi – “sace paccekabuddho bhaveyya, sakkuṇeyya nu kho”ti. “Sopi na sakkuṇeyyo”ti ñatvā “sakkasuyāmādīsu koci sakkuṇeyyā”ti samannāhari. Sace hi tesu koci sakkuṇeyya, taṃ pucchāpetvā attanā vissajjeyya. Na pana tesupi koci sakkoti. Athassa etadahosi – “mādiso buddhoyeva sakkuṇeyya, atthi pana katthaci añño buddho”ti anantāsu lokadhātūsu anantañāṇaṃ pattharitvā lokaṃ olokento na aññaṃ buddhaṃ addasa. Anacchariyañcetaṃ, idāni attanā samaṃ na passeyya, yo jātadivasepi brahmajālavaṇṇanāyaṃ (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.7) vuttanayena attanā samaṃ apassanto “aggohamasmi lokassā”ti (dī. ni. 2.31) appaṭivattiyaṃ sīhanādaṃ nadi. Evaṃ aññaṃ attanā samaṃ apassitvā cintesi “sace [M 0.0275] ahaṃ pucchitvā ahameva vissajjeyyaṃ, evaṃ tā devatā na sakkhissanti paṭivijjhituṃ. Aññasmiṃ pana buddheyeva pucchante mayi ca vissajjante accherakaṃ bhavissati, sakkhissanti ca devatā paṭivijjhituṃ, tasmā nimmitabuddhaṃ māpessāmī”ti abhiññāpādakaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya “pattacīvaraggahaṇaṃ ālokitaṃ vilokitaṃ samiñjitaṃ pasāritañca mama sadisaṃyeva hotū”ti kāmāvacaracittehi parikammaṃ katvā [P 2.0317] “pācīnayugandharaparikkhepato ullaṅghayamānaṃ candamaṇḍalaṃ bhinditvā nikkhamanto viya āgacchatū”ti rūpāvacaracittena adhiṭṭhāsi. Devasaṅgho taṃ disvā “aññopi nu kho bho, cando uggato”ti āha. Atha candaṃ ohāya āsannatare jāte “na cando, sūriyo uggato”ti. Puna āsannatare jāte “na sūriyo, devavimānaṃ eta”nti. Puna āsannatare jāte “na devavimānaṃ, devaputto eso”ti. Puna āsannatare jāte “na devaputto, mahābrahmā eso”ti. Puna āsannatare jāte “na mahābrahmā, aparopi bho buddho āgato”ti āha.

How? The Buddhas are indeed great, exceptional beings, for whom nothing in the entire world with its gods—whether seen, heard, sensed, known, attained, sought after, or mentally explored—escapes their knowledge. Whether it is forms distinguished by colors like blue, etc., or sounds distinguished by sounds like drumbeats, etc., there is nothing among sense objects that fails to enter the range of their wisdom. As it is said: 'Whatever, monks, in this world with its gods... and humans... has been seen, heard, sensed, known, attained, sought after, or mentally explored—all that I know, all that I have fully understood' (A.N. 4.24). Thus, the Blessed One, with unobstructed knowledge in all respects, divided all those deities into two categories based on their capability and incapability. Those hindered by karmic obstructions, as mentioned in the Puggalapaññatti (Pu.Pa. 12), are called incapable. Even if they dwell in the same monastery, the Buddhas do not regard them. On the other hand, those who are capable, even if they live far away, are embraced. At that gathering of deities, he set aside the incapable ones and took up the capable ones. Having taken them up, he further divided them into six categories based on their temperaments: 'So many here are of lustful temperament, so many of hateful temperament,' and so on. Then, considering the suitable teachings for them, he resolved: 'For the deities of lustful temperament, I will teach the Sammāparibbājanīya Sutta (Sutta Nipāta 361, etc.); for those of hateful temperament, the Kalahavivāda Sutta (Sutta Nipāta 868, etc.); for those of deluded temperament, the Mahābyūha Sutta (Sutta Nipāta 901, etc.); for those of speculative temperament, the Cūḷabyūha Sutta (Sutta Nipāta 884, etc.); for those of faithful temperament, the Tuvaṭaka Sutta (Sutta Nipāta 921, etc.); and for those of intellectual temperament, the Purābheda Sutta (Sutta Nipāta 854, etc.).' Having determined the teaching, he again reflected on the assembly: 'Should I know their inclinations through my own insight, through others' inclinations, through the circumstances, or through questioning?' Realizing it should be through questioning, he considered, 'Is there anyone who is able to discern the deities' inclinations and ask questions accordingly?' He saw that not even one among the five hundred monks was capable. Then, considering the eighty great disciples and the two chief disciples, he saw that even they were incapable. He pondered, 'If there were a Paccekabuddha, would he be able to do it?' Knowing that even a Paccekabuddha could not, he considered whether any among Sakka, Suyāma, and other deities could. If any could, he would have them ask the questions and then answer himself. But none among them could either. Then it occurred to him: 'Only a Buddha like myself can do it. But is there another Buddha somewhere?' Extending his infinite knowledge across the boundless world-systems, he saw no other Buddha. This was no surprise, for even at birth, as described in the Brahmajāla Sutta Commentary (Dī.Nī.Aṭṭha. 1.7), he saw no equal to himself and declared, 'I am the highest in the world' (Dī.Nī. 2.31), with a lion’s roar that could not be challenged. Thus, seeing no equal to himself, he thought: 'If I were to ask and answer myself, the deities would not be able to comprehend it. But if another Buddha were to ask and I were to answer, it would be astonishing, and the deities would be able to understand. Therefore, I will create a Buddha by my power.' Entering the jhāna that is the basis for higher knowledge, he emerged and resolved: 'Let the taking up of the robe and bowl, the looking around, the bending and stretching, be just like mine.' After preparing with sense-sphere consciousnesses, he willed with fine-material-sphere consciousness: 'Let him come forth as if breaking through the moon’s disk from beyond the eastern Yugandhara mountain range.' The assembly of deities, seeing this, exclaimed, 'Has another moon risen, friends?' As it drew nearer, they said, 'No, it is the sun.' Closer still, they said, 'No, it is a celestial mansion.' Even closer, they said, 'No, it is a deva-son.' Then, as it came nearer, they said, 'No, it is Mahābrahmā.' Finally, when it was very close, they declared, 'No, friends, another Buddha has arrived!'

Tattha puthujjanadevatā cintayiṃsu – “ekabuddhassa tāva ayaṃ devatāsannipāto. Dvinnaṃ kīvamahanto bhavissatī”ti. Ariyadevatā cintayiṃsu – “ekissā lokadhātuyā dve buddhā nāma [V 0.0253] natthi, addhā bhagavā attanā sadisaṃ aññaṃ ekaṃ buddhaṃ nimminī”ti. Athassa devasaṅghassa passantasseva nimmitabuddho āgantvā dasabalaṃ avanditvāva sammukhaṭṭhāne samasamaṃ katvā māpite āsane nisīdi. Bhagavato bāttiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇāni, nimmitassāpi, bhagavato sarīrā chabbaṇṇarasmiyo nikkhamanti, nimmitassāpi, bhagavato sarīrarasmiyo nimmitasarīre paṭihaññanti, nimmitassa rasmiyo bhagavato kāye paṭihaññanti. Tā dvinnampi buddhānaṃ sarīrato uggamma bhavaggaṃ āhacca tato tato paṭinivattitvā devatānaṃ matthakamatthakapariyantena otaritvā cakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ patiṭṭhahiṃsu. Sakalacakkavāḷagabbhaṃ suvaṇṇamayavaṅkagopānasivinaddhamiva cetiyagharaṃ virocittha. Dasasahassacakkavāḷadevatā ekacakkavāḷe rāsibhūtā dvinnaṃ buddhānaṃ rasmiabbhantaraṃ pavisitvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Nimmito nisīdantoyeva “kathaṃdassī kathaṃsīlo, upasantoti vuccatī”tiādinā nayena adhipaññādikaṃ pucchanto gāthamāha.

There, the ordinary devas thought: "This assembly of devas is for one Buddha. How much greater would it be for two?" The noble devas thought: "There are not two Buddhas in one world-system. Surely the Blessed One has created another Buddha like himself." Then, as that assembly of devas watched, the emanation Buddha arrived and, without paying homage to the Ten-Powered One, sat down on a seat made equal and placed directly in front. The thirty-two marks of a Great Man were present on the Blessed One, and also on the emanation Buddha. Six-colored rays emanated from the Blessed One's body, and also from the emanation Buddha's. The rays from the Blessed One's body impinged upon the emanation Buddha's body, and the rays from the emanation Buddha's body impinged upon the Blessed One's body. Those rays, issuing from the bodies of both Buddhas, struck the summit of existence and, returning from there, descended upon the devas, reaching the very ends of their heads, and stood fixed at the rim of the world-system. The interior of the entire world-system shone like a shrine-chamber interwoven with curved golden rafters. Devas from ten thousand world-systems, massed together in one world-system, entered the radiance of the two Buddhas and stood there. As the emanation Buddha sat down, he spoke a verse, asking a question concerning higher wisdom and so forth, in the manner beginning with: 'How is one a seer? How is one virtuous? How is one called peaceful?'

Tattha pucchāya tāva so nimmito kathaṃdassīti adhipaññaṃ, kathaṃsīloti adhisīlaṃ, upasantoti adhicittaṃ pucchati. Sesaṃ pākaṭameva.

There, in the question, that emanation Buddha first asks about higher wisdom with 'How is one a seer?', about higher virtue with 'How is one virtuous?', and about higher mind with 'How is one peaceful?'. The rest is evident.

Nimmitabuddhādivibhāvanatthaṃ [P 2.0318][M 0.0276] peṭake –

For the purpose of elucidating the emanation Buddha and so forth, it is stated in the Peṭaka:

“Upeti dhammaṃ paripucchamāno, kusalaṃ atthupasañhitaṃ;

Na jīvati na nibbuto na mato, taṃ puggalaṃ katamaṃ vadanti buddhā. (pari. 479);

“One who approaches the Dhamma, inquiring about the wholesome, connected with the goal; he neither lives nor is extinguished nor dead—what person do the Buddhas declare him to be?”

“Saṃsārakhīṇo na ca vantarāgo, na cāpi sekkho na ca diṭṭhadhammo;

Akhīṇāsavo antimadehadhārī, taṃ puggalaṃ katamaṃ vadanti buddhā.

“One whose cycle of rebirth is exhausted, yet has not abandoned lust; not a learner, nor one who has seen the Dhamma; whose taints are unexhausted, bearing the final body—what person do the Buddhas declare him to be?”

“Na dukkhasaccena samaṅgibhūto, na maggasaccena kuto nirodho;

Samudayasaccato suvidūravidūro, taṃ puggalaṃ katamaṃ vadanti buddhā.

“Not endowed with the truth of suffering, nor with the truth of the path—whence then cessation? Very, very far from the truth of origin—what person do the Buddhas declare him to be?”

“Ahetuko nopi ca rūpanissito, apaccayo nopi ca so asaṅkhato;

Asaṅkhatārammaṇo nopi ca rūpī, taṃ puggalaṃ katamaṃ vadanti buddhā”ti. –

“Without cause, nor dependent on form; without condition, nor unconditioned; not having the unconditioned as object, nor having form—what person do the Buddhas declare him to be?”

Vuttaṃ.

Thus it is stated.

Tattha [V 0.0254] paṭhamagāthā nimmitabuddhaṃ sandhāya, dutiyagāthā pacchimabhavikabodhisattaṃ sandhāya, tatiyagāthā arahattaphalaṭṭhaṃ sandhāya, catutthagāthā arūpe nibbānapaccavekkhaṇamanodvārapurecārikacittasamaṅgiṃ sandhāya vuttāti ñātabbā. Kīdisena dassanenāti kīdisavasena dassanena. Kiṃsaṇṭhitenāti kiṃsarikkhena. Kiṃpakārenāti kiṃvidhena. Kiṃpaṭibhāgenāti kiṃākārena.

Here, it should be understood that the first verse is stated with reference to the emanation Buddha, the second verse with reference to the Bodhisatta in his final existence, the third verse with reference to one established in the fruit of arahantship, and the fourth verse with reference to one endowed with the mind that precedes the mental-door reflection on formless Nibbāna. ‘By what kind of seeing?’ means: ‘By what manner of seeing?’ ‘Of what form?’ means: ‘Of what resemblance?’ ‘In what way?’ means: ‘By what method?’ ‘Of what counterpart?’ means: ‘Of what appearance?’

Yaṃ pucchāmīti yaṃ puggalaṃ pucchāmi, taṃ mayhaṃ viyākarohi. Yācāmīti āyācāmi. Ajjhesāmīti āṇāpemi. Pasādemīti tava santāne somanassaṃ uppādemi. Brūhīti niddesassa uddesapadaṃ. Ācikkhāti desetabbānaṃ “imāni nāmānī”ti nāmavasena kathehi. Desehīti dassehi[P 2.0319]. Paññapehīti jānāpehi. Ñāṇamukhavasena hi appanaṃ ṭhapento “paññapehī”ti [M 0.0277] vuccati. Paṭṭhapehīti paññāpehi, pavattāpehīti attho. Ñāṇamukhe ṭhapehīti vā. Vivarāti vivaṭaṃ karohi, vivaritvā dassehīti attho. Vibhajāti vibhāgakiriyāya vibhāvento dassehīti attho. Uttānīkarohīti pākaṭabhāvaṃ karohi.

‘Whom I ask’ means: ‘The person whom I ask, explain that to me.’ ‘I entreat’ means: ‘I beg.’ ‘I request’ means: ‘I command.’ ‘I please’ means: ‘I generate joy in your continuum.’ ‘Speak’ (brūhi) is the word indicating the topic of exposition. ‘Explain’ (ācikkha) means: ‘State by name the things to be taught, saying, “These are the names.”’ ‘Teach’ (desehi) means: ‘Show.’ ‘Make known’ (paññapehi) means: ‘Inform.’ For indeed, when establishing an application by way of the doorway of knowledge, it is said ‘make known.’ ‘Establish’ (paṭṭhapehi) means: ‘Make known’; the meaning is: ‘Set in motion.’ Or: ‘Establish in the doorway of knowledge.’ ‘Open’ (vivara) means: ‘Make open’; the meaning is: ‘Show after opening.’ ‘Analyze’ (vibhajā) means: ‘Show by way of analysis,’ that is, to show by making distinctions. ‘Make plain’ (uttānīkarohi) means: ‘Make apparent.’

Atha vā ācikkhāti desanādīnaṃ channaṃ padānaṃ mūlapadaṃ. Desanādīni cha padāni etassa atthassa vivaraṇatthaṃ vuttāni. Tattha desehīti ugghaṭitaññūnaṃ vasena saṅkhepato paṭhamaṃ uddesavasena desehi. Ugghaṭitaññū hi saṅkhepena vuttaṃ paṭhamaṃ vuttañca paṭivijjhanti. Paññapehīti vipañcitaññūnaṃ vasena tesaṃ cittatosanena buddhinisānena ca paṭhamaṃ saṃkhittassa vitthārato niddesavaseneva paññapehi. Paṭṭhapehīti tesaṃyeva niddiṭṭhassa niddesassa paṭiniddesavasena vitthāritavasena ṭhapeti paṭṭhapehi. Vivarāti niddiṭṭhassapi punappunaṃ vacanena vivarāhi. Vibhajāti punappunaṃ vuttassāpi vibhāgakaraṇena vibhajāhi. Uttānīkarohīti vivaṭassa vitthārataravacanena vibhattassa ca nidassanavacanena uttāniṃ karohi. Ayaṃ desanā neyyānampi paṭivedhāya hotīti.

Or alternatively, ‘explain’ (ācikkha) is the root word of the six terms beginning with ‘teaching’. The six terms beginning with ‘teaching’ are stated for the purpose of clarifying this meaning. Herein, ‘teach’ (desehi) means to teach briefly at first, by way of an initial statement, for those of quick understanding. For those of quick understanding penetrate what is stated briefly and what is stated first. ‘Make known’ (paññapehi) means to make known in detail, by way of exposition, for those of extensive understanding, to satisfy their minds and sharpen their intellect, what was first stated briefly. ‘Establish’ (paṭṭhapehi) means to establish in detail, by way of counter-exposition, what has already been expounded for them. ‘Open’ (vivara) means to open, even what has been expounded, by repeated utterance. ‘Analyze’ (vibhajā) means to analyze, by way of division, even what has been stated repeatedly. ‘Make plain’ (uttānīkarohi) means to make plain by more detailed utterance of what has been opened, and by illustrative statements of what has been analyzed. This teaching is also for the penetration of those who are to be guided.

84.
