Vissajjane pana bhagavā sarūpena adhipaññādīni avissajjetvāva adhipaññādippabhāvena yesaṃ kilesānaṃ upasamā “upasanto”ti vuccati, nānādevatānaṃ āsayānulomena tesaṃ upasamameva dīpento “vītataṇho”tiādikā gāthāyo abhāsi. Tattha ādito aṭṭhannaṃ gāthānaṃ “taṃ brūmi upasanto”ti imāya gāthāya sambandho veditabbo, tato parāsaṃ “sa ve santoti vuccatī”ti iminā sabbapacchimena padena.

84. In the response, however, the Blessed One, without explaining higher wisdom and so forth in their own nature, pointed out only the pacification of those defilements—a pacification which comes about by the power of higher wisdom and so forth, and on account of which one is called ‘peaceful’—in accordance with the inclinations of various devas, speaking the verses beginning with ‘one without craving’. Here, the connection of the first eight verses should be understood with the verse ‘Him I call peaceful,’ while the subsequent verses are connected with the very last phrase, ‘He indeed is called peaceful.’

Anupadavaṇṇanānayo – vītataṇho purābhedāti yo sarīrabhedā pubbameva pahīnataṇho. Pubbamantamanissitoti [V 0.0255] atītaddhādibhedaṃ pubbaantaṃ anissito. Vemajjhe nupasaṅkheyyoti paccuppannepi addhani “ratto”tiādinā nayena na upasaṅkhātabbo[P 2.0320]. Tassa natthi purakkhatanti tassa arahato dvinnaṃ purekkhārānaṃ abhāvā anāgate addhani purakkhatamapi natthi, taṃ brūmi upasantoti evamettha yojanā veditabbā. Esa nayo sabbattha.

The method of word-by-word explanation: ‘One without craving before the breaking’ means one who has abandoned craving even before the breaking of the body. ‘Not dependent on the former end’ means one who is not dependent on the former end, which is divided into past time and so forth. ‘Not to be reckoned in the middle’ means that even in the present time, one should not be reckoned in the manner of ‘attached’ and so forth. ‘For him there is no anticipation’ means that for that Arahant, due to the absence of the two kinds of placing before, there is no anticipation even in the future time. Thus, the connection with ‘Him I call peaceful’ should be understood here. This method applies everywhere.

Purā kāyassa bhedāti karajakāyassa bhedato pubbeyeva. Attabhāvassāti sakalattabhāvassa. Kaḷevarassa nikkhepāti kaḷevarassa nikkhepato [M 0.0278] sarīrassa ṭhapanato. Jīvitindriyassa upacchedāti duvidhassa jīvitindriyassa upacchedato pubbameva.

‘Before the breaking of the body’ means even before the breaking of the physical body. ‘Of personal existence’ means of the entire personal existence. ‘The laying down of the corpse’ means the laying down of the corpse, the depositing of the body. ‘The cessation of the life faculty’ means even before the cessation of the twofold life faculty.

Pubbanto vuccati atīto addhāti pubbasaṅkhāto anto koṭṭhāso “atīto addhāti, atikkanto kālo”ti kathīyati. Atītaṃ addhānaṃ ārabbhāti atītakālaṃ paṭicca taṇhā pahīnā.

‘The former end is called the past time’ means the former portion, the end, is spoken of as ‘past time’ or ‘elapsed time’. ‘With reference to past time’ means craving has been abandoned in dependence on past time.

Aparampi bhaddekarattapariyāyaṃ (ma. ni. 3.272 ādayo) dassento “atha vā”tiādimāha. Tattha evaṃrūpo ahosinti kāḷopi samāno indanīlamaṇivaṇṇo ahosinti evaṃ manuññarūpavaseneva evaṃrūpo ahosiṃ. Kusalasukhasomanassavedanāvaseneva evaṃvedano. Taṃ sampayuttānaṃyeva saññādīnaṃ vasena evaṃsañño. Evaṃsaṅkhāro. Evaṃviññāṇo ahosiṃ atītamaddhānanti tattha nandiṃ na samannānetīti tesu rūpādīsu taṇhaṃ vā taṇhāsampayuttadiṭṭhiṃ vā nānupavattayati. Aparena pariyāyena mahākaccānabhaddekarattapariyāyaṃ dassento “atha vā iti me cakkhu ahosī”tiādimāha. Tattha cakkhūti cakkhupasādo. Rūpāti catusamuṭṭhānikarūpā. Iminā nayena sesāyatanānipi veditabbāni. Viññāṇanti nissayaviññāṇaṃ. Na tadabhinandatīti taṃ cakkhuñceva rūpañca taṇhādiṭṭhivasena nābhinandati. Iti me mano ahosi iti dhammāti ettha pana manoti bhavaṅgacittaṃ. Dhammāti tebhūmakadhammārammaṇaṃ. Hasitalapitakīḷitānīti dantavidaṃsakahasitañca vācālapitañca kāyakīḷādikīḷitañcāti hasitalapitakīḷitāni. Na tadassādetīti tāni hasitādīni nābhinandati. Na taṃ nikāmetīti kantaṃ na karoti. Na ca tena vittiṃ āpajjatīti tena ca tuṭṭhiṃ na pāpuṇāti.

Furthermore, explaining the Bhaddekaratta exposition (beginning with Majjhima Nikāya 3.272), he says, ‘Or alternatively,’ and so forth. Here, ‘Of such form I was’ (evaṃrūpo ahosiṃ) means: ‘Even though dark, I was of the color of an indigo jewel’—thus, ‘I was of such form’ precisely by way of such pleasing form. ‘Of such feeling’ (evaṃvedano) means: ‘Of such feeling’ precisely by way of wholesome pleasure and joy. ‘Of such perception’ (evaṃsañño) is by way of the perceptions and so forth associated with that. ‘Of such formations’ (evaṃsaṅkhāro). ‘Of such consciousness I was in the past’ (evaṃviññāṇo ahosiṃ atītamaddhānaṃ)—here, ‘he does not cultivate delight’ (nandiṃ na samannāneti) means he does not incite craving or craving-associated views regarding those forms and so forth. In another exposition, presenting the Mahākaccāna Bhaddekaratta exposition, he says, ‘Or alternatively, thus my eye was,’ and so forth. Here, ‘eye’ (cakkhu) means the eye-sensitivity. ‘Forms’ (rūpā) refers to forms originating from the four great elements. The remaining sense bases should be understood in this same way. ‘Consciousness’ (viññāṇaṃ) means dependent consciousness. ‘He does not delight in it’ (na tadabhinandati) means he does not delight in that eye and those forms by way of craving and wrong view. ‘Thus my mind was, thus phenomena’ (iti me mano ahosi iti dhammā)—here, ‘mind’ (mano) means the life-continuum consciousness. ‘Phenomena’ (dhammā) refers to phenomena as objects from the three realms. ‘Laughter, chatter, and play’ (hasitalapitakīḷitāni) means laughter showing teeth, verbal chatter, and bodily play and so forth. ‘He does not relish it’ (na tadassādeti) means he does not delight in that laughter and so forth. ‘He does not desire it’ (na taṃ nikāmeti) means he does not make it attractive. ‘Nor does he find satisfaction in it’ (na ca tena vittiṃ āpajjati) means he does not attain satisfaction through it.

Taṃ [P 2.0321] taṃ paccayaṃ paṭicca uppannoti paccuppanno. Rattoti nupasaṅkheyyoti rāgena rattoti gaṇanaṃ na upanetabbo. Uparipi eseva nayo. Evarūpo siyantiādīsu paṇītamanuññarūpādivaseneva [V 0.0256] taṇhādiṭṭhipavattanasaṅkhātā nandī samannānayanā veditabbā. Na paṇidahatīti patthanāvasena na ṭhapeti. Appaṇidhānapaccayāti na patthanāṭhapanakāraṇena.

Depending on that condition, it arises; thus it is presently arisen. 'Infatuated'—one should not reckon it thus; it means it should not be counted as 'infatuated by lust.' The same principle applies above. In such cases as 'might be of such a kind,' the delight consisting of the arising of craving and wrong views, due to refined, agreeable forms, etc., should be understood as the cultivation of delight. 'He does not fix his mind'—he does not establish through aspiration. 'Due to the condition of non-fixation'—not by the cause of establishing aspiration.

85. Asantāsīti tena tena alābhato asantasanto. Avikatthīti sīlādīhi avikatthanasīlo. Akukkucoti hatthakukkuccādivirahito. Mantabhāṇīti mantāya pariggahetvā vācaṃ bhāsitā. Anuddhatoti [M 0.0279] uddhaccavirahito. Sa ve vācāyatoti so vācāya yato saṃyato catudosavirahitaṃ vācaṃ bhāsitā hoti.

85. "Not trembling" means not trembling, not being agitated by not obtaining this or that. "Not boasting" means not having a nature of boasting about virtues like morality, etc. "Free from remorse" means being devoid of remorse, such as remorse concerning the hands, etc. "Thoughtful in speech" means speaking words after having grasped them with wisdom. "Not restless" means being free from restlessness. "Truly restrained in speech" means he is restrained in speech and speaks words free from the four faults.

Akkodhanoti yañhi kho vuttanti “na kodhano akodhano kodhavirahito”ti yaṃ kathitaṃ, taṃ paṭhamaṃ tāva kodhaṃ kathetukāmo “apica kodho tāva vattabbo”ti āha. Kodho tāva vattabboti paṭhamaṃ kodho kathetabbo. Dasahākārehi kodho jāyatīti dasahi kāraṇehi kodho uppajjati. Anatthaṃ me acarīti avaḍḍhiṃ me akāsi, iminā upāyena sabbapadesu attho veditabbo. Aṭṭhāne vā pana kodho jāyatīti akāraṇe kodho uppajjati. Ekacco hi “devo ativassatī”ti kuppati, “na vassatī”ti kuppati, “sūriyo tappatī”ti kuppati, “na tappatī”ti kuppati, vāte vāyantepi kuppati, avāyantepi kuppati, sammajjituṃ asakkonto bodhipaṇṇānaṃ kuppati, cīvaraṃ pārupituṃ asakkonto vātassa kuppati, upakkhalitvā khāṇukassa kuppati. Idaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “aṭṭhāne vā pana kodho jāyatī”ti. Tattha heṭṭhā navasu ṭhānesu satte ārabbha uppannattā kammapathabhedo hoti.

"Non-anger" means what is said: "not angry, angerless, devoid of anger." First, wishing to speak about anger, he said, "Moreover, anger should first be discussed." "Anger should first be discussed" means anger should be spoken about first. Anger arises due to ten causes—anger arises due to ten reasons. "He has done me harm" means "he has caused me loss." In this way, the meaning should be understood in all instances. "Or anger arises without reason" means anger arises without cause. For some people, they become angry thinking, "It rains too much," or "It does not rain," or "The sun is too hot," or "The sun is not hot." They get angry when the wind blows or when it does not blow. Unable to sweep, they get angry at the Bodhi leaves. Unable to put on their robe, they get angry at the wind. Stumbling, they get angry at the stump. This is what is meant by "or anger arises without reason." There, in the previous nine instances, since anger arises in relation to beings, there is a breach of the path of action.

Aṭṭhānaghāto pana saṅkhāresu uppanno kammapathabhedaṃ na karoti. Cittaṃ āghātento uppannoti cittassa āghāto. Tato balavataro paṭighāto. Paṭihaññanavasena paṭighaṃ. Paṭivirujjhatīti paṭivirodho. Kuppanavasena kopo. Pakopo sampakopoti upasaggavasena padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ. Dussanavasena doso. Padoso sampadosoti upasaggavasena padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ. Cittassa [P 2.0322] byāpattīti cittassa vipannatā viparivattanākāro. Manaṃ padūsayamāno uppajjatīti manopadoso. Kujjhanavasena kodho. Kujjhanākāro kujjhanā. Kujjhitassa bhāvo kujjhitattaṃ. Dussatīti doso. Dussanāti dussanākāro. Dussitattanti dussitabhāvo. Pakatibhāvavijahanaṭṭhena byāpajjanaṃ byāpatti. Byāpajjanāti byāpajjanākāro. Virujjhatīti virodho. Punappunaṃ virujjhatīti paṭivirodho. Viruddhākārapaṭiviruddhākāravasena vā idaṃ vuttaṃ. Caṇḍiko vuccati caṇḍo, thaddhapuggalo, tassa bhāvo caṇḍikkaṃ. Na etena suropitaṃ vacanaṃ hoti, duruttaṃ aparipuṇṇameva hotīti asuropo. Kuddhakāle hi [M 0.0280] paripuṇṇavacanaṃ nāma natthi, sacepi kassaci [V 0.0257] hoti, taṃ appamāṇaṃ. Apare pana “assujananaṭṭhena assuropanato assuropo”ti vadanti, taṃ akāraṇaṃ somanassassāpi assujananato. Heṭṭhāvuttaattamanatāpaṭipakkhato na attamanatāti anattamanatā. Sā pana yasmā cittasseva, na sattassa, tasmā “cittassā”ti vuttaṃ.

However, striking at what is improper, though arisen in relation to formations, does not create a break in the path of action. Resentment, arisen as affecting the mind, is resentment of the mind. From that, aversion is stronger. Aversion is so called because of striking against. Opposition is so called because it is contrary. Anger is so called because of agitation. Intense anger and full anger are so called because the word is intensified by virtue of the prefix. Hatred is so called because of aversive disposition. Intense hatred and full hatred are so called because the word is intensified by virtue of the prefix. Corruption of the mind is the mind's depravity, a state of distortion. Mental corruption is that which arises, corrupting the mind. Exasperation is so called because of irritation. The mode of exasperation is exasperation. The state of being exasperated is exasperation. Aversion is so called because of aversive disposition. Aversive disposition is the mode of aversion. Aversive state is the state of aversion. Malice is rejecting one's natural condition. The mode of malice is maliciousness. Opposition is so called because it is contrary. Repeatedly opposing is counter-opposition. Or this is stated in terms of opposing states and counter-opposing states. A cruel person is called fierce, a stubborn person; the state of such a person is fierceness. Ill-humor means that speech is not well-delivered; it is harsh and incomplete. For in a state of anger, there is no such thing as complete speech; even if anyone has it, it is uncommon. But others say, "It is called ill-humor because it generates tears," but that is unreasonable, since joy also generates tears. Dissatisfaction is so called as the opposite of contentment stated earlier. But since that belongs to the mind, not to a being, therefore it is stated, "dissatisfaction of the mind."

Adhimattaparittatā veditabbāti adhimattabhāvo parittabhāvo ca, balavabhāvo mandabhāvoti attho. Kañci kāleti ekadā. “Kañci kāla”ntipi pāṭho. Cittāvilakaraṇamatto hotīti cittassa āvilakaraṇappamāṇo, cittakiliṭṭhakaraṇappamāṇoti attho. “Cittālasakaraṇamatto”tipi pāṭho, taṃ na sundaraṃ. Tassa cittakilamathakaraṇamattoti attho. Na ca tāva mukhakulānavikulāno hotīti mukhassa saṅkocanavisaṅkocano na ca tāva hoti. Na ca tāva hanusañcopano hotīti dvinnaṃ hanūnaṃ aparāparaṃ calano na ca tāva hoti. Na ca tāva pharusavācaṃ nicchāraṇo hotīti paresaṃ mammacchedakaṃ pharusavācaṃ mukhato nīharaṇena bahi nikkhamano na ca tāva hoti. Na ca tāva disāvidisānuvilokano hotīti parassa abbhukkiraṇatthaṃ daṇḍādiatthāya disañca anudisañca punappunaṃ vilokano na ca tāva hoti.

The extremes of intensity and weakness should be understood—that is, the state of being strong or weak, meaning strength or weakness. "At some time" means on one occasion. There is also a reading as "at some time." It is merely to the extent of disturbing the mind—that is, to the extent of disturbing the mind, meaning to the extent of defiling the mind. There is also a reading as "merely making the mind sluggish," but that is not good. It means merely to the extent of fatiguing the mind. And not yet does the face become contracted or distorted—that is, the contraction or distortion of the face does not yet occur. And not yet does the jaw move—that is, the alternating movement of the two jaws does not yet occur. And not yet is harsh speech emitted—that is, the emitting of cruel, cutting words from the mouth does not yet occur. And not yet is there glancing in all directions—that is, repeatedly looking around in all directions for the purpose of attacking another with a stick or the like, does not yet occur.

Na ca tāva daṇḍasatthaparāmasano hotīti āghātanatthaṃ daṇḍañca ekatodhārādisatthañca ādiyano na ca tāva hoti. Na ca tāva daṇḍasatthaabbhukkiraṇo hotīti vuttappakāraṃ daṇḍasatthaṃ ukkhipitvā paharaṇo na ca tāva hoti. Na ca tāva [P 2.0323] daṇḍasatthaabhinipātano hotīti etaṃ duvidhaṃ parassa paharaṇatthaṃ na ca tāva khipano hoti. Na ca tāva chinnavicchinnakaraṇo hotīti daṇḍasatthādikhipanena parasarīraṃ dvidhākaraṇo ca vividhākārena vaṇakaraṇo ca na tāva hoti. “Chiddavicchiddakaraṇo”tipi pāṭho. Na ca tāva sambhañjanapalibhañjano hotīti sarīraṃ bhañjitvā cuṇṇavicuṇṇakaraṇo na ca tāva hoti. Na ca tāva aṅgamaṅgaapakaḍḍhano hotīti aṅgapaccaṅgaṃ sampaggahetvā apanetvā kaḍḍhano na ca tāva hoti. Na ca tāva jīvitā voropano hotīti jīvitindriyato voropano na ca tāva hoti. Na ca tāva sabbacāgapariccāgāya saṇṭhito hotīti sabbaṃ parassa [M 0.0281] jīvitaṃ nāsetvā attano jīvitanāsanatthāya saṇṭhito na ca tāva hoti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yadā aññaṃ jīvitā voropetvā attānaṃ jīvitā voropanatthāya ṭhito, tadā sabbacāgapariccāgā nāma hoti. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

And he is not yet one who takes up a stick or a weapon—that is, he does not yet take up a stick or a single-edged weapon, etc., for the purpose of harming. And he is not yet one who brandishes a stick or a weapon—that is, he does not yet strike after raising a stick or weapon in the manner described. And he is not yet one who strikes with a stick or a weapon—that is, he does not yet throw these two for the purpose of striking another. And he is not yet one who cuts or dismembers—that is, he does not yet split another’s body in two by throwing a stick or weapon, nor does he yet inflict wounds in various ways. The reading “one who pierces or dismembers” is also found. And he is not yet one who smashes or shatters—that is, he does not yet break the body into fragments or powder. And he is not yet one who pulls apart limbs—that is, he does not yet seize limbs or parts of the body and pull them away. And he is not yet one who deprives of life—that is, he does not yet deprive another of the life faculty. And he is not yet one who is resolved to give up everything—that is, he is not yet resolved to destroy another’s life at the cost of destroying his own life. This is what is meant: when one, having deprived another of life, stands ready to deprive oneself of life, that is called giving up everything. For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Kodhaṃ [V 0.0258] chetvā sukhaṃ seti, kodhaṃ chetvā na socati;

Kodhassa visamūlassa, madhuraggassa brāhmaṇa;

Vadhaṃ ariyā pasaṃsanti, tañhi chetvā na socatī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.187, 267);

“Having cut off anger, one sleeps happily; having cut off anger, one does not grieve. The noble ones praise the slaying of anger—that poison-rooted, sweet-tipped one, O brahmin—for, having cut it off, one does not grieve.” (SN 1.187, 267)

Yatoti yadā. Parapuggalaṃ ghāṭetvāti parapuggalaṃ nāsetvā. Attānaṃ ghāṭetīti attānaṃ māreti. Paramussadagatoti atibalavabhāvaṃ gato. Paramavepullappattoti ativipulabhāvaṃ patto. Kodhassa pahīnattāti anāgāmimaggena vuttappakārassa kodhassa pahīnabhāvena. Kodhavatthussa pariññātattāti kodhassa patiṭṭhābhūtassa kāraṇabhūtassa piyāpiyaaṭṭhānasaṅkhātassa vatthussa ñātatīraṇapariññāhi byāpetvā ñātabhāvena. Kodhahetussa upacchinnattāti kodhassa janakahetuno domanassasahagatacittuppādassa ucchinnabhāvena.

When—that is, when. Having killed another person—that is, having destroyed another person. He kills himself—that is, he kills himself. Having reached the pinnacle—that is, having reached a state of extreme strength. Having attained the utmost abundance—that is, having attained a state of extreme vastness. Because anger has been abandoned—that is, because anger of the type described has been abandoned by the path of the non-returner. Because the basis for anger has been fully understood—that is, because the basis, which is the foundation for anger, the cause consisting of liked and disliked objects, has been known by being encompassed by the full understandings of knowing and investigating. Because the root of anger has been cut off—that is, because the generating cause of anger, the mind-moment accompanied by displeasure, has been cut off.

Tāsīti bhāyanasīlo hoti. Uttāsīti atibhāyanasīlo. Parittāsīti samantato bhāyanasīlo. Bhāyatīti bhayaṃ uppajjati. Santāsaṃ āpajjatīti virūpabhāvaṃ pāpuṇāti. Katthī [P 2.0324] hotīti attano vaṇṇabhaṇanasīlo hoti. Vikatthīti vividhā nānappakārato vaṇṇabhaṇanasīlo. Jātiyā vāti khattiyabhāvādijātisampattiyā vā. Gottena vāti gotamagottādinā ukkaṭṭhagottena vā. Kolaputtiyena vāti mahākulabhāvena vā. Vaṇṇapokkharatāya vāti vaṇṇasampannasarīratāya vā. Sarīrañhi “pokkhara”nti vuccati, tassa vaṇṇasampattiyā abhirūpabhāvenāti attho. Dhanena vātiādīni uttānatthāneva.

He is timid by nature. Excessively timid means exceedingly timid by nature. Terrified all around means timid in all directions. He is afraid means fear arises. He experiences dread means he attains a state of distortion. “He is boastful” means he has a habit of praising himself. “He is excessively boastful” means he has a habit of praising himself in various and diverse ways. By birth means by the accomplishment of birth, such as the condition of being a noble. By clan means by a superior clan, such as the Gotama clan. By family means by the state of having a great family. By physical charm means by having a body endowed with beauty. For the body is called “pokkhara,” meaning here the excellence of its beauty, being attractive. By wealth and so forth—the meanings are straightforward.

Kukkuccanti niddesassa uddesapadaṃ. Tattha kukkuccanti kucchitaṃ kataṃ kukataṃ, tassa bhāvo kukkuccaṃ. Taṃ pacchānutāpalakkhaṇaṃ, katākatānusocanarasaṃ, vippaṭisārapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, katākatapadaṭṭhānaṃ, dāsabyaṃ viya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Hatthakukkuccampīti hatthehi kucchitaṃ kataṃ kukataṃ, tassa bhāvo hatthakukkuccaṃ. Pādakukkuccādīsupi eseva nayo.

The term “remorse” (kukkucca) is the heading for the explanation. Here, “remorse” (kukkucca) means what is badly done, an ill deed; its state is remorse. Its characteristic is subsequent regret, its function is to lament what was done and not done, it manifests as repentance, its proximate cause is what was done and not done, and it should be seen as akin to slavery. Hand-remorse (hatthakukkucca) means what is badly done with the hands, an ill deed; its state is hand-remorse. The same principle applies to foot-remorse (pādakukkucca) and so forth.

Akappiye [M 0.0282] kappiyasaññitāti acchamaṃsaṃ sūkaramaṃsanti khādati, dīpimaṃsaṃ migamaṃsanti khādati, akappiyabhojanaṃ kappiyabhojananti bhuñjati, vikāle kālasaññitāya bhuñjati, akappiyapānakaṃ kappiyapānakanti [V 0.0259] pivati. Ayaṃ akappiye kappiyasaññitā. Kappiye akappiyasaññitāti sūkaramaṃsaṃ acchamaṃsanti khādati, migamaṃsaṃ dīpimaṃsanti khādati, kappiyabhojanaṃ akappiyabhojananti bhuñjati, kāle vikālasaññitāya bhuñjati, kappiyapānakaṃ akappiyapānakanti pivati. Ayaṃ kappiye akappiyasaññitā. Avajje vajjasaññitāti niddose dosasaññitā. Vajje avajjasaññitāti sadose niddosasaññitā. Kukkuccāyanāti kukkuccāyanākāro. Kukkuccāyitattanti kukkuccāyitabhāvo. Cetaso vippaṭisāroti cittassa virūpo paṭisaraṇabhāvo. Manovilekhoti cittassa vilekho.

Perceiving the unallowable as allowable means eating bear meat thinking it is pig meat, eating leopard meat thinking it is deer meat, consuming unallowable food thinking it is allowable, eating at the wrong time thinking it is the right time, drinking unallowable beverages thinking they are allowable. This is perceiving the unallowable as allowable. Perceiving the allowable as unallowable means eating pig meat thinking it is bear meat, eating deer meat thinking it is leopard meat, consuming allowable food thinking it is unallowable, eating at the right time thinking it is the wrong time, drinking allowable beverages thinking they are unallowable. This is perceiving the allowable as unallowable. Perceiving the faultless as faulty means perceiving fault in the faultless. Perceiving the faulty as faultless means perceiving faultlessness in the faulty. Scrupulousness (kukkuccāyana) means the manner of being scrupulous. The state of being scrupulous (kukkuccāyitatta) means the state of scrupulousness. Mental remorse (cetaso vippaṭisāro) means the mind's distorted reflection. Mental disturbance (manovilekho) means the mind's agitation.

Katattā ca akatattā cāti kāyaduccaritādīnaṃ katabhāvena ca kāyasucaritādīnaṃ akatabhāvena ca. Kataṃ me kāyaduccaritanti mayā kāyena kilesapūtikattā duṭṭhu caritaṃ kāyena kataṃ. Akataṃ me kāyasucaritanti mayā kāyena suṭṭhu caritaṃ na kataṃ. Vacīduccaritavacīsucaritādīsupi eseva nayo nirodhapariyosānesu[P 2.0325].

Due to what was done and what was not done—that is, by the doing of bodily misconduct and so forth, and by the not doing of bodily good conduct and so forth. “Bodily misconduct was done by me” means that bad conduct was done by me with the body, due to it being corrupted by defilements. “Bodily good conduct was not done by me” means that good conduct was not done by me with the body. The same principle applies to verbal misconduct, verbal good conduct, and so on, in explanations that conclude with cessation.

Cittassāti na sattassa na posassa. Uddhaccanti uddhatākāro. Avūpasamoti na vūpasamo. Ceto vikkhipatīti cetaso vikkhepo, bhantattaṃ cittassāti cittassa bhantabhāvo bhantayānabhantagoṇādīnaṃ viya. Iminā ekārammaṇasmiṃyeva vipphandanaṃ kathitaṃ. Uddhaccañhi ekārammaṇe vipphandati, vicikicchā nānārammaṇeti. Idaṃ vuccati uddhaccanti ayaṃ uddhatabhāvo kathīyati.

The word ‘of the mind’ (cittassa) means it is not of a being or a person. Restlessness (uddhacca) is the manner of being agitated. Non-tranquility (avūpasamo) means not being pacified. The mind is scattered—this is the scattering of the mind, the wavering of the mind, like that of confused vehicles, confused oxen, and so on. Here, the flickering in a single object is described. For restlessness flickers in a single object, while doubt flickers in multiple objects. This is called restlessness—this agitated state is described.

Musāvādaṃ pahāyāti ettha musāti visaṃvādanapurekkhārassa atthabhañjako vacīpayogo kāyapayogo vā. Visaṃvādanādhippāyena panassa paravisaṃvādakakāyavacīpayogasamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā musāvādo.

Having abandoned false speech—here, ‘false’ (musā) means a verbal or bodily action that destroys meaning, with the intention to deceive. However, false speech (musāvāda) is the volition that gives rise to such verbal or bodily action designed to deceive others.

Aparo nayo – musāti abhūtaṃ atacchaṃ vatthu. Vādoti tassa bhūtato tacchato viññāpanaṃ. Lakkhaṇato pana atathaṃ vatthuṃ tathato paraṃ viññāpetukāmassa tathāviññattisamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā musāvādo, taṃ musāvādaṃ. Pahāyāti imaṃ musāvādacetanāsaṅkhātaṃ dussīlyaṃ pajahitvā[M 0.0283]. Paṭiviratoti pahīnakālato paṭṭhāya tato dussīlyato orato viratova. Natthi tassa vītikkamissāmīti cakkhusotaviññeyyā dhammā, pageva kāyaviññeyyāti iminā nayena aññesupi evarūpesu padesu attho veditabbo.

Another explanation: ‘False’ (musā) means an untrue, unfactual thing. ‘Speech’ (vāda) is the communication of that unfactual thing as true or factual. By way of definition, false speech (musāvāda) is the volition that gives rise to such communication in one who wishes to communicate an untrue thing as true to another; that is false speech. ‘Having abandoned’ means, having given up this misconduct reckoned as volition associated with false speech. ‘Abstaining’ means, from the time it is abandoned, one is restrained, refraining from that misconduct. There is no ‘I will transgress’ for him, regarding things knowable by the eye or ear—how much more so those knowable by the body. In this way, the meaning should be understood in other similar passages as well.

Saccaṃ vadatīti saccavādī. Saccena saccaṃ sandahati ghaṭetīti saccasandho, na antarantarā musā vadatīti attho. Yo hi puriso kadāci musā vadati, kadāci saccaṃ, tassa [V 0.0260] musāvādena antaritattā saccaṃ saccena na ghaṭiyati, tasmā so na saccasandho, ayaṃ pana na tādiso, jīvitahetupi musā avatvā saccena saccaṃ sandahatiyevāti saccasandho.

He speaks the truth; therefore, he is a truth-speaker (saccavādī). He connects truth with truth, he is truth-bound (saccasandho), meaning he does not speak falsehood intermittently. For a person who sometimes speaks falsely and sometimes truthfully, his truth is interrupted by falsehood, so truth is not connected to truth for him; therefore, he is not truth-bound. But this one is not like that; even for the sake of his life, not speaking falsehood, he connects truth with truth; therefore, he is truth-bound.

Thetoti thiro, thirakathoti attho. Eko hi puggalo haliddirāgo viya, thusarāsimhi nikhātakhāṇu viya, assapiṭṭhe ṭhapitakumbhaṇḍamiva ca na thirakatho hoti, eko pāsāṇalekhā viya, indakhīlā viya ca thirakatho hoti, asinā sīsaṃ chindantepi dve kathā na katheti, ayaṃ vuccati theto.

Steadfast (theta) means firm, that is, of firm speech. One person is like a turmeric-dyed cloth, like a stake planted in a heap of chaff, or like a gourd placed on a horse’s back—he is not firm in speech. Another is like an inscription on stone, like Indra’s pillar—he is firm in speech. Even if his head is cut off with a sword, he does not utter two words. This is called steadfast.

Paccayikoti pattiyāyitabbako, saddhāyitabbakoti attho. Ekacco hi [P 2.0326] puggalo na paccayiko hoti, “idaṃ kena vuttaṃ, asukenā”ti vutte “mā tassa vacanaṃ saddahathā”ti vattabbataṃ āpajjati. Eko paccayiko hoti, “idaṃ kena vuttaṃ, asukenā”ti vutte “yadi tena vuttaṃ, idameva pamāṇaṃ, idāni upaparikkhitabbaṃ natthi, evameva ida”nti vattabbataṃ āpajjati, ayaṃ vuccati paccayiko.

One who is trustworthy (paccayika) means one who should be relied upon, that is, one who should be believed. For some individuals are not trustworthy; when it is said, "Who said this? So-and-so," they become the kind of person about whom one would say, "Do not believe his words." But one is trustworthy; when it is said, "Who said this? So-and-so," they become the kind of person about whom one would say, "If he said it, this is the standard, now there is nothing further to investigate, it is just so." This is called trustworthy.

Avisaṃvādako lokassāti tāya saccavāditāya lokaṃ na visaṃvādetīti attho.

He does not deceive the world (avisaṃvādako lokassa) means that by speaking the truth, he does not mislead the world.

Pisuṇaṃ vācaṃ pahāyātiādīsu yāya vācāya yassa taṃ vācaṃ bhāsati, tassa hadaye attano piyabhāvaṃ parassa ca suññabhāvaṃ karoti, sā pisuṇā vācā. Yāya pana attānampi parampi pharusaṃ karoti, yā vācā sayampi pharusā, neva kaṇṇasukhā na hadayaṅgamā, ayaṃ pharusā vācā. Yena samphaṃ palapati niratthakaṃ, so samphappalāpo. Yā tesaṃ mūlabhūtā cetanāpi pisuṇavācādināmameva labhati, sā eva ca idha adhippetā.

In passages like 'Having abandoned malicious speech,' the speech by which one speaks to someone, creating affection for oneself in that person's heart and a sense of emptiness regarding the other, is malicious speech. But the speech that makes both oneself and others harsh, or speech that is inherently harsh, neither pleasing to the ear nor touching the heart, this is harsh speech. That by which one chatters aimlessly and meaninglessly is frivolous talk. The underlying intention that is the root of these—malicious speech and the like—is itself what is intended here.

Imesaṃ [M 0.0284] bhedāyāti yesaṃ ito vuttānaṃ santike sutaṃ, tesaṃ bhedāya. Bhinnānaṃ vā sandhātāti dvinnaṃ mittānaṃ vā samānupajjhāyakādīnaṃ vā kenacideva kāraṇena bhinnānaṃ ekamekaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “tumhākaṃ īdise kule jātānaṃ evaṃ bahussutānaṃ idaṃ na yutta”ntiādīni vatvā sandhānaṃ kattā anukattā.

To cause division among these (imesaṃ bhedāya) means for the division of those from whom one has heard something. Or, one who reunites those who are divided (bhinnānaṃ sandhātā) is one who—approaching individually two friends, or those with the same preceptor and so on, who have been divided for some reason, and saying, “For those born in such a family and so learned, this is not proper,” and so on—is a maker and promoter of reconciliation.

Anuppadātāti sandhānānuppadātā. Dve jane samagge disvā “tumhākaṃ evarūpe kule jātānaṃ evarūpehi guṇehi samannāgatānaṃ anucchavikameta”ntiādīni vatvā daḷhīkammaṃ kattāti attho. Samaggo ārāmo assāti samaggārāmo, yattha samaggā natthi, tattha vasitumpi na [V 0.0261] icchatīti attho. “Samaggarāmo”tipi pāḷi, ayamevettha attho. Samaggaratoti samaggesu rato, te pahāya aññatra gantumpi na icchatīti attho. Samagge disvāpi sutvāpi nandatīti samagganandī. Samaggakaraṇiṃ vācaṃ bhāsitāti yā vācā satte samaggeyeva karoti, taṃ sāmaggiguṇaparidīpikameva vācaṃ bhāsati, na itaranti.

Anuppadātā means one who promotes reconciliation. Seeing two people in harmony, one says, “For those born in such a family and endowed with such virtues, this is fitting,” and so on, thereby strengthening their bond—this is the meaning. One whose delight is harmony (samaggārāmo) is one for whom harmony is his pleasure ground; where there is no harmony, one does not even wish to dwell—this is the meaning. The reading ‘samaggarāmo’ is also found, and it has this same meaning. Rejoicing in harmony (samaggarato) means delighting in those who are harmonious; abandoning them, one does not even wish to go elsewhere—this is the meaning. Delighting in harmony (samagganandī) means feeling joy upon seeing or hearing about harmony. Speaking words that create harmony means speaking words that only create harmony among beings—uttering speech that only illuminates the virtue of harmony, and nothing else.

Parassa mammacchedakakāyavacīpayogasamuṭṭhāpikā ekantapharusacetanā pharusā vācā, nelāti elaṃ vuccati doso, nassā elanti nelā, niddosāti attho “nelaṅgo setapacchādo”ti ettha (udā. 65; peṭako. 25) vuttanelaṃ viya. Kaṇṇasukhāti byañjanamadhuratāya [P 2.0327] kaṇṇānaṃ sukhā, sūcivijjhanaṃ viya kaṇṇasūlaṃ na janeti. atthamadhuratāya sakalasarīre kopaṃ ajanetvā pemaṃ janetīti pemanīyā. Hadayaṃ gacchati apaṭihaññamānā sukhena cittaṃ pavisatīti hadayaṅgamā. Guṇaparipuṇṇatāya pure bhavāti porī, pure saṃvaḍḍhanārī viya sukumārātipi porī, purassa esātipi porī, nagaravāsīnaṃ kathāti attho. Nagaravāsino hi yuttakathā honti, pitimattaṃ pitāti bhātimattaṃ bhātāti vadanti. Evarūpī kathā bahuno janassa kantā hotīti bahujanakantā. Kantabhāveneva bahuno janassa manāpā cittavuḍḍhikarāti bahujanamanāpā.

Harsh speech (pharusā vācā) is the utterly harsh intention that gives rise to bodily or verbal action that cuts the vital parts of another. ‘Nelā’ means that ‘elaṃ’ (fault) is absent, thus it means ‘faultless,’ like the ‘nela’ mentioned in ‘nelaṅgo setapacchādo’ (Udā. 65; Peṭako. 25). Pleasing to the ear (kaṇṇasukhā) means that, due to the sweetness of its expression, it is pleasing to the ears and does not produce an earache like a needle prick. Due to the sweetness of its meaning, it does not provoke anger throughout the entire body but instead generates affection—thus, it is endearing (pemanīyā). It enters the heart unimpeded, effortlessly entering the mind—thus, it is heart-touching (hadayaṅgamā). Because it is full of virtues, it is urbane (porī), as it is found in the city (pure bhavā). It is also ‘porī’ because it is delicate like a well-bred woman of the city. It is also ‘porī’ because it is ‘of the city’ (purassa esā)—meaning the speech of city-dwellers. For city-dwellers speak appropriately, saying ‘father’ to one who is like a father and ‘brother’ to one who is like a brother. Such speech is pleasing to many people—thus, it is beloved by the multitude (bahujanakantā). Simply by being pleasing, it is agreeable to many people and gladdens the mind—thus, it is cherished by the multitude (bahujanamanāpā).

Anatthaviññāpikā kāyavacīpayogasamuṭṭhāpikā akusalacetanā samphappalāpo. Kālena vadatīti kālavādī, vattabbayuttakālaṃ sallakkhetvā vadatīti attho. Bhūtaṃ tathaṃ tacchaṃ sabhāvameva vadatīti bhūtavādī[M 0.0285]. Diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikatthasannissitameva katvā vadatīti atthavādī. Navalokuttaradhammasannissitaṃ katvā vadatīti dhammavādī. Saṃvaravinayapahānavinayasannissitaṃ katvā vadatīti vinayavādī.

Frivolous chatter (samphappalāpa) is unwholesome volition that gives rise to bodily and verbal action, making known what is not beneficial. A speaker at the right time (kālavādī) is one who speaks after discerning the appropriate time to speak. A truth-speaker (bhūtavādī) is one who speaks what is factual, true, actual, and in its very nature. A speaker on the meaning (atthavādī) is one who speaks based on the benefit connected with this life and future lives. A speaker on the Dhamma (dhammavādī) is one who speaks based on the nine supramundane Dhammas. A speaker on the discipline (vinayavādī) is one who speaks based on the discipline of restraint and the discipline of abandonment.

Nidhānaṃ vuccati ṭhapanokāso, nidhānamassa atthīti nidhānavatī, hadaye nidhātabbayuttakaṃ vācaṃ bhāsitāti attho. Kālenāti evarūpiṃ bhāsamānopi ca “ahaṃ nidhānavatiṃ vācaṃ bhāsissāmī”ti na akālena bhāsati, yuttakālaṃ pana apekkhitvāva bhāsatīti attho. Sāpadesanti saupamaṃ, sakāraṇanti attho. Pariyantavatinti paricchedaṃ dassetvā yathāssā paricchedo paññāyati, evaṃ bhāsatīti attho. Atthasaṃhitanti anekehipi nayehi vibhajantena pariyādātuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya atthasampannaṃ bhāsati. Yaṃ vā so atthavādī atthaṃ vadati, tena atthena sahitattā atthasaṃhitaṃ vācaṃ bhāsati, na aññaṃ nikkhipitvā aññaṃ bhāsatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Catuddosāpagataṃ vācaṃ bhāsatīti musāvādādīhi catūhi dosehi apagataṃ vācaṃ bhāsati. Dvattiṃsāya tiracchānakathāyāti dvattiṃsāya saggamokkhānaṃ tiracchānabhūtāya kathāya.

Nidhāna is said to be a place of deposit. Nidhānavatī means 'possessing a deposit,' meaning one speaks words fit to be deposited in the heart. 'At the proper time' means that even when speaking in this manner, one does not speak at an inappropriate time, but speaks only after considering the appropriate moment. Sāpadesa means 'with an analogy,' 'with a reason.' Pariyantavatī means 'with limits,' meaning one speaks in such a way as to indicate the limits, so that the limit is understood. Atthasaṃhita means 'connected with the meaning,' meaning one speaks words full of meaning, which cannot be exhausted even when analyzed in many ways. Or, because that speaker speaks about meaning, the words spoken are connected with that meaning; it means not setting aside one thing and speaking about another. Speaking words free from the four faults means speaking words devoid of the four faults, such as false speech. 'Of the thirty-two frivolous topics' refers to the thirty-two topics that are an obstruction to heaven and liberation.

Dasa [V 0.0262] kathāvatthūnīti appicchatādīni dasa vivaṭṭanissitāya kathāya vatthubhūtāni kāraṇāni. Appicchakathanti ettha appicchoti [P 2.0328] icchāvirahito aniccho nittaṇho. Ettha hi byañjanaṃ sāvasesaṃ viya, attho pana niravaseso. Na hi khīṇāsavassa aṇumattāpi icchā nāma atthi.

The ten topics of discussion are the ten grounds, such as having few desires, which are the basis for discourse connected with turning away from saṃsāra. Appicchakathā means 'discourse on having few desires.' Here, 'having few desires' (appiccho) means being devoid of desire, without wish, without craving. Here, indeed, the expression is as if with a remainder, but the meaning is without remainder. For in one whose taints are destroyed, there is not even the slightest thing called desire.

Apicettha atricchatā pāpicchatā mahicchatā appicchatāti ayaṃ bhedo veditabbo – tattha sakalābhe atittassa paralābhapatthanā atricchatā nāma, tāya samannāgatassa ekabhājane pakkapūvepi attano patte patite na supakko viya khuddako viya ca khāyati, sveva pana parassa patte pakkhitto supakko viya mahanto viya ca khāyati. Asantaguṇasambhāvanatā pana paṭiggahaṇe ca amattaññutā pāpicchatā nāma, sā “idhekacco asaddho samāno saddhoti maṃ jano jānātū”tiādinā (vibha. 851) nayena atreva āgatāyeva. Tāya ca samannāgato puggalo kohaññe patiṭṭhāti. Santaguṇasambhāvanatā pana paṭiggahaṇe [M 0.0286] ca amattaññutā mahicchatā nāma, sāpi “idhekacco saddho samāno saddhoti maṃ jano jānātūti icchati, sīlavā samāno sīlavāti maṃ jano jānātū”ti (vibha. 851) iminā nayena āgatāyeva. Tāya samannāgato puggalo dussantappayo hoti, vijātamātāpissa cittaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkoti. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

Moreover, here, this distinction should be understood: excessive desire, evil desire, great desire, and modest desire. Among these, insatiability regarding all gains and longing for the gains of others is called excessive desire. For one endowed with this, even a cooked cake that falls into his own bowl appears as if it were small and not well-cooked, but that very same cake placed in another's bowl appears as if it were large and well-cooked. Now, the display of non-existent qualities and immoderation in receiving is called evil desire. This has been stated right here in the Vibhaṅga (Vibh 851) by the method beginning with: 'Here, someone without faith wishes, “May people know me as faithful,”' and so on. A person endowed with this is established in deceitfulness. Now, the display of existent qualities and immoderation in receiving is called great desire. This too has been stated by the method in the Vibhaṅga (Vibh 851): 'Here, someone with faith wishes, “May people know me as faithful”; being virtuous, he wishes, “May people know me as virtuous,”' and so on. A person endowed with this is hard to satisfy, and even his own mother cannot grasp his mind. Therefore, it is said—

“Aggikkhandho samuddo ca, mahiccho cāpi puggalo;

Sakaṭena paccaye detu, tayopete atappayā”ti. (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.252; a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.63; udā. aṭṭha. 31);

“A mass of fire, the ocean, and a person of great desire; though one give requisites by the cartload, these three are never satisfied.”

Santaguṇanigūhanatā pana paṭiggahaṇe ca mattaññutā appicchatā nāma, tāya samannāgato puggalo attani vijjamānampi guṇaṃ paṭicchādetukāmatāya saddho samāno “saddhoti maṃ jano jānātū”ti na icchati. Sīlavā… pavivitto… bahussuto… āraddhavīriyo… samādhisampanno… paññavā… khīṇāsavo samāno “khīṇāsavoti maṃ jano jānātū”ti na icchati seyyathāpi majjhantikatthero. Evaṃ appiccho ca pana bhikkhu anuppannaṃ lābhaṃ uppādeti, uppannaṃ thāvaraṃ karoti, dāyakānaṃ cittaṃ ārādheti, yathā yathā hi so [P 2.0329] attano appicchatāya appaṃ gaṇhāti, tathā tathā tassa vatte pasannā manussā bahū denti.

Now, the concealing of existent qualities and moderation in receiving is called modest desire. A person endowed with this, desiring to conceal even an existent quality in himself, though faithful, does not wish, 'May people know me as faithful.' Similarly, though virtuous... secluded... learned... energetic... accomplished in concentration... wise... or a taint-destroyer, he does not wish, 'May people know me as a taint-destroyer,' just like the Elder Majjhantika. Thus, a bhikkhu of modest desire generates unarisen gains, stabilizes arisen gains, and pleases the minds of donors. For the more he takes little due to his modest desire, the more people, pleased with his conduct, give abundantly.

Aparopi catubbidho appiccho paccayaappiccho dhutaṅgaappiccho pariyattiappiccho adhigamaappicchoti[V 0.0263]. Tattha catūsu paccayesu appiccho paccayaappiccho. So dāyakassa vasaṃ jānāti, deyyadhammassa vasaṃ jānāti, attano thāmaṃ jānāti. Yadi hi deyyadhammo bahu hoti, dāyako appaṃ dātukāmo, dāyakassa vasena appaṃ gaṇhāti. Deyyadhammo appo, dāyako bahuṃ dātukāmo, deyyadhammassa vasena appaṃ gaṇhāti. Deyyadhammopi bahu, dāyakopi bahuṃ dātukāmo, attano thāmaṃ ñatvā pamāṇeneva gaṇhāti.

There is also another fourfold person of modest desire: one with modest desire regarding requisites, one with modest desire regarding ascetic practices, one with modest desire regarding learning, and one with modest desire regarding attainment. Among these, one with modest desire regarding requisites is a person with modest desire regarding the four requisites. Such a person knows the donor’s capacity, knows the nature of the gift, and knows their own strength. If the gift is abundant but the donor wishes to give little, they take little out of regard for the donor’s capacity. If the gift is meager but the donor wishes to give much, they take little out of regard for the nature of the gift. If both the gift is abundant and the donor wishes to give much, they take only what is appropriate, knowing their own strength.

Dhutaṅgasamādānassa attani atthibhāvaṃ na jānāpetukāmo dhutaṅgaappiccho nāma. Yo pana bahussutabhāvaṃ na jānāpetukāmo, ayaṃ pariyattiappiccho nāma. Yo pana sotāpannādīsu aññataro hutvā sotāpannādibhāvaṃ jānāpetuṃ na icchati, ayaṃ adhigamaappiccho nāma. Khīṇāsavo [M 0.0287] pana atricchataṃ pāpicchataṃ mahicchataṃ pahāya sabbaso icchāpaṭipakkhabhūtāya alobhasaṅkhātāya parisuddhāya appicchatāya samannāgatattā appiccho nāma. “Āvuso, atricchatā pāpicchatā mahicchatāti, ime dhammā pahātabbāti, tesu ādīnavaṃ dassetvā evarūpaṃ appicchataṃ samādāya vattitabba”nti vadanto appicchakathaṃ katheti nāma.

One who does not wish to make known that he has undertaken ascetic observances is called one with modest desire regarding ascetic practices. One who does not wish to make known his extensive learning is called one with modest desire regarding learning. One who, having become a stream-enterer or the like, does not wish to make known his state as a stream-enterer or the like, is called one with modest desire regarding attainment. A taint-destroyer, however, having abandoned excessive desire, evil desire, and great desire, is called one with modest desire because he is fully endowed with pure modest desire, which is known as non-greed and is the complete opposite of desire. One who says, 'Friends, excessive desire, evil desire, and great desire—these things are to be abandoned,' and, having shown the danger in them, says, 'One should live having undertaken such modest desire,' is said to give a talk on modest desire.

Santuṭṭhīkathantiādīsu visesatthameva dīpayissāma, yojanā pana vuttanayeneva veditabbā. Santuṭṭhīkathanti itarītarapaccayasantosaṃ nissitaṃ kathaṃ. So panesa santoso dvādasavidho hoti. Seyyathidaṃ – cīvare yathālābhasantoso, yathābalasantoso, yathāsāruppasantosoti tividho. Evaṃ piṇḍapātādīsupi.

In the discussion on contentment and so forth, we will clarify only the distinctive meanings, but the connection should be understood by the method already stated. A talk on contentment is a talk based on satisfaction with any kind of requisite. This contentment is of twelve kinds. Namely, regarding robes, there are three kinds: contentment with what is obtained, contentment according to one's strength, and contentment with what is suitable. The same applies to almsfood and other things.

Tassāyaṃ pabhedavaṇṇanā – idha bhikkhu cīvaraṃ labhati sundaraṃ vā asundaraṃ vā. So teneva yāpeti, aññaṃ na pattheti, labhantopi na gaṇhāti. Ayamassa [P 2.0330] cīvare yathālābhasantoso. Atha pana yo pakatidubbalo vā hoti, ābādhajarābhibhūto vā, garucīvaraṃ pārupanto kilamati. So sabhāgena bhikkhunā saddhiṃ taṃ parivattetvā lahukena yāpentopi santuṭṭhova hoti. Ayamassa cīvare yathābalasantoso. Aparo paṇītapaccayalābhī hoti. So pattuṇṇacīvarādīnaṃ aññataraṃ mahagghacīvaraṃ, bahūni vā pana cīvarāni labhitvā “idaṃ therānaṃ cirapabbajitānaṃ, idaṃ bahussutānaṃ anurūpaṃ, idaṃ gilānānaṃ, idaṃ appalābhīnaṃ hotū”ti datvā tesaṃ purāṇacīvaraṃ vā saṅkārakūṭādito vā nantakāni uccinitvā tehi saṅghāṭiṃ katvā dhārentopi santuṭṭhova hoti. Ayamassa cīvare yathāsāruppasantoso.

This is its detailed explanation: Here, a bhikkhu obtains a robe, whether beautiful or not. He maintains himself with just that, does not long for another, and does not accept one even if he obtains it. This is his contentment with robes as obtained. However, if one is naturally weak or overcome by illness and old age, wearing a heavy robe causes fatigue. Such a bhikkhu, having exchanged it with a suitable bhikkhu for a lighter one, remains content even while maintaining himself with the lighter robe. This is his contentment with robes according to his strength. Another may gain excellent requisites. Having obtained an expensive robe, such as one of woven wool, or many robes, he thinks, 'Let this be for the elders who have long been ordained, this is suitable for the learned, this for the sick, and this for those who receive little.' Having given them away, he picks out their old robes or discarded cloths from a dust heap, makes a patched robe from them, and wears it, yet remains content. This is his contentment with robes as suitable.

Idha pana bhikkhu piṇḍapātaṃ labhati lūkhaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā, so teneva yāpeti, aññaṃ na [V 0.0264] pattheti, labhantopi na gaṇhāti. Ayamassa piṇḍapāte yathālābhasantoso. Yo pana attano pakativiruddhaṃ vā byādhiviruddhaṃ vā piṇḍapātaṃ labhati, yenassa paribhuttena aphāsu hoti, so taṃ sabhāgassa bhikkhuno datvā tassa hatthato sappāyabhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā samaṇadhammaṃ karontopi santuṭṭhova hoti. Ayamassa piṇḍapāte yathābalasantoso. Aparo bahuṃ paṇītaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ [M 0.0288] labhati, so taṃ cīvaraṃ viya theracirapabbajitabahussutaappalābhīgilānānaṃ datvā tesaṃ vā sesakaṃ piṇḍāya vā caritvā missakāhāraṃ bhuñjantopi santuṭṭhova hoti. Ayamassa piṇḍapāte yathāsāruppasantoso.

Here, a bhikkhu receives almsfood, whether coarse or fine. He maintains himself with just that, does not long for another, and does not accept it even if he obtains it. This is his contentment with almsfood as obtained. However, if he receives almsfood that is contrary to his nature or illness, by consuming which he becomes uncomfortable, he may give it to a bhikkhu of similar condition and, having eaten suitable food from that bhikkhu's hand, remains content even while practicing the ascetic's duties. This is his contentment with almsfood according to his strength. Another may receive much fine almsfood. He gives it away just like robes—to elders, long-ordained monks, learned monks, those who receive little, or the sick. Then, either eating what remains of it, or going for alms and consuming mixed food, he remains content. This is his contentment with almsfood as suitable.

Idha pana bhikkhu senāsanaṃ labhati manāpaṃ vā amanāpaṃ vā, so tena neva somanassaṃ na domanassaṃ uppādeti, antamaso tiṇasanthārakenāpi yathāladdheneva tussati. Ayamassa senāsane yathālābhasantoso. Yo pana attano pakativiruddhaṃ vā byādhiviruddhaṃ vā senāsanaṃ labhati, yatthassa vasato aphāsu hoti, so taṃ sabhāgassa bhikkhuno datvā tassa santake sappāyasenāsane vasantopi santuṭṭhova hoti. Ayamassa senāsane yathābalasantoso.

Here, a bhikkhu obtains a dwelling, whether agreeable or disagreeable. He does not give rise to either joy or sorrow because of it. Even with just a grass mat, he is content with whatever he has received. This is his contentment with dwellings as obtained. However, if he obtains a dwelling that is contrary to his nature or harmful to his health, where dwelling causes him discomfort, he may give it to a bhikkhu of similar condition and, dwelling in a suitable dwelling belonging to that bhikkhu, he is still content. This is his contentment with dwellings according to his strength.

Aparo mahāpuñño leṇamaṇḍapakūṭāgārādīni bahūni paṇītasenāsanāni labhati, so taṃ cīvaraṃ viya theracirapabbajitabahussutaappalābhīgilānānaṃ datvā yattha katthaci vasantopi santuṭṭhova hoti. Ayamassa senāsane yathāsāruppasantoso. Yopi [P 2.0331] “uttamasenāsanaṃ nāma pamādaṭṭhānaṃ, tattha nisinnassa thinamiddhaṃ okkamati, niddābhibhūtassa puna paṭibujjhato pāpavitakkā pātubhavantī”ti paṭisañcikkhitvā tādisaṃ senāsanaṃ pattampi na sampaṭicchati, so taṃ paṭikkhipitvā abbhokāsarukkhamūlādīsu vasantopi santuṭṭhova hoti. Ayamassa senāsane yathāsāruppasantoso.

Another highly meritorious person obtains many excellent dwellings such as caves, pavilions, gabled houses, and so on. Yet, just as with robes, he gives them to elders, those long ordained, the learned, those of little gain, or the sick, and he remains content wherever he stays. This is his suitable contentment with lodging. And one who reflects thus: “An excellent lodging is a place for heedlessness; sitting there, sloth and torpor overcome one, and when one wakes up after being overcome by sleep, evil thoughts arise”—such a person does not even accept such a lodging when obtained. Having rejected it, he remains content even while living in the open air or at the foot of a tree. This is his suitable contentment with lodging.

Idha pana bhikkhu bhesajjaṃ labhati lūkhaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā, so yaṃ labhati, teneva tussati, aññaṃ na pattheti, labhantopi na gaṇhāti. Ayamassa gilānapaccaye yathālābhasantoso. Yo pana telena atthiko phāṇitaṃ labhati, so taṃ sabhāgassa bhikkhuno datvā tassa hatthato telaṃ gahetvā aññadeva vā pariyesitvā bhesajjaṃ karontopi santuṭṭhova hoti. Ayamassa gilānapaccaye yathābalasantoso.

Here, a bhikkhu obtains medicinal requisites, whether coarse or refined; he is content with what he obtains, does not crave anything else, and does not accept another even if he receives it. This is his contentment with medicinal requisites according to what is obtained. But if one who needs oil obtains molasses, he gives it to a fellow bhikkhu and takes oil from his hand, or, having sought something else, is content even while preparing the medicine. This is his contentment with medicinal requisites according to his capacity.

Aparo [M 0.0289] mahāpuñño bahuṃ telamadhuphāṇitādipaṇītabhesajjaṃ labhati, so taṃ cīvaraṃ viya theracirapabbajitabahussutaappalābhīgilānānaṃ datvā tesaṃ ābhatena yena kenaci yāpentopi santuṭṭhova [V 0.0265] hoti. Yo pana ekasmiṃ bhājane catumadhuraṃ ṭhapetvā ekasmiṃ muttaharītakaṃ “gaṇha, bhante, yadicchasī”ti vuccamāno “sacassa tesu aññatarenapi rogo vūpasammati, atha muttaharītakaṃ nāma buddhādīhi vaṇṇita”nti catumadhuraṃ paṭikkhipitvā muttaharītakena bhesajjaṃ karonto paramasantuṭṭhova hoti. Ayamassa gilānapaccaye yathāsāruppasantoso. Imesaṃ pana paccekapaccayesu tiṇṇaṃ tiṇṇaṃ santosānaṃ yathāsāruppasantosova aggo. Arahā ekekasmiṃ paccaye imehi tīhipi santuṭṭhova.

Another highly meritorious person obtains many refined medicinal requisites such as oil, honey, and molasses. Just as with robes, he gives these to elders, those long ordained, the learned, those of little gain, or the sick, and remains content sustaining himself with whatever is brought to him by them. But one who, having the four sweets placed in one bowl and myrobalan in another, is told, “Take, venerable sir, whatever you wish,” and reflecting, “Even if his illness is assuaged by any one of these, myrobalan is praised by the Buddhas and so forth,” rejects the four sweets and makes medicine with the myrobalan—he is extremely content. This is his suitable contentment with medicinal requisites. Among these three kinds of contentment regarding each requisite, suitable contentment is the foremost. An arahant is content with all three of these kinds of contentment regarding each requisite.

Pavivekakathanti pavivekanissitaṃ kathaṃ. Tayo hi vivekā kāyaviveko cittaviveko upadhivivekoti. Tattha eko gacchati, eko tiṭṭhati, eko nisīdati, eko seyyaṃ kappeti, eko gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pavisati, eko paṭikkamati, eko abhikkamati, eko caṅkamaṃ adhiṭṭhāti, eko carati, eko viharatīti ayaṃ kāyaviveko nāma. Aṭṭha samāpattiyo pana cittaviveko nāma. Nibbānaṃ upadhiviveko nāma.

Talk on seclusion means talk connected with seclusion. For there are three kinds of seclusion: bodily seclusion, mental seclusion, and seclusion from the substrata of existence. Here, one goes alone, one stands alone, one sits alone, one lies down alone, one enters a village for alms alone, one retreats alone, one advances alone, one undertakes walking meditation alone, one moves about alone, and one dwells alone—this is called bodily seclusion. The eight attainments, however, are mental seclusion. Nibbāna is seclusion from the substrata of existence.

Vuttampi hetaṃ [P 2.0332] – “kāyaviveko ca vivekaṭṭhakāyānaṃ nekkhammābhiratānaṃ. Cittaviveko ca parisuddhacittānaṃ paramavodānappattānaṃ. Upadhiviveko ca nirupadhīnaṃ puggalānaṃ visaṅkhāragatāna”nti (mahāni. 57).

This has also been said: “Bodily seclusion is for those whose bodies are established in seclusion and who delight in renunciation. Mental seclusion is for those with purified minds who have attained supreme cleansing. Seclusion from the substrata of existence is for those persons who are without substrata of existence and have gone to the unconditioned” (Mahāniddesa 57).

Asaṃsaggakathanti ettha pana savanasaṃsaggo dassanasaṃsaggo samullapanasaṃsaggo sambhogasaṃsaggo kāyasaṃsaggoti pañcavidho saṃsaggo. Tesu idha bhikkhu suṇāti “amukasmiṃ gāme vā nigame vā itthī vā kumārī vā abhirūpā dassanīyā pāsādikā paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya samannāgatā”ti, so taṃ sutvā saṃsīdati visīdati, na sakkoti brahmacariyaṃ sandhāretuṃ, sikkhādubbalyaṃ anāvikatvā hīnāyāvattati. Evaṃ parehi kathiyamānarūpādisampattiṃ attanā vā hasitalapitagītasaddaṃ suṇantassa sotaviññāṇavīthivasena uppanno rāgo savanasaṃsaggo nāma.

Talk on non-association. Here, there are five kinds of association: association through hearing, association through seeing, association through conversation, association through enjoyment, and association through bodily contact. Among these, when a bhikkhu hears, “In such and such a village or town, there is a woman or a maiden who is beautiful, pleasing, graceful, endowed with supreme beauty and comeliness,” having heard this, he sinks down, he is dejected, unable to maintain the holy life. Without revealing his weakness in the training, he reverts to the lower state. Thus, the lust that arises by way of the ear-consciousness process when he hears about the perfection of beauty and so forth being spoken of by others, or when he himself hears sounds of laughter, chatter, or song, is called association through hearing.

“Idha [M 0.0290] bhikkhu na heva kho suṇāti, api ca kho sāmaṃ passati itthiṃ vā kumāriṃ vā abhirūpaṃ dassanīyaṃ pāsādikaṃ paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya samannāgataṃ, so taṃ disvā saṃsīdati visīdati, na sakkoti brahmacariyaṃ sandhāretuṃ, sikkhādubbalyaṃ anāvikatvā hīnāyāvattati. Evaṃ visabhāgarūpaṃ olokentassa pana cakkhuviññāṇavīthivasena uppannarāgo dassanasaṃsaggo nāma.

Here, a bhikkhu does not merely hear, but also sees for himself a woman or a maiden who is beautiful, pleasing, graceful, endowed with supreme beauty and comeliness. Upon seeing her, he sinks down, he is dejected, unable to maintain the holy life. Without revealing his weakness in the training, he reverts to the lower state. Thus, the lust that arises by way of the eye-consciousness process upon seeing a disparate form is called association through seeing.

Aññamaññaṃ [V 0.0266] allāpasallāpavasena uppannarāgo pana samullapanasaṃsaggo nāma. Bhikkhuno bhikkhuniyā santakaṃ bhikkhuniyā vā bhikkhussa santakaṃ gahetvā paribhogakaraṇavasena uppannarāgo sambhogasaṃsaggo nāma. Hatthaggāhādivasena uppannarāgo pana kāyasaṃsaggo nāma. Arahā imehi pañcahi saṃsaggehi catūhipi parisāhi saddhiṃ asaṃsaṭṭho, gāhamuttako ceva saṃsaggamuttako ca. Asaṃsaggassa vaṇṇaṃ bhaṇanto asaṃsaggakathaṃ katheti nāma.

Lust arising by way of mutual talk and conversation is called association through conversation. When a bhikkhu takes what belongs to a bhikkhunī, or a bhikkhunī takes what belongs to a bhikkhu, for the purpose of enjoyment, the lust that arises is called association through enjoyment. Lust arising by way of physical contact such as holding hands is called association through bodily contact. An arahant is unassociated with these five kinds of association and with the four assemblies, released from grasping and released from association. One who praises non-association is said to be giving talk on non-association.

Vīriyārambhakathanti ettha yo paggahitavīriyo paripuṇṇakāyikacetasikavīriyo hoti, gamane uppannaṃ kilesaṃ ṭhānaṃ [P 2.0333] pāpuṇituṃ na deti, ṭhāne uppannaṃ kilesaṃ nisajjaṃ, nisajjāya uppannaṃ kilesaṃ sayanaṃ pāpuṇituṃ na deti, daṇḍena kaṇhasappaṃ uppīḷetvā gaṇhanto viya amittaṃ gīvāya akkamanto viya ca vicarati, tādisassa āraddhavīriyassa vaṇṇaṃ bhaṇanto vīriyārambhakathaṃ katheti nāma.

Talk on the arousal of energy. Here, one who has aroused energy, possessing complete bodily and mental energy, does not allow a defilement that arises while walking to reach the standing posture, a defilement that arises while standing to reach the sitting posture, or a defilement that arises while sitting to reach the lying-down posture. He moves about as if seizing and pressing down a black snake with a stick, or as if treading on the neck of an enemy. One who praises such a person with aroused energy is said to be giving talk on the arousal of energy.

Sīlakathantiādīsu sīlanti catupārisuddhisīlaṃ. Samādhīti vipassanāpādakā aṭṭha samāpattiyo. Paññāti lokiyalokuttarañāṇaṃ. Vimuttīti arahattaphalavimutti. Vimuttiñāṇadassananti ekūnavīsatividhaṃ paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ. Sīlādīnaṃ guṇaṃ pakāsento sīlādikathaṃ katheti nāma.

In the talk on virtue, and so forth: “Virtue” refers to the fourfold purity of virtue. “Concentration” refers to the eight attainments that are the basis for insight. “Wisdom” refers to mundane and supramundane knowledge. “Liberation” refers to the liberation of the fruit of arahantship. “Knowledge and vision of liberation” refers to the nineteen kinds of reviewing knowledge. One who reveals the qualities of virtue and so forth is said to be giving talk on virtue and so forth.

Satipaṭṭhānakathantiādīni saṅgajālamaticca so munītipariyosānāni pubbe vuttānusārena veditabbāni.

The talks on the foundations of mindfulness and so forth, which conclude with the phrase 'having transcended the net of attachment, that sage,' should be understood in accordance with what was previously stated.

86. Nirāsattīti nittaṇho. Vivekadassī phassesūti paccuppannesu cakkhusamphassādīsu attādibhāvavivekaṃ passati. Diṭṭhīsu ca na nīyatīti dvāsaṭṭhiyā diṭṭhīsu kāyaci diṭṭhiyā na nīyati.

86. “Free from attachment” means without craving. “One who sees detachment in contacts” means one sees detachment from selfhood and so forth in present eye-contact and so forth. “And is not led by views” means one is not led by any of the sixty-two views.

Vipariṇataṃ [M 0.0291] vā vatthuṃ na socatīti pakatibhāvaṃ jahitvā naṭṭhe kismiñci vatthusmiṃ na sokaṃ āpajjati. Vipariṇatasmiṃ vāti vinassamāne vatthumhi.

“One does not grieve over what has changed” means one does not fall into sorrow over any object that has perished, having abandoned its natural state. “Or over what is changing” means over an object that is perishing.

Cakkhusamphassoti cakkhuṃ vatthuṃ katvā cakkhuviññāṇasahajāto phasso cakkhusamphasso. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Ettha ca purimā cakkhupasādādivatthukāva, manosamphasso hadayavatthukopi avatthukopi sabbo catubhūmako phasso. Adhivacanasamphassoti pariyāyena etassa nāmaṃ hotiyeva[V 0.0267]. Tayo hi arūpino khandhā sayaṃ piṭṭhivaṭṭakā hutvā attano sahajātasamphassassa adhivacanasamphassoti nāmaṃ karonti. Paṭighasamphassoti nippariyāyena pana paṭighasamphasso nāma pañcadvārikaphasso. Adhivacanasamphasso nāma manodvārikaphasso. Sukhavedanīyo phassoti sukhavedanāya hito uppādako phasso. Itaradvayepi eseva nayo. Kusalo phassoti ekavīsatikusalacittasahajāto phasso. Akusaloti dvādasaakusalasahajāto phasso. Abyākatoti chappaññāsaabyākatasahajāto phasso. Kāmāvacaroti catupaññāsakāmāvacarasahajāto phasso. Rūpāvacaroti kusalādipañcadasarūpāvacarasampayutto[P 2.0334]. Arūpāvacaroti kusalābyākatavasena dvādasaarūpāvacarasampayutto.

“Eye-contact” is contact arising together with eye-consciousness, taking the eye as its base. The same method applies to the rest. Here, the former contacts are based on eye-sensitivity and so forth, while mind-contact is based on the heart-base or is without a base, encompassing all contact of the four planes. “Designation-contact” is a name for this by way of designation. For the three immaterial aggregates, acting as a support, give the name “designation-contact” to the contact arising together with them. “Resistance-contact,” however, without designation, is the name for five-door contact. “Designation-contact” is the name for mind-door contact. “Contact resulting in pleasant feeling” is contact that is conducive to and productive of pleasant feeling. The same method applies to the other two. “Wholesome contact” is contact arising together with the twenty-one wholesome consciousnesses. “Unwholesome contact” is contact arising together with the twelve unwholesome consciousnesses. “Indeterminate contact” is contact arising together with the fifty-six indeterminate consciousnesses. “Sense-sphere contact” is contact arising together with the fifty-four sense-sphere consciousnesses. “Form-sphere contact” is contact associated with the fifteen form-sphere consciousnesses, including wholesome and so forth. “Formless-sphere contact” is contact associated with the twelve formless-sphere consciousnesses, by way of wholesome and indeterminate.

Suññatoti anattānupassanāvasena vipassantassa uppanno maggo suññato, tena sahajāto phasso suññato phasso. Itaradvayepi eseva nayo. Animittoti ettha aniccānupassanāvasena vipassantassa uppanno maggo animitto. Appaṇihitoti dukkhānupassanāvasena vipassantassa uppanno maggo appaṇihito. Lokiyoti loko vuccati lujjanapalujjanaṭṭhena vaṭṭo, tasmiṃ pariyāpannabhāvena loke niyuttoti lokiyo, tebhūmako dhammo. Lokuttaroti lokato uttaro uttiṇṇoti lokuttaro, loke apariyāpannabhāvenapi lokuttaro. Attena vāti attabhāvena vā. Attaniyena vāti attāyattena vā.

“Empty” refers to the path that arises in one who contemplates non-self by way of insight; this path is empty. The contact that arises simultaneously with it is empty contact. The same method applies to the other two. “Signless” refers to the path that arises in one who contemplates impermanence by way of insight; this path is signless. “Undirected” refers to the path that arises in one who contemplates suffering by way of insight; this path is undirected. “Mundane.” The world (loka) is so called in the sense of breaking up and disintegrating—the round of existence. Because it is included within that, it is “mundane,” the Dhamma of the three planes. “Supramundane” means transcending the world, having gone beyond the world; it is also “supramundane” because it is not included within the world. “By self” means or by way of self-nature. “By what belongs to self” means or by way of what is dependent on self.

87. Patilīnoti rāgādīnaṃ pahīnattā tato apagato. Akuhakoti avimhāpako tīhi kuhanavatthūhi. Apihālūti apihanasīlo, patthanātaṇhāya [M 0.0292] rahitoti vuttaṃ hoti. Amaccharīti pañcamaccheravirahito. Appagabbhoti kāyapāgabbhiyādivirahito. Ajegucchoti sampannasīlāditāya ajegucchanīyo asecanako manāpo. Pesuṇeyye ca no yutoti dvīhi ākārehi upasaṃharitabbe pisuṇakamme ayutto.

87. “Withdrawn” (patilīna) means that because lust and so forth have been abandoned, one has departed from them. “Not deceitful” (akuhaka) means not misleading, being free from the three grounds for deceit. “Not concealing” (apihālu) means not inclined to conceal; it is said that one is devoid of the craving of longing. “Not stingy” (amaccharī) means devoid of the five kinds of stinginess. “Not impudent” (appagabbha) means free from bodily impudence and so forth. “Not loathsome” (ajeguccha) means not to be loathed due to being endowed with virtue and so forth, being agreeable and pleasing. “And not engaged in malicious talk” (pesuṇeyye ca no yutto) means not involved in malicious actions, to be understood in two ways.

Rāgassa pahīnattāti arahattamaggena rāgakilesassa pahīnabhāvena. Asmimāno pahīno hotīti asmīti unnatimāno samucchedavasena pahīno hoti.

“Through the abandonment of lust” means through the abandonment of the defilement of lust by the path of arahantship. “The conceit ‘I am’ is abandoned” means the conceit ‘I am,’ the conceit of superiority, is completely eradicated.

Tīṇi kuhanavatthūnīti tīṇi vimhāpanakāraṇāni. Paccayapaṭisevanasaṅkhātaṃ kuhanavatthūtiādīsu cīvarādīhi nimantitassa tadatthikasseva sato pāpicchataṃ nissāya paṭikkhipanena te ca gahapatike attani suppatiṭṭhitapasāde ñatvā puna tesaṃ “aho ayyo appiccho, na kiñci [V 0.0268] paṭiggaṇhituṃ icchati, suladdhaṃ vata no assa, sace appamattakampi kiñci paṭiggaṇheyyā”ti nānāvidhehi upāyehi paṇītāni cīvarādīni upanentānaṃ tadanuggahakāmataṃyeva avikatvā paṭiggahaṇena ca tato pabhuti api sakaṭabhārehi upanāmanahetubhūtaṃ vimhāpanaṃ paccayapaṭisevanasaṅkhātaṃ kuhanavatthūti veditabbaṃ. Pāpicchasseva pana sato sambhāvanādhippāyena katena iriyāpathena [P 2.0335] vimhāpanaṃ iriyāpathasaṅkhātaṃ kuhanavatthūti veditabbaṃ. Pāpicchasseva pana sato uttarimanussadhammādhigamaparidīpanavācāya tathā tathā vimhāpanaṃ sāmantajappanasaṅkhātaṃ kuhanavatthūti veditabbaṃ.

“Three grounds for deceit” are three means of deception. The ground for deceit known as the use of requisites (paccayapaṭisevana): When invited by householders with robes and other offerings, a person with evil desires, though he himself needs them, rejects them relying on his evil wishes. Knowing that those householders have strong faith in him, and knowing they think, “Ah, this venerable one is content, he does not wish to accept anything. How fortunate we would be if he would accept even a little!” he later allows them to bring fine robes and other items through various means. Without revealing his desire to favor them, he accepts the offerings. From then on, even cartloads of gifts are brought to him. This deception, known as the use of requisites, should be understood as a ground for deceit. The ground for deceit known as manner of behavior (iriyāpatha): A person with evil desires deceives others through behavior done with the intention of being esteemed. The ground for deceit known as insinuating talk (sāmantajappana): A person with evil desires deceives others through speech depicting the attainment of superior human qualities.

Katamaṃ paccayapaṭisevanasaṅkhātanti ettha paccayapaṭisevananti evaṃ saṅkhātaṃ paccayapaṭisevanasaṅkhātaṃ. Nimantentīti idha gahapatikā “bhikkhaṃ gaṇhathā”ti bhikkhū nimantenti. Ayameva vā pāṭho. “Nimantetī”ti vā “vadantī”ti vā keci paṭhanti. Tādise nimantāpenti. Nimantentīti pāṭhassa sambhavo daṭṭhabbo. Cīvaraṃ paccakkhātīti cīvaraṃ paṭikkhipati. Etaṃ sāruppaṃ, yaṃ samaṇoti yaṃ cīvaradhāraṇaṃ samaṇo karoti, etaṃ sāruppaṃ anucchavikaṃ. Pāpaṇikā vā nantakānīti āpaṇadvāre patikāni antavirahitāni pilotikāni. Uccinitvāti saṃkaḍḍhitvā. Uñchācariyāyāti bhikkhācaraṇena. Piṇḍiyālopenāti piṇḍaṃ katvā laddhaālopena. Pūtimuttena vāti gomuttena [M 0.0293] vā. Osadhaṃ kareyyāti bhesajjakiccaṃ kareyya. Tadupādāyāti tato paṭṭhāya. Dhutavādoti dhutaguṇavādī. Bhiyyo bhiyyo nimantentīti uparūpari nimantenti. Sammukhībhāvāti sammukhībhāvena, vijjamānatāyāti attho. Pasavatīti paṭilabhati. Saddhāya sammukhībhāvena sakkā kātunti “saddhāya sammukhībhāvā”tiādimāha. Deyyadhammā sulabhā dakkhiṇeyyā ca, saddhā pana dullabhā. Puthujjanassa hi saddhā athāvarā, padavāre padavāre nānā hoti. Tenevassa mahāmoggallānasadisopi aggasāvako pāṭibhogo bhavituṃ asakkonto āha “dvinnaṃ kho nesaṃ āvuso dhammānaṃ pāṭibhogo bhogānañca jīvitassa ca, saddhāya pana tvaṃ pāṭibhogo”ti.

What is meant by “acceptance of requisites”? Here, “acceptance of requisites” is thus designated. “They invite”—here, householders invite the monks, saying, “Accept alms.” Or this is the reading. Some read it as “invites” or “speak.” They cause such to invite. The occurrence of the reading “They invite” should be seen. “Refuses the robe” means rejects the robe. “This is suitable” means that the wearing of the robe by a monk is suitable and appropriate. “Or shopkeepers’ rags” means rags at the shop door, without edges or borders, cast-off cloths. “Having picked up” means having gathered together. “By the alms-gathering practice” means by means of wandering for alms. “With a lump of almsfood” means with a lump of food obtained. “Or with rotten urine” means or with cow urine. “Would make medicine” means would perform the duty of medicine. “Depending on that” means starting from that. “A speaker on asceticism” means a speaker on the qualities of the ascetic practices. “They invite more and more” means they invite repeatedly. “Presence” means by means of presence; the meaning is existence. “Attains” means obtains. “It is possible to do” (sakkā kātuṃ) by the presence of faith—thus he said, beginning with “by the presence of faith.” “Offerings are easily obtained, and recipients are worthy, but faith is difficult to obtain. For an ordinary person, faith is unsteady; it varies at every step.” Therefore, even a chief disciple like the venerable Mahāmoggallāna, being unable to be a guarantor, said, “Friend, I can be a guarantor for two things: possessions and life, but you are a guarantor for faith.”

Evaṃ tumhe puññena paribāhirā bhavissathāti ettha puññenāti [P 2.0336] nissakkatthe karaṇavacanaṃ. Puññato parihīnā parammukhā bhavissatha. Bhākuṭikāti mukhānaṃ padhānapurimaṭṭhitabhāvadassanena bhākuṭikaraṇaṃ, mukhasaṅkocoti vuttaṃ hoti. Bhākuṭikaraṇaṃ sīlamassāti bhākuṭiko, bhākuṭikassa bhāvo bhākuṭiyaṃ. Kuhanāti vimhāpanā. Kuhassa āyanā kuhāyanā. Kuhitassa bhāvo kuhitattaṃ.

“Thus, you will be excluded from merit”—here, “by merit” (puññena) is in the instrumental case, meaning “without merit.” Deprived of merit, you will turn away. “Frowning” (bhākuṭikā) refers to the act of making a frown, showing the primary state of the face being contracted—it is called “facial contraction.” One whose habit is to frown is a frowner (bhākuṭiko); the state of a frowner is “frowning” (bhākuṭiyaṃ). “Deceit” (kuhanā) means deception. The source of deceit is “deceptive practice” (kuhāyanā). The state of being deceitful is “deceitfulness” (kuhitattaṃ).

Pāpicchoti [V 0.0269] asantaguṇadīpanakāmo. Icchāpakatoti icchāya apakato, upaddutoti attho. Sambhāvanādhippāyoti bahumānajjhāsayo. Gamanaṃ saṇṭhapetīti abhikkamādigamanaṃ abhisaṅkharoti, pāsādikabhāvaṃ karotīti vuttaṃ hoti. Itaresupi eseva nayo. Paṇidhāya gacchatīti patthanaṃ ṭhapetvā gacchati. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Samāhito viya gacchatīti upacārappatto viya gacchati. Sesesupi eseva nayo.

“One of evil desires” (pāpiccho) is one who wishes to display qualities that are not present. “Icchāpakato” means overcome by desire; afflicted is the meaning. “Sambhāvanādhippāyo” means having the intention of respect. “Gamanaṃ saṇṭhapeti” means he prepares his going forth, etc., making a pleasing impression, it is said. The same applies to the rest. “Paṇidhāya gacchati” means he goes having established an aspiration. The same applies to the rest. “Samāhito viya gacchati” means he goes as if composed. The same applies to the rest.

Āpāthakajjhāyīva hotīti sammukhā āgatānaṃ manussānaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajjanto viya santabhāvaṃ dasseti. Iriyāpathassāti catuiriyāpathassa. Āṭhapanāti ādiṭṭhapanā, ādarena vā ṭhapanā. Ṭhapanāti ṭhapanākāro. Saṇṭhapanāti abhisaṅkharaṇaṃ, pāsādikabhāvakaraṇanti vuttaṃ hoti. Ariyadhammasannissitanti lokuttaradhammapaṭibaddhaṃ. Kuñcikanti avāpuraṇaṃ. Mittāti sinehavanto. Sandiṭṭhāti diṭṭhamattā. Sambhattāti daḷhamittā. Uddaṇḍeti eko patissayaviseso.

“Āpāthakajjhāyīva hoti” means he displays a peaceful demeanor as if entering jhāna in the presence of people who have come before him. “Iriyāpathassa” refers to the four postures. “Āṭhapanā” means initial placing, or placing with care. “Ṭhapanā” means the manner of placing. “Saṇṭhapanā” means preparation; that is, making it dignified. “Ariyadhammasannissita” means connected with the supramundane Dhamma. “Kuñcikā” means unlocking. “Mittā” means affectionate ones. “Sandiṭṭhā” means merely seen. “Sambhattā” means firm friends. “Uddaṇḍa” is a particular kind of support.

Korajikakorajikoti [M 0.0294] saṅkocasaṅkocako, atisaṅkocakoti vuttaṃ hoti. “Koracakakoracako”ti vā pāṭho. Bhākuṭikabhākuṭikoti ativiya mukhasaṅkocanasīlo. Kuhakakuhakoti ativiya vimhāpako. Lapakalapakoti ativiya sallāpako. Mukhasambhāvikoti attano mukhavasena aññehi saha sambhāviko, appitacittoti eke. Santānanti kilesasantatāya santānaṃ. Samāpattīnanti samāpajjitabbānaṃ. Gambhīranti ninnapatiṭṭhānaṃ. Gūḷhanti [P 2.0337] dassetuṃ dukkhaṃ. Nipuṇanti sukhumaṃ. Paṭicchannanti padatthena duppaṭivijjhādhippāyaṃ. Lokuttaranti dhammadīpakaṃ. Suññatāpaṭisaññuttanti nibbānapaṭisaññuttaṃ. Atha vā lokuttarasuññatāpaṭisaññuttanti lokuttaradhammabhūtanibbānapaṭisaññuttaṃ.

“Korajikakorajiko” means shrinking and shrinking; that is to say, extremely shrinking. Alternatively, the reading is “Koracakakoracako.” “Bhākuṭikabhākuṭiko” means one who is very prone to contracting the face. “Kuhakakuhako” means very deceptive. “Lapakalapako” means very talkative. “Mukhasambhāviko” means sociable through one’s own speech; some say it means “with an applied mind.” “Santāna” means the continuity by way of the continuity of defilements. “Samāpattīnaṃ” means of those to be attained. “Gambhīra” means deep-seated. “Gūḷha” means difficult to show. “Nipuṇa” means subtle. “Paṭicchanna” means hidden, with the intention of being hard to penetrate through its meaning. “Lokuttara” means supramundane, illuminating the Dhamma. “Suññatāpaṭisaññutta” means associated with Nibbāna. Or alternatively, “lokuttarasuññatāpaṭisaññutta” means associated with the supramundane Dhamma, which is Nibbāna.

Kāyikaṃ pāgabbhiyanti kāye bhavaṃ kāyikaṃ. Vācasikacetasikesupi eseva nayo. Acittīkārakatoti bahumānakiriyarahito. Anupāhanānaṃ caṅkamantānanti upāhanavirahitānaṃ caṅkamantānaṃ samīpe, anādare vā sāmivacanaṃ. Saupāhanoti upāhanārūḷho hutvā caṅkamati. Nīce caṅkame caṅkamantānanti akataparicchedāya bhūmiyā caṅkamante paricchedaṃ katvā vālukaṃ ākiritvā ālambanaṃ yojetvā katacaṅkame nīcepi caṅkame caṅkamante. Ucce caṅkame caṅkamatīti iṭṭhakacayanasampanne vedikāparikkhitte ucce caṅkame caṅkamati. Sace pākāraparikkhitto hoti dvārakoṭṭhakayutto, pabbatantaravanantarabhūmantarassa vā suppaṭicchanno, tādise caṅkame caṅkamituṃ vaṭṭati, appaṭicchannepi upacāraṃ muñcitvā vaṭṭati. Ghaṭṭayantopi tiṭṭhatīti atisamīpe tiṭṭhati. Puratopi [V 0.0270] tiṭṭhatīti puratthimatopi tiṭṭhati. Ṭhitakopi bhaṇatīti khāṇuko viya anonamitvā bhaṇati. Bāhāvikkhepakoti bāhuṃ khipitvā khipitvā bhaṇati.

“Bodily insolence” is that which occurs in the body. The same method applies to verbal and mental cases. “Without respect” means devoid of respectful action. Regarding “in the presence of those walking without sandals”: this means near those walking without sandals; or, the genitive case is used here in the sense of disrespect. “Wearing sandals” means one walks having put on sandals. Regarding “while they are walking on a low walking path”: this refers to when they are walking on ground with an unmarked boundary, or even on a low walking path that has been prepared by marking a boundary, scattering sand, and setting up a support. “Walks on a high walking path” means one walks on a high walking path well-paved with bricks and enclosed by a railing. If it is enclosed by a wall with gates and gatehouses, or well-concealed between mountains, forests, or lands, it is proper to walk on such a walking path. Even if not concealed, it is proper after leaving the immediate vicinity. “Stands jostling” means one stands excessively near. “Stands in front” means one stands directly in front. “Speaks while standing” means one speaks without bending, like a post. “Waving the arms” means one speaks while repeatedly flinging their arm.

Anupakhajjāti sabbesaṃ nisinnaṭṭhānaṃ pavisitvā. Navepi bhikkhū āsanena paṭibāhatīti attano pattāsane anisīditvā pure vā pacchā vā pavisanto āsanena paṭibāhati nāma.

“Anupakhajja” means having intruded upon the place where all are seated. “Obstructs even new monks with a seat” means that by not sitting in the seat allotted to oneself, but entering before or after, one is said to obstruct with a seat.

Anāpucchampi kaṭṭhaṃ pakkhipatīti anāpucchitvā anapaloketvā aggimhi dāruṃ khipati. Dvāraṃ pidahatīti jantāghare pidahati.

“Without asking, he throws the wood” means without asking permission, without informing, he throws wood into the fire. “He closes the door” means he closes it in the steam room.

Otaratīti [M 0.0295] udakatitthaṃ pavisati. Nhāyatīti sarīraṃ sineheti. Uttaratīti udakatitthato tīraṃ uggacchati.

“He goes down” means he enters the watering place. “He bathes” means he wets his body. “He comes up” means he rises from the watering place to the bank.

Vokkammāpīti atikkamitvāpi. Ovarakānīti gabbhe patiṭṭhitasayanagharāni.

“Vokkammāpi” means even having transgressed. “Inner rooms” are the sleeping rooms established in an interior chamber.

Gūḷhānīti [P 2.0338] paṭicchannāni. Paṭicchannānīti aññehi paṭicchāditāni.

“Gūḷhāni” means concealed. “Paṭicchannāni” means covered by others.

Anajjhiṭṭho vāti therehi “dhammaṃ bhaṇāhī”ti anāṇatto anāyācito ca.

“Or uninvited” means not commanded by the elders with “Teach the Dhamma,” and not requested.

Pāpadhammoti lāmakadhammo. Asucisaṅkasarasamācāroti aññehi “ayaṃ dussīlo”ti saṅkāya saritabbo ācāro saṃyogo etassāti asucisaṅkasarasamācāro. Saṅkassarasamācāroti sakāraṃ saṃyogaṃ katvāpi paṭhanti. Paṭicchannakammantoti paṭicchāditakāyavacīkammanto. Assamaṇoti na samaṇo. Samaṇapaṭiññoti “ahaṃ samaṇo”ti paṭijānanto. Abrahmacārīti seṭṭhacariyā virahito. Brahmacāripaṭiññoti vuttapaṭipakkho. Antopūtīti abbhantare kusaladhammavirahitattā antopūtibhāvamāpanno. Avassutoti rāgena tinto. Kasambujātoti saṅkārasabhāvo.
