Ācāragocarasampannoti ettha bhikkhu sagāravo sappatisso hirottappasampanno sunivattho supāruto pāsādikena abhikkantena paṭikkantena ālokitena vilokitena samiñjitena pasāritena okkhittacakkhu iriyāpathasampanno indriyesu guttadvāro bhojane mattaññū jāgariyamanuyutto satisampajaññena samannāgato appiccho santuṭṭho āraddhavīriyo ābhisamācārikesu sakkaccakārī garucittīkārabahulo viharati, ayaṃ vuccati ācāro. Evaṃ tāva ācāro veditabbo.

“One of evil nature” means one of a base nature. “One whose conduct is impure and suspect” means one whose conduct is connected with what should be remembered with suspicion by others, who think, “This one is immoral.” Some also read this as `Saṅkassarasamācāro`, making a conjunct with the letter 's'. “One with concealed actions” means one whose bodily and verbal actions are concealed. “Not a recluse” means not a recluse. “Claiming to be a recluse” means one who professes, “I am a recluse.” “Not celibate” means one devoid of the noble conduct. “Claiming to be celibate” is the opposite of what has been said. “Rotten within” means one who has reached a state of inner rottenness because of being devoid of wholesome qualities within. “Leaky” means soaked with lust. “A rubbish-heap” means one who has the nature of refuse. “Accomplished in conduct and resort”: Here, a bhikkhu dwells respectful, deferential, possessed of moral shame and fear of wrongdoing, properly attired and robed, graceful in his advancing and returning, in his looking ahead and looking aside, in his bending and stretching; with downcast eyes, accomplished in deportment, with guarded sense faculties, moderate in eating, devoted to wakefulness, possessed of mindfulness and clear comprehension, of few wishes, content, with energy aroused, scrupulous in the elementary rules of conduct, and full of reverence and respect. This is called conduct. Thus, conduct should be understood in this way.

Gocaro [V 0.0271] pana tividho upanissayagocaro ārakkhagocaro upanibandhagocaroti. Tattha katamo upanissayagocaro? Dasakathāvatthuguṇasamannāgato kalyāṇamitto, yaṃ nissāya assutaṃ suṇāti, sutaṃ pariyodāpeti, kaṅkhaṃ vitarati, diṭṭhiṃ ujuṃ karoti, cittaṃ pasādeti; yassa vā pana anusikkhamāno saddhāya vaḍḍhati, sīlena, sutena, cāgena, paññāya vaḍḍhati. Ayaṃ vuccati upanissayagocaro.

The resort, however, is threefold: the resort of support, the resort of protection, and the resort of binding. Herein, what is the resort of support? A good friend endowed with the qualities of the ten topics of talk, by relying on whom one hears what has not been heard, clarifies what has been heard, dispels doubt, straightens one's view, and gladdens the mind; or one who, by training in conformity with him, grows in faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom. This is called the resort of support.

Katamo [M 0.0296] ārakkhagocaro? Idha bhikkhu antaragharaṃ paviṭṭho vīthiṃ paṭipanno okkhittacakkhu yugamattadassāvī susaṃvuto gacchati, na hatthiṃ olokento, na assaṃ, na rathaṃ, na pattiṃ, na itthiṃ, na purisaṃ olokento, na uddhaṃ ullokento, na [P 2.0339] adho olokento, na disāvidisaṃ pekkhamāno gacchati. Ayaṃ vuccati ārakkhagocaro.

What is the resort of protection? Here, a bhikkhu who has entered a village or is walking along a street goes with his eyes lowered, seeing only a yoke's length ahead, well-restrained. He does not go along looking at an elephant, a horse, a chariot, an infantryman, a woman, or a man; he does not go along looking up, looking down, or gazing around in the various directions. This is called the resort of protection.

Katamo upanibandhagocaro? Cattāro satipaṭṭhānā yattha cittaṃ upanibandhati. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā – “ko ca, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno gocaro sako pettiko visayo? Yadidaṃ cattāro satipaṭṭhānā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.372), ayaṃ vuccati upanibandhagocaroti. Iti iminā ca ācārena iminā ca gocarena upeto…pe… samannāgato. Tenapi vuccati ācāragocarasampannoti.

What is the resort of binding? The four establishments of mindfulness, to which the mind is bound. For this has been said by the Blessed One: “And what, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu's own resort, his native ancestral domain? It is these four establishments of mindfulness” (SN 47.6). This is called the resort of binding. Thus, he is endowed with this conduct and this resort... possessed of it. Therefore, he is called one who is accomplished in conduct and resort.

Aṇumattesu vajjesu bhayadassāvīti aṇuppamāṇesu asañcicca āpannasekhiyaakusalacittuppādādibhedesu vajjesu bhayadassanasīlo. Samādāya sikkhati sikkhāpadesūti yaṃkiñci sikkhāpadesu sikkhitabbaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ sammā ādāya sikkhati. Ettha ca “pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto”ti ettāvatā ca puggalādhiṭṭhānāya desanāya pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlaṃ dassitaṃ. “Ācāragocarasampanno”tiādi pana sabbaṃ yathāpaṭipannassa taṃ sīlaṃ sampajjati, taṃ paṭipattiṃ dassetuṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

“One who sees danger in the slightest faults”: this refers to one who is disposed to see danger in even the slightest faults, such as unintentionally incurred training rules or the arising of unwholesome states of mind. “He trains by undertaking the training rules”: whatever has to be trained in among the training rules, all that he undertakes properly and trains in. Here, by “restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha,” the Pātimokkha-restraint virtue is shown as a teaching based on the person. But “accomplished in conduct and resort,” and so on, should all be understood as stated to show the practice by which that virtue is accomplished for one who practices accordingly.

88. Sātiyesu anassāvīti sātavatthūsu kāmaguṇesu taṇhāsanthavavirahito. Saṇhoti saṇhehi kāyakammādīhi samannāgato. Paṭibhānavāti pariyattiparipucchādhigamapaṭibhānehi samannāgato. Na saddhoti sāmaṃ adhigatadhammaṃ na kassaci saddahati. Na virajjatīti khayā rāgassa virattattā idāni na virajjati.

88. "Not drawn to pleasures" means being devoid of the intimacy of craving for pleasant things, the cords of sensual pleasure. "Gentle" means endowed with gentle bodily actions and so forth. "Possessed of ready wit" means endowed with the ready wit of learning, questioning, and realization. "Not credulous" means not placing faith in anyone concerning the Dhamma one has realized for oneself. "Does not become dispassionate" means that because one is already dispassionate through the destruction of lust, one does not become dispassionate now.

Yesaṃ esāti yesaṃ puggalānaṃ sātavatthūsu kāmaguṇesu icchā taṇhā. Appahīnāti santhavasampayuttā [V 0.0272] taṇhā arahattamaggena appahīnā. Tesaṃ cakkhuto rūpataṇhā savatīti etesaṃ cakkhudvārato pavattajavanavīthisampayuttā rūpārammaṇā taṇhā uppajjati. Āsavatīti okāsato yāva bhavaggā dhammato yāva gotrabhū savati. Sandatīti nadīsotaṃ viya adhomukhaṃ sandati. Pavattatīti punappunaṃ uppattivasena [M 0.0297] pavattati. Sesadvāresupi eseva nayo. Sukkapakkhe vuttavipariyāyena taṇhā arahattamaggena suppahīnā. Tesaṃ cakkhuto rūpataṇhā na savati.

"For whom this exists": for those persons in whom there is desire and craving for pleasant things, the cords of sensual pleasure. "Is not abandoned": the craving associated with intimacy is not abandoned by the path of arahantship. "For them, craving for forms flows from the eye": for these persons, craving having visible forms as its object arises, associated with the cognitive process of impulsion occurring through the eye-door. "It flows out": in terms of location, it flows up to the peak of existence; in terms of phenomena, it flows up to the change-of-lineage moment. "It streams": it streams downwards like a river current. "It occurs": it continues by way of repeated arising. The same method applies to the remaining sense-doors. In the bright counterpart, by the reverse of what was said, craving is well abandoned by the path of arahantship. For them, craving for forms does not flow from the eye.

Saṇhena [P 2.0340] kāyakammena samannāgatoti apharusena mudunā kāyakammena samaṅgībhūto ekībhūto. Vacīkammādīsupi eseva nayo. Saṇhehi satipaṭṭhānehītiādīsu satipaṭṭhānādayo lokiyalokuttaramissakā. Pariyāpuṇanaatthādiparipucchālokiyalokuttaradhammādhigamavasena sallakkhaṇavibhāvanavavatthānakaraṇasamatthā tisso paṭibhānappabhedasaṅkhātā paññā yassa atthi, so paṭibhānavā. Tassa pariyattiṃ nissāya paṭibhāyatīti tassa puggalassa pariyāpuṇanaṃ allīyitvā ñāṇaṃ jāyati ñāṇaṃ abhimukhaṃ hoti. Cattāro satipaṭṭhānāti sattatiṃsa bodhipakkhiyadhammā lokiyalokuttaramissakavasena vuttā. Maggaphalāni nibbattitalokuttaravasena. Catasso paṭisambhidāyo cha ca abhiññāyo vimokkhantikavasena vuttāti ñātabbā.

"Endowed with gentle bodily action" means being possessed of and united with non-harsh, soft bodily action. The same method applies to verbal action and so on. Regarding "with gentle establishments of mindfulness," etc., the establishments of mindfulness and so on are a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane. One who possesses the three kinds of wisdom reckoned as the varieties of ready wit—being capable of discerning, analyzing, and defining by way of learning, questioning about meaning, and realizing mundane and supramundane states—is "possessed of ready wit." "For that person, it becomes clear in reliance on their learning": for that person, knowledge arises and becomes manifest, adhering to their learning. "The four establishments of mindfulness" refers to the thirty-seven aids to enlightenment, spoken of as a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane. The paths and fruits are spoken of by way of the produced supramundane. The four analytical knowledges and the six direct knowledges should be known as being spoken of as culminating in liberation.

Tattha catasso paṭisambhidāyoti cattāro ñāṇappabhedāti attho. Iddhividhādiāsavakkhayapariyosānāni adhikāni cha ñāṇāni. Tassāti parassa, attho paṭibhāyatīti sambandho. Atthoti saṅkhepato hetuphalaṃ. Tañhi yasmā hetuanusārena arīyati adhigamīyati pāpuṇīyati, tasmā atthoti vuccati. Pabhedato pana yaṃkiñci paccayuppannaṃ nibbānaṃ bhāsitattho vipāko kiriyāti ime pañca dhammā atthoti veditabbā, taṃ atthaṃ paccavekkhantassa so attho pabhedato ñāto pākaṭo hoti. Dhammoti saṅkhepato paccayo. So hi yasmā taṃ taṃ vidahati pavatteti ceva pāpeti ca, tasmā dhammoti vuccati. Pabhedato pana yo koci phalanibbattako hetu ariyamaggo bhāsitaṃ kusalaṃ akusalanti ime pañca dhammā dhammoti veditabbā, taṃ dhammaṃ paccavekkhantassa so dhammo pabhedato ñāto pākaṭo hoti, tasmiṃ atthe ca dhamme ca yā sabhāvanirutti abyabhicārī vohāro, tassa abhilāpe bhāsane udīraṇe taṃ lapitaṃ bhāsitaṃ udīritaṃ sabhāvaniruttisaddaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā paccavekkhantassa sā nirutti ñātā pākaṭā hoti.

Herein, "the four analytical knowledges" means the four kinds of knowledge. The six supernormal knowledges are the additional knowledges beginning with the kinds of spiritual power and ending with the destruction of the taints. The connection is: "the meaning becomes clear to that one (tassa)," that is, to another. "Meaning" (attha), in brief, is effect. Since it is approached (arīyati), attained (adhigamīyati), and reached (pāpuṇīyati) in accordance with a cause, it is called "meaning." In detail, these five things should be understood as "meaning": whatever is conditionally arisen, Nibbāna, the meaning of what is spoken, result, and functional consciousness. When one reviews that meaning, it becomes known and manifest in detail. "Dhamma," in brief, is cause. Since it determines (vidahati), sets going (pavatteti), and brings about (pāpeti) this and that, it is called "Dhamma." In detail, these five things should be understood as "Dhamma": any cause that produces a result, the noble path, what is spoken, the wholesome, and the unwholesome. When one reviews that Dhamma, it becomes known and manifest in detail. Regarding that meaning and Dhamma, there is the natural language (sabhāvanirutti), the unerring mode of expression. When one reviews this by making the utterance, the speech, the articulated sound of that natural language the object, that language becomes known and manifest.

Ettha [M 0.0298] atthe ñāte attho paṭibhāyatīti idāni tassa saddaṃ āharitvā vuttappabhede atthe pākaṭībhūte vuttappabhedo [P 2.0341] attho tassa puggalassa paṭibhāyati ñāṇābhimukho hoti. Dhamme ñāte [V 0.0273] dhammo paṭibhāyatīti vuttappabhede dhamme pākaṭībhūte vuttappabhedo dhammo paṭibhāyati. Niruttiyā ñātāya nirutti paṭibhāyatīti vuttappabhedāya niruttiyā pākaṭāya vuttappabhedā nirutti paṭibhāyati. Imesu tīsu ñāṇesu ñāṇanti atthadhammaniruttīsu imesu tīsu sabbatthakañāṇamārammaṇaṃ katvā paccavekkhantassa tesu tīsu ñāṇesu pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ, yathāvuttesu vā tesu tīsu ñāṇesu gocarakiccādivasena vitthāragataṃ ñāṇaṃ paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā. Imāya paṭibhānapaṭisambhidāyāti imāya vuttappakārāya yathāvuttavitthārapaññāya upeto hoti. So vuccati paṭibhānavāti nigamento āha. Yassa pariyatti natthīti pariyatti nāma buddhavacanaṃ. Tañhi uggaṇhantassa paṭisambhidā visadā honti. Yassa puggalassa evarūpā pariyatti natthi. Paripucchā natthīti paripucchā nāma pāḷiaṭṭhakathādīsu gaṇṭhipadaatthapadavinicchayakathā. Uggahitapāḷiādīsu hi atthaṃ kathentassa paṭisambhidā visadā honti. Adhigamo natthīti adhigamo nāma arahattappatti. Arahattañhi pattassa paṭisambhidā visadā honti. Yassa vuttappakārā tividhā sampatti natthi. Kiṃ tassa paṭibhāyissatīti kena kāraṇena tassa puggalassa pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ upaṭṭhahissati.

Here, when the meaning is known, the meaning becomes manifest. Now, having adduced the word for it, when the meaning with its stated distinctions becomes evident, the stated distinctions of meaning become manifest to that person, and they become directed towards knowledge. When the Dhamma is known, the Dhamma becomes manifest. When the Dhamma with its stated distinctions becomes evident, the stated distinctions of the Dhamma become manifest. When the language is known, the language becomes manifest. When the language with its stated distinctions becomes evident, the stated distinctions of the language become manifest. Among these three knowledges—knowledge of meaning, Dhamma, and language—the knowledge that becomes manifest in its distinctions to one who reviews, having made all-encompassing knowledge its object, or the knowledge that is detailed in terms of its scope, function, etc., in these three knowledges as stated, is the analytical knowledge of discernment (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā). Endowed with this analytical knowledge of discernment—that is, with the wisdom detailed as stated—one is called 'one with discernment,' as the concluding statement says. For one who has no learning—learning here refers to the words of the Buddha. Indeed, for one who learns that, the analytical knowledges become clear. For a person who has no such learning, who has no questioning—questioning here refers to discussions on resolving the meaning of difficult words and phrases in the Pali, commentaries, and so on. Indeed, for one who explains the meaning in the learned Pali texts, the analytical knowledges become clear. Who has no attainment—attainment here refers to the realization of arahantship. Indeed, for one who has attained arahantship, the analytical knowledges become clear. For one who lacks these threefold accomplishments as described—what will become manifest to them? By what means will the knowledge in its distinctions arise for that person?

Sāmanti sayameva. Sayaṃ abhiññātanti sayameva tena ñāṇena avagamitaṃ. Attapaccakkhaṃ dhammanti attanā paṭivijjhitaṃ paccavekkhitaṃ dhammaṃ. Na kassaci saddahatīti attapaccakkhatāya paresaṃ na saddahati, saddhāya na gacchati. Avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārātiādikaṃ dvādasapadikapaccayākāradassanavasena vuttaṃ. Avijjānirodhātiādayo saṃsāranivattiṃ sandhāya vuttā. Idaṃ dukkhantiādi saccadassanavasena. Ime āsavātiādayo aparena pariyāyena kilesavasena paccayadassanavasena. Ime dhammā abhiññeyyātiādayo abhiññeyyapariññeyyapahātabbabhāvetabbasacchikātabbadhammānaṃ dassanavasena. Channaṃ phassāyatanānantiādayo phassāyatanānaṃ uppattiñca atthaṅgamañca assādañca [P 2.0342] upaddavañca nissaraṇañca dassanavasena. Pañcannaṃ upādānakkhandhānaṃ pañcavīsatividhena udayañca vayañca, tesu chandarāgavasena [M 0.0299] assādañca, tesaṃ vipariṇāmaṃ ādīnavañca, nissaraṇasaṅkhātaṃ nibbānañca. Catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ avijjādisamudayañca, avijjādinirodhe atthaṅgamañca evamādidassanavasena vuttā. Ete dhammā tattha tattha vuttanayena veditabbā.

"Sāma" means by oneself. "Self-directly known" (sayaṃ abhiññāta) means it is understood by that very knowledge. "Directly experienced Dhamma" (attapaccakkhaṃ dhamma) refers to the Dhamma personally penetrated and contemplated. "Does not believe anyone else" (na kassaci saddahati) means that, due to direct personal experience, one does not believe others, nor does one proceed by faith. "Dependent on ignorance, formations arise" (avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā) and so forth is stated to show the mode of conditionality through the twelve factors. "With the cessation of ignorance" (avijjānirodha) and so on refers to the cessation of the cycle of existence. "This is suffering" (idaṃ dukkhaṃ) and so on is stated to show the truth. "These taints" (ime āsavā) and so on, in another way, show the defilements as the mode of conditionality. "These phenomena are to be directly known" (ime dhammā abhiññeyyā) and so on show the phenomena to be directly known, fully understood, abandoned, developed, and realized. "The six sense bases" (channaṃ phassāyatanānaṃ) and so on show the arising and passing away of the sense bases, their gratification, danger, and escape. "The five aggregates subject to clinging" (pañcannaṃ upādānakkhandhānaṃ) show their twenty-fivefold arising and passing away, their gratification through desire and lust, their drawback through change, and the escape, which is Nibbāna. "The four great elements" (catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ) show their origin through ignorance and so on, and their cessation through the cessation of ignorance, and so on. These phenomena should be understood in the way they are explained in each case.

Amatogadhanti natthi etassa maraṇasaṅkhātaṃ matanti amataṃ. Kilesavisapaṭipakkhattā agadantipi amataṃ. Tasmiṃ ninnatāya amatogadhaṃ. Amataparāyananti vuttappakāraṃ amataṃ paraṃ ayanaṃ [V 0.0274] gati patiṭṭhā assāti amataparāyanaṃ. Amatapariyosānanti taṃ amataṃ saṃsārassa niṭṭhābhūtattā pariyosānamassāti amatapariyosānaṃ.

"Plunged into the Deathless" (amatogadha) means: that for which there is no such thing as death is the Deathless (amata). Because it is an antidote (agada) to the poison of the defilements, it is also the Deathless. Being plunged into that, it is "plunged into the Deathless." "The Deathless as ultimate resort" (amataparāyana) means that the Deathless, as described, is one's ultimate resort, destination, and support; thus, it is "the Deathless as ultimate resort." "The Deathless as final end" (amatapariyosāna) means that the Deathless is the final end of saṃsāra for one; thus, it is "the Deathless as final end."

89. Lābhakamyā na sikkhatīti lābhapatthanāya suttantādīni na sikkhati. Aviruddho ca taṇhāya, rasesu nānugijjhatīti virodhābhāvena ca aviruddho hutvā taṇhāya mūlarasādīsu gedhaṃ nāpajjati.

89. "One does not train out of a desire for gain" (lābhakamyā na sikkhati) means one does not study the discourses and so on with a desire for gain. "And, not being in conflict through craving, one is not greedy for flavors" (aviruddho ca taṇhāya, rasesu nānugijjhati) means that, being without conflict due to an absence of opposition, one does not, through craving, become greedy for root-flavors and so on.

Kena nu khoti lābhapatthanāya kāraṇacintena pihassa pariyesane nipāto. Lābhābhinibbattiyāti catunnaṃ paccayānaṃ visesena uppattiyā. Lābhaṃ paripācentoti paccaye paripācayanto.

The phrase "Kena nu kho" is a particle indicating a search or longing, with consideration of the cause for desiring gain. "By the generation of gain" (lābhābhinibbattiyā) means by the special arising of the four requisites. "Ripening gain" (lābhaṃ paripācento) means causing the requisites to ripen.

Attadamatthāyāti vipassanāsampayuttāya paññāya attano damanatthāya. Attasamatthāyāti samādhisampayuttāya paññāya attano samādhānatthāya. Attaparinibbāpanatthāyāti duvidhenāpi ñāṇena attano anupādāparinibbānatthāya. Vuttañhetaṃ “anupādāparinibbānatthaṃ kho āvuso bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.259). Appicchaññeva nissāyāti ettha paccayaappiccho adhigamaappiccho pariyattiappiccho dhutaṅgaappicchoti cattāro appicchā, tesaṃ nānatthaṃ heṭṭhā vitthāritaṃ eva, taṃ appicchaṃ allīyitvā. Santuṭṭhiññevāti catūsu paccayesu ca tividhaṃ santosaṃ allīyitvā, etesaṃ vibhāgo heṭṭhā vitthāritoyeva. Sallekhaññevāti kilesalekhanaṃ. Idamatthitaññevāti imehi kusaladhammehi [P 2.0343] atthi idamatthi, tassa bhāvo idamatthitā, taṃ idamatthitaṃyeva nissāya allīyitvā.

"For self-taming" (attadamatthāya) means for the purpose of taming oneself with wisdom associated with insight. "For self-composure" (attasamatthāya) means for the purpose of composing oneself with wisdom associated with concentration. "For self-extinguishment" (attaparinibbāpanatthāya) means for the purpose of one's own extinguishment without clinging, through both kinds of knowledge. For this is said: "Indeed, friend, the holy life is lived under the Blessed One for the purpose of extinguishment without clinging" (MN 29). "Relying solely on having few desires" (appicchaññeva nissāya): here, there are four kinds of having few desires—having few desires regarding requisites, attainments, learning, and ascetic practices; their different meanings have been explained in detail below; this means adhering to that quality of having few desires. "Relying solely on contentment" (santuṭṭhiññevāti): this means adhering to contentment with the four requisites and the threefold contentment; their distinctions have been explained in detail below. "Relying solely on effacement" (sallekhaññevāti): this means the effacement of defilements. "Relying solely on this being the case" (idamatthitaññevāti): by means of these wholesome qualities, 'there is this'; the state of that is 'this-ness' (idamatthitā); this means relying solely on and adhering to that state of 'this being the case'.

Rasoti niddesassa uddesapadaṃ. Mūlarasoti yaṃkiñci mūlaṃ paṭicca nibbattaraso. Khandharasādīsupi eseva nayo. Ambilanti takkambilādi. Madhuranti [M 0.0300] ekantato gosappiādi. Madhu pana kasāvayuttaṃ ciranikkhittaṃ kasāvaṃ hoti, phāṇitaṃ khāriyuttaṃ ciranikkhittaṃ khāriyaṃ hoti. Sappi pana ciranikkhittaṃ vaṇṇagandhe jahantampi rasaṃ na jahatīti tadeva ekantamadhuraṃ. Tittakanti nimbapaṇṇādi. Kaṭukanti siṅgiveramaricādi. Loṇikanti sāmuddikaloṇādi. Khārikanti vātiṅgaṇakaḷīrādi. Lambikanti badarāmalakakapiṭṭhasālavādi. Kasāvanti harītakādi. Ime sabbepi rasā vatthuvasena vuttā. Taṃtaṃvatthuko panettha raso ca ambilādīni nāmehi vuttoti veditabbo. Sādūti iṭṭharaso. Asādūti aniṭṭharaso. Iminā padadvayena sabbopi raso pariyādinno. Sītanti sītaraso. Uṇhanti [V 0.0275] uṇharaso. Evamayaṃ mūlarasādinā bhedena bhinnopi raso lakkhaṇādīhi abhinnoyeva. Sabbopi hesa jivhāpaṭihananalakkhaṇo, jivhāviññāṇassa visayabhāvaraso, tasseva gocarapaccupaṭṭhāno. Te jivhaggena rasaggānīti ete samaṇabrāhmaṇā pasādajivhaggena uttamarasāni. Pariyesantāti gavesamānā. Āhiṇḍantīti tattha tattha vicaranti. Te ambilaṃ labhitvā anambilaṃ pariyesantīti takkādiambilaṃ laddhā anambilaṃ gavesanti. Evaṃ sabbaṃ parivattetvā parivattetvā yojitaṃ.

"Taste" (rasa) is the introductory word for the explanation. "Root taste" (mūlarasa) refers to any taste that arises dependent on a root. The same method applies to the tastes of the trunk and so forth. "Sour" (ambila) refers to sour buttermilk and the like. "Sweet" (madhura) refers exclusively to cow’s ghee and such. However, honey mixed with astringency, when left for a long time, becomes astringent; molasses mixed with alkali, when left for a long time, becomes alkaline. But ghee, even when left for a long time and losing its color and smell, does not lose its taste—thus, it remains purely sweet. "Bitter" (tittaka) refers to neem leaves and the like. "Pungent" (kaṭuka) refers to ginger, pepper, and the like. "Salty" (loṇika) refers to sea salt and the like. "Alkaline" (khārika) refers to eggplant, bamboo shoots, and the like. "Acidulous" (lambika) refers to jujube, emblic myrobalan, wood apple, sālava fruit, and the like. "Astringent" (kasāva) refers to myrobalan and the like. All these tastes are mentioned based on their substances. Here, the taste should be understood as being named according to its respective substance, such as sour and so on. "Pleasant" (sādu) refers to an agreeable taste. "Unpleasant" (asādu) refers to a disagreeable taste. With these two terms, all tastes are encompassed. "Cool" (sīta) refers to a cool taste. "Hot" (uṇha) refers to a hot taste. Thus, although taste is divided by distinctions such as root taste and so on, it remains undifferentiated in terms of characteristics and so forth. For all these have the characteristic of striking the tongue, the function of being the object of tongue-consciousness, and the manifestation as the domain of that same consciousness. "They, with the tip of their tongues, the best of tastes" (Te jivhaggena rasaggāni): these ascetics and brahmins, with the sensitive tongue, seek the highest tastes. "Searching" (pariyesantā) means seeking. "Wandering about" (āhiṇḍanti) means moving from place to place. "Having obtained sour, they seek the non-sour" means having obtained sour buttermilk and other sour things, they search for the non-sour. In this way, everything should be applied by turning it over and over.

Paṭisaṅkhā yoniso āhāraṃ āhāretīti paṭisaṅkhānapaññāya jānitvā upāyena āhāraṃ āhāreti. Idāni upāyaṃ dassetuṃ “neva davāyā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

"Reflecting wisely, one consumes food" (paṭisaṅkhā yoniso āhāraṃ āhāreti) means that, knowing by the wisdom of reflection, one consumes food by means of a proper method. Now, to explain this method, the phrase "neither for amusement" and so forth is stated.

Tattha neva davāyāti davatthāya na āhāreti. Tattha naṭalaṅghakādayo davatthāya āhārenti nāma. Yañhi bhojanaṃ bhuttassa naccagītakabbasilokasaṅkhāto davo atirekatarena paṭibhāti, taṃ bhojanaṃ adhammena visamena pariyesitvā te āhārenti. Ayaṃ pana bhikkhu na evamāhāreti.

Here, "not for amusement" (neva davāya) means one does not eat for the sake of amusement. In this regard, dancers, acrobats, and the like are said to eat for the sake of amusement. For they seek out food that, when eaten, excessively stimulates amusement consisting of dancing, singing, poetry, and verses—food obtained through improper and unrighteous means. But this monk does not eat in such a way.

Na [P 2.0344] madāyāti mānamadapurisamadānaṃ vaḍḍhanatthāya na āhāreti. Tattha rājarājamahāmattā madatthāya āhārenti nāma. Te hi attano mānamadapurisamadānaṃ vaḍḍhanatthāya piṇḍarasabhojanādīni paṇītabhojanāni bhuñjanti. Ayaṃ pana bhikkhu evaṃ nāhāreti.

"Not for intoxication" (na madāya) means one does not eat to increase pride, arrogance, or stoutness. Here, kings and royal ministers are said to eat for the sake of intoxication. They consume fine foods, such as rich dishes and other delicacies, to inflate their pride, arrogance, and stoutness. But this monk does not eat in such a way.

Na [M 0.0301] maṇḍanāyāti sarīramaṇḍanatthāya na āhāreti. Tattha rūpūpajīviniyo mātugāmā antepurikādayo ca sappiphāṇitādīni pivanti, siniddhamudumaddavabhojanaṃ āhārenti. Evaṃ no aṅgalaṭṭhi susaṇṭhitā bhavissati, sarīre chavivaṇṇo pasanno bhavissatīti. Ayaṃ pana bhikkhu evaṃ na āhāreti.

"Not for adornment" (na maṇḍanāya) means not eating for the sake of bodily adornment. Here, women who live by their beauty, such as palace women and the like, drink ghee, molasses, and so on, and eat rich, soft, and tender food, thinking, "Thus our bodies will be well-formed, and the complexion of our skin will be clear." But this monk does not eat in such a way.

Na vibhūsanāyāti sarīre maṃsavibhūsanatthāya na āhāreti. Tattha nibbuddhamallamuṭṭhikamallaceṭakādayo susiniddhehi macchamaṃsādīhi sarīraṃ pīṇenti “evaṃ no maṃsaṃ ussadaṃ bhavissati pahārasahanatthāyā”ti. Ayaṃ pana bhikkhu evaṃ sarīre maṃsavibhūsanatthāya na āhāreti.

"Not for beautification" (na vibhūsanāya) means one does not eat to enhance the flesh of the body. Here, wrestlers, boxers, athletes, and the like nourish their bodies with very rich fish, meat, and so on, thinking, "Thus our flesh will be abundant and able to endure blows." But this monk does not eat for the sake of beautifying the body with flesh.

Yāvadevāti āhārāharaṇapayojanassa paricchedaniyamadassanaṃ. Imassa kāyassa ṭhitiyāti imassa [V 0.0276] catumahābhūtikassa karajakāyassa ṭhapanatthāya āhāreti, idamassa āhārāharaṇe payojananti attho. Yāpanāyāti jīvitindriyayāpanatthāya āhāreti. Vihiṃsūparatiyāti vihiṃsā nāma abhuttapaccayā uppajjanakakhuddā, tassā uparatiyā vūpasamanatthāya āhāreti. Brahmacariyānuggahāyāti brahmacariyaṃ nāma tisso sikkhā sakalasāsanaṃ, tassa anuggaṇhatthāya āhāreti.

"Only for..." (yāvadeva) shows the limit and rule regarding the purpose of consuming food. "For the maintenance of this body" means one eats for the support of this material body composed of the four great elements; this is the purpose in consuming food. "For its continuance" means one eats for the continuation of the life faculty. "For the cessation of affliction" means one eats for the cessation and appeasement of the affliction, namely the hunger that arises from not having eaten. "For the support of the holy life" means one eats for the support of the holy life, which consists of the three trainings and the entire teaching.

Itīti upāyanidassanaṃ, iminā upāyenāti attho. Purāṇañca vedanaṃ paṭihaṅkhāmīti purāṇavedanaṃ nāma abhuttapaccayā uppajjanakavedanā, taṃ paṭihanissāmīti āhāreti. Navañca vedanaṃ na uppādessāmīti navavedanā nāma atibhuttapaccayena uppajjanakavedanā, na taṃ uppādessāmīti āhāreti. Atha vā navavedanā nāma bhuttapaccayā na uppajjanakavedanā, tassā anuppannāya anuppajjanatthameva āhāreti.

"Thus" (iti) is a demonstration of the method; the meaning is "by this method." "I shall ward off old feeling": old feeling means the feeling that arises from not having eaten; one eats thinking, "I shall ward it off." "And I shall not generate new feeling": new feeling means the feeling that arises from overeating; one eats thinking, "I shall not generate it." Or alternatively, "new feeling" means a feeling that should not be produced on account of eating; one eats for the very purpose of not producing that which has not yet arisen.

Yātrā ca me bhavissatīti yāpanā ca me bhavissati. Anavajjatā cāti ettha atthi sāvajjaṃ, atthi anavajjaṃ. Tattha adhammikapariyesanā adhammikapaṭiggahaṇaṃ adhammena paribhogoti idaṃ sāvajjaṃ nāma. Dhammena pana pariyesitvā [P 2.0345] dhammena paṭiggahetvā paccavekkhitvā paribhuñjanaṃ anavajjaṃ nāma. Ekacco anavajjeyeva sāvajjaṃ karoti, “laddhaṃ me”ti katvā pamāṇātikkantaṃ [M 0.0302] bhuñjati, taṃ jīrāpetuṃ asakkonto uddhaṃvirecanaadhovirecanādīhi kilamati, sakalavihāre bhikkhū tassa sarīrapaṭijagganabhesajjapariyesanādīsu ussukkaṃ āpajjanti, “kiṃ ida”nti vutte “asukassa nāma udaraṃ uddhumāta”ntiādiṃ vadanti. “Esa niccakālampi evaṃ pakatikoyeva, attano kucchippamāṇaṃ nāma na jānātī”ti nindanti garahanti. Ayaṃ anavajjeyeva sāvajjaṃ karoti nāma. Evaṃ akatvā “anavajjatā ca me bhavissatī”ti āhāreti.

'And there will be sustenance for me' means 'and there will be maintenance for me'. And regarding 'blamelessness'—here, there is what is blameworthy and what is blameless. In this regard, seeking unrighteously, receiving unrighteously, and consuming unrighteously—this is called blameworthy. But seeking righteously, receiving righteously, and consuming after careful consideration—this is called blameless. Some, even with what is blameless, do what is blameworthy. Thinking, 'I have obtained,' they consume beyond measure. Unable to digest it, they suffer, struggling with emetics, purgatives, and so on. Throughout the monastery, monks become anxious, tending to his body, searching for medicine, and so on. When asked, 'What is this?' they say, 'So-and-so's stomach is bloated,' and so forth. They criticize and reproach him, saying, 'This one is always like this by nature. He does not even know the measure of his own stomach.' This is called doing what is blameworthy even with what is blameless. Not acting thus, one eats with the thought, 'May there be blamelessness for me.'

Phāsuvihāro cāti etthāpi atthi phāsuvihāro, atthi na phāsuvihāro. Tattha āharahatthako alaṃsāṭako tatravaṭṭako kākamāsako bhuttavamitakoti imesaṃ pañcannaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ bhojanaṃ na phāsuvihāro nāma. Etesu hi āharahatthako nāma bahuṃ bhuñjitvā attano dhammatāya uṭṭhātuṃ asakkonto “āhara hattha”nti vadati. Alaṃsāṭako nāma accuddhumātakucchitāya uṭṭhitopi sāṭakaṃ nivāsetuṃ na sakkoti. Tatravaṭṭako nāma uṭṭhātuṃ asakkonto tatreva parivaṭṭati. Kākamāsako nāma yathā kākehi āmasituṃ sakkoti, evaṃ yāva mukhadvārā āhāreti. Bhuttavamitako nāma mukhena sandhāretuṃ asakkonto tattheva vamati. Evaṃ [V 0.0277] akatvā “phāsuvihāro ca me bhavissatī”ti āhāreti. Phāsuvihāro nāma catūhi pañcahi ālopeti ūnūdaratā. Ettakañhi bhuñjitvā pānīyaṃ pivato cattāro iriyāpathā sukhena pavattanti. Tasmā dhammasenāpati evamāha –

And regarding 'comfortable living,' there is comfortable living and there is uncomfortable living. Here, the eating of five brahmins—the 'bring-hand' brahmin, the 'enough-cloth' brahmin, the 'turn-around' brahmin, the 'crow-pecked' brahmin, and the 'eaten-vomit' brahmin—is called uncomfortable living. For among them: the 'bring-hand' brahmin, after eating much, is unable to rise in his normal way and says, 'Bring a hand!'; the 'enough-cloth' brahmin, with a bloated belly, even when he has risen, cannot wrap his cloth around himself; the 'turn-around' brahmin, unable to rise, just rolls around in the same place; the 'crow-pecked' brahmin eats until his mouth is so full that crows could peck at the food; the 'eaten-vomit' brahmin, unable to hold it in his mouth, vomits right there. Not acting thus, one eats thinking, 'May there be comfortable living for me.' Comfortable living is eating so as to be less than full by four or five mouthfuls. For when one eats this much and drinks water, the four postures proceed with ease. Therefore, the General of the Dhamma has said:

“Cattāro pañca ālope, abhutvā udakaṃ pive;

Alaṃ phāsuvihārāya, pahitattassa bhikkhuno”ti. (theragā. 983; mi. pa. 6.5.10);

Leaving four or five mouthfuls uneaten, one should drink water; this is sufficient for the comfortable abiding of a resolute bhikkhu.

Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne aṅgāni samodhānetabbāni. Neva davāyāti hi ekaṃ aṅgaṃ, na madāyāti ekaṃ, na maṇḍanāyāti ekaṃ, na vibhūsanāyāti ekaṃ, yāvadeva imassa kāyassa ṭhitiyā yāpanāyāti ekaṃ, vihiṃsūparatiyā brahmacariyānuggahāyāti ekaṃ, iti purāṇañca vedanaṃ paṭihaṅkhāmi navañca [P 2.0346] vedanaṃ na uppādessāmīti ekaṃ, yātrā ca me bhavissatīti ekaṃ aṅgaṃ, anavajjatā ca phāsuvihāro cāti ayamettha bhojanānisaṃso.

In this context, the factors should be combined: 'Not for pleasure' is one factor; 'not for intoxication' is another; 'not for adornment' is another; 'not for embellishment' is another; 'merely for the maintenance and sustenance of this body' is another; 'for the cessation of harm and for the support of the holy life' is another; 'thus I shall dispel old feelings and not arouse new feelings' is another; and 'there will be sustenance for me' is another factor. As for 'blamelessness and comfortable living,' this is the benefit of the meal here.

Mahāsivatthero [M 0.0303] panāha – “heṭṭhā cattāri aṅgāni paṭikkhepo nāma, upari pana aṭṭhaṅgāni samodhānetabbānī”ti. Tattha yāvadeva imassa kāyassa ṭhitiyāti ekaṃ aṅgaṃ, yāpanāyāti ekaṃ, vihiṃsūparatiyāti ekaṃ, brahmacariyānuggahāyāti ekaṃ, iti purāṇañca vedanaṃ paṭihaṅkhāmīti ekaṃ, navañca vedanaṃ na uppādessāmīti ekaṃ, yātrā ca me bhavissatīti ekaṃ, anavajjatā cāti ekaṃ, phāsuvihāro pana bhojanānisaṃsoti. Evaṃ aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgataṃ āhāraṃ āhāreti.

The elder Mahāsiva said: 'The first four factors are called rejection; the latter eight factors are to be combined.' Here, 'just for the maintenance of this body' is one factor; 'for sustenance' is another; 'for abstaining from injury' is another; 'for supporting the holy life' is another; thus, 'I ward off old feelings' is one factor; 'and I will not arouse new feelings' is another; 'and there will be sustenance for me' is another; 'and blamelessness' is another. Comfortable abiding, however, is the benefit of the meal. Thus, one partakes of food endowed with these eight factors.

90. Upekkhakoti chaḷaṅgupekkhāya samannāgato. Satoti kāyānupassanādisatiyutto.

90. 'Equanimous' means endowed with six-factored equanimity. 'Mindful' means endowed with mindfulness such as the contemplation of the body.

Upekkhakoti chaḷaṅgupekkhāya samannāgatoti ettha chaḷaṅgupekkhādhammo nāma koti? Ñāṇādayo. “Ñāṇa”nti vutte kiriyato cattāri ñāṇasampayuttāni labbhanti, “satatavihāro”ti vutte aṭṭha mahācittāni labbhanti, “rajjanadussanaṃ natthī”ti vutte dasa cittāni labbhanti. Somanassaṃ āsevanavasena labbhati. Cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvāti kāraṇavasena cakkhūti laddhavohārena rūpadassanasamatthena cakkhuviññāṇena rūpaṃ disvā. Porāṇā panāhu – cakkhu rūpaṃ na passati acittakattā, cittampi na passati acakkhukattā. Dvārārammaṇasaṅghaṭṭanena pana pasādavatthukena cittena passati. Īdisesu pana ṭhānesu “dhanunā vijjhatī”tiādīsu [V 0.0278] viya sasambhārakathā nāma hoti. Tasmā cakkhuviññāṇena rūpaṃ disvāti ayamevettha attho.

As for 'endowed with six-factored equanimity,' what is this state of six-factored equanimity? Knowledge and so on. When 'knowledge' is mentioned, four functional cittas associated with knowledge are obtained. When 'constant abiding' is mentioned, eight great wholesome cittas are obtained. When 'there is no delighting or aversion' is mentioned, ten unwholesome cittas are obtained. Joy is obtained by way of cultivation. 'Having seen a form with the eye'—by means of the cause which has received the designation 'eye,' the eye-consciousness, capable of seeing form, sees the form. But the ancients said: The eye does not see form because it is non-conscious, and the mind does not see because it lacks the eye. However, seeing occurs through the contact of the sense door and the object, by the mind based on the sensitive matter. In such cases, this is what is called 'speaking inclusively of the requisites,' as in expressions like 'one shoots with a bow.' Therefore, 'having seen a form with the eye-consciousness'—this indeed is the meaning here.

Neva sumano hotīti lobhuppattivasena chandarāguppattivasena somanasso na hoti. Na dummanoti paṭighuppattivasena duṭṭhacitto na hoti. Upekkhakoti upapattito ikkhako hoti, apakkhapatito hutvā iriyāpathaṃ pavatteti. Sato sampajānoti satimā ñāṇasampanno. Manāpaṃ nābhigijjhatīti manavaḍḍhanakaṃ iṭṭhārammaṇaṃ nābhigijjhati na pattheti. Nābhihaṃsatīti na tussati. Na rāgaṃ janetīti tattha tattha rañjanaṃ na uppādeti. Tassa [P 2.0347] ṭhitova kāyo hotīti tassa khīṇāsavassa cakkhādikāyo kampārahitattā ṭhito niccalo hoti. Amanāpanti aniṭṭhārammaṇaṃ[M 0.0304]. Na maṅku hotīti domanassito na hoti. Appatiṭṭhitacittoti kodhavasena ṭhitamano na hoti. Alīnamanasoti alīnacitto. Abyāpannacetasoti byāpādarahitacitto.

'He is not joyful' means: due to the arising of greed, due to the arising of desire and lust, gladness does not arise. 'He is not sorrowful' means: due to the arising of aversion, he does not have an ill-willed mind. 'Equanimous' means: he becomes an impartial observer, and being unbiased, he maintains his posture. 'Mindful and clearly comprehending' means: he is mindful and endowed with wisdom. 'He does not covet the pleasant' means: he does not crave or long for a pleasing object that increases desire. 'He does not delight' means: he is not pleased. 'He does not generate lust' means: he does not produce attachment here and there. 'His body remains steady' means: for him, whose defilements are destroyed, the body—such as the eye—is steady, unmoving, free from agitation. 'The unpleasant' means: an undesirable object. 'He is not dejected' means: he does not become sorrowful. 'His mind is not established' means: his mind is not established by way of anger. 'His mind is not sluggish' means: his mind is not withdrawn. 'His mind is free from ill will' means: his mind is devoid of ill will.

Rajanīye na rajjatīti rajanīyasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ na rāgaṃ uppādeti. Dussanīye na dussatīti dosuppāde vatthusmiṃ na dosaṃ uppādeti. Mohanīye na muyhatīti mohanīyasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ na mohaṃ uppādeti. Kopanīye na kuppatīti kodhanīyasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ na calati. Madanīye na majjatīti madanīyasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ na saṃsīdati. Kilesanīye na kilissatīti upatapanīyasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ na upatappati. Diṭṭhe diṭṭhamattoti rūpārammaṇe cakkhuviññāṇena diṭṭhe diṭṭhamatto. Sute sutamattoti saddāyatane sotaviññāṇena sute sutamatto. Mute mutamattoti ghānajivhākāyaviññāṇena pāpuṇitvā gahite gahitamatto. Viññāte viññātamattoti manoviññāṇena ñāte ñātamatto. Diṭṭhe na limpatīti cakkhuviññāṇena diṭṭhe rūpārammaṇe taṇhādiṭṭhilepena na limpati. Diṭṭhe anūpayoti rūpārammaṇe nittaṇho hoti. Anapāyoti apaduṭṭhacitto.

'He is not attached to what is attractive' means: he does not generate lust toward attractive objects. 'He is not repelled by what is offensive' means: he does not generate aversion toward offensive objects. 'He is not deluded by what is confusing' means: he does not generate delusion toward confusing objects. 'He is not angered by what is provoking' means: he does not waver toward provoking objects. 'He is not intoxicated by what is maddening' means: he does not sink into maddening objects. 'He is not defiled by what is defiling' means: he does not become afflicted by afflicting objects. 'In the seen, only the seen' means: in a visible object seen by eye-consciousness, only the seen. 'In the heard, only the heard' means: in a sound object heard by ear-consciousness, only the heard. 'In the sensed, only the sensed' means: in what is sensed having been contacted via nose-, tongue-, or body-consciousness, only what is sensed. 'In the cognized, only the cognized' means: in what is known by mind-consciousness, only what is known. 'He does not adhere to the seen' means: he does not adhere to a visible object seen by eye-consciousness with the stain of craving and wrong view. 'He is not dependent on the seen' means: he is without craving toward visible objects. 'He is without animosity' means: his mind is without ill will.

Saṃvijjatīti labbhati. Passatīti oloketi. Chandarāgoti sineho. Rūpārāmanti rūpaṃ ārāmaṃ assāti rūpārāmaṃ. Rūpe ratanti rūparataṃ. Rūpe santuṭṭhīti rūpasammuditaṃ.

'It exists' means: it is found. 'He sees' means: he looks at. 'Lustful desire' means: affection. 'Delighting in forms' means: one for whom form is a delight. 'Rejoicing in forms' means: one who takes pleasure in forms. 'Greatly delighted in forms' means: being content with forms.

Dantaṃ nayanti samitinti uyyānakīḷāmaṇḍalādīsu mahājanamajjhaṃ gacchantā dantameva goṇajātiṃ vā assajātiṃ vā yāne yojetvā nayanti. Rājāti tathārūpāneva ṭhānāni gacchanto rājāpi dantameva abhiruhati. Manussesūti manussesupi catūhi ariyamaggehi danto nibbisevanova [P 2.0348] seṭṭho. Yotivākyanti yo evarūpaṃ atikkamavacanaṃ punappunaṃ vuccamānampi titikkhati na paṭipphandati na vihaññati, evarūpo danto seṭṭhoti attho.

They lead the tamed: when going into the midst of a great crowd in parks, pleasure grounds, and so forth, they lead only a tamed ox or horse by yoking it to a vehicle. The king: a king too, when going to such places, mounts only a tamed animal. Among humans: among humans too, one who is tamed by the four noble paths, being unattached, is the best. The phrase 'One who...': one who, even when repeatedly spoken to with abusive words, endures without reacting or becoming distressed—such a tamed one is the best. This is the meaning.

Assatarāti [V 0.0279] vaḷavāya gadrabhena jātā. Ājānīyāti yaṃ assadammasārathi kāraṇaṃ kāreti, tassa khippaṃ jānanasamatthā. Sindhavāti sindhavaraṭṭhe jātā assā. Mahānāgāti kuñjarasaṅkhātā mahāhatthino. Attadantoti [M 0.0305] ete assatarā vā ājānīyā vā sindhavā vā kuñjarā vā varā dantā, na adantā. Yo pana catumaggasaṅkhātena attadantena dantatāya attadanto nibbisevano, ayaṃ tatopi varaṃ, sabbehipi etehi uttaritaroti attho.

Mules: those born of a mare and a donkey. Thoroughbreds: those capable of quickly understanding the training a horse-trainer gives. Sindh horses: horses born in the Sindh country. Great nāgas: great elephants, known as 'kuñjara.' Self-tamed: these mules or thoroughbreds or Sindh horses or elephants are excellent when tamed, not when untamed. But one who, by the self-taming consisting of the four paths, is self-tamed through tameness and is unattached—this one is superior to them, more excellent than all of these. This is the meaning.

Na hi etehi yānehīti yāni etāni hatthiyānādiyānāni, na hi etehi yānehi koci puggalo supinantenapi agatapubbattā “agata”nti saṅkhātaṃ nibbānadisaṃ, taṃ ṭhānaṃ gaccheyya. Yathā pubbabhāge indriyadamena dantena aparabhāge ariyamaggabhāvanāya sudantena danto nibbisevano sappañño puggalo taṃ agatapubbaṃ disaṃ gacchati, dantabhūmiṃ pāpuṇāti. Tasmā attadamanameva varanti attho.

Not by these vehicles: that is, vehicles such as those drawn by elephants and others. Indeed, by these vehicles no person could go, not even in a dream, to that place known as 'the ungone-to'—the destination of Nibbāna—because it has not been gone to before. Just as a wise person, tamed in the earlier stage by the restraint of the faculties, and well-tamed in the later stage by the cultivation of the noble path, being tamed and unattached, reaches that previously ungone-to destination, attaining the ground of the tamed. Therefore, self-taming alone is the best; this is the meaning.

Vidhāsu na vikampantīti seyyassa seyyohamasmītiādīsu mānavidhāsu na calanti nappavedhanti. Vippamuttā punabbhavāti punabbhavapaṭisandhiyā punappunaṃ uppattito suṭṭhu muttā muñcitvā ṭhitā. Dantabhūmimanuppattāti ekantadamanaṃ arahattaphalabhūmiṃ pāpuṇitvā ṭhitā. Te loke vijitāvinoti te arahanto sattaloke vijitavijayā vijitavanto nāma honti.

Unshaken in conditions: they do not stir or tremble in the various kinds of conceit, such as 'I am superior to the superior.' Freed from rebirth: they are completely released and stand liberated from the repeated arising of rebirth-linking. Having reached the ground of the tamed: having attained the ground of absolute taming, the fruition of Arahantship, they stand firm. They are conquerors in the world: these Arahants are called conquerors in the world of beings, having won the victory.

Yasmā ca bhāvitindriyo nibbhayo nibbikāro danto hoti, tasmā tamatthaṃ dassento “yassindriyānī”ti gāthamāha. Tassattho – yassa cakkhādīni chaḷindriyāni gocarabhāvanāya aniccāditilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā vāsanābhāvanāya satisampajaññagandhaṃ gāhāpetvā bhāvitāni, tāni ca kho ajjhattagocarabhāvanāya, evaṃ pana bahiddhā ca sabbaloketi yattha yattha indriyānaṃ vekallatā vekallato vā sambhavo, tattha nābhijjhādivasena bhāvitānīti evaṃ nibbijjha ñatvā paṭivijjhitvā imaṃ parañca lokaṃ sakasantatikhandhalokaṃ parasantatikhandhalokañca [P 2.0349] dantamaraṇaṃ maritukāmo kālaṃ kaṅkhati, jīvitakkhayakālaṃ āgameti patimāneti, na bhāyati maraṇassa. Yathāha –

And because one whose faculties are developed is fearless, unchanging, and tamed, to show that meaning, the verse beginning 'Whose faculties...' was spoken. Its meaning is this: one whose six faculties, beginning with the eye, have been developed by applying the three characteristics of impermanence and so on to their object-domains, and by developing the latent tendencies, causing them to acquire the fragrance of mindfulness and clear comprehension—and these faculties are developed with regard to the internal object-domain, and likewise externally in the entire world; wherever there is a deficiency of the faculties or a possibility arising from deficiency, they are developed there not by way of covetousness and so on. Thus, having thoroughly known and penetrated this world and the next—the world of one’s own continuum of aggregates and the world of others' continuum of aggregates—one who desires to die a tamed death awaits his time, anticipates the moment of life’s end, and does not fear death. As it is said:

“Maraṇe me bhayaṃ natthi, nikanti natthī jīvite”. (theragā. 20);

I have no fear of death, nor longing for life.

“Nābhikaṅkhāmi [V 0.0280] maraṇaṃ, nābhikaṅkhāmi jīvitaṃ;

Kālañca patimānemi, nibbisaṃ bhatako yathā”ti. (theragā. 606, 654, 1002; mi. pa. 2.2.4 thokaṃ visadisaṃ);

I do not long for death, I do not long for life; I await my time, like a hireling his wages.

Bhāvito [M 0.0306] sa dantoti evaṃ bhāvitindriyo so danto.

Developed, he is tamed: thus, he whose faculties are developed is tamed.

91. Nissayatāti taṇhādiṭṭhinissayā. Ñatvā dhammanti aniccādīhi ākārehi dhammaṃ jānitvā. Anissitoti evaṃ tehi nissayehi anissito. Tena aññatra dhammañāṇā natthi nissayānaṃ abhāvoti dīpeti. Bhavāya vibhavāya vāti sassatāya ucchedāya vā. Imissā gāthāya niddeso uttāno.

91. Dependent: the dependencies of craving and views. Having known the Dhamma: having known the Dhamma through its aspects, such as impermanence. Independent: thus independent of those dependencies. This shows that, apart from knowledge of the Dhamma, there is no absence of dependencies. For existence or for non-existence: for eternalism or for annihilationism. The explanation of this verse is straightforward.

92. Taṃ brūmi upasantoti taṃ evarūpaṃ ekekagāthāya vuttaṃ upasantoti kathemi. Atarī so visattikanti so imaṃ visatādibhāvena visattikāsaṅkhātaṃ mahātaṇhaṃ atari.

92. Him I call peaceful: I declare such a one, spoken of in each and every verse, to be peaceful. He has crossed over attachment: he has crossed over this great craving, known as 'attachment,' due to its nature as poison and so forth.

Attano diṭṭhiyā rāgo abhijjhākāyaganthoti sayaṃ gahitadiṭṭhiyā rañjanasaṅkhāto rāgo abhijjhākāyagantho. Paravādesu āghāto appaccayoti paresaṃ vādapaṭivādesu kopo ca atuṭṭhākāro ca byāpādo kāyagantho. Attano sīlaṃ vā vataṃ vāti sayaṃ gahitamethunaviratisaṅkhātaṃ sīlaṃ vā govatādivataṃ vā. Sīlabbataṃ vāti tadubhayaṃ vā. Parāmāsoti iminā suddhītiādivasena parato āmasati. Attano diṭṭhi idaṃsaccābhiniveso kāyaganthoti sayaṃ gahitadiṭṭhiṃ “idameva saccaṃ moghamañña”nti (udā. 54; ma. ni. 3.27, 301) ayoniso abhiniveso idaṃsaccābhiniveso kāyagantho. Ganthā tassa na vijjantīti tassa khīṇāsavassa dve diṭṭhiganthā sotāpattimaggena na santi. Byāpādo kāyagantho anāgāmimaggena. Abhijjhākāyagantho arahattamaggena.

Lust for one's own view is the bodily fetter of covetousness: the lust, characterized as delight in one's own adopted view, is the bodily fetter of covetousness. Resentment and displeasure towards others' doctrines: anger and a state of displeasure towards others' arguments and counterarguments is the bodily fetter of ill will. One's own virtue or vow: one's own adopted virtue, characterized as abstinence from sexual intercourse, or a vow, such as the cow-vow. Or virtue and vows: or both of them. Clinging: one grasps at it based on another's teaching, by way of thinking 'purity is by this,' and so on. The bodily fetter of adherence that 'this alone is true' regarding one's own view: the unwise adherence to one's own adopted view, thinking, 'This alone is truth, the rest is worthless,' is the bodily fetter of adherence to this as the truth. For him, these fetters do not exist: for the one whose cankers are destroyed, the two fetters of views are absent by means of the path of stream-entry; the bodily fetter of ill will, by means of the path of non-returning; the bodily fetter of covetousness, by means of the path of Arahantship.

93. Idāni tameva upasantaṃ pasaṃsanto āha “na tassa puttā”ti evamādi. Tattha puttā atrajādayo cattāro. Ettha ca puttapariggahādayo puttādināmena vuttāti veditabbā. Te hissa na vijjanti, tesaṃ vā abhāvena puttādayo na vijjantīti. Attāti [P 2.0350] “attā atthī”ti gahitā sassatadiṭṭhiṃ natthi. Nirattāti “ucchijjatī”ti gahitā ucchedadiṭṭhi.

93. Now, praising that same peaceful one, he says, 'He has no sons,' and so on. Herein, 'sons' refers to the four kinds, beginning with those born from oneself. And here it should be understood that possessions such as sons are spoken of by the term 'sons' and so on. For him, these do not exist; or, due to the absence of these possessions, sons and so on do not exist. Self: the eternalist view, grasped as 'a self exists,' does not exist for him. Not-self: the annihilationist view, grasped as 'it is annihilated.'

Natthīti [M 0.0307] gahetabbaṃ natthi. Muñcitabbaṃ natthīti mocetabbaṃ natthi. Yassa natthi gahitanti yassa [V 0.0281] puggalassa taṇhādiṭṭhivasena gahitaṃ na vijjati. Tassa natthi muñcitabbanti tassa puggalassa muñcitabbaṃ na vijjati. Gāhamuñcanasamatikkantoti gahaṇañca mocanañca vītivatto. Vuddhiparihānivītivattoti vuḍḍhiñca hāniñca atikkanto.

There is nothing: there is nothing to be grasped. There is nothing to be released: there is nothing to be let go of. For whom there is no grasping: for that person for whom there is no grasping by way of craving and views. For him there is nothing to be released: for that person there is nothing to be released. Having transcended grasping and releasing: he has overcome grasping and releasing. Having overcome growth and decline: he has transcended growth and decline.

94. Yena naṃ vajjuṃ puthujjanā, atho samaṇabrāhmaṇāti yena taṃ rāgādinā vajjena puthujjanā sabbepi devamanussā itova bahiddhā samaṇabrāhmaṇā ca rattoti vā duṭṭhoti vā vadeyyuṃ. Taṃ tassa apurakkhatanti taṃ rāgādivajjaṃ tassa arahato apurakkhataṃ. Tasmā vādesu nejatīti taṃkāraṇā nindāvacanesu na kampati.

94. By which ordinary people, and also ascetics and brahmins, might speak of him: by which fault, such as lust, ordinary people—all devas and humans—and ascetics and brahmins outside this teaching might say he is 'lustful' or 'hateful.' That is not put before him: that fault of lust and so on is not put before that Arahant. Therefore, he does not tremble in disputes: for that reason, he does not tremble at words of blame.

Nejatīti niddesassa uddesapadaṃ. Na iñjatīti calanaṃ na karoti. Na calatīti na tattha namati. Na vedhatīti kampetuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya na phandati. Nappavedhatīti na kampati. Na sampavedhatīti na parivattati.

Nejati: this is the term to be explained in the exposition. Na iñjati: he does not make a movement. Na calati: he does not incline thereto. Na vedhati: he does not quiver, being unable to be shaken. Nappavedhati: he does not tremble. Na sampavedhati: he does not turn about.

95. Na ussesu vadateti visiṭṭhesu attānaṃ antokatvā “ahaṃ visiṭṭho”ti atimānavasena na vadati. Esa nayo itaresu dvīsu. Kappaṃ neti akappiyoti so evarūpo duvidhampi kappaṃ na eti. Kasmā? Yasmā akappiyo, pahīnakappoti vuttaṃ hoti. Imissāpi gāthāya niddeso uttānova.

95. He does not speak among superiors: having included himself among the distinguished, he does not speak out of excessive pride, thinking, 'I am distinguished.' This is the method for the other two cases as well. He does not go to a conception, being unsuitable: such a one does not go to either of the two kinds of conception. Why? Because he is unsuitable for them; it means he has abandoned conceptions. The explanation of this verse is also straightforward.

96. Sakanti mayhanti pariggahitaṃ. Asatā ca na socatīti avijjamānādinā asatā ca na socati. Dhammesu ca na gacchatīti sabbadhammesu chandādivasena na gacchati. Sa ve santoti vuccatīti so evarūpo naruttamo “santo”ti vuccati. Imissāpi gāthāya niddeso uttānova. Arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi. Desanāpariyosāne koṭisatasahassadevatānaṃ arahattappatti ahosi, sotāpannādīnaṃ gaṇanā natthīti.

96. Sakaṃ means that which is grasped as 'mine.' And he does not grieve for what is non-existent means, because of its non-existence, he does not grieve for what is non-existent, etc. And he does not go to phenomena means he does not go to all phenomena by way of desire and the like. He is indeed called peaceful means such a foremost man is called 'peaceful.' The explanation of this verse is also straightforward. He concluded the teaching with the culmination of Arahantship. At the end of the teaching, a hundred thousand crores of deities attained Arahantship, and there was no counting of those who became stream-enterers and so forth.

Saddhammappajjotikāya mahāniddesaṭṭhakathāya

From the Saddhammappajjotikā, the Commentary on the Mahāniddesa.

Purābhedasuttaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Niddesa on the Purābheda Sutta is finished.

11. Kalahavivādasuttaniddesavaṇṇanā

11. The Elucidation of the Exposition of the Kalahavivāda Sutta

97. Ekādasame [V 0.0282][P 2.0351][M 0.0308] kalahavivādasuttaniddese kutopahūtā kalahā vivādāti kalaho ca tassa pubbabhāgo vivādo cāti ime kuto jātā. Paridevasokā sahamaccharā cāti paridevasokā ca sahamaccharā ca kuto pahūtā. Mānātimānā sahapesuṇā cāti mānā ca atimānā ca pesuṇā ca kuto pahūtā. Teti te sabbepi aṭṭha kilesadhammā. Tadiṅgha byūhīti taṃ mayā pucchitamatthaṃ brūhi, yācāmi taṃ ahanti. Yācanattho hi iṅghāti nipāto.

97. In the eleventh exposition of the Kalahavivāda Sutta: "From where do quarrels and disputes originate?" means: from where are these born—quarrels and disputes, the preceding stage thereof? "Lamentations and sorrows, together with stinginess" means: from where do these originate? "Conceit and excessive conceit, together with malicious talk" means: from where do these originate? "These" refers to all those eight defiled states. "Explain that to me" means: reveal to me that meaning which I have asked; I beseech you. For the particle "iṅgha" conveys the sense of entreaty.

Ekena ākārenāti ekena kāraṇena. Aparena ākārenāti aparena kāraṇena. Āgārikā daṇḍapasutāti gahapatino vihesamānā. Pabbajitā āpattiṃ āpajjantāti anagārikā sattasu āpattikkhandhesu aññataraṃ āpajjamānā.

"By one way" means by one reason. "By another way" means by another reason. "Householders prone to violence" means householders harming others. "The renunciates incur an offense" means the homeless incurring one of the seven groups of offenses.

Kutopahūtāti kutobhūtā. Kutojātāti kuto paṭiladdhabhāvā. Kutosañjātāti upasaggena padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ. Kutonibbattāti kuto nibbattalakkhaṇaṃ pattā. Upasaggena padaṃ vaḍḍhetvā “kutoabhinibbattā”ti vuttaṃ. Kutopātubhūtāti kutopākaṭībhūtā. Kiṃ nidānātiādīsu attano phalaṃ nidetīti nidānaṃ. Etasmā phalaṃ samudetīti samudayo. Etasmā phalaṃ jāyatīti jāti. Etasmā phalaṃ pabhavatīti pabhavo. Mūlaṃ pucchatīti kalahassa kāraṇaṃ pucchati. Kāraṇañhi patiṭṭhaṭṭhena mūlaṃ. Attano phalanipphādanatthaṃ hinoti pavattatīti hetu. “Handa naṃ gaṇhathā”ti dassentaṃ viya attano phalaṃ nidetīti nidānaṃ. Etasmā phalaṃ sambhavatīti sambhavo. Pabhavati phalaṃ etasmāti pabhavo. Samuṭṭhāti ettha phalaṃ, etena vā samuṭṭhātīti samuṭṭhānaṃ. Attano phalaṃ āharatīti āhāro. Apaṭikkhipitabbaṭṭhena attano phalaṃ ārametīti ārammaṇaṃ. Etaṃ paṭicca apaṭikkhipitvā phalaṃ [P 2.0352] eti pavattatīti paccayo. Etasmā phalaṃ samudetīti samudayoti evametesaṃ padānaṃ vacanattho veditabbo. Taṃ sandhāya “kalahassa ca vivādassa ca mūlaṃ pucchatī”tiādinā nayena desanā vuttā.

"From where is it brought forth?" means "from where has it come to be?" "From where is it born?" means "from where has its existence been obtained?" "From where is it produced?" is a word augmented by a prefix. "From where has it arisen?" means "from where has it attained the characteristic of arising?" By augmenting the word with a prefix, it is said, "from where has it been completely produced?" "From where has it appeared?" means "from where has it become evident?" In phrases like "what is the cause?": "It indicates its own result," thus it is a cause. "From this, the result comes into existence," thus it is origin. "From this, the result is born," thus it is birth. "From this, the result proceeds," thus it is source. "He asks about the root" means he inquires about the cause of the quarrel. For a reason is the root in the sense of being the foundation. "It functions for the purpose of producing its own result," thus it is a cause. As if showing, "Come, take this," it indicates its own result—thus it is a cause. "From this, the result comes into being," thus it is origination. "The result proceeds from this," thus it is source. "The result arises here, or by this the result arises," thus it is arising. "It brings its own result," thus it is nutriment. "In the sense that it is not to be rejected, it takes its own result as an object," thus it is an object. "Depending on this, without rejecting, the result proceeds," thus it is condition. "From this, the result comes into existence," thus it is origin—in this way, the meaning of these words should be understood. Referring to this, the teaching is stated in the manner of, "He asks about the root of quarrel and dispute," and so on.

98. Piyappahūtāti [V 0.0283] piyavatthuto jātā. Maccherayuttā kalahā vivādāti iminā kalahavivādādīnaṃ na kevalaṃ piyavatthumeva, macchariyampi paccayaṃ [M 0.0309] dasseti. Kalahavivādasīsena cettha sabbepi te dhammā vuttāti veditabbā. Yathā ca etesaṃ macchariyaṃ, tathā pesuṇānañca vivādaṃ. Tenāha “vivādajātesu ca pesuṇānī”ti. Imissā gāthāya niddeso uttānatthoyeva.

98. "Originating from the dear" means originating from objects of affection. "Quarrels and disputes connected with stinginess" indicates that not only are objects of affection a cause for quarrels, disputes, and so on, but also stinginess. It should be understood that all those states are included here under the heading of quarrels and disputes. And just as stinginess is a cause for these, so dispute is a cause for slander. Therefore, it is said, "and slander is among what is born from disputes." The explanation of this verse is clear in meaning.

99. Piyā su lokasmiṃ kutonidānā, ye cāpi lobhā vicaranti loketi “piyappahūtā kalahā”ti ye ettha vuttā, te piyā lokasmiṃ kutonidānā, na kevalañca piyā, ye cāpi khattiyādayo loke vicaranti lobhahetu lobhenābhibhūtā vicaranti, tesaṃ so lobho ca kutonidānoti dve atthe ekāya pucchāya pucchati. Kutonidānāti cettha kiṃnidānā kiṃhetukāti paccattavacanassa toādeso veditabbo, samāse cassa lopābhāvo. Atha vā nidānāti jātā, uppannāti attho. Tasmā kuto jātā kuto uppannāti vuttaṃ hoti. Āsā ca niṭṭhā cāti āsā ca tassā āsāya samiddhi ca. Ye samparāyāya narassa hontīti ye narassa samparāyāya honti, parāyanā hontīti vuttaṃ hoti. Ekā evāyampi pucchā.

99. "What is the source of what is dear in the world? And those who wander the world with greed": those things mentioned here as "quarrels originating from the dear," what is the source of those dear things in the world? And not only the dear things, but also those such as warriors and others who wander the world because of greed, overpowered by greed—what is the source of that greed? Thus, he asks about two meanings in one question. Herein, "what is the source?" means "what is its cause? what is its reason?" The suffix "-to" should be understood as a substitute for the case ending, and its non-elision in a compound. Alternatively, "source" means "born" or "arisen." Thus, it means, "From where are they born? From where have they arisen?" "Hope and fulfillment" means hope and the success of that hope. "Those that are for a person's future" means those that are a person's destination in the next life. This too is a single question.

Dīpā hontīti patiṭṭhā bhavanti. Saraṇā hontīti dukkhanāsanā honti. Niṭṭhāparāyanā hontīti samiddhiparāyanā honti.

"They become islands" means they become a support. "They become refuges" means they are the destruction of suffering. "They have fulfillment as their ultimate goal" means they have prosperity as their final aim.

100. Chandānidānānīti kāmacchandādichandanidānāni. Ye cāpi lobhā vicarantīti ye cāpi khattiyādayo lobhā vicaranti, tesaṃ lobhopi chandanidānoti dvepi atthe ekato vissajjeti. Itonidānāti chandanidānā evāti vuttaṃ hoti. “Itonidānā”ti hi chandaṃ sandhāyāha. Chandanidānā hi lobhādayo. “Itonidānā”ti saddasiddhi [P 2.0353] cettha “kutonidānā”ti ettha vuttanayena veditabbā. Āsāya samiddhi vuccati niṭṭhāti ajjhāsayanibbattipaṭilābho kathīyati.

100. "Having desire as their source" means having sensual desire and other desires as their source. "And those who wander with greed" refers to warriors and others who wander with greed; their greed also has desire as its source. Thus, he answers both meanings together. "From this source" means precisely "having desire as their source." For by "from this source" he refers to desire. For greed and the like have desire as their source. The grammatical formation of "from this source" should be understood in the same way as explained for "what is the source" earlier. "The success of hope is called fulfillment" means the attainment of the result of one’s inclination is spoken of.

101. Vinicchayāti taṇhādiṭṭhivinicchayā. Ye cāpi dhammā samaṇena vuttāti ye ca aññepi kodhādīhi sampayuttā, tathārūpā vā akusalā dhammā buddhasamaṇena vuttā, te kutopahūtāti.

101. "Discriminations" means the discriminations of craving and views. "And those states spoken of by the ascetic" means whatever other unwholesome states are connected with anger and so on, or such unwholesome states spoken of by the Buddha, the ascetic—from where are they produced?

Aññajātikāti [M 0.0310] aññasabhāvā. Aññavihitakāti aññenākārena ṭhitā. Samitapāpenāti nibbāpitapāpena. Bāhitapāpadhammenāti pahīnalāmakadhammena. Bhinnakilesamūlenāti kilesamūlāni [V 0.0284] bhinditvā ṭhitena. Sabbākusalamūlabandhanā pamuttenāti dvādasaakusalabandhanaṃ mocetvā ṭhitena. Vuttāti kathitā. Pavuttāti pakārena kathitā.

"Of another kind" means of a different nature. "Established differently" means established in another manner. "With evil quenched" means with evil extinguished. "Having abandoned evil qualities" means having abandoned inferior qualities. "With the root of defilements shattered" means standing with the roots of defilements shattered. "Freed from all bonds of unwholesome roots" means standing freed from the twelve unwholesome bonds. "Spoken" means said. "Proclaimed" means said in a special way.

102. Tamūpanissāya pahoti chandoti taṃ sukhadukkhavedanaṃ tadubhayavatthusaṅkhātaṃ sātāsātaṃ upanissāya saṃyogaviyogapatthanāvasena chando pahoti. Ettāvatā “chando nu lokasmiṃ kutonidāno”ti ayaṃ pañho vissajjito hoti. Rūpesu disvā vibhavaṃ bhavañcāti rūpesu vayañca uppādañca disvā. Vinicchayaṃ kubbati jantu loketi apāyādike loke ayaṃ jantu bhogādhigamatthaṃ taṇhāvinicchayaṃ “attā me uppanno”tiādinā nayena diṭṭhivinicchayañca kurute. Ettāvatā “vinicchayā cāpi kutopabhūtā”ti ayaṃ pañho vissajjito hoti.

102. "Based on that, desire arises": based on that pleasant and painful feeling, that which is designated as the basis for both, desire arises by way of longing for union and separation. To this extent, the question, "What is the source of desire in the world?" is answered. "Having seen in forms both destruction and existence" means having seen in forms both dissolution and arising. "A being in the world makes discriminations": in the world, including the realms of misery, this being makes discriminations based on craving for the sake of attaining enjoyments, and makes discriminations based on views in the manner of "a self has arisen for me," and so on. To this extent, the question, "And from what do discriminations originate?" is answered.

Sātāsātaṃ nissāyāti madhurañca amadhurañca upanissayaṃ katvā. Iṭṭhāniṭṭhanti iṭṭhārammaṇañca aniṭṭhārammaṇañca.

"Relying on the pleasant and unpleasant" means having made both the sweet and the unsweet a basis. "Liked and disliked" means both agreeable and disagreeable objects.

Surāmerayamajjappamādaṭṭhānānuyoganti ettha surāti piṭṭhasurā pūvasurā odanasurā kiṇṇapakkhittā sambhārasaṃyuttāti pañca surā. Merayanti pupphāsavo phalāsavo madhvāsavo guḷāsavo sambhārasaṃyuttoti pañca āsavā. Taṃ sabbampi madakaraṇavasena majjaṃ. Pamādaṭṭhānanti pamādakāraṇaṃ, yāya cetanāya taṃ majjaṃ pivati, tassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Anuyoganti taṃ surāmerayamajjappamādaṭṭhānānuyogaṃ [P 2.0354] anuāyogaṃ punappunaṃ karaṇaṃ. Yasmā ca pana taṃ anuyuttassa me uppannā ceva bhogā parihāyanti, anuppannā ca nuppajjanti, tasmā “me bhogā parikkhayaṃ khīṇabhāvaṃ gacchantī”ti jānāti. Evaṃ sabbattha. Vikālavisikhācariyānuyoganti avelāya visikhāsu cariyānuyuttaṃ. Samajjābhicaraṇanti naccādidassanavasena samajjābhigamanaṃ. Ālasyānuyoganti kāyālasiyatāya yuttappayuttataṃ. Apāyamukhāni na sevatīti bhogānaṃ vināsadvārāni na sevati.

“Indulgence in intoxicants, the basis of heedlessness”—here, ‘liquor’ (surā) refers to five kinds: grain liquor, flour liquor, rice liquor, liquor mixed with yeast, and liquor mixed with ingredients. ‘Fermented drinks’ (meraya) refers to five kinds: flower wine, fruit wine, honey wine, molasses wine, and wine mixed with ingredients. All of that is an ‘intoxicant’ (majja) in the sense that it causes intoxication. ‘The basis of heedlessness’ (pamādaṭṭhāna) means the cause of heedlessness—a designation for the intention with which one drinks that intoxicant. ‘Indulgence’ (anuyoga) means the repeated practice of that indulgence in liquor and fermented drinks, the basis of heedlessness. And because for one who is devoted to that, existing possessions decline and new ones do not arise, therefore he knows, “My possessions are heading to decay and destruction.” Thus it is in all cases. “Indulgence in wandering the streets at unseasonable times” means being devoted to wandering in the streets at the wrong time. “Frequenting shows” means going to shows for the sake of seeing dances and so on. “Indulgence in laziness” means being yoked to bodily laziness. “He does not cultivate the ways to ruin” means he does not frequent the doors to the destruction of possessions.

Kasiyā vāti kasikammena vā. Vaṇijjāya vāti dhammikavaṇijjakammena vā. Gorakkhena vāti gopālakammena vā. Issatthena vāti dhanusippena [M 0.0311] vā. Rājaporisena vāti rājasevakakammena vā. Sippaññatarena vāti kumbhakārādisippānaṃ aññatarena vā. Paṭipajjatīti payogaṃ karoti. Cakkhusmiṃ uppanne jānātīti sasambhāracakkhusmiṃ uppanne jānāti. “Attā me uppanno”ti diṭṭhiṃ gaṇhāti. Cakkhusmiṃ antarahiteti tasmiṃ vinaṭṭhe. Attā [V 0.0285] me antarahitoti “mama attā vinaṭṭho”ti diṭṭhiṃ gaṇhāti. Vigato me attāti vītikkanto mama attā. Sotasmintiādīsupi eseva nayo.

‘By farming’ means by the work of farming. ‘By trade’ means by the work of lawful trading. ‘By cattle-tending’ means by the work of a herdsman. ‘By archery’ means by the skill of the bow. ‘By royal service’ means by the work of serving a king. ‘By some other craft’ means by any other craft such as that of a potter. ‘He undertakes it’ means he makes an effort. ‘When the eye arises, he knows’ means he knows when the eye with its conditions has arisen. He takes up the view, “A self has arisen for me.” ‘When the eye has disappeared’ means when it has perished. ‘My self has disappeared’—he takes up the view, “My self has perished.” ‘My self is gone’ means my self has passed away. In the case of the ear and so on, the same method applies.

103. Etepi dhammā dvayameva santeti ete kodhādayo dhammā sātāsātadvaye sante eva honti uppajjanti. Ettāvatā tatiyapañhopi vissajjito hoti. Idāni yo evaṃ vissajjitesu etesu pañhesu kathaṃkathī bhaveyya, tassa kathaṃkathāpahānūpāyaṃ dassento āha “kathaṃkathī ñāṇapathāya sikkhe”ti, ñāṇadassanañāṇādhigamanatthaṃ tisso sikkhā sikkheyyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Kiṃkāraṇā? Ñatvā pavuttā samaṇena dhammā. Buddhasamaṇena hi ñatvā dhammā vuttā, natthi tassa dhammesu aññāṇaṃ, attano pana ñāṇānubhāvena te ajānanto na jāneyya, na desanādosena. Tasmā kathaṃkathī ñāṇapathāya sikkhe, ñatvā pavuttā samaṇena dhammāti.

103. ‘These phenomena, too, exist only in pairs’ means these phenomena, such as anger and so forth, arise only when the pair of pleasant and unpleasant exists. By this much, the third question is also answered. Now, if someone were to remain doubtful even after these questions have been answered, to show the way to dispel their doubt, it is said: “The doubtful person should train for the path of knowledge.” This means they should train in the threefold training for the attainment of knowledge and vision. For what reason? The ascetic proclaimed the teachings after knowing them. Indeed, the ascetic Buddha proclaimed the teachings after knowing them; there is no ignorance in him regarding the teachings. But one who does not know them might not understand them through his own lack of knowledge, not due to any fault in the teaching. Therefore, the doubtful person should train for the path of knowledge, for the ascetic proclaimed the teachings after knowing them.

Pakkhepabandhanena vā baddhoti nāgarikabandhena baddho. Parikkhepabandhanena vāti vatiparikkhepabandhanena vā. Gāmabandhanenātiādīsu tasmā tasmā [P 2.0355] ṭhānato nikkhamituṃ alabhanto gāmabandhanādīhi baddho nāma hoti. Tassa bandhanassa mokkhatthāyāti etassa vuttappakārassa bandhanassa mocanatthaṃ.

‘Bound by an enclosing bond’ means bound by a townsman’s bond. ‘Or by an encircling bond’ means by a fence-encircling bond. In phrases like ‘by a village bond’ and so forth, one is said to be bound by a village bond and so on because one is unable to leave this or that place. ‘For the sake of release from that bondage’ means for the purpose of being released from the kind of bondage mentioned.

Ñāṇampi ñāṇapathoti pure uppannaṃ ñāṇaṃ aparāparuppannassa ñāṇampi ñāṇassa sañcaraṇamaggoti ñāṇampi ñāṇapatho. Ñāṇassa ārammaṇampi ñāṇapathoti ñāṇassa paccayopi taṃ ālambitvā uppajjanato ñāṇapatho. Ñāṇasahabhunopi dhammā ñāṇapathoti ñāṇena sahuppannā avasesā cittacetasikā dhammāpi ñāṇapatho. Idāni upamāya sādhento “yathā ariyamaggo ariyapatho”tiādimāha.

‘Knowledge itself is the path of knowledge’: previously arisen knowledge is the path for subsequently arisen knowledge, as it is the path along which knowledge proceeds; thus, knowledge itself is the path of knowledge. ‘The object of knowledge is also the path of knowledge’: because the object is a condition for knowledge, which arises in dependence on it, it is the path of knowledge. ‘Phenomena co-arisen with knowledge are also the path of knowledge’: the remaining mind and mental factors that arise together with knowledge are also the path of knowledge. Now, to establish this through a simile, he says: ‘Just as the Noble Path is the Noble Way,’ and so on.

Kathaṃkathī [M 0.0312] puggaloti vicikicchāvanto puggalo. Sakaṅkhoti sadveḷhako. Savilekhoti cittarājivanto. Sadveḷhakoti kaṅkhāvanto. Savicikicchoti sandehavanto. Ñāṇādhigamāyāti ñāṇapaṭilābhatthāya. Ñāṇaphusanāyāti ñāṇapaṭivijjhanatthāya. Atha vā ñāṇavindanatthāya. Ñāṇasacchikiriyāyāti ñāṇassa paccakkhakaraṇatthāya. Sanidānāhanti ahaṃ sanidānaṃ sapaccayaṃ katvā dhammadesanaṃ karomi. Sappāṭihāriyanti niyyānikaṃ katvā. No appāṭihāriyanti aniyyānikaṃ akatvā dhammadesanaṃ karomi.

‘A doubtful person’ means a person who has doubt. ‘Uncertain’ means perplexed. ‘Wavering’ means having a streaked mind. ‘Perplexed’ means possessing doubt. ‘Doubtful’ means possessing uncertainty. ‘For the attainment of knowledge’ means for the purpose of acquiring knowledge. ‘For the realization of knowledge’ means for the purpose of penetrating knowledge, or for the purpose of finding knowledge. ‘For the direct experience of knowledge’ means for the purpose of directly realizing knowledge. ‘With a cause’: I teach the Dhamma by presenting it with a cause and condition. ‘With a wonder’ means making it lead out. ‘Not without a wonder’ means I teach the Dhamma, not making it something that does not lead out.

104. Sātaṃ asātañca kutonidānāti ettha sātāsātanti sukhadukkhavedanā eva adhippetā[V 0.0286]. Na bhavanti heteti na bhavanti ete. Vibhavaṃ bhavañcāpi yametamatthaṃ, etaṃ me pabrūhi yatonidānanti sātāsātānaṃ vibhavaṃ bhavañca etampi yaṃ atthaṃ. Liṅgabyattayo ettha kato. Idaṃ pana vuttaṃ hoti – sātāsātānaṃ vibhavo bhavo cāti yo esa attho, etaṃ me pabrūhi yatonidānanti. Ettha ca sātāsātānaṃ vibhavabhavavatthukā vibhavabhavadiṭṭhiyo eva vibhavabhavāti atthato veditabbā. Tathā hi imassa pañhassa vissajjanapakkhe “bhavadiṭṭhipi phassanidānā, vibhavadiṭṭhipi phassanidānā”ti upari niddese (mahāni. 105) vakkhati. Imāya gāthāya niddese vattabbaṃ natthi.

104. ‘What is the source of the pleasant and the unpleasant?’ Here, ‘pleasant and unpleasant’ is specifically intended to mean feelings of pleasure and pain. ‘They do not exist, these’ means these do not exist. ‘Annihilation and existence, whatever this meaning is, tell me its source’ means: ‘whatever meaning there is of the annihilation and existence of the pleasant and unpleasant, tell me its source.’ Here, a change of gender is made. But this is what is said: ‘Tell me the source from which this meaning arises: the annihilation and existence of the pleasant and unpleasant.’ And here, by ‘annihilation and existence,’ one should understand in meaning the views of annihilation and existence which are based on the annihilation and existence of the pleasant and unpleasant. For in the section answering this question, it will be stated further on in the exposition (Mahāni. 105): ‘The view of existence has contact as its source, and the view of annihilation has contact as its source.’ There is nothing to be said in the exposition of this verse.

105. Itonidānanti phassanidānaṃ. Imāyapi vattabbaṃ natthi.

105. ‘From this source’ means having contact as its source. About this too, there is nothing to be said.

106. Kismiṃ [P 2.0356] vibhūte na phusanti phassāti kismiṃ vītivatte cakkhusamphassādayo pañca phassā na phusanti. Imāyapi vattabbaṃ natthi.

106. ‘When what has ceased do contacts not impinge?’ means when what has been transcended do the five contacts, such as eye-contact, not impinge? About this too, there is nothing to be said.

107. Nāmañca rūpañca paṭiccāti sampayuttakanāmañca vatthārammaṇarūpañca paṭicca. Rūpe vibhūte na phusanti phassāti rūpe vītivatte pañca phassā na phusanti.

107. ‘Dependent on name and form’ means dependent on associated name and on form as basis and object. ‘When form has ceased, contacts do not impinge’ means when form is transcended, the five contacts do not impinge.

Tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phassoti cakkhurūpaviññāṇānaṃ tiṇṇannaṃ saṅgatiyā phasso jāyati. Cakkhu ca rūpā ca rūpasminti pasādacakkhuñca rūpārammaṇāni ca rūpabhāge rūpakoṭṭhāse katvā. Cakkhusamphassaṃ ṭhapetvāti tiṇṇaṃ saṅgatiyā uppannaphassaṃ muñcitvā. Sampayuttakā dhammā nāmasminti avasesā vedanādayo [M 0.0313] phassena sahajātā dhammā nāmabhāge. Sotañca paṭiccātiādīsupi eseva nayo.

‘The coming together of three is contact’ means contact arises from the coming together of the three: eye, form, and consciousness. ‘Eye and forms are in the form aspect’ means the eye faculty and form objects, having placed them in the form division, the form category. ‘Setting aside eye-contact’ means leaving aside the contact that arises from the coming together of the three. ‘Associated phenomena are in the name aspect’ means the remaining phenomena born together with contact, such as feeling and so on, are in the name category. In cases such as ‘Dependent on the ear,’ the same method applies.

Catūhākārehi rūpaṃ vibhūtaṃ hotīti catūhi kāraṇehi rūpaṃ vītivattaṃ hoti. Ñātavibhūtenāti pākaṭaṃ katvā vītivattena. Tīraṇavibhūtenāti aniccādito tīrayitvā vītivattena. Pahānavibhūtenāti chandarāgapahānato vītivattena. Samatikkamavibhūtenāti catunnaṃ arūpasamāpattīnaṃ paṭilābhavasena vītivattena.

‘Form is transcended in four ways’ means form is transcended due to four causes. ‘Transcended by knowing’ means transcended by making it evident. ‘Transcended by discerning’ means transcended by discerning it as impermanent, etc. ‘Transcended by abandoning’ means transcended through the abandonment of desire and lust. ‘Transcended by overcoming’ means transcended through the power of attaining the four formless attainments.
