'Sunīla' means perfectly blue, without any interval. 'Pāsādika' means inspiring delight. 'Dassaneyya' means lovely to behold. 'Umāpupphasamāna' means similar to the cool water-lily flower. By 'tassa parato' is meant all around its outer surface. 'Pītaka' is all-inclusive. 'Supītaka' means perfectly yellow, without any interval. By 'ubhayato ca akkhikūṭāni' is meant the two eye-corners. 'Lohitaka' is spoken of in an all-inclusive sense. 'Sulohitaka' means perfectly red, without apparent gaps. In the middle, 'kaṇha' means the central part of the eyes, black like collyrium. 'Sukaṇha' means perfectly black, without any interval. 'Alūkha' means pleasing. 'Siniddha' means refined. 'Bhaddāriṭṭhakasamāna' means similar to the bhaddāriṭṭhaka fruit with the skin removed. The text also reads 'addāriṭṭhakasamāna,' the meaning of which is similar to the tintakāka fruit. 'Odāta' is spoken of in an all-inclusive sense. 'Suodāta' means perfectly white, without any interval, like a silver disc. 'Seta paṇḍara' conveys extreme whiteness through both terms. By 'pākatikena maṃsacakkhunā' is meant with the natural fleshly eye. By 'attabhāvapariyāpannenā' is meant dependent on one's own body. By 'purimasucaritakammābhinibbattena' is meant generated by wholesome actions such as bodily good conduct and so forth in past existences wherever they arose. By 'samantā yojanaṃ passati' is meant he sees forms beyond walls and so forth, unobstructed, within a range of approximately four gāvutas (a yojana) all around him, with his natural fleshly eye.

Divā [V 0.0306] ceva rattiñcāti divasabhāge ca rattibhāge ca. Caturaṅgasamannāgatoti catūhi aṅgehi samannāgato paripuṇṇaandhakāro ālokavirahito. Sūriyo vā atthaṅgatoti sūrabhāvaṃ janayanto uṭṭhito sūriyo [M 0.0332] vigato. Kāḷapakkho ca uposathoti kāḷapakkhe cātuddasīuposathadivaso ca. Tibbo ca vanasaṇḍoti gahano ca rukkharāsi. Mahā ca kāḷamegho abbhuṭṭhitoti mahanto kāḷamegho abbhapaṭalo ca uṭṭhito hoti. Kuṭṭo vāti iṭṭhakācayo vā. Kavāṭaṃ vāti dvāravātapānādikavāṭaṃ vā. Pākāro vāti mattikādipākāro vā. Pabbato vāti paṃsupabbatādipabbato vā. Gacchaṃ vāti taruṇagacchādigacchaṃ vā[P 2.0378]. Latā vāti karavindādi latā vā. Āvaraṇaṃ rūpānaṃ dassanāyāti rūpārammaṇānaṃ dassanatthāya paṭisedhaṃ natthi. Ekañce tilaphalaṃ nimittaṃ katvāti sace ekaṃ tilabījaṃ saññāṇaṃ katvā. Tilavāhe pakkhipeyyāti dve sakaṭe tilarāsimhi khipeyya. Keci pana “vāho nāma kumbhātirekadvesakaṭa”nti vadanti. Taññeva tilaphalaṃ uddhareyyāti taṃnimittakataṃ tilabījaṃyeva uddharitvā gaṇheyya.

By 'divā ceva rattiñca' is meant both during the day and at night. By 'caturaṅgasamannāgato' is meant endowed with four factors, being complete darkness and devoid of light. By 'sūriyo vā atthaṅgato' is meant the sun, having risen to create daylight, has disappeared. By 'kāḷapakkho ca uposatho' is meant the fourteenth observance day of the dark fortnight. By 'tibbo ca vanasaṇḍo' is meant a dense mass of trees. By 'mahā ca kāḷamegho abbhuṭṭhito' is meant a massive dark cloud and a layer of clouds has arisen. By 'kuṭṭo vā' is meant a pile of bricks or the like. By 'kavāṭaṃ vā' is meant a door, a window, or the like. By 'pākāro vā' is meant a wall made of clay or other materials. By 'pabbato vā' is meant a mound of earth or the like. By 'gacchaṃ vā' is meant a young tree or the like. By 'latā vā' is meant a vine like the karavinda or the like. By 'āvaraṇaṃ rūpānaṃ dassanāya' is meant there is no obstruction to seeing forms as objects. By 'ekaṃ ce tilaphalaṃ nimittaṃ katvā' is meant if one were to take a single sesame seed as a mark. By 'tilavāhe pakkhipeyya' is meant one might throw it into two carts filled with sesame seeds. Some, however, say, 'A 'vāha' refers to more than one or two carts.' By 'taññeva tilaphalaṃ uddhareyya' is meant one could then retrieve that very sesame seed marked as the sign.

Dibbena cakkhunāti idaṃ vuttatthameva. Visuddhenāti cutūpapātadassanena diṭṭhivisuddhihetuttā visuddhena. Yo hi cutimattameva passati na upapātaṃ, so ucchedadiṭṭhiṃ gaṇhāti. Yo upapātameva passati na cutiṃ, so navasattapātubhāvasassatadiṭṭhiṃ gaṇhāti. Yo pana tadubhayaṃ passati, so yasmā duvidhampi taṃ diṭṭhigataṃ ativattati, tasmāssa taṃ dassanaṃ diṭṭhivisuddhihetu hoti, ubhayañcetaṃ buddhaputtā passanti. Tena vuttaṃ – “cutūpapātadassanena diṭṭhivisuddhihetuttā visuddha”nti. Manussūpacāraṃ atikkamitvā rūpadassanena atikkantamānusakaṃ, mānusakaṃ vā maṃsacakkhuṃ atikkantattā atikkantamānusakanti veditabbaṃ.

By 'dibbena cakkhunā' is meant the same meaning as stated before. By 'visuddhena' is meant purified by seeing the passing away and arising of beings, because it is the cause for the purification of views. For one who sees only the passing away and not the arising grasps the view of annihilation. One who sees only the arising and not the passing away grasps the view of eternalism regarding the new appearance of beings. But one who sees both—because they transcend both these views, their vision becomes a cause for the purification of views. And both are seen by the disciples of the Buddha. Therefore, it is said: 'purified by seeing the passing away and arising of beings, because it is the cause for the purification of views.' By 'manussūpacāraṃ atikkamitvā rūpadassanena atikkantamānusakaṃ' is meant transcending the human, by seeing forms surpassing the human sphere, or because the human fleshly eye is surpassed, it should be understood as transcending the human.

Tena dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passatīti manussamaṃsacakkhunā viya satte oloketi. Cavamāne upapajjamāneti ettha cutikkhaṇe upapattikkhaṇe vā dibbacakkhunā daṭṭhuṃ na sakkā. Ye pana āsannacutikā idāni cavissanti, te cavamānā. Ye ca gahitapaṭisandhikā sampatinibbattāva, te upapajjamānāti adhippetā. Te evarūpe cavamāne upapajjamāne ca passatīti dasseti. Hīneti mohanissandayuttattā hīne. Tabbiparīte paṇīte. Suvaṇṇeti adosanissandayuttattā iṭṭhakantamanāpavaṇṇayutte. Tabbiparīte dubbaṇṇe, abhirūpe virūpeti attho. Sugateti sugatigate, alobhanissandayuttattā vā aḍḍhe mahaddhane. Duggateti [M 0.0333] duggatigate, lobhanissandayuttattā vā dalidde appannapāne. Yathākammūpageti yaṃ yaṃ kammaṃ upacitaṃ, tena tena upagate[V 0.0307]. Tattha purimehi “cavamāne”tiādīhi dibbacakkhukiccaṃ vuttaṃ[P 2.0379]. Iminā pana padena yathākammūpagañāṇakiccaṃ.

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, he sees beings passing away and reappearing—just as one might observe beings with the human eye. To see beings at the very moment of death or the moment of rebirth with the divine eye is not possible. Here, 'passing away' refers to those near death who will soon depart. And 'reappearing' refers to those who have taken rebirth and are newly arisen. He sees such beings passing away and reappearing. He sees them as inferior—those connected with the outflow of delusion—or as superior, their opposite. He sees them as beautiful—those connected with the outflow of non-aversion, endowed with lovely, pleasing, and agreeable forms—or as ugly, their opposite; the meaning is comely and uncomely. He sees them as well-faring—those who have gone to a good destination, or who are wealthy and prosperous due to the outflow of non-greed—or as ill-faring—those who have gone to a bad destination, or who are poor and destitute due to the outflow of greed. He sees them as faring according to their kamma—faring according to whatever kamma has been accumulated. In the earlier passage, with terms like 'passing away,' the function of the divine eye was described. But with this phrase, the function of the knowledge of beings faring according to their kamma is explained.

Tassa ca ñāṇassa ayamuppattikkamo – idha bhikkhu heṭṭhānirayābhimukhaṃ ālokaṃ vaḍḍhetvā nerayike satte passati mahādukkhaṃ anubhavamāne, taṃ dassanaṃ dibbacakkhukiccameva. So evaṃ manasi karoti “kiṃ nu kho kammaṃ katvā ime sattā etaṃ dukkhaṃ anubhavantī”ti, athassa “idaṃ nāma katvā”ti taṃ kammārammaṇaṃ ñāṇaṃ uppajjati. Tathā uparidevalokābhimukhaṃ ālokaṃ vaḍḍhetvā nandanavana missakavana phārusakavanādīsu satte passati mahāsampattiṃ anubhavamāne. Tampi dassanaṃ dibbacakkhukiccameva. So evaṃ manasi karoti “kiṃ nu kho kammaṃ katvā ime sattā etaṃ sampattiṃ anubhavantī”ti. Athassa “idaṃ nāma katvā”ti taṃ kammārammaṇaṃ ñāṇamuppajjati. Idaṃ yathākammūpagañāṇaṃ nāma. Imassa visuṃ parikammaṃ nāma natthi. Yathā ca imassa, evaṃ anāgataṃsañāṇassāpi. Dibbacakkhupādakāneva hi imāni dibbacakkhunā saheva ijjhanti.

This is the sequence of the arising of that knowledge: Here, a monk extends light downwards towards the hell realm and sees beings undergoing great suffering. That seeing is merely the function of the divine eye. He then reflects, 'What kamma have these beings done to experience such suffering?' Then the knowledge arises in him, 'Having done this kamma.' Thus, knowledge having that kamma as its object arises. Similarly, he extends light upwards towards the heavenly realm and sees beings in the Nandana Grove, the Missaka Grove, the Phārusaka Grove, and other places, experiencing great prosperity. That seeing too is merely the function of the divine eye. He reflects, 'What kamma have these beings done to experience such prosperity?' Then the knowledge arises in him, 'Having done this kamma.' Thus, knowledge having that kamma as its object arises. This is called the knowledge of beings faring according to their kamma. There is no separate preliminary practice for this. And just as with this, so too with the knowledge of the future. For these are accomplished together with the divine eye, since the divine eye is their basis.

Ime vata bhontotiādīsu imeti dibbacakkhunā diṭṭhānaṃ nidassanavacanaṃ. Vatāti anusocanatthe nipāto. Bhontoti bhavanto. Duṭṭhu caritaṃ, duṭṭhuṃ vā caritaṃ kilesapūtikattāti duccaritaṃ; kāyena duccaritaṃ, kāyato vā uppannaṃ duccaritanti kāyaduccaritaṃ. Itaresupi eseva nayo. Samannāgatāti samaṅgībhūtā.

'These indeed, venerable ones,' etc.—here, 'these' is a demonstrative term referring to those seen with the divine eye. 'Indeed' is a particle expressing regret. 'Venerable ones' means 'honorable ones.' 'Misconduct' is conduct that is bad, or conduct that is bad because it is foul with defilements. 'Bodily misconduct' is misconduct done by the body or misconduct arisen from the body. The same method applies to the rest. 'Endowed with' means 'possessed of.'

Ariyānaṃ upavādakāti buddhapaccekabuddhabuddhasāvakānaṃ ariyānaṃ antamaso gihisotāpannānampi anatthakāmā hutvā antimavatthunā vā guṇaparidhaṃsanena vā upavādakā, akkosakā garahakāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha “natthi imesaṃ samaṇadhammo, assamaṇā ete”ti vadanto antimavatthunā upavadati. “Natthi imesaṃ jhānaṃ vā vimokkho vā maggo vā phalaṃ vā”tiādīni vadanto guṇaparidhaṃsanena upavadatīti veditabbo. So ca jhānaṃ vā upavadeyya ajhānaṃ vā, ubhayathāpi ariyūpavādova hoti; atibhāriyaṃ kammaṃ, anantariyakammasadisaṃ, saggāvaraṇaṃ maggāvaraṇañca, satekicchaṃ pana hoti. Tasmā yo ariyaṃ upavadati, tena gantvā sace attanā vuḍḍhataro hoti[P 2.0380], ukkuṭikaṃ nisīditvā “ahaṃ āyasmantaṃ [M 0.0334] idañcidañca avacaṃ, taṃ me khamāhī”ti khamāpetabbo. Sace pana navakataro hoti, vanditvā ukkuṭikaṃ nisīditvā añjaliṃ paggahetvā “ahaṃ, bhante, tumhe idañcidañca avacaṃ, taṃ me khamathā”ti khamāpetabbo. Sace so nakkhamati, disāpakkanto vā hoti, sayaṃ vā gantvā saddhivihārike vā [V 0.0308] pesetvā khamāpetabbo. Sace nāpi gantuṃ na pesetuṃ sakkā hoti, ye tasmiṃ vihāre bhikkhū vasanti, tesaṃ santikaṃ gantvā sace navakatarā honti, ukkuṭikaṃ nisīditvā sace vuḍḍhatarā, vuḍḍhe vuttanayeneva paṭipajjitvā “ahaṃ, bhante, asukaṃ nāma āyasmantaṃ idañcidañca avacaṃ, taṃ khamatu me so āyasmā”ti vatvā khamāpetabbo. Sammukhā akhamantepi etadeva kātabbaṃ. Sace ekacārikabhikkhu hoti, neva tassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ na gataṭṭhānaṃ paññāyati, ekassa paṇḍitassa bhikkhuno santikaṃ gantvā “ahaṃ, bhante, asukaṃ nāma āyasmantaṃ idañcidañca avacaṃ, taṃ me anussarato anussarato vippaṭisāro hoti, kiṃ karomī”ti vattabbaṃ. So vakkhati “tumhe mā cintayittha, thero tumhākaṃ khamati, cittaṃ vūpasamethā”ti. Tenapi ariyassa gatadisābhimukhena añjaliṃ paggahetvā “khamathā”ti vattabbaṃ. Yadi so parinibbuto hoti, parinibbutamañcaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā yāva sivathikaṃ gantvāpi khamāpetabbo. Evaṃ kate neva saggāvaraṇaṃ na maggāvaraṇaṃ hoti, pākatikameva hotīti.

'Those who disparage the noble ones' refers to those who, wishing harm to the noble ones—Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of the Buddha, even down to lay stream-enterers—disparage them either by attacking their ultimate basis or by belittling their virtues. This is to say, they are revilers or censurers. Here, one who says, 'These have no qualities of a samaṇa, they are not true samaṇas,' disparages by attacking their ultimate basis. It should be understood that one who says, 'They have no jhāna, no liberation, no path, no fruit,' and so on, disparages by belittling their virtues. And whether one disparages one with jhāna or one without jhāna, in both cases, it is disparagement of a noble one. This is an extremely heavy kamma, akin to an action with immediate retribution, obstructing heaven and the path, but it can be remedied. Therefore, one who has disparaged a noble one should go to them. If the noble one is senior to oneself, the offender should sit on their heels and say, 'Venerable sir, I said such and such to you; please forgive me.' If, however, the noble one is more junior, the offender should pay respects, sit on their heels, raise their hands in añjali, and say, 'Venerable, I said such and such to you; please forgive me.' If the noble one does not forgive, or has departed to another region, one should go oneself or send a fellow monk to seek forgiveness. If it is not possible either to go or to send someone, one should approach the monks residing in that monastery. If they are more junior, one should sit on their heels; if they are more senior, one should act in the way stated for seniors, and say, 'Venerable sirs, I said such and such to the venerable so-and-so; may that venerable one forgive me.' Even if forgiveness is not granted face-to-face, this same thing should be done. If the monk is a solitary wanderer, and neither his dwelling place nor his destination is known, one should approach a wise monk and say, 'Venerable, I said such and such to the venerable so-and-so; remembering it again and again fills me with remorse—what should I do?' He will say, 'Do not worry; the elder forgives you. Calm your mind.' Even so, the offender should face the direction the noble one has gone, raise their hands in añjali, and say, 'Forgive me.' If the noble one has attained final nibbāna, one should go to the place of his funeral pyre, even to the charnel ground, and seek forgiveness. When this is done, there is no obstruction to heaven or the path—it becomes an ordinary matter.

Micchādiṭṭhikāti viparītadassanā. Micchādiṭṭhikammasamādānāti micchādiṭṭhivasena samādinnanānāvidhakammā, ye ca micchādiṭṭhimūlakesu kāyakammādīsu aññepi samādapenti. Ettha ca vacīduccaritaggahaṇeneva ariyūpavāde, manoduccaritaggahaṇena ca micchādiṭṭhiyā saṅgahitāyapi imesaṃ dvinnaṃ punavacanaṃ mahāsāvajjabhāvadassanatthanti veditabbaṃ. Mahāsāvajjo hi ariyūpavādo ānantariyasadiso. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

'Wrong view' means seeing things perversely. 'Undertaking kamma based on wrong view' refers to various actions undertaken due to wrong view, and also includes inciting others to bodily actions, etc., rooted in wrong view. And here, although disparaging the noble ones is included by the statement of verbal misconduct, and wrong view by the statement of mental misconduct, the repetition of these two is to show their exceedingly blameworthy nature. For disparaging the noble ones is exceedingly blameworthy, similar to an action with immediate retribution. And it was said:

“Seyyathāpi, sāriputta, bhikkhu sīlasampanno samādhisampanno paññāsampanno diṭṭheva dhamme aññaṃ ārādheyya, evaṃsampadamidaṃ, sāriputta, vadāmi. Taṃ vācaṃ appahāya taṃ cittaṃ appahāya taṃ diṭṭhiṃ appaṭinissajjitvā yathābhataṃ nikkhitto evaṃ [P 2.0381] niraye”ti (ma. ni. 1.149).

'Just as, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu accomplished in virtue, accomplished in concentration, and accomplished in wisdom might attain final knowledge in this very life—this, Sāriputta, I call an accomplishment. Without abandoning that speech, without abandoning that thought, without relinquishing that view, as if carried there, so he is placed in hell.'

Micchādiṭṭhito ca mahāsāvajjataraṃ nāma aññaṃ natthi. Yathāha –

And there is nothing more blameworthy than wrong view. As it is said:

“Nāhaṃ[M 0.0335], bhikkhave, aññaṃ ekadhammampi samanupassāmi, yaṃ evaṃmahāsāvajjaṃ yathayidaṃ, bhikkhave, micchādiṭṭhi. Micchādiṭṭhiparamāni bhikkhave, mahāsāvajjānī”ti (a. ni. 1.310).

"Monks, I do not see even one other thing that is so greatly blameworthy as this, that is, wrong view. Wrong view is the foremost of great blameworthinesses."

Kāyassa bhedāti upādinnakkhandhapariccāgā. Paraṃ maraṇāti tadanantarābhinibbattakkhandhaggahaṇe[V 0.0309]. Atha vā kāyassa bhedāti jīvitindriyassupacchedā. Paraṃ maraṇāti cuticittato uddhaṃ. Apāyanti evamādi sabbaṃ nirayavevacanameva. Nirayo hi saggamokkhahetubhūtā puññasammatā ayā apetattā, sukhānaṃ vā āyassa abhāvā apāyo. Dukkhassa gati paṭisaraṇanti duggati, dosabahulatāya vā duṭṭhena kammunā nibbattā gatīti duggati. Vivasā nipatanti tattha dukkaṭakārinoti vinipāto, vinassantā vā ettha nipatanti sambhijjamānaṅgapaccaṅgātipi vinipāto. Natthi ettha assādasaññito ayoti nirayo.

"Upon the breakup of the body" means the abandonment of the aggregates of clinging. "After death" refers to the seizing of aggregates arising immediately thereafter. Alternatively, "upon the breakup of the body" means the termination of the life faculty, and "after death" refers to what is subsequent to the passing-away consciousness. "The lower realms," and so forth, are all synonymous terms for hell. Hell is called "apāya" because it is devoid of the gain known as merit, which is the cause of heaven and liberation, or because there is an absence of the gain of happiness. "Duggati" (bad destination) is a destination or refuge of suffering, or a destination produced by wicked kamma due to an abundance of hatred. "Vinipāta" (downfall) is where wrongdoers fall helplessly, or where beings fall perishing, with limbs and minor limbs breaking apart. "Niraya" (hell) is where there is no gain called pleasure.

Atha vā apāyaggahaṇena tiracchānayoniṃ dīpeti, tiracchānayoni hi apāyo sugatito apetattā. Na duggati, mahesakkhānaṃ nāgarājādīnaṃ sambhavato. Duggatiggahaṇena pettivisayaṃ dīpeti, so hi apāyo ceva duggati ca sukhato apetattā dukkhassa ca gatibhūtattā, na tu vinipāto, asurakāyasadisaṃ avinipatitattā. Vinipātaggahaṇena asurakāyaṃ dīpeti. So hi yathāvuttena atthena apāyo ceva duggati ca sabbasamussayehi ca vinipatitattā vinipātoti vuccati. Nirayaggahaṇena avīciādianekappakāraṃ nirayameva dīpetīti. Upapannāti upagatā, tattha abhinibbattāti adhippāyo. Vuttavipariyāyena sukkapakkho veditabbo. Ayaṃ pana viseso – tattha sugatiggahaṇena manussagatipi saṅgayhati. Saggaggahaṇena devagatiyeva. Tattha sundarā gatīti sugati. Rūpādīhi visayehi suṭṭhu aggoti saggo. So sabbopi lujjanapalujjanaṭṭhena lokoti ayaṃ vacanattho. Iti dibbena cakkhunātiādi sabbaṃ nigamanavacanaṃ.

Alternatively, by the term “apāya,” the animal realm is indicated, for the animal realm is indeed a lower realm, being departed from a good destination. It is not a woeful state (duggati) because powerful beings like nāga kings exist there. By the term “duggati,” the realm of spirits is indicated, for it is both a lower realm and a woeful state, being departed from happiness and a destination of suffering. Yet, it is not a state of utter ruin (vinipāta), as it is not ruined like the asura realm. By the term “vinipāta,” the asura realm is indicated, for by the meaning stated, it is both a lower realm and a woeful state, and it is called “vinipāta” because it is utterly ruined in all its constituents. By the term “niraya,” hell itself, of many kinds including Avīci, is specifically indicated. “Upapannā” means “approached,” the intention being “reborn therein.” The bright side should be understood in the opposite manner to what has been stated. Here, however, there is a distinction: by the term “sugati,” the human destination is also included. By the term “sagga,” only the deva destination is meant. There, “sugati” means a beautiful destination, and “saggo” means “most excellent” because of the excellence in forms and other objects. All of this, in the sense of breaking up and dissolving, is called “loka”—this is the meaning of the term. Thus, “with the divine eye,” and so forth—all this is a concluding statement.

Evaṃ dibbena cakkhunā passatīti ayamettha saṅkhepattho – dibbacakkhuñāṇaṃ [P 2.0382] parittapaccuppannaajjhattabahiddhārammaṇavasena catūsu ārammaṇesu pavattati[M 0.0336]. Yathākammūpagañāṇaṃ parittamahaggatātītaajjhattabahiddhārammaṇavasena pañcasu ārammaṇesu pavattati. Anāgataṃsañāṇaṃ parittamahaggataappamāṇamaggaanāgataajjhattabahiddhānavattabbārammaṇavasena aṭṭhasu ārammaṇesu pavattatīti.

“Thus, with the divine eye, one sees”—this is the brief meaning here. The knowledge of the divine eye functions with respect to four objects: limited, present, internal, and external. The knowledge of beings’ destinations according to their kamma functions with respect to five objects: limited, sublime, past, internal, and external. The knowledge of the future functions with respect to eight objects: limited, sublime, immeasurable, path, future, internal, external, and the unspecifiable.

Ākaṅkhamāno ca bhagavāti bhagavā icchamāno. Ekampi lokadhātuṃ passeyyāti ekaṃ cakkavāḷaṃ olokeyya. Sahassimpi cūḷanikanti ettha yāvatā candimasūriyā pariharanti, disā bhānti virocamānā, tāva sahassadhā loko, esā sahassicūḷanikā nāma. Cūḷanikanti khuddakaṃ. Dvisahassimpi majjhimikaṃ lokadhātunti ettha sahassacakkavāḷānaṃ sahassabhāgena gaṇetvā dasasatasahassacakkavāḷaparimāṇā dvisahassī majjhimikā lokadhātu nāma. Ettakena buddhānaṃ jātikkhettaṃ [V 0.0310] nāma dassitaṃ. Bodhisattānañhi pacchimabhave devalokato cavitvā mātukucchiyaṃ paṭisandhiggahaṇadivase ca mātukucchito nikkhamanadivase ca mahābhinikkhamanadivase ca sambodhidhammacakkapavattanaāyusaṅkhārossajjanaparinibbānadivasesu ca ettakaṃ ṭhānaṃ kampati.

“And the Blessed One, desiring” means the Blessed One wishing. “He could see even a single world-system” means he could survey one universe (cakkavāḷa). “Even a thousand small world-systems (cūḷanikā)”: here, as far as the moon and sun revolve, illuminating and shining in the directions, so far is the thousandfold world. This is called the small thousandfold world-system. “Cūḷanikā” means small. “Even a two-thousandfold intermediate world-system (majjhimikā lokadhātu)”: here, counting by a thousandfold portion of a thousand universes, amounting to ten hundred thousand universes, this is called the two-thousandfold intermediate world-system. By this much, the birth-sphere of the Buddhas is shown. For on the day the Bodhisatta, in his final existence, passes away from the deva-world and takes conception in his mother’s womb, and on the day he emerges from his mother’s womb, and on the day of the Great Renunciation, and on the days of his perfect enlightenment, the turning of the Dhamma-wheel, the relinquishing of the life-span, and his final Nibbāna—on these days, this much of the place shakes.

Tisahassimpi. Mahāsahassimpi lokadhātunti sahassito paṭṭhāya tatiyāti tisahassī, paṭhamasahassiṃ sahassadhā katvā gaṇitaṃ majjhimikaṃ sahassadhā katvā gaṇitattā mahantehi sahassehi gaṇitāti mahāsahassī. Ettāvatā koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷaparimāṇo loko dassito hoti. Gaṇakaputtatissatthero pana evamāha – “na hi tisahassimahāsahassilokadhātuyā etaṃ parimāṇaṃ[P 2.0383]. Idañhi ācariyānaṃ sajjhāyamūlakaṃ vācāya parihīnaṭṭhānaṃ, dasakoṭisatasahassacakkavāḷaparimāṇaṃ pana ṭhānaṃ tisahassimahāsahassilokadhātu nāmā”ti. Ettāvatā hi bhagavato āṇākkhettaṃ nāma dassitaṃ. Etasmiñhi antare āṭānāṭiyaparitta- (dī. ni. 3.275 ādayo) isigiliparitta- (ma. ni. 3.133 ādayo) dhajaggaparitta- (saṃ. ni. 1.249) bojjhaṅgaparittakhandhaparitta- (a. ni. 4.67) moraparitta- (jā. 1.2.17-18) mettaparitta- (khu. pā. 9.1 ādayo; su. ni. 143 ādayo) ratanaparittānaṃ (khu. pā. 6.1 ādayo; su. ni. 224 ādayo) āṇā pharati.

“Even a three-thousandfold great thousand world-system.” Starting from a thousand, the third is the three-thousandfold (tisahassī). Because the intermediate is reckoned by making the first thousandfold a thousandfold, and this in turn is reckoned by making the intermediate a thousandfold, it is reckoned with great thousands and is called the great thousandfold (mahāsahassī). By this much, a world whose extent is a thousand million universes is shown. However, the elder Gaṇakaputtatissa said thus: “This is not the measure of the three-thousandfold great thousand world-system. This is a passage from the teachers’ recitation that is deficient in its wording. But the extent of ten thousand million universes is called the three-thousandfold great thousand world-system.” By this much, the Buddha’s sphere of authority is shown. For within this range, the command of the Āṭānāṭiya Paritta, the Isigili Paritta, the Dhajagga Paritta, the Bojjhaṅga Paritta, the Khandha Paritta, the Mora Paritta, the Mettā Paritta, and the Ratana Paritta extends.

Yāvatakaṃ vā pana ākaṅkheyyāti yattakaṃ vā iccheyya. Iminā visayakkhettaṃ dassitaṃ. Buddhānañhi visayakkhettassa pamāṇaparicchedo nāma natthi[M 0.0337], natthikabhāve cassa imaṃ upamaṃ āharanti – koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷamhi yāva brahmalokā sāsapehi pūretvā sace koci puratthimāya disāya ekacakkavāḷe ekaṃ sāsapaṃ pakkhipanto āgaccheyya, sabbepi te sāsapā parikkhayaṃ gaccheyyuṃ. Na tveva puratthimāya disāya cakkavāḷāni. Dakkhiṇādīsupi eseva nayo. Tattha buddhānaṃ avisayo nāma natthi. Tāvatakaṃ passeyyāti tattakaṃ olokeyya. Evaṃ parisuddhaṃ bhagavato dibbacakkhūti dibbacakkhukathaṃ niṭṭhāpesi.

“Or as far as he might wish” means as much as he might desire. By this, the sphere of the object is shown. For there is indeed no limit or determination to the Buddhas’ sphere of object. To illustrate its boundlessness, they give this simile: If one were to fill a thousand million universes up to the Brahma-world with mustard seeds, and if someone were to come from the eastern direction, dropping one mustard seed into each universe, all those mustard seeds would eventually be exhausted, but not the universes in the eastern direction. The same method applies to the southern and other directions. In this way, there is no place that is not within the Buddhas’ sphere of object. “He could see that far” means he could survey that much. Thus, the Blessed One’s divine eye is perfectly pure. This concludes the discourse on the divine eye.

Kathaṃ bhagavā paññācakkhunāpi vivaṭacakkhūti kenappakārena paññācakkhunā apihitacakkhu? Mahāpañño puthupaññotiādikaṃ tattha atirocati yadidaṃ paññāyāti pariyosānaṃ heṭṭhā vuttatthameva.

“How is the Blessed One one with an opened eye of wisdom?” means in what way is his eye of wisdom not closed? The phrases “great wisdom,” “broad wisdom,” and so forth, excel there, ending with “that is, by wisdom.” The meaning is the same as stated below.

Buddhacakkhunāti indriyaparopariyattañāṇena ca āsayānusayañāṇena ca. Imesaṃ dvinnaṃ ñāṇānaṃ buddhacakkhūti nāmaṃ, sabbaññutaññāṇassa samantacakkhūti, tiṇṇaṃ maggañāṇānaṃ dhammacakkhūti[V 0.0311]. Lokaṃ volokento addasa satteti satte addakkhi. Apparajakkhetiādīsu yesaṃ vuttanayeneva paññācakkhumhi rāgādirajaṃ appaṃ, te apparajakkhā. Yesaṃ taṃ mahantaṃ, te mahārajakkhā. Yesaṃ saddhādīni indriyāni tikkhāni, te tikkhindriyā. Yesaṃ tāni mudūni, te mudindriyā. Yesaṃ teyeva saddhādayo ākārā sundarā, te svākārā. Ye kathitakāraṇaṃ sallakkhenti, sukhena sakkā honti viññāpetuṃ te suviññāpayā. Ye paralokañceva vajjañca bhayato passanti, te paralokavajjabhayadassāvino nāma.

“With the Buddha-eye” means with the knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties of others and with the knowledge of inclinations and underlying tendencies. The name “Buddha-eye” is given to these two knowledges; the knowledge of omniscience is called the “all-around eye” (samantacakkhu); and the three path knowledges are called the “Dhamma-eye” (dhammacakkhu). “Surveying the world, he saw beings” means he perceived beings. In phrases like “those with little dust,” those whose dust of passion and so forth in the eye of wisdom is little, in the manner stated, are “those with little dust.” Those for whom it is great are “those with much dust.” Those whose faculties of faith and so forth are keen are “those with keen faculties.” Those whose faculties are weak are “those with weak faculties.” Those whose very qualities of faith and so forth are beautiful are “those with beautiful qualities.” Those who discern the stated reason and can easily be made to understand are “easy to instruct.” Those who see the next world and faults as fearful are called “those who see fear in the next world and in faults.”

Uppaliniyanti [P 2.0384] uppalavane. Itaresupi eseva nayo. Antonimuggaposīnīti yāni antonimuggāneva posiyanti. Udakaṃ accuggamma tiṭṭhantīti udakaṃ atikkamitvā tiṭṭhanti. Tattha yāni yāni accuggamma ṭhitāni, tāni tāni sūriyarasmisamphassaṃ āgamayamānāni ṭhitāni ajja pupphanakāni. Yāni samodakaṃ ṭhitāni, tāni sve pupphanakāni. Yāni udakā anuggatāni antonimuggaposīni, tāni tatiyadivaseva pupphanakāni. Udakā pana anuggatāni aññānipi sarogauppalāni nāma atthi, yāni neva pupphissanti, macchakacchapabhakkhāneva bhavissanti, tāni pāḷiṃ nārūḷhāni, āharitvā pana dīpetabbānīti dīpitāni.

“Uppalinī” means in a lotus grove. The same method applies to the others. “Antonimuggaposīnī” means those that are nourished while submerged within. “Udakaṃ accuggamma tiṭṭhantī” means they stand having risen above the water. Here, those that stand having risen above the water, awaiting the touch of the sun’s rays, are the ones that will bloom today. Those that stand level with the water will bloom tomorrow. Those that have not risen from the water, nourished while submerged within, will bloom only on the third day. However, there are other lotuses called “diseased lotuses” (sarogauppalāni) that have not risen from the water, which will never bloom but will only become food for fish and turtles. These are not included in the Pāli text, but they are explained here because they should be brought forth for explanation.

Yatheva [M 0.0338] hi tāni catubbidhapupphāni, evameva ugghaṭitaññū vipañcitaññū neyyo padaparamoti cattāro puggalā. Yassa puggalassa udāhaṭavelāya dhammābhisamayo hoti, ayaṃ vuccati puggalo ugghaṭitaññū. Yassa puggalassa saṃkhittena bhāsitassa vitthārena atthe vibhajīyamāne dhammābhisamayo hoti, ayaṃ vuccati puggalo vipañcitaññū. Yassa puggalassa uddesato paripucchato yoniso manasikaroto kalyāṇamitte sevato bhajato payirupāsato dhammābhisamayo hoti, ayaṃ vuccati puggalo neyyo. Yassa puggalassa bahumpi suṇato bahumpi bhaṇato bahumpi dhārayato bahumpi vācato na tāya jātiyā dhammābhisamayo hoti, ayaṃ vuccati puggalo padaparamo. Tattha bhagavā uppalavanādisadisaṃ dasasahassilokadhātuṃ olokento ajja pupphanakāni ugghaṭitaññū, sve pupphanakāni vipañcitaññūti evaṃ sabbākārato ca addasa. Tattha tiṇṇaṃ puggalānaṃ imasmiṃyeva attabhāve bhagavato dhammadesanā atthaṃ sādheti, padaparamānaṃ anāgatatthāya vāsanā hoti.

Just as there are those four kinds of flowers, so too are there four types of individuals: the one who understands quickly (ugghaṭitaññū), the one who understands through explanation (vipañcitaññū), the one who needs guidance (neyya), and the one who is only learned in the words (padaparama). The individual who has an awakening to the Dhamma at the moment it is spoken is called an “ugghaṭitaññū” individual. The individual who has an awakening to the Dhamma when a teaching given in brief is explained in detail is called a “vipañcitaññū” individual. The individual who has an awakening to the Dhamma through instruction, repeated questioning, thorough reflection, and associating with, frequenting, and attending on good friends, is called a “neyya” individual. The individual who, even having listened much, spoken much, retained much, and recited much, does not have an awakening to the Dhamma in that existence, is called a “padaparama” individual. There, the Blessed One, surveying the ten-thousandfold world-system as if it were a lotus pond, saw fully in every way: “Today, those ready to flower are the ugghaṭitaññū; tomorrow, those ready to flower will be the vipañcitaññū.” For the first three types of individuals, the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma accomplishes its purpose in this very life; for those who are padaparama, it serves as a foundation for future benefit.

Rāgacaritotiādīsu rajjanavasena ārammaṇe caraṇaṃ etassa atthīti rāgacarito. Dussanavasena ārammaṇe caraṇaṃ etassa atthīti dosacarito. Muyhanavasena ārammaṇe caraṇaṃ etassa atthīti mohacarito. Vitakkanavasena ūhanavasena ārammaṇe caraṇaṃ etassa atthīti vitakkacarito[V 0.0312]. Okappanasaddhāvasena ārammaṇe caraṇaṃ etassa atthīti saddhācarito. Ñāṇameva caraṇaṃ, ñāṇena vā caraṇaṃ, ñāṇassa vā caraṇaṃ, ñāṇato vā caraṇaṃ etassa atthīti ñāṇacarito. Rāgacaritassāti [P 2.0385] rāgussadassa rāgabahulassa. Paratopi eseva nayo.

Among 'one of lustful character' and so forth, 'one of lustful character' means one whose movement among objects is by way of attachment. 'One of hateful character' means one whose movement among objects is by way of aversion. 'One of deluded character' means one whose movement among objects is by way of delusion. 'One of speculative character' means one whose movement among objects is by way of thinking and pondering. 'One of faithful character' means one whose movement among objects is by way of conviction and faith. 'One of wise character' means one for whom knowledge itself is movement, or movement is by knowledge, or movement belongs to knowledge, or movement is from knowledge. 'Of one of lustful character' means of one who is excessive in lust, who is abundant in lust. The same method applies to the others as well.

Asubhakathaṃ kathetīti uddhumātakādidasavidhaṃ asubhapaṭisaṃyuttakathaṃ ācikkhati. Vuttañhetaṃ – “asubhā bhāvetabbā rāgassa pahānāyā”ti (a. ni. 9.1). Mettābhāvanaṃ ācikkhatīti mettābhāvanaṃ cittasinehanaṃ katheti. Vuttañhetaṃ – “mettā bhāvetabbā byāpādassa pahānāyā”ti. Uddeseti sajjhāyane. Paripucchāyāti aṭṭhakathāya. Kālena dhammassavaneti yuttappattakāle uttari pariyattidhammassavane. Dhammasākacchāyāti aññehi saddhiṃ sākacchāya. Garusaṃvāseti garūnaṃ payirupāsane. Nivesetīti ācariyānaṃ santike patiṭṭhāpeti. Ānāpānassatiṃ ācikkhatīti [M 0.0339] ānāpānassatisampayuttakammaṭṭhānaṃ katheti. Vuttañhetaṃ – “ānāpānassati bhāvetabbā vitakkupacchedāyā”ti (a. ni. 9.1). Pasādanīyaṃ nimittaṃ ācikkhatīti cūḷavedalla- (ma. ni. 1.460 ādayo) mahāvedallā- (ma. ni. 1.449 ādayo) dipasādajanakaṃ suttaṃ katheti. Buddhasubodhinti buddhassa bhagavato buddhattapaṭivedhaṃ. Dhammasudhammatanti navavidhalokuttaradhammassa svākkhātataṃ. Saṅghasuppaṭipattinti aṭṭhavidhaariyasaṅghassa suppaṭipannatādisuṭṭhupaṭipattiṃ. Sīlāni ca attanoti attano santakasīlāni ca. Ācikkhati vipassanānimittanti udayabbayādipaṭisaṃyuttaṃ katheti. Aniccākāranti hutvā abhāvākāraṃ. Dukkhākāranti udayabbayapaṭipīḷanākāraṃ. Anattākāranti avasavattanākāraṃ.

He speaks of the foul discourse—that is, he explains a talk connected with the ten kinds of foulness, such as the bloated corpse. For this is said: "The foul should be developed for the abandoning of lust." He explains the development of loving-kindness—that is, he speaks of the softening of the heart through loving-kindness. For this is said: "Loving-kindness should be developed for the abandoning of ill will." 'He recites' means recitation. 'By questioning' means by way of commentary. 'Listening to the Dhamma at the proper time' means listening to further teachings of the Dhamma at the fitting time. 'Discussing the Dhamma' means conversing with others. 'Associating with the venerable' means attending upon the venerable ones. 'He establishes' means he settles near the teachers. 'He explains mindfulness of breathing' means he speaks of the meditation subject connected with mindfulness of breathing. For this is said: "Mindfulness of breathing should be developed for the cutting off of discursive thinking." 'He explains an inspiring sign' means he speaks of a discourse that generates inspiration, such as the Cūḷavedalla Sutta and Mahāvedalla Sutta. 'The Buddha's perfect enlightenment' means the Blessed One Buddha's realization of Buddhahood. 'The Dhamma's well-taught nature' means the well-proclaimed nature of the ninefold supramundane Dhamma. 'The Sangha's good practice' means the good practice, etc., of the eightfold Noble Sangha. 'And his own virtues' means his own virtuous conduct. 'He explains the sign of insight' means he speaks of what is connected with arising and passing away, etc. 'The aspect of impermanence' means the aspect of having come into being and then ceasing to be. 'The aspect of suffering' means the aspect of oppression by arising and passing away. 'The aspect of non-self' means the aspect of not being subject to control.

Sele yathā pabbatamuddhaniṭṭhitoti selamaye ekagghane pabbatamuddhani ṭhitova, na hi tattha ṭhitassa dassanatthaṃ abhimukhe gīvukkhipanapasāraṇādikiccaṃ atthi. Tathūpamanti tappaṭibhāgaṃ selapabbatūpamaṃ. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepattho – yathā selapabbatamuddhanti ṭhitova cakkhunā puriso samantato janataṃ passeyya. Sumedha sundarapañña sabbaññutaññāṇena samantacakkhu bhagavā dhammamayaṃ paññāmayaṃ pāsādamāruyha sayaṃ apetasoko [P 2.0386] sokāvatiṇṇaṃ jātijarābhibhūtañca janataṃ avekkhassu upadhārayatu upaparikkhatu.

Just as 'one standing on a mountain peak' means standing on a mountain peak made of rock, a single solid mass; for one standing there, there is no need for craning the neck or stretching forward to see in front. 'Similarly' means its counterpart, the simile of the rocky mountain. Here, the concise meaning is this: just as a person standing on the peak of a rocky mountain could see the people all around with their eye. O Sumedha, O one of beautiful wisdom, the Blessed One, the All-Seeing One with omniscient knowledge, having ascended the palace made of Dhamma and wisdom, himself free from sorrow, should observe, consider, and carefully examine the people overwhelmed by sorrow, afflicted by birth and aging.

Ayaṃ panettha adhippāyo – yathā hi pabbatapādasāmantā mahantaṃ khettaṃ katvā tattha kedārapāḷīsu kuṭiyo katvā rattiṃ aggiṃ jāleyya, caturaṅgasamannāgatañca andhakāraṃ assa, atha tassa pabbatassa matthake ṭhatvā cakkhumato purisassa bhūmiṃ olokayato neva khettaṃ na kedārapāḷiyo [V 0.0313] na kuṭiyo na tattha sayitamanussā paññāyeyyuṃ, kuṭikāsu pana aggijālamattameva paññāyeyya. Evaṃ dhammapāsādaṃ āruyha sattakāyaṃ olokayato tathāgatassa ye te akatakalyāṇā sattā, te ekavihāre dakkhiṇajāṇupasse nisinnāpi buddhacakkhussa āpāthaṃ nāgacchanti, rattiṃ khittasarā viya honti. Ye pana katakalyāṇā veneyyapuggalā, te evassa dūrepi ṭhitā āpāthaṃ gacchanti, te eva aggi viya himavantapabbato viya ca. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Here is the intended meaning: Just as if, near the foot of a mountain, someone were to prepare a large field, and having built huts within its boundary ridges, were to light a fire at night, and there were darkness endowed with four factors, then a man with good eyesight, standing on the mountain peak and looking down at the ground, would not see the field, the boundary ridges, the huts, or the people sleeping there—only the light of the fires in the huts would be visible. Similarly, when the Tathāgata ascends the palace of the Dhamma and observes the mass of beings, those beings who have not done good deeds, even if seated near him in one dwelling with their right knee beside him, do not come into the range of the Buddha's vision—they are like arrows shot at night. But those teachable individuals who have done good deeds, even if standing far away, come into his range—they are like a fire, like the Himalayas. And this has been said:

“Dūre santo pakāsenti, himavantova pabbato;

Asantettha na dissanti, rattiṃ khittā yathā sarā”ti. (dha. pa. 304; netti. 11);

“From afar the good are visible, like the Himalayas; but here the bad are not seen, like arrows shot at night.”

Sabbaññutaññāṇanti [M 0.0340] ettha pañcaneyyapathappabhedaṃ sabbaṃ aññāsīti sabbaññū. Saṅkhatāsaṅkhatādibhedā sabbadhammā hi saṅkhāro vikāro lakkhaṇaṃ nibbānaṃ paññattīti pañceva neyyapathā honti. Sabbaññussa bhāvo sabbaññutā, sabbaññutā eva ñāṇaṃ “sabbaññutāñāṇa”nti vattabbe “sabbaññutaññāṇa”nti vuttaṃ. Sabbaññūti ca kamasabbaññū sakiṃsabbaññū satatasabbaññū sattisabbaññū ñātasabbaññūti pañcavidhā sabbaññuno siyuṃ. Tesu kamena sabbajānanakālāsambhavato kamasabbaññutā na hoti, sakiṃ sabbārammaṇaggahaṇābhāvato sakiṃsabbaññutā na hoti, cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ yathārammaṇacittasambhavato bhavaṅgacittavirodhato yuttiabhāvato ca satatasabbaññutā na hoti, parisesato sabbajānanasamatthatāya [P 2.0387] sattisabbaññutā vā siyā, viditasabbadhammattā ñātasabbaññutā vā, sattisabbaññuno sabbajānanattaṃ natthīti tampi na yujjati, “na tassa adiṭṭhamidhatthi kiñci…pe… samantacakkhū”ti vuttattā ñātasabbaññutā eva yujjati. Evañhi sati kiccato asammohato kāraṇasiddhito āvajjanapaṭibaddhato sabbaññutameva hotīti. Tena ñāṇenāti tena sabbajānanañāṇena.

The knowledge of omniscience—here, 'omniscient' means one who knows all that is divided into the five kinds of objects of knowledge. For all phenomena, divided into conditioned, unconditioned, and so forth—namely, formations, transformations, characteristics, Nibbāna, and concepts—are just five paths of knowledge. The state of an omniscient one is omniscience; omniscience itself is knowledge. What should be called 'omniscience-knowledge' is here stated as 'omniscience-knowledge'. Moreover, the omniscient ones may be of five kinds: successive omniscient, momentary omniscient, perpetual omniscient, potential omniscient, and known omniscient. Among these, successive omniscience does not exist because it is impossible to know everything in succession. Momentary omniscience does not exist because there is no single grasp of all objects. Perpetual omniscience does not exist because the arising of consciousness depends on its object, conflicts with the life-continuum consciousness, and its occurrence is thus not feasible. Potential omniscience might exist due to the capacity to know all that remains, or known omniscience might exist because all phenomena are known. However, since a potential omniscient one does not possess the state of knowing everything, that too is not fitting. For it is said, 'There is nothing unseen by him... he is all-seeing.' Therefore, only known omniscience is fitting. Thus, this being so, omniscience truly exists due to non-delusion regarding its function, the establishment of its cause, and its connection with adverting. 'By that knowledge' means by that knowledge which knows all.

Puna aparena pariyāyena sabbaññubhāvasādhanatthaṃ “na tassā”ti gāthamāha. Tattha na tassa addiṭṭhamidhatthi kiñcīti tassa tathāgatassa idha imasmiṃ tedhātuke loke imasmiṃ paccuppannakāle vā paññācakkhunā adiṭṭhaṃ nāma kiñci appamattakampi na atthi na saṃvijjati. Atthīti idaṃ vattamānakālikaṃ ākhyātapadaṃ, iminā paccuppannakālikassa sabbadhammassa ñātabhāvaṃ dasseti. Gāthābandhasukhatthaṃ panettha da-kāro payutto. Atho aviññātanti ettha athoti vacanopādāne [V 0.0314] nipāto. Aviññātanti atītakālikaṃ aviññātaṃ nāma kiñci dhammajātaṃ nāhosīti pāṭhaseso. Abyayabhūtassa atthi-saddassa gahaṇe pāṭhasesaṃ vināpi yujjatiyeva. Iminā atītakālikassa sabbadhammassa ñātabhāvaṃ dasseti. Ajānitabbanti anāgatakālikaṃ ajānitabbaṃ nāma dhammajātaṃ na bhavissati natthīti. Iminā anāgatakālikassa sabbadhammassa ñātabhāvaṃ dasseti. Jānanakiriyāvisesamattameva vā ettha a-kāro. Sabbaṃ abhiññāsi yadatthi neyyanti ettha yaṃ tekālikaṃ vā kālavinimuttaṃ vā neyyaṃ jānitabbaṃ kiñci dhammajātaṃ atthi, taṃ sabbaṃ tathāgato abhiññāsi adhikena sabbaññutaññāṇena [M 0.0341] jāni paṭivijjhi, ettha atthi-saddena tekālikassa kālavimuttassa ca gahaṇā atthi-saddo abyayabhūtoyeva daṭṭhabbo. Tathāgato tena samantacakkhūti kālavasena okāsavasena ca nippadesattā samantā sabbato pavattaṃ ñāṇacakkhu assāti samantacakkhu, tena yathāvuttena kāraṇena tathāgato samantacakkhu sabbaññūti vuttaṃ hoti[P 2.0388]. Imissā gāthāya puggalādhiṭṭhānāya desanāya sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ sādhitaṃ.

Again, in another way, to establish omniscience, the verse 'na tassā' is spoken. Herein, 'na tassa addiṭṭhamidhatthi kiñcīti' means that for the Tathāgata, there is nothing—not even the slightest thing—unseen by the eye of wisdom in this triple world, in this present time, that does not exist or is not found. 'Atthīti' is a present-tense verb, indicating the knowability of all phenomena in the present moment. For the sake of ease in poetic composition, the syllable 'da' is used here. And 'aviññātaṃ' (unknown)—here 'atho' is a particle for introducing a word. 'Aviññātaṃ' means that no dhamma-element in the past was unknown; this is the implied remainder of the text. When the word 'atthi' is taken as indeclinable, it is fitting even without the implied remainder. This shows the knowability of all phenomena in the past. 'Ajānitabbaṃ' refers to the future—no dhamma-element in the future will be unknowable or non-existent. This demonstrates the knowability of all phenomena in the future. Or, here, the prefix 'a-' is merely a qualification of the act of knowing. 'Sabbaṃ abhiññāsi yadatthi neyyaṃ' means whatever knowable dhamma-element exists—whether pertaining to the three times or is timeless—the Tathāgata has fully comprehended it with his supreme omniscient knowledge. Here, since the word 'atthi' encompasses all three times and the timeless, the word 'atthi' should be understood as indeclinable. 'Tathāgato tena samantacakkhū' means that because he possesses the knowledge-eye that operates everywhere without limitation in terms of time or space, he is called 'the All-Seeing One (Samantacakkhu).' Thus, for the reasons stated, the Tathāgata is declared to be the All-Seeing, the Omniscient. Through this verse, which is a teaching focused on the individual, the knowledge of omniscience is established.

Na itihitihanti “evaṃ kira āsi, evaṃ kira āsī”ti na hoti. Na itikirāyāti “evaṃ kira eta”nti na hoti. Na paramparāyāti paramparakathāyāpi na hoti. Na piṭakasampadāyāti amhākaṃ piṭakatantiyā saddhiṃ sametīti na hoti. Na takkahetūti takkaggāhenapi na hoti. Na ākāraparivitakkenāti “sundaramidaṃ kāraṇa”nti evaṃ kāraṇaparivitakkenapi na hoti. Na diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyāti amhākaṃ nijjhāyitvā khamitvā gahitadiṭṭhiyā saddhiṃ sametītipi na hoti.

Not by hearsay: 'Thus it was, thus it was,' it is not so. Not by tradition: 'Thus it is said,' it is not so. Not by lineage, not even by the talk of lineage, it is not so. Not by the collections of scripture: 'This agrees with our collection of texts,' it is not so. Not by mere logic, not even by the grasp of reasoning, it is not so. Not by considering appearances: 'This reason is beautiful,' not even by pondering reasons, it is not so. Not by the acceptance of a view after reflection: 'This agrees with the view we have adopted after pondering and accepting it,' it is not so.

Atha vāpi samādhinti ettha samādhinti kusalacittekaggatā samādhi. Kenaṭṭhena samādhīti? Samādhānaṭṭhena. Kimidaṃ samādhānaṃ nāma? Ekārammaṇe cittacetasikānaṃ samaṃ sammā ca ādhānaṃ, ṭhapananti vuttaṃ hoti. Tasmā yassa dhammassa ānubhāvena ekārammaṇe cittacetasikā samaṃ sammā ca avikkhippamānā avippakiṇṇā ca hutvā tiṭṭhanti, idaṃ samādhānanti veditabbaṃ. Tassa kho pana samādhissa –

Or else, concentration—here, concentration is the one-pointedness of wholesome consciousness. In what sense is it concentration? In the sense of settling. What is this settling? It is said to be the even and right placing and establishing of mind and mental factors on a single object. Therefore, by the power of which phenomenon the mind and mental factors, being undistracted and unscattered, stand evenly and rightly placed on a single object—this should be understood as settling. And of that concentration—

“Lakkhaṇaṃ tu avikkhepo, vikkhepaddhaṃsanaṃ raso;

Akampanamupaṭṭhānaṃ, padaṭṭhānaṃ sukhaṃ pana”. (paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 1.1.3);

The characteristic is non-distraction; the function is the destruction of distraction; the manifestation is non-wavering; and the proximate cause is happiness.

Samādhi anāvilaacalabhāvena ārammaṇe tiṭṭhatīti ṭhiti. Parato padadvayaṃ upasaggavasena [V 0.0315] vaḍḍhitaṃ. Api ca sampayuttadhamme ārammaṇamhi sampiṇḍetvā tiṭṭhatīti saṇṭhiti. Ārammaṇaṃ ogāhetvā anupavisitvā tiṭṭhatīti avaṭṭhiti. Kusalapakkhasmiñhi cattārova dhammā ārammaṇaṃ ogāhanti saddhā sati samādhi paññāti. Teneva saddhā “okappanā”ti vuttā, sati “apilāpanatā”ti, samādhi “avaṭṭhitī”ti, paññā “pariyogāhanā”ti. Akusalapakkhe pana tayo dhammā ārammaṇaṃ ogāhanti taṇhā [M 0.0342] diṭṭhi avijjāti. Tenevete “oghā”ti vuttā. Cittekaggatā panettha na balavatī hoti. Yathā [P 2.0389] hi rajuṭṭhānaṭṭhāne udakena siñcitvā sammaṭṭhe thokameva kālaṃ rajo sannisīdati, sukkhante sukkhante puna pakatibhāveneva vuṭṭhāti, evameva akusalapakkhe cittekaggatā na balavatī hoti.

Concentration stands in the object with an unstirred and unshaken state—this is stability. Further, two terms are augmented by way of prefixes. Moreover, having compacted associated states together, it stands in the object—this is consolidation. It plunges into and settles in the object—this is immersion. Indeed, in the wholesome group, four qualities plunge into the object: faith, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. Therefore, faith is called 'inclining towards,' mindfulness 'non-drifting,' concentration 'immersion,' and wisdom 'thorough plunging.' In the unwholesome group, however, three qualities plunge into the object: craving, wrong view, and ignorance. Therefore, these are called 'floods.' Here, one-pointedness of mind is not strong. Just as when dust is sprinkled with water in a dusty place and smoothed, the dust settles only briefly, and as it dries, it rises again to its original condition—so too, in the unwholesome group, one-pointedness of mind is not strong.

Uddhaccavicikicchāvasena pavattassa visāhārassa paṭipakkhato avisāhāro. Uddhaccavicikicchāvaseneva gacchantaṃ cittaṃ vikkhipati nāma. Ayaṃ pana tathāvidho vikkhepo na hotīti avikkhepo. Uddhaccavicikicchāvaseneva cittaṃ visāhaṭaṃ nāma hoti, ito cito ca harīyati, ayaṃ pana evaṃ avisāhaṭamānasassa bhāvoti avisāhaṭamānasatā. Samathoti tividho samatho cittasamatho adhikaraṇasamatho sabbasaṅkhārasamathoti. Tattha aṭṭhasu samāpattīsu cittekaggatā cittasamatho nāma. Tañhi āgamma cittacalanaṃ cittavipphanditaṃ sammati vūpasammati, tasmā so “cittasamatho”ti vuccati. Sammukhāvinayādisattavidho samatho adhikaraṇasamatho nāma. Tañhi āgamma tāni tāni adhikaraṇāni sammanti vūpasammanti, tasmā so “adhikaraṇasamatho”ti vuccati. Yasmā pana sabbe saṅkhārā nibbānaṃ āgamma sammanti vūpasammanti vūpasammanti, tasmā taṃ “sabbasaṅkhārasamatho”ti vuccati. Imasmiṃ atthe cittasamatho adhippeto. Samādhilakkhaṇe indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti samādhindriyaṃ. Uddhacce na kampatīti samādhibalaṃ. Sammāsamādhīti yāthāvasamādhi niyyānikasamādhi.

Non-distraction is the opposite of the distraction that proceeds by way of restlessness and doubt. The mind that wanders due to restlessness and doubt is called distracted. But since this kind of distraction is not present, it is non-distraction. The mind is called agitated when, due to restlessness and doubt, it is carried here and there. But this is the state of a mind not so agitated; hence, it is non-agitation of mind. Tranquility is of three kinds: tranquility of mind, tranquility of disputes, and tranquility of all formations. Therein, one-pointedness of mind in the eight attainments is called tranquility of mind. For, depending on it, the movement and agitation of the mind cease and subside; therefore, it is called 'tranquility of mind.' The sevenfold settlement of disputes, such as by face-to-face procedure, is called tranquility of disputes. For, depending on it, those disputes cease and subside; therefore, it is called 'tranquility of disputes.' And because all formations cease and subside upon reaching Nibbāna, that is called 'tranquility of all formations.' In this context, tranquility of mind is intended. It exercises sovereignty in the characteristic of concentration, thus it is the faculty of concentration. It is unshaken by restlessness, thus it is the power of concentration. Right concentration is concentration as it truly is, concentration that leads out.

157. Athassa bhagavā yasmā indriyasaṃvaro sīlassa rakkhā, yasmā vā iminānukkamena desiyamānā ayaṃ desanā tāsaṃ devatānaṃ sappāyā, tasmā indriyasaṃvarato pabhuti paṭipadaṃ dassento “cakkhūhī”tiādi āraddho. Tattha cakkhūhi neva lolassāti adiṭṭhadakkhitabbādivasena cakkhūhi lolo neva assa. Gāmakathāya āvaraye sotanti tiracchānakathāya sotaṃ āvareyya.

157. Then the Blessed One, because sense restraint is the protection of virtue, and because this teaching, being taught in this gradual sequence, was suitable for those deities, therefore, showing the practice beginning from sense restraint, began with 'With the eyes,' and so on. Therein, 'with the eyes, he should not be greedy' means he should not be greedy with the eyes for things unseen that are to be seen, and so on. 'He should block the ear from village talk' means he should block the ear from worldly talk.

Cakkhuloliyenāti cakkhudvāre uppannalolavasena cakkhuloliyena. Adiṭṭhaṃ dakkhitabbanti adiṭṭhapubbaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ passituṃ yuttaṃ. Diṭṭhaṃ samatikkamitabbanti diṭṭhapubbarūpārammaṇaṃ atikkamituṃ [V 0.0316] yuttaṃ. Ārāmena ārāmanti pupphārāmādiārāmena [M 0.0343] phalārāmādiṃ [P 2.0390] vā pupphārāmādiṃ vā. Dīghacārikanti dīghacaraṇaṃ. Anavaṭṭhitacārikanti asanniṭṭhānacaraṇaṃ. Anuyutto hoti rūpadassanāyāti rūpārammaṇadassanatthāya punappunaṃ yutto hoti.

'With eye-greed' means by way of the greed that has arisen at the eye-door. 'Unseen, to be seen' means a visual object not seen before that is fit to be seen. 'Seen, to be overcome' means a visual object seen before that is fit to be transcended. 'From park to park' means from a park such as a flower garden to a fruit garden or another such park. 'Long wandering' means lengthy wandering. 'Unsettled wandering' means wandering without a fixed determination. 'Devoted to seeing forms' means being repeatedly engaged for the purpose of seeing visual objects.

Antaragharaṃ paviṭṭhoti ummārabbhantaraṃ paviṭṭho. Vīthiṃ paṭipannoti antaravīthiṃ otiṇṇo. Gharamukhāni olokentoti gharadvārāni avalokento. Uddhaṃ ullokentoti uparidisaṃ uddhaṃmukho hutvā vilokento.

'He has entered inside the house' means he has entered inside the threshold. 'He has set out on the street' means he has descended into the street. 'Looking at the fronts of houses' means looking at the doors of houses. 'Looking upwards' means looking in the upward direction, having become upward-faced.

Cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvāti kāraṇavasena cakkhūti laddhavohārena rūpadassanasamatthena cakkhuviññāṇena rūpaṃ disvā. Porāṇā panāhu – “cakkhu rūpaṃ na passati acittakattā, cittaṃ na passati acakkhukattā. Dvārārammaṇasaṅghaṭṭe pana pasādavatthukena cittena passati. Īdisī panesā ‘dhanunā vijjhatī’tiādīsu viya sasambhārakathā nāma hoti. Tasmā cakkhuviññāṇena rūpaṃ disvāti ayamettha attho”ti. Nimittaggāhīti itthipurisanimittaṃ vā subhanimittādikaṃ vā kilesavatthubhūtaṃ nimittaṃ chandarāgavasena gaṇhāti, diṭṭhamatteyeva na saṇṭhāti. Anubyañjanaggāhīti kilesānaṃ anuanubyañjanato pākaṭabhāvakaraṇato anubyañjananti laddhavohāraṃ hatthapādasitahasitakathitaālokitavilokitādibhedaṃ ākāraṃ gaṇhāti. Yatvādhikaraṇamenantiādimhi yaṃkāraṇā yassa cakkhundriyāsaṃvarassa hetu etaṃ puggalaṃ satikavāṭena cakkhundriyaṃ asaṃvutaṃ apihitacakkhudvāraṃ hutvā viharantaṃ ete abhijjhādayo dhammā anvāssaveyyuṃ anuppabandheyyuṃ ajjhotthareyyuṃ. Tassa saṃvarāya na paṭipajjatīti tassa cakkhundriyassa satikavāṭena pidahanatthāya na paṭipajjati. Evaṃbhūtoyeva ca na rakkhati cakkhundriyaṃ. Na cakkhundriye saṃvaraṃ āpajjatītipi vuccati. Tattha kiñcāpi cakkhundriye saṃvaro vā asaṃvaro vā natthi. Na hi cakkhupasādaṃ nissāya sati vā muṭṭhassaccaṃ vā uppajjati. Apica yadā rūpārammaṇaṃ cakkhussa āpāthaṃ āgacchati, tadā bhavaṅge dvikkhattuṃ uppajjitvā niruddhe kiriyāmanodhātu [P 2.0391] āvajjanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā uppajjitvā nirujjhati, tato cakkhuviññāṇaṃ dassanakiccaṃ, tato manodhātu sampaṭicchanakiccaṃ, tato vipākāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātu santīraṇakiccaṃ, tato kiriyāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātu [M 0.0344] voṭṭhabbanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā uppajjitvā nirujjhati, tadanantaraṃ javanaṃ javati.

'Having seen a form with the eye' means having seen a form with the eye-consciousness, which is capable of seeing forms; the term 'eye' is a conventional designation used by way of cause. The ancients, however, say: 'The eye does not see forms, for it is without mind; the mind does not see, for it is without an eye. But upon the impact of the door and the object, one sees with the mind that has the eye-sensitivity as its basis. This is like the expression “one shoots with a bow,” which is a conventional way of speaking involving the necessary equipment. Therefore, the meaning here is that one sees a form with eye-consciousness.' 'A grasper of signs' means one who grasps a sign that is a basis for defilements—such as the sign of a woman or a man, or a sign of beauty—with desire and lust, not stopping at the mere sight. 'A grasper of details' means one who grasps those features—such as hands, feet, smiling, laughing, speaking, looking at, and looking away—which are conventionally called 'details' because they make the defilements manifest by following them up. Regarding 'On account of which…': for which reason, that is, on account of this lack of restraint of the eye faculty, these states of covetousness and so on would flow into, follow, and overwhelm this person who dwells with the eye faculty unrestrained, with the eye-door unclosed. 'He does not practice for its restraint' means he does not practice for the purpose of closing the door of the eye faculty with mindfulness. Such a person does not guard the eye faculty, and it is said that he does not exercise restraint over the eye faculty. Therein, although there is no restraint or lack of restraint in the eye faculty itself—for neither mindfulness nor forgetfulness arises dependent on the eye-sensitivity—yet when a visual object comes into the range of the eye, the life-continuum arises twice and ceases. Then, the functional mind-element arises, performing the function of adverting, and ceases. Next, eye-consciousness arises, performing the function of seeing; then, the mind-element arises, performing the function of receiving; then, the resultant rootless mind-consciousness-element arises, performing the function of investigating; then, the functional rootless mind-consciousness-element arises, performing the function of determining, and ceases. Immediately afterward, the impulsions run.

Tatrāpi neva bhavaṅgasamaye na āvajjanādīnaṃ aññatarasamaye saṃvaro vā asaṃvaro vā atthi. Javanakkhaṇe pana sace dussīlyaṃ vā muṭṭhassaccaṃ vā aññāṇaṃ vā akkhanti vā kosajjaṃ [V 0.0317] vā uppajjati, asaṃvaro hoti. Evaṃ honto pana so “cakkhundriye asaṃvaro”ti vuccati. Kasmā? Yasmā tasmiṃ asaṃvare sati dvārampi aguttaṃ hoti, bhavaṅgampi āvajjanādīnipi vīthicittāni. Yathā kiṃ? Yathā nagare catūsu dvāresu asaṃvutesu kiñcāpi antogharadvārakoṭṭhakagabbhādayo saṃvutā, tathāpi antonagare sabbaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ arakkhitaṃ agopitameva hoti. Nagaradvārena hi pavisitvā corā yadicchanti taṃ kareyyuṃ, evameva javane dussīlyādīsu uppannesu tasmiṃ asaṃvare sati dvārampi aguttaṃ hoti bhavaṅgampi āvajjanādīnipi vīthicittāni.

Even there, neither during the life-continuum moment nor during any of the moments of adverting and so on, is there restraint or lack of restraint. However, during the impulsion moment, if immoral conduct, forgetfulness, ignorance, impatience, or laziness arises, then there is lack of restraint. When this occurs, it is called 'lack of restraint in the eye faculty.' Why? Because when such lack of restraint exists, the door is unguarded, as are the life-continuum, the adverting and other moments, and the process-cognitions. To what is this comparable? Just as when the four gates of a city are unguarded, even if the inner doors, storerooms, and chambers are secured, still everything inside the city remains unprotected and unguarded. For thieves, entering through the city gates, can do whatever they wish. Even so, when immoral conduct and the like arise in the impulsion, then when that lack of restraint exists, the door is unguarded, as are the life-continuum, the adverting and other moments, and the process-cognitions.

Saddhādeyyānīti kammañca phalañca idhalokañca paralokañca saddahitvā dinnāni. “Ayaṃ me ñātīti vā, mittoti vā, idaṃ vā paṭikarissati, idaṃ vānena katapubba”nti vā evaṃ na dinnānīti attho. Evaṃ dinnāni hi na saddhādeyyāni nāma honti. Bhojanānīti ca desanāsīsamattametaṃ, atthato pana saddhādeyyāni bhojanāni bhuñjitvā cīvarāni pārupitvā senāsanāni sevamānā gilānapaccayabhesajjaṃ paribhuñjamānāti sabbametaṃ vuttameva hoti.

“Given out of faith” refers to those things given with faith in kamma and its result, in this world and the next. The meaning is that they are not given with thoughts like, “This is my relative,” or “This is my friend,” or “This person will repay me,” or “This person has done something for me before.” For gifts given in this way are not called “given out of faith.” “Foods” is mentioned here merely as a heading for the discourse, but in essence, it includes all things given out of faith—eating foods, wearing robes, using lodgings, and making use of medicines for the sick. All of this is indeed stated.

Seyyathidanti nipāto. Tassattho, katamo hoti. Naccaṃ nāma yaṃkiñci naccaṃ, taṃ maggaṃ gacchantenāpi gīvaṃ pasāretvā daṭṭhuṃ na vaṭṭati. Gītanti yaṃkiñci gītaṃ. Vāditanti yaṃkiñci vāditaṃ. Pekkhanti naṭasamajjaṃ. Akkhānanti bhāratarāmāyanādikaṃ. Yasmiṃ ṭhāne kathīyati, tattha gantumpi na vaṭṭati. Pāṇissaranti kaṃsatāḷaṃ, “pāṇitāḷa”ntipi vadanti. Vetāḷanti ghanatāḷaṃ, “mantena matasarīruṭṭhāpana”ntipi eke. Kumbhathūṇanti caturassaambaṇakatāḷaṃ[P 2.0392], “kumbhasadda”ntipi eke. Sobhanakanti naṭānaṃ abbhokkiraṇaṃ; sobhanakaraṃ vā, paṭibhānacittanti vuttaṃ hoti. Caṇḍālanti ayoguḷakīḷā, “caṇḍālānaṃ sāṇadhovanakīḷā”tipi vadanti. Vaṃsanti veṇuṃ ussāpetvā kīḷanaṃ.

‘Such as’ is a particle, meaning ‘What are they?’ Dancing means any kind of dancing; even while walking, it is not proper to crane one’s neck to watch it. Singing means any kind of song. Instrumental music means any kind of musical instrument. Shows mean theatrical performances. Storytelling means recitations such as the Mahābhārata or Rāmāyaṇa; it is not proper even to go to the place where it is recited. Hand-sounds mean the clashing of cymbals; some also call it ‘hand-clapping.’ Ghostly performances mean solid drumming; some say it is ‘raising a dead body with a mantra.’ Pot-drumming means playing a square tambourine; some also call it ‘pot sound.’ Grand displays mean the sprinkling of actors; or that which makes things splendid, that is to say, a display of wit. Outcaste games mean playing with iron balls; some say it is ‘the game of outcastes washing hemp.’ Bamboo games mean playing with raised bamboo poles.

Dhovananti [M 0.0345] aṭṭhidhovanaṃ, ekaccesu kira janapadesu kālaṅkate ñātake na jhāpenti, nikhaṇitvā ṭhapenti. Atha tesaṃ pūtibhūtaṃ kāyaṃ ñatvā nīharitvā aṭṭhīni dhovitvā gandhehi makkhetvā ṭhapenti. Te nakkhattakāle ekasmiṃ ṭhāne aṭṭhīni ṭhapetvā ekasmiṃ ṭhāne surādīni ṭhapetvā rodantā paridevantā suraṃ pivanti. Vuttampi cetaṃ “atthi bhikkhave dakkhiṇesu janapadesu dhovanaṃ nāma, tattha hoti annampi pānampi khajjampi bhojjampi leyyampi peyyampi naccampi gītampi vāditampi. Atthekaṃ bhikkhave dhovanaṃ, netaṃ natthīti vadāmī”ti (a. ni. 10.107). Ekacce pana “indajālena aṭṭhidhovanaṃ dhovana”nti vadanti. Hatthiyuddhādīsu [V 0.0318] bhikkhuno neva hatthiādīhi saddhiṃ yujjhituṃ, na te yujjhāpetuṃ, na yujjhante daṭṭhuṃ vaṭṭati. Nibbuddhanti mallayuddhaṃ. Uyyodhikanti yattha sampahāro diyyati. Balagganti balagaṇanaṭṭhānaṃ. Senābyūhanti senāniveso, sakaṭabyūhādivasena senāya nivesanaṃ. Anīkadassananti “tayo hatthī pacchimaṃ hatthānīka”ntiādinā (pāci. 324) nayena vuttassa anīkassa dassanaṃ.

‘Washing’ refers to bone-washing. In some countries, it is said, when a relative dies, they do not cremate them but bury them. Then, knowing that the body has decayed, they exhume it, wash the bones, anoint them with perfumes, and keep them. At an auspicious time, they place the bones in one spot and alcoholic drinks in another, and weeping and lamenting, they drink the liquor. This has also been said: “Monks, in the southern countries there is what is called a washing ceremony. There, food and drink, sweets and meals, delicacies and beverages, dancing, singing, and music are provided. Monks, there is indeed such a washing ceremony; I do not say there is not” (AN 10.107). Some, however, say that this bone-washing is a kind of magic. In elephant battles and the like, a monk should not fight with elephants and the like, nor should he make them fight, nor is it proper for him to watch them fighting. Nibbuddha refers to wrestling matches. Uyyodhika is where combat takes place. Balagga is a place for counting troops. Senābyūha is the arrangement of an army, the deployment of troops in formations like the cart formation. Anīkadassana is the viewing of the battle array, as mentioned in the phrase “three elephants at the rear of the elephant division,” and so on (Pāc. 324).

Na nimittaggāhī hotīti chandarāgavasena vuttappakāraṃ nimittaṃ na gaṇhāti. Evaṃ sesapadānipi vuttapaṭipakkhanayena veditabbāni. Yathā ca heṭṭhā javane dussīlyādīsu uppannesu tasmiṃ asaṃvare sati dvārampi aguttaṃ hoti, bhavaṅgampi āvajjanādīnipi vīthicittānīti vuttaṃ, evamidha tasmiṃ sīlādīsu uppannesu dvārampi guttaṃ hoti, bhavaṅgampi āvajjanādīnipi vīthicittāni. Yathā kiṃ? Yathā nagaradvāresu saṃvutesu kiñcāpi antogharādayo asaṃvutā honti, tathāpi antonagare sabbaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ surakkhitaṃ sugopitameva hoti, nagaradvāresu pihitesu corānaṃ paveso [P 2.0393] natthi. Evameva javane sīlādīsu uppannesu dvārampi guttaṃ hoti, bhavaṅgampi āvajjanādīnipi vīthicittāni. Tasmā javanakkhaṇe uppajjamānopi “cakkhundriye saṃvaro”ti vutto. Ito paraṃ heṭṭhā ca upari ca vuttapariyāyena attho veditabbo.

‘He does not grasp at signs’ means he does not take up a sign of the kind described, by way of desire and lust. The remaining terms should be understood in the same way, according to the method of counteracting what has been explained. Just as, in the previously discussed case, when during the impulsion unwholesome states like misconduct arise, if there is no restraint, then the sense doors are unguarded, and even the life-continuum, adverting, and other cognitive processes are said to be unguarded—so too here, when during the impulsion wholesome states like virtue arise, the sense doors are guarded, and so are the life-continuum, adverting, and other cognitive processes. How so? Just as when the city gates are closed, even if the inner houses and so on are not secured, all the goods within the city remain well-protected and well-guarded, for when the city gates are shut, thieves cannot enter. In the same way, when during the impulsion wholesome states like virtue arise, the sense doors are guarded, and so are the life-continuum, adverting, and other cognitive processes. Therefore, even though it arises at the moment of impulsion, it is called “restraint of the eye faculty.” From here onward, the meaning should be understood in the manner explained before and after.

Visūkadassanāti paṭāṇīdassanato. Gāmakathāti gāmavāsīnaṃ kathā. Bāttiṃsāti dvattiṃsa. Aniyyānikattā saggamokkhamaggānaṃ tiracchānabhūtā kathāti tiracchānakathā. Tattha rājānaṃ ārabbha “mahāsammato [M 0.0346] mandhātā dhammāsoko evaṃ mahānubhāvo”tiādinā nayena pavattā kathā rājakathā. Esa nayo corakathādīsu. Tesu “asuko rājā abhirūpo dassanīyo”tiādinā nayena gehassitakathāva tiracchānakathā hoti. “Sopi nāma evaṃ mahānubhāvo khayaṃ gato”ti evaṃ pavattā pana kammaṭṭhānabhāve tiṭṭhati. Coresupi “mūladevo evaṃ mahānubhāvo, meghamālo evaṃ mahānubhāvo”ti tesaṃ kammaṃ paṭicca “aho sūrā”ti gehassitakathāva tiracchānakathā. Yuddhepi bhāratayuddhādīsu “asukena asuko evaṃ mārito evaṃ viddho”ti kāmassādavaseneva kathā tiracchānakathā. “Tepi nāma khayaṃ gatā”ti evaṃ pavattā pana sabbattha kammaṭṭhānameva hoti.

The sight of shows means seeing various displays. Village talk refers to the conversations of village dwellers. ‘Thirty-two’ means thirty-two. Because it does not lead to the paths to heaven and liberation, it is called animal-like talk, that is, idle talk. Here, talk concerning kings—such as “The great elected one, Mandhātā, and Dhammāsoka were of such great power,” and so on—is called royal talk. The same principle applies to talk about thieves and so on. Among these, statements like “That king is handsome and pleasing to behold” are merely talk connected with the household life, which is idle talk. However, when the discussion proceeds thus, “Even he, of such great power, passed away,” it becomes a basis for meditation. Similarly, regarding thieves—“Mūladeva was of such great power, Meghamāla was of such great power”—to speak of their deeds with admiration, saying, “Ah, such heroes!” is merely talk connected with the household life, which is idle talk. Even in discussions of battles like the Bhārata war, to say, “So-and-so was killed in such a way, so-and-so was struck down,” is, on account of its sensual relish, idle talk. But when it proceeds thus, “Even they passed away,” then in every case it becomes a basis for meditation.

Api ca annādīsu “evaṃ vaṇṇavantaṃ gandhavantaṃ rasavantaṃ phassasampannaṃ khādimha bhuñjimha pivimha paribhuñjimhā”ti kāmassādavasena kathetuṃ na vaṭṭati, sātthakaṃ pana katvā “pubbe evaṃ vaṇṇādisampannaṃ annaṃ pānaṃ vatthaṃ sayanaṃ mālaṃ gandhaṃ sīlavantānaṃ adamha, cetiyapūjaṃ akarimhā”ti [V 0.0319] kathetuṃ vaṭṭati. Ñātikathādīsu pana “amhākaṃ ñātakā sūrā samatthā”ti vā, “pubbe mayaṃ evaṃ vicitrehi yānehi vicarimhā”ti vā assādavasena vattuṃ na vaṭṭati, sātthakaṃ pana katvā “tepi no ñātakā khayaṃ gatā”ti vā, “pubbe mayaṃ evarūpā upāhanā saṅghassa adamhā”ti vā kathetuṃ vaṭṭati. Gāmakathāpi suniviṭṭhadunniviṭṭhasubhikkhadubbhikkhādivasena “asukagāmavāsino sūrā samatthā”ti vā evaṃ assādavasena vattuṃ na vaṭṭati, sātthakaṃ pana katvā [P 2.0394] “saddhā pasannā”ti vā, “khayavayaṃ gatā”ti vā vattuṃ vaṭṭati.

Moreover, regarding food and so on, it is not proper to speak with sensual relish, saying, “We ate, drank, consumed, and enjoyed such colorful, fragrant, tasty, and delightful things.” However, it is proper to speak meaningfully, saying, “In the past, we gave such excellent food, drink, clothing, bedding, garlands, and perfumes to the virtuous, and we performed offerings at shrines.” Regarding talk of relatives and so on, it is not proper to speak with delight, saying, “Our relatives are brave and capable,” or, “In the past, we traveled in such splendid vehicles.” But it is proper to speak meaningfully, saying, “Those relatives of ours, too, have perished,” or, “In the past, we gave such sandals to the Saṅgha.” Similarly, regarding village talk—whether of well-situated or poorly situated villages, of abundance or famine—it is not proper to speak with delight, saying, “The residents of such-and-such a village are brave and capable.” Instead, it is proper to speak meaningfully, saying, “They are faithful and devout,” or, “They have met with decay and dissolution.”

Nigamanagarajanapadakathāsupi eseva nayo. Itthikathāpi vaṇṇasaṇṭhānādīni paṭicca assādavasena na vaṭṭati, “saddhā pasannā, khayavayaṃ gatā”ti evameva vaṭṭati. Sūrakathāpi “nandimitto nāma yodho sūro ahosī”ti assādavasena na vaṭṭati. “Saddho ahosi, khayavayaṃ gato”ti evameva vaṭṭati. Visikhākathāpi “asukā visikhā suniviṭṭhā dunniviṭṭhā sūrā samatthā”ti assādavasena na vaṭṭati. “Saddhā pasannā, khayavayaṃ gatā”icceva vaṭṭati.

The same principle applies to talk about market towns, cities, and districts. It is not proper to talk about women with delight in their beauty, form, and so on; it is proper only to say: “She was faithful and devout; she has met with decay and dissolution.” It is not proper to talk about heroes with delight, saying, “There was a brave warrior named Nandimitta”; it is proper only to say: “He was faithful; he has met with decay and dissolution.” It is not proper to talk about a street with delight in its layout or its people, saying, “Such-and-such a street is well-laid-out, and its people are brave and capable”; it is proper only to say of its people: “They were faithful and devout; they have met with decay and dissolution.”

Kumbhaṭṭhānakathāti [M 0.0347] udakaṭṭhānakathā, “udakatitthakathā”tipi vuccati, kumbhadāsikathā vā. Sāpi “pāsādikā, naccituṃ gāyituṃ chekā”ti assādavasena na vaṭṭati, “saddhā pasannā”tiādinā nayena vaṭṭati. Pubbapetakathāti atītañātikathā. Tattha vattamānañātikathāsadisova vinicchayo.

Talk about pot-stands means talk about water-stands, also called ‘talk about watering places,’ or talk about water-carrying slave girls. Regarding the latter, it is not proper to speak with delight, saying, ‘She is graceful, and skilled in dancing and singing’; it is proper only to speak in the manner of ‘She is faithful and devout,’ and so on. Talk about deceased ancestors means talk about past relatives. There, the judgment is the same as for talk about present relatives.

Nānattakathāti purimapacchimakathāhi vimuttā avasesā nānāsabhāvā niratthakakathā. Lokakkhāyikāti “ayaṃ loko kena nimmito? Asukena nāma nimmito. Kāko seto aṭṭhīnaṃ setattā, balākā rattā lohitassa rattattā”ti evamādikā lokāyatavitaṇḍasallāpakathā.

Talk of diversity means the remaining meaningless talks of various natures, distinct from the former and latter talks. Talk about the world means discussions such as: “By whom was this world created? It was created by so-and-so. A crow is white because its bones are white; a heron is red because its blood is red,” and so on—such worldly, sophistical, and idle talk.

Samuddakkhāyikā nāma kasmā samuddo sāgaro? Sāgaradevena khatattā sāgaro, “khato me”ti hatthamuddāya sayaṃ niveditattā samuddoti evamādikā niratthakā samuddakkhānakathā. Bhavoti vuddhi. Abhavoti hāni. Iti bhavo iti abhavoti yaṃ vā taṃ vā niratthakakāraṇaṃ vatvā pavattitakathā itibhavābhavakathā.

Talk about the ocean is: Why is the ocean called ‘samudda’ or ‘sāgara’? It is called ‘sāgara’ because it was dug by the deity Sāgara; and it is called ‘samudda’ because it declared itself with a hand gesture, saying, “It was dug for me.” Such is the meaningless talk narrating about the ocean. ‘Bhava’ means growth. ‘Abhava’ means decline. The talk that proceeds by stating whatever meaningless reason, saying ‘thus growth’ or ‘thus decline,’ is the talk of ‘thus growth, thus decline.’

Āvareyyāti āvaraṇaṃ kareyya. Nivāreyyāti ārammaṇato vāreyya. Saṃvareyyāti sammā nissesaṃ [V 0.0320] katvā vāreyya. Rakkheyyāti rakkhaṃ kareyya. Gopeyyāti saṃgopeyya. Pidaheyyāti pidahanaṃ kareyya. Pacchindeyyāti sotaṃ chindeyya.

‘He would obstruct’ means he would create an obstruction. ‘He would restrain’ means he would restrain from the object. ‘He would completely restrain’ means he would thoroughly and completely restrain. ‘He would guard’ means he would provide protection. ‘He would watch over’ means he would thoroughly guard. ‘He would close off’ means he would create a covering. ‘He would cut off’ means he would sever the stream.

Tena [P 2.0395] tena na tussantīti tena tena ambilādinā rasena na santosaṃ āpajjanti. Aparāparaṃ pariyesantīti uparūpari gavesanti.

“They are not satisfied with this or that” (tena tena na tussanti) means they do not find contentment with this or that taste, such as sourness. “They keep searching for further and further” (aparāparaṃ pariyesanti) means they seek higher and higher.

158. Phassenāti rogaphassena. Bhavañca nābhijappeyyāti tassa phassassa vinodanatthāya kāmabhavādibhavañca na pattheyya. Bheravesu ca na sampavedheyyāti tassa phassassa paccayabhūtesu sīhabyagghādīsu bheravesu ca na sampavedheyya, avasesesu vā ghānindriyamanindriyavisayesu na sampavedheyya. Evaṃ paripūro indriyasaṃvaro ca vutto hoti. Purimehi vā indriyasaṃvaraṃ dassetvā iminā “araññe vasatā bheravaṃ disvā vā sutvā vā nappavedhitabba”nti dasseti.

158. “By contact” (phassena) means by the contact of disease. “And one should not long for existence” (bhavañca nābhijappeyya) means one should not desire any state of existence, such as sensual existence, etc., in order to eliminate that contact. “And one should not tremble at terrors” (bheravesu ca na sampavedheyya) means one should not tremble at terrors such as lions and tigers, which are the causes of that contact, nor should one tremble at the remaining objects of the nose and mind faculties. Thus, the complete restraint of the senses is explained. Alternatively, having shown the restraint of the senses with the previous explanations, this indicates that “one should not tremble upon seeing or hearing terrors while living in the forest.”

Ekenākārenāti [M 0.0348] ekena kāraṇena. Bhayampi bheravampi taññevāti bhayanti ca bheravanti ca khuddakampi mahantampi uttāsanimittameva. Tamevatthaṃ dassetuṃ “vuttaṃ heta”ntiādimāha. Bhayanti tappaccayā uppannabhayaṃ. Bhayānakanti ākāraniddeso. Chambhitattanti bhayavasena gattacalanaṃ. Lomahaṃsoti lomānaṃ haṃsanaṃ uddhaggabhāvo. Iminā padadvayena kiccato bhayaṃ dassetvā puna “cetaso ubbego utrāso”ti sabhāvato dasseti. Ubbeggoti bhīruko, utrāsoti cittakkhobho. Jātibhayanti jātiṃ paṭicca uppannabhayaṃ. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Rājato uppannabhayaṃ rājabhayaṃ. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Attānuvādabhayanti pāpakammino attānaṃ anuvadantassa uppajjanakabhayaṃ. Parānuvādabhayanti parassa anuvādato uppajjanakabhayaṃ.

“By one cause” (ekena ākārena) means by one reason. “Fear and terror are just that” (bhayampi bheravampi taññeva) means fear and terror, both small and great, are merely signs of alarm. To explain this meaning, he said: “It has been said thus.” “Fear” (bhayaṃ) means the fear that arises due to that condition. “Terrifying” (bhayānakaṃ) describes its characteristic. “Trembling” (chambhitattaṃ) means the movement of limbs due to fear. “Horripilation” (lomahaṃsa) means the bristling of hairs, an uplifted state. With these two terms, fear is shown by its function, and then again, “mental agitation and terror” describes its inherent nature. “Agitation” (ubbegga) means being timid, and “terror” (utrāsa) means disturbance of the mind. “Fear of birth” (jātibhayaṃ) means the fear arising dependent on birth. The same method applies to the rest. “Fear of kings” (rājabhayaṃ) means the fear arising from kings. The same method applies to the rest. “Fear of self-reproach” (attānuvādabhayaṃ) means the fear that arises for the evil-doer when self-reproaching. “Fear of others' reproach” (parānuvādabhayaṃ) means the fear that arises from others' reproach.

Daṇḍabhayanti āgārikassa raññā pavattitadaṇḍaṃ, anāgārikassa vinayadaṇḍaṃ paṭicca uppajjanakabhayaṃ. Duggatibhayanti cattāro apāye paṭicca uppajjanakabhayaṃ. Ūmibhayanti mahāsamudde udakaṃ orohantassa pavattabhayaṃ. Mahāsamudde kira mahindavīci nāma saṭṭhi yojanāni uggacchati, taraṅgavīci nāma paṇṇāsa yojanāni, rohaṇavīci nāma cattālīsa yojanāni uggacchati. Evarūpā ūmiyo paṭicca pavattaṃ ūmibhayaṃ[P 2.0396]. Kumbhīlato pavattaṃ bhayaṃ kumbhīlabhayaṃ. Udakāvaṭṭato bhayaṃ āvaṭṭabhayaṃ. Susukā vuccati caṇḍamaccho, tato bhayaṃ susukābhayaṃ. Ājīvikabhayanti jīvitavuttito bhayaṃ ājīvikabhayaṃ. Asilokabhayanti garahato bhayaṃ.
