“Fear of punishment” (daṇḍabhayaṃ) means the fear arising dependent on punishment inflicted by a king for a householder, or disciplinary punishment for a renunciant. “Fear of bad destinations” (duggatibhayaṃ) means the fear arising dependent on the four states of deprivation. “Fear of waves” (ūmibhayaṃ) means the fear that arises for one descending into the water of the great ocean. In the great ocean, it is said that the great Indra waves rise sixty yojanas, the Taranga waves rise fifty yojanas, and the Rohaṇa waves rise forty yojanas. The fear that arises dependent on such waves is called “fear of waves.” The fear that arises from crocodiles is “fear of crocodiles.” The fear from whirlpools is “fear of whirlpools.” “Susukā” is called a fierce fish; the fear from it is “fear of Susukā.” “Fear of livelihood” (ājīvikabhayaṃ) means the fear from one's means of living. “Fear of disgrace” (asilokabhayaṃ) means the fear from censure.

159. Laddhā [V 0.0321] na sannidhiṃ kayirāti etesaṃ annādīnaṃ yaṃkiñci dhammena labhitvā “araññe ca senāsane vasatā dullabha”nti cintetvā sannidhiṃ na kareyya.

159. “Having obtained, one should not hoard” (laddhā na sannidhiṃ kayirā) means that whatever food, etc., one obtains righteously, one should not hoard it, thinking, “Living in the forest or in a dwelling, this is difficult to obtain.”

Odanoti sāli vīhi yavo godhumo kaṅgu varako kudrūsakoti sattannaṃ dhaññānaṃ dhaññānulomānañca taṇḍulehi nibbatto. Kummāsoti yavehi nibbatto. Sattūti sāliādīhi katasattu. Maccho dakasambhavo. Maṃsaṃ pākaṭameva. Ambapānanti āmehi vā pakkehi vā ambehi katapānaṃ. Tattha āmehi karontena ambataruṇāni bhinditvā udake pakkhipitvā ātape ādiccapākena pacitvā parissāvetvā tadahu paṭiggahitehi [M 0.0349] madhusakkarakappūrādīhi yojetvā kātabbaṃ. Jambupānanti jambuphalehi katapānaṃ. Cocapānanti aṭṭhikehi kadaliphalehi katapānaṃ. Mocapānanti anaṭṭhikehi kadaliphalehi katapānaṃ. Madhukapānanti madhukānaṃ jātirasena katapānaṃ. Taṃ pana udakasambhinnaṃ vaṭṭati, suddhaṃ na vaṭṭati. Muddikapānanti muddikā udake madditvā ambapānaṃ viya katapānaṃ. Sālūkapānanti rattuppalanīluppalādīnaṃ sālūke madditvā katapānaṃ. Phārusakapānanti phārusakehi ambapānaṃ viya katapānaṃ. Kosambapānanti kosambaphalehi katapānaṃ. Kolapānanti kolaphalehi katapānaṃ. Badarapānanti mahākolaphalehi ambapānaṃ viya katapānaṃ. Imāni ekādasa pānāni, tānipi ādiccapākāni vaṭṭanti.

“Rice” (odana) is made from the grains of seven kinds of cereals—sāli, vīhi, barley, wheat, kaṅgu, varaka, and kudrūsaka—and from their allied grains. “Kummāsa” is made from barley. “Sattu” is flour made from sāli and other grains. Fish comes from water. Meat is self-explanatory. “Ambapāna” is a drink made from raw or ripe mangoes. To prepare it with raw mangoes, one should crush young mangoes, place them in water, cook them in the sun by sun-heat, strain the mixture, and on the same day, mix it with honey, sugar, camphor, etc., before consuming. “Jambupāna” is a drink made from jambu fruits. “Cocapāna” is a drink made from banana fruits with seeds. “Mocapāna” is a drink made from banana fruits without seeds. “Madhukapāna” is a drink made from the natural essence of madhuka fruits. However, this is permissible only when mixed with water; pure, it is not allowed. “Muddikapāna” is a drink made by crushing grapes in water, similar to ambapāna. “Sālūkapāna” is a drink made by crushing the stalks of red or blue lotuses and the like. “Phārusakapāna” is a drink made from phārusaka fruits, similar to ambapāna. “Kosambapāna” is a drink made from kosamba fruits. “Kolapāna” is a drink made from kola fruits. “Badarapāna” is a drink made from large kola fruits, similar to ambapāna. These eleven drinks are permissible when cooked by the sun's heat.

Ghatapānanti sappipānaṃ. Telapānanti tilatelādīnaṃ pānaṃ. Payopānanti khīrapānaṃ. Yāgupānanti sītalādiyāgupānaṃ. Rasapānanti sākādirasapānaṃ. Piṭṭhakhajjakanti sattannaṃ tāva dhaññānaṃ dhaññānulomānaṃ aparaṇṇānañca piṭṭhaṃ panasapiṭṭhaṃ labujapiṭṭhaṃ [P 2.0397] ambāṭakapiṭṭhaṃ sālapiṭṭhaṃ khīravallipiṭṭhañcāti evamādīnaṃ piṭṭhehi kataṃ piṭṭhakhajjakaṃ. Pūvakhajjakampi etehiyeva kataṃ. Mūlakhajjakanti mūlakamūlaṃ khārakamūlaṃ cuccumūlanti evamādi. Tacakhajjakanti ucchutacādayo. Pattakhajjakanti nimbapaṇṇakuṭajapaṇṇapaṭolapaṇṇasulasapaṇṇādayo. Pupphakhajjakanti mūlakapupphakhārakapupphasetavaraṇasigguuppalapadumakādayo. Phalakhajjakanti panasalabujatālanāḷikeraambāṭakatintiṇikamātuluṅgakapiṭṭhaphalaalābukumbhaṇḍaphussa- phalatimbarūsakatilavātiṅgaṇacocamocamadhukādīnaṃ phalānaṃ khajjakaṃ.

“Ghee drink” (ghatapāna) means drinking ghee. “Oil drink” (telapāna) means drinking sesame oil and the like. “Milk drink” (payopāna) means drinking milk. “Gruel drink” (yāgupāna) means drinking cooled gruel and the like. “Juice drink” (rasapāna) means drinking vegetable juices and the like. “Flour-based snacks” (piṭṭhakhajjaka) refers to snacks made from the flour of seven kinds of grains, allied grains, and pulses, such as jackfruit flour, rose-apple flour, hog-plum flour, sal flour, milk-vine flour, and so on. “Cake-like snacks” are also made from these same ingredients. “Root-based snacks” include radish roots, khāraka roots, cuccu roots, and so on. “Bark-based snacks” include sugarcane bark and the like. “Leaf-based snacks” include neem leaves, kuṭaja leaves, pointed gourd leaves, sulasā leaves, and so on. “Flower-based snacks” include radish flowers, khāraka flowers, white varaṇa flowers, moringa flowers, lotus flowers, and so on. “Fruit-based snacks” include jackfruit, rose-apple, palmyra fruit, coconut, hog plum, tintiṇika, citron, wood apple, gourd, pumpkin, phussa fruits, timbarūsaka, sesame, eggplant, cocamoca, madhuka, and so on.

Na kuhanāyāti na vimhāpanāya. Na lapanāyāti paccayatthaṃ na lapanāya. Vihāraṃ āgate manusse disvā “kimatthāya bhonto āgatā”ti bhikkhū nimantetunti. “Yadi evaṃ gacchatha, ahaṃ pacchato gahetvā āgacchāmī”ti evaṃ na [V 0.0322] lapanāya. Atha vā attānaṃ upanetvā “ahaṃ tisso, mayi rājā pasanno, mayi asuko rājā asuko ca rājamahāmatto pasanno”ti evaṃ na lapanāya. Na nemittikatāyāti yena kenaci paresaṃ paccayadānasaññājanakena kāyavacīkammena na nemittikatāya. Na nippesikatāyāti yā paresaṃ akkosanādikiriyā yasmā veḷupesikā viya abbhaṅgaṃ parassa guṇaṃ nippeseti nipuñchati, yasmā vā gandhajātaṃ nipisitvā gandhamagganā viya paraguṇe nipisitvā vicuṇṇetvā [M 0.0350] esā lābhamagganā hoti, tasmā “nippesikatā”ti vuccati. Na evarūpāya nippesikatāya. Na lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanatāyāti ettha nijigīsanatāti magganā, aññato laddhañhi aññattha haraṇavasena lābhena lābhamagganā nāma hoti. Na evarūpāya lābhena lābhamagganāya.

"Not for deceit" (na kuhanāya) means not for causing astonishment. "Not for cajolery" (na lapanāya) means not for cajolery for the sake of requisites. Upon seeing people who have come to the monastery, one should not say, "For what purpose have you come, sirs?" with the expectation that they will say, "To invite the monks." Nor should one say, "If so, please go on, I will come after you"; this is cajolery. Or, presenting oneself, one should not say, "I am Tissa, the king is pleased with me, such-and-such a king and such-and-such a royal minister are pleased with me"; this is cajolery. "Not for hinting" (na nemittikatāya) means not by any bodily or verbal action that generates in others a sign to give requisites. "Not for disparaging" (na nippesikatāya) refers to actions such as reviling others. For just as a bamboo splinter scrapes away and wipes off another's polish, or just as one seeking perfume grinds fragrant substances, so too this seeking of gain occurs by grinding and crushing another's good qualities. Therefore, it is called "disparaging." Not for such disparaging. "Not for desiring to win gain with gain" (na lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanatāya): here, "desiring to win" (nijigīsanatā) means seeking. For taking what is obtained from one place and carrying it to another is called seeking gain with gain. Not for such seeking of gain with gain.

Na dārudānenāti na paccayahetukena dārudānena vihāre uṭṭhitañhi araññato vā āharitvā rakkhitagopitadāruṃ “evaṃ me paccayaṃ dassantī”ti upaṭṭhākānaṃ dātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Evañhi jīvikaṃ kappento anesanāya micchājīvena jīvati, so diṭṭheva dhamme garahaṃ pāpuṇāti, samparāye ca apāyaparipūrako hoti. Attano puggalikaṃ dāruṃ kusalaṅgahatthāya [P 2.0398] dadanto kuladūsakadukkaṭaṃ āpajjati, parapuggalikaṃ theyyacittena dadanto bhaṇḍagghena kāretabbo. Saṅghikepi eseva nayo. Sace pana taṃ issaratāya deti, garubhaṇḍavissajjanaṃ āpajjati. Kataraṃ pana dāru garubhaṇḍaṃ hoti, kataraṃ na hotīti? Yaṃ tāva aropimaṃ sayaṃjātaṃ, taṃ saṅghena paricchinnaṭṭhāneyeva garubhaṇḍaṃ, tato paraṃ na garubhaṇḍaṃ. Ropimaṭṭhāne ca sabbena sabbaṃ garubhaṇḍaṃ, pamāṇato sūcidaṇḍakappamāṇaṃ garubhaṇḍaṃ.

"Not by means of wood-gifts" (na dārudānena) means not by wood-gifts for the sake of requisites. For it is not proper to give wood that has arisen in the monastery or has been brought from the forest and protected and stored to supporters, thinking, "In this way, they will provide me with requisites." For one who makes a living in this way lives by wrong livelihood through improper seeking; in this very life, one meets with blame, and in the next life, one becomes a filler of the states of loss. Giving one's personal wood to curry favor, one commits a dukkaṭa offense of corrupting families. Giving another's personal wood with a thieving mind, one should be dealt with according to the value of the goods. The same principle applies to what belongs to the Sangha. But if one gives it out of a sense of authority, one commits an offense for disposing of heavy goods. Now, which wood is considered heavy goods and which is not? Firstly, naturally grown wood is heavy goods only in the place designated by the Sangha; beyond that, it is not heavy goods. In a planted area, all of it is entirely heavy goods; by measure, even that which is the size of a needle-stick is heavy goods.

Na veḷudānenātiādīsupi na veḷudānenāti na paccayahetukena veḷudānenātiādi sabbaṃ na dārudānenāti ettha vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Veḷu pana pamāṇato telanāḷippamāṇo garubhaṇḍaṃ, na tato heṭṭhā. Manussā vihāraṃ gantvā veḷuṃ yācanti, bhikkhū “saṅghiko”ti dātuṃ na visahanti, manussā punappunaṃ yācanti vā tajjenti vā, tadā bhikkhūhi “daṇḍakammaṃ katvā gaṇhathā”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭati, veḷudānaṃ nāma na hoti. Sace te daṇḍakammatthāya vāsipharasuādīni vā khādanīyaṃ vā bhojanīyaṃ vā denti, gahetuṃ na vaṭṭati.

"Not by giving bamboo," etc. (Na veḷudānenātiādi): Here, "not by giving bamboo" means not by giving bamboo for the sake of requisites, and so on. All of this should be understood in the same way as explained in the case of "not by giving wood." However, as for bamboo, by measure, a bamboo the size of an oil-tube is considered a heavy item, but not anything smaller than that. When people go to the monastery and ask for bamboo, the monks, thinking, "It belongs to the Sangha," are unable to give it. If the people repeatedly ask or even threaten, then it is proper for the monks to say, "Take it after performing a service (daṇḍakamma)." This is not considered a gift of bamboo. If, for the purpose of the service, they give items such as adzes and axes, or soft or hard food, it is not proper to accept them.

Vinayaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “daḍḍhagehā manussā gaṇhitvā gacchantā na vāretabbā”ti vuttaṃ. Sace saṅghassa veḷugumbe veḷudūsikā uppajjati, taṃ akoṭṭāpentānaṃ veḷu nassati. “Kiṃ kātabba”nti bhikkhācāre manussānaṃ ācikkhitabbaṃ. Sace koṭṭetuṃ na icchanti, “samaṃ bhāgaṃ labhissathā”ti [M 0.0351] vattabbā. Na icchantiyeva, “dve koṭṭhāse labhissathā”ti vattabbā. Evampi anicchantesu naṭṭhena attho natthi, “tumhākaṃ khaṇe sati daṇḍakammaṃ karissatha, koṭṭetvā gaṇhathā”ti [V 0.0323] vattabbā, veḷudānaṃ nāma na hoti. Veḷugumbe aggimhi uṭṭhitepi udakena vuyhamānaveḷūsupi eseva nayo.

However, in the Vinaya commentary, it is said: "People whose houses have burned down, when taking things and going, should not be prevented." If a blight arises in the Sangha's bamboo grove, the bamboo will be lost if it is not cut down. "What is to be done?"—this should be told to the people during the alms round. If they do not wish to cut it, they should be told, "You will receive an equal share." If they still do not wish to, they should be told, "You will receive two shares." Even if they are unwilling, as there is no point in it being lost, they should be told, "When you have a moment, perform a service; cut it down and take it." This is not considered a gift of bamboo. The same principle applies when a fire breaks out in the bamboo grove or when bamboo is being carried away by water.

Pattadāne garubhaṇḍatāya ayaṃ vinicchayo – pattampi hi yattha vikkāyati, gandhakārādayo gandhapaliveṭhanādīnaṃ atthāya gaṇhanti, tādise dullabhaṭṭhāneyeva garubhaṇḍaṃ hoti. Esa tāva kiṃsukapattakaṇṇapiḷandhanatālapattādīsu [P 2.0399] vinicchayo. Tālapaṇṇampi imasmiṃyeva ṭhāne kathetabbaṃ – tālapaṇṇampi hi sayaṃjāte tālavane saṅghena paricchinnaṭṭhāneyeva garubhaṇḍaṃ, na tato paraṃ, ropimatālesu sabbampi garubhaṇḍaṃ, tassa pamāṇaṃ heṭṭhimakoṭiyā aṭṭhaṅgulappamāṇopi rittapotthako. Tiṇampi ettheva pakkhipitvā kathetabbaṃ. Yattha pana tiṇaṃ natthi, tattha tālanāḷikerapaṇṇādīhipi chādenti. Tasmā tānipi tiṇeneva saṅgahitāni. Iti muñjapalālādīsu yaṃkiñci muṭṭhippamāṇaṃ tiṇaṃ. Nāḷikerapaṇṇādīsu ca ekapaṇṇampi saṅghassa dinnaṃ vā tattha jātaṃ vā bahiārāme saṅghassa tiṇavatthumhi jātatiṇaṃ vā rakkhitagopitaṃ vā garubhaṇḍaṃ hoti. Taṃ pana saṅghakamme ca cetiyakamme ca kate atirekaṃ puggalikakamme dātuṃ vaṭṭati. Heṭṭhā vuttadāruveḷūsupi eseva nayo.

Regarding the giving of leaves, this is the determination of what constitutes a heavy item: leaves, where they are sold and perfumers and others take them for wrapping perfumes and so on, are considered a heavy item only in such places where they are scarce. This is the determination concerning Kimsuka leaves, ear-ornaments made of leaves, palm leaves, and so on. Palm leaves should also be discussed in this context: in a naturally grown palm grove, palm leaves are a heavy item only in the area designated by the Sangha, not beyond it. Among cultivated palms, all are heavy items. Their measure, at the lower limit, is even an empty book of eight finger-breadths. Grass should also be included and discussed here. Where grass is unavailable, they thatch with palm leaves, coconut leaves, and the like. Therefore, these too are included under the category of grass. Thus, regarding muñja grass, straw, and so on, any amount of grass the size of a fistful is a heavy item. And regarding coconut leaves and the like, even a single leaf given to the Sangha or grown there, or grass grown on the Sangha's grass plot in an outer park, or that which is protected and stored, is a heavy item. However, after it has been used for the work of the Sangha and the work of a cetiya, the excess may be given for personal work. The same principle applies to the wood and bamboo mentioned previously.

Pupphadāne “ettakesu rukkhesu pupphāni vissajjitvā yāgubhattatthāya upanentu, ettakesu senāsanapaṭisaṅkharaṇe upanentū”ti evaṃ niyamitaṭṭhāneyeva pupphāni garubhaṇḍāni honti. Yadi sāmaṇerā pupphāni ocinitvā rāsiṃ karonti, pañcaṅgasamannāgato pupphabhājako bhikkhu bhikkhusaṅghaṃ gaṇetvā koṭṭhāse karoti. So sampattaparisāya saṅghaṃ anāpucchitvāva dātuṃ labhati. Asammatena pana āpucchitvā dātabbaṃ. Bhikkhuno pana kassa pupphāni dātuṃ labbhati, kassa na labbhatīti? Mātāpitūnaṃ gehaṃ haritvāpi gehato pakkosāpetvāpi “vatthupūjaṃ karothā”ti dātuṃ labbhati, piḷandhanatthāya na labbhati. Sesañātīnaṃ pana haritvā na dātabbaṃ, pakkosāpetvā pūjanatthāya dātabbaṃ. Sesajanassa pūjanaṭṭhānaṃ sampattassa apaccāsīsantena dātabbaṃ, pupphadānaṃ nāma na hoti.

Regarding the giving of flowers, flowers are heavy items only in a place designated thus: "Let them set aside the flowers on so many trees and bring them for gruel and meals; let them bring those on so many trees for the repair of lodgings." If novices gather flowers and make a heap, a monk who is the flower-distributor, endowed with five qualities, counts the community of monks and makes portions. He is permitted to give them to the assembled community without asking the Sangha. However, one who is not appointed must give them only after asking. Now, to whom is a monk permitted to give flowers, and to whom is he not? He is permitted to take them to his parents' house, or to summon them from their house, and give them, saying, "Make a material offering." He is not permitted to give them for the purpose of adornment. To other relatives, however, he should not take them, but having summoned them, he may give them for the purpose of offering. To other people who have arrived at a place of offering and are not expecting them, they may be given; this is not considered a "gift of flowers."

Vihāre [M 0.0352] bahūni pupphāni pupphanti, bhikkhunā piṇḍāya carantena manusse disvā “vihāre bahūni pupphāni pūjethā”ti vattabbaṃ, vacanamatte doso natthi, “manussā khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ ādāya āgamissantī”ti cittena pana na vattabbaṃ. Sace vadati, khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ na paribhuñjitabbaṃ. Manussā attano dhammatāya “vihāre pupphāni atthī”ti pucchitvā “asukadivase vihāraṃ āgamissāma, sāmaṇerānaṃ [P 2.0400] pupphāni ocinituṃ mā [V 0.0324] dethā”ti vadanti. Bhikkhu sāmaṇerānaṃ kathetuṃ pamuṭṭho, sāmaṇerehi pupphāni ocitāni, manussā bhikkhuṃ upasaṅkamitvā mayaṃ tumhākaṃ asukadivase evaṃ ārocayimha “sāmaṇerānaṃ pupphāni ocinituṃ mā dethā”ti, kasmā na vārayitthāti? “Sati me pamuṭṭhā, pupphāni ocinitamattāneva, na tāva pūjā katā”ti vattabbaṃ, “gaṇhatha pūjethā”ti na vattabbaṃ. Sace vadati, āmisaṃ na paribhuñjitabbaṃ. Aparo bhikkhu sāmaṇerānaṃ ācikkhati “asukagāmavāsino ‘pupphāni mā ocinitthā’ti āhaṃsū”ti manussāpi āmisaṃ āharitvā dānaṃ datvā vadanti “amhākaṃ manussā na bahukā, sāmaṇere amhehi saha pupphāni ocinituṃ āṇāpethā”ti. “Sāmaṇerehi bhikkhā laddhā. Ye bhikkhācāraṃ na gacchanti, te sayameva jānissanti upāsakā”ti vattabbaṃ. Ettakaṃ nayaṃ labhitvā sāmaṇere putte vā bhātike vā katvā pupphāni ocināpetuṃ doso natthi, pupphadānaṃ nāma na hoti.

In the monastery, many flowers bloom. When a monk sees people while going for alms, he should say, 'Offer the many flowers in the monastery.' There is no fault in merely speaking. However, he should not speak with the thought, 'People will bring food and edibles.' If he speaks thus, the food and edibles should not be consumed. People, as is their way, ask, 'Are there flowers in the monastery?' and say, 'On such-and-such a day, we will come to the monastery—do not allow the novices to pick the flowers.' If a monk forgot to tell the novices, and the novices picked the flowers, the people approach the monk and say, 'We informed you on such-and-such a day, saying, "Do not let the novices pick the flowers"—why did you not stop them?' The monk should reply, 'My memory lapsed; the flowers were merely picked, and the offering has not yet been made.' He should not say, 'Take them and offer them.' If he says so, the material gifts should not be consumed. Another monk informs the novices, 'The villagers of such-and-such a place said, "Do not pick the flowers."' The people bring material gifts, give alms, and say, 'We are few in number; please instruct the novices to pick the flowers together with us.' The monk should reply, 'The novices have received alms. The lay followers will know for themselves those who do not go on almsround.' Having understood this principle, there is no fault in having novices, whom one treats as sons or brothers, pick flowers. This is not called a gift of flowers.

Phaladāne phalampi pupphaṃ viya niyamitameva garubhaṇḍaṃ hoti. Vihāre bahukasmiṃ phalāphale sati aphāsukamanussā āgantvā yācanti, bhikkhū “saṅghika”nti dātuṃ na ussahanti, manussā vippaṭisārino akkosanti paribhāsanti, tattha kiṃ kātabbanti? Phalehi vā rukkhehi vā paricchinditvā kathikā kātabbā “asuke ca rukkhe asuke ca rukkhe ettakāni phalāni gaṇhantā, ettakesu vā rukkhesu phalāni gaṇhantā na vāretabbā”ti. Corā vā issarā vā balakkārena gaṇhantā na vāretabbā. Kuddhā hi te sakalavihārampi nāseyyuṃ, ādīnavo pana kathetabboti.

In the giving of fruits, fruits too, like flowers, are considered heavy items only when regulated. In a monastery where there are many fruits and other produce, if ailing people come and ask, the monks hesitate to give, saying, 'This belongs to the Sangha.' The people, becoming displeased, scold and revile. What should be done in that case? One should demarcate by fruits or by trees and make an agreement: 'Those taking so many fruits from such-and-such a tree and such-and-such a tree, or taking fruits from so many trees, should not be prevented.' Thieves or rulers taking them by force should not be prevented. For if angered, they might destroy the entire monastery. However, the danger should be explained.

Sinānadāne sinānacuṇṇāni koṭṭitāni na garubhaṇḍāni, akoṭṭito rukkhe ṭhitova rukkhataco garubhaṇḍaṃ, cuṇṇaṃ pana agilānassa rajananipakkaṃ vaṭṭati. Gilānassa yaṃkiñci cuṇṇaṃ dātuṃ vaṭṭatiyeva.

In the giving of bathing requisites, crushed bathing powders are not heavy items. Uncrushed, the bark of a tree still on the tree is a heavy item. However, for one who is not ill, powder prepared for dyeing is allowable. For one who is ill, it is allowable to give any kind of powder.

Na [M 0.0353] cuṇṇadānenāti vuttanayena sirīsacuṇṇādīnaṃ dānena. Mattikādānemattikā hi yattha dullabhā hoti, tattheva garubhaṇḍaṃ. Sāpi heṭṭhimakoṭiyā tiṃsapalaguḷapiṇḍappamāṇāva, tato heṭṭhā na garubhaṇḍanti.

‘Not by giving powder’ means by giving powder from the sirīsa tree and the like, in the manner described. ‘By giving clay’: clay is a heavy item only where it is scarce. Even so, at the lower limit, it must be the size of a lump of molasses weighing thirty palas; below that, it is not a heavy item.

Dantakaṭṭhadāne [P 2.0401] dantakaṭṭhaṃ acchinnakameva garubhaṇḍaṃ. Yesaṃ sāmaṇerānaṃ saṅghato dantakaṭṭhavāro pāpuṇāti, te attano ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ dātuṃ na labhanti. Yehi pana “ettakāni dantakaṭṭhāni āharitabbānī”ti paricchinditvā vārā gahitā, te atirekāni ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ [V 0.0325] dātuṃ labhanti. Ekena bhikkhunā dantakaṭṭhamāḷakato bahūni dantakaṭṭhāni na gahetabbāni, devasikaṃ ekekameva gahetabbaṃ. Pāṭiyekkaṃ vasantenāpi bhikkhusaṅghaṃ gaṇayitvā yattakāni attano pāpuṇanti, tattakāneva gahetvā gantabbaṃ. Antarā āgantukesu vā āgatesu disaṃ vā pakkamantesu āharitvā gahitaṭṭhāneyeva ṭhapetabbāni. Na mukhodakadānenāti na mukhadhovanaudakadānena.

In the giving of tooth sticks, an uncut tooth stick is a heavy item. Those novices whose turn it is to receive tooth sticks from the Sangha are not permitted to give them individually to their own teachers and preceptors. However, those who have taken their turns after the quantity was determined with the instruction, 'This many tooth sticks should be brought,' are permitted to give the extra ones to their teachers and preceptors. A single monk should not take many tooth sticks from the tooth stick rack; only one should be taken daily. Even one dwelling separately should, after counting the community of monks, take and go with only as many as is his portion. If, in the meantime, guests arrive or some depart for another region, the excess should be brought back and placed where they were taken from. ‘Not by giving water for the mouth’ means not by giving water for washing the mouth.

Na cāṭukamyatāyātiādīsu cāṭukamyatā vuccati attānaṃ dāsaṃ viya nīcaṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā parassa khalitavacanampi saṇṭhapetvā piyakāmatāya paggayhavacanaṃ. Na muggasūpyatāyāti na muggasūpasamānatāya. Muggasūpasamānatāti saccālikena jīvikaṃ kappanatāya etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Yathā hi muggasūpe paccante bahū muggā pākaṃ gacchanti thokā na gacchanti, evameva saccālikena jīvikakappake puggale bahu alikaṃ hoti, appakaṃ saccaṃ. Yathā vā muggasūpassa apavisanaṭṭhānaṃ nāma natthi, evameva saccālikavuttino puggalassa appatiṭṭhānaṃ nāma natthi. Siṅghāṭakaṃ viya icchiticchitaṭṭhānassa patiṭṭhāti. Tenassa sā musāvāditā “muggasūpyatā”ti vuttā. Na pāribhaṭyatāyāti na paribhaṭakammabhāvena. Paribhaṭassa hi kammaṃ pāribhaṭyaṃ, tassa bhāvo pāribhaṭyatā, alaṅkārakaraṇādīhi dārakakīḷāpanassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Na pīṭhamaddikatāyāti na sahasā gharaṃ pavisitvā pīṭhake nisīdanakatāya.

In the phrase 'nor by flattery,' and so on, 'flattery' is defined as speaking in an ingratiating manner out of a desire to be liked, placing oneself in a low position like a slave, and even composing another's faulty speech. 'Nor by being like mung-bean soup' means not having the quality of mung-bean soup. 'Having the quality of mung-bean soup' is a term for making a living through deception. For just as in a pot of mung-bean soup, many beans become cooked while a few do not, so too for a person who makes a living through deception, much is false and little is true. Or, just as there is no place where mung-bean soup does not enter, so too for a person who lives by deception, there is no place where he does not gain a footing. Like a crossroads, he is established in whatever place he wishes. Therefore, this false speech of his is called 'being like mung-bean soup.' 'Nor by being a retainer' means not by the state of being a retainer. The work of a retainer is 'retainership'; the state of that is 'being a retainer.' This is a term for amusing children by adorning oneself and so on. 'Nor by being a seat-presser' means not by the act of entering a house uninvited and sitting on the seats.

Na vatthuvijjāyātiādīsu vatthuvijjā nāma gāmanigamanagarādīnaṃ suniviṭṭhadunniviṭṭhajānanasatthaṃ. Tiracchānavijjā [P 2.0402] nāma aniyyānikattā saggamokkhamaggānaṃ tiracchānabhūtā aṅgasatthanimittādikā avasesavijjā. Aṅgavijjā [M 0.0354] nāma itthipurisānaṃ subhagadubbhagalakkhaṇajānanaṃ. Nakkhattavijjā nāma nakkhattānaṃ yogajānanasatthaṃ.

In the phrase 'nor by the science of sites,' and so on, the science of sites is the treatise for knowing whether villages, market towns, cities, and so on, are well-situated or poorly-situated. The base sciences are the remaining sciences, such as the science of bodily marks, omens, and so on, which are considered 'animal-like' with respect to the paths to heaven and liberation because they are not conducive to release. The science of bodily marks is the knowledge of the fortunate and unfortunate characteristics of men and women. The science of stars is the treatise for knowing the conjunctions of the constellations.

Na dūtagamanenāti na dūteyyaṃ katvā gamanena. Na pahiṇagamanenāti na gihīnaṃ sāsanaṃ gahetvā gharā gharaṃ pahitassa gamanena. Na jaṅghapesaniyenāti gāmantaradesantarādīsu tesaṃ tesaṃ gihīnaṃ sāsanapaṭisāsanaṃ haraṇena. Idañhi jaṅghapesaniyaṃ nāma attano mātāpitūnaṃ, ye cāssa mātāpitaro upaṭṭhahanti, tesaṃ sāsanaṃ gahetvā katthaci gamanavasena vaṭṭati. Cetiyassa vā saṅghassa vā attano vā kammaṃ karontānaṃ vaḍḍhakīnampi sāsanaṃ harituṃ vaṭṭati. Manussā “dānaṃ dassāma, pūjaṃ karissāma, bhikkhusaṅghassa ācikkhathā”ti ca vadanti; “asukattherassa nāma dethā”ti piṇḍapātaṃ vā bhesajjaṃ vā cīvaraṃ vā denti, “vihāre pūjaṃ karothā”ti mālāgandhavilepanādīni [V 0.0326] vā dhajapaṭākādīni vā niyyātenti. Sabbaṃ harituṃ vaṭṭati, jaṅghapesaniyaṃ nāma na hoti. Sesasāsanaṃ gahetvā gacchantassa padavāre padavāre doso.

‘Nor by going as a messenger’ means not by going having undertaken the duty of a messenger. ‘Nor by going on a mission’ means not by going from house to house as one sent, having received a message from laypeople. ‘Nor by running errands’ means by carrying messages and counter-messages for various laypeople in other villages, other regions, and so on. This running of errands, however, is permissible by way of going somewhere carrying a message for one’s own mother and father, or for those who attend to one’s mother and father. It is also permissible to carry a message even for carpenters who are doing work for a stupa, for the Sangha, or for oneself. People may say, 'We will give a donation, we will make an offering, please inform the community of monks'; or they give almsfood, medicine, or a robe, saying, 'Give this to the elder so-and-so'; or they dispatch garlands, perfumes, ointments, banners, flags, and so on, saying, 'Make an offering at the monastery.' It is permissible to carry all of this; it is not called running errands. For one who goes carrying other messages, there is an offense at every footstep.

Na vejjakammenāti na vejjena hutvā kāyatikicchanādibhesajjakaraṇena. Bhesajjaṃ pana pañcannaṃ sahadhammikānaṃ kātabbaṃ bhikkhussa bhikkhuniyā sikkhamānāya sāmaṇerassa sāmaṇeriyā. Samasīlasaddhāpaññānañhi etesaṃ tīsu sikkhāsu yuttānaṃ bhesajjaṃ akātuṃ na labbhati. Mātāpitūnaṃ tadupaṭṭhākānaṃ attano veyyāvaccakarassa paṇḍupalāsassāti etesaṃ pañcannampi kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Jeṭṭhabhātu, kaniṭṭhabhātu, jeṭṭhabhaginiyā, kaniṭṭhabhaginiyā, cūḷamātuyā, mahāmātuyā, cūḷapituno, mahāpituno, pitucchāya, mātucchāyāti etesaṃ pana dasannampi karontena tesaṃyeva santakaṃ bhesajjaṃ gahetvā kevalaṃ yojetvā dātabbaṃ. Sace nappahoti, attano santakaṃ tāvakālikaṃ dātabbaṃ. Etesaṃ puttaparamparā yāva sattamā kulaparivaṭṭā, tāva cattāro paccaye āharāpentassa akataviññatti vā, bhesajjaṃ karontassa vejjakammaṃ vā, kuladūsakāpatti vā na hoti.

“Nor by medical practice” means not acting as a physician by preparing medicines for bodily treatments and so on. However, medicine may be prepared for five kinds of fellow Dhamma-farers: a monk, a nun, a female probationer, a novice monk, and a novice nun. Indeed, for these who are equal in virtue, faith, and wisdom, and engaged in the three trainings, it is not permissible to refuse them medicine. It is also permissible to prepare medicine for one’s parents, their attendants, one’s own attendant, or a person like a withered leaf—for these five as well. However, for these ten—one’s elder brother, younger brother, elder sister, younger sister, lesser mother, greater mother, lesser father, greater father, paternal aunt, and maternal aunt—when preparing medicine, one should take their own medicinal substances, and merely combine and give it. If that is not sufficient, one may give from one’s own resources temporarily. For their descendants, up to the seventh generation of the family lineage, having them bring the four requisites does not constitute an improper request, preparing medicine for them is not considered the offense of medical practice, and there is no offense of corrupting a family.

Na [P 2.0403] piṇḍapaṭipiṇḍakenāti ettha piṇḍapāto kassa dātabbo, kassa na dātabbo? Mātāpitūnaṃ tadupaṭṭhākānaṃ veyyāvaccakarassa paṇḍupalāsassa sampattassa dāmarikacorassa issarassāpi dātabbo. Etesaṃ datvā pacchā laddhampi piṇḍapaṭipiṇḍaṃ nāma na hoti. Na dānānuppadānenāti attano [M 0.0355] dinnakānaṃ na puna dānena. Dhammenāti dhammena uppannaṃ. Samenāti kāyasucaritādinā. Laddhāti kāyena laddhā. Labhitvāti cittena pāpuṇitvā. Adhigantvāti sampāpuṇitvā. Vinditvāti ñāṇena vinditvā. Paṭilabhitvāti punappunaṃ labhitvā.

“Nor by exchanging food portions”: Here, to whom should almsfood be given, and to whom should it not be given? It should be given to one’s parents, their attendants, one who performs services, one who is like a withered leaf, a brigand who has arrived, and even a ruler. After giving to these, even what one later receives is not called exchanging food portions. “Nor by giving after giving” means not giving again what one has already given. “Righteously” means arisen by Dhamma. “Equitably” means through good conduct of body and so on. “Obtained” means obtained by the body. “Gained” means attained by the mind. “Achieved” means fully attained. “Discovered” means discovered through wisdom. “Acquired” means repeatedly obtained.

Annasannidhinti ettha duvidhā annakathā vinayavasena ca sallekhavasena ca. Vinayavasena tāva yaṃkiñci annaṃ ajja paṭiggahitaṃ aparajju sannidhikārakaṃ hoti, tassa paribhoge pācittiyaṃ. Attanā laddhaṃ pana sāmaṇerānaṃ datvā tehi laddhaṃ ṭhapāpetvā dutiyadivase bhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati, sallekho pana na hoti.

Regarding “the accumulation of food”: here there are two discussions about food, one according to the Vinaya and one according to the practice of effacement. According to the Vinaya, any food whatsoever received today that is stored for the next day involves a Pācittiya offense in its consumption. However, if one gives what one has obtained to novices, and has them keep what they have received, it is allowable to eat it on the second day, but this does not constitute effacement.

Pānasannidhimhipi eseva nayo. Ettha pānaṃ nāma ambapānādīni aṭṭha pānāni, yāni ce tesaṃ anulomāni.

The same principle applies to the accumulation of drinks as well. Here, “drink” means the eight kinds of juices beginning with mango juice, and those which are in conformity with them.

Vatthasannidhintiādimhi anadhiṭṭhitāvikappitaṃ sannidhi ca hoti sallekhañca kopeti. Ayaṃ [V 0.0327] pariyāya kathāva, nippariyāyato pana ticīvarasantuṭṭhena bhavitabbaṃ, catutthaṃ labhitvā aññassa dātabbaṃ. Sace yassa kassaci dātuṃ na sakkoti, yassa pana dātukāmo hoti, so uddesatthāya vā paripucchatthāya vā gato, āgatamatte dātabbaṃ, adātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Cīvare pana appahonte satiyā paccāsāya anuññātakālaṃ ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati. Sūcisuttacīvarakārakānaṃ alābhena tato parampi vinayakammaṃ katvā ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati. “Imasmiṃ jiṇṇe puna īdisaṃ kuto labhissāmī”ti pana ṭhapetuṃ na vaṭṭati, sannidhi ca hoti, sallekhañca vikopeti.

In the phrase “regarding the accumulation of robes,” and so on: what is unassigned and unallocated is an accumulation and corrupts the practice of effacement. This is a figurative statement; in a non-figurative sense, one should be content with three robes. Having obtained a fourth, it should be given to another. If one is unable to give it to anyone, but there is someone to whom one desires to give it, and that person has gone away for learning or questioning, it should be given as soon as they return; it is not proper not to give it. But when a robe is not sufficient, it is allowable to keep it for the permitted period in anticipation of receiving more. If a needle, thread, or robe-makers are unavailable, it is allowable to keep it even beyond that, having performed the Vinaya procedure. But it is not proper to keep it thinking, “When this one is worn out, where will I get another like this?”; this is an accumulation, and it corrupts the practice of effacement.

Yānasannidhimhi yānaṃ nāma vayhaṃ ratho sakaṭaṃ sandamānikā sivikā pāṭaṅkīti netaṃ pabbajitassa yānaṃ. Upāhanā pana pabbajitassa yānaṃyeva. Ekabhikkhussa hi eko araññatthāya, ekā dhotapādakatthāyāti ukkaṃsato dve upāhanasaṅghāṭā [P 2.0404] vaṭṭanti, tatiyaṃ labhitvā aññassa dātabbo, “imasmiṃ jiṇṇe aññaṃ kuto labhissāmī”ti hi ṭhapetuṃ na vaṭṭati, sannidhi ca hoti, sallekhañca vikopeti.

Regarding the accumulation of vehicles: a “vehicle” means a conveyance such as a palanquin, chariot, cart, sedan chair, or litter—these are not vehicles for one who has gone forth. Footwear, however, is indeed a vehicle for one who has gone forth. For a single monk, two pairs of sandals are permissible at most: one for going to the forest, and one for when the feet are washed. If a third pair is obtained, it should be given to another, for it is not allowable to keep it thinking, “When this one wears out, where will I get another?” This constitutes an accumulation, and it corrupts the practice of effacement.

Sayanasannidhimhi sayananti mañco. Ekassa bhikkhuno eko gabbhe eko divāṭṭhāneti ukkaṃsato dve mañcā vaṭṭanti, tato uttari labhitvā aññassa bhikkhuno vā gaṇassa vā dātabbo, adātuṃ na vaṭṭati, sannidhi ceva hoti, sallekhañca kopeti.

Regarding the accumulation of beds: “bed” means a couch. For one monk, one in the sleeping chamber and one in the day-residence, at most two couches are allowable. Having obtained more than that, it should be given to another monk or to the Sangha. It is not allowable not to give it away, as this constitutes an accumulation and corrupts the practice of effacement.

Gandhasannidhimhi [M 0.0356] bhikkhuno kaṇḍukacchuchavidosādiābādhe sati gandho vaṭṭati. Tena gandhena tasmiṃ roge vūpasante aññesaṃ vā ābādhikānaṃ dātabbo. Dvāre pañcaṅgulagharadhūpanādīsu vā upanetabbo. “Puna roge sati bhavissatī”ti ṭhapetuṃ na vaṭṭati, gandhasannidhi ca hoti, sallekhañca kopeti.

Regarding the accumulation of perfumes: if a monk suffers from ailments such as itching, scabies, skin diseases, and so on, perfume is allowable. When that illness subsides with that perfume, it should be given to other sick monks. Or it should be used for things such as fumigating a latrine at the door. It is not allowable to keep it thinking, “It may be needed again when illness arises,” for this constitutes accumulating perfumes and corrupts the practice of effacement.

Āmisanti annādivuttāvasesaṃva daṭṭhabbaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ – idhekacco bhikkhu “tathārūpe kāle upakārāya bhavissantī”ti tilataṇḍulamuggamāsanāḷikeraloṇamacchamaṃsavallūrasappitelaguḷa- bhājanādīni āharāpetvā ṭhapeti. So vassakāle kālasseva sāmaṇerehi yāguṃ pacāpetvā bhuñjitvā “sāmaṇera udakakaddame dukkhaṃ gāmaṃ pavisituṃ, gaccha asukakulaṃ gantvā mayhaṃ vihāre nisinnabhāvaṃ ārocehi, asukakulato dadhiādīni āharā”ti peseti. Bhikkhūhi “kiṃ, bhante, gāmaṃ pavisathā”ti vuttepi “duppaveso āvuso idāni gāmo”ti vadati. Te “hotu, bhante, acchatha tumhe, mayaṃ bhikkhaṃ pariyesitvā āharissāmā”ti gacchanti. Atha sāmaṇeropi dadhiādīni āharitvā bhattañca byañjanañca sampādetvā upaneti, taṃ bhuñjantasseva [V 0.0328] upaṭṭhākā bhattaṃ pahiṇanti, tatopi manāpaṃ manāpaṃ bhuñjati. Atha bhikkhū piṇḍapātaṃ gahetvā āgacchanti, tatopi manāpaṃ manāpaṃ gīvāyāmakaṃ bhuñjatiyeva. Evaṃ catumāsampi vītināmeti. Ayaṃ vuccati bhikkhu “muṇḍakuṭumbikajīvikaṃ jīvati, na samaṇajīvika”nti. Evarūpo āmisasannidhi nāma hoti.

“Material goods” should be understood as what remains from what was said about food and so on. For example, a certain monk here thinks, “Such things will be useful at a time of need,” and so he has sesame seeds, rice, mung beans, other beans, coconuts, salt, fish, meat, dried meat, ghee, oil, molasses, vessels, and so on, brought and stored. During the rainy season, he has novices prepare rice-gruel early in the morning, eats it, and then sends them, saying, “Novices, it is difficult to enter the village now because of the water and mud. Go to such-and-such a family, inform them that I am sitting in the monastery, and bring back yogurt and other items from such-and-such a family.” Even when other monks ask him, “Venerable sir, are you going into the village?” he says, “Friends, the village is difficult to enter now.” They say, “So be it, venerable sir. You stay here. We will go to seek almsfood and bring it back.” Then the novice brings back yogurt and other items, prepares the rice and curry, and offers it to him. While he is eating, his supporters send food, and from that too he eats whatever is delicious. Then the monks return with the almsfood they have collected, and from that too he eats whatever is delicious, stretching his neck to eat. In this way he passes the entire four months. Such a monk is said to be “one who lives the life of a shaven-headed householder, not the life of a recluse.” This is called the hoarding of material goods.

Bhikkhuno pana vasanaṭṭhāne ekā taṇḍulanāḷi eko guḷapiṇḍo catubhāgamattaṃ sappīti ettakaṃ nidhetuṃ vaṭṭati akāle sampattacorānaṃ atthāya. Te hi ettakampi āmisapaṭisanthāraṃ alabhantā jīvitāpi voropeyyuṃ, tasmā [P 2.0405] sacepi ettakaṃ natthi, āharāpetvāpi ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati. Aphāsukakāle ca yadettha kappiyaṃ, taṃ attanāpi paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Kappiyakuṭiyaṃ pana bahuṃ ṭhapentassāpi sannidhi nāma natthi.

However, in a monk's dwelling place, it is allowable to store one nāḷi of husked rice, one lump of molasses, and a quarter-measure of ghee. This much is permitted for the sake of thieves who might arrive at an inopportune time. For if they do not receive even this much of a material welcome, they might even take his life. Therefore, even if this much is not available, it is allowable to have it brought and stored. And in a time of discomfort, whatever herein is allowable may also be consumed by oneself. But even if much is stored in an allowable storeroom, there is no hoarding.

160. Jhāyī na pādalolassāti jhānābhirato ca na ca pādalolo assa. Virame kukkuccā nappamajjeyyāti hatthakukkuccādikukkuccaṃ vinodeyya, sakkaccakāritāya cettha nappamajjeyya.

160. “A meditator should not be restless with his feet” means: one who delights in jhāna should not be restless with his feet. “He should desist from scrupulousness and not be heedless” means: he should dispel scrupulousness, such as scrupulousness about the hands, and in this he should not be heedless in regard to acting respectfully.

Ekattamanuyuttoti [M 0.0357] ekībhāvaṃ anuyutto. Paramatthagarukoti uttamatthagaruko. “Sakatthagaruko”ti vā pāṭho.

“Devoted to solitude” means devoted to being alone. “Respecting the ultimate goal” means respecting the highest goal. Or the reading is “respecting one’s own welfare.”

Paṭisallānārāmoti āramaṇaṃ ārāmo, tato tato ārammaṇato paṭisaṃharitvā ekībhāve paṭisallāne ārāmo yassa so paṭisallānārāmo. Assāti bhaveyya. Tasmiṃ ratoti paṭisallānarato. Etehi sīlesu paripūrakāritaṃ dasseti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Sīlavipannassa ekaggatāpi na sampajjati. Ajjhattaṃ cetosamathamanuyuttoti attano cittasamathe yutto. Ettha hi ajjhattanti vā attanoti vā etaṃ ekatthaṃ, byañjanameva nānaṃ. Bhummatthe panetaṃ upayogavacanaṃ. Anūti iminā upasaggena yoge siddhaṃ.

‘Delighting in seclusion’: seclusion is his resort. Having withdrawn from this and that object, he for whom seclusion—the state of being alone—is his resort, is one who delights in seclusion. ‘He should be’ means he would be. ‘Delighting in that’ means delighting in seclusion. By these words, the fulfillment of the training in virtue is shown. For what reason? For one whose virtue is defective, even one-pointedness is not accomplished. ‘Devoted to the internal calming of the mind’ means devoted to the calming of his own mind. Here, ‘internal’ or ‘of oneself’ has the same meaning; only the expression is different. This is an expression in the locative sense, and the connection is established by the prefix `anu`.

Anirākatajjhānoti bahi anihatajjhāno avināsitajjhāno vā. Nīharaṇavināsatthañhi idaṃ nirākaraṇaṃ nāma. “Thambhaṃ niraṃkatvā nivātavuttī”tiādīsu (su. ni. 328) cassa payogo daṭṭhabbo. Vipassanāya samannāgatoti sattavidhāya anupassanāya yutto. Sattavidhā anupassanā nāma aniccānupassanā dukkhānupassanā anattānupassanā nibbidānupassanā virāgānupassanā nirodhānupassanā paṭinissaggānupassanāti. Tā visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 2.741 ādayo, 849 ādayo) vitthāritā[V 0.0329]. Byūhetā suññāgārānanti vaḍḍhetā suññāgārānaṃ. Ettha ca samathavipassanāvasena kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā rattindivaṃ suññāgāraṃ pavisitvā nisīdamāno bhikkhu “brūhetā suññāgārāna”nti [P 2.0406] veditabbo. Ekabhūmakādibhede pāsāde kurumānopi suññāgārānaṃ brūhetāti daṭṭhabbo.

‘Not having rejected jhāna’ means not having cast out jhāna, or not having destroyed jhāna. For this word `nirākaraṇa` has the meaning of removal and destruction. Its usage is to be seen in such passages as: ‘Having removed the pillar, he lives sheltered from the wind’ (Snp 328). ‘Endowed with insight’ means endowed with the seven kinds of contemplation. The seven kinds of contemplation are: the contemplation of impermanence, the contemplation of suffering, the contemplation of non-self, the contemplation of disenchantment, the contemplation of dispassion, the contemplation of cessation, and the contemplation of relinquishment. These are explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga. ‘A developer of empty abodes’ means an augmenter of empty abodes. Here, a bhikkhu who has taken up a meditation subject by way of serenity and insight, and who enters an empty abode day and night and sits, should be understood as ‘a developer of empty abodes.’ Even one who is building a mansion with one or more stories should be seen as a developer of empty abodes.

Sakkaccakārītiādīsu dānādīnaṃ kusaladhammānaṃ bhāvanāya puggalassa vā deyyadhammassa vā sakkaccakāritāvasena sakkaccakārī. Assāti bhaveyya. Satatabhāvo sātaccaṃ, sātaccakāritāvasena sātaccakārī. Nirantarakāritāya aṭṭhitakārī. Yathā nāma kakaṇṭako thokaṃ gantvā thokaṃ tiṭṭhati, na nirantaraṃ gacchati, evameva yo puggalo ekadivasaṃ dānaṃ datvā pūjaṃ vā katvā dhammaṃ vā sutvā samaṇadhammaṃ vā katvā puna cirassaṃ karoti, taṃ na nirantaraṃ pavatteti. So “asātaccakārī, ṭhitakārī”ti vuccati. Yo pana evaṃ na hoti, so aṭṭhitakārī. Anolīnavuttikoti nirantarakaraṇasaṅkhātassa [M 0.0358] vipphārassa atthitāya na olīnavuttiko. Anikkhittacchandoti kusalakiriyāya vīriyacchandassa anikkhittabhāvena anikkhittacchando. Anikkhittadhuroti vīriyadhurassa anoropako, anosakkitamānasoti attho.

In such phrases as ‘one who acts respectfully,’ he is one who acts respectfully by way of acting with respect towards the person or the gift in the development of wholesome states such as giving. ‘He should be’ means he would be. Persistence is the state of being constant; he is one who acts persistently by way of acting with persistence. He is one who acts without stopping because he acts uninterruptedly. Just as a chameleon goes a little way and stops a little way, not going uninterruptedly, so too a person who gives a gift, makes an offering, listens to the Dhamma, or undertakes the ascetic’s duties for one day and then does so again only after a long time, does not maintain it uninterruptedly. He is called ‘one who does not act persistently,’ ‘one who acts intermittently.’ But one who is not like this is one who acts without stopping. ‘One whose conduct is not sluggish’ means he is not sluggish in conduct because of the presence of diffusion, which is defined as uninterrupted action. ‘One who has not thrown off the desire’ means he has not thrown off the desire because he has not abandoned the desire for energy in wholesome action. ‘One who has not laid down the yoke’ means one who does not set down the yoke of energy; the meaning is that his mind has not shrunk back.

Appaṭivānīti anivattanaṃ. Adhiṭṭhānanti kusalakaraṇe patiṭṭhābhāvo. Anuyogoti anuyuñjanaṃ. Appamādoti satiyā avippavāso.

‘Not turning back’ means not returning. ‘Determination’ means the state of being established in doing what is wholesome. ‘Application’ means applying oneself. ‘Heedfulness’ means the non-absence of mindfulness.

161. Tandiṃ māyaṃ hassaṃ khiḍḍanti ālasiyañca māyañca hassañca kāyikaṃ vācasikaṃ khiḍḍañca. Savibhūsanti saddhiṃ vibhūsāya.

161. ‘Lethargy, deceit, laughter, and amusement’: this means lethargy, deceit, laughter, and bodily and verbal amusement. ‘Together with adornment’ means along with adornment.

Rattindivaṃ chakoṭṭhāsaṃ karitvāti purimayāmamajjhimayāmapacchimayāmavasena rattiṃ tayo tathā divāti chabbidhaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ katvā. Pañcakoṭṭhāsaṃ paṭijaggeyyāti rattiṃ majjhimayāmaṃ vissajjetvā avasesapañcakoṭṭhāsesu na niddaṃ okkameyya. Ekakoṭṭhāsaṃ nipajjeyyāti ekaṃ majjhimayāmakoṭṭhāsaṃ sato sampajāno nipajjitvā niddaṃ okkameyya.

‘Having divided the day and night into six parts’: having made six portions by dividing the night into three—the first, middle, and last watches—and the day similarly. ‘He should be vigilant for five parts’: having set aside the middle watch of the night, he should not give in to sleep during the remaining five parts. ‘He should lie down for one part’: for the one part, the middle watch, he should lie down and give in to sleep, mindful and clearly comprehending.

Idha bhikkhu divasampi pubbaṇhe majjhanhe sāyanheti tayopi divasakoṭṭhāsā gahitā. Caṅkamena nisajjāyāti sakalaṃ divasaṃ iminā iriyāpathadvayeneva viharanto cittassa āvaraṇato āvaraṇīyehi dhammehi pañcahi nīvaraṇehi sabbākusaladhammehi vā. Cittaṃ parisodheyyāti tehi dhammehi [V 0.0330] cittaṃ [P 2.0407] visodheyya. Ṭhānaṃ panettha kiñcāpi na gahitaṃ, caṅkamanisajjāsannissitaṃ pana katvā gahetabbameva. Paṭhamaṃ yāmanti sakalasmimpi paṭhamayāme.

Here, as to the day, the three portions of the day are taken: morning, midday, and evening. ‘By walking and by sitting… he should cleanse his mind’: while spending the entire day in only these two postures, he should purify his mind of obstructive states, that is, of the five hindrances or of all unwholesome states that obstruct the mind. Although the posture of standing is not mentioned here, it should be included as being associated with walking and sitting. ‘The first watch’ means during the entire first watch.

Seyyanti ettha kāmabhogīseyyā petaseyyā sīhaseyyā tathāgataseyyāti catasso seyyā. Tattha “yebhuyyena, bhikkhave, kāmabhogī vāmena passena sentī”ti (a. ni. 1.4246) ayaṃ kāmabhogīseyyā. Tesu hi yebhuyyena dakkhiṇapassena sayāno nāma natthi. “Yebhuyyena, bhikkhave, petā uttānā sentī”ti (a. ni. 4.246) ayaṃ petaseyyā. Appamaṃsalohitattā hi aṭṭhisaṅghāṭaghaṭṭitā ekena passena sayituṃ na sakkonti, uttānāva senti. “Sīho, bhikkhave, migarājā dakkhiṇena passena seyyaṃ kappeti…pe… attamano hotī”ti (a. ni. 4.246) ayaṃ sīhaseyyā. Tejussadattā hi sīho migarājā dve purimapāde ekasmiṃ pacchimapāde ekasmiṃ ṭhāne [M 0.0359] ṭhapetvā naṅguṭṭhaṃ antarasatthimhi pakkhipitvā purimapādapacchimapādanaṅguṭṭhānaṃ ṭhitokāsaṃ sallakkhetvā dvinnaṃ purimapādānaṃ matthake sīsaṃ ṭhapetvā sayati. Divasampi sayitvā pabujjhamāno na utrasto pabujjhati, sīsaṃ pana ukkhipitvā purimapādādīnaṃ ṭhitokāsaṃ sallakkheti. Sace kiñci ṭhānaṃ vijahitvā ṭhitaṃ hoti, “nayidaṃ tuyhaṃ jātiyā, na sūrabhāvassa anurūpa”nti anattamano hutvā tattheva sayati, na gocarāya pakkamati. Avijahitvā ṭhite pana “tuyhaṃ jātiyā ca sūrabhāvassa ca anurūpamida”nti haṭṭhatuṭṭho uṭṭhāya sīhavijambhitaṃ vijambhitvā kesarabhāraṃ vidhunitvā tikkhattuṃ sīhanādaṃ naditvā gocarāya pakkamati. Catutthajjhānaseyyā pana tathāgataseyyāti vuccati. Tāsu idha sīhaseyyā āgatā. Ayañhi tejussadairiyāpathattā uttamaseyyā nāma.

Here, there are four kinds of lying down: the lying down of one who indulges in sensual pleasures, the lying down of a departed one, the lion’s posture, and the Tathāgata’s posture. Among these, ‘For the most part, bhikkhus, those who indulge in sensual pleasures lie on their left side’ (AN 4.245)—this is the lying down of one who indulges in sensual pleasures. For among them, there is hardly anyone who lies on the right side. ‘For the most part, bhikkhus, the departed lie on their backs’ (AN 4.246)—this is the lying down of a departed one. Because they have little flesh and blood, their bone-frames knock together and they cannot lie on one side; they lie only on their backs. ‘The lion, bhikkhus, the king of beasts, lies down on its right side… and is content’ (AN 4.246)—this is the lion’s posture. Because it abounds in energy, the lion, the king of beasts, places its two front paws in one place and its back paws in another, tucks its tail between its thighs, notes the place where its paws and tail are resting, places its head on its front paws, and lies down. Having slept, when it awakens, it awakens without being startled. It lifts its head and observes the place where its paws and so on were resting. If any of them have shifted from their place, it becomes displeased, thinking, ‘This is not befitting your birth, not befitting your brave nature,’ and lies down right there again; it does not go out for its prey. But if they have not shifted, it is happy and delighted, thinking, ‘This is befitting your birth and your brave nature.’ It gets up, gives a lion’s stretch, shakes its mane, gives three lion’s roars, and goes out for its prey. The lying down in the fourth jhāna is called the Tathāgata’s posture. Of these, the lion’s posture is intended here. For because this posture abounds in energy, it is called the supreme way of lying down.

Pāde pādanti dakkhiṇapāde vāmapādaṃ. Accādhāyāti atiādhāya īsakaṃ atikkamma ṭhapetvā. Gopphakena hi gopphake, jāṇunā vā jāṇumhi saṅghaṭṭiyamāne abhiṇhaṃ vedanā uppajjati, cittaṃ ekaggaṃ na hoti, seyyā aphāsu hoti. Yathā pana na saṅghaṭṭeti, evaṃ atikkamma ṭhapite vedanā nuppajjati, cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti, seyyā [P 2.0408] phāsu hoti. Tena vuttaṃ – “pāde pādaṃ accādhāyā”ti. Sato sampajānoti satiyā ceva sampajānapaññāya ca samannāgato hutvā. Iminā supariggāhakaṃ satisampajaññaṃ kathitaṃ. Uṭṭhānasaññaṃ manasikaritvāti “asukavelāya nāma uṭṭhahissāmī”ti evaṃ uṭṭhānavelāparicchedakaṃ uṭṭhānasaññaṃ citte ṭhapetvā. Evaṃ katvā nipanno hi yathāparicchinnakāleyeva uṭṭhāti.

‘Foot on foot’ means the left foot on the right foot. ‘Placing slightly above’ means placing it a little beyond, slightly overlapping. For when ankle touches ankle, or knee touches knee, frequent pain arises, the mind is not concentrated, and the lying down is uncomfortable. But when they do not touch, no pain arises, the mind is concentrated, and the lying down is comfortable. Therefore it is said: ‘foot on foot, placing slightly above.’ ‘Mindful and clearly comprehending’ means being endowed with mindfulness and the wisdom of clear comprehension. By this, well-guarded mindfulness and clear comprehension are described. ‘Having attended to the perception of rising’ means establishing in the mind the perception of rising, which determines the time for rising, thinking, ‘At such and such a time, I will rise.’ Having done so, one who lies down rises exactly at the predetermined time.

Vīriyindriyaniddese cetasikoti idaṃ vīriyassa niyamato cetasikabhāvadīpanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, idañhi [V 0.0331] vīriyaṃ “yadapi, bhikkhave, kāyikaṃ vīriyaṃ, tadapi vīriyasambojjhaṅgo, yadapi cetasikaṃ vīriyaṃ, tadapi vīriyasambojjhaṅgoti. Itihidaṃ uddesaṃ gacchatī”ti evamādīsu suttesu (saṃ. ni. 5.233) caṅkamādīni karontassa uppajjanatāya kāyikanti vuccamānampi kāyaviññāṇaṃ viya kāyikaṃ nāma natthi, cetasikameva panetanti dīpetuṃ “cetasiko”ti vuttaṃ. Vīriyārambhoti vīriyasaṅkhāto ārambho. Ayañhi ārambhasaddo kamme āpattiyaṃ kiriyāyaṃ vīriye hiṃsāyaṃ vikopaneti anekesu atthesu āgato.

In the exposition of the faculty of energy, the term ‘mental’ (cetasika) is stated to indicate that energy is invariably mental. For this energy is described in suttas such as: ‘Bhikkhus, whatever physical energy there is, that too is the enlightenment factor of energy; whatever mental energy there is, that too is the enlightenment factor of energy. Thus, this is included in the summary’ (SN 5.233). Even when it is called ‘physical’—arising as it does in one engaged in walking meditation and so on—there is no such thing as physical energy in the way that there is bodily consciousness; rather, it is purely mental. To clarify this, it is called ‘mental.’ ‘Vīriyārambha’ means initiative characterized as energy. For this term ‘ārambha’ (initiative) has come to be used in many senses: in action, in transgression, in activity, in energy, in harm, and in destruction.

“Yaṃ [M 0.0360] kiñci dukkhaṃ sambhoti, sabbaṃ ārambhapaccayā;

Ārambhānaṃ nirodhena, natthi dukkhassa sambhavo”ti. (su. ni. 749) –

‘Whatever suffering arises, all is conditioned by initiative; with the cessation of initiatives, there is no arising of suffering.’ (Snp 749)

Ettha hi kammaṃ ārambhoti āgataṃ. “Ārambhati ca vippaṭisārī ca hotī”ti (a. ni. 5.142; pu. pa. 191) ettha āpatti. “Mahāyaññā mahārambhā, na te honti mahapphalā”ti (a. ni. 4.39; saṃ. ni. 1.120) ettha yūpussāpanādikiriyā. “Ārambhatha nikkamatha, yuñjatha buddhasāsane”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.185; kathā. 333; netti. 29; peṭako. 38; mi. pa. 5.1.4) ettha vīriyaṃ. “Samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ uddissa pāṇaṃ ārambhantī”ti (ma. ni. 2.51) ettha hiṃsā. “Bījagāmabhūtagāmasamārambhā paṭivirato hotī”ti (dī. ni. 1.10; ma. ni. 1.293) ettha chedanabhañjanādikaṃ vikopanaṃ. Idha pana vīriyameva adhippetaṃ. Tenāha “vīriyārambhoti vīriyasaṅkhāto ārambho”ti. Vīriyañhi ārambhanavasena ārambhoti vuccati. Idamassa sabhāvapadaṃ. Kosajjato nikkhamanavasena nikkamo. Paraṃ paraṃ ṭhānaṃ akkamanavasena parakkamo. Uggantvā yamanavasena [P 2.0409] uyyāmo. Vāyamanavasena vāyāmo. Ussahanavasena ussāho. Adhimattussahanavasena ussoḷhī. Thirabhāvaṭṭhena thāmo. Cittacetasikānaṃ dhāraṇavasena avicchedato vā pavattanavasena kusalasantānaṃ dhāretīti dhiti.

Here, indeed, ‘kamma’ is what is meant by ‘initiative.’ In ‘One initiates and then regrets’ (AN 5.142; Pp 191), it means a transgression. In ‘Great sacrifices, great initiatives, they do not bear great fruit’ (AN 4.39; SN 1.120), it means activities like erecting sacrificial posts. In ‘Strive, go forth, apply yourselves to the Buddha’s teaching’ (SN 1.185; Kv 333; Ne 29; Pe 38; Mil 5.1.4), it means energy. In ‘They kill living beings for the ascetic Gotama’ (MN 2.51), it means harm. In ‘He abstains from destroying seed-life and plant-life’ (DN 1.10; MN 1.293), it means cutting, breaking, and other forms of destruction. Here, however, only energy is intended. Therefore, it is said: ‘Vīriyārambha means initiative characterized as energy.’ For energy is called ‘ārambha’ in the sense of initiating. This is its natural term. In the sense of departing from laziness, it is ‘nikkamo’ (exertion). In the sense of advancing to a further and further position, it is ‘parakkamo’ (advancing). In the sense of rising up and striving, it is ‘uyyāmo’ (endeavor). In the sense of exerting, it is ‘vāyāmo’ (striving). In the sense of making an effort, it is ‘ussāho’ (effort). In the sense of intense effort, it is ‘ussoḷhī’ (vigor). In the sense of a firm state, it is ‘thāmo’ (steadfastness). Because it sustains the continuity of wholesome states by upholding the mind and mental factors, or by their uninterrupted occurrence, it is called ‘dhiti’ (fortitude).

Aparo nayo – nikkamo ceso kāmānaṃ panudanāya. Parakkamo ceso bandhanacchedāya. Uyyāmo ceso oghassa nittharaṇāya. Vāyāmo ceso pāraṃ gamanaṭṭhena. Ussāho ceso pubbaṅgamaṭṭhena. Ussoḷhī ceso adhimattaṭṭhena. Thāmo ceso palighugghāṭanatāya. Dhiti ceso aṭṭhitakāritāyāti.

Another method: This ‘nikkamo’ is for dispelling sensual pleasures. This ‘parakkamo’ is for cutting bonds. This ‘uyyāmo’ is for crossing the flood. This ‘vāyāmo’ is in the sense of going to the far shore. This ‘ussāho’ is in the sense of being a forerunner. This ‘ussoḷhī’ is in the sense of being exceedingly intense. This ‘thāmo’ is for lifting the crossbar. This ‘dhiti’ is for acting steadfastly.

“Kāmaṃ taco ca nhāru ca, aṭṭhi ca avasissatū”ti (a. ni. 2.5) evaṃ pavattikāle [V 0.0332] asithilaparakkamavasena asithilaparakkamatā, thiraparakkamo daḷhaparakkamoti attho. Yasmā panetaṃ vīriyaṃ kusalakammakaraṇaṭṭhāne chandaṃ na nikkhipati, dhuraṃ na nikkhipati, na otāreti na vissajjeti, anosakkitamānasataṃ āvahati, tasmā “anikkhittacchandatā anikkhittadhuratā”ti vuttaṃ. Yathā pana tajjātike udakasambhinnaṭṭhāne dhuravāhagoṇaṃ “gaṇhathā”ti vadanti, so jāṇunā bhūmiṃ uppīḷetvāpi dhuraṃ vahati, bhūmiyaṃ patituṃ na deti, evameva [M 0.0361] vīriyaṃ kusalakammakaraṇaṭṭhāne dhuraṃ na nikkhipati paggaṇhāti, tasmā “dhurasampaggāho”ti vuttaṃ. Paggahalakkhaṇe indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti vīriyindriyaṃ. Kosajje na kampatīti vīriyabalaṃ. Yāthāvaniyyānikakusalavāyāmatāya sammāvāyāmo.

‘Let only skin, sinews, and bones remain’ (AN 2.5)—thus, at the time of its occurrence, it is unslackening effort due to unrelaxed persistence; the meaning is firm effort, steadfast effort. Furthermore, because this energy does not lay aside zeal in the place of performing wholesome actions, does not lay aside the burden, does not lower it or release it, and brings about a state of mind that does not retreat, it is therefore called ‘not laying aside zeal, not laying aside the burden.’ Just as, in a muddy place broken up by water, they say to a draft ox, ‘Take it!’ and it pulls the burden even while pressing its knees to the ground, not letting it fall to the ground, so too energy does not lay aside the burden in the place of performing wholesome actions but takes it up—therefore it is called ‘taking up the burden.’ Because it exercises control in the characteristic of exertion, it is the faculty of energy (vīriyindriya). Because it is unshaken by laziness, it is the power of energy (vīriyabala). Because it is the wholesome striving that leads to deliverance, it is right effort (sammāvāyāmo).

Tandīti jātiālasiyaṃ. Tandiyanāti tandiyanākāro. Tandimanakatāti tandiyā abhibhūtacittatā. Alasassa bhāvo ālasyaṃ, ālasyāyanākāro ālasyāyanā. Ālasyāyitassa bhāvo ālasyāyitattaṃ. Iti sabbehi imehi padehi kilesavasena kāyālasiyaṃ kathitaṃ.

‘Tandī’ (sluggishness) is innate laziness. ‘Tandiyanā’ (being sluggish) is the state of being sluggish. ‘Tandimanakatā’ is the state of having a mind overcome by sluggishness. The state of a lazy person is ‘ālasyaṃ’ (laziness); the state of being lazy is ‘ālasyāyanā’ (laziness). The state of one who is lazy is ‘ālasyāyitattaṃ’ (the state of being lazy). Thus, by all these terms, bodily laziness as a defilement is described.

Vañcanikā cariyāti vañcanikā kiriyā. Mā maṃ jaññāti vācaṃ bhāsatīti jānaṃyeva paṇṇattiṃ vītikkamanto bhikkhu bhāriyaṃ karoti, amhākaṃ pana vītikkamaṭṭhānaṃ nāma natthīti upasanto viya bhāsati. Kāyena parakkamatīti [P 2.0410] “mayā kataṃ idaṃ pāpakammaṃ mā keci jāniṃsū”ti kāyena vattaṃ karoti. Vijjamānadosapaṭicchādanato cakkhumohanamāyā viyāti māyā, māyāvino bhāvo māyāvitā. Katvā pāpaṃ puna paṭicchādanato ati assarati etāya sattoti accasarā. Kāyavācākiriyāhi aññathā dassanato vañcetīti vañcanā. Etāya sattā nikarontīti nikati, micchā karontīti attho. “Nāhaṃ evaṃ karomī”ti pāpānaṃ nikkhipanato nikiraṇā. “Nāhaṃ evaṃ karomī”ti parivajjanato pariharaṇā. Kāyādīhi saṃvaraṇato gūhanā. Sabbato bhāgena gūhanā parigūhanā. Tiṇapaṇṇehi viya gūthaṃ kāyavacīkammehi pāpaṃ chādiyatīti chādanā. Sabbato bhāgena chādanā paricchādanā. Na uttānaṃ katvā dassetīti anuttānīkammaṃ. Na pākaṭaṃ katvā dassetīti anāvikammaṃ. Suṭṭhu chādanā vocchādanā. Katapāpapaṭicchādanavasena punapi pāpassa karaṇato pāpakiriyā. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ katapaṭicchādanalakkhaṇā māyā nāma vuccati. Yāya samannāgato puggalo bhasmāpaṭicchanno viya aṅgāro, udakapaṭicchanno viya khāṇu, pilotikāya paliveṭhitaṃ viya ca satthaṃ hoti. Ativelaṃ dantavidaṃsakaṃ hasatīti pamāṇātikkantaṃ dantaṃ vivaritvā paresaṃ dassetvā hāsaṃ somanassaṃ uppādetvā hasati.

‘Deceptive conduct’ means deceptive action. He speaks with the thought, ‘Let no one know me.’ Thus a bhikkhu, knowingly transgressing a rule, makes it a serious matter, yet he speaks as if he were restrained, saying, ‘For us, there is no such thing as a place of transgression.’ He strives with his body, thinking, ‘Let no one know this evil deed done by me,’ and so he puts on a bodily pretense. Because it conceals existing faults, like a magic trick that deludes the eye, it is called ‘māyā’ (deception). The state of being deceptive is ‘māyāvitā’ (deceitfulness). Having done evil, one conceals it again; because a being thereby goes too far, it is called ‘accasarā’ (transgression). Because one deceives by presenting things differently through bodily and verbal actions, it is ‘vañcanā’ (deception). By this, beings act wrongly—this is ‘nikati’ (trickery), meaning to act falsely. From casting off evil deeds by saying, ‘I do not do thus,’ it is ‘nikiraṇā’ (repudiation). From avoiding by saying, ‘I do not do thus,’ it is ‘pariharaṇā’ (evasion). From covering up with the body and so on, it is ‘gūhanā’ (concealing). Concealing completely in every way is ‘parigūhanā’ (thorough concealing). Just as one covers excrement with grass and leaves, so one covers evil with bodily and verbal actions—this is ‘chādanā’ (covering). Concealing completely in every way is ‘paricchādanā’ (thorough covering). Not making it plain is ‘anuttānīkammaṃ’ (non-disclosure). Not making it manifest is ‘anāvikammaṃ’ (non-revelation). Thoroughly covering is ‘vocchādanā’ (complete concealment). Because of concealing an evil deed that has been done, one does evil again—this is ‘pāpakiriyā’ (evil action). This is called—this characteristic of concealing what has been done is called ‘māyā’ (deception). A person endowed with this is like an ember covered with ashes, a stump hidden by water, or a sword wrapped in a rag. ‘He laughs excessively, displaying his teeth’ means that, exceeding the proper measure, he laughs by opening his mouth, showing his teeth to others, and producing laughter and gladness.

Kāyikā [V 0.0333][M 0.0362] ca khiḍḍāti kāyena pavattā kīḷā. Eseva nayo vācasikāyapi. Hatthīhipi kīḷantīti hatthīhi kīḷitatthāya purato dhāvanaādhāvanapiṭṭhanisīdanādikīṭṭhāya kīḷanti. Eseva nayo assarathesupi. Aṭṭhapadepi kīḷantīti ekekāya pantiyā aṭṭha aṭṭha padāni assāti aṭṭhapadaṃ, tasmiṃ aṭṭhapade. Dasapadepi eseva nayo. Ākāsepīti aṭṭhapadadasapadesu viya ākāseyeva kīḷanti. Parihārapathepīti bhūmiyaṃ nānāpathamaṇḍalaṃ katvā tattha pariharitabbapathaṃ pariharantā kīḷanti. Santikāyapi kīḷantīti santikakīḷāya kīḷanti, ekajjhaṃ ṭhapitā [P 2.0411] sāriyo vā pāsāṇasakkharāyo vā acālentā nakheneva apanenti ca upanenti ca. Sace tattha kāci calati, parājayo hotīti.

‘Bodily play’ is amusement enacted by the body. The same principle applies to verbal play. ‘Playing with elephants’ means they play for amusement with elephants by running before them, running after them, sitting on their backs, and so on. The same principle applies to horses and chariots. ‘Playing on the eight-square board’ means playing on a board which has eight squares in each row. The same principle applies to the ten-square board. ‘Playing in the air’ means they play as if in the air, just as on the eight-square or ten-square boards. ‘Playing on the encircling path’ means they draw various circular paths on the ground and play by traversing the path that must be traversed. ‘Playing santikā’ means they play the game of santikā: without moving the game pieces or pebbles that have been placed together, they remove them or place them with just a fingernail. If any piece there moves, it is a defeat.

Khalikāyāti jūtaphalake pāsakakīḷāya kīḷanti. Ghaṭikāyāti ghaṭikā vuccati dīghadaṇḍakena rassadaṇḍakaṃ paharaṇakīḷā, tāya kīḷanti. Salākahatthenāti lākhāya vā mañjaṭṭhiyā vā piṭṭhodakena vā salākahatthaṃ temetvā “kiṃ hotū”ti bhūmiyaṃ vā bhittiyaṃ vā taṃ paharitvā hatthiassādirūpāni dassentā kīḷanti. Akkhenāti guḷena. Paṅkacīrenāti paṅkacīraṃ vuccati paṇṇanāḷikā, taṃ dhamantā kīḷanti. Vaṅkakenāti gāmadārakānaṃ kīḷanakena khuddakanaṅgalena. Mokkhacikāyāti samparivattakakīḷāya, ākāse vā daṇḍaṃ gahetvā bhūmiyaṃ vā sīsaṃ ṭhapetvā heṭṭhupariyabhāvena parivattantā kīḷantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Ciṅgulakenāti ciṅgulakaṃ vuccati tālapaṇṇādīhi kataṃ vātappahārena paribbhamanacakkaṃ, tena kīḷanti. Pattāḷhakenāti pattāḷhakaṃ vuccati paṇṇanāḷi, tāya vālikādīni minantā kīḷanti. Rathakenāti khuddakarathena. Dhanukenāti khuddakadhanunā. Akkharikāyāti akkharikā vuccati ākāse vā piṭṭhiyaṃ vā akkharajānanakīḷā, tāya kīḷanti. Manesikāyāti manesikā vuccati manasā cintitajānanakīḷā, tāya kīḷanti. Yathāvajjenāti yathāvajjaṃ vuccati kāṇakuṇikhujjādīnaṃ yaṃ yaṃ vajjaṃ, taṃ taṃ payojetvā dassanakīḷā, tāya kīḷanti. Mukhabherikanti mukhasaddena bherī viya vādanaṃ. Mukhālambaranti mukhānulittabherisaddakaraṇaṃ. Mukhaḍiṇḍimakanti mukhena pahatabherisaddakaraṇaṃ. Mukhavalimakanti oṭṭhamaṃsaṃ jimhaṃ katvā saddakaraṇaṃ. “Mukhatalika”ntipi pāṭho, mukhaṃ parivattetvā dhamanaṃ[M 0.0363]. Mukhabheruḷakanti mukhena bherivādanaṃ. Nāṭakanti abhinayaṃ dassetvā uggaṇhāpanaṃ. “Naṭṭaka”ntipi pāṭho. Lāpanti ukkuṭṭhitakaraṇaṃ. Gītanti gāyanaṃ. Davakammanti [P 2.0412] hassakīḷākaraṇaṃ. Ayaṃ vācasikā khiḍḍāti ayaṃ kīḷā vācāya jātā vacīdvāre uppannā.

They play with dice on a game board, which is called 'khalikā.' They play with a 'ghaṭikā,' which is a game of hitting a short stick with a long stick. They play by dipping their hands in lac, red dye, or flour paste, then pressing them on the ground or walls to make shapes like elephants and horses, saying, 'What will it be?' They play with balls. They play with a 'paṅkacīra,' which is a leaf-tube, by blowing into it. They play with a 'vaṅkaka,' a small plow, a toy of village boys. They play the 'mokkhacikā' game, which involves spinning around—either holding a stick in the air or placing their head on the ground and turning upside down. They play with a 'ciṅgulaka,' a wheel made of palm leaves that spins when blown by the wind. They play with a 'pattāḷhaka,' a leaf-tube, by measuring sand and such. They play with small toy chariots. They play with small toy bows. They play the 'akkharikā' game, which involves recognizing letters in the air or on one's back. They play the 'manesikā' game, which involves guessing what is in another’s mind. They play the 'yathāvajja' game, mimicking the defects of the one-eyed, crippled, hunchbacked, and so on for amusement. They make drum sounds with their mouths. They make drum-like sounds with a smeared mouth. They strike their mouths to make drum sounds. They make sounds by twisting the flesh of their lips. (Another reading is 'mukhatalika,' which means blowing while twisting the mouth.) They play the drum with their mouths. They perform plays, teaching through acting. (Another reading is 'naṭṭaka.') They engage in shouting. They sing. They engage in making laughter and play. This is vocal play—games born from speech, arising through the door of speech.

Kesā ca massu cātiādīsu kesānaṃ kattarikāya ṭhānātirittāni akatvā kattarikāya chedanaṃ [V 0.0334] massūnaṃ dāṭhikaṃ ṭhapetvā kappāsanañca ekatovaṇḍikādimālā ca mūlagandhādigandhā ca chavikaraṇavilepanā ca. Gīvādīsu piḷandhanaābharaṇā ca sīse paṭimuñcanapasādhanapiḷandhanā ca sarīranivāsanavicitravatthā ca saṃvelliyabandhanapasādhanañca. “Parāsana”ntipi pāṭho. Sīsaveṭhanapaṭasaṅkhātaveṭhanañca.

Regarding hair and beard, etc.: cutting the hair with scissors without making it exceed its proper place; trimming the beard, leaving a dāṭhika; garlands like single-strand garlands, etc.; scents like root perfumes, etc.; and skin-beautifying ointments. Also, ornaments worn on the neck, etc.; head ornaments for tying on, adorning, and wearing; various colored clothes for covering the body; and pleated girdles and adornments. 'Parāsana' is also a reading. And head-wrappings known as turbans.

Ucchādanādīsu mātukucchito nikkhantadārakānaṃ sarīragandho dvādasamattavassakāle nassati, tesaṃ sarīragandhaharaṇatthāya gandhacuṇṇādīhi ucchādenti, evarūpaṃ ucchādanaṃ na vaṭṭati. Puññavante pana dārake ūrūsu nipajjāpetvā telena makkhetvā hatthapādaūrunābhiādīnaṃ saṇṭhānasampādanatthaṃ parimaddanti, evarūpaṃ parimaddanaṃ na vaṭṭati.

Regarding rubbing with powders and the like: the bodily odor of children who have emerged from their mother's womb disappears around the age of twelve years. To remove their bodily odor, they rub them with fragrant powders and the like; such rubbing is not permissible. However, for fortunate children, having them lie on one's thighs and anointing them with oil, then massaging their hands, feet, thighs, navel, and so on to accomplish their proper shape—such massaging is not permissible.

Nhāpananti tesaṃyeva dārakānaṃ gandhādīhi nhāpanaṃ. Sambāhananti mahāmallānaṃ viya hatthapāde muggarādīhi paharitvā bāhuvaḍḍhanaṃ. Ādāsanti yaṃkiñci ādāsaṃ pariharituṃ na vaṭṭati. Añjanaṃ alaṅkārañjanameva. Mālāti baddhamālā vā abaddhamālā vā. Vilepananti yaṃkiñci chavirāgakaraṇaṃ. Mukhacuṇṇakaṃ mukhalepananti mukhe kāḷapīḷakādīnaṃ haraṇatthāya mattikākakkaṃ denti. Tena lohite calite sāsapakakkaṃ denti, tena dose khādite tilakakkaṃ denti, tena lohite sannisinne haliddikakkaṃ denti, tena chavivaṇṇe ārūḷhe mukhacuṇṇakena mukhaṃ cuṇṇenti, taṃ sabbaṃ na vaṭṭati.

Bathing refers to bathing those same children with fragrances and the like. Massage means striking the hands and feet with clubs and the like, as with great wrestlers, to increase the strength of their arms. Mirrors: it is not permissible to use any kind of mirror. Eye cosmetic refers only to that for adornment. Garlands: whether tied garlands or loose garlands. Ointments: anything that colors the skin. Face powder and facial applications: they apply clay paste to the face to remove black spots and the like. When the blood is agitated by this, they apply mustard paste; when the ailment is aggravated by this, they apply sesame paste; when the blood is settled by this, they apply turmeric paste; when the skin color has been restored by this, they powder the face with face powder—all this is not permissible.

Hatthabandhādīsu hatthe vicitrasaṅkhakapālādīni bandhitvā vicaranti, taṃ vā aññaṃ vā sabbampi hatthābharaṇaṃ na vaṭṭati. Apare sikhaṃ bandhitvā vicaranti, suvaṇṇacīrakamuttāvaḷiādīhi ca taṃ parikkhipanti, taṃ sabbaṃ na vaṭṭati. Apare catuhatthadaṇḍaṃ vā aññaṃ vā pana alaṅkatadaṇḍakaṃ gahetvā vicaranti[P 2.0413], tathā itthipurisarūpādivicittaṃ bhesajjanāḷikaṃ suparikkhittaṃ vāmapasse olaggenti, apare [M 0.0364] anekacitrakosaṃ atitikhiṇaṃ asiṃ, pañcavaṇṇasuttasibbitaṃ makaradantakādivicittaṃ chattaṃ, suvaṇṇarajatādivicitrā morapiñchādiparikkhittā upāhanā, keci ratanamattāyāmaṃ caturaṅgulavitthataṃ kesantaparicchedaṃ dassetvā meghamukhe vijjulataṃ viya nalāṭe uṇhīsapaṭṭaṃ bandhitvā cūḷāmaṇiṃ dhārenti, cāmaravālabījaniṃ dhārenti, taṃ sabbaṃ na vaṭṭati.

Regarding hand ornaments and the like: they wear various conch shells, skulls, and the like on their hands and wander about; that or any other hand ornament is not permissible. Others tie their top-knots and wander about, encircling them with golden strips, pearl necklaces, and the like—all this is not permissible. Others carry a staff four cubits long or some other decorated staff and wander about. Similarly, they hang a well-adorned medicine tube decorated with figures of men and women on their left side. Others carry a very sharp sword in a sheath of many designs; a parasol stitched with five-colored threads and decorated with designs like crocodile teeth; sandals decorated with gold, silver, and the like, and surrounded by peacock feathers. Some, displaying a division at the hairline the length of a jewel and four fingers' width, tying a turban cloth on their forehead like a flash of lightning on the face of a cloud, wear a crest jewel, and carry a yak-tail whisk—all this is not permissible.

Imassa vā pūtikāyassāti imassa cātumahābhūtamayassa kuṇapasarīrassa. Keḷanāti kīḷāpanā[V 0.0335]. Parikeḷanāti sabbato bhāgena kīḷāpanā. Gedhitatāti abhikaṅkhitatā. Gedhitattanti giddhabhāvo abhikaṅkhitabhāvo. Capalatāti alaṅkārakaraṇaṃ. Cāpalyanti capalabhāvaṃ.

'Of this foul body' means of this body composed of the four great elements, this corpse-like body. 'Keḷanā' means causing to play. 'Parikeḷanā' means causing to play in every way. 'Gedhitatā' means the state of longing. 'Gedhitatta' is the state of greed, the state of longing. 'Capalatā' means making adornments. 'Cāpalya' is the state of being fickle.

Savibhūsantiādīsu vibhūsāya saha savibhūsaṃ. Chavirāgakaraṇasaṅkhātena parivārena saha saparivāraṃ. Paribhaṇḍena saha saparibhaṇḍaṃ. Parikkhārena saha saparikkhāraṃ.

In phrases like 'savibhūsaṃ': 'savibhūsaṃ' means 'together with ornaments.' 'Saparivāraṃ' means 'together with a retinue,' where the retinue is defined as that which causes passion for the skin. 'Saparibhaṇḍaṃ' means 'together with paraphernalia.' 'Saparikkāraṃ' means 'together with requisites.'

162. Āthabbaṇanti āthabbaṇikamantappayogaṃ. Supinanti supinasatthaṃ. Lakkhaṇanti maṇilakkhaṇādiṃ. No vidaheti nappayojeyya. Virutañcāti migādīnaṃ vaṭṭetvā vassitaṃ.

162. 'Āthabbaṇa' refers to the application of Atharvanic mantras. 'Supina' means the science of dreams. 'Lakkhaṇa' refers to the characteristics of gems and the like. 'No vidaheti' means one should not employ them. 'Virutañca' refers to the cries of animals like deer.

Āthabbaṇikāti parūpaghātamantajānanakā. Āthabbaṇaṃ payojentīti āthabbaṇikā kira sattāhaṃ aloṇakaṃ bhuñjitvā dabbe attharitvā pathaviyaṃ sayamānā tapaṃ caritvā sattame divase susānabhūmiṃ sajjetvā sattame pade ṭhatvā hatthaṃ vaṭṭetvā vaṭṭetvā mukhena vijjaṃ parijappanti, atha tesaṃ kammaṃ samijjhati. Evarūpaṃ sandhāya “āthabbaṇaṃ payojentī”ti āha. Tattha payojentīti yuttappayuttā honti. Nagare vā ruddheti nagare samantato rundhitvā āvaritvā gahite. Saṅgāme vā paccupaṭṭhiteti raṇe upagantvā ṭhite. Paccatthikesu paccāmittesūti paṭāṇībhūtesu verīsu. Ītiṃ uppādentīti sarīracalanaṃ kampanaṃ, tassa uppādanaṃ karonti. Upaddavanti kāyapīḷanaṃ karonti. Roganti [P 2.0414] byādhiṃ. Pajjarakanti jaraṃ. Sūlanti uddhumātakaṃ. Visūcikanti vijjhanaṃ. Pakkhandikanti lohitapakkhandikaṃ. Karontīti uppādenti.

'Āthabbaṇikā' refers to those who know mantras for harming others. It is said that those who employ Atharva mantras ('āthabbaṇikā') abstain from salt for seven days, spread out grass, lie down on the ground, practice austerities, prepare a cremation ground on the seventh day, stand on the seventh step, wave their hands around and around, and chant spells with their mouths; then their actions succeed. It is with reference to such a practice that it is said, 'they employ Atharva mantras.' Here, 'payojenti' means they are yoked and engaged. 'When a city is besieged' means when a city has been besieged from all sides, blockaded, and taken. 'When present in battle' means when one has approached and stands in battle. 'Among enemies and adversaries' refers to hostile foes. 'They cause calamities' means they cause the arising of bodily movement and trembling. 'Affliction' means they inflict bodily suffering. 'Disease' means sickness. 'Pajjaraka' means fever. 'Sūla' means flatulence. 'Visūcikā' means piercing pain. 'Pakkhandikā' means bloody flux. 'They do' means they cause to arise.

Supinapāṭhakāti supinabyākaraṇakā. Ādisantīti byākaronti. Yo pubbaṇhasamayaṃ supinaṃ passatītiādīsu accantasaṃyoge upayogavacanaṃ, pubbaṇhasamayeti attho. Evaṃ vipāko hotīti iṭṭhāniṭṭhavasena evarūpo [M 0.0365] vipāko hoti. Avakujja nipannoti adhomukho hutvā nipanno passati. Evaṃ supinapāṭhakā supinaṃ ādisanti.

'Supinapāṭhakā' means dream interpreters. 'Ādisantīti' means they explain. In phrases like 'yo pubbaṇhasamayaṃ supinaṃ passatīti' (who sees a dream in the morning time), the word indicating time is used in an absolute sense; the meaning is 'in the morning time.' 'Evaṃ vipāko hotīti' means a result of this kind, favorable or unfavorable, will occur. 'Avakujja nipannoti' means lying face down when seeing the dream. Thus, dream interpreters explain dreams in this way.

Tañca pana supinaṃ passanto catūhi kāraṇehi passati dhātukkhobhato vā anubhūtapubbato vā devatopasaṃhārato vā pubbanimittato vāti. Tattha pittādīnaṃ khobhakaraṇapaccayayogena khubhitadhātuko dhātukkhobhato supinaṃ passati, passanto ca nānāvidhaṃ supinaṃ passati. Anubhūtapubbato passanto pubbe anubhūtapubbaṃ ārammaṇaṃ passati. Devatopasaṃhārato passanto devatānaṃ ānubhāvena ārammaṇāni passati. Pubbanimittato passanto puññāpuññavasena uppajjitukāmassa atthassa vā anatthassa vā pubbanimittabhūtaṃ supinaṃ passati[V 0.0336]. Tattha yaṃ dhātukkhobhato anubhūtapubbato ca supinaṃ passati, na taṃ saccaṃ hoti. Yaṃ devatopasaṃhārato passati, taṃ saccaṃ vā hoti alikaṃ vā. Kuddhā hi devatā upāyena vināsetukāmā viparītampi katvā dassenti. Yaṃ pana pubbanimittato passati, taṃ ekantasaccameva hoti. Etesaṃ catunnaṃ mūlakāraṇānaṃ saṃsaggabhedatopi supinabhedo hotiyeva. Tañca panetaṃ catubbidhaṃ supinaṃ sekkhaputhujjanāva passanti appahīnavipallāsattā. Asekkhā na passanti pahīnavipallāsattā.

When one sees a dream, one sees it for four reasons: due to a disturbance of the elements, due to past experience, due to divine influence, or due to a portent. Herein, one whose elements are agitated by factors causing agitation of bile and so forth sees a dream due to a disturbance of the elements, and while seeing it, one sees various kinds of dreams. One who sees a dream due to past experience perceives an object previously experienced. One who sees a dream due to divine influence perceives objects through the power of deities. One who sees a dream due to a portent perceives a dream that serves as a portent for some benefit or harm that is about to arise as a result of merit or demerit. Herein, a dream seen due to a disturbance of the elements or past experience is not true.
