That seen due to divine influence may be true or false, for angry deities, wishing to destroy by means of a stratagem, may even show things in reverse. But that seen due to a portent is absolutely true. The variety of dreams certainly arises even from the combination and differentiation of these four root causes. Moreover, this fourfold kind of dream is seen only by trainees and ordinary people, since their perversions are not abandoned. Those beyond training do not see them, since their perversions are abandoned.

Kiṃ panetaṃ passanto sutto passati, udāhu paṭibuddho, udāhu neva sutto na paṭibuddhoti? Kiñcettha – yadi tāva sutto passati, abhidhammavirodho āpajjati. Bhavaṅgacittena hi supati, taṃ rūpanimittādiārammaṇaṃ rāgādisampayuttaṃ vā na hoti, supinaṃ passantassa ca īdisāni cittāni uppajjanti. Atha paṭibuddho passati, vinayavirodho āpajjati. Yañhi paṭibuddho passati, taṃ sabbohārikacittena passati, sabbohārikacittena ca kate vītikkame [P 2.0415] anāpatti nāma natthi, supinaṃ passantena pana kate vītikkame ekantaṃ anāpatti eva. Atha neva sutto na paṭibuddho passati, ko nāma passati. Evañca sati supinassa abhāvova āpajjati, na abhāvo. Kasmā? Yasmā kapiniddāpareto passati. Vuttañhetaṃ – “majjhūpagato, mahārāja, kapiniddāpareto supinaṃ passatī”ti (mi. pa. 5.3.5).

Now, does one see this while asleep, or while awake, or neither asleep nor awake? Herein, if one sees it while asleep, a contradiction of the Abhidhamma arises. For one sleeps with the life-continuum consciousness, and that consciousness does not take a form-object or the like as its object, nor is it associated with lust and so on, whereas such kinds of consciousnesses arise for one who sees a dream. If one sees it while awake, a contradiction of the Vinaya arises. For what one sees while awake is seen with conventional consciousness, and when a transgression is committed with conventional consciousness, there is certainly an offense, but when a transgression is committed by one seeing a dream, there is absolutely no offense. If one sees it neither asleep nor awake, who is it that sees? In that case, the absence of a dream would follow, but it is not absent. Why? Because one sees while overcome by monkey-sleep. For this was said: “Great king, one who is in an intermediate state, overcome by monkey-sleep, sees a dream.”

Kapiniddāparetoti [M 0.0366] makkaṭaniddāya yutto. Yathā hi makkaṭassa niddā lahuparivattā hoti, evaṃ yā niddā punappunaṃ kusalādicittavokiṇṇattā lahuviparivattā. Yassā pavattiyaṃ punappunaṃ bhavaṅgato uttaraṇaṃ hoti, tāya yutto supinaṃ passati. Tenāyaṃ supino kusalopi hoti akusalopi abyākatopi. Tattha supinante cetiyavandanadhammassavanadhammadesanādīni karontassa kusalo, pāṇātipātādīni karontassa akusalo, dvīhi antehi mutto āvajjanatadārammaṇakkhaṇe abyākatoti veditabbo. Svāyaṃ dubbalavatthukattā cetanāya paṭisandhiṃ ākaḍḍhituṃ asamattho, pavatte pana aññehi kusalākusalehi upatthambhito vipākaṃ deti.

'Overcome by monkey-sleep' means endowed with monkey-sleep. Just as a monkey's sleep is light and restless, so too is the sleep that is quickly changing due to being interspersed with wholesome consciousness and so forth. One who is endowed with that sleep, in the occurrence of which there is repeated rising from the life-continuum, sees a dream. Therefore, this dream can be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate. Herein, for one dreaming of doing things such as paying homage to shrines, listening to the Dhamma, or teaching the Dhamma, it is wholesome; for one dreaming of doing things such as killing living beings, it is unwholesome; free from both extremes, it is to be understood as indeterminate in the moments of adverting and registering. This volition, due to its weak basis, is incapable of drawing forth rebirth-linking; but in the course of existence, supported by other wholesome or unwholesome deeds, it yields a result.

Maṇilakkhaṇādīsu evarūpo maṇi pasattho, evarūpo apasattho, sāmino ārogyaissariyādīnaṃ hetu hoti, na hotīti evaṃ vaṇṇasaṇṭhānādivasena maṇiādīnaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ ādisantīti attho. Tattha āvudhalakkhaṇanti ṭhapetvā asiādīni avasesaṃ āvudhaṃ[V 0.0337]. Itthilakkhaṇādīnipi yamhi kule itthipurisādayo vasanti, tassa vuddhihānivaseneva veditabbāni. Ajalakkhaṇādīsu pana “evarūpānaṃ ajādīnaṃ maṃsaṃ khāditabbaṃ, evarūpānaṃ na khāditabba”nti ayampi viseso veditabbo.

In the characteristics of gems and so forth, it is said that a gem of such a kind is praised, while one of such a kind is not praised; it may be the cause of the owner’s health, sovereignty, and so on, or it may not—thus, the characteristics of gems and the like are explained in terms of color, shape, and so on. Herein, 'the characteristics of weapons' refers to the remaining weapons, excluding swords and the like. Similarly, the characteristics of women and others are to be understood simply by whether the family in which the women, men, and so on dwell prospers or declines. In the characteristics of goats and so forth, it is further explained that “the meat of certain types of goats is to be eaten, while others are not”—this distinction also should be understood.

Api cettha godhāya lakkhaṇe cittakammapiḷandhanādīsupi “evarūpāya godhāya sati idaṃ nāma hotī”ti ayampi viseso veditabbo. Kaṇṇikālakkhaṇaṃ piḷandhanakaṇṇikāyapi gehakaṇṇikāyapi vasena veditabbaṃ. Kacchapalakkhaṇampi godhalakkhaṇasadisameva. Migalakkhaṇaṃ sabbasaṅgāhikaṃ sabbacatuppadānaṃ lakkhaṇavasena vuttaṃ. Evaṃ lakkhaṇapāṭhakā lakkhaṇaṃ ādisantīti evaṃ lakkhaṇasatthavācakā lakkhaṇaṃ ādisanti kathenti.

Moreover, in the characteristics of the monitor lizard, even regarding painted ornaments and so forth, this distinction should also be understood: 'when a monitor lizard of such a kind is present, such and such a thing happens.' The characteristics of the 'kaṇṇikā' should be understood in terms of both the ear-ornament and the gable-finial of a house. The characteristics of a tortoise are similar to those of a monitor lizard. The characteristics of beasts is a comprehensive term, spoken in the sense of the characteristics of all quadrupeds. 'Thus, those who recite the characteristics point out the characteristics' means that those who teach the science of characteristics explain and declare them.

Nakkhattānīti [P 2.0416] kattikādīni aṭṭhavīsati nakkhattāni. Iminā nakkhattena gharappaveso kātabboti gehappavesamaṅgalaṃ kātabbaṃ. Makuṭaṃ bandhitabbanti pasādhanamaṅgalaṃ kātabbaṃ. Vāreyyanti “imassa dārakassa asukakulato asukanakkhattena dārikaṃ ānethā”ti āvāhakaraṇañca “imaṃ dārikaṃ asukassa nāma dārakassa asukanakkhattena detha, evaṃ etesaṃ vuḍḍhi bhavissatī”ti vivāhakaraṇañca vatvā vāreyyasaṅkhātaṃ āvāhavivāhamaṅgalaṃ kātabbanti ādisanti. Bījanīhāroti bījānaṃ vappatthāya bahi nīharaṇaṃ. “Niharo”tipi [M 0.0367] pāḷi. Migavākkanti idaṃ sabbasaṅgāhikanāmaṃ, sabbasakuṇacatuppadānaṃ rutañāṇavaseneva vuttaṃ. Migavākkapāṭhakāti sakuntacatuppadānaṃ saddabyākaraṇakā. Migavākkaṃ ādisantīti tesaṃ saddaṃ sutvā byākaronti. Rutanti saddaṃ. “Ruda”nti vā pāḷi. Vassitanti vācaṃ. Gabbhakaraṇīyāti vinassamānassa gabbhassa puna avināsāya osadhadānena gabbhasaṇṭhānakārakā. Gabbho hi vātena pāṇakehi kammunā cāti tīhi kāraṇehi vinassati. Tattha vātena vinassante vātavināsanaṃ sītalaṃ bhesajjaṃ deti. Pāṇakehi vinassante pāṇakānaṃ paṭikammaṃ karoti. Kammunā vinassante pana buddhāpi paṭibāhituṃ na sakkonti. Tasmā na taṃ idha gahitaṃ. Sālākiyanti salākavejjakammaṃ. Sallakattiyanti sallakattavejjakammaṃ. Kāyatikicchanti mūlabhesajjādīni yojetvā kāyatikicchavejjakammaṃ. Bhūtiyanti bhūtavejjakammaṃ. Komārabhaccanti komārakavejjakammaṃ. Kuhāti vimhāpakā. Thaddhāti dārukkhandhaṃ viya thaddhasarīrā. Lapāti paccayapaṭibaddhavacanakā. Siṅgiti maṇḍanapakatikā. Unnaḷāti uggatamānanaḷā. Asamāhitāti upacārappanāsamādhivirahitā.

'Constellations' are the twenty-eight constellations beginning with Kattikā. 'By this constellation, the house-entering should be performed' means the auspicious house-entering rite should be performed. 'A crown should be tied' means the auspicious adornment ceremony should be performed. 'Vāreyya' means that they point out that the auspicious rites of betrothal and marriage, so called, should be performed, saying: 'Bring a girl from such-and-such family for this boy under such-and-such constellation' (this is the act of betrothal), and 'Give this girl to such-and-such boy under such-and-such constellation, so that their prosperity may grow' (this is the act of marriage). 'Bījanīhāra' means taking seeds outside for sowing. 'Nīhāra' is also a reading in the Pāli. 'Migavākka' is an all-encompassing name, spoken in the sense of the knowledge of the cries of all birds and quadrupeds. 'Migavākkapāṭhakā' means interpreters of the sounds of birds and quadrupeds. 'They point out the migavākka' means they interpret after hearing their sounds. 'Ruta' means sound. 'Ruda' is also a reading in the Pāli. 'Vassita' means speech. 'Gabbhakaraṇīyā' are those who cause the fetus to take hold by administering medicine to prevent the destruction of a failing fetus. For a fetus is destroyed by three causes: by wind, by minute creatures, and by kamma. Herein, when it is being destroyed by wind, one gives a cooling medicine that eliminates wind. When it is being destroyed by minute creatures, one applies a counter-measure against the minute creatures. But when it is being destroyed by kamma, even the Buddhas cannot prevent it. Therefore, that case is not included here. 'Sālākiya' is the medical practice using a probe. 'Sallakattiya' is the medical practice of surgery. 'Kāyatikicchā' is the medical practice of treating the body by combining root-medicines and so forth. 'Bhūtiya' is the medical practice of exorcism. 'Komārabhacca' is the medical practice of pediatrics. 'Kuhā' means deceivers. 'Thaddhā' means those with rigid bodies like wooden logs. 'Lapā' means those whose speech is dependent on material gains. 'Siṅgī' means those by nature fond of adornment. 'Unnaḷā' means those with an uplifted banner of pride. 'Asamāhitā' means those devoid of access and absorption concentration.

Na gaṇheyyātiādīsu uddesaggahaṇavasena na gaṇheyya. Sajjhāyavasena na uggaṇheyya. Citte [V 0.0338] ṭhapanavasena na dhāreyya. Samīpaṃ katvā ṭhapanavasena na upadhāreyya. Upaparikkhāvasena na upalakkheyya. Aññesaṃ vācanavasena nappayojeyya.

Regarding 'One should not take up,' and so on: one should not take up by way of receiving instruction. One should not learn by way of recitation. One should not bear in mind by way of placing it in the mind. One should not keep near by way of placing it nearby. One should not examine by way of investigation. One should not employ by way of recitation for others.

163. Pesuṇiyanti [P 2.0417] pesuññaṃ. Sesaniddeso ca vuttatthoyeva.

163. `Pesuṇiya` means slander. The remaining explanation is as has been stated.

164. Kayavikkayeti pañcahi sahadhammikehi saddhiṃ vañcanavasena vā udayapatthanāvasena vā na tiṭṭheyya. Upavādaṃ bhikkhu na kareyyāti upavādakare kilese anibbattento attani parehi samaṇabrāhmaṇehi upavādaṃ na janeyya. Gāme ca nābhisajjeyyāti gāme ca gihisaṃsaggādīhi nābhisajjeyya. Lābhakamyā janaṃ na lapayeyyāti lābhakāmatāya janaṃ na lapayeyya.

164. Regarding buying and selling: one should not engage in it with the five fellow practitioners, either by way of deceit or with the desire for profit. Regarding 'A bhikkhu should not cause reproach': by not generating the defilements that cause reproach, one should not give rise to reproach for oneself from other ascetics and brahmins. Regarding 'And one should not be attached to a village': one should not be attached to a village through association with householders and so on. Regarding 'Out of desire for gain, one should not talk to people': one should not talk to people out of a desire for gain.

Ye kayavikkayā vinaye paṭikkhittāti ye dānapaṭiggahaṇavasena kayavikkayasikkhāpade (pārā. 593 ādayo) na vaṭṭatīti paṭikkhittā, idhādhippetaṃ kayavikkayaṃ dassetuṃ “pañcannaṃ saddhiṃ pattaṃ vā cīvaraṃ vā”tiādimāha. Tattha pañcannaṃ saddhinti [M 0.0368] pañcahi sahadhammikehi saha. Pañca sahadhammikā nāma bhikkhubhikkhunīsikkhamānasāmaṇerasāmaṇeriyo. Vañcaniyaṃ vāti paṭirūpakaṃ dassetvā vañcaniyaṃ vā. Udayaṃ vā patthayantoti vuḍḍhiṃ patthento vā. Parivattetīti parivattanaṃ karoti.

Those transactions of buying and selling that are prohibited in the Vinaya are those prohibited in the training rule on buying and selling (Pārājika 593, etc.) as not being permissible by way of giving and receiving. To show the kind of buying and selling intended here, it is said, 'with five, a bowl or a robe,' and so on. Therein, 'with five' means with five fellow practitioners. The five fellow practitioners are: a bhikkhu, a bhikkhunī, a female probationer, a male novice, and a female novice. 'Or deceitfully' means deceiving by showing a counterfeit. 'Or desiring profit' means desiring an increase. 'Exchanges' means one makes an exchange.

Iddhimantoti ijjhanapabhāvavanto. Dibbacakkhukāti dibbasadisañāṇacakkhukā. Atha vā dibbavihārasannissayena laddhañāṇacakkhukā. Paracittavidunoti attano cittena paresaṃ cittajānanakā. Te dūratopi passantīti ekayojanatopi yojanasatatopi yojanasahassatopi yojanasatasahassatopi cakkavāḷatopi dvetīṇicattāripañcadasavīsaticattālīsasahassatopi tato atirekatopi cakkavāḷato passanti dakkhanti. Āsannāpi na dissantīti samīpe ṭhitāpi nisinnāpi na paññāyanti. Cetasāpi cittaṃ pajānantīti attano cittenāpi paresaṃ cittaṃ pajānanti. Devatāpi kho santi iddhimantiniyoti devatāpi evaṃ saṃvijjanti ijjhanapabhāvavantiniyo. Paracittaviduniyoti paresaṃ cittaṃ jānantiyo. Oḷārikehi vā kilesehīti kāyaduccaritādikehi vā upatāpehi. Majjhimehi vāti kāmavitakkādikehi vā. Sukhumehi vāti ñātivitakkādikehi vā. Kāyaduccaritādayo kammapathavasena[P 2.0418], kāmavitakkādayo vaṭṭamūlakakilesavasena veditabbā.

'Possessing psychic power' means possessing the power of accomplishment. 'With the divine eye' means possessing a knowledge-eye similar to the divine. Or, it means possessing a knowledge-eye attained through reliance on a divine abiding. 'Knowers of others' minds' means those who know the minds of others with their own mind. 'They see even from afar' means they see and perceive from one yojana, a hundred yojanas, a thousand yojanas, a hundred thousand yojanas, a world-system, or from two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, forty thousand, or even more world-systems. 'Even when near, they are not seen' means even when standing or sitting nearby, they are not discerned. 'They know mind with their own mind' means they know the minds of others with their own mind. 'There are also deities possessing psychic power' means there are indeed deities who exist, possessing the power of accomplishment. 'Knowers of others' minds' means those who know the minds of others. 'With coarse defilements' means with torments such as bodily misconduct, etc. 'With middling' means with thoughts of sensual pleasure, etc. 'With subtle' means with thoughts about relatives, etc. Bodily misconduct and so on should be understood by way of the paths of action; thoughts of sensual pleasure and so on should be understood by way of the root defilements of the round of existence.

Ñātivitakkādīsu [V 0.0339] “mayhaṃ ñātayo sukhajīvino sampattiyuttā”ti evaṃ pañcakāmaguṇasannissitena gehasannissitapemena ñātake ārabbha uppannavitakko ñātivitakko. “Mayhaṃ ñātayo khayaṃ gatā vayaṃ gatā saddhā pasannā”ti evaṃ pavatto pana ñātivitakko nāma na hoti.

Regarding thoughts about relatives and so on: a thought that arises concerning relatives, such as, 'May my relatives live happily and be endowed with prosperity,' based on affection rooted in the household and connected with the five strands of sensual pleasure, is a thought about relatives. However, a thought that proceeds thus, 'My relatives have gone to decay and old age; they have faith and are devout,' is not called a thought about relatives.

“Amhākaṃ janapado subhikkho sampannasasso”ti tuṭṭhamānasassa gehassitapemavasena uppannavitakko janapadavitakko. “Amhākaṃ janapade manussā saddhā pasannā khayaṃ gatā vayaṃ gatā”ti evaṃ pavatto pana janapadavitakko nāma na hoti.

A thought that arises for one with a pleased mind, by way of affection based on the household, thinking, 'Our country is prosperous, abundant in crops,' is a thought about one's country. However, a thought that proceeds thus, 'In our country, people have faith, are devout, and have gone to decay and old age,' is not called a thought about one's country.

Amarattāya vitakko, amaro vā vitakkoti amaravitakko. Tattha ukkuṭikappadhānādīhi dukkhe nijiṇṇe samparāye attā sukhī hoti. Amaroti [M 0.0369] dukkarakārikaṃ karontassa tāya dukkarakārikāya paṭisaṃyutto vitakko amarattāya vitakko nāma. Diṭṭhigatiko pana “sassataṃ vadesī”tiādīni puṭṭho “evantipi me no, tathātipi me no, aññathātipi me no, notipi me no, no notipi me no”ti vikkhepaṃ āpajjati, tassa so diṭṭhigatapaṭisaṃyutto vitakko, yathā amaro nāma maccho udake gahetvā māretuṃ na sakkā, ito cito ca dhāvati gāhaṃ na gacchati, evameva ekasmiṃ pakkhe asaṇṭhahanato na maratīti amaro nāma hoti, taṃ duvidhampi ekato katvā “amaravitakko”ti vuttaṃ.

'A thought for immortality, or an immortal thought' is a thought of immortality. In this regard, when suffering is overcome through exertions such as the squatting posture, the self becomes happy in the future life. The thought connected with one performing such a difficult practice is called 'a thought for immortality.' On the other hand, one holding speculative views, when asked such things as, 'Do you say it is eternal?', resorts to equivocation: 'It is not so for me, it is not thus for me, it is not otherwise for me, it is not not so for me, nor is it not not so for me.' That thought of his, connected with speculative views, is like a fish called 'immortal.' Just as a fish called 'immortal' cannot be caught and killed in the water, as it darts here and there and evades capture, so too, because one does not settle on a single position, one is called 'immortal.' Combining both of these, it is called the 'thought of immortality.'

Parānuddayatāpaṭisaññuttoti anuddayatāpaṭirūpakena gehassitapemena paṭisaṃyutto. Upaṭṭhākesu nandakesu socantesu ca tehi saddhiṃ diguṇaṃ nandati diguṇaṃ socati, tesu sukhitesu diguṇaṃ sukhito hoti, dukkhitesu diguṇaṃ dukkhito hoti. Uppannesu kiccakaraṇīyesu attanā voyogaṃ āpajjati. Tāni tāni kiccāni sādhento paññattiṃ vītikkamati, sallekhaṃ kopeti. Yo tasmiṃ saṃsaṭṭhavihāre tasmiṃ vā voyogāpajjane gehassito vitakko, ayaṃ parānuddayatāpaṭisaññutto vitakko nāma.

'Connected with compassion for others' means connected with a household-based affection that is a counterfeit of compassion. When one's attendants and supporters rejoice, one rejoices doubly with them; when they grieve, one grieves doubly. When they are happy, one is doubly happy; when they are afflicted, one is doubly afflicted. When duties and obligations arise, one personally undertakes the effort. While accomplishing these various duties, one transgresses the regulations and damages the practice of effacement. Whatever household-based thought arises in that living in association or in that undertaking of effort, this is called the 'thought connected with compassion for others.'

Lābhasakkārasilokapaṭisaññuttoti cīvarādilābhena ceva sakkārena ca kittisaddena ca saddhiṃ ārammaṇakaraṇavasena paṭisaññutto. Anavaññattipaṭisaññuttoti [P 2.0419] “aho vata maṃ pare na avajāneyyuṃ, na sodhetvā visodhetvā katheyyu”nti evaṃ anavaññātabhāvapatthanāya saddhiṃ uppajjanakavitakko[V 0.0340]. So tasmiṃ “mā maṃ pare avajāniṃsū”ti uppanne vitakke pañcakāmaguṇasaṅkhātagehanissito hutvā uppannavitakko anavaññattipaṭisaññutto vitakko.

'Connected with gain, honor, and fame' means connected by way of making an object of the gain of robes and so on, of honor, and of the sound of praise. 'Connected with non-contempt' is a thought that arises together with the desire for a state of not being despised, thus: 'Oh, may others not despise me, may they not speak of me after scrutinizing and thoroughly scrutinizing!' That thought, which arises based on the household—that is, the five strands of sensual pleasure—when the thought 'May others not despise me!' has arisen, is the thought connected with non-contempt.

Tatra tatra sajjatīti tesu tesu ārammaṇesu laggati. Tatra tatra gaṇhātīti vuttappakāraṃ ārammaṇaṃ pavisati. Bajjhatīti tehi tehi ārammaṇehi saddhiṃ bajjhati ekībhavati. Anayabyasananti tattha tattha avaḍḍhiṃ vināsaṃ. Āpajjatīti pāpuṇāti.

'He clings here and there' means he is attached to those various objects. 'He grasps here and there' means he enters into an object of the kind described. 'He is bound' means he is bound together with those various objects, he becomes one with them. 'Ruin and disaster' means decline and destruction in those various places. 'He incurs' means he attains.

Āmisacakkhukassāti [M 0.0370] cīvarādiāmisalolassa. Lokadhammagarukassāti lokuttaradhammaṃ muñcitvā rūpādilokadhammameva garuṃ katvā carantassa. Ālapanāti vihāraṃ āgatamanusse disvā “kimatthāya bhonto āgatā, kiṃ bhikkhū nimantetuṃ, yadi evaṃ gacchatha, ahaṃ pacchato bhikkhū gahetvā āgacchāmī”ti evaṃ āditova lapanā. Atha vā attānaṃ upanetvā “ahaṃ tisso, mayi rājā pasanno, mayi asuko ca asuko ca rājamahāmatto pasanno”ti evaṃ attupanāyikā lapanāti ālapanā. Lapanāti puṭṭhassa sato vuttappakārameva lapanaṃ.

'Of one with an eye for material things' means of one who is greedy for material things such as robes. 'Of one who esteems worldly things' means of one who, having abandoned the supramundane Dhamma, fares along esteeming only worldly things such as forms. 'Accosting' means seeing people who have come to the monastery and speaking from the outset, 'For what purpose have you gentlemen come? To invite the bhikkhus? If so, you go, I will bring the bhikkhus and come behind.' Or else, it is self-referential talk, bringing oneself forward by saying, 'I am Tissa, the king is pleased with me, such-and-such a royal minister is pleased with me.' 'Talking' means, when one is asked, talking in the very manner described.

Sallapanāti gahapatikānaṃ ukkaṇṭhane bhītassa okāsaṃ datvā suṭṭhu lapanā. Ullapanāti “mahākuṭumbiko mahānāviko mahādānapatī”ti evaṃ uddhaṃ katvā lapanā. Samullapanāti sabbato bhāgena uddhaṃ katvā lapanā. Unnahanāti “upāsakā pubbe īdise kāle navadānaṃ detha, idāni kiṃ na dethā”ti evaṃ yāva “dassāma bhante, okāsaṃ na labhāmā”tiādīni vadanti, tāva uddhaṃ uddhaṃ nahanā, veṭhanāti vuttaṃ hoti. Atha vā ucchuhatthaṃ disvā “kuto ābhataṃ upāsakā”ti pucchati. Ucchukhettato bhanteti. Kiṃ tattha ucchu madhuranti. Khāditvā bhante jānitabbanti. Na upāsakā “bhikkhussa ucchuṃ dethā”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭatīti yā evarūpā nibbeṭhentassapi niveṭhanakakathā, sā unnahanā. Sabbato bhāgena punappunaṃ unnahanā samunnahanā. Ukkācanāti [P 2.0420] “etaṃ kulaṃ maṃyeva jānāti, sace ettha deyyadhammo uppajjati, mayhaṃyeva detī”ti evaṃ ukkhipitvā kācanā ukkācanā, uddīpanāti vuttaṃ hoti. Sabbato bhāgena pana punappunaṃ ukkācanā samukkācanā. Anuppiyabhāṇitāti paccayavasena punappunaṃ piyavacanabhaṇanā. Saṇhavācatāti muduvacanatā. Sakhilavācatāti mandapamāṇayuttavacanatā sithilavacanatā vā. Sithilavācatāti allīyavacanatā. Apharusavācatāti madhuravacanatā.

"Ingratiating talk" (sallapanā) means giving an opportunity to householders who are anxious and afraid, and then speaking well with them. "Flattery" (ullapanā) means praising them by saying, "You are a great householder, a great ship-owner, a great donor," and so on. "Excessive flattery" (samullapanā) means praising them in every possible way. "Coaxing" (unnahanā) means urging them by saying, "In the past, lay followers gave new gifts at such times; why don’t you give now?" and so on, until they say, "We will give, venerable sir, but we haven’t found the opportunity yet," and similar things—this is called pressing and urging. Alternatively, seeing a lay follower with sugarcane in hand, one asks, "Where did you get this, lay follower?" They reply, "From the sugarcane field, venerable sir." Then one asks, "Is the sugarcane there sweet?" They say, "You can know by tasting it, venerable sir." Such talk, which is like saying, 'It is not proper for a lay follower to have to be told, "Give the monk some sugarcane,"' and which winds around even one who tries to escape, is coaxing (unnahanā). Repeatedly pressing in every possible way is called "excessive coaxing" (samunnahanā). "Boasting" (ukkācanā) means saying, "This family knows only me; if anything worthy of offering arises here, they give it only to me," and so on—this is called inciting. Repeatedly inciting in every possible way is called "excessive inciting" (samukkācanā). "Speaking ingratiatingly" (anuppiyabhāṇitā) means repeatedly speaking pleasing words because of gain. "Gentle speech" (saṇhavācatā) means soft-spokenness. "Friendly speech" (sakhilavācatā) means measured speech, or loose speech. "Loose speech" (sithilavācatā) means clinging speech. "Unharsh speech" (apharusavācatā) means sweet speech.

Purāṇaṃ mātāpettikanti pure uppannaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ santakaṃ. Antarahitanti paṭicchannaṃ tirobhūtaṃ[V 0.0341]. Ñāyāmīti pākaṭo homi. Asukassa kulūpakoti asukassa amaccassa kulapayirupāsako. Asukāyāti asukāya upāsikāya. Maṃ ujjhitvāti maṃ vissajjitvā.

"Purāṇaṃ mātāpettikaṃ" means what was previously possessed by parents. "Antarahitaṃ" means covered, disappeared. "Ñāyāmi" means I become manifest. "Asukassa kulūpako" means a family attendant of such-and-such a minister. "Asukāya" means of such-and-such a female lay follower. "Maṃ ujjhitvā" means having abandoned me.

165. Payuttanti [M 0.0371] cīvarādīhi sampayuttaṃ, tadatthaṃ vā payojitaṃ. Imissā gāthāya niddeso sabbo heṭṭhā vuttanayova.

165. "Payuttaṃ" means connected with robes and so on, or employed for that purpose. The explanation of this verse is entirely in accordance with the method stated previously.

166. Mosavajje na niyyethāti musāvāde na niyyetha.Jīvitenāti jīvikāya.

166. "Mosavajje na niyyetha" means one should not persist in false speech. "Jīvitena" means by livelihood.

Saṭhoti asantaguṇadīpanato na sammā bhāsitā. Sabbato bhāgena saṭho parisaṭho. Yaṃ tatthāti yaṃ tasmiṃ puggale. Saṭhanti asantaguṇadīpanaṃ kerāṭiyaṃ. Saṭhatāti saṭhākāro. Sāṭheyyanti saṭhabhāvo. Kakkaratāti padumanāḷassa viya aparāmasanakkhamo pharusabhāvo. Kakkariyantipi tasseva vevacanaṃ. Parikkhattatā pārikkhattiyanti padadvayena nikhaṇitvā ṭhapitaṃ viya daḷhakerāṭiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Keci pana “kakkaratāti sambhāvayitvā vacanaṃ. Kakkariyanti sambhāvayitvā vacanabhāvo. Parikkhattatāti alaṅkaraṇākāro. Pārikkhattiyanti alaṅkaraṇabhāvo”ti atthaṃ vaṇṇayanti. Idaṃ vuccatīti idaṃ attano avijjamānaguṇappakāsanalakkhaṇaṃ sāṭheyyaṃ nāma vuccati. Yena samannāgatassa puggalassa kucchiṃ vā piṭṭhiṃ vā jānituṃ na sakkā.

"Saṭho" means one who does not speak properly, due to displaying non-existent virtues. "Parisaṭho" means one who is deceitful in every way. "Yaṃ tattha" means what is in that person. "Saṭhaṃ" means displaying non-existent virtues, deceit. "Saṭhatā" means a deceitful manner. "Sāṭheyyaṃ" means the state of deceit. "Kakkaratā" means harshness, like the rough nature of a lotus stalk that cannot be handled. "Kakkariyanti" is a synonym for the same. By the two words "Parikkhattatā pārikkhattiyaṃ," firmly established deceit is meant, like something buried and fixed in place. Some, however, explain the meaning thus: "Kakkaratā" means speaking presumptuously. "Kakkariyanti" means the state of speaking presumptuously. "Parikkhattatā" means a manner of adornment. "Pārikkhattiyaṃ" means the state of adornment. This is called "sāṭheyyaṃ," which is characterized by displaying one's own non-existent virtues. One cannot know the belly or back of a person endowed with this.

“Vāmena [P 2.0421] sūkaro hoti, dakkhiṇena ajāmigo;

Sarena nelako hoti, visāṇena jaraggavo”ti. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.296; vibha. aṭṭha. 894) –

“On the left, it is a pig; on the right, a goat-deer. By its sound, it is a mongoose; by its horn, an old ox.”

Evaṃ vuttayakkhasūkarasadiso hoti. Atimaññatīti atikkamitvā maññati.

Thus, he is like the aforementioned yaksha and boar. ‘Atimaññati’ means he thinks having surpassed.

Kiṃ panāyaṃ bahulājīvoti ayaṃ pana puggalo ko nāma bahulājīvako. Sabbaṃ saṃbhakkhetīti laddhaṃ sabbaṃ khādati. Appapuññoti mandapuñño. Appesakkhoti parivāravirahito. Paññāsampannoti sampannapañño paripuṇṇapañño. Pañhaṃ vissajjetīti pañhaṃ katheti byākaroti.

‘Kiṃ panāyaṃ bahulājīvo’ means what kind of person is this one with a varied livelihood? ‘Sabbaṃ saṃbhakkheti’ means he eats everything he obtains. ‘Appapuñño’ means of little merit. ‘Appesakkho’ means lacking followers. ‘Paññāsampanno’ means endowed with wisdom, of complete wisdom. ‘Pañhaṃ vissajjeti’ means he explains or answers a question.

167. Sutvā rusito bahuṃ vācaṃ, samaṇānaṃ vā puthujanānanti rusito ghaṭṭito parehi tesaṃ [V 0.0342] samaṇānaṃ vā khattiyādibhedānaṃ vā aññesaṃ puthujanānaṃ bahumpi aniṭṭhaṃ vācaṃ sutvā. Na paṭivajjāti na paṭivadeyya. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Na hi santo paṭiseniṃ karonti.

167. ‘Sutvā rusito bahuṃ vācaṃ, samaṇānaṃ vā puthujanānaṃ’ means having heard much unpleasant speech from ascetics or from other ordinary people of various kinds, such as nobles, and being angered and provoked by it. ‘Na paṭivajjati’ means he should not retaliate in speech. Why? For the good do not retaliate.

Kakkhaḷenāti [M 0.0372] dāruṇena. Santoti nibbutakilesā. Paṭiseninti paṭisattuṃ. Paṭimallanti paṭiyodhaṃ. Paṭikaṇṭakanti paṭiveriṃ. Paṭipakkhanti kilesapaṭipakkhaṃ, kilesavasena saṅgaṃ na karontīti attho.

‘Kakkhaḷena’ means harshly. ‘Santo’ means those whose defilements are extinguished. ‘Paṭiseniṃ’ means a counter-enemy. ‘Paṭimallaṃ’ means a counter-fighter. ‘Paṭikaṇṭakaṃ’ means a counter-foe. ‘Paṭipakkhaṃ’ means the opposite of defilements; the meaning is that they do not form an attachment by way of defilements.

168. Etañca dhammamaññāyāti sabbametaṃ yathāvuttaṃ dhammaṃ ñatvā. Vicinanti vicinanto. Santīti nibbutiṃ ñatvāti nibbutiṃ rāgādīnaṃ santīti ñatvā.

168. ‘Etañca dhammamaññāya’ means having known all this Dhamma as stated. ‘Vicinanti’ means discriminating. ‘Santīti nibbutiṃ ñatvā’ means having known peace, that is, having known Nibbāna as the stilling of greed and so on.

Samañcāti kāyasucaritādiṃ. Visamañcāti kāyaduccaritādiṃ. Pathañcāti dasakusalakammapathaṃ. Vipathañcāti dasaakusalakammapathaṃ. Sāvajjañcāti akusalañca. Anavajjañcāti kusalañca. Hīnapaṇītakaṇhasukkaviññūgarahitaviññūpasatthanti idampi kusalākusalameva. Tattha kāyasucaritādi samakaraṇato samaṃ. Kāyaduccaritādi visamakaraṇato visamaṃ. Dasakusalakammapathā sugatigamanapathattā pathaṃ. Dasaakusalakammapathā sugatigamanapaṭipakkhattā apāyagamanapathattā vipathaṃ. Akusalaṃ sadosattā sāvajjaṃ. Kusalaṃ niddosattā anavajjaṃ. Tathā mohena vā dosamohena vā lobhamohena vā sampayuttattā hīnaṃ[P 2.0422]. Alobhaadosaamohasampayuttattā paṇītaṃ. Kaṇhavipākattā kaṇhaṃ. Sukkavipākattā sukkaṃ. Buddhādīhi viññūhi garahitattā viññūgarahitaṃ. Tehi eva thomitattā viññūpasatthanti ñātabbaṃ.

‘Samañca’ means good bodily conduct and so on. ‘Visamañca’ means bad bodily conduct and so on. ‘Pathañca’ means the ten wholesome courses of action. ‘Vipathañca’ means the ten unwholesome courses of action. ‘Sāvajjañca’ means the unwholesome. ‘Anavajjañca’ means the wholesome. ‘Hīnapaṇītakaṇhasukkaviññūgarahitaviññūpasattha’—this too is just the wholesome and unwholesome. Herein, good bodily conduct and so on are straight because they make things straight. Bad bodily conduct and so on are crooked because they make things crooked. The ten wholesome courses of action are a path because they are a path to a good destination. The ten unwholesome courses of action are a wrong path because they oppose going to a good destination and are a path to a woeful state. The unwholesome is blameworthy because it is faulty. The wholesome is blameless because it is faultless. Similarly, what is associated with delusion, or hatred and delusion, or greed and delusion is inferior. What is associated with non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion is superior. What has dark results is dark. What has bright results is bright. What is censured by the wise, like the Buddhas, is censured by the wise. What is praised by them is praised by the wise—this should be understood.

169. Kiṃ kāraṇā nappamajjeyya iti ce – abhibhū hi soti gāthā. Tattha abhibhūti rūpādīnaṃ abhibhavitā. Anabhibhūtoti tehi anabhibhūto. Sakkhidhammamanītihamaddasīti paccakkhameva anītihaṃ dhammaṃ addakkhi. Sadā namassa’manusikkheti sadā namassanto tisso sikkhāyo sikkheyya.

169. If it is asked, ‘For what reason should one not be heedless?’ — the verse ‘For he is a conqueror’ explains. Herein, ‘abhibhū’ means one who conquers forms and so on. ‘Anabhibhūto’ means not conquered by them. ‘Sakkhidhammamanītihamaddasī’ means he has seen the Dhamma directly, not from hearsay. ‘Sadā namassa’manusikkhe’ means always revering, one should train in the three trainings.

Kehici kilesehīti kehici rāgādiupatāpakarehi kilesehi. Abhibhosi neti te kilese abhibhavi. Sesaṃ sabbattha pākaṭameva.

‘Kehici kilesehi’ means by some defilements, that is, by some defilements such as greed, which cause affliction. ‘Abhibhosi ne’ means he conquered those defilements. The rest is clear everywhere.

Kevalaṃ pana ettha “cakkhūhi neva lolo”tiādīhi indriyasaṃvaro, “annānamatho pānāna”ntiādīhi sannidhipaṭikkhepamukhena paccayapaṭisevanasīlaṃ, methunamosavajjapesuṇiyādīhi pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlaṃ[V 0.0343], “āthabbaṇaṃ supinaṃ lakkhaṇa”ntiādīhi ājīvapārisuddhisīlaṃ, “jhāyī na pādalolassā”ti iminā samādhi, “vicinaṃ bhikkhū”ti iminā paññā, “sadā sato [M 0.0373] sikkhe”ti iminā puna saṅkhepato tissopi sikkhā, “atha āsanesu sayanesu, appasaddesu bhikkhu vihareyya, niddaṃ na bahulīkareyyā”tiādīhi sīlasamādhipaññānaṃ upakārānupakārasaṅgaṇhanavinodanāni vuttānīti. Evaṃ bhagavā nimmitassa paripuṇṇapaṭipadaṃ vatvā arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi, desanāpariyosāne purābhedasutte (mahāni. 83 ādayo) vuttasadisoyevābhisamayo ahosīti.

Here, indeed, the restraint of the senses is indicated by such phrases as ‘not greedy with the eyes’; the virtue of using the requisites, by way of rejecting accumulation, by such phrases as ‘of food and drink’; the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha by abstaining from sexual intercourse, falsehood, malicious speech, and so on; the virtue of purity of livelihood by avoiding such practices as spells, dreams, and omens; concentration by ‘the meditating one is not restless with his feet’; wisdom by ‘a monk investigating’; and again, in brief, all three trainings by ‘always mindful, he should train.’ Furthermore, by such phrases as ‘then a monk should dwell in seats and beds, in quiet places, and should not indulge in much sleep,’ the gathering of supporting factors and the dispelling of opposing factors for virtue, concentration, and wisdom are stated. Thus, the Blessed One, having explained the complete practice for the created one, concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of arahantship. At the end of the teaching, a realization occurred just like the one described in the Purābheda Sutta (Mahāniddesa 83ff.).

Saddhammappajjotikāya mahāniddesaṭṭhakathāya

In the Saddhammappajjotikā, the Commentary on the Mahāniddesa.

Tuvaṭakasuttaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Tuvaṭaka Sutta Niddesa is finished.

15. Attadaṇḍasuttaniddesavaṇṇanā

15. The Explanation of the Exposition of the Attadaṇḍa Sutta

170. Pannarasame [V 0.0344][P 2.0423] attadaṇḍasuttaniddese attadaṇḍā bhayaṃ jātanti paṭhamagāthāya attho – yaṃ lokassa diṭṭhadhammikaṃ vā samparāyikaṃ vā bhayaṃ jātaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ attadaṇḍā bhayaṃ jātaṃ attano duccaritakāraṇā jātaṃ, evaṃ santepi janaṃ passatha medhagaṃ, imaṃ sākiyādijanaṃ passatha aññamaññaṃ medhagaṃ hiṃsakaṃ bādhakanti. Evaṃ taṃ paṭiviruddhaṃ vippaṭipannaṃ janaṃ paribhāsitvā attano sammā paṭipattidassanena tassa saṃvegaṃ janetuṃ āha “saṃvegaṃ kittayissāmi, yathā saṃvijitaṃ mayā”ti. Pubbe bodhisatteneva satāti adhippāyo.

170. In the fifteenth chapter, the Exposition of the Attadaṇḍa Sutta, the meaning of the first verse, 'Fear is born from taking up the rod,' is as follows: Whatever fear is born in the world, whether pertaining to this life or the next, all that fear is born from taking up the rod, born from the cause of one's own misconduct. Even so, behold the people engaged in quarrels; behold these people, the Sakyans and others, quarreling with, harming, and oppressing one another. Thus, having rebuked those hostile and wrongly practicing people, in order to inspire a sense of spiritual urgency in them by showing his own right practice, he said, 'I will declare the spiritual urgency, as it was felt by me.' The intended meaning is: when he was formerly the Bodhisatta.

Tayoti gaṇanaparicchedo. Daṇḍāti duccaritā. Kāyadaṇḍoti kāyaduccaritaṃ. Vacīdaṇḍādīsupi eseva nayo. Tividhaṃ kāyaduccaritanti pāṇātipātādikāyato pavattaṃ duṭṭhuṃ caritaṃ, kilesapūtikattā vā duṭṭhu caritanti laddhanāmaṃ tividhaṃ duccaritaṃ kāyaduccaritaṃ. Catubbidhanti musāvādādicatubbidhaṃ. Tividhanti abhijjhāditividhaṃ. Diṭṭhadhammikanti diṭṭheva dhamme imasmiṃyeva attabhāve paṭisaṃvedanīyaṃ. Samparāyikanti anāgate attabhāve paṭisaṃvedanīyaṃ. Āgucārīti pāpakārī aparādhakārī. Tamenaṃ rājā paribhāsatīti pāpakāriṃ rājā paribhāsati, bhayaṃ uppādeti. Dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedetīti kāyikaṃ dukkhaṃ cetasikaṃ domanassaṃ vindati. Etaṃ bhayaṃ dukkhaṃ domanassanti evarūpaṃ bhayañca dukkhañca domanassañca. Kuto tassāti [M 0.0374] tassa corassa kuto uppannaṃ. Attadaṇḍato jātanti attanā kataduccaritato uppannaṃ.

'Three' is a numerical classification. 'Rods' means misconducts. 'Bodily rod' means bodily misconduct. The same method applies to 'verbal rod' and the rest. Threefold bodily misconduct: 'misconduct' (duccarita) is bad conduct that proceeds from the body, such as the destruction of life, etc., or it is so-called because it is putrid with defilements; thus, the threefold misconduct is bodily misconduct. 'Fourfold' refers to the four types, such as false speech. 'Threefold' refers to the three types, such as covetousness. 'Pertaining to the present life' means to be experienced in this very life, in this very existence. 'Pertaining to the future' means to be experienced in a future existence. 'A wrongdoer' means an evil-doer, an offender. 'The king rebukes him' means: the king rebukes the wrongdoer, instilling fear. 'He experiences pain and displeasure' means: he experiences bodily pain and mental displeasure. 'This fear, pain, and displeasure' means: such fear, pain, and displeasure. 'Whence for him?' means: from where has it arisen for that thief? 'Born from taking up the rod' means: arisen from the misconduct committed by himself.

Antamasoti heṭṭhimato. Savacanīyampi karoti “na [P 2.0424] te labbhā ito pakkamitu”nti ito imamhā gāmādinā gantuṃ na labbhā. Na sakkā bahi nikkhamitunti palibodhaṃ saṅgaṃ karoti. Dhanajānipaccayāpīti dhanaparihānikāraṇāpi. Rājā tassa vividhā kammakāraṇā kārāpeti. Kasāhipi tāḷetīti kasādaṇḍakehi potheti. Vettehipi tāḷetīti sakaṇṭakavettalatāhi potheti. Aḍḍhadaṇḍakehītiādayo heṭṭhā vuttanayāyeva. Sunakhehipi khādāpetīti [V 0.0345] katipayāni divasāni āhāre adatvā chātasunakhehi khādāpeti. Te muhuttena aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikameva karoti. Sūle uttāsetīti sūlaṃ āropeti. Rājā imesaṃ catunnaṃ daṇḍānaṃ issaroti imāsaṃ catunnaṃ āṇānaṃ kātuṃ rājā samattho.

'At the very least' means 'from the lowest'. He also makes him subject to his command: 'You are not allowed to depart from here'—meaning, it is not permitted to go from this village or such. 'It is not possible to go outside'—he creates an obstruction, an impediment. 'Even because of loss of wealth'—meaning, even for the reason of the decline of wealth. The king has various punishments inflicted upon him. 'He beats him with whips'—meaning, he strikes him with whip-sticks. 'He beats him with canes'—meaning, he strikes him with thorny cane-creepers. The rest, like 'with half-sticks,' follows the same method as explained previously. 'He even has him devoured by dogs'—meaning, after depriving them of food for several days, he has him devoured by hungry dogs. In a moment, they reduce him to a mere chain of bones. 'He impales him on a stake'—meaning, he raises him onto a stake. 'The king is the lord of these four punishments'—meaning, the king is capable of enacting these four commands.

Sakena kammenāti sayaṃkatena kammena. Tamenaṃ nirayapālāti ettha ekacce therā “nirayapālā nāma natthi, yantarūpaṃ viya kammameva kāraṇaṃ kāretī”ti vadanti. Tesaṃ taṃ “atthi nirayesu nirayapālāti, āmantā. Atthi ca kāraṇikā”tiādinā nayena abhidhamme (kathā. 866 ādayo) paṭisedhitameva. Yathā hi manussaloke kammakāraṇakārakā atthi, evameva nirayesu nirayapālā atthīti. Tattaṃ ayokhilanti tigāvutaṃ attabhāvaṃ sampajjalitāya lohapathaviyā uttānakaṃ nipajjāpetvā dakkhiṇahatthe tālappamāṇaṃ ayasūlaṃ pavesenti, tathā vāmahatthādīsu. Yathā ca uttānakaṃ nipajjāpetvā evaṃ urenapi vāmapassenapi dakkhiṇapassenapi nipajjāpetvā taṃ kammakāraṇaṃ karontiyeva.

'By one's own kamma' means by kamma done by oneself. Regarding 'the hell-wardens,' here some elders say, 'There are no so-called hell-wardens; kamma itself inflicts the punishment, like a machine.' But their view is refuted in the Abhidhamma (as in Kathāvatthu 866ff.) by the method beginning: 'Are there hell-wardens in the hells? Yes. And are there punishers?' For just as in the human world there are inflictors of punishment, so too in the hells there are hell-wardens. 'The heated iron stake'—they lay the body, three gāvutas in size, face-up on the blazing iron ground and drive an iron stake the size of a palmyra palm into the right hand; similarly, they do so to the left hand and other limbs. And just as they lay the body face-up, so too they lay it on its chest, left side, and right side, and inflict that punishment.

Saṃvesetvāti jalitāya lohapathaviyā tigāvutaṃ attabhāvaṃ nipajjāpetvā. Kuṭhārīhīti mahatīhi gehacchādanassa ekapakkhamattāhi kuṭhārīhi tacchenti, lohitaṃ nadī hutvā sandati, lohapathavito jālā uṭṭhahitvā tacchitaṭṭhānaṃ gaṇhāti, mahādukkhaṃ uppajjati, tacchantā pana suttāhataṃ karitvā dāru viya aṭṭhaṃsampi chaḷaṃsampi karonti. Vāsīhīti mahāsuppapamāṇāhi [M 0.0375] vāsīhi. Rathe yojetvāti saddhiṃ yugayottaupakkharacakkakubbarapājanehi sabbato [P 2.0425] pajjalite rathe yojetvā. Mahantanti mahākūṭāgārappamāṇaṃ. Āropentīti sampajjalitehi ayamuggarehi pothentā āropenti. Sakimpi uddhanti supakkutthitāya ukkhaliyā pakkhittataṇḍulaṃ viya uddhaṃ adho tiriyañca gacchati. Mahānirayeti avīcimahānirayamhi.

'Having made him enter' means having laid his body, three gāvutas in extent, on the blazing iron ground. 'With axes' means they plane him with large axes, each the size of one side of a house roof, causing a river of blood to flow. Flames rise from the iron ground and seize the place where he is being planed, producing immense suffering. As they plane him, having marked him with a line like wood, they make him eight-sided or six-sided. 'With adzes' means with large adzes the size of a large winnowing basket. 'Having yoked him to a chariot' means harnessing him to a chariot blazing on all sides, complete with yoke, straps, equipment, wheels, axle-box, and goad. 'Great' means as large as a great gabled hall. 'They make him ascend' means they strike him with blazing iron hammers to force him up. 'Tossed up once' means like rice thrown into a well-boiling pot, he goes up, down, and across. 'In the great hell' refers to the Avīci great hell.

Catukkaṇṇoti caturassamañjūsāsadiso. Vibhattoti catudvāravasena vibhatto. Bhāgaso mitoti dvāravīthīnaṃ vasena bhāge ṭhapetvā ṭhapetvā vibhatto. Pariyantoti parikkhitto. Ayasāti upari navayojanikena ayapattena chādito. Samantā yojanasataṃ pharitvā tiṭṭhatīti evaṃ pharitvā tiṭṭhati, yathā samantā yojanasate ṭhatvā olokentassa akkhīni yamakagoḷakā viya nikkhamanti. Kadariyātapanāti sabbepi te ussadehi saddhiṃ aṭṭha mahānirayā kadariyā niccaṃ tapantīti kadariyātapanā. Balavadukkhatāya ghorā. Kappaṭṭhikānaṃ accīnaṃ atthitāya accimanto. Āsādetuṃ ghaṭṭetuṃ dukkaratāya durāsadā. Diṭṭhamattā vā sutamattā vā lomāni haṃsentīti lomahaṃsanarūpā. Bhīsanatāya bhismā. Bhayajananatāya paṭibhayā. Sukhābhāvena dukhā.

'Four-cornered' means like a square chest. 'Divided' means divided by way of four doors. 'Measured out in parts' means divided by establishing partitions according to the doorways and streets. 'Bounded' means enclosed. 'Of iron' means covered above with an iron plate nine yojanas in extent. 'It stands pervading a hundred yojanas all around' means it stands so pervading that, for one standing a hundred yojanas away and looking, their eyes would pop out like twin balls. 'Kadariyātapanā' means all eight great hells, along with their surrounding minor hells, are called 'kadariyā'; because they burn constantly, they are 'kadariyātapanā.' They are dreadful due to the intense suffering. They are blazing because of the existence of flames that last for an eon. They are hard to access, being difficult to approach or encounter. Merely seeing or hearing about them makes one's hair stand on end, hence they are of a hair-raising nature. They are horrible due to their frightfulness. They are terrifying due to their fear-inducing nature. They are painful due to the absence of happiness.

Puratthimāya [V 0.0346] bhittiyātiādigāthānaṃ evaṃ avīcinirayoti pariyantaṃ katvā ayaṃ saṅkhepattho – aggijālānaṃ vā pana sattānaṃ vā tesaṃ dukkhassa vā vīci antaraṃ natthi etthāti avīci. Tatra hi puratthimādīhi bhittīhi jālārāsi uṭṭhahitvā pāpakammino puggale jhāpento pacchimādīsu bhittīsu paṭihaññati paharati, tā ca bhittiyo vinivijjhitvā parato yojanasataṃ gaṇhāti, heṭṭhā uṭṭhitā upari paṭihaññati, upari uṭṭhitā heṭṭhā paṭihaññati. Evaṃ tāvettha jālānaṃ vīci nāma natthi. Tassa pana anto yojanasataṭṭhānaṃ khīravallipiṭṭhassa pūritanāḷi viya sattehi nirantaraṃ pūritaṃ catūhi iriyāpathehi paccantānaṃ sattānaṃ pamāṇaṃ natthi, na ca aññamaññaṃ byābādhenti, sakasakaṭṭhāneyeva paccanti. Evamettha sattānaṃ vīci nāma natthi. Yathā pana jivhagge cha madhubindūni sattamassa tambalohabinduno anudahanabalavatāya abbohārikāni honti, tathā tattha [P 2.0426] anudahanabalavatāya sesā [M 0.0376] cha akusalavipākupekkhā abbohārikā honti, dukkhameva nirantaraṃ paññāyati. Evamettha dukkhassa vīci nāma natthi. Nirassādaṭṭhena nirayo.

Of the verses beginning 'The eastern wall,' up to 'the Avīci hell,' this is the meaning in brief: There is no interval (vīci) here for the flames, or for the beings, or for their suffering; hence, it is called Avīci (without interval). There, indeed, masses of flames rise up from the eastern and other walls, burning the evil-doers, and strike against the western and other walls. Having pierced through those walls, they extend a hundred leagues beyond. Flames rising from below strike above, and those rising from above strike below. Thus, there is no interval for the flames. Moreover, its interior space of a hundred leagues is continuously filled with beings, like a tube filled with a paste of milk-rice. There is no measure for the beings burning in the four postures, and they do not obstruct one another; each burns in their own place. Thus, there is no interval for the beings. Just as six drops of honey on the tip of the tongue become unperceivable due to the overpowering strength of a seventh drop of molten copper that follows, so too, due to the overpowering strength of the subsequent burning, the other six kinds of equanimity that are the result of unwholesome kamma are unperceivable. Only suffering is perceived continuously. Thus, there is no interval for suffering. It is a 'hell' (niraya) in the sense of being devoid of savor (nirassāda).

Tattha sattā mahāluddāti tasmiṃ nibbattā sattā mahantā luddā. Mahākibbisakārinoti mahantadāruṇakammakārino. Accantapāpakammantāti ekaṃsena pāpakammino. Paccanti na ca miyyareti channaṃ jālānamantare paccanti, na ca miyyanti. Jātavedasamo kāyoti tesaṃ sarīraṃ aggisadisaṃ. Tesaṃ nirayavāsinanti tesaṃ pāpakammānaṃ nirayavāsīnaṃ. Passa kammānaṃ daḷhattanti pāpakammānaṃ thirabhāvaṃ olokehi. Na bhasmā hoti napī masīti chārikāpi na hoti aṅgāropi. Puratthimenāti yadā taṃ dvāraṃ apārutaṃ hoti, atha tadabhimukhā dhāvanti, tesaṃ tattha chaviādīni jhāyanti. Dvārasamīpaṃ pattānañca tesaṃ taṃ pīdhīyati, pacchimaṃ apārutaṃ viya khāyati. Esa nayo sabbattha. Abhinikkhamitāsā teti nirayā nikkhamituṃ āsā etesanti nikkhamitāsā. Mokkhagavesinoti muñcanupāyaṃ esantā gavesantāpi. Na te tato nikkhamituṃ, labhanti kammapaccayāti te sattā nirayato nikkhamanadvāraṃ pāpakammapaccayā nādhigacchanti. Tesañca pāpakammantaṃ, avipakkaṃ kataṃ bahunti tesañca sattānaṃ lāmakaṃ dāruṇakammaṃ avipākaṃ bahuvidhaṃ nānappakāraṃ adinnavipākaṃ kataṃ upacitaṃ atthi.

As for 'there, the beings are exceedingly cruel,' it means the beings born there are exceedingly cruel. As for 'great evildoers,' it means performers of extremely dreadful deeds. As for 'their actions are absolutely wicked,' it means they are solely given to evil. As for 'they burn but do not die,' it means they burn between the six flames, yet they do not die. As for 'their body is like fire,' it means their body is similar to fire. As for 'those hell-dwellers,' it means those hell-dwellers who are evil-doers. As for 'see the firmness of their deeds,' behold the steadfastness of evil deeds. As for 'neither ash nor soot,' it means neither ash nor charcoal. As for 'from the east,' it means when that gate is opened, they rush towards it; there their skin and so forth burns. And for those who have reached the vicinity of the gate, it closes, and the western gate appears as if open. This is the pattern everywhere. As for 'they long to escape,' it means they have hope to escape from hell, thus 'longing to escape.' As for 'seeking liberation,' it means seeking and searching for a means of release. As for 'they cannot escape due to karmic causes,' it means those beings do not find a gate of exit from hell due to their evil kamma. And as for 'their evil deeds, much unripened, done,' it means that for those beings, there exists wretched, dreadful kamma, which is unripened, of many kinds and various sorts, whose result has not yet been given, having been done and accumulated.

Saṃveganti vinilanaṃ. Ubbeganti ṭhitaṭṭhānato gamanaṃ. Utrāsanti ubbejanaṃ asanniṭṭhānaṃ. Bhayanti cittutrāsanaṃ. Pīḷananti ghaṭṭanaṃ. Ghaṭṭananti pīḷākaraṇaṃ. Upaddavanti ītiṃ. Upasagganti rundhanaṃ.

Saṃvega means agitation. Ubbega means being unsettled from one's position. Utrāsa means terror and irresolution. Bhaya means terror of the mind. Pīḷana means oppression. Ghaṭṭana means causing affliction. Upaddava means calamity. Upasagga means obstruction.

171. Idāni [V 0.0347] yathānena saṃvijitaṃ, taṃ pakāraṃ dassento “phandamāna”ntiādimāha. Tattha phandamānanti taṇhādiṭṭhīhi kampamānaṃ. Appodaketi appe udake. Aññamaññehi byāruddhe [P 2.0427] disvāti nānāsatte ca aññamaññehi saddhiṃ viruddhe disvā. Maṃ bhayamāvisīti maṃ bhayaṃ paviṭṭhaṃ.

171. Now, showing the manner in which he was stirred, he said 'trembling' and so forth. Therein, 'trembling' means quivering with craving and views. As for 'in little water,' it means in a small amount of water. As for 'seeing them hostile to one another,' it means seeing various beings in conflict with one another. As for 'fear overcame me,' it means fear entered me.

Kilesaphandanāya phandamānanti rāgādikilesacalanāya calamānaṃ. Payogoti kāyavacīmanopayogo.

'Quivering with the quivering of the defilements' means being stirred by the stirring of defilements such as lust and so on. 'Effort' means the application of body, speech, and mind.

Viruddhāti virodhamāpannā. Paṭiviruddhāti paṭimukhaṃ hutvā virodhamāpannā, suṭṭhu viruddhā vā. Āhatāti kodhena āhatā pahatā. Paccāhatāti [M 0.0377] paṭimallā hutvā āhatā. Āghātitāti ghaṭṭitā. Paccāghātitāti visesena ghaṭṭitā. Pāṇīhipi upakkamantīti hatthehipi paharanti.

Viruddhā means having entered into opposition. Paṭiviruddhā means having come face to face and entered into opposition, or being strongly opposed. Āhatā means struck, beaten with anger. Paccāhatā means struck back, having become an opponent. Āghātitā means collided. Paccāghātitā means violently collided. 'They attack even with their hands' means they strike with their hands.

172. Samantamasāro lokoti nirayaṃ ādiṃ katvā samantato loko asāro niccasārādirahito. Disā sabbā sameritāti sabbā disā aniccatāya kampitā. Icchaṃ bhavanamattanoti attano tāṇaṃ icchanto. Nāddasāsiṃ anositanti kiñci ṭhānaṃ jarādīhi anajjhāvuṭṭhaṃ nāddakkhinti.

172. As for 'the world is entirely without essence,' it means, starting with hell, the world all around is without essence, devoid of permanent essence and so forth. As for 'all directions are shaken,' it means all directions are agitated by impermanence. As for 'seeking only a refuge for myself,' it means desiring a refuge for oneself. As for 'I saw nothing unassailed,' it means I saw no place unassailed by aging and so forth.

Asāroti na sāro, sāravirahito vā. Nissāroti sabbena sabbaṃ sāravirahito. Sārāpagatoti sārato apagato. Niccasārasārena vāti satatasārasaṅkhātena sārena vā. Uparipadadvayepi eseva nayo. Ye puratthimāya disāya saṅkhārāti ye puratthimāya disāya paccayehi saṅgamma samāgamma katā saṅkhārā. Tepi eritāti tepi saṅkhārā kampitā. Sameritāti sammā kampitā. Calitāti calanaṃ gatā. Ghaṭṭitāti udayabbayena pīḷitā. Aniccatāyāti hutvā abhāvatāya. Jātiyā anugatāti nibbattiyā anupaviṭṭhā. Jarāya anusaṭāti paripakkatāya anupatthaṭā. Byādhinā abhibhūtāti cātuvisamena uppannabyādhinā ajjhotthaṭā. Maraṇena abbhāhatāti maccunā abhiāhatā pahatā. Atāṇāti rakkhavirahitā. Aleṇāti leṇavirahitā. Asaraṇāti natthi etesaṃ saraṇanti asaraṇā. Asaraṇībhūtāti sayaṃ saraṇakiccaṃ na karontīti asaraṇībhūtā.

Asāro means not essence, or devoid of essence. Nissāro means completely and in every way devoid of essence. Sārāpagato means departed from essence. By 'permanent essence' or 'substantial essence' is meant the essence designated as continuous. The same method applies to the two subsequent terms. 'The formations in the eastern direction' means those formations made by conditions converging and combining in the eastern direction. 'They too are shaken' means those formations are also agitated. 'Completely shaken' means thoroughly agitated. 'Moving' means they have gone into motion. 'Struck' means oppressed by arising and passing away. 'By impermanence' means by the state of having come to be and then ceasing to be. 'Followed by birth' means entered into by origination. 'Pursued by aging' means pervaded by decay. 'Overcome by sickness' means overwhelmed by sickness arisen from the imbalance of the four elements. 'Struck by death' means assailed and smitten by death. 'Without protection' means devoid of a protector. 'Without shelter' means devoid of a refuge. 'Without sanctuary' means there is no sanctuary for them. 'Having become no sanctuary' means they do not perform the function of a sanctuary themselves.

Attano bhavananti niddesapadassa uddesapadaṃ. Tāṇanti pālanaṃ. Leṇanti leṇaṭṭhānaṃ. Saraṇanti [V 0.0348] dukkhanāsanaṃ. Gatinti patiṭṭhaṃ. Parāyananti paraṃ ayanaṃ. Ajjhositaṃyeva [P 2.0428] addasanti jarādīhi madditaṃyeva addakkhiṃ. Sabbaṃ yobbaññanti yobbanabhāvo yobbaññaṃ, sacetanānaṃ sabbaṃ yobbaññaṃ. Jarāya ositanti paripākāya jarāya avasitaṃ madditaṃ. Evaṃ sabbattha.

'A dwelling for oneself' is the subject term for the following descriptive terms. Tāṇa means protection. Leṇa means a place of shelter. Saraṇa means the destruction of suffering. Gati means a foundation. Parāyana means the ultimate resort. 'I saw it as overcome' means I saw it as crushed by aging and so forth. 'All youthfulness' means the state of being young is youthfulness; it refers to the youthfulness of all sentient beings. 'Beset by aging' means finished, crushed by the aging that is decay. And so for all cases.

173. Osāne tveva byāruddhe, disvā me aratī ahūti yobbaññādīnaṃ osāneyeva antagamake eva vināsake eva jarādīhi byāruddhe āhatacitte [M 0.0378] satte disvā arati me ahosi. Athettha sallanti atha etesu sattesu rāgādisallaṃ. Hadayassitanti cittanissitaṃ.

173. 'Seeing them conflicted at the very end, discontent arose in me' means: seeing beings with hearts struck—that is, conflicted—by aging and so forth, which are the very end-makers and destroyers of youth and so on, discontent arose in me. 'Then, herein, the dart' means the dart of lust and so forth in these beings. 'Lodged in the heart' means based in the mind.

Yobbaññaṃ jarā osāpetīti jarā atthaṅgameti vināseti. Evaṃ sabbattha.

'Aging brings youth to an end' means aging causes it to disappear, it destroys it. The same applies in all cases.

174. “Kathaṃ ānubhāvaṃ salla”nti ce? Yena sallena otiṇṇoti gāthā. Tattha disā sabbā vidhāvatīti sabbā duccaritadisāpi puratthimādidisāpi vidisāpi dhāvati. Tameva sallamabbuyha, na dhāvati na sīdatīti tameva sallaṃ uddharitvā tā ca disā na dhāvati, caturoghe ca na sīdati.

174. If it is asked, 'What is the power of the dart?' the answer is the verse beginning, 'Pierced by which dart…' Therein, 'he runs about in all directions' means he runs in all the directions of misconduct, in the cardinal directions such as the east, and in the intermediate directions. 'Having drawn out that very dart, he does not run about, he does not sink' means that having extracted that very dart, he does not run about in those directions, and he does not sink in the four floods.

Aññāṇantiādīsu ñāṇadassanapaṭipakkhato aññāṇaṃ adassanaṃ. Abhimukho hutvā dhammena na sameti na samāgacchatīti anabhisamayo. Anurūpato dhamme bujjhatīti anubodho. Tappaṭipakkhatāya ananubodho. Aniccādīhi saddhiṃ yojetvā na bujjhatīti asambodho. Asantaṃ asamañca bujjhatītipi asambodho. Catusaccadhammaṃ na paṭivijjhatīti appaṭivedho. Rūpādīsu ekadhammampi aniccādisāmaññato na saṅgaṇhātīti asaṅgāhaṇā. Tameva dhammaṃ na pariyogāhatīti apariyogāhaṇā. Na samaṃ pekkhatīti asamapekkhanā. Dhammānaṃ sabhāvaṃ pati na apekkhatīti apaccavekkhaṇā.

In terms like 'non-knowledge,' non-knowledge is non-vision, being the opposite of knowledge and vision. Not coming face-to-face with the Dhamma, not meeting it—this is non-comprehension. Awakening to the Dhamma in a way that corresponds to it—this is understanding. Its opposite is non-understanding. Not understanding even when connecting with impermanence and so forth—this is non-awakening. Understanding what is unreal and untrue—this too is non-awakening. Not penetrating the four noble truths—this is non-penetration. Not grasping even a single phenomenon among forms and so forth in terms of the general characteristic of impermanence and so forth—this is non-grasping. Not thoroughly scrutinizing that very phenomenon—this is non-thorough-scrutiny. Not seeing equally—this is non-equal-seeing. Not reflecting upon the nature of phenomena—this is non-reflection.

Kusalākusalakammesu viparītavuttiyā sabhāvagahaṇābhāvena vā ekampi kammaṃ etassa paccakkhaṃ natthi, sayaṃ vā kassaci dhammassa paccakkhakaraṇaṃ nāma na hotīti apaccakkhakammaṃ. Yaṃ etasmiṃ anuppajjamāne cittasantānaṃ mejjhaṃ bhaveyya suci vodānaṃ, taṃ duṭṭhuṃ mejjhaṃ imināti dummejjhaṃ. Bālānaṃ bhāvo bālyaṃ. Muyhatīti moho. Balavataro moho pamoho. Samantato [P 2.0429] muyhatīti sammoho. Vijjāya paṭipakkhabhāvato na vijjāti avijjā. Oghayogattho vuttoyeva. Thāmagataṭṭhena anusetīti anusayo. Cittaṃ pariyuṭṭhāti abhibhavatīti pariyuṭṭhānaṃ. Hitaggahaṇābhāvena hitābhimukhaṃ gantuṃ na sakkoti aññadatthu laṅgatiyevāti laṅgī, khañjatīti [V 0.0349] attho. Durugghāṭanaṭṭhena vā laṅgī. Yathā hi mahāpalighasaṅkhātā laṅgī durugghāṭā hoti, evamayampi laṅgī viyāti laṅgī. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva.

In wholesome and unwholesome kamma, due to contrary behavior or the absence of grasping their nature, not even a single kamma is directly evident to him; or, the direct realization of any phenomenon by oneself does not occur, thus it is non-direct-realization. That which, when not arising, would make the stream of consciousness pure and bright—but because of this, it becomes foul and turbid—this is dullness. The state of fools is foolishness. He is deluded, thus delusion. Stronger delusion is confusion. He is utterly deluded, thus total delusion. Because it opposes knowledge, it is called ignorance. The meaning of being bound by the floods has already been stated. Due to being deeply rooted, it persists—this is the underlying tendency. The mind is overwhelmed and dominated—this is obsession. Unable to move toward what is beneficial due to the absence of grasping benefit, it merely limps—this is lameness, meaning it hobbles. Or, it is called lameness because it is hard to dislodge. Just as a massive iron bar known as a `laṅgī` is hard to dislodge, so too this, being like a `laṅgī`, is thus called `laṅgī`. The rest is clear in meaning.

Yā [M 0.0379] evarūpā kaṅkhāti ettha kaṅkhanavasena kaṅkhā. Kaṅkhaṃ ānayatīti kaṅkhāyanā. Purimakaṅkhā hi uttarakaṅkhaṃ ānayati nāma. Ākāravasena vā etaṃ vuttaṃ. Kaṅkhāsamaṅgicittaṃ kaṅkhāya āyitattā kaṅkhāyitaṃ nāma. Tassa bhāvo kaṅkhāyitattaṃ. Vimatīti vigatā mati vimati. Vicikicchāti vigatā cikicchā vicikicchā, sabhāvaṃ vā vicinanto kicchati kilamati etāyāti vicikicchā. Sā saṃsayalakkhaṇā, kampanarasā, anicchayapaccupaṭṭhānā, anekaṃsaggāhapaccupaṭṭhānā vā, ayonisomanasikārapadaṭṭhānā, paṭipattiyā antarāyakarāti daṭṭhabbā.

`Yā evarūpā kaṅkhā` means, here, `kaṅkhā` is so called because of its nature of doubting. `Kaṅkhaṃ ānayatīti kaṅkhāyanā` means it brings about doubt—this is doubtfulness. For an earlier doubt indeed brings about a later doubt. Or, this is said in terms of its aspect. `Kaṅkhāsamaṅgicittaṃ kaṅkhāya āyitattā kaṅkhāyitaṃ nāma` means a mind associated with doubt, being inclined toward doubt, is called affected by doubt. `Tassa bhāvo kaṅkhāyitattaṃ` means its state is being affected by doubt. `Vimatīti vigatā mati vimati` means uncertainty is the absence of certainty. `Vicikicchā` means the absence of decision. Or, while investigating its own nature, one struggles and is wearied by it—this is indecision. It has the characteristic of doubt, the function of wavering, manifests as irresolution or as taking hold of multiple alternatives, has unwise attention as its proximate cause, and should be seen as obstructing the path of practice.

Kampanaṭṭhena dvidhā eḷayatīti dveḷhakaṃ. Paṭipattinivāraṇena dvidhāpatho viyāti dvedhāpatho. “Niccaṃ vā idaṃ aniccaṃ vā”tiādipavattiyā ekasmiṃ ākāre saṇṭhātuṃ asamatthatāya samantato setīti saṃsayo. Ekaṃsaṃ gahetuṃ asamatthatāya na ekaṃsaggāhoti anekaṃsaggāho. Nicchetuṃ asakkontī ārammaṇato osakkatīti āsappanā. Ogāhituṃ asakkontī parisamantato sappatīti parisappanā. Pariyogāhituṃ asamatthatāya apariyogāhaṇā. Nicchayavasena ārammaṇe pavattituṃ asamatthatāya chambhitattaṃ cittassa, thaddhabhāvoti attho. Vicikicchā hi uppajjitvā cittaṃ thaddhaṃ karoti, yasmā pana sā uppajjamānā ārammaṇaṃ gahetvā manaṃ vilikhantī viya, tasmā manovilekhoti vuttā.

By the meaning of shaking, because it wavers in two ways, it is `dveḷhakaṃ`. It is like a two-fold path, obstructing the practice, thus `dvedhāpatho`. Due to the inability to settle on one aspect in the arising of thoughts such as 'Is this permanent or impermanent?' it wavers all around, and is thus `saṃsayo`. Because it cannot grasp one side, it is `anekaṃsaggāho`—not grasping one side. Being unable to decide, it shrinks back from the object, and this is `āsappanā`. Being unable to plunge in, it creeps all around, and this is `parisappanā`. Due to the inability to fully grasp, it is `apariyogāhaṇā`. Due to the mind's inability to proceed decisively towards the object, there is bewilderment of the mind, which means stiffness. For doubt, when it arises, makes the mind stiff. And because, when it arises, it seizes the object and as it were scrapes the mind, it is therefore called `manovilekho`.

Viddhoti sallena laddhappahāro. Phuṭṭhoti ghaṭṭito. Paretoti pīḷito. Dhāvatīti purato gacchati. Vidhāvatīti anekavidhena [P 2.0430] gacchati. Sandhāvatīti vegena dhāvati. Saṃsaratīti ito cito ca carati.

`Viddho` means struck by a dart. `Phuṭṭho` means rubbed. `Pareto` means tormented. `Dhāvati` means goes forward. `Vidhāvati` means goes in various ways. `Sandhāvati` means runs swiftly. `Saṃsarati` means moves here and there.

Acelakoti niccolo, naggoti attho. Muttācāroti visaṭṭhācāro, uccārakammādīsu lokiyakulaputtācārena virahito ṭhitakova uccāraṃ karoti, passāvaṃ karoti, khādati bhuñjati. Hatthāpalekhanoti hatthe piṇḍamhi ṭhite jivhāya hatthaṃ apalikhati, uccāraṃ vā katvā hatthamhiyeva daṇḍakasaññī hutvā hatthena apalikhati. Te kira daṇḍakaṃ “satto”ti paññapenti. Bhikkhāgahaṇatthaṃ “ehi bhadante”ti vutto na etīti na ehibhadantiko. Tena hi “tiṭṭha [V 0.0350] bhadante”ti vuttopi na [M 0.0380] tiṭṭhatīti na tiṭṭhabhadantiko. Tadubhayampi kira so “etassa vacanaṃ kataṃ bhavissatī”ti na karoti.

`Acelaka` means unclothed, that is, naked. `Muttācāro` means unrestrained in behavior; he stands still while performing bodily functions like urination and defecation, devoid of the manners of worldly sons of good family. He eats and drinks. `Hatthāpalekhano` means that when food is placed in his hand, he licks the hand with his tongue. Or after defecating, having the perception of his hand as a stick, he wipes with his hand. They indeed declare that a stick is a 'being.' When told, 'Come, venerable sir,' for the purpose of receiving alms, he does not come—thus, he is `na ehibhadantiko`. Similarly, when told, 'Stay, venerable sir,' he does not stay—thus, he is `na tiṭṭhabhadantiko`. Indeed, he does neither, thinking, 'This would be an act of obedience to his word.'

Abhihaṭanti puretaraṃ gahetvā āhaṭaṃ bhikkhaṃ. Uddissakatanti “idaṃ tumhe uddissa kata”nti evaṃ ārocitaṃ bhikkhaṃ. Na nimantananti “asukaṃ nāma kulaṃ vā vīthiṃ vā gāmaṃ vā paviseyyāthā”ti evaṃ nimantitabhikkhampi na sādiyati na gaṇhāti. Na kumbhimukhāti kumbhito uddharitvā diyyamānaṃ bhikkhaṃ na gaṇhāti. Na kaḷopimukhāti kaḷopīti ukkhali vā pacchi vā, tatopi na gaṇhāti. Kasmā? Kumbhikaḷopiyo maṃ nissāya kaṭacchunā pahāraṃ labhantīti. Na eḷakamantaranti ummāraṃ antaraṃ karitvā diyyamānaṃ na gaṇhāti. Kasmā? Ayaṃ maṃ nissāya antarakaraṇaṃ labhatīti. Daṇḍamusalesupi eseva nayo.

`Abhihaṭa` refers to almsfood that has been brought after being previously fetched. `Uddissakata` means almsfood that has been announced with the words, 'This has been prepared especially for you.' `Na nimantana` means he does not accept almsfood even when invited with the words, 'You may enter such-and-such a family, street, or village.' `Na kumbhimukha` means he does not accept almsfood given by scooping it out from a pot. `Na kaḷopimukha` means he does not accept almsfood given from a cooking pot or a basket. Why? Because pots and baskets may receive a blow from a ladle on my account. `Na eḷakamantara` means he does not accept almsfood given across a threshold. Why? Because on my account, this threshold is made into a boundary. The same principle applies to sticks and pestles.

Na dvinnanti dvīsu bhuñjamānesu ekasmiṃ uṭṭhāya dente na gaṇhāti. Kasmā? Kabaḷantarāyo hotīti. Na gabbhiniyātiādīsu pana “gabbhiniyā kucchiyaṃ dārako kilamatī”ti, pāyantiyā dārakassa khīrantarāyo hotī”ti, “purisantaragatāya ratiantarāyo hotī”ti na gaṇhāti. Na saṃkittīsūti saṃkittetvā katabhattesu. Dubbhikkhasamaye kira acelakasāvakā acelakānamatthāya tato tato taṇḍulādīni samādapetvā bhattaṃ pacanti, ukkaṭṭho acelako tatopi na paṭiggaṇhāti. Na yattha sāti yattha sunakho “piṇḍaṃ labhissāmī”ti upaṭṭhito hoti, tattha tassa adatvā āhaṭaṃ na gaṇhāti. Kasmā? Etassa piṇḍantarāyo hotīti. Saṇḍasaṇḍacārinīti samūhasamūhacārinī[P 2.0431]. Sace hi acelakaṃ disvā “imassa bhikkhaṃ dassāmā”ti manussā bhattagehaṃ pavisanti, tesu ca pavisantesu kaḷopimukhādīsu nilīnā makkhikā uppatitvā saṇḍasaṇḍā caranti. Tato āhaṭaṃ bhikkhaṃ na gaṇhāti. Kasmā? Maṃ nissāya makkhikānaṃ gocarantarāyo jātoti. Thusodakanti sabbasassasambhārehi kataṃ sovīrakaṃ. Ettha ca surāpānameva sāvajjaṃ, ayaṃ pana sabbesupi sāvajjasaññī.

`Na dvinnaṃ` means that when two are eating, if one gets up and offers, he does not accept. Why? Because it would obstruct the other's mouthful. Regarding a pregnant woman and so on, he does not accept, thinking, 'For a pregnant woman, the child in the womb suffers,' 'For a nursing mother, there is an obstruction to the child's milk,' 'For one engaged with a man, there is an obstruction to pleasure.' `Na saṃkittīsu` means from meals prepared by prior arrangement. It is said that during a famine, disciples of naked ascetics collect rice and other provisions from various places to cook a meal for the naked ascetics; the most eminent naked ascetic does not accept even from that. `Na yattha sā` means where a dog is present and waiting, thinking 'I will get alms,' he does not accept food brought from there if it is brought without first giving some to the dog. Why? Because it would obstruct that one's alms. `Saṇḍasaṇḍacārinī` means moving in swarms. If people see a naked ascetic and think, 'We will give alms to him,' and enter the eating hall, then flies hiding in pot-mouths and so on fly up and move in swarms. He does not accept the alms brought from there. Why? Because, on my account, an obstruction to the flies' feeding ground has occurred. `Thusodaka` refers to sour gruel made from the ingredients of all grains. Here, only the drinking of liquor is blameworthy, but this one perceives all of it as blameworthy.

Ekāgārikoti yo ekasmiṃyeva gehe bhikkhaṃ labhitvā nivattati. Ekālopikoti yo ekeneva ālopena yāpeti. Dvāgārikādīsupi eseva nayo. Ekissāpi dattiyāti ekāya dattiyā. Datti nāma ekā khuddakapāti hoti, yattha aggabhikkhaṃ pakkhipitvā ṭhapenti. Ekāhikanti [M 0.0381] ekadivasantarikaṃ. Aḍḍhamāsikanti aḍḍhamāsantarikaṃ. Pariyāyabhattabhojananti vārabhattabhojanaṃ[V 0.0351], ekāhavārena dvīhavārena sattāhavārena aḍḍhamāsavārenāti evaṃ divasavārena ābhataṃ bhattabhojanaṃ.

A one-house alms-seeker is one who, having received alms in only one house, turns back. A one-morsel eater is one who subsists on just one morsel. The same principle applies to a two-house alms-seeker and so on. 'By one offering' means by a single offering. A 'datti' is a small bowl where the choicest almsfood is placed and kept. 'Ekāhika' means with an interval of one day. 'Aḍḍhamāsika' means with an interval of half a month. Eating by turns means eating a meal by rotation; that is, eating a meal brought according to a rotation of days, whether by a one-day rotation, a two-day rotation, a seven-day rotation, or a half-month rotation.

Sākabhakkhotiādīni vuttatthāneva. Ubbhaṭṭhakoti uddhaṃ ṭhitako. Ukkuṭikappadhānamanuyuttoti ukkuṭikaṃ vīriyaṃ anuyutto. Gacchantopi ukkuṭikova hutvā uppatitvā uppatitvā gacchati. Kaṇṭakāpassayikoti ayakaṇṭake vā pakatikaṇṭake vā bhūmiyaṃ koṭṭetvā tattha cammaṃ attharitvā ṭhānacaṅkamādīni karoti. Seyyanti sayantopi tattheva seyyaṃ kappeti. Phalakaseyyanti rukkhaphalake seyyaṃ. Thaṇḍilaseyyanti thaṇḍile ucce bhūmiṭṭhāne seyyaṃ. Ekapassayikoti ekapasseneva sayati. Rajojalladharoti sarīraṃ telena makkhetvā rajuṭṭhānaṭṭhāne tiṭṭhati, athassa sarīre rajojallaṃ laggati, taṃ dhāreti. Yathāsanthatikoti laddhaṃ āsanaṃ akopetvā yadeva labhati, tattheva nisīdanasīlo. Vekaṭikoti vikaṭakhādanasīlo, vikaṭanti gūthaṃ vuccati. Apānakoti paṭikkhittasītudakapāno. Sāyaṃ tatiyaṃ assāti sāyatatiyakaṃ. Pāto majjhanhike sāyanti divasassa tikkhattuṃ “pāpaṃ [P 2.0432] pavāhessāmī”ti udakorohanānuyogaṃ anuyutto viharati.

Eating leaves, etc., is as previously explained. 'Ubbhaṭṭhako' means one who stands upright. 'Devoted to the practice of squatting' means one is devoted to the exertion of squatting. Even while walking, being one who squats, one proceeds by repeatedly jumping up. 'A thorn-bed user' means one who, having hammered iron spikes or natural thorns into the ground, spreads a hide over them and there performs standing, walking, and so on. 'Seyya' means that even when lying down, one arranges one's bed right there. 'A plank-bed user' means one who makes their bed on a wooden plank. 'A bare-ground sleeper' means one who makes their bed on a high spot of bare ground. 'One who lies on one side' means one who sleeps on one side only. 'A dust-and-dirt wearer' means one who smears the body with oil and stands where dust rises, so that dust and dirt adhere to one's body, and one wears it. 'One who uses whichever seat is offered' means one who, not changing the seat one has received, is in the habit of sitting on whatever one gets. 'A filth-eater' means one who has the habit of eating what is repulsive; 'repulsive' refers to excrement. 'A non-drinker' means one who has refused to drink cold water. 'One whose third bathing is in the evening' means one who dwells devoted to the practice of descending into water three times a day—morning, noon, and evening—with the thought, 'I will wash away evil.'

Te salle abhisaṅkharotīti te rāgādisattasalle abhinibbatteti. Abhisaṅkharontoti abhinibbattento. Sallābhisaṅkhāravasenāti sallābhinibbattāpanakāraṇā. Puratthimaṃ disaṃ dhāvatīti purimaṃ disaṃ gacchati. Te sallābhisaṅkhārā appahīnāti ete rāgādisallā payogā nappahīnā. Sallābhisaṅkhārānaṃ appahīnattāti sallapayogānaṃ appahīnabhāvena. Gatiyā dhāvatīti gatiyaṃ dhāvati. Gatiyā gatinti gatito gatiṃ.

'He generates those darts' means he produces those seven darts, such as lust. 'Generating' means producing. 'By way of generating darts' means for the reason of producing the darts. 'He runs to the eastern direction' means he goes to the eastern direction. 'Those formations of darts are not abandoned' means these applications concerning the darts, such as lust, are not abandoned. 'Because the formations of darts are not abandoned' means due to the state of non-abandonment of the applications concerning the darts. 'He runs in a realm of existence' means he runs towards a realm of existence. 'Going in a realm of existence' means going from one realm of existence to another.

Na sīdatīti na nimujjati. Na saṃsīdatīti na samantato mujjati. Na osīdatīti na osakkati. Na avasīdatīti na paccosakkati. Na avagacchatīti na heṭṭhā gacchati.

'He does not sink' means he does not submerge. 'He does not sink completely' means he does not submerge entirely. 'He does not settle down' means he does not withdraw. 'He does not sink down' means he does not retreat. 'He does not go down' means he does not go below.

175. Evaṃ mahānubhāvena sallena otiṇṇesu ca sattesu – tattha sikkhānugīyanti, yāni loke gadhitānīti gāthā. Tassattho – ye loke [M 0.0382] pañca kāmaguṇā paṭilābhāya gijjhantīti katvā “gadhitānī”ti vuccanti, cirakālasevitattā vā “gadhitānī”ti vuccanti. Tattha taṃ nimittaṃ hatthisikkhādikā anekā sikkhā kathīyanti, uggayhanti vā. Passatha yāva samattho vāyaṃ loko, yato paṇḍito kulaputto tesu vā gadhitesu tāsu vā sikkhāsu [V 0.0352] adhimutto na siyā, aññadatthu aniccādidassanena nibbijjha sabbaso kāme. Attano nibbānameva sikkheti.

175. Thus, when beings are overwhelmed by the dart of great power, there is the verse: 'Therein trainings are praised, which in the world are objects of greed.' Its meaning is: the five strands of sensual pleasure in the world are called 'objects of greed' because beings are greedy to obtain them, or because they have been indulged in for a long time. There, as a sign of this, many trainings such as elephant training are discussed or undertaken. See how capable this world is, such that a wise clansman would not be attached to those objects of greed or those trainings, but rather, having become utterly disenchanted with all sensual pleasures through seeing impermanence and so on, trains only for his own Nibbāna.

Paṭivijjhitvāti ñāṇena nikkhametvā vā nibbijjhitvā vā.

'Having penetrated' means either having escaped by means of knowledge, or having become disenchanted.

176. Idāni yathā nibbānāya sikkhitabbaṃ, taṃ dassento “sacco siyā”tiādimāha. Tattha saccoti vācāsaccena ñāṇasaccena maggasaccena ca samannāgato. Rittapesuṇoti pahīnapesuṇo. Vevicchanti macchariyaṃ.

176. Now, showing how one should train for Nibbāna, he says, 'One should be truthful,' and so on. Here, 'truthful' means endowed with truth of speech, truth of knowledge, and truth of the path. 'Free from slander' means having abandoned slander. 'Veviccha' means stinginess.

177. Niddaṃ tandiṃ sahe thīnanti pacalāyikañca kāyālasiyañca cittālasiyañcāti ime tayo dhamme abhibhaveyya. Nibbānamānasoti nibbānaninnacitto.

177. 'One should overcome sleep, drowsiness, and sloth' means one should overcome these three things: nodding, bodily sluggishness, and mental sluggishness. 'One whose mind is on Nibbāna' means one whose mind is inclined towards Nibbāna.

Kāyassa akalyatāti khandhattayasaṅkhātassa nāmakāyassa gilānabhāvo. Gilāno hi akallakoti vuccati. Vinayepi (pārā. 151) vuttaṃ – “nāhaṃ, bhante, akallako”ti. Akammaññatāti kāyagelaññasaṅkhāto [P 2.0433] akammaññatākāro. Megho viya ākāsaṃ kāyaṃ onayhatīti onāho. Sabbato bhāgena onāho pariyonāho. Abbhantare samorundhatīti antosamorodho. Medhatīti middhaṃ, akammaññabhāvena vihiṃsatīti attho. Supanti tenāti suppaṃ. Akkhidalādīnaṃ pacalabhāvaṃ karotīti pacalāyikā. Suppanā suppitattanti ākārabhāvaniddesā. Olīyanāti olīyanākāro. Dutiyaṃ upasaggavasena vaḍḍhitaṃ. Līnanti avipphārikatāya paṭikuṭikaṃ. Itare dve ākārabhāvaniddesā. Thinanti sappipiṇḍo viya avipphārikatāya ghanabhāvena ṭhitaṃ. Thiyanāti ākāraniddeso. Thiyitassa bhāvo thiyitattaṃ, avipphāravasena thaddhatāti attho.

'Unwieldiness of body' is the sickness of the mental body, which is designated as the three aggregates. For a sick person is called 'unwieldy.' In the Vinaya too it is said: 'I am not unwieldy, venerable sir.' 'Unworkability' is the mode of unworkability designated as bodily illness. It covers the body like a cloud covers the sky, thus it is 'covering.' Covering in every part is 'complete covering.' It obstructs within, thus it is 'internal obstruction.' It harms, thus it is 'torpor' (middha); the meaning is that it injures by way of unworkability. One sleeps because of it, thus it is 'sleep' (soppa). It causes the eyelids and so on to droop, thus it is 'drowsiness' (pacalāyikā). 'Sleeping' and 'the state of having slept' are indications of its mode and state. 'Shrinking' is the mode of shrinking. The second term is augmented by way of a prefix. 'Shrunken' means contracted due to lack of diffusion. The other two are indications of its mode and state. 'Sloth' (thīna) is remaining in a dense state, like a lump of ghee, due to lack of diffusion. 'Sluggishness' is an indication of its mode. 'The state of being sluggish' is the state of one who is sluggish; the meaning is rigidity due to lack of diffusion.

Sabbasaṅkhāradhātuyāti [M 0.0383] nibbānaninnamānaso sabbatebhūmikasaṅkhātadhātuyā. Cittaṃ paṭivāpetvāti cittaṃ nivattāpetvā. Etaṃ santanti etaṃ nibbānaṃ. Kilesasantatāya santaṃ. Atappakaṭṭhena paṇītaṃ.

'From the entire element of formations' means, with a mind inclined to Nibbāna, from the element designated as all three planes of existence. 'Having made the mind turn away' means having made the mind turn back. 'This is peaceful' means this is Nibbāna. It is peaceful because the continuity of the defilements has been stilled. It is sublime on account of its un-tormented nature.

Na paṇḍitā upadhisukhassa hetūti dabbajātikā kāmasukhassa kāraṇā dānāni na denti. Kāmañca te upadhiparikkhayāyāti ekaṃsena te paṇḍitā kāmakkhayāya kāmakkhepanatthaṃ dānāni denti[V 0.0353]. Apunabbhavāyāti nibbānatthāya. Jhānāni bhāventīti paṭhamajjhānādīni vaḍḍhenti. Punabbhavāyāti punabbhavakāraṇā. Te paṇḍitā nibbānaṃ abhimukhaṃ hutvā dānaṃ dadanti.

'Not for the sake of happiness based on acquisitions do the wise give' means that those of a foolish nature do not give gifts for the sake of sensual pleasure. 'But for the utter destruction of acquisitions' means that those wise ones definitely give gifts for the destruction of sensual pleasure, for the purpose of dispelling sensual pleasure.
