'For no renewed existence' means for the sake of Nibbāna. 'They develop the jhānas' means they cultivate the first jhāna and so on. 'For renewed existence' means for the cause of renewed existence. Those wise ones give gifts with Nibbāna as their aim.

178. Sāhasāti rattassa rāgacaritādibhedā sāhasākāraṇā. Niddeso uttānatthoyeva.

178. 'Rashness': The causes of rashness are the various states of an impassioned person, such as a lustful disposition. The explanation has a plain meaning.

179. Purāṇaṃ nābhinandeyyāti atītaṃ rūpādiṃ nābhinandeyya. Naveti paccuppanne. Hīyamāneti vinassamāne. Ākāsaṃ na sito siyāti taṇhānissito na bhaveyya. Taṇhā hi rūpādīnaṃ ākāsanato “ākāso”ti vuccati.

179. 'One should not delight in the old' means one should not delight in past form and so on. 'In the new' means in the present. 'When it is diminishing' means when it is perishing. 'One should not be dependent on space' means one should not be dependent on craving. For craving is called 'space' (ākāsa) because it makes room (ākāsanato) for form and so on.

Vemāneti [P 2.0434] abhavamāne. Vigacchamāneti apagacchamāne.

'In disrespect' means when it is not arising. 'When departing' means when it is going away.

“Ākāsatī”ti “ākassatī”ti ca duvidho pāṭho.

There are two readings: 'ākāsatī' and 'ākassatī'.

180. Kiṃ kāraṇā ākāsaṃ na sito siyāti ce? Gedhaṃ brūmīti gāthā. Tassattho – ahañhi imaṃ ākāsasaṅkhātaṃ taṇhaṃ rūpādīsu gijjhanato gedhaṃ brūmi “gedho”ti vadāmi. Kiñca bhiyyo – avahananaṭṭhena “ogho”ti ca ājavanaṭṭhena “ājava”nti ca “idaṃ mayhaṃ, idaṃ mayha”nti jappakāraṇato “jappana”nti ca dummuñcanaṭṭhena “ārammaṇa”nti ca kampakaraṇaṭṭhena “kampana”nti ca brūmi, esāva lokassa palibodhaṭṭhena duratikkamanīyaṭṭhena ca “kāmapaṅko duraccayo”ti.

180. If it is asked, for what reason 'should one not be dependent on space'? The verse says: 'I call it greed.' Its meaning is this: I call this craving, which is designated as 'space,' 'greed' (gedha) because it is greedy (gijjhanato) for form and so on. Furthermore, because of its nature of carrying down, I call it 'flood' (ogha); because of its nature of impelling, 'current' (ājava); because it is the cause of muttering 'this is mine, this is mine,' 'muttering' (jappana); because of its nature of being difficult to release, 'a hold' (ārammaṇa); and because it causes trembling, I call it 'trembling' (kampana). This itself, because it is an obstruction to the world and is difficult to cross, is called 'the mire of sensual pleasure, difficult to get past'.

Ājavanti āpaṭisandhito javati dhāvatīti ājavaṃ, vaṭṭamūlatāya punabbhave paṭisandhidānataṇhāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Jappananti patthanā, taṇhāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Ārammaṇampi vuccati taṇhāti rūpādīsu ārammaṇesu uppannataṇhā muccituṃ asakkuṇeyyaṭṭhena ārammaṇāti kathīyati. Kāmapaṅkoti osīdanaṭṭhena kalalaṃ. Kaddamoti saṅgaṭṭhena kaddamo. Tāpanaṭṭhena kileso[M 0.0384]. Niyyāsaṃ viya laggāpanaṭṭhena palipo. Rundhitvā dhāraṇaṭṭhena palirodho. Evametaṃ gedhādipariyāyaṃ ākāsaṃ anissito.

'Current' (ājava) means it runs or rushes on to renewed existence; because it is the root of the round, this is a designation for the craving that gives rebirth in a future existence. 'Muttering' (jappana) means longing (patthanā); this is a designation for craving. 'Object' (ārammaṇa) is also a name for craving; craving that has arisen in regard to objects such as form is called 'object' because of the impossibility of being released from it. 'Mire of sensual pleasure' (kāmapaṅka) is a bog (kalala) because it sinks down. 'Mud' (kaddama) is mud because it sticks. 'Defilement' (kilesa) is so called because it torments. 'Smearing' (palipa) is so called because it makes things stick like sap. 'Obstruction' (palirodha) is so called because it obstructs and holds back. Thus this [craving] has these synonyms beginning with greed. [Such a one] is not dependent on space.

181. Saccā avokkamanti gāthā. Tassattho – pubbe vuttā tividhāpi saccā avokkamaṃ moneyyapattiyā munīti saṅkhaṃ gato nibbānathale tiṭṭhati brāhmaṇo, sa veevarūpo sabbāni āyatanāni nissajjitvā “santo”ti vuccati. Niddese vattabbaṃ natthi.

181. The verse is: 'Having gone beyond the truths.' Its meaning is this: Having gone beyond the threefold truths previously mentioned, through the attainment of sagehood he has gone to the state called 'sage' (muni); a brahmin, he stands on the ground of Nibbāna. Such a one, having relinquished all bases, is called 'peaceful' (santa). There is nothing more to be said in the explanation.

182. Kiñca [V 0.0354] bhiyyo – sa ve vidvāti gāthā. Tattha ñatvā dhammanti aniccādinayena saṅkhatadhammaṃ aññāya. Sammā so loke iriyānoti asammāiriyanakarānaṃ kilesānaṃ pahānā sammā so loke iriyamāno.

182. Furthermore, the verse: 'He indeed is a wise one.' Therein, 'having known the Dhamma' means having understood conditioned phenomena by the method of impermanence and so on. 'He fares rightly in the world' means that because he has abandoned the defilements that cause wrong faring, he fares rightly in the world.

183. Evaṃ [P 2.0435] apihento ca – yodha kāmeti gāthā. Tattha saṅganti sattavidhaṃ saṅgaṃ yo accatari. Nājjhetīti na abhijjhāyati.

183. And for one who is not covetous, there is the verse: 'Whoever here has overcome desires…' Therein, 'a bond' means he has crossed over the sevenfold bond. 'He does not long' means he does not covet.

184. Tasmā tumhesupi yo evarūpo hotuṃ icchati, taṃ vadāmi – yaṃ pubbeti gāthā. Tattha yaṃ pubbeti atīte saṅkhāre ārabbha uppajjanadhammaṃ kilesajātaṃ atītaṃ kammañca. Pacchā te māhu kiñcananti anāgatepi saṅkhāre ārabbha uppajjanadhammaṃ rāgādikiñcanaṃ mā ahu. Majjhe ce no gahessasīti paccuppannarūpādidhammepi na gahessasi ce. Evaṃ upasanto carissasi.

184. Therefore, to whichever of you wishes to be of such a kind, I say this: the verse 'Whatever in the past…' Therein, 'whatever in the past' means the mass of defilements that are liable to arise in dependence on past formations, and past kamma. 'And may you have no impediment in the future' means: may no impediment such as lust, which is liable to arise in dependence on future formations, exist for you. 'And if you will not grasp at what is in the middle' means if you will not grasp at present phenomena such as form. Thus you will fare calmed.

Abījaṃ karohīti maggañāṇena na bījaṃ karohi. Rāgakiñcananti rāgaphandanaṃ. Dosakiñcanādīsupi eseva nayo.

'Make it seedless' means: with the knowledge of the path, do not make a seed. 'The impediment of lust' means the agitation of lust. The same method applies also to the impediments of hatred and so on.

185. Evaṃ arahattappattiṃ dassetvā idāni arahato thutivasena ito parā gāthāyo abhāsi. Tattha sabbasoti gāthāya mamāyitanti mamattakaraṇaṃ. “Mama ida”nti gahitaṃ vā vatthu. Asatā ca na socatīti avijjamānakāraṇā asantakāraṇā na socati. Na jīyatīti jāniṃ nādhigacchati.

185. Having thus shown the attainment of arahantship, he now uttered the subsequent verses by way of praising the arahant. Therein, in the verse 'He makes nothing “mine” at all…', 'my-making' (mamāyita) means the act of making 'mine' (mamattakaraṇa). Or it means an object that has been grasped as 'this is mine.' 'And he does not grieve over what is non-existent' means he does not grieve because of a non-existent cause, an unreal reason. 'He is not overcome' means he does not come to loss.

Ahu [M 0.0385] vata meti mayhaṃ ahosi vata. Taṃ vata me natthīti yaṃ atīte ahosi, taṃ mayhaṃ idāni na santi. Siyā vata meti yaṃ mayhaṃ bhavissati, taṃ vatāhaṃ na labhāmīti idāni ahaṃ ekaṃsena na pāpuṇāmi.

'Alas, it was mine' means 'Alas, it was mine.' 'Alas, that is not mine' means 'what was mine in the past, that is not mine now.' 'Alas, would that it were mine' means 'what might be mine in the future, alas, I do not get it,' which means 'I certainly do not attain it now.'

186. Kiñca bhiyyo – yassa natthīti gāthā. Tattha kiñcananti kiñci rūpādidhammajātaṃ.

186. Furthermore, the verse: 'For whom there is nothing…' Therein, 'anything' (kiñcana) means any kind of phenomenon such as form.

Abhisaṅkhatanti kammena saṅkharitaṃ. Abhisañcetayitanti cittena rāsikataṃ. Avijjāya tvevāti avijjāya tu eva. Asesavirāganirodhāti virāgasaṅkhātena maggena niravasesanirodhā.

'Fabricated' means fabricated by kamma. 'Willed' means accumulated by mind. 'But by ignorance' means 'by ignorance indeed.' 'Through the complete fading away and cessation' means through the complete cessation by means of the path designated as 'fading away'.

Suññato [V 0.0355] lokaṃ avekkhassūti avasavattisallakkhaṇavasena vā tucchasaṅkhārasamanupassanavasena vāti dvīhākārehi suññato lokaṃ passa. Attānudiṭṭhiṃ ūhaccāti sakkāyadiṭṭhiṃ uddharitvā. Evaṃ maccutaro siyāti evaṃ maraṇassa [P 2.0436] taraṇo bhaveyya. Evaṃ lokaṃ avekkhantanti evaṃ khandhalokaṃ passantaṃ. Maccurājā na passatīti maraṇarājā na oloketi na dakkhati.

'Look upon the world as empty' means: see the world as empty in two ways: either by way of the characteristic of being without mastery, or by way of contemplating conditioned formations as void. 'Having rooted out the view of self' means having extracted the identity view. 'Thus one may cross over death' means thus one would be a crosser-over of death. 'One who looks upon the world thus' means one who sees the world of the aggregates thus. 'The King of Death does not see him' means the King of Death does not look at or see him.

Nāññaṃ patthayate kiñcīti aññaṃ appamattakampi na patthayati na pihayati. Aññatra appaṭisandhiyāti nibbānaṃ ṭhapetvā. “Aññatrappaṭisandhiyā”ti ekapadaṃ katvāpi paṭhanti.

'He does not long for anything else' means he does not long for, does not yearn for, even the slightest other thing. 'Except for non-rebirth' means except for Nibbāna. Some also recite it as one compound word: 'aññatrappaṭisandhiyā'.

187. Kiñca bhiyyo – aniṭṭhurīti gāthā. Tattha aniṭṭhurīti anissukī. “Aniṭṭharī”tipi keci paṭhanti. Sabbadhī samoti sabbattha samo, upekkhakoti adhippāyo. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yo so “natthi me”ti na socati, tamahaṃ avikampinaṃ puggalaṃ puṭṭho samāno aniṭṭhurī ananugiddho, anejo sabbadhī samoti imaṃ tasmiṃ puggale catubbidhaṃ ānisaṃsaṃ brūmīti.

187. Furthermore, the verse: 'Not harsh…' Therein, 'not harsh' means not envious. Some also read it as 'aniṭṭharī.' 'Impartial in every way' means impartial everywhere; the intention is 'equanimous.' What is said? It is this: 'When asked about that unshakeable person who does not grieve thinking, "There is nothing for me," I declare this fourfold benefit in that person: not harsh, not greedy, not agitated, and impartial in every way.'

Niṭṭhuriyoti issukī. Niṭṭhurabhāvo niṭṭhuriyaṃ, taṃ nissāya ettakampi natthīti kheḷapātanti attho. Niṭṭhuriyakammanti niṭṭhuriyakaraṇaṃ. Gahaṭṭho vā hi gahaṭṭhaṃ bhikkhu vā bhikkhuṃ nissāya vasanto appamattakeneva kujjhitvā taṃ nissāya ettakampi natthīti kheḷaṃ pātetvā pādena maddanto viya niṭṭhuriyaṃ nāma karoti. Tassa taṃ kammaṃ “niṭṭhuriyakamma”nti vuccati. Issāti sabhāvaniddeso[M 0.0386]. Tato parā dve ākārabhāvaniddesā. Itarattayaṃ pariyāyavacanaṃ. Lakkhaṇādito panesā parasampattīnaṃ usūyanalakkhaṇā issā; tattha ca anabhiratirasā; tato vimukhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā; parasampattipadaṭṭhānā.

'Harshness' (niṭṭhuriya) means envy. The state of being harsh is harshness; its meaning is spitting, thinking: 'Relying on him, I get not even this much!' 'The act of harshness' means doing a harsh act. For when a householder lives in dependence on a householder, or a bhikkhu on a bhikkhu, he gets angry over some trifle and performs an act of harshness, as it were, by spitting and crushing it with his foot, thinking: 'Relying on him, I get not even this much!' That action of his is called 'an act of harshness.' 'Envy' is an explanation of its nature. The next two are explanations of its manner of being. The other three are synonyms. But from the point of view of its characteristic, etc., envy has the characteristic of jealousy towards others' success; its function is displeasure therein; its manifestation is turning away; its proximate cause is others' success.

Lābhepi na iñjatīti paccayalābhe na calati. Alābhepīti paccayānaṃ alābhepi.

'Even in gain he is not stirred' means he does not waver at the gain of requisites. 'And in non-gain' means even in the non-gain of requisites.

188. Kiñca bhiyyo – anejassāti gāthā. Tattha nisaṅkhatīti puññābhisaṅkhārādīsu yo koci saṅkhāro. So hi yasmā nisaṅkhariyati, nisaṅkharoti vā, tasmā “nisaṅkhatī”ti vuccati. Viyārambhāti vividhā puññābhisaṅkhārādikā ārambhā. Khemaṃ passati sabbadhīti sabbattha abhayameva passati.

188. Furthermore, the verse: 'For the unshaken…' Therein, 'unfabricated' refers to any formation whatsoever, such as meritorious formations. For since it is not fabricated, or it does not fabricate, therefore it is called 'unfabricated.' 'Various undertakings' means various undertakings such as meritorious formations. 'He sees security everywhere' means he sees only fearlessness everywhere.

Ārambhāti [V 0.0356] kammānaṃ paṭhamārambhā. Viyārambhāti uparūpari [P 2.0437] vividhaārambhanavasena vīriyārambhā. Tīsu bhavesu paṭisandhijanakakammānaṃ etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tasmā viyārambhā ārato.

'Undertakings' means the initial undertakings of actions. 'Various undertakings' means energetic undertakings in the sense of various repeated efforts. This is a designation for kamma that generates rebirth in the three realms. Therefore, one is averted from such undertakings.

189. Evaṃ passanto na samesūti gāthā. Tattha na vadateti “sadisohamasmī”tiādinā mānavasena samesupi attānaṃ na vadati omesupi ussesupi. Nādeti na nirassatīti rūpādīsu kañci dhammaṃ na gaṇhāti na nissajjati. Sesaṃ sabbattha tattha tattha vuttanayattā pākaṭameva. Evaṃ arahattanikūṭeneva desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesīti.

189. Thus seeing, 'he does not compare'—this is the verse. Therein, 'he does not say' means he does not declare himself as 'I am equal,' and so on, due to conceit, even among equals, inferiors, or superiors. 'He does not grasp nor reject' means he neither takes up nor rejects any phenomenon among forms and so forth. The rest is evident everywhere, according to the method stated in each instance. Thus, the teaching is concluded with arahantship as its apex.

Saddhammappajjotikāya mahāniddesaṭṭhakathāya

From the Saddhammappajjotikā, the Commentary on the Mahāniddesa.

Attadaṇḍasuttaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Exposition of the Attadaṇḍasutta is completed.

16. Sāriputtasuttaniddesavaṇṇanā

16. The Explanation of the Exposition of the Sāriputta Sutta

190. Soḷasame [V 0.0357][P 2.0438] na me diṭṭhoti sāriputtasuttaniddeso. Tattha ito pubbeti ito saṅkassanagare otaraṇato pubbe. Vagguvadoti sundaravado. Tusitā gaṇimāgatoti tusitakāyā cavitvā mātukucchiṃ āgatattā tusitā āgato. Gaṇācariyattā gaṇī[M 0.0387]. Santuṭṭhaṭṭhena vā tusitasaṅkhātā devalokā gaṇiṃ āgato, tusitānaṃ vā arahantānaṃ gaṇiṃ āgatoti.

190. The exposition of the Sāriputta Sutta is the sixteenth, [beginning with the phrase] 'Not seen by me.' Therein, 'before this' means before the descent in the city of Saṅkassa. 'Of pleasant speech' means of beautiful speech. 'From Tusita he came to the group' means having passed away from the Tusita realm and arrived in his mother's womb, thus having come from Tusita. He is a 'leader of a group' because he is a teacher of a group. Or, he came as a leader from the Tusita devaloka, which is so called in the sense of 'contented'; or he came to the group of the Tusita ones, that is, the arahants.

Iminā cakkhunāti iminā attabhāvapariyāpannena pakatimaṃsacakkhunā. Iminā attabhāvenāti iminā pacchimena attabhāvena. Tāvatiṃsabhavaneti tāvatiṃsadevaloke. Pāricchattakamūleti koviḷārarukkhassa heṭṭhā. Paṇḍukambalasilāyanti rattakambalasadisapāsāṇapiṭṭhe. Vassaṃ vuṭṭhoti vuṭṭhavasso. Devagaṇaparivutoti devasaṅghena parivārito. Otiṇṇoti avatiṇṇo. Imaṃ dassanaṃ pubbeti aññatra imamhā dassanā pubbe. Na diṭṭhoti aññadā na diṭṭhapubbo.

With this eye: with this ordinary fleshly eye included within his own existence. With this body: with this last existence. In the Tāvatiṃsa realm: in the world of the Tāvatiṃsa devas. At the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree: beneath the koviḷāra tree. On the Paṇḍukambala stone: on the stone seat resembling a red blanket. Having passed the rains: one who has spent the rainy season. Surrounded by a host of devas: encircled by a group of devas. Descended: descended. Before this sight: before, other than this sight. Not seen: not seen previously.

Khattiyassa vāti khattiyassa vadantassa na suto. Brāhmaṇādīsupi eseva nayo.

Of a Khattiya: it was not heard from a Khattiya speaking. The same principle applies to brahmins and so on.

Madhuravadotiādīsu byañjanasampannaṃ madhuraṃ vadatīti madhuravado. Pemajanakaṃ pemārahaṃ vadatīti pemanīyavado. Hadayaṅgamacitte ṭhapanayogyaṃ vadatīti hadayaṅgamavado. Karavīkasakuṇasaddo viya madhuraghoso assāti karavīkarutamañjughoso. Vissaṭṭho cāti apalibuddho tattha tattha apakkhalano. Viññeyyo cāti suvijāneyyo ca. Mañju cāti madhuro ca. Savanīyo cāti kaṇṇasukho ca. Bindu cāti ghano ca. Avisārī cāti na patthaṭo ca. Gambhīro cāti na uttāno ca. Ninnādi cāti ghosavanto ca. Assāti assa satthuno. Bahiddhā parisāyāti parisato bahi. Na niccharatīti na nikkhamati. Kiṃkāraṇā? Evarūpo madhurasaddo nikkāraṇā mā vinassatūti. Brahmassaroti [P 2.0439] aññe chinnassarāpi bhinnassarāpi kākassarāpi honti, ayaṃ pana mahābrahmuno sarasadisena sarena samannāgato. Mahābrahmuno hi pittasemhehi apalibuddhattā saro visuddho hoti, bhagavatāpi katakammaṃ vatthuṃ sodheti, vatthuno suddhattā nābhito paṭṭhāya samuṭṭhahanto saro [V 0.0358] visuddho aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgatāva samuṭṭhāti. Karavīko viya bhaṇatīti karavīkabhāṇī, mattakaravīkarutamañjughosoti attho.

Sweet-spoken: speaks with pleasing and well-formed words, thus sweet-spoken. Speaking words that inspire affection: speaks words that inspire affection and are worthy of love, thus speaks affectionately. Speaking words that captivate the heart: speaks words that captivate the heart and are fit to be retained in the mind, thus speaks captivatingly. His voice is as melodious as the karavīka's: like the call of the karavīka bird, his voice is sweet and melodious, thus his voice is as melodious as the karavīka's. Clear and distinct: unobstructed, not faltering here and there. Intelligible: easily understood. Pleasant: sweet. Pleasing to the ear: delightful to hear. Compact: solid. Not scattered: not diffused. Profound: not shallow. Resounding: full of sound. His: the Teacher's. Outside the assembly: beyond the gathering. Does not emanate: does not spread outward. Why? So that such a sweet voice may not be lost without cause. Brahma-like voice: others may have cut, broken, or crow-like voices, but his voice is endowed with a tone like that of the Great Brahmā. For the Great Brahmā’s voice is pure, being unobstructed by bile and phlegm; and the Blessed One also purifies the physical basis produced by past deeds. Due to the purity of this basis, his voice, arising from the navel, emerges pure and endowed with the eight qualities. He speaks like the karavīka: he is a speaker like the karavīka, meaning his voice is as sweet as the call of an enraptured karavīka.

Tāretīti akhemantaṭṭhānaṃ atikkāmeti. Uttāretīti khemantabhūmiṃ upanento tāreti. Nittāretīti akhemantaṭṭhānato nikkhāmento tāreti[M 0.0388]. Patāretīti pariggahetvā tāreti, hatthena pariggahetvā viya tāretīti attho. Sabbampetaṃ tāraṇuttāraṇādikhemantaṭṭhāne ṭhapanamevāti āha – “khemantabhūmiṃ sampāpetī”ti. Satteti veneyyasatte. Mahāgahanatāya mahānatthatāya dunnittariyatāya ca jātiyeva kantāro jātikantāro, taṃ jātikantāraṃ.

He ferries across: he makes one transcend the place of insecurity. He brings across: leading to the place of security, he ferries across. He rescues: leading out from the place of insecurity, he ferries across. He delivers: taking hold, he ferries across; the meaning is that it is like taking one by the hand and ferrying them across. All this, beginning with ferrying across and bringing across, is just establishing in the place of security—thus it is said: 'he brings to the place of security.' Beings: beings who are able to be trained. Due to its great depth, great peril, and the difficulty of crossing it, birth itself is a wilderness—the wilderness of birth. That wilderness of birth.

Gaṇassa sussūsatīti gaṇo assa vacanaṃ sussūsati suṇāti upalakkheti. Sotaṃ odahatīti sotukāmatāya sotaṃ avadahati patiṭṭhāpeti. Aññā cittaṃ upaṭṭhapetīti ñātukāmaṃ cittaṃ paṇidahati. Gaṇaṃ akusalā vuṭṭhāpetvāti janasamūhaṃ akosallasambhūtā akusalā uṭṭhāpetvā. Kusale patiṭṭhāpetīti kosallasambhūte kusale ṭhapeti. Saṅghīti rāsivasena saṅgho assa atthīti saṅghī. Parisavasena gaṇo assa atthīti gaṇī. Gaṇassa ācariyoti gaṇācariyo.

The group wants to listen to him: thus, the group wants to hear, listens to, and takes note of his words. He inclines his ear: that is, out of a desire to listen, he applies and establishes his ear. He prepares his mind for understanding: that is, he directs his mind with the wish to know. Having roused the group from the unwholesome: that is, having roused the assembly from unwholesome qualities born of unskillfulness. He establishes them in the wholesome: that is, he establishes them in wholesome qualities born of skillfulness. One who has a Saṅgha: he has a saṅgha in the sense of a multitude, thus he is called 'Saṅghī.' One who has a group: he has a group in the sense of an assembly, thus he is called 'Gaṇī.' The teacher of the group: thus, he is called 'Gaṇācariyo.'

191. Dutiyagāthāya sadevakassa lokassa, yathā dissatīti sadevakassa lokassa viya manussānampi dissati. Yathā vā dissatīti tacchato aviparītato dissati. Cakkhumāti uttamacakkhumā. Ekoti pabbajjāsaṅkhātādīhi eko. Ratinti nekkhammaratiādiṃ.

191. In the second verse, 'as seen by the world with its gods' means it is seen by humans as well, just as by the world with its gods. 'As it is seen' means seen accurately, without distortion. 'One with vision' means one with supreme vision. 'Alone' means one who is solitary due to renunciation and so forth. 'Delight' refers to delight in renunciation and so forth.

Patirūpakoti suvaṇṇapatirūpako kuṇḍalo. Mattikākuṇḍalovāti mattikāya katakuṇḍalo viya. Lohaḍḍhamāsova suvaṇṇachannoti suvaṇṇena paṭicchanno lohamāsako viya. Parivārachannāti parivārena chāditā. Anto asuddhāti [P 2.0440] abbhantarato rāgādīhi aparisuddhā. Bahi sobhamānāti cīvarādīhi bāhirato sundarā.

A counterfeit: a counterfeit gold earring. Like a clay earring: like an earring made of clay. Like a half-māsa of iron covered with gold: like an iron māsa covered with gold. Covered with a retinue: concealed by a retinue. Impure within: internally impure due to lust and so on. Beautiful on the outside: outwardly beautiful with robes and so on.

Akappitairiyāpathā cāti asajjitairiyāpathā. Paṇidhisampannāti paripuṇṇapatthanā.

Uncontrived postures: postures that are not deliberately arranged. Accomplished in aspiration: complete in aspiration.

Visuddhasaddoti parisuddhakittisaddo, yathābhūtathutighosoti attho. Gatakittisaddasilokoti kittisaddañca silokañca gahetvā caraṇasīlo. Kattha visuddhasaddoti ce? “Nāgabhavane ca supaṇṇabhavane [V 0.0359] cā”tiādinā [M 0.0389] nayena vitthāretvā vuttaṭṭhāne. Tato ca bhiyyoti tato vuttappakārato ca veneyyavasena atirekataropi dissati.

The pure sound: the sound of pure fame, meaning the proclamation of praise for what is in accordance with reality. 'One to whom fame and renown have gone': one who is accustomed to going about having acquired fame and renown. If it is asked, 'Where is this pure sound heard?' In the places stated and explained in detail by the method beginning with 'in the abode of the nāgas and in the abode of the supaṇṇas.' And more than that: even more excellent than what has been described is seen, according to the disposition of those to be trained.

Sabbaṃ rāgatamanti sakalaṃ rāgandhakāraṃ. Dosatamādīsupi eseva nayo. Andhakaraṇanti paññālokanivāraṇakaraṇaṃ. Acakkhukaraṇanti paññācakkhuno akaraṇaṃ. Aññāṇakaraṇanti ñāṇena ajānanakaraṇaṃ. Paññānirodhikanti paññānayananāsakaṃ. Vighātapakkhikanti pīḷākoṭṭhāsikaṃ. Anibbānasaṃvattanikanti apaccayaamatanibbānatthāya na saṃvattanikaṃ.

'All is the darkness of lust': the entire darkness of lust. The same principle applies to the darkness of hatred and the rest. It creates darkness: it obstructs the light of wisdom. It creates blindness: it prevents the arising of the eye of wisdom. It creates ignorance: it causes not-knowing through knowledge. It stifles wisdom: it destroys the eye of wisdom. It belongs to the side of affliction: it is a part of oppression. It does not lead to Nibbāna: it does not lead to the unconditioned, deathless Nibbāna.

Sabbaṃ taṃ tena bodhiñāṇena bujjhīti taṃ sakalaṃ tena catumaggañāṇavasena bujjhi. Paṭhamamaggavasena jāni anubujjhi. Dutiyamaggavasena puna aññāsi paṭivijjhi. Tatiyamaggavasena paṭivedhaṃ pāpuṇi sambujjhi. Catutthamaggavasena nissesapaṭivedhena sammābujjhi. Adhigacchi phassesi sacchākāsīti etaṃ tayaṃ phalavasena yojetabbaṃ. Paṭhamadutiyavasena paṭilabhi. Tatiyavasena ñāṇaphassena phusi. Catutthavasena paccakkhaṃ akāsi. Atha vā ekekaphalassa tayopi labbhanti eva.

'All that, he awakened to with that knowledge of enlightenment': all of it he awakened to by means of the knowledge of the four paths. By means of the first path, he knew and subsequently awakened. By means of the second path, he again understood and penetrated. By means of the third path, he attained penetration and fully awakened. By means of the fourth path, he perfectly awakened with complete and utter penetration. 'He attained, touched, and directly experienced': this triad should be connected with the fruits. By means of the first two, he obtained. By means of the third, he touched with the touch of knowledge. By means of the fourth, he made it directly evident. Alternatively, all three can be obtained for each fruit.

Nekkhammaratinti pabbajjādīni nissāya uppannaratiṃ. Vivekaratinti kāyavivekādimhi uppannaratiṃ. Upasamaratinti kilesavūpasame ratiṃ. Sambodhiratinti maggaṃ paccavekkhantassa uppannaratiṃ.

'Delight in renunciation' refers to the delight that arises in dependence on going forth and the like. 'Delight in seclusion' refers to the delight that arises in bodily seclusion and so on. 'Delight in peace' refers to the delight in the subsiding of defilements. 'Delight in enlightenment' refers to the delight that arises for one reflecting on the path.

192. Tatiyagāthāya bahūnamidha baddhānanti idha bahūnaṃ khattiyādīnaṃ sissānaṃ. Sissā hi ācariyapaṭibaddhavuttittā “baddhā”ti vuccanti. Atthi pañhena āgamanti atthiko pañhena āgatomhi[P 2.0441], atthikānaṃ vā pañhena āgamanaṃ, pañhena atthi āgamanaṃ vāti.

192. In the third verse, 'of the many bound ones here' refers here to the many disciples of the khattiyas and others. Disciples are called 'bound' because their way of life is bound to their teachers. 'They come with a question' means: 'Being in need, I have come with a question'; or, 'the coming with a question of those in need'; or, 'there is a coming with a question.'

Buddhoti padassa abhāvepi taṃ buddhanti pade yo so buddho, taṃ niddisitukāmena “buddho”ti vuttaṃ. Sayambhūti upadesaṃ vinā sayameva bhūto. Anācariyakoti sayambhūpadassa atthavivaraṇaṃ. Yo hi ācariyaṃ vinā saccāni paṭivijjhati, so sayambhū nāma hotīti. Pubbe ananussutesūtiādi anācariyakabhāvassa atthappakāsanaṃ. Ananussutesūti ācariyato ananussutesu. Sāmanti sayameva. Abhisambujjhīti bhusaṃ sammā paṭivijjhi. Tattha ca sabbaññutaṃ pāpuṇīti tesu ca saccesu sabbaññubhāvaṃ pāpuṇi. Yathā saccāni paṭivijjhantā sabbaññuno honti[M 0.0390], tathā saccānaṃ paṭividdhattā evaṃ vuttaṃ. “Sabbaññutaṃ patto”tipi pāṭho. Balesu [V 0.0360] ca vasībhāvanti dasasu ca tathāgatabalesu issarabhāvaṃ pāpuṇi. Yo so evaṃ bhūto, so buddhoti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha sabbadhammesu appaṭihatañāṇanimittānuttaravimokkhādhigamaparibhāvitakhandhasantānaṃ upādāya paṇṇattiko, sabbaññutapadaṭṭhānaṃ vā saccābhisambodhimupādāya paṇṇattiko sattaviseso buddho. Ettāvatā atthato buddhavibhāvanā katā hoti.

Even if the word 'Buddha' did not exist, in the phrase 'that Buddha,' the word 'Buddha' is spoken by one who wishes to indicate him who is the Buddha. 'Self-become' (sayambhū) means one who has become by oneself, without instruction. 'Without a teacher' (anācariyaka) is an explanation of the meaning of the term 'self-become.' For one who penetrates the truths without a teacher is called 'self-become.' 'Previously unheard' (pubbe ananussutesu), and so on, is an exposition of the meaning of being 'without a teacher.' 'Unheard' means unheard from a teacher. 'By oneself' (sāmaṃ) means by oneself. 'Fully awakened' (abhisambujjhi) means he thoroughly and rightly penetrated. And therein, 'he attained omniscience' (sabbaññutaṃ pāpuṇi) means he attained the state of omniscience regarding those truths. Just as those who penetrate the truths become omniscient, so it is said because of his penetration of the truths. There is also the reading 'he attained omniscience' (sabbaññutaṃ patto). And 'mastery over the powers' (balesu ca vasībhāvaṃ) means he attained sovereignty over the ten powers of the Tathāgata. One who is thus is called the Buddha. Herein, the Buddha is a distinguished being, designated on account of a continuum of aggregates cultivated by the attainment of unsurpassed liberation, which is the mark of unobstructed knowledge regarding all phenomena; or designated on account of the full awakening to the truths, which is the basis for omniscience. To this extent, the exposition of the meaning of 'Buddha' is accomplished.

Idāni byañjanato vibhāvento “buddhoti kenaṭṭhena buddho”tiādimāha. Tattha yathā loke avagantā “avagato”ti vuccati, evaṃ bujjhitā saccānīti buddho. Yathā paṇṇasosā vātā “paṇṇasusā”ti vuccanti, evaṃ bodhetā pajāyāti buddho. Sabbaññutāya buddhoti sabbadhammabujjhanasamatthāya buddhiyā buddhoti vuttaṃ hoti. Sabbadassāvitāya buddhoti sabbadhammānaṃ ñāṇacakkhunā diṭṭhattā buddhoti vuttaṃ hoti. Anaññaneyyatāya buddhoti aññena abodhanīyato sayameva buddhattā buddhoti vuttaṃ hoti. Visavitāya buddhoti nānāguṇavikasanato padumamiva vikasanaṭṭhena buddhoti vuttaṃ hoti. Khīṇāsavasaṅkhātena buddhotiādīhi chahi pariyāyehi cittasaṅkocakaradhammappahānena niddāya vibuddho puriso viya sabbakilesaniddāya vibuddhattā buddhoti vuttaṃ hoti. Saṅkhā [P 2.0442] saṅkhātanti atthato ekattā saṅkhātenāti vacanassa koṭṭhāsenāti attho. Taṇhālepadiṭṭhilepābhāvena nirupalepasaṅkhātena savāsanānaṃ sabbakilesānaṃ pahīnattā ekantavacanena visesetvā vuttaṃ. Ekantanikkilesoti rāgadosamohāvasesehi sabbakilesehi nikkileso.

Now, explaining in terms of the letter, he said, 'Buddha—in what sense is he called Buddha?' and so forth. Herein, just as in the world one who understands is called 'one who has understood,' so too, one who has awakened to the truths is a Buddha. Just as winds that dry leaves are called 'leaf-dryers,' so too, as the awakener of the populace, he is a Buddha. He is a Buddha by omniscience: it is said he is a Buddha because of his wisdom, which is capable of awakening to all phenomena. He is a Buddha by all-seeing: it is said he is a Buddha because all phenomena have been seen by him with the eye of knowledge. He is a Buddha by not being led by others: it is said he is a Buddha because he awakened by himself, not needing to be awakened by another. He is a Buddha by blossoming: it is said he is a Buddha in the sense of blossoming with various virtues, like a lotus. He is called a Buddha, designated as one whose taints are destroyed, because, having abandoned the states that constrict the mind, he has awakened from the sleep of all defilements, just as a person awakens from sleep. 'Saṅkhā' and 'saṅkhāta' are one in meaning; the meaning is that 'saṅkhāta' is a component of the word. Because all defilements together with their latent tendencies have been abandoned, he is designated as 'unstained' (nirupalepa) due to the absence of the stain of craving and the stain of views; this is stated emphatically to distinguish him. 'Completely stainless' (ekantanikkileso) means stainless from all defilements, with no remainder of lust, hatred, or delusion.

Ekāyanamaggaṃ gatoti buddhoti gamanatthānaṃ dhātūnaṃ bujjhanatthattā bujjhanatthāpi dhātuyo gamanatthā honteva, tasmā ekāyanamaggaṃ gatattā buddhoti vuttaṃ hoti. Ekāyanamaggo cettha –

He is called a Buddha because he has gone the one-way path (ekāyanamagga), for since roots meaning 'to go' have the meaning 'to awaken,' roots meaning 'to awaken' also certainly have the meaning 'to go'; therefore, it is said he is a Buddha because he has gone the one-way path. Herein, the one-way path is—

“Maggo pantho patho pajjo, añjasaṃ vaṭumāyanaṃ;

Nāvā uttarasetū ca, kullo ca bhisi saṅkamo”ti. (cūḷani. pārāyanatthutigāthāniddesa 101) –

“The path, the way, the road, the course, the straight path, the track, the way; the boat and the crossing-bridge, the raft and the float, the passage.”

Maggassa [M 0.0391] bahūsu nāmesu ayananāmena vuttamagganāmena vutto. Tasmā ekamaggabhūto maggo, na dvedhāpathabhūtoti attho. Atha vā ekena ayitabbo maggoti ekāyanamaggo. Ekenāti gaṇasaṅgaṇikaṃ pahāya pavivittena. Ayitabboti paṭipajjitabbo, ayanti vā etenāti ayano, saṃsārato nibbānaṃ gacchantīti attho. Ekesaṃ ayanoti ekāyano. Ekesanti seṭṭhānaṃ. Sabbasattaseṭṭhā ca sammāsambuddhā, tasmā ekesaṃ maggabhūto sammāsambuddhānaṃ ayanabhūto maggoti [V 0.0361] vuttaṃ hoti. Ayatīti vā ayano, gacchati pavattatīti attho. Ekasmiṃ ayano maggoti ekāyanamaggo. Ekasmiṃyeva buddhasāsane pavattamāno maggo, na aññatthāti vuttaṃ hoti. Api ca ekaṃ ayatīti ekāyano. Pubbabhāge nānāmukhabhāvanānayappavattopi aparabhāge ekaṃ nibbānameva gacchatīti vuttaṃ hoti, tasmā ekāyanamaggoti ekanibbānagamanamaggoti attho.

Among the many names for 'path' (magga), it is here called by the name 'ayana' and by the name 'magga.' Therefore, the meaning is that the path is a single path, not a forked path. Alternatively, 'ekāyana magga' means the path to be traveled by one. 'By one' (ekena) means by one who is secluded, having abandoned crowds and company. 'To be traveled' (ayitabba) means to be practiced; or, 'ayana' is that by which one goes—the meaning is, they go from saṃsāra to Nibbāna. 'Ekāyana' means the way of the foremost. 'Of the foremost' (ekesaṃ) means of the best. And the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones are the best of all beings; therefore, it is said that the path is the path for the foremost, the way for the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones. Or, 'ayana' means 'it goes'—the meaning is it goes, it proceeds. 'Ekāyana magga' means the path that goes in one place. It means the path proceeds solely within the Buddha’s dispensation, not elsewhere. Moreover, 'ekāyana' means it goes to one. Though in the earlier stages it proceeds through various methods and approaches of development, in the later stages it goes solely to the one Nibbāna—thus, the meaning is that the 'ekāyana magga' is the path that goes to the one Nibbāna.

Eko anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddhoti na parehi buddhattā buddho, kintu sayameva anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddhattā buddhoti vuttaṃ hoti. Abuddhivihatattā buddhipaṭilābhattā buddhoti buddhi buddhaṃ bodhoti pariyāyavacanametaṃ. Tattha yathā [P 2.0443] “nīlarattaguṇayogā nīlo paṭo, ratto paṭo”ti vuccati, evaṃ buddhaguṇayogā “buddho”ti ñāpetuṃ vuttaṃ.

He is called a Buddha because he alone is fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect self-enlightenment, not because he was awakened by others, but because he himself is fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect self-enlightenment. He is a Buddha because he has obtained wisdom (buddhi), having dispelled ignorance (abuddhi); 'wisdom' (buddhi), 'Buddha,' and 'awakening' (bodho) are synonymous expressions. Herein, just as it is said, 'a cloth is blue, a cloth is red' because of its connection with the quality of blue or red, similarly, the word 'Buddha' is used to make it known that he is connected with the qualities of a Buddha.

Tato paraṃ buddhoti netaṃ nāmantiādi “atthamanugatā ayaṃ paññattī”ti ñāpanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha mittā sahāyā. Amaccā bhaccā. Ñātī pitupakkhikā. Sālohitā mātupakkhikā. Samaṇā pabbajjupagatā. Brāhmaṇā bhovādino, samitapāpabāhitapāpā vā. Devatā sakkādayo brahmāno ca. Vimokkhantikanti vimokkho arahattamaggo, vimokkhassa anto arahattaphalaṃ, tasmiṃ vimokkhante bhavaṃ vimokkhantikaṃ nāmaṃ. Sabbaññubhāvo hi arahattamaggena sijjhati, arahattaphalodaye siddhaṃ hoti. Tasmā sabbaññubhāvo vimokkhante bhavo hoti. Taṃ nemittikampi nāmaṃ vimokkhante bhavaṃ nāma hoti. Tena vuttaṃ – “vimokkhantikametaṃ buddhānaṃ bhagavantāna”nti. Bodhiyā mūle saha sabbaññutaññāṇassa paṭilābhāti mahābodhirukkhamūle yathāvuttakkhaṇe sabbaññutaññāṇassa paṭilābhena saha. Sacchikā paññattīti arahattaphalasacchikiriyāya sabbadhammasacchikiriyāya [M 0.0392] vā jātā paññatti. Yadidaṃ buddhoti paññatti. Ayaṃ byañjanato buddhavibhāvanā. Ito paraṃ vahassetaṃ bhāranti pariyosānaṃ tattha tattha vuttanayattā yathāpāḷimeva niyyāti.

Furthermore, the statement beginning 'Buddha is not a name...' is spoken to make known that 'this is a meaningful designation.' Herein, 'mittā' are friends and 'sahāyā' are companions. 'Amaccā' are ministers and 'bhaccā' are servants. 'Ñātī' are relatives on the father’s side. 'Sālohitā' are relatives on the mother’s side. 'Samaṇā' are those who have gone forth into homelessness. 'Brāhmaṇā' are those who address others as 'bho,' or those who have pacified or banished evil. 'Devatā' are Sakka and other deities, and also Brahmās. 'Vimokkhantika' means: liberation (vimokkha) is the path of arahantship; the end (anta) of liberation is the fruit of arahantship; the name for what exists at that end of liberation is 'vimokkhantika.' For the state of omniscience is accomplished through the path of arahantship and is perfected with the arising of the fruit of arahantship. Therefore, the state of omniscience exists at the end of liberation. That causal name is also a name for what exists at the end of liberation. Hence it is said: 'This is the vimokkhantika name of the Blessed Buddhas.' 'At the foot of the Bodhi tree, together with the attainment of omniscient knowledge' means: at the foot of the great Bodhi tree, at the aforementioned moment, together with the attainment of the knowledge of omniscience. 'A designation based on realization' (sacchikā paññatti) is a designation that arises from the realization of the fruit of arahantship or the realization of all phenomena—that is, the designation 'Buddha.' This is the exposition of 'Buddha' according to the letter. From this point on, the conclusion of the section beginning 'Carry this burden' should be understood according to the Pāli text itself, following the method stated in each place.

193. Catutthagāthāya vijigucchatoti jātiādīhi aṭṭīyato. Rittamāsananti vivittaṃ mañcapīṭhaṃ. Pabbatānaṃ guhāsu vāti pabbataguhāsu vā rittamāsanaṃ bhajatoti sambandhitabbaṃ.

193. In the fourth verse, 'vijigucchato' (expressing disgust) means being repelled by birth and so on. 'An empty seat' (rittamāsanaṃ) refers to a secluded couch or bench. 'Or in mountain caves' (pabbatānaṃ guhāsu vā) should be connected thus: 'or resorts to an empty seat in mountain caves'.

Jātiyā vijigucchatoti jātiṃ vijigucchato. Jarāya. Byādhinātiādīsupi eseva nayo. Bhajatoti evamādīsu bhajatoti bhajantassa. Sevatoti sevantassa. Nisevatoti sammā sevantassa[V 0.0362]. Saṃsevatoti punappunaṃ sevantassa. Paṭisevatoti upagantvā sevantassa. Pabbatapabbhārāti pabbatakucchiyo.

'Disgusted with birth' (jātiyā vijigucchato) means one who is disgusted with birth (jātiṃ vijigucchato). The same method applies to 'aging' (jarāya), 'illness' (byādhinā), and so on. In phrases such as this, 'bhajati' (resorts to) means 'of one who resorts to' (bhajantassa). 'Sevati' (frequents) means 'of one who frequents' (sevantassa). 'Nisevati' (devotes oneself to) means 'of one who properly frequents' (sammā sevantassa). 'Saṃsevati' (repeatedly devotes oneself to) means 'of one who frequents again and again' (punappunaṃ sevantassa). 'Paṭisevati' (partakes of) means 'of one who approaches and frequents' (upagantvā sevantassa). 'Mountain slopes' (pabbatapabbhārā) means mountain interiors (pabbatakucchiyo).

194. Pañcamagāthāya uccāvacesūti hīnapaṇītesu. Sayanesūti vihārādīsu senāsanesu. Kīvanto tattha bheravāti kittakā tattha bhayakāraṇā. “Kuvanto”tipi pāṭho, kūjantoti cassa attho.

194. In the fifth verse, 'uccāvacesu' (in high and low) means in inferior and superior things. 'In resting places' (sayanesu) means in dwellings and lodgings, such as monasteries. 'How many terrors are there?' (kīvanto tattha bheravā) means how many causes of fear are there. There is also a reading 'kuvanto,' and its meaning is 'cooing'.

Kuvantoti [P 2.0444] saddāyanto. Kūjantoti abyattasaddaṃ karonto. Nadantoti ukkuṭṭhiṃ karonto. Saddaṃ karontoti vācaṃ bhāsanto. Katīti pucchā. Kittakāti pamāṇapucchā. Kīvatakāti paricchedapucchā. Kīvabahukāti pamāṇaparicchedapucchā. Te bheravāti ete bhayajananupaddavā bhayārammaṇā. Kīvabahukāti pucchite ārammaṇe dassetuṃ “sīhā byagghā dīpī”tiādīhi vissajjeti.

'Kuvanto' means making a sound. 'Kūjanto' means producing an indistinct sound. 'Nadanto' means making a roaring sound. 'Saddaṃ karonto' means speaking words. 'Kati' is a question. 'Kittakā' is a question about quantity. 'Kīvatakā' is a question about extent. 'Kīvabahukā' is a question about both quantity and extent. 'Te bheravā' (those terrors) means these fear-producing dangers and objects of fear. When asked 'how many?' he answers with 'lions, tigers, leopards,' and so on, to show the objects.

195. Chaṭṭhagāthāya kati parissayāti kittakā upaddavā. Agataṃ disanti nibbānaṃ. Tañhi agatapubbattā agataṃ, niddisitabbato disā cāti. Tena vuttaṃ – “agataṃ disa”nti. Amataṃ disa”ntipi pāṭho. Abhisambhaveti abhisambhaveyya. Pantamhīti pariyante.

195. In the sixth verse, 'kati parissayā' (how many dangers?) means how many calamities. 'The unreached direction' (agataṃ disaṃ) is Nibbāna. For it is 'unreached' because it has never been reached before, and it is a 'direction' because it is to be pointed out. Hence it is said: 'the unreached direction.' Another reading is 'the deathless direction' (amataṃ disaṃ). 'Abhisambhaveti' means one should be able to realize. 'Pantamhi' (in a remote place) means on the periphery.

Agatapubbā sā disāti yā disā supinantenapi na gatapubbā. Na sā disā gatapubbāti esā disā vuttanayena na gatapubbā. Iminā dīghena addhunāti anena dīghakālena.

'That direction never gone to before' (agatapubbā sā disā) means a direction never gone to before, even in a dream. 'That direction has not been gone to before' (na sā disā gatapubbā) means that, in the manner stated, this direction has not been gone to before. 'By this long stretch of time' (iminā dīghena addhunā) means by this long period.

Samatittikanti [M 0.0393] antomukhavaṭṭilekhaṃ pāpetvā samabharitaṃ. Anavasekanti anavasiñcanakaṃ aparisiñcanakaṃ katvā. Telapattanti pakkhittatelaṃ telapattaṃ. Parihareyyāti hareyya ādāya gaccheyya. Evaṃ sacittamanurakkheti taṃ telabharitaṃ pattaṃ viya attano cittaṃ kāyagatāya satiyā gocare ceva sampayuttasatiyā cāti ubhinnaṃ antare pakkhipitvā yathā muhuttampi bahiddhā gocare na vikkhipati, tathā paṇḍito yogāvacaro rakkheyya gopayeyya. Kiṃkāraṇā? Etassa hi –

“Samatittika” means filled evenly up to the inner line of the rim. “Anavaseka” means without allowing any to be spilled or sprinkled. “Telapatta” refers to a bowl of oil. “Parihareyya” means one should carry, take, or go. Thus, one should guard one’s own mind—just as one would carry that oil-filled bowl, placing one’s own mind between the range of mindfulness of the body and associated mindfulness, so that not even for a moment does it stray outside its range. In this way, a wise meditator should guard and protect it. For what reason? Because of this:

“Dunniggahassa lahuno, yatthakāmanipātino;

Cittassa damatho sādhu, cittaṃ dantaṃ sukhāvahaṃ”. (dha. pa. 35);

“Hard to restrain, flighty, alighting where it wishes—the taming of the mind is good. A tamed mind brings happiness.” (Dhp. 35)

Tasmā [V 0.0363] –

Therefore:

“Sududdasaṃ sunipuṇaṃ, yatthakāmanipātinaṃ;

Cittaṃ rakkhetha medhāvī, cittaṃ guttaṃ sukhāvahaṃ”. (dha. pa. 36);

“Hard to see, extremely subtle, alighting where it wishes—the wise one should guard the mind. A guarded mind brings happiness.” (Dhp. 36)

Idañhi –

For this:

“Dūraṅgamaṃ ekacaraṃ, asarīraṃ guhāsayaṃ;

Ye cittaṃ saṃyamessanti, mokkhanti mārabandhanā”. (dha. pa. 37);

“Far-ranging, solitary, bodiless, lying in a cave—those who will restrain the mind will be freed from Māra’s bonds.” (Dhp. 37)

Itarassa pana –

But for the other:

“Anavaṭṭhitacittassa[P 2.0445], saddhammaṃ avijānato;

Pariplavapasādassa, paññā na paripūrati”. (dha. pa. 38);

“For one whose mind is not steadfast, who knows not the true Dhamma, whose confidence is wavering, wisdom does not come to perfection.” (Dhp. 38)

Thirakammaṭṭhānasahāyassa pana –

But for one who has a stable meditation subject as a companion:

“Anavassutacittassa, ananvāhatacetaso;

Puññapāpapahīnassa, natthi jāgarato bhayaṃ”. (dha. pa. 39);

“For one whose mind is not drenched with lust, whose heart is not afflicted by hate, who has abandoned both merit and demerit, there is no fear for one who is awake.” (Dhp. 39)

Tasmā etaṃ –

Therefore, this:

“Phandanaṃ capalaṃ cittaṃ, dūrakkhaṃ dunnivārayaṃ;

Ujuṃ karoti medhāvī, usukārova tejanaṃ”. (dha. pa. 33);

“Flickering, unsteady, hard to guard, hard to restrain—the wise one straightens the mind, as a fletcher straightens an arrow shaft.” (Dhp. 33)

Evaṃ ujuṃ karonto sacittamanurakkhe.

Thus, making it straight, one should protect one's own mind.

Patthayāno [M 0.0394] disaṃ agatapubbanti imasmiṃ kāyagatāsatikammaṭṭhāne kammaṃ ārabhitvā anamatagge saṃsāre agatapubbaṃ disaṃ patthento vuttanayena sakaṃ cittaṃ rakkheyyāti attho. Kā panesā disā nāma –

“Longing for a direction never before reached”—having undertaken the work in this meditation subject of mindfulness of the body, one longs for that direction, unreached in beginningless saṃsāra, and should guard one’s mind in the manner stated—this is the meaning. But what is this direction called?

“Mātāpitā [V 0.0364] disā pubbā, ācariyā dakkhiṇā disā;

Puttadārā disā pacchā, mittāmaccā ca uttarā.

“Parents are the eastern direction, teachers the southern direction, children and spouse the western direction, friends and associates the northern direction.

“Dāsakammakarā heṭṭhā, uddhaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇā;

Etā disā namasseyya, alamatto kule gihī”ti. (dī. ni. 3.273) –

“Servants and workers are below, ascetics and brahmins are above; these are the directions a competent householder in the family should venerate.” (DN 31)

Ettha tāva mātāpitādayo “disā”ti vuttā.

Here, first, parents and so on are called “directions.”

“Disā catasso vidisā catasso, uddhaṃ adho dasa disā imāyo;

Katamaṃ disaṃ tiṭṭhati nāgarājā, yamaddasā supine chabbisāṇa”nti. (jā. 1.16.104) –

“The four directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below—these are the ten directions. In which direction does the Nāga king stand, the one with six tusks whom I saw in my dream?” (Jā. 1.16.104)

Ettha puratthimādibhedā disāva “disā”ti vuttā.

Here, the directions distinguished as east and so forth are themselves called “directions.”

“Agārino annadapānavatthadā, avhāyikā tampi disaṃ vadanti;

Esā disā paramā setaketu, yaṃ patvā dukkhī sukhino bhavantī”ti [P 2.0446]. (jā. 1.6.9) –

“Householders who give food, drink, and clothing, the hospitable—that too they call a direction. This is the supreme direction, O Setaketu, having reached which the sorrowful become happy.” (Jā. 1.6.9)

Ettha nibbānaṃ “disa”nti vuttaṃ. Idhāpi tadeva adhippetaṃ. Taṇhakkhayaṃ virāgantiādīhi dissati apadissati tasmā “disā”ti vuccati. Anamatagge pana saṃsāre kenaci bālaputhujjanena supinenapi agatapubbatāya “agatapubbā disā nāmā”ti vuccati. Taṃ patthayantena kāyagatāsatiyā yogo karaṇīyoti. Vajatotiādīsu ettha magguppādato samīpaṃ vajato. Ṭhitikkhaṇe gacchato. Phalodayato atikkamato.

Here, Nibbāna is called “direction.” Here too, the same is intended. Because it is seen and indicated by the destruction of craving, dispassion, and so on, it is called “direction.” However, in beginningless saṃsāra, it has never been reached even in a dream by any foolish ordinary person; hence, it is called “the direction never gone before.” For one who aspires to it, the practice of mindfulness of the body should be done. In “he proceeds” and so on, here it means: going near to the arising of the path; going at the moment of standing still; surpassing by the arising of the fruit.

Anteti antamhi ṭhite. Panteti vanagahanagambhīre ṭhite. Pariyanteti dūrabhāvena pariyante ṭhite. Selanteti pabbatānaṃ ante. Vananteti vanaghaṭānaṃ ante. Nadanteti nadīnaṃ ante. Udakanteti udakānaṃ pariyante. Yattha na kasīyati na vapīyatīti yasmiṃ kasanañca vapanañca na karīyati. Janantaṃ [M 0.0395] atikkamitvā ṭhite. Manussānaṃ anupacāreti kasanavapanavasena manussehi anupacaritabbe senāsane.

“Anta” means standing at the boundary. “Panta” means standing in the deep, dense forest. “Pariyanta” means standing at the remote boundary, being far away. “Selanta” means at the edge of the mountains. “Vananta” means at the edge of the forest thickets. “Nadanta” means at the edge of the rivers. “Udakanta” means at the limit of the waters. “Where there is no plowing or sowing” means where no plowing or sowing is done. Standing having gone beyond the inhabited area. “Manussānaṃ anupacāra” means a dwelling not frequented by people for the purpose of plowing and sowing.

196. Sattamagāthāya [V 0.0365] kyāssa byappathayo assūti kidisāni tassa vacanāni assu.

196. In the seventh verse, 'kyāssa byappathayo assu' (what might his expressions be?) means: what kind of words would his be?

Musāvādaṃ pahāyāti ettha musāti visaṃvādanapurekkhārassa atthabhañjanako vacīpayogo kāyapayogo vā. Visaṃvādanādhippāyena panassa paravisaṃvādakakāyavacīpayogasamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā musāvādo. Aparo nayo – musāti abhūtaṃ atacchaṃ vatthu, vādoti tassa bhūtato tacchato viññāpanaṃ. Lakkhaṇato pana atathaṃ vatthuṃ tathato paraṃ viññāpetukāmassa tathāviññattisamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā musāvādo. So yamatthaṃ bhañjati, tassa appatāya appasāvajjo, mahantatāya mahāsāvajjo. Api ca gahaṭṭhānaṃ attano santakaṃ adātukāmatāya “natthī”tiādinayappavatto appasāvajjo, sakkhinā hutvā atthabhañjanatthaṃ vutto mahāsāvajjo. Pabbajitānaṃ appakampi telaṃ vā sappiṃ vā labhitvā hasādhippāyena “ajja gāme telaṃ nadī maññe sandatī”ti pūraṇakathānayena pavatto appasāvajjo, adiṭṭhaṃyeva pana diṭṭhantiādinā nayena vadantānaṃ mahāsāvajjo.

Regarding 'abandoning false speech'—here, 'false' (musā) means a verbal or bodily effort aimed at deceiving and breaking the truth. With the intention of deceiving, however, the volition that gives rise to a bodily or verbal effort to deceive another is false speech. Another method: 'false' (musā) means an untrue, unreal matter, and 'speech' (vāda) is the communication of that as true and real. By definition, however, the volition that gives rise to such a communication in one who desires to communicate an untrue matter as true to another is false speech. Depending on the significance of the matter one breaks, it is a minor or major offense. Moreover, for householders, when one says “I have nothing” and so forth, out of unwillingness to give one's own possessions, it is a minor offense. But when spoken with the intent to break the truth as a witness, it is a major offense. For monastics, having obtained a small amount of oil or ghee and then jokingly saying, “Today, I think a river of oil flows in the village,” in an exaggerated manner, is a minor offense. However, claiming to have seen what was not seen, and so forth, is a major offense.

Tassa cattāro sambhārā honti – atathaṃ vatthu [P 2.0447] visaṃvādanacittaṃ tajjo vāyāmo parassa tadatthavijānananti. Eko payogo sāhatthikova. So ca kāyena vā kāyapaṭibaddhena vā vācāya vā paravisaṃvādakakiriyākaraṇe daṭṭhabbo. Tāya ce kiriyāya paro tamatthaṃ jānāti, ayaṃ kiriyasamuṭṭhāpikā cetanākkhaṇeyeva musāvādakammunā bajjhati.

It has four components: an untrue fact, a deceptive intention, the corresponding effort, and another's understanding of that fact. The application is a single, direct one. And it should be understood as the performance of an action that deceives another, whether by body, by what is connected with the body, or by speech. And if, through that action, another understands that matter, then at the very moment of the volition that initiated the action, one is bound by the kamma of false speech.

Saccaṃ vadatīti saccavādī. Saccena saccaṃ sandahati ghaṭetīti saccasandho, na antarantarā musā vadatīti attho. Yo hi puriso kadāci musā vadati, kadāci saccaṃ, tassa musāvādena antarikatāya saccaṃ saccena na ghaṭiyati, tasmā na so saccasandho. Ayaṃ pana na tādiso, jīvitahetupi musā avatvā saccena saccaṃ sandahatiyevāti saccasandho.

He speaks the truth; therefore, he is a speaker of truth. He connects truth with truth, he joins truth to truth—this means he is one who adheres to truth, not speaking falsely intermittently. For a person who sometimes speaks falsely and sometimes speaks truthfully, his truth is not joined to truth because of the falsehood that intervenes. Therefore, he is not one who adheres to truth. But this one is not like that; even for the sake of his life, he does not speak falsely—he connects truth with truth alone. Thus, he is one who adheres to truth.

Thetoti thiro, thirakathoti attho. Eko puggalo haliddirāgo viya thusarāsimhi nikhātakhāṇu viya assapiṭṭhe ṭhapitakumbhaṇḍamiva ca [M 0.0396] na thirakatho hoti. Eko pāsāṇalekhā viya indakhīlo viya ca thirakatho hoti, asinā sīsaṃ chindantepi dvekathā na katheti. Ayaṃ vuccati theto.

“Theta” means firm, meaning firm in speech. One person is like turmeric dye, like a post sunk in a heap of chaff, or like a pot placed on a donkey's back—not firm in speech. Another is like an inscription on stone, like an Indakhila pillar—firm in speech, not speaking a second word even when his head is being cut off with a sword. This one is called “theta” (steadfast).

Paccayikoti pattiyāyitabbo, saddhāyitabbakoti attho. Ekacco hi puggalo na paccayiko hoti, “idaṃ kena vuttaṃ, asukenā”ti vutte “mā tassa vacanaṃ saddahathā”ti vattabbataṃ [V 0.0366] āpajjati. Eko paccayiko hoti, “idaṃ kena vuttaṃ, asukenā”ti vutte “yadi tena vuttaṃ, idameva pamāṇaṃ, idāni upaparikkhitabbaṃ natthi, evameva ida”nti vattabbataṃ āpajjati, ayaṃ vuccati paccayiko. Avisaṃvādako lokassāti tāya saccavāditāya lokaṃ na visaṃvādetīti attho.

“Paccayika” means to be relied upon, meaning to be believed. For some individuals are not trustworthy; when it is said, “This was said by whom? By so-and-so,” they are liable to be told, “Do not believe his words.” But one who is trustworthy, when it is said, “This was said by whom? By so-and-so,” is liable to be told, “If it was said by him, this is the authority; now there is nothing further to investigate; it is just so.” This one is called “paccayika” (trustworthy). “He does not deceive the world” means that through his truthfulness, he does not deceive the world.

Pisuṇaṃ vācaṃ pahāyātiādīsu yāya vācāya yassa taṃ vācaṃ bhāsati, tassa hadaye attano piyabhāvaṃ parassa ca suññabhāvaṃ karoti, sā pisuṇavācā. Yāya pana attānampi parampi pharusaṃ karoti, yā vācā sayampi pharusā, neva kaṇṇasukhā na hadayaṅgamā, ayaṃ pharusavācā. Yena samphaṃ palapati niratthakaṃ, so samphappalāpo. Tesaṃ mūlabhūtāpi [P 2.0448] cetanā pisuṇavācādināmameva labhati, sā eva idha adhippetāti.

In 'Having abandoned divisive speech,' and so on: divisive speech is that speech by which one, in speaking to a person, creates in that person's heart affection for oneself and estrangement from another. Harsh speech is that by which one makes both oneself and others harsh, speech that is itself harsh, neither pleasing to the ear nor endearing to the heart. Frivolous talk is that by which one babbles uselessly. Even the underlying volition for these receives the name of divisive speech, and so on; this is what is intended here.

Tattha saṃkiliṭṭhacittassa paresaṃ vā bhedāya attano piyakamyatāya vā kāyavacīpayogasamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā pisuṇavācā. Sā yassa bhedaṃ karoti, tassa appaguṇatāya appasāvajjā, mahāguṇatāya mahāsāvajjā.

Herein, divisive speech is the volition, arising from a defiled mind, that instigates bodily and verbal action for the purpose of causing division among others or out of a desire to be liked. It is of little fault when it causes division in someone of little virtue, but of great fault when it causes division in someone of great virtue.

Tassā cattāro sambhārā honti – bhinditabbo paro, “iti ime nānā bhavissanti vinā bhavissantī”ti bhedapurekkhāratā vā, “iti ahaṃ piyo bhavissāmi vissāsiko”ti piyakamyatā vā, tajjo vāyāmo, tassa tadatthavijānananti.

It has four components: another person to be divided; either the aim of division, thinking, “Thus, these will become separate, they will be disunited,” or the desire to be liked, thinking, “Thus, I will become dear and trusted”; the corresponding effort; and that person understanding the meaning.

Imesaṃ bhedāyāti yesaṃ itoti vuttānaṃ santike sutaṃ, tesaṃ bhedāya. Bhinnānaṃ vā sandhātāti dvinnaṃ mittānaṃ vā samānupajjhāyakādīnaṃ vā kenacideva kāraṇena bhinnānaṃ ekamekaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “tumhākaṃ īdise kule jātānaṃ evaṃ bahussutānaṃ idaṃ na yutta”ntiādīni vatvā sandhānaṃ kattā. Anuppadātāti sandhānānuppadātā, dve jane samagge disvā [M 0.0397] “tumhākaṃ evarūpe kule jātānaṃ evarūpehi guṇehi samannāgatānaṃ anucchavikameta”ntiādīni vatvā daḷhīkammaṃ kattāti attho.

“For the division of these” means for the division of those from whom he has heard something. “Or a reconciler of those who are divided” means one who approaches each of two friends, or those with the same preceptor, and so on, who have become divided for some reason, and saying, “This is not fitting for you who were born into such a family, who are so learned,” and so on, thus effects a reconciliation. “One who encourages” means one who encourages reconciliation. Seeing two people in harmony, he says, “This is suitable for you who were born into such a family and are endowed with such qualities,” and so on, thus strengthening their bond—this is the meaning.

Samaggo ārāmo assāti samaggārāmo, yattha samaggā natthi, tattha vasitumpi na icchatīti attho. “Samaggarāmo”tipi pāḷi, ayamevattho. Samaggaratoti samaggesu rato, te pahāya aññatra gantumpi na icchatīti attho. Samagge disvāpi sutvāpi nandatīti samagganandī[V 0.0367]. Samaggakaraṇiṃ vācaṃ bhāsitāti yā vācā satte samaggeyeva karoti, taṃ sāmaggiguṇaparidīpakameva vācaṃ bhāsati, na itaranti.

“Samaggārāmo” means one whose pleasure-ground is harmony; where there are no harmonious ones, one does not even wish to dwell there—this is the meaning. “Samaggarāmo” is also a reading in the Pāli, with the same meaning. “Samaggarato” means one who delights in the harmonious, and does not wish to go elsewhere, abandoning them—this is the meaning. “Samagganandī” means one who rejoices on seeing or hearing of the harmonious. “He speaks words that create harmony” means that he speaks only words that make beings harmonious, words that illuminate the quality of unity, and no other.

Parassa mammacchedakakāyavacīpayogasamuṭṭhāpikā ekantapharusacetanā pharusavācā. Mammacchedakopi payogo cittasaṇhatāya pharusavācā na hoti. Mātāpitaro hi kadāci puttake evampi vadanti “corā vo khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ karontū”ti, uppalapattampi ca nesaṃ upari patantaṃ na icchanti. Ācariyupajjhāyā ca kadāci nissitake evaṃ vadanti “kiṃ ime ahirikā anottappino caranti, niddhamatha ne”ti. Atha ca nesaṃ āgamādhigamasampattiṃ icchanti. Yathā ca cittasaṇhatāya pharusavācā na hoti, evaṃ [P 2.0449] vacanasaṇhatāya apharusavācāpi na hoti. Na hi mārāpetukāmassa “imaṃ sukhaṃ sayāpethā”ti vacanaṃ apharusavācā hoti, cittapharusatāya panesā pharusavācāva, sā yaṃ sandhāya pavattitā. Tassa appaguṇatāya appasāvajjā, mahāguṇatāya mahāsāvajjā. Tassā tayo sambhārā – akkositabbo paro kupitacittaṃ akkosanāti.

Harsh speech is an exclusively harsh volition that instigates bodily or verbal action that cuts another to the quick. Yet even an action that cuts to the quick is not harsh speech if the mind is gentle. For instance, parents may sometimes say to their children, “May thieves cut you to pieces!” yet they would not wish even a lotus petal to fall upon them. Similarly, teachers and preceptors may sometimes say to their dependents, “Why do these shameless and reckless ones behave so? Drive them away!”—yet they still desire their attainment of learning and realization. And just as speech is not harsh when the mind is gentle, so too speech is not non-harsh when the words are gentle. For the words of one wishing to have another killed, saying, “Let him sleep peacefully,” are not non-harsh speech; rather, because of the harshness of the mind, this is indeed harsh speech. It is uttered with reference to a certain person. Due to that person's lack of good qualities, it has little fault; due to their great good qualities, it has great fault. It has three components: another person to be reviled, an angry mind, and the act of reviling.

Nelāti elaṃ vuccati doso, nāssā elanti nelā, niddosāti attho. “Nelaṅgo setapacchādo”ti (udā. 65; peṭako. 25) ettha vuttanelaṃ viya. Kaṇṇasukhāti byañjanamadhuratāya kaṇṇānaṃ sukhā, sūcivijjhanaṃ viya kaṇṇasūlaṃ na janeti. Atthamadhuratāya sakalasarīre kopaṃ ajanetvā pemaṃ janetīti pemaniyā. Hadayaṃ gacchati apaṭihaññamānā sukhena cittaṃ pavisatīti hadayaṅgamā. Guṇaparipuṇṇatāya pure bhavāti porī. Pure saṃvaddhanārī viya sukumārātipi porī. Purassa esātipi porī, nagaravāsīnaṃ kathāti attho. Nagaravāsino hi yuttakathā honti, pitimattaṃ pitāti bhātimattaṃ bhātāti vadanti. Evarūpī kathā bahuno janassa kantā [M 0.0398] hotīti bahujanakantā. Kantabhāveneva bahuno janassa manāpā cittavuḍḍhikarāti bahujanamanāpā.

“Nelā”: “ela” is said to be a fault; “n’assā ela” means “it has no fault,” thus “nelā” means “faultless.” This is like the word “nela” in the phrase “Nelaṅgo setapacchādo” (Ud 65; Peṭ 25). “Pleasing to the ear” means it is pleasant to the ears due to the sweetness of the expression; it does not produce an earache like the piercing of a needle. “Affectionate” means that due to the sweetness of its meaning, it does not generate anger in the whole body but generates affection. “Going to the heart” means it enters the mind with ease, unobstructed. “Urbane” (`porī`): because of its fullness of qualities, it is of the city (`pure bhavā`); hence it is called `porī`. It is also `porī` because it is very refined, like a woman raised in the city. Or, it is `porī` because it belongs to the city (`purassa esā`); that is, it is the speech of city-dwellers. City-dwellers, indeed, use appropriate speech, calling one who is like a father “father,” and one who is like a brother “brother.” Speech of this kind is dear to many people; hence it is “dear to the multitude.” Precisely because it is dear, it is pleasing to many people and gladdens their minds; hence it is “pleasing to the multitude.”

Anatthaviññāpikā kāyavacīpayogasamuṭṭhāpikā akusalacetanā samphappalāpo. So āsevanamandatāya appasāvajjo, āsevanamahantatāya mahāsāvajjo. Tassa dve sambhārā – bhāratayuddhasītāharaṇādiniratthakakathā purekkhāratā, tathārūpīkathākathanañca.

Frivolous talk is an unwholesome volition that instigates bodily and verbal actions that make known what is unbeneficial. When indulged in moderately, it is of little fault; when indulged in excessively, it is of great fault. It has two components: prioritizing pointless talk such as tales of the Bharata war, the abduction of Sita, and so on; and the act of telling such tales.

Kālena vadatīti kālavādī, vattabbayuttakālaṃ sallakkhetvā vadatīti attho. Bhūtaṃ tacchaṃ sabhāvameva vadatīti bhūtavādī. Diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikatthasannissitameva katvā vadatīti atthavādī[V 0.0368]. Navalokuttaradhammasannissitaṃ katvā vadatīti dhammavādī. Saṃvaravinayapahānavinayasannissitaṃ katvā vadatīti vinayavādī. Nidhānaṃ vuccati ṭhapanokāso, nidhānamassā atthīti nidhānavatī, hadaye nidhātabbayuttaṃ vācaṃ bhāsitāti attho. Kālenāti evarūpiṃ bhāsamānopi ca “ahaṃ nidhānavatiṃ [P 2.0450] vācaṃ bhāsissāmī”ti na akālena bhāsati, yuttakālaṃ pana apekkhitvāva bhāsatīti attho. Sāpadesanti saupamaṃ, sakāraṇanti attho. Pariyantavatinti paricchedaṃ dassetvā yathāssā paricchedo paññāyati, evaṃ bhāsatīti attho. Atthasaṃhitanti anekehi nayehi vibhajantena pariyādātuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya atthasampannaṃ. Yaṃ vā so atthavādī atthaṃ vadati, tena atthena sahitattā atthasaṃhitaṃ vācaṃ bhāsati, na aññaṃ nikkhipitvā aññaṃ bhāsatīti vuttaṃ hoti.

“Kālavādī” means one who speaks at the right time; the meaning is that one speaks after discerning the appropriate time to speak. “Bhūtavādī” means one who speaks what is true, factual, and in accordance with reality. “Atthavādī” means one who speaks making it connected with benefit in this present life and in the future life. “Dhammavādī” means one who speaks making it connected with the nine supramundane Dhammas. “Vinayavādī” means one who speaks making it connected with the discipline of restraint and the discipline of abandonment. “Nidhānavatī” means having a treasure; ‘nidhāna’ is called a place for depositing, and `nidhānavatī` means it has a treasure; the meaning is that one speaks words worthy of being deposited in the heart. Regarding ‘at the right time’: even when speaking in such a way, one does not speak at the wrong time, thinking, ‘I will speak words worthy of being treasured’; rather, the meaning is that one speaks only after considering the appropriate time. “Sāpadesa” means with a simile; the meaning is with a reason. “Pariyantavatī” means speaking in such a way as to show a boundary, so that its boundary is understood—this is the meaning. “Atthasaṃhita” means endowed with meaning, such that it cannot be exhausted by one who analyzes it in many ways. Or, because that speaker of meaning speaks meaning, his speech is connected with that meaning; it is said that he does not put aside one thing to speak of another.

Catūhi vacīsucaritehīti “musāvādaṃ pahāyā”tiādinā nayena vuttehi catūhi vācāhi yuttehi suṭṭhu caritehi. Samannāgatoti aparihīno. Catudosāpagataṃ vācaṃ bhāsatīti appiyādīhi catūhi dosehi apagataṃ parihīnaṃ vācaṃ bhāsati.

“Endowed with the four kinds of right speech” means being well-practiced in these four kinds of speech, as explained by the phrase “having abandoned false speech” and so on. “Endowed” means not deficient. “One speaks speech free from the four faults” means one speaks speech that is devoid of or untainted by the four faults, such as being unpleasant.

Atthi agocaroti kiñcāpi thero samaṇācāraṃ samaṇagocaraṃ kathetukāmo “atthi agocaro, atthi gocaro”ti padaṃ uddhari, yathā pana maggakusalo puriso maggaṃ ācikkhanto “vāmaṃ muñca, dakkhiṇaṃ gaṇhā”ti paṭhamaṃ muñcitabbaṃ sabhayamaggaṃ uppathamaggaṃ ācikkhati, pacchā gahetabbaṃ khemamaggaṃ ujumaggaṃ, evameva maggakusalapurisasadiso dhammasenāpati paṭhamaṃ pahātabbaṃ [M 0.0399] buddhapaṭikuṭṭhaṃ agocaraṃ ācikkhitvā pacchā gocaraṃ ācikkhitukāmo “katamo agocaro”tiādimāha. Purisena hi ācikkhitamaggo sampajjeyya vā na vā, tathāgatena ācikkhitamaggo apaṇṇako indavissaṭṭhaṃ vajiraṃ viya avirajjhanako nibbānanagaraṃyeva samosarati. Tena vuttaṃ – “puriso maggakusaloti kho tissa tathāgatassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ arahato sammāsambuddhassā”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.84).

“There is an improper range.” Even though the elder wished to speak about the proper conduct and range of a monk, he introduced the topic by saying, “There is an improper range; there is a proper range.” Just as a skilled guide, when showing the way, first warns, “Let go of the left, take the right,” pointing out the dangerous and crooked path that should be abandoned before directing one to the safe and straight path that should be taken, so too the General of the Dhamma, like a skilled guide, first explains what should be abandoned—the improper range rejected by the Buddha—before explaining the proper range, asking, “What is the improper range?” and so on. For a path shown by an ordinary person may or may not succeed, but the path shown by the Tathāgata is unerring, like a thunderbolt hurled by Indra, leading unfailingly to the city of Nibbāna. Therefore, it is said: “Indeed, ‘a person skilled in the path’ is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.84).

Yasmā vā sasīsaṃ nhānena pahīnasedamalajallikassa purisassa mālāgandhavilepanādivibhūsanavidhānaṃ viya pahīnapāpadhammassa kalyāṇadhammasamāyogo sampannarūpo hoti, tasmā sedamalajallikaṃ viya pahātabbaṃ paṭhamaṃ agocaraṃ ācikkhitvā pahīnasedamalajallikassa mālāgandhavilepanādivibhūsanavidhānaṃ viya pacchā gocaraṃ ācikkhitukāmopi “katamo agocaro”tiādimāha.

Or, just as for a man who has abandoned sweat, dirt, and grime through bathing including the head, the adornment with garlands, perfumes, and various kinds of embellishments becomes fully fitting, so too, for one who has abandoned unwholesome states, the association with wholesome states becomes fully accomplished. Therefore, having first pointed out the improper range as something to be abandoned like sweat, dirt, and grime, and wishing later to point out the proper range—just as the adornment with garlands, perfumes, and various kinds of embellishments is for one who has abandoned sweat, dirt, and grime—he begins by saying, “What is the improper range?” and so on.

Tattha [V 0.0369][P 2.0451] gocaroti piṇḍapātādīnaṃ atthāya upasaṅkamituṃ yuttaṭṭhānaṃ. Ayuttaṭṭhānaṃ agocaro. Vesiyā gocaro assāti vesiyāgocaro, mittasanthavavasena upasaṅkamitabbaṭṭhānanti attho. Tattha vesiyā nāma rūpūpajīviniyo yena kenacideva sulabhajjhācāratā mittasanthavasinehavasena upasaṅkamanto vesiyāgocaro nāma hoti. Tasmā evaṃ upasaṅkamituṃ na vaṭṭati. Kiṃkāraṇā? Ārakkhavipattito. Evaṃ upasaṅkamantassa hi cirarakkhitagopitopi samaṇadhammo katipāheneva nassati. Sacepi na nassati, garahaṃ labhati. Dakkhiṇāvasena pana upasaṅkamantena satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā upasaṅkamitabbaṃ.

There, “gocara” means a suitable place to approach for the purpose of alms-food and other things. An unsuitable place is “agocara.” “Vesiyā gocara” means the range of courtesans; that is, a place to be approached on the basis of friendship and intimacy—this is the meaning. Here, “vesiyā” are women who live by their beauty, easily accessible for any kind of improper conduct. Approaching them on the basis of friendship, intimacy, and affection is called “vesiyāgocara.” Therefore, it is not proper to approach them in this way. Why? Because of the failure of protection. For one who approaches in this way, even the monastic practice long-guarded and protected is destroyed in just a few days. Even if it is not destroyed, one receives blame. However, if one approaches them for the sake of offerings, one should approach with mindfulness established.

Vidhavā vuccanti matapatikā vā pavuṭṭhapatikā vā. Thullakumāriyoti mahallikā anibbiddhakumāriyo. Paṇḍakāti lokāmisanissitakathābahulā ussannakilesā avūpasantapariḷāhā napuṃsakā. Tesaṃ sabbesampi upasaṅkamane ādīnavo vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Bhikkhunīsupi eseva nayo. Api ca bhikkhū nāma ussannabrahmacariyā honti, tathā bhikkhuniyo. Te aññamaññaṃ santhavavasena katipāheneva rakkhitagopitasamaṇadhammaṃ nāsenti. Gilānapucchakena pana gantuṃ vaṭṭati. Bhikkhunā pupphāni labhitvā pūjanatthāyapi ovādadānatthāyapi gantuṃ vaṭṭatiyeva.

“Widows” are called those whose husband has died or is away from home. “Elderly maidens” refers to older, unmarried women. “Eunuchs” are those who are talkative, dependent on worldly pleasures, abound in defilements, with unallayed burning passions, and are impotent. The danger in approaching all of these should be understood in the same way as previously explained. The same principle applies to nuns. Moreover, monks are those for whom the holy life is paramount, and so are nuns. Through intimacy with each other, in just a few days they destroy the ascetic's conduct which should be guarded and protected. However, it is allowable to go to inquire after the sick. It is indeed allowable for a monk to go for the purpose of offering flowers or for giving advice.

Pānāgāranti [M 0.0400] surāpānagharaṃ, taṃ brahmacariyantarāyakarehi surāsoṇḍehi avivittaṃ hoti. Tattha tehi saddhiṃ sahasoṇḍavasena upasaṅkamituṃ na vaṭṭati, brahmacariyantarāyo hoti. Saṃsaṭṭho viharati rājūhītiādīsu rājānoti abhisittā vā hontu anabhisittā vā, ye rajjamanusāsanti. Rājamahāmattāti rājūnaṃ issariyasadisāya mahatiyā issariyamattāya samannāgatā. Titthiyāti viparītadassanā bāhiraparibbājakā. Titthiyasāvakāti bhattivasena tesaṃ paccayadāyakā, etehi saddhiṃ saṃsaggajāto hotīti attho.

A drinking hall is a tavern, which is not free from drunkards who are an obstacle to the holy life. It is not proper to approach such places in the manner of a fellow drunkard, for it is an obstacle to the holy life. By 'associating with kings' is meant those who govern the realm, whether consecrated or unconsecrated. Royal ministers are those endowed with great authority, similar to the power of kings. Heretics are external wanderers with wrong views. Disciples of heretics are those who provide them with requisites as devotees. The meaning is that one becomes associated with these.

Ananulomikena saṃsaggenāti ananulomikasaṃsaggo nāma tissannaṃ sikkhānaṃ ananulomo paccanīkasaṃsaggo. Yena brahmacariyantarāyaṃ paññattivītikkamaṃ sallekhaparihāniñca pāpuṇāti. Seyyathidaṃ? Rājarājamahāmattehi saddhiṃ sahasokitā sahananditā samasukhadukkhatā uppannesu kiccakaraṇīyesu [P 2.0452] attanā yogaṃ āpajjanatā titthiyatitthiyasāvakehi saddhiṃ ekacchandarucisamācāratā ekacchandarucisamācārabhāvāvaho vā sinehabahumānasanthavo. Tattha rājarājamahāmattehi saddhiṃ saṃsaggo brahmacariyantarāyakaro, itarehi titthiyasāvakehi tesaṃ laddhiggahaṇaṃ[V 0.0370]. Tesaṃ pana vādaṃ bhinditvā attano laddhiṃ gaṇhāpetuṃ samatthena upasaṅkamituṃ vaṭṭati.

By 'improper association' is meant an association uncongenial and contrary to the threefold training, whereby one incurs an obstacle to the holy life, a transgression of the rules, and a decline in spiritual practice. For example, associating with kings and royal ministers by sharing their sorrows and joys, their pleasures and pains, and engaging oneself in their affairs; or associating with heretics and their disciples by sharing the same inclinations and conduct, or by cultivating affection, respect, and intimacy that leads to such conduct. Here, association with kings and royal ministers is an obstacle to the holy life, while association with heretics and their disciples involves adopting their doctrines. However, it is permissible for one who is capable to approach them in order to refute their doctrines and establish one's own.

Idāni aparenapi pariyāyena agocaraṃ dassetuṃ “yāni vā pana tāni kulānī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha assaddhānīti buddhādīsu saddhāvirahitāni. Tāni “buddho sabbaññū, dhammo niyyāniko, saṅgho suppaṭipanno”ti na saddahanti. Appasannānīti cittaṃ pasannaṃ anāvilaṃ kātuṃ na sakkonti. Akkosakaparibhāsakānīti akkosakāni ceva paribhāsakāni ca. “Corosi, bālosi, mūḷhosi, oṭṭhosi, goṇosi, gadrabhosi, āpāyikosi, nerayikosi, tiracchānagatosi, natthi tuyhaṃ sugati, duggatiyeva tuyhaṃ pāṭikaṅkhā”ti evaṃ dasahi akkosavatthūhi akkosanti. “Hotu, idāni taṃ paharissāma, bandhissāma, vadhissāmā”ti evaṃ bhayadassanena paribhāsanti cāti attho.

Now, to show what is out of bounds by yet another method, the passage beginning, 'Or whatever families,' is introduced. Therein, 'faithless' means those devoid of faith in the Buddha and so forth. They do not believe thus: 'The Buddha is omniscient, the Dhamma leads to deliverance, the Sangha is practicing well.' 'Lacking confidence' means they are unable to make their minds clear and serene. 'Abusive and insulting' means they both abuse and insult. They abuse with the ten grounds for abuse, saying: 'You are a thief, a fool, a deluded one, a camel, an ox, a donkey, one bound for the lower realms, one destined for hell, one reborn as an animal; there is no good destination for you, only a bad destination is to be expected for you.' And they insult by making threats, saying: 'Wait, now we will strike you, bind you, kill you'—this is the meaning.

Anatthakāmānīti [M 0.0401] atthaṃ na icchanti, anatthameva icchanti. Ahitakāmānīti ahitameva icchanti, hitaṃ na icchanti. Aphāsukāmānīti phāsukaṃ na icchanti, aphāsukameva icchanti. Ayogakkhemakāmānīti catūhi yogehi khemaṃ nibbhayaṃ na icchanti, sabhayameva icchanti. Bhikkhūnanti ettha sāmaṇerāpi saṅgahaṃ gacchanti. Bhikkhunīnanti ettha sikkhamānāsāmaṇeriyopi. Sabbesampi hi bhagavantaṃ uddissa pabbajitānañceva saraṇagatānañca catunnampi parisānaṃ tāni anatthakāmāniyeva. Tathārūpāni kulānīti evarūpāni khattiyakulādīni kulāni. Sevatīti nissāya jīvati. Bhajatīti upasaṅkamati. Payirupāsatīti punappunaṃ upasaṅkamati. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ vesiyādigocarassa vesiyādiko rājādisaṃsaṭṭhassa rājādiko assaddhakulādisevakassa assaddhakulādiko cāti tippakāropi ayuttagocaro “agocaro”ti veditabbo.

'Those who wish for what is not beneficial' means they do not desire benefit; they only desire what is not beneficial. 'Those who wish for what is not for one's welfare' means they only desire what is not for one's welfare, not what is for one's welfare. 'Those who wish for discomfort' means they do not desire comfort; they only desire discomfort. 'Those who wish for non-security' means they do not desire security from the four yokes, which is freedom from fear; they only desire what is fraught with fear. 'Of monks'—here novices are also included. 'Of nuns'—here female probationers and female novices are also included. For all those who have gone forth for the sake of the Blessed One and for those who have gone for refuge, for all four assemblies, such families are indeed those who wish for what is not beneficial. 'Families of such a kind' means families like these, such as noble families and others. 'Associates with' means lives in dependence on. 'Frequents' means approaches. 'Attends upon' means repeatedly approaches. 'This is said' means this: this unsuitable resort, being of three kinds—the resort of courtesans and the like, association with kings and the like, and serving faithless families and the like—is to be understood as 'out of bounds.'

Tassa imināpi pariyāyena agocaratā veditabbā – vesiyādiko tāva pañcakāmaguṇanissayato agocaro veditabbo. Yathāha – “ko ca, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno agocaro paravisayo, yadidaṃ pañca kāmaguṇā”ti[P 2.0453]. Rājādiko jhānānuyogassa anupanissayato lābhasakkārāsanicakkanipphādanato diṭṭhivipattihetuto ca, assaddhakulādiko saddhāhānicittapadosāvahanato agocaro.

Its being out of bounds should be understood by this method as well: the resort of courtesans and the like is to be understood as out of bounds due to its dependence on the five strands of sensual pleasure. As it is said: 'And what, monks, is a monk's non-resort, the domain of others? It is these five strands of sensual pleasure.' The resort of kings and the like is out of bounds because it is unsupportive of the practice of absorption, leads to the production of gain, honor, and esteem, and is a cause for the corruption of view. The resort of faithless families and the like is out of bounds because it leads to the loss of faith and to corruption of mind.

Antaragharappavesādiko ca cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā nimittaggāhādiko ca saddhādeyyāni bhojanāni [V 0.0371] bhuñjitvā visūkadassanānuyogo ca pañca kāmaguṇā cāti catubbidhopi pana kilesuppattivasena agocaroti veditabbo.

Furthermore, these four should be understood as out of bounds because they lead to the arising of defilements: entering the inner house and the like; seeing a form with the eye and grasping at its signs and features; indulging in worldly shows after eating food offered in faith; and the five strands of sensual pleasure.
