Mā bhikkhave agocare carathāti carituṃ ayuttaṭṭhāne mā caratha. Paravisayeti sattuvisaye. Agocare bhikkhave caratanti ayuttaṭṭhāne carantānaṃ. “Cara”ntipi pāṭho. Lacchatīti labhissati passissati. Māroti devaputtamāropi maccumāropi. Otāranti randhaṃ chiddaṃ vivaraṃ.

'Monks, do not wander in a non-resort,' means do not wander in an unsuitable place. 'In the domain of others' means in the domain of the enemy. 'For those wandering in a non-resort, monks,' refers to those wandering in an unsuitable place. There is also the reading 'wander.' 'Will get an opportunity' means will obtain, will see. 'Māra' means both Māra the devaputta and Māra as death. 'Opportunity' means a flaw, a fissure, an opening.

Gocaraniddese na vesiyāgocaro hotītiādīni vuttapaṭipakkhavasena veditabbāni. Ayaṃ pana viseso – cattāro satipaṭṭhānā gocaroti [M 0.0402] carituṃ yuttaṭṭhānavasena catusatipaṭṭhānā gocaro. Saketi attano santake. Pettike visayeti pitito āgatavisaye.

In the explanation of the proper resort, statements such as 'one should not have the resort of courtesans' should be understood as the opposite of what has been said. This, however, is the specific point: the four establishments of mindfulness are the proper resort. 'Proper resort' means a suitable place to dwell; thus the four establishments of mindfulness are the proper resort. 'One's own' means in one's own possession. 'Paternal domain' means the domain that comes from one's father.

Āraddhavīriyassāti sammāupaṭṭhitacatusammappadhānavīriyavantassa. Thāmagatassāti balappattassa. Daḷhaparakkamassāti thiravīriyassa. Yassatthāya pesitoti yena arahattatthāya attabhāvo pariccatto. Attatthe cāti attano atthe arahattaphale ca. Ñāye cāti ariye aṭṭhaṅgike magge ca. Lakkhaṇe cāti aniccādilakkhaṇapaṭivedhe ca. Kāraṇe cāti hetumhi ca. Ṭhānāṭhāne cāti ṭhāne ca aṭṭhāne ca, kāraṇākāraṇe cāti attho. Idāni vitthāretvā dassetuṃ “sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā”tiādimāha.

'Of one who has aroused energy' means of one endowed with the energy of the four right strivings that are rightly undertaken. 'Of one who is strong' means of one who has attained strength. 'Of one with resolute exertion' means of one with firm energy. 'For the purpose for which one was sent forth' means for the sake of arahantship, for which this individual existence has been relinquished. 'And for one's own good' means for one's own benefit and for the fruit of arahantship. 'And in the method' means in the noble eightfold path. 'And in the characteristic' means in the penetration of the characteristics of impermanence and so on. 'And in the cause' means in the reason. 'And in the possible and impossible' means in the possible and the impossible, that is, in cause and non-cause. Now, to show this in detail, it says, 'All formations are impermanent,' and so on.

197. Aṭṭhamagāthāya ekodi nipakoti ekaggacitto paṇḍito.

197. In the eighth verse, 'unified' means having a one-pointed mind; 'alert' means wise.

Jātarūpassa oḷārikampi malaṃ dhamatīti suvaṇṇassa thūlaṃ jallaṃ aggisaṃyogena nīharati. Sandhamatīti sammā nīharati. Niddhamatīti apunabhavappattikaṃ katvā nīharati. “Jhāpetī”ti keci vadanti. Majjhimakampīti tato sukhumatarampi. Sukhumakampīti atisukhumatarampi. Evamevāti [P 2.0454] opammasampaṭipādanaṃ. Attano oḷārikepi kilese dhamatīti kāyaduccaritādike thūlakilese vīriyātapena nīharati. Majjhimakepi kileseti kāmavitakkādike oḷārikasukhumānaṃ majjhimakepi. Sukhumakepīti ñātivitakkādike atisaṇhakepi kilese. Sammādiṭṭhiyā micchādiṭṭhiṃ dhamatīti saha vipassanāya maggasampayuttāya sammādiṭṭhiyā viparītasaṅkhātaṃ micchādiṭṭhiṃ nīharati. Sammāsaṅkappādīsupi eseva nayo.

'One blows away even the gross impurity of gold' means one removes the coarse dross of gold through contact with fire. 'Blows away thoroughly' means removes completely. 'Blows out' means removes it having made it non-recurrent. Some say 'burns away.' 'The middling' means that which is more subtle than that. 'The subtle' means that which is extremely subtle. 'Even so' is for the purpose of presenting the simile. 'One blows away even the gross defilements in oneself' means one removes coarse defilements, such as bodily misconduct, by the heat of energy. 'The middling defilements' refers to those that are intermediate between the gross and the subtle, such as thoughts of sensuality. 'The subtle defilements' means extremely fine defilements, such as thoughts about relatives. 'Right view blows away wrong view' means that with right view associated with the path, together with insight, one removes wrong view, which is characterized as perverted. This same method applies to right intention and the others.

198. Evaṃ āyasmatā sāriputtena tīhi gāthāhi bhagavantaṃ thometvā pañcahi gāthāhi pañcasatānaṃ [V 0.0372] sissānamatthāya ca senāsanagocarasīlavatādīni pucchito tamatthaṃ pakāsetuṃ “vijigucchamānassā”tiādinā nayena vissajjanamāraddhaṃ. Tattha paṭhamagāthāya tāvattho – jātiādīhi jigucchamānassa rittāsanaṃ sayanaṃ sevato ve sambodhikāmassa sāriputta bhikkhuno yadidaṃ phāsu yo phāsuvihāro yathānudhammaṃ yo ca anudhammo, taṃ te pavakkhāmi yathā pajānaṃ yathā pajānanto [M 0.0403] vadeyya, evaṃ vadāmīti. Yaṃ phāsuvihāranti yaṃ sukhavihāraṃ. Asappāyarūpadassanenāti itthirūpādisamaṇāsappāyarūpadassanena. Taṃ bodhiṃ bujjhitukāmassāti taṃ catumaggañāṇasaṅkhātaṃ bodhiṃ bujjhituṃ icchantassa. Anubujjhitukāmassāti anurūpāya paṭipattiyā bujjhitukāmassa. Paṭivijjhitukāmassāti abhimukhe katvā nibbijjhitukāmassa. Sambujjhitukāmassāti pahīnakilese apaccāgamanavasena sammā bujjhituṃ icchantassa. Adhigantukāmassāti pāpuṇitukāmassa. Sacchikātukāmassāti paṭilābhasacchikiriyāya pattukāmassa. Atha vā bujjhitukāmassāti sotāpattimaggañāṇaṃ ñātukāmassa. Anubujjhitukāmassāti sakadāgāmimaggañāṇaṃ puna ñātukāmassa. Paṭivijjhitukāmassāti anāgāmimaggañāṇaṃ paṭivedhavasena ñātukāmassa. Sambujjhitukāmassāti arahattamaggañāṇaṃ sammā ñātukāmassa. Adhigantukāmassāti catubbidhampi adhigantukāmassa. Phassitukāmassāti ñāṇaphusanāya phusitukāmassa. Sacchikātukāmassāti paccavekkhaṇāya paccakkhaṃ [P 2.0455] kattukāmassa.

198. Thus, the Venerable Sāriputta, having praised the Blessed One with three verses, then, for the sake of five hundred disciples, asked with five verses regarding lodgings, alms-resorts, virtuous conduct, and so on. To explain that meaning, the reply began with “for one who is disgusted” and so on. Therein, the meaning of the first verse is as follows: For a monk, Sāriputta, who is disgusted by birth and so forth, who frequents an empty seat and bed, who desires full enlightenment—what is ease, what is an easeful dwelling, and what is in accordance with the Dhamma—that I will declare to you as I understand it. As one who understands would speak, so I speak. “What is an easeful dwelling?” means what is a pleasant abode. “By seeing unsuitable forms” means by seeing forms unsuitable for an ascetic, such as the form of a woman. “For one who desires to awaken to that enlightenment” means for one who wishes to awaken to the enlightenment consisting of the four path knowledges. “For one who desires to awaken accordingly” means for one who wishes to awaken through appropriate practice. “For one who desires to penetrate” means for one who wishes to penetrate by becoming disenchanted after facing it directly. “For one who desires complete awakening” means for one who wishes to awaken rightly without returning to abandoned defilements. “For one who desires to attain” means for one who wishes to reach. “For one who desires to realize” means for one who wishes to achieve direct realization through attainment. Alternatively, “for one who desires to awaken” means for one who wishes to know the knowledge of the stream-entry path. “For one who desires to awaken accordingly” means for one who wishes to know again the knowledge of the once-returner path. “For one who desires to penetrate” means for one who wishes to know the knowledge of the non-returner path through penetration. “For one who desires complete awakening” means for one who wishes to rightly know the knowledge of the arahant path. “For one who desires to attain” means for one who wishes to attain all four kinds. “For one who desires to touch” means for one who wishes to touch through the touch of knowledge. “For one who desires to realize” means for one who wishes to make directly evident through reviewing.

Catunnaṃ maggānaṃ pubbabhāge vipassanāti catunnaṃ ariyamaggānaṃ purimakoṭṭhāse uppannaudayabbayādivipassanāñāṇāni.

Insight in the preliminary stage of the four paths means the insight knowledges, such as that of arising and passing away, which arise in the initial phase of the four noble paths.

199. Dutiyagāthāya sapariyantacārīti sīlādīsu catūsu pariyantesu caramāno. Ḍaṃsādhipātānanti piṅgalamakkhikānañca sesamakkhikānañca. Te hi tato tato adhipatitvā khādanti, tasmā “adhipātā”ti vuccanti. Manussaphassānanti corādiphassānaṃ.

199. In the second verse, “one who walks within limits” refers to walking within the four limits of virtue and so forth. “Attacks of gadflies and other flies” refers to both gadflies and other kinds of flies. For they swoop down from here and there and bite, thus they are called “attackers.” “Human contact” refers to contact with thieves and the like.

Cattāro pariyantāti cattāro mariyādā paricchedā. Antopūtibhāvaṃ paccavekkhamānoti abbhantare kucchitabhāvaṃ sīlavirahitabhāvaṃ olokayamāno. Anto sīlasaṃvarapariyante caratīti sīlasaṃvaraparicchedabbhantare carati vicarati. Mariyādaṃ na bhindatīti sīlamariyādaṃ sīlaparicchedaṃ na kopeti.

The four boundaries are the four limits, the four demarcations. Reflecting on the state of inner impurity means observing the foulness within, the lack of virtue. He dwells within the boundary of virtue's restraint means he moves and acts within the confines of virtue's restraint. He does not break the boundary means he does not violate the boundary of virtue, the demarcation of virtue.

Ādittapariyāyaṃ paccavekkhamānoti ādittadesanaṃ (mahāva. 54; saṃ. ni. 3.61; 4.28) olokento. Akkhabbhañjanavaṇapaṭicchādanaputtamaṃsūpamaṃ paccavekkhamānoti sākaṭikassa [V 0.0373][M 0.0404] akkhabbhañjanaupamañca, kuṭṭhabyādhino vaṇānaṃ paṭicchādanatelapilotikaupamañca, kantārapaṭipannānaṃ jāyampatikānaṃ puttamaṃsakhādanaupamañca (saṃ. ni. 2.63; mi. pa. 6.1.2) olokento. Bhaddekarattavihāraṃ paccavekkhamānoti –

Reflecting on the Fire Sermon means contemplating the discourse on burning (Mahāvagga 54; Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.61; 4.28). Reflecting on the simile of axle grease, the dressing for sores, and a child’s flesh means observing the simile of the cart’s axle grease, the oily rag covering a leper's sores, and the simile of parents eating the flesh of their child in a wilderness (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.63; Milindapañha 6.1.2). Reflecting on the Bhaddekaratta practice means contemplating:

“Atītaṃ nānvāgameyya, nappaṭikaṅkhe anāgataṃ;

Taṃ ve ‘bhaddekaratto’ti, santo ācikkhate munī”ti. (ma. ni. 3.280; netti. 103) –

“One should not pursue the past, nor long for the future. Such a one the peaceful sage calls ‘one with an auspicious night.’”

Evaṃ vuttaṃ bhaddekarattavihāraṃ olokento. Tā uppatitvā uppatitvā khādantīti nippatitvā nippatitvā khādanti.

Thus, he contemplates the Bhaddekaratta practice spoken of in this way. “They leap up again and again and devour,” means “they repeatedly leap down and devour.”

200. Tatiyagāthāya paradhammikā nāma sattasahadhammikavajjā sabbepi te bāhirakā. Kusalānuesīti kusaladhamme anvesamāno.

200. In the third verse, “those of other doctrines” refers to all those who are external, excluding the seven fellow Dhamma-farers. “Seeking the wholesome” means seeking after wholesome qualities.

Satta sahadhammike ṭhapetvāti bhikkhubhikkhunīsikkhamānāsāmaṇerasāmaṇerīupāsakaupāsikāyo vajjetvā. Athāparānipi [P 2.0456] atthi abhisambhotabbānīti aparānipi madditabbāni atthi saṃvijjanti.

“Except for the seven companions in the Dhamma” means excluding monks, nuns, female probationers, male novices, female novices, laymen, and laywomen. “And there are still others to be fully awakened” means there are still others to be subdued, others that exist.

201. Catutthagāthāya ātaṅkaphassenāti rogaphassena. Sītaṃ athuṇhanti sītañca uṇhañca. So tehi phuṭṭho bahudhāti so tehi ātaṅkādīhi anekehi ākārehi phuṭṭho samāno. Anokoti abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇādīnaṃ anokāsabhūto. Abbhantaradhātupakopavasena vāti sarīrabbhantare āpodhātukkhobhavasena vā aññadhātukkhobhavasena vā. Uṇhanti sarīrabbhantare tejodhātukkhobhavasena uṇhaṃ bhavati. Abhisaṅkhārasahagataviññāṇassāti kusalākusalacetanāsampayuttacittassa. Okāsaṃ na karotīti avakāsaṃ patiṭṭhaṃ na karoti. Avatthitasamādānoti otaritvā gāhako.

201. In the fourth verse, “by the touch of disease” means by the touch of illness. “Cold and heat” means both cold and heat. “Afflicted by them in many ways” means he, being afflicted by disease and so on, in many ways. “Without shelter” means not a place for formations, consciousness, etc. “Due to the disturbance of the internal elements” means due to the disturbance of the water element within the body, or the disturbance of other elements. “Heat” means heat arises due to the disturbance of the fire element within the body. “Consciousness accompanied by formations” means the mind associated with wholesome or unwholesome volition. “Does not provide shelter” means it does not make a place or support. “Unsteady in commitment” means one who descends and grasps.

202. Evaṃ “bhikkhuno vijigucchato”tiādīhi tīhi gāthāhi puṭṭhamatthaṃ vissajjetvā idāni “kyāssa byappathayo”tiādinā nayena puṭṭhaṃ vissajjento “theyyaṃ na kāre”tiādimāha. Tattha phasseti phuseyya. Yadāvilattaṃ manaso vijaññāti yaṃ cittassa āvilattaṃ vijāneyya, taṃ sabbaṃ “kaṇhassa pakkho”ti vinodayeyya.

202. Thus, having answered the question posed by the three verses beginning with “For a monk who is disgusted,” now answering the question posed in the manner beginning with “What are his wrong paths,” he says, “He should not steal,” and so on. Here, `phasseti` means he should touch. `Yadāvilattaṃ manaso vijaññāti` means he should recognize the turbidity of the mind. Whatever turbidity of the mind he recognizes, he should dispel it all as “the side of darkness.”

Adinnādānaṃ [V 0.0374][M 0.0405] pahāyāti ettha adinnassa ādānaṃ adinnādānaṃ, parasaṃharaṇaṃ, theyyaṃ corikāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha adinnanti parapariggahitaṃ, yattha paro yathākāmakāritaṃ āpajjanto adaṇḍāraho anupavajjo ca hoti; tasmiṃ parapariggahite parapariggahitasaññino tadādāyakaupakkamasamuṭṭhāpikā theyyacetanā adinnādānaṃ. Taṃ hīne parassa santake appasāvajjaṃ, paṇīte mahāsāvajjaṃ. Kasmā? Vatthupaṇītatāya. Vatthusamatte sati guṇādhikānaṃ santake vatthusmiṃ mahāsāvajjaṃ, taṃ taṃ guṇādhikaṃ upādāya tato tato hīnaguṇassa santake vatthusmiṃ appasāvajjaṃ.

Abandoning taking what is not given—here, taking what is not given is called adinnādāna, seizing another's property, theft, or stealing. In this context, “what is not given” refers to what is possessed by another, in which the owner, if using it as they please, would not deserve punishment or reproach; in that which is possessed by another, one perceiving it as belonging to another, the volition to steal arising as one initiates an attempt to take it, is adinnādāna. This act is of minor fault when the object belonging to another is of little worth, and of major fault when it is of great worth. Why? Because of the worth of the object. When the object is of equal worth, the fault is greater in the case of an object belonging to those of superior qualities; according to those respective superior qualities, the fault is less in the case of an object belonging to one of inferior qualities.

Tassa pañca sambhārā honti – parapariggahitaṃ, parapariggahitasaññitā, theyyacittaṃ, upakkamo, tena haraṇanti. Pahāyāti imaṃ adinnādānacetanāsaṅkhātaṃ dussīlyaṃ pajahitvā. Paṭiviratoti pahīnakālato paṭṭhāya tato dussīlyato orato viratova. Dinnameva ādiyatīti dinnādāyī. Cittenapi dinnameva paṭikaṅkhatīti dinnapāṭikaṅkhī. Thenetīti [P 2.0457] theno, na thenena athenena. Athenattāyeva sucibhūtena. Attanāti attabhāvena, athenaṃ sucibhūtaṃ attabhāvaṃ katvā viharatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Ito paraṃ vuttanayameva.

There are five factors involved: something possessed by another, the perception that it is possessed by another, the intention to steal, the attempt, and the removal by that means. “Abandoning” means abandoning this immoral conduct consisting of the intention of taking what is not given. “Refraining” means from the time of abandoning, one is refraining, abstaining from that immoral conduct. “Taking only what is given” means one who takes only what is given. “Expecting only what is given even in thought” means one who anticipates only what is given. One who steals (`theneti`) is a thief (`theno`); `athenena` means by one who is not a thief. By not being a thief, one has become pure. “By oneself” means by one's own being; it is said that having made one's own being pure and not a thief, one dwells. The rest is as has been said before.

Mettāyanavasena metti. Mettākāro mettāyanā. Mettāya ayitassa mettāsamaṅgino cittassa bhāvo mettāyitattaṃ. Anudayatīti anudayā, rakkhatīti attho. Anudayākāro anudayanā. Anudayitassa bhāvo anudayitattaṃ. Hitassa esanavasena hitesitā. Anukampanavasena anukampā. Sabbehipi imehi padehi upacārappanāppattāva mettā vuttā. Vipulenāti ettha pharaṇavasena vipulatā daṭṭhabbā. Bhūmivasena pana taṃ mahaggataṃ. Paguṇavasena appamāṇaṃ. Sattārammaṇavasena ca appamāṇaṃ. Byāpādapaccatthikappahānena averaṃ. Domanassappahānato abyāpajjaṃ, niddukkhanti vuttaṃ hoti.

Loving-kindness is so called in the sense of loving. The mode of loving is loving. The state of a mind endowed with loving-kindness, possessed of loving, is the state of having loving-kindness. Compassion is so called because it sympathizes; the meaning is that it protects. The mode of compassion is compassion. The state of one who is sympathetic is the state of being compassionate. Wishing well is so called in the sense of seeking the welfare of others. Sympathy is so called in the sense of commiseration. By all these terms, loving-kindness that has reached access and absorption is spoken of. As for 'extensive,' here its extensiveness should be understood in terms of pervasion. But in terms of plane, it is exalted. In terms of proficiency, it is immeasurable. And in terms of having beings as its object, it is immeasurable. It is without enmity because of the abandonment of ill-will as its adversary. Through the abandonment of mental distress, it is without malice; thus it is said to be without suffering.

Āvilanti appasannaṃ. Luḷitanti kalalaṃ. Eritanti asanniṭṭhānaṃ. Ghaṭṭitanti ārammaṇena ghaṭṭanamāpāditaṃ. Calitanti kampamānaṃ. Bhantanti vibbhantaṃ. Avūpasantanti anibbutaṃ.

'Turbid' means unclear. 'Agitated' means stirred up. 'Wavering' means without resolve. 'Disturbed' means brought into collision with an object. 'Trembling' means shaking. 'Bewildered' means distracted. 'Unpeaceful' means not stilled.

Yo [M 0.0406] so māroti evamādīsu mahājanaṃ anatthe niyojetvā māretīti māro. Kaṇhakammattā kaṇho. Kāmāvacarissarattā adhipati. Maraṇaṃ pāpanato antagū. Muñcituṃ appadānaṭṭhena namuci. Mārassa baḷisanti mārabaḷisaṃ. Vaṭṭasannissitaṭṭhena mārassa āmisanti mārāmisaṃ. Vasavattanaṭṭhena mārassa visayoti māravisayo. Gocaraṭṭhena mārassa nivāsoti māranivāso[V 0.0375]. Kāmacāraṃ caraṭṭhena mārassa gocaroti māragocaro. Duppamuñcanaṭṭhena mārassa bandhananti mārabandhanaṃ. Dukkhuddayoti dukkhabandhano.

In 'He who is Māra,' and so on: he is Māra because he kills by engaging a great multitude in what is unwholesome. Because of black deeds, he is Black. Because he is the lord of the sense-sphere, he is the Overlord. Because he brings to death, he is the End-maker. Because of not granting release, he is Namuci. 'Māra's fishhook' is the fishhook of Māra. 'Māra's bait' is the bait of Māra, in the sense of being dependent on the round of rebirth. 'Māra's domain' is the domain of Māra, in the sense of bringing under his power. 'Māra's dwelling-place' is the dwelling-place of Māra, in the sense of being a pasture. 'Māra's range' is the range of Māra, in the sense of wandering in the sphere of sensual pleasures. 'Māra's bond' is the bond of Māra, in the sense of being difficult to be released from. The arising of suffering is the bond of suffering.

203. Mūlampi tesaṃ palikhañña tiṭṭheti tesaṃ kodhātimānānaṃ yaṃ avijjādikaṃ mūlaṃ, tampi palikhaṇitvā tiṭṭheyya. Addhā bhavanto abhisambhaveyyāti etaṃ piyāpiyaṃ abhibhavanto ekaṃseneva abhibhaveyya, na tattha sithilaṃ parakkameyyāti adhippāyo.

203. Regarding 'Even their root, having dug it up, one should stand firm': whatever is the root of their anger and pride, namely ignorance and so on, that too one should dig up and stand firm. Regarding 'Surely one would overcome them': this means that, overcoming the liked and disliked, one should conquer them completely; one should not make a slack effort there—this is the meaning.

Avijjā mūlantiādayo [P 2.0458] avijjā kodhassa upanissayasahajātādivasena mūlaṃ hoti. Anupāyamanasikāro ca asmimāno ca ime dve upanissayavaseneva. Ahirikaanottappauddhaccā ime tayo upanissayasahajātādivasena mūlāni honti, tathā atimānassāpi.

Regarding 'Ignorance is the root,' and so on: ignorance is a root of anger in the sense of being a condition of dependence, co-nascence, and the like. Unwise attention and the conceit 'I am'—these two are roots only in the sense of being a condition of dependence. Shamelessness, fearlessness of wrongdoing, and restlessness—these three are roots in the sense of being conditions of dependence, co-nascence, and the like; likewise for excessive pride.

204. Paññaṃ purakkhatvāti paññaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ katvā. Kalyāṇapītīti kalyāṇapītiyā samannāgato. Caturo sahetha paridevadhammeti anantaragāthāya vuccamāne paridevanīyadhamme saheyya.

204. 'With wisdom put first' means having made wisdom the forerunner. 'With wholesome joy' means endowed with wholesome joy. 'He should endure the four conditions for lamentation' means he should endure the lamentable conditions mentioned in the immediately following verse.

Vicayabahuloti parivīmaṃsanabahulo. Pavicayabahuloti visesena vīmaṃsanabahulo. Pekkhāyanabahuloti ikkhaṇabahulo. Samekkhāyanabahuloti esanabahulo. Vibhūtavihārīti pākaṭaṃ katvā ñātavihārī.

'Abounding in investigation' means abounding in thorough examination. 'Abounding in detailed inquiry' means abounding in examination in a special way. 'Abounding in observation' means abounding in seeing. 'Abounding in reflection' means abounding in seeking. 'Dwelling clearly' means dwelling with clear knowledge, having made it manifest.

Abhikkante paṭikkanteti ettha tāva abhikkantaṃ vuccati gamanaṃ. Paṭikkantaṃ nivattanaṃ. Tadubhayampi catūsu iriyāpathesu labbhati. Gamane tāva purato kāyaṃ abhiharanto abhikkamati nāma. Paṭinivattento paṭikkamati nāma. Ṭhānepi ṭhitakova kāyaṃ purato onamento abhikkamati nāma. Pacchato apanāmento paṭikkamati nāma. Nisajjāyapi nisinnakova āsanassa purimaaṅgābhimukho saṃsaranto abhikkamati nāma. Pacchimaaṅgappadesaṃ pacchā saṃsaranto paṭikkamati nāma. Nipajjāyapi eseva nayo.

In 'advancing and retreating': here, first, 'advancing' is called going forward. 'Retreating' is turning back. Both are found in the four postures. In walking, moving the body forward is called 'advancing.' Turning back is called 'retreating.' In standing, even while standing still, bending the body forward is called 'advancing.' Moving it backward is called 'retreating.' In sitting, even while seated, shifting forward toward the front of the seat is called 'advancing.' Shifting backward toward the back part is called 'retreating.' The same method applies to lying down.

Sampajānakārī [M 0.0407] hotīti sampajaññena sabbakiccakārī, sampajaññameva vā kārī hoti. So hi abhikkantādīsu sampajaññaṃ karoteva, na katthaci sampajaññavirahito hoti. Ālokite vilokiteti ettha pana ālokitaṃ nāma purato pekkhanaṃ. Vilokitaṃ nāma anudisāpekkhanaṃ. Aññānipi heṭṭhā upari pacchato pekkhanavasena olokitaullokitaapalokitāni [V 0.0376] nāma honti. Tāni idha na gahitāni. Sāruppavasena pana imāneva dve gahitāni, iminā vā mukhena sabbāni gahitānevāti.

'He is one who acts with clear comprehension' means he performs all activities with clear comprehension, or he acts with clear comprehension itself. For he practices clear comprehension in advancing, retreating, and so on, and is never devoid of clear comprehension. In 'looking ahead and looking around,' 'looking ahead' means looking forward. 'Looking around' means looking in the various directions. Other actions, in the sense of looking down, up, and back, are called 'looking down,' 'looking up,' and 'looking back.' These are not included here. However, on account of their suitability, only these two are included; or by this expression, all are included.

Samiñjite pasāriteti pabbānaṃ samiñjanapasāraṇe. Saṅghāṭipattacīvaradhāraṇeti ettha saṅghāṭicīvarānaṃ nivāsanapārupanavasena[P 2.0459], pattassa bhikkhāpaṭiggahaṇādivasena paribhogo dhāraṇaṃ nāma. Asitādīsu asiteti piṇḍapātabhojane. Pīteti yāguādipāne. Khāyiteti piṭṭhakhajjakādikhādane. Sāyiteti madhuphāṇitādisāyane. Uccārapassāvakammeti uccārassa ca passāvassa ca karaṇe. Gatādīsu gateti gamane. Ṭhiteti ṭhāne. Nisinneti nisajjāya.

'In bending and stretching' refers to the bending and stretching of the joints. 'In wearing the outer robe, bowl, and inner robe' means the use of the outer and inner robes by way of dressing and covering, and the use of the bowl by way of receiving almsfood and so on; this is called 'wearing.' In 'in eating, etc.,' 'eating' refers to the eating of almsfood. 'Drinking' refers to the drinking of beverages like gruel. 'Chewing' refers to the chewing of hard foods like cakes. 'Tasting' refers to the tasting of lickables like honey and molasses. 'In the act of defecating and urinating' means in the act of defecating and urinating. In 'in going, etc.,' 'going' refers to going. 'Standing' refers to standing. 'Sitting' refers to sitting.

Sutteti sayane. Jāgariteti jāgaraṇe. Bhāsiteti kathane. Tattha upādārūpassa saddāyatanassa appavatte sati bhāsitā nāma na hoti, tasmiṃ pavattante hotīti pariggāhako bhikkhu bhāsite sampajānakārī nāma hoti. Vimuttāyatanasīsena dhammaṃ desentopi bāttiṃsatiracchānakathaṃ pahāya dasakathāvatthunissitaṃ kathaṃ kathentopi bhāsite sampajānakārī nāma. Tuṇhībhāveti akathane. Tattha upādārūpassa saddāyatanassa pavattiyaṃ tuṇhībhāvo nāma natthi, appavattiyaṃ hotīti pariggāhako bhikkhu tuṇhībhāve sampajānakārī nāma hoti. Aṭṭhatiṃsaārammaṇesu cittaruciyaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā nisinnopi dutiyajjhānaṃ samāpannopi tuṇhībhāve sampajānakārī nāma. Ettha ca eko iriyāpatho dvīsu ṭhānesu āgato. So heṭṭhā abhikkante paṭikkanteti ettha bhikkhācāragāmaṃ gacchato āgacchato ca addhānagamanavasena kathito. Gate ṭhiteti ettha vihāre cuṇṇikapāduddhāravasena kathitoti veditabbo. Buddhānussativasenātiādayo heṭṭhā tattha tattha pakāsitā eva.

'In sleeping' means in lying down. 'In being awake' means in waking. 'In speaking' means in talking. Here, when the sound-base, which is derived materiality, is not occurring, there is no speech; when it is occurring, there is. Thus, a monk who comprehends this is called one who acts with clear comprehension in speaking. One who teaches the Dhamma with the topic of the sphere of liberation as the heading, having abandoned the thirty-two kinds of animal talk and speaking on topics based on the ten subjects of discussion, is also called one who acts with clear comprehension in speaking. 'In being silent' means in not talking. Here, when the sound-base, which is derived materiality, is occurring, there is no silence; when it is not occurring, there is. Thus, a monk who comprehends this is called one who acts with clear comprehension in silence. Even one who is seated having taken up a meditation subject from among the thirty-eight objects according to the inclination of his mind, or one who has attained the second jhāna, is called one who acts with clear comprehension in silence. And here, one posture is mentioned in two places. Previously, in 'in advancing and retreating,' it was described in terms of a journey, of going to and returning from a village for alms. In 'in going, standing,' it should be understood as described in terms of pacing and washing the feet in the monastery. 'By way of recollection of the Buddha,' and so on, have already been explained in their respective places.

Aratīti [M 0.0408] ratipaṭikkhepo. Aratitāti aramanākāro. Anabhiratīti anabhiratabhāvo. Anabhiramanāti anabhiramanākāro. Ukkaṇṭhitāti ukkaṇṭhanākāro. Paritassitāti ukkaṇṭhanavaseneva paritassanā.

'Discontent' (arati) is the rejection of delight. 'Discontent' (aratitā) is the mode of not delighting. 'Displeasure' (anabhirati) is the state of not being delighted. 'Not delighting' (anabhiramanā) is the mode of not delighting. 'Restlessness' (ukkaṇṭhitā) is the mode of agitation. 'Torment' (paritassitā) is trembling on account of restlessness.

205. Kiṃ sū asissanti kiṃ bhuñjissāmi. Kuva vā asissanti kuhiṃ vā asissāmi. Dukkhaṃ vata settha kuvajja sessanti imaṃ rattiṃ dukkhaṃ sayiṃ, ajja āgamanarattiṃ kattha sayissaṃ. Ete vitakketi ete piṇḍapātanissite dve, senāsananissite dveti cattāro vitakke. Aniketacārīti apalibodhacārī nittaṇhacārī.

205. 'What will one eat tomorrow?' means 'What shall I consume?' 'Or where will one eat?' means 'Or where shall I eat?' 'Alas, one slept badly! Where will one sleep today?' means 'I slept badly this night; where shall I sleep today, on this coming night?' 'These thoughts' means these four thoughts: two concerning almsfood, and two concerning lodging. 'One who wanders without a home' means one who wanders without impediments, one who wanders without craving.

Phalake [V 0.0377][P 2.0460] vāti vaṅkādiphalakapīṭhe ca. Āgāmirattinti āgamanirattiyaṃ. Ādevaneyyeti visesena devaniyye. Paridevaneyyeti samantato devaniyye.

'Or on a plank' means on a bench or plank, such as a slanted one. 'In the coming night' means on the night of arrival. 'To be lamented' means especially to be lamented. 'To be greatly lamented' means completely to be lamented.

206. Kāleti piṇḍapātakāle piṇḍapātasaṅkhātaṃ annaṃ vā, cīvarakāle cīvarasaṅkhātaṃ vasanaṃ vā laddhā dhammena samenāti adhippāyo. Mattaṃ sa jaññāti pariggahe ca paribhoge ca so pamāṇaṃ jāneyya. Idhāti sāsane, nipātamattameva vā etaṃ. Tosanatthanti santosatthaṃ, etadatthaṃ mattaṃ jāneyyāti vuttaṃ hoti. So tesu guttoti so bhikkhu tesu paccayesu gutto. Yatacārīti saññatavihāro, rakkhitairiyāpatho rakkhitakāyavacīmanodvāro cāti vuttaṃ hoti. “Yaticārī”tipi pāṭho, esoyevattho. Rusitoti rosito. Ghaṭṭitoti vuttaṃ hoti.

206. "Kāle" means: at the time for alms-food, having obtained food designated as alms-food, or at the time for robes, having obtained clothing designated as robes, righteously and properly—this is the intention. "Mattaṃ sa jaññāti" means he should know the measure in both acquisition and use. "Idha" means in this teaching, or it is merely a particle. "Tosanatthaṃ" means for the sake of contentment; for this purpose, it is said, he should know moderation. "So tesu gutto" means that bhikkhu is guarded in those requisites. "Yatacārī" means one of restrained conduct, with guarded deportment, and with the doors of body, speech, and mind protected, it is said. The variant reading "Yaticārī" has the same meaning. "Rusito" means angered. "Ghaṭṭito" means struck, it is said.

Dvīhi kāraṇehi mattaṃ jāneyyāti dvīhi bhāgehi pamāṇaṃ jāneyya. Paṭiggahaṇato vāti parehi diyyamānaggahaṇakālato vā. Paribhogato vāti paribhuñjanakālato vā. Thokepi diyyamāneti appakepi diyyamāne. Kulānudayāyāti kulānaṃ anudayatāya. Kulānurakkhāyāti kulānaṃ anurakkhaṇatthāya. Paṭiggaṇhātīti thokampi gaṇhāti. Bahukepi diyyamāneti anappakepi diyyamāne. Kāyaparihārikaṃ cīvaraṃ paṭiggaṇhātīti ettha kāyaṃ pariharati posetīti kāyaparihārikaṃ. Kucchiparihārikanti kucchiṃ pariharati posetīti kucchiparihārikaṃ. Itarītarapaccayasantosena samannāgatassa bhikkhuno aṭṭha parikkhārā vaṭṭanti tīṇi cīvarāni patto dantakaṭṭhacchedanavāsi ekā sūci kāyabandhanaṃ parissāvananti. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

"He should know moderation for two reasons" means he should know the measure in two ways: either at the time of receiving or at the time of using. "Paṭiggahaṇato vā" means from the time of receiving what is given by others. "Paribhogato vā" means from the time of consumption. "Even if little is given" means even if a small amount is given. "For compassion towards the families" means for not offending the families. "For the protection of families" means for the purpose of protecting the families. "He accepts" means he accepts even a little. "Even if much is given" means even if a not-small amount is given. Regarding the phrase "he accepts a robe for maintaining the body": here, `kāyaparihārikaṃ` means that which maintains and nourishes the body. `Kucchiparihārikaṃ` means that which maintains and nourishes the stomach. For a bhikkhu endowed with contentment with any requisite whatsoever, eight requisites are suitable: three robes, a bowl, an adze for cutting tooth-sticks, a needle, a belt, and a water strainer. And this has been said:

“Ticīvarañca [M 0.0409] patto ca, vāsi sūci ca bandhanaṃ;

Parissāvanena aṭṭhete, yuttayogassa bhikkhuno”ti. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.215; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.294; 2.349; a. ni. aṭṭha. 2.4.198);

"Three robes and a bowl, an adze, a needle, and a belt; with a water strainer—these eight are fitting for a diligent bhikkhu."

Te sabbe kāyaparihārikāpi honti kucchiparihārikāpi. Kathaṃ? Ticīvaraṃ tāva nivāsetvā ca pārupitvā ca vicaraṇakāle kāyaṃ [P 2.0461] pariharati posetīti kāyaparihārikaṃ hoti. Cīvarakaṇṇena udakaṃ parissāvetvā pivanakāle khāditabbaphalāphalaggahaṇakāle ca kucchiṃ pariharati posetīti kucchiparihārikaṃ hoti.

All of them are both for the maintenance of the body and for the maintenance of the stomach. How? Firstly, the three robes, having been worn as a lower garment and draped as an upper garment, maintain and nourish the body while one is wandering about; thus they are for the maintenance of the body. And when drinking water after straining it with the corner of a robe, or when taking edible fruits and non-fruits, they maintain and nourish the stomach; thus they are for the maintenance of the stomach.

Pattopi tena udakaṃ uddharitvā nhānakāle kuṭiparibhaṇḍakaraṇakāle ca kāyaparihāriko hoti[V 0.0378]. Āhāraṃ gahetvā bhuñjanakāle kucchiparihāriko. Vāsipi tāya dantakaṭṭhacchedanakāle mañcapīṭhānaṃ aṅgapādacīvarakuṭidaṇḍakasajjanakāle ca kāyaparihārikā hoti. Ucchucchedananāḷikerāditacchanakāle kucchiparihārikā. Sūci cīvarasibbanakāle kāyaparihārikā hoti. Pūvaṃ vā phalaṃ vā vijjhitvā khādanakāle kucchiparihārikā. Kāyabandhanaṃ bandhitvā vicaraṇakāle kāyaparihārikaṃ. Ucchuādīni bandhitvā gahaṇakāle kucchiparihārikaṃ. Parissāvanaṃ tena udakaṃ parissāvetvā nhānakāle senāsanaparibhaṇḍakaraṇakāle ca kāyaparihārikaṃ, pānīyapāṇakaparissāvanakāle teneva tilataṇḍulaputhukādīni gahetvā khādanakāle ca kucchiparihārikaṃ.

The bowl, too, is for the maintenance of the body when one draws water with it for bathing or for preparing the hut's furnishings. It is for the maintenance of the stomach when one takes food and eats. The adze, too, is for the maintenance of the body when used for cutting tooth-sticks or for preparing the legs of beds and chairs and robe-racks. It is for the maintenance of the stomach when used for cutting sugarcane or trimming coconuts and the like. The needle is for the maintenance of the body when sewing robes. It is for the maintenance of the stomach when used to pierce a cake or fruit for eating. The belt is for the maintenance of the body when one fastens it and walks about. It is for the maintenance of the stomach when one uses it to tie up and carry sugarcane and other such items. The strainer is for the maintenance of the body when one strains water with it for bathing or for preparing the lodging's furnishings. It is for the maintenance of the stomach when one strains drinking water and living creatures, and when one uses it to take and eat sesame seeds, rice, flattened rice, and the like.

Paṭisaṅkhāyonisoti upāyena pathena paṭisaṅkhāya ñatvā, paccavekkhitvāti attho. Ettha ca “sītassa paṭighātāyā”tiādinā nayena vuttapaccavekkhaṇameva yoniso paṭisaṅkhāti veditabbaṃ. Tattha cīvaranti antaravāsakādīsu yaṃkiñci. Paṭisevatīti paribhuñjati nivāseti vā pārupati vā. Yāvadevāti payojanāvadhiparicchedaniyamavacanaṃ. Ettakameva hi yogino cīvarapaṭisevane payojanaṃ, yadidaṃ sītassa paṭighātāyātiādi, na ito bhiyyo. Sītassāti ajjhattadhātukkhobhavasena vā bahiddhā utupariṇāmanavasena vā uppannassa yassa kassaci sītassa.

“Wisely reflecting” means having known by reflecting by means of a method, by a path; the meaning is “having reviewed.” Here, the reviewing spoken of in the manner of “for warding off cold,” and so on, should be known as “wise reflection.” In this context, “robe” refers to any garment, such as the inner robe and so on. “Uses” means makes use of, or wears as a lower garment, or drapes as an upper garment. “Only for” is a word indicating the purpose, the limit, the demarcation, and the restriction. For a yogī, the purpose in using a robe is just this much—namely, that it is for warding off cold, and so on—no more than that. “Of cold” refers to any cold whatsoever that has arisen, whether due to a disturbance of the internal elements or due to an external change of season.

Paṭighātāyāti paṭihananatthaṃ. Yathā sarīre ābādhaṃ na uppādeti, evaṃ tassa vinodanatthaṃ. Sītabbhāhate hi sarīre vikkhittacitto yoniso padahituṃ na sakkoti. Tasmā sītassa paṭighātāya cīvaraṃ sevitabbanti [M 0.0410] bhagavā anuññāsi. Esa nayo sabbattha. Kevalañhettha uṇhassāti aggisantāpassa, tassa vanadāhādīsu sambhavo veditabbo. Ḍaṃsamakasavātātapasarīsapasamphassānanti ettha pana ḍaṃsāti ḍaṃsanamakkhikā. “Andhamakkhikā”tipi vuccanti. Makasāti makasā eva. Vātāti sarajaarajādibhedā[P 2.0462]. Ātapoti sūriyātapo. Sarīsapāti ye keci sarantā gacchanti dīghajātikā sappādayo, tesaṃ daṭṭhasamphasso ca phuṭṭhasamphasso cāti duvidho samphasso; sopi cīvaraṃ pārupitvā nisinnaṃ na bādhati. Tasmā tādisesu ṭhānesu tesaṃ paṭighātatthāya paṭisevati. Yāvadevāti puna etassa vacanaṃ niyatapayojanāvadhiparicchedadassanatthaṃ. Hirikopīnapaṭicchādanatthanti niyatapayojanaṃ, itarāni kadāci honti. Tattha hirikopīnanti taṃ taṃ sambādhaṭṭhānaṃ. Yasmiṃ yasmiñhi aṅge vivariyamāne hirī kuppati vinassati, taṃ taṃ hiriṃ kopanato hirikopīnanti vuccati. Tassa ca hirikopīnassa paṭicchādanatthanti hirikopīnapaṭicchādanatthaṃ. “Hirikopīnaṃ paṭicchādanattha”ntipi pāṭho.

“For warding off” means for the purpose of repelling. So that it does not cause an affliction in the body, thus it serves to dispel it. For when the body is afflicted by cold, the mind becomes distracted and one cannot strive wisely. Therefore, the Blessed One permitted that robes should be used to ward off cold. This principle applies everywhere. Only here, “of heat” refers to the scorching heat of fire; its occurrence should be understood in forest fires and the like. Regarding “the contact of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things”: here, “gadflies” (ḍaṃsa) refers to biting flies; they are also called “blind flies.” “Mosquitoes” (makasa) means mosquitoes. “Wind” includes the varieties with and without dust. “Sun” means the sun’s heat. “Creeping things” refers to any long-bodied creatures that move by slithering, such as snakes. Their contact is twofold: contact by being bitten and contact by being touched. Even this does not trouble one who is seated wrapped in a robe. Therefore, in such places, one uses the robe for the purpose of warding them off. The repetition of the word “only for” is for showing the limitation to a definite purpose. “For the purpose of covering the private parts out of modesty” is the definite purpose; the others are occasional. Here, “private parts” (hirikopīna) refers to this or that private area. For whichever limb, when exposed, causes modesty to be agitated or lost, that is called the “private parts” because it agitates modesty. “For the purpose of covering those private parts” is the meaning of `hirikopīnapaṭicchādanatthaṃ`. There is also the reading: `Hirikopīnaṃ paṭicchādanattha`.

Piṇḍapātanti [V 0.0379] yaṃkiñci āhāraṃ. Yo hi koci āhāro bhikkhuno piṇḍolyena patte patitattā “piṇḍapāto”ti vuccati. Piṇḍānaṃ vā pāto piṇḍapāto, tattha tattha laddhānaṃ bhikkhānaṃ sannipāto, samūhoti vuttaṃ hoti. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayameva.

“Almsfood” means any food whatsoever. For whatever food has fallen into a bhikkhu’s bowl by way of lumps of alms is called “almsfood.” Or, `piṇḍapāto` is the “falling of lumps,” meaning the gathering, the collection of alms obtained here and there, it is said. The rest is just as will be explained below.

Senāsananti sayanañca āsanañca. Yattha yattha hi seti vihāre vā aḍḍhayogādimhi vā, taṃ senaṃ. Yattha yattha āsati nisīdati, taṃ āsanaṃ, taṃ ekato katvā “senāsana”nti vuccati. Utuparissayavinodanapaṭisallānārāmatthanti parisahanaṭṭhena utuyeva utuparissayo. Utuparissayassa vinodanatthañca paṭisallānārāmatthañca. Yo sarīrābādhacittavikkhepakaro asappāyo utu senāsanapaṭisevanena vinodetabbo hoti, tassa vinodanatthaṃ ekībhāvasukhatthañcāti vuttaṃ hoti. Kāmañca sītapaṭighātādināva utuparissayavinodanaṃ vuttameva. Yathā pana cīvarapaṭisevane “hirikopīnapaṭicchādanaṃ niyatapayojanaṃ, itarāni kadāci kadāci bhavantī”ti vuttaṃ, evamidhāpi niyatautuparissayavinodanaṃ sandhāya idaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Atha vā ayaṃ vuttappakāro utu utuyeva. Parissayo pana duvidho pākaṭaparissayo ca paṭicchannaparissayo ca. Tattha [M 0.0411] pākaṭaparissayo sīhabyagghādayo, paṭicchannaparissayo rāgadosādayo. Te yattha apariguttiyā ca asappāyarūpadassanādinā ca ābādhaṃ na karonti, taṃ senāsanaṃ evaṃ jānitvā paccavekkhitvā paṭisevanto [P 2.0463] bhikkhu paṭisaṅkhā yoniso senāsanaṃ utuparissayavinodanatthaṃ paṭisevatīti veditabbo.

‘A dwelling place’ means a place for lying down and a place for sitting. Wherever one lies down, whether in a monastery or in a half-gabled house and so on, that is a place for lying down. Wherever one sits down, that is a place for sitting. Combining these, it is called ‘senāsana’ (a dwelling place). ‘For dispelling the discomfort of the seasons and for delight in seclusion’ means that the seasonal discomfort is the season itself, in the sense of that which is to be endured. The aim is both to dispel the discomfort of the seasons and to find delight in seclusion. Any unsuitable season that causes bodily affliction or mental distraction is to be dispelled by using a dwelling place; thus, it is said to be for dispelling that and for the happiness of solitude. And indeed, the dispelling of seasonal discomfort has already been stated by way of warding off cold and so on. Just as in the use of robes it was said, ‘covering the sense of shame and the private parts is the definite purpose, while the others occur occasionally,’ so too here, this should be understood as having been said with reference to the definite dispelling of seasonal discomfort. Or alternatively, the season is just the season of the kind described. Discomfort, however, is of two kinds: manifest discomfort and concealed discomfort. Manifest discomfort includes dangers like lions and tigers, while concealed discomfort includes defilements like lust and hatred. A monk who uses a dwelling place, having known and reflected upon it as a place where these do not cause affliction through lack of protection or through seeing unsuitable forms and so on, should be understood as one who, with wise reflection, uses the dwelling place for the purpose of dispelling the discomfort of the seasons.

Gilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhāranti ettha rogassa paṭiayanaṭṭhena paccayo, paccanīkagamanaṭṭhenāti attho. Yassa kassaci sappāyassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Bhisakkassa kammaṃ tena anuññātattāti bhesajjaṃ. Gilānapaccayova bhesajjaṃ gilānapaccayabhesajjaṃ, yaṃ kiñci gilānassa sappāyaṃ bhisakkakammaṃ telamadhuphāṇitādīti vuttaṃ hoti. Parikkhāroti pana “sattahi nagaraparikkhārehi suparikkhattaṃ hotī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 7.67) parivāro vuccati. “Ratho sīlaparikkhāro, jhānakkho cakkavīriyo”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 5.4) alaṅkāro. “Ye ca kho ime pabbajitena jīvitaparikkhārā samudānetabbā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.191-192) sambhāro. Idha pana sambhāropi parivāropi vaṭṭati. Tañca gilānapaccayabhesajjaṃ jīvitassa parivāropi hoti, jīvitanāsakābādhuppattiyā antaraṃ adatvā rakkhaṇato sambhāropi. Yathāciraṃ pavattati, evamassa kāraṇabhāvato; tasmā “parikkhāro”ti vuccati. Evaṃ gilānapaccayabhesajjañca taṃ parikkhāro cāti gilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhāro, taṃ [V 0.0380] gilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhāraṃ. Gilānassa yaṃ kiñci sappāyaṃ bhisakkānuññātaṃ telamadhuphāṇitādijīvitaparikkhāranti vuttaṃ hoti.

‘Requisites of medicine for the sick’: here, ‘requisite’ (paccaya) means that which counteracts illness, that is, that which opposes it. This is a designation for whatever is suitable. ‘Medicine’ (bhesajja) is so called because it is permitted by that which is the physician's work. Medicine that is a requisite for the sick is ‘requisite-medicine for the sick’; this means whatever is suitable for the sick and is the work of a physician, such as oil, honey, and molasses. As for ‘requisite’ (parikkhāra): in passages such as ‘well-fortified with seven city requisites,’ it means ‘retinue’ (parivāra). In passages such as ‘virtue is the chariot’s requisite, meditative absorption the axle, energy the wheel,’ it means ‘adornment’ (alaṅkāra). In passages such as ‘these are the requisites for life that a renunciant should collect,’ it means ‘equipment’ (sambhāra). Here, however, both ‘equipment’ and ‘retinue’ are applicable. And this requisite-medicine for the sick serves both as a retinue for life and as equipment for it, because it protects life by not giving an opportunity for the arising of life-destroying ailments. Because it is a cause for life to last long, it is therefore called a ‘requisite’ (parikkhāra). Thus, it is both medicine that is a requisite for the sick and a requisite (parikkhāra); hence, ‘requisites of medicine for the sick.’ This means whatever is suitable for the sick, permitted by a physician, such as oil, honey, and molasses, which are requisites for life.

Uppannānanti jātānaṃ bhūtānaṃ nibbattānaṃ. Veyyābādhikānanti ettha byābādhoti dhātukkhobho taṃsamuṭṭhānā ca kuṭṭhagaṇḍapīḷakādayo, byābādhato uppannattā veyyābādhikā. Vedanānanti dukkhavedanā, akusalavipākavedanā, tāsaṃ veyyābādhikānaṃ vedanānaṃ. Abyābajjhaparamatāyāti niddukkhaparamatāya. Yāva taṃ dukkhaṃ sabbaṃ pahīnaṃ hoti, tāvāti attho.

‘Uppannānaṃ’ means of those that have arisen, come into being, or been produced. ‘Veyyābādhikānaṃ’: here, ‘byābādha’ (affliction) means a disturbance of the elements and the conditions arising therefrom, such as leprosy, boils, and pimples. Because they arise from affliction, they are called ‘veyyābādhikā’ (afflicting). ‘Vedanānaṃ’ means of painful feelings, of feelings that are the result of unwholesome kamma; thus the full phrase means ‘of those afflicting feelings’. ‘Abyābajjhaparamatāya’ means for the supreme state of non-affliction, which is the supreme state of being without suffering. The meaning is: until all that suffering is abandoned.

Santuṭṭho hotīti paccayasantosena santuṭṭho hoti. Itarītarena cīvarenāti thūlasukhumalūkhapaṇītathirajiṇṇānaṃ yena kenaci. Atha kho yathāladdhādīnaṃ itarītarena yena kenaci santuṭṭho hotīti [M 0.0412] attho. Cīvarasmiñhi tayo [P 2.0464] santosā yathālābhasantoso yathābalasantoso yathāsāruppasantosoti. Piṇḍapātādīsupi eseva nayo.

‘He is content’ means he is content with regard to the requisites. ‘With any kind of robe’ means with any whatsoever, whether coarse, fine, rough, refined, firm, or worn out. Moreover, the meaning is that he is content with whatever is obtained and so on, with any kind whatsoever. For regarding robes, there are three kinds of contentment: contentment with what is obtained, contentment according to one’s ability, and contentment with what is appropriate. The same principle applies to almsfood and other requisites.

Vaṇṇavādīti eko santuṭṭho hoti, santosassa vaṇṇaṃ na katheti, eko na santuṭṭho hoti, santosassa vaṇṇaṃ katheti, eko neva santuṭṭho hoti, na santosassa vaṇṇaṃ katheti, eko santuṭṭho ca hoti, santosassa vaṇṇaṃ katheti, taṃ dassetuṃ “itarītaracīvarasantuṭṭhiyā ca vaṇṇavādī”ti vuttaṃ. Anesananti dūteyyapahīnagamanānuyogappabhedaṃ nānappakāraṃ anesanaṃ. Appatirūpanti ayuttaṃ. Aladdhā cāti alabhitvā. Yathā ekacco “kathaṃ nu kho cīvaraṃ labhissāmī”ti puññavantehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ ekato hutvā kohaññaṃ karonto uttassati paritassati, santuṭṭho bhikkhu evaṃ aladdhā ca cīvaraṃ na paritassati. Laddhā cāti dhammena samena labhitvā. Agadhitoti vigatalobhavanto. Amucchitoti adhimattataṇhāya mucchaṃ anāpanno. Anajjhāpannoti taṇhāya anotthaṭo apariyonaddho. Ādīnavadassāvīti anesanāpattiyañca gadhitaparibhoge ca ādīnavaṃ passamāno. Nissaraṇapaññoti “yāvadeva sītassa paṭighātāyā”ti (ma. ni. 1.23) vuttaṃ nissaraṇaṃ eva pajānanto. Itarītaracīvarasantuṭṭhiyāti yena kenaci cīvarena santuṭṭhiyā. Nevattānukkaṃsetīti “ahaṃ paṃsukūliko, mayā upasampadamāḷeyeva paṃsukūlikaṅgaṃ gahitaṃ, ko mayā sadiso atthī”ti attukkaṃsanaṃ na karoti. Na paraṃ vambhetīti “ime panaññe bhikkhū na paṃsukūlikā”ti vā “paṃsukūlikamattampi etesaṃ natthī”ti vā evaṃ paraṃ na vambheti.

‘A speaker of praise’: one person is content but does not speak praise of contentment; another is not content but speaks praise of contentment; another is neither content nor speaks praise of contentment; and another is both content and speaks praise of contentment. To show this last one, it is said: “and is a speaker of praise for contentment with any kind of robe.” ‘Improper seeking’ means the various kinds of improper seeking, such as engaging in messenger work or going on errands. ‘Unsuitable’ means improper. ‘Not having obtained’: just as a certain person, thinking, “How shall I obtain a robe?” associates with virtuous monks and, acting deceitfully, becomes agitated and anxious, a contented monk, not having obtained a robe, does not become anxious. ‘Having obtained’ means having acquired it rightfully and properly. ‘Not greedy’ means being without greed. ‘Not infatuated’ means not having fallen into the swoon of excessive craving. ‘Not attached’ means not being overwhelmed or enveloped by craving. ‘Seeing the danger’ means seeing the danger both in an offense of improper seeking and in the greedy use of requisites. ‘Wise about the escape’ means understanding the escape stated as: “only for the purpose of warding off the cold.” ‘Contentment with any kind of robe’ means contentment with whatever robe. ‘He does not exalt himself’: he does not exalt himself by thinking, “I am a rag-robe wearer; I undertook the rag-robe practice right at the time of my higher ordination. Who is like me?” ‘He does not disparage others’: he does not disparage others by thinking, “These other monks are not rag-robe wearers,” or “They do not even have the slightest practice of wearing rag-robes.”

Yo [V 0.0381] hi tattha dakkhoti yo tasmiṃ cīvarasantose vaṇṇavādī, tāsu vā dakkho cheko byatto. Analasoti sātaccakiriyāya ālasiyavirahito. Sampajāno paṭissatoti sampajānapaññāya ceva satiyā ca yutto. Porāṇeti na adhunuppattike. Aggaññeti “aggo”ti jānitabbe. Ariyavaṃse ṭhitoti ariyānaṃ vaṃse patiṭṭhito. Ariyavaṃsoti ca yathā hi khattiyavaṃso brāhmaṇavaṃso vessavaṃso suddavaṃso [M 0.0413] samaṇavaṃso kulavaṃso rājavaṃso, evaṃ ayampi aṭṭhamo ariyavaṃso ariyatanti ariyapaveṇī nāma hoti. So kho panāyaṃ ariyavaṃso imesaṃ vaṃsānaṃ mūlagandhādīnaṃ kāḷānusārigandhādayo viya aggamakkhāyati. Ke pana te ariyā yesaṃ eso vaṃsoti? Ariyā vuccanti buddhā ca paccekabuddhā ca tathāgatasāvakā ca, etesaṃ ariyānaṃ vaṃsoti ariyavaṃso. Ito pubbe hi satasahassakappādikānaṃ catunnaṃ asaṅkhyeyyānaṃ [P 2.0465] matthake taṇhaṅkaro meṅkero saraṇaṅkaro dīpaṅkaroti cattāro buddhā uppannā, te ariyā, tesaṃ ariyānaṃ vaṃsoti ariyavaṃso. Tesaṃ buddhānaṃ parinibbānato aparabhāge ekaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ atikkamitvā koṇḍañño nāma buddho uppanno…pe… imasmiṃ kappe kakusandho koṇāgamano kassapo amhākaṃ bhagavā gotamoti cattāro buddhā uppannā, tesaṃ ariyānaṃ vaṃsoti ariyavaṃso. Api ca atītānāgatapaccuppannānaṃ sabbabuddhapaccekabuddhasāvakānaṃ ariyānaṃ vaṃsoti ariyavaṃso, tasmiṃ ariyavaṃse patiṭṭhito.

Yo hi tattha dakkho: whoever is skilled in that, whoever is a speaker of praise regarding contentment with robes, or is skilled, expert, and accomplished in those matters. Analaso: free from laziness in continuous effort. Sampajāno paṭissato: endowed with clear comprehending wisdom and mindfulness. Porāṇa: not newly arisen. Aggañña: should be understood as “the best.” Ariyavaṃse ṭhito: established in the lineage of the noble ones. And what is the noble lineage? Just as there are the lineages of warriors, brahmins, merchants, laborers, ascetics, families, and kings, so too this eighth lineage is called the noble lineage, the noble tradition. Indeed, this noble lineage is declared the foremost among these lineages, just as the scent of black sandalwood and others is foremost among root scents and others. But who are these noble ones whose lineage this is? The noble ones are called the Buddhas, the Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Tathāgata; this is their lineage, the noble lineage. For before this, at the head of four incalculable ages and a hundred thousand eons, four Buddhas arose: Taṇhaṅkara, Medhaṅkara, Saraṇaṅkara, and Dīpaṅkara. They were noble, and their lineage is the noble lineage. After the parinibbāna of those Buddhas, one incalculable age passed, and then the Buddha named Koṇḍañña arose… and so on… in this age, four Buddhas have arisen: Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, Kassapa, and our Blessed One Gotama. Their lineage is the noble lineage. Moreover, the lineage of all past, future, and present Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples is the noble lineage. He is established in that noble lineage.

Itarītarena piṇḍapātenāti yena kenaci piṇḍapātena. Senāsanādīsupi eseva nayo. Āyatanesūti cakkhādīsu āyatanesu.

Itarītarena piṇḍapātena: with any kind of almsfood. The same principle applies to lodgings and so forth. Āyatanesu: in the sense bases, such as the eye and so on.

Yatoti saññato. Yattoti yattavā. Paṭiyattoti ativiya yattavā. Guttoti rakkhito. Gopitoti mañjūsāya viya paṭṭhapito. Rakkhitoti paṭisāmito. Saṃvutoti dvārasaṃvaraṇena pihito. Khuṃsitoti garahito. Vambhitoti apasādito. Ghaṭṭitoti ghaṭṭanamāpādito. Garahitoti avamaññito. Upavaditoti akkosito.

Yato: controlled. Yatto: restrained. Paṭiyatto: exceedingly restrained. Gutto: protected. Gopito: placed as if in a casket. Rakkhito: secured. Saṃvuto: closed by the restraint of the sense doors. Khuṃsito: censured. Vambhito: rejected. Ghaṭṭito: subjected to friction. Garahito: scorned. Upavadito: insulted.

Pharusenāti mammacchedanavacanena. Kakkhaḷenāti dāruṇena. Nappaṭivajjāti paṭippharitvā na katheyya.

Pharusena: with speech that cuts to the quick. Kakkhaḷena: with fierce speech. Nappaṭivajja: does not reply in kind.

207. Jhānānuyuttoti anuppannuppādanena uppannasevanena ca jhānena anuyutto. Upekkhamārabbha samāhitattoti catutthajjhānupekkhaṃ uppādetvā samāhitacitto. Takkāsayaṃ kukkuccañcupacchindeti [V 0.0382] kāmavitakkādivitakkañca kāmasaññādikaṃ vitakkassa āsayañca hatthakukkuccādikukkuccañca upacchindeyya.

207. Jhānānuyutto: being devoted to jhāna by arousing the unarisen and cultivating the arisen. Upekkhamārabbha samāhitatto: having a mind composed by arousing the equanimity of the fourth jhāna. Takkāsayaṃ kukkuccañcupacchindeti: he should cut off thoughts such as sensual thoughts, the basis of thought such as sensual perceptions, as well as remorse, such as remorse over actions and the like.

Anuppannassa [M 0.0414] vā paṭhamassa jhānassa uppādāyāti tasmiṃ attabhāve anuppannassa vā uppajjitvā parihīnassa vā paṭhamajjhānassa uppādanatthaṃ attano santāne paṭilābhatthaṃ. Uppannaṃ vā paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ āsevatītiādīsu ettha ādarena sevati paguṇaṃ karoti bhāveti vaḍḍheti bahulīkaroti punappunaṃ karoti.

Anuppannassa vā paṭhamassa jhānassa uppādāya: to arouse the first jhāna, which has not yet arisen in that existence, or to regain the first jhāna, which having arisen, has declined, for the sake of attaining it in one’s own continuity. Uppannaṃ vā paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ āsevati, and so on, means here: he attends to it carefully, makes it practiced, develops it, increases it, makes it abundant, practices it repeatedly.

Upekkhāti [P 2.0466] catutthajjhāne uppannā tatramajjhattupekkhā. Upekkhāti sabhāvapadaṃ. Upekkhanāti upapattito ikkhanākāro. Ajjhupekkhanāti adhikā hutvā ikkhanā. Cittasamatāti cittassa samatā cittassa ūnātirittataṃ vajjetvā samabhāvo. Cittappassaddhatāti cittassa appagabbhatā, athaddhabhāvoti attho. Majjhattatā cittassāti na sattassa na posassa, cittassa majjhattabhāvoti attho. Catutthe jhāne upekkhaṃ ārabbhāti catutthasmiṃ jhānasmiṃ uppannaṃ tatramajjhattupekkhaṃ paṭicca. Ekaggacittoti ekārammaṇe pavattacitto. Avikkhittacittoti uddhaccavirahito na vikkhittacitto.

Upekkhā: refers to the equanimity of impartiality arisen in the fourth jhāna. Upekkhā: is a term denoting its intrinsic nature. Upekkhanā: means the mode of seeing by way of occurrence. Ajjhupekkhana: means seeing with dominance. Cittasamatā: is the evenness of mind, the state of the mind being balanced, avoiding deficiency or excess. Cittappassaddhatā: means the mind's non-agitation, meaning its non-rigidity. Majjhattatā cittassa: refers to the mind, not a being or a person; it means the mind's state of neutrality. Catutthe jhāne upekkhaṃ ārabbha: means depending on the equanimity of impartiality arisen in the fourth jhāna. Ekaggacitto: means the mind is focused on a single object. Avikkhittacitto: means free from restlessness; the mind is not scattered.

Nava vitakkā vuttanayā eva. Kāmavitakkānaṃ kāmasaññāsayoti kāmavitakkaṃ vitakkentassa uppannā kāmasaññā tesaṃ vitakkānaṃ āsayo vasanokāsoti kāmasaññāsayo. Byāpādavitakkādīsupi eseva nayo.

The nine kinds of thoughts are as previously explained. Kāmavitakkānaṃ kāmasaññāsayo: means the sensual perception that arises in one who thinks a sensual thought is the basis, the dwelling place, for those thoughts; thus it is the basis of sensual perception. The same principle applies to thoughts of ill-will and the like.

208. Cudito vacībhi satimābhinandeti upajjhāyādīhi vācāhi codito samāno satimā hutvā taṃ codanaṃ abhinandeyya. Vācaṃ pamuñce kusalanti ñāṇasamuṭṭhitaṃ vācaṃ pamuñceyya. Nātivelanti ativelaṃ pana vācaṃ kālavelañca sīlavelañca atikkantaṃ nappamuñceyya. Janavādadhammāyāti janaparivādakathāya. Na cetayeyyāti cetanaṃ na uppādeyya.

208. Cudito vacībhi satimābhinandeti: when admonished by the words of his teacher or others, being mindful, he should welcome that admonishment. Vācaṃ pamuñce kusalaṃ: he should utter speech arisen from knowledge. Nātivelaṃ: he should not utter speech that is beyond the proper time or beyond moral bounds. Janavādadhammāya: for talk that leads to public criticism. Na cetayeyya: he should not give rise to intention.

Idaṃ te appattanti idaṃ tava na pattaṃ. Asāruppanti tava payogaṃ asāruppaṃ. Asīlaṭṭhanti tava payogaṃ na sīle patiṭṭhanti asīlaṭṭhaṃ, sīle ṭhitassa payogaṃ na hotīti vuttaṃ hoti. Keci “asiliṭṭha”nti paṭhanti, amaṭṭhavacananti atthaṃ vaṇṇayanti.

Idaṃ te appattaṃ: this has not been achieved by you. Asāruppaṃ: your effort is unsuitable. Asīlaṭṭhaṃ: your effort is not established in virtue, or is unvirtuous; it is said that for one established in virtue, such a practice does not occur. Some read it as “asiliṭṭha,” explaining it as meaning unpolished speech.

Nidhīnanti tattha tattha nidahitvā ṭhapitānaṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇādipūrānaṃ nidhikumbhīnaṃ. Pavattāranti [V 0.0383] kicchajīvike [P 2.0467] duggatamanusse anukampaṃ katvā “ehi sukhena te [M 0.0415] jīvanupāyaṃ dassessāmī”ti nidhiṭṭhānaṃ netvā hatthaṃ pasāretvā “imaṃ gahetvā sukhaṃ jīvā”ti ācikkhitāraṃ viya. Vajjadassinanti dve vajjadassino “iminā naṃ asāruppena vā khalitena vā saṅghamajjhe niggaṇhissāmī”ti randhagavesako ca aññātaṃ ñāpanatthāya ñātaṃ anuggaṇhatthāya sīlādinā cassa vuddhikāmatāya taṃ taṃ vajjaṃ olokanena ullapanasabhāvasaṇṭhito ca. Ayaṃ idha adhippeto. Yathā hi duggatamanusso “imaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti tajjetvā poṭṭhetvāpi nidhiṃ dassente kopaṃ na karoti, pamuditova hoti, evameva evarūpe puggale asāruppaṃ vā khalitaṃ vā disvā ācikkhante kopo na kātabbo, tuṭṭheneva bhavitabbaṃ. “Bhante mahantaṃ vo kataṃ kammaṃ, mayhaṃ ācariyupajjhāyaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā ovadantehi punapi maṃ vadeyyāthā”ti pavāretabbameva. Niggayhavādinti ekacco hi saddhivihārikādīnaṃ asāruppaṃ vā khalitaṃ vā disvā “ayaṃ me mukhodakadānādīhi sakkaccaṃ upaṭṭhahati, sace naṃ vakkhāmi, na maṃ upaṭṭhahissati, evaṃ mama parihāni bhavissatī”ti vattuṃ avisahanto na niggayhavādī nāma hoti, so imasmiṃ sāsane kacavaraṃ ākirati. Yo pana tathārūpaṃ vajjaṃ disvā vajjānurūpaṃ tajjetvā paṇāmento daṇḍakammaṃ karonto vihārā nīharanto sikkhāpeti, ayaṃ niggayhavādī nāma seyyathāpi sammāsambuddho. Vuttañhetaṃ – “niggayha niggayhāhaṃ, ānanda, vakkhāmi, pavayha pavayhāhaṃ, ānanda, vakkhāmi, yo sāro so ṭhassatī”ti (ma. ni. 3.196). Medhāvinti dhammojapaññāya samannāgataṃ. Tādisanti evarūpaṃ paṇḍitaṃ bhajeyya payirupāseyya. Tādisañhi ācariyaṃ bhajamānassa antevāsikassa seyyova hoti, na pāpiyo, vuḍḍhiyeva hoti, no parihānīti.

"Of treasures" refers to pots of treasure filled with gold, silver, and other valuables, which have been buried and stored here and there. "One who points out" is like someone who, out of compassion for a poor and struggling person, says, "Come, I will show you a means to live comfortably," leads them to the place where the treasure is, extends their hand, and says, "Take this and live happily." "One who sees faults": there are two kinds of fault-seers. The first is a fault-finder who seeks an opportunity, thinking, 'I will reprimand them in the midst of the Sangha for this impropriety or mistake.' The second is one who—for the purpose of making known what is unknown, for reinforcing what is known, and out of a desire for that person's growth in virtue and so on—is established in the nature of pointing out faults by observing them. The latter is intended here. Just as a poor person does not get angry when someone threatens or even strikes them while showing them a treasure, but instead rejoices, in the same way, when such a person points out an impropriety or a mistake, one should not become angry but should be pleased. One should say, "Venerable sir, you have done me a great service. Standing in the place of my teachers and preceptors, you have advised me. Please speak to me again." One should make such an invitation. "One who speaks reprovingly": a certain person, upon seeing an impropriety or a mistake in their co-residents, thinks, "This person attends to me respectfully with offerings of water for washing the face and so on. If I speak to them, they will no longer attend to me, and thus I will suffer a loss." Being unable to speak, they are not called "one who speaks reprovingly." Such a person scatters rubbish in this dispensation. But one who, upon seeing such a fault, trains them by reproving, disciplining, imposing a penalty, or expelling them from the monastery in accordance with the fault—this one is called "one who speaks reprovingly," just like the Perfectly Enlightened One. For it is said: "Reproving and reproving, Ānanda, I shall speak; sifting and sifting, Ānanda, I shall speak. What is sound will remain." "Wise" means endowed with wisdom that has the essence of the Dhamma. "Such a one" refers to such a wise person whom one should associate with and attend upon. For a disciple who associates with such a teacher, it is better, not worse; there is only growth, not decline.

Ovadeyyāti uppanne vatthusmiṃ vadanto ovadati nāma, anuppanne “ayasopi te siyā”tiādivasena anāgataṃ dassento anusāsati nāma. Sammukhā vadantopi ovadati nāma, parammukhā [P 2.0468] dūtaṃ vā sāsanaṃ vā pesento anusāsati nāma. Sakiṃ vadantopi ovadati nāma, punappunaṃ vadanto anusāsati nāma. Ovadanto eva vā anusāsati nāmāti evaṃ ovadeyya anusāseyya. Asabbhāti akusaladhammā nivāreyya, kusaladhamme patiṭṭhapeyyāti attho. Satañhi so piyo hotīti so evarūpo puggalo buddhādīnaṃ sappurisānaṃ piyo hoti. Ye [M 0.0416] pana adiṭṭhadhammā avitiṇṇaparalokā āmisacakkhukā jīvikatthāya pabbajitā, tesaṃ asataṃ so ovādako anusāsako “na tvaṃ amhākaṃ upajjhāyo, na ācariyo, kasmā amhākaṃ ovadasī”ti evaṃ mukhasattīhi vijjhantānaṃ appiyo hotīti.

One should advise: when speaking about a matter that has arisen, it is called advising; when showing what has not yet arisen with words like, 'Disrepute might come to you,' it is called instructing. Speaking face-to-face is called advising; sending a messenger or a message in one's absence is called instructing. Speaking once is called advising; speaking repeatedly is called instructing. Or, one who advises is also said to instruct. Thus, one should advise and instruct. 'From what is evil': one should restrain from unwholesome states and establish one in wholesome states—this is the meaning. 'For he is dear to the good': such a person is dear to the virtuous, such as the Buddhas and other good persons. But to those who have not seen the Dhamma, who have not crossed beyond the next world, who have an eye for material gain, and who have gone forth for the sake of a livelihood—to such unvirtuous ones, the advisor and instructor becomes displeasing, as they pierce him with the spears of their mouths, saying, 'You are not our preceptor, nor our teacher—why do you advise us?'

Ekakammanti [V 0.0384] apalokanakammādikaṃ ekakammaṃ. Ekuddesoti nidānuddesādiko ekuddeso. Samasikkhatāti samānasikkhatā. Āhatacittatanti kodhena pahatacittabhāvaṃ. Khilajātatanti thaddhabhāvaṃ. Pañcapi cetokhileti buddhadhammasaṅghasikkhāsabrahmacārīsu pañcasupi cittassa thaddhabhāve.

A single act: a single act such as the act of announcement. A single recitation: a single recitation such as the recitation of the Nidāna. Same training: having the same training. Struck mind: the state of a mind struck by anger. Hardened nature: a state of stiffness. The five mental barrennesses: the five states of stiffness of mind regarding the Buddha, Dhamma, Sangha, the training, and fellow practitioners.

Ñāṇasamuṭṭhitaṃ vācanti ñāṇasampayuttacittena uppāditaṃ vākyaṃ. Muñceyyāti vissajjeyya. Atthūpasaṃhitanti atthasahitaṃ kāraṇasahitaṃ. Dhammūpasaṃhitanti dhammena yuttaṃ. Kālātikkantaṃ vācaṃ na bhāseyyāti kālātītaṃ vācaṃ na katheyya tassa kālassa atikkantattā. Velātikkantanti mariyādātītaṃ vacanaṃ na bhaṇeyya vacanamariyādassa atikkantattā. Ubhayavasena kālavelā.

Speech arisen from knowledge: it is speech produced by a mind associated with knowledge. "Should release" means should utter. "Connected with meaning" means connected with purpose, connected with reason. "Connected with the Dhamma" means connected with the Dhamma. "One should not speak words that have missed the time" means one should not speak words that have passed their time, because that time has elapsed. "One should not speak words that have exceeded the limit" means one should not speak words that go beyond the boundary, because the boundary of speech has been crossed. By 'both' is meant time and limit.

Yo ve kāle asampatteti attano vacanakāle asampatte. Ativelanti velātikkantaṃ katvā atirekappamāṇaṃ bhāsati. Nihato setīti nigghātito sayati. Kokilāyeva atrajoti kākiyā paṭijaggito kokilāya abbhantare jāto kokilapotako viya.

`When the time has not come`: this means when one's own time for speaking has not arrived. `Excessively`: this means speaking in excess measure, having gone beyond the proper time. `He lies down defeated`: this means he lies down, struck down. `Like a cuckoo's own offspring`: this means like a young cuckoo born inside a crow's nest and cared for by a female crow.

209. Athāparanti atha idāni ito parampi. Pañca rajānīti rūparāgādīni pañca rajāni. Yesaṃ satīmā vinayāya sikkheti yesaṃ upaṭṭhitassati hutvāva vinayanatthaṃ tisso sikkhā sikkheyya. Evaṃ sikkhanto hi rūpesu…pe… phassesu sahetha rāgaṃ, na aññeti.

209. `Then further`: now, moreover, beyond this. `The five defilements`: the five defilements are lust for form, etc. `For the removal of which a mindful one trains`: one should train in the three trainings for their removal while being established in mindfulness. For one training thus would indeed overcome lust for forms... contacts, not otherwise.

Rūparajoti [P 2.0469] rūpārammaṇaṃ paṭicca uppanno rāgādirajo. Saddarajādīsupi eseva nayo.

`The dust of form`: this is the dust of lust and so on that arises in dependence on a form-object. The same method applies to the dust of sounds and so forth.

210. Tato so tesaṃ vinayāya sikkhanto anukkamena – etesu dhammesūti gāthā. Tattha etesūti rūpādīsu. Kālena so sammā dhammaṃ parivīmaṃsamānoti so bhikkhu yvāyaṃ “uddhate citte samathassa [M 0.0417] kālo”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 5.234) nayena kālo vutto, tena kālena sabbaṃ saṅkhatadhammaṃ aniccādinayena parivīmaṃsamāno. Ekodibhūto vihane tamaṃ soti so ekaggacitto sabbaṃ mohāditamaṃ vihaneyya, natthi ettha saṃsayo.

210. Then, training for their removal, he gradually...—the verse begins, `In these phenomena`. Therein, `in these` means in forms and so on. `At the proper time, rightly investigating the Dhamma`: this means that monk, at the time spoken of by the method beginning, 'When the mind is agitated, it is time for serenity,' etc., investigates all conditioned phenomena in terms of impermanence and so on. `Having become unified, he would dispel the darkness`: this means that, with a one-pointed mind, he would dispel all the darkness of delusion and so on; there is no doubt about this.

Uddhate citteti vīriyindriyavasena citte avūpasante. Balavavīriyañhi mandasamādhiṃ vīriyassa uddhaccapakkhattā uddhaccaṃ abhibhavati. Evaṃ uddhate citte. Samathassa kāloti samādhissa bhāvanāya kālo. Samāhite citteti upacārappanāhi citte samāhite. Balavasamādhi hi mandavīriyaṃ samādhissa kosajjapakkhattā kosajjaṃ abhibhavati. Samādhi vīriyena saññojito kosajje patituṃ na labhati. Vīriyaṃ samādhinā saññojitaṃ uddhacce patituṃ na labhati[V 0.0385]. Tasmā tadubhayaṃ samaṃ kātabbaṃ. Ubhayasamatāya hi appanā hoti. Vipassanāya kāloti evaṃ samāhite aniccādivasena vividhāya passanāya kālo, samādhikammikassa balavatīpi saddhā vaṭṭati. Evaṃ saddahanto okappento appanaṃ pāpuṇāti. Samādhipaññāsu pana samādhikammikassa balavatī ekaggatā vaṭṭati. Evañhi so appanaṃ pāpuṇāti. Vipassanākammikassa pana paññā balavatī vaṭṭati. Evañhi so lakkhaṇappaṭivedhaṃ pāpuṇāti. Ubhinnaṃ pana samattepi appanā hoti eva.

`When the mind is agitated`: this means when the mind is unsettled on account of the energy faculty. For strong energy, when concentration is weak, overcomes agitation, due to energy's siding with agitation. Thus, `when the mind is agitated`. `It is time for serenity`: time for developing concentration. `When the mind is serene`: when the mind is composed through access and full absorption. For strong concentration, when energy is weak, overcomes sloth, due to concentration's siding with sloth. Concentration, yoked with energy, cannot fall into sloth. Energy, yoked with concentration, cannot fall into agitation. Therefore, both should be balanced. For absorption is attained through the balance of both. `It is time for insight`: when the mind is thus composed, it is time for diverse seeing in terms of impermanence, etc. For one whose work is concentration, strong faith is fitting. Thus, believing and trusting, one attains absorption. But regarding concentration and wisdom, for one whose work is concentration, strong one-pointedness is fitting. Thus one attains absorption. For one whose work is insight, however, strong wisdom is fitting. Thus one penetrates the characteristics. But when both are balanced, absorption is indeed attained.

Kāle paggaṇhati cittanti yasmiṃ samaye atisithilavīriyatādīhi līnaṃ cittaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ samaye dhammavicayavīriyapītisambojjhaṅgasamuṭṭhāpanena taṃ cittaṃ paggaṇhāti. Niggaṇhatīti yasmiṃ samaye accāraddhavīriyatādīhi uddhataṃ cittaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ samaye passaddhisamādhiupekkhāsambojjhaṅgasamuṭṭhāpanena taṃ cittaṃ niggaṇhāti. Sampahaṃsati kālenāti yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ paññāpayogamandatāya vā upasamasukhānaṃ vigamena vā nirassādaṃ hoti[P 2.0470], tasmiṃ samaye aṭṭhasaṃvegavatthupaccavekkhaṇena saṃvejeti. Aṭṭha saṃvegavatthūni nāma – jātijarābyādhimaraṇāni cattāri, apāyadukkhaṃ pañcamaṃ, atīte vaṭṭamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ anāgate vaṭṭamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ, paccuppanne āhārapariyeṭṭhimūlakaṃ dukkhanti. Ratanattayaguṇānussaraṇenāssa pasādaṃ janeti. Ayaṃ vuccati “sampahaṃsati kālenā”ti. Kāle cittaṃ samādaheti yasmiṃ samaye [M 0.0418] saddhāpaññānaṃ samādhivīriyānañca samabhāvo, tasmiṃ kāle cittaṃ samādaheyya.

He arouses the mind at the proper time: at the time when the mind is sluggish due to excessive laxity of energy and the like, at that time he arouses that mind by developing the enlightenment factors of investigation of phenomena, energy, and joy. He restrains: at the time when the mind is restless due to excessive energy and the like, at that time he restrains that mind by developing the enlightenment factors of tranquility, concentration, and equanimity. He gladdens at the proper time: at the time when the mind is listless due to dullness in the application of wisdom or the fading away of the bliss of tranquility, at that time he stirs it by reflecting on the eight grounds for a sense of urgency. The eight grounds for a sense of urgency are: birth, aging, sickness, and death (four); the suffering of the lower realms as the fifth; suffering rooted in the past round of existence; suffering rooted in the future round of existence; and suffering rooted in the present search for food. He generates confidence by recollecting the qualities of the Triple Gem. This is called 'he gladdens at the proper time.' He steadies the mind at the proper time: at the time when there is a balance of faith and wisdom, and of concentration and energy, at that time he should steady the mind.

Ajjhupekkhati kālenāti yasmiṃ samaye sammā paṭipattiṃ āgamma alīnaṃ anuddhataṃ anirassādaṃ ārammaṇe samappavattaṃ samathavīthipaṭipannaṃ cittaṃ hoti, tadāssa paggahaniggahasampahaṃsanesu na byāpāraṃ āpajjati sārathi viya samappavattesu assesu. Ayaṃ vuccati “ajjhupekkhati kālenā”ti. So yogī kālakovidoti eso vuttappakāro kammaṭṭhānayoge niyutto paggahaniggahasampahaṃsanasamādahanaajjhupekkhanakālesu cheko byatto. Kimhi kālamhītiādinā paggahādikālaṃ pucchati.

He looks on with equanimity at the proper time: when the mind, having undertaken proper practice, is neither sluggish nor restless, without zest, and evenly engaged with the object, progressing along the path of serenity. At that time, he does not engage in arousing, restraining, or gladdening, like a charioteer with horses moving evenly. This is called 'he looks on with equanimity at the proper time.' That yogi is skilled in timing: this one, engaged in the meditation practice in the way described, is skilled and expert in the times for arousing, restraining, gladdening, steadying, and looking on with equanimity. With 'At what time?' and so on, he asks about the time for arousing and so forth.

Idāni paggahādikālaṃ vissajjento “līne cittamhī”tiādimāha. Atisithilavīriyatādīhi citte līnabhāvaṃ gate dhammavicayavīriyapītisambojjhaṅgasamuṭṭhāpanena paggaho. Uddhatasmiṃ viniggahoti accāraddhavīriyatādīhi uddhate citte passaddhisamādhiupekkhāsambojjhaṅgasamuṭṭhāpanena niggaho. Nirassādagataṃ cittaṃ, sampahaṃseyya tāvadeti paññāpayogamandatāya vā upasamasukhānaṃ [V 0.0386] vigamena vā assādavirahitaṃ gataṃ aṭṭhasaṃvegavatthupaccavekkhaṇena vā ratanattayaguṇānussaraṇena vā tasmiṃ khaṇe cittaṃ sampahaṃseyya.

Now, explaining the time for arousing and so on, he says, 'When the mind is sluggish,' and so forth. When the mind has become sluggish due to excessive slackness of energy and the like, there is arousing by developing the enlightenment factors of investigation of phenomena, energy, and joy. When it is restless, there is restraining: when the mind is restless due to excessive energy and the like, there is restraining by developing the enlightenment factors of tranquility, concentration, and equanimity. 'When the mind has become devoid of zest, one should gladden it at that very moment' means: when it has become devoid of zest due to weakness in the application of wisdom or due to the passing away of the bliss of tranquility, at that moment one should gladden the mind by reflecting on the eight grounds for a sense of urgency or by recollecting the qualities of the Triple Gem.

Sampahaṭṭhaṃ yadā cittanti yasmiṃ kāle vuttanayeneva sampahaṃsitaṃ cittaṃ hoti. Alīnaṃ bhavati nuddhatanti vīriyasamādhīhi saññojitattā līnuddhaccavirahitañca hoti. Samathanimittassāti samatho ca nimittañca samathanimittaṃ, tassa samathanimittassa. So kāloti yo so līnuddhaccavirahitakālo vutto, so kālo. Ajjhattaṃ ramaye manoti jhānasampayuttaṃ cittaṃ kasiṇādigocarajjhatte toseyya abhiramāpeyya.

'When the mind is gladdened' means: at the time when the mind is gladdened in the manner described. 'It is not sluggish nor restless' means: it is free from sluggishness and restlessness because it is yoked with energy and concentration. 'Of the sign of serenity' means: serenity and the sign are the sign of serenity; of that sign of serenity. 'That is the time' means: that time which was spoken of as free from sluggishness and restlessness, that is the time. 'One should delight the mind internally' means: the mind associated with jhāna should be pleased and delighted internally with an object such as a kasiṇa.

Etena [P 2.0471] mevupāyenāti etena vuttaupāyena eva. Ma-kāro padasandhivasena vutto. Ajjhupekkheyya tāvadeti yadā upacārappanāhi taṃ cittaṃ samāhitaṃ, tadā “samāhitaṃ citta”nti jānitvā paggahaniggahasampahaṃsanesu byāpāraṃ akatvā tasmiṃ khaṇe ajjhupekkhanameva kareyya.

'By this very means' means: by this very method stated. The letter 'm' is spoken for the sake of euphonic connection. 'One should simply look on with equanimity' means: when that mind is concentrated through access and absorption, then, knowing 'the mind is concentrated,' without engaging in arousing, restraining, or gladdening, at that moment one should just practice equanimity.

Idāni [M 0.0419] “kimhi kālamhi paggāho”ti puṭṭhagāthaṃ nigamento “evaṃ kālavidū dhīro”tiādimāha. Kālena kālaṃ cittassa, nimittamupalakkhayeti kālānukālaṃ samādhisampayuttacittassa ārammaṇaṃ sallakkheyya, upaparikkheyyāti attho. Sesaṃ sabbattha pākaṭameva. Evaṃ arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesīti.

Now, concluding the verse that was asked, 'At what time is arousing?', he said, beginning with 'Thus, the wise one who knows the time.' 'From time to time, one should observe the sign of the mind' means: from one occasion to the next, one should mark and investigate the object of the mind associated with concentration. The rest is clear everywhere. Thus, he concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of arahantship.

Saddhammappajjotikāya mahāniddesaṭṭhakathāya

In the Saddhammappajjotikā, the commentary on the Mahāniddesa.

Sāriputtasuttaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Sāriputta Sutta Niddesa is completed.

Aṭṭhakavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Aṭṭhakavagga is completed.

Saddhammappajjotikā nāma mahāniddesa-aṭṭhakathā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Mahāniddesa, named Saddhammappajjotikā, is completed.
